## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library**, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the most holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, very diligently corrected by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscript codices; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following the individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily ascertain which Fathers, and in which places in their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the completeness of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient form of the volumes—uniform throughout the entire course of the work—the low price, and above all this single, systematic, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time united in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clerical Library, or of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been issued in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—The 360 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,300 francs; the 1,000 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800.—The wholly Latin edition embraces all authors, Western as well as Eastern; the latter, however, are provided there only in a Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 1197: Peter the Chanter

[Col. 0009]

## Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., vol. VII, col. 78.)

[Col. 0009A] After the death of Bishop Maurice, if credence is due to Ralph, abbot of Coggeshall, in his English Chronicle (*Amplissima collectio*, vol. V, p. 846), Peter, Chanter of the Church of Paris, was elected bishop by the whole clergy and people, with the king’s assent. He refused the dignity of the episcopate, lest a fall from a higher rank should be more grievous.

Celebrated in the writings of almost all authors of that age, he was born at Paris, or, according to Ralph, at Reims. As a youth he devoted his mind to letters; having become learned beyond his years, he taught them publicly in the University of Paris with great distinction. Yet what was the outstanding adornment of his character was this: he was a defender of ancient morals and a most diligent enforcer of stricter discipline. Since he shone with these virtues, he readily obtained the highly honorable office of precentor of the Church of Paris. Once summoned to the see of Tournai, he humbly declined the call (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 214).

Finally, after likewise refusing [Col. 0009B] the bishopric of Paris, Ralph reports that, when William, Archbishop of Reims, together with the clergy and citizens, requested him to accept the deanship of that Church, he set out for Paris in order to obtain permission for this from the chapter. He reached the Cistercian monastery of Longpont, where, laid low by grave illness, he received the habit of holy religion and ended his life in a blessed death. When his body was moved from the place where it had been buried for the construction of buildings, it exhaled a most sweet fragrance.

His epitaph is read in the cloister of Longpont monastery, in which his death is entered as the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 1180; but the epitaph is more recent. Therefore William of Nangis, Vincent of Beauvais, Alberic, and the monk of Saint-Marianus—the authors of these times—speak more correctly of Peter’s death under the year 1197; Ralph likewise assigns his death to 1198, since Peter is still mentioned in a charter of Odo in 1197. The Paris Necrology says of him: “On the seventh day before the Kalends of October died Peter, precentor and deacon, who gave us forty pounds for purchasing revenues.”

He composed various works, still preserved in manuscript in different libraries. Of all these, only his *Summa*, called *The Abbreviated Word*, was printed at Mons in 1639. Some maintain that his [Col. 0010B] teaching was tainted with certain defects. Caesarius relates that Peter and his disciples fell into the error of believing that bread consecrated in the Eucharist was not consecrated unless the consecration of wine were also added, and conversely.

[Col. 0009]

## Historical-Literary Notice

(Oudin, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 1661.)

[Col. 0009C] Peter, canon and Chanter of Blessed Mary of Paris, director of the theological school for several years, acquired great renown for learning in Gaul at this time. The surname “the Chanter” commonly adheres to him in manuscript codices, from the office of precentor which he held as a chief dignity in that Church.

We do not know his actual family name, but only that he was a Frenchman by nation and a Parisian by birthplace. Aegidius of Paris mentions him in his *Carolinus* in these words:

> And Peter, whom we lament to have grown lukewarm in divine matters,  
> following lofty things merely in words.

Gabriel Naudé is therefore mistaken in the addition to his *History of Louis XI* when he says that Peter Abelard is intended here. For Aegidius commemorates only Parisian professors, to remove the reproach commonly cast by others that few professors of any [Col. 0010C] distinction came from the city of Paris. Abelard, however, was from Nantes and an Armorican by nationality. Nor would Aegidius have substituted our Peter the Chanter here, and thereby easily exposed himself to conviction of falsehood, unless Peter had truly been Parisian by birth.

Aegidius says there that Peter had grown lukewarm in divine matters, perhaps because, devoting himself wholly to disputatious theology, he devoted himself little or not at all to preaching the divine word. John Trithemius, however, in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says that he was a man most learned in the Holy Scriptures and nobly trained in secular philosophy; that he gloriously presided over the Parisian theological school for many years; and that he excellently instructed many disciples.

While he thus flourished in Gaul, he was elected bishop of the Church of Tournai in 1191. When his election was challenged, Stephen, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, wrote to William, Archbishop of Reims, then chief administrator of the realm, asking him to support the elect. [Col. 0011A] I shall transcribe his words, in which the exceptional merits of Peter the Chanter are commended. Thus Letter 173:

> “To the lord of Reims, concerning Peter, Chanter of Paris, elected bishop of Tournai. May your gentleness, a common refuge open to all, extend itself to individuals in such a way that it gathers all together. They come from East and West and recline in your bosom. Nor is anyone once admitted easily dismissed, unless he happens to commit something which does not deserve to be forgiven.
>
> “These are the grounds that give me and many others confidence to ask that an entrance for supplication may be opened to us on behalf of your devoted son, Master Peter, Chanter of Paris. Let not one who does not claim dignity for himself incur your displeasure; let not another’s act harm one whose own merit is sufficient. He is a man whose reputation for sweetness is spread throughout all the Churches, who, shining most effectively in a twofold knowledge, adorns doctrine by exhortations and discipline by conduct. In some respect, we believe him the equal of Origen: he teaches as he lives, and lives as he teaches.
>
> “Such lamps should be on your lampstand [Col. 0011B]; such stones in the diadem upon Aaron’s head; such suffragan bishops in the holy Church of Reims, that neighboring provinces may be stirred by holy emulation to promote similar men, and that the charge committed to you may be more easily and more frequently assisted through their religion and prudence.
>
> “If anything was done less than properly in his election by the clergy of Tournai, it ought neither to touch the ignorance of one absent nor to injure the innocence of a just man, since, if it please you, whatever was wrongly done can most easily be corrected: to you God has committed both the power of correcting errors and the knowledge to correct them. For, if I may state my conclusion without prejudice and with your favor preserved, four things concur in that election which Leo I named: the wishes of the citizens, the testimony of the people, the judgment of the honorable, and the election of the clergy. To these are added the integrity of the man, the cheerfulness of his reputation, and both the need and the benefit of the widowed Church.
>
> “Moreover, it is often and solemnly said that the lord king—may God [Col. 0011C] preserve him and restore him to us—expressly named this man, expressly asked for him, and expressly wished and intended that he should preside over the Church of Tournai. If the matter is otherwise handled, it is to be feared—and perhaps it is true—that he may conceive indignation and wrath and visitations through evil angels, and inflame royal and youthful anger against those who have impeded the advancement of so great a man. In all these matters, holy Father, provide for your honor, take counsel for the sound testimony of your reputation, defer to the royal command, and, after first correcting as was fitting the error of the electors, confirm the election and receive your elect and beloved one in your fatherly bosom.”

Among all writers who mention Peter the Chanter, James of Vitry surpasses them in praise. He could know him especially well, since he studied at Paris while Peter was still living and teaching. He adorns Peter the Chanter with this eulogy:

> “Like a lily among thorns and a rose among nettles; like an angel [Col. 0011D] in Pergamum, where Satan’s throne is; like incense fragrant in summer days; like a solid vessel of gold adorned with every precious stone; like a budding olive and a cypress lifting itself on high; like a heavenly trumpet and the Lord’s lyre-player, such at that time was Master Peter, the venerable Chanter of Paris—a man mighty in deed and word, likewise refining his gold and silver, making a balance with his words, and lending weight and gravity to his doctrine by the integrity of his conduct. For he began to do and to teach, like a lamp burning and shining, a city set upon a mountain, and a golden lampstand in the house of the Lord. From his most limpid spring the most blessed man Fulk drank deeply.”

Much more could be collected in praise of Peter the Chanter from various writers of the same age, but these matters are omitted for brevity, so that we may come to his writings, both printed and manuscript.

He therefore wrote the *Summa* called *The Abbreviated Word*, because it begins with these words: “The Lord shall make an abbreviated word upon the earth,” etc. (Rom. [Col. 0012A] 9:28). It is the only one of all Peter the Chanter’s works printed at Mons in Hainaut, in 1639, in quarto, by François Vandre, with notes by Georges Galopin, monk of Saint-Ghislain of the Order of Saint Benedict. It also exists in manuscript in the library of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris; at Cambridge, in the College of Saint Benedict, codex 223; and in the Cistercian monastery of Longpont in the diocese of Soissons.

The *Summa* called *The Abbreviated Word*, according to Bunderius’ testimony in the *Catalogue of Belgian Manuscripts*, is called in many manuscript codices *Summa on the Rebuke of Vices and the Commendation of Virtues*. In this connection one must observe that nothing is more common in libraries than for one and the same work of Peter the Chanter to bear various and poorly corresponding titles. Thus the unwary very easily suppose that this writer has as many different works as they find different titles in manuscripts. To establish a reliable distinction between works, one must judge by their incipits, or their first sentences, and never by their varying headings, as we shall say presently.

This *Abbreviated Word* is particularly common in manuscript libraries. I know that I saw it three times in the library of Saint-Victor outside the walls of Paris, under the shelfmarks MM. 13, PP. 6, and QQ. 17; also in the Colbert Library, codices 1345, 1414, 2069, 3609, and 4448; in the royal library, codex 4827; and elsewhere [Col. 0012B].

He also wrote the *Summa* called *Abel*, because, proceeding in alphabetical order, it begins with the name Abel. I saw it in manuscript in the aforementioned monastery of Longpont and in the library of Prémontré at Braine, both in the bishopric of Soissons; also in manuscript at Cambridge in the college of the House of Saint Peter, codex 97. This same work is often simply titled in manuscript library codices: *Distinctions of the Chanter of Paris*: “Abel is called the beginning of the Church,” etc. Or again: *Distinctions in Alphabetical Order, of Master Peter, Chanter of Paris*. A manuscript under this title is found in many libraries in England, and in Belgium in the libraries of Dunes and Aulne, both Cistercian.

Yet it is frequently titled *Summa Called Abel*, in order to distinguish it from other *Summae* beginning differently which the same Peter the Chanter composed. The same *Distinctions of the Chanter of Paris* are in manuscript at Cambridge in the College of Saint Benedict, codices 219 and 371, and in the college of the House of Saint Peter, codices 72 and 78; at Oxford, in the library of Merton College, codex 164; and in the library of Conches, of the Order of Saint Benedict in Normandy, shelfmark T. 2 [Col. 0012C].

He wrote a *Great Summa on the Sacraments*, beginning: “A question is raised concerning the legal ordinances, which were given as a sign for the perfect, a yoke for the proud, and a pedagogue for the weak,” etc. It was partly drawn from the holy Fathers, and I saw it in manuscript in the Cistercian monasteries of Longpont in the diocese of Soissons, Clara Vallis in the diocese of Laon, and Clairvaux in the diocese of Langres.

This work *On the Sacraments* is sometimes titled *Summa on the Sacraments and the Counsels of the Soul*; indeed, it is not infrequently attributed erroneously to Peter of Reims, as in the Victorine manuscript shelfmark GG. 13, fol. 149: *Summa of Master Peter of Reims, on the Sacraments and the Counsels of the Soul*. Incipit: “A question is raised concerning the legal sacraments, which were given as a sign for the perfect, a yoke for the proud, and a pedagogue for the weak,” etc. This is also the work which Philippe Labbe promised to bring to light from a manuscript codex. In the library of Dunes it is titled *Book of Sentences*: “A question is raised concerning the legal sacraments,” etc.

But it is certain that this *Summa* belongs to Peter the Chanter of Paris, not to Peter of Reims, since Peter the Chanter of Reims, surnamed de Riga, advanced in writing no farther than the art of poetry. Charles Visch, in his *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, p. 263, attributes to the said Peter the Chanter of Paris three manuscript books *On the Sacraments*, at Villers and Aulne, both very celebrated Cistercian abbeys in Belgium. Their incipit is: “The people went about,” etc. I have nothing to say concerning these [Col. 0013A], since I have not seen them. Yet I can scarcely persuade myself that Peter the Chanter wrote more than once on the same subject.

The celebrated Colbert Library of Paris possesses two manuscript codices, numbered 2208 and 1419, under the title *Counsellor of Master Peter the Chanter*, or *Summa on the Sacraments and the Counsels of the Soul*. Yet from an extensive reading of the work itself, where the author cites and refutes Peter the Chanter in certain chapters, it is evident that it does not belong to Peter the Chanter. I later discovered that this *Summa* most certainly belongs to Robert of Courson, a most learned theologian somewhat later than the Peter of whom we speak. The same work is found falsely under Peter the Chanter’s name in manuscript in the Cistercian library of Longpont, shelfmark D. 6, with the Penitentials of Bartholomew of Oxford and Robert of Flamborough; and finally in the library of Vallis Lucensis of the same order, lectern 16, shelfmark Z. Thus scarcely any manuscript work of Peter the Chanter in libraries fails to have several titles or headings [Col. 0013B].

He also wrote a short work *On the Contrarieties of Theology*, beginning: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma,” etc., in manuscript in the Library of Navarre at Paris, in a quarto codex, and at Cambridge in the College of Saint Benedict, codex 371, though anonymous and entitled *Treatise on the Contrariety of Scripture*. The same work is titled in a manuscript of Villers, a Cistercian monastery in Brabant, *On Theological Contrarieties*, because at the beginning of the work it speaks of apparent contradictions in Holy Scripture. For this reason scribes gave the whole work that name, in accordance with the custom of ancient scribes, who gave books titles from the subject treated in their opening chapters.

The same work is titled *Grammar of Theologians* in many other libraries: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma,” etc., as in the libraries of the abbeys of Afflighem and Ninove in Flanders. Henry of Ghent speaks of this work as follows in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 15: “He also wrote another book, which he called the *Grammar of Theologians*, useful in many places for understanding Holy Scripture.”

The same work is titled in manuscript *Master Peter the Chanter of Reims, On Figures of Speech*, in the celebrated library of Saint-Victor outside the walls of Paris, shelfmark GG. 13, fol. 270: “We see through a mirror and in an enigma,” etc., after the *Summa on the Sacraments and the Counsels of the Soul* of the Chanter himself, fol. 149, discussed above. The same work in the same library, shelfmark B. 6, fol. 162, is titled: *Treatise of Master Peter the Chanter, On Figures of Speech*, its incipit written in red letters: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma,” etc.

In the same codex is his short work *On the Proprietary Monk*, fol. 189, beginning: “Judas, because he was a thief and had the purse, carried away the things put into the common purses,” etc. Finally, the same work is also entitled *On the Solutions of Contrarieties*, sometimes *On Theological Figures of Speech*, and sometimes *Figures and Phrases of Holy Scripture*. Thus in libraries one finds almost as many titles and varying headings as manuscript codices [Col. 0013D].

At Paris, in the hands of Jacques Hommey, an Augustinian hermit, we also saw Peter the Chanter’s *Allegories on Scripture*, or on the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments. Hommey had borrowed them from the Library of Navarre at Paris. Their incipit is: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” etc. They are also in manuscript at Cambridge, in the library of Pembroke Hall, codex 76, together with sermons of Peter Comestor, to whom they are wrongly attributed.

For the works of Peter the Chanter and Peter Comestor are often confused in manuscript codices because only their first initial letter was written. Since this is found in manuscripts of better standing, other and later persons added, at will or conjecturally, now the heading “Peter the Chanter,” now “Peter Comestor.” There survive in manuscript Peter the Chanter’s commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy in the library of Golden Valley of the same Cistercian Order, codices 9 and 10, which we held in our hands. His commentaries on Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, and Ruth are in manuscript at Oxford in the Balliol Library, codex 22; likewise, his commentary on the Psalms there, codex 30.

Peter the Chanter’s commentary on the Psalter is in manuscript in the library of Saint-Michel-in-Peril-of-the-Sea, shelfmark E. 28. It begins: “John wept because no one was found to open the book,” etc.; and its commentary on the first Psalm begins: “Ezra, restorer of the library in the Babylonian captivity,” etc. I saw the same work in manuscript in the renowned library of the Regular Canons of Saint-Victor at Paris, shelfmark D. 2, entitled: *Notes of Peter of Reims on the Psalter*. Thus very many works of Peter the Chanter of Paris are found in libraries under the name Peter of Reims, as we have already said [Col. 0014B].

His gloss on the Gospels is in manuscript at Oxford in the library of Merton College, codex 144; likewise in the Cluniac Library, under the heading *Peter the Chanter on the Four Gospels*, shelfmark G. 2. His gloss on the New Testament is in manuscript at Cambridge in Pembroke Hall, codex 179. But let us set forth in a little more detail this author’s particular labors on Holy Scripture.

Sixtus of Siena, of the Order of Preachers, testifies in his *Sacred Library* that he saw the following in the library of the Dominican friars at Lyons:

- One book on the Psalter, beginning: “John wept, and there was no one to open the book,” etc.
- One book on Proverbs, beginning: “The Proverbs of Solomon according to the Hebrew truth,” etc.
- One book on Ecclesiastes: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you,” etc.
- One book on Wisdom: “The palace of the supreme King,” etc.
- [Col. 0014C] Two books on Ezekiel: “And it came to pass in the third year,” etc.
- One book on the Acts of the Apostles: “The earth was melted,” etc.
- One book on the Catholic Epistles: “My mouth shall speak wisdom,” etc.
- One book on the Apocalypse: “This alone among the books of the New Testament is called prophecy,” etc.

John Bunderius, in his *Index of the Manuscript Books of Belgium*, when listing the works of this Peter—whom he calls Peter of Reims, Chanter of Paris, as he is also called in the Chronicle of Longpont—sets forth, in the following terms, whatever further items he found in various monasteries, besides those already listed and distinguished above:

- Annotations and brief commentaries on the whole Old and New Testament, among the Dominicans at Valenciennes.
- Commentary on Genesis, beginning: “The first principle of words, the first principle of eternal works,” etc.
- On Exodus: “Moses made the first covering,” [Col. 0014D] etc.
- On Leviticus: “Ezekiel pierced through the wall,” etc.
- On the Psalter: “John wept, and there was no one to open the book,” etc., at Clairmarais, Baudelo, and Saint Martin’s at Louvain.
- On the Epistles of Paul: “At your rebuke they shall flee,” etc., at Clairmarais, Saint Martin’s at Louvain, and among the Friars Minor at Bruges and Valenciennes.

These are the statements of John Bunderius in the cited place.

The Necrology of the Church of Tournai testifies that this good man declined episcopal mitres and put on the monastic habit in the Cistercian monastery of Longpont, where he completed a holy life with a holy death. He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, in 1197, as the necrology of the same abbey in which he died records.

[Col. 0015]

# Eulogies of Peter the Chanter

(*The Abbreviated Word*, ed. Georges Galopin, quarto.)

James of Vitry, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, *Western History*, chapter 8.

[Col. 0015A]

“The Lord had left for himself a few upright and God-fearing men, who had not stood in the way of sinners and had not sat in the seat of pestilence. One of these was like a lily among thorns,” etc. See above in the *Historical-Literary Notice*.

Thomas of Cantimpré, Book II of *The Bees*, chapter 1, no. 9.

Concerning this good man—John, a regular canon at Cantimpré—his fellow canons told me that, while he was in Paris and a hearer of the blessed and great man, Master Peter the Chanter of Paris, he was troubled by certain doubts and temptations, etc.

The same, Book I, chapter 19, no. 8.

“It is mortal and damnable, when one suitable benefice is sufficient, to retain several benefices. This same thing Master Peter the Chanter of Saint Mary of Paris both said and wrote.” (*The Abbreviated Word*, chapters 31 and 32.)

The same, Book II, chapter 30 (otherwise chapter 29), according to the manuscript exemplar of the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai, in the notes of Georges Colvenerius, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Chancellor of Douai, etc.

[Col. 0015B]

“Master Peter of blessed memory, formerly Chanter of Paris, told a certain acquaintance of mine,” etc.

Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, Book XXIX of the old edition, chapter 59.

“In the same year (1197), Peter the Chanter of Paris, distinguished alike by life and doctrine, died: a lover of piety and justice, he departed from the body at the monastery of Longpont in great devotion and holy confession.”

Saint Antoninus, *Chronicle*, part II, title 17, chapter 9, §§55 and 29 (has the same words as Vincent of Beauvais). Caesarius of Heisterbach, of the Cistercian Order, Book II of *Memorable Histories*, chapter 34.

In the time of Philip, King of the Franks, who reigns today, there was in the city of Paris a very wealthy usurer [Col. 0015C] named Theobald. Since he possessed many estates and innumerable sums gathered from usury, he was divinely moved to compunction and came to Master Maurice, bishop of the same city, entrusting himself to his counsel. Because Maurice was exceedingly zealous in building the Church of Blessed Mary, he advised him to hand over his money for the construction of the work that had been begun.

Theobald, somewhat suspicious of such advice, went to Master Peter the Chanter and told him the bishop’s words. Peter replied: “This time he has not given you good counsel. Go instead and have it proclaimed through the streets by a herald that you are ready to restore to everyone from whom you have taken anything above the principal.” And so it was done.

Then Theobald returned to the master and said: “With conscience as witness, I have restored all that was taken to everyone who came to me, and much still remains.” Then Peter said: “Now you may give alms securely.”

Lord Daniel, abbot of Scone, related to me that, at the advice of the same Chanter, Theobald went naked through the streets of the city in his breeches, while a servant drove him on with a rod and said: “Behold this is the man whom the nobility honored for his wealth, who held the sons of nobles as hostages,” etc.

The same, Book VIII, chapter 69.

[Col. 0016A]

Some called Saint Thomas of Canterbury condemned as a traitor to the realm; others, a martyr as defender of the Church. The same question was debated among the masters at Paris. For Master Roger swore that he had deserved death, though not such a death, judging the blessed man’s steadfastness to be obstinacy. On the other hand, Master Peter the Chanter swore that he was a martyr worthy of God, since he had been slain for the liberty of the Church. Christ resolved their question when he glorified Thomas by many great signs.

The same, Book XII, chapter 48.

Master Peter the Chanter of Paris had edified many by word, life, and example. He became a novice at Pontenella, a house of our Order, and died before the year of probation was complete; he was buried in the chapter house. Later, when necessity of building required that his body be transferred, the grave was opened and such a great and sweet fragrance poured forth from it [Col. 0016B] that its scent refreshed the nostrils of all. That fragrance was a sign of his exceptional doctrine, the reward of which he had received in heaven. How much grace and glory teachers or preachers deserve after this life, the following discourse shows.

The Chronicle of Marchiennes, in the *Paralipomena of the Franco-Merovingian Synopsis*, under the year 1194, fol. 987, states:

“Peter the Chanter of Paris, an outstanding doctor, who wrote *The Abbreviated Word*, departed from the body in great devotion and holy confession in the monastery called Longpont, not far from Soissons.”

Henry of Ghent, in the book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 15.

“Peter the Chanter of Paris, himself also director of the theological school, wrote a book which is called *The Abbreviated Word* from its beginning, a work full of great usefulness. He also wrote another book, which I call the *Grammar of Theologians*, quite useful in many places for the understanding [Col. 0016C] of Holy Scripture.”

John Trithemius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, around the year 1200.

Peter the Chanter of Paris, and afterward, as is reported, a bishop, a man most learned in the Holy Scriptures and nobly trained in secular philosophy, gloriously presided over the theological school at Paris for many years and excellently trained many outstanding disciples. He also wrote certain distinguished short works, of which I remember that few have come into our hands. The volume listed is:

- *The Abbreviated Word*, one book: “The Lord shall make an abbreviated word.”
- Another work of *Distinctions*, one book: “Abel is called the beginning.”
- *Grammar of Theologians*, one book.
- Various sermons, one book.
- *On Certain Miracles*, one book.
- *On the Sacraments* also, three books: “The people went about.”

He flourished in the time of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Sixtus of Siena, Book IV of the *Sacred Library*.

Peter the Chanter of Paris, and afterward bishop of the same city, among other distinguished works which he published, wrote a scholastic gloss on the whole most holy [Col. 0017A] Bible. From this I myself saw the following books in the library of the Order of Preachers at Lyons:

- On the Psalter: “John wept because there was no one to open [the book].”
- On Proverbs: “The Proverbs of Solomon according to the Hebrew truth.”
- On Ecclesiastes: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you,” etc.
- On Wisdom: “The palace of the supreme King.”
- On Ezekiel: “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year,” etc.
- On the Acts of the Apostles: “The earth was melted,” etc.
- On the Catholic Epistles: “My mouth shall speak wisdom,” etc.
- On the Apocalypse: “This alone among the books of the New Testament is called prophecy.”

To these items repeated from Sixtus of Siena, Antonio Possevino of the Society of Jesus adds in his *Sacred Apparatus*, vol. II, under the letter P:

“Some testify that he also wrote on the Twelve Prophets and that this work existed in Germany in our time; he also wrote three books on the sacraments; another which he entitled *The Abbreviated Word*; a *Grammar of Theologians*; another work on certain miracles; and several sermons. A manuscript moral work of the same Peter the Chanter, or *On Cases of Conscience*, exists both at Louvain and Bordeaux in our colleges. Our Martin Delrio obtained that work in the very ancient monastery of La Sauve-Majeure in the district of Bordeaux, among other books which had decayed beneath a skylight.” Thus he.

What he says about a commentary by the same author on the Twelve Prophets having existed in Germany, I believe he takes from the epitome of Gesner’s library, where one reads: “Peter the Chanter’s exposition on the Twelve Prophets.” Also: “Discourses in alphabetical order on every subject of theology. M. Dresserus, that is, Matthäus Dresser.”

Besides the materials found in Sixtus of Siena and Possevino, Pierre Crespet cites his sermon 2 on the Blessed Virgin, found toward the end of *The Abbreviated Word*, on Isaiah 40: “Behold, the nations are as a drop from a bucket,” etc., in *The Triumph of Blessed Mary*, day 2.

On day 23, Crespet cites sermon 1 of the same author on the Annunciation.

Georgius Cassander, at the end of his *Roman Order concerning the Office of the Mass*, writes as follows:

A few centuries ago, too, in Gaul there was much use of masses commonly called double-faced, triple-faced, and four-faced: that is, several masses on different subjects, repeatedly performed as far as the offertory, were finally concluded with a single canon. Against these Peter the Chanter writes vigorously in the *Verbum abbreviatum*. I believe that they have altogether fallen into disuse, etc.

In the catalogue of manuscript books of the Library of Cambron, published by the Friar Minor Bosquier, of pious memory, the following occurs: “Expositions by Master Peter the Chanter on one of the four [Gospels]. Also, a book of Master P. the Chanter called the *Verbum abbreviatum*. Also, an exposition on Job.”

[Col. 0018A] Moreover, Peter the Chanter seems to have written on Matthew, according to Ludolph of Saxony in the *Life of Christ*, Part I, chapters 17, 38, and 42. He is cited in those places, and the margin of the latest edition notes: “On Matthew.”

The same Ludolph, in the same work, chapter 68, speaks of him thus: “The same thing—namely, that it is mortal and damnable—Peter the Chanter of Paris both said and wrote.”

Georgius Colvenerius, doctor and professor of sacred theology and chancellor of Douai, in his notes on chapter 19 of Book I of Thomas of Cantimpré’s *Universal Good, or the Bees*, on the words, “The same Master Peter, Chanter of St Mary of Paris, both said and wrote,” says:

“This is the reading of manuscript B and of the third printed edition; two other manuscripts concur, reading: ‘Master Peter, of holy memory, Chanter of Paris.’ But in manuscript P, the word *Comestor* has been added above the line to the name Peter—perhaps from older printed editions, both of which read, though incorrectly: ‘The same Master Peter Comestor, Chanter of St Mary of Paris, said and wrote.’ Certainly those who add *Comestor* conflate two distinct authors into one. For Peter Comestor, who, according to Trithemius, was a priest of the Church of Troyes, does not appear to have been Chanter of the Church of St Mary at Paris.

“Moreover, as Trithemius himself attests, Peter the Chanter lived about forty years after Comestor. For Comestor flourished in 1160; the Chanter died, according to Vincent in the *Mirror* and Antoninus in the *Chronicles*, in 1197.

“The same variation of reading,” he says, “occurs in Book II, chapter 1, page 9, where two printed editions add the name *Comestor*. But this is wrongly done, as is proved by the fact that Cantimpré can scarcely seem to have been able to see a disciple of Peter Comestor; and because all the manuscripts, together with the third printed edition, show no trace whatever of this reading in that passage.”

But in chapter 30, Part XII, all read without any variation: Peter the Chanter of Paris.

John Cognatus, Book IV of the *History of Tournai*, chapter 1, from the obituary book of the same church:

On the tenth day before the Kalends of October died the distinguished doctor Peter the Chanter of Paris. Once elected bishop of this church, he humbly declined the vacancy; and, after serving for no small time as a model of learning and morals to his hearers, he assumed the Cistercian habit and, in the monastery of Longpont, brought his holiness of life to completion in a blessed end.

Thomas James, in his catalogue of manuscript books still preserved in England, printed at London in 1600:

Peter the Chanter wrote on the Book of Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, and Ruth. One copy: Oxford, Balliol Library, vol. 22. On the Psalms, one copy there, vol. 30. *Verbum abbreviatum*, one copy: Cambridge, Benet Library, vol. 223. A gloss on the Gospels, one copy: Oxford, Merton College Library, vol. 144. *Distinctions*, one copy: Cambridge, Benet Library, vol. 219.

[Col. 0019]

# NAMES OF AUTHORS

Whose works the author employed in this book called the *Verbum abbreviatum*.

## A

Alan the poet. Alberic of Rheims. Agellius, or Aulus Gellius. Pope Alexander III. Ambrose. Anselm. Appendix to the Third Lateran Council. Aquila, translator of Scripture. Arator the poet. Aristippus. Aristotle. Athanasius. Augustine. Ausonius the poet.

## B

Basil. Bede. Benedict, in the Rule. Bernard. The Holy Bible, both according to the Septuagint and the Vulgate edition. Boethius.

## C

Institutes of the Carthusians. Cassiodorus. Cato. Cicero. Constitutions of the Cistercians. Claudian. *Conferences of the Fathers*. The Lateran Council under Alexander III. The Council of Rheims under Eugenius III. The Council of Tours. Constitutions of Pope Gregory VII.

## D

Pope Damasus. Demosthenes. Diogenes. Dionysius the Areopagite.

## E

Epicurus. Pope Eugenius III. Eusebius of Caesarea.

## F

Fulco of Rheims.

## G

Gallus the poet. Pope Gelasius. *Lives of the Philosophers* by Laertius. Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers. The Interlinear Gloss. The Ordinary Gloss. Gratian. Gregory the Great. Gregory VII.

## H

Jerome. Hilary. Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans. [Col. 0020] *Tripartite History*. Horace.

## I

Innocent II. Isidore. Ivo of Chartres.

## J

Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*. Canon and civil law. Juvenal.

## L

Legends of the saints. Pope Leo I. Lucan.

## M

Macrobius. The Master of the *Sentences*, or Peter Lombard. Martial. Milo of Thérouanne.

## O

Origen. Ovid.

## P

Peter the Dialectician, or Master Abelard. Plato. Porphyry. The Porretan, or Gilbert of Poitiers. Propertius. Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*. Prudentius. Pulanus.

## Q

Quintilian. Quintus Curtius.

## R

Rabanus. Remigius. Robert of Cambrai.

## S

Samson, archbishop of Rheims. Sallust. The two Senecas. Sidonius IX [uncertain reading]. Statius the poet. Strabus. Suetonius. Symmachus.

## T

Pope Telesphorus. Terence. Thomas of Canterbury. Theophylact.

## V

Valerius Maximus. Virgil. Lives of the saints, such as: the *Life of St Fursa*, the *Life of St Launomarus*, and the *Life or Legend of St Sebastian*.

[Col. 0021]

# THE ABBREVIATED WORD OF THE VENERABLE PETER THE CHANTER, OF THE CHURCH OF BLESSED MARY AT PARIS, DOCTOR AND PROFESSOR OF SACRED THEOLOGY

A moral work most useful to all theologians, pastors, confessors, preachers, jurists, and persons of every condition. Now for the first time brought out of darkness and illustrated with notes through the study and labour of the Reverend Father Dom George Galopin, monk and librarian of the monastery of St Ghislain, of the Order of St Benedict, Province of Hainaut.

(Mons, from the press of Francis Waudraeus, “Under the Bibles,” 1639, quarto.)

# TO GOD THE WORD, THE INCARNATE WORD, THE ABBREVIATED WORD, OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST

All my labour spent upon elucidating this *Abbreviated Word*, composed by the venerable Peter the Chanter, I offer and consecrate to you, good Jesus. I pray that you may have eternal mercy upon me and upon all who read this work fruitfully.

# GREETING TO THE CHRISTIAN READER

Christian reader, the *Abbreviated Word*, long and greatly desired, at last comes to light—but only after much toil had first been expended. For since manuscripts are commonly seen both covered in grime and corrupted by devouring age, there is no doubt that they require a diligent reader, and, if I may say so, an indefatigable one, who, before committing them to the press, examines them again and again to determine whether the words and sentences have been corrupted by scribes’ carelessness and hasty writing. Therefore, as far as possible, one should use not a single copy but a second and third, so that one may correct another’s error and one may supply another’s mutilation, and thus a sounder reading, easier to understand, may emerge.

This was what I had to do. When I began to make a transcript from one copy sent to me, I observed in it such a mass of letter-forms, and such obscure and unfamiliar abbreviations of words, that I immediately judged that I needed several copies if I wished to establish the genuine reading.

Accordingly, for this purpose I obtained three manuscripts from three monasteries of our Low Countries, flourishing in virtue and learning: namely, Saint-Vaast, Marchiennes, and Cambron. I often sought a fourth in our own region, but could not find it, because it had disappeared. In addition, I used another manuscript from Cambron in which, among the works of Anselm of Canterbury, several chapters of our *Abbreviated Word* were contained. Whenever I mention this manuscript in the notes, I call it the Cambron fragment. For brevity’s sake I have marked the other copies—namely, that of Saint-Vaast—by V; that of Marchiennes by M; and that of Cambron by C.

The margins and outer edges of these three manuscripts are burdened with certain notes, but these were added not by the venerable author Peter, but by students for the sake of elucidation. This is plainly inferred from the Saint-Vaast margin cited in the notes to chapter 97. For there one reads: “This entire member of the distinction must therefore be removed; nor should it be believed that Peter the Chanter of Paris inserted this fault, and the other things found in this book. Rather, scholastics copying him and adding their own little notes at pleasure corrupted the whole.”

The Marchiennes manuscript agreed in some fashion with that of Cambron as to the text and collateral notes; but from chapter 66 to 80 it departed from both the Saint-Vaast and the Cambron copies in an almost continuous variation of reading. [Col. 0023] I therefore judged that it ought to be transcribed word for word and, once transcribed, placed at the end of the work, that is, after all the notes.

The variation of which I have spoken consisted not only in words, but also in examples. The more numerous and extensive these are, the more they contribute, above others, to fuller understanding and proof of the subject in question. These examples are partly the author’s and partly those of some scholiast, who in chapter 80—at the end, after all the notes—quotes Peter the Chanter’s words and calls him “the Master.” This cannot be supposed to have been said by the author about himself.

The Saint-Vaast manuscript is written in an elegant hand, but it must be regretted that it has much too much in the text and also lacks much. It has too much when it admits into the text things belonging to the margin, namely notes. It is deficient, and not rarely, when it omits portions of the true text. This seems at times to have been noticed, together with me, by a monk of the same monastery, as I suppose, who marked these deficiencies in lead pencil and wrote in the side margins: “Here it is deficient.”

Now, as to the notes, I would have you know, reader, that I faithfully recorded those belonging to either manuscript; but where the matter required it—as frequently happened—I sometimes added my own, according to the measure of my ability and judgment, in order to explain obscure words and to restore and clarify corrupted citations of passages. Yet I treated these matters as briefly as I could, lest I should produce, in place of an *Abbreviated Word*, a *Prolonged Word*. If in these notes I have said anything less correctly, I wish that the saying of blessed Augustine might be applied to me (*On the Trinity*, Book I, chapters 3 and 2): “I shall not be reluctant, where I hesitate, to inquire; nor ashamed, where I err, to learn. Therefore, whoever reads these things: where he is equally certain, let him proceed with me; where he equally hesitates, let him inquire with me; where he recognizes his own error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back. Thus let us enter together upon the way of charity,” etc.

Reader, make use of this *Abbreviated Word*, and I promise that you will reap abundant fruit. Its reading is wholesome and fruitful for fleeing and guarding against every kind of sin, for shaping morals, acquiring virtues, instilling in the mind love of God and contempt for the world; and, to conclude in the words of a certain wise man—in the Marchiennes text, chapter 80, after all the notes—“The *Abbreviated Word* is clear for attaining faith and knowledge of morals.” Farewell in the Lord; and if, through this reading, some spur to virtue takes deeper root than usual in your mind, assist me with your prayers to God as the reward for the labour I have undertaken.

# PETER THE CHANTER’S *ABBREVIATED WORD*

[Col. 0023]

## CHAPTER I. Against the excess and prolixity of glosses and useless questions

[Col. 0023A]

“The Lord made a short word upon the earth” (Rom. 9). For if the Word sent to us from the bosom of the Father—indeed, if the uncontainable Son of God, “whom the whole world cannot contain”—willed to be enclosed within the narrowness of a virgin’s womb, how much more did he will the Word of the sacred page—which he granted us and left us as the earnest and pledge of his love—to be abbreviated, so that in it we might discover his ways and paths, and read set forth briefly and succinctly the route of our course toward eternal blessedness?

An excess—indeed, an infinity—of words exists in other writings when compared with Holy Scripture; and Scripture rejects it. Rebuking this prolixity and excess of words and showing that it should be cut away, the philosopher says (Seneca, Letter 2): “The multitude of books distracts us. Therefore, since you cannot read as much as you possess, it is enough to possess as much as you can read.” [Col. 0024A] “But now,” you say, “I want to unroll this book, now that one.” It is the stomach of a fastidious person to taste many things; when they are varied and diverse, they soil rather than nourish. Therefore always read approved books; and if you ever wish to turn aside to others, return to the earlier ones, obtaining for yourself some aid against every vice and every plague. And when you have run through many things, select one that you may digest on that day. This too is what I do: from the many things I have read, I seize and select something.

Again (Letters 48, 16, 45): “Even if much of life remained, it would have to be dispensed sparingly, so that it might suffice for necessary things. For it is great madness to devote oneself to excess amid such scarcity of time. What is needed is not words but things.” This is knowledge of things, which more effectively forms the mind, orders life, directs actions, shows what must be done and omitted, and guides the course toward the stern and through the hazards of the tossing waves. No one is safe without it.

2 (Letter 19.) Therefore, since time is short, since the span in which we live is a point, indeed less than a point, and since death already holds the time that has passed, let us serve the Lord at least for an hour. [Col. 0025A] Imitating brevity, let us gather together the more useful chapters, drawn both from the body of Holy Scripture and from the good sayings of other writings.

“For whatever has been well said anywhere is mine,” says the Theologian (Letter 16): for rebuking individual vices, commending virtues and morals, directing our works, and resolving matters that arise in the Church.

The exercise of Holy Scripture, therefore, consists in three things: reading, disputation, and preaching. Excessive prolixity is the mother of forgetfulness and the stepmother of memory in each of these. Reading is like the foundation and substructure of what follows, [Col. 0025B] because through it the remaining benefits are gained. Disputation is like the wall in this exercise and building, because nothing is fully understood or faithfully preached unless it has first been broken by the tooth of disputation. Preaching, to which the preceding things minister, is like a roof sheltering the faithful from the heat and whirlwind of vices. Therefore, after reading Holy Scripture and investigating doubtful matters by disputation and inquiry—and not before—one should preach, so that one curtain may draw another, and so forth.

## CHAPTER II. On brevity in reading

Gregory, commending brevity in reading and cutting away from it prolixity and superfluous exposition, says (Homily 15 on Luke 8): “This reading”—that is, “A sower went out to sow his seed,” etc.—“does not need exposition, but admonition.” Therefore passages that admonish, because they are evident in themselves, should be read separately in a private place; but explanatory and difficult passages should be heard in the schools. “For this,” says Jerome (on Isaiah 1), “the thresholds of teachers must be worn down.”

Again, the same author says (on Ezekiel 16): “When, before the offense of idolatry, the Lord had entrusted to that people only the Decalogue, sufficient for salvation, after that offense he gave them multiple ceremonies, by which, as their deserts required, they were burdened and afflicted.” By their example we ought to fear that, although the Lord entrusted to the primitive Church only the text of Matthew’s Gospel, containing all things necessary for salvation, we have, as our deserts require—namely, by vain exercises, superfluous investigations, and other sins—been burdened with a multitude of glosses and with excessive and prolix reading. In these there is only “labour and affliction of spirit” (Eccles. 1): namely, in those glosses which speak not within the text but around it.

Again, Isaiah says: “Why do you spend your money, not for bread?” (Isa. 55)—that is, not for the actual nourishment 3 of spiritual utterances that satisfy and are necessary—“and your labour,” namely study, “not for fullness,” but upon leaves of words and upon a multitude which passes over the ear and does not satisfy the mind.

Again, the same prophet says: “Where is the learned man? Where is he who weighs the words of the law?” (Isa. 33)—namely, the scribe and Pharisee who burdens the law with superfluous exposition?

Again: Jerome expounds text by text, judging another gloss superfluous; and for that reason he is harder for us to understand.

Again: just as Jerome and Origen placed asterisks and obeli before passages to be illuminated, pierced, and deleted, so now it seems still more necessary that we should place them before passages for explaining difficult matters and for cutting down and deleting the prolixity and superfluity of glosses.

Again: as in the Temple there were pouring vessels, extinguishers, and snuffers for the lampstand (Exod. 25), so in Holy Scripture there were pourers—those who expounded it, Jerome and Gregory; extinguishers—those who extinguished heresies, namely Augustine and Hilary, mighty hammers against heretics; and snuffers—those who uprooted superfluities, such as Jerome and Origen. Following their example, let us also snuff out and cut away some superfluities from its reading.

Again: it ought to cause us the greatest shame that Jerome, aided only by a library, when summoned and consulted by Pope Damasus, answered sufficiently all the Church’s consultations and questions. Again: in the space of one year he expounded the whole Bible to Paula and Eustochium historically, allegorically, tropologically, and anagogically.

Again, Augustine says (*Against Maximus*, Book III, chapter 114, and on Psalm 57): “Do not believe my words unless I prove what I say through the Old or New Testament.” The Apostle also says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the utterances of God” (1 Pet. 4). The Gloss: Not contrary to God’s will, but in accordance with the authority of sacred utterance and for the neighbour’s benefit.

Again: armed only outwardly and not inwardly, we are unarmed against the Jew and the heretic, both in making objections and in answering them.

Again: Holy Scripture is our ship, by which we must cross “this great and wide sea” (Ps. 103), etc. It must be burdened not with ballast and superfluous expositions, but only with sufficient and necessary ones.

Again (Sulpicius Severus, Dialogue I, chapter 12): “Useful and necessary things must often be passed over, lest we be weighed down by a multitude of useful things.” Again, in the *Legend of St Martin*: “For one to whom few things are not enough, even more will not be useful.” Again, Solomon: “Let your actions be few” (Ecclus. 11). Therefore, if there should be few things, this should be still more the case with words.

Again: this is precious gum, which flows from the eyes [Col. 0026D] of the Lord; nothing superfluous, nothing adulterated, nothing contrary ought to be mixed with it.

Again: we again stop up with the Philistines the mouth of Abraham’s well, from which Isaac removed the stone (Gen. 26).

Again: when the children of Israel were commanded to depart from Egypt, they were to take only a little flour and fine flour with them (Exod. 12).

Again:

> Everything is covered with jewels and gold;  
> the girl herself is the smallest part of herself.  
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, Book I.)

4 Gregory: “Just as it is the part of an idle or vicious reader to explain what is plainly said, so it is the part of a prudent reader to clarify obscure sayings with few words.”

Again: “This is the tree that has been planted”—and so forth, as far as “it shall make,” that is, “shall teach to make”—“whose leaf shall not fall” (Ps. 1), [Col. 0027A] because it is the word of life; but “the leaves will fall,” by which we overshadow the tree’s fruit, lest it appear. If we are forbidden to gather the fruit of this tree except in the amount sufficient for us, much more are its useless leaves forbidden.

Again: just as the text is the shadow of eternal life, so the gloss applied to it is and ought to be a word of eternal life.

Again, in Deuteronomy, chapter 16: “You shall not plant a grove or any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God.” This is a tree not leafy; this is a vine not rich in shoots but fruitful, having more fruits than leaves. It does, indeed, have leaves, by which promises and threats are covered.

Again: the book sealed with seven seals was opened by Christ, the Key of David; for its opening John wept (Rev. 5). Let us not force him to weep again by rendering it obscure, tedious, and burdensome to read through superfluous expositions and useless glosses.

Again: the dark water of the clouds was made drinkable, as is evident in the eunuch (Acts 8). When Philip showed him the passage of Isaiah written about the Lord’s Passion, “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter” (Isa. 53), etc., he immediately understood.

Again: “The rocks were split and the tombs were opened” (Matt. 27) in the Lord’s Passion, because the writings of the prophets, hard to understand, were made open and plain by their fulfilment; yet we render them obscure by a multitude of glosses.

Again: we seem to mend the veil of the Temple that was torn and to restore ceremonies, although Christ is the end of the promises, who brings all things to fulfilment.

Again: we seem like those feeling their way at Lot’s door and not entering (Gen. 19), like the Egyptians groping at noon (Exod. 10); of this the Book of Wisdom speaks in its final chapter (Wis. 19).

Again: we seem to veil Moses’ face (Exod. 10), that is, Holy Scripture, so that it may appear horned to us, as to the Jews (Exod. 24), although God has uncovered and revealed it.

Again: we seem to veil Christ’s face and say, “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (Matt. 26)—or, “who understands [you]?”

Again, Leviticus 26: “You shall eat the very oldest of old things,” that is, you shall use and imitate the ancient way of reading; “and you shall cast away the old,” that is, the reading practice of the moderns, who are now old and therefore “old things,” once the “new”—that is, the most ancient things of the ancients—has been renewed [Col. 0027D] and then introduced for use.

Again, Isaiah says (chapter 1): “Your wine-sellers mix water with wine.” Let us not mix water and dregs with wine, olive-lees with oil, chaff with grain.

Again: to attain brevity, we ought especially to be moved by the loss involved in writing so many and such great volumes, because of excessive expense; by the loss in reading, because of lesser progress and delay in moving on to more useful things; by the loss in correcting, because of the waste of time, bodily weariness, and labour; and by the loss in carrying them, because of the weight and encumbrance of books.

Again: we wear ourselves out in reading superfluities—such as the locations of places, numerical counts of years and times, genealogies, mechanical arrangements 5 in buildings, as in the layout of the Tabernacle [Col. 0028A] and even of the imagined Temple. Holy Scripture was not given to us that we might seek vain and superfluous things in it, but faith, instruction in morals, and counsel and answers for the countless matters arising in the Church.

## CHAPTER III. On the brevity and usefulness of questions

After this, we must discuss the brevity of questions or disputation, and show which questions, and of what kind, ought to be treated. To this end, Ephesians chapter 4: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but whatever is good for the building up of faith, that it may give glory to those who hear.”

Again, 1 Timothy chapter 1: “I urged you to warn certain brethren not to teach otherwise, nor to attend to fables and endless genealogies, which produce ruin rather than God’s edification, which is in faith.”

Again, in the same letter, chapter 6: “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that accords with godliness, he is proud and knows nothing, but is sick concerning questions and battles of words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemies,” etc.

Again, in the same letter, chapter 4: “Avoid foolish and old wives’ fables. Rather train yourself in godliness,” which consists in faith and good morals.

Again, in the same letter, chapter 6: “Avoid profane novelties of language and oppositions of falsely named knowledge; by professing it some have fallen away from the faith.” True knowledge consists only in instruction in faith [Col. 0028C] and morals.

Again, 2 Timothy chapter 1: “Hold the pattern of sound words which you have heard from me, in faith and love in Christ Jesus.” In the same letter, chapter 2: “Do not contend in words, for it is useful for nothing except the overthrow of the hearers.”

Again, in the same letter, chapter 2: “Present yourself unashamed, rightly handling the word of truth; but avoid profane and empty talk, for they advance greatly toward ungodliness, and in them there is no fruit.”

Again, in the same letter, chapter 2: “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they produce quarrels; but the servant of the Lord must not quarrel.”

Observe the difference between foolish questions and rash ones. The former are vain and useless; the latter are dangerous, overthrowing the mind and quickly generating their error.

Again, chapter 3: “But continue in the things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them, and because from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which can instruct you for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. For all Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.”

Again, in Psalm 58: “My mouth shall speak wisdom.” Gloss: “Concerning faith and heavenly things.” “And the meditation of my heart, understanding.” 6 Gloss: “Concerning good morals.”

Again, in Psalm 67: “Yet the Lord shall crush”—by humbling or punishing—“the heads of his enemies,” that is, pride, “and the hairy crown,” that is, the subtleties [Col. 0029A] of empty questions. For there are people who pursue such minute quibbles of calumnies and questions that they seem even to examine individual hairs.

Again, Leviticus chapter 1: “He who offers a turtledove or pigeon shall throw away the crop,” that is, every swelling—“a swelling repels what is poured in; therefore let your altar be hollow”—“and the feathers,” that is, throw away superfluous and useless questions.

Again, in the same book, chapter 26: “If you keep my commandments, I shall give you rain in its seasons; if not, I shall give you from above a heaven of iron”—that is, Scripture which will not rain doctrine upon you—“and a bronze earth,” that is, divine Scripture unfruitful for you. “Your labour shall be consumed in vain.” Gloss: the labour you expend upon the divine Scriptures, because you understand them perversely and occupy yourselves with superfluities.

Again, Deuteronomy chapter 28: “May God give rain,” that is, doctrine, which does not bring forth the shoots of virtues but pronounces eternal destruction; “and may ashes descend from heaven upon you,” that is, a burning, subtle, and confused doctrine, “until you are destroyed.” Gloss: eternal punishment. That which is reduced to ash and dust is like what is confused. Nothing is subtler than a straw; nothing harms usefulness as much as excessive subtlety. Do not stir up and scatter dust, lest, once stirred, it envelop and darken—indeed blind—the eye of your mind.

Again, Seneca says (Letter 20): “One purpose belongs to declaimers and seekers of the crowd’s applause; another to those who hold the ears of idle people by varied or fluent disputation. Heavenly philosophy teaches us to act, not to chatter or talk volubly. For it is concerned with things, not words. It is not a popular art—although now, through our fault, it has been given over to glory, gain, and litigation. Do not rest content amid the winding meanders and twists of words and the labyrinthine dwellings of quibbles; rather, flee them” (Letter 16).

Again: “Why do you twist words for me and arrange syllables? Surely I cannot distinguish what must be sought from what must be avoided unless I construct the most crafty questions and establish by a false conclusion a lie arising from truth. We ought to be ashamed that, in a matter so serious, old men play games. O childish follies! Is this why we have grown our beards? Is this what we teach, grave and pale? Heavenly philosophy promises something: namely, to make me obedient in some way to God. This is no place for joking. You have been summoned as counsel for the wretched. You have promised aid to shipwrecked persons, captives, the sick, the needy, and those offering their heads to the raised axe” (Letter 48).

“Our battle is against vices, against the plagues of Erebus, against the monster of this sea. Why then do you shoot such tiny darts against death? Do you meet a lion with an awl? These things you say are sharp. Nothing is sharper than a straw; but subtlety itself makes certain things useless and ineffectual” (Letter 82).

The example of Polemon is pertinent here. While he was living a thoroughly dissolute life, crowned with garlands of roses, drenched in perfumes, and surrounded by a crowd of rakes and procurers, he entered Xenocrates’ school. Accordingly all the disciples were greatly indignant; 7 but the master alone, taking pity on his wretchedness, departed from the course of his proposed disputation [Col. 0030A] and began to discourse on frugality and good morals, commending each virtue and rebuking and condemning the vices opposed to them. At last Polemon, deeply moved, took one leg off the other and cast away every badge of luxury and vice—his scarves, nets, little crowns, and such things. Thus, through one most pointed disputation, the man who entered as a most shameful procurer emerged as a most serious philosopher (Valerius Maximus, Book VI, chapter 11).

Again, Seneca: “Why do you construct captious arguments for me? Why do you bind the questioner with chains”—namely, of disputation? “Great monsters”—that is, vices—“are struck with great weapons” (Letter 82).

Again: “It is shameful to descend armed with an awl into the battle undertaken for gods and men”—for gods, that is, for faith; for men, that is, for good [Col. 0030B] morals—undertaken against vices, “armed with an awl,” that is, with a light and frivolous argument or disputation (ibid.).

Again: “We should have found many necessary things, had we not sought superfluous ones. Quibbling about words has taken much time from us, as have captious disputations, which exercise an unproductive sharpness. We tie knots and investigate the ambiguous meaning of words, as though we had leisure, as though we already knew how to live and how to die” (Letter 45). And below: “We must take greater care that things, not words, deceive us. Who defines for me differences of terms by which no one has ever been caught except while disputing? Things deceive; therefore distinguish them.”

Again: “The person to whom you prove that he has horns is not so foolish as to test and touch his own forehead.” [Col. 0030C] Thus such things deceive harmlessly, like the cups of conjurers and the little stones of Pygmies, in which the very deception gives pleasure. “But I have no leisure for these follies. A great task is in my hands. Now lethal matters surround me, death follows me, life flees; teach me against these things” (Letter 52).

Again: “Nothing is more shameful than heavenly philosophy seeking applause. It is something between the shouting of a theatre and a school. Disputations prepared and poured forth into the ears of the people have more noise and less usefulness. No one gives counsel clearly. Quiet words enter and adhere more easily; not many are needed, but effective ones” (Letter 38).

Therefore one should not shout in theological disputations; nor should one dispute about trifles. Rather, as Seneca says [Col. 0030D] (Letter 49), “Discourse to me concerning justice, piety, frugality, and each of the two kinds of chastity, namely chastity of mind and body.” The tragedian likewise says: “The speech of truth is simple”; therefore it ought not to be entangled. For nothing is less fitting than this crafty subtlety of mind for those attempting great things (Euripides, *Phoenician Women*).

Let us therefore put aside the refined constructions of this sharp declamation and useless little questions, lest we seem longer to circle Mount Seir with the Jews in a manifold and vain circuit (Deut. 2), and, wandering so long in Rameses, remain unable to arrive at the land of promise—that is, at the truth of theology (Exod. 12; Num. 33). Since you were born for greater things, apply yourself to realities rather than words, so that whatever you read, dispute, [Col. 0031A] or preach, you may direct toward forming morals in yourself and in others through your example. For example: awaken what languishes within you; tame what is swollen; restrain what is uncontrolled; bind what is loose; harass and uproot your desires; enlighten your ignorance (Seneca, Letter 89).

We are instructed concerning the usefulness of disputation and against its uselessness by the example of the ancients. The patriarchs fought against idolatry by deed and example. The prophets rebuked the children of Israel for disobedience by word and example. The apostles preached against unbelief by word, example, and even death. The doctors of the Church disputed against heresies in defence of the Gospel and the faith. But we, barren in the Church and bearing no fruit in it, fail while languishing amid superfluous and vain questions.

## CHAPTER IV. On the rashness of questions and rash disputations
“Together the foolish and the stupid shall perish” (Ps. 48). This has been said of foolish disputations: although they are useless, yet because they seem to possess a certain subtlety, they entice and deceive. Although fools perish, the more so do the senseless, who inquire into heavenly matters beyond their powers and beyond what suffices for salvation, and who seem to harass the Lord Jesus with wasps and daggers. Against such persons the Apostle inveighs, saying: “Do not be wise beyond what is fitting,” etc. (Rom. 12).

Likewise, Jeremiah, chapter 15 [Col. 0031C]: “Woe is me, my mother! Why have you borne me, a man of strife,” or of judgment? Another reading: “a man of discord,” or one who judges, “in all the earth? I have neither lent at interest, nor has anyone lent to me, and all curse me”—by contradicting me, and I them. Thus we too curse one another in words and contradict one another, agreeing on scarcely anything.

Likewise, Job, chapter 19: “Yet even if I have been ignorant, my ignorance shall remain with me”—concerning non-necessary matters; and so too knowledge, not knowledge as such, which causes one to vanish away and grow proud.

Likewise, Ecclesiasticus, chapter 16: “The giants of old did not pray for their sins”; the curious are compared and likened to them. And in the same place: “He who is diminished,” that is, divided among many things, “in heart thinks vain things.”

Likewise [Col. 0031D], Psalm 63: “They have searched out iniquities,” etc.; and Luke, chapter 2: “Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign that shall be contradicted.” For when he was born, Herod immediately contradicted him concerning the kingdom (Matt. 2); when he suffered, the Scribes and Pharisees contradicted him concerning the title of the inscription (John 19); and now his humanity is disputed, as are other sacraments, since different persons hold differing and opposed opinions about them.

Likewise, Psalm 50: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” Uncertain things are those for which some indications are available, though we are ignorant of more concerning them than we know. Hidden things are those which are wholly concealed and of which we have no indications; and the Lord had revealed both the one and the other to David. But do we presume to surpass David [Col. 0032A], or to equal him in merits, so that the Lord should similarly reveal these things to us? Such people disdain to say: “Your knowledge has become wonderful to me, and I shall not be able to attain it” (Ps. 138); rather, they think they can.

Likewise, they do not deign to say: “My eyes have failed for your word” (Ps. 118). Jerome (Epistle 104, §8): “I am not so foolish as to believe that I can fully pluck the fruits of that tree whose roots are fixed in heaven.”

Likewise, such persons “squeeze the breasts so that they draw out blood instead of milk” (Prov. 30), or pour it forth.

Likewise, they make the waters “of one manner,” with which “we ought to walk in the house in harmony,” into “waters of contradiction” (Ps. 67): waters which they contradict, and by which they contradict one another, the Lord himself, and the waters themselves.

Jeremiah, chapter 33 [Col. 0032B]: “My heart is broken within me,” he says; “my bones have trembled. I have become like a drunken man, and like one drenched with wine, before the face of the Lord, before the face of his holy words”; and therefore: “Because the land is full of adulterers, because before the face of the curse the land has mourned” (ibid.). If, therefore, before his primary “face,” which is the divine essence, I “have become like a drunken man,” etc., in seeking to understand and know it, so likewise before his secondary “face,” namely, “his words,” which concern that essence and teach us to recognize it.

Likewise, the Hebrews were commanded with consideration and discernment that no one under thirty years of age should read the beginning of Genesis, the end of Ezekiel, or the Song of Songs. Therefore the food of sacred Scripture ought to be dispensed in classes and by measure, by a faithful and prudent steward [Col. 0032C].

“Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth, because your magnificence is exalted above the heavens” (Ps. 8)—that is, above the heavens of sacred Scripture; and he says, “We cannot attain it” (Ps. 138). Thus his name is inexplicable and admirable, and likewise his greatness, which has no end.

Likewise, the ark is to be covered out of reverence, although it has been uncovered with respect to the ceremonies (Lev. 16). Likewise, the smoke of compounded incense moderated the priest’s sight, lest, entering the temple, he should behold the naked “Holy of Holies” (ibid.). So we too must now moderate our sight.

The angel in Tobit, chapter 12: “Bless the God of heaven,” etc. “For it is good to conceal the secret of a king, but honorable to reveal and confess his works.” Gloss: The mysteries of the Lord are to be concealed, but his works proclaimed. Hence, on that verse of the Psalm, “Your knowledge has become wonderful to me” (Ps. 138), etc., the Gloss—and elsewhere the text itself—says: “Your works are wonderful, and my soul shall know them exceedingly” (ibid.). Therefore inquire into the Lord’s works, and treat of them, of repentance, and of giving counsel in the Church.

Likewise [Col. 0032D]: “You shall not break a bone thereof” (Exod. 12; John 19); and: “Do not reduce the bones of the king of Edom to ashes” (Amos 2:1). Let the pit be closed, lest an ox or an ass fall into it (Exod. 21).

“Give me understanding according to your word” (Ps. 118). M. Not below it, not against it, not above it. I do not even dare to say “with” your word, but “according to” it, lest I seem to contend with you as an equal. Therefore: “I have clung to your testimonies, O Lord” (Ps. 118)—not above them, as those who are likened to Simon Magus, who flew, but not “above the wings of the winds” (Ps. 17), as Christ alone did, “who made darkness his hiding-place,” until “we see him” hereafter “face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

Likewise [Col. 0033A], of those flying above: “They have set their mouth in heaven, and their tongue has passed through the earth” (Ps. 72): that is, they treat and dispute of heavenly things in a human manner. They “set their eyes to stoop down to the earth” (Ps. 16), whereas they ought rather, with Martin, to look toward heaven than to “set their mouth in heaven.” The Lord “turned the rivers” of such persons “into blood,” that is, into a carnal sense and exposition, “that they might not drink their rains” (Ps. 77).

Likewise, it is dreadful to gather dust, refuse, and worthless twigs concerning heavenly things and the highest good, the author of all. Hence the philosopher (Epistle to Eustochium on the guardianship of virginity): “He who is timid in the greatest and doubtful matters is worth nothing.” And Jerome: “It is foolish to be anxious about what cannot be known without danger.”

Likewise: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1). “For he who walks simply walks confidently” (Prov. 10). I do not mean a feigned and heretical simplicity, or a simplicity akin to folly, but simplicity without the fold of error, the fold of curiosity, and rash inquiry.

Likewise [Col. 0033C], “Like newborn infants,” yet rational, “desire the milk” of doctrine (1 Pet. 2): namely, such sufficient and lesser matters as you can grasp. We are therefore warned not to inquire into foolish matters; much more into curious ones—indeed, we are forbidden.

“Do not lift up your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God” (Ps. 74): either by blaspheming through heresy; by teaching evil conduct; by investigating too much through pride and curious disputation; or by asserting that the Lord’s commands are general, particular, local, and temporal, and thereby smoothing down the bow of sacred Scripture by a carnal exposition. “Do not speak lofty” and rash things, boasting; “but let old things depart from your mouth” (1 Sam. 2): that is, superfluous and rash investigations and the false doctrines of philosophers.

Likewise: Manoah said to the angel [Col. 0033D] who appeared to him, “What is your name?” The angel replied: “Why do you ask my name, which is wonderful” (Judg. 13), and inexplicable? M. If we are forbidden to inquire concerning the name of the Deity, much more are we forbidden to inquire curiously and proudly concerning the reality signified by that name. Every name of God is ineffable. Let it suffice, then, that he himself is “Wonderful, Strong, Mighty” (Isa. 9), etc.—that these, namely, are his names.

Likewise Jerome: “It is said with no less wickedness that God is not what he is, than it is denied that he is what he is.” Moses placed boundaries around the mountain, lest a beast touching it should be stoned (Exod. 19). Thus Christ and our Fathers “set a boundary upon the mountain” and around the mountain of sacred Scripture, “which we must not transgress” (Ps. 103; Heb. 12) by useless, rash, and superfluous inquiry [Col. 0034A]. For those who touched the mountain in a beastly manner were stoned.

Likewise, Proverbs, chapter 25: “My son, have you found honey”—namely, of doctrine? “Eat what is sufficient for you, lest perhaps, having been filled, you vomit it up” (Prov. 25). Gloss: That is, by seeking beyond your powers, you lose what you have understood.

Likewise, with Jonathan dip only the tip of the rod into honey, and your eyes will be made bright as his were (1 Sam. 14); and you will rightly pursue your enemies as he did, because “The unfolding of your words, O Lord, gives light” (Ps. 118). It does not darken or entangle, as curious inquiry does.

Likewise, Ecclesiasticus, chapter 3: “My son, do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not search things stronger than yourself; but think always upon the things God has commanded, and do not be curious concerning his many works. For it is not necessary for you to see with your eyes the things that are hidden” [Col. 0034B]—much less to search out his majesty.

Likewise, in the same place: “Do not investigate superfluous matters repeatedly, and do not be curious concerning his many works. For very many things beyond human understanding have been shown to you; for their own suspicion has overthrown many” (Ecclus. 5).

Likewise, Ecclesiastes, chapter 7: “Why is it necessary for a man to seek things greater than himself, when he does not know what is advantageous to him in his life?” Likewise: “I said, ‘I shall become wise’; and wisdom itself withdrew farther from me—farther than it was—and there is another depth: who shall find it?” Likewise, chapter 8: “Who is like the wise man, and who knows the solution of the divine word?” Likewise: “I understood that of all the works of the Lord, man cannot discover the reason of those things that are under the sun; and the more he labors to seek, the less he will find” [Col. 0034C].

Likewise: “My son, let your words be few” (Ecclus. 5), concerning God, of whom diverse things are dangerously said. Likewise, Ecclesiasticus: “He who seeks the law shall be filled by it, but he who acts” curiously and “deceitfully shall be scandalized by it” (Ecclus. 32), and shall not find it.

Likewise Aristotle: “Never is it fitting for us to be more reverent and more sober than when we speak about the gods.” M. Much more when we speak of the one true God.

## CHAPTER V. On the manner of disputing: that one should dispute without contention

[Col. 0034D] There follows the manner of disputing, which requires that it be done without quarrel and contention. Hence Isaiah: “The waters of Siloam flow with silence” (Isa. 8), not with litigation, not with violence, nor with a tragic gaping mouth.
