Likewise, in Deuteronomy, in the song of Moses: “Let my speech flow as dew” (Deut. 32): falling drop by drop, without noise and excessive outpouring.

Likewise, 2 Kings, chapter 22: “He made darkness his hiding-place; round about him, filtering waters,” namely, of sacred Scripture, “from the clouds of heaven.” We must therefore treat of them by filtering them, and not by pouring them forth violently, so that they may descend from the clouds of sacred Scripture.

Likewise, 2 Timothy 2: “The servant of God must not strive”—so as to make a din through zeal for wrangling and defend his error with a tragic gaping mouth—“but must be gentle toward all” [Col. 0035A], correcting and disputing “with modesty.”

Likewise: “Not in contention” (Rom. 13). Gloss: For wrangling does not befit saints, but conference does. In contention the inferior envies the superior and strives to set himself before him.

Likewise, 2 Timothy 2: “Do not contend in words, for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of the hearers.” Gloss: Contention can do nothing but ruin, while the verbose adversary appears equal or superior to the humbly speaking Catholic; and in it one cannot avoid bringing forth something contrary to conscience.

Delivery ought to be orderly, like one’s life; and what is precipitate and hurried is not orderly. Swiftness of speech is neither under its own control nor sufficiently friendly to philosophy, which ought to place words, not throw them forth, and proceed step by step (Seneca, Epistle 40).

Likewise, the philosopher: “In short, I command you to be slow-speaking, sparing of speech, and to speak in a low voice. For to move the head, twist the arms, stretch out the fingers, stamp the feet, and shake the whole body—what else is this but a certain likeness to madness, displaying you as like a boxer?” (ibid.).

Likewise Isaiah: “When you cease to stretch out the finger and to speak what does no good, then you shall please my soul” (Isa. 58).

Likewise, as it is shameful for one raising a question in disputation to resemble an actor by proposing it with gestures, so it is shameful and dangerous for one answering to be excessively hasty—especially when resolving questions in which the peril of souls is involved [Col. 0035C] (Heb. 10). Hence Ecclesiasticus, chapter 32: “My son, do nothing without counsel, and after the deed you will not repent.”

Likewise: “He who makes a question manifest”—namely, by resolving it—“will prepare a word” (Ecclus. 33). Gloss: by praying, meditating, and working well; “and thus, having prayed, he shall be heard, shall preserve discipline, and then shall answer.” “The inward parts of a fool are like a cartwheel,” etc.

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 32: “A man of counsel will not destroy understanding; a stranger and proud man will not fear fear, even after he has acted without counsel and is rebuked for his own pursuits.”

Likewise, chapter 37: “My son, in all things establish within yourself the heart of good counsel, for you have nothing more valuable than it.” Likewise, chapter 37: Before every work let a true word go before you, and before every action stable counsel.

Likewise: “The lips of the imprudent will relate foolish and unconsidered things, but the words of the prudent will be weighed in a balance. The heart of fools is in their mouth, and the mouth of the wise is in their heart” (Ecclus. 21).

Likewise, by the example of the saints of the primitive Church, as well as of the righteous who preceded them and other elders who followed them: they resolved nothing and answered no questions unless deliberation and counsel had first been held and had preceded.

Likewise, by analogy: when a question concerning some small plot of land or other earthly trifle is brought before a judge, such solemnity of judgment is employed—in the approval of witnesses, the production of advocates [Col. 0036A], the delay and waiting for adjournments, the integrity of the accused, and finally the rendering of sentence. How much more should this be so in matters concerning heavenly things, the sacraments of the Church, and matters—namely, whether counsel should or should not be given—in which the peril of souls is at stake.

Likewise, Aristotle answered no question put to him, even an easy one, without a period of delay. Thus, when a difficult question was proposed to him, Theophrastus, still impelled by youthful heat, promised that he would solve it. When he failed in solving it and was deeply ashamed, Aristotle said to him: “You need a bridle.” But to another disciple, namely Eudemus—who resolved questions proposed to him too slowly and only after long delays—Aristotle said: “You need spurs.” Yet he had a rich vein of talent.

## CHAPTER VI. On preaching, which holiness of life ought to precede

There follows the third exercise of sacred Scripture, namely preaching, whose foundation—as with the two preceding exercises (above, chapter 1)—is holiness of life and good conduct, through which one comes to those exercises. Hence in the Psalm: “It is good for me to cleave to God” through faith, good life, and the working of faith (Ps. 72); then: “To place my hope in the Lord God, that thus I may proclaim all your praises,” or preachings, “in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9).

For preaching is manifold: instruction, correction, exhortation, stirring up, consolation, and the support of benefaction. And because the voice serves the three things mentioned above as though necessary to them and as their prelude, one must know that voice too is manifold. There is the voice of weeping: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Ps. 5); and there is the voice of confession; then the voice of exultation issuing from a serene conscience, followed by the voice of preaching. Hence the Psalm: “In the voice of exultation and confession is the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41). And elsewhere: “We will confess to you, O God”—our sins, for the removal of evils; “we will confess to you”—praises, for the bestowal of goods; and then, living and acting well, “we will call upon your name,” so that we may preach good and useful things to others. Hence follows: “We will recount your wonders” (Ps. 74), the works of creation and re-creation [Col. 0036D], to stir up the people.

This order is observed also in the order of healing. Harmful things and the rest must first be removed. Likewise, addressing preachers on the same point, the Lord says: “You,” seasoned with wisdom, “are the salt of the earth”—life; “you are the light of the world”—doctrine (Matt. 5). For a good life precedes knowledge—not, I say, knowledge of words, but of things. Thus by life, and not otherwise, you will attain knowledge, namely knowledge of deeds. This is knowledge of things; whoever loves does not lack it.

Likewise Solomon: “My son, desiring wisdom, keep his commandments, and the Lord will give it to you” (Ecclus. 10). Likewise: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 118): namely, by fulfilling them through works, I have obtained understanding in doctrine. The Gloss says on that passage: “Through keeping the commandments one comes to the secrets of the mysteries.”

Likewise: “Good understanding to all who do it” (Ps. 110), first; likewise: “Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge” (Ps. 118). Discipline first, knowledge afterwards. Likewise: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord; blessed are they who search his testimonies” (ibid.). As if to say: first possess the foundation of life—namely innocence, “walking in the law of the Lord,” by working well—then search his testimonies, in order to acquire greater knowledge.

Likewise the Apostle: “Take heed to yourself and to doctrine” (1 Tim. 4). And in the apostolic rule he puts first the requirements of pure life: “A bishop must be sober, chaste” (Tit. 1) [Col. 0037B], and the like; and last, what concerns doctrine, saying: In a teacher, a good life should precede doctrine and preaching (Gregory, Homily 2 on the Gospels). For the preaching of one whose life is despised is necessarily held in contempt.

Likewise, by the example of the Lord, “who began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). Likewise, the legal priest first put on the ephod, then the breastplate. For one must first bear one’s own burdens and those of one’s neighbors, and fulfill the works of the law, before approaching reasoning and doctrine—as if one must first possess a pure life.

Likewise, in figure of these things, “the shoulder of separation and the breast of elevation” (Exod. 29, 39) belonged to the priests. One must first labor and work, so as to be separated from evil, before being raised to knowledge and mental contemplation.

Likewise, on the priest’s tunic were “pomegranates”—signifying the fervor of charity, which comes first—and “bells” (Exod. 39), signifying the resonance of doctrine and preaching, which follows. Eloquence is struck dumb where a sick conscience lies beneath.

Likewise, concerning virtues: “The Lord shall give the word to those who proclaim the gospel with great power” (Ps. 67). For the phrase “with great power” must refer to both parts.

Likewise, in sacred Scripture things rather than words speak: “Act in reality, and you will be safe” (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*). In it things persuade more than words. This is inferred from the example of Bernard preaching to nuns and becoming silent at the beginning of his sermon because of their sins (see his *Life*, book 3, chapter 3). When they repented and confessed, he rained upon them the shower from heaven of sacred Scripture [Col. 0037D].

Likewise, the same man preached to German laypeople and moved them to tears, though they did not understand him. After him, an excellent monk-interpreter unfolded the sermon; but while he spoke, they were not at all moved. For whoever does not burn does not kindle. Indeed, God often closes the mouths of prophets because of the people’s sins.

Likewise, the philosopher: “A discourse delivered in a coarse garment and on a pallet, with a pale face, is more magnificent” (Seneca, Epistle 20). But we preach the word of God with swollen and ruddy cheeks; therefore it is despised.

Likewise, it is read in the *Lives of the Fathers* (book 5, booklet 3, no. 18): Certain hermits, together with some secular persons, came to Abbot Felix, asking him to give them an address; but he answered them nothing. They knocked again, and again he was silent. When they knocked a third time, he replied: “There is no discourse today.” For there is no discourse unless the life of the speaker and the merit of the hearer correspond to it. At the least, it requires holiness of life in the speaker, which must come first as a foundation.

Likewise [Col. 0038A], those who handle the word of God—by reading, disputing, or preaching—without the foundation of holiness and life are like the Sodomites knocking on Lot’s door, wishing to enter in order to commit shameful acts; but, struck with blindness, they could not find the door (Gen. 19). So too, those seeking glory, gain, and such things in sacred Scripture, turning it into a popular art, are blinded by curiosity and other sins and are not permitted to enter.

Likewise, if Mary Magdalene, fervent in love, was forbidden by the Lord to touch his feet because he had not yet ascended to the Father in her heart (John 20), how much more should we be forbidden to touch these feet, namely sacred Scripture—we who love less and whose life, deformed by crimes, stinks before the Lord!

Likewise, Job, chapter 8: “The hope of the hypocrite shall perish, and his folly shall not please him.” Gregory, on this passage, says of Origen: “This is the man who does what he speaks and speaks what he does.” For a hypocrite is one who says one thing and does another. Hypocrites indeed utter the word, but they do not kindle their hearers to desire what is above.

## CHAPTER VII. On the commendation of sacred eloquence

[Col. 0038C]

A word bursting forth from a cold breast does not inflame, because whoever does not burn does not kindle. Likewise: “Your utterance is exceedingly fiery” (Ps. 6): namely, seasoned with the fire of charity and brought forth from charity, so that fire may speak fire.

Likewise, for this reason, at the sending of the Holy Spirit, he appeared above the heads of the Apostles in tongues of fire (Acts 25 [probably Acts 2]), so that, kindled with more fervent love, they might utter fiery words in all languages.

Likewise: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12).

Likewise, when Basil the Great preached, it seemed to his hearers that a fiery tongue came forth from his mouth [Col. 0038D], for he spoke from the fire of charity.

Likewise, when Sebastian preached, Zoe, wife of Nicostratus, said to him: “I see before you an angel of the Lord holding for you an open book, from which all your preaching proceeds.”

Likewise the Apostle: “My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, because my heart is enlarged” by charity (2 Cor. 6). Otherwise it is not opened in preaching; but, possessing charity, the Lord says: “Open wide your mouth, and I shall fill it” (Ps. 80).

Likewise David: “My heart has been enlarged, and my tongue has exulted,” etc. (Ps. 15).

Likewise the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, eat this scroll” (Ezek. 3), on which were written Lamentation, Song, and Woe. Song for the justified, lamentation for the impenitent, woe for the damned or reprobate. Preaching ought therefore to concern the reward of the heavenly homeland, repentance, and the punishment of Gehenna alone [Col. 0039A]. “And I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey” (Ezek. 3). He who most sweetly loves the word of God in his heart preaches it sweetly and most pleasantly with his mouth; but he preaches it uselessly and bitterly when conscience opposes and contradicts his tongue.

Likewise: “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my justices?” (Ps. 49). Since you do not fulfill them in deed, why do you utter something concerning my majesty in common discourse to the people? “And why do you take up my covenant” (ibid.)—that is, though you are irreverent, you presume to preach it to others “through your polluted mouth” (ibid.)? Private reading, indeed, is not forbidden. As if to say: nor should your mouth presume to teach holy words.

Cassiodorus says upon this passage [Col. 0039B]: God forbids a tongue to presume publicly to preach when an evil conscience opposes it; yet praise is not forbidden to those converted to repentance. But see that you do not sing well and live badly.

Likewise the Apostle: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest perhaps, after I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9). He does not say: “Lest, after I have read to others,” namely privately. Therefore wicked persons should not mingle themselves with divine discourses.

Likewise, for this reason in the Old Testament there was a bronze basin at the entrance of the tabernacle, where priests washed their hands when entering and leaving the tabernacle (Exod. 30). Hence: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). In the same basin were mirrors, in which those entering and leaving [Col. 0039C] the tabernacle could see whether there was any stain in themselves needing purification. M. For this purpose alone.

Note that one kind of preaching is gain-seeking (Blessed Gregory, Homily 12 on the Gospels); another is vain and proud, seeking glory; another is curious and foolish; another deceitful and heretical; another insulting and full of scandals—when, namely, one preaches whose life is despised—and these latter two are by no means tolerated. Another is official, when someone preaches by virtue of office; another charitable, when someone, being a private person, preaches out of charity and not from office.

A hidden sinner who is not a prelate may preach well; but a sinful prelate, even if his sin is hidden, sins mortally if he preaches. Jerome proves this (Epistle 1 to Heliodorus) [Col. 0039D], addressing such a man in these words: “Not all bishops are bishops. You who live badly in office, why do you occupy another’s place and ground? Beware lest you withhold from the people, on account of your sin, preaching and prayer owed to them, and lest you be punished eternally with the people. For he who is weighed down by his own sins does not cleanse those of others.”

“For such a one hinders a common work and therefore sins mortally” (Matt. 15). But an impenitent person remaining resolved to sin ought not to preach even by virtue of office, since he acts contrary to the office and sins mortally in exercising it; how much more one whose life is full of scandals!

Likewise: Unless you are an imitator of Samson, you will not draw a honeycomb from the lion’s mouth (Judg. 14).

Likewise, Jeremiah, chapter 1, God says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you, and I gave you as a prophet among the nations.” And Jeremiah said: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” [Col. 0040A]; that is, more ignorant in the ABCs—namely, in life, knowledge, and eloquence.

Likewise, 2 Timothy 2: “Therefore, my son, the things you have heard from me, and through many witnesses, commit them to faithful persons who will be capable of teaching others also.” Capable in life, knowledge, and eloquence. For this third thing—eloquence—is necessary to the first two; otherwise, insofar as someone benefits by example, so far does he harm by silence.

Likewise, in the same epistle: “Take diligent care to present yourself approved,” first “a workman not ashamed,” and afterwards “rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Tim. 2).

Likewise the Lord in the Gospel: “Who do you think is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appoints over his household to give them their measure of wheat in due season?” (Luke 12). Thus he knows what things, for whom, of what kind, and when they ought to be served.

Likewise the philosopher (Seneca, Epistle 24): “Nothing so afflicts us philosophers as the reproach that we deal in words, not works, and that we are called by those who make witty jests ‘animals of the clod’ [perhaps *gloriae*, ‘of glory’].”

Likewise, holy Gideon, about to fight the Midianites, broke the jars, lit the lights or lamps, sounded the trumpets, and the Midianites were terrified and defeated (Judg. 7).

Likewise, the Lord commanded Isaiah (chapter 32) and Jeremiah (chapter 1) that they should not preach until they had first girded their loins and reins.

Likewise [Col. 0040C], the children of Israel besieging Jericho (Josh. 6) went around it seven times; and on the seventh circuit they sounded the trumpets, and Jericho’s walls fell. Jericho is interpreted “defect.” Therefore, one who is going to preach should first go around all his own defects together with the world, which is in defect; and on the seventh circuit—that is, when he does so fully and perfectly, in a perfect circuit—the vices of worldly people to whom he will preach will fall.

Likewise: “I went around and offered in his tabernacle a sacrifice of shouting,” etc. (Ps. 26).

## CHAPTER VIII. On curious preaching, and against it

The philosopher (Seneca, Epistles 71 and 108): O reader, disputant, and likewise preacher, who seek the good and uprightness of life, do not expect magnificent utterances from those wandering performers and hunters of words [Col. 0040D], who adulterate the word of God with little flowers and artificial colors, borrowed translations and comparisons, and shameless discourses that are pleasing rather than useful and produce an itching of the ears.

Can such a preacher help me more than a nauseated ship’s captain who can scarcely stand, stunned and vomiting, and is unable to govern either himself or others? Human life in this world ought to be governed with no less care than a ship at sea.

“But,” you say, “Aristotle, Socrates, Plato, Philo, and others say that these things ought to be followed and observed.” Do not concern yourself with their sayings in such matters; rather, in order to live well, do what you say.

Likewise, by the example of Abbot William of Clairvaux, who refused to compose a sermon but preferred [Col. 0041A] to discuss business and matters to be done in the monastery, saying that a sermon of this sort produced only an itching of the ears—though he was greatly urged to preach in many chapters.

Likewise, he who commands: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. 6), likewise says: “Do not think about how or what you shall speak” (Luke 12; Matt. 10). Therefore, one who thinks about how or what he will say opposes and empties the Lord’s command, because, studying with frenzy, he beats the lectern, and his discourse tastes of bitten nails. If such a man's life preached, his tongue too would preach without labor and premeditated discourse. For to such a man “it shall be given in that hour what he shall speak” (ibid.).

In Acts of the Apostles, chapter 17, Luke rebuking curious preachers and hearers says: “All the Athenians and the strangers who were there devoted themselves to nothing else than either telling or hearing something new”—not in order that they might believe or do it, but that they might marvel at it.

Likewise the Apostle: “I did not come to you in wisdom of speech, not in the learned words of human wisdom” (1 Cor. 2:13), but in simplicity of speech, “lest the cross of Christ should be emptied” (1 Cor. 1:17). For when truth is plain, ornament of language is not required, lest faith be produced more by words than by the truth of the Passion. That Passion, as it was accomplished, is to be narrated in simple speech, lest what we believe be attributed rather to the words of human wisdom than to truth and grace, and thus “the cross of Christ be emptied” [Col. 0041B].

Truth does not seek corners, because it suffices for itself. Heavenly philosophy is not like human philosophy, that shameless harlot which does not suffice for itself unless it is colored and painted with artificial colors and Jezebel’s eye-paint (4 Kings 9)—that is, with verbal flowers and trappings—so that it may appear wise rather than be wise.

Likewise Jerome (vol. 1, Epistle to Gallus): “A friend ought not to bait a friend, but should rather set before him what benefits than what delights.”

Likewise the philosopher (Seneca, Epistle 115): “I command you not to be anxious about the composition and polish of discourse; for do not expect a solid and sound word from such a person. Whenever you see speech that is carefully wrought, elegant, polished, trimmed close, and rhythmically balanced, know that the mind is devoted to trifles and weakened. But a great mind speaks more freely, using its own words, indeed, but more sincerely [Col. 0041C] and securely.

“You see these young men with their hair plastered down, their beards gleaming, wholly formed from a little box? Tripping over a syllable, they often fall away from the whole discourse, moving others to laughter like the jackdaw, whose borrowed feathers had been taken from individual birds.”

Such persons ruin the solid word of the Lord. Having bread stored in the ark but not established in the heart, they spoil and prepare the bread in diverse ways, so that it tastes not of its own flavor but of an alien and adulterated one.

Likewise, Jerome, showing how a faithful and prudent preacher ought to preach, says in his consolatory letter to Julian on the death of his daughters: “Thus, not with a writer’s carefulness but with the rashness of one dictating, I break a long silence toward you, offering you the bare and temporary good will of duty; and, for temporal things and amid temporal things, bringing consolation.” A spontaneous letter is one without an arrangement of thoughts, without embellishment or composition of words, so that throughout it you may find or discover nothing of the orator, but may think it poured out in marching order, and a provision for the journey thrust upon one who is eager to depart. Holy Scripture speaks in a living voice, simply and usefully: “Music in mourning is an untimely tale” (Ecclus. 22). Therefore, despising the charm of rhetorical art and the grace of childish, applause-seeking eloquence, we flee to the gravity of the holy Scriptures, where there is true medicine for wounds and sure remedies for griefs; in them a mother receives back her only son upon the bier; there it is said to the crowd standing round, “The girl is not dead, but sleeps” (Luke 8); there a man dead three days and already stinking, at the voice of the Lord crying aloud, comes out and breaks forth, still bound with bands (John 11).

Such, therefore, ought preaching to be, because such is Scripture: so that the aforesaid dead in sins may be raised by it and through it; and so that it may work miracles and heal the sick rather than delight the curious. Likewise: A wise preacher, on the testimony of the wise man, ought to attend to all his own deceptions and circumstances and those of all his hearers, lest he run through one sermon only, but rather through many; so that, according to those attending, he may alter and shape his discourse, subtracting and adding if need be, according to what suits each person. For one who uses a single fixed sermon to cure every vice is like a physician giving one pill for every disease. He is also like an orator who knows one single kind of case and certain common devices for making a peroration, which he employs in every case and every affair.

Likewise: Such a person is like a householder who sets before his guest cold, insipid, and rotten foods, by which he is not nourished, when fresh food ought to be set before him. Likewise: To preachers of this kind, who begin well because they begin from a good principle, but proceed and end their sermon badly, following their own ornate words remote from the beginning, that poetic saying may be objected:

> [lacuna] The amphora began  
> To be fashioned; why, as the wheel runs, does a little jar come out?  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*)

And again:

> [lacuna] Perhaps you know how to paint a cypress.  
> ([Horace], ibid.)

And likewise:

> One purple patch, and another, shining broadly,  
> Is sewn on.  
> ([Horace], ibid.)

And likewise:

> [lacuna] But at his right hand lay  
> A monster.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 4)

For these preachers begin thus: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). Then they ask: “What accidents belong to a word?” And they preach and allegorize beds and fireplaces. Likewise, the Athenians say to the Apostle speaking serious matters: “Brother, if you have any words of exhortation, speak to us” (Acts 13). He likewise, when he concluded his discourse at Ephesus (Acts 18), spoke only a few words at his departure. So also at Athens, in which nevertheless all things necessary for the Christian soul are found, both for prelates in relation to prelacy and governance, and for subjects in attaining humility.

Jerome likewise, in the above-mentioned letter: “The Lord lives; his word lives; his words are living, by which your son will be restored to you, he himself bearing witness who says: ‘He who believes in me, though he be dead, shall live’” (John 11). Or are you sorrowful and ignorant concerning those who sleep, “as are the rest who have no hope?” (1 Thess. 4). Far be it! For “if you believe that Jesus died and rose again, so we believe,” etc. (ibid.). By this voice and through this voice I shall drive from your heart the death which you had contracted as death and grief for your son, so that you may now revive and receive consolation. Likewise: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching and piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts of the heart” (Heb. 4).

## Chapter IX. On the Humility of Preaching

The philosopher [Seneca] (*Epistle* 114): The speech of a wise man ought to be such as his life is: not polished, not painted, not applause-seeking, moving people to laughter and the like, but simply unfolding meaning without verbal ornaments in plain speech.

Likewise (the same, *Epistle* 75): Why does your heart take pleasure in a polished rather than a true word? Why this itching of the ear? You must be burned; you must be cut. You must be burned in heart and cut in ear, so that you may cut off and remove such things from yourself, lest your heart turn such things over and your ear listen to them. For they are dangerous, even though pleasant.

Likewise: The art concerning heavenly things is transmitted purely; the other arts serve for the exercise of talent, but this one concerns the business of souls. A sick man does not seek an eloquent, handsome, polished physician, but a prudent one who knows how to heal, who is kindly disposed and restrained in humble speech, moderate in dress, and short in stature, lest he presume greatly. So too, a ship does not seek a handsome helmsman, but one who knows how to steer.

Likewise, Jerome, inviting us to the humility of holy Scripture, says: This is that rustic ploughshare by which Shamgar slew six hundred Philistines (Judg. 3); and you too, if you preach in rustic and humble speech, will kill so many vices and demons. For by this sword they are slain rather than by Cicero’s sword. This is the jawbone of an ass upon which the Lord sat, by which Samson killed a thousand Philistines (Judg. 15). This is the milk-pail from which David drew five most clear stones, by which he struck down Goliath (1 Sam. 17). I mean clear and natural stones, not painted or artfully furnished. For artificially furnished speech is suspect, just as a suborned judge, witness, or advocate is suspect. Therefore, turning away from inflated words, and from words more dutiful than useful, let us, as poor persons and exiles, pursue humble things, the poet inviting us to this when he says:

> Telephus and Peleus, when each is poor and in exile,  
> Cast aside their bombast and words a yard and a half long.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*)

Likewise: Let us not resemble one who defends himself with a tragic gaping of the mouth. Likewise:

> What worthy thing will this man, who promises with such a huge gape, produce?  
> As human faces smile at those who smile, so they respond to those who weep.  
> If you wish me to weep, you yourself must first feel grief;  
> Then your misfortunes will wound me  
> ([Horace], ibid.)

and move me.

Likewise: Do not despair, because:

> There are words and tones by which you may soothe this pain  
> And in some measure lay aside the sickness.

Thus the philosopher speaks to a grieving friend. You too, preacher, should say:

> There are words and tones by which you may soothe this pain  
> And entirely lay aside the sickness.  
> ([Horace], *Epistles* 1.1)

Likewise: These are childish words, signified by the saliva running down David’s beard (1 Sam. 21), and therefore manly, because “what is foolishness with God is wiser than all human beings” (1 Cor. 1).

Gregory likewise: The discourse of truth does not issue from manufacture, but from nature. And Jerome: He who does not penetrate the unsearchable and secret things of God—both what is manifest and what is not manifest are open to one who lives humbly and rightly in the utterance of the divine word.

Up to this point we have laid the seeds and foundations of the exercise of reading, disputation, and preaching, to which a diligent reader may add whatever he sees to pertain to the same subject. Yet I give this one warning: let him add only useful and sufficient things. Otherwise, as Solomon testifies: “There will be no end to the making of books” (Eccl. 12). And John says in the Apocalypse (ch. 22): “To this,” he says, “you shall add nothing.” And in the Life of St. Martin it is read that, if a few examples of saints do not suffice someone for the formation of his life, many will not profit him.

## Chapter X. On the Rebuke of Pride

All the foregoing serves two ends: namely, that we may know “to turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36). And, since evil cannot be avoided unless it is first known, we must begin with the rebuke of pride—which, according to blessed Augustine (*Exposition 2 on Psalm* 18), is the cause and beginning of all evils and sins. Whoever lacks it is pure, because this sin is the last for those returning to God which was the first for those withdrawing from him.

Jerome says of it: Pride, by a heavenly logic, seeks heavenly minds; flying back to its own origin, it attempts to break into the glory and purity of human beings—the pride which broke forth from the glory and purity of angels—so that those whom it finds sharers in nature, it may make partners in ruin. For when the righteous person’s spiritual building has been constructed and all things duly perfected, pride is often born and stealthily creeps in, on account of the excellence of works and virtues which he possesses. Thus he becomes such a person that he now speaks with the Pharisee, raising his eyes to heaven and saying: “I am not as other people; I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke 18), etc.; whereas the Publican, humble in contrast, resolved to lower his eyes to earth, beating his breast and saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (ibid.).

Jerome likewise (*Letter to Antony on Modesty*, vol. 1): This is what cast the angel from the lofty rank and glory of angels into the dark air, assigned to him as a prison until the day of judgment. This is what cast the first human being from the heavenly paradise into the world, “into a pit of misery and a mire of dregs” (Ps. 39). This is what preferred the people of the Gentiles—formerly not reckoned as a drop from a bucket (Isa. 40)—to the Jewish people, puffed up because God “had not dealt thus with every nation” (Ps. 147); and so “the head was turned into the tail, and the tail into the head” (Deut. 28).

David likewise: “I counted all the sinners of the earth transgressors” (Ps. 118). For there are sinners of heaven and sinners of earth. Sinners of heaven are like him who said, “I will set my throne in heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14); and like him who said, “I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15); and those of whom it is said, “They have set their mouth in heaven” (Ps. 72); and all inhabitants of heaven who abandon heaven—such as those who diminish the grace they had received through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

But sinners of earth are those entangled in earthly offenses, such as lust, gluttony (*gastrimargia*), and the like. David likewise: “The Lord, who is just, will cut down the necks of sinners” (Ps. 128), that is, he will crush stiff-necked and proud sinners. He does not say the wandering foot directed toward evil, the harmful hand, the wanton eye, or whatever limbs are used to go toward evil, but the neck, because nothing displeases God so much as an erect neck after sin. Likewise: “If my own sins do not rule over me, then I shall be spotless and cleansed from the great transgression” (Ps. 18), that is, pride. For nothing is more serious than “to apostasize from God” (Ecclus. 10), which pride causes. Likewise: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. 35). The foot of pride means proud affection; and thus the hand of the sinner—that is, of anyone urging me to sin—will not be able to move me. The order is right: pride is the root of sin, through which one proceeds to other sins. This is what is said in another psalm: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others; if my own sins do not rule over me, then I shall be spotless” (Ps. 18).

Jerome likewise: Pride is compared to spittle. It is not enough for the proud that they offend God, unless they also spit in his face. For they rise up and strike themselves against him, whereas by other vices they withdraw from God. Hence: “Cursed are those who fornicate away from you” (Ps. 72); these rush against him and grow fat upon him. Likewise: Pride began with injury to God; therefore God, detesting this vice above all vices, says: “Let this enemy of mine be reserved for me; my contest is with him.” Hence it is said: “God resists the proud” (1 Pet. 5), etc.:

> [lacuna] God breaks every proud person.  
> (Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 4)

It is not said that he resists the lustful or gluttonous, though he abominates those vices too, but not as greatly as pride. Likewise: Pride is depicted as horned. For it has two horns: one against the love of God, the other against love of neighbor. Against these are the horns of humility, namely love of God and love of neighbor. Hence this vice especially attacks God. David says of these horns: “The horns of the righteous shall be exalted, and I will break all the horns of sinners” (Ps. 74).

Jerome likewise (*Letter to Abigaus*, vol. 1): Nothing have I recoiled from since my earliest age as I have from the monster of pride, an erect neck, lofty eyes, a weighty brow, and insulting humility. David likewise: “O Lord my God, if I have done this” (Ps. 7), as though the sin of pride were shameful, a sin even to name which is dreadful, since it is especially opposed to the Lord. Ecclesiasticus likewise (ch. 10): “Pride is hateful before God and human beings, and every iniquity of the nations is execrable.” Likewise: “An arrogant and proud man is hateful in the city.”

Holy Scripture detests pride above all vices. Therefore the Psalmist complains of it in almost every psalm, as there: “The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me” (Ps. 118); and there: “The proud acted wickedly in every way,” or “exceedingly” (ibid.), because in sinning they surpass other sinners. Or “in every way,” even to the consummation of sin. For the consummation of every sin is pride. Thus no graver or further sin remains than to sin through pride. Likewise: “Their heart has curdled like milk” (ibid.), that is, the heart of the proud. For just as milk is bound and hardened by rennet and leaven, so the milk of the proud is bound by the leaven of pride, so that their love may not extend to neighbor and enemy, to whom it ought to extend, and therefore not to God either.

Gregory likewise (*Morals*, book 8, ch. 30, and book 34, ch. 18): Just as humility weakens every vice, gathers together all virtues, and strengthens them, so pride destroys and scatters all virtues, and heaps up and consolidates all vices. Likewise: At the gateway of the Christian religion, the catechumen professes under attestation that he renounces the devil as prince and author of all evils, and all his works, and especially his pomps, which are more difficult to avoid and are not avoided except with the greatest caution. For his works, consisting in unlawful things, are more plainly evident and therefore more easily avoided. But his pomps are in lawful things and in the use of lawful things, which become unlawful when pride is added: as in the excess and costly display of clothing, in gilded saddles, and in spurs and bridles, where gold shines and glitters more than upon altars.

But is there not, in the use of temporal things, a defined goal, a sure measure, and boundaries which one may not exceed without sin? Did not nature establish these distinctions? Did not the saints also, as the Apostle says: “Having clothing and food, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6)? Would anyone, feeding and clothing himself as is done today, have sinned mortally in the primitive Church? Would he not have been rebuked for such things? And if it was then a mortal sin, how has it ceased to be sin?

But you will object: Everyone ought to live according to the measure of his station and according to the good customs and usages of those among whom he lives, so that they may not strive to stir up desire, whether in themselves or in others, through these things. But how far will this custom extend? Will it not be able to stretch as far as excess? Yet who is wise enough to identify that honest, lawful, and bounded custom of which the authority speaks and which it is to be understood to mean, when every day something is added to former customs—both to the custom of clothing oneself and to others?

Likewise: The origin of pride shows how monstrous it is. It sometimes arises from a gift of fortune, and in many ways: for example, from wealth, because “an abundance of bread and pride of life were the cause of the sin of Sodom.” Likewise: “They shut up their fat; their mouth spoke pride” (Ezek. 16). Likewise, see what idleness and another’s food do: “They are not in the labor of human beings,” etc. (Ps. 16). “Their iniquity came forth as though from fat” (Ps. 72).

Pride also sometimes proceeds from outward and inward bearing: from clothing, food, horses, servants, and the like. Hence Sebastian: “This man was never a Christian, because he loved the luxury of flavors.” So too the philosopher [Seneca] (*Epistle* 87), riding in a broken-down carriage drawn by weak and lean asses that testified to life by motion alone, with a barefoot and almost naked driver, replied to those whom he met and who asked whether the carriage was his: “No; it is borrowed from someone else.” But returning to humility and to his own heart, he said: “What have I done in denying my modest means, as though proudly and with a bad excuse?” For whoever is ashamed of what is shabby will sometimes boast of what is costly.

Pride sometimes arises from a gift of nature: knowledge, talent, memory, diligence, a pleasing voice, reason, and the like. Hence Benedict, fearing at Rome the monster of pride when he saw that in talent and learning he surpassed the young men of his own age, “withdrew from study, prudently ignorant and wisely unlearned” (St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 2). The Apostle likewise says: “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8). And Augustine, writing to Jerome: “I would rather that this knowledge which puffs up should cease than that the knowledge which builds up—namely charity—should perish.”

Pride also arises from nobility of birth. But take away your Hannibal, I pray; it is wretched to rely on another’s fame. What benefit is lineage if one lives badly before the refined?

> Nobility of spirit alone is the one and only virtue.  
> Tell me, offspring of the Trojans: who would judge dumb animals  
> [lacuna] noble, unless they are brave? But you  
> Are nothing but an Athenian, and most like a trunk of Hermes.

Pride also arises from beauty. Hence:

> Arrogance belongs to the beautiful, and pride follows beauty.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 8)

It sometimes arises from the gift of grace. Hence Jerome (St. Jerome, vol. 2, Letter 93): Beneath ashes and sackcloth, beneath fasting, beneath a tunic and sleeved garment of coarse cloth, great pride often lies hidden; because:

> When you have fought well, when you think all things subdued,  
> Pride, the more troublesome foe, remains to be conquered.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti*, book 2)

Likewise: “The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me” (Ps. 118). It did not profit them that human nature, after the sin of the first human being, was humbled both by what it suffered and by its many afflictions—namely, Christ in that nature. Therefore neither Christ’s death, nor the cross, nor the lance, nor the nails, nor such things profit the proud, since they oppose humility; indeed, they strive to destroy it and wish it not to exist, and thus wish Christ to be neither God nor man.

Likewise, because pride arises from good things and gifts of fortune, such as wealth, the Apostle commands in 1 Timothy, chapter 6: “Let the rich of this world not think highly of themselves, nor hope in the uncertainty of riches,” which now come and now depart. Likewise, pride arises from powers and dignities, whether possessed or desired, when someone becomes proud in them. Hence the blessed Virgin: “He has cast down the powerful from their seat,” that is, the proud, “and exalted the humble” (Luke 1). “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6). “For the Lord will repay abundantly those who act proudly” (Ps. 30).

Likewise: The Apostle was not afraid of riches for himself, but for others, when he said: “I know how to abound and how to suffer want” (Phil. 4); but he feared their disease, namely pride or greed, the two vices which are always joined, as Bede testifies in his commentary on Ecclesiasticus. Likewise, Wisdom says: “O Lord, give me neither riches nor poverty”: poverty, “lest,” through lack, “I steal what belongs to another”; riches, “lest I say, ‘Who is the Lord?’” (Prov. 30).

Jerome likewise: “The Lord is sweet to all” (Ps. 144); nevertheless, he heals and drives out the monster and dung of pride by filth and by other evils, though venial ones. These are “ox-dungs that pelt [it]” (Ecclus. 22); remedies so vile are not applied to other vices. Hence Deuteronomy, chapter 7: “You shall devour and consume the seven peoples” who are in the land into which you will go, but “little by little and in portions, because you cannot destroy them all at once, lest perhaps the beasts of the earth multiply against you.” Beware lest bears and lions arise from the beasts and devour you. For there are certain vices tributary to us, by means of which greater ones are avoided; of these it may be said:

> [lacuna] And someone made bad use of him.

Thus Paul too was healed from pride by an evil, namely a tributary evil. Hence: “Lest the greatness of revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan,” etc. (2 Cor. 12). If you consider more subtly, you will observe that the most filthy vice of pride is often healed by a most filthy remedy, and a mortal vice by a mortal remedy. Hence: “Their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened,” etc. (Ps. 15). Likewise: “Satan casts out Satan,” etc. (Matt. 12). Likewise: “You shall come to Babylon, and there you shall be healed” (Mic. 4). Likewise: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Ps. 118).

This monster is also often cured by a kind of good feigning and self-contempt. Thus Gregory tells of a certain hermit whom a citizen, to whom he sold his small works, asked to enter his house and lay hands upon his sick son. When he approached the city and saw the citizens and a pomp coming to meet him, he felt shudders and certain preliminaries and beginnings of pride within himself because of the honor shown him. To prevent pride from arising, he stripped himself and threw himself into a river, and the citizens despised him as though he were mad. Leaving behind his half-garments, he returned naked to his cell.

Thus Master Lanfranc (*Book 1 on Eutropius*) cured himself of pride: by shortening syllables that should be lengthened and lengthening syllables that should be shortened. Yet afterward he disputed so subtly and acutely at the Council of Tours against the Berengarian heresy. Of such people it may be said:

> There are times when excessive self-contempt is useful.  
> To feign folly in its place is the highest prudence.  
> (Cato, *Distichs*)

Jerome likewise: “Pride is a mountain placed between us and the sun, which does not permit us to see the sun of righteousness.” Likewise: “This is the frying-pan placed between us and Jerusalem, lest we see it” (Ezek. 4). This is the intervening cloud of which it is said: “You have opposed a cloud, lest prayer pass through” (Lam. 3). Likewise: “O Lord, my heart has not been lifted up” (Ps. 130).

For there is pride of heart, mouth, the whole body, and action. Pride claims all the limbs of the body for itself and compels them to serve it, and then for the first time it agrees and harmonizes with itself. Of the pride of heart, which intoxicates and causes the other kinds of pride to sprout like a root, David says: “O Lord, my heart has not been lifted up.” But the human mouth is twofold: the mouth of the face and the countenance.

> He gave humankind an uplifted face.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1)

And the brow is the dwelling and sign of either modest humility or shameless elevation. Of this mouth the poet says:

> What threats he bears in his face! With how great an arrogance he crushes all things!  
> (Statius, *Thebaid* 1)

In this face there is manifold pride: for example, pride of the raised nostril. Hence Isaiah: “Take heed of the human being who has breath in his nostrils” (Isa. 2). There is also pride of the eyes. Hence “lofty eyes” (Prov. 6), and the Prophet: “Nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. 130). And Job, or Wisdom: “Do not give me the loftiness of my eyes” (Ecclus. 23). And there is an erect neck also. Hence: “The Lord will cut down the necks of sinners” (Ps. 128).

Cassiodorus the senator likewise, speaking of the young Julian the Apostate: “There is no hope for one who in youth has these traits: an inflexible neck, wandering and roving eyes, threatening nostrils breathing insults, swaggering shoulders, and mocking gestures.” There is also the mouth of the proud tongue. Hence: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things” (Ps. 11). Likewise: “They have set their mouth in heaven, and their tongue has passed through the earth” (Ps. 72). The proud tongue likewise sometimes claims all the limbs for itself, as though it compelled them to speak and serve it. Hence:

> When foot, hand, and all the other limbs speak,  
> For what reason is the lower throat silent?

There is also pride of the entire body—excepting only the private parts, of which we are ashamed and which for that reason we cover with greater honor. Some aid their height with their feet, placing calf upon calf; they walk with distended bellies, although neither bodily bulk nor gluttony compels them to do this. Others are puffed out in the chest, as though bent into an arch:

> And they strongly resemble reclining Maecenas.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 1)

Some spread themselves with their hands in every direction. Hence:

> With sweating fingers he fans the summer gold.  
> ([Juvenal], ibid.)

Some walk with neck erect and extended, as though fixed to a stake. Hence Isaiah: “The daughters of Israel are lifted up, and walk with stretched-out neck” (Isa. 3).

Of pride in action David says: “He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. 100). Likewise: “The Lord will repay abundantly those who practice pride” (Ps. 30). Likewise: “I have not walked in great things nor in things too wonderful for me,” etc. (Ps. 130). Individual vices possess individual limbs in which they have their dwellings; but this vice rules in almost every limb. Because of these many kinds of pride, the Prophet says in the plural: “Lift up your hands against the prides of those who speak wickedly against me” (Ps. 73).

This vice is also so pestilential and dominant that it claims for itself the dominion and kingdom of another vice. Hence the philosopher [Seneca] (*Epistle* 60): “I see a single forest suffice for many elephants, and powerful bulls content with a single field. What then is it that a human being, smaller than these, feeds upon earth, sky, and sea? Is it because of the magnitude of his hunger, by which he surpasses other animals, or to satisfy his voracious appetite? Not at all. For it is not the use of the belly that is valued, but ambition.”

Likewise in 2 Kings: “Yet he did not remove the high places.” Likewise: “God resists the proud” (1 Pet. 5). “God breaks every proud person” (Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 4). For he swiftly takes vengeance on such people; others he awaits more patiently for repentance. Likewise, reproving this vice, the Apostle says: “Not disorderly” (Rom. 1), namely neither in gait nor in outward or inward bearing, because bodily disorder is a sign of inward disorder. Likewise, Ecclesiasticus 35. Likewise, Job 15: “For he stretched out his hand against God,” etc. Likewise, “and as giants the proud stood against me.” Likewise: “These are the giants building the tower of Babel against the Lord, that they may ascend into heaven” (Gen. 1). Likewise: “These say with the devil: ‘I will ascend into heaven,’” etc. (Isa. 14).

Likewise, Job 18: “Let death, the firstborn, devour his beauty and his arms,” that is, pride, which was born first among vices in heavenly beings and killed the first creature of God, namely the angel. Cassiodorus likewise (on Ps. 18): There is no third origin of sin besides the hidden sin by which the devil fell, the sin of another by which the human being was deceived, and custom, which made the sin one’s own. Hence it was said in the psalm: “And I shall be cleansed from the great transgression” (Ps. 18), namely the transgression of pride, which truly is the greatest. For there is no greater sin than “to apostasize from God,” which is the vice of pride in human being and angel. “Pride is the beginning” and cause “of every sin” (Ecclus. 10), that is, of every kind of sin; whoever lacks it is indeed free from every sin.

Therefore the same psalm says: “And the words of my mouth shall be pleasing,” etc. (Ps. 18). For the words of my mouth will be such “as are always pleasing in your sight” (ibid.), not in the sight of human beings. But if I am not clean from pride, my words will not be pleasing in your sight. If, however, I am clean, not only my words but also “the meditation of my heart” (ibid.) will be such—not to please human beings, but you, who see within and examine human consciences.

## Chapter XI. Against Envy

Pride is the mother of envy; and would that, once the mother had been thoroughly stifled and crushed, the daughter too might be stifled and crushed! Through pride the first angel fell, becoming Satan from an angel. He retained pride in act and perhaps in affection; but envy both in act and affection. Through his envy death entered into the world (Wis. 2). For because the devil envied in humanity what he had lost, he strove, through his suggestion, that the human being too should fall from that good, saying through the serpent: “On whatever day you eat, you shall be as gods” (Gen. 3).

But how great this vice is appears from its root, namely pride, and from its effect: for it produces brotherly hatred. How great and how grievous this hatred is appears from the authorities of the saints, who say that on account of it all sins, even forgiven sins, return and are demanded again to the last farthing; which is especially irremediable when it has envy as its root. For it sometimes arises from insult or injury: from insult in two ways, namely from the insult of a hidden word, such as a slanderous word, or of an open and abusive word; and from injury in two ways, namely injury involving loss, or injury inflicted upon the body. In that case this vice, namely brotherly hatred, is remediable, because it has an impelling cause.

Likewise: If, according to the quality of their merits, the good are assigned to the orders of angels, then according to the quality of their merits the wicked will be assigned to the orders of demons: so that, just as those demons will envy forever, so these wicked persons may remain envious forever. Therefore, since envy will reign after death, the poet’s statement is not true:

> Envy feeds on the living; after death it rests.  
> (Ovid, *Elegies* 1.15)

Yet I do not know whether human beings will envy after death.

Likewise: So great is the malice of envy that it persecutes even the Holy Spirit. For what else do I persecute in my neighbor’s good than the gift of the Holy Spirit? Thus I persecute the giver himself in his gift and strive to extinguish him. Likewise: What is diminishing or besmirching one’s neighbor’s good except ascribing it to Beelzebub, prince of demons? Thus we do not wish the Lord to be the giver of the good, when we pervert it in our neighbor, as though ascribing it to the devil.

Likewise: Just as envy attacked the first Adam (Gen. 3), through which “death entered the world” (Rom. 5), so it attacked the second Adam also. For Christ was crucified through envy by the Scribes and Pharisees. This is “the wild beast that devoured Joseph” (Gen. 37), because he was loved more than all his brothers by his father: both the historical Joseph and the spiritual Joseph, namely Christ. This is the whale that swallowed Jonah (Jonah 2).

Envy consists in two things, namely joy and grief. Hence the poet:

> To exult in misfortunes and grieve at happy events.  
> (Statius, *Thebaid* 2)

But there the poet marks only one cause, where another poet says:

> The envious person wastes away at another’s abundant fortunes.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* 1.2)

And another says:

> A smile is never present except one produced by sorrows.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 2)

Both are contained in this: “O you who shall see the sweet heavens, but then enter darkness once again.”

Likewise, Job (ch. 5): “Pride kills the fool, envy kills the little one.” Solomon likewise in Proverbs (Prov. 14): “Purity,” or “the life of the heart, is health to the flesh; envy is rottenness to the bones.” Isaiah likewise (ch. 33): “You shall conceive the fire of ardor and bring forth stubble, and your spirit shall consume and devour you.” Hence the poet:

> Nothing is more just than envy,  
> Which immediately consumes its own author, who is nearest to it.

Likewise: Just as pride has its signs, so that it does not remain hidden—such as lofty eyes, and others in other limbs—so envy too has its signs. For it is:

> Perpetual anxiety, which does not cease even at mealtime,  
> With dry and pallid jaws as though in sickness, and between the molars,  
> As the food grows with difficulty [lacuna]  
> You may discover the torments of the hidden mind in the sick  
> Body; you may discover joys too: the face takes its appearance from both.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 14 and 15)

It is also:

> An old and ancient quarrel between neighbors,  
> Immortal hatred, and a wound never to be healed.  
> ([Juvenal], ibid.)

[Col. 0053A] Likewise: envy, born of pride, is the mother of treachery, murder, and fratricide. Driven by it, Cain deceitfully said to his brother, “Let us go out into the field.” When “God looked upon Abel and his offerings, but did not look upon Cain or his offerings,” Cain, all the more envious of his brother, killed him, and received from the Lord the sign of his envy and crime: namely, fear in his mind and trembling of his head. Fearing that he would be killed by the Lord for his crime, Cain received the Lord’s reply: “You shall not die at once, but shall be trembling and a wanderer upon the earth” (Gen. IV), as punishment for sin.

Likewise: driven by this, Joab murdered Amasa with a dagger (II Kings XX), and also Abner, out of envy and fear—because they were David’s intimates—that David would remove from him the command of the army, so that one or the other of them might succeed him (II Kings III).

[Col. 0053B] Likewise: this is the evil spirit by which Saul, with the Lord’s permission, was agitated in envy against David, because David prospered; and because he heard little women singing David’s praise: “Saul struck down thousands, and David tens of thousands.” While David was singing psalms and playing the lyre before him, Saul was restored to his former state of mind. But again the evil spirit, permitted by the Lord, began to trouble him against David (I Kings XVIII and XIX), because, although the poison of envy may cease for a time, it can scarcely be extinguished without sprouting again.

Likewise: envy the daughter, and pride the mother, conspired together for the ruin of the whole world. For just as the former arises from good, prosperous, and superior things, so the latter arises from natural goods and from the goods of one’s neighbour and another person, especially better goods. Hence:

> Gold, wealth, and estates a generous friend will often give;  
> But one willing to yield in talent will be rare.  
> (MARTIAL, VIII, epigram 15.)

Likewise: envy is the mother of detraction. For it either strips a person entirely of his good qualities, or detracts from them in part by smearing them, if it cannot erase them altogether; and unless it had injured someone, it would be extinguished.

[Col. 0053C] Likewise Solomon, detesting envy, says in Proverbs: “Do not eat with an envious man, and do not desire his foods”—that is, his bites, slanders, and gnawings—“for, in the likeness of a diviner and soothsayer, he judges what he does not know. ‘Eat and drink,’ he will say to you, but his heart is not with you. You will vomit up the foods you had eaten,” through repentance, [Col. 0053D] “and lose your fair words” (Prov. XXIII), by which you rebuked and admonished him so that he might be corrected.

Likewise: envy is all the more detestable because it arises from the goods of nature as well as those of fortune. Envy opposes learning when someone has acquired it by natural ability and exercise, because:

> One willing to yield in talent will be rare, etc.

Hence Jerome, in the Prologue to Isaiah (*Commentary on Isaiah*, book XI, to Eustochium), says: “I am not unaware that we too suffer the bites of many who, goaded by envy, despise, scorn, and defame what they cannot attain. But let them first read, and afterward despise, lest they seem to condemn what they do not know, not from judgment, but from the presumption of hatred.”

30. Likewise: if envy arises from gifts of grace, it is contempt—for the good are despised by the envious, who say: “They are good, but unskilled and unlearned.” Or it is holy imitation: learn holy pride, likewise holy envy. Hence:

> … and emulous of such great deeds.

And Joshua was emulous of Moses. Before him, when it was said that certain persons—“I do not know who they are”—were prophesying there, Moses said: “Would that all might prophesy, just as we do!” (Num. XI). Likewise the Apostle: “But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. V). Likewise: through envy, the Hebrew truth has been taken away from us, according to Jerome’s interpretation, which envied his translation.

## CHAPTER XII. Against detraction

[Col. 0054B] As envy is the daughter of pride, so detraction is the daughter of envy and a “most evil tooth” (Prov. XXV). Rebuking it after pride and envy, the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter I: “Therefore God gave them over to passions of dishonour, filled with every iniquity, strife, proud, haughty, whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God.” This must be carefully noted. Although God hates all evil persons, nevertheless these are called “hateful to God,” as though in this respect their own epithet were attributed to them.

Likewise, Galatians V: “But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another”—that is, with the unity of faith torn apart, which happens through envy and detraction.

Likewise, Psalm C: “A perverse heart”—that is, a slanderous one—“did not cleave to me;” [Col. 0054C] “a proud eye and an insatiable heart.” Likewise Proverbs IV: “Put away from yourself a perverse mouth, and let slandering lips be far from you.” Likewise chapter XXIV: “The thought of a fool is sin, and the slanderer is an abomination to men.” Likewise Leviticus XIX: “You shall not curse the deaf,” that is, you shall not slander one who is absent. For foolish is the person who insults someone present, though he is more excusable; but treacherous, deceitful, and more blameworthy is the one who harms and gnaws at an absent person.

Likewise Ecclesiastes X: “If a serpent bites silently, he who secretly slanders is no less harmful.” Therefore the slanderer is a serpent, possessing a serpentine bite and a venomous tongue. Likewise Solomon: “He who slanders his neighbour binds himself” to God and [Col. 0054D] man (Prov. XIII). Or he binds himself to God for the future, so that through contrition of heart he may make satisfaction to Him, and thus his sin be forgiven; and also to a human being, so that he may make bodily satisfaction if he has inflicted bodily loss upon him, because “sin is not forgiven unless what has been taken away is restored.”

But if he has inflicted a spiritual wound—for example, hatred through detraction, or induced him by suggestion to seek illicit love, and the like—must he make bodily satisfaction? Must he, that is, be bound to visit him bodily wherever he may be and remove the spiritual wound which he inflicted, humbly saying: “Forgive me, because by detraction or in another way I injured you thus,” or: “Do not burn with love for this person, because, persuading you, I deceived you”? It seems from the Gospel that satisfaction must indeed be made in this way to those so injured.

[Col. 0055A] For the Lord says: “If you offer your gift at the altar and your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there and first go to be reconciled to your brother; and then, when you come, you shall offer” (Matt. V). “When you come”: not only by the inward steps of faith and devotion, but bodily, as the exclusive expression indicates.

What if I have injured someone’s reputation before a prelate, so that he is not given a prebend which otherwise would have been given? Am I bound to confess to him that I injured him thus and, by slandering him, took away his prebend? For to detract is to take something away from someone, from his fullness. Am I bound to grant him a prebend such as I took from him by detraction? This is a question.

Likewise in the Psalm: “And he gave their fruits to blight” (Ps. LXXVII). [Col. 0055B] Blight is a defect which a harmful breeze secretly produces in fruits. This is envy, which blights, scorches, and consumes the goods of others. This is the locust. For the locust, injuring with its mouth and consuming fruits and trees, is malice which gnaws away, by detraction, the testimony of a good person. This is also the dog-fly (*cynomyia*), that is, the canine fly which stings sharply.

Likewise: for reproving this plague, the example of Augustine, most gentle and modest, ought to suffice. Though he might have inscribed many epigrams above his table—for instance, against gluttony and talkativeness, which often attend meals—namely: “Let not your hearts be weighed down with revelry and drunkenness” (Luke XXIV); and: “Food should be taken as medicine”; and: “Remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke XVI); and: “This house is not mine, but Christ’s poor people’s”—[Col. 0055C] he chose especially to set up this metrical epigram, which would exclude detraction from his table:

> Whoever loves to gnaw at the lives of the absent with words,  
> Let him know that this table is unworthy of him.

Likewise James, in the Catholic Epistle, chapter IV: “Do not speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother or judges his brother speaks against the law and judges the law; but if he judges the law, he is not a doer of the law but a judge. For there is one lawgiver and judge, who can destroy and deliver. But who are you, who judge your neighbour?” Every slanderer speaks against the law and judges the law, because he does what the law forbids—namely, speaking against another. Or he speaks against the law [Col. 0055D] and judges it who deprives it of its office: for example, one who publicly rebukes a hidden sin, or does so with rancour or a desire for revenge and without prior warning, or omits something among the relevant circumstances. For the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him” (Luke XVII).

Likewise Proverbs XXIV: “Do not lie in wait and seek wickedness in the house of the righteous”—that is, do not seek an occasion by which you may disparage and slander a righteous person. Likewise Solomon, detesting the slanderer in the same passage, calls everyone who speaks against his neighbour a sword, a spear, and a sharp arrow (Prov. XXV): that is, the false testimony which the slanderer gives.

[Col. 0056A] But does one slander less by speaking the truth about someone? Answer: even if the slanderer says what is true about him, it is nevertheless, as regards the slanderer, a lie and falsehood, because he says it contrary to his intention. Thus detraction is plainly present whether through established truth or virtue, or through falsehood, even though something true is said of someone with a biting tooth and malicious tongue, in order to induce hatred and contempt for him, diminish his reputation in some respect, or lessen any good belonging to him.

But if, out of compassion and grief, and in detestation of vice—not so that you may lead into hatred the person of whom you have spoken truthfully—you disclose his public sin before those who know it, or disclose a secret matter “between you and him alone” (Matt. XVIII), or before persons who know it equally with you, so that at least, through their compassion and rebuke, he may be corrected, you will not be a slanderer. For will and intention distinguish an evil act.

Likewise in the Psalm: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows,” etc. (Ps. LVI). The teeth—that is, the gnawings of slanderers—are weapons and arrows, etc.

[Col. 0056B] Likewise: “Their throat is an open grave” (Ps. XIII), because the words of flatterers are foul and corrupting. “With their tongues they acted deceitfully; the venom of asps, incurable, is beneath their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (I Cor. XI).

Likewise, a saying of a certain wise man: Observe and consider the harmony of all bodily members: how all suffer with one injured fellow-member, support and cherish it, and do not wish its stain or defect to be exposed, any more than their own. How much more should this harmony be observed by spiritual members—that is, the faithful, who are members of Christ’s body, of which He Himself is the head—so that they support one another, suffer together, and no one member exposes the shame of its weak fellow-member, but rather covers it, following the example of the Apostle speaking to the Corinthians: “Those members of the body which we consider less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour” (I Cor. XII).

[Col. 0056C] Also by the example of a mother who more greatly cherishes and indulges her weaker and younger child; and by the example of the father of a household who calls his prodigal son back to his own table (Luke XV).

Likewise—as may be inferred from the verse of Psalm XIV, “Neither did he do evil to his neighbour, nor receive reproach against his neighbours”—there are three kinds of slanderers. One invents and conceives the slander, having material and an opportunity for speaking against another; or, lacking these, falsely fabricates something against his neighbour, which is more cruel. Hence the poet:

> Cruel in inventing every sort of reproach against anyone.  
> (HORACE, book I, epistle 15.)

Another hears it and repeats it; a third, however, receives the slander. The first finds the material; the second enlarges and multiplies it; the third lends authority to the slander and so strengthens it. For if there were no listener, there would be no slanderer. Hence the Psalmist: “And he did not receive reproach against his neighbours” (Ps. XIV): he did not invent it, he did not fabricate it.

[Col. 0057A] “He did not receive,” that is, he did not regard it as acceptable to repeat reproach and detraction; nor did he “receive” it even to hear it. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “Fear God, my son, and do not associate with slanderers” (Prov. XXIV), by taking part through possessing, repeating, or hearing it; “for suddenly their destruction will arise, and who knows the ruin of them both?” (ibid.)—that is, of the slanderer and of the one who supports him, namely, the listener.

Therefore, lest you share in the offence of slanderers, “hedge your ears with thorns” (Ecclus. XXVIII), lest they hear detraction; and open your mouth also to rebuke the slanderer. Hence Solomon: “The north wind scatters the rain, and a sorrowful face a slanderous tongue” (Prov. XXV).

Likewise Jerome, in the letter to Nepotian: “My son, beware of having a slanderous tongue and itching ears. For the excuse which you offer—that you cannot use force upon people, shut their mouths, or hedge in your ears—is of no avail. You speak to no one against his will. An arrow is not fixed in a rock, but, rebounding, is often sent back against the one who aimed it. Therefore, as you keep your loins chaste, so keep your mouth, eyes, and ears most chastely.”

[Col. 0057B] Likewise Psalm XLIII: “You have made us a reproach to our neighbours, a mockery and derision”—or “contempt,” in another reading—“to those who are around us.”

Likewise Bernard, in Homily 24 on the Song of Songs: “In slanderers,” he says, “is fulfilled what is read in the Gospel: ‘On that day Herod and Pilate became friends’” (Luke XXIII). For such persons walk apart, sit together, agree and meet with one another in order to utter whispers and slanders, so that in this they are found discordantly concordant and concordantly discordant.

But this plague of detraction attacks and wounds charity more sharply than other vices. For the slanderer extinguishes or kills charity in himself, if he had it before; if not, he shows himself empty of it. In the listener too, so far as he is able, he extinguishes charity; and he draws his neighbour into hatred and contempt, not only among those present but also among the absent, and among all persons to whom that poisonous and irrevocable word flies.

[Col. 0057C] Now there are two kinds of slanderers: the open and the concealed. The first, without shamefacedness, without a modest mouth, and irreverently, emits whatever poisonous venom comes into his mouth, with biting tooth and cursing tongue. The second disguises and cloaks detraction under the counterfeit paint of modesty and a certain appearance of reserve, uttering it in words of mourning and lamentation, in a subdued voice, with lowered face and eyes fixed upon the ground. He says: “It would not become known from me, were it not that others had disclosed it. I praise him in every respect; but in this matter, which grieves me, I do not praise him. For he might have acted better,” and such like.

And this kind is more cruel than the former, because such detraction is more persuasive precisely because it appears to proceed from an affection of compassion; and it is thus crueler than open detraction, which pours out all its poison without disguise.

Three punishments of slanderers are recorded. The punishment of God’s ecclesiastical judgment, concerning which one reads in Distinction 46, chapter *Clericus*. The punishment also of God’s hidden judgment, which with seeing faith we daily see and read: namely, deprivation of the function of speech. This occurs in heretics, blasphemers, those who sell by means of their tongue, those vainly boastful in speech [Col. 0058A] (“who set their mouth against heaven” [Ps. LXXII]), unbelievers—for Zacharias too lost for a time “the ready measures of speech” (Luke I)—and slanderers and whisperers hateful to God. There is also the punishment of the future and manifest judgment. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “Do not associate with slanderers, for suddenly their destruction will arise, and who knows the ruin of them both?” (Prov. XXIV).

34. Likewise in Ecclesiasticus: “Have you heard a word against your neighbour? Let it die with you, trusting that it will not burst you apart” (Ecclus. XIX).

## CHAPTER XIII. On humility

[Col. 0058B] As we have said, envy is the daughter of pride and detraction its granddaughter; and as through pride “death first entered the world” (Rom. V), so through Christ’s humility life first entered the world. “For the Magi returned to their own country by another way” (Matt. II). For just as through pride we first withdraw from God, so through humility we first approach Him.

And although the Lord Jesus Christ excels and is commended in every virtue, He is commended especially in humility—so much so that on this subject above all other virtues He conducted [perhaps: founded, *erexerit*] the schools of heaven, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI).

Likewise Augustine, commending this virtue, says: “This is water which is not read of in the books of foreigners,” namely, the philosophers. For rhinoceroses, enraged, killed themselves from anger alone.

Likewise Jerome, to the monk Antony, who was unwilling to reply to him: “Our Lord, the master of humility, when His disciples were disputing about rank, placed a little child in their midst, saying: ‘Unless someone humbles himself as this little child, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven’” (Matt. XVIII).

[Col. 0058C] Lest He should seem merely “to teach and not to do” (Acts I), He fulfilled by example what He taught in word: when He washed the fishermen’s feet (John XIII); when He received the traitor with a kiss; when He spoke with the Samaritan woman; when, with Mary the sinner sitting at His feet, He discoursed concerning the kingdom of heaven (Luke XXII); when, rising from the dead, He first appeared to that same woman (John XX).

But Satan fell from the archangelic height for no other reason than pride, the opposite of humility. The Jewish people likewise, once preferred to “a drop of a bucket” (Isa. XL), was destroyed through claiming for itself “the first seats and greetings in the marketplace” (Matt. XXIII), while the Gentile people took its place. Thus the tail was turned into the head (Deut. XXVIII), and conversely.

Against the sophists of the age and the wise of the world, Peter and James, fishermen, are sent; and Scripture gives the reason: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” [Col. 0059A] (I Pet. V). See, brother, what and how great an evil pride is: namely, that it has God as its adversary. Therefore in the Gospel the arrogant Pharisee is rejected and the humble Publican heard (Luke XVIII).

“I have already sent you, unless I am mistaken, ten letters full both of duty and of prayers, while you, on the contrary, are deaf to them, do not even deign to make a gesture, and while the Lord speaks with servants, a brother does not speak with his brother. If you do speak rarely, then, I say, it is exceedingly insulting. Believe me: unless the modesty proper to a pen restrained me, I would send you such an injury that you would begin to answer me, even in anger. But since it belongs to a human being to grow angry and to a Christian not to commit injury, returning to the old custom, I again beg that you love one who loves you and, as a fellow servant, grant speech to a fellow servant.”

[Col. 0059B] Likewise the Lord proposes another teaching on humility: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, quiet, and trembling at my words?” (Isa. LXVI). As if He said: Humility alone makes for me a dwelling quiet and trembling at my words.

Likewise Psalm XV: “You have made known to me the ways of life,” that is, of humility. For although the other virtues too are ways of life, the general name of them all is assigned and made proper to humility, which is the foundation of all other virtues; just as the general name of vices is assigned to pride, as in: “I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin” (Ps. XVIII). And it is indicated generally there: “O Lord my God, if I have done this” (Ps. VII), that is, a work of pride, which is the fountain and source of other vices.

Likewise the Blessed Virgin, the imitator of her Son, in her song sets humility above all the other virtues that she possessed, saying: “The Lord has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed.
