He has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke I).

[Col. 0059C] Likewise David, in Psalm CXXX: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; neither have I walked in great matters nor in things wonderful beyond me.” David is commended especially in this virtue.

Likewise: we read that a certain hermit saw in a vision the world in the air, full of snares, and asked an angel familiar to him: “Who shall escape all these snares?” The angel answered: “Prudent humility alone.” For there is an imprudent humility, akin to foolishness.

Likewise it should be noted that there are three stages in acquiring and preserving humility. The first is to consider what you do not possess; the second, that you possess nothing from yourself; the third, to reflect that you can lose what you possess. In the first you find yourself imperfect, both in natural goods and in gratuitous gifts. In the second, you find that you have nothing of your own: “For what have you, O man, that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV). “And from his fullness we have all received” (John I). In the third, you fear ruin and falling—namely, lest that which you appeared to possess be taken away from you.

[Col. 0059D] Likewise, at the beginning of His discourse, the Lord commends humility as especially necessary to the religion of the Christian faith, saying in Matthew: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” that is, the humble, “for theirs is the kingdom [Col. 0060A] of heaven” (Matt. V).

Likewise David, perceiving the usefulness of humility and commending it for this reason, says in Psalm XVII: “For you will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud.” Likewise: “I said in the excess of my mind: ‘I am cast away from before your eyes,’” because I have been made exceedingly humbled and abject, with a good abjection; “therefore you heard the voice of my prayer.” Likewise in the same Psalm: “For you have regarded my humility; you have saved my soul from necessities” (Ps. XXX). Likewise Psalm CI: “He has regarded the prayer of the humble.” Likewise Psalm XXIV: “See my humility and my labour, and forgive all my sins.” For humility precedes the labour of repentance so that sins may be forgiven.

Likewise in the Gospel: “He who exalts himself [Col. 0060B] shall be humbled” (Luke XIV): that is, “he who exalts himself” with the exaltation of pride “shall be humbled” by the abasement of punishment; while “he who humbles himself” by virtue “shall be exalted,” in the present and in the future—in the present by increase of virtues and good works, and in the future by the bestowal of glory.

Likewise Samuel says to Saul in I Kings XV: “When you were little in your own eyes, were you not made head and king in Israel? But now, because you have become great in your own eyes and have cast away the words of the Lord”—by preserving Agag, king of Amalek, and whatever was fat from the flock—“the Lord has cast you away, so that you shall not be king over Israel”; but your rival shall succeed you.

And Gregory says on this passage (*Morals*, book XVIII, chapter 20; book XXVI, chapter 19; [Col. 0060C] book XXXIV, chapter 17): “When you were little in your own eyes, you were great to me; when you regard yourself as great, you are reckoned little by me.” Conversely David, when he despised the power of his kingdom by dancing before the ark of the Lord, said: “I will play before the Lord and become more lowly, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (II Kings VI).

Likewise, II Kings VI: Michol, his wife, mocking him as he danced, leaped, whirled himself about, twisted his arms, and sang before the ark, said: “How glorious was the king of Israel today and yesterday, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants; he was stripped as one of the buffoons would be stripped [Scriptural text: ‘as one of the buffoons might be stripped’].” David replied to her: “I shall play before my Lord, who chose me. I shall play and become more lowly than I have become, and I shall be humble in my own eyes; and with the maidservants of whom you spoke I shall appear more glorious.”

[Col. 0060D] On this passage Gregory says (*Morals*, book XXVII, chapter 27): “I delight to consider how many and how great were the gifts of virtues David received, and how strongly he preserved himself by humility amid them all. Whom would it not puff up to break the jaws of lions, to tear apart the limbs of bears, to hear everyone say: ‘Saul struck down thousands, and David tens of thousands’ (I Kings XVIII); after his elder brothers had been despised, to be chosen ‘from behind the ewes heavy with young’ (Ps. LXXVII); when the king was rejected, to be anointed for the reins of royal power; to have David, feared by all, lay Goliath low with one stone; after the king’s proposal, to bring back many foreskins once the Philistines had been slain; finally to receive the promised kingdom and possess all Israel without opposition? (I Kings XVII.)

“And yet, when he brings the ark of God back to Jerusalem, as though forgetting that he had been set above all, he dances before the ark among the people and, as though in a festive dance, whirls himself around with leaps. [Col. 0061A] Set over all, he despises himself, making himself equal to the least beneath the Lord and displaying what is lowly (II Kings VI). He does not recall the power of the kingdom; he does not fear becoming lowly in the eyes of his subjects by dancing; before the ark of Him who had given him honour, he does not recognize himself as set above others in honour. Before God he performed weak and utterly lowly things, so that by humility he might strengthen those mighty things which he had done before men. I marvel more at David dancing than fighting. In fighting he subdued an enemy; in dancing before the Lord he conquered himself—David whose humility Michol, mad with the swelling pride of royal descent, despised.”

## CHAPTER XIV. On two kinds of evil humility

[Col. 0061B] It should be noted that there are two kinds of evil humility, which David removes from himself. Some people established in high position acknowledge that they are ash and dust, but do not endure being regarded as lowly by others. Others, established in high position, confess that they are both dust and ash and endure being regarded as lowly by others, but inwardly swell on that account.

Therefore, against these two swellings of proud humility David says: “I shall play and become more lowly before the Lord in my own eyes” (II Kings VI): that is, both that I may endure being considered lowly by others, and that, because of this lowliness, I may not inwardly swell—that is, in the eyes of my heart.

[Col. 0061C] Likewise it should be noted that humility is fourfold. There is humility of nature, humility of grace, humility of fault, and humility of punishment. The first two are conjoined, related, and alike; yet one of them is meritorious.

Of humility of nature it is said: “Unless someone humbles himself as this little child, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII). Of humility of grace it is said: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX): namely, those who possess through grace what the others have by nature. And again: “I will confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent of the world and revealed them to little children” (Matt. XI).

Of humility of fault—there are two kinds of humility of fault—that proceeding from pretence, it is said: [Col. 0061D] “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. VII). But of humility of fault proceeding from servile fear, the poet says:

> Nothing is harsher than when the lowly man rises to power:  
> He strikes at all while fearing all; he rages against everyone.  
> (CLAUDIAN, book II, *Against Eutropius*.)

Of humility of punishment it is said: “He who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke XIV), namely by shame, abasement, and the punishment of Gehenna. And again, Proverbs XXIX: “Humility follows the proud”—namely, the punishment of Gehenna, shame, and abasement—“but glory shall receive the humble in spirit” (Prov. XXIX).

Likewise: I delight to consider with how many and how great examples of humility [Col. 0062A] Holy Scripture is strewn, in order that we may gather from them a few things, as though seed.

You see, then, Jacob obedient to his mother and remaining at home with her, chosen by the Lord; while Esau, hunting and seeking great things, is rejected (Gen. XXV). You see Saul, little, taken from behind the she-asses and made king, then becoming wicked and proud and afterward cast down (I Kings XVI). You see David, little, chosen after his elder brothers had been passed over, “from behind the ewes heavy with young” (Ps. LXXVII). The Lord likewise chose a fisherman from behind his nets to be an apostle (Matt. IV). “He chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (I Cor. I). He chose fishermen, not philosophers.

When at Rome some wished to choose a certain nobleman as pope, someone said: “We seek a successor to Peter the fisherman, the son of a craftsman [Matt. XIII], not a successor to Augustus:

> For this man rules souls; Caesar has bodies.”

[Col. 0062B] Therefore the Law commanded that the altar of burnt offering be made hollow—because a swelling repels what is poured into it—and square, because of the squareness of the four cardinal virtues (Exod. XXVII).

Likewise, though in one and the same majesty He was God with the Father, the Lord “bowed the heavens and came down” (Ps. XVII), took the form of a servant (Phil. II), chose as His putative father a poor craftsman, and was born from the womb of a poor and wage-earning virgin, in a lodging-place; He was wrapped in swaddling-clothes and placed in a small manger. He was first manifested to shepherds—keeping watch by night over their flock [Col. 0062C] and humble people—as though even then saying: “I hide these secrets of my birth from the wise and reveal them to little children” (Matt. XI). He was also offered in the Temple with the offering of the poor, suckled and fed with a little milk, by which not even a bird is left hungry (Luke II); He preached lowly things in lowly words, suffered on a mean gibbet, and was laid in another’s tomb (Matt. XXVII).

Therefore, whoever you are, following the example of the Lord, “the greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III), not only in words but also in deeds and in every member of your body: in bearing and dress. Wherever pride can have its dwelling, set the response of humility against it, saying with the Prophet: “You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop” (Ps. L), etc.

[Col. 0062D] For this reason we are also exhorted in the psalm, as children, to praise the Lord; namely there: “Praise the Lord, children” (Ps. 112), that is, the humble. For God “regards the lowly alone” (Ps. 137), and is worthily praised by them alone, because “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15), and of the proud, because “the Lord knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137). To inculcate humility, God also wished to be called King and praised by the children of the Hebrews, not by the Scribes and Pharisees (Matt. 21). As they went forth to meet him, he sat upon an ass, that is, a humble and gentle animal, so that everything might resound with humility: the praisers, because “out of the mouth of infants and nursing children thou hast perfected thy praise” (Ps. 8); [Col. 0063A] the one praised, because he humbled himself both in himself and in the beast upon which he rode (Matt. 21). For this reason too, the words *Let us bless the Lord* are sung in the Church by children, at least in age: that all our works may be shown to be performed in humility, and ought to be seasoned by it; otherwise they are to be deemed fruitless and tasteless.

Likewise, James says in the Catholic Epistle, chapter 4: “Humble yourselves in the sight of God, and he shall exalt you.” And the Apostle says: “Not setting your minds on high things, but consenting to the lowly” (Rom. 12). Likewise the same Apostle: “Do not be high-minded, but rather fear” (Rom. 11 [the source reads II]), that is, humble yourself. For where pride is, there is ruin; but where humility is, there is moderation. Pride is followed by ruin and abasement; humility by glory and exaltation. “It is better to be humble with the humble than to divide spoils with the proud” [Col. 0063B] (Prov. 16). Likewise: “Better is a little to the righteous than the great riches of sinners” (Ps. 36).

Likewise Gregory: Whoever does not possess humility is a hypocrite—if this is understood of humility as a virtue rather than as a civic quality, which indeed is true; therefore every sinner who lacks charity is a hypocrite. This seems especially so because everyone desires to appear to be what he is not, and to conceal within himself what he is. God “will appoint such a one his portion with the hypocrites,” who are censured in many places of Holy Scripture, especially in the Gospel. Job also says of them: “This I know: that the praise of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite lasts but a moment. Though his pride rise up to heaven and his head [Col. 0063C] touch the clouds, in the end he shall perish like dung” (Job 20). Here the hypocrite is compared to dung: he is a whitewashed wall, concerning whom it is said, “The sluggard shall be stoned with his own dung” (Ecclus. 22). When such people are deprived of their dung—that is, temporal goods—they are tormented and distressed by their loss; and thus the things that had been their delights are turned into torments for them.

Likewise Jerome, on the Epistle to the Galatians (on 5:26), reproving the proud humility of scholars, says: What else is God’s work than to read the Scriptures, preach in the Church, desire the priesthood, and minister before the altar of the Lord? Yet even these things arise from a desire for praise unless a man “keeps his heart with all diligence” (Prov. 4). You may see very many people—as Cicero also says—entitle their books *On the Contempt of Glory*, while prefixing titles for the glory of their own name; and, as though speaking and writing of humility, they are proud, turning both the subject and language of humility into glory. We interpret the Scriptures, frequently turn the stylus [write and revise], and compose things worthy of reading; but unless these are done for Christ’s sake, rather than for remembrance among posterity and fame among peoples, all the labor will be futile, “and we shall be as sounding brass and a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13). You may see many people contend with one another over the Scriptures and make God’s discourse an athletic contest: they challenge one another, and, if defeated, they envy. For they are desirous of empty glory.

Likewise, Philippians 2: “If therefore there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort [Col. 0064A] of charity, any fellowship of the Spirit,” etc. Likewise 2 Corinthians 4: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s and not from us”; for you are an earthen, corruptible vessel, a sack of dung and food for worms. Humble yourself, because you possess in this vessel a treasure—namely, the soul, marked with the light of the countenance of your God. O man, acknowledge your dignity, in which “you were created in the image of God” (Gen. 1), and thus learn a holy pride. For how glorious was the ardor of martyrdom present in the Theban Legion!

Likewise, Ecclesiasticus, rebuking the humility of self-abasement and faint-heartedness, says in chapter 13: “Take heed, lest, deceived in folly, you be humbled. Do not be humble in your wisdom, lest, humbled, you be led into folly.” Likewise, concerning the same matter the Apostle says to [Col. 0064B] Titus, chapter 2: “Let no one despise you; but rebuke with all authority.” On this passage Jerome says: Nothing so destroys and corrupts the Church as the assertion that laymen are better than clerics.

Likewise, Ecclesiasticus, reproving the humility of pretense and falsity, says in chapter 19: “There is one who wickedly humbles himself, while his inward parts are full of deceit.” Therefore fear what is said in Psalm 93: “The Lord, the God of vengeance, the God of vengeance, has acted freely. Rise up, O judge of the earth; render recompense to the proud. How long shall sinners, O Lord, how long shall sinners glory? They shall utter and speak iniquity; all who work injustice shall speak.” Fear also, and behold what [Col. 0064C] is said in Psalm 88: “You have humbled the proud one like a wounded man; in the arm of your strength you have scattered your enemies.” Embrace what is said in another psalm: “I am poor and in labors from my youth; having been exalted, I was humbled and troubled” (Ps. 87); therefore, “You heard the voice of my prayer when I cried to you” (Ps. 30).

Likewise, attend to Jerome’s saying: He who gathers and heaps up virtues without humility does just as if he carried fine dust to the brow of a mountain, to be scattered by the breath of a light breeze. Likewise, when the Lord had gathered his disciples and was teaching upon the mountain, sitting there and constructing the seven-rung ladder of Jacob, he placed humility, as it were the foundation of holiness, on the first step; and, opening [Col. 0064D] his mouth, he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5). Poverty of spirit is humility.

## Chapter XV. On Gentleness

Against the most evil triad—namely pride, envy, and detraction—we have argued, setting against it the antidote of humility. It is good to linger over this: “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17), that is, in humility. And certain things must be gathered concerning its foster-sister, the virtue of gentleness; for no one is gentle who is not humble, and conversely. Thus the Lord joins gentleness to humility, as a foster-sister virtue, adjoining and neighboring it, immediately afterward on Jacob’s ladder, saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. [Col. 0065A] 5), namely, the earth of the living. And elsewhere: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

This is commended by the origin of the word. For *mansuetus* [gentle] is said as though *manu suetus*, a person, that is, who is companionable, tractable, and kindly in adversity and even toward personal injuries. Likewise, it is commended by Christ’s example, who appeared most gentle: “The Lord is gracious and gentle,” etc. (Ps. 35). Likewise, it is commended in Moses (Num. 12), who was the gentlest of men—understand, apart from Christ. Likewise by the example of the Apostle Andrew, who is recorded to have been the gentlest of the saints. Likewise by the authority of Scripture: “The meek shall inherit the earth and delight in the abundance of peace” (Ps. 36). “The Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners to [Col. 0065B] the ground” (Ps. 146). And: “He shall guide the meek in judgment; he shall teach the gentle his ways” (Ps. 24).

Likewise by the authority of the poet:

> Unlovely savagery does not enter into these manners,  
> Nor is it less at variance with their pursuits.  
> —Ovid, *Epistles from Pontus*, I

Therefore it ought especially to be at variance with the pursuits of a Christian, if it is so at variance with those of a pagan:

> Add that faithfully studying the liberal arts  
> Softens manners and does not allow them to be savage.  
> —Ovid, *Epistles from Pontus*, II

Likewise James says in chapter 1 of his Epistle: “Receive with meekness the implanted word, which [41] is able to save your souls.” Likewise 1 Chronicles, chapter 18: “Moreover, the sons of David were chief ministers at the king’s hand.”

## Chapter XVI. On Poverty

[Col. 0065C]

The rule of heavenly teaching, “which can save your souls” (Jas. 1), is said to have consisted in humility and gentleness: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). He joins a third thing to these on Jacob’s ladder—not a virtue, but an increase of virtues—namely poverty. By word and example he governed schools concerning it, especially because it is the nurse that guards virtues, saying: “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6).

I speak of visible poverty, with which, as also with spiritual poverty, all Holy Scripture is sprinkled, and of which almost every psalm most strongly breathes. The Lord commended it not only by word but by example, so that it might be imitated and sought for the safeguarding of virtues; and he commended or dedicated it to himself and to his household, saying in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8), except the wretched manger, the womb of a poor and wage-earning virgin, the gibbet of the cross, and the tomb—yet even that was another’s. Hence too the Lord chose gentle and poor fishermen, upon whom he might found his Church (Matt. 4). Hence too, when the crowds wished to seize him and make him king, he fled away (John 6). Hence too, though asked three times, he did not wish to enter the house of the royal official, lest he seem to honor riches, whereas he went down to the house of the centurion (John 4); for poverty is rather to be honored and loved. Hence too he said to a certain rich young man: [Col. 0066A] “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess, give to the poor, and follow me” (Matt. 8 [the source’s citation]); which rich people cannot fulfill, as Jerome testifies (*Letter* 150, to Hebidia). For they cannot offer a whole burnt offering—understand, not easily. Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “It is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). Yet whether the word expressing possibility, when joined with a negative particle, denies possibility or merely ease is a question. But this is certain, Jerome says in the cited place: it is safer neither to possess riches nor to love them, since they can scarcely be possessed without being loved.

Likewise, for the detestation of riches, riches themselves are designated by the name of a certain demon; hence: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16). But *Mammon*, or *mammona*, a demon’s name, is interpreted “riches,” either because they are acquired wickedly, distributed most badly, not distributed when they ought to be distributed, or make their distributor proud. Likewise Jerome, in the place cited above.

To commend poverty and its choice, it is pleasing to consider these verses of Lucan:

> O safe resource of life—  
> Small, scanty homes! O gifts of the gods not yet  
> Understood, to whom was it granted, within what walls  
> Or temples, that, while no tumult shook with fear,  
> Caesar’s hand might beat at their gates?  
>
> [lacuna]  
>
> He knows that cottages are no prize for civil wars.  
> —*The Pharsalian War*, V

[Col. 0066C] Likewise in the same work:

> [lacuna] Fruitful poverty, mother of men, is fled;  
> And from the whole world is summoned that by which  
> Each nation perishes.  
> —Ibid., book I

But riches nurture effeminate and soft people, not men. Likewise Jerome: according to Quintilian, orators sometimes use verses from poets or poems to tickle and delight the ears. This does not befit a Christian; yet it is permitted to introduce material from pagan writings—after spoiling the Egyptians and enriching the Hebrews—provided the maiden’s nails are cut and her hair shorn, so that the truth commending virtue or crushing vice may be more fully recommended and confirmed by the testimony of opponents.

[Col. 0066D]

> The empty traveller will sing before a robber.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires*, X

> A man lives better on little; Fortune has granted all to be happy,  
> If anyone has learned how to use what he has.  
> —Claudian, *Against Rufinus*, I

Cato: “Remember to bear patiently the burden of poverty.” It is no burden except to those who bear it.

Likewise Seneca, in commendation of poverty—or rather, in commendation of losing riches—says (*Letter* 42): Therefore, in the things we desire and strive for with great labor, we ought to consider whether there is no advantage in them, or more disadvantage. Some are superfluous; some are not worth so much. But we do not foresee this, and things that [Col. 0067A] cost us most dearly seem to us free. Our stupidity may be seen from this: we think that only those things are bought for which we pay money; we call free the things for which we expend ourselves. Things we would not wish to buy if we had to give our house for them, or some pleasant and productive estate, we are most ready to obtain with anxiety, danger, and the sacrifice of modesty, freedom, and time. So true is it that nothing is cheaper to anyone than himself. Let us therefore do in every deliberation and matter what we are accustomed to do whenever we approach a seller of goods. Let us see at what price the thing we desire is offered. Often what costs most has no stated price. I can show you many things which, once acquired and accepted, have wrested freedom from us. We should be our own masters if these things were not ours. What is more foolish than to rush into one’s own danger through the dangers of others, and not to consider how burdensome are the things we seek, even if they were not superfluous?

Likewise Tobias’s wife says: “Would that this money had never existed, for which we sent you to travel abroad, child, light of our eyes and staff of our old age. For our poverty was enough for us, so that we counted it riches that we saw our son” (Tob. 5). Likewise Jerome, on the passage, “God, in thy sweetness thou hast provided for the poor” (Ps. 67), says that the explanation of this verse never shines forth more clearly than in the apologue of Horace, called Flaccus:

> A stag, superior in battle, drove a horse  
> From their common pasture, until, the weaker in the long contest,  
> [Col. 0067C] He begged man’s aid and accepted the bridle.  
> But after the violent victor had departed from the foe,  
> He could not drive the rider from his back nor the bridle from his mouth.  
> So he who, fearing poverty, lacks liberty more precious than metals,  
> Wickedly bears a master and will serve for ever,  
> Because he does not know how to be content with little.  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, I.10

Likewise, in the saying of a wise man: a poor man laughs more often, more sincerely, and more truly than a rich man rests and sleeps. Hence Juvenal, *Satires*, I:

> [lacuna] And we  
> Advised Sulla to sleep deeply  
> As a private man.

Likewise Jerome (*Exhortatory Letter to Exsuperantius*): Poverty is for this reason to be embraced with a more generous vow: those who have left everything for Christ and follow naked the naked one will come with him as judges in a certain higher dignity. Hence: “You who have left all things and followed me shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). Likewise, by the example of the apostles, who left boats, nets, and even the desire to possess, for Christ’s name (Matt. 4).

Likewise, its truth and usefulness are made clear even by its opposite, namely abundance. The sin of the Sodomites was “abundance of bread and pride” of life (Ezek. 16), which arose from the abundance of temporal goods; because:

> Minds commonly grow wanton in prosperous circumstances.  
> —Ovid, *The Art of Love*, II

Likewise the poet:

> Humble fortune made Latin women chaste.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires*, VI

[Col. 0068A] Likewise Gregory: Those whom the weakness of character and riches wounds are healed by poverty’s medicine. Likewise Jerome: Poverty is to be loved for this reason, that it shows by whom you are loved. Likewise the same writer: This one thing is lacking to a person who has everything: there is no one to tell him the truth, whether in rebuking, advising, or imposing penance. Moreover, on account of the rich we transgress this precept: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him” (Luke 17); for it is difficult for them to confess rightly or to “bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3).

Likewise, as an example: When Xerxes, king of the Persians, was setting out against the Lacedaemonians with an innumerable army, toadies and flatterers from the inner rooms of his palace blinded him through flattery, saying that not even the air itself would suffice to contain the hail of his missiles, and other things of that sort. At last Demaratus, an exile and poor man, likewise a Lacedaemonian, was summoned and said to the king: “Those who promise you victory because of the number of your army lie to you. It will not happen so. The very mass of your army will crush you, and you will be conquered by yourself.” And so it happened. Likewise, the reason why those “who have left all things shall sit as judges” (Matt. 19) is that voluntary poverty is often both the nurse and sign of greater charity, although one may be poor amid riches.

Likewise, to signify that riches are to be despised, “the young man left behind the linen cloth and fled naked” (Mark 14). Likewise, to figure the same thing, Joseph left his cloak to the Egyptian harlot (Gen. [Col. 0068C] 39). Unless we abandon many things, even necessary things, to the harlot’s pleasures, she herself will entangle and overwhelm us. Hence the Apostle says: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from all things” (1 Cor. 9), even lawful things. Likewise Jeremiah: “Nebuzaradan,” king of the “Coci” [uncertain; probably an OCR-corrupted ethnic designation], left poor “vinedressers” and farmers in their native land, but carried off the rich and powerful and transferred them into exile (Jer. 52; 4 Kings 25). Likewise David: “He shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the poor” (Ps. 71). Likewise, in the Gospel God calls the poor man by name: “There was a beggar named Lazarus”; but he does not give the rich man’s name, as though it were unworthy and shameful, saying: “There was a certain rich man,” etc. (Luke 16).

Likewise Saint Bernard, when asking a certain religious abbot how matters stood with him and his community, received this answer: “Well, because we have still been left poor.” Likewise: “The Lord heard the poor and did not despise his chosen ones” (Ps. 68). Likewise Jerome: Poverty is greatly to be praised in this, that it hears and frees “his prisoners.” There are chains of nature and chains of fortune—namely poverty and what adheres to it. There are also chains of guilt, and chains of grace and perfection. Of these Augustine says: He burdens them excessively who heaps up beyond necessities.

Likewise the philosopher says: I remember Attalus saying this to the great admiration of everyone: “For a long time riches deceived me. I was astonished whenever some of them gleamed in one place or another. I thought that the things concealed were like those [Col. 0069A] displayed; but at a spectacle I saw the entire wealth of the City worked in relief, in silver and gold and in things surpassing the value of gold and silver: exquisite dyes, gems, and garments brought from beyond not merely our borders but even beyond those of our enemies. Here were troops of boys conspicuous in dress and form; there women, and other things which the fortune of the highest empire had produced while reviewing its possessions. ‘What,’ I said, ‘is this but inciting human desires, already aroused of themselves? What does this display of money mean? Have we assembled to learn avarice?’ Yet, by Hercules, I carry away from there less desire than I brought. I despised riches, not because they are superfluous, but because they are insignificant in their effect. Did you see how, within a few hours, that carefully arranged procession of riches passed slowly by? Will that which could not occupy a whole day occupy our whole life?”

There was added also his saying that riches “seemed to me as superfluous to their possessors as they had been to their spectators” (Seneca, *Letter* 110). This, therefore, I say to myself whenever something of this sort strikes my eyes—whenever a splendid house appears, a well-appointed train of servants, a litter borne by handsome bearers. What do you marvel at? What do you stare at? It is a display. These things are exhibited, not possessed; and while they delight, they pass away. Turn rather to true riches; learn to be content with little. And, great and high-spirited man, cry out also that saying: “Let us have water; let us have porridge.” It is shameful to place the happy life in gold and silver; it is equally shameful to place it in water and porridge. [Col. 0069C] “What, then, shall I do if I do not have these?” Do you ask what is the remedy for want? Hunger ends hunger. Otherwise, what difference does it make whether the things that compel you to serve are great or small? What does it matter how little the thing is, if Fortune can deny it to herself? Even this water and porridge fall under another’s control. But free is not the person over whom Fortune is allowed little power, but the person over whom it is allowed none. This is so if you desire none of these things. Nature has spoken sufficiently to all. If you wish to ponder this frequently, you are acting so as to be happy, not to seem so; and so as to seem so to yourself, not to others.

Likewise, to the same effect, the poet says:

> [lacuna] Put away complaints.  
> For he is not poor who has the use of things at hand.  
> If your belly, your side, and your feet are well provided for,  
> Royal riches can add nothing greater.  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, I.12

Likewise: The rich man who is not content with necessities is a wolf, who strangles many little sheep though he can scarcely devour and eat one.

Likewise Seneca, at the end of *Letter* 4: This is taken from another’s little garden: poverty governed by nature’s law is great wealth. But do you know what limits that law of nature sets or establishes for us? Not to hunger, not to thirst, not to be cold. To drive away hunger and thirst, you need not sit at proud thresholds, nor endure a haughty brow and humanity that is insulting even when it is civilized; you need not venture upon seas or follow armies. What nature desires is peaceful and readily available. [Col. 0070A] But now we sweat for superfluities. Those are the things that wear out the toga, make us grow old under a tent, and drive us upon foreign shores. What is enough is at hand.

Likewise the same writer (*Letter* 2): “Cheerful poverty,” he says, “is an honorable thing.” But if it is cheerful, it is not poverty, since one who gets along well with poverty is rich. A poor man is not one who has little but one who desires more. For what does it matter how much lies in his chest, how much in his granaries, how much he feeds or lends at interest, if he covets another’s possessions; if he counts not what he has acquired but what remains to be acquired? You ask what is the limit of riches? The first is to have what is necessary. The second is to possess what is enough, or sufficient. He has satisfaction who possesses however small an amount—namely, what necessity requires—even in time of necessity. For nature is content with necessity, even when hunger and thirst are restrained and moderate; but it is sated with what is over and above hunger and thirst.

## Chapter XVII. Against Those Who Seek and Retain Superfluities

[Col. 0070B]

But Augustine objects to this, saying: “If we do not give to the poor not only superfluous things but even necessary things, we are robbers.” Likewise Jerome: “He is proved to seize another’s property who is shown to retain for himself more than necessities.” It is as though he said: You may retain necessities, provided that from these you give according to the time, place, and need of the person asking. Augustine also allows sufficiency to the rich, saying: “Let the rich use superfluities, provided that from them they distribute necessities to the poor” [Col. 0070C].

Solomon seems, on the contrary, to speak against the good of poverty when he prayed: “Give me neither riches nor poverty” (Prov. 30). The answer is that he did not shrink from poverty, but from its occasion—namely, lest by occasion of it he commit theft. Nor did he fear riches, but their disease—namely pride. But if you cannot bear poverty patiently, choose the mean, according to the poet, who says:

> Whoever loves the golden mean, safe from harm,  
> Lacks the squalor of an abandoned roof  
> And, soberly, lacks the envy-provoking  
> Palace.  
> —Horace, *Odes*, II.10

## Chapter XVIII. On Moderation

[Col. 0070D]

David, commending the golden mean, says: “Better is a little to the righteous than the great riches of sinners” (Ps. 36). For, as Augustine says, whoever is rich needs many things; and where there are great riches, there too are many people in need. And there are present people who can devour in a moment’s hour the riches which the rich had unjustly heaped together.

Likewise, concerning this moderation, a certain wise man says: “A morsel of bread with joy is better” (Prov. 18) than riches, abundance, and the banquets of kings and princes. Likewise Seneca, commending this, says (*Letters* 95, 98, 104): When Roman citizens were about to dine together publicly in honor of Jupiter, some brought golden vessels, others jeweled or silver vessels, and tapestries and silk garments of most elaborate weaving, and spread them in public. Among these it is pleasing to behold the harmony and likeness of another Cato, distinguished in action at home and abroad: Tubero, while others spread silver couches for public use, spread wooden ones, goat skins for coverings and tapestries, and earthenware vessels set before the guests in front of Jupiter’s very shrine. What else could he consecrate in the Capitol but poverty? If I have no other deed by which to enroll him among the Catos, do we think this little thing? That banquet-display was rather a censorship than a banquet; it was more like a school and instruction for seeking moderation than a dinner for filling and satisfying [Col. 0071B] the belly. O how ignorant are people greedy for glory of what glory is or how it should be sought! On that day the Roman people looked upon the furnishings of many, but marveled at one alone. The gold and silver of all the others was broken up, melted a thousand times, and still to be melted again; it would pass through filthy hands and be handled and handled again. But Tubero’s earthenware will endure through all ages.

Likewise the same writer, more fully defining and limiting moderation, says—and Augustine also says, though something like theft seems to lurk in Augustine’s definition when he says, “According to the measure of your person and means, according to the custom of the Church and of the country in which you must live”—I warn you not to do, after the fashion of those who wish not to improve but to be noticed, anything remarkable in your dress or manner of life. Avoid rough clothing, uncut hair, a rather neglected beard, a proclaimed hatred of silver, a bed placed on the ground, and whatever else ambition pursues by a perverse path. The very name of philosophy, even heavenly philosophy, is sufficiently unpopular even when handled modestly. What if we begin to set ourselves apart from ordinary human society? Let everything within be unlike; let our outward appearance conform to the people. Let the toga neither shine nor be dirty. Let us not possess silver upon which a design in solid gold has been chased; but let us not think it a sign of frugality to have lacked gold and silver. Let us strive to follow a better life than the crowd, not a contrary one. Otherwise we drive away and turn aside from ourselves those whom we wish to correct. [Col. 0071D] We also bring about this result: our own people will be unwilling to imitate anything, because they fear that everything must be imitated.

This is the first thing philosophy leaves to us: a more common sense, humanity not offensively at odds with human customs, and the gathering of money—that is, from which profession our distinctiveness will separate us. Certainly our purpose is to live according to nature. It is against nature to torture our bodies, hate easy cleanliness, seek squalor, and use foods not merely cheap but dirty and disgusting. Just as desiring delicate things belongs to luxury, so fleeing things customary and not expensive to procure belongs to madness. Philosophy requires frugality, not punishment. Frugality need not be unkempt [Col. 0072A]. This measure pleases me: let life be tempered between good customs and public ones; let all approve our life, but not recognize it. What then? Shall we do the same things as others? Will there be no difference between us and them? Very much indeed. Let anyone who looks at us more closely, anyone who enters our house, know us to be unlike the crowd; let him admire us rather than our furnishings. Great indeed is the man who uses earthenware as he would silver; nor is he less great who uses silver as he would earthenware. It is the mark of a weak spirit not to be able to endure riches. Are riches therefore to be sought? No; but neither are they to be despised, according to the saying of Attalus, the great philosopher, who did not despise riches but allowed others to possess them (Seneca, *Letter* 110).

## Chapter XIX. Against the Worm and Evil of Riches

[Col. 0072B]

As visible poverty is the nurse and encouragement of spiritual poverty—that is, humility—so its opposite, riches, nurture and bring forth covetousness. The Apostle testifies to this when, in 1 Timothy 6, speaking against those who labor to acquire riches, he says: “Godliness with sufficiency is great gain,” namely, when a person has as much as is necessary to sustain life and as befits his station, so as to be suitable among those with whom he must live honorably. And he adds there: “For we brought nothing into this world; without doubt neither can we carry anything out. Having food”—simple food, not delicacies or incentives to gluttony—[Col. 0072C] “and clothing, with which we may be covered,” not adorned and given over to luxury, “let us be content with these. But those who wish to become rich”—he does not say “are rich,” but “wish to become rich”—beyond the purpose, bounds, and limits established by nature, “fall into many temptations and the snare of the devil, and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge men into destruction and perdition.”

## Chapter XX. Against Covetousness and Avarice

“The root of all evils is covetousness” (1 Tim. 6), which is wishing to have anything more than is enough; in Greek this is called πλεονεξία, “greed” or “the desire for more.” By this the devil fell, who loved not money but his own power; and so did the first human beings, who wished to be like gods. Therefore covetousness, in this sense, seems to include certain species of vices: pride, self-exaltation, *gastrimargia* [gluttony], and some others. To this question and argument belongs what Augustine proposes (*On Free Choice of the Will*, III.17, and on Psalm 118): “Some books read, ‘The root of all evils is avarice,’” which is understood specifically as love of money. Hence in Greek it is called φιλαργυρία, “love of silver” or “love of money”; but here the species is put for the genus. For avarice is a species of covetousness. Gregory, on the other hand, does not distinguish between them, saying in Homily 16 on the Gospels: “The devil tempted the first human being in three ways.”

[Col. 0073A] First, by gluttony, in the persuasion concerning food, when he said: “In whatever day you eat” (Gen. 3). Second, by vain glory, in the promise of divinity, when he said: “You shall be as gods” (ibid.). Third, by avarice, in the promise of knowledge, when he said: “Knowing good and evil.” Gluttony is an immoderate appetite for food.

Vain glory is love of one’s own excellence. Avarice is an immoderate desire to possess, concerning not only money but also high station and knowledge, whenever exaltation beyond measure is sought; indeed it concerns any thing whatever, whenever it is desired beyond what is enough, according to Augustine. Likewise, to the same effect, the philosopher says (Seneca, *Letter* 16): “Just as in other things, so we suffer from intemperance in letters. For we do not learn for life, but for the school.” Likewise the philosopher says: “Do not wonder that my mind is generous; I am still generous from another’s property.” But why did I say “another’s”? Whatever has been well said by anyone is mine, like this saying of Epicurus: “If you live according to nature, you will never be poor; if according to opinion, you will never be rich. Nature desires little; opinion, immeasurably much.” Let everything that many wealthy people possessed be heaped upon you; let Fortune raise you above the private measure of wealth, cover you with gold, clothe you in purple, and bring you to such a degree of luxurious abundance that you hide the ground under marble—not only so that you may possess riches, but also tread them beneath your feet. Let statues, paintings, and everything that art has produced beyond the demands of luxury be added, and from these you will learn to desire still greater things. Natural desires are limited; but those born of false opinion have no point at which to stop. For falsehood has no limit: a road has an end for the traveler; error is boundless. Withdraw therefore from vain things; and when you wish to know whether what you seek is prompted by natural or blind desire, consider whether it can stop anywhere. If, when you have gone far, something farther always remains, know that it is not natural, because:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires*, XIV.15

If we did not have riches, we would not be avaricious and covetous. Likewise Solomon, Proverbs 30: “The leech has two daughters” of the devil, incessantly crying, “Bring, bring.” Lust is incessant, and covetousness more incessant still. For lust can be checked by age or some medicine; covetousness by none.

Likewise covetousness is compared to dropsy, because:

> The more water is drunk, the more it is thirsted for.  
> —Ovid, *Fasti*

Likewise it is compared to the tale of Narcissus, because:

> While he sought to quench his thirst, another thirst grew.  
> —The same author, *Metamorphoses*, III.6

Likewise, in the saying of a certain wise man: Though we old men are wiser than others in all other matters, in avarice alone we become foolish and fail; and the less of the road remains, the more provision for the journey is sought.

## Chapter XXI. On Avarice
Avarice, a species of covetousness—although Gregory does not distinguish species from genus (*Homilies on the Gospels*)—is censured and detested by Ecclesiasticus, chapter 10: “Nothing is more wicked than a miser.” And because, on account of avarice and greedily amassed money, the miser is often proud, it adds: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” It then says concerning avarice: “For nothing is more unjust than to love money. Such a man has his very soul—not merely his tongue—for sale, because in his lifetime he has cast away his inward parts,” disembowelling himself, like a spider spinning useless webs, through anxiety to acquire and preserve money. Hence David: “You made his soul waste away like a spider” through envy [perhaps: avarice, or anxiety] (Ps. 38), because

> The tireless merchant runs to the farthest Indies.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, I.1.)

Likewise Jerome, in his letter to Paulinus, from Proverbs 17 [Col. 0074B], according to the Septuagint, after verse 6, at the end of the “helmeted prologue”: “For the believer the whole world is wealth; but the unbeliever lacks even an obol”—and is more concerned with what he does not have than with what he does have.

Likewise, it is an epithet of avarice either to make the miser proud, polished, and somewhat more elegant, or else that nothing is more filthy than he. Hence Juvenal: “filthy down to the ankle.” Let that deadly epithet of Horace suffice (*Satires*, I):

> Tantalus, thirsty, tries to catch the streams that flee from his lips.  
> Why do you laugh? Change the name, and the tale is told of you:  
> piled-up stones all about, you sleep greedily gaping,  
> as though you were compelled to spare sacred things,  
> or to delight, as it were, in painted pictures.

Likewise, pertinent here is the saying of a certain poor and honourable [Col. 0074C] cleric: “I would cast away that rich man’s wealth, even if it were increased a hundredfold or a thousandfold, rather than endure such anxiety in acquiring, keeping, and looking upon it. For I possess and behold it without anxiety. I enter a monastery, look upon its gold and silver in the vessels of the church, and feast my eyes. It is preserved for me without the trouble of appointing guards, so that, whenever I please, I may again feast my eyes by seeing it.”

Jerome, in his letter to Nepotian on the life of clerics: “A wealthy cleric ought to be rich in conscience and poor in money; for he has been taken into the portion or inheritance of the Lord—indeed, he is the Lord’s portion. For we are those of whom he says: ‘The lines have fallen to me in splendid places’” (Ps. 15) [Col. 0074D]; “we ought to have eyes before and behind, providing both for ourselves and for others.”

Likewise Sebastian, in his *Legend*: “If you object, ‘Why did God give riches, if we cannot and ought not possess them?’—they were bestowed upon you,” he says, “for the work of generosity. If you wish to lend them at interest and multiply them, lend them rather to Christ’s brother. Put them into the hands of Christ’s poor. ‘You shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life’” (Matt. 19). “Would not a man be welcome to you who, when you were travelling to market through a dangerous place infested with robbers, carried your money to a safer place, so that you might receive it back unharmed?” Certainly. “Put it, then, into the hands of the poor, ‘by whom it may be carried into heavenly treasures, where thieves neither steal nor dig through’” (ibid.).

[Col. 0075A]

> The wealth that you alone shall always possess is that which you have given.  
> (Martial, V.43.)

Likewise Ecclesiasticus, censuring the vice of avarice, says in chapter 14: “For a man greedy and grasping, wealth is irrational.” For it is acquired by right or wrong, and thus without reason.

> If you can do it rightly; if not, get wealth by whatever means.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, I.1.)

He continues: “And for the envious man, what use is gold?” Therefore every miser seems to be envious. For he envies others’ riches in order to possess them. “He who unjustly heaps up wealth for himself gathers for others, and another shall luxuriate in his goods. He who is wicked to himself, for whom shall he be good? Nor,” therefore, “shall he take delight in his own goods.” And David says: “He heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it” [Col. 0075B] (Pss. 38, 48). And: “They shall leave their riches to strangers” (Ecclus. 14). “He who envies himself—nothing is more wicked than he; and this is the recompense of his malice. Even if he does good, he does it unknowingly and unwillingly, and in the end he reveals his malice. The eye of the greedy man is insatiable in its pursuit of iniquity; it shall not be satisfied until it consumes,” dries up, “its own soul. An evil eye is bent upon evil; it shall not be satisfied with bread, but shall be needy; the miser shall be sorrowful at his own table” (Ecclus. 14).

Likewise, according to a certain wise man: “No heavier curse can be wished upon anyone than avarice: while it torments his heart in the present, he suffers dreadful torments, and thereby earns eternal punishments in the future.”

Likewise the Apostle, Ephesians 5: “Know that no fornicator, or unclean person, [Col. 0075C] or miser—which is the service of idols—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” For as an idolater renders to an idol the worship and service due to God, so the miser, serving money rather than God, renders to money and coin the worship owed to God.

Likewise the Apostle, Colossians 3: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth,” fleeing “fornication, lust, evil concupiscence, and avarice, which is the service of images.” Augustine likewise rightly compares avarice to idolatry, because their evil is not dissimilar, and each is fully accomplished by one work. Each strives to take from God what is his: the former, namely, the glory of divinity, so that God may not possess it alone; the latter, God’s things, so that she alone may possess what the Lord made for all [Col. 0075D].

Likewise Jerome to the monk Heliodorus: “By a false estimation of the weight of sins, avarice seems to some a lighter sin than idolatry; but they err greatly. For he who throws two grains of incense upon Mercury’s altar does not sin more gravely than he who greedily, covetously, and uselessly gathers and heaps up money.”

Likewise the Lord in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters, God and Mammon” (Matt. 6:24), that is, avarice—so called either from the name of pleasures or riches, which produce and foster it, or rather from the name of the demon who presides over ill-gotten riches.

Likewise, when the devil tempted the Lord through avarice, he said: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4:9). Therefore he who seeks riches [Col. 0076A] and the glory of the world falls down and worships the devil. For avarice brings about a greater fall than other vices, because it takes from God the service and worship owed to him.

Likewise the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 5: “If anyone called a brother among you is a fornicator, or a miser, or a worshipper of idols, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one it is not lawful even to eat.” Therefore misers must be avoided; above all, moneylenders must be excluded from communion in the Church’s sacraments unless they repent and restore what they have taken away.

At Saint-Denis, a certain such man, when dead, was cast upon a dungheap. At length, through the greed of a certain monastery, he was buried in the church’s cemetery. When honourable men protested lest this become an example, his corpse was dug up and thrown back on the dungheap.

Objection concerning soldiers who retain tithes.

Likewise the Lord in the Gospel: “Beware of all avarice. For a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” (Luke 12). For his possession is the loss of grace and glory.

Likewise Proverbs 15: “He who follows avarice troubles his own house; but he who hates gifts shall live. But fire shall devour the tents of those who gladly receive gifts.” Likewise chapter 28: “He who hates avarice shall have long days. But the man who hastens to become rich and envies others does not know that poverty shall come upon him.”

Likewise Ecclesiastes 5: “The miser shall not be filled with money, and he who loves riches shall derive no fruit from them. Where there are many riches, there are many to consume them. And what [Col. 0076C] advantage has their owner, except to look upon them?” Likewise in chapter 6: “A man to whom God has given riches, substance, and honour, and whose soul lacks nothing of all that it desires—yet God has not granted him power to eat of it, but a stranger shall consume it: this is vanity and a great misery.”

Likewise Horace (*Epistles*, I.16):

> I do not see how the miser is better off or freer than a slave.  
> For whoever desires will also fear; and furthermore,  
> he who lives in fear shall never be free to me.

Because:

> He has lost his weapons and abandoned the post of virtue,  
> who always hastens to increase his wealth and is overwhelmed by it.

Likewise Jerome, in his commentary on Proverbs 30 [Col. 0076D]: “Avarice is like hell and the mouth of a harlot’s womb. For it is insatiable; and the more it snatches and devours, the more it thirsts to snatch and to destroy.” Hence the poet:

> Whatever perishes in the world  
> is bestowed upon the greedy in riches.

Likewise:

> Even a rich miser is always poor.

But he is rich who is poor with Christ. Likewise: Since the leech has two daughters, namely lust and avarice, the worse and more detestable daughter is avarice. For lust is relieved by the benefit of age and the passage of time; but no antidote cures avarice. Rather, the less of the road remains, the more it grows in acquisition.

Hence Claudian:

[Col. 0077A]

> What good is it to cut the sinews? No force castrates  
> blood-stained avarice, though exercised in petty thefts,  
> [lacuna] but it rages more fiercely for gold;  
> mutilated lust enjoys this one thing alone.  
> (*In Eutropius*, I.)

Likewise: At judgment, above all monsters, the Lord will detest the one monster of avarice, as the cause of our condemnation; and its opposite, namely merciful generosity or liberality, he will approve above all our works, as though it were the cause of our salvation, when he says: “I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink” (Matt. 25), and so forth. And what is the reason why you did not give? Avarice. What is the reason why you gave? Generosity. Yet it is easier to give—because this is to unload oneself—than to fulfil the works of the other virtues. Hence it is a small thing to enjoin upon a penitent that he distribute his substance to the poor, unless he has suffered from avarice, so that he may thereby be cured of it.

Likewise Jerome: “Avarice is all the more detestable because it itself nourishes and fosters the vice contrary to itself; for avarice almost always accompanies prodigality.” Hence the poet Claudian:

> Whatever profound avarice has drawn in,  
> worse extravagance pours back out.  
> (*On the Gildonic War.*)

How then are they opposites?

Likewise, Genesis 31: Rachel, fleeing with Jacob from the presence of her father Laban, stole his idols, which she hid beneath the camel’s bedding and sat [Col. 0077C] upon. When Laban sought them and did not find them in her tent, she said: “Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, because what happens according to the custom of women has now come upon me.” But Jacob later, discovering that foreign gods—namely Laban’s idols—were in his house, buried them beneath a terebinth tree, although they were of gold and silver, with their earrings, ornaments, and phylacteries.

By Jacob, Christ and the perfectly penitent person are understood: one who buries beneath Christ’s cross every worldly and ancient covetousness and its philosophy—that is, every occasion and circumstance of avarice—following naked the naked Crucified One, whose poverty appeared most fully upon the cross. For as he hung upon it, he had only a loincloth, the covering of his private parts. Who can say with Christ [Col. 0077D]: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14), and with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6)?

By Rachel, whose name is interpreted “sheep,” is signified one who repents gently and imperfectly. What happens to her according to the custom of women occurs when, pursuing the uncleanness of avarice, she suffers, as it were, female ailments. Yet in repenting she hides the idols, that is, avarice, beneath the camel’s bedding—namely beneath dung—and under the camel’s covering, that is, beneath the humility of repentance; concealing every swelling, exaltation, and avarice that come from riches. Thus she sits upon the dung in which the idols were hidden, because she sets God above all things, even if she has riches beside her [Col. 0078A]. Her possessions, however, serve her; she does not serve her possessions, as Horace says of himself:

> I strive to make things subject to me, not myself to things.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, I.1.)

Likewise pertinent here is the example of Joseph, who left behind to the Egyptian harlot not only his cloak but also her lust. That is, we ought to leave behind to worldly pleasure not only covetousness, but every occasion and circumstance of it.

Likewise pertinent is the example of “the young man who, leaving behind the linen cloth, fled from them naked” (Mark 14), namely from the Jews.

Likewise pertinent is the example of the molten calf, which Moses ordered to be reduced to the finest dust. For through repentance we must not merely condemn and abolish avarice itself and the substance of sin, [Col. 0078B] but utterly consume all its circumstances and slightest occasions, and condemn them as the foul dung of most unclean excrement, with the Apostle who says: “I have counted all these things as dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3; 12, question 2, *Gloria*).

Likewise Jerome, from his letter to Paulinus on the monastic institution: Crates of Thebes, once a very wealthy man, set out for Athens to study philosophy, taking with him a great weight of gold. On the journey, deliberating with himself and considering that he could not possess virtues and riches at once, since he was going to unlearn avarice and saw that riches were its encouragement and nourishment, he cast away the gold, saying: “O riches, depart; be far from us.” But now we follow the poor Christ laden [Col. 0078C] with gold and silver; and, clinging to our former wealth under the pretext of almsgiving, how can we faithfully distribute others’ goods when we timidly preserve our own?

Likewise pertinent is the example of that Cynic and philosopher Diogenes, who lived in a jar and, empty of hope and free from fear, passed a rich poverty.

When a certain courtier, Aristippus, came upon him while he was cleaning and washing his vegetables, he said: “You are wise and a philosopher; if you had wished to serve kings, you would not wash your vegetables.” He replied: “If you knew how to use moderate poverty, you would not need to lie to kings through begging flattery.” Hence Horace (*Epistles*, I.17):

[Col. 0078D]

> If Aristippus could patiently dine on vegetables,  
> he would not wish to make use of kings; if he knew how to make use of kings,  
> he who finds fault with me would despise vegetables.

## CHAPTER XXII. Against those who receive gifts

We do not detest and condemn avarice and every acceptance of gifts only by examples of pagans, but also by many examples from Holy Scripture.

First, by the example of Abraham. When, returning from the slaughter of the four kings, he was bringing back Lot and Lot’s possessions, the king of Sodom said to him: “Give me the persons; take the rest for yourself.” Abraham answered: “I lift up my hand to the Lord God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, that from a thread of the warp even to the strap [Col. 0079A] of a sandal I shall receive nothing of all that is yours, lest you say: ‘I made Abraham rich’—except what the young men have eaten and the portions of the men who came with me; for they shall receive their portions” (Gen. 14).

Likewise, Genesis 23. When his wife Sarah had died, Abraham said to the sons of Heth: “I am a stranger and sojourner among you; give me a right of burial among you, that I may bury my dead.” The sons of Heth replied: “You are a prince of God among us; bury your dead in our choicest tombs.” Abraham rose, gave thanks, and bowed to them, and said: “If it pleases you that I bury my dead, intercede with Ephron son of Seor, that for a fitting sum he may give me the double cave which he has at the far end of his field as a burial possession.” Ephron answered in the hearing of all: “It shall not be so; rather, I freely give you the field and the cave in it.” Abraham replied [Col. 0079B]: “I shall not receive it freely, but shall give money for the field. Receive it, and so I shall bury my dead in it.” And Abraham weighed out the money that Ephron requested: four hundred shekels of silver, of approved and current coinage.

Likewise, Genesis 33, by the example of Esau. When his brother Jacob offered him gifts of cattle, asses, male and female servants, Esau said: “What are these companies that I met?” Jacob answered: “That I might find favour before my lord.” And he said: “I have much, my brother; keep what is yours for yourself.” Jacob said: “Please do not say so; but if I have found favour in your eyes, receive this small gift from my hands. For I have seen your face as though I saw the face of God; be gracious to me, and receive the blessing which I have brought you.” Only with difficulty, when his brother urged him, did he accept it.

Yet this acceptance, although compelled, is in him and people like him a sign of divine reprobation. For there are some who wish to be compelled to accept, and nevertheless do accept: “That force is welcome to him, and he deserves to be compelled.”

Likewise, Exodus chapters 34 and 35. For the construction of the tabernacle all the men and women, with devout minds, offered gifts so that the works commanded by the Lord through Moses might be made; and all the children of Israel freely dedicated offerings to the Lord. “But when the craftsmen pressed on with the work, they said to Moses: ‘The people offer more than is necessary.’ Therefore Moses ordered proclamation to be made by a herald: ‘Let neither man nor woman offer anything further for the work of the sanctuary.’ Thus they ceased offering gifts, because what had been offered was sufficient and more than sufficient.”

Likewise, Numbers 16. When Moses rebuked Dathan and Abiram for murmuring against Aaron, they answered him: “Is it too little for you that you have brought us out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, unless you also rule over us? Do you also wish to put out our eyes?” Moses, greatly angered, said to the Lord: “Do not regard their sacrifices, Lord; you know that I have never received from them even an ass, nor afflicted any one of them.”

Likewise, Numbers 22: “The elders of Moab and its senior princes, having the price of divination in their hands, sent by Balak, [Col. 0080A] said to Balaam: ‘Thus says Balak, son of Sephor, king of the Moabites: Do not delay to come to me; I am prepared to honour you and to give you whatever you desire. Come and curse this people.’ Balaam answered: ‘If Balak should give me a house full of silver or gold, I could not alter the word of my God, to speak either less or more.’”

Likewise, when Balak presented and offered him gifts, he said (Num. 23–24): “Curse Jacob; denounce Israel.” He answered: “How shall I curse one whom God has not cursed? On what ground shall I denounce one whom the Lord does not denounce? Can I speak anything other than what God commanded me? He who blesses Jacob shall himself be blessed, and he who curses him shall be counted under a curse. Yet, as I go to my people, I shall give you counsel about what your people [Col. 0080B] shall do to this people.” And he fulfilled it, as John testifies in Revelation 2, saying that Balaam, having accepted the price of divination, although compelled, “taught Balak to place a stumbling-block before the children of Israel,” namely “to eat” of sacrifices to idols “and to commit fornication.”

Likewise, 1 Samuel 12: “Samuel said to all Israel: ‘I have heard your voice in all that you said to me, and have appointed over you a king who goes before you. And now I have grown old, having lived among you from my youth until this day. Behold, I stand ready. Speak concerning me before the Lord and before his Christ,’” namely Saul: “‘Whether I have taken anyone’s ox or ass; whether I have slandered anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have received a gift from anyone’s hand. I shall despise it today and restore it to you.’”

Likewise, by the example of David at the end of 2 Samuel: “It shall not be as you wish; rather, I shall buy the threshing-floor from you at a price, where a temple may be built to the Lord; and I shall not offer free holocausts to my Lord.”

Likewise, by the example of Addo the prophet, 1 Kings 13: “The king said to the man of God: ‘Come home with me and dine, and I will give you gifts.’ The man of God answered the king: ‘If you gave me half your house, I would not come with you, nor eat bread nor drink water in this place.’”

Likewise, 2 Esdras 5: “I and my brothers and my servants have lent money and grain to many; let us not demand this debt back together; let us remit what is owed to us,” etc.

Likewise, Acts of the Apostles [Col. 0080D] 20: “You know, from the first day when I entered Asia, how I lived among you at all times, serving the Lord in humility and tears.” And, developing a most moral discourse, at its close he adds concerning the office of prelates, teaching them by his own example to beware of avarice: “I have not coveted silver, gold, or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands supplied what was needed for me and for those who were with me.”

Likewise, the Epistle of Jude (chap. 5, 8, 9): “Woe to those who have gone in the way of Cain, poured themselves out in Balaam’s error for reward, and perished in Korah’s rebellion.”

Likewise, 2 Corinthians 11: “I preached the Gospel to you freely; and when I was with you and in need, I was burdensome to no one, but in all things I kept myself, and shall keep myself, free of burden to you. [Col. 0081A] The truth of Christ is in me: this boasting, that I do not accept, shall not be hindered in me in the regions of Achaia. What I do and shall do is to cut off an opportunity” for preaching to those who preach for gain.

Likewise Ezekiel 22: “You have accepted gifts, interest, and excess; you greedily extorted from your neighbours, and have forgotten me, says the Lord. Behold, I have clapped my hands over the avarice you have practised.”

Likewise the Apostle, Acts 20: “I have shown you all things: that by labouring thus one must support the weak and remember the word of the Lord Jesus, which he himself said”—and frequently had upon his lips—“‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

Likewise, by the example of blessed Thomas, who, when appointing [Col. 0081B] his chancellor, bound him by an oath never to receive anything in administering the chancellery, even so much as a little dog.

Likewise Ecclesiasticus 20: “Presents and gifts blind the eyes of judges, and, like a mute thing in the mouth, turn aside their rebukes.” Corrupted by a gift, they are struck dumb by ceasing from rebuke.

Likewise Isaiah, chapter 33: “Who walks in righteousness and speaks truth, who casts away gain from extortion and shakes his hands free from every gift? He shall dwell on high.” Note the word “shaking.” Through a loosening of the hands, large gifts readily fall to the ground; but small ones, unless they are shaken off, adhere to the hands like dust.

Likewise Strabo, on Exodus: Covetousness is a little branch cast into a dog’s mouth, which [Col. 0081C] makes it mute.

Likewise, the greedy man resembles that foolish Virgilian shepherd, of whom:

> The wolves saw Moeris first.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogue* 9.)

Of wolves it is said that, if they see people first, they make them mute.

Likewise Job 15: “In the end fire shall devour the tents of those who gladly receive gifts.”

Likewise, 4 Kings 5. Naaman the Syrian, cured of leprosy through Elisha, said to him: “I beseech you, my lord, receive a blessing from your servant.” But he answered: “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand, I shall not receive it.” When Gehazi, in his master Elisha’s absence, had accepted gifts from him, Elisha said to him upon his return: “Now, therefore, you have received silver and garments, in order to buy olive-groves, vineyards, sheep and oxen, [Col. 0081D] male and female servants; but Naaman’s leprosy also shall cling to you and to your seed for ever” (4 Kings 5).

Likewise Demosthenes, asked to open his mouth in defence of the republic’s liberty, wrapped his head in wool, pretending to be sick, and said: “I cannot, brother; for I suffer from *synanche* [quinsy].” The reply was: “Not *synanche*, I say, but *argyranche* [silver-quinsy].”

Likewise: “Gifts blind the eyes of the wise” (Deut. 16) and bend the force of authority.

Likewise, by the example of Cyriacus, deacon of Pope Marcellus. Having authority to command demons, he cured the daughter of the Emperor Diocletian, who was possessed by a demon; after leaving her, the demon leapt into the daughter of Sapor, king of the Persians. When Sapor heard that Cyriacus had cured Diocletian’s daughter, he sent a great legion with gifts to [Col. 0082A] Diocletian, asking that Cyriacus come at his request and cure his daughter. When Cyriacus was asked, he granted the request; and when carriages and horses were prepared for him to travel upon, he said: “It does not become a Christian to travel so pompously; go on ahead, and I will follow.” When he had cured Sapor’s daughter and baptized him and his entire household, the king offered him gifts. He replied: “I shall not receive these gifts. Far be it that Christ’s grace should be, or be reckoned, for sale.”

Likewise Jerome: As a married woman is not chaste if she receives gifts, especially from her lover and bridegroom—since these are signs of her frivolity and future adultery—so neither is a judge who receives small gifts from a fellow brother; they are signs of his corruption and of the judgment he is to render.

Likewise Jeremiah 6 [Col. 0082B]: “From the least even to the greatest, all pursue avarice; from prophet even to priest, all practise deceit. They treated the brokenness of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace.”

Likewise Exodus 23: “Do not accept gifts, which blind even the prudent and overthrow the words of the just.”

Likewise Quintilian tells of a certain orator trained at Athens and made eloquent at the expense of a rich man. Later, when asked to speak for the republic, he appeared in a case against his own patron, that rich man; and in it the rich man prevailed. He therefore summoned that orator to court, accusing him of ingratitude. When accused, the orator said to the rich man: “My lord, you know that I directed nothing cruel against you, nothing prompted by hatred, but I stood for the liberty of the republic and the honour of my own person—indeed, of yours also. But now I see that nothing is more dangerous than gifts received, if they bind us to every kind of slavery.”

Likewise Jerome, writing to a wealthy matron and knowing that, by slandering him, her dogs said that he sought intimacy with princes, replied to them: “Far be it from me to seek such things! For one to whom cheap vegetables and coarse bread are enough does not seek such things.” For contempt of gifts and wealth is a trustworthy testimony that one has no reasons for lying, flattering, begging, or seeking the intimacy of powerful persons.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Against those who receive gifts for justice done, to be done, expedited, or omitted

[Col. 0082D] The acceptance of gifts is manifold. The first kind is simple: the acceptance of lawful gifts for no unjust cause. Yet it is dangerous, because by them we sell our freedom, of which we spoke above at the end of the chapter on avarice (chapter 21).

The second is for justice already done—which is Gehazi-like—or justice to be done—which is simoniacal; for justice omitted or to be omitted, expedited or to be expedited—which is unjust; and even for injustice to be done—which is diabolical.

The third is from hidden or open robbery: for example, violent robbery, usury, theft, exactions, extortions of money, tallages received in excess of the prescribed stipend, and the like.

The fourth is for spiritual things: for orders, sacraments, ecclesiastical benefices, offices, and things attached to these, whether conferred or to be conferred, or withheld—not given, when someone has proposed to grant an ecclesiastical benefice to a worthy person. This is also, and more cruelly, an insult done to the Holy Spirit, and an impediment preventing his grace from running its course.

The fifth is when someone receives through tricks, curiosities, mumming, and theatrical art, or when he possesses abundance and is not needy. Hence Jerome, to Paulinus: “O monk, if you are needy and receive, you give rather than receive; if you receive and are not needy, you rob.”

The sixth is accepting gifts from unlawfully acquired goods, even if they are spent upon pious causes—for example, in building monastic granges, workshops, and the like.

The following are collected against the second heading. Those who receive gifts for justice done, to be done, expedited [Col. 0083B] or omitted, or for injustice to be done, if they are pastors and prelates of the Church, are like foolish Nabal, who, while shearing sheep, paid no heed to David and had no compassion for Joseph’s affliction. They are not shepherds of sheep but shearers, flayers, pluckers, wolves, and squeezers of money; seeking milk and wool from the sheep, gaping after profit rather than attending to the salvation of souls.

For it is read in 1 Kings 25 that, “when David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep, or his flock, he sent ten young men to him, saying: ‘Whatever your hand finds, give to your servants and to your son David.’” He replied: “Who is David? And who is the son of Jesse? Today slaves have multiplied [Col. 0083C] upon the earth, who flee from their masters.” Hearing this, David was very angry and ordered his servants to gird themselves with swords, as though intending to take vengeance upon him.

When Abigail, his prudent and wise wife, heard this, she met David—without her husband’s knowledge—with bread, wine, and cooked rams. Descending from her ass, she fell at his feet and said: “Let this iniquity be upon me, my lord; I beg you, receive this blessing which your maidservant has brought to you, my lord. Let no malice be found in you. Let it not become a groaning of heart and a scruple to you that you have shed my husband’s blood, when the Lord has appointed you leader over Israel.” David therefore received what she offered and said: “Go peacefully to your house.” Yet after ten days the Lord, taking vengeance for David, struck Nabal the shearer, and he died (ibid.).

Likewise, such persons are like Laban (Gen. 29), who deceived Jacob while he served him, changed his wages ten times, sold his daughters and counted them as strangers, and consumed their price. For this reason, when he had gone to shear the sheep, Rachel stole the idols of her father—things most precious to him among all—and fled (Gen. 31).

Likewise, they are great shearers of sheep down to the flesh, indeed shearers down to blood; if they cannot do that, they are pluckers down to the skin—that is, in lesser gifts. Outwardly they appear beautiful, but in their works and inwardly they are ravening wolves. They are like Absalom (2 Kings 14), whose hair grew more abundantly the more he cut it, and who ordered Joab’s field, which had a barley harvest, to be burned because Joab refused to come to him [Col. 0084A]. What they are ashamed to do themselves, they accomplish through their subordinate officials: pimps and agents of shearing, investigators and trackers of their plunder. It would be more prudent for these men to lead about little prostitutes in procuring than to concern themselves with robbery and participation in their superiors’ sin, since they cannot restore anything of what has been taken.

Likewise, such persons are like Judah (Gen. 38), who, after his wife’s death, went up to the shearers of his sheep.
