As he went up to shear the sheep, Tamar his daughter-in-law, changing her widow’s clothing, sat at a crossroads. Seeing her, Judah supposed that she was a prostitute; and, giving her gifts as to a prostitute, he had intercourse with her.

Likewise Psalm 13: “Shall not all who work iniquity,” manifold iniquity, “know” in the future? And who are they, and why do they “work iniquity”? Namely those “who,” and because “they devour my people” [Col. 0084B] by daily and manifold plunder, “as bread for food”: that is, those who use their ministry in order to receive gifts from men, not for human salvation or God’s glory. For bread is a daily and pleasant food; likewise they delight in daily robbery, as they swallow up simple Christians. Their becoming such derives from the fact that “they did not call upon the Lord,” but upon temporal things.

Likewise Psalm 25: “Their right hand is filled with gifts,” when, for justice, the price of money, praise, fear, or unjust favour is sought.

Likewise Psalm 143: “Their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” It ought rather to be called a left hand than a right, because for things of the right hand they seek temporal things, and change the right into the left; being not ambidextrous with Ehud but “both-left-handed,” and therefore unable to pierce the very fat King Eglon (Judg. 3).

Likewise, because of avarice such persons cannot fulfil this commandment: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6), since they do the things of the right hand for the left and for temporal goods. Nor can they fulfil this: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). Rather: “His left hand is under my head, and his left hand embraces me”; for they have only a left hand, acting only for the left.

Likewise, at judgment such persons shall be placed with the foul goats on the left [Col. 0084D], not with the sweet-smelling lambs on the right (Matt. 25), since here they sought nothing but the left hand.

Likewise Zechariah 5: “The angel said to me: ‘See what this is that goes forth.’ And I said: ‘What is it?’ And he said: ‘This is the amphora that goes forth.’ And I said: ‘This is the eye of everyone on earth’; and behold, a talent of lead was being carried, and behold, a woman sitting in the midst of the amphora. And he said: ‘This is wickedness.’ And he cast her into the midst of the amphora, and I put the mass of lead upon its mouth.’”

Jerome, in his commentary on Zechariah and Nahum: “Formerly iniquity sat upon a talent of lead, but now upon a talent of gold.” Now that saying of the poet is fulfilled:

> Now indeed are the ages golden: the greatest honour  
> comes through gold.

[Col. 0085A]

> By gold is accomplished whatever is unjustly sought,  
> and no one asks vain things under the pretext of a gift.  
> (Propertius, III.11.)

Likewise Arator, *On the Acts of the Apostles*, I:

> [lacuna] With shrewd mind, this with yourself …

Turn over in your thoughtful mind what it means that a lump of gleaming metal is placed beneath the feet, not entrusted to sacred hands; they show that it ought to be despised [ed.: abandoned] by refusing to touch it, and teach that the gold they put beneath their steps should be trampled underfoot. From it earthly cares come into hearts; upon like ground, where it may rest, O miserly mind, learn that you eagerly guard what you press down in its place, what you burn to look upon more often, and to whose embraces you return in every dream. The devout shrink from handling it, nor do they carry it even when they prepare good works, so greatly do they perceive that wickedness lies in it; gold, though bearing gifts, is despised.

Likewise Claudian (*Against Eutropius*, book I) [Col. 0085B]:

> [lacuna] He wishes shared marks of disgrace to be consolations for his own lot; and, himself sold, he desires to sell everything, when the differing burden of two men often hangs in the balance, when the judge inclines under its weight and a province wavers in the two pans of the scales.

Hence Jerome: A judge ought not to be like a balance, which is tipped to one side by the small weight of an obol and is thereby unjust. So too a judge who has regard to a gift, or to a person, or to anything apart from the judgment of the Lord, and is thereby inclined to one side, examines less justly. Hence Solomon: “Weight and balance are the judgments of the Lord” (Prov. 16) [Col. 0085C]. But whoever, because of a gift or something of that kind, bends just judgment, whether in its circumstances and appendages or in the substance of the sentence, “has weight and weight in his house” (Deut. 25).

Hence Solomon: “Weight and weight are an abomination before God; a deceitful balance is abominable to the Lord. An equitable weight is his will” (Prov. 20). Likewise, Deuteronomy, chapter 25: “You shall not have different weights in your bag; there shall not be a greater and a lesser in your house. For the Lord abominates him who does these things.” Likewise: “Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. 33). Augustine says: from money, praise, fear, private favour, unjust mercy.

Hence the Lord in Leviticus (chapter 19): “Do not consider the person of the poor man.” Augustine adds: in judgment; because one who spares the poor man’s purse, pitying him in an unjust cause, strikes his heart. Likewise, Exodus chapter 23: “You shall not turn aside in the judgment of the poor” [Col. 0085D]. But today this need not be commanded: for now the poor are despised in judgment, indeed even by their brethren. Hence Solomon: “The brothers of a poor man hate him” (Prov. 19).

Likewise, Jeremiah (chapter 48): “Cursed is everyone who does the work of God deceitfully.” Gregory explains: for the reward of a bodily thing, or for a word of praise, or for the favour of human judgment. Likewise Jerome: As wine, taken too abundantly, even if fine, dulls the intellect, so too a small gift dulls a judge’s judgment, so that he cannot see the truth. Likewise: As a matron who has received a small gift sent from elsewhere gives evidence of her corruption, so from a judge who receives a small gift nothing but a corrupt judgment will issue.

Likewise, Exodus chapter 18 [Col. 0086A]: “Jethro said to Moses: What is this that you are doing among the people? Why do you sit alone” to judge, “while all the people wait from morning until evening? You are not doing a good thing,” he said. “You and your people with you will be consumed by foolish labour. The business is beyond your strength; you cannot bear it alone. But listen to my words and counsels, and the Lord will be with you,” namely, if you remove from yourself the multitude of business matters, lest you be weighed down. It is especially important if you choose as judges such men as are noble and powerful and feared. If they are humble, justice and the Church are better provided for thereby; but if they are proud and wicked, oil is added to the furnace.

“Wise men and men who fear God, in whom truth is found, and who hate avarice. Appoint from among them tribunes, centurions, and heads of tens, who may judge the people at all times” (Exod. 18) [Col. 0086B]. And command them, saying: “Hear them and judge what is just, whether the man be a citizen or a stranger. There shall be no distinction of persons: you shall hear the small as the great, and shall accept no one’s person, because the judgment is God’s. But if anything in the case seems too difficult to you, refer it to me” (Deut. 1); and thus you will dismiss the people in peace.

Likewise, Deuteronomy chapter 16: “You shall appoint judges and masters,” steadfast ones, “in all your gates, which God has given you throughout your tribes, that they may judge the people with righteous judgment and not turn aside to either side. Nor shall you accept a person or gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the just” [Col. 0086C] before men. “You shall pursue justly that which is just, so that you may live for ever.”

Likewise Caesar in Sallust: O all you men who ought to render just judgment, it is necessary that you be free from private love or hatred, fear or desire, or special favour; otherwise you will easily turn aside from right judgment.

Likewise Cicero, *On Duties* (book III, before the middle): Duties are especially disturbed in friendships, in which both failing to grant what may rightly be granted, and granting what is not equitable, are contrary to duty. But for this entire class of things—that is, things that may be granted—the rule is brief and not difficult. Things that seem advantageous—honours, riches, pleasures, and such things—are never to be preferred to friendship [Col. 0086D]. Yet a good man will do nothing against the republic, against an oath, against justice, or against good faith for a friend’s sake, even if he is a judge in the case of that friend himself. For he lays aside the character of a friend when he puts on that of a judge. He will grant friendship only this: that he prefer his friend’s case to be true, and that he allow time for settlement of the suit, so far as the law permits; but he will grant him absolutely nothing except what can be fulfilled without violating good faith. In rendering judgment he should have God alone in mind, not his friend. For if everything friends wish must be done, such relationships should be called not friendships but conspiracies. Therefore let him be a judge, and such a one, as “says to his father,” and to every man: “I do not know you” (Deut. 33).

Likewise Amos (chapter 5) [Col. 0087A]: “Seek the Lord and you shall live, lest the house of Joseph be consumed as by fire. You who turn your judgment into wormwood and leave justice upon the ground”—that is, for the earth, namely earthly things—“the Maker, namely God, of Arcturus and Orion,” who smiles upon devastation against the strong man,” namely upon the mighty and great man who oppresses and despoils the people, “or brings devastation upon the powerful.” Hence: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6). “They hated him who reproved in the gate, and abominated him who spoke perfectly. Therefore, because you despoiled the poor and took from him choice spoil, you shall build houses of squared stone but shall not dwell in them. You shall plant most lovely vineyards but shall not drink their wine; because [Col. 0087B] I have known your many crimes and your grievous sins: enemies of the just,” and of just judgment, “receiving gifts. Therefore the prudent man shall be silent in that time, because it is an evil time” (Amos 5): when a man does not receive correction, for which reason the prudent person is silent, “lest he give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7). “Seek good and not evil, and the Lord shall be with you. Hate evil and love good, and establish judgment in the gate, if perhaps the Lord may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph” (Amos 5).

Likewise Amos: “I saw the Lord standing upon the altar, and he said: Strike the lintel, and let the thresholds be shaken. For avarice is at the head of them all, and I shall slay the last of them with the sword. There shall be no escape for them; he who flees shall flee and shall not be saved. If they descend as far as hell, from there my hand shall bring them out; and if they ascend to heaven, from there I shall pull them down” [Col. 0087C].

Likewise he says in chapter 2: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I shall not turn him back, because he sold the just man for silver and the poor man for shoes; they crush upon the dust of the earth the heads of the poor and turn aside the way of the humble; they reclined upon garments taken in pledge and drank the wine of the condemned.”

Likewise he says in chapter 3: “Will the lion roar in the forest unless he has prey? Will the lion’s cub give voice from his den unless it has seized something? Will a bird fall into a snare upon the ground without a fowler? Will a snare be taken from the ground before it has caught something?”

Likewise he says in chapter 4: “Hear this word, you fat cows, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who have brought false accusation against the needy and crushed the poor, who say to your officers: Bring it, bring it, and we shall drink. The Lord has sworn that you and your remnant shall be cast in boiling pots into Armon” [Col. 0087D].

Likewise he says in chapter 6: “Woe to you who are rich in Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria, chief men, heads of the peoples. Cross over to Calneh; go down to Gath, and see whether their territory is broader than yours.” As if he said: You will not see so many wicked deeds among idolaters as among yourselves, who “enter in pomp into the house of Israel.” A terrible word. “You who are set apart for an evil day, who draw near to the throne of iniquity, who sleep upon ivory beds and wanton upon your couches, eating lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery; like David they thought themselves to possess instruments of song; drinking wine from bowls, anointed with the finest ointment, and feeling no compassion for the affliction of Joseph” (Amos 6) [Col. 0088A]. Thus says the Lord: “Indeed, you shall go into exile at the head of those who go into exile” (Joel 3).

Likewise Joel chapter 3: “I shall contend with them in judgment, because they put a boy into a brothel and sold a girl for wine, that they might drink”—namely, softening and corrupting for a gift effeminate, tender, and childlike souls, which they sell into the slavery of the devil.

Likewise Hosea (chapter 4): “There is no truth in the land, no mercy, no knowledge; but cursing, lying, theft, and murder have overflowed” [Col. 0088B], having forgotten the law of the Lord their God; “and I shall forget them and their children. I shall change their glory into disgrace. They would eat the sins of my people”—I do not mean merely by eating offerings for sins, or by absorbing and destroying them through prayer, teaching, and confession, which would be good—but by justifying the wicked for gifts and condemning the devout.

Likewise he says in chapter 5: “Hear this, priests; attend, house of Israel; and listen, house of the king, because judgment concerns you, since you have become a snare for a watchtower and a net spread over Tabor,” to catch birds—and would that they were only little birds.

Likewise Amos (chapter 6): “Woe to you who turn judgment into bitterness and the fruit of justice into wormwood, who rejoice in nothing” [Col. 0088C]. Nothingness is acceptance of persons, fear, lax mercy, corruption by a gift, the poor man’s purse, and things of that kind. “Who say: Have we not by our own strength taken horns for ourselves?” (Mic. 6), namely horns of prelacy and dominion. “But no one takes honour to himself,” etc. (Heb. 5).

Likewise Hosea (chapter 4): “If you commit fornication, Israel, at least let Judah not offend; and do not enter Gilgal,” namely the rolling-place of vices, “and do not go up to Beth-aven” (ibid.), namely to the mountain of pride, “after Ephraim.” For “Ephraim, suffering false accusation and broken by judgment, began to go after filth.”

Likewise Malachi (chapter 1): “O priests, who despise my name, who offer polluted bread upon my altar and say: The table of the Lord is contemptible. If you offer the blind or the lame, is that not evil? Offer it to your governor, and see whether it will please him.” And below: “Who is there among you who will shut the doors and kindle my altar without payment? I have no pleasure in these things; therefore neither will I receive a gift from your hand. You have polluted my name, contaminated my table, saying: Behold, what labour! And you brought from plunder the lame and the sick, and brought a gift” (ibid.) [Col. 0088D]; but I blew it away and despised it.

Likewise he says in chapter 2 [Col. 0089A]: “O priests, if you do not lay it to heart to give glory to my name, I shall send want upon you and curse your blessings; I shall cast your arms”—and your right shoulder—“away, and scatter upon your faces the dung of your feasts. My covenant was with Levi, and he kept it,” and so did the primitive Church, the command and Gospel of the Lord. The remaining words may be applied to the praise of the primitive Church and the reproach of the modern one. “And thus you covered the altar of the Lord with tears and weeping; I shall not receive anything pleasing from your hand” (ibid.).

Likewise Micah (chapter 2): “Woe to those who devise useless things and work evil upon their beds; in the morning light they do it, because their hand is against God. They coveted fields and violently took them, and seized houses; they falsely accused a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.”

Likewise he says: “Are not my words good to him [Col. 0089B] who walks uprightly? But on the contrary, my people have risen up as an enemy; from above the tunic, you have taken away the poor men’s cloak; you have turned those who passed by innocently toward war. You have cast the women of my people from the house of their delights; from their little children you have taken away my praise for ever.”

Likewise, chapter 3: “Hear, princes of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel. Is it not yours to know judgment—you who hate good and love evil, because you violently take their skins from them and their flesh from their bones; who eat the day of my people, flay their skin from them, break their bones, and cut them to pieces as in a cauldron, like flesh in the midst of a pot—acting wickedly in their devices.”

Likewise he says: “Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who deceive my people, who bite with their teeth and preach peace; but if anyone does not put something in their mouths, they sanctify war against him. Night shall be to them instead of vision, and darkness instead of divination, because there is no answer of God in them” (Mic. 3) [Col. 0089C].

Likewise he says: “Hear this, princes of the house of Jacob and judges of the house of Israel, who abominate judgment and pervert everything straight: because you build Zion in blood and Jerusalem in iniquity. Her princes judged for gifts, her priests taught for payment, and her prophets divined for money; yet they rested upon the Lord, saying: Is not the Lord in our midst? Evils shall not come upon us” (ibid.).

Likewise, chapter 6: “Hear, O tribes; and who will approve it?” As if to say: Who will be the author of these words?—God, understand. “Still there is fire in the house of the wicked, and treasures of iniquity, and a scant measure full of wrath. Shall I justify an impious balance, and bags of deceitful weights, by which her rich men are filled with iniquity, while her inhabitants speak lies and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth?”

Likewise, chapter 7: “The holy man has perished from the earth, and there is no upright man among men. All lie in wait for blood; each hunts his brother unto death. They call the evil of their hands good; the prince demands, the judge is for repayment, and the great man has spoken the desire of his soul.”

Likewise, the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10; Amos, chapter 8 [Col. 0090A]; Malachi, chapter 2; the Epistle to the Laodiceans, chapter 1.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Against clerics who use superfluities and excuse themselves on the ground that they chant in church

So far concerning the corruption and avarice of judges. Let us now proceed—though would that we might prosecute—the flesh-hooks, little doors, and a thousand other contrivances of fraud employed by prelates, by which they drain the purses of the poor, having become fishers of money rather than of souls.

Of these flesh-hooks and tridents it is read in 1 Kings, chapter 2, concerning the sons of Eli, that they thrust flesh-hooks and hooks into pots, kettles, and caldrons; and whatever the flesh-hook drew up, the priest took for himself. His servant said to the sacrificer: “Give me flesh, that I may cook it for the priest.” But the sacrificer said: “Let the fat first be burned today according to the custom, and then take for yourself whatever your soul desires.” He replied: “By no means; for you shall give it now, otherwise I shall take it by force” [Col. 0090B].

Here are struck at those prelates who, not content with their stipends, spread their nets for the capture of money through their flesh-hooks and officials, “casting the net into the deep” (Luke 5), that is, into the depth of money, and saying to their flesh-hooks: “Empty, empty, even to the foundation of the purses” (Ps. 136).

There are three classes of these officials. First, the confessor, to whom the bishop commits his office in spiritual matters, in hearing confessions and caring for souls. Second, the quaestor of his palace, the dean, archpriest, and the like, who keep watch by fair means or foul over the increases and profits of the bishop’s causes and affairs [Col. 0090C]. Third, the chief rural provost: although more worthy before God, he is nevertheless of less account to the bishop. With the former the bishop has rare conversation and rare consultation concerning the account to be rendered of his stewardship and the governance of souls; by this it is evident how much he loved those souls, their Redeemer, and their supreme Shepherd. But with the torturer and the provost he has frequent conversation, accounting, and consultation. By this it is evident how much he loved money.

Moreover—and this is more detestable—he sends the first man to perform his office without first making a thorough examination of his fidelity, without administering an oath that he will preserve fidelity to him in the governance of souls. But he examines the second and third to the fingernail [Col. 0090D]: whether they know well how to squeeze the purses of the poor and return with carried-off profit to their masters. He does not entrust them with the care of money without an intervening oath, so that they may learn to be faithful to him in the pursuit and profit of money and plunder. And, what is more astonishing and detestable, he sells to them tax-farming, torture, exaction, and prelacy; he commits these things to them for a fixed price. To avoid loss or damage to their own money, through every wickedness of exactions, false accusations, and plundering, they “spread their nets for the capture” (Luke 5) of money, becoming robbers rather than officials.

Of these two, namely the quaestor and the provost, the quaestor is the more violent. For the provost more often punishes the guilty person with a fixed and defined penalty; but the steward imposes an uncertain and arbitrary one, inflicting the greatest punishment for a small fault [Col. 0091A]. His judgment and snares are feared merely by hearing of them, for he appears merciless in all his ways.

Because we are permitted to profit and learn from whatever source, let us rebuke such men by this example. A certain cleric, after losing at dice everything he had except five shillings, began to curse himself, blaspheme God, and promise those five shillings to the man who would teach him how he might offend God more grievously. Someone was present to teach him, affirming and approving his instruction before the testimony of all, and said: If you wish to offend God above every sinner, become an official or quaestor of a bishop’s palace.

Likewise: The ministers and officials of prelates are hidden little doors, beneath the table of Bel, underground passages through which his priests entered secretly to carry off and devour the things placed by the king upon the table: “When King Cyrus discovered their fraud, he killed them and gave Bel into Daniel’s power; Daniel immediately overthrew him and his temple” (Dan. 14) [Col. 0091B]. These hidden little doors have now been turned into open gates and doors. For whereas then the goods of poor and rich alike were secretly stolen, now they are publicly, before everyone, seized through their innumerable contrivances, frauds, and new devices invented for extorting money, now established in the place of law and custom.

Because of these little doors—that is, the officials of prelates and ministers of princes—the Lord says through John the Baptist to soldiers and ministers of princes: “Do violence to no one” (Luke 3). Augustine (*Sermon 19, On the Words of the Lord*): The crime of extortion is committed when money is demanded and wrung from subjects by officials through fear or violence [Col. 0091C]. The legal penalty for this crime is fixed at fourfold restitution; would that today it were fixed at double. Likewise Jerome: It was for this reason that soldiers and ministers were assigned fixed stipends, lest, while they sought their expenses, they should range abroad as robbers.

Likewise: For this reason the Lord said to the apostles and ministers of the Church: “I have chosen you that you may go,” without delay, not that you may eat, but that you may “bear fruit” (John 15)—not plunder, not temporal profit, but the most peaceable fruit. Hence it follows: “And that your fruit may remain” (ibid.). But is not “the labourer worthy of his wages” (Luke 10)? Certainly; but only of that which the Lord specifies: “Eating and drinking such things as they have” (ibid.), not things that they do not have—not so as to receive, daily through their deputy, luxurious and elaborate dishes.

Likewise: When the anathemas of the Old Testament were accursed and set apart from every use—as the anathema of Jericho, of which Joshua chapter 6 speaks—the anathemas of the New Testament are today consecrated and loosened for the capture of money; indeed, today men are excommunicated in order that money may be extorted. Detesting this, the Lord says to Joshua concerning Achan: The people have been polluted by the anathema. “For they have taken from the anathema, stolen and lied, and hidden it among their goods” (Josh. 7). Hence “Israel shall not be able to stand [Col. 0092A] before its enemies, but shall flee from them, until he who has been polluted by this crime is destroyed from among you” (ibid.). Achan was found guilty for carrying off certain very small things: “At Joshua’s command he was stoned by all the people, and everything that belonged to him was consumed with the anathema” (ibid.).

Likewise, and what is more execrable, an excommunicated man today is not absolved unless he first has given an oath that he will stand ready, at the prelate’s judgment, to make satisfaction for his contumacy and transgression. Once absolved, he is immediately condemned to a monetary penalty for private uses; whereas an agreement concerning money, made in absolution, before it, or for the sake of absolution, produces simony. For absolution is a spiritual thing pertaining to the power of the keys. But if he adjudged that the man should distribute his anathema to the poor [Col. 0092B], this would indeed be tolerable and good.

If they object that it is not simony because power to punish excommunicated persons in this way has been granted them by secular authority, that is indeed true as regards the imposition of punishment, but not as regards absolution. For that comes from God. Nor is punishment imposed by such a prince unless the person has been separated from the Church for a year and a day. Why then do they themselves anticipate this period? Indeed, why do they convert even a brief suspension into a monetary penalty?

Likewise: Since a provincial governor is prohibited by the laws, beyond necessary maintenance, from receiving from fellow provincials presents and small gifts that grow as far as the value of a substantial gift, how much more should this be forbidden to ministers of the Church? And if some prefect of a commune, after his administration has ended, is compelled under secular laws to restore what he wrongly received in office, how much more must this be observed in ecclesiastical administration [Col. 0092C], which today is offered for sale and converted into plunder?

Likewise: In a case of injuries, an agreement between the parties and pardon granted by the opposing party both settle the litigation before a civil judge and remove every monetary payment. How much more harshly is it treated before an ecclesiastical judge! Even the fear of the archdeacon today blows away a settlement, unless the hand has first been anointed; and it likewise blows away forgiveness and remission of injuries, to which we are bound by the Lord’s command: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6).

Likewise, to give an execrable example concerning such little doors: A certain man, in a money case, had to undergo the ordeal of water. The water was blessed; after he had been stripped, bound, and seated upon the board of a tub, ready to be lowered into the water, his adversary remitted to him every injury and complaint. Then the quaestor of the palace appeared, demanding from him—though he had neither been moved (*commoto*) [perhaps *commonito*, “warned”] nor confessed—nine and a half pounds belonging to the prince’s right [Col. 0092D]. When he refused to give them, a long dispute arose between them over whether a larger or smaller sum of money should be paid. Seeing that he could not leave freely, he said: “I shall give you no money, not even a small amount; but I shall undergo the ordeal, and, if found just, shall give fifty shillings to the poor for food.” He accordingly underwent the ordeal and was found clean.

When the priest demanded five shillings from him for the blessing of the water [Col. 0093A], he and the palace quaestor were mocked by everyone together.

Likewise Jerome: The plague of avarice has so invaded the Church that it is to be feared that it may be said of her: “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head” (Isa. 1)—that is, from least to greatest—“there is no health in her” from avarice.

Likewise: What surpasses the crime of the priests of Baal (3 Kings 18) is that today even lesser priests swear to their prelate that they will report to him every case from which money may be extorted and conceal none, even when they could easily settle peace between the parties themselves. Thus, if certain persons summoned (below, chapter 52) disregard the summons, they are excommunicated as contumacious; if they appear in order to clear themselves, they incur perjury [Col. 0093B]. But is such an oath of priests lawful and prudent? It seems so, since the Church for the most part tolerates this, and since their administration depends upon the superior prelate, so that such cases seem rather to belong to him. Yet Pope Alexander wrote in a certain decretal that such an oath is imprudent and unlawful.

Likewise: Certain canons prohibiting persons related in the second or third degree of affinity from marrying, yet allowing those already married not to be separated, belong incidentally to these little doors. Abusing these canons like flesh-hooks and tridents for the capture of money, we join whom we please and separate them when we please [Col. 0093C]. But if we remained within the boundaries and limits set by the Lord, we would not so dispense, at our own will, against the sacrament of marriage.

Likewise: To this purpose belongs that double-edged decree, cutting both ways, which is as follows: “Let no one marry the wife of his godfather or of his godmother; I neither forbid nor permit it.”

Likewise: These little doors are the cormorants which blessed Martin, near the end of his life, saw on a river, intent upon continual catches of fish and greedily gaping after them; he said: “This is the form of demons.” He commanded them to fly away from the river.

Likewise: These are the “flies that destroy the sweetness of ointment” (Eccles. 10) and of ecclesiastical peace; would that Abraham had driven them from the sacrifices with a fan (Gen. 15). But now they have grown into ravens [Col. 0093D], and, enticed by corpses, do not return to the ark (Gen. 8).

Likewise: These are hawks and all birds of prey, the flesh of all of which is forbidden in the law (Lev. 11). A hawk is called *accipiter* from *accipiendo*, “taking,” that is, plundering. For so the word is understood there: “You shall not take as pledge another millstone or the garment of a widow” (Deut. 24), that is, you shall not plunder. And in the Apostle: “You endure it if anyone devours, if anyone takes” (2 Cor. 11), that is, plunders.

Likewise: Ecclesiastical men today are so devoted to avarice that the Lord cannot say of them: “The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places” (Ps. 15), but rather in plunderings, flesh-hooks, and the cords of sins; they are worse than thieves. For thieves plunder and keep the booty for themselves; but these are not for themselves: they are pimps [Col. 0094A] and carriers of another’s money, driving beasts and cattle into the nets of others.

Likewise: These are the unclean dogs of whom David says in Psalm 58: “They scatter themselves to eat” and devour; “if they are not satisfied, they will murmur”—they will accuse, extort, and plunder.

Likewise: How detestable it is that we turn Christ’s spittle, scourges, lance, nails, and cross into snares and nets of money, forging them in the furnace of avarice!

Likewise: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9), as though that sowing claims this harvest as its due. But if you have not sown and yet receive what is due, you no longer receive even that as a due, but plunder it and turn a due into sacrilege. For if you have not sown [Col. 0094B], how will you receive? “In the account of giving and receiving” (Phil. 4) lies the peace of the Church. You give spiritual things and receive temporal things. Even from this due the Apostle, though he could have received it, abstained: to repel false brethren, to remove the curious, because of the avarice of subjects, lest he receive anything from the greedy and uncorrected or incorrigible, and lest they think that, if he received it, they had bought for themselves impunity in sinning.

But why today is payment received only from the uncorrected and wicked, while from the good nothing is received except through false accusation?

Likewise: “The labourer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10); but if “he does not work or labour, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3). If he does work, “he is worthy of his food” (Matt. 10) [Col. 0094C], that is, of food due and necessary to him, not superfluity, luxury, and a multitude of dishes. “His own” also means what is necessary for his own person and household, in proportion to his person and the administration owed to him—not for a retinue of serving boys, in whom the ruin and destruction both of a poor monastery and of a poor priest are impending.

Likewise, the example is relevant that, when the apostles preached and saw that certain persons did not wish to receive spiritual things and correction, “they shook the dust from their feet as a testimony against them” (Mark 6). As if they said: We have shaken our hands, and the dust from our feet, free of your hands; from you who are incorrigible we shall receive not even something small, comparable to dust.

Likewise: “You shall not bind,” or bridle, “the mouth of the ox treading out the grain” (1 Cor. 9)—that is, the preacher who tills the land of the Church with the plough of preaching, chews over the law of God, and threshes in the barn of the Church, separating chaff from grain—because such a one is owed fodder. But would that God bridled the mouths of modern preachers—not that they might not eat, but that they might not plunder and devour [Col. 0094D].

When the Gospel is to be preached, a cushion is placed beneath the Gospel, as though to say: “His left hand is under my head,” etc. (Song 2); to the preacher all these things shall be added. Why then is a cushion placed beneath the Gospel? Why do you receive—indeed, plunder—these things, when you do not proclaim it?

Likewise: The officials of prelates are not only their leeches, swelling so that they may disgorge, but also strainers which strain out for them the milk of plunder [Col. 0095A] while retaining for themselves the filth of sin.

Likewise, this example is relevant concerning a prelate who confessed through the mouths of all his subordinates. For as each confessed his particular false accusations, plunderings, and other sins, he said: “I am guilty of all these things.” Therefore such men sin with a long and numerous hand.

> Do you not know that kings have long hands?  
> (*Ovid, Heroides* 16.)

By kings I mean the prelates of the Church. Hence: “And now, O kings, understand” (Ps. 2). Likewise Psalm 61: “Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire plunder; if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.” Likewise Augustine: The same thing happens to the mouse, the thief, and the robber. Do you prey? You too shall become prey. Do you hold? You shall be held. Do you plunder? You shall be caught in the mousetrap [Col. 0095B]. As a mouse desires booty for bait, which it receives from trappers. Likewise Job chapter 31: “If my land cries out against me,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXV. Against simony occurring in the exercise of ecclesiastical offices, or of any spiritual things whatsoever, which are forbidden to be performed for temporal goods

Justice and the administration of the commonwealth consist not only in the determination of cases, but also in the celebration and conferral of sacraments and in the exercise of ecclesiastical offices or of any spiritual things whatsoever. Holy Scripture forbids these things to be done for temporal goods, reproving in many places the avarice of those who receive unlawfully in this way, and those who, with Judas, sell justice and God [Col. 0095C].

First, in the Gospel it says: “God is spirit, and those who worship him [must worship] in spirit and truth” (John 4): that is, he must be worshipped for spiritual and true goods, so that worship includes the performance of every spiritual thing. It does not say, for temporal things, but for eternal things. Otherwise, unless “your eye is single, your whole body will be dark” (Luke 11).

Likewise Cicero, *On Duties* (book II, after the middle): No vice is more foul than avarice in rulers and those governing the commonwealth. For to hold the commonwealth as a source of profit is not merely shameful but criminal, impious, and sacrilegious. Therefore, what the Pythian Apollo gave forth as an oracle—that Sparta would perish through no cause but avarice—seems to have been predicted not only to the Lacedaemonians but to all wealthy peoples. For those who govern the commonwealth can win the goodwill of the multitude more easily by nothing than by abstinence and self-restraint.

Whoever wish to be popular and attempt the administration of the commonwealth, so as to pursue profit and glory, undermine the foundations of the commonwealth. Likewise, the same author: “Self-restraint, abstinence, and the flesh were born from the same womb of nature.” (Cato.) How much more, from the same womb of grace and evangelical doctrine, ought self-restraint, abstinence, and the Christian people to be born?

Likewise the Apostle: “Seek the things that are above [Col. 0096A], not those upon the earth” (Col. III), nor seek earthly things. Likewise the Lord: “First,” and most especially, “seek the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matt. VI). He did not say, “Seek these things, and seek those things,” but chiefly seek this, “and those things shall be added unto you.”

Likewise: “His left hand is under my head,” not above it, “and his right hand shall embrace me” (Cant. II). The right hand is eternal blessedness and all things that prepare the way and path to it; thus, as it were, let the left be made for the right, not the right for the left. Hence: “Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” (Matt. VI). Hence also the distinction is established between the Old and the New Testament, because the latter promised eternal things, whereas the former promised temporal things. For this reason the reading of the latter is raised at the end, as a sign of this matter, whereas the reading of the former [Col. 0096B] is lowered.

Likewise, for this reason the sandals of apostles and bishops have soles below and openings above: as though it were said, Preaching, and whatever spiritual thing is joined to it, should never touch or look toward earthly gain; nor should it be hidden under the earth in the vessel of worldly fear; but it should freely consider heavenly things alone, without hope of any earthly advantage.

Likewise, for this reason the censer has solidity at its base, but holes and openings in its upper part: namely, so that the smoke of prayer may rise, not descend by looking toward any earthly advantage. But if it looks back, the sandals and the censer are inverted.

And note that spiritual things are done for three causes: the cause for the sake of which they are done, which ought to be God alone; the cause without which they could not [Col. 0096C] be done; and the cause without which they would not be done. If a spiritual thing is done solely for a temporal object and not for God’s sake, it is execrable and diabolical. But if God is the cause, and earthly profit is the cause without which it would not be done, although it could be done, then the cause without which becomes the cause for the sake of which.

“For my cloak is short,” etc. (Isa. XXVIII)—“and my bed is narrow,” etc. (ibid.)—“You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. VI)—“How long halt ye between two sides?” (III Kings XVIII). You cannot “enter the land by two ways” (Ecclus. II). Human necessity arising from frailty excuses the third cause. “For the labourer is worthy of his food” (Matt. X).

Likewise the Apostle, II Corinthians IV: “Not adulterating the word of God.” [Col. 0096D] Augustine: For gain, as those who preach falsehood or vain glory, “but out of sincerity and out of God,” for God’s cause alone, “and before God we speak” (II Cor. II) and work—so that in “word” every good and spiritual work may be understood.

Likewise: There are two ends between which every work ought to be bounded: fear of punishment (not wholly an improper end, because it excuses and removes one from sin; nor wholly a proper one, because it does not worthily bring one to perfection), and the love of God, namely, the right eye. The left eye is for punishment; the right eye for loving God. Where then is the third eye, for loving money, for whose sake you work?

Likewise, these are the two millstones of which the Lord speaks in Deuteronomy, chapter XXIV: “Thou shalt not take in pledge” [Col. 0097A] either millstone; namely, do not remove from any work of yours the millstone of fear, but especially the millstone of the love of God. Therefore, since the first is not meritorious without the second—indeed, without it, in a certain manner, it is forbidden to exist—much more is the third millstone, of covetousness, or the fourth, of various glory, forbidden from every work, so that not even the third may be mixed with either of the two.

For just as a divided mind obtains nothing, so neither does a work thus divided, in which the division is not under God nor for God’s sake, but against God; so that it is no longer division and participation, but the devil’s total appropriation of that work.

But since a work of the right hand performed for the purpose or love of acquiring money, or receiving new money, produces simony, will it also be simoniacal if it is done through anxiety and fear of losing money already possessed, or of receiving [Col. 0097B] it? Clearly, that is a lesser evil.

Likewise, we read (Exod. II) that Amram, a man of the house of Levi, begot his son Moses by his wife; and, seeing him beautiful, hid him for three months. Therefore hide your works from covetousness and vain glory, lest they be seized by the Egyptians and drowned; and lest, made feminine by the admixture of the left hand, they be preserved for the devil’s work.

Likewise: “Enter into thy chamber, and, having shut the door”—against covetousness and vain glory—“pray” by doing good works, “to thy Father” (Matt. VI).

Likewise: Whereas a twofold invitatory is read, Psalm and signal-call, a third is found in the Church more effective than the others: a money-gift.

Likewise, the Lord commands that Passover be celebrated “with the unleavened bread of sincerity [Col. 0097C] and truth” (I Cor. V). Augustine: without every corruption of vices, in the truth of good works, which belong to the right hand. If the left hand is mixed with this, Passover is now celebrated in the old leaven. A priest celebrates Passover whenever he approaches the altar to immolate the Paschal Lamb.

Likewise: “Therefore I have loved thy commandments above gold and topaz” (Ps. CXVIII). Augustine, on this psalm, verse 1: Not for gold and topaz, or for anything temporal, as a Jew is enticed by temporal things. How much inferior is the Christian if he performs spiritual acts for temporal things, when he is bound to love God’s commandments above such things, not for their sake. His life ought to be a cross and martyrdom, so that here he may heed: “Ye shall weep and lament” (John XVI), not earthly consolation, in expectation of eternal blessedness to be bestowed upon him [Col. 0097D] in the future.

Likewise Augustine (*Enchiridion*, ch. 66, and book II of *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, ch. 34): For this reason the Lord did not will that punishment, as well as guilt, be removed through baptism, lest one should believe in God delicately—that is, rather with a view to the removal of punishment than through love of faith and justice.

73

## CHAPTER XXVI. Against those who seek temporal advantage in spiritual things

By a similar argument, I say that temporal things must not be set up as inducements in spiritual matters, whether to cause them to be done or to cause them to be done more readily and swiftly; lest men run to them from love of money rather than zeal for justice, and, according to their opinion, listen more gladly to the pleasant voice promising temporal things than to the voice speaking [Col. 0098A] the blood of Christ (Jerem. XII, XXIV).

Likewise, on Psalm CXXXV: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.” Augustine: This is the primary reason for thanksgiving. “For his mercy endureth for ever”: this is the secondary reason. For he is a hireling who praises God for something other than God himself.

Likewise: “He will praise thee when thou hast done him good” (Ps. XLVIII). Gregory: In God’s sight the sacrifice of confession which temporal prosperity produces is despised . . . Jerome: One who thus confesses with his mouth eats the iniquity of his heart, which he will digest amid the torments of hell.

Likewise the Lord says in the Gospel: “You seek me, not for my own sake, but because I filled you with loaves” (John VI).

Likewise: “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and they that have power over [Col. 0098B] you are called benefactors” (Luke XXII), because of benefits bestowed upon them by those rulers. “But ye shall not be so. For this is what heathens and publicans do” (Matt. V).

Likewise, relevant to condemning this is the example of clerics playing at dice and then rushing to Vespers disorderly and indecently when they heard that the “evening coins” were at hand for the chanting of Vespers and were first to be distributed in the church.

Likewise, the example of a prelate who asked the choir in church that the feast of St. Stephen be made a double feast, with silken vestments and ecclesiastical chants, but could not obtain this unless he promised the clerics an annual meal and refreshment, and, in addition, that the morning coins for that night should be doubled: so that they might celebrate the feast of doubled money rather than the feast of St. Stephen.

Likewise, the example of Lombard male and female mourners, [Col. 0098C] hired solely for payment to weep and lament at the funerals of the dead. Similar to them are certain persons chanting in church and singing for pay, of whom any one might say:

> O money, money, to you he pays this honour.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires*, V.)

Brothers—indeed, men for whom money is discipline, money the dean, and even god: they are idolaters, worshipping money rather than God, and would never otherwise sing to God except for money.

Likewise the Apostle, I Thessalonians, chapter V: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good; abstain from every appearance of evil.” Augustine: Not only from things unlawful in themselves, but also, if any things which may lawfully be done or not done appear evil to persons of lesser understanding, abstain from these also, “providing things honest, not only before God, but also before men” [Col. 0098D] (Rom. XII). But the appearance is shameful and evil because it scandalizes one’s neighbour through the left hand while enticing someone by the right hand.

If you object that the appearance is good for this reason, that many men frequently chant and sing thus, and serve God in church, hear Augustine disapproving it when he says: It is better for spiritual things to be omitted altogether than for them to be done, handled, or touched impurely and insincerely. In performing ecclesiastical offices, the Lord approves not the multitude of participants but the devotion of their souls.

Likewise: When the last bell of the money-hour was ringing in a certain church, and a barrier had been put in place at the little choir-door [Col. 0099A] in preparation, the clerics ran as though to a solemnity and as old women to ointment: some stooping, some jumping over the barrier to get in; others entering disorderly through the larger door, although by it none but the persons of the church were permitted to enter. Because of the disgracefulness of this cheap gain, a certain layman said to a cleric and begged him not to attend that hour, lest it bring dishonour. But what could he do? If he entered the choir, laymen would mark him as touched by greed; if not, clerics would mark him as proud.

Likewise: A certain prebendary in two neighbouring churches attended the night offices in one and the day offices in the other, and thus, with Oliver running and answering for him in both places, rapidly enriched himself.

Likewise, a man appointed as a fixed [Col. 0099B] pensioner to distribute such payment, when he saw a multitude of clerics attending the hours, grumbled and was distressed, and began to reproach the clerics because they attended the hours regularly and in great numbers.

Likewise: What is more base than for laymen in a certain church to call two hours “the Lord’s hours,” because no fixed money is appointed for chanting them, and the others “the pennies’ hours”—indeed, the devil’s? Indeed, clerics are not present for chanting these hours, nor even for chanting the Hours of the Blessed Virgin; but, while they are present at others, they flee from these, so that the Holy Spirit may claim no work for himself in the Church, since nothing is done there freely, but money claims everything for itself.

And, in sum: just as before this wretched trafficking was established it was honourable and praiseworthy to enter the choir, [Col. 0099C] celebrate ecclesiastical offices, and be assiduous in them, so now it is dishonourable and unpraiseworthy, because by such assiduity we are judged more greedy than devout. And so now:

> The once-venerable name of noble Church  
> Is offered for sale, and sits for profit as a prostitute.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Against simony existing in the substances of the sacraments, especially the Eucharist

If the venality, leprosy of Gehazi, and simony of Simon are so shameful and damnable in the appendages of the sacraments, as was shown above, how much more so are they in the very substances of the sacraments, especially in the Eucharist? For there the whole Christ is received, the fountain and origin of all graces, whereas graces are distributed in the other sacraments [Col. 0099D].

For no shamefulness or enormity of sin do we read that the Lord was so angry and inflamed as for the sale of the dove, especially of the Eucharist. For the cleansing and expulsion of this pest from the Church, the Lord, stirred by the ardour of the Spirit, is recorded as having for a moment set aside his inborn and ineffable meekness and patience—though he could not cast them off, “because he is very merciful” (Joel II), etc.—and, “having made a scourge of cords, cast out of the Temple those selling and buying sheep and doves, and overthrew the tables of the money-changers” (John II; Matt. XXI). He calls them God’s altars on account of the priests’ greed.

Likewise, inflamed with zeal for the house of God, [Col. 0100A] concerning which it is written, “The zeal of thy house hath consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII), he says to them: “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. XXI). In a den, plunder is both seized and divided. A thief is one who pursues temporal gains in exchange for the Church’s spiritual things; he also physically pursues those who give nothing and offer nothing, attempting to obtain and seize gifts from them. He spiritually kills those who give, since, while he contemplates harm and the plundering of his neighbour’s goods, he sits like a thief in a den.

Likewise Augustine (*Tractate 10 on John*): All those “who seek in the Church what is their own, and not what is Jesus Christ’s” (Phil. II), make the Church a house of trade. Augustine also says of it: Let no one do anything in an oratory except [Col. 0100B] that for which it was made, whence it has its name.

Likewise, Peter, inflamed with this same zeal for the Lord’s house and imitating his Master in punishing the madness and Simoniacal heresy, said to Simon Magus, who supposed the grace of the Holy Spirit saleable: “Thy money perish with thee” (Acts VIII). He spoke this either as a wish, or as one caught up into the sublime judgment of God and foreseeing in him the future pest of the Church. With the same zeal he struck Ananias and Sapphira, so that they were carried out dead before him, saying to those still alive: “How have you dared to lie to the Holy Spirit?”

Likewise, it should be especially observed that, while still a young man, not possessing authority for public administration and being quite lowly and insignificant among them, the Lord “cast out those selling and buying” (John II), etc. In this he gave everyone a pattern [Col. 0100C] and example for accusing, rebuking, and, insofar as we can, casting out every form and pestilence of simony, especially the sale of the Eucharist.

Likewise, he is recorded as having cast sellers and buyers out of the Temple twice, giving us a pattern and example that not once only, but always, whenever we see the dove sold, we must rebuke and censure the seller and buyer, so that this pest may be expelled from the Church (John II and Matt. XXI).

Likewise, if the Lord so punished bodily the figure of the sale of the dove, how much more incomparably will he punish its very reality, the leprosy of simony?

Likewise: “If then, having made a scourge of cords” (John II), he punished the sale of the dove, how much more should it now be punished—not merely with a scourge, but even with nails, [Col. 0100D] swords, and every other weapon, and assailed with all one’s strength?

Likewise, how great the enormity of this crime is appears from the fact that, whereas the Lord waited for men entangled in other crimes to repent, as Judas the traitor, instructing us that without judicial procedure we should not accuse or publicize, but cover and endure our neighbours’ other sins, as he endured Judas’s betrayal—he could not endure this crime alone without immediately punishing it bodily, whereas he rebuked and punished the others by word.

Likewise, in casting out those selling doves and overturning the tables of the money-changers, whom the priests’ avarice had placed there so that they might lend to those without offerings and thus have offerings more readily available, [Col. 0101A] he also showed that every occasion for simony, and every facility for receiving even trifling gifts for spiritual things, must be rooted out and extirpated from the Church.

Likewise, what is more dangerous than that we, as though blind, allow God himself to be sold more shamefully than he was sold by Judas—openly perceiving venality in other sacraments but not in this? Thus certain persons wholly double and duplicate a Mass in one day, while others, through shame and fear not daring to make two whole Masses, make one two-faced, three-faced, or many-faced—that is, celebrate one of many faces.

Likewise, what is more shameful than, if no offering is made at the first face and first introit, to assume another face—indeed a third and fourth—in order that an offering may be made? These are like those who sing tales and deeds. Seeing that a song [Col. 0101B] about Landric does not please their listeners, they immediately begin to sing of Narcissus; and if that too does not please, they sing of someone else. It is plain that the reason why all other ecclesiastical offices remain in their simplicity, purity, and institution and are not doubled, while this alone is doubled against its institution, is the offering made for this and not for that.

Likewise, that we may still persist in uprooting the root—that is, Simoniacal greed—“Thus will I bless thee in my life, namely in thy name,” not in the name of money, not of greed; “I will lift up my hands” (Ps. LXII). He lifts them in the Lord’s honour and glory who, persevering in good works, seeks not his own glory or the world’s but the Lord’s.

As though he said: I begin with myself, “because I crucify myself with my vices and concupiscences” (Gal. V); I [Col. 0101C] preach the Crucified, adore the Crucified, and, what is more, sincerely consecrate, receive, and distribute to others for eating the Crucified One. How then shall I lift hands crucified to the world, hands consecrating thee, O Christ, toward any price other than you, O price of the world? How toward profit, especially toward sin?

Likewise Simon Magus, who wished to be a Christian and work miracles for profit, suffered repulse from Simon Peter. As though seeking to avenge this, he said to him: You drive me away, and I shall triumph over you—indeed over the whole body of the Church (Acts VIII). “In the altars themselves I shall set my seat, bed, and throne” (Isa. XIV), and my dominion; so that even while angels are present, and men are, as it were, gathered together in one corner of the altar to consecrate the Lord’s body, I, in another, with the altar-minister—indeed rather with my own minister—shall have it consecrated for payment. Greed rules in this sacrament, which is nevertheless beyond price.

Likewise: If I am driven away from the altar, Simoniacal greed, my daughter—the daughter of the high priest—will no less, but rather more, burst into the Holy of Holies, setting everything on the altars out for sale. And, what is impious, from those offerings are raised altars, sacred places adorned, and monasteries of religious built—men thus abusing this apostolic precept: “Asking no question for conscience’ sake” (I Cor. X), whereas the Apostle spoke only to those who at times ate with idolaters in order to preach to them.

Likewise, we sell Christ more shamefully than Judas because we are worse than he (Matt. XXVI). He [Col. 0102A] sold him when he believed him to be a mere man, and when even his household was in need; but we sell him whom we know to be true God and man. He did so for thirty pieces of silver; we for a penny and a most trifling price.

Likewise, though not truly repentant, he returned and cast away the “thirty pieces of silver”; but among us in the Church there is no one who casts away what has been shamefully acquired.

Likewise, since the thirty pieces of silver “were the price of blood, they were not put into the treasury” (Matt. XXVII); now, from offerings and gains even more shamefully acquired, altars are raised, churches built, and the like.

Likewise, whereas all other vices tremble and flee from sacred places, simony itself has invaded the altars.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Against the sale and multiplication of Masses

[Col. 0102B] To uproot the sale and multiplication of Masses, which the sale of altars and the greed of ministers have produced: If Christ was immolated for us only once, let him be represented as immolated only once in a day by one of his vicars (Heb. IX).

Likewise, if Christ, offered once, was a sufficient victim and redemption for the human race, it suffices for a single priest to represent once in a day him who suffered once and was immolated once. “What is more than this is from evil” (Matt. V).

Likewise, those who consecrate twice in a day “crucify again to themselves the Son of God and put him to open shame” (Heb. VI).

Likewise Augustine: I neither praise nor blame daily reception of communion in the Eucharist; nevertheless, I leave this to each person’s conscience, provided he is conscious of no sin, is [Col. 0102C] of a contrite spirit, and of a broken heart (*On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 53). If, therefore, Augustine scarcely permits a single reception in a day even to one so humbled, contrite in heart, and devout, would he, if asked, have permitted anyone to consecrate twice in a day? Far from it! Rather, he would have repelled such a person with all his strength, and perhaps struck him with an anathema.

Likewise, receiving the Eucharist belongs to all Christians; consecrating it belongs to few. Therefore consecrating is greater than receiving. But it is detestable and most disorderly to repeat it in a day, namely, that the Lord’s body should be given to anyone more than once in a day. Therefore it is disorderly and dangerous to repeat in a day what is greater, namely to consecrate twice, especially when necessity does not compel it.

Likewise, [Col. 0102D] in Exodus the children of Israel were commanded that only one gomor of manna should be gathered daily for each head, except on the sixth day: “For then they were to gather double food, that is, two gomors for each person” (Exod. XVI), so that the gomor gathered on the Preparation Day might suffice on the Sabbath, when they were not permitted to gather or do any work. But whatever one had gathered beyond a gomor and beyond what sufficed for eating putrefied and bred worms.

Thus one must fear lest the sacrament of the altar, consecrated twice in a day by one man, should rot—not, I say, in the sacrament, but in the consecrator’s conscience because of his sins and crimes in thus doubling it.

At the Lord’s Nativity, however, because of the solemnity and as it were a Sabbath, and also because of the mystery, [Col. 0103A] a country priest was permitted to consecrate three times. But a higher prelate in one church consecrates once that day, in another twice; yet now, by multiplying Masses, we celebrate the Lord’s Nativity every day.

Likewise, if frequent preaching does not bear fruit but becomes cheap, how much more does this sacrament, repeated in a day, become cheap and turn into weariness and the detriment of devotion? At that time the word of the Lord was precious because rare; so also was the consecration of the Eucharist because rare. But now it is cheap because so often repeated.

Likewise, if in the figure one Lamb was offered, immolated, wholly eaten, and eaten quickly in one house, once at Passover for the Lord (Exod. XII), how do you, a sinner, dare irreverently and repeatedly to double, triple, [Col. 0103B] and multiply the very reality of the figure under the mark and guise of venality, “when they have no right to eat from this altar who serve the tabernacle” (Heb. XIII)?

Likewise, if the legal priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year with blood, and the holy place once daily with incense (Exod. XXX; Heb. IX), how do you, a sinner and evangelical priest, dare to enter daily—and, what is abominable, twice in a day—into the most holy of holies, the holy things of all holy things and heavenly pledges, so irreverently and with too little fear because so frequently, and perhaps without blood and incense?

One approaches these holy things “with blood”—that is, with faith in the Passion and sorrow of heart, issuing from it as a kind of blood through the eyes—“and with bitter herbs” [Col. 0103C] (Exod. XII), with the incense of prayer. For tears make this cup sweeter.

Likewise, if the holy Carthusian order, offered as a holocaust to God and purified from the stain of the world through abstinence and mortification of the flesh, “already flying upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII), dares to consecrate only on feasts and weekdays marked by a spiritual office, how do you, a sinful priest, fearlessly dare so irreverently to handle things so holy, by doing so twice in a day?

Likewise, a certain righteous man, observing and considering that the Lord on Friday was placed in a new tomb and in a clean linen cloth (Matt. XXVII), and did not change his sepulchre but rested in it through the whole Sabbath and rose on Sunday, the third day, [Col. 0103D] proposed that he would consecrate only on the third day, with one day interposed as though for rest, in which he would cleanse his linen cloth—that is, his conscience—with tears and penitence, so that more strongly and devoutly he might rise on the third day to consecrate the Lord’s body.

Likewise, if during a fast one approaches the bodily table only once a day, how much more the spiritual table? If then there is a single food, the spiritual food is now spiritually multiplied by certain external seasonings of introits, unto nausea and drunkenness.

Likewise, some badly interpret that place in the Lord’s Prayer: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke XI): he did not say “twice this day.”

Likewise, the Hebrew has, in place of “daily,” *sogolla*, which is interpreted as ἐπιούσιον, “supersubstantial,” and has a double interpretation. [Col. 0104A] Hence Matthew translated thus: “Give us our supersubstantial bread” (Matt. V); Luke, “daily”; Mark, “special.” But they do not make it “supersubstantial,” “special,” and “daily”; rather, as far as lies in them, they make it cheap, saleable, two-day-old, and three-day-old.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Against Masses of many faces

Every falsehood seeks corners, etc.:

> While fools avoid one fault, they rush into its opposite.  
> (Horace, book I, satire 20.)

Thus, while certain people avoid the multiplication of Masses, seeking a refuge and covering for their greed, they fall not merely into a fault but into a monstrosity, monstrously making Masses two-faced and three-faced. And whereas in the Apostle [Col. 0104B] the Church is said to consist of persons of many faces, nowhere do we read of a Mass of two or three faces.

Likewise, among poets we read of two-headed Janus, the seven-headed hydra, hundred-handed Briareus, two-bodied Geryon, and another three-bodied being; nowhere do we read of a two-headed, two-faced, or many-faced Mass. For it is more monstrous than every monster to make Masses two-faced, three-faced, and the like.

Likewise, such persons contradict the mystery of the Mass, because:

> It expresses office, sighs, glory, praises,  
> The *Kyrie eleison* thrice tripled, prayers.

But now in the Mass it is repeated threefold seven times or more, and the mystery and order of the Mass are confused.

Likewise, to which of the two introits will a two-faced Mass be assigned, and from which [Col. 0104C] will it receive its name? If from the second, which is for the faithful, then the kiss of peace ought not to be given in it; or, if it is given, the general institution and custom of the Church are contradicted. If from the first, which is in memory of the sending of the Holy Spirit, then one thus celebrating does not celebrate Mass for the faithful, and so is not discharged from celebrating an anniversary or thirty-day Mass.

But if he acknowledges this by saying, “Under one canon I celebrate two Masses,” what sort of Masses are they? Merely a Mass of catechumens? So it seems, because the victim is not yet represented as having been sent. Thus it would be more proper to say that under two canons one Mass is celebrated, because there is one representation of the victim sent, than that two Masses are celebrated under one canon.

Likewise, such persons contradict the ordinance of a synod or council—provincial [Col. 0104D] indeed, but held by authority of a legate of the Roman See—in which it was commanded that no one should consecrate twice in a day unless under the greatest necessity, such as if a body were present, a woman after childbirth required purification, or another case of necessity arose.

But it was entirely forbidden that, even under any urgent necessity, Masses should be made two-faced in this fashion. Rather, after the victim had been sent, the chasuble was to be laid aside and the introit of the Mass of the catechumens begun, one introit and then another, as the priest pleased.

Likewise, the mystery of the Mass, usefully approved by the Church, is contradicted. For when the priest first stands in the Mass at the right corner of the altar, he signifies Christ’s coming to the Jewish people, at the right and peculiarly his own. His first return from the right corner to the left signifies Christ’s coming to the idolatrous Gentiles, in whose gathering [Col. 0105A] he still remains. His return from the left corner to the right signifies the gathering of the remnant to faith, which will be in the time of Elijah and Enoch; he anticipates and hastens it—indeed, represents it as accomplished—by repeatedly returning from corner to corner. Yet he does not thereby signify or represent that the victim has been sent.

Likewise, through the Mass is represented the passion of the Lord, who “came from the bosom of the Father” (John I), as it were from the right corner of the altar, “into the left-hand and evil world” (I John V). And “when his hour had come, that he should pass from this world” through the Passion “to the Father” (John XIII), he was sent as a victim for us into heaven; and “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive” (Eph. IV).

Such persons destroy this principal figure of the Mass, or show it to be false and empty, [Col. 0105B] when they go back from corner to corner, to the left from the right and to the right from the left, although Mass has not yet been celebrated.

Likewise, it was not the Church’s authority but greed that instituted the interpolations or insertions of Masses. The proof is that the more favoured Masses are inserted, not others, such as a Mass of blessed Linus or Sebastian and the like.

Likewise, since the other ecclesiastical offices are not inserted, why is the office of the Mass inserted for greed? The multiplication of prayers is not an insertion of offices: prayers may be multiplied at any hours, without therefore being grafted into them.

Likewise, a Mass thus inserted resembles Nebuchadnezzar’s idol, described in Daniel’s first vision (Dan. II): its head was of gold, its breast and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, some part [Col. 0105C] of its feet iron and some clay.

Likewise, examples should be taken from good things. We know that conventual churches do not have this custom of inserting Masses.

Likewise, there is the example of the revenue from the first Mass owing to certain monks and from the second to priests: did the monks’ greed therefore compel such a priest to consecrate twice in a day?

Likewise, the example of a woman needing purification, who at the second offertory of the Mass for the faithful made her offering at the priest’s prompting rather than at the first, while a monk sat in ambush awaiting the offerings of the first introit, and thus departed deceived.

Likewise, the example of soldiers gradually resisting by making offerings at individual introits; one of them said to a priest thus inserting a Mass: “Even if you begin individual Masses in this way until [Col. 0105D] Vespers, I shall not cease from offering until you have consecrated the holy Eucharist.”

Likewise, the example of a priest who, before he had even put on his chasuble, began multiplying introits lest the assembled people depart.

Likewise, this injures souls. They are defrauded of the promised due, since the Church holds that the more frequently and more specially the sacrament of the altar is offered for them, the greater refreshment they receive.

Likewise, since the Church knows that special prayers surpass general ones, if one person’s thirty-day observance or anniversary is numbered and aggregated with another’s thirty-day observance, is not injury done to the other—indeed, to both—when each soul expects, by promise, to be helped not merely by a general prayer but by its special one?

Likewise, would [Col. 0106A] a Mass thus inserted free from purgatory the soul of a righteous person from Aachen, who asks that a Mass be celebrated for it by a righteous priest and thereby attain deliverance?

Likewise, the example of Master Fulk, dean of Reims, unwilling that his father’s anniversary should be aggregated with the bishop’s anniversary.

Likewise, the example of a woman refusing Masses offered by a priest to be sung in Lent for the faithful; though they had been imposed on her as a penance, she nevertheless did not wish them to be sung by a priest bound to the Lenten service.

But what is a priest to do when asked by this person and that person to perform thirty-day observances, if he cannot suffice to discharge the special thirty-day observances? Let him say to those requesting: “Therefore I shall remember your loved ones in so many Masses.” Let him not say: “I shall perform a thirty-day observance for them,” unless he intends a special one. For in performing general observances [Col. 0106B] he is not discharged from the special observances which the petitioner understood him to promise.

Likewise, if such insertion and multiplication of Masses is lawful, a priest is bound to grant every person who requests it any number of Masses to be sung for him, since he can easily fulfil what is requested by such grafting.

Likewise, a dry Mass, which is without the grace and moisture of consecrating the Eucharist, is not celebrated for the faithful. Therefore, if two introits precede the victim, one will be a dry Mass and will thus help after Mass just as much as the one preceding the victim. Why, then, is it made to precede the victim in an inserted Mass? Is it because of greed and to defraud souls?

Likewise, besides the doubling and insertion of Masses, greed has invented novel Masses, such as a single Mass of all the Apostles to be sung. Likewise, a Mass of the Epiphany, or of another solemnity, to be sung every day, even on Easter Day (when [source ends incomplete).

…that each individual thing may fittingly hold the place allotted to it.) Thus, if in the Easter season Masses and praises pertaining to another occasion are sung, so too in other seasons, in order that the variety of offices may increase the devotion of the ministers and remove the weariness caused by sameness. Yet I do not condemn the devotion of those who celebrate a Mass of the angels even on Easter Day, except because of scandal. Likewise, certain persons while still alive have anniversary services celebrated for themselves, thereby obstructing the suffrages and prayers instituted for the dead. Likewise—and I say this weeping—some have turned so great a sacrament into an art of magic, [Col. 0106D] celebrating Masses over waxen images in order to curse someone; indeed, while cursing a person, they sing the Mass of the faithful ten times or more, so that before the tenth day, or shortly thereafter, he may die and be buried with the dead. Likewise, some have now devised a Mass for the slaughter of those killed, as though they were new martyrs struck down “round about Jerusalem” (Ps. 78 [Vulgate]), imagining it to be an effective lure for offerings because of the favour enjoyed by the slain.

For expelling this manifold disease from the Church, I believe there is one remedy: namely, that there should be few churches, few altars in them, few persons to be ordained and a careful selection of them; likewise, a selection of those ordained and admitted; and, above all, a selection of those set over the lesser priests. [Col. 0107A] The supreme remedy, considered by Gregory VIII, would be the removal of offerings, except three times a year—namely, on Christmas Day, Easter, and Pentecost—and on the feast day of the church’s patron, in the presence of the body of a deceased person, and on anyone’s anniversary day.

Observe that in all Israel there was only one Temple, one tabernacle, and likewise only one altar for offerings in the open court of the Temple (3 Kings [1 Kings] 6). There was indeed an altar of incense in the holy place, but upon it only a small amount of incense was offered (Exod. 27). Detesting this multiplication of altars, Hosea says (ch. 8): “Because my people multiplied altars for sinning, altars became for him an offence. They offer sacrifices, but the Lord will not receive them.” Therefore, following the example of the one Temple, there ought to be one church in each city, [Col. 0107B] or, if the city were populous, a few churches, but so that they should be under one greater church. For the multiplication of chapels has produced illegitimate ministries, and many other monsters and irregularities.

## CHAPTER XXX. Against those who consecrate or receive Christ’s body unworthily

Since the aforesaid plurality, multiplication, and novelty of Masses proceeds from the greed and irreverence of those who consecrate them, it remains to speak of those who consecrate and receive Christ’s body unworthily. Accordingly, writing against unworthy consecration as well as unworthy reception, the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11: “Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For he who eats [Col. 0107C] and drinks unworthily,” etc. Augustine: this is done without devotion, or by celebrating the mystery otherwise than it was handed down by the Lord or by the Church, or by remaining in the will to sin (AUGUSTINE, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 53). “He eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body”—that is, not distinguishing it from other foods with the reverence due to it, through the habitual practice of consecrating or receiving Christ’s body.

Likewise, Gregory says concerning everyone who consecrates or receives Christ’s body unworthily, as the Lord says of Judas: “Nevertheless, behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke 22). For, following Judas’s example, he “betrays the Son of Man” who presumes to violate that inviolable sacrament of the Lord’s body. By consecrating contrary to the rite [Col. 0107D] of the Church, or by receiving unworthily, such a person is a betrayer.

He sells Christ who, neglecting fear and love of him, is shown to love perishable and criminal things. Likewise Augustine: those sin more grievously who hand Christ over to sinful members than Judas, who handed him over to the Jews who crucified him. Likewise, commenting on Psalm 68: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink,” Augustine says that those who consecrate and receive unworthily are like them. For they sin more grievously by despising Christ reigning in heaven than did those who crucified him while he walked upon earth.
