For they, now that truth has been placed plainly in the noonday light, are manifestly without excuse. “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had the sin of unbelief; [Col. 0108A] but now,” etc. (John 15). Those others crucified the Lord through ignorance; hence he prayed for them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

Likewise: if John, who had lived in the desert from childhood and had been sanctified in his mother’s womb (Luke 1), even when invited by the Lord, did not dare to touch that head of the Lord, terrible to angels and worthy of reverence (Mark 1), how do you, a sinner and defiled person, presume not merely to touch his head but to enclose and imprison the whole Christ, God and man, in the prison-house of your defiled body? Or if he feared to baptize Christ, by whom he himself ought to have been baptized, how does your sinful soul, which ought wholly to be inhabited by him, not fear to enclose him wholly in the vile little lodging of your body?

[Col. 0108B] Likewise: if it was said to Mary, who loved the Lord with such ardour and served him so devoutly in life and death, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20)—in your heart, that is—if, I say, she was not permitted to touch the outward “footstool of his feet” (Ps. 109 [Vulgate]), because she did not believe that he was equal to the Father, whose “going forth is from the height of heaven” (Ps. 18 [Vulgate]), how do you, a sinner, believe it lawful and permitted to you not merely to touch the whole God, but to place him in your wholly unclean body? Fear lest not only “Do not touch me” be said to you, but also, “Friend, how did you enter here”—that is, into the heavenly banquet—“without a wedding garment” (Matt. [Col. 0108C] 22), that is, charity?

Likewise, 2 Kings [2 Samuel] 6: if Uzzah, because he stretched out his hand to the figurative ark lest it be overturned by the oxen kicking back, was struck dead by the Lord, how much more ought he to be struck by the Lord who unworthily consecrates or receives the true ark, namely, the Lord’s body? Yet Uzzah approached to support the ark as part of his due office, because he was of the tribe of Levi and a priest, but he did so unworthily. For the Hebrews relate that on the previous night he had lain with his wife. How much more, then, will those who approach Christ’s body be punished—men who lie with concubines or prostitutes?

Likewise, 2 Chronicles 26: Uzziah, who presumed to offer incense to the Lord against the office of the priests, was struck with leprosy by the Lord. How much more will he be struck by the Lord with leprosy—or rather, with eternal death—who has presumed unworthily to immolate the heavenly victim to the Lord? Likewise: by the institution of the primitive Church, after the Gospel had been read, it was said to catechumens, “Go out, go out.” If, therefore, even the members of Christ—that is, those possessing charity—were not permitted to be present at the consecration of the Lord’s body, then those who are members of the devil and lack charity have utmost cause to fear [Col. 0108D] to consecrate or receive so great a sacrament.

I say without hesitation that ministers of the altar who consecrate or receive in this way sin mortally, as do also those who minister at the altar in this matter. It is written: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). But whether those who are in the churchyard and choir, who nevertheless ought through devotion and consent to consecrate Christ’s body with the ministers of the altar and to receive it spiritually, though not sacramentally, sin mortally, I do not determine. Yet they have much to fear, while they are still members of the devil, because they attend the consecration of Christ’s body, whereas catechumens, even sanctified ones, were not permitted to be present.

Likewise: “Appoint a solemn day amid the dense throngs, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117 [Vulgate]). Note the firmness and stability of the mind in good. The “day” is that of virtues, so that you may say: “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Ps. 75 [Vulgate]); “and solemn,” so that “the remnant of thought may keep a feast day unto the Lord”—that is, in serenity of conscience—and this “amid the dense throngs” of all the articles of faith, virtues, good works, tears, which make this drink sweeter, and penitential abstinences, if you desire to approach [Col. 0109B] “even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117 [Vulgate]), that is, to consecrate or receive Christ’s body.

Likewise, Exodus chapter 12: if the Lord commands that the figurative paschal lamb be eaten “roasted with fire and with wild lettuces,” and by men “with loins girded and staffs in their hands,” how much more does he command that no one approach the eating of the true paschal Lamb unless with bitterness of heart and penitence; baked also in the oven of the Holy Spirit; chaste; conscious of no guilt in himself; strong; wholly clothed in virtues; not barefoot even upon his feet—hence, “Your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6)—but firm in faith, virtues, affections, and good works.

Likewise, as a means of striking fear into those approaching the Eucharist, there is the example [Col. 0109C] of that holy Egyptian sinner who, doing penance in the desert, was visited by the Lord in this sacrament once in forty years, through Abbot Zosimas, a hermit of that desert (*Her Life is in Surius*, vol. II). She first made confession to him; when he came to her a second time to give her the Eucharist, at the coming of the Lord’s body she dissolved wholly into tears. Although she wept every day, then she did so more abundantly, almost until her eyes poured themselves out.

[lacuna]

Therefore, these things having been done, she came to the cup of mercy.

She sacrifices herself wholly in tears and joins herself to the cup.  
(HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans)

[Col. 0109D] Likewise, concerning those who approach this altar unworthily, the Lord complains, saying: “They gave me gall for food” (Ps. 68 [Vulgate]), the bitterness of their sin; “and in my thirst,” in which I thirsted to drink them and incorporate them into myself, “they gave me vinegar to drink,” the sharpness of their wickedness. But observe that, “when the Lord had tasted the vinegar, he would not drink” (Matt. 27); likewise, he does not incorporate such people into himself, even though they receive the Eucharist sacramentally: they belong to the Church in name, but not in divine power.

Likewise Augustine: whoever has not first been crucified with Christ to the flesh, the world, and its concupiscences (Gal. 5), before approaching to consecrate or receive Christ’s body, so far as lies within him crucifies Christ anew and must be numbered among those of whom the Apostle says: “Crucifying again in themselves [Col. 0110A] the Lord, and holding him up” to mockery and derision (Heb. 6).

Likewise: Mark cut off his thumb in order to be unfit for priesthood, fearing that he might be seized and made a priest. So greatly did he reverence the consecration of Christ’s body, though he had often received it sacramentally.

But now men about to be ordained do not remove from themselves what is natural; rather, they bring forward both lawful and unlawful things so that they may be ordained, and this more for profit than for devotion and divine service. Likewise, in the *Lives of the Fathers*: when a certain elder among the hermits was chosen by them for the priesthood and forcibly ordained by the bishop of Egypt, he said: “Although I am a priest, I shall not consecrate during my lifetime,” considering himself unworthy to consecrate Christ’s body, though, without consecrating it, he received it from another. But now [Col. 0110B] some consecrate Christ’s body far too frequently, as though it were a daily banquet, because of greed; others do so far too rarely, because of sloth.

Likewise, in the Psalm: “Send forth your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me first into your tabernacles; and so I shall enter unto the altar of God,” by consecrating or receiving Christ’s body, “unto God, who makes my youth joyful” (Ps. 42 [Vulgate])—that is, who grants me in actual possession the joyful youthfulness of grace, and in hope the youthfulness of glory. Natural youth, too, should be considered in ordaining someone, unless gravity of character and holiness of life compensate for age. But one who consecrates and serves at the altar, while he consecrates, is as though in Paradise, forgetful of all things behind.

Likewise: “I will wash my hands among the innocent”; and so, innocent and [Col. 0110C] clean, as an angel through their example and imitation, “I will go around your altar, O Lord” (Ps. 25 [Vulgate]), in order to consecrate your body. Likewise, when Joshua was walking in the plain of Jericho, meditating upon something, “he saw an angel with a drawn sword,” and said to him: “Who are you? Are you one of us or of our adversaries?” He answered: “I am prince of the host of heaven. Take off the shoes from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground” (Josh. 5).

Therefore you who approach the altar to consecrate and receive the Eucharist should consider that “the place where you stand is holy ground; a dreadful place, the house of God and gate of heaven” (Gen. 28). Fear “the angels ascending and descending there by the ladder,” with drawn sword, lest they cut down [Col. 0110D] your latter parts (3 Kings [1 Kings] 21); fear lest “the axe has already been laid to the root of the tree” (Matt. 3), because you approach unworthily. Fear the choir of angels standing against you, bearing witness to your injury of them and ready to avenge the Lord’s wrath if you have approached unworthily; or, if you have offered worthily, carrying the sacrifice of your praise and prayers on high before God’s sight. Hence:

> At the time when the priest stands suppliantly at the altars,  
> And the Son himself, remaining, is sacrificed to the Father,  
> The heavens lie open, the heavenly choir is present, things below  
> Are joined to things above, and agent and act become one.  
> (HILDEBERT of Le Mans, *On the Mystery of the Mass*)

A similar thing is read to have been said to Moses in Exodus: “When Moses was driving the sheep of Jethro into the inner desert [Col. 0111A] and came to Mount Horeb, the mountain of God, the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush; and he saw that the bush burned and was not consumed” (Exod. 3). When he went to see that great vision, the Lord said: “Do not come near here, but take off the shoe from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 12 [probably 3]). If Moses, therefore, was forbidden to approach the burning and figurative bush, how much more are you forbidden to approach the true body of Christ unless you have first cast away from yourself and your affections all dead and carnal works?

Likewise: when the Lord forbade a stranger, foreigner, or unclean person to eat of the paschal lamb, how much more does he forbid the sinner—not yet made a citizen and member of God’s household—from eating of the true Lamb, being himself stained while the Lamb is unstained? [Col. 0111B] Likewise David: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in hands and clean of heart,” etc. (Ps. 23 [Vulgate]).

Likewise: if you have not yet watered Christ’s feet with tears of penitence and cherished them with Magdalene (Luke 7); if you have not yet sat down “to eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126 [Vulgate]); if you have not yet humbled yourself to kiss the Lord’s feet; if you have not yet risen to strong works, as though to kiss the Lord’s hands: how do you presume to approach the kiss of his head—indeed, the consecration, reception, and kiss of the whole Christ? “These things come by their numbers and their proper degrees, just as do the orders.” In this sacrament, by omitting any degree, one sins more grievously than by omitting a grade of order before receiving an order.

Likewise Solomon: “When you sit at the table [Col. 0111C] of a rich man, know that you ought to set before him such things as have been set before you” (Prov. 23, according to the Septuagint). The Lord has set before us countless dishes and gifts, all of which are nevertheless comprised under these three. He set before us himself as the price for us on the cross; as provision for the journey on the altar; and as the future reward in heaven.

We set the first before him if “we crucify our flesh with its vices and concupiscences; if we have been crucified to the world and the world to us” (Gal. 5, 6); if we deny ourselves, daily take up Christ’s cross, and follow him (Luke 9); if, with the Apostle, “we bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in our body” (Gal. 6); if we mortify our flesh for Christ; if it is granted us from above to die for him; if we have compassion on our neighbour. We set before him the second dish if we live according to the Gospel; if we feed our very head, not in himself but in his members, by giving whatever alms to the poor, whether bodily or spiritual. “For what we have done to one of his least ones, we have done to him” (Matt. 25).

We cannot set the third dish before him, “because he has no need of our goods” (Ps. 15 [Vulgate]); but he himself will set this before us in the future. Yet we are his inheritance, and for this inheritance he sanctified himself; concerning it the Father says to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance” (Ps. 2). But for those who approach Christ’s table otherwise, unless the two aforesaid dishes have been set before him, “their table will become before them a snare, [Col. 0112A] a recompense, and a stumbling-block” (Ps. 68 [Vulgate]). “They eat and drink judgment upon themselves” (1 Cor. 11), and die from a good odour.

Likewise, the Epistle to the Hebrews: “We have an altar of which those who serve the tabernacle” of the body “have no right to eat” (Heb. 3 [probably 13]); namely, those who do not mortify and “crucify their flesh with its vices and concupiscences” (Gal. 5), and who “do not open their hands to the needy,” etc. (Prov. 31). Likewise, the Apostle declares in 1 Corinthians 11 who ought to approach the Eucharist for consecration or reception, and how worthily and fearfully they ought to do so, saying: “When you come together in one, it is no longer”—that is, it is not fitting—“to eat the Lord’s supper,” unless you have first been examined and prepared, as is shown below in the same place.

Likewise, if when we pray, “having also been instructed by saving [Col. 0112B] precepts, we scarcely dare say, ‘Our Father’” (Matt. 6), unless we are his children by adoption and have fulfilled all the petitions that follow, how much more difficult is it to dare to consecrate and receive him whole, since greater devotion and purity of conscience are required here? Therefore this prayer is placed before the reception of the holy Eucharist.

See that you do not gather and receive this heavenly manna beyond one *gomor*, that is, the measure of sobriety, lest it cause your conscience to breed worms through sins (Exod. 16). See that you wrap the Lord’s body “in a clean and new linen cloth” (Matt. 27), that is, in a pure conscience. See “that you place it in a tomb in which no one has yet been laid” (John 19); or, if the devil has been placed there, do not bury the Lord in your clean tomb until he has been cast out. See that you do not put “new wine into old wineskins” (Matt. 9) of sins. See that you carry the heavenly ark of the Lord upon a new cart (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 6). If you yoke cows to it, yoke such cows as yourself and others who do not know how to turn back their necks after calves (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 7), that is, their affections after carnal desires, but who go forward straight on and, though lowing, carry the Lord’s ark to the land of promise, to the heavenly house of Abinadab. Likewise Psalm 117: “Appoint a solemn day amid the dense throngs, even to the horn of the altar.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. Against Geryons: two-bodied, two-headed beasts in several churches

[Col. 0112D]

Not unlike or discordant with the plurality, two-facedness, and three-facedness of Masses is the plurality of ecclesiastical persons, dignities, and offices held by the same person, whether in one Church or in different ones. For there are some who, like Geryons, Briareuses, two-bodied or three-bodied creatures, monstrous beasts with many heads, strive to resemble God, three in persons and one in substance. For each of them, though one in substance and person, nevertheless desires to be several persons in ecclesiastical offices and dignities.

The Lord rebukes this race of monstrous men, this monster of greed, in the Law and in Numbers chapter 4, distinguishing and dividing the offices of the tabernacle’s ministers: assigning the Merarites to one office, the Kohathites to another, the Gershonites to another, and the Levites and Aaronites to another. If in the Synagogue and in the figure no interchange of offices, no confusion of order or alternation, could be made, [Col. 0113A] how much more ought this interchange and indistinction of offices, ecclesiastical persons, and dignities to be forbidden and eliminated in the Church, where there is truth. It has disfigured and confused the Church so greatly that one does not know how, or under what title, such beasts should be entered in writing.

Likewise, if offices, dignities, and ecclesiastical persons were distinct, the Church would truly be “a dreadful place” (Gen. 28), and “an army drawn up in battle order” (Song 6), against which the gates of hell would not prevail (Matt. 16). But if in a material battle and army it is not permitted that the same man be both captain of the first rank, armour-bearer, constable, commander of the army, and seneschal; that the same man be keeper both of the right wing and the left wing in battle, both northern and southern: how much more ought offices not to be mingled in the Church and spiritual warfare, where battle must be fought not only against visible enemies but against invisible ones, namely demons and vices?

Because of this failure to divide ecclesiastical persons and offices, the Church is easily conquered by the devil, the world, and vices, so that it now says: “Though an army stand against me, my heart shall not fear” (Ps. 25 [Vulgate]), because my members are confused, undistinguished, and disordered. Likewise Augustine: “Under secular laws, a man who sought for himself two or more guardianships would be regarded as suspect and therefore excluded from all of them. [Col. 0113C] How much more ought he who seeks and usurps several offices in the Church to be excluded and regarded as suspect, lest, while attempting both of two offices, he perform neither well.”

Likewise, Jethro, though a gentile, is read in Exodus and Deuteronomy to have said to Moses, who was judging case after case from morning until evening and, being occupied with all, had no time for himself: “You will wear yourself out with foolish labour” (Deut. 1); divide your burden among many, etc. Augustine says there: “It seems to me that a mind too much occupied with many human activities is in some fashion deprived of leisure for God; yet it becomes fuller in proportion as it extends itself more freely to things above and eternal.” How much more, then, is one deprived of leisure for God who is occupied by several offices? For:

> A mind directed to many things is less attentive to each individual thing.

Therefore Solomon says: “My son, let not your activities be many” (Ecclus. 11).

> A wise man sets bounds even to honourable pursuits.  
> (JUVENAL, *Satires*, VI)

Moses therefore, on Jethro’s advice, appointed some as rulers of tens, others of fifties, others of hundreds, others of thousands; some as *pentecontarchs* [commanders of fifty], others as *chiliarchs* [commanders of a thousand], all without mixture (Exod. 18). Why, then, are the same men deans and archdeacons in the Church, the same men two archdeacons, and the like? Only major cases were referred to Moses; he did not judge minor ones unless he suspected a dean or another official whose office it was [Col. 0114A] to judge them. Thus it seems that no appeal should be made in minor cases. But now, even an unjust appeal made in the smallest cases holds good.

“But,” they say, “we do not labour or bear burdens as Moses did, even if we are attached to several dignities and offices. We discharge them through vicars, hired servants, and concubinary clerics. Therefore they need not be divided, for we rest in those men.”

To such people one ought to reply: “Therefore, because you do not work, neither should you eat” (2 Thess. 3). A certain people said to one such bishop: “Do not appoint over us a concubinary priest so that you may roam and wander about the country, devoted to idleness.” Likewise, if Jethro said in his counsel to Moses, “Divide your burden among many,” etc. (Exod. 18), today it is said in the Church: “Gather burdens together and unite several offices in one person, and the Lord will depart from you.”

Likewise, in Numbers the heads of the families of Gilead, from the tribe of the sons of Joseph, approached Moses, saying: “The Lord commanded you to divide the land among the children of Israel and to give the daughters of Zelophehad, our brother, the inheritance due to their father. He forbade men of another tribe to take them as wives, lest the allocation of lots be confused and the possession of some pass to others.” Moses said to them: “Let them marry only men of their own tribe, lest their possession pass from tribe to tribe; let these things remain as they were separated by the Lord” (Num. 27, 36).

How much more ought the children of the Church to say to their prelate: “Give our Church [Col. 0114C] a man from its own tribe, and let not the minister of one Church be transferred to the ministry of another: a dean in one Church to an archdeaconry in another, and so onward; so that the distribution of offices and ecclesiastical persons is confused and he who was useful to one Church becomes useless to both.”

Likewise, observe that Christ had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9). Do you seek various resting-places—namely, ecclesiastical offices—in which you may lay your head and rest? Such resting-places will be for you a punishment unto eternity rather than rest. Likewise, in the Psalm (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]): “The King of powers is of the beloved, of the beloved,” that is, for “dividing the spoils of the beauty of the house”—that is, for making the house beautiful. Hence: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (Ps. 25 [Vulgate]).

The Apostle likewise teaches this division of the spoils for the beauty of the house in Ephesians chapter 4: “And the Lord himself gave some to be apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers,” etc. Likewise Luke says in the Gospel, chapter 2: “When a strong man armed guards his court, all that he possesses is in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he will take away all his armour in which he trusted and distribute his spoils.” These spoils are faithful souls, ecclesiastical dignities, and offices.

Likewise Isaiah: “They shall rejoice before you as those rejoice in harvest, as victors exult when they divide captured spoil” (Isa. 9). Likewise, it is written of Paul: “Benjamin, a ravening wolf, gathering prey in the morning and dividing spoils in the evening” (Gen. 49). For he ordained some persons and, according to the distinct ranks of men, assigned them different offices in the Church—Timothy, Titus, and others. David, observing this pleasant variety and beautiful house of the Lord, says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, surrounded with variety, and thus clad around with varieties in golden fringes” (Ps. 44 [Vulgate]). The variety of chants, readings, responsories, antiphons, and ornaments makes this variety commendable. But the variety of harmonious ecclesiastical persons and offices makes it especially pleasant and beautiful; to correspond with their variety, there ought to be a variety of ministers.

When these things are observed in the Church, it may rightly and truly be said of her: “You are beautiful and fair, daughter of Jerusalem, like an army drawn up in battle order” (Song 6). [Col. 0115B] Likewise, in James chapter 3: “Do not become many teachers, my brethren.” The interlinear gloss says: that is, ministers of several churches, “knowing that you receive a greater judgment.” For indiscriminate activities disturb the offices of churches.

Likewise, in the appendix to the Third Lateran Council, under Alexander III: if it is forbidden for one church, one prebend, or one bishopric to be divided among several persons, then similarly, by the contrary inference, several churches or offices ought not to be assigned to one person—except perhaps because of a shortage of ministers and a multitude of cases; and this because of the shameful and disgraceful enormities that result. Indeed, one thing should belong to one person, not several things to one person. If your father was content [Col. 0115C] with one wife, why are you not content with one Church?

Consider what the Apostle says: “He who serves the altar should live by the altar” (1 Cor. 9). He does not say: “He who serves altars should live by altars”; nor does he say: “He who serves altars should live by the altar”; nor: “He who does not serve an altar or altars should live by an altar or altars.” For he says: “He who does not work shall not eat” (2 Thess. 3). Therefore, where he does not work, or when he does not work, neither should he eat. If someone objects that he serves in several churches, I answer that he cannot serve several churches at one and the same time; and therefore, in proportion to the time, he should receive a benefice from each church in which and to the extent that he serves.

Let everyone consult his conscience, understanding the form of words used by the giver and receiver of an ecclesiastical benefice, concerning how he ought to conduct himself in the church. For a book is handed to him and it is said: “I give you this church, or prebend, for the honour of God and the service of this church.” This is as though it said: “Be constant in the office of this church.” In some churches this form is supplied more expressly: “I give you this church, or prebend, for the honour of God and the service of this church, on condition that you reside and hold a residence in this church.”

Likewise, such persons seem badly to interpret: “Seven women shall lay hold of one man” (Isa. 4). Let them see that they do not incur that amusing invention of a youth who, after remaining for a long time with the senators in the Capitol, was asked by his mother what had been decided. Not wishing to reveal the senators’ counsel, he devised a new trick and replied to his mother that he had heard that henceforth one man would have several wives. When she heard this, his mother called together the matrons at the entrance of the Capitol and cried: “Not two women for one man, but one woman for two men” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, I). But it is not two women for one man, but two men for one [church]—indeed today more than two, as at the church of Saint Medericus and many others.

Likewise, it should be noted that, in secular jurisdictions, one knight cannot serve two lords in two legions unless his service in the former legion is preserved, and so the other’s jurisdiction is diminished. How much less can someone divide himself in order to serve God in several churches, when he ought to offer himself wholly and always, in order to serve in each one? Someone also reproached another because he had undertaken the guardianship of more peoples [Col. 0116B] than he himself had parsons in his parish. “I have heard,” he said, “that, when a certain dean severely rebuked his subordinate for the *marrancies* [failures of attendance or service] which he committed every hour, by day and by night, the subordinate replied: ‘Why do you rebuke me, when in all the churches in which you hold dignities and from which you receive daily revenues and emoluments, you cause so many defects and *marrancies* by your absence?’” Thus that dean was silenced, and thereafter dared not rebuke him or another man for such defect and *marrancy*, perceiving in himself a greater cause for rebuke.

I have also heard that when two men were canons of two churches, one being dean in one and the other in the other, it was asked which was the other’s spiritual father and which was the other’s obedient subject. The answer was that, so long as they were in one of those churches, the man who was dean in the church in which they were was the other’s spiritual father, and the other was his obedient subject.

[Col. 0116C] But if they were not in one of those churches, but perhaps in another church or others, which would be father and which spiritual son? Such fatherhood and sonship are contrary to nature and monstrous. Likewise, a physician who undertook the care of a hundred or thirty sick persons in the same town—much less in different towns—would be deemed infamous. Much more ought the man who has undertaken the care of so many souls, not in one town but in different ones, not in one region but in different regions, to be branded with infamy.

Likewise John says in his Gospel: “The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep; but the hireling, who is not the shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees,” etc. (John 10). If he sees the wolf coming, then he is present. Likewise, if he flees, he is present. Often he does not flee, but drives away the sheep and brings them back to the folds; sometimes he preaches. Thus the hireling sins less than the man whose church it is, since the latter is always absent. But by what name shall the man who is always absent be called? He is not a shepherd, because he does not feed the sheep; he is not a hireling, because the hireling is always present, whereas he is not. Therefore let monstrous greed devise a new name for this new monster.

To expose this monster, it is sufficient that the Lord distributes diverse gifts of the grace of the Holy Spirit in the spiritual body, as the Apostle teaches in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 12: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Lord,” etc. He immediately adds: “To one indeed is given through the Spirit the word of knowledge, and to another the word of wisdom,” etc. He did not confer all things upon one person, so that the individual members might serve one another. Likewise, in the same place, the Apostle assigns different offices to the individual members in the human body: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be?” etc. He immediately adds: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of your works’; nor again the head to the feet, ‘You are not necessary to me.’”

Likewise, in the house of a householder there are different offices required by human necessity. He appoints one as swineherd, another as oxherd, another as charioteer, another as courier, and so on, according to each one’s proper ability, lest he incur some loss to his possessions. How much more ought a distinction of offices and dignities be made in the spiritual body—that is, in the Church—so that charity may bind all things together and spread more widely? Hence that distinguished versifier:

> The eyes are the watchmen of the head; the ears, of melody;  
> The feet, leaders; and the hands, makers of all things.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Against bigamists and Lamech-like men in several churches
It is shameful that certain bishops borrow eyes from other bishops. And when there are four bishops who have only two eyes, they have thus become not merely blind or one-eyed, but monstrously deprived of eyes, although they ought to be living creatures full of eyes before and behind, as is read in Ezekiel (ch. I). For each ought to be an Argus, so as to see spiritually and make others see. For, according to the poet:

> Argus had his head ringed with a hundred lights.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I, fable 10.)

Such persons are worse than Julius Caesar. After Lucan had enumerated Caesar’s individual vices, he said of him at the end:

> Caesar was everything.  
> (*Pharsalia*, book III.)

That is, he usurped for himself all the dignities of Rome. For he was consul, quaestor, and so forth, all in the same city. [Col. 0117D] Worse, therefore, is he who wishes to possess all honours in different places: a beast with many heads, like that monster concerning which theologians dispute, which appears uniform below the navel but manifold above. Thus those who say that Gaul alone lacks monsters are lying.

Observe that nothing disfigures a body or head more than absent eyes; no bodily parts are more necessary. It is also doubtful whether this person of many faces ought similarly to have several seals, or different seals: how he should write, or how one should write to him; whether with the title of a dignity; whether all titles of dignity should be appended, or one alone; whether his personal name should be used, so that the names of his dignities are omitted—in which perhaps he would take offence. If it is said that only the name of the greater dignity [Col. 0118A] should be placed first, what if he possesses several equal dignities? If it is said that he should be designated by the title of the church which he visits more frequently, what if he runs now here, now there?

> With what knot shall I hold Proteus as he changes his face?  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, I.1.)

Ask him what he is called, or under what name he wishes letters to be addressed to him: he himself will not know. Someone, writing to such a many-headed beast, had prefixed in the greeting the names of all his dignities and prebends; he heard from another: “This must still be added: ‘Servant and peasant of Sancerre.’”

This person of many faces must also possess a multiple wardrobe, and many breviaries on account of the [Col. 0118B] diverse usages of the churches over which he presides. But what is he to do when, in one church, all who possess such-and-such garments are excommunicated? What if everyone is excommunicated in that church who has anything except garments rejected by another? He is likewise Horace’s many-formed idol, whose model cannot be found in nature. Hence:

> If a painter wished to join a horse’s neck  
> To a human head, and add varied feathers.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*.)

The same poet elsewhere:

> …the little crow, stripped of its stolen colours,  
> Would provoke laughter.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, I.3; reading uncertain.)

For it is theft—or robbery—that he appropriates and usurps for himself so many goods belonging to the poor. [Col. 0118C] Against such persons the Lord speaks in the Gospel of Luke: “Into whatever city you enter, choose who in it is worthy, and remain in his house; and do not move from house to house” (Luke X). If, then, a guest for one night must choose a worthy host, and must not pass “from house to house,” how much more ought one who is to be a permanent resident and minister in one and the same church to do so?

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On holy unity

This monstrous plurality of dignities and similar things, in the same or in different churches, concentrated upon one person, is also rebuked by a threefold and holy unity, lest such a person be able to say with David: “Look [Col. 0118D] upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor” (Psalm XXIV). If, by analogy, you object riches, I shall answer: one may be poor amid riches. The Apostle did not dread riches, but their character.

The first unity is that of faith, sacraments, and morals; those divided by heresies and schisms lack it. “For there is one faith, one baptism, one Lord,” etc. (Ephesians IV). “One thing have I asked of the Lord,” etc. (Psalm XXVI). “My dove is one” (Song of Songs II). The ark was completed in one cubit.

The second unity is unity of actions. Hence Solomon: “My son, let not your actions be many” (Ecclesiasticus XI).

> The wise man sets a limit even to honourable pursuits.

And elsewhere:

> The mind intent upon many things is less attentive to each particular.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires*, VI.)

“Divide your burden among many,” etc. By analogy, a third unity follows from this: namely, unity of dignities, offices, and revenues. If the consequent is denied, so is the antecedent. If plurality of actions is denied and forbidden, then plurality of dignities and similar things is also forbidden. For to possess several dignities or revenues is antecedent to performing several actions in them. “For he who does not work, neither should he eat” (II Thessalonians III).

Even before a secular judge, one who seeks the office of guardian for two wards is regarded with suspicion, lest, while undertaking both, he perform neither well. If, then, it is forbidden: “Let not your actions be many,” much more is the antecedent forbidden, namely: [Col. 0119B] “Let not your actions be in several churches, revenues, dignities.” Take care that you do not possess things from all churches, or from many churches, revenues, and the like, in such a way that you no longer possess yourself.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On bad unity

There is also a fourth unity, namely a bad one, by which someone seeks singularity among others, establishing justice for himself, “thinking himself to be something when he is nothing” (Galatians VI), arrogant beyond measure, or arrogating to himself what he does not possess: isolated, savage, unicorn-like, proud. Of him it is said: “Woe to one alone, because if he falls”—falling through pride—“he has no one to lift him up” (Ecclesiasticus IV).

Likewise, all the questions which may be raised concerning Jacob’s double marriage to wives, and concerning the maidservants introduced to him, and concerning these matters (Genesis XXIX), and against such persons: Jacob is nevertheless excused because he took two wives in order to procure offspring for the worship of God and to multiply the people of one faith. Let them themselves consider whether they have undertaken several churches or dignities for the spiritual fruitfulness and benefit of the Church, rather than for income and temporal profit; whether they have undertaken them to multiply the people in God’s worship and to multiply in them children and the fruit of good works.

This indeed does not seem likely, because Rachel—that is, some church more fruitful in revenues and temporal fruits—is preferred to Leah, though Leah is more fruitful in spiritual fruit. Leah is despised; Rachel is chosen in preference. Rachel also says to Leah: “Give me [Col. 0119D] some of the mandrakes of your son Reuben.” Leah answered: “Does it seem a small thing to you that you have taken my husband from me, unless you also take the mandrakes of my son?” Rachel said: “Let him sleep with you and rest with you tonight in exchange for the mandrakes of your son” (Genesis XXX).

But now those who are titled to two churches take care neither to sleep, rest, read, nor sing with one of them, in that one church, even for one night, “in exchange for the many mandrakes and revenues” which they exact from it. Yet the Church would be more fruitful if individual ministers were assigned to individual churches. If you object the scarcity of clerics and ministers: today several churches are entrusted to several unlearned persons, while learned and prudent men have none; although not even one church ought to be entrusted to one such unlearned person, whereas several might be entrusted to a prudent man because of the scarcity of good men.

Yet several sick persons are not entrusted to one physician, nor several guardianships to one guardian, when that entails difficulty and danger; much less should several churches be entrusted to one person, where the danger concerns souls—there, bodies and possessions. Likewise, upon such persons falls the curse of God, recorded in Deuteronomy, chapter XXVIII: “You shall take a wife, and another shall sleep”—rest, [Col. 0120A] sing, and minister—in the church. What follows does not suit them, but is the opposite of their situation: “You shall plant a vineyard and not harvest it; you shall sow a field and not reap its fruit” (Deuteronomy XXVIII).

These men, by contrast, do not plant, dig, stake, or manure the vineyard, and yet harvest it and drink its wine. They do not sow the field, yet gather its fruit, so that they may be likened to him of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are a harsh man: you reap where you did not sow, and gather where you did not scatter” (Matthew XXV).

Again, if offence is caused in a church by the failure and absence for one day of someone who ought to read or sing there, how much greater is it if someone is absent for a year—indeed for a decade, or a still longer period—from the church in which he ought to minister? But a very great offence and failure occurs when one man reads or sings twice in one night in a church; how much greater ought it to be considered when one man is assigned to two churches, since he cannot read, sing, and minister in both on one day or night?

But in one distinguished [Col. 0120C] church—more shamefully still—there are five or more dignities extremely rich in revenues and income. Though these revenues are received there, no service is rendered there by proxy or by anyone else. I do not say merely that no singing or reading takes place: not even counsel is given to the church. Indeed, none of the five persons is found there once in the year.

Again, such persons are more detestable than Lamech, who first introduced bigamy (Genesis IV). For they are found not merely bigamists but trigamists, tetragamists, pentagamists, and so on. Yet when such a man leaves as heir of all that has been amassed in one of his churches any one of his churches, it will be difficult to distribute and leave to the individual churches what belongs to them. Isaiah, chapter V: “Woe to those who join house to house,” coupling church to church, “and field to field unto the boundary of the larger estate. Shall you dwell alone in the midst of the earth?” As if to say: “Are you alone wise, or do you alone know how to sing in church, that you usurp several?”

## CHAPTER XXXV. Against external simony, namely in the offices, dignities, and revenues of the Church

We have already stigmatized above the plague and leprosy of simony, which concerns the interior sacraments, even “unto the horn” and the sacrament “of the altar” (Psalm XVII). The Lord similarly stigmatizes its form which consists in external matters—namely ecclesiastical offices, churches, dignities, revenues, personates, and whatever is annexed to spiritual things. In the Gospel of John, chapter X, he says: “He who does not enter through the door”—Christ, that is, humbly, lest standing erect he strike against the low doorway, Christ, and otherwise fall from on high—“and who does not enter” when called by God through canonical election, otherwise hearing, “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” “into the sheepfold” (Matthew XXII), that is, into the Catholic Church and the fellowship of the faithful, whatever assembly of saints it may be, “but climbs in by another way,” in any manner apart from Christ—whether by thinking wrongly about him, as a heretic does, or by “seeking in the Church his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians II), as does the false man, hireling, or simoniac—then:

> Himself sold,  
> He desires to sell all things.

For things begun from an evil principle are scarcely carried on by a good means or concluded with a good end. “He is a thief” (John X), because he calls his own what belongs to another: that is, if the governance of souls has been entrusted to him, he calls God’s sheep his own. If not, he usurps for himself, like a hidden robber, what is not his—namely the patrimony of the Crucified One and the goods of the poor. “He is also a robber” (ibid.), because he has stolen God’s sheep. If he has the governance of souls, he kills himself; if not, he both kills himself and violently seizes and retains the goods of the poor.

“But he who enters through the door” (John X), that is, through Christ, sincerely, “seeking not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians II), “is the shepherd of the sheep.” [Col. 0121C] “To him the doorkeeper”—that is, sacred Scripture, which leads to Christ and to his eternal blessedness; or the Holy Spirit, “who teaches all truth” (John XIV)—“opens” a fuller way to blessedness through the hidden things of Scriptures, questions, confessions, and counsels. “For he who follows me does not walk in darkness” (John VIII), whether of ignorance or sin.

“And the sheep”—that is, those predestined to life and subject to him—hear his voice humbly and devoutly in obedience, because he preaches Christ and seeks nothing else. And he “calls his own sheep” (John X): he summons and raises them to offices and dignities in the Church, calling them by name, namely by the name of merit, predestination, or spiritual grace (Philippians IV). Of names of this sort it is said: “Rejoice, because your names are written in the book of life” (Numbers IV).

Likewise, Moses called each person by his own name—not by the name of the crowd, not by the name of money counted out, not by carnal affection, nor by any private consideration such as lineage and the like. “For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven,” whether Greek, Scythian, or whatever barbarian, “is fit for the kingdom of God” (Matthew VII). And the poet says:

> You raise up men chosen from every region,  
> And seek their character, not the cradle from which they come.  
> (Claudian, *On the Praise of Stilicho*, II.)

He “leads the sheep out” (John X) and sends them forth by word and [Col. 0122A] example, “from Egypt” (Exodus XIII), that is, from sin; “and goes before them” in counsel of perfection, in the merit and example of his life. “And the sheep follow him” (John X), even to the kingdom of God, by obeying and persevering to the end, because they know his voice, “wherever he goes” (Revelation XIV). But they “do not follow a stranger”—one in whom, that is, there is not Christ’s voice but that of temporal gain, even if he otherwise seems good—“but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers” (ibid.).

As Christ is the “door” for entering the Church militant and triumphant, so also he is “the way: I am the way” in example, “the truth” in promise, and “the life” in reward (John XIV); and he is a bridge, making a bridge for us and a way of entering the present and future Church. Hence Hebrews IX: “Christ, appearing as high priest of good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands,” that is, “not of this creation,” etc.

There is a fourfold bridge, way, or manner of entering the Church, the assembly of saints, through Christ. The first was the burning of Aaron’s rivals, the flowering and fruit-bearing of his rod, by which it was shown that he was called by the Lord. Of this calling one reads in Numbers XVII and XVIII and Hebrews V: “No one takes the honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was.” I do not mean miracles as the basis of calling, but signs of works, learning, and virtues by which a person is shown to please God.

The second bridge was the voice falling from heaven by which the Son was glorified by the Father: “This is my [Col. 0122C] beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III); and through the Prophet: “You are a priest forever” (Psalm CIX).

Nicholas was called by this calling. The third bridge was the casting of lots, by which “Matthias received the place of the ministry and apostleship from which Judas transgressed, that he might go to his own place” (Acts I). It should especially be observed that, among Christ’s disciples, the apostles selected only two whom they recognized as most suitable for the apostolic office; they did not presume to name either one apostle, but left this to divine grace.

Moreover, if Simon Peter had selected seven deacons as administrators of the poor’s goods (Acts VI) out of private love and carnal affection, so that the apostles might devote themselves more freely to prayer, the disciples would doubtless have rejected those selected as useless to them. But lots have now been removed because of their proximity to divination; canonical election has succeeded them. Unless it is pure, sincere, and holy, it is apart from Christ and sacrilegious. But if people do not now trust lots, and fear that an unworthy person might be selected for an archdeacon or similarly minor office in the Church by a blind judgment, how can they trust lots for the perpetration of homicide through strange and blind judgments?

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On those who hinder the sincerity of canonical election

The leprosy of Gehazi (IV Kings V), Simon’s greed (Acts VIII), the violence of the rebels and great men (Numbers XVI), and many other causes which we shall pursue, hinder and destroy the sincerity and purity of canonical election. Jerome touches on some of them in his letter, namely in Cause VIII, Question I, saying:

“Moses, the friend of God, ‘to whom the Lord spoke face to face’ (Exodus XXXIII), could certainly have made his sons successors to his authority and left his own dignity to his descendants. But Joshua, a stranger from another tribe, is chosen, so that we may know that leadership over peoples is to be granted not to blood but to merit of life (Numbers XXVII). But now we see very many making this matter a favour: they do not seek to set up as pillars in the Church those whom they have known best to benefit the Church, but those whom they themselves love with private affection, or whose services have won them over, or for whom some great man has made request; and, to pass over worse things, those who obtained clerical status through gifts.”

It should also be added that nowhere is the Lord read to have raged and burned with indignation over any crime as he did over the monster of simony. For, about to fight against this monster and cast it out of the Church, armed “with a whip made of cords” (John II), setting aside, as it were for an hour, his native gentleness according to his humanity, “he drove from the temple those selling doves and overturned the tables of the money-changers” (John X). As if he said: “One must enter my house through me. For ‘I am the door’ (ibid.); you do not approach churches, spiritual things, or things annexed to spiritual things through yourselves. Thus you make my house, a house of prayer, into a den of robbers and a house of trade” (Matthew XXI).

If, then, the Lord blazed and raged thus against the figure, how much more against the reality and monster of simony, which—if it were to be expelled today from the Church together with the monsters it has spawned—would require not merely cords but swords, spears, and thunderbolts falling from heaven?

The Lord, setting forth in the Gospel canonical election as the successor and imitator of the aforesaid three modes of choosing, says: “Come after me,” etc. (Luke IX): by fulfilling “the commandments,” without which there is no salvation, and “crucifying your flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians V). For “if anyone wishes to come after me,” it is necessary that “he deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke XVI). Therefore a prelate of the Church must be chosen from among the crucified.

Because the preceding qualifications, common to all, are insufficient for those to be chosen, he adds: “I will make you,” through authority and the infusion of gifts and virtues, so that he who presides in dignity may preside in uprightness of character and excel in learning. Thus, when these things have been fulfilled and bestowed, “I will make you become,” through the ministry and canonical election of those electing, “fishers of men” (Matthew IV)—of souls, not of money.

Those otherwise chosen or who obtain a spiritual benefice are like the priests of Jeroboam, who made priests of idols from the lowest and meanest of the people: “For whoever wished filled his own hand, and became a priest of the high places. [Col. 0124A] For this cause the house of Jeroboam sinned, and was overthrown and wiped from the face of the earth” (III Kings XIII). But was this simoniacal? It is certain that selling the legal priesthood was simony. If it was the priesthood of idols, there is a question—unless perhaps we say that simony existed there because even “the priests of the high places,” on account of the dignity of the priesthood, necessarily had to preach by virtue of their office and possess upright character, as true priests do.

Likewise, the Lord in Luke, chapter XII: “Who do you think is the faithful servant,” or “the faithful and prudent steward?” (Luke XII). “Faithful,” by fulfilling what is necessary for salvation. Hence the Apostle: “Entrust these things to faithful persons, who will be able also to teach others” (II Timothy II): capable in life, learning, and eloquence.

“And prudent,” lest he give “what is holy to dogs” (Matthew VII). “Whom God has appointed,” through his authority and the ministry of the electors, namely through canonical election. Otherwise he is not sent by the Lord, of whom and of his like it is said: “All who came”—that is, not sent by God—“are thieves and robbers” (John X). It follows: “Over his household,” so that as he presides in dignity, so he may preside in uprightness of character. “That he may give them”—he is not placed over them in order to receive from them milk and wool, oil and dregs—but rather “that he may give them their measure of wheat,” that is, of the divine word, according to his hearers’ capacity, and this “in due season. For everything has its time: a time to keep silence and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes III). Constant preaching, however, becomes cheap.

Those otherwise set over the Lord’s household are like the priests of Bel (Daniel XIV), who, having broken the true door—Christ—as far as in them lies, enter by stealthy little doors, through filthy gifts, counted money, carnal affection, and the like, into the sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, eating, devouring, and carrying away the offerings of princes and peoples.

The words in Deuteronomy, chapter XX, may also be applied to such persons: “Who is the man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest perhaps he die in battle and another dedicate it. Who has planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common, so that all may be permitted to eat from it? Let him go and return to [Col. 0124D] his house, lest perhaps he die in battle and another perform his office. Or who is the man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go and return to his house, lest perhaps he die in battle and another take her.”

But these men undertake churches and ecclesiastical benefices and do not dedicate them through any work or service, and thus die in battle. They often plant within themselves good conduct and learning, but have not yet made it common to others by example and preaching; therefore, if they have not done these things, let them return to their house and church before being chosen for another. But now men are chosen who need teachers; although they ought to teach others, they themselves rather need to be taught by them—“like newborn infants,” who betroth churches to themselves while others know them carnally, by ministering and preaching in them.

Again, how great ought to be the purity and sincerity of canonical election is evident from the words and figures of Truth itself. See how purely and sincerely Joshua was chosen; how purely and sincerely the other judges were chosen (I Kings X); Saul also, though reprobate, was chosen as king, but given to the people in God’s anger, because they had asked for him (II Kings V). See most holy David, most sincerely “chosen from behind the nursing ewes” (Psalm LXXVII), and anointed king with a horn of oil. See Gideon reject the gluttons who drank in bovine fashion and the pleasure-loving, but choose the few and sober men—those who advanced in strength to battle against the Amalekites and lapped the ground (Judges VII). See in Numbers men aged twenty years and above chosen to fight valiantly against the Midianites (Numbers I). How much more should prelates, mature in age, spirit, and gravity of character, who advance valiantly to battle against invisible enemies, be chosen in the Church?

Likewise, this is evident from the word “to choose” itself. To choose is to select better things from among good things. Otherwise the chooser neglects, or rather prefers and casts down, than chooses. To show simony more clearly branded, let us posit the following definition, by which its roots may be made known. Simony occurs whenever something is done by a human being whereby a spiritual benefice is given not freely, or less than freely. I say “is done,” not “is.” For consanguinity is from nature and from God; it is not done by a human being. When a spiritual benefice is given to nature rather than grace, “flesh and blood reveals this” (Matthew XVI) to the giver, not the Spirit. This is not simony but a mortal sin of another kind. Whether one who thus receives a spiritual benefice in a church in preference to a worthier person is bound to resign it, I do not determine; for, if this were said, very great havoc would arise in the Church.

I say that something undue is done, such as a gift or a base service rendered or to be rendered. Due service is excluded: for example, when a person called to share responsibility for a bishop’s expenses serves the Church, so that the bishop may thereby ascertain his dignity, learning, virtues, and good character; if endowed with these, he confers an ecclesiastical benefice on him, and it is no less freely conferred on that account. The adverb “freely,” however, excludes expectation of a gift, service, or spiritual benefice to be conferred or already conferred, whether or not an agreement has intervened. “For God sees the heart” (I Kings XVI).

An agreement about the condition without which priestly office cannot be exercised in a church is not excluded. Before the church’s dedication, a bishop or priest makes an agreement with its patron for the provision of necessities of life for the ministers of the altar. This definition, then, includes the simoniacal plague and Gehazi’s leprosy, but not Korah’s violence, which breaks open the door of the Church. It is worse than the first two plagues. I would rather be a thief than a robber, a simoniac than a Korahite acting through the entreaties and extortions of princes.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the four kinds of spiritual things

[Col. 0126A]

There are four kinds of spiritual things.

1. Spiritual things through which the Holy Spirit is possessed, or is presumed to be possessed: such as virtues and miracles.

2. Spiritual things through which the grace of the Holy Spirit is conferred upon someone, or increased when already conferred: such as ecclesiastical sacraments—see the notes—apart from marriage; also orders and ecclesiastical offices.

3. Things annexed to spiritual things: things attached to ecclesiastical persons or churches, such as dignities, tithes, first-fruits of the field, and church revenues.

4. Consecrated vessels and vestments of the Church are called spiritual things.

The first are unobtainable by purchase, both in law and in fact. The second are unobtainable by purchase in law, though not in fact: they are sold, but produce simony. The third are unobtainable by purchase in law, except in cases to be discussed elsewhere. The fourth, if they can be melted down, may be sold when melted down to anyone; but otherwise only to ecclesiastical persons, not to laymen. For in the fifth distinction on consecration we are forbidden to convert into common uses things once dedicated to God, even consecrated timbers and stones of a church.

That temporal things may be offered for spiritual things appears from the end of Numbers XXXI. The children of Israel, approaching Moses, said: “For this reason we offer as gifts to the Lord, each man whatever gold he was able to find in the spoil: anklets, bracelets, rings, armlets, necklaces, that you may entreat the Lord for us.” Therefore, may money lawfully be demanded and given for trentals, anniversaries, [Col. 0126C] and such things? It is not so.

The answer is drawn from what follows: “Moses and Eleazar the priest received all the gold offered and brought it into the tabernacle of testimony as a memorial of the children of Israel before the Lord.” From this it is clear that money may be given to the Church as a memorial and encouragement, as a sign of the devotion of one seeking the Church’s intercessions and as an example to others; it is not given for spiritual things. Thus Peter too prays in heaven for someone, seeing that he draws near to God in devotion and deed, just as the Church prays for one who, as a sign of devotion and deed, requests its prayers and intercessions.

Therefore may I, for that reason, give to the Church so that I may be enrolled in it and receive prebends and revenues? It is not so. For a different reason on each side removes the agreement. The Church’s intercessions and prayers are necessary to salvation; salvation is possible without ecclesiastical revenues. One who gives little or nothing should be included in the Church’s intercessions equally with one who gives more, provided he seeks them devoutly and sincerely; otherwise shameful gain and venality would appear in the Church.

Second, money is given to a church for its need, for the sustenance of the ministers’ bodily necessities, for providing church lights, and similar purposes without which the divine office cannot rightly be celebrated there.

Third, money is sometimes given in a church—which must then be spent on pious causes, otherwise greed rather than justice demands it—not for spiritual things or an absolution to be conferred, [Col. 0127A] but as a penalty for sin, for punishment. In the first case every agreement and condition is excluded. In the second, an agreement is admitted: namely, that the priest may agree with the patron for the provision of necessities of life. Likewise, a priest lacking an ecclesiastical benefice may agree with another that he will minister in his church while he remains in the schools, concerning the provision of necessities sufficient for performing such an office: namely, that he may have not merely the means to live, but also the means to feed the poor, so that he may confirm by deed what he preaches by word.

Similarly, in the third case an agreement is admitted; but whether it occurs—perhaps is made—in the second or third case, it must be made so that the weak are not scandalized by it. A shameful, dishonourable, and greedy agreement is always excluded.

Since ecclesiastical offices belong to the class of spiritual things, a priest who sells his office—for example, by hiring out himself, his services, his work, and the church’s instruments—even for a nuptial blessing, commits simony. Likewise, one who takes in a church a poor dignity insufficient for his person, by attaching to it temporal emolument, when otherwise he would not submit his neck to the yoke, burden, and duty of performing that dignity, unless on account of an external addition or expected addition to the revenues, displays and declares not only the venality of the office but of his own person for performing it. Yet it is more shameful to sell oneself than something external. Likewise, on the same point, Cause I, Question 2: “With what pious disposition of mind,” etc.

Whether a dignity or ecclesiastical benefice acquired in this way must be resigned is a question. Just as an oral agreement concerning spiritual things is evidence of venality and actual simony before men, so a mental agreement is such before God and the angels, who speak only mentally. Simony, therefore, consists in expectation of a gift to be received, in the conception of giving that gift, and in the hope of each party: the giver of an ecclesiastical benefice hoping for recompense, and the recipient—or one hoping to receive—an ecclesiastical benefice. To give, however, is sometimes also to receive.

Whether one who has acquired an ecclesiastical benefice in this way is bound to resign it is asked. But since expectation and conception of gifts produce simony, what difference will there be in this case between simony and Gehazi’s leprosy? Simony is committed in the will, both of the one conceiving the intention to give and of the one expecting to receive; Gehazi’s leprosy, however, exists only in the act, namely when something is given or received.

Again, if expectation alone intervenes, when the recipient of an ecclesiastical benefice knows from indications that the giver expects recompense, even though the recipient has not conceived an intention to give, the recipient’s entry into that benefice is shameful, because it was not freely conferred upon him. But is he bound to resign it? If he did not know that a gift was expected, then, if the prelate is in need, he may and ought to give him aid.

But if a priest grants someone a portion or small fragment of ecclesiastical revenues as an annual pension for life, and that person sells it, will he be a simoniac? No; for such money belongs equally to a layman and a cleric. Even if church money is given by a priest to someone, that person is not thereby bound to perform divine or ecclesiastical office.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. In how many ways is simony committed?

Simony is committed by breaking the door, which is Christ, in three ways: by a gift from the hand, from the tongue, or from service. This distinction may be found in Gregory’s *Morals* (book IX, chapter 17), on the passage in Jeremiah (chapter XLVIII): “Cursed is everyone who does the work of God deceitfully,” namely, for the reward of a material thing, for a word of praise, or for the favour of human judgment.

For there is the coin of vainglory, the coin of pride, the coin of greed, and the coin of base service. But concerning this last, it is asked whether, without an express agreement, it produces simony. Certainly it does. But what of the rendering of honourable service? The philosopher seems indeed to intend this, saying (Seneca, *Letters*, 42):

> Therefore, in the things we pursue, toward which we strive with great labour, we must consider whether they contain no benefit at all, or more disadvantage than benefit.

Some things are superfluous; some are not worth so much. Yet we do not take this into account, and things that cost us exceedingly dearly seem free to us. Our folly may be seen from this: we think only those things are bought for which we pay money; we call free those [Col. 0128C] for which we expend ourselves—things which we would not wish to buy if we had to give our house for them, or a pleasant and fruitful estate. To attain them we are fully prepared to undergo anxiety, danger, loss of modesty, freedom, and time. So true is it that nothing is cheaper to anyone than himself. Therefore, in all plans and undertakings let us do what we are accustomed to do whenever we approach a dealer in some merchandise. Let us see at what price that which we desire is offered. Often the greatest price is that for which no money is paid. I can show you many things which, once acquired and received, have wrested freedom from us. We would be our own masters if those things were not ours.

But he seems to speak of labour following a conferred benefit, not of labour preceding it. Again: the coin of avarice, whether with an express [Col. 0128D] agreement or without one—when there is the wrongful hope, expectation, and intention of both giver and recipient—produces simony. Therefore does usury, and the coin of service rendered, [produce simony] without an agreement? Certainly, if the service rendered has been base. If it is honourable—for example, if the giver of an ecclesiastical benefice, in the recipient, considers favour, learning, uprightness, that is, Christ, rather than a temporal advantage rendered to himself through service—there will not be simony; provided that the recipient himself does not render the service with the intention of receiving a temporal reward.

Again: it is asked whether a mental agreement, with the hope of both parties—the giver and the recipient—which is at least wrongful before God, constitutes a fraudulent form of simony and produces a defective entry into a spiritual benefice. For example, [Col. 0129A] if an elderly uncle gives his church to his worthy, indeed honourable, nephew—though otherwise he would not give it—only in the hope of receiving the revenues and fruits of that church for as long as he lives; and if the nephew would not otherwise receive the spiritual benefice unless he gave the attached fruits to the giver: is one who thus holds an ecclesiastical benefice bound to resign it?

It is nevertheless clear that, if an oath has been sworn or is to be sworn concerning the concession of the fruits’ proceeds, and thus a verbal agreement intervenes, such an entry is defective. But what if someone’s election rests upon his having sworn, or promised to swear, that he will observe the customs of that church, and the like? “Blessed is he who is fearful in such matters” (Prov. 28).

Again: what if someone confers the administration of an ecclesiastical dignity upon another—though otherwise he would not confer it, nor would the other accept it—unless he grants that person its revenues for up to three years, in order to marry off the recipient’s sister: so that a spiritual thing is received and a temporal thing given?

Again: what of one resigning a church or prebend in order to confer it upon his nephew, whom the prelate compels to swear that he will not injure his uncle, [Col. 0129B] but will provide him with the necessities of life from its revenues? Many approve this and consider ungrateful one who refuses to provide necessities to his impoverished uncle—as though the uncle had received this benefice in that hope and with that intention, and another had conferred it upon him with the same intention.

Again: what if a prelate would not otherwise give ecclesiastical benefices to his younger nephews, and if the flesh also somewhat compels him to do this, unless he receives the revenues and fruits? In all these cases it is asked whether the entry is defective and simoniacal.

Again: whoever sells one of two things—the spiritual benefice and that which is attached to it—leaves neither unsold; and whoever buys one leaves neither unbought. Therefore whoever gives one gives the other also, and whoever receives one receives the other also. But suppose a prelate confers an ecclesiastical dignity on someone, though otherwise he would not confer it, unless he pledges its fruits for purchasing or redeeming the church’s lands or revenues, or grants them for a time for its building works or expenses. Then the other receives one thing and not the remainder, because he does not receive it immediately. The same objection applies to annual, biennial, triennial, and similar arrangements, [Col. 0129D] all of which seem to constitute an evasion of simony.

Here some distinguish, saying that sequestration of ecclesiastical goods effected by the common authority of the Church and for its benefit is lawful; but that which proceeds from a bishop’s private advantage and avarice is simoniacal.

Again: by this same rule, “Whoever sells one,” etc., others are convicted of receiving simoniacally—or at least unjustly—the fruits of some prebend for a year, together with another spiritual thing to which the fruits are attached, whether the appointed canon has served in the church during that year or not. If he has not served, then those who thus receive the fruits deprive that church for a whole year both of a servant and of service. If he has served, then they take away what is attached to the spiritual office and “muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain” (1 Cor. 9); and thus [Col. 0130A] one serving at the altar does not live by the altar, and one sowing spiritual things does not reap material things.

I think that, if this case were argued before a just judge, he would assign such a man at least a share of the revenues on which he could live. For it is unjust that someone should possess the whole spiritual office—singing in choir, entering chapter, ministering at the altar—yet not possess the whole of the things attached to it. Such things may not be expended even for pious causes. From the common portion of the church, indeed, such an annual alms might be assigned to monasteries or other religious places; but from the spiritual and individual portion belonging to a particular person in the church, it could not be.

But although a mental agreement arising on the part of both parties makes an entry defective, it makes it more defective when it comes from the one giving the ecclesiastical benefice. For it lies within his power and will to give or not give it. He is the door through which entry is made well or badly; let him see that it is not corrupted, so that the gift is not made freely. But if the recipient had intended to give a gift, either personally or through another, yet did not give it, and the prelate conferred the ecclesiastical benefice upon him sincerely and without any hope of a gift, let him receive it while doing penance for his wrongful intention; his entry will not be defective, since the integrity of the door remains. [Col. 0130B] For he received freely, and the other gave freely. Even if he had a wrongful and simoniacal intention before God, by repenting of it, since he did not bring it into effect, he acquires or possesses nothing simoniacally.

[Col. 0130C] Just as, if I intended to buy your daughter as my wife, but you gave her to me freely, I would have her as wife freely and without purchase.

Again: if theft from a church is hidden from its secret judgment—that is, the judgment of confession—it is nevertheless simply theft; and the confessor therefore commands what was taken to be restored. Hence hidden mental simony, that is, simony before the Church’s inward judgment rather than its outward judgment, is simony; and the benefice thus acquired must be resigned as one acquired by theft and in secret. For the confessor, as inward judge, ought to judge it to require restitution, since simony has been committed before God. But the judge of external cases will not judge this to be simony unless the accused publicly confesses it or is convicted of it.

Again: suppose someone approaching a church or monastery says: “I offer myself and my possessions to this church or monastery, to serve in it forever.” If he is received without distinction, his entry will be sound. But if more than he has offered is demanded from him, or if a distinction is made between his goods and himself, such that his goods are the reason why he is received, his entry will be defective. If, however, a distinction is made between his goods and himself, such that he is the reason why his goods are received together with him, his entry will be sound and lawful.

But if the monastery is so needy that it cannot receive or support one offering himself without money, it should grant him spiritual fraternity, not bodily incorporation; or, owing to its poverty and for his livelihood, it may require from him, in order to receive him, temporal revenues by which [Col. 0131A] he alone may be maintained for life. But if it demands perpetual revenues, manifest avarice then makes the entry defective. From this it is clear that no monastery ought to be built or founded without a definite number of lands, livestock, and persons. For when these have increased, it will be able to avoid the snares and avarices of simony only with difficulty.

What if I give something to members of the bishop’s household who are not well disposed toward me, so that they do not harm my reputation before him but keep silent, and do not help secure for me an ecclesiastical benefice? Since they have the sign of silence, advising the bishop makes the entry defective. What if they are not members of the bishop’s household, and yet I give them something so that they do not blacken my reputation? My entry will not be defective for that reason.

But what if I give something to the bishop’s doorkeeper so that I may enter his chapel, where I am to be ordained? No: since ordination is already due to me on account of the examination and my admission to the register that preceded it. Even if neither examination nor admission preceded, yet if I entered for this purpose in hope of ordination, because I am worthy to be ordained, my entry will not be defective if I give him something for this reason, because he has no responsibility for ordinations.

But simony spreads its branches from the altars in which it is rooted and nests, even to the doors and entrance into orders to be conferred. For the chaplain of the ordainer stands by, [Col. 0131B] so that, once the order has been conferred, he immediately snatches the forceps and towel from his hands, alleging that he receives them by custom; he also complains that he does not receive individual towels from every ordinand, and often, with sacrilegious hand, seizes from a widow what she borrowed.

The archdeacon likewise, for presenting one to be ordained, demands for his meal three solidi for a subdeacon, five or four for a deacon, and seven for a priest. But just as selling or buying the principal thing is simony, so also is selling or buying an accessory and all things joined to it which are due by reason of ecclesiastical office to the person upon whom the principal thing is conferred. Therefore selling a seal, a bell-rope (*canipulum*), justice, wax, and the like, unless poverty excuses it, is simony.

Hence Gregory, in Homily 39 on Luke 19, at the words, “And entering into the temple, he began to cast out those who sold and bought in it”: “Many, when they receive a place among the sacred orders because of the religious habit, turn the office of religion into the merchandise of earthly trade. He ‘sells a dove in the temple’ [John 2] who bestows as a reward that which is rightfully due to some persons. He ‘sells justice’ who observes it for the sake of receiving a reward. He ‘buys in the temple’ who, while withholding from his neighbour what he owes him by right, gives a reward to patrons so that they may support an unjust cause: he buys sin.” To such people it is said: “You have made my house a den of thieves” (Matt. 21; Luke 19). For through malice and avarice they kill where they ought to give life.

Again: it is asked whether it is simony to buy admission to this common fraternity, from which someone is expelled if he does not pay what he promised. It seems so, since spiritual things are joined to it, such as the solemn celebration of Masses, suffrages, and the prayers of the faithful; yet we do not determine this. [Col. 0132A]

Again: whether it is simoniacal for an abbot to buy a mitre, exemptions, and the like, so that he may not be subject to the bishop. It seems so, because these things are attached to spiritual matters—which indeed they are. Yet everyone, even in spiritual matters, may redeem his own right.
