Hence: throw away money, in order that you may buy paradise for yourself.

Again: it is asked whether it is simony to give a procuration or revenues to a college so that it may celebrate the feast of some saint with double rites, whereas previously it celebrated it only simply; or even to pay for the singing of a new and unaccustomed hymn, and the like. Here too there is no complete purity. Blessed Thomas of Canterbury, in order wholly to remove simony from his household, when appointing Master Arnulf as chancellor, bound him by oath that he would accept nothing, whether by agreement or without agreement, even as far as a bell-rope, for administering the office of chancellor. [Col. 0132B]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the punishment of simoniacs

The punishment of simoniacs follows. Gehazi was struck with leprosy because of the enormity of his crime (4 Kings 5). Simon was condemned to Gehenna. In the present life the sentence of his condemnation was pronounced: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8).

One man, in order to redeem the freedom of the Church, sold ecclesiastical rights and benefices to princes, and was deprived of his customary grace of preaching. Another, while conferring orders and saying, “In the name of the Father and of the Son,” failed at the third sign. For he became mute when he ought to have invoked “the Holy Spirit,” as though it were said to him: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10).

The accessory also is punished, just like the principal. Thus Cyriacus the deacon, when gifts were offered him so that he might come to cure the daughter of King Sapor, said: “Far be it from me that Christ’s grace should be made saleable through me! Go on ahead,” he said to the messengers; “I shall not mount a horse, as Christ did not, but shall follow you on foot.” [Col. 0132C]

A certain religious woman also, who ate almost nothing at all and was often carried away into ecstasy and angelic vision, accepted gifts from those making offerings, under the pretext of building a chapel and purchasing lands for the use of her monastery. She lost her former grace, her prophetic spirit, and the speech of angels. Many others too have been severely punished by God in many different ways.

## CHAPTER XL. On the exchange of spiritual things

[Col. 0132D]

The exchange of spiritual things follows, an exchange which is akin to the contract of buying and selling, and therefore seems to bear the mark of simony. In certain provinces, where money is scarce, the exchange of commodities takes the place of a contract of buying and selling: merchandise is received for merchandise, an animal for an animal. Thus exchange in spiritual matters does not seem very unlike buying and selling, nor unlike that which produces simony.

For this reason, by this commerce, an agreement of exchange—on account of which an ecclesiastical benefice is resigned, and on account of which and through which entry into another is opened—produces simony between the bishop who gives, provided that he knows of [Col. 0133A] this exchange, and the man resigning the benefice which the bishop confers upon his own nephew. Therefore it also produces simony between those resigning, even without the knowledge of the giving bishop. In that case—that is, when the bishop does not know of the agreement for this exchange—he will not give the benefice simoniacally to his nephew, but the latter will nevertheless acquire it simoniacally.

Again: by an exchange of this sort, especially of tithes redeemed from lay hands and of revenues derived from money-chests, any ecclesiastical benefice whatever could be obtained; and so all the prebends of some church could be acquired without simony through the exchange of such things. But this is false.

Again, Deuteronomy 22: “If anyone has taken a wife and seeks an occasion to dismiss her, after the elders of the city have learned this,” they shall punish him according to the law and adjudge her to him as wife, “so that he may not dismiss her all the days of his life.” Therefore, by analogy: if this man has lawfully obtained a church and seeks an occasion to leave it because another is richer and more productive, he ought to be punished according to the penalty established in the canons and remain in it all the days of his life. [Col. 0133B]

Nevertheless, note that the exchange both of persons and of benefices, when made by the authority of the Church and for its benefit, is permitted; but that which is made for temporal advantage, where one considers one’s own benefit more than that of the Church, seems to have a blemish. Yet I do not wish to “set my mouth against heaven” (Ps. 72), by asserting that this is simoniacal, since Pope Alexander II allowed an exchange of this kind to be made by dispensation, whether in writing or without writing, I do not know.

Again, the Lord says: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10). And again elsewhere: “If you have been invited to a dinner, recline in the lowest place, awaiting the moment when it may be said to you: Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14). And the Apostle: “No one takes the honour to himself,” etc. (Heb. 5). From these three passages it is gathered that “grace, unless given freely, is not grace” (Rom. 11).

But will there be some middle ground between being “called by God” and taking honour to oneself? Far from it! For you are not called by God unless you ascend through him, unless you receive freely; that is, in construing nothing as your own, you take honour to yourself. Whoever enters “by another way than through the door” (John 10), ascending by another way, is called by someone other than God.

But what if the breaking of the door exists only in the will and not in action? Repent of the intention, and retain the benefice received—received though it was with a bad intention, but nevertheless given freely. For I shall receive your book no less freely if you give it to me freely, even if I had intended to buy it. Therefore it is clear from this that an agreement concerning an increased pension—especially among regular clergy, since they do not have the care of souls and have a permanent vicar appointed or to be appointed—produces simony, if the question lies between a secular cleric and a permanent vicar. It would be safer for the pensions of both to be assigned and fixed. But an agreement between such a cleric and a temporary vicar does not produce simony, because necessity excuses it. [Col. 0134A]

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Korites

The Korites follow. They are those who intrude themselves into the Church through the entreaties and violence of secular or ecclesiastical princes, either because loss of temporal goods is feared, or bodily harm, or because princes are feared slavishly. Those so intruded commit a greater sin than simoniacs. For just as a robber is worse than a thief, because the latter is commanded to be put to death and the former to be flogged, so a Korite is worse than a simoniac: the latter enters the Church peacefully, namely by giving money; the Korite by violence, breaking the door.

Therefore, if where we do not offend we are equals, and if we are commanded not to lord it over the clergy, but are told: “Rule over the fish of the sea and the beasts of the earth” (Gen. 1)—that is, only over those who live beastly lives, not over those who live rightly and have committed nothing for which they ought to be rebuked—then even a greater lord cannot give the fiefs of a lesser lord or command him to give them; nor can a greater prelate command a lesser to give an ecclesiastical benefice. Nor can he himself give it, since it is the lesser’s to give, except in a particular case: namely, [Col. 0134B] as punishment for one who gives an ecclesiastical benefice badly. Then he could command that it be given to a better person.

Otherwise, those who issue commands of this sort, and who procure such exemptions and releases from the obedience due to a lesser prelate, do not seem to preserve the holiness or integrity of the door, but introduce particular schisms, from which will be forged that universal schism and separation from the Roman Church of which the Apostle says: “Unless the falling away comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2).

Yet I say this rather in fear and doubt than by assertion, “lest I set my mouth against heaven” (Ps. 72), especially since all the Church’s goods are in the power of the greater prelate—but only when the lesser prelate is at fault. [Col. 0134C]

## CHAPTER XLII. On the punishment of the Korites

The punishment of the Korites follows. Korah was consumed by fire sent from heaven, as a temporal sign of the eternal fire to follow (Num. 16), because he violently usurped the priestly office. Uzziah also, because he improperly touched the censer as if he were a priest, was struck with leprosy (2 Chron. 26); likewise Uzza, for touching the ark (2 Kings 6), and Miriam, Aaron’s sister, for slander alone (Num. 12). [Col. 0134D]

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the blood-relations who build Zion in blood

Just as the leprosy of Gehazi (4 Kings 5) corrupts the integrity of the door through which entry is made into the Church and into a spiritual benefice, so too do flesh and blood. For when something is given to blood, it is not given to grace but to nature. “For grace, unless it is given freely, is not grace” (Rom. 11). Therefore, just as Gehazi’s leprosy is an impediment preventing an ecclesiastical benefice from being given freely, so flesh and blood here also seem to be an impediment. I present these points more as objections and opinions than as assertions.

It may thus be objected against such givers that they are like Judas, who had two purses: the Lord’s purse, containing the possessions of the poor, and his own, into which he put things that he carried off for his wife and children. If he, because of theft as it were of one day, committed sacrilege and deserved to hang by a noose (John 12), how much more does one commit theft and sacrilege who gives the inheritance of the Crucified—intended for distribution to the poor—not merely for a time, to flesh and blood, but entrusts to his nephew for life the office of administering the possessions of the poor? He knows that his nephew will expend these things [Col. 0135B] not for the needs of the poor but upon ambition, vanity, and worldly luxury, and will thus defraud and despoil the poor—or rather Christ—of his possessions and goods.

Again: while it is said of those entering the Church through the door, “Who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John 1), it may be said of those entering through flesh and blood: they were born of blood and of the will of the flesh, not of God, in receiving ecclesiastical orders and benefices. There are, moreover, several births of ours. Just as in baptism we are born to God, so also in receiving the other sacraments. Such people cannot say: “My lots are in your hands” (Ps. 30). For the Lord’s will and good pleasure are not considered when Christ’s lot and inheritance are conferred upon them.

Again: in their case no lot is cast for the seamless garment of the Lord, to determine whose it shall be; rather, they tear it apart and seek no lot (John 19). For no lot is cast when an inheritance is left to a certain successor, and persons of blood succeed to the inheritance of the Crucified by something like hereditary right, rather than by the Lord’s lot.

Again: these people, as though crucifying the Lord in his members by distributing little or nothing, would at least divide his garments, casting lots upon them to determine who should take what. Of such people Micah says: “Woe to those who build Zion,” that is, the Church, “in blood” (Mic. 3), in sins; and who, through fleshly affections, give to flesh and blood, tending more to the destruction [Col. 0135D] of the Church than to its building. They are like hoopoes, which nest in their own dung.

Thus it may be objected to one giving an ecclesiastical benefice: because “flesh and blood reveal” to him that he ought to give in this way, not “my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16). Again: “Whoever does not hate father and mother for my sake”—that is, whoever does not set aside carnal affections and thus gives a spiritual office to nature—“is not worthy of God” (Luke 14).

Again the Lord says: “Who are my father and mother and brothers? And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: These are my mother and sister and brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father is himself brother and sister,” etc. (Matt. 10; Matt. 12). It is as though he said: the spiritual man does not know carnal relations. As if saying to father and mother: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25), he shows himself to us as especially to be imitated in conferring spiritual things. For this reason also he placed Peter above John, though Peter was born from another tribe (John 21).

Again, Jerome: “Moses, the friend of God,” etc., above, almost at the beginning under this same heading.

Again: if one of the seven deacons, during the week of his turn, did not distribute to the poor “according as each had need,” those goods of which “all things were common” (Acts 4), but held them back, or part of them, so that the poor might not be fed, for his wife and children: who is so devoid of reason as not to believe that he would immediately be struck by Peter with the same thunderbolt and terror by which Ananias and Sapphira were struck, and with the same curse that struck Simon Magus? (Acts 5.)

Therefore do not establish your nephew as a pillar of the Church; nevertheless, you may assign him an ecclesiastical benefice from which he may be supported. But what if he is as honourable and worthy as a stranger? Even this is dangerous unless his uprightness requires it and excludes every suspicion of disgrace, scandal, and bad example—a thing not easily achieved. [Col. 0136B] For an example is drawn not from the good deeds we perform but from their outward bark, appearance, and surface, not from their truth. If I have given to my nephew out of favour, others will use my example to give to theirs from natural affection rather than grace, saying: “Shall I not give to my own as he gave to his? I gave from grace; let him give from nature.”

From the foregoing it is apparent how far we have departed from the cradle of the primitive Church in conferring the administration and stewardship of the poor’s goods, following custom rather than the ancient saints, as though defending ourselves by prescription. But can one who has acquired an ecclesiastical benefice in this way die securely while retaining it, that is, without resigning it? It is not mine to determine this, lest “I set my mouth against heaven.” [Col. 0136C]

## CHAPTER XLIV. Against those who withdraw themselves from the jurisdiction of their prelates

Those are like the Korites who, as if through a kind of violence, exempt and withdraw themselves from the jurisdiction and obedience of their lesser prelate by the authority of a greater one (Ps. 72). Against such quasi-schismatics stands the Apostle’s passage in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 12, concerning the unity and mutual, due performance of office by the members of the human body serving one another. Since the human body has many necessary and mutually serviceable members, lest the body perish—as it would if all its members were a single member—“the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of your works; nor the head to the feet, You are not necessary to me.” Nor can the more excellent member command the inferior not to be necessary to the others, nor to serve and obey the intermediate members. Therefore this unity should much more be observed among the spiritual members of the Church, so that no member’s office or obedience may be exempted or withdrawn from the jurisdiction, service, and rule of the lesser [Col. 0136D] prelate by the authority and for the advantage of the greater.

Again, Saint Bernard, in the authoritative and useful little book entitled *On Consideration* (Book III, at the end), says: “If a Seraph wished to command thrones and dominions not to be inferior to cherubim, nor subject to that order as superior, but to answer directly to themselves as though in the first rank, would the monk who ordered them thus, namely so that one order should be inferior to another, endure this? Far from it! Rather, I think, he would punish such a one more severely than Lucifer was punished, when he desired dominion and exemption from the Lord’s jurisdiction” (Isa. 14). Though he was first “in the delights of paradise” (Ezek. 28), he remains, on that account, last amid the punishments of hell.

Again, it is related and read that this same Bernard was very eager, in zeal for uprooting this enormity and exemption from the Church, to sit in the papal see for three years, chiefly for three reasons: namely, to summon bishops back to their metropolitan, that they might be subject and obedient to him; and exempt abbots back to their bishops, that they might serve under their jurisdiction. [Col. 0137B] Second, that no one in the Church should hold two dignities. Third, that no monk should live in a cell or elsewhere outside the community.

Again: at Jethro’s counsel Moses appointed leaders of tens, hundreds, fifties, and thousands over the people (Exod. 18); but all these things were done as a figure of the Church. Would Moses not have sinned had he confused the offices and jurisdictions of individuals? Nor did he permit appeals from one to another, lest they should be defrauded or deprived of the offices assigned to them; only when some question arose did he command that it be referred to himself, or to Hur, or to Aaron. Therefore this exemption from the jurisdiction of the ordinary prelate must much more be avoided in the Church, lest confusion and the rending of offices through exemptions of this kind produce schisms and divisions of ecclesiastical unity.

Again, Romans 13: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.” He does not say “to the power,” but “to the powers ordained by God” in the Church; those “who resist” them “resist God’s ordinance.” Again, Hebrews 13: “Obey your rulers and be subject to them,” whether lesser or greater. How, then, does a greater prelate emancipate someone from the jurisdiction and power of a lesser, so that he is not bound to obey him?

Again: if an exemption and emancipation of this kind is not lawful to secular power, it is much less lawful to ecclesiastical power, since spiritual affairs ought to possess greater equity than secular ones. For example, a greater prince cannot emancipate anyone from the jurisdiction, power, fief, and homage of a lesser lord except after investigation of the case, as when he has committed a crime deserving either hanging or exile. But neither is the Church a person capable of being punished personally; and, if its prelate has sinned, even if the whole present Church itself has sinned, the sin of the prelate—or even of the present Church—ought not to redound to the loss of the future Church or its future prelates, since they too may be good. Therefore such emancipation in spiritual matters is not lawful even if the prelate has sinned.

Therefore, since one person is bound by homage to a secular and lesser lord, from whom he cannot be released by a greater except after investigation of the cause, and another is bound by obedience to the lesser prelate appointed over him, [Col. 0138A] even if the greater releases him through favouritism or for some other such reason—

Again: a greater prelate cannot permanently deprive a church of its office or of the conferral of sacraments, saying, “I do not wish you ever to confer this or that sacrament on anyone”; therefore neither can he deprive it of jurisdiction, of the conferral of orders, and especially of a noble member of that Church.

Again: when someone justly excommunicated by a lesser prelate is bound in such a way that he cannot be absolved by a greater, either before God or before the Church, except after investigation of the cause, worthy satisfaction, and the consent of the lesser prelate who bound him, then one who is justly subject to a church by ecclesiastical ordering cannot be emancipated and exempted from the jurisdiction and power of the lesser by the authority of the greater, except with the consent of the lesser and also of his church, and for a definite reason, such as the benefit of both. [Col. 0138B]

Again, Wisdom 1: “Love justice, you who judge the earth,” that is, earthly things, in which you are appointed judges and superiors over offenders, subjects, and inferiors.

What is heavenly and holy you neither possess nor can judge, in which respect you are equals of just lesser persons; for where we do not sin, we are equals. Therefore neither may a superior ordain anything in the diocese of an inferior, nor emancipate anyone from his jurisdiction, unless the latter has sinned gravely through negligence or in some other way. Yet even then the personal fault does not redound [Col. 0138C] to the harm of the Church. This equality of the lesser with the greater—except where the lesser has sinned—is also shown by the name of brotherhood. For the greater writes to the lesser as to a fellow brother. Again (II Cor. XIII): “We who are greater can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.” But the truth is that this church was, or is, subject to that one; therefore a superior prelate can do nothing against this truth.

Again, in Judges VIII: the private ephod which Gideon made from the earrings and spoil of the children of Israel, which they had taken from the Ishmaelites and Ammonites, became the ruin of Gideon and of his whole household. This private ephod is a private ring, a private mitre, an abbatial mitre, and things of this sort pertaining to private exemptions.

Again, Joshua, chapter XXII: the Lord commanded the children of [Col. 0138D] Israel to set up for him a single altar in the land of promise; but the Reubenites set up another beyond the Jordan. Israel, offended at this, marshalled an army against their Reubenite brothers, saying to them through priestly envoys: “Why have you erected a sacrilegious altar against the altar of the Lord? For this we shall fight against you and cast down the sacrilegious altar.” They answered: “We erected an altar as a memorial of the Lord, not that we might sacrifice to the Lord upon it, but as a testimony that the Lord is with us and that we might invoke his name there; for it is burdensome for us to go so often to Shiloh, to Gilgal, where there is that small altar for sacrifices made by Moses, to which nevertheless they used to come when they wished to sacrifice.” But now not merely one altar is erected against the greater [Col. 0139A] and episcopal altar, but three or five, so that justice may perish and obedience perish as well.

Again: since every province has its metropolitan and every diocese its bishop, it seems absurd and monstrous that a church or an abbot should be within the bishopric of a given bishop and belong to his bishopric, yet not be under the bishop of that diocese and subject to him, although he belongs to, and is within, that bishop’s bishopric.

Again, according to the order and nature of things, the most general genus cannot command the most specific species without that species being subject to the intermediate genus.

Again, concerning the mystical significance of the abbatial mitre, the question is asked: if the horns of the mitre on the abbot’s head signify the Old and New Testaments, then, if any question should arise (Exod. XXIV), must it be referred to him as to a [Col. 0139B] bishop? Likewise, he seems to be the leader of the flock who scatters enemies with the horns of the Old and New Testaments. But if they signify nothing, then the abbot’s mitre is empty, superfluous, and childish, like the mitre made from a slip of paper for a boy during the recitation of a miracle-story. If his ring likewise has the same significance as a bishop’s ring, is he then the Church’s bridegroom and paranymph? Concerning the lappets of the mitre and his sandals too, it is asked what meaning they have, and likewise concerning the blessing by which he is blessed as abbot—what kind it is, and whether it may be repeated.

Master Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, says of this blessing that it is simple, like a blessing spoken over food; for it is not conferred with the laying on [Col. 0139C] of hands, and therefore may be repeated. Or an abbot who has once been blessed and then deposed may exercise the office of abbot without a repetition of the blessing. But how does he lay hands on others, up to the diaconate? He seems almost to send men ordained by himself into the Lord’s vineyard (Matt. XX), like a bishop. How also does he have power over convening and celebrating a synod of priests or a chapter, as Saint Bernard and other religious men maintained?

It is to be feared that these exemptions and particular divisions may produce a universal separation from the Roman spiritual realm—a separation already made in part from the Roman material realm—of which the Apostle says: “Unless the apostasy comes first, and the man of sin, the son of [Col. 0139D] perdition, is revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God,” etc. (II Thess. II). Master Gilbert used to call exempt abbots of this kind schismatics.

But someone will say to me: “You set your mouth against heaven” (Ps. LXXII). I answer: No. I introduce these points not by asserting them, but by raising objections. For I may not say to the lord pope, “Why do you do thus?” For it is sacrilege to rebuke and censure his actions. Nevertheless, I do not see the resolution of these matters, or the way in which they may be answered. Yet I know that no such division and exemption exists in the Church by the authority of either the old or the new canon, but by the special authority of the Apostolic See, which the Lord does not permit to err. Perhaps, led by the prompting and familiar counsel of the Holy Spirit and by a private law, it [Col. 0140A] does this, as Samson killed himself together with his enemies (Judg. XVI); but in this way consuls and proconsuls have been removed from the midst, so that few or none may rule, and Caesar alone may be everything, ruling everything as though he ruled all.

## Chapter XLV. Against flatterers

As Gregory testifies (*Morals*, book XII, ch. 25), just as payment by gift or money amounts to simony, so too does payment for obsequious or base service—namely, flattery. For a gift is conferred freely; but that is not a gift of grace which is bestowed as much through fault as through money or natural advantage.

The Prophet, condemning the plague of flattery, says in Psalm CVIII: “He clothed himself with cursing as with a garment, and it entered [Col. 0140B] like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones.” Flattery, says Augustine, is both oil and a curse, because it gives pleasure and prepares torments. And Psalm CXL: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat.” Augustine: the oil is the flatterer’s false praise and feigned affection, which softens minds from the rigor of truth. These are the sellers of oil, who lift up falling words.

Seneca (*Letters*, 20): “Oh, when will that day come when no one will lie in your honor?” For this reason poverty is to be loved: it finds no flattery, whereas riches foster it. Hence David, Psalm CIV: “Their land brought forth frogs in the inner chambers of their kings.” Frogs are babbling and talkative flatterers. The poet, execrating their chattering [Col. 0140C] and flattery, says:

> A crowd of greeters makes your spacious halls resound;  
> Here, the song of birds; there, the murmurs of a gliding stream.  
> —Claudian, *Against Rufinus*, book I

These are gnats. Hence it follows: “He spoke, and there came dog-flies and gnats,” which sting secretly and yet do more harm than dog-flies; likewise flattery does more harm than detraction. Hence Psalm LXIX: “Let them immediately be turned back and ashamed who say to me, ‘Well done, well done!’” Augustine: there are two kinds of persecutors, namely those who blame and those who flatter; but the flatterer’s tongue persecutes more than the murderer’s hand.

Both blame—that is, detraction—and praise are a fire in which a man, like gold, is tested in a furnace: he is tried by reproach or praise. He comes out whole who is carried away by neither. And Psalm XXXIX: “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ immediately bear their confusion”—those who applaud me flatteringly for what is good in me. Again, in Lamentations, first chapter, Aleph, He: “Her enemies have become the head,” because flatterers blind the rulers and heads of the Church, and:

> When the head is sick, the other members suffer.

For the error of a ruler is drawn into example. Again: that the sweetness and levity of flattery do more harm than the bitterness of detraction is evident, because no one is so stern, hard, and secure that he is not sometimes caught by this plague, in which he seems to delight if he does not immediately repel it. You may also argue this [Col. 0141A] from Psalm CXIX: “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips,” which detract and discourage what ought to be done, “and from a deceitful tongue,” which presses and harms more by praising, under the disguised appearance of advice, so that you fall when you have begun to ascend. Hence the Prophet, seeking a remedy against it—or the Lord speaking to him—adds: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against the deceitful,” that is, flattering, “tongue? Sharp arrows of a mighty one with desolating coals.” This is the remedy.

Again, Psalm XXXIII: “Keep your tongue from evil,” namely detraction, “and your lips from speaking deceit,” namely flattery. By this deceit the first human being fell, whose root remains in his descendants because he consented to the flattering devil when he said to him, under the disguised appearance of counsel: “On whatever [Col. 0141B] day you eat of it, you shall be like gods” (Gen. III). By this deceit diabolical pride is exalted in man, so that, presuming upon himself, he says: “I shall ascend into heaven, and set my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). Hence:

> And consume your turbot, preserved for ages to come.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires*, IV

The poet says:

> He wanted to be caught—what could be clearer? Yet his crests  
> rose high: there is nothing that a person cannot believe about himself  
> when power equal to the gods is praised.

These are the actors, of whom the same poet says:

> It is an actor-nation. You laugh? It is shaken by a louder roar  
> of laughter. It weeps if it sees a friend’s tears;  
> it does not feel cold, but if you ask for a little fire in winter,  
> it takes a cloak; if you say, “I am hot,” it sweats.  
> Therefore we are not equals: the better man is he who always,  
> night and day, can assume another’s face,  
> toss his hand from his face, and stand ready to praise  
> if his master has belched well.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires*, III

But they also teach others to flatter, saying:

> Even if there is no dust, nonetheless shake off no one.  
> —Ovid

And the philosopher says (Seneca, *On Benefits*, VI.30): riches are to be feared for this one reason, because flattery accompanies them, and a rich man finds no one to tell him the truth. For this reason poverty is especially to be loved, because it reveals by whom you are loved (the same author, *Letters*, 20). For a man’s fortune has no flattery as its companion: it loves his condition, not his person.

The same author (*On Benefits*, VI.31): not even in Xerxes’ vast army was anyone found who would tell him the truth, except one. Some asserted that the seas were not sufficient to contain his fleet; others, that the air was insufficient for the hail of his missiles; and so forth. Demaratus the philosopher alone approached and told him the truth in these words: “You will be defeated by yourself and will not perceive it. For this mass of yours will crush you. Things without limit can scarcely be ruled.” These are Sirens, sweet even unto destruction (Ps. LVII). Jerome says of them: “As we journey toward our homeland, we must pass the deadly songs of the Sirens with a deaf ear,” “stopping our ears like the asp,” smearing them with pitch, as Ulysses and his companions did.

These are theatrical little harlots, whom human philosophy drove away from itself in Boethius [Col. 0142A] (*Consolation of Philosophy*, I, prose 1), and much more should heavenly philosophy do so. Solomon says of them: “Honey and milk are under the harlot’s tongue” (Prov. V), “but in the mouth of the holy is a sword and death.” And Boethius (*Consolation of Philosophy*): “No plague is more effective for harm than a familiar enemy.” Such are all friends and all enemies: “A man’s enemies are his own household” (Matt. X)—his flatterers. Of them the Lord says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV). And David: “They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him” (Ps. LXXVII). And again: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul,” by the flatterer, “and the wicked man is blessed,” etc. (Ps. IX, v. 24). Again: “Unjust witnesses rose up against me” (Ps. XXVI)—[Col. 0142B] flatterers, worse than false accusers, detractors, and revilers—“and iniquity lied to itself.”

Again, the poet Juvenal, on the blind flatterer who blinded others:

> No one was more astonished at the turbot. For he said many things  
> to the left; but the monster lay at his right.  
> —*Satires*, IV

Hence Jerome: every flatterer is blind in mind, who for earthly gain, favor, and glory kills both his own soul and another’s. They are like Joab, who, taking Amasa by the chin and pretending friendship in a kiss of peace, struck him in the groin with a marvelously fashioned and hidden sword, and poured out his entrails (II Kings XX). For flattery is a hidden poison [Col. 0142C] and sword: it harms greatly and is not feared.

Again, Jeremiah XXXVIII: “O Zedekiah! Your peaceful men”—that is, the prophets, your flatterers—“have deceived you and prevailed against you, saying: ‘Let there be peace in our days.’ They have sunk your feet in mire and slipperiness, and have withdrawn from you.” For:

> While you are fortunate, you will count many friends;  
> when times have become cloudy, you will be alone.  
> —Ovid, *Tristia*, I.8

Again, in Proverbs, chapter I: “My son, if sinners”—that is, flatterers—“entice you, do not consent to them.”

Again: just as Joab deceitfully killed Amasa, so Abner son of Ner, as though about to kiss him (II Kings XX), called him aside from David’s army, as though to speak with him more privately, and killed him out of envy because David had appointed him commander of the army over Abner’s own force. The flatterer is like him. For every flatterer is a traitor, a Judas and a Joab (II Kings III): the traitor in a kiss, the flatterer in a word. “For the harsh wounds of a friend are better than the kisses” of a flatterer (Matt. XXVI).

Again: that flattery is detestable is clear from the fact that it is the tinder and nurse of pride, which is the greatest sin (Prov. XXVII). Hence David: “And I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin” (Ps. L). Again, because it is the tinder and nurse of ignorance, which is a most dangerous sin. For a disease that is not exposed is not healed.

Again, the plague of flattery has so broken in and advanced that it corrupts even words and the art of composition, introducing tropes, solecisms, and certain metaplasms contrary to the rules for joining words and to the nature of speech: using the plural for the singular; and when we speak to God in the singular, speaking to a human being in the plural. For we lie to lords so thoroughly that, flattering them, we corrupt the authorities of sacred Scripture by applying them to them. This plague has even gained such strength that it corrupts the most effective argument by which the Trinity of persons is proved: namely, “Let us make [Col. 0143A] man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I.25). When it says “let us make,” it requires a plurality of persons; when it says “image,” unity of essence. But now we put this word “let us make” in the plural number, and similarly other words, where there is no plurality or distinction of persons, nor even a concept—unless you choose to call it a concept of flattery, of several dignities, or of excellence. Thus this most pernicious metaplasm has become established, so that the plurality of persons can no longer be proved when “let us make” is said, since we use the plural indiscriminately for one person and one nature, as though for several persons and several natures.

Hence also in the Fourth Council of Carthage, distinction 56, it is read: “A cleric found to occupy himself with flatteries or betrayal shall be degraded from office.” And Jerome, in the letter beginning “Hear, daughter, and see,” etc. (Ps. XLIV), says: “Do not incline your ear to words of wickedness” (*Letter to Eustochium, On the Guarding of Virginity*). For one who speaks something indecent often tests the judgment of the mind: whether you willingly hear such things, namely that you are called a virgin and the like; whether you should by chance lapse at some time into a ridiculous word. Whatever [Col. 0143C] you say, they praise; whatever you deny, they deny. They call you quiet, holy, and one in whom there is no deceit: “Behold, truly a handmaid of God,” they say; “behold, complete simplicity—not like that dreadful, ugly, rustic, terrifying woman, who perhaps has no husband because she could not find one.” We are led by a natural evil when we gladly favor our flatterers. And although we answer that we are unworthy in those things for which they praise us, and a hot blush covers our faces when we hear a lie spoken in our praise, nevertheless the soul inwardly rejoices at its own praise.

Again, Ecclesiasticus, chapter XIII: “When the rich man is deceived, many come to his aid; he has spoken proudly, and they have justified him. The humble man is deceived,” or falls, “and is further rebuked; he has spoken sensibly, and no place is given him. The rich man has spoken, and all are silent, and they raise his word to the clouds. The poor man has spoken, and they say, ‘Who is this?’ And if he stumbles, they will overthrow him.”

Again, Psalm LIV: “His words were smoother than oil, and yet they are darts.” Cassiodorus: flatterers shall be separated from the wrath of the Lord’s countenance in the future, when in the final winnowing he separates the chaff from the grain. And why? Because they “made their words smoother” by flattery “than oil”: so that, as nothing is lighter than oil, the smoothness of flattery is said to surpass even this; and conversely it is to be understood that no equal can be found for so great a crime.

Again, Deuteronomy XIV: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.” And Exodus XXIII; likewise II Kings XX; Song of Love, chapter I: “O beautiful one, if you do not know yourself”—that is, because you do not know yourself, delighting in falsehood and flattery—“go out” from my company “and go after the tracks of your flocks, and feed your kids.” Again, Isaiah III: “My people, those who call you blessed,” etc.

## Chapter XLVI. On recipients of unlawfully acquired gifts

It has been said (chapters 21 and 22) concerning the principal and primary recipients of unlawful gifts, and also of lawful gifts, by which freedom seems to be sold. It remains to speak of secondary recipients, namely those who receive something from the first recipients. That the matters to be proposed may be clearer, a distinction must be made among unlawfully acquired things.

Some things are unlawfully acquired and unjustly retained, and cannot be spent even on pious causes. For we cannot transfer to others things over which we have no right of ownership. How can we confer upon others what we are bound to restore? Sin is not remitted unless what has been taken is restored; nor is repentance performed while such things are retained—it is feigned (Augustine, *Letter* 54, to Macedonius; also found in 14, question 6, *Si res aliena*). Such are things acquired through simony, theft, usury, and robbery. Concerning these, see *First Cause*, question 1, “Non est putanda,” and Cause 14, question 5, chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4.

But some things are unjustly acquired and not unjustly retained once the fault is purged—that is, when a person repents of what he acquired wrongly. Since [Col. 0144C] the thing is no longer tainted, because it is acquired with the willing and knowing consent of its owner, once the evil manner of acquisition has been purged, and thus its cause has ceased, the effect also ceases: namely, the obstacle to its being expended on pious causes. Where there is shamefulness on both sides, namely of giver and receiver, the possessor’s case is stronger, because neither does the giver have a right of recovery nor the receiver an obligation of restitution. Even under human laws, if someone contracts with a prostitute, advocate, or the like to give ten shillings, he is compelled by a civil judge to pay it. Therefore things acquired by an actor, mime, prostitute, advocate, physician, or soldier, under the terms of the profession or military service, according to its proper art, and without subsequent fraud, may be spent on pious causes.

But if someone receives ten [Col. 0144D] in order to kill a person with a sword or administer poison to him, may I receive from this gift so received? By that rule it appears that I may: “Where shamefulness is equal, the possessor’s case is stronger,” especially after the fault has been purged. And it likewise appears that one may receive from a simoniac. But this is not so; nor is it the same in homicide, the administering of poison, and similar most atrocious crimes.

That no one may receive from secondary recipients of unlawful gifts whose restitution is commanded will thus be evident. First, by the example of Stephen, the second abbot in the Cistercian order. When the brothers had no sustenance for one day, he went with one lay brother to a neighboring village. As they begged separately and sought food for the brothers, one man gave cakes to the lay brother, another cheeses, another a cask of wine. The abbot received these from him and loaded them upon the ass on which he rode. On their return, while chanting psalms and praying, he carefully asked the lay brother from whom he had received alms. After naming many, the lay brother said that he had received alms from the priest of that village. When the abbot heard this, he immediately distributed all the goods to shepherds and poor people whom they encountered. The lay brother said to him: “Far be it, my abbot, that you should do this. The brothers at home are dying of hunger.” The abbot replied: “That priest is a simoniac, and we ought to receive nothing from such persons, after the example of Tobit. Though in extreme poverty, when he heard the bleating of a kid which his wife had brought home to make him a dish, he said: ‘See whether it is stolen; but return it to its owners, for we are children of the saints, and it is not permitted us to eat or touch anything from theft’” (Tob. II).

But modern religious persons everywhere receive offered gifts from anyone whatever, misusing that apostolic authority: “Asking no questions for conscience’ sake” (I Cor. X). To condemn this form of avarice more sharply, one must examine its root, which consists in the acquisition of a thing first acquired or retained corruptly. Rebuking primary recipients of this kind through John the Baptist, the Lord says in Luke to the tax collectors who came to him to be baptized. They said to him: “Master, what shall we do, lest we fall away and be cast into the fire?” “Do nothing beyond what has been appointed for you” (Luke III). Ambrose and Bede read [Col. 0145C] another translation: “Exact nothing beyond what has been prescribed,” whether money, compulsory services (*angariae*), or by means of forced labor. But how “beyond what has been prescribed” or appointed? Do you understand the prescription or appointment of divine or human law? If divine law, then in the passage, “That they may perform the judgment written” (Ps. CXLIX), you will make all possessors of houses, villages, and fields transgressors. If human law, made by the authority of the ruler with the people’s consent, you will find no boundary or limit in law of this sort; rather, you will turn our avarice, evil customs, snares, and nets of avarice into law. This too has been done today.

The soldiers also asked, saying: “What shall we do?” And he said to them: “Do violence to no one”—for you have this power, which the crowd does not—“and make no false accusation; and be content with your wages” (Luke III), the wages assigned to military service. Do not seek plunder through false accusation or exaction, “but be content with your wages.” But to the crowds he said: “He who has two tunics, let him give one to him who has none” (ibid.). As though saying: no office, sex, condition, or age is excluded from performing mercy. For this is commanded to all.

This, therefore, will be your form and rule for distinguishing from whom it is permissible to receive and from whom it is not. Receive nothing from anyone which you know that person has received beyond what is prescribed. Nor receive it even if it has passed through a hundred hands, so long as it remains tainted and must be restored. This is apparently proved by Tobit’s words when he says: “See whether it is stolen, but return it to its owners” (Tob. II). He does not say, “See whether you have stolen it,” but “whether it is stolen”—that is, whether it was first taken by theft by you or by any other person. “For we are children of the saints, and it is not permitted us to eat, consume, or touch anything from theft” (ibid.).

Likewise by the example of Saint Fursey, who had received a funeral garment from someone. But should I not receive wages from my lord, or payment of a debt from money that is mixed—tainted and untainted money mingled together? It appears that I should not, by the example of Saint Launomarus, mentioned above in the first heading on avarice.

Again, Jerome: “Nothing is to be received from those whom we know to live upon the tears of the poor, lest it be said to you: ‘If you saw a thief, you ran with him’” (Ps. XLIX). And Isaiah says: “Woe to the sinful nation, to the people weighed down with iniquity, to the wicked seed, to criminal children: they have forsaken the Lord, blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, and turned away backward” (Isa. I). Thus Jerome excludes persons when he says “those whom,” not “things which,” we know to live on the tears of the poor—“those whom,” etc. He excludes the utterly corrupt giver only when his offering is small; sometimes he is not even repelled from the Eucharist and private communion among others, unless he persists. But if he were not going to offer a large sum of money, he would be excluded, as would a notorious and publicly known person through whom, if anything were received, scandal would arise.

Again, by the example of Master Peter Abelard, who refused to receive from Count Theobald anything to distribute among his companions unless it had been taken from unalloyed revenues; he said that goods coming from other sources he would give to dogs, beasts, and the birds of heaven.

Again, Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXXIV: “The offering of one who sacrifices from unjust gain is defiled, and the mockeries of the unjust are not pleasing to God”—that is, offerings for which the Lord mocks them—because “the Most High does not approve the gifts of the unjust, nor look upon the offerings of the wicked. [Col. 0146C] For he who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who slays a son before his father’s eyes.” The gloss: “How detestable is the sacrifice which is compared to the bereaved father’s grief!”

Again, Jerome (*Letter to Nepotian, On the Life of Clerics*, chapter 11): those who receive gifts from robbers, simoniacs, and usurers are like those who devour and eat smaller fish that have been swallowed by larger ones. For just as fish thus swallowed are fit for no use, so the offering of such persons is fit for no use or religious purpose.

Again: such persons are like Achan and his companions, who, contrary to the Lord’s command, stole a gold bar from the accursed spoil of Jericho (Josh. VII). What has been unjustly acquired should not be offered but anathematized—that is, suspended and removed from human use—because it must be restored. Good use does not justify what has been badly acquired. Jerome (question 5, *Neque enim*): “It must be carefully examined and guarded against, lest anyone take anything from what is accursed, lest many perish because of it.”

Again: those who, under the pretext of religion or poverty, receive gifts from such persons are like Gideon, who accepted from the people earrings and every kind of [Col. 0147A] gold from the spoil of the Midianites in order to make from it an ephod and teraphim; “and this became the ruin of Gideon and of his whole household” (Judg. VIII). Again: they are like Saul, whom “the Lord cast away from his presence, that he should not be king in Israel” (I Kings XV), because contrary to his command he had kept Agag, the very fat king, and the choicest things from the Amalekites’ spoil in order to sacrifice them to the Lord.

Again Isaiah, chapter I: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord? I am full. I have not desired your burnt offerings.” Jerome, expounding this passage in chapter I of Isaiah in two ways, says: “This may also be understood of those who offer robbery or avarice upon altars or distribute it to the poor.” Again: “Honor the Lord from all your substance” (Prov. [Col. 0147B] III), that is, from what has been lawfully acquired. For what has been unlawfully acquired is not yours, because it must be restored. Nor is even lawfully acquired property yours, if you have not otherwise retained enough to restore what you have taken. For only that is counted among someone’s goods which remains to him after his debt has been deducted.

Therefore the rule is this: what has been unlawfully acquired must never be accepted from anyone, except for the sake of preaching by which he may be converted, or except in extreme necessity; nor may even lawfully acquired goods be accepted unless there remains to him sufficient and safe means from which to restore what he has taken or pay his debts. Things received against this rule, I believe, must be restored by the recipient.

But if they object with the Apostle’s authority, namely, “Asking no questions for conscience’ sake” (I Cor. X), we say that this is to be understood concerning food sacrificed to idols. Moreover, such people are like those sitting and eating in an idol’s temple, because, to the scandal of their brothers, they receive from those who offer them robberies and similar unlawfully acquired goods, when these ought rather to be restored. Again: those who act and those who consent sin alike; and consenting parties who receive from such unrebuked persons are to be punished with equal punishment. Again, Ephesians IV: “Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, that he may have something to give to one suffering need.”

## Chapter XLVII. Against those who give to persons not in need
To receive goods unlawfully acquired under the pretext of religion or poverty has been discussed. We shall now show that it is unlawful for one who is not in need to receive even lawfully acquired goods [Col. 0147D], or for anyone to give them to such a person. Since these two matters are connected, we shall first show that one ought not give to those who are not needy. Hence Prosper, in his book *On the Contemplative Life* (book II, ch. 10): “A pastor of the Church ought not distribute anything to those for whom their own resources suffice, since to give to those who already possess is nothing other than to waste.”

Likewise Jerome (letter to Pammachius, *To the Wounded Sanatus*): “It is sacrilege to give the goods of the poor to those who are not poor.” And again (letter to Nepotian, at the end): “One should give to the poor, not to those who belch after eating; not to those who cook pheasant birds in slow vapours; not to parasites, not to loafers, not to those living in idleness and on another’s food.” Another’s food is food not earned by one’s own labour.

Likewise [Col. 0148A], the Prophet says of Christ: “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111 [112]). And the Blessed Virgin says in her canticle: “He has filled the hungry with good things, and has sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1). Likewise, by the example of Elisha, who filled empty vessels until the oil stopped—that is, until he had sufficiently shown mercy to the widow (4 Kings 4). But now we fill vessels already full, not in order that the oil may stop, but that it may overflow and run out: we bestow mercy on persons who are not needy but abound in temporal goods. This is to add wood to forests and water to the sea.

Likewise, the Lord says in Luke, chapter 14: “When you give a dinner or a supper, do not invite your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbours, lest perhaps they also invite you again and repayment be made to you. [Col. 0148B] But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind; and you shall be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you.” Likewise in the same chapter: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame; and compel them to come in.”

The rich wish to enter the Lord’s wedding-feast, but not through the narrow gate. One excuses himself, saying: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I beg you, hold me excused,” and so forth. Another: “I have taken a wife,” and so forth.

Likewise John says in the Third Catholic Epistle: “Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brethren,” and especially “for strangers” and the poor, from whom you expect no reward, “who will bear witness to your charity in the presence of the Church.”

Likewise, a monk of a very wealthy monastery advised a certain man who wished to enter his cloister with much money that he should enter the cloister of a poor monastery, so that Christ’s poor living there might have food. For giving this advice, when reproved by the brethren, he obtained forgiveness from God. There is no one today who says to one offering gifts: “Give to the needy, not to me. For I do not need them, because what is mine suffices for me.”

Likewise Isaiah, chapter 1: “Help the oppressed,” by supporting him with food and delivering him from his oppression. “Judge for the orphan, defend the widow, and come, and rebuke me, says the Lord.” Now, however, gifts are given to the rich, and repayments or reciprocal exchanges follow in rewarding and avenging; they “do not judge for the orphan” and the needy [Col. 0148D], but for the rich. “The cause of the widow,” or of a pitiable person, “does not come before them” (ibid.), so that they may uphold her cause, aid her by patronage, award her what is just, or feed the needy person.

Likewise David: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 21 [22]). And elsewhere: “Blessing I will bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Ps. 131 [132]), not those who belch after eating. Likewise the Apostle, 1 Timothy 5: “Honour widows who are truly widows”—that is, who, just as they are deprived and bereft of husbands, are also deprived of worldly concerns and assistance—by supplying their necessities and comforting them with support. “But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household.” That is: if she is useful to someone, or has support from which she may be maintained, whether from her own property or that of her relatives, she should not be fed from the goods of the Church.

[Col. 0149A] “But if she is truly a widow and desolate,” then let her be supported from Church property, provided that she does not enter a monastery unless she has reached the suitable age of sixty years. “But if any believer has widows” related to him by blood, or younger widows, “let him provide for them, lest the Church be burdened, so that it may suffice for those who are truly widows.” Observe that the Apostle admits freely, and without any temporal recompense whatsoever, into the fellowship of the Church widows “who are truly widows” and of suitable age. To other true widows, below that age, he does not allow entry, but orders that sustenance be supplied to them from the Church’s goods.

Likewise, Psalm 102 [103]: “The Lord performs mercies and judgment for all who suffer wrong.” The interlinear gloss: “Therefore mercy must be shown to all.” [Col. 0149B] Hence elsewhere: “Give to everyone who asks you, and give to everyone who asks” (Luke 6). And again: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him” (Prov. 25).

But Augustine objects to himself (*On Christian Doctrine*, book III, ch. 16) the saying of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 12: “Give to the good man, and do not receive a sinner; do good to the humble, and do not give to the ungodly.” But in this conflict of words you must attend to two things—indeed three: nature, grace, which restores corrupted nature, and vice.

Give to nature, because he is a human being, if, that is, he is needy. Yet we sometimes call nature “flesh and blood”; and to blood-relations you should give from what is your own, from your patrimony, not from that acquired by Christ’s blood, whose administration has been entrusted to churchmen so that they may distribute it to the poor. For this reason the Lord commanded in the Law that such a priest and Levite should be chosen as would say to father and mother: “I do not know you” (Deut. 33).

“But shall I not give, from the patrimony of the Crucified One, to my good and upright kinsman?” No: not so as to raise him up as a pillar in the Church, because of the destructive force of the example. For men do not consider that you gave to a good man, but that you gave to a kinsman, and they will make it an example. Give to grace, and especially from the patrimony of the Crucified One. For grace is bestowed freely. Hence it ought rather to be given to grace—indeed, to grace alone—not to nature, that is, to carnality. Hence in the *Lives of the Fathers* (book V, little book 10, no. 101): “My abba, should I give alms to a parent, son, or kinsman?” The abba answered: “No.” “Why, my abba?” “Because a little blood draws you.”

[Col. 0149D] **124.** Never give to vice, because giving to sinners and sacrificing to demons are alike. Sinners are to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved or fostered. Likewise, if the stewards of the possessions of the multitude “whose heart and soul were one” (Acts 4) had distributed more lavishly to certain persons because they were their kinsmen, I believe that they would have been struck by Peter with the same thunderbolt as Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5).

Likewise, if, according to the philosophers (Seneca, *On Benefits*, book IV, ch. 10), in bestowing secular benefits one must consider what one gives, to whom, why, and how, much more must this be done with ecclesiastical benefactions and their revenues. What? Here one must understand and consider how much should be given, and according to the principle that distribution should be made according to what “each one needs” (Acts 2).

[Col. 0150A] Alexander failed to observe this and was blameworthy. For when an old soldier, a paid veteran who had completed his service, came to him seeking compensation for his military service, because he had long served with him and had often, by his help, won the glory of triumph over enemies, Alexander said to him (book II, ch. 16): “I give you that city.” He answered: “I am not worthy of so great a gift.” Alexander replied: “I do not consider what is fitting for you to receive, but rather what is proper for me to give.”

Seneca says in his books *On Benefits*: “O most swollen creature, creature of glory! You ought to have measured yourself wholly by the person and modest means of the recipient, so as to proportion both yourself and your gift to his condition.” Likewise (ibid.): “A certain person approached another and asked a small gift from him. He replied: ‘You deserve something greater, and it does not befit me to give so little.’ When he asked for something greater, he replied: ‘You have not deserved so much, and therefore I shall not give you so much.’ O greedy creature, who craftily withholds both the lesser and the greater gift” (ibid., ch. 17).

One must also consider to whom one gives, according to the poet’s saying:

> Consider carefully to whom you give.

And again: “Let your alms sweat in your hand,” and so forth (Ecclus. 29). And again: “It is no less shameful to give to shameful persons than to give for shameful purposes.” It is evil to give Christ’s patrimony to the unworthy; it is dangerous to appoint them stewards of the poor’s goods. For through such persons, since they cannot be removed, Christ is defrauded for a long time; through the others, only for a time.

Why one gives must also be considered. This is the Christian consideration in bestowing every gift: namely, with what intention one gives—simply, that is, solely for God’s sake, who considers not how much is given but from what disposition it is given. Give, therefore, because he is a prophet, because he is good, even because he is a human being and is needy; never because he is a sinner or an actor.

[Col. 0150C] How should one give? Without grumbling, without boasting, without reproach. “Let your gift and your speech flow like dew” (Deut. 32). Give also quickly, because he who received only after asking did not receive freely. Again: “He gives twice who gives quickly.” Likewise: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” (Matt. 15) to eat. Likewise: “Do not increase the wealthy man’s abundance, nor make the rich richer.”

Jerome prescribed for us the pattern for assigning or bestowing ecclesiastical benefices in that letter, “Moses, friend of God,” and so forth. The pattern for distributing spiritual revenues, such as daily bread and wine, should be that blessed communion in which, from what was laid at the apostles’ feet, “distribution was made according as each had need” (Acts 2). When we give from these same goods, whether to neighbour, stranger, or anyone else, we should look to need, so as to bestow nothing in excess.

[Col. 0150D] “But should I here prefer a kinsman to a stranger?” No, if both are equally needy, because of the destructive example; just as the seven deacons would not for that reason have preferred their own kinsmen to others. If you object that the times are different now, they indeed are; but we, like them, are stewards, not masters, of what is cast at the apostles’ feet [Col. 0151A] (Acts 6). Give, therefore, to need, not to blood.

But what of those who enrich their parents from the temporal and secular resources of spiritual persons, even changing their station? I do not presume to assert that they thereby sin mortally. Yet it would be safer for them to follow the pattern and example of Joseph in such cases. When Joseph had become ruler of Egypt, and Pharaoh wished to exalt and enrich his brothers, they said to him by Joseph’s counsel: “Far be it, lord, that we should be so exalted. For we are shepherds, and pasturelands suffice us for feeding our livestock.” He gave them the fertile pastureland of Goshen, separated from the Egyptians, which was not struck by certain of the plagues of Egypt (Gen. 46–47; Exod. 8–9).

For this purpose the example of Master Anselm also pleases us. When Stephen, Seneschal of France, wished to advance Anselm’s nephews, make them knights, and marry them to noble maidens, Anselm said: “Far be it, lord, that you should do this. Rather let them remain in the same condition and calling in which the Lord called them, lest they be lifted up into pride. They were born of poor and rustic men. I beg that they remain such. I would rather never have read Holy Scripture than see them, once advanced in this way, abandon humility.”

Likewise the Archbishop of Canterbury says: “Some things are in themselves lawful and not vicious, even lawfully acquired, yet wrongly retained—for the luxury of those who use them rather than for necessity. Or they are improperly distributed, as to kinsmen. Since they are the goods of the poor, they make their stewards sacrilegious tax-gatherers and robbers.”

[Col. 0151C] Hence Jerome, on Isaiah chapter 3, at the passage, “The exactors of my people have despoiled them,” says: “Exacters, not teachers—namely scribes and Pharisees, demanding their first-fruits and tithes, who ought to teach but do not teach.” It is as if he said: because they “reap carnal things,” or exact them from their subjects, and do not “sow spiritual things” for them, they are exactors (1 Cor. 9). “For the peace of the Church consists in the account of giving and receiving” (Phil. 4); otherwise there is no peace.

Likewise, on the passage: “You have fed upon my vineyard,” that is, by violently demanding tithes and such things, and thus “the spoil of the poor is in your house” (Isa. 3), Jerome says: “Of the poor in understanding or spirit, who was unable to pay and unable to resist giving what he had to give.” Therefore, if you demand additional tithes and such things from a poor subject burdened by debt, who has nothing from which to pay what he owes, you are a robber, and “the spoil of the poor is in your house.”

[Col. 0151D] Likewise, on the passage, “Why do you crush my people and grind the faces of the poor?” (ibid.), Jerome says: “Our own rulers likewise, when they publicly accuse and put poor offenders to shame while wealthy men commit worse sins, do not make a loan.” “In their houses is the spoil of the poor,” while they heap the Church’s riches up for themselves and abuse them in luxuries, although they are given for the support and need of the poor; **126** they reserve them for their own excessive uses, or distribute them to kinsmen [Col. 0152A], making the poverty of other poor persons the wealth of themselves or their own people.

Therefore the Apostle also says: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9). It is as though he said: if you do not sow, do not reap. And again: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). Likewise Jerome (*Letter to Nepotian*, at the end): “It is the greatest danger not to give the poor from the patrimony of the Crucified One.”

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On those who receive gifts though they are not in need

Against those who receive though they are not needy, Jerome writes (1, 4, 2, *Clerics*, and 16, question 1) to Pope Damasus: “Clerics who can be supported from the goods and wealth of their parents, if they receive what belongs to the poor, certainly commit sacrilege; and by abuse of such things, ‘they eat and drink judgment to themselves’” (1 Cor. 11).

Likewise Prosper, in *On the Contemplative Life* (chapter “Since,” at the end): “Those who have means of support receive, not without great sin on their part, that from which a poor person would have lived.” Likewise he says (book II, ch. 10): “The Holy Spirit indeed says of clerics: ‘They eat the sins of my people’” (Hos. 4); “but, as having nothing of their own, they receive not sins but provisions which they appear to need. So possessors receive not provisions in which they abound, but the sins of others.”

Likewise Jerome [Col. 0152C] in a certain letter: “O monk, if you are needy and receive, you give rather than receive; if you are not needy and receive, you rob, because you appropriate for yourself what ought to be distributed to the poor.” Likewise: “Many people deceive others into believing what is not true poverty, when under the cover of poverty or religion they receive gifts.”

But it should be observed that there are three classes of persons who receive gifts under the cover of poverty. Some, in a time of famine, though they have means from which they could support themselves, hide their possessions; they cry through the streets under the appearance of poverty. When discovered to be such, they are punished, because their concealed goods are taken from them.

But I ask why this same diligence is not applied to clerics, so that, when discovered to receive beyond their need, [Col. 0152D] they too might be punished in the same manner. The reason and ground for punishment seems greater here.

Likewise, there are others who are wretched at all times and, as enemies, puff themselves up cheaply; trembling, they put on various appearances of sick persons and change their face like Proteus. Some of these conceal themselves because they do not wish to be found out by men. Others, once gifts have been received, immediately show themselves as they were, resuming their former and natural appearance and even mocking those who gave to them. These are more excusable, and less bad, than those who conceal themselves, in that they expose their shamefulness and buffoonery.

**127.** The third class consists of false preachers, and this class is twofold. Some are hirelings, seeking gifts through lies, false relics, seals, and letters. Others, through false miracles, pretend to be Nicholases or whatever saints sent by God, so as to deceive people and thus rob them of their goods. All such people do two evils in the Church: they secretly steal the goods of the poor, often even from poor people; and they cause true poor persons not to be believed.

It is asked whether they are bound to restore what they have thus received. Those of the first class, when discovered, are punished; and if they are not discovered, I approve of their restoring it or distributing it to the poor. I give the same advice to concealed mimes and pseudo-entertainers, for they defraud the genuinely poor. The same I say concerning things acquired by lies.

[Col. 0153B] “Then will a church built by lies be destroyed?” No; because stones and similar materials are of lesser value and, once dedicated to God, cannot become common property again. But concerning copes and other valuable items acquired in this way, I approve of their being sold and the proceeds restored, if one can remember what was received and from whom.

That this should be done appears from this rule (*Regula* 66, in the sixth): “Where there is disgrace on both sides, the possessor’s case is stronger, because you have no right of recovery if you gave to an actor or a prostitute knowingly and deliberately; for you act more shamefully in giving than the other does in receiving.” By analogy: where disgrace is only on one side, the other side’s case is stronger. If I gave unknowingly to such a beggar, receiving him in the name of a prophet, the disgrace lies on one side alone; therefore he who received in this way is bound to restore it. For here the disgrace lies only on the recipient’s side.

Likewise, no one’s deceit, lie, or fraud ought to aid him. Therefore he is bound to restore what was thus received, at least into the bishop’s hands, so that it may be distributed to the poor by his counsel.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Against those who give to entertainers

To these remarks must be added something concerning actors, prostitutes, mimes, jesters, magicians, gamblers, and *tyrocinatores* [an uncertain term, perhaps persons practising a novice’s trade]. The Apostle urges the correction of actors and busybodies in this way, 1 Thessalonians chapter 5: “We beseech you, brethren, correct the disorderly”—that is, busybodies. He who ceases from correcting them lest he lose what they used to give him [Col. 0153D] is a hireling.

Likewise 2 Thessalonians 3, concerning excommunicating and avoiding the same persons in fellowship: “We have confidence concerning you, brethren, in the Lord, that you both do and will do the things which we command you”—concerning the avoidance of busybodies and magicians. If anyone refuses to obey you, let him be excommunicated.

And, in the same epistle, chapter 3, he writes the final canon of a sentence already pronounced, or at least to be pronounced, against them: “But we command you, brethren,” concerning busybodies, “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ”—we command through Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to whom honour belongs—that, if a diseased sheep is excluded, “you withdraw yourselves,” that you do not have fellowship with them. “Withdraw yourselves,” namely, “from every brother walking disorderly,” [Col. 0154A] contrary to what the order of nature or grace requires, “and not according to the tradition which they received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us,” namely, “because we were not disorderly” as those are who attend to others’ affairs, wandering here and there among you; “nor did we eat bread from anyone for nothing,” that is, without labour, “but, labouring and toiling night and day, so that we might not burden any of you. Not because we did not have the right” to receive from you, as subjects, the necessities of life, “but in order to give ourselves to you as a pattern for imitating us.”

Against idle busybodies Augustine says (*On the Work of Monks*, ch. 2): “The Apostle wishes Christ’s servants to do bodily work, so that they may not be compelled by need to ask anyone for necessities.” Nor is this contrary to the Lord’s command, “Do not be anxious what you shall eat,” and so forth (Matt. 6). For from what follows it is clear that this was said so that they should not preach the Gospel for that purpose, not that they should fail to provide what suffices for necessity. It is as though he said: “I worked among you as an example for you, and in this way taught that this ought to be done.”

“For even when we were with you, we gave you this command: if anyone is unwilling to work” bodily and with his own hands, “neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3). “For we have heard that some among you walk disorderly,” namely, “doing no work, but busying themselves with curious matters,” living idly upon the labour of others. “But to those who are such we command and exhort in [Col. 0154C] the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly”—gloss: “not noisily, not ridiculously, not grumblingly, not singing ditties”—“they should eat their own bread,” earned by their own labour (ibid.).

And lest on this occasion they should cease ministering to the poor, he added: “But you, brethren, do not grow weary in doing good” to the poor. “And if anyone does not obey our word”—that is, this word by which we command him to work, and so forth—“make him known to me by letter,” so that I may excommunicate him; or “mark him by my letter,” namely this letter—gloss: “correct him, or declare him marked by sentence.” “And do not associate with him” in shared living, “so that he may be put to shame,” ashamed at being rejected; “yet do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother,” namely, out of love.

Observe that the Apostle abstained from receiving anything from his subjects for five reasons: lest he burden any of them, as stated above; because of their avarice; to repel false preachers; to prevent impunity in sin, lest by giving to him they imagine they had purchased preaching; and to remove busybodies from idleness, so that by his example they might seek food by the labour of their hands.

Likewise 1 Thessalonians 4: “We beseech you, brethren, that you abound more and more and make it your aim to be quiet”—gloss: “free from curiosity”—“and to attend to your own business,” leaving others’ affairs aside; namely, “that you work with your hands, as we commanded you,” lest you languish in idleness, from which busyness especially comes, “and desire nothing from anyone” [Col. 0155A].

Likewise Ecclesiasticus chapter 12: “If you do good, know to whom you do it, and great thanks will be yours. Give to the good man, and do not receive a sinner. Do good to the humble, and do not give to the ungodly; forbid bread to be given to him.” Likewise Tobit chapter 4: “Set your bread and your wine upon the burial of the righteous,” so that the righteous person may be buried, “and do not eat or drink from it with sinners and entertainers.” That is, do not share it with them because they are sinners, as those do who feed entertainers and idle persons while Christ’s poor go hungry.

Likewise Seneca, Letter 29: “First,” he says, “one must consider with whom one eats and drinks, rather than what one eats and drinks. For a feast without a friend is the life of a lion and a wolf. But this will not happen to you unless you withdraw; otherwise you will have as dinner-guests those whom the nomenclator has selected from the crowd of callers. He errs who seeks a friend in the vestibule and tests him at the dinner-table. No greater evil belongs to the busy man, besieged by his possessions, than that he thinks those are his friends to whom he himself is not one; that he judges his benefits effective for gaining friends, although some people hate him more the more they owe him. A light debt makes a debtor; a heavy one, an enemy. What then? Do benefits not produce friendships? They do, if it has been possible to choose those who will receive them; if they have been bestowed, not scattered abroad. Therefore, while you are of sound mind, use this counsel of the wise: think it more important who receives than what he receives.”

Likewise Jerome: “Giving to actors and sacrificing to demons are alike, if you give because they are actors, not because they are human beings.” Likewise a certain versifier:

> Before Jupiter’s statue a full-fed actor made a foul noise;  
> Jupiter ordained that he should live from his own resources.

Likewise, by reasoning itself: there is no class of people in which some useful service for human necessities is not found—of which it cannot be said, “There was some use even in that evil”—except this class of people, which is a monstrosity, redeemed from its vices by no virtue, fitted for no use serving human necessity.

If you say that it is suited to gain praise for someone, far be that thought; for it is no less shameful to be praised by shameful people than to be praised for shameful things. Likewise, this class of people has declared war on nature and the world; nothing suffices for it, it devours everything, it is enemy both to itself and to others, and therefore it must especially be repelled.

[Col. 0155D] Jerome prohibits not only such persons but also their supporters from being promoted, saying: “Yesterday in the forum, today in the choir; yesterday a patron of actors, today a consecrator of virgins.” Indeed, today and every day of his life, he is simultaneously both a patron of actors and a consecrator of virgins.

Likewise, they are as it were pierced by their own arrows through their own accounts.
