One of them says: “They boast that this rich man serves them each year with so great a sum of money, as though it were rent owed to them; another, and a third, with so much.” Then he cursed them all, especially wealthy clerics, because they had encouraged his worst habits by supplying him excessive expenses, praising his verses, tales, and gestures, and thus neither correcting him nor allowing him to come to repentance.

Likewise, another, received into a poor man’s house, asked him to buy and prepare necessities for his supper. The host bought what was necessary, not excessive. When the actor saw this—one accustomed to live off constant abundance, though never satisfied, that is, off another’s goods—he said: “You do not know whom you have received as guests. Buy for us richer and excessive foods, beyond what is enough for us and your household.” He replied: “By this I know that you are a glutton and a lickspittle.” He expelled him, throwing the purchased meat upon his shoulders.

[Col. 0156A] As he departed, the entertainer blessed him, saying that he had found only one host who was a man; if others had imitated his example, he would long ago have abandoned his profession of entertainment and repented.

Likewise another, having received fifteen pounds from a powerful man, while a knight had received from the same man sixty shillings of very inferior coin—although it had first been established that he was a knight and that he had been captured—said: “To me, an entertainer, you gave so great a sum without objection or proof; but to a free-born man of the same condition as yourself, braver than you and perhaps more useful to the commonwealth if he were placed at the summit of government, you gave so small a sum, although he is needy, and not without proof?” Indignant, he gave the knight the fifteen pounds he had received.

Likewise the nature of bees, which drives out drones, shows that such persons must be kept from homes. Hence Virgil:

> They drive the lazy herd of drones from the stalls.  
> (*Georgics* IV.167)

## CHAPTER L. Against usurers

[Col. 0156C]

After the foregoing kinds of greed, we shall in this chapter stigmatize its worst kind: usury. Hence David: “From usuries and iniquity you have redeemed their souls” (Ps. 71 [72]). The Lord commands the talent of nature and the talent of grace to be multiplied by putting it out at interest (Matt. 25), so that we may receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life (Matt. 19).

Hence Augustine, on Psalm 36 [37], sermon 3, verse 26: “Wretched man, why do you lend at interest to a human being? Lend at interest to God, and you will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.” Do not be the wicked servant who hides his lord’s talent, like an advocate selling his tongue or his learning—which is worse than hiding it. For if the servant who hid his lord’s talent is rebuked by the Lord as wicked (Matt. 25), much more worthy of rebuke, and more wicked, is one who distributes it wrongly by selling it.

But the Lord forbids the talent of fortune or money, just as also the talent of sin, from being lent at interest; likewise the talent of punishment. Augustine, on Psalm 54 [55], verse 12: “Usury is when more is exacted in punishment than was committed in guilt.” From the usuries of punishment and guilt “the Lord will redeem their souls” (Ps. 71 [72])—the souls of those who redeem their own souls by refraining from the usuries of money, and from punishment imposed beyond the measure of guilt. Those who do not refrain from these are made like the devil.

For just as the devil lends sin to a human being so that he may receive another sin from him, because “blood has touched blood” [Col. 0157A] (Hos. 4), and a sin not immediately washed away through repentance draws another after itself by its own weight, so a human usurer lends the talent of money at interest (Ps. 14 [15]) in order to receive another.

And just as the devil does not wish the talent of sin to be repaid to him, because the longer it is retained the more it multiplies, so neither does the usurer wish the talent of money lent to his neighbour to be repaid. Indeed, one who lends at interest is worse than the devil’s tax-collector, because the devil, author of all malice, lends his own talent, not another’s; whereas the usurer, when he makes a loan of the talent of money, lends not his own but God’s, though it was bestowed upon him in order that his neighbour might be helped freely. He wickedly lends it at interest, and even sells time, so that by reason of the longer delay he may receive a greater profit.

[Col. 0157B] David also says of him: “The sinner shall borrow”—from God, the talent of nature and grace; from the devil, the talent of guilt—“and shall not pay back. But the righteous man shows mercy and gives” (Ps. 36 [37]), because “pleasant is the man who shows mercy and lends” (Ps. 111 [112]): he disposes freely, and so forth. But the needy person “shall borrow” the talent of money from a usurer “and shall not pay back,” because he has nothing with which to do so, nor does the creditor wish him to pay it, thinking that he will receive more.

And because one cannot pronounce a worse curse upon someone than that he should fall into the devil’s hands, the Prophet, judging it a still greater imprecation to pray that someone should fall into the hands and snares of a usurer, says: “Let the usurer search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder his labours” (Ps. 108 [109]). Hence Isaiah, chapter 5: “Strangers shall consume their labours.” A stranger is one who does not lend freely to his neighbour.

Therefore, whenever anything greatly increases through delay of time, or whenever punishment is added beyond guilt, usury is committed. It is compared to a serpent and a cancer because it creeps and grows gradually until it occupies the whole body. Hence the poet:

> Hence devouring usury and interest greedy with time.  
> (Lucan, book I)

It is also compared to holy fire—that is, accursed and unquenchable fire—and likewise to the disease called “Touch me not.” Usury has many coverings and little cloaks by which it is concealed and, as it were, excused. Among these the chief is that something cheap is sold on credit as expensive—for example, dyed cloth or another cheap commodity presented as a costly item. Such a seller, increasing the price of the object sold and lent on credit because of the delay of time, sins more than one who lends a costly item at interest in exchange for a costly item. For the former, under the cloak and appearance of trade, has not, as he claims, sold a cheap thing as an expensive one, but has lent it at interest so as to receive it back with an increase.

[Col. 0157D] Likewise, a usurer sins more than a thief, who merely strips a person of his goods by night or secretly, or than a robber who does so by day and openly. For the usurer makes a continuing practice and profession of seizing his neighbours’ goods; the others do not.

Likewise, this disease has become cancerous and pestilential through the passage of time. In former times scarcely one usurer was found in an entire city; and he was hidden. He lent at interest only to poor people, and even then only secretly, after being given assurance that they would not reveal it. If any evil suspicion arose concerning him, his house was called the devil’s house, vineyard, well, or field; thereafter the kiss of peace was not given him at Mass. No fire was taken from his house by his neighbours, nor did anyone have any association with him.

[Col. 0158A] Even children were terrified when he approached and pointed him out to one another. So detestable was the vice of usury at that time. But now, in the dregs of our age:

> These things are now done openly, and men desire them to be entered in the public records.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* II)

Alas for grief! Men so detestable now become chamberlains of princes and prelates. Through usurious money, they have advanced their sons into princes and prelates of the Church, “that they may sit with princes and hold the chair and throne of glory” (1 Kings 2). They are also the purses and leeches of princes, because after sucking everything dry they vomit it into the treasury, so that the prince may say to such a leech:

“Lean, you will return to the narrow hollow which, lean, you entered.” (Horace, *Epistles* I.7.) These men have also acquired the name of Jews. For the princes who protect them do not allow them to be accused of any crime, saying: “These are our Jews.” Indeed, they are worse than Jews, because the Jew, by the prescription of the Law, “does not lend at interest to his brother” (Deut. 23), [Col. 0158C] but only to a foreigner, by permission; whereas this man lends at interest both to his neighbour and to a stranger, contrary to the Lord’s commandment. Such persons, if they are clerics, cannot be protected by clerical privilege against princes, because of the abhorrence of the crime. For when they die, all their goods are confiscated, so that neither the bishop nor they themselves have any power over them, even if they should wish to make a testament concerning them.

An example concerning monks carrying a moneylender’s corpse to burial, and a knight, the moneylender’s lord, meeting him, appears above under the heading: “On those who receive gifts unlawfully acquired” (see notes on ch. 46). Such persons incur this curse: “Woe to you who despoil, for you yourself shall be despoiled” (Isa. 33). But above all, [Col. 0158D] the prelates of our own time ought to be ashamed: although Alexander III, in the Third Lateran Council (1180), issued a decree that this plague was to be utterly rooted out by a sentence of anathema, they nevertheless still flatter those pestilent men and cherish them in their vices.

Accordingly, when certain persons present at the council asked who and what sort of people were struck by the sentence that had been pronounced, a certain prelate replied: only notorious offenders. And when the question was pursued as to who were notorious, it was said: those who publicly confessed themselves usurers, or indicated it by some recognized sign—for example, those who carried money to be lent at interest in a halter for sale at the top of a rod. And thus that decree was rendered ineffectual.

Again: the saying addressed by the Lord to Adam may be turned against these men in the contrary sense: [Col. 0159A] “In labour and the sweat of your brow you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 31). But to such a person it is said: In the labour and sweat of another’s face you shall eat another’s bread. And Isaiah says: “Strangers devour your land before your eyes” (Isa. 1). And Jeremiah, chapter 17: “The partridge cries out; she brooded over what she did not lay; he made riches, but not with judgment; in the midst of his days he shall leave them, and at his end he shall be a fool.”

The partridge is an unclean bird, by which, just as a heretic, so also a moneylender may be understood: one who gathers another’s riches. “But not with judgment,” because unjustly; and, even if justly, nevertheless “by whatever means the thing [is acquired]” (Horace, *Epistles* I), at his end he will be found a fool. For this is the first punishment awaiting such people. Scarcely does the inheritance of such men pass to a third heir, as very many examples [Col. 0159B] have shown. And because

> “A sordid prize has no good outcome,”  
> (Ovid, *Elegies* I),

things wrongly acquired are wrongly dissipated.

Their second punishment is that they will scarcely be able to restore what they have taken away. For this sin is so corrupting and tenacious beyond all others that, even if they have the means to make restitution, they prefer to be donors rather than restorers of what they have taken.

Their third punishment will be in Gehenna: boiling gold will be poured abundantly over them as they sit with Nero, and from every side.

Their fourth punishment (see below, ch. 52) is that the father who lent at interest wickedly for his son, and the son who, after his father’s death, entered into his plunder, will reproach one another in dialogue, [Col. 0159C] curse one another, tear one another to pieces, and each will rush upon the other.

It is also cruel and dangerous to receive money lent at interest from a moneylender, or indeed anything else, once we know him to be such. This is shown by the example of blessed Tobias, who said (ch. 8): “We are children of the saints, and we cannot join ourselves in this way, like the nations that do not know God.” And by the authority of blessed Jerome, who says: We must take the greatest care not to receive gifts from those whom we know to live on the tears of the poor, lest it be said to us: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him” (Ps. 41). Also by the example of blessed Fursa (Surius, vol. I, 16 January), who was struck with a stain of leprosy or morphea because he had received a tunic from a moneylender—though [Col. 0159D] he did not know him to be such—as is related in his life.

## CHAPTER LI. Against Advocates

Another class of men resembles the aforesaid class, namely moneylenders, in greed: that is, advocates. For just as “the sinner borrows many talents and will not repay” (Ps. 36), so the advocate receives freely from God the talent of nature, the talent of knowledge, and of grace, yet gives nothing freely in return. Rather, he makes his tongue saleable, although it is a small member, set in moisture and easily slipping.

That an advocate may sell his service Augustine attests, saying (*Letter* 54 to Macedonius): A judge ought not therefore to sell a just judgment, [Col. 0160A] nor a witness true testimony, because an advocate sells just legal assistance and a jurist true counsel. If you are a judge, see that you have the means to live. For to sell judgment, even if you are needy, since judgment belongs to the office of judge and to justice, is simony. If you are a patron and receive a salary from the Church, you are a soldier maintained at the Church’s expense; or, if you are not needy, you may not sell legal assistance, which in that case must be given freely.

If you are needy, “the labourer is worthy of his hire” (Luke 10), provided it is moderate, not excessive. Therefore I pursue the vice exercised in the office of advocacy, not the office itself, nor the art; for:

> Even under error itself, evils lie close beside goods;  
> virtue has often borne the blame for vice.  
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love* I.)

[Col. 0160B]

> It is not things, but evil deeds, that fall into vice.  
> (Gallus the poet, *Elegies* I.)

Antiquity reproves this class of men not only because of their greed, but also because of the lowliness of their office. Just as boxers, runners, heralds, and other such public functionaries were base and despised, so too were advocates. No one became an advocate except as a remedy for his poverty, seeking food by the occupation. But today this class of men is especially blameworthy because of its greed and self-neglect. For, abandoning the liberal arts and heavenly disciplines, everyone reads the code and seeks forensic affairs, so that they may appear abroad and in outward matters, and thus beg for glory and gain.

The Apostle, reproving them for the lowliness of the office, says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, [Col. 0160C] chapter 6: “Therefore, if you have secular judgments, appoint as judges those who are contemptible,” that is, lowly, “in the Church”; but let those of greater prudence and a more subtle natural capacity devote themselves to preaching, reading, contemplation, and prayer.

Again, the poet says of this:

> If Fortune wishes, an orator will become consul [printed correction: “you will become”];  
> if that same Fortune wishes, a consul will become an orator.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* VII.)

That is, he will become base, poor, and despised.

Again: I have seen an incurable disease for whose cure no physician could be found, because the patient’s recovery was despaired of; but I have never seen a cause so ruined or unjust that an advocate could not be found to defend it.

[Col. 0160D] Again: it is read in the *Tripartite History* (book X, ch. 3) that John Chrysostom was invited by his friends to the office of advocacy, perhaps because of its profit, and because he was suited to the office—that is, by nature, eloquence, and learning. But he immediately rejected it as a plague, unjust, and contrary to life.

Again, Sidonius says: These are they who fear even those whom they make afraid; they are those accustomed to bring accusations, utter threats, and take away possessions. They are those who delay lawsuits when admitted, obstruct them when overlooked, disdain them when reminded, forget them when drunk, and become haughty when enriched. They are those who buy lawsuits, sell interventions, dictate judgments to be rendered, overthrow judgments already dictated, draw litigants in, drag those to be heard onward, lead away the condemned, call back those making settlements, and reopen settlements. They envy reverence to clerics, lineage to nobles, precedence to superiors, association to equals, rights to those girded for office, privileges to the ungirded, schools to founders, fees to teachers, and honour to the educated. They are harpies in exactions, statues in contributions, beasts in investigations; wise in understanding, wooden in judging, fiery in inflaming, iron in forgiving, foxes in deceiving, tigers in anger, bulls in cruelty, minotaurs in consuming.

If at any point the smell of a rusty purse blows upon their nostrils, or if the appearance of a glittering deceitful coin shines forth, immediately you will see the eyes of Argus, the claws of Sphinxes, the hands of Briareus, the perjuries of Laomedon, [Col. 0161B] the cunning of Ulysses, the deceits of Sinon, the fidelity of Polymnestor, the devotion of Pygmalion, the counsels of Ahithophel (2 Sam. 17), and the kisses of Absalom (2 Sam. 15).

## CHAPTER LII. That in Their Cases Judgment Should Be Made Rather by Divine than Human Laws

Proverbs, chapter 23: “Buy truth, and do not sell wisdom, instruction, and understanding”; rather, “give freely, because you have received freely” (Matt. 10; Rom. 3). Do not say, as arrogant faith says: If I have justification by faith, how is it free?

Again: as is read in a certain tragedy of Seneca, a man thought that he saw Nero in the underworld [Col. 0161C] bathing, while attendants around him poured boiling gold over him. Seeing a company of advocates approaching him, Nero said: “Come here, you saleable race of men. O my advocate friends, come and bathe with me in this vessel; for there is still room left in it, which I have reserved for you.”

Again: it is shameful and dishonourable for a man to be reproached because his tongue—or any limb whatsoever—is saleable. For it belongs to prostitutes to expose their limbs for sale, to have limbs that are saleable.

Again: from the saying of a wise man who was hearing cases but was prevented from seeing the truth by the throng of chattering advocates: “Well done,” he said, “to the princes who have removed these brains from the Church; if they had cleansed it of the little retinues of advocates, they would have accomplished a better and more useful work.”

[Col. 0161D] Again: at their end these men are found especially foolish, and die disgracefully. Some, because they had had saleable tongues, were preceded in death by muteness and loss of speech. As one man was dying, his tongue was seen to move more swiftly than the wind, as though it said: “I sinned grievously and readily with my tongue, like a reed shaken by the wind.” Another man’s lower lip was seen to move more quickly than the lip of a crocodile. Another, when the Eucharist was offered to him at the last, said: “Let it first be judged whether it is right for me to receive it.” Those standing by said to him: “We judge it both right and just.” But he replied: “It is not, I say, a right judgment. For since you are not my equals, you cannot judge me justly.”

Again: an advocate pleads either with regard to God, or from favour toward a friend, or for profit. But today one who pleads with regard to God is rare; for this reason, if he did plead, he could do so lawfully and meritoriously. Hence the Lord says: “Let the cause of the widow come before you” (Deut. 10; Isa. 1): before you as judge, to be heard or decided; before you as advocate, to be defended. Job too was an advocate of the poor in lawsuits. Hence: “I was a foot to the lame and an eye to the blind. I was a father to the poor, and I diligently investigated the cause which I did not know. I broke the jaws of the wicked man, and drew the prey from his teeth” (Job 29). He resembles the one who says: “Rescuing the needy and poor from the hand of those stronger than him,” etc. (Ps. 34).

[Col. 0162B] Today, since few or no pitiable persons come into litigation, but the rich dispute over estates and useless matters; and since even pleading in a cause for God’s sake is dangerous—because the glory and ambition of the forum often blind us, and we so greatly fear losing even an unjust case lest we seem ignorant—we ought to abstain altogether from advocacy, since we can devote ourselves to more honourable and useful studies, unless the cause of a widow or some pitiable person, whom the Lord commands us to protect, comes before you as judge or advocate.

But to plead for a friend’s favour is more dangerous. For even though in this way you obtain your friend’s favour, perhaps gaining it for a time, from the opposing party, when you solicit many persons, you gather much and lasting hatred. If you say: “I defend my friend’s cause so that I may urge him and his adversary toward peace”—but what [Col. 0162C] if you learn that his cause is unjust? “Then I shall urge him toward peace.” By settlement, then, you urge him to bargain over another’s property, so that he may receive what is another’s, and thus seize it; and it will be said that this is done with another’s loss. And if you are hired, you will receive your fee and wages out of plunder, when you take something from what has been extorted and acquired in this way.

But a certain just and prudent man, when he discovered that his friend’s cause, which he had earlier supported, was unjust, abandoned it and transferred himself to defend the opposing side—not, however, as a traitor.

If you plead for profit, and are needy, it is permitted to you as an exception and remedy for your poverty, provided that you receive according to the proportion of a just price: not more than half the just price, and not a very great fee for slight labour. But if you are not needy [Col. 0162D] and nevertheless take payment, you sin mortally, because justice gives freely to each person what belongs to him.

If you sell to a man the counsel owed to him, especially when you are not occupied in a more honourable or useful pursuit, you are selling his right, a thing owed to him. Thus you commit theft or robbery when you do not give freely what you ought to have given freely. As Proverbs, chapter 23, says: “Buy truth, and do not sell wisdom, instruction, and understanding.” But the buyer does not sin, because he redeems what is his own.

## CHAPTER LIII. That Positive Justice Has Nothing Firm in It

The danger of this office is increased by the fact that advocates rely more upon the positive justice of men—which has nothing firm in it—than upon divine justice, although David, in the person of every faithful person, said through the Holy Spirit: “I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice” (Ps. 118). And again: “I have not declined from your judgments” (ibid.).

Again, the Lord says to Moses in Deuteronomy, chapter 16: “You shall appoint judges and masters throughout [Col. 0163A] all the tribes, that they may judge the people with just judgment”—that is, by divine law, not Justinian’s. Again, the Lord in Exodus, chapter 20, and Leviticus, chapter 18, gave Moses laws sufficient to judge between neighbour and neighbour in their cases. Therefore, especially in their spiritual cases, one must not depart from them, since they are not ceremonial matters but are to be observed literally, as is plainly proved by the gloss on that passage in Numbers, chapter 27: “You shall give them possession among their father’s relatives, and let them succeed him in inheritance.”

Origen (*Homilies on Numbers*, homily 22, opening): It is evident to all who know these laws, according to the historical sense, what force they possess: they are observed not only among the children of Israel but among all persons who live under laws. Hence it is apparent that the liberty of the daughters of Zelophehad not only conveyed inheritance to them, but also gave enduring legal rights to the world. You see how great is the usefulness of history. Who, then, can dissolve these laws, which the whole world employs?

Again, in Numbers, chapter 18: “Behold, I have given you the charge of my firstfruits; everything sanctified by the children of Israel I have delivered to you and to your sons, [Col. 0163C] for the priestly office, as everlasting ordinances.” We shall set forth, by Scriptural authority, which of these things are to be observed literally and which are not.

Origen (*Homilies on Numbers*, homily 11): For it is written: “The law of the Lord is undefiled,” blameless, “converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones” (Ps. 18); it is not [the same as] “the commandment of the Lord, bright, enlightening the eyes; the chaste fear of the Lord, holy, enduring for ever and ever; the justices of the Lord, right, rejoicing hearts; the judgments of the Lord, true, justified in themselves.” Unless each of these things were distinct, Scripture would not have assigned a distinct difference to each. Therefore law is one thing, commandment another, testimony another, justification another, judgment another.

[Col. 0163D] Hence elsewhere: “These are the law, and the commandments, and the justifications,” and the precepts, and the testimonies, “and the judgments which the Lord commanded Moses” (Num. 36). But everything written under the title of law—for example, “This is the law of the Passover,” the law of circumcision, the law of leprosy, and so forth—is “a shadow of things to come” (Heb. 10), and is not to be observed literally. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law” (Gal. 3), not from the curse of commandment, testimony, or judgment; wishing us to be subject not to the law but to its shadowy judgments and commandments.

Again, Leviticus, chapter 23: “After you have harvested the crop,” etc. Gloss: Things full of piety are commanded to be observed literally. Again, chapter 18: “Keep my laws,” etc. Gloss: It is not enough to keep part of the law. We must observe all the precepts and judgments. These are to be observed not only by Jews but by all nations, if they wish to serve God.

That positive justice has nothing firm in it is clear from this: the Lord gave certain and inviolable laws concerning marriage, excluding only twelve persons from marriage (Lev. 20); to these we add, by exception, the fifth, sixth, and seventh degrees (see 35, q. 3, *Contradicim.*). Yet we join some persons together and separate those joined, according to our own pleasure. But persons in the sixth degree are lawfully joined; therefore they must not be separated except for fornication. If, however, no marriage exists between them and we knowingly tolerate some persons joining in this way, we become authors of their fornication, since [Col. 0164B] we can separate them.

Again (above, ch. 23): to these we add the second and third kind of affinity, through which more snares and deceptions are supplied to more people for craftily joining or separating whom they wish. Again (30, q. 3, *Illud etiam*): to this purpose serves that crafty decree, namely: “That someone may marry the daughter of his co-godfather; I neither praise nor blame, neither forbid nor command it; but if he marries her, I shall not separate those who are joined.”

Again: it is dangerous to bind oneself to general rules and judicial definitions, for something outside rule and generality is frequently found. Again: decrees are manifestly changeable, since they exist in the heart of the lord pope, so that he may interpret them at his pleasure. If he judges according to them, he judges justly; if against them, he will likewise be said to have judged justly. For it lies within his power to frame, interpret, and abrogate canons.

Again: it is asserted that Pope Alexander III said that, if moved by equal reasons and equally probable arguments, he was prepared to judge for the negative whenever he had judged for the affirmative. Therefore all positive justice depends on the judge’s will, provided he judges piously and reasonably. For this reason, because positive justice is so changeable, and in individual cases one reason after another refashions the agreement, you cannot be fully instructed in it. In indignation Master Ivo of Chartres threw a book of decrees at his feet, as though it were worthless and useless.

Again, Agellius says: The laws of cities are spiders’ webs: they allow stronger [Col. 0164D] animals to pass through, but hold back the weaker and more feeble.

> “Censure pardons ravens, but harasses doves.”  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* II.)

Again, from the saying of a wise man: Positive justice is extremely changeable because arguments in it are drawn from certain remote probabilities and analogies. But a prudent judge never judges except by an express canon, law, or manifest reason. Yet even an express canon or law has no force before the supreme secular or ecclesiastical judge, because it depends upon their institution and will. Therefore, according to Isaiah (Isa. 8), one must have recourse to divine testimony and law, so as to argue from it; and from the examples of saints, or manifest equity, or living reason, [Col. 0165A] against which no authority can ever prevail.

Again (dist. 4, ch. *Statuimus*): [consider] the formalities of judicial procedure—such as delays, the production of witnesses, citations, and the like—which are changed and varied as the judge thinks expedient. The Bolognese have already thrown away half of them after revising them, establishing that every civil case should be concluded by the consuls, bound to this by oath, within twenty days.

Again (Third Lateran Council under Alexander III, title 1, ch. 3): A canon is derogated from by a contrary canon, by the tacit consent of the Roman Church and by the contrary usage of those employing it. If such usage is sufficient to abrogate any canon whatever—as the canon of Telesphorus concerning beginning the fast from Septuagesima is a canon; as the canon of the Lateran Council (title 1, chs. 13 and 14, [Col. 0165B] and in the appendix, part XXX) concerning not promising to anyone an ecclesiastical benefice not yet vacant is a canon; as the most useful canon against conferring several dignities or churches to one person entitled to them is a canon; as also the canon concerning the bishop’s house (dist. 41, *Episcopus*)—which is to be built humbly beside the church, in which he is to feed himself and the poor—is a canon; and similarly the other such canons, especially those in which no dispensation has been made, though the Roman Church permits them to be violated by contrary usage and tacit consent, because it neither rebukes nor condemns nor dispenses, as it would dispense in the case of ordaining a bigamist, who could not be promoted without its permission—then canons and human laws have no force and no stability, but are to be abrogated and erased at the will of those using the contrary practice.

But if this does not suffice—which seems likely, because a cleric ignorant of the canons is blameworthy for carelessness and negligence, while one who knows them and does not observe them is blameworthy for disobedience—then the contrary usage of persons acting without dispensation makes all who act against any canon, where no dispensation has been granted and no contrary chapter has derogated from it, transgressors and disobedient persons.

## CHAPTER LIV. Against the Ambitious

Having cut down the aforementioned branches of greed, let us now apply the axe to its greatest and chief branch, ambition. Ecclesiasticus, chapter 7, says in reproving it: “Do not seek leadership from a man, nor a seat of honour from a king; and do not desire to seem wise in the presence of a king. Do not seek to become a judge unless you are able, by the virtue and wisdom given you, to break through the iniquities of the people; lest perhaps you fear the face of the powerful and place a stumbling-block in your zeal” and office. “Do not sin among the multitude of a city, nor throw yourself into the people; neither bind” and gather “double sins to yourself, so that you will not be free even in one.”

First, because among the people no single sin is found from which you are free; rather, you will bear the iniquities of all. Whereas you ought to be the scapegoat, bearing each person’s sins out of the city, you bring each person’s individual sins into the city. If, through negligence or ignorance, you omit anything that concerns your office, you will be punished for every iniquity of your subjects (Lev. 16). Hence the Apostle, 1 Timothy [Col. 0166A] 5: “Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, nor share in the sins of others.” Gloss: In all that a person ordained by you later does, if [you ordained him] without careful, discerning, and prolonged examination.

The vice of ambition is likewise reproved at the beginning of the book: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1)—nor sought a secular or ecclesiastical dignity, whether temporal, or teaching from a chair; a chair which, like a creeping pestilence and disease, has invaded everyone and the whole flock, by which they mock and deceive both themselves and others. Hence the Hebrew truth has: “Blessed is he who has not sat in the seat of scoffers,” to whom woe will come. For because they mock both themselves and others, entering the sanctuary of God “not by the door” (John 10) “but another way,” they will be mocked. “Woe to you who despoil, because you shall be despoiled” (Isa. 33).

Again, the bishop of Le Mans:

> Although very many things are accustomed to corrupt human character,  
> a woman, wealth, and honour overthrow it more powerfully.  
> (Hildebert.)

That is: lust or carnal pleasure, love of money—“the accursed hunger for gold” (Virgil, *Aeneid* III)—and the ambition for honour. But how much ambition surpasses the other plagues and does greater harm with the poison of its malice, the same bishop writes:

> Unhappy is he whom neither possessions nor a woman can conquer,  
> but whom ambition subjugates.  
> (Hildebert.)

Again, 1 John 2: “All that is in the world is [Col. 0166C] either the concupiscence of the flesh, or the concupiscence of the eyes, or the pride of life”; the daughter of the latter is “the concupiscence of the eyes,” that is, ambition. Rebuking it with its mother, the Prophet says: “Not so the ungodly, not so; but they are like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1).

Again, the philosopher Seneca (*Letters* 73): Ambition has this greatest evil or vice: it considers neither God, nor itself, nor others, but through right and wrong, and “through a thousand perils of death” (Virgil, *Aeneid* II), both of soul and body, it strives and labours to acquire the dignity it desires.

Again, 1 Corinthians, chapter 3: “Charity is not ambitious,” that is, it does not wish to be preferred to another; “it does not seek its own things.” Gloss: but those of another. Thus it sometimes wishes to be preferred, not for its own sake or temporal pleasure, but for the common benefit of all.

Again (Possidius, *Life of St Augustine*, ch. 4): Augustine fled from every city that lacked a bishop, lest he be made bishop. Again, he says: “In nothing do I perceive God to have been so angry with me as when, although I was unworthy to be put to the oar, I was placed at the helm”—that is, at the summit—“of governance of the Church.”

Again, Ovid, *Tristia* III.4:

> Believe me: he who has hidden well has lived well, and each person ought  
> to remain beneath his own fortune.  
>
> Live for yourself, and, as far as you can, avoid a conspicuous life. For the higher the rank, the more grievous the fall.

> There are times when excessive contempt is useful.  
> (Claudian, *Against Eutropius* I.)

Again: after Pope Sixtus died, the papacy long remained vacant; no one was found willing to take up that burden, when it did not have [Col. 0167A] wealth and secular pomp attached to it. But when these were attached in the time of Sylvester, ambition immediately arose, and the love of ruling spread far and wide—although one “who presides” ought to do so “with solicitude” (Rom. 12), ought rather to be subject, and rather a servant than a master.

Hence the Lord says in Luke 22: “There arose also a contention among them, which of them seemed to be greater. And he said to them: ‘The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; but you are not so. Rather, let the greater among you become as the lesser, and the one who goes before’ in rank of dignity ‘as the servant.’ For who is greater according to the world’s judgment: the one who reclines, or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am in the midst of you as one who serves.” Therefore one who presides ought rather to be subject, except in regard to a certain dignity—that is, the obedience and reverence to be shown to him.

Again, Gregory in the *Pastoral Rule* (part I, ch. 9): One powerful in virtues should come unwillingly and under compulsion to the rule of souls; one not powerful in virtues should not come. But what of one who is powerful now—that is, who could now be powerful if he repented, though a small weakness and frailty prevents him, while in all other respects he has knowledge, reputation, and the like? Or one who was previously powerful, but is hindered by slight frailty, so that he could not approach with a serene conscience? What is he to do? Will he accept the honour unwillingly and under compulsion against his conscience, or wholly reject what is offered because of his bad conscience, and endure being struck with a sentence of anathema because [Col. 0167C] he has neglected the care of his neighbours?

Again, Gregory: Each person ought to consider and weigh the measure of his own strength, and take on the care of souls according to his powers, lest, while he boasts, he become in a place of honour a cause of ruin to others. Therefore one whose conscience is gnawed by his own crimes should not wish to be the judge of others.

The poet confirms this in saying:

> You who write, choose matter equal to your strength,  
> and ponder long what your shoulders refuse to bear  
> and what they are able to bear.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, opening.)

What one aspiring to ecclesiastical dignity ought to consider Augustine describes on the Apostle’s words: “Entrust these things to faithful persons who are able to teach them” (2 Tim. 2): life, learning, and eloquence.

Again, the poet:

> Caesar can no longer endure anyone before him,  
> nor Pompey anyone equal to him.  
>
> . . . impatient of a second rank in power.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.)

Ambition destroyed the republic and killed the senate. It must especially be guarded against among ecclesiastics, and one must not ascend rashly to ecclesiastical honour. Hence the Lord said to the Apostles: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20). As though he said: How will you minister the sacraments of the Holy Spirit to others unless you have first received him? Or how will you bestow his gifts on others [Col. 0168A] unless you have them yourselves?

Again: many who have been promoted repented with tears at their end of having accepted honours, saying that such honours are acquired with the greatest danger, possessed and governed with still greater danger, and that they would rather have lived all the days of their life simply, without the pinnacle of dignity.

Again: Geoffrey of Péronne, prior of Clairvaux, was elected bishop of Tournai. When Pope Eugenius and his abbot, Saint Bernard, compelled him to take up the burden of the episcopate, he lay prostrate in the form of a cross at the feet of the abbot and of the clerics who had elected him, and said: “If you cast me out, I can be a fugitive monk; but I shall never be a bishop.”

As he was suffering at his end, a certain monk, his closest friend, attended him as guardian in his illness and said: “My dear brother, since we shall now be separated in body, I ask you, if it may be done in peace and consistently with the saving will of God, to reveal to me after death what your state is.” After his death, in a secret oracle before the altar, [Col. 0168B] Geoffrey’s soul appeared to him in a vision and said: “Behold, I am here, Geoffrey your brother.” The other said to him: “My dear one, how are you?” He answered: “Well. But the Holy Trinity has revealed to me that if I had been promoted to be bishop, I would without doubt have been among the reprobate.”

## CHAPTER LV. Against the Promotion of the Unworthy

The evil of ambition is followed by the promotion of fools, unlearned persons, useless persons, and, to speak in one word, the unworthy. Writing against this, Jerome says: “A degenerate bull does not lead the herd, but one who surpasses the others in size and sinews. The most eminent elephant leads the herd of elephants.” Human nature has become so foolish that, turning its back upon the sun of justice, “turning aside judgment, setting its eyes to look down upon the earth” (Ps. 118), it does not observe, in choosing the guide and ruler of souls for their eternal salvation, what nature, acting as guide, does among brute creatures for bodily preservation.

Again, Solomon says: “Like one who casts a stone into Mercury’s heap is one who gives honour to a fool” (Prov. 26). Again: the Church ought to be “like an ordered army in battle array” (Song 6): that is, its strongest and most discerning members should be placed at the front and at the extremity of the wedge, while the feeble are in the middle. Otherwise it will be neither formidable nor ordered, but the gates of hell will prevail against it (Matt. 16).

Again, Leviticus, chapter 21: “A man of the seed of Aaron who has a blemish shall not offer bread or sacrifices to his God, nor approach his ministry: if he is blind or lame, if his nose is small, large, or crooked, if his foot or hand is broken, if he is hunchbacked, or bleary-eyed,” etc. If, then, in ordaining a Levite for ministry under the Law, a bodily blemish was forbidden and guarded against without dispensation, how much more is a spiritual blemish forbidden by the Lord in evangelical ministry?

Again: Jerome (*Apology against Rufinus*, book 4, ch. 4), introducing verses of Horace in mockery of promoters of the unworthy, says:

> He who does not know how to play abstains from weapons of the field.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry.*)
>
> . . . No one but one who has learned dares  
> give southernwood to the sick. What belongs to physicians  
> physicians promise; craftsmen handle craftsmen’s work.  
> We, unlearned and learned alike, write poetry everywhere.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* II.1, to Augustus.)

So now we, learned and unlearned alike, run to the governance of souls, saying:

> Let the itch seize the last place; it is shameful for me to be left behind,  
> and shameful indeed to admit that I do not know what I have not learned.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry.*)

Again, Jerome to Pammachius the monk: Today conspicuous honour is cheapened by the crowd, and among good men dignity becomes unworthy because so many wicked men possess it.

[Col. 0169B] 143 There are four causes of this unworthy promotion of unworthy persons: love of the flesh; nobility of lineage; the favour of flattery that caresses the ears of princes; and avarice, which is the cause of the preceding causes, because it is “the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6). For suppose that the royal revenues of kings and the great benefactions conferred upon the Church by princes were removed from the Church: no one would be found to approach its labours and works. Why? Because all who are in ecclesiastical dignity seek honour, not burden; pleasures, not work; milk and wool, not the care of souls.

Likewise the same Jerome: Joseph was made lord of Egypt only after his wisdom had been proved (Gen. 41). Psalm 104: “The word of the Lord kindled him,” and therefore “the king,” [Col. 0169C] Pharaoh, “sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free. He appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions.” And for what purpose? Not to provide for royal necessities, not to move armies, not to live and ride in pompous equipment or dress, not to be idle and take pleasure, but “that he might instruct his princes as himself, and teach wisdom to his elders”—much less, then, to the young. How much maturity and prudence, therefore, ought there to be in a ruler? If Joseph was appointed to the temporal government of Egypt only after his wisdom had been proved, how much more ought no one to be appointed to the lordship and spiritual governance of the Church except one whose wisdom and life have been proved?

Likewise: Only after a threefold confession of love for the Lord [Col. 0169D] was the primacy of the apostolate entrusted to Peter. It is as though the Lord were saying to him—and, in him, to others to be set over the governance of the Church—“Because you love me more than these.” That is, you love me more than your own people; you also love me more than your possessions; you also love me more than yourself: “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs; feed my kids” (John 21). Therefore, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16), that is, I will appoint you ruler of the people.

Likewise: The Philistines placed Dagon—what they regarded as precious—beside the ark of the Lord (1 Kings 5). Those who promote unworthy persons, on the contrary, are like the Philistines, indeed worse than they: they place the ark of the Lord beside Dagon, entrusting the Church to an idol that is deaf, mute, and weak, whereas the ark ought to be entrusted to those fit to bear it, govern it, [Col. 0170A] and disclose it through the worthy administration of the Church’s sacraments. Therefore let those who promote unworthy persons beware lest such mice gnaw their entrails [Latin *extales*; uncertain] and lest they be struck by a punishment like that of the Philistines; and let those thus promoted fear lest they fall like Dagon, their heads cut off and the extremities of their hands and feet severed, so that they become wholly useless.

Likewise: It must be feared today lest what happened in the time of the Judges should occur. For if at that time the Philistines took measures that there should be no smith in Israel able to make spear or sword, even as far as an ox-goad (1 Kings 13), such a smith is still lacking: there is no one to rouse or spur on his neighbour. Indeed, even [perhaps: a whistle, a goad] is lacking today for the oxen of the Church—not only the spear and sword of doctrine—and those who have it, if any do, fear [Col. 0170B] to use it, having become “dumb dogs unable to bark” (Isa. 56), or even to mutter before princes, lest they lose their useless burdens.

But you will object: There are indeed many smiths in the Church, namely private persons, 144 such as scholars and masters of schools. But why do I make this objection? Such people are now considered cheap and useless and are not chosen as artisans of the Church; consequently they have little or no place in it from which they may benefit it. Likewise Ecclesiastes (ch. 10): “There is an evil which I saw under the sun, like an error proceeding from the presence of the ruler: a fool set in lofty dignity, and wise men sitting below.”

Likewise: How can this be said of the prelates of the Church: “Where is the seer? Where is the house of the seer of the Lord?” (1 Kings 9). It must be feared [Col. 0170C] that, because our sins demand it, we shall be deprived of seers, just as the Jews were deprived of prophets.

Likewise: If Belshazzar—because he misused the symbolic vessels brought from the temple of the Lord by Nebuchadnezzar his father, placing them in the temple of his idol, while he himself, his nobles, and his concubines drank wine from them drunkenly on feast-days—was punished by the destruction of his city and the loss of his kingdom (Dan. 5), how much more will those be punished who misuse the living vessels of the Lord, entrusting holy souls to unworthy persons to govern and ecclesiastical sacraments to them for administration?

Likewise, Matthew, chapter 24: “When you see the abomination of desolation”—namely, the deaf and mute idol, which is the cause and sign of the destruction of Jerusalem and of the holy Church, especially of the one who presides over it—“standing in [Col. 0170D] the holy place” (Mark [13]: in the temple of God, “where it ought not”), then, “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing. For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world” (Matt. 24). This proceeds from ambition for dignities and honours, which began in the time of the Law, when the Jews sought the high priesthood from Roman rulers. Yet not even in that dregs of times—namely, the time of perverse mediocrity—did just anyone everywhere “sit upon the chair of Moses”; only “the scribes,” teachers of the Law, “and the Pharisees,” set apart from others, possessing at least externally the sign of religion, and mature in age. Thus the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon the chair of Moses. Do all that they say, [Col. 0171A] but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). But now young men and fools sit in the chair of Moses, so that you should do what they say, while not wishing to do even what they do.

If a skilled person, though ambitious or otherwise evil, is promoted, there is nevertheless hope for him, because “who knows whether he may turn” (Joel 2), repent, and become good today though he was evil yesterday. But for a foolish and ignorant person promoted, there is no hope. For the Lord rarely raises up an unwise and ignorant man and makes him wise, as he makes a sinner penitent.

Likewise Leviticus, chapter 4: “If the synagogue,” or the people, or a ruler, or a private person, “sins through ignorance,” he shall do this and this, “and when the priest prays for them, the Lord will be merciful to him.” From this, Augustine says, the difference between the sin of the priest and the sin of the people is evident, [Col. 0171B] namely that the priest is not said to sin through ignorance. For he is not permitted to be ignorant of the Lord’s commandments; and we do not read that anyone prays for the priest, because, as Solomon says: “If a serpent strikes the enchanter, who will heal him?” (Ecclus. 12).

Likewise the Lord says of Peter and his successors: “Put out the net into the deep” (Luke 5), that is, into the deep understanding and inquiry of sacred Scripture, through disputation, if doubtful cases arise, so that you may thus see what ought to be done and what ought not.

Likewise, to the apostles: “Gather up the fragments lest they perish” (John 6), that is, the tiny fragments, the subtle meanings and hidden mysteries which the unlearned cannot grasp, and also those which escape the hands of those eating—that is, the understanding and inquiry of those disputing—investigate these and retain them in memory, as baskets and the perfect are full of the nourishment of the word of God, so that in due time and place [Col. 0171C] you may distribute them to the poor, even to the unlearned.

Likewise: In distinguishing the ministers of the Church as “apostles, evangelists, etc., pastors and teachers” (Eph. 4), the Lord joins pastors and teachers. For this reason too, when the Apostle describes a “pastor” of the Church, at the end of his description he sets down “teacher,” as though this were the vital and substantial difference: namely, one who knows how to resist anyone contradicting sound faith, and who is prepared “to give an account to everyone who asks” concerning faith and hope (1 Pet. 3), and concerning the Church’s good morals.

Likewise: Jerome speaks of Helvidius (Letter, *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*), that unique and horrible monster in Gaul, the only lay priest in the whole world. Yet, although he wrote certain things about the Blessed Virgin Mary with propriety in the ordering of his words, he did so impiously in their meaning.

Likewise: If, by the Lord’s command, an overnight guest must be selected with such diligence, lest the reputation of preaching be stained by the guest’s disgrace, how much more carefully must a priest be selected who is to be not a guest but the ruler of a Church for a longer time? And if he must be ordained with such maturity and care, with how much care must he be deposed?

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Office of Prelates

To repel and refute the unworthy promotion of unworthy persons—or rather, their intrusion—it is fitting to consider the office of prelates, a term that includes the parish priest as well. Since courageous and perfected men fear to undertake it, let unworthy and presumptuous men cease being forced into its exercise, or even being canonically elected to it.

Of this Moses says, Numbers chapter 27: “May the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over this multitude, who may go out and come in before them.” He is to go out as a shepherd on their behalf against visible and invisible enemies; to come into the tabernacle and church in order to pray for them; “and lead them” into battle “against spiritual wickednesses” (Eph. 6), by word and example as their leader; “and bring them in,” at last, into the heavenly Jerusalem, “lest the people of the Lord be like sheep without a shepherd.”

Likewise, in the same place: [Col. 0172B] “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of God, and lay your hand upon him, that he may give the precepts of life to the children of Israel. When he consults the Lord, at His word he shall go out to battle and enter the tabernacle, he first, and all his sons with him, and the rest of the multitude.”

Likewise Genesis chapter 46: “Joseph said to his brothers: When Pharaoh calls you and says, 146 ‘What is your occupation?’ you will answer: ‘We are shepherds from childhood. We have come to sojourn in your land’” (Gen. 47). Behold how in every case manliness precedes the rank of prelacy. For the greater part of religious life rests in courage of spirit; courage is especially necessary to a prelate, for if he is afraid, [Col. 0172C] all is over with him. Horace:

> Though the shattered world should fall upon him,  
> Its ruins will strike him unafraid.  
> (*Odes*, III.3)

Likewise: Although Jeremiah was sanctified from the womb and even commanded by the Lord, he feared to undertake the pastoral office and burden—“For this place is terrible” (Gen. 23)—saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” (Jer. 1), and elementary in life. But when a man’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is scorned. He was elementary also in learning; yet a prelate must be a teacher. He was elementary also in eloquence; for an ineloquent man harms by his silence as much as he benefits by example. The fury of wolves must be driven away by the barking of the dog and the shepherd’s staff. [Col. 0172D] “And the Lord said to me: Do not say, ‘I am a child’; for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and you shall speak whatever I command you. Do not fear their face, for I am with you. Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, that you may root up”—by rebuking vices—“and destroy”—by rejecting them on the authority of Scripture—“and overthrow”—by making them renounce those things and the world—“and build”—by preaching, consoling, and encouraging—“and plant” (ibid.)—by hearing confessions and imposing satisfaction.

Likewise Psalm 102: “Bless the Lord, all you his angels,” the ministers and prelates of the Church, “mighty in strength, who do”—not merely preach—“his word.” For what purpose? “To hear the voice of [Col. 0173A] his words.” That is: by your good life, make His commandments audible. For a preacher who acts and lives as he preaches is readily heard; one who lives one way and preaches another makes the word of God neither heard nor believed.

Jeremiah, chapter 1: “Therefore gird your loins, arise, and speak to them all that I command you. Do not be terrified at their face, for I will not make you fear their countenance”; rather, as to Ezekiel in chapter 3: “I have made your forehead” bronze, “harder than their foreheads, like adamant and flint”; and “I have made your face stronger than their faces.” And Jeremiah (ch. 1): “For behold, today I have made you a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall against all the land of Judah.” It is especially to be noted that Job, Elijah, Jeremiah, and John were sent to preach only with their loins girded: some in garments of skin, some with leather belts, some through harshness of life and mortification of the flesh. The Lord gave the same command to the apostles: “Let your loins be girded,” and afterwards, “your lamps burning” (Luke 12). For one going to war must first bridle the beast of the body, crucifying it “with its vices and concupiscences” (Gal. 5), through abstinence and continence, lest the man fall into a precipice and so that, with steady step, it may carry only its rider, namely the Holy Spirit. A rigid and austere life, not a soft and effeminate one, therefore befits a preacher.

A prelate is a city fortified by virtues, a pillar 147 supporting the Church, and a wall protecting it; subjects should flee to him as to a city of refuge, because: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God” (Ps. 86). This is the city—that is, the prelate—which cannot be conquered.

Likewise: Let the one approaching the pastoral office consider that among the judges no one wished to judge the people unless the Lord first stirred up his spirit to perform this task. Thus the Lord stirred up the spirit of Othniel (Judg. 1), and also the spirit of Deborah the prophetess before she judged the people (Judg. 4); likewise the spirit of Gideon, who would not judge the people until he had been given the sign of the fleece made wet and the threshing-floor dry, and then, conversely, the threshing-floor wet and the fleece dry (Judg. 6). Nor should you approach this office unless you have first been given—not, I say, signs of miracles, but signs of virtues and good works.

Likewise, Exodus [Col. 0173D] 3: The Lord says to Moses, “Come, I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may bring my people out of Egypt.” Moses replies, “Who am I”—namely, insufficient and nothing—“that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” The Lord replies, “You shall have this sign that I have sent you”: namely, the transformation of the staff into a serpent, and conversely of the serpent into a staff; also the sign of the hand placed in the bosom and made leprous, then drawn out and cleansed; and also the sign of water changed into blood. Moses replies: “I beseech you, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you have spoken to your servant; rather, I am slow and impeded in speech.” “I beseech you,” he says, “Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4), namely Aaron, one worthier and more eloquent [Col. 0174A] than I.

Augustine (*Book II, Questions on Exodus*): According to the Hebrews, Moses had a thin and weak voice, and it was necessary for him to use a loud voice because, owing to royal pride, he was not allowed to approach closely. The conclusion is that he was neither slow of speech nor professed himself ineloquent, since the Lord “put His words in his mouth.” Yet, with regard to the Egyptians, he possessed a resonant voice and incomparable eloquence, but considered himself insufficient for this office. He who believes himself sufficient is insufficient; and he who thinks and believes himself insufficient is sufficient, patient in suffering, and humble, to proclaim: “For what is wiser and stronger among men is foolish to God; and what is foolish to God is wiser and stronger than any man” (1 Cor. 1).

Likewise, 2 Timothy 2: “Take care to present yourself [Col. 0174B] to God as an approved worker,” that is, by the merit of your life show yourself before God to be such that the people obey you; “unashamed,” so that deeds accord with words, and that you neither blush nor fear to preach the Gospel. The same Apostle, in his first letter to him: “Attend to yourself” first, “and then to doctrine.” By this expression understand the whole office of a prelate. And in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 20: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God. Rightly handling the word of truth”: rightly teaching one’s neighbour, namely by word and example and according to the capacity of each individual, so that the pastoral staff may thus be bent back upon itself, “and the mouth of the turtledove turned back as far as the shoulders” (Lev. 1).

Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel [Col. 0174C] (Luke 12): “Who do you think is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household,” free of every private affection, namely fear or gain, “over his household, to give them at the proper time” 148—for preaching, if it is continual, becomes cheap—“a measure of wheat,” according to the capacity of the hearers or of each one. “Blessed is that servant,” etc.

Augustine (*On the Exposition Begun of the Epistle to the Romans*, before the middle): What is the reason that the Apostle, in greeting a prelate, places three things—“mercy,” that is, remission of sins; “peace,” that is, tranquillity of mind and, as it were, a foretaste of eternal peace; and “grace”—whereas in greeting private persons, as in both Epistles to Timothy, he gives only the first two? It is because, besides these, grace is necessary to a prelate for strength and fortitude. Accordingly, as to Joshua, Moses’ successor, it is said three times: “Be strong and courageous” (Josh. 1).

Likewise: When the Church is handed over to an unworthy person, Eli with the children of Israel may lament and say: “Alas! The glory of the Lord has departed from Israel, because the ark of the Lord has been captured. For the Philistines carried it from the stone of help into Ashdod” (1 Kings 4), that is, from “the fire of my father” into the fire of concupiscence, “and brought it into the temple of Dagon” (1 Kings 5), “the fish of sadness,” seeking secular business and profits in the Church. Then let Jacob weep for Joseph sold and bound in the prison of Potiphar the eunuch (Gen. 39), when the Church and its ecclesiastical sacraments are entrusted for dispensation to soft, barren, and unlearned eunuchs. [Col. 0175A] Jeremiah laments the same thing in the Lamentations, saying (ch. 10): “All her splendour has departed from the daughter of Zion. All her princes have become like rams finding no pasture, and they have gone away without strength”—namely, the strength of a shepherd—“before the face of the pursuer,” the devil driving them away. Thus, because “her enemies have become head, her little ones have been led into captivity before the face of the oppressor.” When the shepherd is struck, the sheep of the flock are scattered (Matt. 26).

Likewise the same prophet: “The enemy stretched out his hand over all her desirable things, because she saw the nations”—that is, those living as Gentiles—“entering her sanctuary,” that is, promoted in the Church, “concerning whom God commanded that they should not enter your Church.” In it, “because [Col. 0175B] the enemy has risen up, she has been greatly cast down, having no consolation or comforter” (Lam. 1), so that now, because of the promotion of unworthy persons, one says in lament with the Prophet: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem,” the holy Church, “a watch-house for fruit” (Ps. 78).

Indeed, concern today is less for appointing guardians to govern souls than for appointing guards over worthless fruit—fruit now left to pigs for eating—not the fruits of which the Song of Songs says (ch. 7): “All fruits, new and old, I have kept for you, my beloved.” Concern for Peter’s keys is less than concern for cellar keys.

Likewise Romans 1: “I desire to see you, that I may impart to you [Col. 0175C] some spiritual grace.” For it is more the prelate’s concern to give to subjects than to receive from them; yet if he has served well, he will receive a golden crown for himself and a lesser crown for those whom he has kept. Concerning this grace he adds: “I may come to you,” namely, to strengthen you in faith, that is, to be mutually consoled among you through the faith shared by you and me.

Likewise in the same chapter 1: “I have purposed to come to you, that I may have some fruit among you, as among the other nations,” giving to you rather than receiving. Confirming this, the Lord says in the Gospel: “You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” (John 15). It is as though He said: Seek for yourselves fruit among your subjects, everlasting [Col. 0175D] and abiding, not temporal fruit that does not remain.

Likewise in the same passage: “I am debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to wise and foolish; so, as far as lies in me, I am ready to preach the Gospel also to you who are at Rome.” The Apostle was ready to preach before he entered upon this office. He did not enter it in order to become ready for it afterwards, as do those who must apply themselves to learning when they ought to be teaching.

Likewise 4 Kings 11: “Jehoiada the priest therefore made a covenant between the Lord and the king, between God and the people, between the king and the people, that the people might be the Lord’s people,” obedient to God and king. For the prelate is mediator between God and those aforesaid; he must make a covenant and establish peace between the Lord and his subjects. But who is to mediate for him if he becomes [Col. 0176A] a wolf and a hireling is not stated; instead, without a guardian, under the pretext of office and protecting himself by certain frivolous arguments, he rages against his subjects.

Yet he has succeeded to the place and ministry of Elijah. When Elijah was taken up to heaven in a fiery chariot resting on four wheels, Elisha said: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its driver” (4 Kings 2). The repetition of the word denotes paternal affection and the paternal office to be performed for sons. For a prelate ought to rest upon and be carried by four wheels, namely the four cardinal virtues. A prelate must be just, brave, temperate, and prudent: he is the chariot of God and of the Church, not of Pharaoh.

For he must govern, bear, and sustain her by the example of holy conduct; by the word of preaching; by the benefit of temporal consolation; and by the assistance of service and devout prayer. As the driver of the Church, he ought to possess a whistle, song, and other soothing means by which he may caress and console her. He should have only one goad in his hand, to spur and whip the oxen—that is, the flesh—when they kick back, so that with steady step it carries its rider, namely its spirit. This too is signified in the episcopal staff. But now our ox-drivers possess many goads and reasons for pricking, and no soothing remedy. Hence someone says:

> Shepherd, care for the sheep, as this figure teaches:  
> Draw by the first part; govern by the middle; prick by the lower end.  
> Draw, support, spur on the wandering, the sick, the sluggish.

Likewise Ezekiel chapter 3: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel,” etc.; and chapter 13: “Son [Col. 0176C] of man, prophesy against the prophets,” etc.; and chapter 22: “Son of man, the house of Israel has become dross to me,” etc.; and chapter 44: “They shall teach my people what is the difference between holy and profane, and shall show them the difference between clean and unclean”; and in the same place: “Son of man, set your heart upon it, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears all that I say to you,” etc.

## CHAPTER LVII. Against the Negligence of Prelates

The Apostle, writing against the negligence of prelates in 1 Timothy 4, says: “Attend,” shepherd, “to reading,” and afterwards “to exhortation” for those now willing, “and to doctrine” for those who do not know; and “do not neglect [Col. 0176D] the grace” of your office “that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy,” that is, by the canonical election of holy men, in which from past things they seem to declare what kind of person you will be.

And in the same Epistle, chapter 1: “This commandment”—concerning the forming and governing of Christ’s Church vigilantly, carefully, and vigorously—“I entrust to you, my son Timothy, according to the prophecies that went before concerning you”; that is, according to what I knew you possessed before this, the knowledge of sacred letters, which are called prophecies; or according to what the Holy Spirit showed me concerning you through inspiration or through the grace of expounding those letters, which I knew you possessed, since from childhood you have known the sacred writings; and also according to your preceding life, which ought to have been, as it were, a prophecy of what you would be if afterward [Col. 0177A] promoted: “that you may wage” in act “a good warfare in them, holding faith,” sound doctrine, “and a good conscience.”

Likewise 1 Maccabees chapter 5: “Judas Maccabaeus,” secular power, “was gathering together the rear of the army and exhorting the people throughout all the way, until they came into the land of Judah and went up to Mount Zion with joy and gladness and offered burnt offerings, because none of them had fallen until he returned in peace to Jerusalem.” How much more ought an ecclesiastical prelate, by virtue of his office, to gather the weak and infirm from the Church, encourage them throughout the whole way of this life, and guard and govern them vigilantly and vigorously until they ascend to the mountain of the Lord, the heavenly Jerusalem, and praise the Bridegroom for ages of ages in peace, because none of them has fallen—though they had fallen away from his side—through the guarding of the shepherd, who leads them safely on their threatening journey through the desert into the land of Judah?

4 Kings 22 and 23: If Josiah king of Judah, still a boy, upon hearing the words of the Law of the Lord and having Deuteronomy read before him, was terrified in heart, “tearing his garments,” humbling himself as he sat and wept before the Lord because he had not observed His commandments; if he “made a covenant before the Lord to walk after Him” in all His commandments with all his heart and all his soul, “and to uphold the words of the covenant and law read” before him; commanding also that all unclean vessels be cast out of the temple, that effeminate men and unclean persons be removed from the city, that altars and groves be destroyed, and that the rite of the Law be observed in everything: [Col. 0177C] how much more carefully and vigilantly should a spiritual prelate—to whom this office belongs—provide for these matters in the aforesaid Church of God, and not neglect them or pass them by, as though with a deaf ear, failing to awaken at the thunderings and words of the Lord?

Likewise Jeremiah, threatening prelates because of their lethargy, torpor, and negligence, says in chapter 50: “My people have become a lost flock; their shepherds led them astray and caused them to wander in the mountains” of 151 pride; “from mountain to hill they passed,” from sin to sin; “they have forgotten their resting-place,” from which three things drive a man: smoke, dripping water, and a quarrelsome wife. “All who found them devoured them, and their enemies said: ‘We have not sinned, because they sinned against the Lord, the beauty of righteousness.’”

Likewise: The Lord went throughout all Galilee preaching, healing the sicknesses of the people, and thereby teaching the office of a prelate, in whose exercise he ought to be watchful, useful, diligent, energetic, and vigorous (Matt. 4).

Likewise Isaiah, chapter 52: “My people have been taken away for nothing,” through the neglect of their shepherds; “their rulers act wickedly, says the Lord, and continually all day long my name is blasphemed.”

Therefore Ezekiel chapter 36: “Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations,” because the people today are not like the priest—indeed, are better than the priest—and the priest is less than, not like, the people. Against such priests the Apostle writes in 1 Timothy chapter 4: “Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word,” [Col. 0178A] and preaching, “and conduct,” so that, seeing your continence even in many lawful things, they may judge themselves, by comparison with you, to be unworthy. For nothing harms the Church more than seeing laypeople better than clerics.

Likewise Isaiah chapter 28: “Hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men who rule over my people. For you have said”—by deed, if not by word—“‘We have made a covenant with death’” (whence Solomon: “They have made pledges even unto death” [Wis. 1]), “and we have made a pact with hell. When the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon” them, or “us.” Isaiah says this of them: “Because we have made falsehood our hope and are protected by falsehood. But woe to you who [Col. 0178B] have erred through drunkenness,” that is, indiscretion and negligence. “Priest and prophet have not known; overwhelmed by wine, they have been swallowed up by drunkenness,” namely by luxury, cheerfulness, and delight in temporal things. “They have erred in drunkenness,” through indiscretion and excess, and have caused others to err. “They did not know the seer; they did not understand judgment. For all tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there is no place left.” For the Church has been filled to the mouth, in its prelates, with the filth of temporal concerns, sloth, and avarice, so that they leave no room in these matters even for laypeople, but surpass them.

Therefore: “Woe to you, deserters of my people, who have made a plan, but not from me; and have woven a web, but not through my Spirit; who add [Col. 0178C] sin upon sin; who walk” pompously “down into Egypt and have not consulted my mouth, hoping for help in Pharaoh’s strength and trusting in Egypt’s shadow” (Isa. 30): in riches and secular pomp. Thus Amos, chapter 6: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion, chief men of the heads of the people, entering pompously into the house of Israel.” Therefore “I will send a famine upon the land: not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God.” “For little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. 4). Indeed, there is one present who removes spiritual bread by word and example, and bodily bread as well by robbery.

Thus Psalm 104: “He called a famine upon the land and broke all the staff of bread. He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold into slavery. They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul, until his word came.” Behold what 152 a prelate must suffer for the people, so that the word he may preach to them may come to him—and before it comes to him. “The word of the Lord kindled him” (Ps. 104), because one who does not burn does not set others on fire: a “fiery word” (Ps. 118) does not enter a cold breast. The Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles in tongues of fire before they preached (Acts 2). When Basil preached, a fiery tongue was also seen to proceed from his mouth; and when Sebastian preached, an angel was seen holding a book for him, from which all his preaching proceeded.

After this: “The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples dismissed him. He appointed him lord of [Col. 0179A] his house and ruler of all his possessions, that he might instruct his princes as himself and teach wisdom to his elders,” etc. After him: “He sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he chose” (Ps. 104). “No one takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5). “He who takes the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26). “He placed among them the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Ham” (Ps. 104).

Note in all these things the order, degrees, and office of a prelate, who, like Joseph in Egypt, ought to feed the people of God (Gen. 41), and, like Moses, lead them out of Egypt (Exod. 12).

Likewise Luke, briefly setting out in the speech delivered by the Apostle to the bishops and priests of Asia summoned to Miletus—the speech written in Acts of the Apostles [Col. 0179B] chapter 20—the whole care and pastoral duty owed to subjects, says: “So that there might be no delay for him in Asia, he was hurrying, if possible, to keep the day of Pentecost at Jerusalem.” Therefore a prelate ought not to be absent from his church on the greater solemnities. “But from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders,” the aged men, “of the Church. When they had come and were gathered together, he said to them: You know, from the first day when I entered Asia, how throughout all the time I was with you, serving the Lord in all humility, and with tears and trials which befell me” from the Jews; “how I withheld nothing profitable, but announced to you” the previously unknown things of salvation, “and taught you publicly,” in church, “and [Col. 0179C] from house to house, testifying to Jews and Gentiles repentance and faith,” and other conduct, “in the Lord Jesus Christ. And now, bound by the Spirit, I go to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying that bonds and tribulations await me. But I fear none of these things, nor do I count my soul,” or life, “more precious than myself”—still less his own possessions, since he had none—“provided I may finish my course and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the Gospel of the grace of God.”

Of this ministry the Apostle says in 2 Timothy chapter 4: “But you, be watchful and labour in all things,” teaching both the perverse and the good rightly; “do the work [Col. 0179D] of an evangelist”; confirm by deed what you preach by mouth; “fulfil your ministry” thus: “be sober,” discerning in all your work, without every excess, rejecting even lawful things. “For everyone who strives in the contest abstains from all things” (1 Cor. 9).

He continues: “And now I know that you all, among whom I have gone about preaching the kingdom of God, will see my face no more. Therefore I call you to witness this day that I am clean from the blood of all of you. For I did not shrink”—that is, omit—“from announcing to you the whole counsel of God”: any teaching necessary to salvation.
