Therefore, had he failed to announce it to them, he would have been guilty of their souls. For if brother is bound to be the keeper of brother, and neighbour of neighbour [Col. 0180A]—otherwise the voice of a brother’s blood will cry to the Lord from the earth (Gen. 4)—how much more is a prelate bound to be the guardian of souls, for whom he has pledged that he will bring even the infirm sheep, carrying them upon his shoulders, into the heavenly fold, preferring all things to them, indeed exposing his own body to death for their sake.

Concerning the same passage, Jeremiah, chapter 48: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood,” that is, from the slaughtering of sin. Gregory (Part III of the *Pastoral Rule*, Admonition 26): This curse can apply to all, but how much more to prelates? To withhold one’s sword from blood is to restrain the word of preaching from killing the carnal life. Likewise, 3 Kings, chapter 20: “Thus says the Lord: Because you released from your hand a man worthy of death [Col. 0180B], your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.” It follows: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood. I know that after my departure ravenous wolves will enter among you, sparing not the flock. And from among yourselves men will arise speaking perverse things, in order to draw disciples after themselves. Therefore watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease with tears to admonish every one of you. And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace” (Acts 20): to the incarnate Word, who preached to you, or to the word which he himself—and I through him—preached to you, that it may be your guardian. Hence, 2 Peter [Col. 0180C], chapter 1: “We have the more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawn and the morning star arise in your hearts. I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing” (Acts 20).

Gloss: In this wolves are recognized and distinguished: that they covet and demand such things; true prelates do not. “You yourselves know that these hands supplied what was necessary for me and for those who were with me.” This is an example of working, a sign for bishops by which they are distinguished from wolves. “I have shown you all things: that by thus laboring one ought to support the weak and remember the word of the Lord Jesus—for he himself said: It is more blessed to give than [Col. 0180D] to receive. And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all,” commending them to God. “And there arose great weeping among them all; and falling upon Paul’s neck, they kissed him, grieving especially over the word which he had spoken, that they would see his face no more. And they escorted him to the ship” (Acts 20). A good ruler and rector is one at whose departure his subjects grieve and weep, especially because they will see him no longer.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the spiritual patience of prelates

The chief virtue and adornment of a prelate is patience. Commending it as exceedingly necessary for prelates, the Apostle says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 12: “And though I am nothing among you, nevertheless the signs of my apostleship [Col. 0181A] were performed among you in all patience.” Note: “all.”

Likewise, the Lord says: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves; therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.” And again: “Whoever strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also; and whoever takes your tunic, offer him your cloak as well” (Matthew 10); and, when your horse has been taken, say with the hermit: “Indeed, take the whip also.”

Likewise, 4 Kings 2: Elisha says to Elijah: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its driver,” that is, its supporter and ruler. On this Gregory says in Book 20 of the *Morals* and in Homily 21, Book 2 (in *dial.*, reading 12, Book 20, chapter 28), on Ezekiel: Impatience is almost always a companion of power, and it rules power badly subjected to it, because power readily carries out what impatience feels. But holy prelates [Col. 0181B] subject themselves inwardly to the yoke of patience more than they preside outwardly over other people. Thus they endure the disturbances of certain seditious persons all the more because they are more able to avenge themselves upon them; and lest they ever proceed to unlawful acts, they often do not even choose to execute for their own sake what is lawful. They bear the clamors of their subjects; through love they rebuke those whom they carry through gentleness; nor do they cease to teach, knowing that it is written: “A man’s teaching is recognized through patience” (Proverbs 19).

If, then, teaching consists in patience, each person is shown to be the more learned the more patient he is. Hence the good disciple, seeing his master taken up into the air, cries: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its driver” (4 Kings 2). What does it mean that he is called [Col. 0181C] both chariot and driver, except that the driver urges on while the chariot carries? Therefore the teacher who bears the people’s morals through patience and teaches with the words of sacred speech is called both “chariot” and “driver”:  “chariot,” because by enduring evils he carries them; “driver,” because by exhorting he urges and stirs them up. “Chariot,” because he sustains evils; “driver,” because he exercises the people by good admonitions.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the diligence and humility of prelates

On pastoral diligence and humility, whose nurse is poverty: when poverty is despised it greatly harms, but when observed it is of the highest benefit. Hence the Lord, commanding the apostles and their successors [Col. 0181D] to be free from worldly cares and temporal riches, says: “Do not possess gold or silver, nor 155 money in your purses” (Matthew 10). For the preacher, who ought to exhort others to despise riches, needs almost necessarily to be cut off from them, lest, carrying out worldly works and the burden of secular business, he have less leisure for his office. For he ought to have such trust in God that, even if he does not foresee the means of the present life, he may nevertheless know with absolute certainty that they will not fail him.

He adds why he gives them this command—because all necessities are owed them by those to whom they preach: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (ibid.). Note: *his*. And what sort of food is his? Hear Luke defining this: “Eating and drinking whatever they have” (Luke 10). And lest more luxurious and [Col. 0182A] costly things than “what they have” be sought, he adds: “Whatever is set before you.” If, therefore, you seek food, it is necessary that you embrace the moderation of apostolic preaching, so that you keep the beginning of the command: “Do not possess gold or silver” (Matthew 10). If, as successor of the apostles, you expect that food should be provided for you by the subjects among whom you labor, how can the end of the command be observed—indeed, observed or confirmed by many canons—without its beginning? It is uncivil to disclose one part of a law and affirm that it must be observed, while concealing another part or disputing concerning it as though it need not be observed.

Or by what authority will the first part of the command be set aside? If you say, by the custom and practice of those who do the contrary, asserting that ecclesiastical commands are local, temporal, and personal, the Gospel will have no firmness; against this the Lord says: “What I say to one, I say to all” (Mark 13). If you say that you do not possess these things but reserve them for the use of the poor, the layperson does the same. Therefore this command imposes nothing more on you in this matter than on a layperson.

Likewise, the Lord says: “How difficultly those who have money will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 18); “It is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19). When the disciples wondered and were astonished at his words, Simon Peter said to him: “Behold, we have left all things”—even the desire to possess them. For one who desires riches is counted among the rich, even if he does not possess them. It follows: “And we have followed [Col. 0182C] you. What then shall we have?” He answered: “In the renewal, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid.).

For this reward John, leaving behind the linen cloth, fled from them; Joseph left his cloak behind (Genesis 39); Matthew too, leaving the tax office and abandoning the accounts of the revenues—even at risk—followed the Lord. That Gospel man who wished to bury his father was commanded by the Lord to leave his father’s burial and follow him (Matthew 8). Therefore, much more is a prelate commanded to leave behind the noise of war, its burden, and the care of temporal affairs.

But how can the prelates of this age, the successors of the apostles, say: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you,” when they abound in temporal goods even beyond laypeople; when “they seek all these things which the Gentiles seek” (Matthew 6); when, contrary to the Lord’s command, they lay up treasures by multiplying gold and silver, horses and trappings, and the pomp of the world—which was forbidden even to the kings of Israel, lest they return to Egypt? (Deuteronomy 17). If they say that “they have left all things” because they have no patrimony or private possessions, but only an entrusted administration of the goods of the poor, many emperors and kings likewise left all things behind, such as those who succeed to a kingdom by election rather than inheritance. If they say: “Behold, we have left all things,” because we set all things after God, married persons are likewise bound to this [Col. 0183A]. Or how will they preach to their subjects that they should scatter and distribute their goods to the poor, when they do not cease to gather and store up what has been scattered? It would be safer not even to have something from which they might distribute to others. Or, if they have not left all things, how will they come with the Lord as judges?

Likewise, in the Gospel of John: “The Samaritan woman left her water-jar and went into the city, announcing all that Jesus had said to her” (John 4). Let those who are about to evangelize learn from this first to leave behind the water-jar—that is, covetousness—and to lay aside the burden and care of the world before undertaking evangelization.

Likewise, in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 22: “A dispute arose among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be the greater.” To them the Lord said: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power”—the power of bestowing—[Col. 0183B] “over them are called benefactors. But you are not so.” For even of the things which you distribute, you are not authors or lords, but stewards. Therefore, if an ecclesiastical prelate confers a benefice upon someone who is worthy and does so freely, he receives rather than gives; but if he confers it upon one who is unworthy or not needy, he steals and defrauds the goods of the poor, while that other person plunders them. How, then, do prelates suppose that those whom they have promoted are bound to serve them in all things, and shamefully reproach them by claiming to have been benefactors to them? If they bestow worthily—that is, assign an ecclesiastical benefice—they receive rather than give anything.

Or how do secular princes exercise dominion more than prelates of churches? If you say that they are lordly but do not exercise lordship: do they not actually possess servants and maidservants, fiefs and burdens, and titles of dignity, just as worldly rich men do? Do they not serve Caesar as well as God? Indeed, more than God. Yet concerning them, by the shameful removal of the negative particle, it is truer today to say: “The kings of the Gentiles—but you, more than so”; for in both secular and spiritual matters they are girded with the material sword as with the spiritual one.

## CHAPTER LX. On the state of clerics and the lower orders

After the priestly rank, a few things must be touched upon concerning the dignity and rank of deacons. The Apostle passes to them from the rank of bishops, using the name of bishops to signify the remaining [Col. 0183D] priests, while showing what sort of persons they ought to be. Thus, writing of deacons in the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3, he says: “Deacons” ought always to be chaste in body and mind, “modest,” like bishops, “not double-tongued, not given to much wine,” not drunken, “not pursuing shameful gain,” not buying in order to sell more dearly; “holding the mystery of faith in a pure conscience,” believing soundly and possessing works of faith. Of them may be repeated the things already said concerning bishops, since the same things are appropriate to them.

“And these”: he does not simply say “these,” but “and these”—namely deacons, as also bishops—“must first be proved” before being ordained; and, when ordained, in life, knowledge, and eloquence, “and thus,” having been tested and ordained, “let them minister, having no crime.” Hence Ambrose (*On Duties*, Book 1, chapter 50): The Apostle commands that a holy and honorable man be chosen as priest and Levite. And Jerome (Epistle 128, to Fabiola, beginning *Usque hodie*): No one except one perfect in knowledge and morals is to be chosen as priest and Levite. And the Lord said to Moses (Numbers 3): Finally, let that man be chosen priest and Levite who says to his father: “I do not know you.” For Levites are the watchmen and guards of the temple and bearers of its vessels. Therefore: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52).

Likewise, the Apostle, 1 Timothy chapter 5: “Lay hands on no one”—even if he appears wise and religious—“hastily,” without prior judgment and examination. The first laying on of hands is due to deacons to be ordained. For it is a recent institution that the subdiaconate should be a sacred order. He adds why hands should not hastily [Col. 0184B] be laid on anyone: “Neither share in the sins of others”—by consenting to everything that he may do, unless you have tested him once and again. For a man ought to be ordained with as much maturity as he is deposed—indeed, with more. For:

> A guest is more shamefully expelled than he is not admitted.  
> (*Ovid, Tristia*, Book 5, Elegy 6.)

How then are cloistered persons ordained without examination, even clerics of another diocese by dimissory letters, and boys possessing titles contrary to apostolic commands—which, because they are evangelical, admit no dispensation? And boys too are given prebends in churches. For this reason it seems that their institution is null, or conditional, and wholly dependent upon the future: namely, that when they reach years of discretion, they should be examined, ordained further if found suitable, and then minister; but if not, they should resign and others be substituted in their place.

Likewise Lawrence says to Sixtus (from the *Life* in Surius, vol. 4, and Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book 1, chapter 41): “Where are you going without your son, Father? Whither, holy priest, do you hasten without your deacon?” For the deacon ought to be ready to go with the priest to the sacrifice of the altar, to martyrdom, and to evangelize. Test certainly whether you have chosen a suitable minister, to whom you entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood: not to effect it, but to assist. As secretary of the altar, he shares in the priest’s making of the Eucharist—not because he receives or consecrates it, nor because it cannot be done without him, but because the Lord’s body is consecrated more solemnly and with greater reverence in the presence, ministry, and witness of the deacon. This ought to be observed especially in greater churches, and also in rural ones which have sufficient temporal means to provide for two ministers.

But that it belongs to the deacon’s office to preach by authority cannot be inferred, except perhaps from the example of blessed Vincent, who preached in place of his bishop—whereupon blessed Valerius said to him: “Now to you, dearest son, [belongs] the divine word,” etc.—and even from the ordination itself. For the Gospel is committed to him, as though it were said to him: “But you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). The Apostle’s saying might likewise be applied to this: “Entrust this to faithful men, who are suitable” (2 Timothy 2) in life, knowledge, and eloquence, to teach these things. [Col. 0185A] On the other hand, those first seven deacons were instituted to dispense and distribute food to the poor, so that the apostles might more freely devote themselves to contemplation, prayer, and preaching. But did not Stephen preach? Did not Philip? (Acts 6.) Certainly—but the others, especially those scattered abroad, did so equally with the apostles. Jerome writes sufficiently concerning the state of clerics to Nepotianus (Epistle 12).

## CHAPTER LXI. Against boy-prelates or novices

For priestly reverence, age is especially necessary and is almost of the substance of priestly rank. Hence the bishop of Le Mans writes to a certain man elected: There is an age which canonical rigor excludes from consecration because it fears it in those consecrated. If these things are so, an endless labor lies upon you, and things which have been begun with an evil principle will not easily find good outcomes. For in high priests sound age is required, so that religion may fear no danger and priestly dignity may not lose its reverence. Hence it is that in Ezekiel’s thirtieth year the heavens are opened, he sees visions of God, and prophesies; the prophet’s age is first described in order to show at what years preaching ought to be entrusted to a person (Ezekiel 1).

Christ likewise loved John above Peter; yet to Peter—not to John, though a virgin and perhaps more learned—was granted the power of binding and loosing (John 21). For he who said through Isaiah (chapter 57), “Remove stumbling-blocks from the way of my people,” did not wish to place a stumbling-block before his disciples, nor to set a young man before his elders, although he had made John especially intimate with himself through the prerogative of chastity. He therefore deferred to age, not to merits; nor did he prefer a married man to a virgin, but the more advanced to the younger.

Finally, Luke teaches us that the blessed Virgin found Christ seated in the temple among the doctors, listening to them and questioning them (Luke 2).

Therefore, until the fullness of years was lacking, the teacher of all did not exceed the limits of a disciple. But when full days came, he became a master by right, who had been a disciple by example. In all this is set forth the explicit pattern which the Church should follow, and a fixed boundary of age is appointed below which it is not permissible to make a bishop; once it is done, it is subject to judgment.

[Col. 0185D] But Solomon is objected, who was anointed king at twelve years of age (1 Chronicles 29); likewise Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1), Daniel (Daniel 13), and Timothy (2 Timothy 4), who as boys and before manhood became prophets and doctors of the Church. Yet this raises no objection. For perhaps even Solomon therefore had no good outcomes in his kingdom. Of the others we say that the privileges of a few do not make a common law; hence they should not be drawn into a consequence. Or, if you wish to draw this into a consequence, let persons like those mentioned be sought and chosen.

Likewise, Isaiah chapters 2–3: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, because he is accounted exalted.” If he should rise, he might strike the earth for the sin of the Church. “For behold, the Lord, the ruler of hosts, will remove from Jerusalem and Judah the strong and mighty man, [Col. 0186A] every support of spiritual bread and support of water”—that is, of teaching—“the strong man and the warrior, the judge and prophet and elder; the prince, the honorable of countenance, the counselor, the wise man, and the prudent interpreter of mysterious speech. And I will give boys as their princes, and effeminate men”—that is, wanton, unstable, and weak men—“shall rule over them; and the people shall fall upon [Vulgate: rush upon] one another, each man upon his neighbor. For the boy shall rage against the elder,” that is, he will dispute without reason, “and the base man against the noble. A man shall seize his brother, one of his father’s household, and say: ‘You have clothing’”—that is, all necessities—“‘be our ruler; this ruin’”—namely, that of our race—“‘is under your hand,’” that is, let it be, as it were, under your protection: if you wish to rise up, you can restore our race. “He shall answer,” excusing himself as unequal to the burden: “I who do not suffice for myself, how shall I suffice for others? I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor clothing; do not appoint me ruler of the people.”

Jeremiah excuses himself thus in chapter 1; Moses likewise in Exodus 4. Therefore the Apostle commanded that one should be chosen “not a novice, lest, being chosen, he be lifted up into pride” (1 Timothy 3). Hence Ecclesiastes, chapter 2: “Put away anger and malice from your heart. For youth and pleasure are vain.” And what else is it to entrust the governance of souls to youths than to sell and hand over Joseph—that is, Christ—to barren, soft, and effeminate eunuchs? (Genesis [Col. 0186C] 27.) Or to leave the ark of the Lord to idolatrous Philistines, that it may be housed beside Dagon? (3 Kings 5.) Or to give the vessels of the Lord to Belshazzar’s concubines and boys so that they may drink from them? (Daniel 5.) For this reason the king was killed and Babylon destroyed. Rehoboam, having abandoned the counsel of the elders, yielded to the young men and therefore lost the kingdom (3 Kings 12). Hence Ecclesiastes, chapter 10: “Woe to you, O land, whose king is a boy and whose prince eats in the morning.”

Likewise, in the First Book of Kings the Lord says to Eli: “I plainly declared that your house and the house of your father should minister before me forever. But now the Lord says: Far be this from me! Rather, whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be dishonored. Behold, days are coming when I shall cut off your arm and the arm [Col. 0186D] of your father’s house, so that there shall be no old man in your house. And this shall be a sign to you: your two sons shall both die on one day; and I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to my heart and my soul” (1 Kings 2).

Likewise Isaiah (chapter 22): “Enter,” says the Lord, “to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna, overseer of the temple, and say to him: ‘What have you here? Or who are you here, that you have cut out for yourself a tomb here?’” For he thought that he would remain in that place permanently. “Behold, the Lord,” he says, “will carry you away as a cock is carried away.” A cock is one who presides well over the temple, awakening others from sleep. But this man, like a cock, pursued womanish things, a lover of pleasures rather than of God. “And as one lifts up a garment, he will lift you up; as a ball he will throw you into [Col. 0187A] a broad and spacious land.” “Broad is the way and gate that leads to death” (Matthew 7).

Likewise Jerome, on Isaiah chapter 3: The Septuagint call the effeminate and the youths “mockers,” such as the concubines of the Levite mocked at Gibeah (Judges 19): namely, effeminate, luxurious men, weakened into womanhood. Teachers of peoples too are mockers when they “devour the people of God like bread” (Psalm 13), not knowing the Scriptures or interpreting them perversely.

It follows in Isaiah, chapter 3: “And the base in birth or life shall rage against the noble. For a man shall seize his brother and one of his father’s household.” Men will not elect others commonly, but will seize those dear to them from carnal affection, forcing them in, and say: “You have clothing; therefore [Col. 0187B] be our ruler. This ruin is under your hand.” Likewise Jerome, in the same place: Let us not immediately acquiesce in the judgment of the multitude choosing us; but, once chosen to authority, let us know the measure of our own strength, because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5). Many who are hungry and naked, because they possess neither spiritual food nor Christ’s tunic—that is, virtues—promise clothing and nourishment to others; and, being ulcerous, boast that they are physicians, not fearing the saying in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 7: “Do not seek to become a judge, lest perhaps you may be unable to remove the wickedness of the people.”

But when the episcopate was a burden and labor, the person elected answered: “I am not a physician,” one sufficient to heal your miseries; “and in my house there is neither bread nor clothing; do not appoint me ruler of the people.” A similar passage is read in First Question, First [Distinction/Chapter; reference uncertain]. But modern elect do not imitate these examples.

Likewise: “Young men and virgins, old men with the younger, praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148). It is common to all to praise with heart, mouth, and deed. But to praise in the chair and in government belongs only to elders. Hence: “Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the chair of the elders” (Psalm 106). But whoever praises “in the chair” of the elders while lacking old age in years presumptuously declares that he possesses old age of manners and gravity. It is as though he said: “I am another Daniel, another Timothy; I am such a man that, because of my life and merits, spiritual right ought to be conceded to me and the general right [Col. 0187D] of the canons broken.”

Likewise, the Lord says to Eli: “Because you were lax in correcting your sons, I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there shall be no old man in your house all your days. Yet I will not wholly remove a man from my altar, and you shall see your rival”—that is, a young man—“in the temple amid all Israel’s prosperity” (1 Kings 2).

Likewise, 1 Timothy chapter 5: If the Apostle commands that “younger widows” should be avoided—because the blood burns in them and they quickly grow wanton when fed at another’s expense—so that they are not admitted to the Church’s provision, to be fed from ecclesiastical goods, how much more does he prohibit young men and adolescents from being admitted to the government of the Church, so that they may feed others—especially since they are more prone to become wanton in ecclesiastical goods, because the rich may do everything [Col. 0188A] and can do everything?

Likewise: Under human law, a person younger than twenty-five excused himself from undertaking another person’s guardianship; today, under the same law, such a person is not only not admitted to guardianship but is excluded, lest those who need a guardian and defender become administrators and guardians of another’s property. Otherwise that comic saying would be shamefully applied to those appointing such a person: “For one who needs a patron, they provide me a defender; for one who needs a pedagogue, they appoint me a teacher.” And what is more unseemly and indiscreet than to admit a man below mature age as ruler and guardian of souls, when the Apostle admits no woman under sixty to the administration of temporal matters and the guardianship of virgins? (1 Timothy 5.)

How will one who needs bread broken for him break bread for others? (Jerome, at the end of the letter to Oceanus beginning *Nunquam, fili Oceane*.) How do those still nursing and needing milk become nurses who offer milk to others? How do those become teachers who do not know how to be disciples? How shamefully the Church which admits such a man is reproached: yesterday he was in the theater, today in the choir; yesterday at the circus, today at the altar; yesterday a supporter of actors, today a consecrator of virgins.

Let such men fear the deed of Mark, who cut off his own thumb so that he would be disqualified from priesthood. Likewise, the Lord commands in the law (Deuteronomy 20) that no man younger than twenty, no fainthearted man, no man attached to a wife, no man who had built a house and had not yet dedicated it, nor one who had planted a vineyard and had not yet drunk from it, should go forth to bodily war. How much more ought these things [Col. 0188C] be guarded against and forbidden in those going forth to spiritual warfare, who are to fight “against the spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6). For the instability of a younger age breaks reverence and destroys the priestly order.

Likewise, Moses and Aaron were not sent by the Lord to speak to Pharaoh until they were eighty years old (Exodus 7). Likewise, if people’s age is considered in the representation of miracles, as though in a play, yet such representations move human affections; if it is considered in comedies and tragedies, why not in serious matters and in presenting truth—namely, in choosing true pastors of the Church?

Likewise Isaiah (chapter 1): “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good.” Jerome says: For this purpose, one must wear down the thresholds of teachers. But whoever has not frequented the thresholds of teachers and assumes the office of preaching somehow says, with Paul: “I was taught the Gospel not by man but by the Holy Spirit” (Galatians 1); therefore believe me, because I am another Paul. Likewise, if among the Hebrews the reading of the beginning of Genesis, the end of Ezekiel, and the Songs of Love was forbidden to those under thirty, how much more ought the living reading of the whole of sacred Scripture—which indeed consists more in deed than in speech—to be forbidden in the Church to those under age? “Trust a bearded teacher.”

These points may also be directed against the ambition of teachers gathering a crowd of old men and decrepit soldiers to their theater and spectacle, who, though still boys, presume to teach old men. Likewise, 1 Kings chapter 1: Samuel was brought by his mother only after he was weaned, that he might appear before the Lord, remaining and serving continually in the temple. Hence the Gloss: Anna does not wish to take the boy to the house of God before he is weaned, because the Church advances no one to priesthood while he shares in the “milk” of infancy rather than “solid food,” namely spiritual understanding. It is as though she said: Only one weaned from the milk of childhood, the milk of adolescence, and the milk of more tender teaching. Likewise, Job chapter 32, concerning Elihu.

## CHAPTER LXII. Against evil silence, especially that of prelates

[Col. 0189B] The office of prelates is chiefly strengthened, as though this were part of its substance, by their barking, through which wolves are kept away from the flock, lest they be “dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah 56), “not setting themselves as a wall for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 13). Crying out against their most wicked silence, Isaiah, chapter 62, says: “For Zion”—that is, kings and princes—“I will not be silent; for Jerusalem”—Levites and priests—“I will not rest, until her righteousness goes forth as brightness.” And again: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have stationed guards: all day”—of prosperity—“and all night”—of adversity—perpetually “they shall not be silent. You who call the Lord to remembrance, do not be silent, and give him”—the Lord—“no silence, until he establishes and makes [Col. 0189C] Jerusalem”—that is, the Church—“a praise in the earth,” such as and as great as I see depicted in sacred Scripture. For the Church does not yet seem established, because it is found almost nowhere; but it is such, or ought to be such, as it is not seen but understood to be—not, however, as I perceive it in practice.

And again, chapter 40: “The voice of the Lord saying: Cry out; do not cease. Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem; lift it up, do not fear.” And again: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of one announcing and preaching peace, announcing good things, preaching salvation!” Likewise the same prophet, chapter 6: “Woe is me, because I kept silent! Woe is me, because I am a man of polluted lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people with polluted lips!” Polluted not by lies, not by buffooneries, not by insults, but by silence. As punishment for this sin: “One of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a burning coal, which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth,” and burned my lip, “and said: Behold, I have touched your lips, and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin”—arising from silence—“shall be cleansed.”

Likewise Jeremiah, second alphabet, *Yod* (chapter 2): Alas, alas! “The princes sat upon the earth”—in earthliness, to cultivate the vineyard and defend and possess royal estates and dung-heaps—“and the elders of the daughter of Zion were silent; they sprinkled ashes upon their heads, they girded themselves with haircloth, the virgins of Jerusalem cast down their heads to the ground, because the nursing child failed in the streets.” Likewise Acts of the Apostles, chapter 20: “I testify to you today that I am clean from the blood of all. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.” Likewise Psalm 39: “I have announced and spoken, and they are multiplied beyond number. I have declared your righteousness in the great Church; behold, I will not restrain my lips, Lord, you know. I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have spoken your truth and your salvation. I have not hidden your mercy and your truth from the great assembly.”

Likewise: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door”—not a lock—“of restraint about my lips” (Psalm 140). Likewise Proverbs, chapter 1: “Wisdom preaches abroad; in the streets she gives her voice, and at the head of crowds”—that is, among prelates—“she cries out; at the gates of the city she utters [Col. 0190B] her words,” saying: “How long, little children”—in understanding—“will you love childhood, and fools desire harmful things, and the imprudent hate wisdom?”

Likewise Jeremiah, chapter 26: “Stand in the court of the house of the Lord, and speak to all the cities of Judah all the words which I commanded you to speak to them. Do not withhold a word, if perhaps they may hear and repent and turn from their evil way.” And chapter 3: “Go and cry these words. Return, O rebellious Israel, says the Lord, and I will not turn my face from you, nor will I be angry with you forever. Know your iniquity, because you have transgressed; and return, returning children, to me, because I am your husband, and I will take you.”

Likewise the Apostle, Acts, chapter [Col. 0190C] 20: “You know, from the first day when I entered among you, how I withheld none of the things profitable to you, so as not to announce them to you and teach you publicly and from house to house, testifying to Jews and Gentiles repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Likewise: John too, while in prison and having no hope of the amendment of Herod or Herodias, attacked the crime rather than the persons, as an example to posterity (lest they should abominate the crime of adultery or incest less, had he kept silent). He repeatedly cried: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6). Had he ceased, his head would not have been cut off. He cried out, preferring danger before the king to forgetfulness of the divine commandment—he “who was sent in the spirit and power of Elijah” [Col. 0190D] (Luke 1)—against Herod and Herodias, as Elijah did against Ahab and Jezebel (3 Kings 18).

Likewise, it is read in the *Ecclesiastical History* that, when Pope Athanasius was exiled for the Catholic faith by rulers favouring Arius and the Arians, a certain hermit said inwardly to himself (*Book* 10): “Woe is me, because I keep silent” (Isaiah 6). “Why do I idly eat bread?” (Proverbs 30). Why do I not rather go into exile with the righteous, wandering, and holy Athanasius? Why do I not cry aloud against the rulers on his behalf? Leaving his desert and cave, and imposing this upon himself as penance, he cried through cities, fortified places, villages, and streets: “Athanasius is righteous, Catholic, and holy; he teaches the truth, which I steadfastly maintain and affirm.”

Likewise David: “I believed; therefore I spoke” (Psalm 115). And the Lord in the [Col. 0191A] Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father” (Matthew 10). And the Apostle: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10), in its proper time and place. Hence in the Socratic decree: It is no less impiety to keep silent about the truth at the proper time and place than to speak falsehood. But whoever keeps it silent is like the Cathar, “who speaks truth in his heart” (Psalm 14), saying: “Swear, forswear; do not reveal a secret,” when it is necessary and useful that such matters be disclosed to one’s neighbour rather than concealed.

Likewise Jeremiah cries: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each save his own soul. Do not be silent concerning her iniquity, for it is the time of the Lord’s vengeance” (Jeremiah 51). “And when he had finished speaking all that [Col. 0191B] the Lord had commanded him, the priests seized him, saying: ‘This man must die, because he has prophesied against the city.’ And Jeremiah said to all the princes and to the people: ‘The Lord sent me, saying: Make your ways and your pursuits good; hear the voice of the Lord your God, and he will repent of the evil which he has spoken against you. 164 Behold, I am in your hands: do to me what is good and right in your eyes. Yet know and understand that, if you kill me, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its inhabitants. For in truth the Lord sent me to you, that I might speak all these words in your hearing’” (Jeremiah [Col. 0191C] 26).

Likewise Gregory, on the passage, “Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was dumb” (Luke 11), explains “dumb” by its effect: for certain demons preside over certain persons in order to make them mute when there is need to speak. Thus they may be called dumb demons. In like manner certain demons preside over garrulity, making chatterers of those concerning whom the philosopher says: “What difference is it whether they thunder from above or below?” Some silent people too chatter along with the whole world.

And Susanna (Daniel 13), though silent, cried out; and so did Hannah and Moses (1 Kings 1).

Silence is wrongly maintained in four matters: in confessing sins and praises: “For confession perishes from the dead man, as from one who is no more” (Ecclesiasticus 17). “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me” [Col. 0191D] (Psalm 68). “Confess your sins one to another” (James 5). “In hymns confess him” (Psalm 99).

Silence is also wrong in reproving one’s neighbour, if you see your neighbour’s iniquity and do not rebuke him: “I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezekiel 3). “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him” (Matthew 18), and so forth. Augustine (*Letter* 19, chapter 4): The correction of a brother is commanded from equal to equal, from inferior to superior, from superior to inferior, from anyone to anyone.

Silence is also wrong in preaching. Hence the Lord: “What you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matthew 10). And the Apostle: “Press on and preach, in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4).

[Col. 0192A] Silence is likewise wrong in counselling one’s neighbour when he is in need. Hence Job: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame” (Job 29). Likewise: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6).

But is silence wrong in acting as an advocate? Yes: in the cause of the widow, the ward, and the orphan. Hence the prophet: “Let the widow’s cause come before you. They do not judge for the orphan, and the widow’s cause does not come before them. Seek justice, aid the oppressed, judge for the orphan, defend the widow” (Isaiah 1). But advocacy is wrongly undertaken from greed. Then silence would be better. It is good to be silent in disputing and litigating. But an objection is made: Nothing is fully understood unless it is broken by the tooth of disputation? Yet by disputation he means discussion of the sort fitting for saints.

There are five causes of most pernicious silence. The first is human or worldly fear, under the pressure of which Peter denied him (Matthew 26). “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew 10). If a bishop is afraid, it is all over with him.

**B. CYPRIAN.** The second cause is greed, which accompanies fear. For no one fears unless he desires. Greed is a little frog which, thrown into a dog’s mouth, makes it mute. Thrown into the mouth of Demosthenes—who was the living voice of law—it made him mute when he ought to have pleaded and acted as advocate with the Romans for the republic, and with the Athenians against Philip, king of Macedon, father of 165 Alexander. Hence one of the senators, reproaching him when he kept silent about good causes, said [Col. 0192C]: “Demosthenes suffers not from *squinancia* [quinsy], but from *arginancia* [money-quinsy].” This little frog, thrown into the mouths of judges, and also into the mouths of masters by children, causes punishments, terrors, and threats to be remitted on their account, because gifts blind the eyes and bend the force of authority. Paul even abstained from receiving support and necessities from his subjects, earning his livelihood by his hands (1 Corinthians 9).

The third cause is sloth or negligence. “Jesus went about the cities, preaching and healing every infirmity among them” (Matthew 9). Therefore a prelate ought to be energetic and diligent.

The fourth cause is simplicity and a certain almost natural modesty, by which Jeremiah excused himself, saying (chapter 1): “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God: I am but an alphabet-learner [*abecedarius*], and [Col. 0192D] I do not know how to speak.”

But no prelates say this today, as though prudence in them supplied for age—which is false—but rather through human favour or nobility of birth. Yet this is a fault in a preacher and orator. Hence Quintilian, in the *Institutes of Oratory*: Modesty, the friend of virtue, is a fault in an orator, though at the proper time it is lovable.

The fifth cause—and the worst—is ignorance. Hence Jerome, in his letter against Helvidius: One ignorant of preaching—what voice will a dumb herald utter? O deaf and dumb idol-shepherd, idol of the Church’s desolation, standing in the holy place of Zion, who, unable to speak, gives the peoples answers as though through hired demons and piglets. He is comparable [Col. 0193A] to the Gallic monster Helvidius, who in Gaul—which lacked monsters—alone was discovered to be both priest and layman: not because he did not know many letters, but because he did not know the tropes of speech. Thus, ignorant of the various senses of the name “firstborn,” he erred concerning the Blessed Virgin.

Therefore there is a voice of repentance. Hence: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Psalm 6).

[lacuna]

“And tears have the weight of a voice.” (Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, Elegy 1.) There is also the voice of confession: “The sound of one feasting, in the voice of exultation and confession” (Psalm 41). This is followed by the voice of prayer: “Give heed to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God” (Psalm 5). Afterwards comes the voice of praise and [Col. 0193B] thanksgiving and of a conscience made serene: “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” (Psalm 117). In all these matters silence is dangerous. After this follows, in proper order, “the voice of preaching,” which is the voice of salvation, lest it be said to a preacher who is still entangled in satisfaction for sin: “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your lips?” (Psalm 49), etc.

Hence St Bernard to Bruno, bishop-elect of Cologne: Although you are learned and canonically elected, nevertheless, as you assert, you have not wept, you have not completed penance, and so you are a novice in life, though not in faith. That you should undertake so great a burden I neither commend nor wholly disapprove, because of the necessity and frailty of the pressing time; [Col. 0193C] but if you undertake it, I shall pray for you.

Likewise: “I thought to understand this; it was labour before me, until I entered the sanctuary of the Lord and understood their latter end” (Psalm 72). And: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Psalm 118).

By the first voice: You sit with Mary at the Lord’s feet (Luke 10).

By the second: You rise to kiss the hands.

By the third: To kiss the head.

By the fourth: To anoint the whole Christ. Of this there are five kinds: “correction”—this belongs to students in evil habits and modes of life contrary to Holy Scripture; “instruction,” for prelates; and “exhortation, encouragement, and consolation,” for the saints. The apostles and apostolic men in the primitive Church possessed the voice of calling to faith. Of these voices David says: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God, that I may proclaim all your preachings in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Psalm 72).

For there are several modes of preaching, as we have said, in which silence is wrong, especially for a prelate. But if any other mode beyond those mentioned is added, it arises from the evil of curiosity, display, and delight. Hence the Apostle: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth; but if any is good, let it be only for instruction” (Ephesians 4). And David: “My mouth shall speak wisdom”—concerning faith—“and the meditation of my heart understanding” (Psalm 48), concerning good morals.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On Good Silence

[Col. 0194A]

Having censured the vice of bad silence, let us commend good silence. Let the prelate open his mouth to praise, adore, confess to, counsel, console, preach about, and teach God. For there is “a time for silence and a time for speaking” (Ecclesiastes 3). Hence: “I have hidden your sayings in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Psalm 118).

Augustine: Good silence is the foundation of religion. For I know that you have commanded that what is holy should not be given to dogs, nor pearls scattered before swine (Matthew 7), lest God’s secrets be shown to the unworthy, lest the treasures of God’s house be revealed to Babylonians (Jeremiah 26). Yet someone divulges them in order to please the person to whom he speaks through flattery, [Col. 0194B] or for greed, vain glory, or inquisitive talkativeness. Therefore the discipline of silence must be adopted, so that a person should first be silent before he speaks, according to that saying: “Let every person be swift to hear and slow to speak” (James 1).

There are four causes of good silence with respect to hearers: namely, because they are dogs—detractors, obstinate persons, and unbelievers—or because they are swine, disgusted by the word of God and unclean.

The speaker of slander is bad; the reporter of it worse; the hearer worst. Hence Ezekiel, chapter 3: “Son of man, I will make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you shall be dumb and not like a man who rebukes, because they are a provoking house.” The third cause is frequency: preaching [Col. 0194C] loses its value if it is continual.

> The wise man sets an end even to honourable things.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 6.441.)

The fourth cause is the incapacity of hearers. Hence the Apostle: “I could not speak to you as to 167 spiritual persons; I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3).

Likewise, two causes are considered with respect to the preacher: consciousness of sin, whence: “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you hate discipline” (Psalm 49); and mute eloquence, beneath which lies a sick conscience. “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4). Speak first by deeds rather than words; and also incapacity for divine discourse, or good modesty. Hence: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak” [Col. 0194D] (Jeremiah 1).

Therefore, if it is useful and necessary to speak, consider what, how many things, how great they are, of what kind, when you speak, to whom or to which persons, where, and how. Consider also whether you need to use public preaching or private preaching, which is directed to a private person and takes place in a secret setting. In this latter context correction must sometimes cease. Hence the Apostle: “After a third warning avoid a heretical man” (Titus 3); so also an incorrigible person and an incorrigible ruler.

Hence Jerome, in the prologue to Ezra (letter to Domnion and Rogatian): To strive in vain and to achieve nothing but incur hatred by wearying or rebuking is the height of madness. Thus Paul, lest he provoke Caesar’s anger, so cautiously and under a veil predicted the destruction of the Roman Empire that he did not predict it; he so published it that he did not publish it: “Let him who now holds, hold, until he is removed from the midst” (2 Thessalonians 2).

Likewise Jeremiah, chapter 25, cautiously and prudently foretold and threatened the destruction of Babylon; as Jerome says, lest he provoke the king of Babylon to anger, he used the name “Sheshach” in place of “Babylon,” which was to be destroyed. Jerome himself also says of that passage (in his commentary thereon): When rulers, false prophets, and priests accuse him and seek to impose on him a capital charge, he speaks to the people whom they had stirred up against him, wisely, humbly, and steadfastly. Wisely, urging them to repentance so that the Lord might change his sentence concerning [Col. 0195B] the destruction of the city; humbly, saying: “I, your servant, am also in your hands”; steadfastly, saying: “In truth the Lord sent me to you, and these things will happen unless you repent” (Jeremiah 26).

But in public preaching one must by no means be silent. Hence Jeremiah, chapter 26: “Stand in the court of the Lord’s house, and speak to all the cities of Judah,” etc. Nor should one be silent even in private preaching if a bad example is feared. Hence John did not keep silent even in prison (Mark 6).

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the Vice of the Tongue

The four causes of evil talkativeness or garrulity are flattery, boasting, greed, and [Col. 0195C] reckless loquacity. Talkativeness is therefore contrary to good silence, against which the Prophet cries: “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips. Do not incline my heart to words of malice” (Psalm 140), among which are idle words. Hence Abbot Serapion in the *Lives of the 168 Fathers*: There is no member in my body which I fear as much as the tongue. “If anyone thinks himself religious and does not restrain his tongue” from evil, “but deceives his heart, that person’s religion is vain” (James 1).

Likewise he says: For a long time I wept, endured many labours, and lived a long time in the desert; yet I was never able to attain the measure of humility and silence possessed by my son Zacharias.

Likewise Abbot Pastor: I never uttered a word in an elder’s presence, but praised what he said. Likewise, replying to someone who asked, “How may I live quietly in the place where I live?” he said: “Among those with whom you live, live as a stranger, not as a master; and never let your word have power before you.” Likewise he said: If you wish to be loved and to live quietly, keep much silence. “For in much speaking sin will not be absent” (Proverbs 10).

Therefore the poet (Cato) proclaims:

> Think the first virtue to be the restraint of the tongue.  
> For never having kept silent does harm; having spoken does harm.

Faith is rare for this reason: many people speak many things. And Ecclesiasticus says (chapter 9): “A man of many words is abominable and hateful in a city, and one who often stumbles in speech.” Lantfranc, lest he grow proud because of his learning, [Col. 0196A] always kept silent until a danger to the faith arose.

Some of the Fathers also, lest they sin with the tongue, carried in their mouths almost continually a pebble as a bridle. Likewise: As it is safer to err in the remission of mercy than in the rigour of justice, so it is safer in silence than in talkativeness. Likewise: “Who is the man who desires life and loves to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Psalm 33). For “a man of many words,” who speaks true things beyond necessity, “will not be established on the earth” (Psalm 139).

For, just as through frequent swearing we often fall into perjury, so through frequent idle speech we fall into evil speech. “For in much speaking sin will not be absent; [Col. 0196B] but he who restrains his lips is most prudent” (Proverbs 10). For “a fool is struck by his lips” (ibid.). “The labour of their lips shall cover them” (Psalm 139). He who speaks truth does not labour. “But the bridegroom’s friend stands and hears the bridegroom’s voice with joy” (John 3).

Augustine, on Psalm 50, at “You shall give joy to my hearing”: Therefore let teaching, speaking, and preaching be a necessity for you; but let hearing, keeping silent, and learning be your desire. It is safer for truth to be heard than spoken. For to one who swells outwardly, glorying to burst into speech, it will be said: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22).

In the righteous person, therefore, the heart speaks, the mouth meditates, and the hand signifies work. Hence: “The mouth [Col. 0196C] of the righteous shall meditate justice, and his tongue shall speak judgment” (Psalm 36). Let him not be “like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13), but let his words have a foundation and not proceed from the surface of his lips. Of such a one it is said: “By the understanding of his hands he led them” (Psalm 77). Work, therefore, and you will understand.

To distinguish those who employ evil speech from those who use good speech, observe that the double-minded and deceitful “speak in heart and heart” (Psalm 11); chatterers, “in mouth and mouth”; slanderers and revilers, “in tooth and tooth”; contemplatives, in the heart alone; active persons, in heart and mouth for their neighbour.

To avoid the vice of the tongue, note that one uses evil speech in three ways. First, against oneself through arrogant boasting: “My son, let not the lips of a slanderer praise you” (Proverbs 4). [Col. 0196D] Secondly, against one’s neighbour—and this in three ways: by a manifest word of malice and insult; by a hidden word of detraction; or by a feigned word of flattery. Thirdly, against the Lord: by a word of unbelief, a word of blasphemy, a word of heretical perversity, a word of foolish inquiry, or a word of wandering curiosity.

“Men will render account on the day of judgment for every idle word” (Matthew 12). An idle word is whatever is said apart from the benefit of speaker or hearer: “A man of many words is terrible in his city, and one rash in speech will be hated” (Ecclesiasticus 9). “He who desires life and loves to see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil” (Psalm 33), etc.

He does not say, “from an idle word,” but “from evil,” because the tongue is slippery and easily slides into idle speech, [Col. 0197A] greed, “pride, the wicked way, and a double mouth I hate” (Proverbs 8). “The wise in heart will receive commandments” (Proverbs 10): it is sometimes necessary to speak for the sake of the unlearned. He who always desires to teach always wishes to have unlearned people.

Truth does not ask whether heart, mouth, and hand agree: “Good understanding belongs to all who do it” (Psalm 110). “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Psalm 118). In Ecclesiasticus, chapter 28: “The whisperer,” etc.—almost the whole chapter is against the vice of the tongue; likewise the end of James’s Epistle, chapter 3: “Do not become many teachers,” etc.

## CHAPTER LXV. What Preaching Ought to Be According to the Capacity of Hearers, and against the Evil Talkativeness of Preachers

That we may continue the office of the prelate and examine more fully his [Col. 0197B] reckless talkativeness, we judge that the foregoing should be supplemented by a discussion “On the restraint and moderation of preaching.” It must be moderated according to the quality and quantity of what is to be said, and likewise according to the quality and capacity of the hearers.

Hence David: “Day pours forth speech to day”—that is, the spiritual person to the spiritual person, the greater to the greater: the “Word,” which “was in the beginning with God” (John 1), which God spoke once. “And night declares knowledge to night” (Psalm 18): the weak and imperfect person openly shows a lesser knowledge to the weak and imperfect. Augustine: as historical matters concerning Christ. For not all things are for all persons, but spiritual matters are to be given discerningly to spiritual persons, wisdom to the wise.

But to carnal persons the preacher ought to announce lesser matters, such as historical matters. Likewise: “The mountains ascend” (Psalm 103)—the apostolic men: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1); “the plains descend”—the lesser to the lesser: “The Word was made flesh.”

Likewise the Apostle, 1 Corinthians, chapter 2: “I did not come to you in loftiness of speech or wisdom. For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect and spiritual, in whom charity believes all things in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.” The same, chapter 3: “But I could not speak to you as to 170 spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons, as little children in Christ: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.” “If anyone among you seems wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may become wise.” Likewise, chapter 9: “I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak. And what more? I became all things to all, that I might save all.”

Hence Romans, chapter 1: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the unwise.” First Corinthians, chapter 9: “I made myself the servant of all.” The same, 2 Corinthians 5: “Whether we are beside ourselves”—contemplating things which it is not lawful for a man to speak, and the wisdom which we speak among the perfect—“it is for God.” “Or whether we are sober,” that is, moderate, “it is [Col. 0197D] for you”—among incapable hearers, “I saw that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified”—that is, for your benefit. “For charity constrains us” (2 Corinthians 5) to condescend to those of lesser capacity.

For this reason also, as a figure, “spittle”—that is, saliva-like and infantile words—“ran down David’s beard” (1 Kings 21). A prelate ought to have infantile words for the lesser and manly words for the greater. Likewise this was signified in Jacob’s vision of angels ascending and descending by the ladder (Genesis 28). Its top reached heaven, its feet the earth. The Lord himself also prefigured the same thing when he said: “Henceforth you shall see angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1).

Hence Augustine, commenting on “In the beginning was the Word,” says: A prelate should be like a hen, which clucks, grows hoarse, and wastes away over her chicks, covering and warming them with her wings. He ought likewise to be like an orator—like Cicero or Hortensius—so that in an assembly and on the [Col. 0198B] Capitol he thunders in strong and trumpet-like speech. But when he comes home among little children, he should begin to stammer and break up his words, using childish words, so that by conforming to them he may be understood.

Likewise the Lord: “Who do you think is the faithful servant whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” (Matthew 24). This must be considered in the number, quality, and quantity of matters to be said. Gregory says upon this passage in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part 3, Admonition 36, chapters 5 and 6): The faithful servant is rare; rarer is the prudent servant who does not mingle anything with the divine utterances through an adulterated opinion; rarest are those who know how to dispense to their household a measure of wheat according to the hearers’ capacity and the quality of what is said. Those who irreverently disclose what ought to be hidden, who scatter abroad heavenly secrets before everyone, who intoxicate with wine those who need milk, seeking rather to display their own talent than to benefit their neighbours, are not dispensers but destroyers [Col. 0198C] of the divine word.

Likewise the same author, on Exodus 25: In the Lord’s temple there were vinegar-bowls, bowls, and cups (*Morals*, Book 20, chapter 2); so in the Church there are biting interpretation, abundant preaching, and preaching that is lesser and sweet. For we should not set everything before everyone indiscriminately, but, as it were for a preliminary tasting, offer greater matters to the greater and lesser matters to the lesser.

This preacher is also a physician, a public servant, a beast of burden—upon which the Samaritan placed the wounded man (Luke 10), and of which it is also said: “Let the earth bring forth grass for beasts of burden” (Psalm 103), so called from helping (*iuvando*)—a basket and a dung-vessel; the Church is the stable. Describing his office, Jeremiah, chapter 1, says: “I have appointed you over nations, that you may pluck up and destroy, lose 171 and scatter, build and plant.” He gives four words concerning the casting out of sins—which occurs through rebuke of vices, threats of judgment, hearing confession, and imposing satisfaction—but only two concerning the planting of virtues, which occurs through preaching and example.

Prelates, then, are baskets by which sins should be carried out, not brought in; they are to gather rubbish, chaff, and dung for making Pharaoh’s bricks, in washing and preparing which they become more defiled. [Col. 0199A] Let the confessor possess the Samaritan’s wine and oil: wine, that by piercing rebuke the penitent may conceive, through fear of the Lord, and bring forth the Spirit of salvation; oil, by consolation, that he may not be swallowed up by sorrow, but that “his sorrow may be turned into joy” (John 16).

Let him show himself to the penitent gentle, pleasant, and sweet, cherishing him as it were in his embraces and saying: “You confess to God alone, whose vicar I am, so that I cannot disclose what is revealed to him, whether by word, nod, or sign. You who confess to me bind me in spiritual fatherhood, so that I may bear your sins as those of a son, grieve for them, and make satisfaction for them with you. Therefore trust and do penance. If you follow my counsel, I promise—and pledge myself as guarantor in this matter—that you will be wholly freed.”

But he must never support the penitent in his greed or in withholding another’s property. If the penitent secretly offers an offering, he should refuse it. He must never show favour to the penitent’s person or flatter him, but judge justly in order to heal. Of these baskets it is said: “His hands served in the basket” (Psalm 80). These are the baskets which the Lord commanded to be filled with fragments left over by those eating, fragments which escape the hands of diners (John 6).

In confession the confessor ought especially to enjoin three chief things upon the penitent as most necessary: to avoid, as far as possible, an occasion of sin; to flee delay in confessing if he has suffered a relapse; and not to incur negligence in making satisfaction for sins. He must flee the occasion of sin, [Col. 0199C] because places alone are harmful and occasion sometimes provides matter for sinning. He must banish delay in confessing, because delay is great ruin. Thus, after sin has been committed, one must run immediately to the confessor. Hence Augustine: Why does uncertain tomorrow await today’s salvation? Negligence in satisfaction is incurred because “Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 68).

Nor should this be omitted: someone, with I know not what intention, said to Alexander III: “Lord, you are a good pope. Whatever you do is papal.” Alexander replied in his vernacular: “If I knew how to judge well, preach well, and give penance well, I would be a good pope.” Thus in these three things he expressed the entire office of the prelate.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On the Threefold Office of the Prelate, and against Respect of Persons

The prelate’s threefold office—namely, to judge, give penance, and preach—is especially impeded by respect of persons. Rebuking it, the Apostle says in Romans 2: “Grace and peace to everyone who does good” toward God, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For there is no respect of persons with God.” Augustine: For he does not receive Jews who act wickedly because of their fathers’ merits, nor reject converted Gentiles because of their parents’ sins.

That it may be clear what respect of persons is, we must consider what honour is, which God commands, so that teaching and knowledge of one contrary may be compared with its contrary. Honour is the reverence to be shown to someone for a due cause: for example, because of religious devotion and uprightness of life, age—whence, “before a grey head” [Leviticus 19], etc.—learning, rank, prelacy, sovereignty, superintendence, an office necessary to the Church, nobility of birth, as because one is the king’s son, or an honourable obligation. [Col. 0200A]

But the abuse of this reverence is respect of persons. This is not found with God. Note, therefore, that there are several causes relating to such honour. The first cause is due and honourable; the others are somewhat honourable and, as it were, appendages to honour. But which person possessing one of these should be preferred to another possessing another of them is a question.

[Col. 0200B] Respect of persons, however, is a foolish reverence shown to someone for an undue and unlawful cause—for example, fear, greed, wealth, or any disgraceful consideration, such as because she is a concubine, and the like. Sometimes, however, reverence is not shown to a person for a due cause when it ought to be shown; and this is rejection of the person.

There are also intermediate causes of respect of persons, because they are neither wholly due nor wholly unlawful, such as carnal affection. There is also indiscreet benevolence, whereby I prefer the richer person to the poor in receiving him, and the like. To rebuke this vice, recall the example of Master Garnerius the grammarian; the example of Master Peter Abelard; likewise the example of the mitred prelate receiving a very wealthy usurer; and the example of the pimp [Col. 0200C] mocking certain powerful persons and baring his buttocks at them because they would rise and show reverence to a certain wealthy burgess—that is, citizen.

Likewise James, chapter 2: “My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with respect of persons. For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing enters before you, and a poor man in shabby dress also enters, and, looking at the man dressed in splendid clothing, you say to him: ‘Sit here in a good place’; while to the poor man you say: ‘Stand there,’ or ‘Sit beneath my footstool’—do you not judge among yourselves and become judges with wicked thoughts? Has not God chosen the poor in this world as heirs of the kingdom? But you dishonour the poor. You commit sin, transgressing the Lord’s law.”

Augustine, on this passage: If we apply this difference of seating to ecclesiastical honours, it must not be thought a light sin “to hold the faith of the Lord of glory with respect of persons” (James 2). For who could endure that a rich person be chosen for an honourable seat in the Church while a poorer but more learned and knowledgeable person is despised? (Gloss from Bede, who drew this from Augustine on James 2.) But if he speaks of daily sittings, who does not sin here? Yet he does not sin here unless inwardly he judges within himself that the rich person is better than the poor by as much as he is richer, and seems to signify this by preferring him.

But we believe there is respect of persons in everyday sittings, especially [Col. 0201A] when honour is shown to someone through deliberate decision—not through ignorance or surprise, but knowingly—and solely because of wealth, not because of any due cause present in him. Indeed, it may rather be said to his wealth:

> O money, money, you procure this honour for him;  
> you are his brothers.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 5.136.)

Likewise, for another reason: if, according to Augustine, someone judges within himself that the rich man is better by as much as he is richer and is therefore to be honoured, this is rather error and ignorance than respect of persons. Again: by preferring this man to another because of wealth, you seem to say that he is better than the other. Again: it appears that this must be understood generally concerning everyday sittings, as well as ecclesiastical sittings—indeed, rather concerning everyday ones. For in St James’s time ranks and honours in the Church were not distributed as they are now.

Likewise Deuteronomy, chapter 1: God through Moses: “Judge what is just, whether he is citizen or stranger. There shall be no distinction of persons: you shall hear the small as the great; nor shall you accept anyone’s person, because judgment belongs to God.” Nor should a person be favoured in ordinary seating any more than in judgment, except for a due cause.

Likewise Job 32: “I will not show favour to any man, nor will I make man equal to God.” And Ecclesiasticus says (chapter 35): “The Lord will not show favour against the poor, and he will hear the prayer of the injured.” And the canonical Epistle of Jude says: “These are murmurers and chatterers, walking according to [Col. 0201C] their own desires, speaking proud things, and admiring the persons of men for the sake of gain.” Therefore respect of persons is involved in other matters also, as in the perversion of judgment.

Likewise, by examples. Phinehas, armed with zeal for God, pierced the Midianite woman—though she was the daughter of a prince—while she was coupling with a noble Hebrew of the tribe of Simeon (Num. 25). Moses likewise, because of the molten calf, said: “Whoever is a man of God, let him join me; let him gird himself with the sword alongside me, and let each pass through the midst of the camp, killing with the sword all who worshipped the calf, so that his eye spares neither father, son, brother, nor friend” (Exod. 32). When this had been done, Moses said to them: “Today, I say, you have consecrated your hands to God.” Likewise the Lord said to Moses: “Hang all the leaders on the gallows [Col. 0201D], and spare no one, so that my wrath may thus be turned away from the people” (Num. 25). This too was done.

Bohemond likewise, appointed judge during the expedition when the land of promise was first liberated from the Muhammadan heresy, because the Count of Saint-Gilles had despoiled 174 merchants passing through and, after being summoned three times, refused to restore what he had taken, said to him: “Whoever is a man of God, let him gird himself with the sword alongside me.” Coming before the count, he said with drawn sword: “Either you will restore what was taken, or you will submit your neck to this sword to be cut off. For I shall spare you no more than an obscure man of the common people.” The count replied: “You have judged rightly,” and restored what had been taken.

Likewise (Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Martin*, ch. 23): Blessed Martin offered the cup [Col. 0202A] to a poor priest seated at his side, rather than to the prince seated on the other side.

Likewise, 1 Kings, chapter 14: Jonathan, contrary to the decree of his father and the people, dipped the end of his staff into a honeycomb and ate; and immediately his eyes were brightened and he was refreshed. When he was discovered and seized by lot, Saul said to him: “May God do these things to me, and add these things besides, for you shall surely die, Jonathan.” To this the people replied: “Then shall Jonathan die, who has wrought this great deliverance in Israel? This is a sacrilege. As the Lord lives, not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground, because today he has worked with God.” Thus the people delivered Jonathan and snatched him from his father’s hands, lest he die. See how greatly Saul avoided respect of persons: he would spare not even his son, any more than another transgressor.

Likewise, on the words of Exodus chapter [Col. 0202B] 32, “Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join me; let each man put his sword upon his thigh and pass through the midst of the camp,” Gregory says (*Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 26): To pass through the midst of the camp is to live within the Church with such equity—that is, to judge, rebuke, and preach—that one who reproves the faults of sinners rests in the favor of no one; but a man kills his brother, friend, and neighbor. He kills them when, upon finding matters deserving punishment, he strikes them with the sword of rebuke; nor does he spare those whom he loves by natural affection. Therefore, if only that man is called a man of God who is stirred by zeal of divine love to strike at vices, then surely he denies that he belongs to God who refuses, so far as he is able, to rebuke the life of carnal persons.

[Col. 0202C] Likewise (Gloss on this passage): Haman, to whom King Ahasuerus ordered honor and reverence to be shown by the people, once passed joyfully and briskly before Mordecai, who was seated before the palace gates; Mordecai neither rose for him nor moved from his seat (Esther 5). Likewise, John chapter 4: “A certain royal official asked the Lord to come down and heal his son.” The Lord does not go to the royal official’s son, even when asked, lest he seem to honor wealth.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On maintaining moderation in all things

Often, while a person avoids becoming one who respects persons, he becomes “a rabid dog and grim Procrustes,” an abaser of persons instead; he incurs ingratitude and avoids the sobriety of civilized fellowship, becoming [Col. 0202D] drunk rather than sober. For:

> While fools avoid faults, they rush into their opposites.  
> There is something between Tanais and the father-in-law of Visellus.  
> [lacuna] Safest will you go in the middle.  
> Virtue is a mean, reduced from vices on either side.  
> There is measure in things; finally, there are fixed boundaries,  
> Beyond or short of which the right cannot stand.

(Horace, *Satires*, I.2.24; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, II.136; Horace, *Epistles*, I.18.9; *Satires*, I.1.106–107.)

“The highest law is the highest injustice” (Cicero, *On Duties*, I). “Do not be too righteous, because there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness” (Eccles. 7). The blessed have held the middle course. Therefore: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Deut. 17). For it is safer to err by leniency than by severity. The severe and excessively rigid are [Col. 0203A] like the scribes and Pharisees, who “place unbearable burdens upon others’ shoulders, but are unwilling to move them with their own finger” (Matt. 23). Endure the law that you have imposed.

Luke chapter 5: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins; rather, new wine is put into new wineskins, lest the wine be spilled and the skins perish. And no one sews a new garment onto an old one, or an old patch onto a new one, lest the tear become greater.” “Those who squeeze breasts too hard pour out blood instead of milk; and one who presses too hard draws blood” (Prov. 30). Therefore moderation and restraint must be observed in every good work. For it is a fault to pursue every fault to its utmost, and it is glorious for a ruler to punish short of what is deserved.

When the envoy of a certain prudent prince was asked by another prudent prince—who, finding the envoy unlettered, thought him foolish—what was held in his prince’s kingdom to be the greatest wisdom and prudence, he declined the time given him to formulate an answer and replied: Measure and moderation in every action, especially in that of a prince. Thus the prince, who had first thought him foolish, judged him most prudent; he retained his saying in memory in all his own actions, because “the honor of a king loves judgment” (Ps. 98).

Moderation must also be maintained in laughter. Thus Ecclesiasticus chapter 21 says: “A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely laugh even quietly.” And Proverbs chapter 15: “The rejoicing heart of the saints makes the face glad; but the mouth of fools feeds upon folly.” Saint Bernard says of Saint Malachy, archbishop (in his sermon for that saint’s feast): Sorrow did not darken [Col. 0203C] his face, nor did laughter make it frivolous. Of the abbot of Igny, he says (in his sermon on the death of the monk Humbert): Laughter never appeared upon his face, though for the sake of those present he sometimes brightened his countenance; but, if you recall rightly, he did not allow himself full laughter. The Lord too is recorded to have wept three times, but never to have laughed; he said: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6).

Let us therefore pursue cheerfulness of mind, provided it is not accompanied by wantonness: “Let us rejoice according to the countenance of the saints, having the face of those going” (Judith 16) to Jerusalem. But could God properly have laughed? It seems indeed that, if he had good inward joy arising from a fitting cause, he could have expressed it outwardly in the act of laughter, especially since he assumed all our defects except sin; and since the capacity for laughter, or laughability, is a natural property given to humankind. How then could he not have used it? Perhaps he could, but he is not recorded to have done so.

Likewise, it is asked whether man [176] is called laughable by a property and nature of the soul, by some property of the body, or by the composite of both; and, if this primary capacity for laughter is a quality, whether it is an action or a passion. But moderate laughter, if it is continuous, should be regarded with suspicion. Such laughter is more a sign of treachery than of exultation. Of one who laughs in this way it is said: “Cursed is the man concealed in the city” (Jer. 38), ever ready to weave deceit with a flattering smile. Isaiah also says of him (ch. 29): “Woe to you who are deep in heart, so as to hide your counsel from the Lord and from your neighbor”; and Ecclesiasticus chapter 13: “Do not trust the words of one who smiles while questioning you about your secrets, whose cruel spirit will not refrain from malice.”

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On evil singularity
