The evil of singularity opposes this meditation upon good conduct, good works, and ways of life. Let us therefore root it out, so that, once the contrary of good singularity has been cut away, virtue—that is, good singularity—may shine forth. Singularity, according to the authority of Blessed Bernard, produces notoriety and admiration, and new inventions arise from pride.

Likewise Jerome (*Letter to Eustochium, On the Keeping of Virginity*, ch. 2, after Seneca): Neither affected squalor nor acquired luxuries, whether [Col. 0204B] in food or dress, suit a Christian.

Likewise Augustine: Whoever uses transient things more restrictively than the customs of those among whom he lives permit is either intemperate or suspect; but whoever uses them in such a way as to exceed the bounds of the good customs among which he lives either signifies something or is disgraceful. For in all such matters, the fault lies not in the use of things but in the lust of desire.

Likewise he says: It does not matter what kind of food or clothing you take, nor how much, provided the uprightness of life is preserved and, in respect to the varieties of food or clothing among which you must live, you conform to necessity according to your rank and health, so that you may say with the Apostle: “I know how to abound” (Phil. 4), etc. Thus “wisdom was justified [Col. 0204C] by her children” (Matt. 11). Therefore, as Jerome says, one must not depart from common life, lest, having become a “solitary wild beast” (Ps. 79), when you go out in public you sow murmuring among the people and produce astonishment in onlookers, and deserve to be said of as: “This is he.”

Likewise: “Woe to one alone”—that is, to one who, from pride or superstitious presumption, devises singular practices, new customs, and new ways of living—“because, if he falls, he has no one to raise him up” (Eccles. 4).

Likewise, by the example of the Apostle, who “became all things to all people, that he might win all for Christ” (1 Cor. 9): abstaining from lawful things, circumcising Timothy (Acts 16), making an offering at Cenchreae (Acts 18), and even abstaining from a certain perfection in order that he might be more perfect.

Likewise, by the example of “Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and men” (1 Tim. 2), who, apart from sin, assumed our defects; who bore with weak disciples in his manner of life; and who handed down to them, in word [Col. 0204D] and example, a light and bearable yoke and a rule of life.

Likewise, Seneca, fifth letter to Lucilius: But I warn you not to do anything, after the manner of those who desire not to improve but to be noticed, that is remarkable in your dress or manner of life. Avoid harsh attire, untrimmed hair, an excessively neglected beard, a declared hatred of silver, a bed placed upon the ground, and whatever else ambition pursues by a perverse path. The very name of philosophy is sufficiently unpopular, even if handled modestly. What if we begin to separate ourselves from human custom? Let everything within be different; let our outward appearance conform to the people. Let the toga neither shine nor indeed be dirty. Let us not possess silver on which an engraving of solid gold has been laid down; but let us not suppose that it is evidence of frugality to lack gold and silver. Let us aim to follow a better life than the crowd, not a contrary one. Otherwise, we drive away and alienate those whom we wish to reform. We also bring it about that our own people will wish to imitate nothing, while they fear that everything must be imitated.

This is the first promise of philosophy: common sense, humanity, sociability, and fellowship; deviation from this profession will separate us. Let us see whether those things by which we wish to gain admiration are ridiculous and hateful. Surely our aim [Col. 0205A] is to live according to nature. It is contrary to nature to torture one’s body, hate easy cleanliness, seek squalor, and use foods not merely cheap but foul and disgusting. As desiring luxurious things belongs to extravagance, so fleeing things customary and obtainable without great expense belongs to madness. Philosophy demands frugality, not punishment.

Yet frugality need not be unkempt. This is the measure that pleases me: let life be tempered between good customs and public customs. Let all admire our life, but not recognize it. What then? Shall we do the same things as everyone else? Will there be no difference between us and them? There will be very much. Let one who has examined us more closely know that we differ from the crowd; let one who has entered our house admire us rather than our furnishings. Great is the person who uses earthenware as he would silver; nor is he less great who uses silver as he would earthenware. But it belongs to a weak mind not to be able to endure riches.

Likewise, Saint Bernard, sitting in the chapter-house at Pontigny as judge, when the brethren laid before him a question concerning the singularity of a certain monk, said to him: “Would you believe the word of the Lord, or the word of an angel that did not contradict the Lord’s words?” And he said: “I would indeed believe.” Then the abbot said: “And I say to you in the word of the Lord, though I am a sinner, that you must lay aside your singularity. Although in it you seem to imitate certain saints, you will gain greater merit by sharing the brethren’s common manner of life.” He immediately yielded to the abbot, put off every singular practice, and lived commonly in the flock like a little sheep. Singularity must therefore be avoided with the greatest care in a community. There one sins more grievously than in a private place, especially by that singularity which gives scandal to the weak.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On good singularity

Good singularity, more commonly called good solitude, is commended in many passages of Sacred Scripture. Thus Sarah, daughter of Raguel, in Tobit chapter 3: “You know, Lord, that I never mingled with those at play, nor offered myself as a companion to those who walk in frivolity.” And Jeremiah (*Lamentations* 3): [Col. 0206A] “I sat alone and kept silence.”

And the philosopher says (Seneca, Letter 7): Flee the crowd. You have not yet entrusted yourself safely to it. I indeed confess my own weakness: I never bring back from the crowd the character that I took into it. Something of what I had composed is always disturbed; something that I had driven away returns. What happens to invalids whom long weakness has so affected that they can never be brought out without injury happens to us, whose minds are being restored from a long illness; for intercourse with many people is hostile. No one fails either to commend some vice to us, to impress it upon us, or, without our knowing it, to smear it upon us. Certainly, the greater the crowd with which we mingle, the greater the danger. Nothing is so damaging to good character as to sit at some public spectacle. For then crimes creep in more easily through pleasure.

What do you suppose I mean? Do I return more avaricious, more ambitious, more luxurious? Indeed, rather more cruel and inhuman, because I have been among people. Therefore a tender mind, not yet very tenacious of what is right, must be withdrawn from the crowd; it easily passes over to the majority. A dissimilar multitude could have shaken the mind even of Socrates, Cato, and Laelius. So much is there no one among us who, even when we are most carefully forming our character, can bear the assault of vices coming with so great a retinue. One example of luxury or avarice does much harm. A self-indulgent table-companion gradually weakens and softens one. A wealthy neighbor provokes greed. A malicious companion rubs off his own rust even upon a candid and simple mind. What do you think happens to those habits of character against which a public assault has been made? [Col. 0206C] One must either imitate or hate. Yet both must be avoided: lest you become like the wicked if you conform yourself to them, because they are many; or become an enemy to many if you hate them, because they are unlike you.

Withdraw into yourself as much as you can. Associate with those who will make you better. Admit those whom you can make better. These things occur mutually: while people teach, they learn.

Likewise Jerome: Rarely in public, honorable at home. For whenever I have been among people, I have returned less a human being. There are three kinds of solitude: solitude of place, which belongs to the strong; solitude of heart, which ought to belong to everyone; and solitude in action, which must be avoided in all things, especially when it gives scandal. Likewise Jeremiah chapter 15: “I did not sit with the council of those at play, and I gloried because of the presence of your hand; I sat alone, because you filled me with bitterness.”

## CHAPTER LXX. On keeping good company and fleeing bad

Good solitude depends especially upon the company of good people. Thus Cato says (Book I): Walk with good people, because character is formed by companionship. And the Apostle says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it (Ecclus. 13). And Psalm 100: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.” And how? “I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes; I hated those who commit transgression. A perverse heart did not cleave to me; I did not acknowledge one turning away from me in malice. The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, him I pursued. With one of proud eye and insatiable heart I did not eat.”

What sort of household, then, ought you to have? Hear: “My eyes are upon the faithful of the land, that they may sit with me”—in judgment and at table. “He who walks in the blameless way, he ministered to me”—at the altar, at table, in the house, in every administration and office of mine. “He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house; he who speaks unjust things shall not stand before my eyes” (Ps. 100). And Psalm 25: “I did not sit with the council of vanity, nor will I enter with those who act wickedly. I hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the impious. I will wash my hands among the innocent, and encompass your altar, O Lord” [Col. 0207B].

Ecclesiasticus chapter 9: “Let righteous men be your table-companions.” And the philosopher says (Seneca, Letter 19): One must consider first with whom one eats and drinks, rather than what one eats and drinks. And Augustine says: It is fitting for a prelate to have such chamberlains that he may fear lest, if they are bad, he seem to approve the life of those whose company he keeps. Hence the Apostle says, “Ruling his own household well” (1 Tim. 3), not so as to increase wealth, but so as to have his children, household, and family subject to him in all chastity and sobriety.

But someone may say, as though excusing himself, while nevertheless keeping a bad household: “My nature is indeed with the good, but my life is with the bad.” Yet precisely in this he is bad: he fosters bad people in his house, and both his life and his nature are with the bad. For as a judge or ruler of a people is, so are his ministers; and conversely. The household proves and shows what the master of the house is like.

Thus Ecclesiasticus chapter 13: “Every animal loves its like; so too every person loves one like himself. All flesh will be joined to its like, and every person will associate with his like. Can a wolf ever have fellowship with a lamb? So a sinner with a righteous person. What fellowship has a holy person with a dog?” And when the Lord commands even a guest for one night to be chosen, both because of infamy and because of the corrupting and destructive power of example, how much more must one choose the person with whom one is to live for a long time? Therefore association with the bad must be avoided especially. We can scarcely stand firm on dry ground, much less run upon slippery ground.

Abraham [Col. 0207D] also, on hearing the Lord’s command (Gen. 17), immediately circumcised all the homeborn servants and males of his household. [180] Note that he had not effeminate men in his house, but males, whom he also circumcised. You too, following Abraham’s example, should have the household of your house circumcised in all respects. Origen too, commending Abraham (*Homily 4 on Genesis*), says of him: Observe the diligence of Abraham in inviting angels to a meal. Abraham, though old, runs about; Sarah his wife hastens; the servant hurries. In a wise person’s house, no one is lazy.

Likewise, according to the saying of blessed Thomas of Canterbury, which he used from the poet:

> It is the greatest virtue of a ruler to know his own people.  
> —Martial, *Epigrams* VIII.15

[Col. 0208A] And Cato says of Pompey:

> A chaste household, free from luxury, and never corrupted by Fortune [the final word *Deum* is uncertain].

And Proverbs chapter 13: “He who walks with the wise shall be wise; a friend of fools becomes like them.” And this saying: Fire in the bosom, a serpent in the lap, and a mouse in the purse are destructive neighbors. In very many Psalms the company of the wicked is reproved and the company of the good commended: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the wicked,” etc. (Ps. 1). “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy mountain? He who walks without blemish and works righteousness,” etc. (Ps. 14). “I will confess you in the great assembly; among a weighty people I will praise you” (Ps. 34). “But he glorifies those who fear the Lord” (Ps. 14). “Gather to him his saints, who establish his covenant” (Ps. 49).

Otherwise, on account of the gathering and fellowship of the bad, it will be said to you: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him,” etc. (ibid.). And this will be fulfilled in your house: “I saw wickedness and contradiction in the city. Day and night it shall surround it. Upon its walls are wickedness, and in its midst labor and injustice” (Ps. 54). For this reason the Prophet also prays against such persons, saying: “Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into hell, for wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst. For there is no change in them, and they have not feared God,” etc. (ibid.).

And Augustine: In this every believer ought to imitate God: he should not have bad persons as companions, except for the purpose and hope of their correction; if he finds them incorrigible, he should at least avoid them in private association after much admonition, and expel them from himself if he can.

But someone may say: “Many men are good in themselves, yet have bad entourages.” Far be it! For similarity of character, according to the saying of a certain wise man, produces association, and kindred pursuits are easily joined. And this saying: Scripture compares rulers who are good but have bad entourages to Scyllas and Harpies. Scylla is described as having a human face indeed, but as girded with dogs’ heads; the Harpies as having maidenly faces but most rapacious claws. Thus such people often appear human and gentle on the surface, but, surrounded by depraved retainers and ministers, they are like Scyllas in their scent for prey and like Harpies in the rapacity of their claws.

It is therefore evident that the wealth of the rich and powerful is situated in a dangerous place. For “frogs in the inner chambers of kings” (Ps. 104)—wicked men and companions of thieves—are found especially in the houses of the powerful. They become sinners because of those rich men whom they deceive and by whom they are deceived, since those are not expelled who “prepared snares for the feet” of the powerful and “dug a pit before their face,” and “fell into it” (Ps. 56). This way of theirs is a stumbling-block to themselves, yet afterward “they will take pleasure in their own mouth” (Ps. 48).

And Josephus says: For this reason especially the condition of the powerful is fearful and dangerous: the mass of their affairs does not allow them to be moderately bad. Since they have sinned not with one simple, personal mouth but with another’s and with many mouths—by a long hand, as it were—they must confess their sins. They cannot, like a poor person, say: “Lord, against you alone, and in myself alone, have I sinned” (Ps. 50), but rather: Against you and many neighbors in myself, and through my many attendants.

Therefore flee every association with the bad and every hindrance that prevents your progress in God’s way. Thus the Lord says: “Whoever does not hate father and mother cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14); and “If your eye causes you to stumble, cast it away from you,” etc. (Mark 9). And Jerome (*Letter to Heliodorus, On the Praise of the Solitary Life*): Go on, trampling your father; go on, trampling your mother; even the breasts at which you sucked. “Say to father and mother: I do not know you” (Deut. 33). Likewise, according to the Lord’s counsel with Abraham, “Go out [Col. 0209B] from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12); before you are overthrown, say with the Prophet: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude.” Likewise Psalm 105: “They mingled among the nations and learned their works,” etc.; and Psalm 42: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation; deliver me from the unjust and deceitful man.” Likewise: “For whenever Saul saw a strong man and one fit for battle,” etc. (1 Kings 14); and “It was reported to Saul by those saying,” etc. (1 Kings 19).

Likewise: “I will confess you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the congregation” (Ps. 110): theirs, not that of the unrighteous.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On the prompting of carnal affection

[Col. 0209C]

Just as bad company, so carnal affection impedes good solitude. To rebuke and remove it from more useful works, the Lord, while occupied in preaching, replied to the announcement that his brothers and mother were seeking him outside: “Who are brother, mother, and sister?” And, stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, etc. (Matt. 12).

Likewise, while disputing in the synagogue, having been left by his father and mother, he said to them when they sought him: “Did you not know that I must be in those things which are my Father’s?” (Luke 2). He taught that works arising from carnal affection, as less useful, should be postponed to spiritual and more useful ones.

Likewise, when wine failed at the wedding, he said to his mother: “What is it to me and to you, woman?” (John 2), as though to say: I have nothing from you in spiritual works. Likewise: “Whoever does not hate father and mother” (Luke 14), that is, whoever does not prefer spiritual affections to carnal ones. Likewise: “When you give a dinner, do not invite the rich, but the poor, weak, and lame” (ibid.), in whom you have not carnal affection but the fire of divine love.

Jerome: For Christ’s love, a father’s burial must be omitted—for whose love no one ought to be left unburied. Moses, too, chose Joshua from another tribe, not from his own tribe, as ruler of the people (Num. 11, 13). Likewise: A priest and Levite must never go out from the holy places; let the priest have his head covered with a turban (Lev. 16), he “who says to father and mother: I do not know you” (Deut. 33). Priests also, under the old law, were forbidden to attend the funerals of the dead, even of parents (Num. 19), so that we might thereby be taught that carnal affections must be postponed, especially since we are and ought to be priests “according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). Scripture is silent about his father and mother, as a figure of the priests of the Gospel, so that in spiritual matters they may “say to father and mother: I do not know you” (Deut. 33). For the patrimony entrusted to them is another’s—namely Christ’s and the poor’s—not theirs or their parents’.

Joseph likewise—at whose command all things were done in Egypt—scarcely permitted the land of Goshen to be given to his relatives (Gen. 47); nor did he wish them to be elevated, but to remain in their customary pastoral occupation. Yet, lest we adopt dog-like manners by hating [Col. 0210B] parents, Gregory teaches in this way (*Homily 37 on the Gospels*) how such affection ought to be moderated. The ark of the Lord, captured by the Philistines, was placed on a new cart; cows with calves drew it and led it to Beth-shemesh, not turning their necks back on the road but lowing after their calves (1 Kings 6). We ought to have carnal affection in our mind, not in our action, especially in spiritual matters. Those who, led by carnal affection, turn their necks back after their calves are like Lot’s wife, who looked back and was changed into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19). They are like one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back (Luke 9). They are also like the Hebrews looking back toward Egypt, to the pots of meat, melons, and other things of Pharaoh (Num. 11).

Let those take care not to be punished with a punishment like Judas’s who carry off what was put into the coffers of the Lord and the poor, giving it to wife and children, led by carnal affection. For this he deserved to betray and crucify the Lord, and deserved hanging and eternal punishment for himself (Matt. 27).

Leviticus 21: “The high priest shall not enter at all where any dead person is; he shall not be defiled even for his father and mother, nor shall he go out from the holy places.” Jerome says on this passage (*Letter to Fabiola, On the Priestly Garments*): However powerful and rich a person may be, and though he offer a multitude of victims, if he is dead, he is not touched or seen by the high priest. But if he comes back to life and comes forth from the tomb at the Savior’s call (John 11), walking free from the bonds of sins, the high priest enters to him, remains [Col. 0210D] with him, and dines with him. Carnal affection compels us to do many things; and while we consider bodily kinships, we offend the Creator of body and soul. “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10).

Many monks, by pitying their parents, lose their souls. Let us attend to that Father who never dies, or who dies for us; who, living to God, died so that he might make us dead people alive (Rom. 6). If we have anything from Egypt which the prince of this world may recognize as his own, let us leave it, along with the cloak, in the hand of the Egyptian harlot (Gen. 39). A young man, covered with a linen cloth, followed the bound Lord (Mark 14); he would have fallen into snares unless, unencumbered and naked, he had evaded the attack of his pursuers. Let us render to parents what belongs to parents, provided they live for God (1 Tim. 5).

But this concerns the high priest; some concession is made to lesser persons. To uproot even tenderness of flesh, Abraham was told: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12). Go out in mind: this concerns the necessity of the command. Go out in body: this concerns the safeguard of counsel. For while we are held among relatives in body, we are often held among them also in mind. Therefore Benedict, Giles, and very many saints left their native land, and holy companies of pale men entered the wilderness.

In the book of Numbers (ch. 25), Levites are also commanded to kill all their relatives initiated into Baal-peor, just as those initiated into the calf were killed. For nothing carnal, no carnal affection, ought to touch one who ministers at the altar and lives from the patrimony [Col. 0211B] of the Crucified, so as to prevent him from administering the testament entrusted to him according to the pleasing and perfect will of the testator.

Likewise, Judges chapter 9. Contrary to the counsel of Jotham, who set before the Shechemites the parable of the olive trees, fig trees, vine, and bramble, Abimelech’s fellow-tribesmen and brothers chose Abimelech himself as king and set him over them, led by kinship of the flesh. Once promoted, like fire issuing from the bramble, he burned the city of Shechem and killed seventy brothers, together with many Shechemites who had promoted him.

Likewise, the Lord says in Matthew chapter 17: “So that we may not give offense” to those demanding the tribute: “O Peter, go to the sea, cast in a hook, take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you,” even though I am a son of the kingdom. Augustine says here: In a wonderful way we are instructed and edified by this, since the Lord was of such poverty that he had nothing from which to pay the tribute. Judas indeed held common funds in the coffers, but the Lord judged it wrong to transfer or convert the goods of the poor to his own uses. In this he gave an example to us, especially to those who live from his patrimony. Therefore, if the Lord judged it wrong to convert the goods of the poor to his own necessary uses, how much more wrong is it to spend them on superfluities? From this conclude also that unlawful debts, though confirmed by oath, are not to be paid from the patrimony of the Crucified; rather, as in a shameful cause, the oath must be annulled.

Likewise, brute animals nourish their offspring while they are weak and still small, cherishing and embracing them with every care; but when they have grown larger and reached maturity, they leave them to themselves. Yet we, though human beings, cherish our offspring not only during childhood but at every age; nor only our offspring, but those descended from our side. Indeed, we burden them with superfluities beyond necessity, bestowing very much upon them; and, according to the saying of Pope Alexander [III], “God took sons away from us, and the devil gave us grandsons.”

Likewise Jerome to the monk Heliodorus (*Letter on the Praise of the Solitary Life*): Hear the edict of your King: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11). Remember the day of your enlistment, when you were buried with Christ in baptism and swore in the words of the sacrament that, for his name’s sake, you would spare neither father nor mother. Though a little grandson hangs from your neck, though your mother with disheveled hair and torn garments bares the breasts by which she fed you; [184] though your father lies upon the threshold: go on, trampling your father; with dry eyes fly to the banner of the cross. The only kind of filial devotion in this matter is to be cruel.

The day will come—yes, it will come—when you will return as victor to your native land, when, as a strong man crowned, you will enter the heavenly Jerusalem. I do not know why you should say that you are now hindered by chains. We do not have breasts of iron or hard hearts. Hyrcanian tigresses did not nurse us from stone; and we too have passed through these things. Now your widowed sister clings to your arms with entreaties; now the household servants with whom you grew up [Col. 0212B] say: “To whose service are you leaving us?” And your old nurse, now an aged woman, and your foster-father—second only to your natural father in filial affection—cry out: “Wait a little while for those who are about to die, and bury them.” Perhaps your mother too, her breasts loose and flaccid, her brow plowed with wrinkles, repeats in groaning the old baby-talk from the breast. Let grammarians, if they wish, say also:

> Upon you the whole household, bowed down, leans and rests.  
> —Virgil
The love of Christ and the fear of Gehenna easily break these bonds. Yet Scripture, on the other hand, commands obedience to parents (Exod. 20); but whoever loves them above Christ loses his soul. The enemy holds a sword to kill me, and shall I think of my mother’s [Col. 0212C] tears? Shall I abandon Christ’s military service because of my father—one to whom, for Christ’s sake, I do not owe burial, though for His sake I owe it even to everyone? Peter, timidly advising the Lord who was about to suffer, became a stumbling-block (Matt. 16). Paul, when the brethren tried to hold him back from proceeding to Jerusalem, replied: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 21). This battering-ram of filial affection, by which faith is shaken, must be blunted by the sword-point of the Gospel: “My mother,” he says, “and my brethren are those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 12). If they believe in Christ, let them support me as I fight for His name; if they do not believe, let the dead bury their own dead [Col. 0212D] (Matt. 8).

Moses also, following Jethro’s counsel (Exod. 18), chose as judges and rulers not relatives, but men who were knowledgeable, very wise, and prudent, hating every kind of avarice. In that holy community likewise, the stewards were not told to give better and more lavish portions to their relatives, but “to each according as he had need” (Acts 2). Again: if the administration of a private person’s testament is, because of the suspicion arising from kinship, not entrusted to someone with relatives, how much more ought Christ’s testament not to be entrusted to such persons?

Again, prelates ought to be taught by the example of the Templars not to have their friends as their associates. For the Templars themselves never have a blood-relative [Col. 0213A] serving them, lest they distribute to him the common goods of the brethren. Relevant also is the example of a bishop who summoned only his own relatives and nephews into his church, so that from among them a prelate to succeed him might be chosen and installed as though by hereditary right. And this indeed happened, though with great controversy, no small expense, and the burden of debt. But when the elected successor to the old man fell ill, his own people said to him in conversation: “From what source will this money be paid, which we spent in having you promoted? You have killed us, through whom we hoped to live and be exalted.” To them he replied: “Woe to you, because you killed me when you promoted me to the summit.” Again, 4 Kings 4: “Pour into all these vessels,” etc. And Habakkuk 2: “Woe to those who build [Col. 0213B] Zion in blood.” And David (Ps. 44): “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father’s house.”

## CHAPTER LXXII. Praise of Solitude of Place

After solitude of heart and solitude in action follows solitude of place, which is the nurse, and often the mother, of solitude. There are, indeed, two kinds of solitary life: that of cenobites and that of anchorites. The first is safer, because of the imperfect character of our weakness. The second is loftier, or more excellent, because of the perfection of charity. To it, as to the higher stage according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, one passes from the first when the one passing over has been fully strengthened and “clothed [Col. 0213C] with power from on high” (Luke 24).

Commending their solitude of place, David says: “I have become like a solitary sparrow upon the roof” (Ps. 101). And Solomon: “The locusts have no king” (Prov. 30). And Jerome, flying from the schools of the liberal arts to the desert, writes thus to a former schoolfellow, inviting him to the desert and contempt of the world (Letter to Heliodorus, *On the Praise of the Solitary Life*):

“O desert, blooming with Christ’s flowers! O solitude, in which are born those stones of which, in the Apocalypse, the city of the great King is built! O wilderness, enjoying God’s presence more intimately, what are you doing, brother, in the world—you who are greater than the world? How long are you oppressed by the shadows of roofs? How long does the prison of smoky cities confine you? Believe me: in the desert I see I know not what [Col. 0213D] greater light. I delight, having cast aside the burden of the flesh, to fly to the pure brightness of the ether. Do you fear poverty? But Christ calls the poor blessed (Matt. 5). Are you frightened by labor? No athlete is crowned without sweats. Do you think about food? But faith does not fear hunger. Do you fear that your limbs, worn away by fasting, may strike against the bare ground? But the Lord lies with you. Does the uncultivated growth of your unkempt head horrify you? But Christ is your head. Does the boundless vastness of the desert terrify you? But walk through paradise in your mind. Whenever you pass over there in thought, so often you will not be in the desert. Is your rough skin drawn tight for lack of baths? But one who has once been washed in Christ has no need to be washed again. And, briefly, hear the Apostle’s answer to every objection: ‘The sufferings [Col. 0214A] of this present time,’ he says, ‘are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us’ (Rom. 8). You are a delicate soldier, dearest friend, if you wish to rejoice here in the world and afterwards reign with Christ.”

Again, to Rufinus (Letter *On the Praise of Bonosus*, beginning, “To fear God more”): “We shall tell you something, so that, if you do not know it, you may learn it; but if you have known it, you may rejoice with us. Your Bonosus—indeed mine, and, to speak more truly, since he belongs to Christ, ours—already climbs ‘Jacob’s ladder’ (Gen. 28), bears the cross (Matt. 16), does not look back (Luke 9), ‘sows in tears so that he may reap in joy’ (Ps. 125), and, in the mystery of Moses, raises the serpent in the wilderness (Num. 21). Let fabricated miracles, invented by lies, yield to this truth, whether in Greek or Roman style. [Col. 0214B] Behold a youth educated with us in the honorable arts of the world, a man who had wealth in abundance and outstanding rank among his equals: despising his mother, sisters, and dearly beloved brother, he settled, like some new colonist of paradise, upon an island shipwrecked amid the resounding sea—an island whose harsh cliffs, naked rocks, and solitude inspire terror. No farmers are there; no monks are there—not even that little Onesimus whom you know, in whose embrace he delighted as in that of a brother—clings as a companion to his side in such vast emptiness. There alone—indeed, not alone, since Christ accompanies him—he saw the glory of God, which even the Apostles had not seen except in the desert. He does not, indeed, behold turreted cities; but he has become enrolled as a taxpayer of the new city and has given his name as its citizen. Are his limbs made hideous by a misshapen sackcloth? Yet thus he will better ‘be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ’ (1 Thess. 4). Does he enjoy no southern breeze of the Euripus? Yet from the Lord’s side he drinks the water of life. No grass makes the earth green; no blossoming field is thick with shady groves. Steep rocks enclose something like a prison of horror. But he is secure, fearless, and wholly armed according to the Apostle [Col. 0214C] (Eph. 6): now he hears God while rereading the divine writings; now he speaks to God or prays to God. And perhaps, following the example of John, who saw the Apocalypse in the desert, he sees something of God while dwelling on the island.”

The same author, to Marcella (Letter beginning, “Ambrose”): “Let us enter solitude, as though into certain rural retreats. There food-bread, vegetables watered by our own hands, milk—the delight of country life—will offer us cheap indeed, but innocent foods. Living thus, sleep will not call us away from prayer, nor fullness from reading. If it is hot, the seclusion of a tree will provide shade. If it is autumn, the very mildness of the air and leaves spread beneath us will show us a place of rest. In spring the field is painted with flowers, and among the plaintive birds the psalms will be sung more sweetly. If there is cold and winter snow, I shall not buy wood; I shall keep warm while awake, or at least while asleep, and, what I know is more useful, I shall not be cold. Let Rome keep her tumults; let the arena rage, the circus go mad, the theaters run riot; let her be occupied with gossip and delight in formal calls. ‘But for us it is good to cleave to God and to place our hope in the Lord God’ (Ps. 72), so that, when the kingdoms [Col. 0215A] of heaven have exchanged this poverty for themselves, we may burst forth in the words: ‘For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?’ (Ps. 72).”

Again, Bishop Maximinus: “Thus the distinctive purpose, or struggle, of the anchorites is not deprived of martyrdom, any more than are those who, throughout the various places of the desert, remained in caves and tiny huts of cells, content with scant food on this solemnity. Some kept company with beasts; some were supplied by birds. Despising the delights of food, trampling the luxury of the world underfoot, not loving temporal praise, fleeing human sight, accustomed to converse with angels, they shone forth in very many signs of virtue: ‘They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, distressed—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, [Col. 0215B] and mountains, and caves, and caverns of the earth’ (Heb. 11),” etc.

Again, Jerome (Letter to Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*): “Oh, how often, when I was established in the desert—namely, in the grim dwelling-place of monks—I thought that I was amid the delights of Rome! ‘I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness’ (Jer. 15). My limbs were rough with sackcloth; my skin, misshapen and squalid, had become as though covered with Ethiopian flesh. Daily there were tears, daily groans; and if at any time sleep, struggling against me, pressed down upon me, on the bare ground I scarcely bruised my bones which clung to it. Thus, through fear of Gehenna, I had condemned myself to such a prison; and, made the companion of scorpions and wild beasts, I often attended the choirs of girls. Their faces were pale with fasting, while my mind burned with desires. At the feet of [Jesus] [Col. 0215C] I lay, watered them with tears, wiped them with my hair, and subdued the rebellious flesh by vigils and fasts, using raw food and cold water—for in cooked food there is some luxury.”

(Seneca, Letter 7): “Therefore, if you are imperfect, flee the crowd, because you cannot safely entrust yourself to it; if you are perfect, you may return to the crowd out of necessity for the brethren.” Hence Stilpo (the same, Letters 9 and 10): “The fact is that all folly suffers from weariness of itself. I do not change my judgment: flee the multitude, flee the few, flee even one person. I have no one to whom I should wish you entrusted; and see where my judgment leads: I dare entrust you to yourself.” Crates, Stilpo’s disciple, when he saw a young man walking alone in a secluded place, [Col. 0215D] asked what he was doing there alone. “I am talking with myself,” he said. Crates replied: “Take care, I beg you, and pay close attention not to be talking with a bad man.”

We are accustomed to watch over someone grieving and afraid, angry and furious, lest he make bad use of solitude. No imprudent person should be left to himself. For then they devise evil counsels; then they lay up future dangers either for others or for themselves; then they arrange improper desires; then whatever the mind concealed through shame or fear it exposes; then it sharpens boldness, provokes lust, and incites anger. Finally, the one advantage which solitude has—namely, to entrust nothing to anyone and fear no judge—is lost to the fool. For he betrays himself. See, therefore, what I may hope concerning you—or rather, what I may promise myself. For hope is the name of an uncertain [Col. 0216A] good; nevertheless, I find no one with whom I would rather have you be than with yourself.

Again, Seneca (Letter 11): “One good man ought to be chosen and kept always before one’s eyes, so that we may live as though he were watching, and do everything as though he were seeing. Nor without reason: for a great part of sins is removed if a witness stands by the sinner. Let the mind have someone whom it reveres, and by whose authority it makes even its private chamber more private. O happy is he whom not merely the sight, but even the thought, of such a person corrects! O happy is he who can revere someone so that he composes and orders himself even at that person’s remembrance! He who can so revere someone will soon himself be worthy of reverence. Choose, then, Cato—O Christian, Paul. If Cato seems to you too stern in moral discipline, choose another holy man of gentler temperament and life, whose life, character, and speech please you. Always set him before yourself either as a guardian or as an example. We need, I say, someone to whom our depraved morals may be raised. For unless you have a rule, you will neither correct what is crooked [Col. 0216B] nor straighten what is bent.”

There are three kinds of monks and persons leading a solitary life. The first is that of hermits, anchorites, or recluses. The Lord dedicated this life when the Spirit drove Him into the desert to be tempted by Satan, and He was with the wild beasts: “And angels came and ministered to Him” (Matt. 4), with ostriches, serpents, and beasts as companions. John the Baptist also sanctified it, concerning whom Paul the Deacon says in the hymn:

[Col. 0216C]

> In tender years you sought  
> The caves of the desert, fleeing the throngs of citizens,  
> So that not even the slightest hunger  
> Might be able to stain your life.

Mary the Egyptian repented in the desert; Elijah fled into the desert from the face of Jezebel (3 Kings 19); Jeremiah hid in the desert, saying: “I sat alone and kept silence” (Lam. 3). Again: “Rise, flee, save your souls, and you shall be in the desert like lowly tamarisks” (Jer. 48). Again, chapter 49: “Rise, go up, flee, go away deep into the hollows”—that is, into caves and caverns—“sit down, you inhabitants of Hazor, says the Lord.” Martin, while still twelve years old, immediately desired the desert, and would sufficiently have fulfilled his vow had not the weakness of his age [Col. 0216D] prevented him. Having become a recluse, he proved a remarkable raiser of two dead persons and performer of more miracles than when he became bishop. Yet while living in the episcopate, he had a private cell, in which he often prayed and lived alone, speaking with God and angels, except when the need of his subjects and church compelled him to go out. Blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, lived in a similar manner. Remigius of Rheims was taken from the cell in which he had shut himself up and made bishop.

The second kind of monks is that in which three or four, or a few more, live in common and from common resources, as do the Carthusians. This order originated with John the Baptist, who remained in the desert with his disciples. Others say that it arose from the sons [Col. 0217A] of Jonadab; others, from the Rechabites, who lived thus. (Concerning them, Jeremiah 35 says: “Now Jonadab was the son of Rechab.”) The third kind is that of cenobites. This kind of life is safer because it includes persons of many dispositions, namely the weak and the strong. Of it David says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132).

The first kind is perfect; the second is more moderate than the extremes and more desirable. For through the companionship joined to it, it excludes the danger of the first kind, which lies in isolation: “Woe to him that is alone, because if he falls, he has no one to raise him” (Eccl. 4). For a small number is safe, because well-provided and few bellies are content with little. It also excludes the danger of the third kind, in the number of persons and in the fixed amount of lands, with the weight [Col. 0217B] and measure of all works prescribed. Circumscribed in all things by smallness and poverty, it excludes litigation, because “the servant of God must not strive” (2 Tim. 2). It also excludes envy and the plundering of the powerful and rich. For those who have nothing are not envied; vexatious lawsuits are not raised against them:

> The traveler without possessions sang before the robber.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* 10.22

It also excludes the sin scarcely avoided in a cenobium: namely, when one person is allowed to run about and wander in the necessities of the house, in which he often gives offense and receives it, and his sin redounds upon every individual.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. The Sin of One Often Redounds upon the Whole Community

[Col. 0217C] When Achan sinned, the people were polluted by the curse (Josh. 7). When the Gadites, Reubenites, and half-tribe of Manasseh built an altar in the land of Canaan, it was said: “Because you have erected a great and sacrilegious altar contrary to God’s command, tomorrow God’s wrath will rage against the people” (Josh. 22). The Jewish populace also, not rescuing Christ, “the poor and needy man, from the hand of those stronger than he” (Ps. 34), became guilty of the Lord’s death. And Moses says: “You shall not follow a multitude to do evil, nor in judgment yield to the opinion of the many, lest you depart from truth” (Exod. 23). And the Apostle: “Purge out the old leaven,” and cast it out, “because a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5). You do not sin less because you sin with many, but more; nor will you burn less because you burn with a greater number. Hence that general proverb must be rightly understood: “What is sinned by many goes unpunished”—that is, by man, but not by God. And again: Whoever does not correct when he can rebuke and prevent, consents.

Those, however, who believe themselves excused from sin because of the multitude or the prelate are like Pilate washing his hands with water and saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this man; see to it yourselves” (Matt. 27); not like Daniel, who said: “You have condemned innocent blood; men of Judah, return to judgment” (Dan. 13). They are also like the first parents, casting blame upon God, which these likewise cast upon the multitude and the abbot: because “the woman,” or the serpent, “gave [Col. 0218A] to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3). “The abbot commands this,” or “the convent does this”; hence I do not oppose it:

> Though a thousand take it, nothing is lost thereby.  
> —Ovid

Thus, when a certain man entered a cloister and encountered in the multitude a sin which he had avoided in solitude—namely, a plurality of churches; the establishment in churches of hirelings who possess merely the title, not the care, of governing souls; a harvest where he did not sow; the receipt and enjoyment of revenues where he did not labor (Luke 19); a prelate’s occupation of a better benefice; the defrauding of souls of nourishment; the withholding of the church office, and of its person or minister—he feared for himself, believing that this was no less a sin when done by a multitude, even though through this they did not have seared [Col. 0218B] consciences such as they would have had if, being in solitude, they had done it.

They also consider themselves immune from sin on account of the community, when the community or prelate of the church permits, or gives authority and consent for, things not due to be done or demanded by the Church, such as the exaction of tallages, the payment of accursed tithes, and the like. Again, Gregory, on the Second Book of Kings, chapter 24: “Because David numbered the people, God sent a pestilence into Israel, and seventy thousand men died,” says: “It happens, because of the evil of the flock, that the life of a truly good shepherd often becomes delinquent, and the hearts of rulers are disposed according to the deserts of the peoples.” David numbered the people in sin, and the people received punishment. Again, in the same book, chapter [Col. 0218C] 21: “There was also a famine in the days of David,” etc.

Again, Josephus (*Jewish Antiquities*, book 5, chapters 15–16), on 1 Kings 2, “Now Eli was old, and heard,” etc., says: “Eli was condemned for the iniquity of his sons because he punished them with insufficiently severe correction; indeed, he restrained and rebuked them, but with a father’s indulgence, not with the severity and authority of a high priest.” Therefore let priests learn that they will be punished on account of the crimes of the people, and that the fault of subjects will be imputed to them. Again, 1 Kings 28: “Therefore the Lord has done to you what you suffer.” Again, Numbers 32: “But the sons of Reuben,” at the words “If you will not follow him,” etc.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On Making Oneself Guilty after the Example of a Holy Man for a Slight Occasion of Sin

[Col. 0218D]

“You shall not follow a multitude to do evil” (Exod. 23). For a holy man who fears God, on account of however slight an occasion that he has afforded, considers himself guilty of a sin which nevertheless he did not expressly commit by hand or word. Thus David, after Saul killed eighty-five priests of the Lord and the men of Nob because Ahimelech the high priest had given him, hungry and fleeing, the showbread and Goliath’s sword, said: “I am guilty concerning all these souls” (1 Kings 22). Again, in 2 Kings 23, when the Philistines’ garrison and camp were in Bethlehem, David, being thirsty, said: “Oh, that someone would give me a drink of water from the cistern that is in Bethlehem by the gate!” [Col. 0219A] Therefore three mighty men broke into the Philistines’ camp, drew water from that cistern, and brought it to David. But he would not drink it; instead, he poured it out to the Lord, saying: “Shall I drink the blood of these men who went forth, and the peril of their lives?”

Gregory (*Register*, book 9, Letter 39; and the Ordinary Gloss on 2 Kings, chapter 23): “He who had not feared to desire another man’s wife, taught by his scourging, when he desired water was afraid, rebuking himself because of the soldiers’ peril.” And the Apostle says in Acts, chapter 20: “Therefore I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all” of you. “For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.” Therefore, if he had omitted anything among the matters that arose, he would have considered himself guilty of all their souls.

[Col. 0219B] The Lord says through Moses in Deuteronomy, chapter 19: “You shall set apart for yourself three cities in the land of promise, and three beyond the Jordan in the middle of the land, so that they may be equally spaced from one another. You shall diligently make roads to them, so that one fleeing because of homicide may have a place to escape and take refuge, from nearby and without difficulty or obstruction of the way. You shall thus divide and prepare these cities of refuge, lest you be guilty of anyone’s blood—namely, one who could not flee to one of them because of the length or obstruction of the road.” Therefore, O prelate, unless you remove every difficulty, employ every means of access, and preserve every safeguard of the Church so that one fleeing to her may be delivered, you will be guilty of his blood [Col. 0219C] if it is shed.

Again, chapter 22: “When you build a new house, you shall make”—little railings and supports—“a wall around the roof,” even if it is flat, “lest blood be shed in your house and you be guilty when another slips and falls headlong.” That even a slight occasion of evil is blameworthy is shown by that fabulous statement in which it is said:

> … I killed you, pitiable woman,  
> Because I ordered you to come by night to places full of fear.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 4.4

Thus an advocate, or anyone else—especially one who sends someone to Rome for an unjust cause—can say: “I killed you, pitiable man, because I ordered you,” etc., “to pass through places full of fear, across the Alps, across the Apennines, and through a thousand perils of death.”

Again, Job, chapter 9: “I feared all my works. For even if I shall have been washed as with snow waters, and my hands shall shine as most clean, yet you will dip me in filth, and my garments shall abhor me.” As though to say: Even if my works appear good in themselves, I nevertheless fear lest, because they are done indiscreetly, or in an order, manner, or time in which they ought not to be done, they may be unclean. For a change in the order of merits changes their form, and likewise does the observance of other circumstances. And, as Gregory says (Letter to Augustine, bishop of the English, chapter 10), our good deeds are not pure goods; but evil deeds are not pure evils; and “your righteousnesses are as the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. 64) in the Lord’s sight. It belongs to good minds to recognize fault where there is no fault [Col. 0220A] at all.

Moreover, not only a slight occasion for committing sin makes one a sinner, but also a slight occasion for wrongdoing, a slight occasion for omission, and so forth. Hence in Numbers, chapter 32, when the sons of Reuben and Gad asked that land beyond the Jordan be given them for feeding cattle and for providing houses for their wives and little children, Moses answered: “Will your brethren cross the Jordan and go to war while you sit here? If you will not follow them, the Lord will abandon the people in the wilderness, and you will be the cause of all their deaths.” Again, Exodus 21: “If an ox has been a goring ox yesterday and the day before, and its owner has been warned” by his neighbors, “but has not confined it, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner also shall be killed.”

Therefore let those fear who keep toothed and fierce beasts, especially prelates of the Church, to whom a beast costs less in maintenance than the belly of a poor and needy person. But those excusing themselves from an occasion for sin which they have afforded, and thinking that they are not guilty unless they have sinned by their own hand, are like the first parents; like the Jews who said—when Judas said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood”—“What is that to us? See to it yourself” (Matt. 27). He was betrayed by a disciple, judged by the governor, crucified by Roman soldiers. They did everything in such a way that they seemed to do nothing; and this is what we seek today: not that we may sin, but that we may not seem to sin. These are like the Pharisees saying to the Apostles preaching Christ: “Do you mean to bring [Col. 0220C] this man’s blood upon our heads?” (Acts 5). Yet His blood is still upon them and upon their children.

Fearing this slight occasion, a certain man, though he had sinned at long remove, confessed his sins through the mouths of all his officials, just as through his own mouth. For this reason also Robert, bishop of Amiens, who had said to secular judges concerning a hanging, “Do the work that you have to do,” grieved all the days of his life.

Saint Maurilius, bishop of Angers, was summoned to baptize a child who died before he could perhaps reach him. He suspended himself from his office and fled to England, throwing the keys of the church into the sea, vowing to God that he would never again perform the office of priest [Col. 0220D] until he saw, by signs, that the sin was forgiven which he thought bound him because of this slight occasion. When, having become a gardener in England, the keys were found in the belly of a purchased fish, they were offered to him. Yet he did not return immediately, but only after completing his penance; having returned, he raised the child and baptized him.

## CHAPTER LXXV. Against the Suspicious, and Those Who Rush from Conjectures into Rash Judgments

A just man not only cuts away from himself even a slight occasion of doing evil, but also the root of rash judgment—that is, suspicion. Hence, in order to do what he is taught by the words of God, he prays: “Cut off my reproach which I have suspected” (Ps. 118). Augustine [Col. 0221A] (on the same psalm, sermon 12) explains: that is, make it so that I have no evil or false opinion about the good or evil of others, which is “my reproach”; because I often suppose a thing to be otherwise than it is, and thus show that the fault which I suspect in others is my own. For one whose eye readily sees vanity, whose mouth speaks it, or whose hand does what is done in himself, suspects it of another; so that he may even believe another acts for the reason for which he himself does good things, judging the pure goodness of others to be superficial and like his own, solely from his own mind.

Again, Augustine on the same passage: It must be known that, because men’s hidden things are not seen, room has been given for suspicions. When the Lord in the Gospel (Matt. 6) gave instructions concerning the end or purpose of works—namely, that they should not do their righteousness either for human praise, or for money, or even for food or clothing—He forbade us, because we could suspect that it was done for such reasons, saying: “Do not judge” others from suspicions, “and you shall not be judged” (Luke 6); that is, you shall not be condemned, nor judged by others through suspicion. For our judgments about hidden matters are rash; to judge these belongs only to Him whose judgments are true and hidden. Judgment of manifest facts, however, is allowed to anyone; but judgment of persons belongs to the judge alone, and only of those convicted in court or confessing.

To this the following objection is made: doubtful matters should be interpreted in the better sense. For it is unjust and devilish [Col. 0221C] to incline to the other side and be more prone toward evil than toward good. Hence the Apostle says to the Romans, chapter 14: “Receive him who is weak in faith,” cautiously, “not in disputes,” and suspicions, “about thoughts.” The Gloss says: “For concerning his actions, which may be performed with either a good or evil intention, since it is unknown with what intention they are done, we are forbidden to judge. But if he errs, and you know that he does it knowingly and even with evil intention, bear it patiently; cure the error by prayer or by any other means.” Hence, to the Galatians, chapter 6: “Brethren, if a man be overtaken in some fault, you who are spiritual, instruct,” or restore, “such a person”—one who does not lack everything, but something—not, certainly, by bitterly attacking him, mocking the sinner, smearing over the good things that he possesses by rash [Col. 0221D] and suspicious judgment, or proudly detesting him as incurable, “but in a spirit of gentleness”: giving thanks to God for the good he has, promising pardon and salvation from Christ for the evil, “considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.”

Augustine (*On Baptism against the Donatists*, book 2, chapter 5): “If you think otherwise about a matter than it actually is, this is a human temptation. But to love one’s own opinion too dearly, to rush into rash judgment, and to envy better men to the point of the sacrilege of breaking communion and founding schism, is devilish presumption. To think otherwise about nothing than the matter actually is, is angelic perfection. Therefore, so long as we do not have an angel’s perfection, let us not have a devil’s presumption; rather, ‘let us bear one another’s burdens’ [Col. 0222A] (Gal. 6), forgiving one another’s debts and sympathizing with the evils of our neighbors, lest, if you do not sympathize, they become your own. ‘But if anyone thinks himself to be something’ (ibid.), through the emptiness of arrogance, foolish suspicion, and comparison with spiritual persons, ‘when he is nothing’ (ibid.), pretending to possess what he does not have and rashly judging another not to have what they do possess, ‘he deceives himself. But let each one prove his own work’ (ibid.), and rather judge it ‘in himself and not in another’ (ibid.)—that is, not measuring his own praise by the faults or lesser perfection of others, thereby vainly commending himself and foolishly judging others.”

Again, 1 Corinthians, chapter 4: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes and will illuminate the hidden things of darkness”—that is, make known the sins of the condemned—“and will reveal [Col. 0222B] the counsels of hearts; and then praise will be given to each one from God.” Augustine (*Tractates on John*, 90): “One errs perniciously in matters when one thinks evil good and good evil, when one does not approve virtues and does not detest vices. Certainly, if one errs through some suspicion regarding persons, it is a pardonable and human temptation, and our belief concerning them is often deceived. Nor is this surprising, since history itself sometimes, and rumor much more often, lies even concerning the same people. But if we are tempted in these matters, at least let us hold back our judgments and definitive sentences.”

Again, Romans 14: “Who are you, who judge another’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. Therefore let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that you place no stumbling-block or offense before your brother.” Augustine, *On the City of God*: “Let us not usurp for ourselves what does not concern us. Let us not blame things whose intention we do not know; or, even if they are manifestly evil, let us not despair of healing. For one who is evil today may be good tomorrow. Rash judgment lies in these two things, and comes from the vice of pride or envy in those who love to blame more than to correct.” To them it is said: “Do not judge, lest you be judged” (Matt. 7).

Again, 2 Corinthians 1: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience.” Augustine: “Do not consider this glory by comparison with anyone else, because the Apostle does not say, ‘Our glory is the testimony’ of another’s evil or lesser grace, but says, ‘the testimony of our conscience.’ Since this is hidden, it too is not subject to another’s judgment; and therefore no one should presume either to pronounce or to entertain a judgment against it, saying, ‘Who keeps chastity, or this commandment, or any other?’ For if he thinks that no one does, he himself is no one.”

Again, persons of this sort—suspicious and rash judges, judging the hidden things of hearts—when God alone “knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” (Ps. 93), alone searches hearts and reins (Ps. 7), alone will judge, and “will not judge by the hearing of His ears, neither reprove by the sight of His eyes” (Isa. 11)—presumptuously take up and usurp the divine office, wishing to make themselves equal to God, like him who said: “I will ascend into heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. [Col. 0223A] 14). As though saying: “The heart of man is deep and unsearchable; who knows it? We are counsellors and searchers of hearts.” And again: “The judgments of God are a great abyss” (Ps. 35). “Who knows them? We are God’s counsellors.”

They also usurp for themselves the prophetic spirit of Elisha, saying with him to his servant Gehazi: “Was not our heart present when you received silver and garments from Naaman as he met you?” (4 Kings 5). They are likewise like the Jews shouting and smearing the Lord’s works: “By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, you cast out demons” (Luke 11). This is what those say who invert the work of the right hand, declaring that it is done for a left-hand motive—for example, praise, human favor, gain, and the like.

This is “quenching the Spirit of God” (1 Thess. 5) [Col. 0223B] and sinning against the Holy Spirit: namely, ascribing to the devil a work which ought to be attributed to His goodness (Matt. 12). The Lord alone could truly use the term “hypocrite.” For who knows of another whether inwardly he is gold or golden, or merely gilded and covered with the foil of hypocrisy, except the Lord? Such persons also torment the just by a kind of dilemma, when the just reveal and make known to them the secrets of their household and their manner of life as an example. If they see signs of a stricter life in his way of living—such as a bed of ashes, bedding, sackcloth, and the like—they immediately cry out that he is a hypocrite. But if he conceals these things from them and closes his coffers, they say: “In secret he is a devourer of flesh, a drinker of wine, and lies upon the feathers of Sardanapalus.” [Col. 0223C] These:

Postponing their own concerns, they attend to other people’s affairs. HORACE. They have a gaping mouth, the enclosure of the doorway removed, and itching tongues. Against such people the Lord says: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8). As though he said: Since you are not compelled to do so, why do you judge your brother? And the philosopher SENECA says: “In doubtful matters do not decide quickly; rather keep your judgment suspended for a long time. Just as it must be formed and conceived with deliberation and discernment, so must it be pronounced with great seriousness.” And Jerome says (in the book *On the Four Virtues*, attributed to Martin, bishop of Dume): “If you see the Lord’s anointed caressing a woman’s head, do not immediately suspect evil from this, but say that he did it for the purpose of blessing her.” Likewise James, chapter 4: “He who speaks against a brother or judges his brother speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. But who are you, to judge your neighbour?” Likewise Ecclesiasticus, chapter 11: “Before you inquire, do not reproach anyone; and when you have inquired, rebuke justly.” Likewise: “Remove from me the reproach which I have feared, for your judgments are pleasant” (Psalm 118).

## CHAPTER LXXVI. Against Gossips

Because suspicious people are accustomed to be gossips, the Apostle rebukes persons of this kind in 2 Thessalonians 3: “We charge and exhort those who are such in the Lord,” that is, in Christ, “that, working with silence,” that is, without complaint and petty rumours, “they eat their own bread.” And Cato says (*Distichs*, book 1):

> Avoid rumours, lest you begin to be regarded as their new author;  
> Faith is rare for this reason: many people say many things.

And Horace says (*Epistles*, book 1, epistle 18):

> Flee the inquisitive man, for he is a chatterer.

And Quintus Curtius says: “Moreover, rumour is a vice of the idle soldier.”

> Rumour—an evil than which none is swifter—  
> Flourishes through motion and gains strength as it goes.  
> (VIRGIL, *Aeneid* 4.138.)

He who listens to and circulates it employs unwashed and foul speech; his life is correspondingly dishonourable. Such persons have drunken ears and itching tongues, and dispositions like their kindred speech: rumour-mongers, whisperers, and peddlers of trifles, who report what they do not know. Yet a man’s judgment ought to be a firm conviction of mind and an undoubted response. An uncertain witness does not go unpunished; therefore neither should an uncertain assertor of any matter. It is more dangerous to rush into a judgment by which another person’s reputation is injured and smeared than into one by which that person’s little property is diminished or lost. Socrates directed that time be allowed for resolving every question. And Ecclesiasticus, chapter 32: “My son, do nothing without counsel”—that is, without the file of discernment—say nothing; “and after you have acted, you will not repent.” For repentance often follows hasty speech and action. And Solomon says: “My son, above all have firm counsel” (Ecclesiasticus 37), so that you do or say nothing without judgment—that is, previous judgment, namely discernment and preceding deliberation.

Likewise Ecclesiasticus 33: “He who makes inquiry known will prepare a word”; “he orders his words with judgment” (Psalm 111); “and thus, having prayed to the Lord, he will be heard, will preserve discipline, and then will answer” (Ecclesiasticus 33). Likewise Ecclesiasticus 29: “Confirm your word, and deal faithfully with him; and at every time you will find what is necessary for you.” And Solomon in Proverbs, chapter 4: “Let your eyelids go before your steps,” that is, before your actions, so that you say or do nothing without foresight.

Do not resemble those of whom it is said: “The heart of fools is in their mouth” (Ecclesiasticus 21). Likewise: “The heart of fools will be unlike itself” (Proverbs 15). And likewise: “The tale of a fool is like a burden on a journey; the lips of the imprudent will tell foolish things, and the words of the senseless are unutterable; but the words of the prudent will be weighed in a balance” (Ecclesiasticus 21). The sum of all sums, therefore, is this: I bid you be slow of speech. And the philosopher says (SENECA, *Epistle* 40, at the end): “He who is timid in doubtful matters is worth nothing.” And the poet says (STATIUS, *Thebaid*, book 11):

> Give space and a brief delay: rash impulse brings all things badly to pass.  
> … Here is the madness of wretches: to press on into danger,  
> Not to weigh matters in fear, and to hate what is safe.

The emperor Augustus was deliberate in all his undertakings and did nothing without judgment. Hence Suetonius records his saying: “Whatever is done well is done quickly enough.”

## CHAPTER LXXVII. Against the Inconstant

[Col. 0225A]

Inconstancy accompanies this vice of gossip. For such people are often inconstant, and thus also peddlers of trifles. Rebuking the inconstant, Ecclesiasticus, chapter 33, says: “The heart of a fool is like a cartwheel, and his thought like a turning axle.”

> No one who is at variance with himself will be agreeable to anyone.  
> (CATO, *Distichs*, book 1.)

The first proof of a well-ordered mind is the ability to linger and remain with oneself. And the Apostle says in the final chapter of 1 Corinthians: “Watch; stand firm in the faith; act manfully,” because inconstancy belongs to women. “Woman is always variable and changeable” (SENECA, *Epistle* 2). “Be steadfast, and you shall see the help of the Lord upon you” (2 Chronicles 20). Otherwise, having become inconstant, you will incur the curse and punishment of the sons of Judah. Thus Psalm 108: “Let his sons be driven about,” inconstant and uncertain, “and beg; let them be cast out from their dwellings; let the moneylender search out his substance,” etc. Such people, together with the suspicious, incur Cain’s curse: they have a trembling head, a trembling and inconstant heart, and a trembling tongue, “wandering and fugitives with Cain upon the earth” (Genesis 4). All folly suffers from weariness of itself: the inconstant become wearisome to themselves, because “the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus 27). Their works have neither tail nor head; “they praise different things, following them.” And Isaiah 3: “Women have ruled over my people.” And Proverbs, chapter 4: “Make straight the path for your feet, and all your ways shall be established.” “The Lord is a support for those who fear him” (Psalm 24). And Peter was told: “Strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22). For the inconstant are compared to reeds shaken by every wind (Matthew 11). And David says: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice; be strengthened” (Psalm 104), etc. Likewise: “Perfect my steps in your paths, that my footsteps may not be moved” (Psalm 16). And likewise: “Strengthen, O God, what you have wrought in us” (Psalm 65). “But the Lord set his face firmly to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9).

In whose mouth there “was not yes and no.” Excusing himself from this vice, the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 1: “Did I use fickleness, so that with me there should be yes and no?” Likewise: “Be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 15). Solomon compares the inconstant person to an apostate in Proverbs 6, saying: “An apostate and frivolous man walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot,” etc. The Gloss: “By outward restlessness he shows that he stands inwardly on no root; for movement or inconstancy of mind makes the limbs restless.” Likewise: “The wicked walk in a circle” (Psalm 11). Likewise: “Their soul abhorred every food” (Psalm 106), etc.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. Against Foreign Ordeals of Red-Hot Iron and Cold or Boiling Water

[Col. 0226A]

Just as doubtful judgments are forbidden by the same authority, so too are foreign ordeals—indeed, diabolical temptations by which the Lord is tested. Hence Deuteronomy 18: “Take care that there be found among you no one who consults diviners, observes dreams or omens, practises magic, casts spells, consults pythonic spirits or soothsayers, or seeks truth from the dead.” Therefore, if you are forbidden to seek truth by the sword or battle, by the offices of sacred judgments [perhaps *judiciorum*, “judgments,” rather than *divinorum*, “divine things”], and by fire, water, or air, neither should you test anyone’s innocence by the office of a spell-caster or enchanter. Both the former and the latter are forbidden by the same canonical and apostolic authority.

Likewise, in the same chapter: “The prophet who wishes to speak what I have not commanded shall be put to death. But how shall I know that the Lord has not spoken through him? You shall have this sign: if what that prophet has predicted does not happen, the Lord has not spoken it; rather, the prophet has fabricated it through the swelling of his own heart, and therefore you shall not fear him.” But foreign ordeals and enchantments, or curses of water or red-hot iron, often deceive and fail to achieve their effect. For by these an innocent person is often condemned. Therefore, if what this worker of wonders promises does not occur, neither has God spoken such a judgment.

But if it occurs, and God has not commanded such a judgment to be pronounced in the Law or the Gospel, then the person speaking and enchanting thus against God ought to be put to death. Likewise Deuteronomy, chapter 17: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses, he who is to be put to death shall perish.” The Gloss: “The judge shall judge him only according to the word which I have spoken,” namely the attestations of the Law and the Gospel. And the Apostle says in Hebrews 6: “An oath is the end of every controversy.” And in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1: “Not because we lord it over your faith, but because we are helpers of your joy.” Since, therefore, no one can be compelled to believe, how can one whose faith is deficient be burned, when no human being can lord it over such faith? And David says: “O God, you will not go forth in our powers” (Psalm 43), as of old in the miracles of the ancient fathers.

Likewise the Lord in Matthew, chapter 4: “Command that these stones become bread.” He replied: “It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” He does not employ power but the authority of the Scriptures, teaching us to fight more by doctrine than by miracles. In the same place: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid.). The Gloss: “The devil suggested that he should test by some sign how much power he had with God. But no one ought to tempt God when human reason supplies what he should do.” Thus, although he could do all things, he says to his followers: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10). And he himself fled, though he could have descended from the Temple otherwise than by casting himself down in display (John 6). But once human reason fails, let a person commend himself to God—not by testing him, but by devout confession.

Therefore I would advise giving accused persons the water of jealousy (Numbers 5) and of cursing—because Scripture mentions it—but never the body of the Lord, on account of the excessive *tapeinōsis* (ταπείνωσις), that is, humiliation, of so great a sacrament. Even if I were a priest and commanded by the universal Church, I would not perform a foreign ordeal.

Likewise, certain things once approved by the Lord and permitted for a time—such as the casting of lots among the multitude concerning Saul (1 Samuel 10), or among a few, namely two, concerning Matthias and Barnabas (Acts 1)—are not accepted by the Church today: both because of their proximity to divination, since evils are near to goods (HORACE), and because of the uncertainty of lots (26, question 5, chapter *Sortes*). Even when the lots are kept and cast, especially in a multitude, a wicked and unworthy person might be preferred to one worthy to govern. The Church therefore preferred that the election of a prelate be entrusted to human reason and discernment rather than to the uncertainty of lots.

From this I conclude that, if for the stated reasons the Church does not accept the foreign and uncertain judgment of lots even in a case where no shedding of blood is feared, much less should it, for the same reasons and where bloodshed is involved, accept foreign ordeals for proving anyone’s innocence or guilt. It remains, therefore, that they should be removed from the midst of the Church, just as casting lots should be—especially since they were neither instituted nor received by her authority, but stealthily and greedily introduced.

Likewise, today the truth of lots is not believed in a more important matter, namely in electing a prelate of the Church, upon whose election her welfare especially depends if a good man is elected, while danger to souls threatens if an evil man is chosen. Therefore the truth of a foreign ordeal ought not to be believed in a less important matter. Or, if it is believed in the lesser matter, then in the greater and more useful matter one ought much more to abide by the truth of this judgment.

Likewise, the privileges of a few are not to be drawn into a consequence and made into a common law. We read that Moses crossed the Red Sea on dry ground (Exodus 14); Daniel was drawn unharmed from the lions’ den (Daniel 6); the three youths were delivered from the fiery furnace (Daniel 3); Brixius, to clear himself, carried burning coals in his cloak (*byrrhus*) (GREGORY OF TOURS, *History of the Franks*, book 2, chapter 1; and his *Life*, vol. 6 of Surius); and Ahaz, at Isaiah’s command, asked the Lord for a sign (Isaiah 7). But now, after faith has been preached and received, as some authorities proclaim, this is not the time for performing miracles, but rather for fulfilling and imitating the works of faith and the commandments. Or, if you want miracles to occur, produce for us someone like one of those just named, and let them be worked through him, and for some matter exceedingly useful to the Church.

Likewise, in the ordeal of water the element exercises its nature, office, manifestation, and proof of someone’s innocence; the nature of that element is to receive within itself a heavy body—unless the human body is transformed and compressed, as it were, into a ball or little boat. Thus in this ordeal grace assists nature. Conversely, in the ordeal of red-hot iron the element is deprived, for proof of someone’s innocence, of its own nature and office, which is to burn tender flesh. The contrary likewise takes place in these ordeals regarding the manifestation of someone’s guilt or wickedness. Therefore I conclude that in both these elements their nature and office ought to be preserved in the manifestation of someone’s innocence; where each is miraculously deprived of its nature in showing someone’s guilt—or because the judgments are contrary—both, namely the ordeal of water and the ordeal of fire, must be refuted and rejected.
