Likewise, if the miracles promised by the Lord in the Gospel to the righteous sometimes fail, and are not necessary in the sense that they must always attain their effect (Mark 16)—for example, that the sick be cured by the laying on of hands, and similar things, as the saints testify—how can these miracles of foreign ordeal be necessary, so that they always occur or achieve their effect? If they fail, therefore, they are to be rejected. That such foreign ordeals are stealthy miracles is proved by the fact that the elements are deprived of their nature through incantation.

Moreover, God has granted even wicked persons power to perform miracles, and to perform them on behalf of the wicked. Hence: “Did we not cast out demons in your name?” (Matthew 7), etc. Yet even if miracles are not worked through me or for me, I shall not for that reason believe myself less faithful or innocent. For now the Church relies more upon good works than upon miracles. Likewise the Lord says: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name” (John 14), that is, piously and perseveringly, and those things which are necessary for salvation—“without which there is no salvation”—“shall be done for you.” For you, I say; not for those for whom, or against whom, the request is made. How then does a priest who is a magician and enchanter presume that he will be heard for everyone for whom or against whom he invokes God?

Likewise Peter, in the *Dialogues* (book 1, chapter 2), asks Gregory how someone was raised from the dead by the placing of a shoe upon him: namely, whether because of the merit of the one invoking, the merit of the mother praying for her son, the merit of the person raised, or of the saints to whom the prayers are addressed. Gregory replies: “At one time miracles happen for this cause, at another for that, and at another when all these causes concur.” But for which of these reasons are such things done by a priest of this kind?

Likewise, neither exorcisms invented by Solomon nor those devised by the Church—to expel demons, cure the possessed, and heal diseases—are necessarily always effective in such cases; they often fail. How then can exorcisms—or rather, curses of water or fire, whose origin and authority are wholly unknown—be necessary so that they always attain their effects? Is this through the force of the exorcisms or their authority, or through the force of orders? I say that it is so if they are attached to some order; but their author is unknown. It remains, therefore, that they possess this power by force conferred upon them. But by whom? Thus, by the force of orders. Can anyone, then, always do this because he is a priest or because he is an exorcist?

Likewise Psalm 58: “Attend to my soul and free it; rescue me because of my enemies”—that they may be confounded or converted by my deliverance. But it seems strange that he makes this the ground of his petition, as though he were not to be delivered if neither outcome occurred. Yet it should be observed that there are two kinds of deliverance. One is hidden and takes place for the saints themselves: in this way the seven Maccabees were delivered when consumed by fire, their mother herself urging them to choose death for God’s laws rather than life against them (2 Maccabees 7). The other is manifest and takes place in order that enemies may be punished or converted: in this way the three youths were delivered from the fire even in body, and therefore Nebuchadnezzar himself was converted and proclaimed their God, whom he had despised (Daniel 3).

If, then, you seek someone’s manifest deliverance, and provoke God to grant it and to perform miracles—not for the conversion of brethren or the confirmation of the faith, but by testing God—you attempt to bring the times and state of grace back to the times and state of the Old Testament. Yet in the time of grace the Lord has promised his saints only hidden deliverances, giving them manifest ones in his own time, not as to the ancients, who, like infants at the breast, had to be enticed by miracles and temporal things to love heavenly things.

The Lord also says to his righteous people under the New Testament through Isaiah 43: “Do not remember the former things, and do not look upon things of old. Behold, I make new things, and now they shall spring forth; surely you shall know them.” Likewise Psalm 107: “In God we shall do valiantly”: not by the sword, not by miracles, but in God—namely, by conquering the devil through faith in him and good works.

Likewise, the baptismal form instituted by Christ does not always attain its effect, when even the stain of a single grave sin prevents it. How, then, will the execrable formula of an incantation over iron, invented by I know not whom, necessarily always possess efficacy? Likewise, if a church of unbelievers promised the Church of the faithful that it would receive Christ’s faith if it proved and tested it to be true by an ordeal of red-hot iron, would the Catholic Church undergo such an ordeal in one person in order to gain so many? Far be it from her to entrust Christ’s faith to an uncertain judgment, lest it be endangered by the devil’s cunning and malice, with God’s permission. For this reason the Jews were not allowed to carry their scroll around the city of Reims in a time of drought, when rain had been denied to the Church despite its prayers and processions.

Those who approve, celebrate, or undergo foreign ordeals seem to make themselves equal to John, “who, cast into a vat of boiling oil, emerged unharmed” both in mind and body. They also wish to appear like blessed Marcellus of Paris. When a smith placed a glowing mass of iron upon his hands, and Marcellus asked that the coals be put into a censer, he said: “It is hot from the heat of the fire, and it weighs nine pounds. But may the hand of your sinner never become the balance for weighing red-hot iron.”

Likewise, to use examples: At the Council of Reims in 1148, with Pope Eugenius presiding, a certain Manichaean, convicted and confessing his heresy, was imprisoned by the common decree of the council. He was not killed or mutilated, but, lest he corrupt others and perhaps repent, was placed in the prison of Samson, archbishop of that city, and was sustained on water and a thin diet until he died.

That archbishop also wholly forbade the ordeal of fire to be performed in his diocese. He tolerated the ordeal of water in whatever form, but did not allow any priest of his to celebrate the blessing of water unless the rulers had first guaranteed the priest who was to bless it that no limb would be mutilated and no blood shed. Yet unbelievers of old gave a Christian who had not been convicted or confessed thirty days’ respite to deliberate whether he would sacrifice to idols. But from one convicted or confessing and denying Christ’s name they required nothing further than sacrifice to idols; for it was not proved whether he so believed in his heart. How then does the Church presume to examine human hearts by a foreign ordeal? Or why are lawful periods of deliberation not granted to Cathars, but they are immediately burned?

Indeed, certain honourable matrons who refused to consent to the lust of priests, born of “the seed of Canaan” (Daniel 3), were written in the book of death, accused as Cathars, and condemned by a certain petitioner and foolish zealot for the Christian faith—after he had squeezed the purses of wealthy Cathars and allowed them to depart. One man alone, because poor and pale, though faithfully confessing Christ’s faith in all things and persisting in hope, was burned because he told the assembled bishops that he would by no means undergo the ordeal of red-hot iron unless they first assured him that it could be done without mortal sin and without testing the Lord. On hearing these words, all together abandoned him, telling the king that they were not permitted to take part in a judgment of blood.

Likewise Hebrews, chapter 11: “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms.” Augustine replies: sometimes by a hidden victory and deliverance, sometimes by a manifest one. “They worked righteousness”—this always. “They obtained promises in Christ.” If you are righteous, obtain these preceding things always through faith. For it is not necessary to faith that you should always obtain the following things in the outward appearance of miracles—“that they stopped the mouths of lions,” etc. Therefore one who attempts, of necessity and infallibly, to work miracles presumes that he possesses holiness like theirs, indeed greater.

Likewise, many examples prove that one must not rely on the falsehood and uncertainty of a foreign ordeal: for instance, the sacristan of Orléans who was hanged because he was accused of secretly taking relics from the church of Saint Samson, whereas another person, later discovered, confessed that he had taken them. And the recluse of Compiègne, excessively bold in the case of a similar theft because he knew himself innocent, who carried red-hot iron and was burned. And the female recluse familiar with the Cathars: her name became so despised among the people that there was no one to feed her when she was dying of hunger. On the advice of a certain religious dean, after first confessing to him that she was wholly free from the heretical depravity of the Cathars, she carried the iron in her own purification and was burned twice.

And there is the case of the English pilgrim, who, returning from the regions of Jerusalem without his companion—for his companion had turned aside to Saint James—was charged falsely by his companion’s parents with having killed him on the road. He underwent the ordeal of water and perished; shortly after his hanging, his companion returned to England. Therefore, in doubtful matters judgment must be withheld, especially in a capital case. There one must proceed not merely by conjectural or probable grounds, but judge by reasons clearer than light, lest one who judges otherwise be guilty of the death of the condemned.

Nor should persons convicted by such an ordeal be handed over to death, because this judgment is in a manner ecclesiastical: it is not performed without a priest’s presence, and therefore, when a person is handed over to death, he is handed over by the priest, since it is done by the authority of the person through whose authority it is done. Blessed Thomas of Canterbury likewise refused to allow a degraded cleric to be punished again for the same crime, because “God does not punish twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1 according to the Septuagint; cited at 13, question 2, chapter *Quaesitum est*).

That Cathars, before being convicted or confessing, should not be killed unless the Church has established by practical means that it can resist them, appears from the Apostle’s saying: “After a third admonition, avoid a heretical man” (Titus 3). He does not say, “Kill him.” Likewise David: “Rebuke the beasts of the reeds, and scatter the congregation of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Psalm 67). They should therefore be confined, not killed. Thus Isidore says on 2 Samuel 16, “Go in to your father’s concubines,” etc.: “By David’s concubines corrupted by Absalom we understand heretics and apostates. David no longer goes in to these, nor are such people likewise set over the government of the Church. Yet David commands food to be supplied to them when they have been placed in custody; they must be separated from the fellowship of the good. But he does not refuse food to such people; rather, he commands that it be provided, so that they may be converted through the occasion of benefits.” Likewise 1 Kings 2: “Today I will not put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord,” etc.

The Apostle also, because he despised everything and suffered frequent afflictions, was charged by a pseudo-[apostle] with not believing soundly and not being a man of God. Hence in 2 Corinthians, chapter 4: “Therefore death works in us, because you do not believe as you claim; but life works in you,” because you do believe. For good things succeed for you at your wish, whereas evils and death always threaten us. But David says: “The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonderful works” (Psalm 110). Therefore do not expect him always to do for you what he once did, so that you might have their remembrance.

Likewise, the Apostle in 1 Corinthians, chapter 12, shows the diversity of persons according to offices in the Church and the division of gifts within it: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing in one Spirit; to another the working of powers,” that is, miracles, etc. If, then, the working of powers is granted to everyone, especially in a foreign ordeal, how are there “divisions of gifts”? Or how are some priests not admitted to curse water? If this power is granted only to priests and to all priests, how can there be so many divisions of gifts? Or, when all are one member, where is the body?

Likewise, is this granted to them solely from the gift of the Holy Spirit, or by the force of orders? If from the gift of the Holy Spirit, then someone may lack that gift because of some stain. And since “there are divisions of gifts,” how do all presume to exercise this power? That this is done solely by the force of orders appears from the fact that this kind of judgment is performed contrary to ecclesiastical institution and prohibition.

Likewise, false accusation remains unpunished in this ordeal. Consequently people rush everywhere and rashly into accusing anyone whatsoever. Therefore this judgment is unequal and unjust, since, according to the law, likeness of punishment demands that slanderers receive retribution. Likewise Isaiah, chapter 44: “Thus says God, who makes all things, who alone stretches out the heavens, who establishes the earth—and none is with me—making void the signs of diviners and turning soothsayers to madness, turning the wise backward and making their knowledge foolish.”

Likewise, to provide someone with an opportunity or occasion for fornication when one can prevent it is a mortal sin. Therefore to provide an opportunity or occasion for shedding someone’s blood, when one can prevent it or refuse consent, is a more mortal sin, since this sin is greater than that one. Thus both the priest enchanting the element and the accused person undergoing such an ordeal sin mortally. But you will say: “A multitude is never party to a case, and therefore cannot be resisted.” Could a multitude make simple fornication cease to be a mortal sin, or make it more tolerable, if everyone committed fornication? Far from it! According to the saying: “A multitude provides no defence to the sinner.” Therefore neither does it in this graver matter.

I, therefore, if accused, would clear myself by oath and go no further. Likewise, as a priest, I would not bless water or iron, nor provide relics and holy things upon which someone might swear before undertaking single combat, lest through my authority and occasion I become guilty of bloodshed. Likewise, the truth of this ordeal either rests solely in the priest’s office, or in the will of the accused who wishes to undergo it, or in both. But it does not rest solely in the priest’s office, because it would not be performed for that reason alone; nor in the accused person’s will, because he undergoes it unwillingly. Or, if voluntarily: will this make the ordeal just? If so, will it be unjust because he underwent it unwillingly? Or if he is compelled and forcibly placed in a tub, must the judgment of water be accepted?

What then, if human reason gives you no course of action? Say: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit” (Psalm 30). But let the earth of my body, as you see fit, either be given into the hands of the wicked or, if it pleases you, be delivered. Likewise, the injustice of this type of judgment is evident from the trickery and precaution practised in it: for example, binding a human body into the form of a little boat, bladder, or ball when it is lowered into the water, or holding one’s breath, by which retention the body floats. Thus human blood, “for which the Lord Jesus Christ shed his own blood” (Matthew 26), is committed to the uncertainty and contrivance of the person lowering the accused, or to the fear instilled in him, on account of which he holds his breath.

Likewise, a combatant who is to undertake single combat trusts more either in his own strength and bodily power, in his skill’s exercise, in his complete innocence, or in a miracle to be wrought by God. If in his own strength or skill, the judgment is unequal. If in complete innocence, it is presumption and an anticipation of the divine judgment, in which alone “the hidden things of our heart will be revealed” (1 Corinthians 4). If in a miracle, it is a diabolical temptation, since it was said: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matthew 4), when human reason gives you something to do.

Likewise, this kind of judgment is evidently unjust because different people hold different views of it. Some condemn a person lowered into water if he does not touch the bottom; others justify and acquit him if the water receives, encloses, and covers him completely, including his hair; others pronounce such a person just even if only his hair floats, although hair is an excrescence of the body and not part of its substance.

Likewise, if red-hot iron is carried by three persons, it is less heated and hot when carried by the last. Hence the third person’s hand was found unburned when three carried it, while the others’ hands were burned. Likewise, a hand may be calloused or not. An example is given of a man who prepared one of his sons for the ordeal of water: when six had floated, he put the seventh into the water, and he immediately sank to the bottom. “This one,” he said, “is necessary to me,” and afterward he prevailed through him.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. Against the Burdensomeness and Multitude of Traditions

[Col. 0233C]

Besides the above-mentioned wholly unlawful traditions and diabolical inventions concerning foreign ordeals, there are certain lawful and useful traditions. Yet they often, and in particular cases, seem to create an obstacle and contradiction to divine evangelical and apostolic commands. There are also other lawful traditions that create no obstacle to divine commands, yet by their multitude burden those who institute them and render their transgressors disobedient; these ought to be instituted only sparingly and in small number, and only for a most manifest and useful cause.

They seem to create an obstacle to divine commands. These abolish the evangelical freedom of rebuking a brother—namely, the silence, tranquillity, and religious observance of the cloister—except in venial and less atrocious sins. Thus, in more atrocious sins, this command perhaps sleeps and expires among cloistered persons: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him” (Matthew 18), etc., according to the ecclesiastical form and judicial order.

Likewise, the tradition that one must not return from the contemplative to the active life except for the Church’s benefit conflicts with these commands: the Lord gave his followers authority for every work (Matthew 10). And likewise: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you” (Matthew 5), that is, if the contemplative life has produced in you an obstacle and weariness, return to the active life. I do not mean just any active life, but one that is contemplative in comparison with the lower active life.

[Col. 0234A] There is, then, a higher contemplative life, by which a person clings in mind to contemplation of the Trinity and the heavenly spirits. There is also a less worthy contemplative life, such as reading, writing, and the like; these too are parts of the contemplative life in relation to the lower active life, which is also a remedy for married persons. There is likewise the active life of a prelate, more worthy in merit. Therefore, one wearied by the higher contemplation should return to the middle course.

Likewise, the tradition of shunning property and of not distributing to the poor, not assisting the afflicted except through the person entrusted with administration, seems contrary to these commands: “Be reconciled with your adversary” (Matt. V)—that is, with the Gospel, which is your abbot and adversary on the way, crying: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. LVIII), etc. And likewise: [Col. 0234B] “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke VI). And again: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him” (Rom. XII), etc. Again: “Pure and undefiled religion is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from this world” (Jas. I). Again: “He who has two tunics, let him give one to him who has none, and likewise food” (Luke III). Martin went beyond what was required when he divided his cloak with a poor man. Again: “Whoever sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him?” (I John III). For He says: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. XXV). I believe that, in a necessity which knows no law, Martin—if he were alive—would prefer to obey the evangelical abbot, as the greater adversary, [Col. 0234C] rather than an abbot serving in a cloister.

Thus too a certain devout monk, obeying God rather than men, stole the cloak of an abbot who was his guest and gave it to a naked poor man. He also released and allowed to depart a brother kept in fetters on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, because on that night “the heavens became honey-sweet” (Luke II), and peace and liberty were restored to humankind.

Likewise, the tradition of lying down in a cowl shaped like a cross—because Blessed Benedict said (in the Rule, ch. 22), “Monks should always lie down clothed and girded, so that they may be readier and better prepared to meet the Lord”—seems contrary to this command: “Let your service be reasonable” (Rom. XII). And likewise to the example of Peter sleeping in prison (Acts XIX [probably XII]). But if they would be readier [Col. 0234D] if they lay down wearing shoes—for putting on shoes takes longer than putting on clothing—why has this too not been commanded for the same reason? But is it lawful for a monk to lie naked? Nor is it fitting for a cleric, whose naked flesh ought never to appear.

Whether a monk drowned—because amid waves and peril he refused to take off his tunic, relying more on tradition than on God’s command, namely, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. IV)—and thus uncertain what to do according to human reason, ought to be condemned or buried with Christian burial, is not for me to judge. Perhaps he did not remove his tunic through inward inspiration rather than zeal for holy tradition, or according to common understanding.

[Col. 0235A] Likewise, the tradition of not covering the whole head in a monastery is contrary to the aforementioned command: “Let your service be reasonable” (Rom. XII). But a certain convert, when he was doubtful whether human traditions or divine commands ought more to be obeyed, chose in necessity to prefer works of piety to human commands; and perhaps the Holy Spirit, who had made him doubt what ought to be done in the uncertainty, revealed this to him, lest, by postponing works of mercy, he should appear blameworthy along with the Pharisees, to whom God said: “But you say: If a man should say to father or mother, ‘Corban’—that is, a gift—whatever from me might benefit you; then you no longer permit him to do anything for father or mother, making void the word of God through your tradition” [Col. 0235B] (Mark VII).

Therefore, in fulfilling God’s commandments we ought rather to exercise ourselves with David, who says: “I will exercise myself in your ordinances” (Ps. LXXVI). Yet now, by a multitude of new traditions, we seem to bring back the yoke “and unbearable burden which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts XV), traditions which often supply matter and occasion for sinning. Observe that the Apostle instituted only a few honourable and mystical traditions, such as the veiling of a woman’s head “in prayer because of the angels” (I Cor. XI), and things of that sort. Anthony the hermit likewise, when certain religious persons asked him for a rule and pattern of religious life, handed them a copy of the Gospel.

At the Lateran council, too, when the Fathers were sitting to frame new [Col. 0235C] decrees, John of Chartres said:

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] Under Alexander III, the Third Ecumenical Council.]
>
> “Far be it,” he said, “that new enactments should be made, or that very many of the old ones should be reworked and renewed!”

We are also excessively burdened by the multitude of inventions, although authority says that even some useful things must be set aside, lest we be weighed down by a multitude of useful things. Indeed, the Gospel ought rather to be commanded and laboured for, since few now obey it. Let us fear lest the Lord say to us: “Well do you make void the commandment of God in order to keep your tradition. Such people worship me in vain,” says the Lord (Mark VII).

See also how many transgressors the decree of the last Gregory (Gregory VII) creates, concerning fasting on Wednesday and Friday for five years for the consolation and visitation [Col. 0235D] of the Church of Jerusalem; and concerning fasting in the Advent of the Lord, which some interpret as an exhortation, others as counsel, while others say that it has been abrogated by the contrary custom of those who observe otherwise. See also that the decrees of the Lateran council (title I, chapter 8) create transgressors: for example, the decree that tithes be recalled from lay hands under threat of anathema; and that an ecclesiastical benefice should not be promised before it fell vacant. Today dispensations are granted in these matters with no recollection of the preceding canons (35, question 3, *Porro duorum*).

See [manuscript: “I saw”] also how that most holy sacrament of the Church, namely marriage, is by [Col. 0236A] traditions concerning the third degree of affinity and certain others made now void and now valid, now firm, through the chatter of advocates relying on the nets of traditions in order to fill their own purses and squeeze others dry—so much so that the sacrament of marriage is turned into ridicule among laypeople.

See also how many transgressors would be created if all the traditions handed down concerning the formalities of judicial procedure were observed. While advocates prolong this procedure—while they labour over it and preen themselves over it—a year passes. Yet the Apostle declares: “An oath is the end of every dispute” (Heb. VI); and Moses: “Every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XVII). And Count Theobald, standing on one foot, settled many lawsuits.

That clearer and more certain teaching may be had concerning lawful [Col. 0236B] and unlawful traditions, a distinction must be made. Some traditions are openly contrary to divine commands, such as the tradition of Corban against this command: “Honour your father and mother” (Mark VII). Some put an obstacle and impediment in the way of their fulfilment, as does that canonical tradition of regular clergy, established out of avarice, whereby converts are not to confess certain crimes to their chaplain but to the prior.

So too the tradition of Grandmont, that theft, a lapse of the flesh, and certain other crimes are not to be confessed except to the prior of Grandmont—though a man sent by Barbatus was sinning all the way to him through the cells; and lest his sin be disclosed in this manner to everyone, he often displayed it both to the priest and to all the others.

Other traditions, again, concerning matters [Col. 0236C] in which truth is not endangered—such as keeping silence and the like—produce scruples in the consciences of very many, if failure to observe them makes one a transgressor and less obedient; or whether it does so, when salvation can exist without them. Others again, by their multitude, produce weariness and sloth in those who wish to fulfil them, since it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. XLVIII). And Jerome says: It is better to chant one psalm with gladness of mind than a hundred in sadness and sloth, because God loves one who sings psalms and prays gladly, not from sadness or necessity. Therefore, far be it that Matins, psalms, or prayers should be multiplied by command unless devotion is present!

Likewise, some establish schism and a division of unity, such as the traditions handed down concerning different ways of singing, chanting psalms, and reading in different monasteries and churches of clerics. Yet unity, so far as we can, ought to be preserved in all things; it is the bond of ecclesiastical peace.

Likewise, certain traditions which are fulfilled—such as those concerning the singing of the vocal hours—produce excessive security, as though one who fulfils them were not at all, or less, bound to fulfil the real things: the seven works of mercy. Yet it is written: “These ought you to have done, and not to have omitted those” (Matt. XXIII; Luke XI). If these or those must be omitted, these should rather be omitted. [Col. 0237A] For on account of those omitted things we shall be reproached at judgment, and “cursed is everyone who has not fulfilled all that is written in this book” (Gal. III; Apoc. I), the evangelical book.

But on the “ten-stringed psaltery” (Ps. XCI), in the song of a psalm and the psalm of a song, we are commanded to praise the Lord—not always in a song of a song or a psalm of a psalm. These things should be alternated both according to the needs of brothers and to remove weariness. Therefore, “sing psalms with the spirit; sing psalms also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV), not “straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matt. XXIII). Do not abandon the Spirit that gives life for the letter, on account of a tradition, a determination, or some remote interpretation; but, with Nicholas, cleave closely to it, who always had before the eyes of his mind this evangelical saying: “Unless a man renounces all that he possesses, [Col. 0237B] he cannot,” etc. (Luke XIV).

Moreover, it should be noted that certain traditions and customs concerning oaths to be taken by persons being canonized and instituted in churches are dangerous. For example, in one church a person being canonized swears that, according to his ability and according to his rank and order in the church, he will exact justice and vengeance for losses and injuries inflicted upon himself, the church, or its people. That oath is precipitate, as the supreme pontiff, consulted on this matter, testified. For who would swear, without rashness, even to obey God according to his ability? Yet there is a certain “according to one’s ability” required by necessity, to which we are bound. Hence one raises his hands to God in vain if he does not stretch them out, according to his ability, to the poor.

Likewise, in another church one swears not to remit a fixed sum [Col. 0237C] of goods taken from the church or its people: for one hundred pounds, only one hundred shillings may be forgiven to the despoiler; for one hundred shillings, five shillings. This oath contains injustice. It deprives the swearer of evangelical liberty and mercy: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke VI); and of the ability to fulfil the Apostle’s counsel: “A servant of God ought not to quarrel” (II Tim. II). Therefore, etc., if it is lawful, let him swear (I Cor. VI); yet to bind oneself by oath is dangerous because of cases that may arise. For my due share, I would never bind myself in this way.

Likewise, in another church, one swears that, among the people of the church, an arsonist, thief, murderer, a person convicted or confessed, shall become an exile, be disinherited, or even be expelled from the territory of that Church; and that a suspect must [Col. 0237D] clear himself by the judgment of fire or water. This oath contains a devilish presumption, as Pope Alexander testified in a Decretal—perhaps Alexander III.

Likewise, in another church, one swears concerning free status, and that no slave is to be admitted there. This was done in order to exclude the prince’s slaves and household, because, if they were admitted, action against the wicked prince would be more lenient. But that church now receives that prince’s slaves, while it swears that it will not receive outsiders of the same condition who are more worthy. See how difficult it is to abolish a sticky and inveterate custom.

Likewise, in another church one swears not to accept a pledge except one of gold or silver for goods or losses inflicted upon the church. This is vain, frivolous, or greedy—[Col. 0238A] something the supreme pontiff also condemned.

Likewise, in another, one swears that no one will admit a dispensation, remission, or increase in his own *foraneitas* [outside status], even by command of the lord pope and with the consent of the chapter, should they wish to increase his pension; and thus he forswears works of piety being done to himself in that church.

And, to put an end to traditions—or rather to rebukes of them—there is an almost universal tradition in the Church, dangerous to many, that when a priest is instituted and invested with the care of souls, he is made to swear that he will observe all the laws and commands of the higher prelates; and that he will neither suppress nor conceal it if he sees any of his subjects sinning, litigating, quarrelling, or striking one another in a cemetery or on a feast day, and the like—matters from which the purse [Col. 0238B] can more readily be squeezed than a soul saved—but will report them to the notice of the higher prelates. This oath has produced scruples in many.

It seems lawful on the ground that one who thus swears has the care of souls only as dependent on the higher prelate. Therefore he seems bound to abide by and acquiesce in that prelate’s judgment and the traditions laid down by him for governing those souls. But, conversely, the lesser prelate who so swears disregards this command of the Lord: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone; if he hears you, you have gained your brother” (Matt. XVIII). Here, however, he is immediately compelled to tell the Church.

Likewise, one who thus refers lawsuits and offences to the palace officials—those who squeeze and flay others—will sow discord, destroy the souls of his subjects, and incur their [Col. 0238C] hatred. Likewise, when Moses established chiefs of tens, hundreds, and fifties (Exod. XVIII; Deut. I), he did not bind them by oath, but simply commanded them to refer to himself the greater questions and those which they were unable to resolve. Likewise, according to the laws, no one is bound to accuse.

Likewise, for another reason this oath seems unlawful: namely, because it plainly conflicts with this command of the Lord: “If you remember that your brother has anything against you” (Matt. V), and with the Apostle’s command: “Have peace among yourselves” (I Thess. V). This peace is today disturbed and broken by the greed of prelates, who do not allow persons previously at enmity to be freely reconciled unless the accused first weep for their purse being squeezed dry, rather than for the offence. This [Col. 0238D] is clear from the example of boys, one of whom, while playing, wounded another with an arrow unto death. Their fathers—since the father of the killer was rich—were not permitted to reconcile with one another freely.

But an oath would seem lawful if the lesser official swore that he would perform the duties of the greater according to his ability; that he would not conceal the latter’s rights in pursuit of personal gain in lesser matters; and that he would refer to the greater official enormous offences, for whose treatment a greater physician is required.

The Apostle also appears to void all traditions except those necessary to salvation, in II Corinthians, chapter VIII: “I do not speak as commanding you to make a gift and a sharing of service for the saints, lest perhaps by disobeying you transgress; but through the earnestness of others, proving the genuineness of your charity” [Col. 0239A].

Likewise, when the Lord sent His disciples to preach, He said to them: “Heal the sick, etc. Freely you have received; freely give. Take nothing with you; eat and drink what they have; and stay with a worthy person in the city” (Matt. X). Do not the enactments concerning the reception of legates with so many horses, so large a household, and the exaction of meals consisting of several courses seem contrary to this teaching? Especially since these things “are not in the house,” and since they do not preach or work there. The Apostle also, preaching to the Corinthians and accepting nothing from them, says that he despoiled other churches which meanwhile supplied him with offered expenses. Note that he calls himself a despoiler even for modest provisions without which he could not live. Thus the Apostle “despoiled churches” in necessities (II Cor. XI); these men flay them for superfluities.

### Chapter LXXX. Against those who soften the bow of Holy Scripture

Just as God’s commands are omitted through the invention of new traditions, so also through those who soften and slacken the rigour of Holy Scripture. For the Lord “has bent His bow and made it ready, and in it He has prepared instruments of death” (Ps. VII). But those who lighten and relax this bow—what else do they strive for except that the divine law should depend on their interpretation, will, morals, and custom, when rather all these ought to depend on it?

Therefore the Lord commands the traveller [Col. 0239C] to “be reconciled with his adversary” (Matt. V): he should not rely on or follow his own will, but his adversary. Against men of this sort, who seek comfort for their folly, Augustine says, on the passage, “Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. CXVIII [119]:165):

> They neither cause stumbling nor are themselves caused to stumble; or rather, the law itself is not a stumbling-block to them, because one who loves the law honours whatever he understands in it, and judges that what seems absurd in sound is profound and that he himself does not know it.

Therefore he follows the law rather than the example of any great man, lest, seeing that man struck by scandal, he himself should stumble too—a thing that does not happen to one who follows the law. In cases and human affairs the examples of prudent people should be followed; but in the way [Col. 0239D] of faith, life, and morals one ought rather to imitate and heed the rule and form of living and believing sufficiently prescribed by the Lord. For “his words are spirit and life” (John VI); “his word is living and effectual” (Heb. IV); “his command is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII); and “all his commands are faithful” (Ps. CX), altered by no falsehood or perverse exposition: “Established for ever and ever” (ibid.), not sent in vain like human words, which can be changed or interpreted at our pleasure.

But one who fears the Lord “delights exceedingly in his commandments” (Ps. CXI), so as to rely on them more than on his own will; he does not judge them difficult to fulfil, as Muhammad did, who slackened the Lord’s bow. Those seem like him who, softening it in accordance with their own manners and will, interpret it accordingly. “But the righteous man, who lives by faith” (Heb. X), says: “I have clung closely to your testimonies, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII), [Col. 0240A] placing no superfluous, false, or voluntary interpretation between himself and them like a barrier, lest he should thereby be prevented from “running in the way of your commandments” (ibid.) and they themselves fail to shine upon him. For: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (ibid.).

Jerome says: “Terrified by the authority or example of no one whatsoever, I have consented to no perversity or false exposition of Holy Scripture.” And the philosopher Seneca says: “The greatest of evils is that we live according to examples of evil.” What then? Always consider the law before following anyone’s example, lest you stumble. “For we all stumble in many things” (Jas. III), even prelates, whose life ought to be a lesson for their subjects and an interpretation of Holy Scripture (Gregory, *Morals*, book XXX).

And God says in Psalm XXI: “My heart”—the hidden meaning of Scripture, in which is my will—“has become like melting wax in the midst of my belly”; that is, among soft and effeminate persons it melts and vanishes away.

Because those who wish to live according to their own will annihilate it and cause it to disappear through a false and soft interpretation, although “the veil of the temple was torn” (Mark XV), so that even the weak may see holy things, if they love, if they lift their eyes to heaven, and do not “set their eyes to decline to the earth” (Ps. [Col. 0240C] XVI). And Isaiah I says: “Your wine-merchants mix water with wine.” Jerome: He who softens the precepts of Holy Scripture—which ought to correct his hearers—in accordance with their will, mingling in his own opinion, corrupts the wine. Hence the same writer says: “‘His wine,’ that is, the pure and sincere truth contained in Holy Scripture, ‘is mixed with water,’ corrupted by a false exposition which softens the rigour of Holy Scripture by its insipidity.”

“Your silver,” the silver of your speech, “has turned to dross; its excellent colour has been changed” (Lam. IV), because of you painters and silversmiths, who, though you ought to be bright and silver-like, have become yellowish, filthy, and counterfeit, following your own will in the pure wine of Holy Scripture rather than God’s.

Martin, seeing a shorn sheep, said: “This one has fulfilled the evangelical command: [Col. 0240D] ‘He who has two tunics, let him give one to him who has none’” (Luke III). Going beyond this, Martin divided his cloak in half for it as well. But how does he “agree with his adversary”—that is, Holy Scripture, which opposes the flesh and human sensuality, teaching him “the way of God’s commandments” (Matt. V) and to walk in them—who says that the commandments themselves, “established for ever and ever” (Ps. CX), are temporary, local, and personal, and who adds to and subtracts from precepts and counsels, interpreting and expounding them according to his own will and pleasure?

Such persons, I say, sin grievously because they do not, soundly and sincerely, “ask the mouth of the Lord” (Josh. IX). Solely because they do not wish to fulfil God’s commands in deed, they labour exceedingly in expounding them. But it is heretical to say that they are stated more terrifyingly than truly, for they are stated more truly than terrifyingly. To the saints, indeed, integrity and truth of meanings are of greater concern than integrity and arrangement of words.

Conversely, the philosopher—and especially we—may be challenged: when we say that all things in Christ’s teaching are in the light and open, why have we departed so far from the life-giving Spirit and the plain letter of the Gospel, expounding and allegorizing more than the Jews did from the killing letter? (II Cor. III).

In book VI, chapter 3, of the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius of Caesarea, it is read concerning Origen that he possessed perfect doctrine and a consummate life, so that this could truly be said of him: “This is one [Col. 0241B] who speaks as he lives and lives as he speaks. As is his word, such is his life; and as is his life, such is his word.” He maintains that the sayings and commands of the Saviour are to be observed literally and sincerely as they were delivered, especially these two commands: “He who has two tunics, let him give one to him who has none” (Luke III), and “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. VI).

His disciple Basilides likewise, as is read there, when he was dragged into court and an oath was demanded of him, said (chapter 5, according to Rufinus’s division): “I am a Christian. Far be it from me to swear!” For it is altogether unlawful for a Christian to swear, except concerning things that pertain to salvation, as when hearers are sluggish and weak and less willing to assent to what is said concerning salvation. Thus Paul also swore, not concerning a trivial and earthly matter.

By similarly weakening the Lord’s bow, they make him [Col. 0241C] seem almost a liar when he said: “Enter through the narrow gate, for narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII). We either do not find this gate, or, if we do find it, we have widened it so greatly through superfluous exposition rather than love that it no longer has any narrowness; thus we enter through the broad gate, not the narrow.

But the Lord’s saying in Matthew, chapter V, ought to strike the greatest fear into people of this kind—indeed, into all of us: “Do not think,” he says, “that I came to abolish,” that is, not to fulfil, “the law or the prophets. I came not to abolish but to fulfil”: both as to the truth of what was foretold concerning me by the Law and the Prophets; as to the meaning of figures and ceremonial observances; and [Col. 0241D] as to fulfilment of the commandments. Nor do I say merely “to fulfil,” but “to fulfil completely”: that is, to fulfil them perfectly in myself and in my members.

“For truly I say to you: until heaven and earth pass away” (ibid.)—that is, before they change from this mutable form into immutability—“not one iota,” the least command, such as that one must not be angry with a brother, nor call him “raca” or “fool,” that one must help him, even by raising his ass; that one must not wear soft garments, must not lord it over neighbours, and the like—“or one apex,” the tiniest command, or the least particle of some command, “shall pass from the law until all has been done.” Nothing will remain unfulfilled in me the head or in the body: in the manifestation of the truth of figures, in the spiritual fulfilment of commands, and in the perfection of moral precepts, so that what is imperfect may be perfected.

“Whoever therefore abolishes”—that is, does not fulfil—“one of these least commandments, and teaches people so”: namely, teaches them by example, word, or exposition that slackens and softens the Lord’s bow, “shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.): most despised and foolish; indeed, he is no one in the Church of the saints. He is counted for nothing in the Church triumphant or militant. “But whoever does and teaches”—namely, that the Law must be fulfilled, especially in the least commands—“he shall be called great,” indeed greatest, “in the kingdom of heaven,” though at present rejected and despised.

Therefore, he is small who abolishes and teaches this to be abolished; least, who abolishes and teaches this; great, who does not abolish, even if he does not teach this; greatest, who does not abolish and teaches [Col. 0242B] that it must not be abolished. One who fears God, therefore, fulfils every command even to the smallest stroke, and even the counsels if they become matters of necessity through a vow, knowing that he will render account for abandoning them, down to an idle word. If we shall give an account for an idle word, how much more for idle and superfluous clothing, idle teaching, and the like?

The Lord adds: “But I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees”—I do not mean their supposed righteousness, nor merely its figurative form, but the moral and spiritual righteousness that justifies them, so that you may fulfil to perfection the things added in the Gospel—“you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). For example: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you,” imposing something more, namely not to be angry, “that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (ibid.).

If, then, you are angry at his sin or with him in the first stirrings of emotion, beware lest, by being angrier than is fitting, you incur judgment. He adds also that “whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’” who utters an interjection expressing indignation of mind against him and harms or provokes him by gesture, sign, or a little word, “shall be liable to the council.” How much more someone who, by weakening greater commandments, teaches that they may be abolished? “But whoever says to his brother, ‘You fool!’”—the Gloss says: whoever proceeds so far as insults, reproaches, injurious, particular, and other definite words, even to fury of mind, not merely a sign—“shall be liable to [Col. 0242D] Gehenna”; he is as though already judged.

Likewise, in John, chapter V: “If you do not believe Moses’s writings, how will you believe my words?” As if to say: If you do not fulfil spiritually the things belonging to the Law, how will you fulfil what are evangelical commands? Hence Augustine, on that passage: From this it is gathered that whoever neglects to fulfil the commandments of the Law, which are outward, will be much less able to fulfil the evangelical commandments, which are more perfect and subtler.

Likewise: “My mouth shall speak wisdom,” concerning faith, “and the meditation of my heart understanding” (Ps. XLVIII), concerning good morals.

For two things are necessary to salvation: the way of faith and the light of morals. If, therefore, we call one who departs only a little from the faith a heretic, rebuking him and saying that he is not [Col. 0243A] on the way but outside it, why do we likewise not rebuke one who withdraws even slightly from the light of moral commands, charging him that he is now not in the light but in darkness; not sober but drunk, having exceeded the sobriety of life?

Moreover, since faith has been drawn out from certain cells—that is, small passages—of Holy Scripture, and indeed from obscure ones, in the exposition of which one would easily go astray if they were expounded and interpreted otherwise—by addition, subtraction, or relaxation—than has been set forth and expounded for us by the saints: why, in the light of morals, in matters likewise necessary to salvation and handed down to us in the clarity and plain manifestation of words, is it permitted to bring forward our own interpretation, however much it may relax, obscure, and deprive them of their proper force, without notable error?

For example: “I and the Father are one” (John X). Augustine (*Tractates on John*, tractate 6): See from what sort of honeycomb the honey of faith has been pressed, and by what movements of doctrine. In the words, “I and the Father are one,” Sabellius is confounded; in the word “one,” Arius—so that we may avoid both the Scylla of Sabellius and the Charybdis of Arius. But if, in accordance with such an exposition of this passage, you expounded the text, “I ask, Father, that they may be one, as we also are one” (John XVII), as unity in the same sense as their union, you would immediately fall into a condemned heresy. Lest this happen, do not depart from the established and ancient exposition.

Likewise, from this small cell of words, “This is my body” (Matt. XXVI), the faith concerning Christ’s body is drawn. If you expounded “This is my body” as Manichaeus did—namely, “This is my body,” that is, merely some representation of my body and nothing else—or interpreted it in another way than the Catholic faith holds, you would immediately go astray. So it seems to be with the moral commandments. They are easy and require no exposition if they are fulfilled in deed; indeed, the obligation to fulfil them is as much a matter of faith as the articles of faith. For faith is that what is said is done.

And Augustine, on the passage “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV), says (*Epistle* 19, chapter 2, and *On Lying*): A faithful servant is one who spends and gains what he has received: that is, who speaks and does the truth which he believes, as did this man who says, “I believed, therefore I spoke.” He not only believed the other things which faith requires as articles of faith, but along with them believed that he ought to await [Col. 0243D] or hope for a reward for speaking and acting, and a punishment for remaining silent or omitting commands.

Likewise (chapter 20 on Psalm CXV): See with what discrimination and care that people fulfilled the figurative observances: Daniel abstaining from Gentile foods (Dan. I), the Maccabees abstaining from pork even to the shedding of blood (II Macc. VII). With how much greater care, then, ought spiritual things to be fulfilled, if the Jew exercised such discrimination and care in fulfilling the killing letter? How much greater care must you exercise in the life-giving Spirit? Therefore, if you hear that pork is forbidden to the Jew, understand that gluttony, every impurity, and drunkenness are forbidden to you as well. If the hawk, kite, and other rapacious animals are forbidden to him, understand that every act of robbery is likewise taken away from you [Col. 0244A] (Deut. XIV). For robbery is every unjust detention of another’s property.

Hence Tobit, explaining that passage in chapter II, says: “We are children of the saints; it is not lawful for us to eat or touch what comes from theft.” How then do we impose tallages and exactions? Or if we fear to give anyone an occasion or opportunity for fornication, why do we not shudder still more at giving someone not merely an occasion for robbery, but our own service in it? We must not commit lesser evils so that others may commit greater ones.

Likewise, the Apostle says in II Corinthians X: “In presence,” while I am present, “I seem lowly to you,” because I do not rebuke harshly; “but absent I am confident toward you,” as you say, rebuking you confidently and harshly by letters—as though, drawn by hope of gain or compelled by fear, I soften and weaken the Lord’s bow when present. But it is not so. For as I rebuke when absent, so also when present.

Likewise, against these eunuchs and effeminate persons, who emasculate what is manly and robust in the Lord’s bow, Isaiah inveighs in chapter III, saying: “I will take away from you the strong man and the prudent interpreter of mystical speech, and I will give you boys as rulers, and effeminate men shall rule over you.” Would that they did not rule over Holy Scripture, but allowed it to run freely in its own gravity and maturity.

Likewise the prophet says: “Woe to those who bring false balances” (Mic. IV). Likewise Solomon, Proverbs chapter XX: “Balance and balance, weight and weight—both are an abomination before God.” The worst weighers and assessors of sins have an unjust balance. [Col. 0244C] That they are such happens because they either do not know Holy Scripture or soften its rigour: they possess balance and balance, with which they exaggerate and aggravate crimes in some persons, while they lighten and soothe them in others. Courtly flatterers especially possess a deceitful balance, who just as—
Romulus’ well-fed descendants recite divine poems. (PERSIUS, Satire 1.) They also mislead princes and great men, telling them that they are not bound by all the Lord’s commandments, but may receive dispensations on account of the nobility of their lineage, their rank, their public reputation—lest it decline—and the like. And, 215 that I may show such people to be still more ridiculous by examples, hear the words of one playing many parts. “I thought,” he said, “when I was dangerously ill, that so great and learned a prelate, hearing my confession, would require me to renounce all my dignities except one, since I was ‘reaping where I had not sown and gathering where I had not scattered,’ nor had I ministered.” But he passed this over in silence, rebuked me only for the sins of my youth and certain lesser crimes, and imposed upon me the duty of making satisfaction if I recovered.

Another also [manuscript: “indeed”], though no virgin, maintained that he would rather have sinned a hundred times against the Holy Spirit, provided he repented, than once have fallen into carnal uncleanness. Another preferred to have four concubines rather than four archdeaconries. Another said the opposite. [Col. 0245A] Again, another, though no virgin, said that he would rather have abstained from carnal uncleanness a hundred times out of vainglory, and thus have sinned mortally a hundred times, than have fallen into it once; and thus:

> While fools avoid vices, they run into their opposites.  
> (HORACE.)

Although virginity is most praiseworthy, so too is continence. For virgins draw near to the angelic mode of life; and so, from the softening of this bow and from ignorance, there arises an inability to distinguish good from greater good, evil from greater evil—which is no slight error. Yet although sins must not be made light of, penances are nevertheless discretionary. Thus, while making them light, they often rank lesser crimes—because they are visible, such as carnal uncleanness and the like—[Col. 0245B] above greater ones, because these are invisible and therefore more dangerous. Others, looking more rightly in the opposite direction, do so because of this indiscriminate treatment of crimes and softness.

A certain man made an archdeacon out of a lay robber and a half-cleric, saying that once made archdeacon he would not rob, but would live justly; yet what a grave-digger does, a physician had also done. And what the grave-digger and robber did, this archdeacon does: from being a grave-digger, he has become a greater grave-digger. Again, against interpreters of this utterly wretched kind Isaiah says, chapter 5: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil,” through knowledge or gross ignorance, which amounts to error; “who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter.” Jerome, on this passage: Every truth is sweet in itself and [Col. 0245C] to the good, though not to the wicked; for them “truth begets hatred” (TERENCE, *Andria*), who perish from a good fragrance, while falsehood is bitter. Therefore we must take the greatest care not to follow falsehood in place of truth, darkness in place of light, bitterness in place of sweetness. For “some ways seem right and” altogether just, “yet their last end leads to hell” (Prov. 16). “There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness. Do not be overly righteous” (Eccles. 7). Therefore, lest we incur this curse, let us “turn aside neither to the right nor to the left” (Deut. 5). Aquila, however, translated more pointedly: “Woe to those who say to evil, ‘You are good’; or to good, ‘You are evil’” (JEROME).

[Col. 0245D] Understand this knowingly. Ignorance concerning a person or an act excuses, but ignorance concerning the law does not. For divine law ought to lie open and in the light of knowledge. What then, or how, is one to judge concerning the subtle nets of simony and of lingering delight? Will there be woe to “him who” in these matters “calls good evil” (Isa. 5), 216 where good and evil are difficult to distinguish? Jerome: We avoid the curse with difficulty, because we easily flatter the wicked on account of their power and despise the good on account of their poverty.

Again: The following conclusion must be drawn from this authority: “Woe to those who call good evil,” etc. Likewise, woe to those who, through knowledge or gross ignorance, call a greater good a lesser good in comparison with a lesser good; [Col. 0246A] or a lesser good a greater good in comparison with a greater good, placing more useful things after less useful ones. For Jerome says: “It is no small error to prefer a lesser good to a greater, worthier, or more useful good.” For a change in the order of merits destroys and alters the form. Likewise, “Woe to those” who call a greater evil a lesser evil in comparison with a lesser evil, or a lesser evil a greater evil—not simply, I say, but by comparison and in relation to a greater evil. For we often aggravate sins, so that a person may avoid them more earnestly or, if he commits them, punish them more severely in himself.

Again, Psalm 118, under the letter *Yodh*: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.” Gloss: How profoundly the commandments must be understood. Again, at the end of the Apocalypse: “If anyone adds to these things”—by adding useless [Col. 0246B] or corrupt traditions and soft interpretations—God shall add to him the plagues written in this book. “And if anyone takes away”—by subtracting, or by softening the rigor of this bow—“God shall take away his part from the book of life” (Apoc. 22). Again, Deut., chapters 31, 4, and 12; Acts of the Apostles, chapter 3; likewise Ezekiel, chapter 33; Proverbs, chapter 30; Epistle to the Galatians 1: “Even if an angel should [preach] another [gospel],” etc.; Ecclesiastes, chapter 12.

## Chapter LXXXI. Against the Slothful

To those who weaken the bow of sacred Scripture and are most evil weighers of sins is joined their foster-sister, sloth, on account of which they neither read nor search the sacred Scriptures. Sloth is a most [Col. 0246C] grievous sin. Solomon denounces it in Proverbs, chapter 6: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you rise from your sleep?” Chapter 1: “Hand in hand is not innocent.” The same, chapter 12: “He who tills his land shall be filled with” abundant “bread; but he who pursues idleness is utterly foolish.” Again, chapter 12: “The slack hand shall serve” the tribute “of sin.” Again, chapter 13: “The sluggard desires and does not desire” to work, and the like, because he is unstable in all his ways. Again, chapter 15: “The way of the slothful is like a hedge of thorns,” because they shut him in, fence him about, and prick him so that he cannot work well. The same, chapter 18: “Fear casts down the sluggard” from good work; “but the souls of the effeminate shall hunger. He who is soft and lax in all his work is like one [Col. 0246D] who destroys his own work.” Hence in the following chapter: “Sloth brings on sleep, and the lax soul shall hunger” for pleasures. Again, chapter 20: “The sluggard would not plough because of the cold,” that is, serve God; “therefore he shall beg in summer,” namely on the day of judgment, and “nothing shall be given him,” namely rest. Again, chapter 21: “Desires kill the 217 sluggard, for his hands would not do anything.” Hence: “Every idle person” lives among the desires of his soul (Prov. 13:4, according to the Septuagint). Hence also the poet:

> The question is asked why Aegisthus became an adulterer:  
> The reason is ready at hand—he was idle.  
> (OVID, *Remedies for Love*, I.)

And likewise:

> If you take away idleness, the bows of desire perish—  
> [Col. 0247A] that is, of every desire.  
>
> Love yields to activity; act, and you will be safe.  
> (OVID, *Remedies for Love*, I.)

Again, Solomon, Proverbs chapter 24: “Cultivate your field, lest it be said of you: ‘I passed by the field of a sluggard,’” or drunkard, “and by the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles and thorns had filled it all.” The same, chapter 26: “As a door turns on its hinge, so does the sluggard on his bed. The sluggard hides his hands under his armpits and finds it laborious to bring them to his mouth.” In Ecclesiastes, chapter 4: “The fool” and sluggard “folds his hands and eats his own flesh,” through envy. This is said hyperbolically: the sluggard is often pressed by such great want that, if it were possible, [Col. 0247B] he would eat his own flesh. Or his sloth is the reason why his flesh, which will supply fuel and material for it, is eaten and devoured by eternal fire.

Again, Ecclesiasticus, chapter 22: “The sluggard shall be stoned with a muddy stone, and all shall speak of his contempt. The sluggard is to be stoned with the dung of oxen,” that is, with a harsh rebuke for his sin; “and everyone who touches him shall shake out his hands.” Again, the same: “Torture and fetters are due to an ill-disposed servant; send him therefore to work, lest he be idle. For idleness has taught much wickedness. Loosen his hands, and he seeks freedom;” therefore “set him to continual work; let yoke and strap bend his neck. For this is fitting for him.” But a son will do whatever he can out of love.

Again, the comic poet: See [Col. 0247C] what idleness and another’s food can do. Jerome (on Ezekiel, chapter 16): Abundance of bread, pride of life, and idleness were the origin of the sins of Sodom. Again, the Lord rebuking the idle in the Gospel says: “Why do you stand here idle all day? Go also into my vineyard” (Matt. 20). In digging, manuring, pruning, and planting that vineyard, since greater care ought to be given to the spirit than to the body, more ample diligence is necessary—especially since Christian foresight must always be alert, so that a person may always “live soberly, godly, and justly” (Tit. 2).

Again, at the judgment the Lord reproached omissions rather than acts committed, for which transgressors certainly are to be condemned, saying: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. [Col. 0247D] 26). By the name of hunger understand every want that you yourself or your neighbor suffers, in whom Christ is present; and by the name of food to be distributed, every talent entrusted to you by which you can aid your neighbor. Nor is it enough if on some occasion you have given food to the hungry, since even a bad person often does this, unless you have given as much as you can, as much as you ought, and as often as you ought. Excessive failure to distribute makes you guilty, but a moderate failure does not. But how can these matters be distinguished?

Again, in the Gospel the Lord condemns not only the doer of evil but also the servant who is sluggish in doing good, saying: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down 218 and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3). It belongs to servants, therefore, to sleep, be slothful, and be torpid; but it belongs to sons [Col. 0248A] to love and to keep watch. For the law was revealed to those who watched: while shepherds were watching over their flock, “great joy was announced to them, which shall be for all the people, because a Savior has been born” (Luke 2). Therefore: “Awake, you who sleep, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5). And the bride says in the Song: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5). Let our flesh sleep in such a way that the mind watches in Christ.

And Peter, at the end of his First Epistle, chapter 5, says: “Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour.” The Lord also “promised a crown to those who watch.” And in Luke, chapter 12, distinguishing three watches, he says: “And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those [Col. 0248B] servants.” Three times in that Evangelist he says, “Watch, watch, watch,” signifying the three watches. But why he leaves the first watch unspoken, I leave for the curious to resolve.

He sets three watches against threefold torpor: first, in matters relating to God; second, in matters relating to yourself; third, in matters relating to your neighbor. Watch, therefore, in matters relating to God; watch in matters relating to yourself; watch in matters relating to your neighbor. Or he distinguishes three watches on account of the threefold enemy: the devil, the world, and one’s own body. The world rages, the body presses upon us, and the devil lies in ambush.

In Mark, chapter 15, however, four watches are distinguished, where he says: “You do not know at what hour the Lord will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, [Col. 0248C] or in the morning.” These are classified by the philosopher as: the time of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, and before dawn. Four are distinguished on account of the four cardinal virtues: so that, being watchful, you may prudently and discerningly choose what is necessary; courageously preserve what you have chosen; temperately maintain your watch in adversity; and justly maintain it in prosperity, lest the sleep of sin creep upon you.

There is a fourfold sleep: of nature, for necessity; if it is excessive, it is evil. Hence:

> Always keep greater watch, and do not give yourself to sleep;  
> For prolonged rest supplies nourishment to vices.  
> (CATO, *Distichs*, Book I.)

Of sin: “Those who sleep, sleep by night” (1 Thess. 5); [Col. 0248D] of grace: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5); of glory: “And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord” (Acts 7). The first is in the world and directed toward the world, insofar as necessity requires; the second is in the world and directed toward sin; the third is in the world, but estranged from the world and from sin; the fourth is estranged from the world, from sin, and from every punishment. Hence: “In peace I shall sleep and rest together” (Ps. 4).

The sleep of sin too is threefold. First, some sleep in sin and do not rise again. Second, they doze: now repenting of sin, now falling back into it. Third, they fall asleep finally, dying in their sin. Against this sleep the Prophet prays: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever fall asleep in death” (Ps. 12). He also threatens the slothful, adding in Psalm 72: [Col. 0249A] “They are not in the toil of men, nor are they scourged with other men; therefore pride has taken hold of them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety. Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness; they passed into the desire of their heart; they thought and spoke wickedness,” etc.

These people also resist sacred Scripture and the Lord, who, because of sin, threatened humanity in Genesis. To Eve he says: “In pain and travail” you shall bear children. To Adam: “By the toil and sweat of your face,” not another’s, “you shall eat your bread.” For they are robbers who reap carnal things from those subject to them on the condition that they sow spiritual things for them, and yet do not sow them (1 Cor. 9).

Indeed, they are worse than moneylenders: they confer no benefit on those from whom they reap, but cause them harm if they pray for them. For when the one sent to intercede is displeasing, the mind of the angry party is provoked to [Col. 0249B] worse things. How do those who live in idleness, worldly pomp, and an abundance of worldly delights bring forth spiritual children in pain and travail? Or how do those “eat their bread by the sweat of their face” (Blessed GREGORY, *Pastoral Rule*) who are torpid in idleness and use the people—the feet of the world—as a beast of burden, though they themselves ought to be the people’s beasts and servants?

Arsenius, first a count of the palace and afterward a great hermit (see his *Life* in Surius, vol. IV), when asked in what he placed his confidence, answered: “In this: that I fled from men, kept silent for a time, and wept; above all, I rejoice that I worked with my hands.” And a certain wise man said to someone: “Whom, I ask, do you consider wise?” He replied: “That man,” pointing to [Col. 0249C] a learned, legally skilled, and wealthy man. “No,” he said, “but this man is wise,” pointing to a farmer. A widow also, when dying, refused to be buried in a shift given to her, saying: “I shall indeed be buried in a shift made by the labor of my own hands, not by another’s.”

Again, Isaiah, chapter 56: “His watchmen are blind,” etc. Therefore work, because: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127). But if you do not labor, you will be deprived of this blessing. “Your wife [shall be] like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house” (ibid.). And although sloth may be reproved and found in nearly every class of humankind, it is found especially in the clergy, because clerics have much leisure. There is nothing for them to do, although the Apostle says: “Give them this charge, that they may eat their” [Col. 0249D] “bread,” namely the bread of their own labor (2 Thess. 3). And Solomon says in Ecclesiastes, chapter 6: “All the labor of man is for his mouth.”

Thus too that saying is explained: “By the toil and sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3); by bread, every necessity for the body is understood. Understand the whole body from a part. For human labor consists not only in acquiring food, but also in clothing oneself and preparing a building in which to live. Labor is manifold: that of nature, grace, and sin. The labor of nature is twofold, bodily and spiritual: spiritual in thought, bodily in various ways. Nor does the Lord forbid natural labor directed to necessity, when he says: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. [Col. 0250A] 6), referring to vicious anxiety, not necessary provision.

The labor of grace is for grace and on account of grace. This too is twofold, bodily and spiritual; and each is threefold. There is penitential labor: “I have labored in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears” (Ps. 6). And there is the labor of mortifying one’s flesh: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection” (1 Cor. 9). Penitence has two hands: penitential labor, for blotting out past sins; and chastisement of the flesh, for avoiding future ones. Concerning these labors it is said to us: “God has no need of our goods” (Ps. 15); for we owe these works in order to recover lost salvation. The third labor of grace consists in care for one’s neighbor: that you may instruct him [Col. 0250B] in the way of the Lord and expend for him, according to place and time, every talent entrusted to you, with Paul, who says: “I have labored more abundantly than all” (1 Cor. 15). “My daily burden is concern for all the churches. For who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11.) And again: “Bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things,” or, “godliness has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4).

And this labor ought to follow the two preceding labors of grace, not precede them, nor in any manner accompany them, lest a man be more ready to flow out to others than to retain for himself—as a shell does. Concerning this labor it is said that “God in a certain sense needs our goods.” The labor of sin [Col. 0250C] is labor directed toward sin; it is manifold according to the variety of vices. See how much one person labors for empty glory, another for lust, another for gluttony, and so with the rest, “so that all day long there are iniquity upon the walls of Babylon, and toil and injustice in her midst” (Ps. 54). Certain laboring, such as envying, is not only directed toward sin but itself constitutes sin.

Nevertheless, the good often convert natural labor into labor of grace; often, as among farmers, it is indifferent; but evil people convert even this into labor of sin. For example, just as gluttony and vainglory turn the labor of obtaining necessary food into sin, so we convert the labor connected with clothing and with buildings into the labor of sin.

## Chapter LXXXII. Against the Superfluity and Curiosity of Clothing, Food, and Buildings

[Col. 0250D]

And how? Let us first consider the labor connected with food. The Apostle says: “Having food,” not delicacies, “and clothing,” not ornaments, “let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6). And “he who serves the altar should live from the altar” (1 Cor. 9), not live wantonly. Another authority has: “Those who proclaim the Gospel must live from the Gospel” (ibid.), that is, be sustained by it. And the Lord says: “He who has two tunics should give one to him who has none” (Luke 3).

But see how the necessity of food is now transformed contrary to these precepts, sometimes into gluttony, [Col. 0251A] sometimes into vainglory, sometimes into any other sin—through the excess of courses, their costliness, their elegance, the variety, number, and splendor of attendants, and even through the variety and multitude of instruments by which food may be prepared more quickly and more elegantly. But hear how the philosopher rebukes those who labor thus (SENECA, Epistle 60): A single wood is enough for several elephants; a bull seeks the pasture of a few acres; but man feeds on land and sea, and in such diverse ways. What then? Has nature given us an insatiable belly, so that, while giving us small bodies, we may exceed the voracity of the largest animals? Not at all. For it is not the hunger of the belly that costs us much, but ambition.

See that the first parents used a simple diet—not costly, varied, excessive, or corrupted by artifice. Hence Boethius (*Consolation of Philosophy*, Book II, metre 5):

> Excessively blessed was the former age,  
> Content with faithful fields  
> And not ruined by idle luxury;  
> It was accustomed easily  
> To break its late fast with acorns.  
>
> It knew not how to mix Bacchus’ gifts  
> With liquid honey,  
> Nor to blend the shining fleeces of the Seres  
> With Tyrian dye.  
>
> Health-giving grass gave sleep,  
> A flowing stream gave drink,  
> And a very tall pine gave shade.

Thus: “By toil and sweat you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3), that is, your food; so also, by the toil and sweat [Col. 0251C] of your face, you shall be clothed in your clothing and sheltered beneath your roof.

## Chapter LXXXIII. On the Superfluity and Costliness of Clothing

But consider how far your glory and luxury have departed from the clothing of the first human beings, both in the material, the color, the form, and the arrangement of garments. For the Lord made garments of skin for the first parents to cover their shameful nakedness and disgrace (Gen. 3), though I do not know how these were prepared. Behold the rough and simple material of clothing—from which people have proceeded to the hides of animals, the wool of sheep, and the flax of fields. These are indeed from nature and therefore tolerable. But we would not even stop there: we advanced to birds’ feathers, [Col. 0251D] the excrement of worms, and even to gold embroidery, spinning thread from gold.

From a simple and natural color people came to dark color, though this suits religious life; then to red, reddish, saffron, violet, mixed, and confused colors—so that under the colors of clothing we may strike the eyes of those looking at us and draw them into admiration. Yet nature has given each thing, especially flowers, a color so beautiful by nature that not even “Solomon in all his glory could be clothed” with its like (Matt. 6). But you object that garments of different colors, and skins dyed red and hyacinth-blue, were in the tabernacle (Exod. 25). The answer is:

> The signs have passed away; the things signified remain.

Jerome too, answering this objection, says: Formerly these things were approved, when the blood of animals brought remission of sins. But now the poor [Col. 0252A] Lord has consecrated poverty and simplicity in his Church. Therefore, bishops, tell me: what is gold doing in churches? What is silk doing there? Such things protect against rain better than a poor man does. If you bring these things back into the Temple by Judaizing, bring back sacrificial blood as well.

Would that our times now returned to ancient morals, following the example of the holy Pallid Fathers, who recalled the simplicity of the clothing of the first parents.
