Some covered their shameful nakedness with little mats, others with bark, others with sackcloth, others with haircloth. The Egyptian woman—Mary of Egypt, whose *Life* is found in Surius, vol. II—went beyond them: she lay hidden naked in the wilderness, fleeing the sight of people, whose gaze upon her nakedness would bring her shame.

Further, certain excessively grammatical persons explain this passage—“By the sweat of your [Col. 0252B] face,” etc. (Gen. 3)—wrongly and perversely in this way: “By the toil and sweat of your face,” taking *your* as transferred between the noun *face* and the pronoun *your*: that is, the face of your tenant, your beast of burden, or your servant. Or perhaps [reading uncertain: *caeterum*] “by the toil and sweat” of these persons, not your own.

Tubal-cain is reproved by Jerome on Genesis because, by different strokes of hammers, he discovered the vain and varied consonance of musical sounds: how much more [should] the inventor of superfluities that are more harmful [be reproved]? The preceding syntactical connection is materially uncertain. Hence Boethius (*Consolation of Philosophy*, Book II, metre 5):

> Alas, who was the first  
> To dig up the hidden weights of gold  
> And gems that wished to lie concealed—  
> Precious perils?

[Col. 0252C] And Jerome says: “The practice of that craft which luxury invented for misuse is carried on perilously.” Sin is committed especially in the fashioning of garments. Since nature distinguished man from brute beasts by a notable and honorable mark, what nature denied humanity—namely, a tail—human beings claim for themselves by artifice in tailed clothing, having a tailed mind as well. For:

> You may discern the torments of a hidden mind in a diseased body.  
> (JUVENAL, Satire 9.)

The Apostle rebukes people of this sort (Rom. 1) as “disorderly.” Others have trains and long folds in their clothing, dragging themselves behind them in long garments and falsely increasing their height; though the pagan poet rebukes them, saying:

> Keep far from the country, thin badge of shame,  
> And long border which covers the middle of the feet.  
> (OVID, *Art of Love*, Book I.)

Above all, a trailing and long garment does not suit a Christian: it drags or raises dust behind it, blinding the eyes of those who follow, like Darius and Byrrhus. Hence Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, says in a sermon: “Christian matrons ought not to wear garments reaching below the ankle and trailing behind them, with which they sweep the filth of floors and streets. Know, beloved ladies, that if clothing of this kind were necessary to you, nature would have given you some remedy by which you could cover the ground. But now, since a garment [Col. 0253A] exceeds the size of the body, why should a shoe not do so too, so that a person might drag shoes behind him?” Yet conversely, we make our shoes as tight and close-fitting as possible:

> Let not your wandering foot swim in loose leather.  
> (OVID.)

Some, since they cannot make themselves tailed lower down in their garments, have animal tails sewn on, lest they be entirely without tails. Others wear star-spangled—indeed, lizard-like—garments pierced with holes.

## Chapter LXXXIV. Against the Various Craftsmen of These Vanities

To devise these vanities and superfluities, Christian curiosity employs various craftsmen whom perhaps even idolatry lacks. It is incredible that, if Scipios, Catos, and Laelii had seen such workmen, they would not immediately have driven them away. We must therefore determine which craftsmen [Col. 0253B] are necessary to the Church and which are not; which are to be tolerated in it and which are not.

Farmers are necessary, being, as it were, the foot of the world. Wine-growers also are necessary because of our weakness, though Noah planted the first vineyard (Gen. 9) and was made drunk by the first wine, “in which is luxury” (Eph. 5); and afterward Lot committed incest through drunkenness (Gen. 19). Likewise, furriers, shoemakers, tanners, and simple carpenters are necessary—not Daedalian craftsmen, not makers of costly things; weavers who work simply in materials; dyers too, provided they do not exceed too greatly in expense and perhaps because of the mystery enacted in the Church; painters depicting histories, not frivolities; and makers of musical instruments, so that sadness and weariness may be removed by them, [Col. 0253C] and devotion, not wantonness, may be aroused. For such things are dangerously heard by the wanton.

But goldsmiths, especially those who gild saddles and spurs, or other things without which Christian religion could exist; engravers; makers of perforated garments; makers of dice, especially loaded dice—though I do not mean chessmen, since one may play with these for recreation—these, I say, are not necessary. Unless they had first renounced their craft, I would not impose penance upon them. Pope Alexander [III], in the case of a certain entertainer, neither allowed him to live by his occupation nor forbade it to him altogether.

And since a sword is necessary for a judge, it is permissible for swords to be forged. But does it follow that daggers and missiles piercing double armor may be made as well? Yes. For just as human prudence first rightly invented simple swords against the malice of enemies, so human ingenuity may, against growing and doubled malice, devise and construct two-edged swords and other weapons. But what of the maker of poison? He may be tolerated, provided he gives the Church assurance that he will not cause harm by poison. Yet, once these things have entered customary practice, to rebuke and denounce them is treated with contempt; whereas the Church ought to have resisted them when they first emerged and removed such craftsmen, lest they spread.

The Apostle, rebuking [Col. 0253D] superfluity of clothing and other things, says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 9: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives [Col. 0254A] the prize? So run,” namely, without hindrance and burden, “that you may obtain it. For everyone who competes in the contest abstains from all things” that might impede the prize of the contest, even lawful things.

But if, weighed down and impeded by the number and superfluity of garments, as also of other things, we not only carry them but drag them after us, we become not merely their bearers but also post-horse drivers, charioteers, and pack-animal drivers—though so excellent a prize awaits us if we attain it and vanishes if we fail in this perilous race. To reach the goal, we must be equipped to go through this stadium by prudence, by which we choose what should be done, what should be believed, how one should walk in God’s ways, and in what condition one must be in order to live well.

We must also be girded, to run by temperance against the flowing folds of desire:

> Rash impulse governs all things badly.  
> (STATIUS, *Thebaid*, Book II.)

> Nothing in excess.  
> (TERENCE.)

We must be belted, to serve through justice, which renders to each what is his own. You must have your loins girded for running, that you may, with measured step, carry the Holy Spirit to your neighbor and do to him what you wish to be done to yourself (Tob. 4). We must also be equipped to fight through fortitude against the threefold enemy, because “the life of man upon earth is warfare” [Col. 0254C] (Job 7). Therefore our journey ought to be ready and unencumbered, aided by chariot, running, and leaping. For we ought not merely to be travelers, but Hebrew runners, passers-through—*Dothain* or *Idithun* (Gen. 37)—and leapers like the stag, which assists its running by leaping and springs over every gap and obstacle.

But now the reverse is true. By the superfluity of clothes and other things we block the narrow way, so that we may not find “the way of the commandments,” or, having found it, may not “run” in it (Ps. 118).

## Chapter LXXXV. Against Softness of Clothing

Because this obstacle must be removed from our paths, the Lord in the Gospel rebukes two things in the luxury and superfluity of clothing: softness and pride. He says: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, more than a prophet. But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11).

Softness in clothing is plainly a vice, as Gregory says (*Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 6), since the Lord couples it with the vice of instability, to which pride is joined. Since the body by nature does not need this softness, what is sought in soft clothing except spiritual wickedness—namely pride and pleasure directed toward pride, not necessity? In the use of food the devil strikes us with one hand, namely softness; in the use of clothing, with two hands: softness [Col. 0255A] and pride.

Nevertheless, every religious person is permitted to eat every food according to time and place if necessity requires; but under no necessity, nor at any time, has it been permitted for religious persons to use splendid or superfluous clothing. Yet now those who wear soft garments are in bishops’ and clerics’ houses. If they say that they too are kings, then so indeed were the apostles, who “counted all these things as dung, that they might gain Christ” (Phil. 3).

To softness and pride in clothing a third blameworthy feature may be added: costliness. Hence Bernard:

> *Chisimus* [reading uncertain] climbs up, with the attire of the powerful:  
> marten, and beaver, stripped at no lesser cost,  
> and sable, the robber of the purse.

With these skins and those of other animals we procure artificial beards, so that we may walk about masked, having shaved off our natural ones, for softness, effeminacy, and luxury; though meretricious glitter, theatrical dress, or royal display does not become humility and does not suit a Christian. And the philosopher says: “I am indeed pleased that you pursue this ambitious finery with implacable hatred.”

## Chapter LXXXVI. Against the Superfluity of Buildings

Just as in the superfluity and curiosity of clothing and food the labor of nature is turned into sin, and a thing falls into vice if it lacks art, so too is this true in the superfluity, curiosity, and costliness of buildings. Consider how far people have departed from ancient simplicity [Col. 0255C] in constructing houses. For it is written that Abraham, at the first stage of faith, lived only in huts, not possessing even a foot’s breadth of land. He pitched his tents between Bethel and Ai, as a pilgrim traveler and not a permanent resident or citizen; and upon the summit of his roof—that is, in a hut roofed with straw—he received angelic guests (Gen. 12). Likewise Lot and Noah lived in tents (Gen. 18).

Some of the ancients lived in caves in rocks; others in the bark and hollows of trees. When people saw them emerging from these, some fabulously supposed that they had been born from them. Elisha had not his own lodging but one belonging to another, lent him by a certain widow; in it he had an upper chamber, and in it a table, [Col. 0255D] a bed, and a lampstand (4 Kings 4). Nor, when traveling, did he exchange it for another lodging, now mindful and observant of that evangelical command: “Into whatever city you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain with him; do not depart from there” (Matt. 10).

Again: When
The earth will now produce evil men, and little ones. (JUVENAL, Satire 15.)

And not only in stature, but also in length of life, we have been shortened by manifold excess, and because of our sins; and since even the ends of the ages and the consummation have come upon us, how great is the madness, how great the excess, that we should be so concerned with the bulk, elaboration, and expense of building houses—as though they would never perish! Especially since the ancients, to whom a longer life was granted [Col. 0256A], and who were at the beginning of the world, very far indeed from its end, did not concern themselves with such things. They believed that at the end of the world “the foundations of the earth shall be moved” (Psalm 81), down to its lowest depths—namely, as far down as the works of sins have descended; and the air will be purged as far upward as their works have risen.

Hence a certain cleric of Rheims says: “If these builders believed that the world would have an end, such lofty structures would not be raised to heaven, nor would foundations be laid down to so great an abyss.” In this they resemble the giants building the tower of Babel, striving against the Lord. Therefore let them also fear lest with them they be “scattered from the face of the earth” (Gen. 11), that is, from the Church, and afterward be “confounded” in the fire of Gehenna.

But [Col. 0256B] because of this excess and expense of houses and walls, charity and distribution to the poor are less today. For we provide less adequately for their sustenance because of such superfluous expenses. Likewise Isaiah, chapter 66: “Heaven is my throne, but earth is the footstool of my feet. What is this house that you will build for me? And what is this place of my rest?”

Likewise Jerome (Letter 11 to Ageruchia): “I know,” he says, “that there are peoples—namely the Megarians—who build as though they were always to live, but eat and drink as though they were to die tomorrow, saying: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die’” (Isa. 22).

Likewise: Paul the First Hermit lived in a cave, or underground chamber and subterranean dwelling, fed daily by [Col. 0256C] an angel with half a loaf. Anthony, the father of hermits and archimandrite, having heard of his holiness, visited him and knocked at his door; but Paul thought him a wild beast or a wolf. At last, by divine inspiration, it was revealed to him that it was Anthony, whose name he had previously not known, and he said: “May my lord Anthony be welcome.” And they kissed one another.

When they were about to eat together, an angel brought a whole loaf. Taking it from opposite sides—that is, by pieces and portions facing one another, so that they might both break it—they afterward ate it, after a holy contest beforehand concerning its division and blessing, each wishing to defer the remainder to the other as the greater person. Paul proposed very many questions to Anthony, among which he inserted this one, asking whether [Col. 0256D] idolatry and the obstinacy of the Jews still continued, and whether the Christian religion imitated the practices of the Gentiles in costly buildings, saying: “Do towers and fortifications and palaces, and such lofty and costly buildings, still rise in Rome?” He answered: “Yes.” Then Paul, weeping, lamented this excess still more, complaining that men were given over to such great vanity, when Christians ought mutually to exhort one another, saying: “We have no lasting dwelling here, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13).

Likewise: A certain emperor said to a certain hermit: “Why is your little dwelling so confined and measured to your little body that it neither surpasses nor exceeds it by a single jot?” He replied: “This is enough for a man who is going to die: that he may always remember the foulness of his grave, and from the very necessity by which he knows that he will die may believe himself already, as it were, dead. Thus I have anticipated my tomb and, as it were, buried myself beforehand.” And he added: “One springs into heaven better and more safely from a hut than from a palace.”

Likewise the Lord in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8). Behold: Christ’s moderation and humility teach us that we ought to be content with humble dwellings, he who “had nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9), and therefore nowhere to walk about or to spread out his glory and himself. Therefore let us not be like crafty and foul-smelling foxes; let us not be nearer to the devil and hell; let us not display the sign of our being swallowed up with Dathan and Abiram (Num. 16). Let us by no means build [Col. 0257B] in the bowels of the earth down to its lowest depths, nor in the air assigned as a prison to demons until judgment; nor, by building in pride, let us be their neighbors and “companions” of demons “and ostriches” (Job 30). Rather, let us remain earthly upon the earth, knowing that we shall pass from the earth, yet are to become heavenly both in body and soul; especially because it is written: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men” (Psalm 113).

Likewise, one prelate to another: “What is the meaning of this height of your houses? Why the towers? Why the fortifications in them? You will not be more fortified in these against the devil, but nearer to him.”

Likewise: They detest this lust [Col. 0257C] for building—the palaces of princes built from the tears and plunder of the poor. Monastic or ecclesiastical buildings, moreover, are erected from the loans and usuries of the avaricious, from lies of deceits and deceits of lies, of preachers and hirelings. Built from ill-gotten wealth, they often collapse, because:

Filthy spoil has no good outcome.  
(OVID, Elegy 1.)

Likewise: The example of Saint Bernard, weeping because he saw shepherds’ little huts roofed with straw, like the ancient cells of the Cistercians, while those who had then begun to inhabit such cells were living in star-studded and walled palaces. Yet because of this sickness of building, religious themselves, like others, are often punished by the instrument of their offense. For the construction [Col. 0257D] of beautiful and spacious houses is an invitation to proud guests. Even their granges are often turned into castles for their defense; and so that they may not lose them, they often conceal the truth and neglect God’s justice, not daring to utter a word against princes, because they have lost their liberty, of which it is said:

The traveler with empty pockets will sing before the robber.  
(JUVENAL, Satire 10.)

They have lost it for the riches of their granges and fields, allowing dormitories and refectories to be built for them by robbers and moneylenders, as an everlasting sign and memorial of their own avarice. Nor should they permit this even from the personal money of good men; rather, they should exhort them to convert such money instead to the support of the poor and the ransom [Col. 0258A] of captives.

Likewise: Sin is committed even in the building of churches. For although their heads ought, in accordance with the mystery, to be lower than their bodies—because “our head is Christ” (Eph. 4), namely, Christ is humbler than his Church—they are now raised higher. Rebuking this threefold excess, the pagan philosopher says:

For him it was a feast to have conquered hunger, to have driven winter from the high household gods by a roof, and, in the Roman fashion of Quirinus, to have put a toga—a costly garment—over rough limbs.  
(LUCAN, Book 2.)

Likewise the Psalmist: “They shall leave their riches to strangers, and their tombs, their houses, forever” (Psalm 48)—that is, for a long time, namely until the resurrection. Therefore, since you will dwell longer with worms in the grave than with human beings [Col. 0258B] in an earthly house, if one of the two is to be more carefully arranged, raised, and expensively built, that dwelling seems more deserving in which you must remain longer—though it is evident that it is a fault for that one to be built and adorned excessively. Hence the poet:

He who has no urn is covered by the sky.  
(LUCAN, Book 7.)

The loss of a tomb is easy.  
(VIRGIL, *Aeneid* 2.646.)

Nature buries those who are abandoned.  
(MAECENAS, Book 15.)

And Gregory (*Morals*, ch. 37): “Costly and adorned tombs are for the dead an increase of punishment rather than a remedy.” A man’s first tomb is his own body. Hence: “Those sleeping [Col. 0258C] in the tombs” (Psalm 87). The second is an earthly dwelling, upon the earth or in the earth. The third will be purgatorial fire. The fourth is paradise or hell.

Do not be more concerned with the construction and adornment of an earthly house than of your own body, which is covered with little and in which you will also rise again, “when this mortal shall put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15). Do not imitate Daedalus in skill in building a house, the giants in height (Gen. 11), or Solomon in expense (3 Kings 6). But why not Solomon in wisdom? Because such things are no longer approved as they once were, when, namely, the blood of beasts was the redemption of sins.

Likewise Psalm 73: “Look upon your covenant, because the dark places of the earth have been filled with houses of iniquity,” built from plunder, lies, thefts, and resources that ought to have been distributed to the poor.

Likewise Jerome, on the death of Saint Paula (Letter to Eustochium, *On the Death of Paula*): “She was unwilling,” he says, “to pour out money upon stones which are to pass away with earth and the world, but upon living stones, which move over the earth.” Of these, in the Apocalypse, the city of the great king is built.

Likewise, the same author, Letter 30 (ch. 21): “In what words can I set before you the Savior’s cave and that manger in which the little child wailed? They ought to be honored by silence rather than by mean speech. Yet where about them are broad porticoes? Where gilded ceilings? Where houses clad by the sufferings of the wretched and the labor of the condemned? Where basilicas built [Col. 0259A] after the pattern of private palaces, so that the vile little body of a human being may walk about more splendidly, and, as though anything could be more adorned than the world, may prefer to look upon its roofs rather than heaven? At Bethlehem” (Matt. 2), “in a small opening in the earth, the Creator of the heavens was born. Here he was seen by shepherds, here pointed out by a star, here worshiped by the Magi” (Luke 2).

Likewise Jeremiah, chapter 22: “Woe to him who builds his house in injustice, and his upper rooms not in judgment; who oppresses his friend for nothing and does not render him his wage; who says: ‘I shall build myself a broad house and spacious upper chambers,’ who opens windows for himself, makes cedar ceilings, and paints with red pigment. Whose eyes and heart are set upon avarice and slander and the accomplishing of an evil work.”

Likewise the philosopher, [Col. 0259B] having spoken of those who enlarge their estates and fields, adds: “Now I speak to you, whose luxury spreads out as spaciously as those men’s avarice. To you I say this: How long until there is no lake over which the summits of your villas do not hang? No river whose banks our buildings do not fringe? Wherever veins of hot water gush forth, there new resorts of luxury will be raised. Wherever the shore bends into some bay, you immediately lay foundations, not content with the ground unless you have made it by hand. Though you have built much, though vast things, you are nevertheless each but one body, and a small one. What use are many sleeping chambers? You lie in one. Nothing is yours wherever you are not.”

Likewise the poet:

[Col. 0259C] No place in the world outshines lovely Baiae.  
If a rich man has pronounced that a lake or sea feels the desire  
Of its hurrying master, and if corrupt desire  
Has made him a lodging there, tomorrow, workmen,  
You will carry your tools to Teanum.  
(HORACE, Book 1, Epistle 1.)

Likewise Juvenal (Satire 14):

Centronius was a builder; he diminished his estate,  
Broke his wealth, though no small measure of the remaining  
Portion was left. Yet his mad son ruined it all  
While he raised new villas with finer marble.

Likewise Jerome (Letter to Heliodorus, *On the Praise of the Solitary Life*): “It befits a penitent, and especially one living in enclosure, to dwell—not, I say, in spacious houses, but in dwellings, that is, in haircloth shelters or ruined walls: places which are not houses, but have the likeness and trace [Col. 0259D] of houses. Thus, being confined, he may gather himself together and not extend himself toward forbidden things, mindful of the virginal womb in which the Lord was enclosed and confined; then of his being placed in a little manger, upon a cross, and afterward in a tomb.” Hence David: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like a night-owl in a dwelling” (Psalm 101), or among ruined walls.

Likewise Isaiah, chapter 5; Leviticus 26; Habakkuk 2; likewise Isaiah 26, and Daniel, chapter 8.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Against the prodigal, who acquire badly and spend worse.

Very many people, as they are prodigal, vigilant, and drunken in building and superfluous expenditures, are likewise most avaricious, lethargic, sleepy, and lazy in supplying pious causes and daily necessities [Col. 0260A]. Of such people the poet says:

He restricts the bellies of his slaves by an unjust measure,  
Though hungry himself; for he can never endure  
To consume moldy scraps of blue-green bread.  
(JUVENAL, Satire 14.)

While disputing about goat’s wool and trifles, he scolds his slaves:

Let him neither alleviate poverty nor exalt a kinsman.  
(CATO, 15.)

But the Lord condemns the vice of prodigality in Luke, setting forth the parable of the prodigal son, who by living luxuriously consumed his father’s goods. When these had been consumed, in a far country he fed swine, and himself fed upon the swine’s husks. In him [Col. 0260B] is condemned the prodigality of temporal wealth, which he consumed for his temporal desire, like Esau selling his birthright and his father’s blessing for red lentils (Gen. 25). So too does any believer who gives the priceless price—namely Christ—and the wonderful treasure hidden “in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4), namely the soul made “in the image of God” (Gen. 1), in exchange for smoke, sleep, and shadow.

In him is also condemned the prodigality of nature and the prodigality of grace. For he went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, who corrupted in him what was natural by stripping him of gratuitous gifts (Luke 10). Such persons too are denoted by the woman with the hemorrhage, who, having spent nearly all her goods on physicians, could not be cured until she came [Col. 0260C] to the true physician (Matt. 9).

Now people become prodigal for several reasons. Some because of a passion for building, and other excesses and drunkennesses. Others because of a passion for sexual intercourse: “and all their goods are borne to Cyane,” who with one little tear swallows up the lustful man, disdaining his delicate foods while at home she greedily consumes black, moldy bread with yesterday’s broth. And Juvenal:

What goods he has given to the stables, and he lacks every  
Inheritance of his ancestors.

Others through gluttony. Hence Horace (Book 1, Epistle 15):

After boldly taking possession of his maternal and paternal goods,  
Urbanus began to be regarded as  
A wandering buffoon, not one who held a fixed stall;  
Hungry, one who could not distinguish citizen from enemy,  
[Col. 0260D] Savage in inventing any reproaches against anyone,  
A ruin, tempest, and abyss of the market.

Others through ambition for rank or fame:

So much greater is the thirst for fame than  
For virtue. For who embraces virtue itself  
If you remove its rewards? Yet once the glory  
Of a few, and desire for praise and title, overwhelmed their country.  
What then is fame’s outcome?  
That you may please boys and become a school declamation.

Others, in order to excuse their own misery and sin, give even to actors and the unworthy, so that it may be said of them: “They deny nothing that is demanded of them, but give nothing unless it is demanded.” Therefore they give nothing to a good and honorable man. Of them it is also said: “It is remarkable where and from whom they receive what they spend.” Though it would be truer to say: “It is remarkable where and upon what they spend [Col. 0261A] what they receive—and what they seize from so many people.” For they receive badly and spend worse what they would better preserve in order to repay those from whom they seized it.

Others do so through negligence or ignorance: those who become squanderers of their own goods and petitioners for others’ goods. For prodigality is generally accompanied by covetousness, avarice, and plunder. Hence the poet:

Whatever deep things  
Avarice has drawn forth, worse luxury pours back out.  
(CLAUDIAN, *On the Gildonic War*.)

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On holy prodigality.

There is, however, a certain holy prodigality by which someone gives his life for Christ. Hence: “Paul, lavish with his great soul.” Therefore give not as a prodigal [Col. 0261B] gives, and desire whatever is necessary according to your means, but nothing beyond your means. Hence Tobit (ch. 4): “When you have little, give little.”

It is right for each person to measure himself by his own measure and rule.  
(HORACE, Book 1, Epistle 7.)

The measure of one’s mouth  
Must be known and considered in matters  
Both greatest and least, even when a fish is bought;  
Do not desire a mullet when you have only a goby  
In your purse.  
(JUVENAL, Satire 11.)

Do not become like those who keep for themselves merely the strainer of milk, retaining only the filth of sins while the money runs down to others. Do not seize goods in order to feed many bellies when you have only one belly, and that, according to nature, content with little.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. Against those who avidly immerse themselves in temporal things.

[Col. 0261C]

Rebuking also those who are prodigal—whether in buildings, clothing, foodstuffs, or any superfluous expenses—and especially those who immerse themselves in temporal concerns and in curious, vain, and unnecessary learning, the Prophet says: “The wicked walk in a circle; according to your height you have multiplied the sons of men” (Psalm 11), not the sons of demons. And again, invoking judgment upon them, he adds: “My God, make them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind” (Psalm 82): that they may be light and inconstant, like a reed shaken by every wind of doctrine.

They resemble the children of Israel who offended God and therefore spent forty days “on a journey of three days, [Col. 0261D] around Mount Seir” (Exod. 3), and did not enter the land of promise, though their children did (Deut. 2). So too these people, driven by the gadfly of temporal concerns, do not rest. Dizzy and epileptic, they “walk in a circle with the wicked” (Psalm 11), from vanity to vanity, not heeding that only “one thing is to be asked of the Lord” (Psalm 26) and sought; that “there is none who does good,” until one comes “to one” (Psalm 13); that for one traveling on the road something must be an end, whereas error is boundless.

They also resemble the devil, “who goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 2). These are the lunatics and the frenzied brought to the Lord for healing (Matt. 17), who now fall into the water of lust, now into the fire of anger, covetousness, and other [Col. 0262A] crimes, and do not direct their course toward God. They move in a circular orbit, from vanity to vanity, concerned with superfluous and unnecessary things, not content with the limits of nature or grace; and thus they do not arrive at the eighth beatitude.

Of these Solomon speaks thus in Proverbs, chapter 20 (according to the Septuagint): “A wise king winnows the wicked, and brings upon them the wheel of evils”; they “are always learning and never arriving at the perfection of knowledge” (2 Tim. 3), always laboring and working in vain, never resting, because “they do not walk by the path of life, but their steps wander and are unsearchable” (Prov. 5).

Likewise Isaiah, chapter 19: “The Lord has mingled”—that is, permitted—“in the midst of Egypt a spirit of dizziness, and they have caused Egypt to err in all its work, as a drunken man staggers and vomits. And there shall be no work for Egypt, which head and tail, bending and restraining, may do.” Likewise the same author, chapter 57: “But the wicked are like a boiling sea, which cannot rest,” etc.

Likewise David (Psalm 77): “And he struck them in their hind parts; he gave them everlasting reproach,” as to the Philistines (1 Kings 5). For while they “embrace dung instead of saffron” (Lam. 4), and set aside the ark—that is, the faith and Church of Christ—for temporal things, serving only outwardly and loving the mice that boil up from the earth—that is, cares and anxieties about temporal affairs—these gnaw at their backsides; because they either corrupt or consume their inward parts and interior goods. These people have God’s covenant, not in order to live [Col. 0262C] according to it, but in order that they may cleverly cloak their vanities with it. Setting it beside Dagon—observing it only outwardly, for temporal goods as for eternal ones—they fall with Dagon (1 Kings 5), with their idols and various vanities, their heads cut off. “But the word of the Lord remains forever” (Psalm 32).

Moses compares these foul persons to foul things. He condemned these temporal goods as dung in the gold of the calf, melted down into powder (Exod. 32), and, having given it to those who thirsted for and worshiped it to drink, as the most unclean filth of dung and the vapor of urine.

As though he said to them: “You thirst for dung: you shall drink dung. You thirst for gold: you shall drink gold.”

They also resemble “Lot’s wife, who departed from Sodom” (Gen. 19), and from the burning desire for earthly things, then “looked back” through worldly desire, “and was turned into a pillar of salt.” They are likewise compared to those “who put their hand to the plow but look back: they are not fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). These people resemble those who seize the Lord but cannot bear his majesty and fall backward upon their faces: impregnated and fattened with the dung of temporal things, they are unwilling to expel it for necessary uses, by which the earth may be fertilized, just as the Jews would not do so on the Sabbath unless they covered it; “but they rotted like beasts in their dung” (Joel 1). “They perished in Endor,” that is, in the spring of propagation; “they became [Col. 0263A] like the dung of the earth” (Psalm 82). Like hoopoes, they nest in their dung, and therefore are “to be stoned with cow-dung” (Ecclus. 22): in them the dung of temporal things produces the dung of sins, to be removed by the dung of penitential satisfactions.

Likewise David: “You made his soul waste away like a spider,” etc. (Psalm 38). Avidity for temporal things makes men spiders. A spider is a rotten and venomous worm which devours flies so that it may weave useless webs, and by weaving them disembowels itself. So too certain men are spiders, “devouring as bread” (Psalm 13) the small substance of the poor, who are the foot of the world and merely flies; or the substance of moneylenders and powerful men, who are themselves the flies of the chief and greater spiders—those, namely, of their servants [Col. 0263B], enemies, or flattering courtiers—so that they may be punished by the instrument of their offense, because:

There is no law more just  
Than that the makers of death should perish by their own art.  
(OVID, Book 1, *Art of Love*.)

“Woe to you who plunder, for you shall be plundered” (Isa. 33). Woe to you who squeeze dry, for you shall be squeezed dry—often beyond what you have squeezed from others.

These are Pharaoh’s horses, which are drowned in the sea with their rider (Exod. 14). To such persons the devil and the world say, “Bend down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51). This has resulted in there being scarcely anyone today who does not beg, except a moneylender or one supported by fixed wages and revenues.

Such persons resemble Amalek, that is, those who lick the earth. They not only lick and eat earthly things but, like an ox, lick them up by the roots, devouring and seizing the little substances of the poor. For this reason, when tested by Gideon (Judg. 7), they are excluded from his company, lest they be in battle with him as he fights against the Midianites and demons.

## CHAPTER XC. On those punished by the instrument of their offense.

It is frequent that evil people are punished by the instrument of their offense: punished in that by which they unjustly punish their neighbor, and struck in that by which they offend God. Hence the Psalm: “He opened and dug [Col. 0263D] a pit, and fell into the hole that he made; his sorrow shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his own crown” (Psalm 7). Hence Augustine, on this passage of the Psalm: “The deceiver is first and more grievously harmed by the loss of innocence than his neighbor by the loss of money.”

Likewise Psalm 9: “In this snare which they hid, their foot has been caught; the Lord shall be known as one executing judgments; the sinner is caught in the works of his own hands.” Hence Augustine: “Each person’s own iniquity is his punishment and gallows.” Likewise Psalm 56: “They dug a pit before my face, and fell into it.” And likewise: “Let the snare which he does not know come upon him, and let the trap seize him; and let him fall into that very snare” (Psalm 34). And likewise: “Let their sword enter [Col. 0264A] into their own hearts, and let their bows be broken” (Psalm 36).

Hence Augustine: “He who wishes to harm his neighbor is like one who attempts to strike another with a sword by which he first pierces himself.” Likewise Proverbs, chapter 26: “He who digs a pit shall fall into it; and upon him who rolls a stone it shall return.” Hence Ecclesiasticus, chapter 27: “He who throws a stone on high, it shall fall upon his head; and a treacherous blow will divide the wounds of the treacherous. He who digs a pit shall fall into it; he who sets a stone for his neighbor shall stumble over it; he who lays a snare for another shall perish in it. An evil plan shall roll back upon its maker, and he shall not know whence it comes upon him.” Likewise, according to the saying of Wisdom: “Every deceit, turned back upon itself, is shattered.”

Likewise the Lord: “What a man has sown, this also [Col. 0264B] shall he reap” (Gal. 6); and, “with whatever measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke 6). Likewise, chapter 13 of Luke: “The men building a tower at Siloam were crushed by it.” And Augustine (Saint Severian, in the sermon *On the Innocents*): “Do not seize your neighbor’s goods, for the bait is taken and the soul is lost.”

Likewise through examples. Goliath was killed by the sword with which he thought to kill David (1 Kings 17). Haman was hanged on the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai, whom Mordecai succeeded in the fullness of authority and possession of riches (Esther 7). Saul was killed by the sword by which he had spared the Amalekites against the Lord’s command, teaching that the king of Egypt—who, for the irrigation of land parched by drought, had sacrificed a foreigner for a foreigner—was himself first sacrificed (1 [Col. 0264C] Kings 31).

A certain courtier also, who taught the king of Sicily a new kind of torture by which the accused might be tortured, was the first to suffer the penalty of his invention (Perillus). Hence:

King Phalaris roasted the limbs of violent Perillus in the bull;  
Unhappy inventor, he inaugurated his own work.  
Each was just: for there is no law more equitable  
Than that the makers of death should perish by their own art.  
(OVID, *Art of Love*, Book 1.)

Likewise according to the philosopher (SENECA, Letter 83): “All human pleasures are transformed into individual torments.” Drunkenness makes a man stupid and mad; gluttony makes him lustful and lazy. And why say more? Each dish has produced its own disease. [Col. 0264D] Hence today we suffer from every kind of disease because we live rightly in no way. You may now count as many dishes as cooks.

Thus those who go about resemble him who said: “I have gone around the earth and walked through it” (Job 1). They are “like the birds of heaven and fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (Psalm 8). Opposed to this evil circuit is the righteous circuit of which it is said: “I went around and sacrificed in his tabernacle” (Psalm 26). This is the proper order: that only after a manifold good circuit should one sacrifice an offering, or receive what has been sacrificed.

Therefore we ought to go around all created things, because all cry out: “God made us, that he may be praised in us.” Hence they are invited to his praise, almost in the morning synaxis—that is, at the end of Matins—in that [Col. 0265A] Psalm, “Bless,” etc. We must also survey the benefits of our creation, because “we were created in the image and likeness of God” (Gen. 1); likewise the benefits of our re-creation, the benefits of the Church’s sacraments, the commandments of necessity: “For then I shall not be confounded, when I have considered all your commandments” (Psalm 118). Also the counsels of perfection; likewise that saying of the Apostle, as though a threefold cord: “Soberly, justly, and piously” (Titus 2); the examples of the saints; the rewards of eternal recompense; the punishments of eternal damnation; every category of sins and every kind within those categories; likewise the circumstances of individual sins which aggravate them; and every period and state of our life. Hence: “I shall call to mind all my years [Col. 0265B] in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38).

## CHAPTER XCI. On the manifold face of man.

Such surveying, especially of the benefits of our creation and re-creation, invites us to the love of God.

For, as Pope Leo testifies (Sermon 2, *On the Resurrection*): “Man would have been great if he had remained in that state in which the Lord made him; he is greater if he remains in that state in which the Lord remade him.” For God made him in his image in the face of nature, and in his likeness in the face of grace.

Now man’s face is manifold: first, the face of outward nature, by which in some manner man is also made like God. Hence:

[Col. 0265C] While the other animals look downward upon the earth,  
He gave man an uplifted face and commanded him to behold heaven  
And to raise his countenance, standing erect, toward the stars.  
(OVID, *Metamorphoses* 1.)

Thus Saint Martin too, with eyes and hands always turned toward heaven, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0265D] In his Life by Sulpicius Severus.]

Paul the First Hermit [Note: [Col. 0265] St. Jerome, in the Life of the same Paul; St. Augustine, on the same, in a sermon.] was found by Anthony standing erect and, as it were, dead in prayer. Vincent, under torture, always gazed toward heaven with uplifted eyes.

This face and erectness of nature is especially disfigured by fornication. “For he who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6), because he defiles it and makes the soul the handmaid of the body, so that during that act it is not permitted to think or feel anything else. Thus he is absorbed, so that the face of a human being is as though turned into the face of quadrupeds. Hence the lustful person is compared either to a sow or a pig; or, “he who fornicates sins against his own body,” because, contrary to the beauty and erectness of his body, he bends it down to the mud.

By the face of inward nature too, man is made like God: through natural love, gentleness, kindness, sociability, and the like. There is also the face of grace, by which one is especially made like God, having the face of Christ going to Jerusalem. This consists in virtues, which are all one face in the root of charity, but many faces in the manifestation and a certain aptitude of works. For Job excelled in patience, David in humility, Moses in gentleness, Joseph in [Col. 0266A] chastity, with respect to outward works. Hence too the Church consists of persons with many faces, “surrounded with variety” (Psalm 44). These may say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given gladness in my heart” (Psalm 4).

This face also consists in works and in fulfilling his commandments. Its signs are these: “He who is of God hears the words of God” (John 8); “If anyone loves me, he keeps my commandments” (John 14), because the proof of love is the performance of a work. “For by their fruits you shall know them” (GREGORY, Homily 30 on the Gospel, Matt. 7). And the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5).

This face consists also in the counsels fulfilled by men in bonds and enclosure; but clerics—soldiers in dress, actors in speech, prostitutes in deed and gesture, secular persons in their occupation with temporal concerns—in which of these faces do they follow God, or in what habit will they rise again, who live in none? They do indeed preserve the tonsure, but for glory or gain, and some make it wider than others; they often assume and maintain this clerical liberty for the defense and preservation of temporal possessions. Against them the Apostle says: “Only do not give your liberty as an occasion for the flesh” (ibid.).

There is also a manifold face of sin; nevertheless, “God shall reduce their image to nothing” (Psalm 72). There is also the face of glory that shall be given us [Col. 0266C], when “this mortal shall put on immortality, and this corruptible shall put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15), when “your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm 102). But the face of sin corrupts the face of nature, destroys the face of grace, and takes away the face of glory.

## CHAPTER XCII. In praise of faith.

Faith begins the face of grace and virtue. Hence Prudentius:

First to enter the field under the doubtful lot of battle,  
Faith goes forth to fight.

For just as some valiant soldier among the others first makes assaults upon the assembled enemy, so faith first desires to storm the fortress of vices. For three principal reasons faith has primacy and leadership [Col. 0266D] among the other virtues: first, because it is the mother and begetter of all the others. “For Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac Jacob” (Matt. 1): that is, faith begets hope, and hope charity. Although all are mingled and possessed together in the disposition of a movement, the movement of faith nevertheless precedes the movement of the others.

For because I believe, I hope, I love, I suffer for Christ, I suffer with my neighbour, and so forth. Charity too is called the mother of the virtues, but in the sense of nurture and formation. Faith, therefore, is their first mother and origin; charity is their second mother and, as it were, their nurse. Faith also holds primacy because, with a certain devout blindness and boldness, audacious and unrestrained, it penetrates where intellect does not reach [Col. 0267A]. For it believes God to be three and one; it penetrates the heavens; it believes that the Lord Jesus is received and eaten under the cloud of bread. It does not understand these things, but only believes them, here stripping off all human reason, which proceeds from causes. “For faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof” (Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, hom. 26). Yet in some matters it both believes and to some extent understands; in all articles it seeks words that are faithful and sound rather than courtly and pleasing, or philosophical.

Hence Augustine says: “I would rather be uncouth than unbelieving; I would rather be an uncultivated Catholic with Jerome than a courtly heretic with Sabellius.” Faith has no underlying basis, no nature from which it derives its origin, except grace alone [Col. 0267B]. For it comes from God alone; the other virtues in some way derive their origin from nature. Natural love precedes gratuitous love, and similarly with the rest. Thus they possess an underlying support which faith does not; and therefore it is first among them. It also holds primacy because, without the other virtues, even an untrained person works miracles. Hence: “Have we not healed the sick in your name and cast out demons?” (Matt. VII). And Gregory says in the *Dialogues* (III.7): “I found an empty vessel,” empty, that is, of other virtues, “but well sealed,” because it bore the mark of a slight faith. And in the Apostle, First Corinthians, chapter XIII: “Though I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” [Col. 0267C]. For evil persons often perform such things.

Because of the primacy and dignity of faith, the Apostle, like a wise architect, placing it in the foundation of the spiritual building, says in commendation of it in First Corinthians, chapter III: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus”: that is, faith concerning Christ Jesus. Likewise, Romans, chapter III: “But the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe in him.” And in chapter III: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Likewise, Ephesians VI: “Stand, having your loins girded with truth, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness,” and in all undertakings “taking the shield of faith, by which you may be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked one.”

Hence faith is also compared to the serpent’s head [Col. 0267D], which it conceals and protects while exposing the rest of its body to wounds. So long as its head is unharmed, it is not killed; similarly, neither is one who preserves faith. Even if he falls in other things, yet, faith having been steadfastly preserved, he will revive. Hence the Lord: “Be prudent as serpents” (Matt. X). And the Apostle in the Epistle to the Colossians: “But now Christ has reconciled you in the body of his flesh through death: present yourselves holy and without blemish and blameless before God, provided that you remain founded, firm, and steadfast in faith, and unmoved from the hope of the Gospel” (Col. I). Likewise Habakkuk II: “My righteous one shall live by faith.” And Peter, First Epistle, chapter V: “The devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith.” Likewise [Col. 0268A], First John, chapter V: “Everything born of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that overcomes the world, our faith.” Likewise the Apostle: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI). And Luke in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter XV): “Purifying their hearts by faith.” And the Lord in the Gospel: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark IX).

Again: “If you have faith as large as a mustard seed, you shall say to the mulberry tree, ‘Be transplanted,’ and it shall be transplanted; you shall say to the mountain, ‘Be moved into the sea,’ and it shall be moved” (Matt. XVII). Christ says to the two blind men: “According to your faith be it done to you,” and immediately their eyes were opened (Matt. IX). And he says to the centurion: “Go, and as you have believed, so let it be done for you.” And his servant was healed in that hour (Matt. VIII). Augustine (*Sermon 74, On Time* [Col. 0268B]): How great is one’s own faith if another’s faith is so great that it merits bodily health and the first grace for someone else? And Elizabeth says to the Blessed Virgin: “Blessed are you who believed, because all things spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled in you” (Luke I). For faith bore the Saviour. Because Zacharias did not believe the angel, he “lost the measures of ready speech,” etc.

Likewise the Apostle, Hebrews chapter XI: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.” It is the *hypostasis* and foundation of all virtues, of all good things; indeed, everything contained in this chapter commends faith. An example is that of the hermit who had so highly commended abstinence in preaching that he urged people to fast for two and three days. For this reason, when the brothers took refreshment, they did not invite him. Having fasted until evening, he said to them: “Why did I not take refreshment with you?” They replied: “Lest you do one thing and preach another.” He said to them: “I preached as a fool and without discernment.” They replied: “Then moderate your word, so that both you and others may be able to bear it.” One man said to another: “You are like someone coming from hell.” The other replied: “And you are like someone going to hell—which is worse.”

## Chapter XCIII. On the Defect of Faith

No virtue today suffers such a great deficiency as faith. Hence in Psalm IX: “Why has the wicked provoked God? For he has said in his heart: ‘God will not require it’”—that is, in order to punish. And in the same Psalm: “For he has said in his heart [Col. 0268D]: ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so that he will never see.’” In opposition to him the Lord answers: “Do you wickedly suppose that I shall be like you?” (Ps. XLIX)—supposing evil to please me, since you do not believe me an avenger, while you hope for and promise yourself impunity? It is not so. For in the future “I shall rebuke you,” though until now I have been silent, awaiting your repentance; and in rebuking you, “I shall set you before your own face”: that is, I shall show you to yourself in the book of conscience. You will displease both me and yourself, because now you do not wish to displease yourself so that you may please me.

Likewise Jerome in Origen: If you thought a loss of temporal goods or bodily punishment before a judge threatened you, with what concern and vigilance would you seek out advocates, appease the judge, and win his favour through services and gifts [Col. 0269A], making him favourable to you in a temporal case? But now, when the case of your soul is to be conducted, you are sluggish, though you must “render an account even for an idle word” (Matt. XII), before the eyes of the Judge who sees all things. Why is this? Listen: because you fear and believe this; but you neither fear nor believe the judgment of the highest Judge. Or if you suffered bodily illness, with what care would you summon physicians? But now, when you suffer from a disease of the soul, why do you not run with equal concern to a confessor, to physicians of the soul? Why do you put faith in the words of a physician and not in Christ’s words? Listen: because you diligently believe a liar who is useless, but do not believe Christ, who is true and beneficial; he threatens you, if you do not obey him, not merely with the loss of glory but with the flame of Gehenna. And he says:

> Ah, with how anxious a labour does each person  
> Hasten to the physician out of love for the flesh,  
> While slow healing follows, without complaint,  
> The soul’s disease when it has gone forth.  
> —Hildebert of Le Mans, *On the Fire*

And Jerome (*Letter to Heliodorus, On Praise of the Solitary Life*): Faith does not fear famine: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI). And Habakkuk, chapter II: “Behold, the unbeliever’s soul shall not be upright in himself” (Prov. XX). And Isaiah, chapter XXI: “He who is unbelieving acts unfaithfully.” And Solomon: “Many merciful men are found, but who shall find a faithful man?” And Ecclesiasticus, chapter II: “Woe to the faint-hearted who do not believe God; therefore they shall not be protected [Col. 0269C] by him. Those who fear the Lord will not distrust his word.” Likewise James, chapter II: “What shall it profit, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but has no works?” etc.

Not only the lack of faith, but its smallness, must be feared. Hence the Lord says to Peter: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. XIV). And to the Apostles, who said, “Why could we not cast him out?” he replied: “Because of your unbelief. Amen, I say to you: if you have faith like a mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain, ‘Pass over,’ and it shall pass over; and nothing shall be impossible to you” (Matt. XVII). Likewise Augustine (*On Lying*, chapter 20): Faith means that what is said comes to pass; therefore, where what is said does not come to pass, there is no faith. But why? “Because he does not set God before his sight” (Ps. LIII); “There is no fear of God before his eyes” [Col. 0269D] (Ps. XIII). For they are like Antichrist, saying with him in their heart: “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so that he will never see” (Ps. IX). They are also like Epicurus, saying with him:

> You may believe that God does not care for mortal affairs.

They are also like the Jews who disbelieved the Lord’s words and said in Isaiah, chapter XXII: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” To them God says: “Because you gathered the waters of the lower pool, and counted the houses of Jerusalem and pulled them down to fortify the wall, and did not look to him who made the water of the pool, nor saw its maker from afar—if this iniquity is forgiven you, you shall die, says the Lord.” Likewise chapter XXIX: “Woe to you who are deep of heart [Col. 0270A], that you may hide counsel from the Lord, whose works are in darkness, and who say: ‘Who sees us, and who knows us?’” etc. Likewise chapter XXIV: “‘My secret,’ concerning eternal glory and the inestimable reward, ‘is mine,’ always before my eyes. ‘My secret,’ concerning the fire of Gehenna and unending punishment, ‘is mine,’ because it belongs to none but a few. Hence: ‘Woe is me,’ because others do not possess this secret of faith, ‘but transgressors have transgressed, and have transgressed by the transgression of transgressors.’”

Likewise Psalm XCIII: “And they said: ‘The Lord shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob understand.’” Rebuking them, the Holy Spirit immediately adds through the Prophet: “Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, at last become wise. Shall he who planted the ear not hear?” etc. Likewise Psalm XXIII: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain”—that is, by not believing that inestimable glory is prepared for the righteous and unending punishment for the wicked.

Likewise, it is natural to Adam’s children to seek advantages by desiring them and to avoid disadvantages. Indeed, in seeking a more certain and greater benefit, and avoiding a more certain and greater harm, they become more prudent and more concerned. But nothing is more certain than faith, nor is there any greater benefit than eternal glory or greater harm than eternal punishment. Therefore, whoever is more prudent and vigilant in gaining a lesser advantage—such as a temporal good—or avoiding a temporal harm, has something more certain than faith [Col. 0270C]; faith has become to him something than which nothing is more certain, since according to his own opinion he is more energetic and attentive regarding what is more certain and greater. Such people resemble demons, in whom there is no faith; or, if there is faith, it is dead. Like demons, who believe and tremble, they possess faith in apprehension, but not in devotion; and consequently their faith is dead. It is not faith but pretence, dream, nourishment, and habit. Such people “made nothing of the desirable land” (Ps. CV).

Likewise, the disciples say to the Lord concerning the smallness of their faith: “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII). Likewise the Apostle: “They profess that they know God in words, but deny him in deeds” (Tit. I); they blaspheme, and “the truth of God is not in them” (I John VIII [an erroneous citation as printed]). For those who deny by their actions sin more than those who deny in heart or mouth, just as one sins more by deed than by thought or speech. “To know, or to understand, you is consummate understanding” (Wis. XV and VI). But just as knowing God is consummate understanding, so denying God is consummate folly; as: “The fool has said in his heart”—in mouth and deed—“There is no God.” Therefore such persons “have become corrupt and abominable in their pursuits,” etc. But the Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men to see whether there was one who understood or sought God. “Destruction and unhappiness are in their ways”; and this is because “they have not known the way of peace” (Pss. LII, XIII).

Likewise, First John, chapter II: “He who says that he knows God [Col. 0271A] and does not keep his commandments is a liar.” Likewise the third Epistle: “He who does good is from God; but he who does evil does not see God.” Likewise the Lord in John’s Gospel, chapter V: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that is from God alone?” Augustine: Because pride blinds them, and the ambition for praise, which desires to be judged to possess what it does not possess and to exalt itself above others. Humility alone hates this; it seeks the glory of God alone and desires to please him alone. Likewise in the same place: “He who believes in me shall also do the works that I do”—namely, works of mercy.

Hence in the Catholic Epistle: “He who believes in God ought to walk as he walked” (I John II) [Col. 0271B], who said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart,” etc.; “and he shall do greater works than these” (Matt. XI)—miracles, when necessary and when the Lord sees that it is expedient. Likewise in Luke, chapter VIII: “Those upon the rock are those who, when they have heard, receive the word with joy; and these have no roots of charity, because they believe for a time and in the time of temptation fall away”—from faith. In the same chapter, when a storm arose at sea and the Lord was sleeping, “the disciples came and awakened him, saying: ‘Master, we are perishing.’ He said to them: ‘Where is your faith?’” And in James, chapter I: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask in faith, doubting nothing. But he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, moved and tossed by the wind. Let not such a person receive anything from the Lord.”

For such a person says with the philosopher:

> Fear first made gods in the world.  
> —Petronius, fragment; Statius, *Thebaid* III.361

And likewise:

> Virtue is my divinity and my sword.  
> —Same author

Likewise Romans, chapter IV: “He did not waver through unbelief at God’s promise,” etc. In the same Epistle, chapter XVI: “Do you have faith? Keep it to yourself before God,” etc. Faith is great in three respects: in literary and subtle comprehension, which often edifies and often puffs up; in certainty, because nothing is more certain than faith; and in devotion, which is the seasoning of charity. For sure and devout faith exists in everyone who fears God [Col. 0271D].

## Chapter XCIV. On Hope

Once the foundation of the spiritual building, namely faith, has been laid, its raising follows—that is, hope. For it is raised through hope, and is completed and perfected through charity and the other virtues. And rightly so. For hope, like the other virtues, is a daughter of faith. What we believe, we hope; and because we hope, we love, and through loving we merit in what measure and manner we do so. Hence David: “Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, according as we have hoped in you” (Ps. XXXII).

And the Apostle, commending hope together with faith and charity, says in Romans, chapter V: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God the Father through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access by faith into this grace in which we stand and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God; and not only do we glory” [Col. 0272A] in the hope of glory, “but also in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience, patience testing, and testing hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts.” Rather, it strengthens and confirms, like the anchor of faith.

Hope is a certain assurance proceeding from the grace and merits of each individual. Therefore in evil persons hope is not a virtue; yet they are not children of distrust or despair, for no one on the way is to be despaired of, though neither should much be hoped for in such persons. They are not children of hope, but occupy a kind of middle state, so long as they do not depart from devout tears and are resolved not to sin. Hence David: “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. IV)—threefold, namely, “living soberly, righteously, and piously, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” (Tit. II), etc.—and thus “hope in the Lord”; otherwise, you presume. And again: “Hope in the Lord and do good” (Ps. XXXVI).

From hope and faith arise—or they are identical with hope—a certain holy expectation in adversities and confidence in what is to be done, which are no small consolations in every tribulation. Hence David: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord” (Ps. XXXIX), so as to receive the double robe. Isaiah (chapter XXVIII): “Wait; wait again” [Col. 0272C]. And again David: “I waited for him who saved me from faintness of spirit and the storm” (Ps. LIV), because:

> Hope causes the shipwrecked man to stand amid the waters.

And David: “And now, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?” (Ps. XXXVIII), etc. And again: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord, for I shall yet confess him” (Ps. XLI), etc. And likewise: “I shall act confidently in him and shall not fear” (Ps. XI). “It is good to wait in silence for the salvation of God” (Lam. III).

And the Apostle, Romans, chapter VIII: “The expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God, because it too shall be freed from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that every creature groans and is in labour until now. And not only it”—still unbelieving—“but we ourselves also,” the Apostles, “having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as children of God, the redemption of our body. For we have been saved in hope; but hope of a thing seen is not hope. For what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience”—namely, patience in adversity. And elsewhere: “My little children, eternal life is already in you through hope” (I John III).

Likewise Job, chapter XIX: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and I shall again be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. This hope has been laid up in my breast” [Col. 0273A]. And the Apostle: “For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit until that day” (II Tim. I). The defect of hope, however, resembles the defect of faith. For one who does not believe does not hope, and conversely.

## Chapter XCV. On Charity

If a little child is born but not nourished, it languishes and dies. So faith and hope, as also the other virtues, unless nourished and perfected by charity, languish. Hence the Apostle, setting forth the commendation and marks of charity in First Corinthians, chapter XII, says: “I show you a still more excellent way”—that is, charity, which is the greatest gift among the gifts given on the way [Col. 0273B]. For “if I speak with the tongues of men and angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body so that it burns, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII).

How abundant and great its usefulness is, he shows by adding: “Charity is patient” in injuries; “it is kind,” generous to the needy; “charity is not envious”: it does not begrudge another, but loves another’s good as its own; “it is not puffed up” by its own prosperity; “it does not act improperly,” for an evil conscience does not sting it; “it is not ambitious”: it does not wish to be preferred to others; “it does not seek its own interests,” but rather those of another and those of Christ, nor does it demand back what has been taken; “it is not provoked,” being not stirred to anger; “it does not think evil,” by deliberating how to repay evil with evil; “it does not rejoice in another’s iniquity,” but “rejoices together in truth” and justice. “It bears all things” in action for truth; “it believes all things” concerning promises, after the spirit has been tested; “it hopes all things” which truth has promised; “it endures all things,” patiently awaiting promised things amid adversity. “Charity never fails,” because what serves here for meriting well will in the future be our reward; but the other gifts will not be given to us then.

Hence it follows: “But now faith, hope, and charity, these three, remain; but the greatest of these is charity” [Col. 0273D], because “it never fails, it shall never be made void,” as those other things shall. This is that of which the Prophet says: “Of every perfection”—namely, of a completed work, of virtues, and of the sacraments of our redemption—“I have seen an end” (Ps. CXVIII), and its completion, namely charity. For through charity Christ hanging upon the cross said: “It is finished” (John XIX): namely, the charity which he bore toward us fulfilled all that was said of him, even to the passion of death. “No one has greater charity than that a person lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

Most complete was the Father’s love by which “he loved us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I), by which “he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII). And the Apostle, First Timothy, chapter I, says: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith.” Hence Augustine (*Sermon 39, On Time*): Whoever has no leisure to unfold the wrappings of the divine sayings or penetrate all their secrets, let him hold fast charity, upon which the whole Law and the Prophets hang. Have charity, and do whatever you wish: you have fulfilled all things. And again (*On the Praise of Charity*, tractate, vol. IX): This is a fountain in which an alien—that is, one finally and perseveringly reprobate—has no share. If charity is lacking, the other things are possessed in vain; if it is present, all things are possessed. Whoever possesses it in conduct possesses knowledge both of what is evident and of what is not evident in the Scriptures.

This is the “commandment exceeding broad” [Col. 0274B] (Ps. CXVIII), extending even to enemies. Charity is never solitary: now it is in heaven, now in one’s neighbour. It is never idle, but is the guide toward the common good of the entire human race, regarding nothing human as alien to itself. Broad as Ocean, it comprehends all commandments without error and keeps them without effort.

And Jeremiah in Lamentations I, under the letter Mem, says: “From on high he sent fire into my bones, and taught me.” Likewise (chapter 20): “A flame-bearing fire in my bones.” And the bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs, chapter IV: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart”—you have not merely touched it but penetrated to the innermost recesses of my heart—“with one of your eyes,” namely with one principal virtue, that is, charity. With the other virtues you touch me; with this one alone you wound my heart. And likewise: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish with love” (ibid.).

Likewise, in Octonary XIII, under the letter Mem, which is interpreted “bowels,” or “from the very selves,” or “from the innermost parts,” or “fire from within.” For charity does not love from the surface of the lips or from pretence, but as though from the bowels, from the very innermost and deepest parts of the heart [Col. 0274C]. It is also called “bowels” in the plural because charity is not devoted to a single work. For God has given those who love the power for every kind of work. Charity is the chief of all virtues.

But Adam, in his first state endowed with every natural gift, how did he not possess meritorious charity? Still innocent, he had simple natural love, but not the savour and flame of charity, which no one knows except by experience. Therefore, if Adam, so great a being, did not possess charity, do not presume to say that you possess it unless you are known to possess it from the fruit of works. Likewise: “God is charity, and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him” (I John IV). Great is charity; great is its promise. Charity is great because it is God himself, “and of his greatness there is no end” (Ps. CXLIV). He is he “whom the whole world cannot contain.” Therefore charity is ineffable and uncircumscribable.

Although God is named after a few virtues, he is not designated by the name of any virtue so truly and properly as by the name of charity [Col. 0275A]: “For God is charity.” But the statement “You are my patience” (Job XVII) is figurative, as Augustine attests (*On the Trinity*, XV.17): that is, you yourself are he from whom I have patience. God is not called my sobriety or my chastity, and things of that sort, as he is called my strength, etc. And although God is called charity, this name is verbally appropriated and specified—though in reality it belongs to the whole Trinity—with reference to the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and Son, and the sign and proof of the Father’s inward love for the Son, as offspring are of their parents. For he proceeds from both. Therefore the works of the Trinity in our redemption are attributed and appropriated to the Holy Spirit: “For Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit,” and the like.

From this arose an opinion of certain persons, not to be approved, who say that charity is nothing other than God, from whom alone comes the motion by which we love him. But unless there were a created charity, it would wrongly be said: “Faith, hope, and charity, these three; but the greatest of them is charity” (I Cor. XIII)—the charity from which arises the motion, itself also from God, by which we love him. Great is the promise of charity because “he who abides in charity abides in God” through grace, and will at last abide through glory. “And God in him,” who says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words, and my Father will love [Col. 0275B] him” (I John IV), etc. And again: “I have made known to them your name, and I shall make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them” (ibid.).

Our heart, therefore, must be cleansed with the utmost care and guarded with every watchfulness, as the dining-room and lodging of the whole Trinity.

## Chapter XCVI. On Good and Bad Mourning

Almost all virtues, gifts, and good works are daughters of charity. First, however, we must proceed to its daughters: namely, the seven Beatitudes and the eighth, which returns to the head and cleanses and tests the others. Commending these virtues, or gifts leading to blessedness, the Lord says in the sermon delivered on the mount: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). But because we have discussed above poverty both inward and outward [Col. 0275D], and also meekness, the third Beatitude follows: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (ibid.).

Mourning is not properly a virtue, but rather a little stream proceeding from the fountain of piety and mercy. Tears are manifold: there are tears of despair, whence: “We do not wish you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, who have no hope” (I Thess. IV), etc. And the philosopher Seneca (*Letters*, 63): “One should shed tears for a lost friend, not lament; for this is womanish.” And one should not lament for this reason: reason ought immediately to accomplish what weariness and forgetfulness accomplish through the length of time. And: “Nothing dries more quickly than a tear.” Likewise: “Do not lament your dead man” (Jer. XXII), because he rests; indeed, we lose a living friend more than a dead one.

There are also tears of greed. Hence:

> Lost money is wept for with genuine tears.

Both these and the former tears are detestable and forbidden. There are also tears of natural and human affection; these are tolerable so long as they do not exceed due measure. For we cannot help grieving and shedding tears over a dead friend. Christ “wept” (John XI) over dead Lazarus, though these tears were rather those of charity. Hence: “See how he loved him” (II Kings X [citation as printed]). David also wept for Saul, his enemy, and for Absalom, his son (II Kings XVIII).

There are also tears of piety and compassion, manifold according to their various causes. There are likewise penitential tears, of body and heart, for one’s own sins [Col. 0276B]. For first: “Have mercy on your own soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX), and begin with yourself. “He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?” (Ecclus. XIV). Of these tears it is said: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. VI). There are also tears for the sins of others. Hence: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. XI). The printed text here is corrupt or incomplete: “The sins of neighbours *frix*, etc.” The Apostle was in temptations and a flood of tears for the sins of his neighbours.

There are also tears for the lower watering-place and the upper watering-place: that is, for this miserable sojourning and for longing for the homeland. Hence: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Ps. CXIX), etc. And again: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII). And again: “My tears have been my bread by day and by night,” etc. Of these tears it is said: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation. As they went, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but those who come shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV)—namely, sheaves of merits and rewards. And again: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V).

Arsenius (*Life*, in Surius, 19 July), a decurion and nobleman, fled to the wilderness, where he wept so much for these four causes that he always carried a cloth with him to wipe away his tears. Diogenes also wept continually, but from natural compassion for human folly. Yet it is remarkable where he obtained sufficient moisture. Achsah says to her father Caleb: “You have given me dry land; now give me the upper watering-place and the lower watering-place” (Josh. XV) [Col. 0276D].

## Chapter XCVII. On Good Hunger and Thirst

(Blessed Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, hom. 30): “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V). Hunger or thirst is manifold. There is thirst for grace, or righteousness: toward God, toward yourself, and toward your neighbour, so that you may desire “to live piously, soberly, and righteously” (Tit. II). Commending this thirst, Isaiah, chapter LV, says: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten, buy, and eat,” etc. And David, Psalm XLI: “As the deer longs for fountains of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul has thirsted for God, the strong, the living,” etc.
