And Psalm LXIII: “My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsts for you.” For in many ways it displays this thirst through the ministry of the body: by frequent genuflections, frequent and continual prayers, frequent fasts, vigils, and almsgiving. For the proof of love is the performance of a deed. There is also thirst for glory, which is ineffable to us. Hence: “Into which angels desire to look” (I Pet. I). And likewise Blessed Gregory (*Morals*, XVIII.28): They enjoy without becoming sated; the more they enjoy, the more they thirst to enjoy—not desiring in deprivation what they do not possess, but desiring the continuance of refreshment and delight already possessed [Col. 0277B]. Of this refreshment it is said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI).

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V). “Seek, therefore, the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. VI). For it is not enough to thirst for one without the other. Hence Augustine (*On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, I; *Sermon 92, On Time and the Usefulness of Fasting*, chapter 1): “If you granted me the virtue that I should seek nothing higher, I would reject even that virtue.” Therefore have thirst for righteousness and thirst for glory: the former as merit, which obtains; the latter as reward, which repays and crowns. On account of this manifold thirst Daniel was called “a man of desires” (Dan. IX), namely of righteousness and glory. For a single desire alone is not sufficient.

This thirst is the holy desire of the righteous, of which the Psalm says: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor, that it may remain forever” (Ps. XVII); “but the desire of sinners shall perish” (Ps. CXII). Desire or thirst of sin is manifold according to differing pleasures, but it is principally confined to two things: avarice and lust. These are the two leeches that continually cry: “Bring, bring” (Prov. XXX). Of the thirst of the greedy and the dropsical man it is written:

> Thirsting, Tantalus tries to catch the streams  
> That flee from his lips.  
> —Horace, *Satires* I.1

And:

> The more water is drunk, the more it is thirsted for.  
> —Ovid, *Fasti* I

And:

> While he seeks to quench thirst, another thirst has grown.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.6

And:

> With stones heaped up on every side,  
> You lie sleepless, gaping.  
> —Horace, *Satires* I.1
(QUINTILIAN, book VII.) For greed always opens other gulfs, and needs more what it does not have than what it does have. The thirst of lust, moreover, grows and is stimulated the more lust is exercised. There is also a thirst of nature, which is evident to the perceptive understanding through faith. There is likewise a thirst, or desire, which belongs neither to nature, nor to sin, nor to grace, but to vanity. [Col. 0278A] For it is frivolous and foolish, such as the desire for temporal things and for pleasure. Hence: “Your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Ps. X).—“But do not fear when a man has become rich and when the glory of his house has been multiplied; for when he dies, he will take none of it away, nor will his glory descend with him” (Ps. XLVIII).

Some, too, are at times restrained and hindered from the desire of holy things by sluggishness and ingrained habit. Hence: “Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them” (Ps. CVI). This is the desire of the sluggish, but it is unprofitable. There is also the desire of beginners, who nevertheless do not rise wholly; and this is good. Hence: “Little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. IV). There is also the desire of the perfect [Col. 0278B] and of those who are attaining their end. Hence: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. V). This is a certain strengthening and foretaste of glory through righteousness; in the homeland there will be fullness in the goods of that glory and satiety through the bestowal of the crown.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. On General Mercy

(GREGORY, Homily 30 on the Gospels.) “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). Mercy is a special daughter, and the chief and more express sign, of charity; so much so that it may be said of mercy above the other virtues: the proof of love is the performance of a deed. This is especially commendable [Col. 0278C] both in Christ the head and in his members, who ought to imitate his footsteps in works of mercy. In Christ it is commended because “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV), and because “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXXII). Although he is just, nevertheless “mercy exalts itself over judgment” (Jas. II), because he is “abundant in forgiveness” (Isa. LV), and it is his proper work always to have mercy and to spare; for he does not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live (Ezek. XVIII).

In order that man might live eternally with him through his mercy, he who “was in the form of God emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II); and in that form he especially invited us, by word and example, to works of mercy. His every [Col. 0278D] action is our lesson. “Seeing the city,” moved by mercy, “he wept over it, saying: For if you too had known” (Luke XIX). Mercy is commended in Christ’s members, because without it they do not imitate him. Therefore, if you are imitators of Christ, it is necessary “that you be abundant in forgiving; that mercy may exalt itself in every work of yours” (Jas. II), rise to the surface, and be preferred to every severity and rigor, so that you wholly empty and pour yourself out in works of mercy: beginning first with yourself, carrying it out secondly toward your neighbor, and referring every work to God.

Again, this is commended by the Lord because, at judgment, he promises to reward works of mercy before the works of the other virtues: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and [Col. 0279A] you gave me to drink” (Matt. XXV), and so forth. But works of mercilessness, if one may so speak, committed or carried out, he threatens to condemn and punish before other sins: “I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat,” and so forth.

Likewise, in Luke, chapter III, the Lord says: “Tax collectors came to John, saying: What shall we do, that we may not be cut off and cast into eternal fire? But he said: Do nothing beyond what has been appointed; exact nothing beyond what is prescribed. Soldiers also questioned him, saying: And what shall we do? And he said to them: Extort from no one, make no false accusation, and be content with your pay.” Bede, on Luke chapter III: John restrains each person, in his own rank and office, from committing injury, so that, while they first restrain themselves from the desire for what belongs to others, they may at length proceed to share their own goods with their neighbors. Thus, with just moderation, he warns them beforehand not to seek spoil by false accusation from those whom they ought to benefit by military service, teaching that military pay was established for this reason: lest, while provisions are being sought, a robber run rampant.

“And the crowds asked him, saying: What then shall we do? To them he said: Let him who has two tunics give one to him who has none; and let him who has food do likewise.” Bede: A command is given concerning the sharing of two tunics and of food. For it pertains to the worthy fruit of repentance that we should share with our neighbors not merely outward and less necessary things, but even things most necessary: the food by which we live and the tunic by which we are clothed. [Col. 0279C] See how great is the value of works of mercy, which above all others are prescribed as worthy fruits of repentance. Hence: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke XI).

Likewise Ambrose on the same passage: No office, no class, no age is excluded from the practice of mercy. For all are exhorted together by John to give to one who lacks. Mercy is the fullness of virtues. It is so great that it often, through a certain holy boldness and confidence in God, and through the bond of divine love—of which it is itself both sign and way—strives to oppose obedience and 249 other virtues.

Hence, a Carthusian convert, setting out with forty pounds for the fair, to spend them on the needs of his cell, had as his companion [Col. 0279D] on the road an old soldier, infirm and poor. He asked him, “Where are you going?” The man answered: “Burdened with debt, I am going to ask a certain creditor for a postponement.” The convert said to him: “I will go with you.”

The debtor answered: “May you prosper.” When they had entered the debtor’s house, and he asked for a postponement, the creditor refused it, adding that he would put his son in chains in prison, and that unless he repaid the entire debt that day, on the appointed day his whole inheritance would be made over to him. When the convert intervened for him, the creditor heaped many insults and reproaches upon him. The convert said to him: “Today this righteous man shall be delivered from the prison of this death” (Rom. VII); and, throwing the forty pounds down before him, he redeemed the soldier’s son from prison and freed the man himself [Col. 0280A] from the debt. On his return he told the brethren all that had happened; and they especially commended him for this deed.

Likewise, the bishop of Nola, as Gregory testifies in the *Dialogues* (book III, chapter 1), having exhausted his resources in works of mercy, sold himself into slavery—although bound by pastoral duty—in order to redeem a certain captive; and the Lord, who has mercy on all who show mercy to others, restored him to the fullness of the dignity of the episcopal office.

Likewise, John of Alexandria had, as it were, a contest and compact with the Lord: whatever the Lord gave, he would distribute wholly to the poor, saying: “Thus, Lord: you give, I distribute; let us see who wins.”

Likewise, the bishop of Taranto released, by means of a certain leaden tunic, a man solemnly doing penance and bound by the supreme pontiff. When asked by what authority he did this, he replied: “By this authority, and that of him who said: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy’” (Matt. V). The same man so wholly poured himself out in works of mercy that he secretly took from those who had abundance whatever he could in purple cloth or silver, in order to distribute it to the poor. When he was accused of this as though of theft, he replied: “The law is not made for the righteous; all things ought also to be held in common. Nor do I take away what belongs to another, but I restore to this man what is his and is owed to him.”

But no merciful man, whoever he may be, is recorded (TERENCE, *Adelphoe*, V.3) to have ended his last day except with a good end. And the Lord says through the prophet: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI); he “raised up a horn of salvation for us, to show mercy to our fathers; to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins; through the bowels of mercy of our God, whereby the Dayspring from on high visited us,” and so forth (Luke I).

Likewise James, chapter II: “Judgment without mercy shall be for him who does not show mercy”—without mercy, that is, mercy which sets free, not merely spares. For the Lord always spares, because he is merciful; but he does not always wholly free from punishment, because he is just; or “without mercy,” that is, in return for lack of mercy. Therefore, if you are an imitator of Christ, you are always bound to forgive one who inflicts an injury upon you. For it is no small fault to pursue the whole fault.

## CHAPTER XCIX. On Mercy That Forgives

[Col. 0280D]

There are two kinds of mercy. One consists in forgiving; the other in aiding one’s neighbor. The first is excellent and greater than the second. For one who conquers anger is greater than one who captures a city; and it is greater to escape an injury by keeping silence than to overcome it by answering. Likewise: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. III).

Of the first the Lord says: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke VI). And in the Lord’s Prayer we ask: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). Note the condition: we forgive every debt from the heart—namely, every resentment, injury, and insult; and the thing itself as well, if they are unable to pay. Hence the Apostle, in First Corinthians, [Col. 0281A] chapter VI: “Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded? Why do you not rather accept injury?” And the Lord in the Gospel: “If one strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also. And if one wishes to contend with you in court and take your tunic, surrender your cloak to him as well” (Matt. V). Likewise: “Be quickly reconciled with your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Amen, I say to you: you shall not come out thence until you have paid the last farthing” (ibid.). And again: “Whoever compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him another two thousand paces” (ibid.). And again: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good [Col. 0281B] to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (ibid.).

Likewise the Lord in Matthew, chapter XVIII: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you asked me; ought you not also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” And his lord, angered, handed him over to the torturers until he should pay the whole debt. “So also shall my heavenly Father do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” The Lord punishes mercilessness so severely that because of it he permits all sins to return; he punishes the merciless person even for the last farthing, [Col. 0281C] that is, for original sin previously forgiven.

Likewise, Romans, chapter XII: “Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse; render evil to no one for evil. Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good.” Likewise, by the example of Christ, who prayed for those who crucified him (Luke XXIII); and by the example of Stephen, who prayed for his persecutors (Acts VII).

There is also the example of a certain man who forgave the killer of his son when the killer fell at his feet upon the ground in the form of a cross. The father had caught up with him, armed and accompanied by armed men. The killer, beseeching him, said: “My lord, stop a little and withdraw your sword, that I may say only two words. [Col. 0281D] A just death indeed awaits me; but delay it a little, that I may make confession; or, if you wish to deal more mercifully with me, lest my death become a cause of grief to you. By him who mercifully redeemed you on the cross, I beg you to forgive it me, that you may have something to reproach and set before him at the judgment, should he wish to deal strictly with you; and for as long as I live, I will go on pilgrimage for the deliverance of your son’s soul from its punishments.” At once the father permitted him to depart free and restrained his companions from doing him harm.

But of the second kind of mercy the Lord says in the Gospel: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink,” and so forth (Matt. XXV). Likewise: “Give to him who asks of you; and do not turn away from him who wishes [Col. 0282A] to borrow from you” (Matt. V). And the Apostle says to the Romans (chapter XII): “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink; for in doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head.”

Likewise James, chapter I: “Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from this world.” Likewise Ephesians, chapter IV: “Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and shouting and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice. Be kind to one another, compassionate, merciful, forgiving one another, as God also forgave you in Christ.”

Likewise, in the first chapter of the Song of Songs: “Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the best ointments.” Three ointments flowing from the bride’s breasts are distinguished: [Col. 0282B] the ointment of contrition, the ointment of devotion, and the ointment of mercy or compassion. The first is sweet and pleasant, although crushed and prepared in the mortar of conscience out of the bitterest spices. Hence it is said: “I shall call to mind all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. XXXVIII). Likewise: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. L).

The second is sweeter, because softened: when, after penance has been completed and the Lord’s feet have been watered with tears, the penitent rises with Mary, in serenity of conscience, to kiss the head of the Godhead (Luke VII), giving thanks for the sin forgiven him and saying with the Apostle: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified” (I Cor. IV). [Col. 0282C] And again: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). Of this it is said: “A sacrifice of praise has honored me” (Ps. XLIX).

The third is best and complete, by which the whole Jesus Christ is anointed; it belongs especially to prelates, such as him who said: “My daily pressure is concern for all the Churches” (II Cor. XI). And again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (ibid.). And again: “I die daily, brethren, for your glory” (I Cor. XV). The first and second concern yourself; the third concerns both yourself and your neighbor.

A most excellent example also of forgiving a neighbor’s offenses is Saint Joseph (Gen. L), and many others, who was reconciled to his brothers in such a way that a certain affectionate and playful mockery [Col. 0282D] was an intensification of the compassion shown to them.

## CHAPTER C. On the Clemency of a Judge, or Mercy That Remits

Apart from this common kind of mercy, there is a particular kind of clemency belonging to a judge or powerful person. It is less apparent in a private individual, but especially apparent in a judge, who ought to spare both himself and others by always remitting something of the punishment due. For it is cruel to have dealings with beasts, to take delight in punishments, and to remit nothing of punishment. Showing what this clemency of a judge ought to be, the poet says:

> A ruler is slow to punish, swift to reward,  
> And grieves whenever he is compelled to be stern.
>
> Unlovely savagery does not suit such a character,  
> Nor is it less at variance with your pursuits.
>
> Add that faithfully studying the liberal arts  
> Softens manners and does not allow men to be savage.  
> (OVID, *Epistulae ex Ponto*, I, elegy.)

[Col. 0283A] Likewise, the bishop of Le Mans, reproving a countess (Hildebert, Epistle 25): while you hold power, clemency wins you your husband, and authority the people; from the former you gain a name, from the latter favor. A gentle rule keeps a kingdom safe. The proper place of this virtue is among the powerful, who rule others through justice or by the benefit of election. It is not so among the people, who have no power to punish.

But God from on high detests cruelty and adorns clemency, assigning the former to beasts and the latter to human beings, as nature teaches. He ordained that men ought to be gentle through clemency and beasts feared through cruelty. Therefore to be cruel is to have dealings with beasts and to deny one’s humanity. For reason has absolutely no fellowship with cruelty. Clemency has made her dwelling with God and with the wise of the Lord; cruelty has migrated to the untamed and to those who delight in blood. What fellowship, then, has humanity with cruelty, whose dwelling-place reason so loftily despises, so far abandons, so steadfastly repudiates, so completely ignores?

[Col. 0283B] As nothing is closer to humanity than clemency, so nothing is more glorious in a ruler, by whose discretion he softens harsh powers, summons gentler dispositions, and spares the guilty. It belongs to clemency always to take something away from a vengeful sentence or punishment. Whoever leaves no offense unpunished commits an offense: it is a fault to pursue the whole fault. He declares himself merciless for whom everything permitted is pleasing. It is a glorious virtue in a ruler to punish less than he may lawfully punish. It is virtue to be drawn to vengeance by necessity, not to approach it from choice. One who is offended and yet merciful has something great and divine about him.

A good ruler punishes no one without regret; he proscribes no one without sorrow. A good ruler pursues a crime so as to remember that the person he punishes is a human being. A good ruler rules himself and serves the people; he despises no one’s blood. It is the blood of an enemy, but of one who can become a friend; it is the blood of a wrongdoer, but of a human being, whoever he may be. Because he could not give life, he considers it a crime to take it away. Therefore, whenever blood is shed, he is ashamed. [Col. 0283D] For a teachable mind that loves discipline, these things suffice; from them those who are more diligent may easily perceive how much cruelty harms authority and how much clemency benefits it.

Seneca likewise writes of this to Nero (book II, chapters 3 and 4). What more need be said? Every syllable of Sacred Scripture resounds and breathes mercy. You possess only what you have mercifully bestowed upon your neighbor. Augustine: Mercy alone accompanies the dead. “For their works follow them” (Apoc. XIV)—namely, works of mercy, whether forgiving, remitting punishment, correcting a brother, sustaining and cherishing him bodily, or interceding for him:

> The wealth you have given is the only wealth you will always possess.  
> (MARTIAL, book V, epigram 43.)

## CHAPTER CI. On Mercy That Corrects

[Col. 0284A]

There follows mercy that corrects, which is greater than every manual and bodily work. Commanding that it be shown to neighbors, the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, go and correct him,” and so forth (Matt. XVIII). Carry out all things according to the Lord’s command, which all are commanded to keep, toward all persons and in every sin, except in the matter of a personal injury and in a capital case; and all this is for the preservation of mercy.

Likewise, at the end of Romans, chapter I: “Although they knew the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.” And II Corinthians, chapter II: “If anyone has caused me sorrow, he has caused sorrow not to me, but in part, lest I burden all of you. For such a person, this rebuke by the majority is sufficient; so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and console him, lest one such as this be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.” And in the same epistle, chapter VI: “Therefore go out from among them and be separated from them, says the Lord; do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you.”

Likewise I Corinthians, chapter V: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened.” Likewise Galatians, chapter VI: “Brethren, if a man has been overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted.” Likewise Ephesians, chapter IV: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, let each speak truth [Col. 0284C] with his neighbor, for we are members of one another.” Likewise Acts, chapter XX: “I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.”

Likewise Job, chapter XXIX: “I broke the jaws of lions, 254 and from their teeth I took away the prey.” Likewise Proverbs, chapter XXIV: “Rescue those who are being led to death; and do not cease to deliver those who are being given over to destruction.” And Jeremiah, chapter XLVIII: “Cursed is he who keeps his sword from blood.” And Genesis, chapter IV: “Where is Abel your brother? He answered: I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” And Deuteronomy, chapter XXII: “You shall not see your brother’s ox or sheep straying and pass by; [Col. 0284D] but you shall bring it back to your brother.” Likewise, concerning lifting up a neighbor’s ass. Likewise Ezekiel, chapter III. Likewise Ephesians, chapter V: “Rather, rebuke them. For it is shameful even to speak of those things which are done by them in secret.” Likewise Ecclesiasticus, chapters XIX, XX, and XXI.

Likewise, I am incomparably more bound to love my neighbor’s soul than my own body. Likewise, the proof of compassion is the performance of correction, just as the proof of love is the performance of a work. Likewise, the union or care of souls is holier than that of bodies. Likewise, be a true imitator of the Samaritan, who had mercy on the wounded man and did not pass him by like the priest and Levite, but took care of him (Luke X). Likewise, by the example of the Lord, who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the desert, went to seek the hundredth sheep that had perished (Luke XV). [Col. 0285A] Likewise, feed with not only bodily but also spiritual food those dying from hunger for the word of God, and so forth. Likewise Ephesians, chapter V: “Be imitators of God as most dear children, and walk in love, as Christ also loved us,” namely, so that we lay down our lives for our brethren. For in this we especially know his charity. Therefore, if anyone, according to place and time, is bound “to lay down his life for his neighbor” (John XV)—which is indeed true—much more ought he to correct one whom he sees sinning. Likewise IV Kings, chapter XV, concerning Uzziah. Likewise, all that has been adduced against most wicked silence may be adduced here, especially those things which most directly bear upon this command of the Lord concerning correcting a brother.

## CHAPTER CII. On Mercy That Intercedes for Enemies

[Col. 0285B]

There follows mercy that intercedes even for enemies (Luke XXIII). Apart from the Lord and the protomartyr Stephen (Acts VIII), an outstanding example of it is Samuel interceding for Saul, who wished to kill him. For this reason Samuel deserved that “all from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord” (I Kings III).

Moses likewise provided a wonderful example: praying for the people who enraged and grievously troubled him, he restrained the wrathful Lord, saying: “Either forgive them, or blot me out of the book of life” (Exod. XXXII). Likewise Psalm CV: “And the Lord said that he would destroy them, if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood [Col. 0285C] in the breach before him to turn away his wrath, lest he destroy them.” Moses did not wish to enter the promised land alone without them. Hence the saints compare him to a mother who, invited to a solemn feast, will not enter without a little child left outside—perhaps crying, dirty, and tiresome—but chooses rather to fast outside with her child.

## CHAPTER CIII. On Visible, Bodily, and Manual Mercy, or Mercy That Gives Aid

There follows visible, bodily, and manual mercy. Its most excellent example was Job, who says in chapters XXIX and XXXI: “The ear that heard me called me blessed, and the eye that saw me bore witness to me, because I delivered the crying poor man and the orphan [Col. 0285D] who had no helper. The blessing of him who was perishing came upon me, and I consoled the heart of the widow. I clothed myself with righteousness, and it clothed me as a garment and diadem; I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor; I broke the jaws of the wicked and took prey from his teeth. I was the comforter of mourners. If I denied the poor what they desired; if I made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat from it—for mercy grew with me from my infancy and came forth with me from my mother’s womb; if I despised the passer-by because he lacked clothing, or the poor man without a covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was not warmed by the fleece of my sheep; if a stranger remained outside and beyond my tent; [Col. 0286A] if my door was not open to the traveler.” This is an aposiopesis, as though he said: If I did not do these things, showing mercy to all, may God likewise not have mercy on me.

Likewise Psalm XXXIV: “Lord, who is like you, delivering the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the helpless and poor from those who plunder him?” Mercy often burns so ardently that, through a devout and holy impulse, it does not spare other virtues—especially obedience, of which it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and unwillingness to obey is the sin of divination” (I Kings XV)—as is clear from the example of a certain convert who, though forbidden by his abbot, gave to the needy when occasion and opportunity presented themselves.

Likewise Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXIX: “For the commandment’s sake receive the poor man, and because of his need do not send [Col. 0286B] him away empty.” Likewise Ecclesiasticus in the same chapter: “He who shows mercy lends to his neighbor, and he who is strong in hand keeps the commandments.”

## CHAPTER CIV. On Almsgiving

Mercy’s daughter is almsgiving. Concerning it one must consider what its effect is; what ought to be given; how, in what order, how much, in what manner, and from what resources; and to whom, how many, and what kind of persons it should be given.

Of its effect the Holy Spirit says in Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXIX: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor man, and it itself will pray to the Lord for you, that you may be delivered from every evil.” For almsgiving is one wing of prayer, and fasting the other. Likewise: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. III). Likewise: “The almsgiving of a man, as a purse with him, and the grace of a man, as the apple [Col. 0286C] of the eye, he will preserve against enemies” (Ecclus. XVII). And the Lord says in Luke, chapter XI: “Nevertheless, give what remains as alms; and behold, all things are clean for you.” Likewise: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI). And David, in Psalm CXI: “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever.”

And Lawrence [Note: [Col. 0285D] See his Life in Surius, 10 August]: “The hands of the poor have carried the Church’s resources which you demand into heavenly treasures. What is given here to the poor and needy is received by Christ in heaven.” Hence he himself says: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” [Col. 0286D] (Matt. XXV). And again: “He who receives you receives me” (Matt. X). Likewise: “Martin, while still a catechumen, clothed me with this garment” [Note: [Col. 0286D] Life in Surius, 11 November].

What ought to be given, and in what order, is shown in Luke, chapter VI, where the Lord says: “Give to everyone who asks you”: give the thing he asks for, if you can; if you cannot, give a cup of warm water; if you do not have that, a cup of cold water. If you do not even have cold water, give him correction if he is wicked, prayer if he is good. For a righteous person who possesses all things in the Lord of all never lacks something to give.

How much should be given the Lord shows through the instrument of John in Luke, chapter III: “Let him who has two tunics give one to him who has none, and let him who has food do likewise.” A command concerning the sharing of two tunics and food [Col. 0287A] is suitably and pointedly given (Matt. X), because if one tunic is divided, no one is clothed by it. In half a tunic, both the recipient and the giver remain naked. Therefore keep for yourself and your household what is necessary; distribute what remains to the poor—even from what is necessary, according to place and time—or else you will be a robber.

The Apostle likewise sets forth this moderation in goods to be distributed to the poor, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (chapter VIII): “I do not say this so that your generosity and willingness to give alms may be relief to others but distress to you; but that by equality your abundance may supply their lack, and their abundance in spiritual things may supply your lack, so that there may be equality.” Of this it is written in Exodus [Col. 0287B] (chapter XVI) concerning manna: “He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack,” but had enough. For the peace of Jerusalem consists in the account of giving and receiving: those who abound in temporal goods distribute them to poor persons who abound more greatly in spiritual things, so that, by thus sharing temporal and spiritual goods equally, the one who has much in temporal goods may not abound, because he retains nothing beyond necessities for himself but distributes it equally to the poor; and “he who has little” in temporal goods does not “lack” them, because he receives enough from another.

Thus also with spiritual goods. Martin exceeded this equality of goods by supererogation (see his [Col. 0287C] Life in the place indicated above), when he gave half his cloak to a poor man. Some began to mock him as a disfigured man because of his truncated clothing; others groaned more deeply because nothing like it had ever happened to them. He also gave to a poor man the single tunic he had wholly entrusted to a little sheep [an uncertain OCR reading, perhaps a garment-related term]; the archdeacon bought him another, striped, for five denarii.

It is good and pious that the Lives of both blessed Martin and blessed Nicholas (the Life of St. Nicholas is in Surius, 6 December) begin with works of mercy, in which, as men of mercy, they excelled, so that it may thereby be shown that these works were the foundation of their entire religious life. Each bore compassionate affections toward the afflicted. Thus Nicholas gave three virgins in marriage, lest through want [Col. 0287D] they should be stained by the disgrace of a brothel. For there was extraordinary compassion in his heart, and he bestowed many benefits upon the oppressed.

The bishop of Nola went further (*Dialogues* of blessed Gregory, book III, chapter 1): he sold not only his possessions but himself into slavery, in order to free a widow’s son from prison and captivity. But we are unwilling to follow and approve, by works rather than words, either this apostolic equality in distributing goods to the poor or Martin’s division, or total giving. Indeed, by disputation we oppose it, intending to be able to possess everything ourselves and to have nothing superfluous. But “God is not mocked” (Gal. VI): he created all things for the use of all, not of one person alone.

[Col. 0288A] It remains to say to whom, how many, what sort of persons, and in what manner alms should be given. To whom, then? To everyone, if you can, but “especially to those of the household of faith” (ibid.); and among these, more to the more needy, and among these, more to the more righteous: “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII). “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor” (Ps. CXI), not to those who are belching [i.e. the already satiated]. You will find the other authorities bearing on this above, under the heading (above, chapter 47): “Against Those Who Give to the Non-Needy.” Here, then, is to whom, how many, what sort of persons, and in what manner one should give.

With regard to the character and prudent administration of almsgiving, the following points should be observed. Distribution: lest all be given to one person. “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor” (Ps. CXI). “I wish to do good to this man as to you.” Necessity: necessary things should be given, not superfluities; not luxurious foods, [Col. 0288B] except in the necessity of illness. Cheerfulness: without compulsion. Hence II Corinthians, chapter IX: “Let each give as he has determined in his heart, not from sorrow or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.” For forced services do not please God, but voluntary ones do. Hence: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII). He who gives from embarrassment, or to avoid the importunity of one asking, loses both the thing and the merit.

258 For almsgiving ought to be given solely with a view to God, not for any external thing, such as payment and the like.

The compassion of the giver gives worth to almsgiving, not the quantity given. Likewise Exodus, chapter XXXV: “Let everyone who is willing and of ready heart offer firstfruits [Col. 0288C] to the Lord.” Likewise: the children of Israel, with devout and willing hearts, offered gifts to the Lord for the construction of the tabernacle. But when the craftsmen pressed on with the work, they said to Moses: “The people offer more than is needed” (Exod. XXXVI). He ordered a proclamation to be made that no one should offer anything more for the work of the sanctuary.

Likewise I Esdras, chapters I, II, and VII. This should be urged against collectors, councillors, masters, and teachers who press people to contribute to a work: almsgiving elicited through entreaties and embarrassment ought not to be approved, because it is not sincere.

The Apostle to the Philippians (chap. IV): “No church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving except you alone. For even to Thessalonica you sent once and twice for my need. And it is not the gift that I seek, [Col. 0288D] but I seek the fruit abounding to your account”—that is, the good and upright will by which the inward person is made fruitful. Hence the Lord in the Gospel does not say simply, “He who receives a righteous man,” but adds, “in the name of a righteous man.” To receive a righteous man is the gift; to do so in the name of a righteous man is the fruit (Matt. X). A raven and a widow are recorded to have fed Elijah (III Kings XVI). But the raven, which did not feed “in the name of a righteous man,” did so with a “gift”; the widow, who did feed him in the name of a righteous man, did so with “fruit.” “Therefore I seek this fruit rather than the gift” (Phil. IV). For those who give neither for the right cause nor with the right end; or who give unwillingly, or put the righteous man second, are like the raven: they are ministers, possessing not the fruit of almsgiving but only its service.

## CHAPTER CV. From what alms ought to be given.

[Col. 0289A]

It follows to consider from what alms ought to be given: namely, from what is your own, not from what belongs to another. Hence: “Honor the Lord from your own substance” (Prov. III), not from another’s. And Deuteronomy, chap. XIII: “Nothing of the anathema shall cling to your hand”—that is, of anything which ought to be separated from you, or which it is right for you to separate from yourself—“that the Lord may have mercy on you.” Likewise, chap. VII: “You shall not covet the silver and gold of which they are made, nor take anything from them for yourself, lest you offend; for it is an abomination to the Lord your God.” Likewise (chap. XII), a “lamb without blemish”—of body, not of fleece—was commanded to be offered to the Lord. For the remaining authorities and concordances [Col. 0289B] on this matter, see above under the heading, “On the acceptance of unlawfully acquired gifts.”

Likewise, consider the example of Martin, a poor cardinal-priest who despised gifts. When the lord chancellor had sent to him, as to the other cardinals, the customary offering and blessing of the Roman curia—namely, twenty pounds at Christmas for celebrating the feast—he rejected it, because it had been acquired by robbery and simony. Likewise, when a horse had been lent to him by a certain bishop, his own horse having failed him while he was carrying out a legation, he refused to assist the said bishop in his case until the horse had been returned to him and he had first learned that the bishop’s cause was just.

Likewise, consider the example of Stephen, the second abbot of Cîteaux. He distributed to the poor and to children the loaves and cheeses given by his converted priest, [Col. 0289C] judging that his monks ought not to eat them as stolen and plundered goods, since the “right hand” of very many priests and archdeacons “is filled,” both then and now, “with gifts” (Ps. XXV). And “their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Ps. CXLIII): they seize and receive with the right hand, and for things of the right hand; being worse than lay usurers, who seize with the left hand and for things of the left hand.

## CHAPTER CVI. On the order of giving alms.

A certain order in giving alms must also be observed. But, to begin more deeply, the kinds of almsgiving must be distinguished.

The first is God’s, consisting in our creation and re-creation; in the consolation [Col. 0289D] afforded us through benefits; in instruction through commandments; in our correction through scourges; and finally in the bestowal of rewards in glory.

The second kind is that of Christ as man, who on the cross offered himself to God the Father as a living victim for us, while we were still his enemies. “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). He also daily presents himself to the Father with the insignia of his warfare, praying and interceding for us as our advocate and brother in heaven.

The third is that of a human being toward himself: “Have mercy on your soul, first pleasing” (Ecclus. XXX) God.

The fourth is that of a human being toward his neighbor, and it is manifold: in rebuking a brother in order to correct him; in forgiving one’s own injury; in [Col. 0290A] praying for him; in compassion; in giving holy counsel; and in expending every entrusted talent, whether bodily or spiritual. Yet the outward bestowal of aid has, by common usage, claimed the general name of almsgiving as its own. In this species—namely, bodily almsgiving—a certain order is observed.

The first, sincere, and pure almsgiving is from one’s own labor. Hence: “By labor and the sweat of your own face,” not another’s, “you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III), and give to others to eat. Likewise: “You shall eat the labors of your hands, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII). The Apostle also provides an example, for he sought food by his hands. He says likewise to the Ephesians, chap. IV: “Let him who stole steal no longer; but rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, that he may have something to give to one suffering need.” There is likewise the example of the widow who refused to be buried in any shift other than the one which she had spun and woven.

The second degree of bodily almsgiving is from one’s own patrimony, from which alms may be given; and although it is not so pure as the first, you nevertheless cultivate it by another’s sweat and use a human being as a beast of burden.

The third degree is from the patrimony of the Crucified One, of which we are stewards and, as it were, executors, not masters. Hence it is called almsgiving less properly. Yet equal love commends, or obtains and earns, equal reward in all these cases. But in this last case, unless the stewardship is just, we shall be thieves [Col. 0290C] and robbers. And it often happens that the goods of the poor are given to the wealthy and to priests’ nephews; yet they are not wealthy but impoverished, because:

> Filthy booty has no good outcome.  
> [Note: [Col. 0289D] Festus Pompeius cites this from Naevius.]  
> (OVID, *Amores*, book I, elegy 10.)

And things badly acquired are badly dissipated.

## CHAPTER CVII. On caution in giving alms.

To what has been said should be added what pertains to prudent caution in giving alms: namely, that with your own will and readiness, by free choice and with your own hand, if you can, you distribute alms. This is shown by the example of Christ and of many saints ministering among their subjects; and by the example of Count Theobald, [Col. 0290D] of blessed memory, who with his own hand gave shoes along with ointment to the poor, for this reason: that tears of compunction, greater devotion, and humility might grow in him thereby, and that the poor might pray for him more affectionately, their favor being more fully won through the service of his humility.

While you live, distribute also for yourself, while it is the time for sowing; for a dead person rarely finds a friend. Nothing grows cold more quickly in the heart than friendship for the dead after death. Let us therefore prepare ourselves for entering the kingdom, for only those prepared shall enter. “Let us anticipate the face” of the Judge “with confession, and with psalms”—that is, with good works and praises—“let us make joyful noise to him” (Ps. XCIV), before he comes; [Col. 0291A] remembering that “each of the four living creatures walked before its face” (Ezek. I), teaching the imitators of the Gospel to walk in this way. So too the Apostle stretched himself toward the things before him (Phil. III). And there is likewise the example of a most simple soul which said: the almsgiving of a living person is like a lamp carried before someone; it illuminates him, showing him where he should go. But the almsgiving of a dead person is like a lamp carried behind someone’s back: it does not illuminate him, so as to keep him from falling into a precipice.

There is also this difference between works of mercy done under the Law and works of mercy done under the Gospel. The Law says: “Break your bread for the hungry,” etc. (Isa. LVIII). Hence among some the praiseworthy custom has become established that something is broken from each loaf [Col. 0291B] for the poor.

Tobit likewise says (chap. IV): If you have little, you shall give little. But God, commanding more perfect mercy in the Gospel, says: “Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX)—not only to the needy, but even to one who seizes from you. Hence: “If anyone takes your tunic, give him your cloak also” (Matt. V). Thus, when a hermit, nearly naked and walking in his undergarments, was asked who had stripped him, he said: “This book is the heavenly robber, teaching that all things should be given to the poor.” The questioner said to him: “How have you given everything, when you still have that book?” And immediately he gave it away.

Likewise the Apostle, II Corinthians, chap. VIII: “I make known to you the grace of God which is in the churches of Macedonia: [Col. 0291C] that their deepest poverty abounded unto the riches of their simplicity, because I bear them witness in truth that beyond their means they were first willing, begging us with much exhortation for the grace and participation of the ministry which is for the saints.”

## CHAPTER CVIII. On the commendation of almsgiving.

But what is the cause of such high commendation of almsgiving in Sacred Scripture? Hear the Apostle, I Timothy, chap. IV: “For bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things, having the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come.” Not mortification of the flesh, unkempt dress, frequent vigils, continual and severe fasts, austerity of life, and [Col. 0291D] a dreadful appearance make you a true philosopher and Christian. Rather, these are the signs of almsgiving: that you abound in bowels of mercy; that you covet nothing; that you fear nothing; knowing that “godliness with sufficiency is great gain” (I Tim. VI). For what is sufficient is at hand.

Godliness has the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come. Hence: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI). Likewise: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI). Likewise: “They shall receive a hundredfold in this age” (Matt. XXI), that is, “a hundred times as much,” namely a multiplication of all the riches existing in the world. For these are lacking to no one who has not loved them.

It also has the promise of the life of grace. Hence: “In keeping them there is great reward” (Ps. XVIII), namely serenity of conscience and increase of virtues. “For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). It also has “the promise of life” in glory—that is, of the glorious life which shall be in the future, just as it has the promise of present life—because the one who has performed works of mercy in the present “shall possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX). Likewise: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song II). Likewise: “He who ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also shall my minister be” (John II). Likewise: “I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV). “Come therefore, blessed of my Father, that you may eat and drink in his kingdom” (Luke XXII). “And, passing by, he shall minister to them” (Luke XII).

## CHAPTER CIX. On purity of heart.

[Col. 0292B]

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). Purity of heart, as a general virtue, embraces all virtues, all good works, and thoughts. For whatever is attributed to faith and the other virtues is included in purity of heart, as that from which it arises. It is necessary for every believer, and without it there is no salvation. Hence Solomon: “With all vigilance guard your heart” (Prov. IV), keeping it pure; and this indeed is more difficult than keeping the body pure, because when the mind is corrupted the body is corrupted, and not conversely, as in the foolish virgins (Matt. XXV). Therefore purity of mind is more necessary [Col. 0292C] than purity of body.

“And who can boast that he has a pure heart?” (Prov. XX). Even in angels something of impurity or “perversity” has been found in the sight of the Lord (Job IV). And in Ezekiel, chap. III, the Lord says: “He who hears” with the body, “let him hear” with the mind; and he who “rests” in body, “let him rest” in mind. Gregory (*Homily 12 on Ezekiel*): “For one who keeps the sabbath in body and not in mind may fittingly be described by what Jeremiah says: ‘Her enemies saw her and mocked her sabbaths’” (Lam. I). Outwardly, indeed, he is a “hypocrite and a whitewashed tomb” (Matt. XXIII), but inwardly he is herniated and full of filth.

The heart must therefore be guarded with the utmost care and every vigilance. “For it is not what enters a man’s mouth that defiles him, but what [Col. 0292D] comes out of the heart” (Matt. XXIII): such as thefts, adulteries, murders, and every evil; and likewise every good. Hence: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Luke XI), but only after the heart has first been cleansed by faith. Hence Peter: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts V). Faith, therefore, begins purity of heart; hope and love bring it to perfection.

And David says: “Create a pure heart in me, O God.” For the heart created in him at first had almost ceased to exist through the wounding of natural gifts and the stripping away of gratuitous ones. Hence, because one with an impure heart is without a heart, he prays: “Create a pure heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit”—by which I may direct my thoughts toward you and according to your good pleasure—“within my inmost parts” (Ps. L). And the Apostle says: [Col. 0293A] “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. IV).

Purity of heart is especially necessary for scholars approaching the reading of Sacred Scripture. Hence Augustine: “In so exalted a light, the eye of reason is not fixed unless it has first been cleansed through the purity of faith.” “For the natural man does not receive the things that are of God” (I Cor. II). For this reason the gift of the Holy Spirit which is understanding is adapted to this beatitude, namely purity of heart, so that it may be shown that these ought to be joined and accompany one another; for “from your commandments I have understood” (Ps. CXVIII). But we discussed this small branch of purity more fully at the beginning of our preaching.

This virtue is also especially necessary to a priest. Hence Moses: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII). Just as Abraham, while sacrificing, needed a fan when unclean birds descended upon the sacrifices (Gen. XV), [Col. 0293B] with which he drove them away, so too a priest needs the fan of faith and purity of heart, especially when he stands at the sacrifice of the altar. Then the “dying flies” rise more importunately and attack, seeking “to spoil the sweetness of the ointment” (Eccl. X:1); he must drive them away with this fan and appoint the faithful maidservant to guard the door, lest robbers kill Ish-bosheth (II Kings IV). Thus, with “the door shut, he shall enter his chamber, praying to the Father” (Matt. VI).

## CHAPTER CX. On peace.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V). Since peace is the consummation of all virtues, it is deservedly placed seventh and last in the catalogue of beatitudes. Sacred Scripture seems to attribute greater things to it than to the other virtues, as is shown by the fuller expression of its reward: the “peacemakers shall be called sons of God,” whereas the others “shall possess the kingdom” (ibid.). But sons succeed to the father’s universal right by hereditary title.

There are threefold peace: peace of time, of the breast, and of eternity. Of the first, nothing need be said at present; yet it often harms many, because they grow lax through it, though it also benefits many, such as the weak. The second is virtue and merit; the third is the reward of the second. To show how necessary this virtue is to our salvation, and how greatly the Christian religion ought to seek it, the Lord says to the disciples—and in them to us—“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John XIV). As if he said: “I leave peace with you,” that is, certain remnants of peace, because it is imperfect and not enduring. Therefore he does not add, “my peace”; rather, I leave you the peace of the breast in the present, after which “my peace”—that is, perfect and abiding peace—I give, or shall give, you in the future: the peace of eternity. For God will not give peace except upon peace.

Therefore the Prophet also says in the person of the righteous: “In peace,” only half-full, “I shall sleep”; then in perfect peace, which is “in the selfsame”—unchangeable and perfect—“I shall rest” (Ps. IV), I shall rest perfectly. For the peace of the breast in the present is imperfect, because it is often disturbed. The world rages, the body oppresses, and the devil lies in ambush.

Therefore the true Peacemaker also says: “In the world you will have tribulations, but in me you will have peace” (John XVI). And the Lord, in order firmly to implant peace in the minds of the faithful after the resurrection, announced it to the disciples when “the doors were shut” (John XX), as though it were the sum of virtues, saying: “Peace be with you” (ibid.). Therefore his spiritual vicar, namely the bishop, turning toward the people at Mass, announces it to them. Therefore, too, when the Lord was born, an angel announced to shepherds and simple people that first and chief joy—the message of peace—saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke II).

Therefore, too, in the Church’s chief sacrament, the sacrament of the altar, when the Eucharist has been consecrated, the priest [Col. 0294B] says with the Church: “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy” (John I)—“have mercy”; and, in order that he may have mercy perfectly, gathering all his mercies into one expression and adding the sum and effect of all virtues, he says: “Grant us peace” (ibid.).

Speaking of this, the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II), reconciling the lowest to the highest and earthly things to heavenly, restoring peace between God and man. For we were all enemies of God and hostile to him, though he always loved us. He was also the mediator of peace between human being and human being, namely Jew and Gentile (I Tim. II); and between a human being and himself, when he was divided against himself and was not one, in the unity of faith and morals, whose “ark” “was not completed in one cubit” (Gen. VI); and between a human being and an angel, whose fall through human sin was delayed in being repaired (Isa. XIV). The angels themselves did not serve human beings so readily before Christ’s coming as afterward, as though offended by them because they had offended their Lord.

The devil alone was not reconciled, but was excluded from this peace, because he first sowed discord between Creator and creature. His children and imitators are also apparent in those who do not have peace with their neighbor, and consequently neither with God nor with themselves. Conversely, all peacemakers are children and imitators of Christ. Therefore the Apostle says in Romans, chap. V: “Being justified [Col. 0294D] by faith, let us have peace with God and with our neighbor, through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

This is the virtue which alone excels in the fellowship and company of the saints, making peacemakers lovable, sociable, and approachable; so that, on account of it more than the other virtues, the person who is peaceable is placed over and before all. Because of this, the bride in the Song, praying for what is so useful to her, says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I). The mouth that kisses is the assuming Word; the mouth kissed is assumed human nature. From these comes the effective *electrum* of peace between God and man: the man Christ Jesus, God and man. See how great peace ought to exist between a human being and God, when God united himself, through human nature, to a neighbor; for the sake of that human nature he united it to himself in the unity of supreme peace.

Therefore God says through the Prophet: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXIII), lest it withdraw from you. Showing how it is to be pursued, Augustine says: “Throw away money, that you may buy peace and a tranquil heart.” And the Lord says: “If someone takes your tunic, give him your cloak also” (Matt. V); and, “Be reconciled with your adversary on the way” (ibid.). And the Apostle says, “Redeeming the time” and the peace of the breast, “because the days are evil” (Eph. V), because of the wickedness practiced in them. Likewise: “Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? But you inflict injury and commit fraud—and this against brethren” (I Cor. VI).

Likewise, the Prophet inviting us [Col. 0295B] to peace says: “He has made your borders peace, and filled you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. CXLVII). The heavenly Jerusalem, within whose borders there will be nothing but peace, is a “house of one manner” (Ps. LXVII); but at the borders of Gehenna are pain and discord. Hence, as though this peace were sufficient for salvation, the same Prophet adds in prayer: “Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem, and abundance for those who love you. Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers. For my brethren and neighbors I spoke peace concerning you; for the house of the Lord our God I sought good things for you” (Ps. CXXI). Likewise: “Give peace to those who wait for you, that your prophets may be found faithful” (Ecclus. XXXVI). Likewise the Apostle, Philippians, chap. IV: “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may guard your hearts and [Col. 0295C] your minds.”

The same Apostle, showing how necessary peace is to salvation, writes to all to whom he writes in this form: “Grace be to you, and peace from the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. I), that is, tranquility of mind, without which God is not seen; for “in this peace his place was made” (Ps. LXXV), whence he “will not rest except upon one who is peaceable and quiet” (Isa. LXVI). Likewise David: “Keep innocence and behold equity, because there are remnants for the peaceful person” (Ps. XXXVI). He does not say, “for the innocent and just,” though he could have said so, but “for the peaceful,” showing that the conclusion and sum of the other virtues lie in peace as in their mistress, to whom the others are appendages and toward whom they tend, like attendants and handmaids. Hence [Col. 0295D] he attributes the remnants of rewards, concerning which he says, “The remnants of thoughts shall keep festival for you” (Ps. LXXV), not to the attendant virtues but to their mistress.

## CHAPTER CXI. From whom we ought to have peace.

It has been said with whom we ought to have peace: namely, with God, with our neighbor, and so forth. We must now say from whom we ought to have peace: from our own flesh, so that Delilah may be subdued (Judg. XVI), following the example of the Apostle, who says: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude” (I Cor. IX). And the Lord says: “Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning” (Luke XII).

From the devil, so that we may avoid, insofar as we can, “spiritual wickednesses” (Eph. VI). From the world, lest we be too much devoted to “secular affairs” (II Tim. II) and worldly actions. Hence Jethro says to Moses in Exodus, chap. XVIII: “You will wear yourself out with foolish labor. Divide your burden among more persons, and the Lord will be with you,” etc.

Augustine says on this passage (*Book II, Questions on Exodus*, question 68): “It is evident that a mind too intent upon human activities is emptied of the Lord; and it becomes so much the fuller as it more freely extends itself toward heavenly and eternal things.” And Solomon says: “My son, let your activities not be many” (Ecclus. XI), even honorable ones, because:

> A wise person sets a limit even to honorable pursuits.  
> (JUVENAL, *Satires*, VI.)

Take care that you are not so possessed by all others that you do not possess yourself. Take care that you do not help your neighbor in such a way that you neglect yourself: “He who is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good?” [Col. 0296B] (Ecclus. XIV). “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul?” (Matt. XVI).

The attention directed to many things is less for each individual thing. As eating too much is a vice, so working too much for earthly things is a vice. Therefore bind and reduce yourself to unity as far as you can, because “there is none who does good, no, not even one” (Ps. XIII); “the ark was completed in one cubit” (Gen. VI); “one thing have I asked of the Lord, this I shall seek” (Ps. XXVI); “one thing is necessary for you” (Luke X); “only one was healed in the pool” (John V).

In this way you will have peace from the world, with the Apostle who says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI). And you will have peace not only from [Col. 0296C] the world, but also from every enemy, if you love and keep the commandments of God. Hence: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. CXVIII), because those who live according to God’s law neither suffer nor cause stumbling. They expound it not according to human custom but according to sincerity, and, without the cloud of allegory, simply and nakedly, as it proceeded from the Savior’s mouth. Of such interpreters it is said: “My tongue has clung to my jaws” (Ps. XXI). Likewise, Hebrews, chap. XII: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God.”

## CHAPTER CXII. On the effect of peace.

[Col. 0296D]

It follows to discuss the effect of peace. Peace alone builds a house for the Lord. Hence David, because “he was a man of blood,” was forbidden to build a house for the Lord (I Chron. XXII). But Solomon (III Kings V), though wicked, was nevertheless commanded to build a house for the Lord because, without war, he was peaceable in peace. See how abominable war among the household of faith is to the Lord. If, therefore, you have peace from the things mentioned above, you are peaceable and build a temple for the Lord; but if you are warlike, you destroy his temple against the Lord.

But the Lord’s saying, addressed to the disciples, also bestowed upon peace much strength and authority above the other virtues: “Into whatever house,” he says, “you enter, say: ‘Peace to this house’” [Col. 0297A] (Luke IX). He does not say, “Let charity,” or faith, gentleness, or the like, “be upon this house,” but “peace,” as though gathering all other virtues into the bundle of peace.

Likewise David: “The Lord makes the flood to dwell, and the Lord shall sit as king forever”; for against this flood, “the Lord shall give strength; afterward he shall bless his people with peace” (Ps. XXVIII). And holy Zachariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied and said: “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High,” etc., because you shall do these and these things “to direct our feet into the way of peace” (Luke I), as though including all his works in this work of peace.

## CHAPTER CXIII. On the twofold peace.

[Col. 0297B]

There is the peace of God and the peace of the world. The first is twofold: peace of the breast, whence, “Peace I leave with you” (John XIV); and peace of eternity, whence the Apostle says, “The peace of God which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. IV). The second likewise is twofold.

For there is a feigned peace of the world. This is the peace of traitors and flatterers, concerning which it is said: “The man of my peace, who ate my bread, has greatly increased his treachery against me” (Ps. XL). And Jeremiah, chap. XXXVIII: “O Zedekiah, your peaceable men have deceived you and prevailed against you; they have sunk your feet in mire and slipperiness.” Likewise: “Peace, peace,” from tyrants and heretics, “and there was no peace” (Jer. VI), from false brethren. Likewise: “I came not to send peace upon the earth”—because this is mortal sin—“but a sword” (Matt. X), for in the mouth of saints are sword and death, but in the mouth of the harlot are honey and milk (Prov. V).

There is also the peace of the world, namely present prosperity without disturbance. Hence: “But my feet were almost moved, my steps nearly poured out, because I envied the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII).

This indeed is from God, but it often harms by occasion, because it breeds contempt, laxity, and sloth. Hence: “In peace, behold, my bitterness was most bitter” (Isa. XXXVIII). And the poet:

> Now we suffer the evils of long peace;  
> Luxury, more savage than arms, has settled upon us  
> And avenges the conquered world. For:
>
> [Col. 0297D] Minds generally grow wanton in favorable circumstances.  
> (OVID, book II, *The Art of Love*.)

And elsewhere:

> Why is it asked that Aegisthus became an adulterer?  
> The cause is obvious: he was idle.  
> (ID., book I, *Remedies*.)

For the sake of maintaining this peace, liberty often perishes and virtues are trampled down; and where virtue perishes, neither is there peace. Hence James, chap. III: “The wisdom that is from above is first indeed”—by which no other virtue perishes—“chaste; then peaceable, modest, persuadable, consenting to good things, full of mercy and good fruits, not judging, without simulation. But the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” And the poet says:

> [Col. 0298A] . . . . O gods above, turn this peace far away.
>
> Liberty perishes together with peace.  
> (LUCAN, book III of *The Pharsalian War*; he speaks of Julius Caesar.)

And Cato, seeing that “Caesar was everything” and that the state of the republic was perishing, said: “If you gods dare to endure the Roman commonwealth and liberty being destroyed, I too shall endure it; yet for liberty I shall attempt whatever I can, judging it more honorable that liberty be dragged into slavery than that it go there.” Conversely, King Hezekiah uttered the mildest but worst saying in Isaiah, chap. XXXIX, taking no precaution for the liberty of his descendants that was about to perish: “Let there only be peace and truth in my days” (IV Kings XX).

## CHAPTER CXIV. On patience.

[Col. 0298B]

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for their reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. V). There are only seven perfect beatitudes, completing Jacob’s ladder (Gen. XXVIII), of which we have already spoken. Yet besides these remains patience, which as the eighth returns to the beginning by circling round, purifying, testing, and manifesting all virtues. For as gold is tested in a furnace, so every virtue is tested by patience.

That we may have recourse to it whenever we need it, we must remember God’s patience. Commending it so that we might imitate him in it, the Prophet says in Psalm CXLIV: “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient, long-suffering, and greatly merciful.” And the Apostle, Romans, chap. II: “O man, who do such things, do you despise the riches of the goodness, patience, and long-suffering of God? Do you not know that the goodness and patience of God lead you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works: to those indeed who persevere in good work according to patience, seeking glory and honor and incorruption, eternal life.”

And Isaiah, chap. XLIII: “O Jacob, I formed you for myself as a people, for praise; you have not called upon me, Jacob, nor labored for me, Israel. But you have made me serve your sins; you have given me labor through your iniquities. I am, I am he [Col. 0298D] who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.” Likewise, chap. XLVI: “Hear me, house of Jacob and house of Israel, you who are borne from my womb, carried from my belly. Even to old age I am the same, and to gray hairs I shall carry you; I made you, and I shall bear you; I shall carry you and save you.” See how great God’s patience breathes forth in all these words. Therefore he himself says through Isaiah: “My vineyard, what more ought I to have done for you which I did not do?” (Isa. V). “I have a case against you, because amid all my patience and goodness, you have forgotten me.”

And that we may contemplate more closely the patience of our head and Savior, let us observe that for us, and so that we may deserve to have instruction and an example from his patience, he was made patient even unto the endurance of scourges, blows, spitting, reproaches, and death. (*Collect of the Church for Palm Sunday.*) Hence Isaiah, chap. L: “I did not resist; I did not turn back. I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn away my face from those reviling and spitting upon me. Therefore I set my face like the hardest stone, and I know that I shall not be confounded.” And chap. LIII: “He has neither form nor beauty,” etc. The Lord endured all these things patiently, in order to teach us patience.

Commending its effect to us and showing how necessary it is for a Christian, [Col. 0299B] he says: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke XXI). In other virtues we have our souls; in this we hold them more firmly. And Proverbs, chap. XVI: “The patient person is better than the strong man, and one who rules his spirit than a conqueror of cities.”

> Rule your spirit: unless it obeys, it rules.  
> (HORACE.)

But the Apostle, showing “the more excellent way,” namely charity, at the beginning of its definition (I Cor. XII), placed patience before the other distinctions as its substantial, completing distinction and property, saying: “Charity is patient,” etc. (I Cor. XIII). Likewise, II Corinthians, chap. XII: “Although I am nothing among you, nevertheless the signs of my apostleship were performed among you”—not, I say, in a multitude of retainers, horses, exactions, and worldly display—“but in all patience, in signs, wonders, miracles, and powers.” Thus he put first patience, as the clearer sign of his apostleship and the thing he always needed, as more necessary.

Likewise, in the same epistle, chap. VI: “In all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God: in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in vigils, fasts,” etc. Here also he placed patience first. And the Lord, speaking in Luke of the seed that was sown, says in chap. VIII: “But that which fell on good ground are those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, retain it and bear fruit in patience.” [Col. 0299D] And the poet:

> Patience, greatest of virtues, fights unarmed  
> And often overcomes armed men.  
> (PRUDENTIUS.)

And likewise:

> The serpent, thirst, the heat of the sand—  
> Patience gladly finds harsh things sweet to virtue;  
> What is honorable is sweeter the more greatly it costs one.  
> (LUCAN, *On Cato*, book X.)

Likewise James, chapter V: “Take as an example, brethren, of a grievous penal outcome, long-suffering, labour, and patience, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of Job’s endurance and have seen the end of Christ.” [Col. 0300A] He does not say “the end of Job,” though he could have done so, lest we should expect with Job, in this present life, accumulated prosperity after adversity. He therefore added concerning Christ’s end—of whom it is said, “With the Lord God are the issues of death” (Ps. LXVII)—that he endured adversities and persecutions from birth until death. This is also to be understood of the end of consummation. For Christ, through the end of death, came to the end of consummation. Hence: “O fools, and slow of heart to believe! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer and thus to enter into his glory?” (Luke XXIV). And you, if you wish to enter into glory, must enter it through patience and suffering. “For Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps,” etc. (I Pet. II).

And Jerome says (Letter to Eustochium, *On the Keeping of Virginity*): Only through patience is fulfilled what Scripture says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI). And again: Who among the saints was crowned without patience? From the Church’s cradle there has never been lacking in her iniquity that oppresses, and righteousness that endures. And another Scripture says (Gregory, *Dialogues*, book I, ch. 5): The insult inflicted proves how great each person’s merit is before God.

Likewise Jerome, to Eustochium (in the epitaph of Paula, Eustochium’s mother): To acquire patience, step for a little while outside this prison—that is, the mortal body—and paint before your eyes the reward of eternal recompense, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II); and you will be harder [Col. 0300C] than stone and diamond, unless you have patience, regarding every punishment as “nothing, so that you may gain Christ” (Phil. III); because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII); yet “this momentary affliction produces in us an exceeding weight of glory” (II Cor. IV).

Hence the Apostle says to the Romans, chapter III: “We glory also in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience; and patience, testing; and testing, hope,” etc. And in chapter VIII: “If we hope for what we do not see, through patience amid adversities we await it.” Again: “Be patient toward all, but especially toward those of the household of faith” (Gal. VI).

Likewise the Psalmist David: “For the winepresses” (Ps. VIII), that is, for the churches which in the present age are in winepresses and pressures, like wine, so that, finally clarified through the winepresses and purified, they may be stored in the Lord’s cellar as the finest wine; and lest the Lord should object: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. LXIII). 270 Likewise: “My bone was not hidden from thee, which thou hast made in secret, and my substance in the lower parts of the earth” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Likewise: “The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Ps. XXXIII).

This virtue above all others healed the possessed man and triumphed over the possession. When a hermit came to the city to sell his small wares, and, having offered one cheek, offered the other to be struck, the demon departing from the man uttered this voice: “By patience alone I was conquered; by this alone I lost the vessel which I had firmly possessed.” And this is the test of virtues and of a good man: what no other virtue is.

For he who at an inflicted injury, or a slight or grave insult, grows hot, swells, and bursts, is devoid of this virtue. He is like a scorpion which, when trodden upon, vomits forth its stings and wounds with its curved blow; when it is not trodden upon, it is not at all venomous or to be feared by passers-by. For it lets them go away freely.

Likewise, Psalm XXXVII: “But I, as a deaf man, did not hear; and as a mute man not opening his mouth. And I became as a man who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth.” These are the words [Col. 0301B] of the Saviour, and likewise of every penitent, so that he may know that he is not penitent unless he feels himself patient through the threefold cord of patience: namely, that he has patience against an insult of the mouth, against loss of property, and even against injury to his own body. For it is not enough that you have patience against one of these unless you have it against every one, as did Christ also, “who, when he was reviled, did not revile” (I Pet. II). When he was stripped of his garments, beaten with blows, and crucified (Matt. XXVII), “he became as a lamb that is silent before its shearer and does not open its mouth” (Isa. LIII).

Of this patience it is said: “The patience of the poor shall not perish for ever” (Ps. IX). For no one is known to be a Christian before he is girded and tested with this threefold cord of patience. Hence Satan says to the Lord, Job chapter II: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life; but put forth thy hand and touch his bone and flesh, and then thou wilt see that he will bless thee to thy face.”” Yet even if Job had not thus been tested through bodily injury, he was nevertheless inwardly ready to bear it patiently. Nor can he be said to have had patience against bodily injury which he did not undergo; but if he had died before the event, would he therefore have been judged impatient? Many are patient in mind, yet fail in the very act of injuries; and they seem previously to have lacked patience. Hence:

> He who fell was not himself standing on stable ground.  
> (Boethius, *Consolation*, book I, metre 1.)

“And that house which fell was not founded upon firm rock” (Luke VI).
