Saint Bernard also used to say that, if a sword hung over his head, he believed he would fail in martyrdom; nevertheless, he had the disposition to suffer. Shall such persons then be judged impatient? Far from it! For patience, when provoked by injuries, often perishes; and often, though not previously possessed, it is given and grows amid pressures: “For the judgments of God are hidden” (Rom. II).

Therefore he is patient who “denies himself, takes up his cross daily, and follows” 271 Christ (Luke IX). The cross is borne in four ways. Christ bore it first on his shoulders, like a garment, to the place of suffering. Secondly, Simon of Cyrene bore it under forced service (Matt. XXVII), perhaps in order to hasten the Lord’s passion. Thirdly, the two thieves bore it for their sins; but one of them exchanged the punishment of guilt for the meritorious patience of life. Five points are to be noted concerning him.

First, he accused himself, saying: “We indeed receive the due reward of our deeds” (Luke XXIII).—“The wise man, at the beginning of his speech, is his own accuser” (Prov. XVIII).

Second, he rebuked his neighbour, who blasphemed the Just One.

Third, he commended the Just One, saying: “But what evil has this man done?” (Luke XXIII).

Fourth, he implored pardon: “Remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom” (ibid.).

Fifth, he was heard, in the forgiveness of sins granted to him and in the blessedness soon to be bestowed: “Today,” he says, “thou shalt be with me in paradise” (ibid.).

But he represents the type of every penitent, who ought to imitate him in the matters just mentioned. Fourthly, the Lord bore the cross more closely to himself, because it was fixed to his flesh and sewn to it with nails, for the accomplishment of righteousness. Hence: “Government has been placed upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX).

The two final modes are good, because they are for righteousness. The first is that of penitents: through compassion for one’s neighbour, mortification of the flesh, and endurance of adversities, so that the penitent may say: “I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). For daily I take up my cross and follow Christ. The Church prays that she may have this mode, saying (*Collect of the Church, Friday within Passion Week*):

> Grant, O Lord, that, restraining sins by voluntary chastisement, we may rather be afflicted by temporal punishments than assigned to eternal torments. Burn here; cut here.

The first mode, therefore, belongs to the imperfect—namely, those who are an atom of Christ’s testimonies. The final mode belongs to the perfect, namely martyrs, who are “a heap of witness” (Gen. XXXI). The two middle modes of bearing are evil unless a person converts the punishment of guilt into the testimony of patience. But under forced service the cross is borne for three reasons: either from slavish fear, like a slave; or from shame, like many religious, who are ashamed to leave the cloister because of what people may say; or for human praise, like a hypocrite.

As we have said, therefore, threefold patience must be opposed to threefold persecution. For how will one who cannot endure insulting words endure losses of property? And how will one who cannot endure losses endure death and torments? The philosopher too urges patience with words (Seneca, *On Constancy*), saying: “The insults of the ignorant must be borne with equanimity; and for one proceeding toward honourable things, their contempt must be despised, ‘where contempt is helpful.’” And again: What does it matter whether these *garciones* [see notes; perhaps “boys” or “serving-lads”] thunder above or below? As in their rear, so too they stink in their mouths. Their words also, therefore, should be despised through patience as dung. Nor should you care if you are despised by such people, because to despise the world, to despise no one, to despise oneself, and to despise being despised—these are four good things, but the last is greater.

Of the second [Col. 0303A] and third patience the Apostle says in Hebrews, chapter X: “You were made a spectacle by reproaches and tribulations; you received the plundering of your goods with joy, knowing that you have a better and abiding possession. Do not therefore lose your confidence, which has a great reward. For patience is necessary for you, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise.” And in chapter XII he adds: “Therefore, having so great a cloud of witnesses laid upon us, laying aside every weight and the sin that surrounds us, let us run with patience to the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame. Consider therefore him who endured such contradiction against himself from sinners, lest you grow weary and faint in your souls. For you have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.” You cannot yet say with Christ: “I will receive the cup of salvation” (Ps. CXV), though only there is worthy recompense, where blood is repaid by blood.

Three things, however, aid the patience of grace: natural patience, which comes from a certain natural vigour; habit; and the promise of rewards. By natural patience Alexander found his army enduring hardships (Quintus Curtius and the other writers who recorded the deeds of Alexander the Great should be read), [Col. 0303C] when he tested it by leading it beneath the torrid zone for a day’s march without drink, until they reached a certain river. Of this too a certain righteous man said: “Man is the animal most patient of labours; he can bear more than he thinks. But weariness with easy things has made everything difficult for us. We fear things because they are not difficult; but because we fear them, they are difficult.”

Habit also helps greatly. Hence: “Accustom yourself to what you bear badly, and you will bear it lightly.” And Cicero says in *On Duties*: “Each person must choose a manner of life; habit will make it sweeter and more tolerable.” But we have weakened and enervated ourselves through luxuries, so that we cannot endure even Christian labours and contests. Above all, it may be objected against us that, with patience freely given and for so great a reward, we cannot bear what pagans endured through natural patience, often for an dishonourable cause.

Hence the philosopher says (Seneca, Letter 24): “Metellus endured exile bravely, and Rutilius even willingly. The one endured it in order that he might return to the Republic; the other refused his return to Sulla, to whom at that time nothing was refused. Socrates disputed in prison and, though there were persons promising escape, refused to leave; he remained in order to remove from humankind fear of the two gravest things, death and prison. Mucius put his hand into the fire [manuscript: *imposuit*, ‘placed’]. It is bitter to be burned; how much more bitter if you suffer it by your own act! You see a man uneducated and furnished with no precepts against death or pain, equipped only with military courage, exacting from himself the penalty for an unsuccessful attempt; nor did he remove his hand, running down to the bare bones, before the fire was withdrawn from him by his enemy.” [Col. 0304A] He could have done something more fortunate in that camp, but nothing braver. See how much keener courage is in embracing dangers than cruelty in inflicting them. Porsena more readily pardoned Mucius for wishing to kill him than Mucius pardoned himself for not having killed him.

A similar saying is found in the Legend of Blessed Vincent, who says: “When I am tortured, I can endure more by my resolution than you who torture me can inflict.” 273 Seneca says (Letter 4): “It is difficult to bring the mind to contempt for life”—which, for honour’s sake, is very far from being the case! Do you not see from what trifling causes life is despised? One man hangs himself before his mistress’s door; another throws himself from a roof lest he hear his angry master any longer; another, lest he be brought back from flight, drives a sword into his entrails.

It should be noted that there is patience of nature, patience of grace, as we have said, and patience of sin, which is more properly called remissness. This is asinine patience: namely, bearing what ought not to be borne. Holy and good impatience is opposed to it. Inflamed by this, Jeremiah says in chapter XX: “The word of the Lord has become in my heart as a burning fire, shut up in my bones; and I grew weary, unable to bear the insults and terror of many.” Of this Isaiah says, chapter LXIII: “My indignation itself helped me.” By this Phinehas struck with his dagger those who were coupling together (Num. XXV); by this Moses, armed, killed the idolaters, “going from gate to gate” (Exod. XXXII), lest the whole people should perish; [Col. 0304C] by this Samuel killed Amalek, whom Saul had spared against the Lord’s command (I Sam. XV). With this zeal Peter struck Ananias and Sapphira dead (Acts V); he also cursed Simon Magus: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII). With this the Lord cast buyers and sellers out of the Temple (Matt. XXI). For it is written: “Zeal for thy house has consumed me,” etc. (Ps. LXVIII).

Of this it is written: “Faintness seized me because of sinners who forsake thy law” (Ps. CXVIII). And: “My zeal made me waste away” (ibid.). And again: “Who is weak, and I am not on fire?” etc. (II Cor. XI). And again: “Ready to punish every disobedience and contradiction” (II Cor. X). And in Ezekiel, chapter XI: “The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon me.” And in Ecclesiasticus, chapter II: “Whatever shall be brought upon thee,” etc. Again there: “Woe to those who have lost endurance,” etc. And in Ecclesiastes, chapter VII: “Do not be quick to anger”; and: “The patient man is better than the proud.” In Proverbs, chapter XIV: “He who is patient is governed by much prudence.” Again, chapter XVI: “The patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own mind than a conqueror of cities.” And: “It is better to be humbled with the meek than to divide spoils with the proud.” Likewise Proverbs, chapter XIX: “A man’s wisdom is known by patience.” Again: “He who is impatient will suffer loss.” James, chapter I: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation,” etc. The same, chapter V: “Behold, we call blessed those who endured,” etc. II Kings, chapter XV: “David fled barefoot from Absalom’s presence.” [Col. 0305A] Likewise chapter XVI, in which “Shimei curses David, and David does not allow himself to be avenged.”

## CHAPTER CXV

### On the four cardinal [principal] virtues

As seven is the number of the seven beatitudes (Matt. V), and fifteen that of the fifteen degrees, so four, perfect and solid, is the number of the four cardinal virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, 274 and justice. Prudence is the wise and most orderly choice by which we prefer eternal things to transient things, virtues to vices, our homeland to exile, and freedom to servitude. Concerning this choice Augustine says to Macedonius (Letter 52): “Virtue is nothing other than loving what ought to be loved. Prudence is choosing what ought to be chosen; fortitude is not being turned away from it by any troubles; temperance is not being turned away from it by any enticements; justice is not being turned away from it by any pride.”

In these few words, then, the perfection of the Christian life has been shown. This is the four-horse chariot by which those who have no abiding city here seek the city to come (Heb. XIII).

Blessed indeed was the chariot by which Elijah the Tishbite was carried up into heaven: it deferred death, but did not escape it (IV Kings II). But this one is much more blessed: whoever ascends it “shall not taste death for ever” (John VIII). Nor would the prophet have found that figurative fire unless he had first mounted this chariot.

## CHAPTER CXVI

### On prudence

[Col. 0305C] The first wheel and foot of this saving vehicle is prudence, by which we separate what ought to be loved from what ought not to be loved, and useful things from harmful ones. But it is most difficult to know how to distinguish prudence, discernment, and knowledge; the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; the works of virtues, virtues themselves, and their roots. For all alike make honey of heavenly honey. Yet prudence mingles itself with every virtue and good work; it encompasses, governs, measures, completes, and perfects them all.

Commending it, the Lord says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X). “Who is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household?” (Luke XII). “The prudent virgins took oil in their vessels with their lamps” (Matt. XXV); the foolish did not, because they were imprudent. And the Lord says in Leviticus, chapter II: “Whatever you offer, season with salt; in every offering you shall offer salt.” “The king’s honour loves judgment” (Ps. XCVIII). And Peter says in the first Epistle, chapter IV: “Be therefore prudent, and watch in prayers.” And Ecclesiasticus, chapter XX: “A prudent man will please great men.” And the Apostle: “Let your service be reasonable” (Rom. XII), lest anything be excessive or deficient. Hence Ecclesiastes, chapter VII: “Do not be excessively righteous”; for there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness. And Proverbs, chapter XVIII: “The prudent heart shall possess wisdom.” And chapter XVI: “He who is wise in heart shall be called prudent.” And chapter IX: “The knowledge of holy things is prudence.”

At the council of the holy Pallidores [uncertain reading], when Macarius had placed sobriety as his equal contribution in the symbol of virtues, another fasting and abstinence, another frequent vigils, and the like, Antony, prince of hermits, added discernment, by which all the other things were to be seasoned.

## CHAPTER CXVII

### On fortitude

We know, however, that many who have professed virtue, and who through prudence had chosen what ought to be chosen, have failed when adversity struck. For example, the children of Israel wisely chose to leave Egypt, since they wisely resolved to obey the Lord’s counsel and commandments; but in the wilderness they impatiently endured the discomforts of thirst (Exod. XVI). They also, amid the attacks of enemies and the hardships of the journey, longed for the pots of meat, returning in desire to the melons and garlic of Egypt (Num. XI), though they ought to have forgotten what lay behind and stretched forward to what lay ahead (Phil. III).

Thus adversity breaks many religious; and, as you will find written, unless everything is available at their beck and call, they are cast down by the smallest matters. While poverty burns them, while contempt tortures them, while they behold persons exalted and splendid, whom either choice or law has made heirs, they fly back in disgust to riches; they complain that glory has been taken from them; they envy their own. And, what is a great loss to the religious life they have undertaken, while they sigh for the small things they abandoned, they do not consider how great a reward they expect for what they left behind. Such persons indeed choose uselessly the good things which should be loved, since, terrified by the storms mentioned above, they turn their minds back to things not to be loved.

Fortitude must therefore be added to prudence, so that, in holding fast to what we wisely choose, we may resist most bravely the troubles that arise. By this virtue Paul resisted the thorn of the flesh and the angel of Satan. By it he was armed in prisons and in all the afflictions which he enumerates to the Corinthians, when he said: “For when I am weak, then I am stronger” (II Cor. XII), and powerful.

What, then, is the difference between patience and fortitude? Patience consists in enduring adversities; fortitude in resisting and acting against evils. By this virtue David preserved his innocence amid adversities; by it he spared Saul when Saul persecuted him (I Sam. XXIV); [Col. 0306D] by it, when he heard of the death of the son whom he had begotten by Bathsheba, he consoled himself and ate (II Sam. XII). We too must have recourse to it when we are beset by different things. For it is difficult to resist adversities until victory unless fortitude is joined with prudence.

Commending this, God says: “Be strong in battle. When a strong man armed keeps his court, all that he possesses is in peace” (Luke XI). But “who shall find a strong woman? Her worth is from afar and from the uttermost bounds” (Prov. XXXI). “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII). And I Peter, chapter V: “Your adversary the devil goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith.” And Proverbs, chapter X:

> The wealth of a rich man is the city of his strength, and like [Col. 0307A] a strong wall surrounding him.

And chapter XII: “The hand of the strong shall rule; but that which is slack shall serve tribute.” And chapter X: “The hand of the strong procures riches.” And Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXX: “A healthy poor man, strong in body, is better than a rich man who is weak and scourged by illness.”

## CHAPTER CXVIII

### On temperance

When these have been joined together, temperance must necessarily be added, to preserve virtue in prosperity, as it has been preserved in adversity by fortitude. Nothing is so harmful to virtue as the admixture of pleasure in permitted things. An enemy whose entry is expected to be peaceful is carelessly guarded against. Thus a good purpose often collapses when the mind resists enticements less firmly and recoils; when it is relaxed by prosperity; when it loves honour lavishly bestowed; when it grows insolent through unusual circumstances.

Through this luxury and fall of intemperance, God’s beloved departed from God, of whom it is said: “The beloved grew fat and departed; grown fat, thickened, and enlarged, he kicked; he forsook God his maker and departed from God his saviour” (Deut. XXXII). The Lord also, to instruct us in temperance, withdrew from the crowds who wished to seize him and make him their king, refusing the heights of offered rank (John VI).

Therefore, lest any delights wrest from you the fruit of your religious life, fear to exceed the bounds of temperance—in enticements, in prosperity (such as reputation, eloquence, birth, rank, wealth, and the like), and in virtue and good works. For temperance commonly rests below what is permitted and good, and never proceeds beyond it. If it is lacking, the other virtues either fall from their height or do not rise to it; indeed, they are often in vice. For without temperance, the exercise of any virtue is impulse, not reason:

> … Impulse mismanages all things.  
> (Statius, *Thebaid*, book II.)

Temperance measures one’s strength and does not depart from the mean. Hence it now exerts what is relaxed and now moderates what is arduous; thus it preserves, perfects, and carries the virtues through to their reward. Through it

> The wise person sets a limit even to honourable matters,  
> (Juvenal, *Satires*, VI)

that is, a limit to chastisement. For it is the bridle and matronly band by which breasts overly full of milk are bound and restrained. In the aforesaid chariot it claims the third place for itself, prepared against excess, against every superfluity, and to encounter the robberies of pleasures.

By this you must gradually cut away the habit of luxuries: reject the assiduousness of attendants, festive adornment, and entirely unlearn foreign perfumes. When these things give you a base pleasure in others, or give others a base pleasure in you, they wound the integrity of souls. Habit is hard to unlearn; and most difficult of all to uproot is the habit which has held us for a long time and pleased us with much delight. From it a graver enemy awaits us.

I call “enemy” delights frequented from the cradle, a husband’s affection, children, the diligence of servants, [Col. 0308A] and every temporal happiness. These are disciplined and restrained by temperance when a person begins to be exalted because of the things just mentioned; but restraining pride is justice’s office. There is, however, a difference between the office of justice and that of temperance: a person often grows proud even because of temperance, and justice restrains that pride. Therefore through temperance we resist even permitted enticements, lest in them we exceed measure by doing something useless. This is called sobriety by some, moderation by the Apostle: “Let your moderation be known to all men” (Phil. IV); and “measure” by a certain wise man, just as fortitude is called magnanimity by the philosopher.

## CHAPTER CXIX

### On justice

[Col. 0308B] Perhaps you think the matter accomplished and boast of complete victory if neither adversity nor prosperity has wrested from you your purpose of religious life. But you deceive yourself badly and dream of empty health if the swellings of pride have not yet been subdued by the poultice of justice—that is, humility—which renders to each what is his own, presumes nothing of itself, regards nothing as its own or perfect, and reflects that what it has may be lost.

Pride infects the entire body of virtue; its vital strength withers, and every beautiful thing is deformed (see above, ch. X). Pride, heavenly by origin, seeks lofty minds and, as though returning to its native source, bursts into the glory and purity of human beings—the glory and purity from which it burst forth among angels. It triumphed first in heaven and then on earth. As it was wholly innate in angels, so that it would not depart from them, it infected human beings so as to separate them from God; and, having cast down angel and human being, it proceeds to tempt God, so that him whom it saw as a companion in likeness of nature it might make a companion in ruin as well.

This first and final destruction conquered before all vices and is conquered after all of them. For after the faithful soul, emerging from the abyss of vices, has climbed the saving height of virtues, pride suddenly leaps out as from an ambush and assails it, about to shake down into ruin the entire building of the Lord’s house which had risen toward completion. For what is more ruinous to a righteous person than desiring to seem righteous; than being delighted and exulting at greetings in the marketplace; than being softened by flattering favour; than, almost forsaking humanity, measuring and pretending himself equal to those above? While he glories wrongly and presumes to be what he is not, he is cast down into confusion and loses what he is; and he becomes so much the farther from God through the wall of pride as he had seemed to himself nearer through the height of virtues. Hence: “A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand” (Ps. XC).

You see, therefore, how great a destruction of character pride is, and how necessary humility is in deeds well done. Without humility, choosing through prudence what ought to be loved is erroneous discernment; overcoming adversities through fortitude is boastful victory; resisting enticements through temperance is drunken sobriety. Hence a fourth wheel must be joined to these—the one Augustine (Letter LII) calls justice [Col. 0309A] as the completion and concluding seal of all virtues—by which the Lord’s chariot, in which one ascends to heaven, is completed; by which the lost sheep is returned to the flock; by which the grain is led or brought into the Lord’s granary.

These are the four rivers of paradise (Gen. II), by which the earth of our hearts, drenched and watered, “brings forth fruit in patience” (Luke VIII). These are the four corners of Job’s house (Job I), upon which a wind rushing in crushed his seven feasting sons. So too, when temptation floods and rushes into the house of conscience and good will, though supported by the four virtues, it often overturns that house, killing and suffocating the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit that were nourished in it.

Therefore presume nothing in any respect; and, even with your house founded upon firm rock (Matt. VII), cry fearfully with Peter: “Lord, save me” [Col. 0309B] (Matt. XIV). And cling against every temptation to this threefold cord: presume nothing of yourself, but “cast thy thought upon the Lord” (Ps. LIV); despair of nothing from God, but strengthen your heart in your salvation (Ps. XII); glory and exult not in yourself but in God. “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I). “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. VI).

Remember to make from this cord a scourge, by which the worldly tumult and the crowd of pleasures may be expelled from the temple of your breast (Matt. XXI); through which the itch of luxuries may flee, softness be despised, variety of dishes be scorned, the glitter of gems and elaborate vessels be trampled down, and the pride of lineage and power may fall. Let kings be preferred to palaces, haircloth to linen, contempt to favour, and injuries to services. Delighting in such pursuits, God will be to you the fruit of your labour: in him you will attain all good things, and he will feed and satisfy you in his eternal glory.

## CHAPTER CXX

### On truth

We have spoken above concerning the face of nature, and also the face of grace, to which Truth belongs; and whoever wishes to imitate Christ, the author of truth, must possess it. It is commended in Christ the head, who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV): the way in example, truth in promise, life in reward; or, the way of holy conduct, truth of heavenly and spiritual teaching, and life of eternal blessedness.

Of him also it is said: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV). And: “Mercy and truth have met together” (ibid.). “Because of truth going before, and meekness and righteousness” (Ps. XLIV). “The beginning of thy words is truth,” etc. (Ps. CXVIII). “Thy word is truth” (John XVII). The Father is truthful, the Son is truthful, and the Holy Spirit is truthful. “All thy commandments are truth” (Ps. CXVIII); and: “Thy truth is round about thee” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

But whoever is a liar is a child of the devil, the author of lying; but, O Christ, “thou wilt destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. V). Jerome says (in his commentary on the same Psalm): “I hear something new: namely, that the Lord, who says, ‘I have hated the unrighteous’ (Ps. CXVIII), hates wicked persons and will destroy all who speak falsehood.”

Lamenting the lack of truth, David says: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy man has failed; for truths have been diminished among the children of men,” etc. (Ps. XI). Likewise: “Every man is a liar” (Ps. CXV). Inviting us to this virtue, Ecclesiasticus says in chapter XXXVII: “The soul of a holy man sometimes declares truths more than seven watchmen sitting on high to keep watch. In all things pray to the Most High that he may direct thy way in truth.” Likewise: “Before all your works let a truthful word and steadfast counsel go before you” (ibid.).

Hence concerning Saint Sebastian (see his Life in Surius, 20 January): truthful in speech, prudent in counsel, faithful in things entrusted, outstanding in every honourable quality of character. Likewise Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXV: “My soul hated three kinds: a proud poor man, a lying rich man, and an old man foolish and without understanding. Blessed is he who finds his friend true.” Again, chapter XLI: “Be ashamed before father and mother of fornication; before ruler and powerful man of a lie; before prince and judge of an offence,” etc. For lying is especially unbecoming in a powerful person.

Again, chapter XIII: “Every man loves one like himself, as every animal loves its like”: the liar loves the liar, and the truthful person the truthful. Chapter XV: “Foolish and lying people shall not attain wisdom, nor remember it; but truthful persons shall be found in it and shall prosper until the sight of God.” Proverbs, chapter XVI: “Well-ordered words are a honeycomb”; but truth does not seek corners; plain words befit goodness. Again, chapter XXIX: “A ruler who gladly hears lying words has all his ministers wicked” and lying; for as the ruler of a city is, so is its minister.

Likewise: After an oath especially, truth is greater than religious observance. Likewise, in the saying of a wise man: A lie, like the vice of gluttony, is sticky and clinging. For more mature age often puts an end to other vices, but by no means to lying, just as not to gluttony. For we eat every day, we speak every day, and thus one more easily falls into these vices and more difficultly unlearns them.

There is a twofold truth: namely, truth of statement, which consists [Col. 0310D] in the joining of predicate to subject, so that the thing is as it is said to be; and this is the philosopher’s truth (Aristotle, *On Interpretation*, ch. 5). And there is the truthfulness of the speaker, which consists in the speaker’s intention, whether he has said what is false or what is true. For a wise man often changes his plan for more useful reasons, as did the Apostle; and this is the theologian’s truth. In this sense it is said: “A priest’s words are either true or sacrilegious”: true by truthfulness rather than by the truth which consists in the predicate’s correspondence to the subject. Now someone is often true, yet not truthful, and is therefore a liar. If both are possible, that is well; if not, always be truthful. Likewise, in 2 Corinthians, chapter 1: “When I intended” to come to you and did not come, “did I use fickleness?” Far from it! For it belongs to a wise man to alter even a plan reasonably formed [Col. 0311A] for one that is more useful and more honourable. In me there is not “yes and no,” because “God is faithful,” whose imitator I am (1 Cor. 11), “and in him there is not yes and no”; he “has also sealed us” with truth, as though distinguishing us from others by this his own mark. Likewise, the philosopher says: Truth distinguishes a free man and separates him from a slave. For lying belongs to slaves, not sons. But is not every man a liar? Yes—but only in respect of a lie (*menda*). For “if we say that [280] we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Every human being is also a liar in himself, but truthful in God.

There is also a threefold truth considered in relation to an uncombined thing. First, there is the truth which is the unchangeableness of the divine essence, “with whom there is no change, [Col. 0311B] nor shadow caused by turning” (James 1). There is also truth of nature, rather than grace, such as chastity and similar virtues.

The virtue of a philosopher is genuine according to the truth of nature, not of grace. The sacraments administered by heretics in the Church’s form are likewise true with sacramental truth, though not efficacious truth; yet they eat bread sacrilegiously, apart from its effect, and so forth. There is also the truth of grace, namely created charity. And this twofold truth should, if possible, always be referred to the first. Therefore, since truth is especially the sign of Christian religion, the greatest care and attention must be given lest it be extinguished either in ourselves or in others. “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5). For even by the Socratic principle [Col. 0311C] it is no less a sin to keep silent about truth than to speak falsehood; indeed, it is often the greater sin, according to place and time—for example, in correcting one’s neighbour or giving testimony. Advocates fail to notice this when they forbid their clients to state the plain and unadorned truth in their account, teaching them to conceal one part and colour another. Likewise, 3 John; likewise, 1 John, chapter 3; likewise, Ecclesiasticus, chapters 24 and 27.

## CHAPTER 121. On holy and good violence

Holy violence must be joined to truth: by it we rescue ourselves and our neighbours, just as by speaking truth, from the jaws of the wicked enemy; and in him who conquered the world (John 16), we conquer the world and the flesh. Commending this as highly necessary for every believer, both for himself and for his neighbour, the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). Jerome (*On the Same Chapter according to the Sense*, and throughout Epistle 24, falsely ascribed to him): What greater violence is there than that flesh should will to become what spirit is; that man should become God; and that fragile flesh should be in the place from which angelic and heavenly nature fell? Likewise: Therefore be a plunderer of the kingdom of heaven, not of poor souls, money, and flies. Likewise the Lord: “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, his possessions are in peace” (Luke 11). Likewise Genesis, chapter 49: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf: in the morning [Col. 0312A] he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoil.” This refers to appointing different ministers in the Church to different ranks and offices. Likewise (Ps. 67): “The King of hosts, beloved, beloved, shall divide the spoils of the beauty of the house.” Likewise Numbers, chapter 23: “Behold, this people rises like a lioness, and lifts itself up like a lion. It shall not lie down until the lion’s whelp devours the prey and drinks the blood of the slain,” incorporating them into Christ and the Church with Peter, to whom it was said: “Slay in the commandments and eat” (Acts 10), by transferring the commandments into the body of the Church. Slay [281] and make alive; or, “until it drinks the blood of the slain,” that is, until it destroys the sins of those slain by the devil. For what is drunk is consumed and departs from its former condition. In this word also observe how great [Col. 0312B] should be the thirst and eagerness to plunder the devil and rescue yourself and your neighbour from his jaws—especially if you are a prelate, learned, and instructed. Yet everyone ought to have this thirst. In the name “lioness,” of feminine gender, note maternal affection; in the name “lion,” the father’s blows. The lion’s cub is roused by its father’s roar. So too the Lord now soothes us with prosperity, now frightens us by adversity, by the roar and thunder of the threats of Gehenna, and wakes us from torpor; each of his words is like a separate thunderclap.

Likewise Isaiah, chapter 9: “For every violent plundering with tumult, and a garment mingled with blood, shall be for burning, fuel for the fire.” But holy [Col. 0312C] violence is the daughter of fortitude, and so should more suitably be joined to it: by it we conquer the world—that is, worldly occupations, prosperity, and adversity; also the devil—that is, “spiritual wickednesses” (Eph. 6), envy, and the like; and likewise the flesh—that is, fleshly enticements—“crucifying it with its vices and concupiscences” (Gal. 5), and “bearing the marks of the Lord Jesus in our bodies” (Gal. 6), setting violence against violence. Hence in Psalm 136: “O wretched daughter of Babylon,” yet “blessed” is the penitent “who repays you the recompense” and return “which you rendered to us!”—healing opposites by opposites, laughter by weeping, gluttony by abstinence, and thereafter repaying the flesh with harsh things for the pleasant things it desires.

[Col. 0312D] “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash” your little ones, lest they grow wild and great—your first impulses—“against the rock,” Christ (1 Cor. 10), lest the little foxes destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts (Song 2). “You shall break the heads of the dragons in the waters” (Ps. 73), and crush the head of the serpent lying in wait for your heel (Gen. 3), so that “your chastening may be in the mornings” (Ps. 72), because:

> Too late is the remedy prepared  
> when evils have gained strength through long delay.  
> —Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, bk. 1; Gregory, *Dialogues*, bk. 2, ch. 2

Blessed Benedict employed this holy violence when he threw himself into nettles, in order to restrain and overcome pain by pain. That martyr employed [Col. 0313A] it who cut off his own tongue in order to throw it, bloody, into a prostitute’s mouth and thus conquer lust. You may gather many other examples of the saints concerning this.

(Jerome, *Life of Paul the Hermit*.) This holy violence even extends to God himself, so that a man may dare to contend with him, though piously. Thus Jacob is remembered to have wrestled with an angel; Jacob prevailed, and so was given the name “Israel” (Gen. 32). The angel yielded, as though to say: Do not fear your brother Esau, you who prevail over God in combat. We too in some manner prevail in those matters concerning God which we grasp with the mind; but in those which we cannot grasp, we undoubtedly yield. [Col. 0313B] Therefore, to use the words of blessed Gregory (*Homilies on Ezekiel*, bk. 2, homily 14): Jacob wrestles, and the angel is overcome, when God is apprehended by inward understanding; he wrestles and yields, because, when he strives to comprehend the unbounded light, he fails. And [282] it should be noted that although Jacob prevailed in the wrestling match, the angel nevertheless touched and withered the sinew of his thigh: because when the mind in contemplation apprehends divine delights, through desire for them the affection of the flesh withers. For once the spirit has been tasted, all flesh loses savour. When one sinew has been dried up, one foot remains sound and the other is weak, because when fleshly concupiscence is mortified in us, the right foot, by which we are directed to God, grows strong, while the left, by which we turn away from God, becomes weak. Here too I think it should be noted that [Col. 0313C] Jacob, struck in the thigh, rests more firmly on his sound foot, while the infirm foot neither wholly adheres to the earth nor is wholly raised from it: for Jacob is little supported by it, because it touches the earth little and is suspended a little. For when love or delight in worldly things languishes in us, we lean upon one part of them because of nature and are suspended from the remainder because of the crown. In the former lies what we seek out of necessity; in the latter, what we avoid by counsel. “For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope” (Rom. 8). And: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from all things” (2 Cor. 9). But in the future, when the enticements of our mortality have dried up, the whole human person, made upright, will rest upon and cling to divine love. Yet no one will thus stand erect there unless he has first limped here with a good limp.

There is a threefold limping which is a mortal fault. Thus he limps who accepts one Testament without the other, as the Ebionites accept the New without the Old; or he who worships God for temporal as well as eternal things. Hence: “How long do you limp between two sides? If Baal is God, worship him,” etc. (3 Kings 18). “You cannot serve two masters” (Luke 16). “You cannot enter the land by two ways” (Ecclus. 2). “A short cloak cannot cover both” (Isa. 28). To avoid such limping, the Apostle says: “Lift up your slackened knees and your feeble hands” toward God, “lest anyone who is lame go astray, but rather be healed” (Heb. 12). There is also a lawful limping arising from human weakness. Married persons limp in this way, since [Col. 0314A] they do not follow the Lamb “on both feet,” as virgins do (Rev. 14): not possessing that most excellent bodily integrity which virgins have, although they have integrity of mind. There is also a limping of virtue and grace, by which “Jacob limped” (Gen. 32), and those limp who use temporal things only for nature’s need and suspend themselves from the rest for the crown.

## CHAPTER 122. On obedience

The “face of one going to Jerusalem” (Luke 9) is manifold and one, just as the Church, though one, consists of persons of many faces: manifold in the plurality of effects and works of virtues, but one in their root. For when one is possessed, all are possessed. In the spiritual lyre, no more than in a material one, does [Col. 0314B] one string sound harmoniously without the others. Among these faces obedience is eminent, and without it one does not go to Jerusalem. Obedience is compliance with a just thing; [283] or obedience is the effect or execution, by a deliberating mind, of an honourable and just command: of “God,” through Holy Scripture; of “man,” through prelation and dignity, “set over our heads” (Ps. 65). We have an example and model of this virtue in Christ the head. Writing of Christ’s obedience in 1 Corinthians, chapter 15, the Apostle says: “As we have borne the image of the earthly” man, Adam, “let us bear also the image and marks of the heavenly” through obedience. Concerning it the same Apostle says in Philippians, chapter 2: “Have this mind [Col. 0314C] in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man.” Note humility, the mother that conceives and gives birth to obedience. Hence it follows: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” Note patience, the nurse which cherishes, carries, and supports obedience. And although it would seem more fitting to say, “Have in yourselves the mind which was in Christ Jesus,” he said not merely relatively but demonstratively, “Have this,” so that it might be a visible demonstration, because Christ “was seen among men and conversed with men” (Baruch 3), and also an intellectual demonstration because of the thing’s absence.

Likewise, although there are many things which we can “have in mind in Christ Jesus,” since in him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2), he nevertheless says specifically “this,” not “these,” referring this singularity to our small capacity. It is as though he said: If you cannot possess as great a humility, obedience, and patience as Christ possessed, at least “have this in yourselves” which was in him: namely, have this small measure of humility, obedience, and patience, and thus fear him and obey him. Hence Ecclesiasticus, chapter 7: “He who fears God neglects nothing”; he despises nothing but obeys God in all things. Likewise, 1 Kings, chapter 15: Samuel says to Saul: [Col. 0315A] “Does the Lord desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, rather than obedience to the voice of the Lord? Obedience,” he says, “is better than sacrifices, and listening than offering the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is as the crime of idolatry.” There is a threefold obedience: necessary, superabundant, and pernicious. Necessary obedience concerns things pertaining to salvation, such as the command of divine precepts and the imposition of salutary penance. But whether, when commanded in something directed to the public benefit—for example, undertaking a journey to Rome for the Church, receiving an order, and the like—we are bound to obey a superior, is uncertain. For Gregory says (*Pastoral Rule*, part 1, chs. 6–7): A man strong in virtues should not be promoted or ordained except under compulsion; [Col. 0315B] one not strong in virtues, not even under compulsion. And David says: “I shall sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. 53). And the bride in the Song of Songs: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5). I neither affirm nor deny it. Yet if something of this kind should be commanded you, strive and labour to free yourself from the obligation to fulfil the command, lest a scruple be generated in your conscience. Superabundant obedience occurs when we obey in matters which a superior is not bound to command. But we ought rarely to command anything, lest we make many transgressors. Whether we are bound to obey a superior [284] in giving temporal goods is a question, since the Lord says: “What they say,” namely what pertains to the chair, “do” (Matt. 23). Yet it is safer to obey in these matters, as also to relinquish an ecclesiastical benefice, [Col. 0315C] than to possess it with a scruple of conscience. Especially in view of the fact that Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, withdrew from the construction of an unfinished monastery in Spain because he obeyed the brothers who recalled him. Because he always kept this obedience before his eyes, he gave up many good works, preferring the good of obedience to all of them. The one-eyed abbot of Clairvaux [or: Cîteaux], and many other saints, did likewise, maintaining obedience even in matters bordering upon sin. Pernicious obedience consists both in manifest evils and in things opposed to divine commands, or in matters not evil in themselves but from which ruin easily follows. Therefore one must not obey even in these matters; just as neither things which serve truth, helping and fostering it though they are not truth itself, ought to be abandoned [Col. 0315D] because of scandal—no more than plain truth should be abandoned. “He who despises small things shall fall little by little” (Ecclus. 19).

But it is asked whether, when there is a command to fulfil counsels, we are bound to obey a superior. No. Nor can the superior command anyone to fulfil such a counsel—unless he is bound by vow or oath—in which case he is bound to command him to fulfil the vow. Likewise it is asked: Am I bound to render my ministry—I, a bishop, dean, or the like—to the lord pope when he commands that some unworthy person be ordained by me, granted a prebend, and so forth? Likewise: Are clerics bound to be more subject and obedient to their prelates, or lay brothers and monks to their abbots? I say that monks [Col. 0316A] and lay brothers are more bound to their abbots, because of their greater perfection, which binds them more and in more respects to obedience than we are bound to obey prelates. Likewise, Gregory answers in *Morals*, book 35, chapter 10: It must be known that evil is never done through obedience, but good which is being done ought sometimes to be omitted through obedience. Likewise, Deuteronomy, chapter 13; likewise Ecclesiastes, chapter 4: “Guard your foot when entering the house of God, and draw near to hear. For obedience is far better than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know that they do evil.” Likewise Bede on Ecclesiastes, chapter 9: “Whatever good your hand can do, do it promptly.” For obedience is without delay. Likewise Acts, chapter 9: “Behold, I am here, Lord.” [Col. 0316B] Obedience knows no delay. Likewise, blessed Peter, First Epistle, chapter 1.

## CHAPTER 123. On magnanimity

Magnanimity also belongs to this face: it is strength in resisting the adversaries of the Church, in patiently enduring diverse trials. It belongs especially to prelates, who in magnanimity say: “We cannot but speak the things which we have heard [285] and know” (Acts 4). Of such persons it is said: “The spiritual man judges all things and is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2), because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3). God magnifies these before kings. To them the Lord says in Joshua, chapter 1: “Be strong and very courageous, that you may observe and do all the law which Moses my servant commanded you; [Col. 0316C] do not turn from it to the right or to the left.” It should particularly be observed that when he is told, “Be strong,” and so forth, it is so that he may possess magnanimity in mind, speech, and action. Commending this, the philosopher says (in Seneca, *On the Four Virtues*, ch. 2): Consider that nothing is praiseworthy except the mind, to which nothing is great when it is itself great. Likewise Jerome on Ezekiel (vol. 5): Great faith, great boldness of the prophets: Daniel was great, because he dared to say to the elder who added murder to adultery, “Seed of Canaan and not of Judah,” though he was still a boy (Dan. 13). So too Isaiah, who cries (Isa. 1): “Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of our God, people of Gomorrah.” Great also was [Col. 0316D] Ezekiel, who reproved the whole city of Jerusalem for its baseness, saying (Ezek. 16): “Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite.” He even compares her to a prostitute and adulteress. Some grammarians have interpreted this virtue in blessed Thomas—that is, of Canterbury—to have been *tempestas*, “storm.” But pusillanimity and storm surround and destroy this virtue. Praying to be delivered from them, the Prophet says: “Deliver me from faintness of spirit and storm” (Ps. 54). Pusillanimity belongs to hirelings, who are “dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56), who do not set themselves as a wall for the house of God, who do not stand in opposition on the day of battle (Ezek. 13); like the sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, yet turning back on the day of war [Col. 0317A] (Ps. 77), because they seek only milk and wool (Prov. 31), which they do not wish to lose, “whose sheep are not their own, and therefore they flee when they see the wolf coming,” etc. (John 10). Thus pusillanimity consists in not resisting, in not rebuking when necessary. Storm, however, belongs to fools; it may also be called impetuosity of mind, and consists in reproving without observing any circumstances of time, person, character of what is said, and the like. Magnanimity is the mother of fortitude; fortitude is the mother of patience, which is the nurse and proof of all virtues. According to the testimony of blessed Jerome (*At the End of the Epitaph of Paula, His Mother, to Eustochium; Athanasius Describes the Whole History*), it produced the roses of martyrs and the victorious crowns of confessors. By it saints resisted heretics [Col. 0317B] and opposed tyrants. By it Athanasius did not fail in the persecution carried out by heretics and rulers. By it a hermit, coming out of his cell, publicly proclaimed Athanasius a saint, innocent and just. By it Romanus ran to martyrdom, crying: “I am a Christian.” By it Antony stretched out his thin, long neck and wished to submit it to the sword. By it Urban was twice made a confessor. By it that tutor answered the satrap of Julian, who asked what his ragged Galilean was doing—whether he was sleeping, snoring, awake, or eating: “He is preparing a coffin and digging a grave for you, Julian the apostate, to be buried in hell.” By it Nicholas rescued three boys condemned to death and proved their innocence. By it Ambrose [Col. 0317C] expelled and excommunicated Theodosius from the church, because his edict had involved very many [286] just persons along with the wicked at Thessalonica. By it Phinehas struck those who were coupling (Num. 25), “and the plague ceased” (Ps. 105). Because of this Cyprian says: If a bishop is afraid, he is finished. Exercise, labour, and endurance of adversity assist, foster, and strengthen this virtue. For these make spirits noble and great; leisure and rest make them small and slack. An eye that dwells in shade quickly grows dim in the sun. Hence Dionysius did not fear to seek the ferocity of an unbelieving people, because remembrance of past sufferings strengthened his courage. And the philosopher says (Seneca, Epistle 13; Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. 10, chs. 15–17; Eusebius, bk. 8, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 12): I know that you have great courage. For even before you trained yourself by salutary precepts and by precepts that conquer hardships, you were sufficiently pleased with yourself in opposition to fortune; much more after you joined battle with her and tested your strength. These can never give a person certain confidence in himself unless many difficulties have appeared from this side and that, and sometimes have come still closer. Thus that truly great spirit, which will not come under another’s control, is tested. This is its touchstone, as it were, its proving instrument. An athlete who has never been bruised cannot bring great spirit to the contest. The man who has seen his own blood, whose teeth have cracked beneath a blow, who, tripped up, bore his opponent’s entire weight and did not lose heart when thrown down; who, whenever he fell, rose more stubbornly—he enters the fight with great hope. For proved virtue, experienced in hardships and provoked by injuries, adds much to itself.

## CHAPTER 124. On prayer

Among the works of virtues, prayer is greatest; and the chief sign of the “face of one going to Jerusalem” (Luke 9) is to be frequent and assiduous in prayer. A wandering and unstable mind cannot remain long in it. As Augustine testifies (Augustine on Psalm 85), proving this same point from the inner places of Holy Scripture, the two most excellent and distinctive works of a religious man—and especially one living in a cloister—are prayer and reading. [Col. 0318B] Both are good if both can be done; if not, prayer is better and more useful. He who prays speaks with God about salvation; he who reads has God speaking with him. Commending prayer in the Gospel, the Lord says: “This kind of demon cannot go out except by prayer and fasting” (Mark 9); that is, by abstinence from evil and the devotion of prayer, which nourishes the soul in good. Although every good work is called prayer, according to the saying that he does not cease to pray who does not cease to act well, the term is here made specific and restricted: prayer is a devout affection or movement of the mind toward God which, lest it grow sluggish, sometimes breaks forth into speech. David too, commending it, says: “In return for my love they slandered me, but I gave myself to prayer” (Ps. 108): as though to say, in every [287] tribulation I fled to prayer. And likewise Psalm 34: “Unjust witnesses arose, questioning me about things I did not know. They repaid me evil for good, barrenness to my soul. But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth; I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my own bosom.” Armed with prayer, a person can resist every temptation and adversity. Armed with it, Martin drove away every plague and every harmful thing. He fled to it as to his customary weapon when his house—and even his bed, softer and more pleasant than usual—was set ablaze. Finally, when he had no exit open to him, he threw himself to the ground on his knees and extinguished the fire. In the work of prayer he gave himself so wholly that, with eyes and hands always directed toward heaven, even while dying he did not relax his spirit from unconquered prayer. Paul the first hermit (see the life of him written by St Jerome) prayed while dead, because when St Antony found his holy body supported and leaning against a tree, it had the posture of one praying, with mouth and hands raised to heaven. Jerome says of him: “It is evident how constantly and how greatly he prayed to God while alive, since he does not cease to pray while dead.”

## CHAPTER 125. On the effect of prayer

How great prayer’s effect is, see and consider in the more secret things of God, which are made manifest and opened to us by prayer alone. For after prayer had been made in the upper room, when Peter was at Joppa, he saw a vessel [Col. 0319A] suspended from heaven by its four corners, full of creeping things, and was told: “Slay and eat” (Acts 10). By prayer Cornelius was led to Peter, when an angel appeared to him and said: “Cornelius, your prayers have been heard and your alms have been accepted before God. Send and summon Simon,” etc. (ibid.). Likewise Ecclesiasticus, chapter 35: “The prayer of one who humbles himself shall pierce the clouds; and until it approaches, he shall not be comforted, and he shall not depart until the Most High looks upon him.” Likewise, chapter 18: “Do not be hindered from praying always.” Hence the Apostle: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5). Likewise Luke, chapter 3: “When Jesus had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened”; likewise while Martin was praying. The heaven of Holy Scripture was opened to Hilary as he disputed about the Trinity and refuted heretics. [Col. 0319B] Likewise Luke, chapter 9: “Jesus took Peter, James, and John, and went up onto the mountain to pray; and while he was praying, his appearance was changed and his clothing became white and gleaming.” Likewise chapter 11: “Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey and I have nothing to set before him. And he from within, answering, says: Do not trouble me; the door is now shut and my children are with me in bed. And if he persists in knocking, I tell you that even if he does not give to him” immediately, “rising because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needs. And I say to you: ask and it shall be given you; [288] seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and [Col. 0319C] he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it shall be opened.” Ambrose (on Luke 11): Let no one fear that he will wake one who is asleep, when he knows that he is always awake in prayer. And Bede says (*On Luke*, bk. 4, ch. 27): If a human friend rises and gives, compelled not by friendship but by annoyance, how much more does God give, who without annoyance most generously grants what is asked? Likewise, the Lord says to his disciples in Luke, chapter 18: “It is necessary always to pray and not grow weary.” And he set before them the parable of the unjust judge and the shameless widow, who shamelessly or importunately asked him to vindicate her against her adversary, and whom he heard. Therefore the Lord adds: “Hear what the judge of injustice says” and does: “Will not God do justice for his elect who cry out to him day and night, and will he be patient with them? I tell you that he will quickly do justice for those elect.” From this unjust judge—although he in no way represents God’s person—it may be inferred how much the just and good God cares for those who pray to him, since even an unjust man cannot disregard those who seek him with continual prayers, if only to escape annoyance. Likewise, the Apostle was always mindful of those subject to him, praying for them in all his prayers (Phil. 1). Likewise, he trusted that through the prayers of his subjects he would be restored to them while absent (Philem. 22). Likewise (Eph. 6), he asks to be helped by the prayers of his inferiors in opening his mouth to proclaim God’s word to the people. Likewise Jerome to Paula: At the beginning, he says, of every work, precede it with the Lord’s Prayer and the sign of the cross on your forehead. Likewise Augustine on the passage in Acts, chapter 11: “I, Peter, was praying at Joppa,” at which hour and work God would not allow me to be deceived. Therefore neither would he allow another who prays devoutly to be deceived. Hence doubts are better resolved and opened by prayer than by any other inquiry. Likewise, chapter 12: “Peter was kept in prison, but prayer was made without ceasing by the Church to God for him.” It is clear how great the effect of prayer is: it brings Peter out of prison; Daniel out of the lions’ den (Dan. 6); Cornelius out of unbelief (Acts 10); and very many out of death (James 5). It closes and opens the heavens. Likewise, chapter 9: “Ananias, arise; go into the street called Straight, and seek in the house of Judas one Saul, a Tarsian by name, [Col. 0320B] for behold, he is praying,” etc. The Lord himself applied himself to no work as frequently and continually as to prayer, so much so that he often spent the whole night in prayer (Luke 6). And when his Passion was at hand, “being in agony, he prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22). He said also to his disciples: “Watch and pray”—that is, pray watchfully—“lest you enter into temptation. For the spirit is ready, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26). And in Mark, chapter 14, he says: “See” by hope, “watch” by faith, “and pray” by charity. Therefore you too, instructed by the Lord’s example, exhortation, and command, let no other work hinder you from praying; nor be so occupied by other works that you do not have prayer. Likewise James, chapter 1: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach, and it shall be given him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing.” Likewise chapter 5: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a righteous man is of great power” before God. “Elijah prayed that it might not rain on the earth, and it did not rain [289] for three years and six months. And he prayed again, and heaven gave rain and the earth yielded its fruit.” Likewise 1 Peter, chapter 3: “Finally, be all of one mind” in prayer. Likewise chapter 4: “Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers,” etc. Likewise David: “Blessed be the Lord, who has not removed my prayer or his mercy from me” (Ps. 65)—which mercy will not first be removed unless prayer has first been removed.

[Col. 0320D] Likewise 4 Kings, chapter 4: “When Elisha had prayed, the Lord opened the boy’s eyes,” etc. Likewise on Numbers, chapter 27: Successors are sometimes revealed by God to those praying, as Moses was told: “Take to yourself Joshua son of Nun”; and as blessed Martin was told concerning blessed Brice.

## CHAPTER 126. On things impeding prayer

Sloth and acedia impede both the grace and constancy of prayer. Hence Jerome (on Eph. 5): “I would rather,” he says, “chant one psalm with cheerfulness of mind than the entire Psalter with torpor, weariness, and acedia.” (Gregory, *Dialogues*, bk. 2, ch. 4.) Benedict saw one of his monks failing in constancy in prayer, and prayed [Col. 0321A] that the cause which impeded him might be shown to him. While blessed Benedict prayed, he saw the devil, in the appearance of a black boy, pulling back by his hood a monk who wished to pray. Therefore, because of the weariness of prayer, prescribed observances requiring a multitude of canonical hours and psalms to be chanted are dangerous. For Jeremiah says in chapter 48: “Cursed is everyone who does the work of God negligently”; he who prays without devotion calls judgment down upon himself. Likewise, “flies”—that is, vain and fantastic thoughts—“dying,” while others, male or female, continually succeed them, “spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccles. 10). Evagrius the hermit testified that it is difficult to pray without impediment, and more difficult to chant psalms without impediment. Therefore, to remove impediments to prayer, drive away the birds and the importunity [Col. 0321B] of flies from the Lord’s sacrifices, following Abraham’s example (Gen. 15), “with a whip made of cords” (John 2) of virtues. Shake and beat the milk-pail of your breast, so that the flies may come out. “Enter into your chamber and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. 6). Set a prudent maidservant as door-keeper at the door of your house, not like the one who allowed Ish-bosheth to be killed (2 Kings 4). “Turn away your eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118), because we ought not look upon what we may not lawfully desire.

> As soon as I saw, I was undone; how fatal an error carried me away!  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* 8

“Death entered through the window” (Jer. 9); Eve saw that the fruit was beautiful to behold, etc. (Gen. 3). “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lam. 3). [Col. 0321C] Therefore be like Job (chapter 31), who said: “I made a covenant with my eyes”; and you too should make a covenant with all your members, being “crucified with vices and concupiscences” (Gal. 5) and with reproaches. Do not pray except set upon the cross, following the Lord’s example, who, fixed on the cross, prayed to the Father. Be an imitator of Jacob, sanctified [290] from the womb, who, through the assiduity and frequency of his prayers, had knees calloused and hardened like those of camels. Bartholomew bent his knees to God one hundred times by day and one hundred times by night. “Every kind of demon is especially cast out by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17). If lust or another vice troubles you, set yourself a definite number of genuflections together with a litany, and you will escape every temptation.

Moreover, it should be noted that often what is asked for, because it is not conducive to salvation, prevents the effect of prayer; often also those for whom we ask prevent it, because they are unworthy. Hence, on Luke, chapter XI, and Jeremiah, chapter VII: “Therefore do not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer for them.” The same in chapters XI and XIV; likewise Judith, chapter IV. Bede, on that passage: when the Apostle asked for the “thorn of the flesh” to be removed, the Lord said to him: “Paul, my grace is sufficient for you” (I Cor. XII). Likewise Psalm CVIII, on the verse: “And let his prayer become sin.” Gregory (Homily XXVII on the Gospels): In the house of Jesus you do not seek Jesus if, in the temple of eternity, you importunately pray for temporal things.

## CHAPTER CXXVII. On avoiding oaths.

[Col. 0322A]

He who is accustomed to swear does not have “the face of one going to Jerusalem” (Luke IX). For just as “in much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Prov. X), so neither in much swearing will perjury be lacking. That we are altogether forbidden to swear seems clear from the Lord’s words in Matthew, chapter V: “You have heard that it was said to those of old” (Exod. XX): “You shall not commit perjury; but you shall render your oaths to the Lord”—swearing by Him, not by idols or creatures—“but I say to you, do not swear at all,” etc. Likewise James, chapter V: “Before all things, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven nor by earth,” etc.

Likewise, there is the example of Origen’s disciple—Basilides, concerning whom Eusebius writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 4; [Col. 0322B] Rufinus, chapter 5—who became entangled in the legal arguments of the court. When an oath concerning the faithful administration of a stewardship was demanded from him, he replied: “I have been changed into another man; I am a Christian, and it is not lawful for me to swear at all. But if it is now lawful, ask what has been added to the perfection of the Law. If you say that the Gospel forbids false swearing, and that the Law forbids the same thing where it says, ‘You shall not lie; you shall not bear false witness’: if it forbids swearing except from necessity, and thus forbids frequent swearing, the Law says the same where it says, ‘You shall not take the name of your God in vain.’ Indeed, on the contrary, because of our imperfection, under the Gospel people swear far more often, more frequently, and in lesser causes than under the Law. If one must swear for the hearer’s benefit, because an oath has authority, [Col. 0322C] since people are slow to believe, it is permissible to confirm by an oath what is usefully persuaded; but what sort of useful matter is it? Not a temporal matter, but one of faith and the spirit. In this case it is permissible to swear, after the example of the Apostle (I Cor. XV), but not for a temporal and perishable thing. Thus I speak, if anything has been added to evangelical perfection.”

But when the Apostle adduces that “an oath is the end of every controversy 291” (Heb. VI), he states this not in his own person but in that of others. The Lord also says: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no; whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matt. V)—from the evil of the one who makes others swear, not of the one who swears. Therefore it is from the evil of the canon which compels one to swear, because it also compels one to give testimony; nor is anyone a witness unless sworn. Therefore it is from the evil [Col. 0322D] of whatever prelate compels one to swear, and thus we seem, when coerced, to transgress the Lord’s command.

Likewise, if I can undertake and fulfil by vow all the other evangelical perfections, why not likewise this counsel of perfection? Or why, if someone observes it, do we immediately cry out that he is a Cathar?

One oath is made by surprise; another is made deliberately. They call the first a jesting word, though it seems to be a crime. For a simple word uttered by itself is jesting; therefore, when an oath is added to it, it makes it more than jesting. Likewise, an oath has three companions: truth, judgment, and justice; but this has none of these companions, therefore it is perjury. Yet in the courts of certain princes it has been forbidden, under a penalty of [Col. 0323A] five shillings, for anyone to swear by the limbs of the Lord. Some, however, distinguish themselves from others, as if by a special mark and oath of their own, and an execrable one.

A cleric also, playing a game with a Jew by agreement for money, refrained from swearing so that the Jew might not seize the money. He said to him: “By refraining from an oath, as though compelled, I have uttered greater blasphemies against God in my heart than with my mouth, if you had allowed me to swear.” The Jew at once withdrew from him as from a blasphemer.

Likewise Ecclesiasticus, censuring the habit of swearing, says in chapter XXIII: “Do not let your mouth become accustomed to swearing, for many falls” and ruinous disasters “are in it. Let the naming of God not be continual in your mouth, nor mingle yourself with the names of saints, for you will not be free from them. [Col. 0323B] For as a servant constantly questioned is not diminished by bruising, so everyone who swears and names” the name of God “will not be cleansed altogether from sin. A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the plague will not depart from his house; and if he deceives his brother, his offence will be upon himself; and if he conceals it, he will sin doubly; and if he swears vainly, he will not be justified.” In the same book, chapter XXVII: “Speech that swears much will bring horror upon the head, and its irreverence is a stopping of the ears.” Likewise Wisdom, chapter XIV: “Those who swear unjustly despise justice. For it is not the power of those swearing, but the punishment of sinners, that always visits the transgression of the unrighteous.”

## CHAPTER CXXVIII. On good simplicity.

[Col. 0323C]

Holy simplicity is a certain “face” of one “going to Jerusalem” (Luke IX). There is simplicity of virtue, simplicity of foolishness, and simplicity of pretence and hypocrisy. Of the first the Lord says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X). 292 Prudence accompanies this simplicity. Hence Jerome, on the Apostle’s passage in I Timothy, chapter III, “A bishop must be blameless,” etc., says: “Prudent against those who, under the name of pious simplicity, practise a priest’s foolishness.”

But regarding this it is asked whether it is the same as the simplicity praised here: [Col. 0323D] “If your eye is simple” (Matt. VI), that is, without the fold of error and the fold of perverse love. If it is the same, then every simple person abounds in the works of every virtue, because he is prudent and discerning in all things to be done and omitted; the simpler he is, the more discerning. Yet conversely it seems that the simpler one is, the more remote from discernment and the nearer to foolishness. Hence it is clear how greatly simple was Bishop Valerius, who placed the seed of the divine word in Vincent’s mouth (*Life of St Vincent*, found in Surius under 22 January).

Therefore this dove-like simplicity seems different from the simplicity mentioned above, and different from that of which we read: “There was a man named Job, simple and upright,” and discerning in all the Lord’s ways, [Col. 0324A] “and fearing God” (Job I). Thus simplicity here may be called a certain modesty of mind, which also shines in the countenance, together with a lesser discernment in matters; whereas there it is called simplicity in the sense of prudence and complete discernment in all things. Nevertheless, a sound knowledge of evil neither can nor ought to be lacking.

Simplicity especially befits the theologian, because sacred Scripture is friendly to simplicity. Things open and simple suit goodness. “Be children in malice, but not in understanding” (I Cor. XIV); “as newborn infants desire milk, while yet rational” (I Pet. II). He “who walks simply walks confidently” (Prov. X). And Wisdom, chapter I: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart”—not being scrupulous about questions, [Col. 0324B] but rather concerned about sins and their circumstances. And Proverbs, chapter II: “The Lord will protect those who walk simply.” And in the same book: “The upright shall dwell in the land, and the simple shall remain in it.” Likewise, chapter II: “The simplicity of the just shall guide them.” Likewise Ambrose (*On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, chapter 9): Simple faith in the truth is greater than all the eloquence of ambitious falsehoods, the sophistry of philosophers’ little flowers, and the subtleties of heretics.

Of the simplicity of foolishness it is said: Excessive simplicity is akin to foolishness. Likewise Augustine, on the passage, “A bishop must be prudent” (I Tim. III): lest he be so simple as to be foolish.

[Col. 0324C]

Of the simplicity of pretence it is said: “Beware of false prophets” (Matt. VII), etc. And likewise:

> Remember to avoid those who are downcast in spirit and silent.  
> —Cato, book IV, *Distichs*

And likewise, concerning good simplicity, II Corinthians, chapter IX: “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed, and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that, enriched in all things, you may abound in every simplicity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God.”

293 ## CHAPTER CXXIX. On practising hospitality.

Hospitality is a “face of one going to Jerusalem” (Luke [Col. 0324D] IX), namely one of the daughters of mercy and an outstanding grace among virtues. To those who lack it the Lord will say at judgment: “I was a stranger, and you did not take me in” (Matt. XXV). Commending it, the Apostle also says in Hebrews, chapter XIII: “Do not forget hospitality. For through it some have pleased” God “by receiving angels as guests”—as Lot did, not knowing that they were angels (Gen. XIX). And Abraham: “He saw three and worshipped one.”

Hence Genesis, chapter XVIII: “As Abraham sat in the valley of Mamre, at the entrance of his tent, in the very heat of the day, the Lord appeared to him. And when he lifted up his eyes, three men appeared to him; seeing them, he ran to meet them, and worshipped to the ground, and said: Lord, if I have found favour [Col. 0325A] in your eyes, do not pass by your servant; but let me bring a little water, and let your feet be washed; and rest under the tree, and I shall set forth a morsel of bread, that your heart may be strengthened; afterwards you shall pass on.”

Likewise chapter XIX: “Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the gate of the city. When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them, and worshipped with his face to the ground, and said: I beg you, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant and stay there; wash your feet, and in the morning you shall proceed. They said: No; we shall remain in the street. But he urged them strongly to turn aside to him; and having entered his house, he made them a feast.”

Likewise the Apostle, Romans chapter XII: “Pursuing hospitality.” Note the frequency implied by the word. [Col. 0325B] Likewise Peter, first epistle, chapter IV: “Be hospitable to one another without complaining; each administering to the other the grace he has received, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.” For we ought not to be devoted to one work alone. Likewise the Third Epistle of John: “Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, and especially for strangers.” Likewise, the Apostle, enumerating what are almost the essential distinguishing marks of a bishop, includes this: “A bishop must be hospitable” (Tit. II).

But this grace has departed far from bishops and clerics, and also from laypeople, so that now they give lodging only for payment. Likewise, it was because of their hospitality that the eyes of the two disciples going to Emmaus were opened; formerly they had been held by blindness, [Col. 0325C] “and they recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread. When he pretended to be going farther, they constrained him, saying: Stay with us, Lord, for evening is drawing on and the day is now declining. And he entered with them” (Luke XXIV). Bede, on Luke chapter XXIV: Truth was walking with them, and they invite him to lodging—indeed, compel him. From this example it is gathered that strangers are not merely to be invited to lodging but even drawn in.

Likewise, as is read in the homily on this passage (St Gregory, Homily 39 on the Gospel, on the martyrdom of the monks), a certain householder received a leper as a guest and placed him in his own bed; and he heard from the Lord that he had received the Lord in the leper. Likewise Joshua, chapter VI: “Enter the house of the prostitute woman and bring her out, and all that is hers, [Col. 0325D] as you confirmed to her by oath, 294” etc. Likewise III Kings XVII: “Arise, go to Zarephath of the Sidonians,” etc. Likewise IV Kings IV: “And one day Elisha was passing through Shunem,” etc. Likewise Judges, chapter IV.

295 ## CHAPTER CXXX. On clothing the naked.

There follows among the works of mercy the covering of the neighbour’s nakedness. Hence the Lord: “I was naked, and you covered me” (Matt. XXV)—not only by hospitality but also by clothing—lest you incur my prohibition: “When you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. LVIII), by failing to cover it.

Job, possessing this grace, says (chapter [Col. 0326A] XXXI): “If I despised a passer-by because he lacked clothing, or a poor man without covering; if his sides have not blessed me, and he has not been warmed with the fleece of my sheep.” Likewise the Lord: “He who has two tunics, let him give one to him who has none; and he who has food, let him do likewise” (Luke III). Martin, doing more than was required, divided his cloak with a poor man; indeed, what is more, he gave the poor man his only tunic, and gave it wholly. (He did both, as is related in his *Life* by Sulpicius Severus.) Likewise Acts of the Apostles, chapter IX: “When Peter arrived, many weeping widows stood around him,” etc.

## CHAPTER CXXXI. On visiting the sick and imprisoned.

There follows: “I was sick,” or “in prison, and [Col. 0326B] you visited me” (Matt. XXV). This means not only a visit to provide what is needed and to offer consolation, but also a visit that brings liberation, which is more excellent than the first. Of this the Lord says through David: “Lord, who is like you, delivering the needy and poor man from the hand of those stronger than he?” (Ps. XXXIV).

Job, strong in this grace, says in chapter XXIX: “I was a father to the poor. For I broke the jaws of the wicked man and plucked the prey from his teeth.” And David: “You will be a helper to the fatherless and orphan”—that is, to every wretched person—(Ps. IX). By this more worthy form of visitation (see chapter CXXIII), Nicholas delivered three boys condemned to death; Daniel (chapter XIII) delivered Susanna; and many other saints delivered innocent persons imprisoned.

## CHAPTER CXXXII. On burying the dead.

[Col. 0326C]

The seventh work of mercy is read of in Tobit, chapter II.
