Though he had fasted and been hungry the entire day, when he sat down to table in the evening and heard that one of his fellow-countrymen lay unburied, he rose at once and, at the risk of his own life, buried the man’s body, wholly giving himself to this task.

By this grace Antony—having no implement, while two lions served and helped him—buried Paul (*St Jerome, Life of Paul the First Hermit*), whom he found unburied and leaning against a tree in the posture of prayer. By this grace Zosimas, with a single lion rendering service, [Col. 0326D] buried the body of that holy penitent, Mary of Egypt. Hence that versifier:

> He is borne to the tomb; he is buried with a beast in attendance.  
> —Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans

Very many saints imposed this work of mercy upon themselves as penance. “For it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. VII). But this grace, not only of burying but also of accompanying the funerals of the dead as far as the place of burial, has today almost entirely grown cold; so much so that no one wishes to remember his last things, so that he may never sin (Ecclus. VII).

But since earth returns to earth (Gen. III), it may seem that no concern ought to be taken for the burial of the dead—far be it! By this work many have pleased God. [Col. 0327A] And in burying the dead we benefit ourselves more than them; therefore burial should not be costly. For, as the saints testify, such expense serves more to aggravate the deceased’s sins than to remedy them. It is better for such things to be sold and given to the poor, because:

> He who has no urn is covered by heaven.  
> —Lucan, book VII, near the end

> The loss of a tomb is easy.  
> —Virgil

> Nature buries those left behind.  
> —Maecenas

Likewise II Kings, near the end.

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. On fasting.

Fasting is a chief part of the “face of one going to Jerusalem” (Luke IX). By general fasting one abstains from every mortal sin; by the special fasting discussed here, [Col. 0327B] from food and drink. The Lord consecrated this by “fasting in the wilderness forty days and forty nights” (Matt. IV). It was prefigured by Moses’ fast (Exod. XXIV) and Elijah’s fast (III Kings XIX).

Of this the Prophet says in the Lord’s person: “I humbled my soul in fasting” (Ps. XXXIV). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “This kind of demon cannot be cast out except by prayer 296 and fasting” (Mark XII). And the Apostle: “Let us show ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in fastings, in unfeigned charity” (I Cor. VI). And the Lord in Matthew, chapter VI: “When you fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces so as to appear to men to be fasting. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not [Col. 0327C] appear to men to be fasting, but to your Father,” etc.

There is a detestable fast of the greedy, an indifferent fast of the physician, and an execrable fast of the hypocrite and the proud, discussed above. It was with this fast that the Pharisee fasted, saying: “I fast twice on the Sabbath,” etc. (Luke XVIII). And there is the fast of the Christian: dry and sober, in the mortification of the flesh. Jerome, as if defining it (*Letter to Eustochium, On the Guarding of Virginity*), says: “A belly always hungry and sober is preferable to fasts of two and three days.”

Joel, inviting us to this profitable fast, says in chapter II: “Turn to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; rend your hearts and not your garments.” And Isaiah, [Col. 0327D] chapter LVIII: “Why have we fasted and you have not looked upon us? We have humbled our souls, and you have not known it?” He answered: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found, and you exact payment from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for quarrels and disputes, and strike wickedly with the fist. Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this the fast I have chosen: for a man to afflict his soul for a day? To twist his head about like a circle, and spread sackcloth and ashes? Is not this rather the fast which I have chosen: loosen the bonds of impiety, untie oppressive bundles, let the broken go free, and break every burden,” etc.

Likewise Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXXIV: “He who is washed after touching a dead body, and touches it again, what does his washing profit him? So the man who fasts for his sins and then commits the same things again: what does he gain by humbling himself? Who will hear his prayer?” Likewise Zechariah, chapter VII: “When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months through these seventy years, did you fast a fast for me?” etc. Likewise Jonah, chapter III: “And the Ninevites believed in the Lord, proclaimed a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth from the greatest to the least,” etc.

This was the way of pale and bloodless saints making for their homeland. For Jerome testifies (*Life of St Paul*) that Paul the First Hermit always fasted until bread was sent to him from heaven. It was doubled when [Col. 0328B] Antony came to him. Paul said to him: “Come, brother, let us eat; our ration has been doubled for us.” And, incredible as it seems to us, St Hilarion (the same author, *Life of St Hilarion*) was content with five figs a day for fifteen years. But as an old and weak man he was refreshed with a piece of barley bread. Holy Mary of Egypt lived forty years on two loaves and roots. Jerome (*Letter to Marcella*, beginning “Ambrosius”) was content with cheap vegetables, coarse-sifted bread, and water.

But we cannot attain this most stringent fast because of our sloth and corruption. Let our fast, then, be a strict one of bread and water, yet so that our service may be reasonable (Rom. XII). For we do not wish to be unclothed, [Col. 0328C] but clothed over. Three things are owed to the ass: fodder, that it may be sustained; a rod, that it may not kick; a burden, that it may be useful to its master. Of the first it is said: “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V). For it was created by God, not by the devil, as the Manichaean says. And the Apostle says: “Make provision for the flesh,” provided that it be “not for its desires” (Rom. XIII). Of the second the same Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection,” etc. (I Cor. IX). Of the third he says: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI).

In the first is found the sustenance of nature; in the second, the beginning of grace and law; in the third, the fulfilment and consummation of the law. In the first, nature; in the second, discipline; in the third, charity toward one’s neighbour. But the sobriety of the followers of Muhammad today surpasses that of Christians. [Col. 0328D] Hence their prince Saladin, hearing that Christians used three or four courses, said that such people were not worthy of the earth.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. On rebuking gluttony.

Gluttony utterly destroys sobriety. Praying that this plague might be turned away from the people of God, the Prophet says: “With bit and bridle”—with lesser and greater restraint and curbing—“constrict their jaws,” by giving them provisions more sparingly; “for they,” in abundance, because of gluttony, “do not draw near to you” (Ps. XXXI), but are drawn away.

Hence the Apostle says to the Romans, chapter XII: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies [Col. 0329A] as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your reasonable service; and do not be conformed to this wicked age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind.” And elsewhere: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit? Shall I then take the member of God and make it the member of a prostitute?” (I Cor. VI). For the belly and the genitals are near neighbours. Likewise: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, bearing the marks of the Lord Jesus in their body” (Gal. V, VI), through abstinence and the weapons of penitents. But “they have also received the answer of death” (II Cor. I), having continually the memory of death, or the mortification of the flesh answering them against vices, in accordance with the saying: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted [Col. 0329B] as sheep for the slaughter” (Ps. XLIII). Hence David, in Psalm XXXII: “Give praise to the Lord on the lyre; sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery”—that is, in the mortification of the flesh, from which one must begin.

Therefore the beast must first be tamed and bridled, so that with measured pace it may carry the Holy Spirit. Hence Gregory: “Burn first our loins with the fire of penitential tribulation, restraining Delilah; then burn our heart with the fire of the Holy Spirit and your love.” For this reason the Lord also says to the disciples: “Let your loins be girded” first, “and then let lamps be burning in your hands” (Luke XII). John, Jeremiah, and the others did not preach except with their loins girded.

For “Nebuzaradan,” the chief of the cooks—that is, the belly of dishes—first [Col. 0329C] “destroyed the walls of Jerusalem” (Jer. LII), and all the defences of the soul’s Christian religion.

Therefore first bridle the horse, lest it be “a deceitful thing for salvation” (Ps. XXXII), lest the Lord “cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. XV). “But he who delicately nourishes his servant will find him rebellious” (Prov. XXIX). Rather tame your body, that you may have an obedient servant, with him who says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest, having preached to others, I myself should be found reprobate” (I Cor. IX); and with the Prophet praying thus: “Pierce my flesh with your fear,” etc. (Ps. XVIII).

Hence Jerome on Mark (Commentary on chapter I): Andrew means “manly,” and he is manly who forcibly [Col. 0329D] does violence to the destruction that brings him death—that is, to the body, which, through its fuel, is often the cause of death unless it is restrained. I say that he does violence to it so thoroughly that he “has the answer of death in himself” (II Cor. I), and “always carries his soul in his hands” (Ps. CXVIII).

Likewise Exodus, chapter XXXII: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play”—that is, to commit idolatry—because “they made a calf in Horeb and worshipped a graven image” (Ps. CV). See, therefore, what idleness and foreign, superfluous food do: they gave birth to idolatry, every form of idleness, every pride, and every superstition. Hence the Lord: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke XXI); lest you be like those “whose god is their belly” (Phil. III); and like these:

[Col. 0330A]

> There are those for whom the sole reason for living lies in the palate: they live to eat and do not eat to live.

## CHAPTER CXXXV. Against gluttony and drunkenness.

We join gluttony and drunkenness because, like gluttony, drunkenness distends the belly, inflames the flesh, and fosters and nourishes lust. Thus wines overcame Lot, whom Sodom had not overcome, so that he committed incest with his daughter (Gen. XIX). Drunkenness also exposed the thighs of Noah, ruler of the ark and leader of his generations (Gen. IX).

Gluttony has four attendants: what, how much, of what kind, and when. “What” concerns and is considered in the kind of food; “how much,” in its quantity; “of what kind,” in the seasoning of the food, whether sauce or even its usefulness; “when,” in the suitability [Col. 0330B] and frequency of the time. Hence: “Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. X).

> Marius, an exile, drinks from the eighth hour and enjoys gods  
> angered.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* I

To these attendants, to heighten the provocation of gluttony, cost is added, because things bought at a higher price please more. But:

> Do not crave a mullet when you have only a goby  
> in your purse.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* XI

Hence the poet:

> Wanton  
> and lascivious old men came, whose notable glory  
> is eating, and who think it honourable to vary corrupt dishes.  
> They invite the belly by price and consign to the palate  
>   
> [Col. 0330C] Juno’s birds from the stars, and whatever green creature, skilled  
> in speech, is brought from the coloured Indies.

Even if none of the things named above provokes the householder, yet his table often has a fifth attendant, arising from his pride and vices: namely ambition. Hence the philosopher Seneca (*Letter* 60): Bulls are fed by the grazing of a few acres; a single forest suffices for several elephants; but man feeds upon land and sea. Why is this? Is it because, although nature has given us modest bodies or little bodies, we surpass the voracity of enormous animals? Not at all. For it is not hunger of the belly that costs us greatly, but ambition.

Likewise the philosopher (the same author, *Letter* 89): “I turn to you, whose gluttony is deep and insatiable:

> The ruin, storm, and abyss of the market,  
> whatever it had sought, it had given to the greedy belly.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.15

Hence it searches the seas and the land; it pursues some things with hooks, others with snares, and others with various kinds of nets, with great labour. No creature has peace except from disgust. How little of these banquets, acquired by so many hands, is tasted by a mouth wearied with pleasures! How little does a sickly and nauseated master taste of this beast captured at peril! How little of so many shellfish brought from so far away passes through this insatiable stomach! I say that you are unhappy because you do not understand that you possess a hunger greater than your belly.”

Likewise Jerome (*To Furia, On Preserving Widowhood*): [Col. 0331A] “Some, fattened and enlarged from the estate of the Crucified, confound and distend their bellies with dishes and wine, turning the belly, unaccustomed to its proper function, into a sack. They consume and expel rotten and putrid foods, and soothe and relieve the burning stomach with drink; like Saul, drinking water and becoming drunk every night—see I Kings, chapter XXVI. Since they possess neither frugality nor chastity, they endure losses, the murmuring of servants, and dissensions among those who consider not the resources from which they spend, but how much they consume and devour.

“But if the Apostle, O daughter, ‘chastises his body and brings it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, he himself become reprobate’ (I Cor. IX), how can you, still a young woman in the heat of youth, full of dishes and wine, be secure about chastity? If blazing Vesuvius, fire-spewing Olympus, and Aetna full of steaming heat burn, how much more do youthful marrow, filled and inflamed with wine and dishes? Hence the poet:

> Wines prepare the spirits and make them fit for passion.  
> Care flees and is dissolved by abundant unmixed wine.  
> Then laughter comes; then the poor man takes horns;  
> then pain and cares and the wrinkle of the brow depart:  
> when Venus is in wine, fire is in fire.  
> —Ovid, book I, *Art of Love*

Likewise Deuteronomy, chapter XXXII: “The beloved grew fat and kicked: grown fat, grown stout, grown thick, he abandoned God his maker, withdrew from God his saviour 300, and forgot the Lord his creator.” Likewise in the same book (chapter VIII): “When [Col. 0331C] you have eaten and are full, take careful heed lest you forget the Lord.” Likewise Jeremiah, chapter V: “I satisfied them, and they committed adultery; they indulged in luxury in the prostitute’s house. They became lustful, breeding horses; each neighed after his neighbour’s wife.” Likewise Hosea, chapter XIII: “According to their pastures they were filled and satisfied; they lifted up their heart and forgot me”—“the fat cows of Samaria” (Amos IV).

First, therefore, the body weighs one down; then the world rages; finally the devil lays snares. These three also drive a person from the house. First, a quarrelsome wife (Prov. XXI; XIX), that is, the temptation of the flesh; then smoke, the sin of ignorance; then dripping, an alien suggestion of every kind from without. But first a person is tempted by “the desire of the flesh, then the desire of the eyes” (I John II), and finally “the pride of life” (ibid.).

Likewise Jerome to Furia: Great and watchful virtue is required to overcome what you were born in the flesh, to live in the flesh yet not according to the flesh, but above the flesh to fight with yourself every day, and to guard your soul pure and undefiled as though with the hundred eyes of Argus (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*), and to overcome the enemy enclosed within. The poet too, instructing morals, says:

> Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold.  
> —Terence, *Eunuchus*

And abundance of bread was the cause of the sins of Sodom (Ezek. XVI).

[Col. 0332A]

It is clear, therefore, from the authorities of the saints that abstinence and sobriety are foster-sisters and nurses of continence, while gluttony is the nurse of luxury. For a belly boiling with unmixed wine easily slides into lust. Take care lest, at a banquet among the feasts with Job’s daughters, you be thrown down (Job I).

Gregory (*Morals*, book II, chapter 9): Satan crushed Job’s children at the feast of their elder brother, not because they were devoted to the belly, but because amid banquets the good intention of the mind burns less fervently and watches less carefully. Samson cast down the Philistines amid feasts (Judg. XVI). Nebuchadnezzar, abusing feasts and the vessels of the Lord, heard this terrible voice: *Mane, techel, phares*—“numbered, weighed, divided” (Dan. V)—which was followed by the destruction of his house. When Holofernes was sunk in excessive drunkenness, Judith cut off his head (Judith XXIII).

Drunkenness makes a person forgetful of himself and of God; it gives birth to countless monstrosities, reveals counsels, and does not sympathize with affliction. Thus Saul, drinking water, was drunk every night, as in I Kings, chapter XXVI. For what does drunkenness not signify?

[Col. 0332B]

> It does not know what distance lies between groin and head.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* VI

The devil tempted the first parents by gluttony: “On whatever day you eat, you shall be like gods” (Gen. III). Then he tempted the Lord Jesus: “Command that these stones become bread” (Matt. IV). Gluttony, the desire of the flesh, and lust are associated vices. Therefore gluttony must be avoided with the utmost care because of its associates, especially because of lust, since it seems to be a vice implanted in us and natural.

Hence Jerome [Note: [Col. 0331] Found in the *Rule*, under the heading “On the abstinence of philosophers,” excerpted from the letter to Furia]: “Avarice is trampled down [Col. 0332C] by philosophers and laid aside along with the purse. A slanderous tongue is corrected by imposed silence; bodily adornment and the style of clothing are changed in the space of one hour. All other sins are external, and what is external is easily cast off. Lust alone 301, implanted by God for the creation of children, if it exceeds its limits, overflows into vice and, by a certain law of nature, longs to break forth into intercourse.”

Likewise Joshua, chapter XI: “He hamstrung their horses,” etc. Gluttons are like Esau, who “sold his birthright for red lentils and lost his father’s blessing” (Gen. XXV).

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. On simple fornication.

[Col. 0332D]

From gluttony arise simple fornication, adultery, incest, and shameful lust, or the foulness of the Sodomites. Simple fornication is illicit intercourse between an unmarried man and an unmarried woman, or conversely. This crime is especially detestable because, as the Apostle says: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. XIII). “Neither fornicators nor adulterers shall enter the kingdom of God” (Eph. V).

By this vice a person loses his dignity and the image of God, so that he is wholly swallowed up, becomes earth, and is changed from a rational being into a creeping creature and a beast. Of such people Joel says: “They rotted like beasts in their dung” (Joel I). “For he who fornicates sins against his own body” (I Cor. VI). The desire for fornication is anxiety; satiety is repentance. Hence he who cut out his own tongue so as not to fornicate said: “Far be it from me to buy at such a price that for which I should repent.”

The Lord prohibits it both in deed and in will: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). Hence the prophet Daniel (chapter X) saw a man whose loins were girded with a golden belt. “John saw a man girded about the breasts with a golden band” (Apoc. I), as though saying: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Ps. XXV). Fornication must especially be fled because it is sticky; whereas we can wrestle with other vices, concerning this one it is said: “Flee fornication” (I Cor. VI).

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. On adultery.

[Col. 0333B]

Adultery is of one kind, simple—namely, an unmarried person with a married person, or conversely; and of another kind, double and more serious—namely, a married person with a married person, or conversely. Adultery appears to be a crime equal to homicide. Hence under the Law the Lord commanded the adulteress to be stoned without remedy (Deut. XVII, XXV). For the Law assigns the measure of penalties according to the measure of sins. Therefore it is especially to be feared that the Church may err when she does not observe these ordinances instituted by the Lord. Likewise Augustine [Note: [Col. 0333D] See sermons 244, 245, and 247]: Adulterers hold the second place among those in hell; incestuous persons and deniers of God hold the first. Yet I believe adultery to be a greater crime [Col. 0333C] 302 than incest committed in the fourth degree of consanguinity.

The adulterer alone despises a widow’s pleasures.

Likewise Solomon: “The children of adulterers shall not prosper” (Wis. III). Likewise, Proverbs, chapter VII: “Come, let us be drunk, and enjoy the embraces we desire,” etc. Likewise, it is read in the Life of St. Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0333] Bishop of Paris, ninth in order, by Fortunatus, in Surius under 1 November] that a certain woman, because she was noble, despised her husband and attached herself to another man’s flesh; at last she died. She was solemnly conducted to the tomb with pomp and honorably buried; yet on that very day she was dug up by a fire-vomiting serpent, which lay upon and gnawed the little vessel—that is, the member—which she had withheld from her husband. Thus the devil deprived her of her grave and of the last offices of humanity, indignantly bearing that [Col. 0333D] her body should rest in the earth, because she had withheld her husband’s vessel, which she ought to have “kept in sanctification” (I Thess. IV).

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. On the sin of Sodom

The sin of the Sodomites was “abundance of bread, pride of life, and excess of wine” (Ezek. XVI). Rebuking this sin, the Lord says in Genesis, chapter XIX: “But the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners before the Lord.” Likewise, chapter XVIII: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous. [Col. 0334A] I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry that has come to me.”

Gloss: The novelty of so great and unheard-of a shamefulness produces, as it were, amazement and doubt in the hearer. Hence the Lord is presented as speaking almost in astonishment and doubt at so great a crime: “I will go down and see whether,” etc. For it seems incredible to me that human beings have perpetrated so great an outrage. Gregory (Morals, book XIX, chapter 14): Sin is in a voice when it is in action with a faint note.

It is in a cry when it is committed freely with manifest perpetration of the crime. Thus, concerning only two sins, as being the greatest and equal—namely homicide and the sin of Sodom—it is read that a cry ascended to the Lord from the earth. The Lord is read to complain, [Col. 0334B] namely because he “created male and female for the multiplication of humankind” (Gen. I); but murderers and Sodomites destroy and kill them as enemies, and as the chief adversaries of God and humankind, as though saying: You created human beings that they might multiply; but we shall labor to ensure that your work is diminished and destroyed.

Likewise, whereas the Lord delays inflicting punishment for other sins, for this one he appears to have laid aside the patience and goodness innate to him: not waiting for the Sodomites to repent, but instead punishing them in time with fire sent from heaven (Gen. XIX), and at last completing their punishment through the fire of Gehenna. Likewise, the Lord fashioned man from the mud of the earth in the field of Damascus, intending to form [Col. 0334C] woman from his rib in Paradise. Therefore, lest anyone should believe them to be androgynous, anticipating the formation of woman he says: “He created them male 303 and female” (Gen. I), as if to say: There shall be no union of man with man, or woman with woman, but only of man with woman, and conversely.

Therefore the Church permits an androgynous person—that is, one possessing the organ of each sex, fitted, namely, both for acting and for undergoing—to use the organ by which the person is more inflamed, or by which the person is weaker.

If more inflamed as a man, they permit the person to take a wife; but if the person is softer, as a woman, they permit the person to marry a husband. But if that organ fails, use of the remaining organ is never granted; rather, the person shall remain continent forever, because of the traces of alternation in the Sodomitic vice [Col. 0334D] which God detests. Likewise, Romans, chapter I: “For this reason God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves, to passions of dishonor. For their women exchanged the natural use for that use which is contrary to nature. Likewise also the men, abandoning the natural use of woman, burned in their desires for one another, men committing shamefulness with men, given over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are unfitting.”

Likewise, the Epistle of Jude (v. 7): “Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, because they committed fornication beyond measure and went after other flesh”—men committing shamefulness with men [Col. 0335A], women with women. For man and wife are one flesh—“were made an example, suffering the punishment of eternal fire” (Gen. II), in the present life. Likewise, Leviticus, chapter XVIII: “You shall not lie with a male as with a woman, because it is an abomination,” and shameful and unspeakable. It also punishes intercourse of a male with a male with the same penalty as intercourse of a human being with a beast, namely death. Hence Leviticus, chapter XX: “Whoever lies with a male as with a woman, both have committed an abomination; they shall surely die.”

But how have these matters now fallen into disuse, so that the Church leaves untouched what the Lord punishes severely, while she herself punishes most severely what he punishes lightly? It is to be feared that this proceeds from avarice, while the other is omitted from a cooling of charity. These destroyers of humankind [Col. 0335B] are like Onan, who spilled his seed upon the ground and, unwilling to raise up seed for his brother, was struck by the Lord (Gen. XXXVIII). These, as Isaiah says (chapter I), are like Sodom and Gomorrah—that is, mute in God’s praise and harsh through the enormity of their sins. Likewise, I Timothy, chapter I. Likewise, Colossians III: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth,” etc. Likewise, Joshua, chapter VI: “Cursed be the man who raises up and builds Jericho: in his firstborn he shall lay its foundations, and in the last of his children he shall set up its gates.”

Much more cursed is one who raises up the sin of the Sodomites, thus destroying his firstborn and last of his children, namely faith together with humility, especially because of its enormity. And in detestation of this crime God was angry with that land, turning the Pentapolis [Col. 0335C] into the Dead Sea, so that no fish lives in it, nor does a ship in which a human being is present sail upon it. In that land there are trees bearing fruits which vanish at the touch, emitting dust and ashes (Wis. X). Even for merely looking back at Sodom, Lot’s wife was turned into earth and a pillar of salt (Gen. XIX), as though the Lord said: I do not wish there to be any memory, any looking back, any 304 trace of this crime, because of its enormity.

Persons of this sort are effeminate, enervated men, women reserved by Pharaoh for his pleasures, who turn themselves from males into females, misusing feminine intercourse. These are imitators of Sardanapalus, a man more corrupt than any woman. Jeremiah also, at the end of Lamentations, beyond every lament and sorrow over the ruin and captivity of the city, adds lamentation [Col. 0335D] and groaning over the practice of the sin of Sodom, saying: “They shamelessly abused young men, and boys fell upon the wood” (Lam. VI). Such persons become not only mute but even blind, struck with *aorasia* [blindness], groping at Lot’s door at noon (Gen. XIX), so that while seeing they may not see. Likewise Isaiah, chapter LXVI: “Those who were sanctified and thought themselves clean in the gardens behind the door or behind the inner entrance,” etc. Likewise Joel III: “They set a boy,” etc. Likewise: Where a man marries as a woman, let laws be armed and legal rights drawn forth.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. On ingratitude

The Lord, rebuking ingratitude as the worst form [Col. 0336A] of guilt, says in Matthew, chapter XVIII: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you begged me. Ought you not also to have had mercy upon your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you? And his lord, angered, handed him over to the torturers until he should pay back the whole debt, even to the last farthing.”

Jerome, Augustine, and Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0335D] For the passages, see the Notes]: So great is the plague of ingratitude that, if we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, everything that had been forgiven us through repentance [M. “mercy”] is demanded back and revoked from us. Even according to civil laws, a freedman who had been freed was recalled into slavery for ingratitude. The Athenians (Valerius Maximus, book V, chapter 3) had even the most wicked dispositions, yet most equitable laws, because they punished the ungrateful as they did other criminals [Col. 0336B].

We are bound to be most grateful to God because he created us, and especially because he re-created us; for: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation” (Ps. CXV). The only worthy recompense is that death should be repaid by death: “but you have not yet resisted unto blood” (Heb. XII). If, therefore, in strict justice you are bound to be so grateful to God as to repay death by death, how ungrateful are you to him if by sinning you provoke him to anger!

“Nabal, a foolish man” (I Sam. XXV), was slain by the Lord because of ingratitude. For he denied a blessing to David, who was needy and cold, along with his fellow soldiers, exiles in the wilderness, and who had often kept wolves away from Nabal’s sheep during the sheep-shearing; moreover, he heaped insults and reproaches upon him, saying: [Col. 0336C] “Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse? Today servants who have fled from their masters have multiplied upon the earth” (ibid.). But how grateful David was to those well-disposed toward him is clear from II Kings, chapter XVI. He forgave every injury to Shimei, who reviled, cursed, and insulted him; and he divided his paternal inheritance with Ziba and Mephibosheth. He also elevated the son of aged Barzillai, who had kindly received him in 305 adversity when he was pressed by want (II Kings XIX).

Hezekiah, because he did not give thanks to the Lord for his incredible victory over Sennacherib, fell sick unto death; but, repenting, he was healed by the Lord (IV Kings XX). At last, giving thanks, he burst forth into this Canticle, saying: [Col. 0336D] “I said: In the midst of my days I shall go to the gates of hell,” etc. (Isa. XXXVIII).

Likewise, in the Gospel of Luke, chapter XVII, concerning the ten cleansed lepers, the Lord says: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found who returned and gave glory to God”—by giving him thanks for the health bestowed—“except this foreigner.” Yet members of one’s household and relatives are usually especially ungrateful. Likewise, in Deuteronomy, desiring us to be grateful even to enemies for a small kindness, the Lord says in chapter XXIII: “You shall not abhor an Edomite, because he is your brother; nor an Egyptian, because you were a stranger in his land and he fed you. Those born of them in the third generation shall enter the Church of God.”

Likewise, [Col. 0337A] in II Kings, chapter IX, David says to Mephibosheth: “Do not fear, for I will indeed show you mercy for the sake of Jonathan your father, and I will restore to you all the fields of Saul your father; and you shall always eat bread at my table.” Likewise Valerius Maximus (book V, chapter 3): Popilius Laenas was saved by Cicero, who pleaded for him in a capital charge; afterward Popilius pursued him when he had been proscribed by the senate and Antony, cut off the head which had pleaded for his own head, and carried it to the senate as though it were the finest spoil. Unhappy man, most criminal and most ungrateful of all human beings, who, beginning murder with his own father, killed the father of his country. Yet letters are too feeble to brand this monster. For no one can worthily lament so pitiable a fate for Cicero, because [Col. 0337B] there is now no second Cicero. Popilius hates no one except the person to whom he owes the most. It is dangerous, therefore, to confer many benefits upon someone, because, when it is shameful not to repay, he wishes there to be no one to whom he must repay. Likewise Seneca (Letter 19): A light debt makes a friend; a heavy one, an enemy.

## CHAPTER CXL. Epilogue of the forms of guilt

Since guilt proceeding to Gehenna has many forms, in general, as many vices as we put on, so many faces, countenances, and images of brute animals we impose upon ourselves. Hence the Lord says in Isaiah, chapter L: “I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was none who heard.” And elsewhere: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. LXIII), because “I am alone until I pass over” [Col. 0337C] (Ps. CXL).

Jerome (Letter 18, to Marcella, beginning “Ambrosius”): A person is not a *vir* [a true man] nor even a human being who, through cruelty, assumes the image of a lion. Hence the Apostle says: “The Lord delivered me from the mouth of the lion” (II Tim. IV). And: “Go, tell that fox” (Luke XIII), namely Herod, because of his deceitfulness. To the lustful it is said: “Maddened horses after females” (Jer. V). To the pleasure-loving and unclean: “Do not cast pearls before swine” (Matt. VII). To detractors and slanderers: “Do not give the holy thing 306 of God to dogs” (ibid.). To the proud: “Birds of the air, who set their mouth in heaven” (Ps. LXXII). To the curious and avaricious: “Fishes of the sea, who walk through the paths of the sea” (Ps. VIII). To the rapacious: “I know that after my departure ravening wolves will enter among [Col. 0337D] you, not sparing the flock” (Acts XX). To the malicious and venomous: “Brood of vipers” (Luke III).

And generally, to persons entangled in whatever vice or vices, it is said: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI); because “the Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men” (Ps. XIII), etc. And: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand” (Ps. LVIII). And again: “The beasts rotted in their dung” (Joel I). And Isaiah: “The burden of the beasts of the south, or the vision of the four-footed creatures in the wilderness” (Isa. XXX). But although we put on the faces of so many animals, the devil has used three animals as his vessels and instruments: the serpent, the pig, and the human being, into whom he is read to have entered.

The pig has much [Col. 0338A] resemblance to the human being in body, as appears from its anatomy and dissection; and also in spirit, when the rational spirit of a human being is, as it were, suffocated and changed through uncleanness into the spirit of a brute animal. Thus the prodigal son fed swine in a far country, being fed on the swine’s husks (Luke XV). For this reason the Lord also forbade pork above every food, though under a figure (Lev. I).

It should also be particularly noted that no animal has so departed from God and from its natural state as a human being who goes after other flesh, or who uses natural intercourse without a fixed and appointed time, or who is excessive in clothing, food, and other necessities. Of this manifold image the Psalm says: “Yet you shall bring their image to nothing” (Ps. LXXII). Jerome [Col. 0338B] likewise, summing up this manifold form of guilt, as it were, under an epilogue, says in Letter 18 (to Marcella): Now anger puts upon us the person of a lion; now superfluous anxiety plans ahead for many years to come, and we do not remember the Gospel saying: “Fool, this night they will take your soul from you; and whose shall be those things which you have prepared?” (Luke XII). Garments are sought not merely for use but for luxury. Wherever there is gain, the foot is quicker, speech more rapid, the ear more attentive. If a loss—as often happens in household affairs—has been announced, the face is cast down with sorrow. We rejoice over a coin; we are distressed over a lost penny.

Therefore, since in one human being there are such diverse faces of animals, the Prophet prays to the Lord thus: “Lord, scatter their image in your city” [Col. 0338C] (Ps. LXXII). For although we have been made in the image and likeness of God, through our vice we put many personae upon ourselves. And just as in theatrical performances one and the same actor now presents sturdy Hercules, now is softened into Venus, now trembles as Cybele, so we—who, if we were not of the world, would be hated by the world—have as many likenesses of personae as we have sins.

## 307 CHAPTER CXLI. On repentance

To rebuke vices and commend virtues, we have gathered and excerpted many things for a seedbed of preaching from the little gardens of Holy Scripture, leaving more and greater things from the authorities of that same Scripture concerning the matters stated above [Col. 0338D] to the diligence of the industrious reader, or adding them at the end of our discussion of repentance (above, chapter 9). Repentance destroys vices and builds up and initiates virtues; it is, that is, the second plank after shipwreck, and a remedy and antidote against all sins and the devil’s poisons (Jerome, Letter 8, to Demetrias, *On Preserving Virginity*, chapter 5).

From this most healthful remedy John the Baptist, the Forerunner of the Lord, “a voice crying in the wilderness,” began his preaching, saying in Matthew, chapter III: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near”—as if to say: The gate is about to be opened, because Christ has come. And again (ibid.): “Brood of vipers, who showed you [Col. 0339A] how to flee from the coming wrath? Produce fruits worthy of repentance.” The Savior too, after fasting in the wilderness and being tempted by the devil, began to preach and say in Matthew, chapter IV: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Peter likewise said to the Jews who had crucified the Lord, when they came to him and asked how they might be saved: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts II).

For the sufficiency, perfection, and integrity of repentance four things are necessary: the infusion of grace, contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and worthy satisfaction in deed. The latter three are insufficient without the first. For we are uselessly contrite, confess, make satisfaction, and afflict ourselves with the labor of punishment without the infusion of grace, [Col. 0339B] without faith working through love. Therefore believe, hope, and love, so that you may be fruitfully contrite, confess, and act.

The Prophet sets forth and teaches this fourfold pattern through four short expressions of that penitential Psalm (Ps. L): “Have mercy upon me, O God,” through the infusion of grace; “Blot out my iniquity,” through contrition of heart; “Wash me yet more,” through confession of sin—“yet more” than I know how to ask or am sufficient to ask. Or “yet more,” so that no trace of sin may remain in me, by which we easily relapse into sin. Or “yet more,” with respect to the increase of grace, not to its cause; or with respect to the order of penitential satisfaction. Hence it says: “Cleanse me,” through satisfaction in deed.

This fourfold pattern is also indicated in the Song [Col. 0339C] of Love in the word “Return,” repeated four times: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you” (Cant. XXI). For after worthy satisfaction in repentance—although even earlier, yet especially then, O Bride—“the King desires your beauty” (Ps. XLIV), because then “you are altogether beautiful, my beloved” (Cant. IV), etc. This same fourfold pattern is also expressed in the Psalm where it says: “Sing praises 308 to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises wisely” (Ps. XLVI). The adverb placed last, like the verb, is to be repeated with it four times; as if: “Sing praises” through the infusion of grace, and do so “wisely”; then be contrite “wisely”; afterward confess “wisely”; finally make satisfaction for sins committed [Col. 0339D] “wisely.”

And it should be noted that there is a fourfold washing of a human being from sin. The first is baptism, from original sin, in children; the second is faith, also from actual sin, in adults: “cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV). The third is the shedding of blood through martyrdom, which belongs to few; hence: “Those who washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. XXII). The fourth is repentance, repeated as often as necessary after the baptismal covenant has been broken, and it belongs to all. Hence Isaiah: “Wash yourselves, be clean; put away the evil of your thoughts” (Isa. I).

But the fruits of repentance must be worthy; this will be so if the punishment imposed corresponds to the fault. Hence Gregory: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Homily 20 on the Gospels). For penitence or the fruit of a good work is not the same for one who has sinned little or not at all [Col. 0340A] as for one who has sinned gravely or more greatly.

## CHAPTER CXLII. How great contrition ought to be

Augustine, on chapter XI of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, shows how great contrition and bitterness of heart for sin ought to be: “If we judged ourselves”—ascending the tribunal of our mind, with reason presiding as judge, thought accusing, conscience bearing witness, and fear torturing us as executioner—so that, as it were, through the tears of the soul pain and blood might flow by the severity of repentance, “we should certainly not be judged,” that is, condemned by the Lord. But when we are judged here, we are corrected by the Lord through temporal punishments, so that [Col. 0340B] we may not be condemned with this world.

In this judgment of repentance, or in the future judgment, we read of God alone as advocate, in Hezekiah’s Canticle, Isaiah chapter XXXVIII. As though the penitent said: “Lord, I suffer violence,” oppressed by the habit of sinning, fearing lest fear, the executioner and lictor, drive me into despair; and lest this happen, “Answer for me,” by helping my frailty and forgiving my sins, because “what shall I say, or what shall I answer you, when I myself have done it?” This indeed I shall say: “I shall review all my years in the bitterness of my soul,” and of my repentance.

Likewise John the Baptist, Matthew chapter III: “He who is to come after me shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit,” through the sweetness of baptism and its covenant once broken. “He shall baptize you in fire,” that is, in penitential punishment, [Col. 0340C] inward and outward, tormenting you in the manner of fire. Likewise Psalm XLVII: “There,” that is, in repentance, are “pains as of a woman in labor,” because only “with a vehement spirit will he shatter the ships of Tarshish.” “Of a woman in labor,” that is, trying to give birth, whose pain does not immediately end. He does not say “of one giving birth,” who, when she gives birth, is delivered from pain.

Consider how great a fruit follows the pain of a woman in labor, so that you may repent. “For a woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow; but when she has borne a son, she no longer remembers the distress for joy, because a human being has been born into the world” (John I), that is, into heaven. Likewise: “Going, they went and wept, scattering their seed; but coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” [Col. 0340D] (Ps. CXXV). And again: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). And again: “From fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XXVI), and of repentance.

Likewise the Gloss: Consider how great contrition of heart for sin ought to be in the four things which the Lord did in raising Lazarus: “He troubled himself, groaned in spirit, wept, and cried: Lazarus, come forth” (John XI). If the Lord did these things in raising one dead four days, how much more must you weep and cry, you who are weighed down by the stone of habit, who have not merely for four days but through the course of many years rotted foully in your own dung? Therefore, that you may be raised from the abyss of vices, trouble yourself through sorrow; groan [Col. 0341A] through horror of Gehenna; weep through compassion; “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX); cry out through confession, prayer, and holy action, saying to your soul: “O Lazarus”—or, to yourself as Lazarus—“come forth” from the abyss of vices.

Likewise, that contrition may be stirred up within you, hear Jerome writing to Heliodorus (*On the Praise of the Solitary Life*): What are you doing, brother, in the world, you who are greater than the world? Behold, the trumpet sounds: “Arise, O dead”; for now the Judge, “made drunken with wine” (Ps. LXXVII), proceeds to judge the world in the clouds of heaven. Now the “two-edged sword,” cutting down whatever stands in its way, issues from his mouth. Arise; how long will you be sluggish? Surround yourself with a rampart, gird yourself with a ditch; prepare yourself for the Savior’s judgment, because “at an hour [Col. 0341B] when you do not think, the Son of Man shall come” (Luke XII; Rev. I; Matt. XXIV).

That you may also be contrite, say with the Prophet: “The groans of death surrounded me; the pains of hell encompassed me” (Ps. XVII). And not without reason: “For who shall be able to endure everlasting burnings?” (Isa. XXXIII). Therefore: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury,” that is, in the fire of Gehenna; “nor correct me in your anger,” that is, with the fire of purgatory (Ps. XXXVII); but “have mercy upon me.” Burn here, cut here, so that I may truly be able to say with the Prophet: “All my bones are troubled, and my soul is exceedingly troubled. My eye is disturbed by fury.” Hence: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (ibid.).

Likewise Jeremiah (chapter IV): “My belly pains me,” because of spiritual wickednesses; “my belly pains me,” because of carnal desires; “my senses are troubled within me. I shall not be silent, because my soul has heard the sound of the trumpet, the cry of battle; destruction upon destruction has been summoned, and all the land has been laid waste.” The same author, chapter VI: “Make for yourself mourning for an only son, bitter lamentation, because suddenly the devil, the destroyer, will come upon us,” unless we take precautions. The same author, chapter VII: “Cut off your hair and cast it away, and take up an indirect [that is, for spiritual and eternal goods] lamentation, because the Lord has cast off and abandoned your generation in the wrath of his fury.” The same author, chapters VIII–IX: “My sorrow upon sorrow; within me my heart mourns. Over the destruction of the daughter of my people I am broken and sorrowful; stupefaction has seized me. Who then [Col. 0341D] will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people?”

Likewise Job, chapters VI–VII: “Would that my sins, by which I have merited wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in a balance. This would appear heavier than the sand of the sea. Therefore my words too are full of sorrow, because the arrows of the Lord are in me, whose indignation drinks up my spirit, and the terrors of the Lord wage war against me. Therefore I have numbered laborious nights for myself. If I sleep, I say:” When shall I arise? “And again I await the evening, and I shall be filled with pains until darkness.” Likewise: “Every night,” that is, for every sin, [Col. 0342A] “I shall wash my bed,” the bed of my conscience. “With my tears,” inward or outward, “I shall water my couch,” as Arsenius did; because “my sin is always against,” or before, “me” (Ps. L).

Likewise, the title of Psalm CI: “The prayer of the poor man when he is anxious in the presence of the Lord.” Likewise, a hermit, after falling into the slippery sin of the flesh, said: “I grieve unto death; and, unless I feared scandal and bringing the name of monks into contempt, I would publicly confess this sin to everyone” [Note: [Col. 0341D] The Life is in Surius, under 19 July]. Likewise Deuteronomy, chapter IV: “When you seek God, you shall find him, provided that you seek him with all your heart and with all the tribulation of your soul.”

## CHAPTER CXLIII. On confession of the mouth

After confession of the heart follows confession [Col. 0342B] of the mouth. For confession is threefold: “of the heart,” as David says: “I said, I will confess, and you forgave” (Ps. XXXI); of the mouth; and of deed. Confession of the mouth is one thing for faith and another for repentance. Likewise confession for faith is threefold: of the heart concerning what must be believed—“With the heart one believes unto righteousness”; of the mouth—“With the mouth confession is made unto salvation”; and: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father” (Luke XII). These are “well-sounding cymbals” (Ps. CL), neither of which sounds without the other in a crisis or necessity. Hence such confession is called, as it were, *simul fassio* [a joint acknowledgment], and more properly *professio* [profession].

A profession is a particular pursuit or office in which someone excels through personal merit and the judgment of others. There is also confession of deed for faith, because “the proof of love is the display [Col. 0342C] of a deed. No one has greater love than that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (St Gregory, Homily 30 on the Gospels; John XV). From this alone some persons were formerly called confessors. For in antiquity and in the primitive Church no one was called a confessor except a martyr, or one who had been led and prepared for the trial of the sword and of martyrdom. Thus Urban, accustomed to rest among the tombs of martyrs, was twice made a confessor, having been led to the trial of the sword for confessing Christ’s name, though he was spared.

But the name “confessor” has now been extended to penitential confession, so that any truly penitent person may be called a confessor. Confession for repentance is threefold: of the heart, which is made to God; of the mouth, which is made [Col. 0342D] to Christ’s commanding representative: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke XVII); and of deed. Confession of the mouth for repentance was prescribed and introduced into the Church for three reasons: first, that humility, shame, and embarrassment may be instilled into the proud and stiff-necked person.

For food is grievously taken when it must necessarily be followed by an antidote through the rebuke and correction of the confessor, lest the sinner suffer relapse. It is prescribed also because confession of the mouth itself is a major part of satisfaction. (Hence, as an authority has it: The more priests you confess to in the hope of pardon, the more swiftly you obtain absolution from guilt [Col. 0343A].) It is prescribed also for knowledge of sin and leprosy. For often before confession a person thought a mortal sin venial, and a greater crime a lesser one; from this error the person is cured by a confessor’s instruction.

Hence, as a figure of such knowledge and discernment of leprosies, Moses confined persons suspected of leprosy for seven days, and again for another seven, unless beforehand they appeared either clean or truly leprous (Lev. XIII). But on the fourteenth day he admitted a person found clean to the fellowship of men, and cast the leper outside the camp. If Moses showed such care and diligence toward a figure, frequently and repeatedly inspecting one infected with a spot to determine whether he was leprous, how much greater care ought the priests of the Gospel to take concerning the reality? Would that they did!

For confession of the mouth, and also to express confession of the heart, we beat our breasts, like the woman who beats a pot and shakes out flies, often and repeatedly inspecting it to see whether any remains at the bottom. So too the heart—which is the receptacle of evil thoughts, in which all sins except ignorance are conceived—must be shaken out, beaten, and searched, so that no trace of sin may remain in it.

The Psalmist reveals how confession should be made with the mouth when he says: “I will confess the Lord exceedingly with my mouth” (Ps. CVIII). And again: “I will confess the Lord according to his justice” (Ps. VII)—“according,” namely, to the fact that he is just, indeed “according” to the fact that he is justice itself; not merely “according” to the fact that he is pure, but “according” [Col. 0343C] to the fact that he is purity itself. Flay yourself, that is, so that no circumstance of sin may remain hidden, no sin may be colored by an excuse, but it may be disclosed to the confessor as it was committed.

Concerning confession in deed, it will be spoken of thus. This threefold confession is expressed in the following brief words: “When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people” (Ps. CXIII), through confession of the heart. “Judea became his sanctification,” through confession of the mouth; then, “Israel his dominion,” through confession of deed. For once repentance has been performed, a human being has recovered in great part mastery over himself. Then for the first time the person is powerful over himself. The first confession begins, the second advances, the third completes.

This threefold confession is likewise marked in the brief saying: “God is known in Judea; in Israel his name is great; and his place was made in peace” (Ps. LXXV). First we sit with Mary at the kissing of the Lord’s feet, she who watered his feet with tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment (Luke VII). And you, if you truly desire repentance, anoint his feet on earth with the ointment of compassion and works of mercy, and wipe them with hair—that is, by casting away superfluities and distributing them to the poor. Second, we rise with her to the kissing of his hands. Third, we stand at the kissing of the head.

Likewise David: “Sing before the Lord, and in confession to him” (Ps. CXLVI), first; then, “sing praises to his name, for it is sweet” (Ps. [Col. 0344A] CXXXIV). And again: “Enter his gates,” that is, those of the holy Church, “with confession, his courts” first; then “confess to him in hymns” (Ps. XCIX). For just as there are “rings in their nostrils” (Prov. XI), so there is “praise of God in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV). Likewise Judges: “Who shall go before us to battle?” (Judg. I), against the world, against the devil, against one’s own body. “Judah,” that is, confession: he set the example by first entering the Red Sea, the wilderness, and suffering adversities, so that he might enter the land of promise, which he entered first.

For this is the confession which instructs the penitent to endure every adversity patiently, that the person may deserve to enter the land of the living, receive a royal name, and be enrolled among kings: “You are an elect race, [Col. 0344B] a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II). “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XLIX).

## CHAPTER CXLIV. On the confessor
In order that we may confess, we need a confessor, who in dealing with penitents ought so to fulfill the office of father and mother as both to pierce and to anoint. Let him have a father’s blows and a mother’s breasts, and the oil and wine of the Samaritan with which to heal the wounded man’s wounds (Luke 10). He has been established in the Church for no other purpose than, as a physician, to heal the sick. To one who comes to him to confess, he should say: “My son, know that you confess not to me but to God; yet, by calling me as a witness of your confession, you make your sins mine—sins which I promise both to bear with you, to make satisfaction for, and, now that they are covered, to conceal as though they were my own” [Col. 0344C].

Therefore let the confessor be prudent and discerning, gentle, pleasant, kind, and benevolent, merciful and approachable. At times, however, like a father, let him employ a biting rebuke—as did that man who, when someone was unwilling to restore what he had taken, imposed no satisfaction upon him for that reason. When the latter made an offering upon the Lord’s altar, the priest said: “Far be it from me to be taken by your food placed in a snare.” Following him, he spat and threw the coin after him, saying: “May your money be with you unto destruction” (Acts 8). Like Cain, “a wanderer and fugitive” (Gen. 4), such a man departs irreverently and as a fugitive from the face of the Lord. But, ashamed and contrite, on the following day he returned to him with an abundance of tears [Col. 0344D], promising to make satisfaction for his sin according to the priest’s judgment.

Nor should confessors grow proud as though they were prelates. They are the Church’s dung-baskets: I do not mean that they carry dung, either their own or that of others, within themselves—like beasts rotting in their dung (Joel 1), and the hoopoe, which nests in its dung—but that they are baskets carrying their own sins and those of others “outside the camp” of the Church (Heb. 13), as though carrying them out rather than carrying them. Thus they are worthy to be filled with the fragments left over by those who ate with the Lord, lest they perish (John 6). David also says of such persons: “He turned his back from burdens; his hands served in the basket” (Ps. 80).

The judgments belonging to this office are many, great, and difficult, because they concern the peril and salvation of the soul, the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts [Col. 0345A]. Therefore, lest he judge with insufficient discernment, he should not have an excessive multitude of penitents. Let him often visit those who have confessed to him, and speak privately with them, asking about their condition and whether they have performed penance without relapse.

A wise confessor always enjoins three things, sufficient for penance, especially upon an intelligent penitent: first, according to his ability, to guard against and avoid every occasion of sin, especially in matters which readily draw the mind into consent; second, to flee delay in confessing; third, negligence in making satisfaction. One should also confess frequently, following the example of that most holy abbot of Longpont, who, because of the most exact and frequent confession which he made, was asked: “What does it mean, my abbot, that you confess so often?” He replied: “It seems to me each day that I had not previously confessed; and because I recall something among the things forgotten, I confess something even more purely and sincerely, and often with greater humility than before” [Col. 0345B].

How great the effect of confession is appears from the fact that through it “sins are covered” (Ps. 31) in judgment, and even now miraculously. Thus one reads of a demoniac reproaching a certain man with his sins. Ashamed, the man immediately ran to confession; when the demoniac returned, he said: “I know what you have done. I indeed have your sins beneath my tongue, but I cannot make them public.” Likewise, when a ship was in danger at sea, some people confessed publicly before everyone; but once delivered from the storm, they retained no memory of the sins they had confessed [Col. 0345C].

Job, chapter 7, shows how great and what sort of confession ought to be, when he says: “I will not spare my mouth; I will speak in the tribulation of my spirit; I will converse in the bitterness of my soul.” But for confession to be true, it must be humble, simple, pure, and faithful.

“There are those who glory when they have done evil and rejoice in the worst things” (Prov. 2), who even “proclaim” their sins “like Sodom” (Isa. 3). Clothed in religious dress and professing religion, they often most shamelessly boast of their past evils: for example, of something they once did bravely in a gladiatorial conflict or cleverly in a literary contest, or of some other thing favored according to the vanity of the world but harmful, ruinous, and destructive according to the salvation of the soul [Col. 0345D]. This is still a sign of a worldly mind. The humble garb worn by such people is not the merit of holy newness, but the covering of ancient oldness. They do not put off the old man, but cloak themselves with the new; they do not wash away their deeds, but mock themselves by confessing without humility. “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6).

It is shameful to recall the insolence of some, who are not ashamed, with lamentable rejoicing, to boast that, even after taking up the holy habit, they cunningly tripped up and deceived someone in a business matter—a brother—or that they boldly rendered retaliation for abuse or cursing, that is, “evil for evil, or cursing for cursing” (1 Pet. 3).

[Col. 0346A] Others confess their sin down to every circumstance, in order that they may seem thereby more humble to the confessor. Such confession, however, is harmful and vain, because we are not humble, though we desire to appear so. To seek praise for humility is not the virtue of humility but its overthrow. The truly humble person wishes to be accounted lowly, not proclaimed humble. He rejoices in contempt of himself; his only sound pride is that he despises praise. What could be more perverse or more unworthy than that confession, the guardian of humility, should serve pride, and that you should wish to appear better through that by which you appear worse? It is a marvelous kind of boasting: that you cannot be thought holy unless you appear criminal. But such confession has the appearance of humility, not its virtue; it not only does not deserve pardon, but even provokes wrath [Col. 0346B].

Confession must also be simple. Hence David says: “Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140). Do not cast blame upon another, unless he was a participant in the crime; and even then accuse yourself rather than him. Grieve for him; do not excuse yourself by custom, nobility of birth, nature, companionship, constellation, or fate. For this is to cast blame upon the Creator and to detract from, weaken, and diminish his goodness.

Let confession also be faithful: confess in hope of pardon, never utterly despairing of forgiveness, but trusting, lest by your own mouth you condemn yourself rather than justify yourself. Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, and Cain, the fratricide, confessed and despaired more grievously. One said: “I have sinned, betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27) [Col. 0346C].

The other said: “My iniquity is greater than that I can deserve pardon” (Gen. 4). The confession of both was wholly faithless. But you should possess this threefold cord of confession, which “is not quickly broken” (Eccl. 4), so that you may “go a three-days’ journey and sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness” (Exod. 5).

## CHAPTER 145. On Satisfaction for Sin, Perseverance, and Its Character

In contrition, confession, and satisfaction, frequency and perseverance are necessary. Hence Augustine [Col. 0346D] (*On True and False Penance*, falsely attributed to him, ch. 8) says:

> Penance is a certain vengeance of one who grieves, always punishing in himself what he grieves to have committed.

And again (ibid., ch. 19):

> One must grieve continually over sin, as the force of the very word makes clear. For *paenitentia* [penance] is “holding punishment,” so that it always punishes, avenging in itself what it committed by sinning. He holds punishment who always exacts vengeance for what he grieves to have committed. Penance, therefore, is vengeance always punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed.

What remains for us except to grieve during life? For where grief ends, penance too fails. If penance ends, what remains of pardon? Let a person rejoice and hope in grace for as long as he is sustained by penance [Col. 0347A]. The Lord says: “Go, now sin no more” (John 8). He did not say merely, “Do not sin,” but: let not even the will to sin arise in you. How can this be kept unless grief is continually guarded in penance? Therefore let him always grieve and rejoice in his grief; and let it not suffice that he grieves, but let him grieve from faith, and not always grieve that he has grieved.

Again, in the Psalm: “But I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is always before me,” etc. (Ps. 37). If we do not confess daily, at least once a day let us recall to memory, in bitterness of heart, sins gathered together in a bundle. In this threefold cord a certain holy violence is necessary, which the penitent must inflict upon himself lest he relapse. Hence: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). But inability to undergo the hardships of penance for the salvation of one’s soul is the mark of a soft and effeminate mind. But if:

> To redeem your body, you will endure iron and fires.  
> —Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, book 1

will you not awaken in order to save yourself and your soul? Indeed, you ought to awaken far more, because:

> This is the task; this is the labor.  
> —Virgil

Of this holy violence to be inflicted upon oneself it is written in Psalm 9: “Their memory has perished with a noise.” Augustine says: “No one comes to the highest peace of mind unless he has fought with vices amid great tumult and with all his forces gathered.” Hence Saint Jerome says: “Untie the cord of habit and ingrained sin by which you are bound. If you cannot untie it, break it; if you cannot even break it, cut it” [Col. 0347C]. And again: “Cast out what tears your heart; if these things cannot otherwise be torn away, the heart itself must be torn away with them.”

Hence that martyr [Note: [Col. 0347] Concerning whom Jerome writes in the *Life of St Paul the First Hermit*.], whom tortures did not conquer: when a woman began to soften him, he bit off his own tongue and spat it, bloody, into the prostitute’s mouth, that he might temper pleasure with pain. Hence St Benedict (Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 2, ch. 2), feeling the first stirrings of lust, threw himself into brambles and thorns, so that he might restrain their heat by bodily pain. Hence a hermit threw himself into a river. Another feigned madness by his gestures and manner of eating [Note: [Col. 0347] St Symeon Salos, concerning whom see the Roman Martyrology, 1 July.], so that through false madnesses he might escape the true madness of pride. So also David.

Again, Psalm 76: “My soul refused to be comforted; I remembered God and was delighted; I rose up, and my spirit failed. My eyes anticipated the watches; I was troubled and did not speak” [Col. 0347D]. Behold how great and how continual is the distress of the penitent. It continues: “And I meditated by night with my heart, and I was exercised.” Behold the frequency of penitential labor. “And I swept my spirit”: with the broom of penance I cleansed or scraped it, casting out the scrapings and filth; through penance I purified it, or dug up my spirit with the mattock of penance, which is driven deep so that harmful things may be expelled. For one who wishes to sow a cultivated field first frees it from shrubs.

But where sins have become habitual and ingrained, there is need of a mattock, fire, iron, or a winnowing fan—especially regarding vainglory [Col. 0348A]. Therefore the threshing-floor of the soul must first be threshed with scourges; then cleansed with a broom; afterward cleared with a mattock; then, lest chaff or any trace of sin remain, purified with a winnowing fan before the coming of the Judge, “whose winnowing fan is in his hand” (Matt. 3). With these, as it were, four rods from which the scourge of penance is made, Jeremiah gives four words: “Behold, I have set you over kingdoms, that you may pluck up”—the first rod—“destroy”—the second—“ruin”—the third—“scatter”—the fourth—and thus “build and plant” (Jer. 1). He gives only two words for restoring, planting, and strengthening salvation, but four for acquiring it, because this is more difficult.

Penance must also be fruitful. Hence: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruits worthy of penance” (Luke 3): namely, so that the quality and quantity of punishment may correspond to the quality and quantity of guilt. Again, Romans chapter 6: “As you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification.” Augustine (*Sermons on the Words of the Apostles*, sermon 17, chs. 5–6) says: “I do not say so much in length of time as in the supplement of pure confession and fruitful satisfaction; nevertheless, more is owed to righteousness than to sin—‘I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh’” (Rom. 6) [Col. 0348B]. Again Augustine: “Righteousness of mercy ought now to be loved more than the iniquity then loved, so that for righteousness one may endure pains and despise everything, even death. But if righteousness cannot now be loved more than iniquity was then loved, at least let it now be loved as much as iniquity then was.”

Ambrose, on Romans 6, “For as you presented your members,” says: “He said humanely ‘as,’ and not ‘more,’ which he ought to have said, but did not, lest faith should then be shunned as harsh and unbearable.” Therefore, that you may perform fruitful penance, take up its labors, so that, crushed and afflicted, you may say with the Prophet: “Lord, see my humility”—in contrition and confession—“and my labor”—in satisfaction—“and forgive all my sins” (Ps. 24). And again: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16).

“Make for yourself also”—so that “at all times your garments may be white” (Ecclus. 9)—“a lye” [Col. 0348D], by which they may be washed: from the water of penitential tears, the fire of the Holy Spirit stirring up within you the smoke of good works and tears, and ashes through mortification of the flesh. For ashes and haircloth are weapons of penance. The labor of penance and abstinence consists especially in food and clothing. Thus locusts and haircloth belong to John the Baptist (Matt. 3); sackcloth and coarse bread to Jerome; tunic and brambles to Benedict; handkerchief and tears to Arsenius; chamber-pot and five dried figs to Eulalius; nakedness, roots, and herbs to the Egyptian sinner; pillar and worms to Symeon.

David also, when his sin was announced to him [Col. 0349A], descended from his throne and sat in ashes and haircloth, neither judging nor performing any royal work until he heard from the Lord through Nathan: “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Kings 16). Yet afterward he was punished by his son because of the remnants not, I say, of guilt but of punishment; and he suffered persecution, even from a certain man—namely Shimei—who reproached him (2 Kings 16). Therefore fear for yourself; and, following Jerome’s counsel (*Letter to Rusticus*, “That which is unknown”), sleep in sackcloth, so that you may compensate for former pleasures by austerity of life. At Jonah’s preaching (ch. 3), the Ninevites sat in ashes and haircloth, from greatest to least.

But do not delay penance. For, as Augustine testifies (*On True and False Penance*, and sermons 57 and 58 *On Time*, and tractate 35 on John), “He who waits to repent until the day of death rarely truly repents” [Col. 0349B]. For then sins rather leave him than he leaves sins. Yet by the example of the thief, if penance is true, it is not too late. Therefore, while you live, perform worthy and fruitful penance. This will be so if you despise all the enticements of seductive pleasure, torment yourself more severely through penance, weep more abundantly, support the poor more liberally, burn more ardently in charity, and live “piously, soberly, and justly.” Then you may have some confidence of pardon, because “the Lord is abundant in forgiveness” (Tit. 2); and because you offended your Creator by sinning ungratefully against him, say: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115).

Indeed, first be reconciled to him and restore yourself, whom you had taken away; afterwards, once reconciliation and restoration have been accomplished, say: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (ibid.) [Col. 0349C]. For even for one who has sinned nothing, the sole worthy recompense is that blood be repaid with blood, to him to whom we owe all that “we live and move and are” (Acts 17). “Yet we have not resisted unto blood” (Heb. 12); nor have we performed even slight penance. Ambrose (*On the One Penance*, book 2, ch. 10), showing how great it must be if it is true, says: “I have found more who preserved baptismal innocence than who performed true penance.”

## CHAPTER 146. On the Caution Required in Penance

[Col. 0349D]

In performing it, the greatest caution must be employed: that, having been circumcised and cleansed from sin through confession, in accordance with Joshua’s command (ch. 5), you remain in the same place of the camp until you are perfectly healed. This will happen if you eat the bread of grief and penance in silence, away from the noise of the crowd, withdrawing yourself from spectacles, associations, persons, and every occasion of sin.

Hence Jerome says: “For those who have professed penance, the recollection of past pleasures is dangerous. For the flesh most tenderly breathes after former allurements and urges the spirit brought out of Sodom to look back toward Egypt, to return to Pharaoh’s garlic and melons” (Num. 11). Lest this occur, hide with Rachel [Col. 0350A] Laban’s idols beneath dung—that is, sins beneath the filth of penance (Gen. 31). And not only sins: with Jacob, bury beneath the terebinth tree all the phylacteries of broken idols (Gen. 35). That is, through the memory of the Lord’s cross, mortifying yourself, bury every circumstance and occasion of sin; and permit no little occasion to cause relapse.

For this reason also, with Moses, hide and bury the Egyptian beneath the sand. Reduce the molten calf also to the finest powder (Exod. 2), lest its memory be revived. Take nothing from the accursed thing of Jericho, like the unhappy Achan (Josh. 7), but burn it all, reduce it to ashes; and then confidently say: “You have forgiven, O Lord, the sins of your people”—thus, of the penitent—“you have covered all their sins and cast all my sins behind your back” (Ps. 84) [Col. 0350B].

This caution in penance has strength joined to it as a companion, concerning which there was discussion above (ch. 117). Hence it is also said: “He brings forth the bound in strength” (Ps. 67), both the strength of him who brings forth and of him brought forth or to be brought forth. In order to inflict this strength upon yourself, consider the deed of Ehud, who drove a dagger into the belly of Eglon, the very fat king, so powerfully that the hilt followed the iron (Judg. 3). He did not draw out the sword, but left it in the body as he had struck it; immediately the filth of his belly burst out through the secret passages of nature. He did this after most carefully shutting the doors of the upper chamber and fastening them with a bar.

Therefore drive the iron of penance into the fatness of sins, and persevere even to the hilt [Col. 0350C] and the end of penance—that is, throughout the entire course of life. Do not cease until the filth and circumstances of sins burst forth. Do this with the doors of your mind, and of all your paths and works, closed, lest through an occasion of sin you fall back. Do this also after the example of a certain man who, when he first fell again into his habitual weakness of the flesh, stabbed himself, as it were with a sword, by the vow to enter a monastery—thus abstaining from his customary and ingrained sin. You also will pierce your flesh with “the devouring sword of the Lord” (Jer. 12), if you live according to the Gospel, which will be your cross and martyrdom.

Again, on caution in penance, Genesis chapter 19: “Do not look behind you, nor stand in all the surrounding region”—that is, in any circumstance or occasion of sin—“but save yourself on the mountain.” Again, on the quantity and severity of penance, which must be equivalent to purgatorial fire: for either God punishes or man does. If God, it is in purgatorial fire, whose slightest punishment is heavier and more severe than the most exquisite torments of all martyrs. If man, it is by temporal punishment, which according to human ability must be equivalent to purgatory. This will happen if he kindles, according to his strength, the fire of tribulation and penitential severity; otherwise he will appear to punish himself insufficiently and not to repent truly [Col. 0350D]. Therefore few truly repent.

Again, how great penance ought to be is evident from the fact that a greater and harsher torment, even with equal charity, confers swifter absolution in purgatory [Col. 0351A]; therefore also in penance, which must be equivalent to it. Thus he repents less who is less tormented, even though he has equal charity. But he who is tormented more is more quickly freed from the punishment of sin. Thus, in this case—that is, penance—God delights in human torments; yet by greater torment persons do not merit a greater reward, but swifter deliverance. “Dig around your tree, then, and put in dung,” the filth of penance, lest, with “the axe now laid to the root,” it be cut down (Luke 13).

Against past softness and pleasures of the flesh, sleep in sackcloth; cure excessive sleep with many vigils; relieve gluttony by fasting; dry up drunkenness with thirst.
