Thus cure opposites with opposites, and say: “As things burned by fire”—by wrongly kindled love—“and dug down”—by wrongly humbling fear—“they shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance” (Ps. 79) [Col. 0351B]. Conversely: “Burned by fire,” not only of charity but of penitential tribulation rightly kindled, and “dug down” by divinely given and rightly humbling fear, they shall be saved “by your mercy” and “shall rejoice” (Ps. 30).

For as iron is purified by fire and hammer, so hardened and ingrained sin is purified by tribulation and scourges. Of one thus purified and penitent David says: “He answered him”—that is, the Lord—“in the way of his strength” (Ps. 101): according to his ability, he made temporal punishment equal to purgatorial fire. And because he continually held in his heart the memory of death, the fewness of his days, and the brevity of life—so that this might remain continually fixed in his heart—he adds in prayer: “Make known to me the fewness of my days” (ibid.); that is, make me always hold the brevity of my life in mind [Col. 0351C].

## CHAPTER 147. On Always Keeping in the Heart the Brevity of Human Life

Concerning this brevity of life, which must always be held in memory so that you may repent, David says in Psalm 38: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end,” namely, that I may always hold it in my heart; “and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what is lacking to me. Behold, you have made my days measurable, and my substance as nothing before you,” in comparison with your eternity. “Yet every living man is altogether vanity; yet man passes away in an image. And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance”—not perishable, but enduring for ever—“is with you” (Ps. 38) [Col. 0351D].

Again, the philosopher says: “Every day, every hour, shows that we are nothing, and by some new evidence of our frailty forces us, though forgetful and contemplating eternal things, to look back upon death. How foolish it is to arrange one’s lifetime when you are not master even of tomorrow! O what madness among those who begin long hopes and say: ‘I shall buy, build, lend, collect, hold offices; then at last I shall withdraw a weary and full old age into leisure.’ Believe me, all things are uncertain even for the fortunate; no one should promise himself anything concerning the future. Even what is held slips through the hands; disaster cuts short the very hour which we press.” Therefore let us always form our mind as though we had come to the end.

Again Jerome: “What is the present life? A point. And temporal delight? Sleep, shadow, foam, smoke.” The philosopher: “A brief and unreal pleasure.” It is sleep, because “they slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75). It is foam, because the little fire of a three-day fever disperses and dissolves it. Human life is more perishable than a spider; hence: “You made my soul waste away like a spider” (Ps. 38). It is shadow, because “his day passed like a shadow” (Ps. 143). And the poet says:

> We are a light shadow; we are smoke driven by a whirlwind;  
> We are the hay of the field: first flesh, afterwards mud.

[Col. 0352B]

It is smoke, because it is “a vapor appearing for a little while,” as James says (ch. 4). And David says: “He remembered that we are dust; man is like grass, his days like the flower of the field; so he shall flourish” (Ps. 102). Again: “They shall quickly wither like grass and swiftly fall like green herbs” (Ps. 36), because “as the morning passes, in the evening he falls, hardens, and withers” (Ps. 89).

Again the poet Ovid (*Remedies for Love*):

> The passing years steal each thing from us;  
> He who is not fit today will be less fit tomorrow.

Again, we may be instructed by an apologue. Two men united in friendship made an agreement that the first of them to become wealthy and promoted would immediately raise the other. One was promoted. The other at once approached him, asking to be enriched and exalted. While supper was being prepared, the two went for a walk. By magical art, one clouded the other’s eyes, so that the latter now seemed to himself to be chosen metropolitan and patriarch, conducted with great pomp, and enthroned with musical instruments [Col. 0352C]. Afterwards his companion opened his eyes by withdrawing the magical art and invited him to the lavish supper already prepared. He said to him: “Why have you drawn me away from such great joy? If it had been true joy, I would not compare it with all Croesus’s riches.” The other replied: “But you ought to choose that joy even more than the true one. For, though imaginary, it is truer than present joy and happiness. Both are perishable and transitory. That one, like this one, is sprinkled with no bitterness; no sin, or at least not so much sin, steals in. Therefore it should be chosen rather than this.” Thus contempt for the world was persuaded to both, so thoroughly that they immediately fled to the desert or monastery.

Again: for one lavish supper of a single night you would endure no loss of reputation, disgrace, danger, or injury to the body. Yet the entire banquet of this present life is nothing in comparison with the future; and a banquet of one night is something in comparison with the banquet of the present life. Therefore, lest you lose the future banquet, you must according to your ability avoid everything through which it is lost. Hence diligently strive through penance and contempt of the world to preserve the great treasure hidden “in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4) [Col. 0353A], for which the Lord created you unto such blessedness and such a banquet.

Again Hosea (ch. 13): “Therefore men shall be like a morning cloud, and like the morning dew passing away; like dust swept away from the threshing-floor by a whirlwind, and like smoke from a chimney.” Again Isaiah, chapter 29: “The multitude of those who winnow you shall be like fine dust, and like passing sparks, and like the dream of a night vision.” Hence David says: “I saw the wicked highly exalted; I passed by, and behold he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36). Yet even if you compare and join each individual millennium of time to each grain of sand in the sea, time will nevertheless reach its end, because the number of grains of sand is determinate.

It is therefore certain that all time which can be imagined is but a point of an hour and exceedingly brief in comparison with eternity [Col. 0353B]. How then, in such brevity of time, do you place your soul as though under the cast of a die, by not doing penance? Nor do we dare or can we postpone our case without the judge’s own decision. How, then, when we must render account and explanation to the eternal Judge for all our works, do we defer and delay repenting and doing good—especially since he threatens us that he “will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thess. 5), and exhorts us: “Walk while it is day, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12)?

Again Jerome, on Ezekiel chapter 25: “The world and all its flower and delight are like ‘red lentils’” (Gen. 25). Therefore look, my son: do not sell the right and dignity of the firstborn and the father’s blessing for red lentils. Again Gregory (*Morals*, book 14, ch. 4): “The pleasure of fornication is transitory and brief, but the punishment of the fornicator is everlasting.” From all these considerations fear can be instilled into us, so that we may hasten more urgently to perform penance.

Again David, lamenting the brevity of human life in Psalm 72, says: “How have they been brought to desolation! They suddenly failed; they perished because of their iniquity. As a dream of those who rise, O Lord, in your city you shall reduce their image to nothing.” For this reason a certain rich man, in order to embitter his pleasures as though putting a bridle upon them, kept a servant while he dined who said to him: “You will die, you will die” [Col. 0353D]. For the best definition of philosophy is continual meditation upon death.

And the philosopher, Seneca (*Letters* 24 and 54), says: “Whom will you give me who sets any value upon time, who appraises a day, who understands that he dies daily? For we are deceived in this: that we do not look ahead to death. A great part of it has already passed. Whatever span of life lies behind us, death possesses.”

Therefore embrace every hour; thus you will depend less upon tomorrow if you lay hold upon today. How then, wretch, do you not arrange your household every hour? How, unhappy man, do you not continually set death before your eyes? Think him already dead whom you know must necessarily die. Your childhood has already perished in you; your adolescence is dead in you; youth has departed; now old age torments you [Col. 0354A]. Decrepitude threatens, to extinguish and bury you.

Know that the water-clock does not exhaust only its final drop, but also every drop which flowed out before it. Thus death does not close only the last hour of life, but brings it to completion and consummation. Indeed, we share this very day in which we live with death. Again Jerome: “Our foolishness is especially exposed in this: though we immediately perceive loss of temporal goods, we do not perceive the loss and failing of body and limbs, such as decay, shaking, and the falling of teeth.”

We are alert in noticing loss of provisions, but lethargic and dull in considering and avoiding danger to the soul. We come unprepared and unconcerned to the market of the heavenly King, fearing to approach it; whereas to temporal markets we go only prepared and carefully supplied with necessities by which we purchase perishable goods [Col. 0354B]. Therefore we are lazy servants and wretched merchants, when by a fortunate exchange we ought to trade earthly things for heavenly. How shall we say to the householder: “Lord, you entrusted two or five talents to me; behold, I have gained another two or five,” if we have not put “the Lord’s money out at interest” (Matt. 25) before we must render account of it?

Again, when you have been hired to cultivate the Lord’s vineyard with the blood of the spotless Lamb, how do you stand idle in the eleventh hour? At least work even in the final hour, knowing that you have passed the first, third, and sixth hours idle and fruitless (Matt. 20). In what hour do you believe yourself to be? Why do you wait a little longer? Perhaps the final hour is already present for you: perhaps the Lord is already coming and knocking at your door, saying, “Open, open.”

Therefore, because of the brevity of human life, let the penitent continually say in fear with Hezekiah: “I said: In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of hell. I sought the remainder of my years; I said, I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living. I shall see man no more, nor the inhabitant of rest. My generation has been taken away and folded up from me like a shepherd’s tent. My life has been cut off like cloth from the weaver; while I was still beginning, he cut me off. From morning until evening you will make an end of me. I hoped until morning; like a lion, so he crushed my bones [Col. 0354D]. From morning until evening you will make an end of me. Like a young swallow I shall cry; I shall meditate like a dove,” etc. (Isa. 38).

Let him say also: “Men of blood shall not halve their days” (Ps. 54). Yet the beginning of true penance is, as it were, a halving of days, because “one day in your courts”—and in the courts of the penitent—“is better than thousands” (Ps. 83) spent in sin. Some, however, literally begin their days here; some halve them for God; some end them; some bring them to perfection and consummation.

Again Job, chapter 7: “The life of man upon earth is warfare.” Again, chapter 14: “Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.” Again, chapter 20: “This I know: that the praise of the ungodly is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite like a point” [Col. 0355A], who at the end shall perish like a dung-heap. And below: “They are exalted and strengthened by riches and amusements; their little children hold drum and lyre and rejoice at the sound of the instrument. They spend their days in good things, and in a point of an hour descend to the depths of hell.”

## CHAPTER 148. On Hastening Penance

“He has the face of one going to Jerusalem” (Luke 9) who continually bears in his heart the brevity of human life, mindful of that saying of the Lord: “Pray that your flight may not happen in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24): that is, in the chilling time of old age, or late, or in the time of rest—namely, after judgment, when rest ought to be taken—but rather: “While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be children of light” (John 12) [Col. 0355B]. “Repent” (Acts 3), and make satisfaction for sin in the time of sowing, while you “breathe the vital airs.” “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. 125). “For in its season you shall reap” (Gal. 6).

But: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings and penitential labours will also reap eternal life from blessings” (II Cor. IX). Penance, therefore, must be hastened, and practised throughout the whole time of life—especially after the example of Noah, who for a hundred years built the ark (Gen. VI), in which he might save himself from temporal death, and only for a time. How much more ought you, throughout the whole course of your life, to prepare the ark—that is, your soul—for which Christ died; and, with greater care, to coat it within, in the heart (toward yourself and God), and without, in works (toward yourself and your neighbour), with the indissoluble pitch of charity, in order to avoid eternal death? Nor must one cease coating it because of the reproaches and insults of neighbours and relatives, just as Noah did not cease building the ark. “For as you presented your members, and for however long, to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity” (Rom. VI), so likewise for just as long, etc.

## CHAPTER CXLIX. On the seven reasons for hastening penance.

There are seven reasons why penance must especially be hastened.

The first is the habit of sinning, from which a person can scarcely tear himself away, and whose practice is unlearned with difficulty; for habit carries with it the greatest bond, being, as it were, a second nature. Thus Horace (Book I, Epistle 2):

> The jar, once newly steeped, will long preserve  
> The scent.

And there is no room for a remedy where what were vices have become habits. It is easy to return to familiar practices, but difficult to tear oneself from a habit whose use has held one for a long time and pleased one with great delight (Horace, Book II, Satire 5):

> As a dog is not frightened away from a greased hide.

So neither is one accustomed to sin frightened away from sin. For he who is weighed down by the stone of sinful habit stinks, like Lazarus four days dead (John XI) [Col. 0356A], and “sits in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron” (Ps. CVI): that is, by a habit iron-hard, harsh, and scarcely dissoluble.

Jerome: The people of Israel could scarcely forget, in the wilderness, the more sumptuous Egyptian table—melons, that is, pleasures—and the thousand disgraceful deeds they had committed. For ingrained and evil habit is sticky. Hence Jeremiah, chapter XIII: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard its spots? Then you also will be able to do good, when you have learned evil”—by study and habit. The same, chapter XVIII: “The Lord says: There is no one who does penance for his sin, saying, ‘What have I done?’ But all have turned to their own course, like a horse rushing headlong into battle.” The same, chapter IX: “They taught [Col. 0356B] their tongue to speak falsehood; they have laboured to act wickedly.” Likewise Basil the Great (Book of Responses to Disputed Rules, response 6): As a man cannot unlearn his mother tongue, so he can scarcely unlearn a long habit of sin.

“Blessed, therefore, is he who has borne the Lord’s yoke from his youth, and has lifted himself above himself” (Lam. III), because practice becomes skill when, that is, after, a crime is unlearned from tender years. (Ovid, *Heroides*, Epistle 4.)

The second reason is the collapse from sin into sin. For a sin not immediately washed away by penance draws, by its own weight, toward another sin (Basil, on Isaiah I). “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. IV), “that they may fill up their sins always” (I Thess. II). “The sins of the Amorites are not yet full” (Gen. XV). Woe [Col. 0356C] to those who draw out a long rope of sins. This is “the cord with which they will be bound and cast into outer darkness” (Matt. XXII). “My scars have putrefied and become corrupt because of my foolishness. I have become wretched and bowed down to the end” (Ps. XXXVII), etc. “And when the sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII). Remaining in mortal sin, he “stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the righteous judgment of God, according to his impenitent heart” (Rom. II). For “deep calls to deep” (Ps. XLI).

Therefore fear to remain in sin because of its consequence. For the Prophet, invoking curses on such people, says: “Let their way be darkness and slipperiness, with the angel of the Lord pursuing them” (Ps. XXXIV). And: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bow down their back always,” etc. (Ps. LXVIII). “Therefore God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to dishonourable passions, so that they might do things which are unfitting” (Rom. I). Likewise, Hebrews, chapter XII: “See that no one lacks the grace of God,” etc. Therefore do not borrow a talent from the devil, the exactor, because you will repay it with heavy interest. “For the moneylender will search out all your substance, and strangers will plunder your labours” (Ps. CVIII).

The third reason and danger is sudden, untimely, and uncertain death. For although nothing is more certain than death, nevertheless nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death. Therefore, lest you be “taken beforehand” (Wis. IV), you must forestall it by penance. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Watch, [Col. 0357A] be vigilant, and pray” (Mark XIV), “for you do not know at what hour the Lord will come. Blessed is that servant whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watchful. If the master of the household knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” (Matt. XXIV). “You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect” (Luke XII). Likewise: “Fool, this night they will demand [your soul]” (ibid.), etc. “If the righteous man is taken beforehand by death, he will be at rest” (Wis. IV); but if the unjust man is taken beforehand by death, he will be in eternal punishment. “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. XXXIII); “evils shall seize the unjust man in his destruction” (Ps. CXXXIX). “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord” (Ps. CXIII). “The living, the living, he shall confess you” (Isa. XXXVIII).

In hell there is no [Col. 0357B] redemption and no confession; for “who will confess you in hell?” (Ps. VI). Jerome: Therefore gather in the sixth age a homer of heavenly manna, sufficient for you in the seventh age, that of those at rest. For “henceforth the Spirit says that they may rest from their labours” (Apoc. XIV). Say also with the Prophet: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids,” etc. (Ps. CXXXI). Thus sleep as though you will never wake again; thus keep watch as though you will never sleep again:

> Believe that every day which has dawned for you is your last.  
> —Horace, Book I, Epistle 4

“You do not know what the coming day will bring forth” (Prov. XXVII): excessive is the treasure which we expose to so great a danger. For snares surround us everywhere, from the [Col. 0357C] manifold enemy.

The fourth danger is this: even if, while you are long ill, time is granted you to deliberate and repent, nevertheless, overwhelmed by illness and by its sharpness, you are wholly the servant of illness and attentive to it, not to penance. Indeed, you are so entirely occupied with this that you first ask for and summon a physician of the body rather than one of the spirit; you rejoice more at the arrival of a physician than of a confessor. Hence Hildebert of Le Mans, “On a Fire”:

> Ah! with what anxious labour everyone hastens,  
> Out of love for the flesh, to meet the physician.  
> No complaint follows concerning the diseases of the soul;  
> A tardy remedy follows the soul when it has departed.

Jerome: Therefore do penance while you are well, while you are able to sin, so that you may appear to repent and abandon sins from love, not from fear; and not that the sins themselves abandon you. If you are ill, how do you know that you truly repent? Jerome: You can scarcely think of anything except what you feel. For the whole attention of the mind is drawn where the force of pain lies. Penance, moreover, is a delicate matter, requiring a mind at rest and tranquil; it does not wish to be occupied or hindered by other things. Nor is this surprising. Our own small affairs, to be carried out well, demand an ample and suitable time, with obstacles and other concerns removed. And when we ought to have owed our entire life to God, how shall we, who may live only one hour longer, pay the whole debt? The judge’s suit against us will not be empty, nor can the debtor’s poverty exclude it, when throughout the whole span of life he had the means to pay.

The fifth danger is that, even where true penance is present, though late, we have not forestalled purgatorial fire—which we ought to have forestalled—and which is more grievous than the most exquisite torments of martyrs. We know that either God punishes or man does, and that “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X). Therefore: “Let all my enemies be ashamed and exceedingly troubled; let them turn back and be very swiftly ashamed” (Ps. VI).

The sixth is the difficulty of truly doing penance. Hence Ambrose (*On the Unity of Penance*, Book II, chapter 10): I have found more persons who preserved baptismal innocence than who performed true penance. It is easier to preserve health once possessed than to restore it after it has been lost. For this is achieved only through bitter draughts, fire, flame, and iron.

[Col. 0358B] The seventh is the bitterness and shame of confessing one’s sin, stripped bare with all its circumstances, before a priest. Hence the Apostle: “And now what fruit had you in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI). Yes, yes: through the bitter cup of the remedy one comes to the joy of salvation (Gregory, Homily 27 on the Gospels). But where is the person who does not make himself coverings with Adam (Gen. III), excusing his sin either in its substance or in some other circumstance which he is ashamed to confess? Where is he? “And we shall praise him” (Ecclus. XXXI). For these reasons and many others, we ought, as far as our strength permits, to abstain from sin.

## CHAPTER CL. On eternal punishment.

[Col. 0358C]

Besides the foregoing motives for hastening penance, continual meditation on eternal punishment, together with eternal blessedness or life, is necessary. Between these millstones the Christian soul must always be ground, that it may become bread most pleasing to the Lord. Setting eternal punishment and the state of the future judgment before our eyes, so as to instil horror and fear into us and cause us to hasten penance, the Prophet briefly describes it:

“You will make them, O Lord, like a furnace of fire” (Ps. XX), so that they may have nowhere to go out, nowhere to rest or catch breath from their several sins, while the fire and worm of conscience bite and burn them as in a furnace, “in the time of your countenance”—that is, of your wrathful and angry face—when, “mighty like one drunk with wine” [Col. 0358D] (Ps. LXXVII), you come to judgment, the trumpet being sounded by an angel: “Arise, dead! Arise, you who sleep in the graves!”

Hence: “The Lord shall trouble them in his wrath” (Ps. XX), arguing the case with them: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. XXV)—from whatever bread and talent entrusted to you for distribution. “I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (ibid.), and so concerning the remaining works of mercy, with the seventh added, namely the burial of the dead, the work of holy Tobit. Likewise: “Wicked and slothful servant, who hid your lord’s talent: you knew that I am a harsh man, reaping where I did not sow and gathering where I did not scatter. Ought you not, then, to have entrusted my money to the bankers, so that when I came I might certainly have received [Col. 0359A] what was mine with interest?”

Finally they will be pierced as by a sword by this utterance: “I do not know you”; and by this: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire”; and by this: “Cast them into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid.). Then the eternal fire of Gehenna “will devour them” (Ps. XX), raising in them eternal smoke and tears. “They shall have gnashing of teeth” because of the frost of eternal punishment, for “they shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job XXIV); and thus they will be punished in a threefold hell.

First, upon hearing the “harsh word” (Ps. XC), “Arise, dead,” when they are raised and awake from the sleep of death, conscience immediately tortures and condemns them.

Second, upon hearing the harsher word in reproach of their sins and of the talent not distributed but “hidden” (Matt. XXV).

Third, upon hearing the harshest word, when they fall and descend into the abyss of hell: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (ibid.).

Elsewhere the Prophet expresses this misery of those to be damned: “Then he shall speak to them in his wrath and trouble them in his fury” (Ps. II). Likewise Isaiah, in the last chapter: “The elect shall go out,” not because they delight in those persons’ punishment, but because of their plain sight of it, “and shall see the corpses of those who have transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched; and they shall be unto satiety of vision for all flesh,” because “the righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance” [Col. 0359C] (Ps. LVII).

Likewise John the Baptist, Matthew chapter III: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the wrath to come? Produce fruits worthy of penance. And do not choose to say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; we are from the horn of the altar; the temple of the Lord and Holy Scripture are among us. For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones. Already the axe has been laid to the root of the tree. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire.” “The Ancient of Days shall sit with the elders of the land” (Prov. XXXI), “whose winnowing fan is in his hand; and he shall thoroughly cleanse his threshing-floor, gather his wheat into his granary, but burn the chaff and tares with unquenchable fire” (Matt. III; Luke III).

[Col. 0359D] Likewise Habakkuk, chapter III: “In indignation you will tread down the earth; in wrath you will strike the nations with astonishment”; for who has measured, “or who can number your wrath?” (Ps. LXXXIX). Or, “who can endure everlasting burnings?” (Isa. XXXIII). “Who knows the power of your wrath?” (Ps. LXXXIX). Praying that this fury and wrath might be removed, the Prophet says: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury”—that of eternal punishment—“by punishing me; nor correct me in your anger”—that of purgatorial fire—“which is lesser still, by purging me” (Ps. VI). But burn here; cut here.

Likewise Zephaniah, chapter I: “A voice of crying” from the first “gate,” that is, from the sight of conscience already condemning them; “and wailing” from the second, that is, from the gate of hearing, as they hear that terrible utterance: “Depart, [Col. 0360A] you cursed” (Matt. XXV). And afterward: “Great destruction from the hills” (Zeph. I). Since they did not possess sight and hearing as “windows” for sinning—more confined and sinning less—but as “gates,” widening these senses for sinning, in punishment they will not have these senses as “windows,” so as to suffer narrow and moderate pains, but as “gates,” so that they may be tormented broadly and abundantly.

Likewise: “The fire of Gehenna has been kindled in my fury, and it shall burn unto the lowest parts of hell” (Deut. XXXII). Likewise: “He shall rain snares upon sinners” (Ps. X): fire in the present life, namely sins, by which, bound as with ropes, they “will be cast into outer darkness” (Matt. XXV). And the fire of Gehenna “and sulphur”—that is, the stench of sins and of infernal punishments—will be “the portion [Col. 0360B] of their cup,” that is, of their punishment (Ps. X), because in these they will be punished only partially: their quantity and quality cannot be explained except partially; or they will be punished partially because less than they deserved.

Likewise Proverbs, chapter XIX: “Judgments” of damnation “are prepared for mockers,” that is, for those who despise the divine commandments, and “hammers striking the bodies of fools”; for, as glowing iron, so they will be beaten and struck with hammers upon an anvil. Will they, then, fail away in punishment? By no means. For “they are placed like sheep in hell”; once their wool has been shorn, more grows back. “Death shall feed upon them” (Ps. XLVIII). For they will grow again for punishments, just as the tip of a rod or grass eaten by a sheep nevertheless grows again.

Likewise Hebrews, chapter X: “There is a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a jealous fire of Gehenna which will consume the adversaries of God.” Likewise Job, chapter X: “Why did you bring me forth from the womb? Would that I had been consumed, so that no eye might see me. I should have been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the tomb. Will not the fewness of my days soon come to an end? Leave me, therefore, that I may mourn my pain a little, before I go and do not return to a land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death, 328 a land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwells.”

Likewise: If one guilty of treason against royal majesty is, even under human [Col. 0360D] laws, decreed to suffer capital punishment, what end will there be for those who despise divine omnipotence? “He touches the mountains and they smoke” (Ps. CIII), and does a worthless little particle of dust, to be scattered by a single light breath and utterly incapable of being reconciled or gathered again, dare provoke so fearsome a majesty? He—he is to be feared, “who, after he has killed the body, has power to cast into Gehenna” (Luke XII). I dread Gehenna; I dread the Judge’s face, terrible even to the angelic powers. I tremble “before the wrath of the Mighty One” (Jer. IV), “before the face of his fury” (Jer. XXX), “before the crash of the collapsing world, the conflagration of the elements” (II Pet. III), “the mighty tempest” (Ps. X), “the voice of the archangel” (I Thess. IV), and “the harsh word” (Ps. XC).

[Col. 0361A] I tremble before the teeth of the infernal beast, before the belly of hell, “before the roaring creatures prepared for food” (Ecclus. LI). I shudder at the gnawing worm and rushing fire, smoke, heat, and numbness, “sulphur and the spirit of tempests” (Ps. X). I shudder at “outer darkness” (Matt. XXV). “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. IX), that by weeping I may forestall weeping and gnashing of teeth, the harsh fetters of hands and feet, and the weight of chains pressing, constricting, burning, yet not consuming. Alas for me, my mother! Why did you bear me? (Jer. XV), a son of pain, a son of bitterness, indignation, and eternal lamentation. “Why was I received upon knees? Why suckled at breasts?” (Job III), born “for burning and food for fire” [Col. 0361B] (Isa. IX).

Whoever is thus affected has undoubtedly recovered his senses, and in fear and shame runs to confession, by which the stains of all sins are wiped away.

But you will say: “I cannot fast, weep, keep silence, practise continence, and so forth, in this way.” The answer is: nevertheless, whether you wish it or not, and of necessity, you will abstain from these things in hell. Therefore forestall this, so that you may eat bread in the kingdom of God.

Likewise, from pictures in which you may observe that penalties resembling sins are owed for similar sins, and that people are punished in the limbs with which they sinned: one person is burned in the genitals, another in the tongue, another in the palate; some have their eyes pulled out, others their feet cut off and bound, and such things. One may also see a father attacking his children and reproaching [Col. 0361C] them that because of their sins he had been a sinner and a usurer, and therefore rising against them and tearing their faces with teeth and nails. Conversely, children rise against their father and reproach him in dialogue for having furnished them occasion for robbery and for detaining another’s property.

Likewise Bede (*Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book V, chapter 13), concerning a certain head of a household who led a religious life with his household in Lesser Britain: Having been afflicted with bodily illness, he finally died in the first part of the night; but at daybreak, returning to life and suddenly sitting up, he drove in terrified flight all those who sat weeping beside the body, except his wife, who loved him more than the others. [Col. 0361D] Consoling her in her fear, he said: “Do not be afraid, because I have now truly risen from the death in which I was held among men, and I have been permitted to live again—yet not as before, but I shall live very differently.”

Immediately he sought an oratory; afterward, returning from prayer into the house, he divided all his substance into three portions. One he gave to his wife, another to his children, and the third he retained for himself, immediately distributing it to the poor. Not long afterward, freed from worldly concerns, he came to a monastery situated beside a river. Having received the tonsure, he entered the place of secluded dwelling which the abbot had provided for him. There he remained until the day of his death in such contrition of mind and body that, even if his tongue kept silence, his life declared that he had seen many things, hidden from others, either dreadful or desirable. He related what he had seen in this manner:

“He who led me was bright in appearance and shining in garment.” As we walked silently, we came to a broad, long, and deep valley. On one side it had fires most hot and crackling; on the other, every kind of cold—snow, hail, and frost. Then I began to think that it was hell. My guide answered this thought: ‘This is not,’ he said, ‘the place of hell, as you suppose, but a purgatorial place, where souls to be purified, exhausted by fire, leap into the midst of hostile cold, and conversely.’

“When he led me a little farther inward, I saw before me dark places, and, as it were, tangible darkness. There, as though from certain [Col. 0362B] wells, I saw balls of ashes ascend with smoke and boiling stench pouring forth; then I saw those balls in turn fall back into the depths. While I stood there for a little while in fear, uncertain what I should do or where I should turn, I heard behind my back the sound of immense weeping and wailing, together with a crackling laugh, like that of an uneducated crowd jeering at captured enemies. I saw a crowd of evil spirits mocking with laughter and dragging three souls to hell. Of these, so far as I could discern, one was tonsured like a cleric, one was a layman, and one was a woman. Thus they descended with them into the wells.

“Meanwhile certain spirits ascended from the flame-vomiting abyss, with flaming eyes, breathing foul fire from mouth and nostrils. They strove to seize me with fiery tongs, but did not prevail. For my guide appeared to me with brightness, like a twinkling star ever increasing amid the darkness. Led out into open light, I saw before us a very great wall, high and long without end, having no door, window, or ascent; and by some means unknown to me we were immediately upon its summit.

“And behold: there was there a very broad field, full of the fragrance of flowers in spring and the splendour of unutterable light. In it were innumerable gatherings of persons clothed in white, very many seats, and companies rejoicing. Then I began to think that it was the kingdom of heaven, of which I had often heard. My guide answered [Col. 0362D] this thought: ‘This is not,’ he said, ‘the kingdom of heaven, as you think, but the region of holy spirits; not yet, however, of such perfection that they immediately deserve to be introduced into the kingdom of heaven. The flame-vomiting well which you saw is the very mouth of Gehenna; whoever falls into it even once will never come out of it. But you, because you are now returning to humankind, should strive to live more in simplicity and uprightness, so that you may live eternally among these joyful companies which you behold.’

“Delighted by the sweetness and beauty of the place and the fellowship of the saints, I greatly disliked returning to the body, yet I did not dare ask my guide anything. But amid these things, by some means unknown to me, I suddenly found myself living among people.”

[Col. 0363A] He did not recount his visions to the curious and unlearned, but to religious persons, including King Wilfrid [perhaps Alfred], a religious man. Until the day of his death he lived on sifted bread and a meagre diet, entering the river daily—often while it was frozen—to mortify the flesh, and there pouring prayers and supplications to the Lord. When he was asked why he afflicted himself with so many miseries and such cold, he answered: “That I may avoid the greater things which I saw.” Thus, by the example of his holy way of life, he stirred many to penance.

Likewise Jerome to Heliodorus: “That day will come, will come, on which ‘this corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality’ (I Cor. XV)—blessed is the servant whom the Lord finds watchful” (Luke XII). Then at the trumpet’s voice the earth will fear together with its peoples, [Col. 0363B] but you will rejoice. When the Lord is about to judge, the world will roar mournfully; tribe will strike breast against tribe; once most powerful kings will tremble with naked side. Then fiery Jupiter with his offspring will truly be displayed; foolish Plato will be brought with his disciples; Aristotle’s arguments will not help. Then, rustic and poor man, you will leap for joy, laugh, and say: “Behold my crucified God. Behold the Judge who wailed, wrapped in swaddling cloths in a manger. This is the son of a workman and of a working woman; this is he whom, carried in his mother’s bosom, God as man fled into Egypt; this is he clothed in scarlet and crowned with thorns. This magician, possessed by a demon and called a Samaritan by blasphemers. Look, Jew, at the hands which you pierced; look, Roman, at the side which you opened. See the body: is it the same one which you said the disciples had secretly removed by night?” Brother, your love compelled me to say these things to you; and, so that it may fall to your lot to share in these joys, undertake the labour which is now hard.

## CHAPTER CLI. On the joy and reward of eternal blessedness.

Jerome, at the end of his letter to Eustochium, describing the joys and rewards of eternal blessedness, says (*On Preserving Virginity*):

“Leave the prison for a little while, I pray you, and set before your eyes the reward of your present labour, which ‘eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man’ (I Cor. II). What will that day be like when Mary, the mother [Col. 0363D] of the Lord, comes to meet you, attended by virgin choirs; when, after the Red Sea, Pharaoh having been submerged with his army, she holds a tambourine and begins the song for those who answer:

> Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honoured;  
> Horse and rider he has cast into the sea!  
> (Exod. XV)

“Then Thecla will joyfully fly into your embrace; then the Bridegroom himself will meet you, saying: ‘Arise, come, my near one, my bride, my dove’ (Song II), because ‘behold, winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed’ (ibid.) for her. Then the angels also will marvel and say: ‘Who is this appearing like the dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun? The daughters shall see you, and queens shall praise you, and concubines shall proclaim you’ (Song VI). Then another choir of the chaste will come running. Sarah will come with married women; Anna, daughter of Phanuel, [Col. 0364A] with widows. In different companies of flesh and spirit, those women will be your mothers. One will rejoice that she gave birth to you; the other will exult that she taught you.

“Then the Lord will truly mount the ass and enter the heavenly Jerusalem (Matt. XXI); then the little ones—of whom the Saviour speaks in Isaiah: ‘Behold, I and my children whom God has given me’ (Isa. VIII)—raising palms of victory, will sing with one harmonious voice: ‘Hosanna in the highest! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!’” (Matt. XXI).

“Then the hundred and forty-four thousand, before the throne and the elders, will hold harps and sing a new song. And no one will be able to utter that song” (Apoc. XIV), except the fixed number. “These are those who have not been defiled with women; for they have remained virgins. These are those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (ibid.).

Whenever the vain ambition of the world delights you, whenever you see anything glorious in the world, pass in mind to paradise. Begin here to be what you are going to be, and you will hear from your Bridegroom: “Set me as” a shade or covering “upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song VIII); and, fortified alike in work and thought, you will cry out and say: “Many waters cannot extinguish charity, nor can rivers cover it” (ibid.).

Likewise Jerome, at the end of the letter to Demetrias [volume II begins, “Though endowed with the highest intellect,” but it is not by Jerome]:

“Consider, I pray, the greatness of your reward, if indeed anything that is boundless can be considered. After the soul’s departure, after the body’s dissolution [Col. 0364C], after ashes and dust, you, a virgin, are to be restored to a better state. Your body, committed to the earth, is to be raised to heaven; your mortality is to be changed by the honour of immortality. After these things you are to be granted fellowship with angels, to receive the kingdom of heaven, and to remain eternally with Christ.

“What, therefore, will you return to the Lord for all that he has returned to you?” (Ps. CXV). “What will you do worthy of so great a Rewarder? What labour will you consider hard, when its rewards are so great?” Hence the Apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). And likewise: “This momentary affliction works in us an eternal weight of glory” (II Cor. [Col. 0364D] IV).

“You, therefore, for whom meditation upon Christ’s coming fills days and nights; for whom, because of the purity of your conscience, the Lord’s presence is to be desired; who await the end of the world as the fixed time of your reward—you will receive exultation from that day, not fear. For then, mingled with the choirs of saints and attended by holy virgins, you will fly up to meet the Bridegroom in his embrace, saying: ‘I have found him whom my soul sought’ (Song III). You will no longer fear separation at any time, since, once endowed with the glory of immortality and the splendour of incorruption, you will reign always with Christ. As the Apostle says: ‘For the Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of an archangel, and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who live, who [Col. 0365A] remain, shall be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord’ (I Thess. IV)—‘heirs indeed of God, and co-heirs with Christ’ (Rom. VIII).

“Therefore let this always be your concern and study. Let these things continually turn in a virgin’s heart; let the labour of the whole day be occupied with them, and let even the sleep of night be placed in them. Let the soul awake again to these things. No labour should seem hard, no time long, by which the glory of eternity is acquired.”

## CHAPTER CLII. On eternal delight.

Eternal delight consists in two things: the knowledge of God and the joy of the saints in their homeland. Concerning knowledge [Col. 0365B] we read in the Gospel: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). What is greater than to see God face to face and know him as we too are known? (I Cor. XIII.) Concerning joy we read: “Your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John XVI).

This joy in the vision and fellowship of God is exceedingly great. In wonder, the Prophet cries: “What indeed have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII). The whole world is “red lentil stew” (Gen. XXV), compared with the greatness of your glory, in which we shall share. Then what he says elsewhere will be fulfilled: “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God, upon his holy mountain. God founded it for eternity” (Ps. XLVII). And elsewhere: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting places” (Ps. CXLIX), that is, in their consciences or dwellings.

Tasting this joy beforehand, the Psalmist says elsewhere: “I remembered these things and poured out my spirit within me, because I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. XLI). There, brought to the wedding of bridegroom and bride, we shall feed upon the immaculate Lamb, while the Bridegroom passes among us and ministers to each one. Foreseeing the entrance into these nuptials and bridal chamber, the Prophet says: “I rejoiced at the things said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” [Col. 0365D] (Ps. CXXI). There, “the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you” (Ps. LXXXVI).

Then will be fulfilled what is read in the Song of Songs: “My dove is in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall” (Song II). For the Church will fill and restore the hollow and ruin left by the angels. Now it is said: “You shall weep and lament” (John XVII); and, “As they went, they went and wept” (Ps. CXXV). But then it will be said: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy, and your heart shall rejoice” (John XVII). “But those who come shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV).

Since we are inadequate and unable to explain this joy, which “eye has not seen nor ear heard” (I Cor. II), let us gaze from afar upon our holy mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, and, like children at the breast, babble with holy Isaiah: “My secret”—concerning eternal punishment, because few believe it or because it is inexpressible—“is mine” [Col. 0366A] (Isa. XXIV). And as an orator, depicting the grief of the parents of a dead son of a household, when he came to express the father’s grief for his son, failed because he had no further or greater feelings of grief than those already described to portray; he did what he could, portraying the father with his head covered by a cloth, so that this might be a sign of immeasurable and inexpressible grief. So we place an end to our words concerning the joy of the homeland, thereby indicating that it is immeasurable and inexpressible.

## CHAPTER CLIII. On monks’ private property.

[Col. 0366B]

Judas, “a thief, and having the money-box” (John XII), carried away the goods of the poor; and deservedly, because of theft and sacrilege, became Christ’s betrayer and his own murderer. So too Ananias and Sapphira—who are not, however, read to have renounced all things as explicitly as monks do—lie to the Holy Spirit along with those who do not render the whole of what they vowed, and incur Peter’s curse (Acts V). Since they cannot bring themselves to say even of a shoe, “mine,” how can they say it of a purse, books, a sonorous voice, money, and such things? Those can do so who have only one thing—namely, their own soul. Hence a monk is called the keeper of one thing, namely his own soul.

So too Saul, because, against the Lord’s command, he preserved fat King Agag and the fattest things, and did not destroy Amalek, lost the kingdom (I Kings XV). So likewise monks, to whom all worldly things are anathema, both in respect of possession and in respect of common life: unless they kill within themselves the flesh, the world, and all that belongs to it, all of which they have renounced, they will lose the heavenly kingdom.

Moreover, these men are slain with Achan (because they steal from the anathema of Jericho—that is, from some worldly thing forbidden to them, lest they use it) by the true Joshua (Josh. 7). These are not merely, I say, like, but worse than the priests of Bel who had secret doors (Dan. 14), turning their religious life [Col. 0366D] into snares and nets for money. They are also like Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, who likewise were slain over portions of meat (1 Sam. 2). For their sin both their father was punished and the ark of God was captured (1 Sam. 4). See how great is the sin of such persons. You will scarcely find a multitude punished for any sins except for a sacrilegious sin of this kind.

When Achan sinned, the people were defiled by the anathema (Josh. 7). Likewise: “You have raised a sacrilegious altar, and tomorrow God’s wrath will rage against the people”—that is, Gideon’s ephod (Judg. 8).

Likewise, other thieves steal out of want; these steal out of abundance, while the whole Church supplies them with necessities. These too [Col. 0367A] are like the jackdaw, which hides away what is given to it although it does not need it. Benedict strictly commanded that monks of this kind, with their money, be buried outside the church. Likewise Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium *On Guarding Virginity*, chapter 14, tells of a hermit found at death with one hundred solidi. By the judgment of the other hermits these were tied around his neck, and he was buried with them, with these words: “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8). The same was done concerning Gregory’s monk (*Life of St. Gregory*), who was found to possess one gold coin.

Likewise, in Matthew, chapter 24: “Then those who are in Judaea shall flee to the mountains”—that is, those established in the confession of faith; “and he who is on the roof”—that is, one who rises above the flesh in mind—“shall not come down to take anything from [Col. 0367B] his house.” That is, those who have left all things and ascended to the height of virtues should not return to some attachment of their former way of life. The monk “who is upon the roof” and possesses private property must “not come down to take anything from his house”—or from the house of any private person, which would be more tolerable—but from the house of Christ and of the poor, which belongs to another. Since even a layperson who takes a sacred thing is sacrilegious, one who takes what has been blessed in religious profession takes from what is sacred and insults the Holy Spirit, driving him out of his house. He makes Christ’s members members of money, and makes “the temple of God a den of thieves” (Matt. 21), and a purse of coin:

> O money, money—who bestows upon you this honour?  
> [Col. 0367C] (Juvenal, *Satires*, V.)

“You are gods. O money, you are my teaching!” [variant: “is”].

Likewise, 2 Maccabees 12: “The most valiant Judas, after a collection had been made, sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem,” etc. What then shall be said of the monk who has gold coins in his cowl or even in his chest, like idols? From these they obtain private extra portions in the refectory (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 54). But how can this be, when they may not even possess letters without special permission? It would be safer for them to receive nothing except through the hand of the provost. But concerning those slain under Judas (2 Macc. 8), what wonder if they retained something with which to live, when they were fugitives, daily afflicted by war, hunger, and death [Col. 0367D]? But we, in peace and without necessity, seek superfluities.

Likewise, if Tobit, an exile among the nations—among whom he was permitted to lend at interest—and one who could possess private property, said of the goat which his wife brought him, “See that it is not stolen” (Tob. 2), what is to be said of a monk? See that he is not a thief; see that he is not sacrilegious. Where is the abbot like Tobit, even though blind, who hears the money beneath the cowl—not bleating, but trembling—and says, “See that the money is not stolen”? Likewise, some religious pretend, under cover of brethren or friends whose depositaries and, as they say, agents they are, and hand money over to merchants, although they are permitted to exercise only ecclesiastical ministries. Likewise, if Nadab and Abihu [Col. 0368A] were consumed by fire because they offered strange fire to God (Lev. 10), what of the monk who offers another’s property to the devil, while furtively claiming it for himself [perhaps: appropriating it]? He is worse than another robber who is not sacrilegious and steals from a private person; for this man takes property from many—namely, the entire convent and every poor person—and therefore sins more grievously: “Nor is the sin forgiven unless what has been taken is restored” (*Regulae*, 4, *juris*, in 6; from Augustine).

Likewise, a certain prior forbade a brother who wished to establish a library, saying: “This shall not be done, lest it become your idol, in which you would claim some private ownership and be envious if another should take it.” Yet nowadays monks are tolerated who openly possess private property, and even who steal and share profits with the officials of a count. Likewise, [Col. 0368B] in some manner private ownership is forbidden to all. Hence: “Charity does not seek what is its own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 13); especially the charity of such persons, who have from the common store all necessities without labour, “having the promise of life” (1 Tim. 4), both of the present life and of that to come; who possess all things by despising them. Hence: “They shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19). “For nothing is lacking to the believer; the greedy man needs even a small coin” (Prov. 17, according to the Septuagint). Likewise, a wolf, or holy fire, attacked a hermit collecting money from offerings, etc.

A nun also, labouring at the point of death, had the few coins which she possessed in a chest taken out [Col. 0368C] and returned; yet she could not breathe out her soul until the small coin which had secretly remained at the bottom of the chest was thrown out. Once it was thrown out, she departed in peace to the Lord.

Likewise Jerome: “Just as I have found none better than those who live well in the cloister, so I have found none worse than those who live badly in the cloister”; for they are either “very good figs” or “very bad figs.” Hence Psalm 30: “I have become a reproach beyond measure to all my enemies, and a terror to my acquaintances.” Likewise, Martin, while still a catechumen, was so frugal that he seemed more a monk than a soldier.

Likewise, in the letter to the monk Heliodorus: The monk’s private property [Col. 0368D] is not the anathema of Jericho, but Jerusalem. Even singularity in matters pertaining to religion, without the abbot’s knowledge, is forbidden as sacrilegious; for, as Saint Benedict says, “What is done without the abbot’s knowledge shall be accounted vanity, not reward.” The stronger thing is that which is greedy. Likewise Jerome: “He errs who calls an idolater one who puts down two grains,” etc.

Note also that there are certain things in which even secular persons possess no private ownership, and neither “mine” nor “yours” ought to be said. Hence:

> Nature made neither the sun nor the air private,  
> nor the slender waters.

Likewise, among the counsels of demons, the one who has overthrown and deceived [Col. 0369A] a monk is more highly approved. Thus it is evident how great the order of monks is. Likewise, Luke 9: “No one putting his hand to the plough,” etc. Ambrose’s gloss on this passage: “If a disciple following [Col. 0370A] the Lord is reproved,” etc. Likewise, cells used to be called obediences, because cloistered religious came to them only when compelled by obedience. Nowadays, however, they are objects of sale and purchase.

336–337. NOTES ON *THE ABBREVIATED WORD*, BY THE REVEREND FATHER LORD GEORGE GALOPINUS, RELIGIOUS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GHISLAIN IN HAINAUT.

[Col. 0369]

[Col. 0369B] **“The abbreviated word.”** The author begins from this passage of the Apostle, Romans 9, taken according to the letter, which in what follows he transfers to a mystical, tropological, or moral sense. Thus the “abbreviated word” is the cutting away of excesses and vices, and consequently the introduction of virtues. This accords with the mind of Blessed Augustine. In one place he says: “The Lord will make a finishing and shortening word upon the earth”; that is, he will save believers through the compendiousness of faith by grace, not through the innumerable observances by which that multitude of the children of Israel was oppressed with a servile burden. Vol. IV, Book I, *Questions to Simplicianus*, question 2.

Elsewhere he says: “This is the word which God shortened upon the earth: the observance of the two commandments of charity. For on these hang the whole law and the prophets.” Vol. II, Letter 205 to Boniface, shortly after the beginning.

**“Uncircumscribable.”** As God is.

**“He willed to be circumscribed.”** The Word now made flesh. John 1.

[Col. 0369C] **“Which he grants us.”** This seems, through the carelessness of the copyist, to have been omitted in M. “How,” says Blessed Jerome, “the earnest which is granted us,” etc. On Ephesians, chapter 1.

**“As an earnest and pledge.”** Certainly not “in an ark,” as M has it. Here I hear Blessed Augustine speaking of Christ the bridegroom: “For this purpose let the bridegroom give an earnest: that in his earnest he himself may be loved. Therefore love,” etc., vol. IX, Tractate 2 on the First Epistle of John, after the middle. Blessed Jerome, in the place cited above, teaches the difference between an earnest (*arrha*) and a pledge (*pignus*).

**“That we might apprehend.”** C: “that we might comprehend.”

**“Briefly and succinctly.”** These are plain. Meanwhile M: “briefly and more securely.”

**“It is infinity.”** Nothing is better. For infinity, as Aristotle says in *On the Heavens*, book 1, is considered in three ways: with respect to magnitude, number, and duration. Here it concerns number. Therefore M and C wrongly read: “It is weakness.”

**“It distracts us.”** From Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*, Letter 2, in the middle. V and M: “it distinguishes.” I do not reject this, in the sense of “divides and separates.” But the text of Seneca in our parchment library, together with Justus Lipsius, has *distringit* (“it harasses” or “draws apart”).

**“A multitude of books.”** C had read “a multitude of words,” but corrected it.

**“It is enough to possess.”** Seneca, Letter 2; likewise *On Tranquillity of Mind*, book 1, chapter 9: “Why do I need innumerable books and libraries, whose owner can scarcely read their catalogues through his entire lifetime? A crowd burdens the learner; it does not instruct him.” And below: “Therefore let such a quantity of books be acquired as is enough, nothing for display,” etc.

**“They defile; they do not nourish.”** Aeschylus judges so:

> Ὁ χρήσιμ᾽ εἰδὼς, οὐχ ὁ πολλ᾽ εἰδώς, σοφός.  
> Wise is one who knows useful things, not one who knows many things.

[Col. 0370B] **“Digest on that day.”** Our manuscript text of Seneca has “digest.” Certainly this is good, so that it remains within the image of food, as Lipsius says.

**“I grasp something.”** Laertius speaks well concerning Aristotle: “Just as those who eat and exercise most are not healthier than those who do so moderately, so those who read not the most things but the most useful things are to be judged learned and diligent.”

**“There would remain life.”** The sound reading of Seneca, Letter 48. C: “there would be much life.”

**“Through scarcity of time.”** V: “through the misery of time,” but incorrectly; consult Seneca.

**“Knowledge of things.”** The Stoics maintained the doctrine that vices are ignorances of those things the knowledge of which constitutes virtues. See Lipsius, *Manuduction*, book 2, dissertation 1.

**“But also toward the aplustre.”** C: “but toward the aplustre.” V: “but also aplustre.” Both expressions please me. Festus says: “Aplustria are ornaments of ships; because they were more than was necessary for use, they were also called *amplustria*.” Juvenal:

> The aplustre, and the sad captive upon the summit of the arch.

**“He directs his course.”** V: “course.” C: “step.” Virgil, *On the Naval Contest*, book 5:

> Direct your course here;  
> love the shore.

**“With a point and less.”** V wrongly: “with a point,” etc.

**“Wherever there is something blessed.”** In my judgment, this is the genuine reading. For it is lawful to extract what is useful and good from any authors, even pagan ones. The Apostle used the poet Aratus (Acts 17:28), Menander (1 Cor. 15:33), and Epimenides (Titus 1:12).

Moreover, Blessed Augustine, Stephen of Canterbury, and countless similar authorities teach that this may lawfully be done, provided that the nails are pared away, as Blessed Jerome says in Letter 146 to Damasus, vol. III, and in his address to the Roman orator beginning, “Our Sebesius.” Blessed Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book 2, chapter 4, at the beginning; Stephen of Canterbury, final chapter of *On Virtues and Vices*.

[Col. 0370D] **“It is mine,” says the theologian, etc.** Namely, it is fitting and beneficial to me. V instead reads: “It is necessary,” says the theologian. This certainly pleases me if elsewhere I hear Seneca saying it; for in Letter 45: “What is good is certainly necessary.” Yet I prefer the statement in Letter 16: “Whatever has been well said by anyone is mine.”

**“In the Church.”** Supply “militant.” M omits the word “Church.”

**“Excessive prolixity.”** The order in V is inverted: “For each of these, prolixity is an enemy, the mother of forgetfulness and stepmother of memory.” M, however: “For each of these, prolixity is an enemy and stepmother, the mother of forgetfulness and of memory.” [Perhaps add: “and enemy of memory.”] Is it then the mother of memory? By no means. For just as a stomach weighed down with an excessive quantity of food does not digest healthily, so memory burdened by prolixity is not nourished but confused.

**“And building.”** V rightly has this. Two witnesses wrongly have “building-work,” because of disagreement in case.

**“To which the earlier things minister.”** Namely, reading and disputation. V has “first things” for “earlier things.”

**“And doubtful matters.”** M and C read thus: “Therefore, after reading and disputation, the doubtful matters of Sacred Scripture should be investigated, and one should not preach beforehand.”

**“Curtain to curtain.”** In order and reciprocally; or, as the Gloss says on the chapter *Cum venisset*, *extra*, *On Sacred Unction*: so that a faithful person may draw an unfaithful one.

## CHAPTER II

**“Likewise the same.”** Jerome, on Ezekiel 16, at the words “I clothed thee with colours” (for which the Septuagint has, “I clothed thee with various things”), adds: “With the ceremonies of the Law, occupied in the study of which you might abandon idols.”

**“Likewise Isaiah.”** V adds: “Chapter 163.” C and M have chapter 164 in the margin. There is great variation in the reckoning of numbers. In our large folio manuscript Bible, I counted only 158 chapters of Isaiah, but 1,580 verses, as I saw them counted at the end. The present division into chapters in our Bibles was made four hundred years ago; on it were based the biblical concordances prepared by Cardinal Hugh and Conrad of Halberstadt, a monk, aided by five hundred monks from different monasteries, as Sixtus of Siena reports in *Sacred Library*, book 3, Method 3. But let us return. This passage of Isaiah begins, “Why do you spend?” V, however, has, “Why do we not spend?” M: “Why do you not spend?”

**“Your silver.”** V subsequently: “our silver.”

**“Not on breads.”** M and V, because they inserted the negation at the beginning, now remove it.

**“Scribe and Pharisee.”** This is well supplied by the interlinear gloss on Isaiah 33:18; V wrongly omits “Scribe.”

[Col. 0371C] **“Asterisks and obeli.”** Origen, and after him Blessed Jerome, used these. Blessed Jerome himself testifies concerning Origen in *Apology against Rufinus*, book 2, chapter 8. Saint Augustine writes concerning Blessed Jerome in Letter 88 to him. But you ask what asterisks and obeli are? Hear Blessed Jerome, vol. II, Letter 89 to Blessed Augustine, chapter 6: “Wherever there are little rods, that is, obeli,” etc.; “where there are asterisks, that is, shining little stars,” etc.

**“For illuminating and piercing.”** Genuine and sound readings are illuminated; superfluous readings, or those not received, are pierced. *Obelos* is Greek; in Latin, “an arrow.”

**“They prefixed.”** Not “they proposed,” as C has, because below it says, “that we might prefix these things.”

**“From Pope Damasus.”** The letter with questions to Blessed Jerome, and his reply, are nos. 124 and 125.

**“The whole library.”** The remarkable labour of a monk. “Let books be copied,” he says to Rusticus, “so that the hand may work for food and the mind may be satisfied with reading.” Likewise, there: “Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.”

[Col. 0371D] **“Historically, allegorically.”** Receive this brief account:

> The letter teaches what happened; allegory, what you should believe;  
> the moral sense, what you should do; anagogy, where you should tend.

Do you want more? Consult Blessed Augustine, *On the Usefulness of Belief against the Manichees*, chapter 3.

**“Likewise Augustine: Do not.”** M says in the margin: “Perhaps Gregory.” Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule* has something not dissimilar: “One who prepares himself for the words of true preaching must draw the origins of his arguments from the sacred pages, so that he may refer everything he says to the foundation of divine authority and establish upon it the structure of his speech.” Blessed Jerome, in the letter to Nepotian beginning, “You ask of me,” says: “Let a presbyter’s speech be seasoned with reading of the Scriptures.” The passage is from Blessed Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, book 3, chapter 14, and on Psalm 57. Similar material appears in *On the Unity of the Church*, chapters 3, 6, 10, and 16.

**“With my words.”** M and V: “with my letters.”

**“And the Old Testament.”** M: “and the old character.” V: “or the old canon.” I have also read in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 18, after Origen: “It must not be unknown,” he says, “that there are twenty-two books in the canon of the Old Testament.”

**“Likewise the Apostle says.”** Among theologians, by the simple title “the Apostle” Blessed Paul is understood. But here, and only in this place, understand Saint Peter: First Epistle, chapter 4.

**“Ballast.”** An empty and useless burden. Ships are laden with ballast so that they may be steadier against storms. Hence Virgil, *Georgics* 4:

> Like unstable skiffs, when the surge tosses the ballast,  
> they rise.

**“In the Legend of Saint Martin.”** Written by Sulpicius Severus, Dialogue 1, chapter 12.

[Col. 0372B] **“Rather in words.”** How beautifully Saint Benedict says in chapter 7 of the Rule: “Let the monk speak few and reasonable words.” Saint Gregory, *Morals*, book 30, chapter 7: “He rightly knows how to speak who knows how to be silent in an orderly manner.” And Seneca, Letter 75: “Let our words not please, but benefit.”

**“It is liquefied from the eyes of the Lord.”** In this sense, not “it is not well liquefied,” as V has.

**“From whom Isaac removed.”** Two witnesses wrongly read “Jacob,” for this is said concerning Isaac in Genesis 26: “Again Isaac dug other wells, which the servants of his father Abraham had dug and which the Philistines had formerly stopped up after his death.” M rightly omitted “Jacob,” but would have been still better had it added “Isaac,” as we corrected it from the scriptural text.

**“Until he shall do.”** Up to the words which follow in the same psalm: “And whatsoever he shall do.”

**“Because it is the word of life.”** V and C: “which is the word of life.” I preferred the causal conjunction. In Scripture, says the moral Gloss, leaves sometimes signify the words which were in Christ, not falling away but enduring. Hence Matthew 24: “But my words shall not pass away.”

**“But the leaves shall fall.”** C: “shall kill.”

**“The text is a shadow.”** If I read “words” for “shadow,” as C and V do, what sense is there? The interlinear Gloss on Psalm 17, “Dark waters,” says: “Obscure doctrine is found in the prophets and in all preachers.”

[Col. 0372C] **“The word of eternal life.”** Correctly. The Old Testament is shadow; the New Testament is truth.

**“Deuteronomy, chapter 19. Three, chapter 75.”** I wonder at such a great number of chapters in Deuteronomy, when in our manuscript Bible I have seen only nineteen, though 2,600 verses.

**“A tree without foliage.”** Concerning which, 3 Kings 14:23. C reads “fruitful,” but incorrectly, for that contradicts what follows.

**“Not abounding in vine-leaves.”** So that “the winepresses of eloquence might overflow not with the leaves of words but with expressions of meanings, as it were grapes.” Blessed Jerome, to Rusticus, letter beginning “Nothing [is] Christian,” chapter 2.

**“The book has been opened.”** I do not disapprove of M and V: “The seven seals of the book being opened by Christ, the key of David, for the opening of which John wept.” Let us not force the matter, etc. Blessed Jerome has nearly similar words in his letter to Paulinus beginning, “Brother Ambrose,” before the middle.

**“For which, that.”** From M and V I added “for which,” referring to the seals. C: “for which [singular].”

**“Water of the clouds.”** From Psalm 17. By this the author understands the utterances of the prophets, which are obscure in themselves and thus need an interpreter.

**“Although Christ.”** M: “although only Christ.”

**“Book of Wisdom, final chapter.”** Today chapter 19; formerly chapter 45, or, according to another codex, chapter 41.

**“Or he understands.”** V omits this.

[Col. 0373A] **“Leviticus, chapter 26.”** C has chapter 87 in the margin. From here to “Innkeepers” is absent in V.

**“The most ancient things of the ancients.”** Note the distinction. C: “The most ancient things of the ancients, such as Master Anselm and Gilbert, you shall eat”—that is, imitate; “and old things,” that is, the manner of reading of the moderns, who, etc. M appears in the margin to wish the names Anselm, Alberic of Rheims, Robert Pullen, and Gilbert to be referred, by three dots placed above, to the phrase “the manner of reading of the moderns.” The name Simon, also found in the margin, it refers to the words “the manner of reading of the ancients.”

**“You shall imitate.”** Not “you shall change,” as C has.

**“Your innkeepers.”** The Septuagint translation of Isaiah chapter 1: “Your innkeepers mix wine with water.”

**“Amurca.”** Oil-lees.

**“To the other more useful matters.”** V: “to the other works.” But I would say: “to other more useful works.”

**“And an impediment.”** This comes from V alone, and not without reason, because these books occupy much space and can scarcely be moved elsewhere even with the strength of one very strong man.

[Col. 0373B] **“The situation of places.”** This concerns geography.

**“The numbers of years.”** This concerns chronology.

**“Genealogies.”** Endless genealogies, of which the Apostle speaks in 1 Timothy 1:4.

**“Answers.”** C: “reasons.”

## CHAPTER III

**“Ephesians, chapter 4.”** Three: chapter 19.

**“They produce ruin.”** V and M omit “ruin.”

**“In the same, chapter 6.”** Three: chapter 8.

**“Nevertheless.”** C perversely has: “If well, surely God will destroy such a man, because a crafty man is hateful” (Prov. 17). But this plainly conflicts with the text of the psalm.

**“For there are such persons.”** The Gloss of Cassiodorus.

**“Let the altar be hollow.”** This was commanded in Exodus 27. Consult the Gloss.

[Col. 0373C] **“A heaven of iron.”** Here the author follows the Septuagint translators; otherwise Saint Jerome’s translation reads, “Like iron.”

**“In the same chapter 26.”** Three: chapter 87.

**“That is, divine Scripture.”** C does not read “divine.” The Gloss on this passage understands by “bronze earth,” not Scripture, but dry and unfruitful ground, which is the literal sense.

**“Rain, that is, doctrine.”** Thus Blessed Jerome on Isaiah 55.

**“Shoots of virtues.”** Not “offspring,” as C has.

**“Nothing is subtler.”** This has the flavour of Seneca, Letter 82: “Nothing is sharper than an ear of grain,” etc.

**“It harms usefulness.”** M and C: “subtlety.”

**“Not to chatter.”** Seneca has “not to speak.”

**“Not to talk garrulously.”** V omits this.

**“It is not popular.”** Seneca, Letter 16. V: “not into the popular.”

**“In Maeandrian windings.”** The same Seneca, Letter 104, or 105, before the middle. C: “in Maeandrian watches.”

**“And in the halls of quibbles.”** Added from V alone.

**“What are words to me?”** Seneca, Letter 48: “Words are [nothing] to me,” etc.

**“Most crafty.”** Thus two copies, with Seneca. V incorrectly: “rusty.”

**“We old men play.”** I confess that I restored “old men” in the text from Seneca; otherwise C has “a series,” and M and V “series.” This arose from scribal misuse.

**“You are an advocate.”** From Seneca, Letter 48. C: “you are called.” V: “you are to be made an advocate.”

**“The poised axe.”** A later hand in C wrote above *intentae* (“poised”): *sublatae* (“raised”).

**“The plagues of Erebus.”** Evil demons.

**“Safe against death.”** I restored Seneca’s words from Letter 82, otherwise 83, at the end. C: “such great death, small”; V and M: “the whole death, small.”

**“Such small darts.”** C has the diminutive *jacilla*.

**“On Palaemon.”** C: “On Polemon,” or “Philemon.” See the story in Valerius Maximus, book 6, chapter 11; Saint Jerome on Hosea 1; and Saint Augustine, Letter 130.

[Col. 0374A] **“Of a most depraved life.”** M: “of a most approved life.” Ironically, this is good; for he was especially devoted to luxury.

**“The insignia of luxury.”** Isaiah enumerates them in chapter 3:19.

**“Captious words.”** Thus also Seneca, Letter 82. C: “words of capture.”

**“Undertaken against vices.”** Namely, a battle-line. I do not wholly reject it. C: “against vices, armour is taken up, a light awl,” etc. M in the margin: “they take up armour against vices—an awl, that is, a light [weapon],” etc.

**“Quibbling has robbed.”** Not “con-quibbling,” as C has. *Cavillationes* are sophistries and witticisms.

**“The meaning of words.”** V departs from Seneca in writing “the designation of words.”

**“As though we had leisure.”** Seneca, Letter 45: “Have we so much leisure? Do we now know how to live and how to die?” C is condemned by this reading: “as though we had leisure for words.”

**“And below.”** Letter 45, before the middle.

**“Differences of sounds.”** Seneca: “You distinguish likenesses of sounds.”

**“That he may test his forehead.”** Diogenes the Cynic did this, Lipsius says in his commentary on Seneca.

[Col. 0374B] **“Thus these things are harmless.”** M incorrectly: “thus these things are without harmfulness.”

**“Conjurers’ cups.”** Certainly not “receptacles,” as C has. Lipsius describes this game, still not uncommon today, in his commentary on Seneca, Letter 45.

**“Of the Pygmies.”** This is not found in Seneca. If you seek the Pygmies, you will find them in Blessed Jerome on Ezekiel 27 and Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book 16. Finally hear witty Juvenal, *Satires*, 13:

> At the sudden birds of Thrace and the sounding cloud,  
> the Pygmy warrior runs in tiny armour.  
> Soon unequal to his enemy, and snatched through the air,  
> he is carried in the curved talons of a savage crane. If you saw this  
> among our peoples, you would be shaken with laughter; but there,  
> though the same battles are constantly seen, no one laughs,  
> where the entire cohort is not more than one foot tall.

[Col. 0374C] I have taken this from our manuscript Juvenal. In printed editions the fifth verse was read thus: “You would be shaken with laughter, but there.”

**“Deception delights.”** Thus Seneca. Therefore not “a fable delights,” as C has.

**“I have no leisure for these matters.”** M and C: “I have no leisure toward these matters.” This may be tolerated, in the sense “I do not pursue them professionally.”

**“He gives clear counsel.”** C: “they give clear counsel.”

**“Therefore one must not shout.”** Hear, theologians; and why not you philosophers too? Hear Seneca, alas, not a Christian, Letter 52: “What is more disgraceful than philosophy seeking applause?” Likewise, Letter 75: “Even if I were disputing, I would not stamp my foot, wave my hand, or raise my voice,” etc.

**“On the twofold chastity.”** M: “on the twofold prudence.”

**“Cleverness of mind.”** There is variation here. C: “cleverness of mind, with efforts.” M and V: “cleverness of mind, for those attempting great things.” I preferred Seneca, although this reading can be tolerated: “Cleverness for minds attempting great things.”

[Col. 0374D] **“Of sharp declamation.”** V: “of delirium”; M somewhat better: “of deliberation.”

**“And vain.”** Or “empty,” as V and M have.

**“Take care not [to labour] on words.”** Seneca teaches this in Letters 45 and 115.

**“In yourself and in others.”** Thus M; C: “Refer [it] to reforming others’ morals of life by your example.” V: “To forming morals in yourself and in others by your example,” but a later hand has prefixed *in*, to read “informing.” Does not Seneca speak splendidly in Letter 52? “Let us choose those,” he says, “who teach by life.” Blessed Augustine says: “Many indeed help many people by saying what they do not do, but they would help far more by doing what they say.” *On Christian Doctrine*, book 4, chapter 27; see also chapter 29.

**“Suppose in yourself.”** C incorrectly: “Suppose of life,” as is clear from Seneca, Letter 89, shortly before the end.

**“Afflict your own [faults].”** C: “kill,” for “afflict.”

**“Idolatry.”** Three [copies], as I have seen in all manuscripts, have “idolatry.”
