[Col. 0375A] **“With superfluous and vain things.”** C, omitting “with,” has merely “superfluous,” and otherwise differs.

## CHAPTER IV

**“With wasps and dagger.”** The margins of M and C contain: “The Lord appeared with a torn face to a certain religious person” (M adds “abbot”). It is recorded that the Lord appeared as a leper to a monk who was a martyr, in Homily 40 of Blessed Gregory on the Gospels.

**“Jeremiah, chapter 15.”** Three: chapter 61.

**“Another reading.”** Not “another letter”; rather, it is the interlinear Gloss itself, which reads: “Or, I who am judged.” C comes close: “Or, I who judge.”

**“Job, chapter 19.”** Both the text and margin in three copies read chapter 14. No wonder: the Book of Job was formerly divided into only thirty-six chapters, whereas now it has forty-two.

**“Ecclesiasticus, chapter 16.”** Three: chapter 44.

[Col. 0375B] **“They are likened.”** Not “they are assimilated,” as C has.

**“Book of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 16.”** C and V: “Book of Wisdom, chapter 45.” M is somewhat better but still indefinite: “Book of Solomon, 45.”

**“Is diminished.”** C: “lingers.”

**“That is, divided through many.”** I took this from the text of V and the margin of C.

**“Now concerning humanity.”** Whether he was a true human being. M incorrectly: “concerning humility.”

**“So that likewise.”** C: “unless likewise.”

**“Or they pour out.”** C lacks this.

**“Of one disposition.”** “Of one mind, thinking one thing,” says Blessed Augustine on this passage.

**“Jeremiah, chapter 23.”** Three: chapter 85.

**“A drunken man.”** Both margins: “That is, not understanding.”

**“Wet with wine.”** “Digest the one thing by which you are wet,” 1 Samuel 1. C: “wet in wine”; Jeremiah at this place: “wet from wine.”

**“And therefore because.”** M omitted “and therefore,” but another hand restored it between the lines.

[Col. 0375C] **“If therefore from the face.”** Before “If therefore,” M places an “M,” which, from what follows, I infer means “Master.”

**“And discreetly.”** C is mistaken: “and learn.”

**“Within thirty years.”** Blessed Jerome bears witness to this in the preface to Ezekiel addressed to Eustochium. C and M: “within twenty years,” incorrectly.

**“You shall not break a bone.”** To this the margins of C and M add: “We shall not here extract the marrow from this, however much we have laboured at it.”

**“M not below.”** Understand M as “Master.” Thus below M means Master Anselm, Master of the Sentences, and so forth.

**“Flying above.”** V and C: “thus flying.”

**“With Martin.”** Here: “With eyes and hands always directed toward heaven, he never relaxed his unconquered spirit from prayer.” From the *Life* of the same saint by Sulpicius Severus, vol. VI of Surius.

**“Likewise: Terrible.”** Above *Terrible*, M reads “M,” perhaps “Master.”

**“The philosopher: He who.”** I have not yet found this in Seneca, who is meant by the designation “philosopher,” but it is found well in Plautus, *Mostellaria*, act 5, scene 1, at the beginning.

**“He is worth a trifle.”** M in the margin: “that is, foolish and useless.”

**“What is known without danger.”** C: “What is not known without danger.” From Blessed Jerome’s letter to Eustochium, *On the Guardianship of Virginity*.

**“He who walks simply.”** That is, not by two ways, as in Ecclesiasticus 2.

**“Kindred to folly.”** “Prudence without simplicity is malice, and simplicity without reason is called folly.” Blessed Jerome on Hosea 7. But Blessed Augustine, on 1 Timothy 3, “A bishop must be prudent,” says: “Lest he be so simple as to be foolish.”

[Col. 0376A] **“Existing without a fold.”** V and M: “Being without a fold.” The author commonly uses *ens* (“being”) for *existens* (“existing”) in this work.

**“Of curiosity and.”** V: “of curious and notorious inquiry.” M: “of curious and report inquiry.”

**“Newborn infants.”** M omitted “infants” in the text, but restores it in the margin: “namely, little children.”

**“Rational.”** This is the common reading, *rationabiles* (“rational”), but in the Roman edition corrected under Sixtus V and Clement VIII it now reads *rationabile* (“rational,” agreeing with “milk”). Thus also the Greek, Syriac, Royal Bible, Bede, and four Leuven manuscripts.

**“By speaking ill.”** Not “by cursing,” as C has.

**“Or through proud [conduct].”** I corrected this from V. For C has “or proud and curious,” while M has “or through pride.”

**“And inexplicable.”** Or “ineffable,” as V has. It is called “inexplicable” because, as the Chaldaic paraphrase says, it is secret.

**“M: If therefore.”** In the margin M means Master Anselm.

**“Jerome: Not.”** Hear M in the side margin: “What then concerning relations, which are taken to be persons—what not?”

[Col. 0376B] **“Thus also Christ.”** Distinguish the readings. V: “Thus Christ also set the Fathers as boundaries on the mountain and around the mountain of Sacred Scripture, which we ought not to transgress,” etc. M: “They set boundaries on the mountain”; the remainder as in the text.

**“And superfluous.”** V omits this.

**“Proverbs, chapter 25.”** C: 43; M: 48.

**“By seeking beyond one’s powers.”** Or “inquiring,” as C has. This is absent from V, though it belongs both to the interlinear Gloss and to Blessed Jerome himself.

**“Dip in honey.”** C incorrectly departs from the sacred Bibles: “anoint with honey.”

**“And the eyes shall be gladdened.”** C: “My eyes shall be gladdened, and you shall rightly pursue your enemies” (added between the lines: “as that man [did]”) “because the explanation of your words enlightens me,” etc.

**“That curious inquiry.”** C: “He does not involve [one] in curious inquiry.”

[Col. 0376C] **“You shall not be curious.”** C: “Do not be curious,” as it is in the Bibles.

**“Ecclesiastes.”** C has chapter 14 in the margin; our manuscript has chapter 15.

**“The things that are under the sun.”** Far be it that I should here follow V: “the things that are above the sun.” He says “over all things”; “the things which are done under the sun,” as in Ecclesiastes 8.

**“And he who curiously.”** Thus M and V; C: “and he who incuriously.” Above “and” I see an M, meaning Master, as the margin explains.

**“When we speak concerning the gods.”** From Aristotle; Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book 7, chapter 30, at the beginning.

**“M: Much more.”** Again M means “Master,” between the lines in M and in the text of C.

## CHAPTER V

**“My speech.”** C and M: “your” for “my.”

**“2 Samuel, chapter 22.”** V and C: 94; M: 93.

**“2 Timothy 2.”** V: 2 Timothy 4.

[Col. 0376D] **“So that he may make a noise.”** M and C add a gloss—perhaps by our author or another older than he—of whom Nicholas of Lyra also speaks afterward on this passage.

**“Let him defend himself with gaping.”** To defend oneself loudly and captiously. These words have the flavour of Horace’s *Art of Poetry*.

**“2 Timothy 2.”** Three: 2 Timothy 4.

**“Contention can accomplish nothing.”** The two margins say: “Augustine’s gloss.” It is now the interlinear gloss.

**“Ordered delivery.”** Words of Seneca, though somewhat polished, Letter 40. From the words “ordered delivery” down to “Likewise: The philosopher” are lacking in V and M.

**“In sum.”** From Seneca at the end of Letter 40, which it is pleasant to read. C: “the sum of all philosophy.” But Seneca: “The sum of sums is.”

**“For to move the head.”** Seneca, Letter 75, disapproves of this.

**“Likewise Isaiah.”** V adds chapter 73; C has 63 in the margin.

**“Likewise: Just as it is shameful.”** V puts first: “Likewise Proverbs, chapter 16: Just as it is shameful,” etc. I do not think this can be found in the whole of Sacred Scripture.

[Col. 0377A] **“It is shameful and dangerous.”** And much more shameful is it to be compelled to a palinode, because of words previously uttered or let slip through excessive haste.

**“He who [answers] the question.”** C and M understand in the margin: “namely, the one answering.”

**“Namely, by solving it.”** V has only this in the text; the two others elsewhere.

**“He will prepare his speech.”** M: “He will prepare him.”

**“And thus, having prayed.”** C: “and if he thus prays, he shall be heard.”

**“In the same, chapter 32.”** Three: 84.

**“He shall not scatter.”** M: “he shall not disperse”; V: “he shall not lose.”

**“Likewise, chapter 37.”** V: 98; M and C: 97. The words “Son, in all things” are absent from M, which begins, “Corboni,” etc.

**“Another thing is more for you.”** “For you” occurs only in this text; V: Ecclesiasticus 37, “Another thing is worth more than that.”

**“Chapter 37. Before.”** Three: 99.

**“Steady counsel.”** C: “establish counsel.” After “steady,” the margins of C and M propose that this be read: “Likewise, Job [Col. 0377B] chapter 26 (now 33): Nevertheless, let not a miracle terrify you,” etc.

**“Likewise: Lips.”** V: chapter 60. I noted the place in the margin of the text.

**“Unless with deliberation.”** C also has: “Unless together with deliberation.”

**“For when in a question.”** C: “When a question is raised concerning,” etc.

**“Little earth or little thing.”** The former is a diminutive from *terra* (“earth”), the latter from *res* (“thing”).

**“If so great.”** I found “if” only in C.

**“Finally, in judgment.”** Or “then,” as M and C have.

**“Even easy.”** The word “even” has force. Therefore C and M wrongly omit it.

Unless a truce has been granted.] A custom has become established (by tradition) that one never answers questions proposed by a master, or replies demanded by an opponent in argument, whether in theology or philosophy, unless time has first been allowed the respondent for repetition and reflection. For one must not rush, says Seneca, *Letters* 40. [Col. 0377C]

In the solution of which.] These words are absent from C., which has in their place: “When he was defeated and failed.”

Aristotle said to him.] Among approved authors a great variety of this story is found. Volaterranus, *Anthropology*, book XX, following Suidas, says thus: “The Chian Theopompus and Ephorus, historians and pupils of Isocrates, the one needed a bridle, the other spurs.” Laertius attributes this not to Theopompus, nor to Aristotle, but to Plato teaching pupils in his school, among whom were Aristotle and Xenocrates. Thus Plato said to the impetuous Aristotle: “You need a bridle”; but to the overly slow Xenocrates: “Spurs.”

Meanwhile, I know that Theophrastus (of whom our Author speaks here) was Aristotle’s pupil and successor in the school, as Seneca testifies, *Natural Questions*, book VI, chapter 13, and Volaterranus in the passage cited; but I have not yet read that Eudemus was his pupil.

Eudemus.] V.: Eudemius. M.: Eudonius. Perhaps Eudoxus [Col. 0377D], Aristotle’s fellow-pupil under Plato, whom Libertus Fromondus—formerly professor of philosophy at Louvain in our Falcon College, who in my presence then received the degree of Doctor of Sacred Theology, and today, as I hear, is doctor and censor of books there—mentions in his notes on Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, book VII, chapter 3. Or perhaps Eudemus, or, as Plutarch has it, Eodemus the orator. See him in vol. I, *On Illustrious Men*, under Philopoemen.

Who, being too slow.] M.: “Who too slowly.” C.: “Eudenius slowly and not unless,” etc. The words “who, being too” are absent there.

Yet a vein of talent.] Those possess a rich vein who have imbibed fuller learning from the source of their art—whether Aristotle and Plato in philosophy, or Homer in poetry—or, in a word, who are gifted.

## CHAPTER VI

All praises.] C.: “all hearings.”

That is, of learning.] Of the learned; of the correction of the wicked, that they may repent; of the exhortation of the good, that they may make [Col. 0378A] progress toward better things, says St Benedict in the *Rule*; of stirring up the sluggish; of consoling the faint-hearted; of supporting, or—as C. has it—of “co-supporting” those who fail.

The three aforesaid.] Namely, reading, disputation, and preaching, discussed in chapter 1.

349 Of a serene conscience.] Hence Solomon, Proverbs XV: “A secure mind is like a continual feast.” Such a man is

> Whole in life and free from guilt.  
> (HORACE, book I, Ode 22.)

C. not badly: “The voice of exultation is serenity of conscience.”

And for removing.] Someone, having placed a point beneath *et* (“and”), wished to delete it in V., likewise in the following phrase, “and for conferring,” although it is not superfluous. The sense is: “We shall confess to thee, O God, our sins, that thou mayest forgive what has been committed, and [we shall pray] for the removal of evils”; and, “Lead us not into temptation, but,” etc.

[Col. 0378B] The works of creation.] C.: “of the Creator,” and does not add “of re-creation.”

Harmful.] Sinful humours, as physicians speak.

The Lord speaking to the same effect.] M.: “The Lord adds, speaking.”

For a good life.] The Moral, or Ordinary, Gloss on Matthew V, verses 13 and 14 has: “Salt comes before light, because life comes before doctrine. Life leads to knowledge of the truth. He who fears God does not lack knowledge.” Knowledge of things. Hear Seneca: “What then is good? Knowledge of things. What is evil? Ignorance of things.” And below: “Let this also be added: perfect virtue is equality and a tenor of life wholly harmonious with itself; this cannot exist unless knowledge of things is attained, and the art by which things divine and human are known.” Thus he, *Letters* 31, in the middle.

But he who loves.] From V. I have gathered this reading; C. otherwise: “For this is knowledge of things, which he who first loves does not lack.” M., however: “For this is knowledge, which he who first loves does not lack.” All are bearable in their respective senses. Finally, I add from the Gloss on Matthew V, “You are the salt of the earth”: “He who fears God does not lack knowledge.”

Likewise Solomon: “Son.” C.: “Son, desire.” V.: “Son, have you desired wisdom? Keep,” etc., as Augustine reads it, book XXII *Against Faustus*, chapter 53. The passage is Ecclesiasticus, chapter I. The author of that book is Jesus son of Sirach. Yet the Fathers commonly cite it under Solomon’s name, because it contains many sayings of Solomon.

And it says—the Gloss.] Here M. and V. fail until “Good understanding.” The Gloss, which is St Augustine’s, reads thus: “For one does not attain wisdom concerning hidden things except through obedience to the commandments.” Nor, reader, should you condemn me for restoring *mysteries* in place of *ministries*. For from the aforesaid Gloss this is made clear.

They will make him first.] V. wrongly omits “first.”

First, discipline.] V. also lacks these two words and the two [Col. 0378D] following.

His testimonies.] M. adds *afterward* between the lines after “his.” As though it said: first, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord”; afterward, “Blessed are they who search his testimonies,” which pertain to knowledge. See further St Ambrose on Psalm CXVIII, verse 2.

Attend to yourself and to doctrine.] M. explains more clearly in the margin: “Attend to yourself first, and to doctrine afterward.” That is: attend to yourself, how you live; and to doctrine, how you teach. For Jesus began first to do and afterward to teach, Acts I.

In the teacher, life.] The Apostle, after enumerating what contributes to the upright 350 rule of life for a bishop and teacher, finally admonishes: “that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine,” etc. M. and V. have: “Finally, that which concerns doctrine, saying that good life should, as it were, precede the teacher,” etc. St Gregory states it plainly, *Homily 11 on Ezekiel*: “He knows how to speak truthfully who has first learned to act well.”

[Col. 0379A] V. and M.: “Life is held in contempt.”

The ephod.] St Gregory treats at length of the garments of the Levitical priests, book I, letter 24; from this it is evident that our author drew his material from him.

Is denoted.] V.: “is understood.”

And the bells.] C.: “And whose bells.”

For he is struck dumb.] “When,” says St Gregory, “the guilt of sin bites the conscience, fear of disgrace binds the tongue.” Again, the same author, *Morals* VII: “He receives eloquence in speaking well who enlarges the bosom of his heart through the practice of right living; conscience does not hinder the speaker when life goes before the tongue.”

Likewise, from virtues.] V. and M. read: “To evangelists the Lord will give the word with great power, in great power.” For both things, etc. There is a transposition of words. By “in great power” understand holiness of life and meritorious works, as the margins of C. and M. suggest.

Does not kindle.] How beautifully St Leo says, in his sermon on St Lawrence the Martyr: “Let eloquence be ready for exhortation, let reason be effective for persuasion; yet examples are stronger than words, and it is more to teach by deed than by voice.” [Col. 0379B]

For often God.] V. fails from this point until “Likewise, the philosopher.”

M.: “But we.” By M. understand “Master.”

The word of God.] V.: “the word of faith.”

Aorasia.] Tria has *aurisia*, but incorrectly. For Genesis XIX reads: ἐπάταξαν ἐν ἀορασίᾳ, ἀπὸ μικροῦ ἕως μεγάλου — “they struck them with blindness, from the least even to the greatest.”

To find the door.] V. and M.: “But, struck with blindness, they were unable to enter.”

Whom we love less.] C.: “By which less,” etc.

Madness.] By no means “modesty,” as C. has it.

Concerning Origen.] I have seen these matters concerning Origen in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 3; but not yet in St Gregory.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0379C] V. and M. alone begin a new chapter here, and with some difference. M. gives this title: “Concerning hypocrites,” and begins: “Hypocrites indeed utter the word,” etc. V. as in the text.

The great Basil preaching.] In Surius, volume I: while he was reading the sacred books, St Ephrem saw a fiery tongue speaking through his mouth.

My mouth is open.] Tria has this reading; but II Corinthians VI reads: “Our mouth,” etc.

My heart in charity.] Again II Corinthians VI has “our heart.” Tria has “my.” M., together with C., had omitted the word *charity*, but a recent hand restored it between the lines.

Otherwise it is not open.] Above *otherwise*, I saw in M. the letter M., meaning *magister*, “master.”

It has been enlarged.] So Tria. In Psalm XV: “It has rejoiced.”

Lamentation.] Or “lament,” as the two manuscripts have.

A song of the righteous.] There is variation in M. and V. They have: “Song, lament, and woe, of deliberately impenitent persons [Col. 0379D] and reprobates.” I judged the reading restored in the text sounder, prompted by St Jerome’s letter to Rusticus, beginning *Nothing is more fitting for a Christian*, before the middle, and by St Gregory’s homily on Ezekiel.

Repentance.] C. wrongly omitted this. For that great herald, “A voice crying in the wilderness,” says: “Repent,” etc., Matthew III.

Sweetly and most pleasantly.] “A consciousness of holy love,” says St Gregory, “is more effective for preaching than trained knowledge of speech.”

When you by deed.] From Cassiodorus. V., omitting these words, has: “Why do you recount my righteousnesses in ordinary speech, speaking of majesty, and take up,” etc.

To preach publicly.] V. omits both words, substituting “to praise.” M. likewise, but notes in the margin the words found in the text.

I shall read privately.] I restored *privately* from the margins of M. and C.

[Col. 0380A] Tabernacle.] C. here and shortly before has *temple* for *tabernacle*.

They might see the tabernacle.] Correctly, as is clear from both the Ordinary and the Moral Gloss on Exodus XXXVIII, verse 8. M. and V.: “And, when about to leave the tabernacle, they washed and wiped away tears, if they saw any upon themselves.”

M.: “For this.” Perhaps M. means Master Peter the Chanter, our author. V. does not read M., and has: “Note in addition that preaching is,” etc. “For this alone,” that is, not for curiosity, or complacency in the appearance of one’s face, or its artful arrangement, by which he might arouse lust in those standing around.

Seeking glory.] Added from V. alone.

Private, namely.] V.: “Private concerning charity and not,” etc.

Jerome.] Letter 1 to Heliodorus, *In Praise of the Solitary Life*; his words are cited in II, question 7: “Not all.”

For such a common.] Restored from the margins of M. [Col. 0380B] and C., though warned by V.’s text. For C. read in place of these words: “And if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit,” Matthew XV.

By following mortal sin.] How does he sin mortally, since preaching is not in itself an act of any sacrament? Meanwhile, I acknowledge that preaching instituted by Christ is dishonoured and, as it were, held in contempt by this act, since one must preach not only by word but also by example.

Honeycomb from the lion’s mouth.] The Moral Gloss here understands by “honeycomb” the honey-sweet doctrine of St Paul. But M. and C., in their margins, interpret “honeycomb” as doctrine and “the lion’s mouth” as Scripture.

An *abcedarian* in life.] M. and V. explain more fully: “An abcedarian in life”—that is, in age—“an abcedarian in knowledge, an abcedarian in fluency or eloquence.” This is the interlinear Gloss on II Timothy II, verse 2.

To show yourself approved.] C.: “Show yourself approved, first,” etc. V. omits “first,” and afterwards “consequently.” [Col. 0380C]

Then knowing.] C. has only “then.”

From those who make jests.] The two margins vary the order of the text. C.: “from those making [in the margin: actors] jests [in the margin: *cheres*] animals of the clod.” M. has *chieres* in the margin for *cheres*.

With the pitchers broken.] In M. I saw this interlinear Gloss: “With the pitchers broken, that is, first with the neck subdued”; and above “the lamps kindled,” it adds: “by works.” These words are obscure, but St Gregory illuminates them, *Homily 13 on the Gospels*: “We hold burning lamps in our hands when through good works we show our neighbours examples of light.”

The walls of Jericho.] M. explains in the side margin: “The world and all its concupiscence.”

Preach, therefore, first.] V. has *to the people* for *first*. The sense is certainly good, but foreign to the purpose.

## CHAPTER VIII

C. connects this with the preceding chapter.

[Col. 0380D] Disputer.] C. wrongly omitted this, as is clear from chapter 1.

Magnificent utterances.] Thus Seneca, *Letters* 108. C.: “magical utterances,” perhaps because of an abbreviation.

Itinerant performers.] “Jesters,” says C. in the margin.

The word of God.] C. alone has “God.”

Who can scarcely stand.] C.: “Who is astonished,” etc., omitting the intervening words.

Able to govern.] C.: “is able.”

But you will say.] Two manuscripts have “saying,” except V.

Philo and others.] Seneca enumerates others at the end of *Letters* 108. V., for Philo, reads “philosophers and others.”

Do what you say.] Seneca insists on this in many places. Thus, *Letters* 20: “This is the greatest duty and proof of wisdom, that deeds accord with words,” etc. See further *Letters* 24 and 75, at the beginning. Cicero: “The chief point of the art is to teach what you do.”

He beats the lectern.] Here he is likened more to a madman than to a good man. So M. in the margin.

[Col. 0381A] Unless either to speak.] Acts XVII. C. therefore wrongly has: “Unless to learn and hear.”

Not that they might believe.] The interlinear Gloss on this passage.

Let faith be made.] This reading seemed genuine to me, as I learned from the Gloss, even though C. says “Let them become faithful.”

But truth [has] corners.] Words of St Jerome’s letter to the monk Rusticus, beginning *Nothing is more fitting for a Christian*, near the end.

353 And Jezebel with antimony.] The copyist seems to have been ignorant of this Scriptural passage. For C. has “Jezebel’s study.” M., with V., aimed more nearly at it: “Jezebel’s pipe.”

To bait.] Thus Terence, *Adelphoe*, act II, scene II: “Go,” he says, “do you not know how to bait men?” that is, attract them. Therefore the two manuscripts, M. and C., are not to be followed in reading “to ensnare.”

Given to trifles.] Not “small,” as C. has it. Seneca, in the same letter: “Neatness is not a manly ornament.”

[Col. 0381B] Their heads overloaded.] Tria so reads, for “burdened with a luxuriant growth of hair.” Seneca, however, has otherwise: “You know many young men polished in beard and hair,” etc. Tibullus sang in accordance with the sense of our text, book III, elegy IV:

> Unshorn locks flowed down a long neck.

The chest [adorns] them wholly.] That is, adorned in garments freshly taken from a sweet-smelling coffer.

From the whole discourse.] C.: “from the whole bark.”

With the little crow.] Of which Horace speaks, book I, epistle 3:

> . . . may the little crow provoke laughter,  
> Stripped of its stolen colours.

Of his daughters.] Tria has “of her sons,” but wrongly, as is clear from St Jerome’s letter.

The intention of duty.] V.: “the word of duty.”

The letter is extemporaneous.] Here I did not depart from St Jerome’s text, although Tria wishes *temporal*, which differs from it by the whole sky.

Concerning the orator.] Not “concerning discourse,” as V. has.

And to one wishing to depart.] Again Tria departs from St Jerome’s sound text. C.: “To one wishing to possess.” M.: “To one wishing to conceive.” V.: “To one wishing to possess,” which I [read as] “I offer, at his entrance,” for “food carried in,” etc. [Col. 0381C]

Food brought for the journey.] As the margins say: “I offer a traveller provisions for the road, not amusement for one who is itching.”

By the living voice.] C. removes “living.”

M.: “Such, therefore.” By M. understand “master,” as I said above.

To those arriving.] C. had read “to those hearing,” but corrected itself in the margin.

By which they are not nourished.] C.: “which they do not use.”

Jerome in the above-mentioned [letter].] I have not read this in the above-mentioned letter, which is the consolatory letter to Julian concerning the death of his daughters; nor in the additions to that letter in the edition of 1508. See Erasmus’s scholia.

Your son will be restored to you.] If these words were taken from the aforesaid letter, then surely “daughter,” not “son,” must be read.

I shall now drive out.] V.: “Drive [them] out of your heart, that you may revive [Col. 0381D] and receive consolation.” M., in the lower margin of this page, has material which should be assigned elsewhere, as will appear. It is as follows: “When Pope Alexander was commended by someone, he said: ‘I should be a good pope if I knew how to prescribe penance, to judge, and to preach, and if I first possessed the fountain, namely charity, from which (perhaps *ex quo*, ‘from which [source]’) these things proceed.’”

## CHAPTER IX

C. does not divide the chapter here either.

Such should speech be.] Seneca, *Letters* 114, at the beginning, after Solon and Plato. See Lipsius’s notes on this place.

Not polished.] C.: “not polluted.”

But only meanings.] M.: “so many meanings.” C.: “all meanings.”

In simple speech.] Consult Seneca’s *Letters* 40.

Likewise: Why should the heart.] These too savour of Seneca’s *Letters* 75.

[Col. 0382A] Let it not turn over such things.] V.: “Let neither mouth turn over such things nor ear listen to them.”

Your heart.] M. makes no mention of this.

For they are dangerous.] Why not, with V. and M., “For they are pernicious,” etc.?

Likewise the same.] Seneca, *Letters* 75.

And handsome.] Absent from V.

Well-ordered.] Why do V. and M. have “disordered”?

And well-ordered in speech.] Note the variation. V. first has: “And well-ordered in speech, humble in bearing, moderate in short stature, lest,” etc. C.: “And well-ordered in speech and humble in bearing, moderate in stature, lest,” etc. M. reads in the margin: “Just as a ship needs not a handsome helmsman, but one who knows how to steer.”

Shamgar [slew] six hundred.] Restored from Judges III. Tria has “five hundred Philistines,” though old printed editions have “Sangar,” not Shamgar.

You will kill.] Added from V. alone.

[Col. 0382B] Than with Cicero’s sword.] That is: more quickly will you destroy low things by plain speech and plant virtues than by Cicero’s eloquence.

Or a witness.] I did not see this in V.

Let us pursue humble things.] Or “the humble,” as V. has.

Words a foot and a half long.] From Horace’s *Art of Poetry*. That is, affected and excessively elongated words.

It defends with a gaping mouth.] These too savour of Horace’s *Art of Poetry*.

The philosopher to his friend.] These are verses of Horace, book I, epistle 1, but slightly altered. For his second line is:

> . . . and lay aside a great part of illness.

By David’s beard.] The Gloss adds here: “For just as weakness is shown in saliva, so strength is shown in the beard.” In I Samuel XXI, 13.

Likewise Gregory.] M. omitted this saying, suppressing Gregory’s name as well.

And that which is plain.] M.: “And that which is plain in the utterance of the divine discourse”; the remainder is absent.

[Col. 0382C] 355 Of preaching.] Wrongly absent from C.

They are not sufficient.] V.: “they are available.”

## CHAPTER X

And because he cannot.] C.: “But because not.”

Unless first known.] C. alone omits “unless,” and alone admits “first.”

From a bruising.] Tria has “from the slaughter of pride,” but C.’s margin corrects it to “from a bruising.”

Of all evils.] V. and M.: “of every evil and sin.” I know this occurs in Ecclesiasticus X; but because the author here uses St Augustine, I have preserved Augustine’s words as well, *Exposition on Psalm XVIII*, volume VIII.

When they first depart.] Thus St Augustine on Psalm XVIII, 14.

Those whom it finds.] V. and M.: “And those whom it finds.”

Justly and rightly.] M. and C.: “justly and lawfully.”

He has not done thus.] V. omits this.

[Col. 0382D] Not first reckoned.] Again it omits “first.”

The inhabitants of heaven.] From the Gloss of St Ambrose, as I gather from M. and V.: “The inhabitant of heaven leaves.”

That lust may be *gastrimargia*.] Thus far the Gloss of St Ambrose on Psalm CXVIII. Tria, together with all the manuscripts, reads *castri margia*, incorrectly.

That is, stiff-necked persons.] The Ordinary Gloss, which is also St Augustine’s.

The erect neck.] As in evil things the neck signifies pride, so in good things it signifies the uplifting of freedom: St Gregory, *Morals* XIII, chapter 6.

That is, pride.] St Augustine on Psalm XVIII.

A proud disposition.] The same on Psalm XXXV. V. therefore is not correct in reading “the disposition of pride.”

They dash themselves against.] M. omits “themselves.” C. likewise, but for “they dash” has “they compact.”

They commit fornication away from you.] That is, those who commit fornication depart from you. So C. in the margin.

They grow fat.] C.: “they run about.”

God breaks every proud [person].] A hemistich from Prudentius’s *Psychomachia* IV [Col. 0383A], which is worth reading. “Often,” says the same margin, “the Lord strikes down the proud, as though punishing them himself without the agency of angels or men.”

He abominates vices.] Supply “God.” C.: “Vices are abominated by God.”

Likewise the same: Pride.] Perhaps St Jerome, as I infer below from the notes.

Likewise Jerome.] Letter to Abigaus, volume I. M.: “Likewise the same.” Thus immediately above was also St Jerome.

The insult [against] humility.] M. and C.: “humanity,” incorrectly.

He is opposed.] The two margins note: “The proud man hates God and neighbour.”

Ecclesiasticus, chapter X.] C. and M.: XXXIII.

And abominable.] M. wrongly reads: “Inabominable.”

Whence there remains nothing.] V. and M.: “There is pride, so that nothing remains except to sin more gravely and further,” namely, than through pride.

356 Therefore, neither toward God.] V.: “Even toward neighbour and enemy; therefore neither toward God, toward whom it ought to be extended.”

Likewise Gregory.] *Morals* VIII, chapter 30; more distinctly, book XXXIV, chapter 18. For there: “Anger assaults patience, *gastrimargia* abstinence, lust continence; but pride, which we have called the root of vices, is by no means content with extinguishing one virtue, but raises itself against all the members of the soul,” etc. [Col. 0383B]

At the gate of religion.] In baptism.

He renounces the devil.] M.: “He will renounce.” These appear to be drawn from St Jerome’s letter to Demetrias, beginning *Among all subjects*. At the word “devil,” M. says in the margin: “As the beginning and author of evils.”

His pomps.] “The devil’s pomps are lies and the temporal things which we use,” according to both margins.

They are more plainly evident.] I think this should be read thus; otherwise, “with evident things.”

And the display of garments.] V. and M.: “the desire for garments.” But hear Seneca here, *On Tranquillity*, chapter 9: “Let us accustom ourselves to remove pomp from ourselves and measure the adornments of things by their use,” etc.

And the limits which.] These recall Horace:

> There is a measure in things; finally, there are fixed limits,  
> Beyond or short of which right cannot exist.

The copies vary. C.: “and a fixed measure, which and limits it is not permitted to exceed.” M.: “and a fixed measure, which and limits,” etc.

As the Apostle.] C.: “As the apostles.”

As happens today.] C. alone reads this. If, Peter the Chanter, extravagance in clothing was highly blameworthy in your age, it is so even in ours. Such is the curiosity in its costliness and variety that we cannot distinguish not merely a commoner from a nobleman, but scarcely even a young man from a young woman. The order is perverse.

[Col. 0383D] Common and plebeian people seem, by their elaborate bodily adornment, to have put on nobility of birth; conversely, nobles are content with simple but honourable clothing. Why so? I shall say: virtue and uprightness of character are in them. For, as Juvenal says, *Satires* 8:

> Nobility of soul is the sole and only virtue.

Or: “The highest nobility before God is to be illustrious in virtues.” Thus St Jerome to the matron Celantia. See also Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, prose and metre 6.

Has it ceased to be a sin?] Yet it is not mortal except in certain cases: namely, when it aims to arouse lustful desire or at another mortal end. So teaches St Thomas, II–II, question 169, article 2, replies to 2 and 3; Cajetan, in the *Summula*, under *ornatus*, and on St Thomas at the cited place; Graffius, part 1, book II, chapter 77; Lessius, book IV, *On Justice*, chapter 4, doubt 14; and six hundred similar writers.

So that by these.] Namely, customs and ways of living or dressing. C., not badly: “So that these,” [Col. 0384A] that is, “that they may not strive for an opportunity,” etc.

Concerning which.] V.: “The authority concerning which is to be understood.” M.: “The authority concerning which, and of what sort, is to be understood.” The authority is taken from the Apostle, I Timothy II, verse 9: “Likewise also women in becoming apparel.” Likewise in the same place: “Adorning themselves.” But those who advance such an argument should, I ask, attend to St Augustine’s solution, volume X, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 18, at the end; and book III, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 10. Also Distinction 41: “Whoever.”

The custom of dressing oneself.] V. reads: “It can be tolerated when, namely, this or that manner of dressing oneself has been altered and introduced by custom.”

Its source.] Or “origin,” as V. has. The sources of pride are manifold. Sometimes it arises from a gift of fortune, from inward disposition, and from outward wealth; from a gift of nature; from nobility of birth; from beauty; from a gift of grace; from powers sought; from dignities possessed. Thus the margins.

[Col. 0384B] Abundance of bread.] Or, according to the Seventy Interpreters, “the abundance of pleasures and luxury,” Ezekiel XVI.

Their iniquity.] The copies vary here. C.: “Their iniquity, and also with outward disposition,” etc. Perhaps *inward* disposition should be read. “Pride sometimes proceeds even from outward disposition, such as clothing,” etc. M.: “From outward disposition and of external things”; I do not reject this sense: from outward disposition in itself, namely in bodily clothing, and from external things belonging to oneself, for example horses, mules, and the rest of one’s household goods.

So too the philosopher.] Seneca, *Letters* 87.

By movement alone.] V.: “By movement alone [dative].” It makes no sense.

To humility and heart.] C.: “to his own heart,” excluding the rest.

My moderation.] V. omits *my*, thereby negating it.

Excusing.] The particle is absent from C.

He blushes at a shabby [vehicle].] Supply “vehicle.” See Seneca, *Letters* 87.

Sometimes.] V.: “never.”

Whence Benedict at Rome.] C.: “Whence Benedict by reason.” I understand nothing.

Fearing a monster.] V.: “Avoiding a monster.”

Even from nobility of birth.] Against St Jerome: “Never set yourself above anyone on account of nobility of birth,” letter to Celantia.

In public gatherings I have seen true nobles humbler than false ones. I call false those who wish to be called noble among those noble by birth, though, weighed in the scales of genealogy or paternal descent, they are found to possess less. Boethius speaks plainly on true nobility, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, prose and metre 6. [Col. 0384C]

Take away Hannibal.] From Juvenal, *Satires* 6.

To labour for fame.] From the same, *Satires* 8.

Nobility of soul.] From the same satire.

358 Most like Hermes.] That is, Mercury, says C. in the text and M. in the margin.

Pride is present.] Ovid, *Fasti* II.

Under ashes and sackcloth.] “Far more misshapen is that pride which lies hidden beneath certain signs of humility”; and below: “What profit is it to thin the body by abstinence if the soul swells with pride?” Thus St Jerome, or, as some hold, Paulinus to Celantia.

You will think [it] subdued.] C.: “you will think [it] completed.” In the margin it adds: “Zosimas sinned thus.” His life is found in Surius, volume II.

Which attacks more.] V.: “which [attacks] more.”

Those whom it did not benefit.] V.: “In whom it did not,” etc. See St Augustine’s exposition on Psalm CXVIII, verse 69.

When it opposes humility.] M. adds between the lines after “humility”: “namely Christ in it.”

From power and dignity.] These now come and now depart. You will discover that hateful pride arises from them if you read Boethius attentively at the beginning of prose 6, book III of the *Consolation of Philosophy*. But since powerful people sometimes are degraded, and therefore it is more fitting for them to be content with little, I should like to quote Seneca’s verses:

> Another may wish to be happy and great;  
> Let no crowd call me powerful.  
> Let a slender boat skim the shores,  
> And let no great wind command  
> My little vessels to cleave the midst of the sea.  
> (*HERCULES OETAEUS*)

[Col. 0385A] They are joined.] Besides the Venerable Bede, St Bernard also testifies to this, sermon 37 to his sister.

And dung, above.] V. omits “and dung.”

The oxen stoning [them].] C. makes no mention of this saying.

Deuteronomy, chapter VII.] Tria: XXXV.

Seven peoples.] That is, the seven capital sins. Thus both margins. For more, see Lyra’s Gloss on this passage.

Often cured by a plaster.] As when avarice is cured by detected simony, and pride by lust exposed. Sometimes, by God’s permission, someone falls into lust so that he may be rendered free from pride. St Augustine teaches this, *City of God*, book XIV; St Thomas, II–II, question 162, article 6, reply to 3.

There you will be healed.] V. omits *there*. These words seem to be spoken antiphrastically from Jeremiah 51: “We have healed Babylon, and she has not been healed,” verse 9.

Whence Gregory.] V.: “Whence it is read in the *Lives of the Fathers* concerning a certain man.”

Seeing citizens.] C.: “He saw citizens.”

The bristle-haired.] *Horripilo*, as though bristling with rougher hair. The bristle-haired are those who swell all the more the more they are honoured. The term *horripilatio* occurs in Ecclesiasticus XXVII, verse 15.

359 Pride might arise.] C.: “might spring up.” Incorrect, unless perhaps “might burn,” because afterward he rushes into the river for the sake of cooling.

As though mad.] V. and M.: “as though foolish.” In C.’s margin these words are read concerning this hermit: “I am God and do not change; I do not enter the city.” Likewise the hermit did not wish to enter it.

Half-girdles.] Things which gird the middle of a human being.

Lanfranc.] He was Archbishop of Canterbury, a holy and learned man. At the Roman council under Pope Nicholas II in 1059 he disputed with Berengar, the heresiarch, and refuted him so thoroughly that Berengar gave his book to Vulcan to be devoured. When Berengar returned to his vomit, the aforesaid Lanfranc wrote *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Eucharist*, volume III of the Councils, part 3; Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year noted above; Baronius, volume XI, year 1088. His book *On the Sacrament of the Altar* is extant in volume VI of the second edition of the *Library of the Fathers*. [Col. 0385C]

Subtly.] Not “sublimely,” as C. and M. have.

At the Council of Tours.] Held by order of Pope Victor II, through a legation sent against Berengar. Lanfranc mentions it in his book against the same man; Baronius, volume XI, under the year 1055.

Excess is helpful.] Not “no less,” as C. has, since that is erroneous and contrary to Claudian’s original text.

You placed a cloud in opposition.] V.: “A cloud was placed in opposition,” but contrary to the text of Holy Scripture.

Pride of heart.] C.: “For there is pride of heart, mouth, heart, the whole body, and deed.” Why repeat “heart” twice? Hear the manifold kinds of pride: pride of heart, mouth, eyes, forehead, hands, feet. Thus the margin.

And the forehead is the dwelling-place.] C. explains, not badly: “and above the mouth is the dwelling-place, namely the forehead.”

A sign of modest.] M. divides it thus: “And a sign of modesty, humility, or shameless arrogance.”

And Job, or Wisdom.] C. simply: “And Wisdom,” by which understand Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXIII; Job has nearly the same in chapters VII and XXXI.

Exaltation.] M. and C.: “excellence,” incorrectly.

Threatening nostrils.] V. and M.: “Nostrils breathing threats and injuries.”

Boastful shoulders.] Or “ostentatious,” say M. and V.

Laughing gestures.] V., by way of explanation and note, adds: “Words formed and gestures moving people to laughter”; M. adds *perhaps* in the margin.

Let the limbs speak.] C.: “Let the limbs move.”

By what reasoning he is silent.] M. and V.: “When he is silent with reason.”

[Col. 0386A] *Gastrimargia*.] Tria, with almost all manuscripts, as I said above on chapter 10, reads *castrimargia*, incorrectly.

As if curved like a bow.] The surface of the belly is convex in front and concave behind; to this is sometimes added a tortoise-like gait, with such affected gravity of body that, if you sent before such persons a herald sounding a trumpet, you would at once think an affected prefect was walking by.

With a stake fixed.] V.: “with a heel fixed”; it makes no sense. The poet Prudentius describes this in *Psychomachia* 4.

The Lord and kingdom.] V. and M.: “Dwelling-place and kingdom.”

Of another vice.] Namely, *gastrimargia*, as C. and M. note.

Is it because of?] Why do Tria read “not”? See Seneca in the cited place.

By which other animals.] V.: “Which other,” etc.; this does not please me.

A gluttony to be filled?] V.: “a gluttony to be extinguished?” [Col. 0386B] That is, to be satisfied?

God breaks every [proud person].] A hemistich of Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 4.

Nor in gait.] This is the interlinear Gloss.

Ungainliness of the body.] Correctly. Therefore M. and V. are wrong to have “ungainliness of mind.”

Job XVIII.] Tria: Job XIV. In former times the numbering of chapters was lower than it is today, as I noted above.

The firstborn of death.] V.: “death first-created.” This can be tolerated.

Which among vices first.] V.: “which [is] first among vices” (here it fails): “the first creation.”

Likewise Cassiodorus.] Here M. has a lacuna through the end of the chapter.

Meditation of the heart.] C.: “thought.”

Who [is] within.] C.: “whom you see as just.”

## CHAPTER XI

The mother having been suffocated.] From St Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew*.

[Col. 0386C] Which he retained.] V. omits this through “His envy.”

Into effect and perhaps.] C.: “into affection and into effect,” namely envy. Here I shall note material gathered from a manuscript of the monastery of Cambron, in which, among the works of Stephen of Canterbury, are several chapters from Peter the Chanter’s *Verbum abbreviatum*: “Envy was the first sin after pride, and through it he was made Satan from an angel; but he lost it in effect, I know not whether in affection; and he retains envy in effect and affection. For he envies us what he lost; whence, envying them, he deceived our first parents. And I do not know whether the damned and reprobate are purified of envy by demons, so that after death they envy the good, and thus the saying may be false:

> Envy feeds upon the living; after death it rests.  
> (OVID, book I, Elegy 15.)”

He strove that.] Consult St Augustine, volume VIII, on Psalm LVIII, sermon II, in the middle; likewise on Psalm CXXXIX, at the beginning.

[Col. 0386D] Brotherly hatred.] C.: “for it always produces hatred.” On these matters, St Thomas, II–II, question 34, article 6, in the body of the article.

Those which say.] V.: “those who say,” also well, if the reference is made to the authorities.

Were also rendered.] I gathered these three words from C. alone.

Which especially.] V. and M.: “which also then.”

361 And then this vice.] M.: “and concerning this vice,” namely brotherly hatred.

It has an impelling cause.] M.: “it has a solicitude that impels,” etc.

It will reign afterward.] “That no other sin [will reign afterward],” says the margin of M. and C.

I pursue another.] V.: “he pursues another”; likewise in the immediately following passages.

The giver himself.] V.: “the Holy Spirit himself.”

I strive to extinguish.] “By saying,” say both margins, “he does it out of hypocrisy,” and so forth.

In joy and sorrow.] In joy, because evil happens [Col. 0387A] to one’s neighbour; in sorrow, because good things happen to him.

To exult over evils.] The poet Statius, *Thebaid* II.

It wastes away.] C. and M.: “It withers.” See Horace, book I, epistle 2. Our Waudraeus, canon of St German at Mons, directs this epigram against the envious man:

> Envious man, who would believe it? You waste away amid abundant goods,  
> And grow thin among fattened sheep.  
> Since you can live only by envy, it remains  
> That you die in that part by which you wish to live.  
> (Book I, epigrams.)

Laughter is always absent.] Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, thus:

> Laughter is absent, except such as the sight of sufferings produced.

O you who will see sweet things.] The envious man grieves over his enemy’s prosperity. There follows: “You who will enter darkness”: he rejoices over adversities.

Pride kills.] The biblical codex: “Anger kills.”

Purity or life.] C. omits “or life.”

Health of the flesh.] Of carnal desires, [Col. 0387B] says C.’s margin.

Rottenness of the bones.] The two margins explain: “Of all the virtues, which it makes rot.” Such also is Lyra’s Gloss.

The fire of burning.] Of envy, says the interlinear Gloss.

Straw of the wall.] Vanity, or empty works. The same Gloss.

Juster than envy.] Thus St Jerome on Galatians, chapter V: “Someone among the later Greeks,” he says, “elegantly rendering a Greek verse, played upon envy in elegiac metre, saying:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which at once gnaws  
> Its very author and tortures his mind.”

But we add what we saw in the margin of M.: “As though through him.” Hence:

> Unhappy first author, he stained the work.

Perpetual anxiety.] This verse and those following are from Juvenal, Satires 14 and 15.

It takes both.] The same author, Satire 9.

And trembling of the head.] V.: “And trembling of the body.” [Col. 0387C] Some say that God gave Cain such a horn in his nostril, and eyes so sparkling, that by his appearance he seemed more terrible than a unicorn. Book III, homily 6, chapter 2, of *The Widow of Zarephath*, which we published some years ago.

This is the spirit.] V.: “I also endure.” “This is the spirit,” that is, envy, etc.

362 Because he had also heard.] V.: “had seen.”

Before the one playing the psaltery.] V. and M.: “before the one playing the psaltery,” namely Saul. This certainly makes sense.

To the lyre.] Why do V. and M. read “to the letter”?

Envy, daughter.] C.: “Envy, son.”

From good things that prosper.] C.: “It arises from a man’s own good things, just as this arises from the good things of one’s neighbour and another, and from better things.”

If wholly.] C.: “But he cannot wholly destroy it.”

If he has not harmed someone.] V. and M.: “If he has not harmed in some respect.”

Do not eat.] “Spiritual or material foods,” says the Cambron fragment, of which I spoke above in the notes to this chapter [Col. 0387D].

And you will destroy the fair ones.] The same fragment likewise: as though he were saying, “You will by no means be able to appease an envious man.”

Which arises from good things.] M.: “which arises,” incorrectly.

In the Prologue to Isaiah.] I shall specify the place more exactly: in the prologue of St Jerome to Book XI of the *Commentaries on Isaiah*, addressed to Eustochium.

They despise also.] To them applies this verse, collected from the margins of C. and M.:

> The poems which the *caletes* [reading uncertain] do not know, they say should be despised.

M. reads *omnia* (“all things”) for *carmina* (“poems”). C. has *zelotes* (“zealots, the jealous”) for *caletes*.

Likewise, if it arises.] M.: “Envy obtains.” He has misused the word.

Holy imitation.] C.: “Holy invitation.” V.: “Holy pride.” Why not “holy emulation”? For the Apostle says, “I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God” [2 Cor. 11]. I say “holy,” since elsewhere I observe a perverse emulation: “Do not emulate evil men” [Prov. 24]. Cicero in the *Rhetoric* teaches that emulation is understood in two ways, as praise and as fault. [Col. 0388A]

They prophesy here.] They were Medad and Eldad, Numbers 11:26–27.

Which for the interpretation.] C.: “who for the interpretation.”

## CHAPTER XII

He is mistaken in the heading.] C. has “against tradition” for “for detraction.”

Worst tooth.] M. differently: “And detraction is most evil to God.” That is, detraction itself is hateful to God. Cassiodorus says thus on Psalm 3: “They are called teeth from taking away (*demendo*). Therefore the tongues of detractors are very aptly called teeth; for, as teeth take away portions of foods, so these persons, through added detraction, gnaw away men’s reputations.”

Romans, chapter I.] V.: three [instead of one].

Contention.] This has been discussed sufficiently above, chapter V.

[Col. 0388B] As though in this matter to them.] V. is defective through “likewise, epistle.”

Galatians V.] II: three.

You bite one another.] “By derogating in part,” say the two margins.

363 You are consumed.] “By abolishing altogether.” The same margins, C. and M.

Namely, torn apart.] M.: “you are consumed, namely in the unity of faith.” C.: “you are consumed—schism, namely, in the unity of faith.” This is perhaps what the ordinary Gloss intends in this place, namely: “You are consumed through schism from the Christian religion.”

In the Psalm, chapter C.] V. and M.: Psalm 99. Incorrectly.

That is, one who detracts.] V. and M. read thus: “A perverse heart did not cleave to me,” etc.; “the one detracting from his neighbour,” etc.; “one of proud eye,” etc.—all from the same Psalm.

Of proud eye.] “For envy,” say the margins C. and M. But the Cambron fragment is clearer: “Of proud eye,” pride; “of insatiable heart,” envy; “the one detracting,” etc., detraction.

Proverbs, chapter IV.] Three: XIV. Our Bible formerly had chapter XII.

[Col. 0388C] Likewise, chapter XXIV.] Three: XLV. The aforesaid Bible: XLIV.

The thought of a fool.] M.: “a foolish thought.” Above this, between the lines, I read: “and his whole life.”

That is, not to one absent.] This is Leviticus 19: “You shall not curse the deaf.” St Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part 3, Admonition 36, explains it in the same manner and sense.

He who detracts from his neighbour.] C. adds: “from God, from his neighbour, and from man.”

V. and M. do not repeat “and from his neighbour,” because it is sufficiently evident that he binds himself to him insofar as he detracts from him.

But also from man.] Only C. has *but*. Meanwhile it might be absent without altering the meaning.

By speaking humbly.] M.: “by speaking, humbled.” V.: “humbled, saying.”

Coming, not merely.] I wish that, instead of “coming,” one read, “Go first,” etc. For it is abundantly clear, both from the ordinary Gloss and from the Lyra Gloss, that it ought to be read thus. There “Go” is expounded in two ways: first, by the feet of the body; second, of the mind. I mean of the mind when one has the purpose [Col. 0388D] of making satisfaction at a fitting place and time. Injury must first be repaired; then sacrifice must be offered to the immortal God, and you must understand that he is to be propitiated only after the brother has first been reconciled.

For detraction is.] Observe the variation. C.: “For detraction is to take something from someone, and something from the fullness of someone.” M.: “For detraction is to take from someone the fullness of someone.” But M. makes no sense thus. The Cambron fragment defines it thus: “Detraction is a drawing away from someone.”

The question is.] These words could have been understood from the question asked; but since V. had them in the text, we could by no means exclude them from the text. Meanwhile, instructed by the teaching of many, I myself would say that such a detractor ought both to restore the benefice and to repair the reputation he has torn apart before the prelate. But prelates themselves, when they favour informers, readily believe accusers, and lend an attentive ear to detractors, are by no means excused from sin. For St Augustine, [Col. 0389A] tome VIII, on Psalm 108, verse 4, says: “If you listen to a detractor with a cheerful countenance, you give him fuel for detraction,” 364 etc. See further 6, question 1, *Ex merito*, and 11, question 3, *Non solum*.

Foods are to be taken.] I once read this in the same St Augustine, *Confessions*, book 10, chapter 31.

Let him know her unworthy.] M.: “Let him judge her unworthy of himself.” This epigram occurs in tome X, Sermon 26 *To the Brothers in the Desert*.

Catholic Epistle, chapter 4.] Three: chapter 9. Among ancient authors it is called not “canonical” but “Catholic.” Origen in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 19; Dionysius of Alexandria, ibid., book VII, chapter 10; St Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under James. It is called Catholic, together with the Epistles of St Peter and the others, because it was not sent to one particular city, as the Epistle to the Romans, nor to one private person, as the same author’s Epistle to Timothy; but was sent generally to the faithful scattered abroad, as is evident from chapter 1. It is also called canonical because it contains canons [Col. 0389B] and precepts for establishing the Christian life, or because, equally with the Pauline Epistles, it belongs to the canon of books.

He who [—] hidden sin.] M. determines nothing, and therefore reads badly: “He who [—] a sinner publicly,” etc. Those who sin publicly must be corrected publicly as an example. Thus the Venerable Bede on Luke 8: “A public fault requires a public remedy.” [“let it be removed.”]

Proverbs 24.] Copy: XLVI.

But does false testimony less.] C. blunders: “But does false testimony detract less by speaking true devil of something?”

Or by virtue.] C. alone.

Words of flatterers.] By no means: “Words of detractors,” as C. has it. For this is evident from the interlinear Gloss, which is also Augustine’s.

Of a certain wise man.] See the Gloss.

When one member suffers injury.] V.: “all suffer compassion when one member is injured.”

To be observed.] C.: “to be preserved.”

[Col. 0389C] Less honourable members.] Cambron fragment: “dishonourable members.”

By the example also of a mother.] From here through “by the example also of the householder,” etc., V. is defective.

The younger.] C.: “the smaller.” It makes sense, certainly, if you understand lesser age rather than merely lesser size. Thus the Cambron fragment reads: “She cherishes the weaker son with greater care.”

The prodigal son.] After the example of the prodigal son, the Cambron fragment rightly adds: “For he who is bad today will be good tomorrow; and therefore no one is to be disparaged.”

For someone invents.] Three agree, but the Cambron fragment states it more clearly thus: “For one person invents detraction without any basis, or with some basis, because there is no one whose foot does not sometimes slip, of whom that poetic saying may be spoken:

> Savage in inventing every reproach against anyone.

Another listens in order to report it, and of him this may be said:

[Col. 0389D]

> Savage in speaking every reproach against anyone.”

The margins C. and M.: “Rare is the man whose foot does not at some time slip.” C. adds: “so that it slips.”

365 Savage in inventing.] A verse of Horace, *Epistles*, I.15. C.: “savage in speaking.”

It scatters the rains.] “Of flattery and detraction,” say the aforesaid margins.

A sad face.] Namely, one rebuking, says M. between the lines; or one indicating that he abhors detraction as a rotten stench, contracting his nostrils, wrinkling his brow, or drawing down his eyebrow.

To Nepotian.] Tome I, *On the Life of Clerics*, near the end. The epistle begins: “You ask of me.” Similar things are found in the epistle to Rusticus in the same tome, beginning: “Nothing [is] to a Christian,” after the middle.

Not into a rock.] I myself would prefer “into a rock,” “from its force,” and this on the basis of Jerome’s text. For he says: “An arrow is never fixed in a stone.” V. here varies thus: “For you speak to none unwillingly, so that an arrow may be fixed in a rock, but, rebounding,” etc.

Contempt, another reading.] Three do not understand here. For it is not another reading but a Gloss, namely Cassiodorus’s Gloss on this place. For he there distinguishes mockery from contempt. “Contempt,” he says, “is abject worthlessness.”

It extinguishes or destroys.] C. omits “or destroys.” M.: “it extinguishes or punishes.” This is not pleasing. St Bernard, in the same homily: “It kills utterly and extinguishes.” It would be greatly beneficial to read it.

There are, however, two kinds.] The same author discusses them at length in the same place.

Saying thus: “Through me.”] Almost the same things are in St Jerome’s epistle to Rusticus, “Nothing [is] to a Christian.” “But,” he says, “you will say: I myself do not detract; what can I do when others are speaking? We offer this as a pretext for excusing excuses in sins,” etc.

The chapter ‘A cleric.’] It reads there: “A slanderous cleric is to be compelled to seek pardon; and if he refuses, he is to be deposed, and not restored [Col. 0390B] to his office except with the fullest satisfaction.”

By evident faith.] Manifest and open faith. M. and C. incorrectly: “by hidden faith.”

We see daily.] “It is evident,” says the Cambron fragment, “because many detractors and advocates have been deprived of the use of their tongue.”

Among those who sell their tongue.] By “those who sell their tongue” understand advocates, pleaders, and others of the same profession, who, in their doubled or tripled replies, hurl insults at witnesses and at the opposing side, introducing calumnies wholly irrelevant to the matter from malice and vindictiveness of mind. Shameful indeed! That counsellors do not take action against such detractors, known and caught in deed, word, and writing; that they do not pronounce sentence against them by due process, condemning them either to removal from office for a year or to perpetual incapacity for holding it. V. and M.: “among those who sell a grandiloquent tongue.” C.: “among those who sell a vain and grandiloquent tongue.” Hear Lucan, book X of the *Pharsalian War*:

[Col. 0390C]

> No faith or piety belongs to men who follow the camp,  
> And whose hands are for sale: there right is, where the reward is greatest.

Punishment also to come.] See 6, question I, *Deteriores*; *On Penance*, distinction I, *Homicidium vero*.

366 ## CHAPTER XIII

Life first.] C.: “Life entered afterwards.” In the sense meant here, this cannot be tolerated.

First we approach.] Again C.: “after we approach.” In Lyra, *post* is written with such an abbreviation that I am almost led to read *prius* (“first”), and thus I would not condemn this reading or the former one.

So that concerning it.] The author appears to have taken this from St Augustine, tome X, Sermon 2, *On the Vigil of Pentecost*. C. divides the adverb *adeo* into two words, *a Deo* (“from God”), incorrectly.

[Col. 0390D] He has humbled himself.] “By nature,” say the margins C. and M.

Like this little child.] “By grace.” The same.

To the same little women.] “He first appeared to women,” says St Jerome. C., omitting “to the little women,” reads only “to the same [one].” V. and M. do the opposite.

The text infers that Mary Magdalene, to whom the risen Saviour first appeared, is identical with Mary the sinner. Guillaume Estius takes the contrary view in *Theological Orations*, 14, and in his notes on this place.

First prelate of the drop.] V. omits “first.” Concerning “of the drop,” the margins say after St Jerome: that is, of the Gentile people, base and idolatrous.

The chief seats for themselves.] Not “the worst,” as C. has. See St Jerome’s epistle to the monk Antony.

How much of prayers.] The same author again incorrectly: “how much of price.”

Not make a gesture.] V.: “not make you mute.” M.: “and compel you to make yourself mute, and [before] the Lord,” etc. C.: “Compel yourself to be mute.” I restored “gesture” from St Jerome.

Unless the modesty of the pen.] The margins C. and M.: “A spoken word flies away; a written word remains. Therefore the greatest reverence is due to the pen in writing, lest anything be written except what is honourable and useful.” V. has this in the text after the words, “To reply while angry.” But I judged that later persons had annotated it—as V. suggests in the notes to chapter 97—and therefore that it should be deleted from the text.

He saw the world in the air.] C.: “He saw the air full,” etc. But M.: “He saw the world”—though above it adds, “read: air”—“full of snares,” etc. These things were said of St Antony, as is read in the Life of the same composed by St Athanasius.

Unwary humility.] The Cambron fragment reads: “For excessive humility is akin to folly.” Correctly so: humility without reason is regarded as folly.

Akin to folly.] M.: “akin to justice.” Absurdly.

And to be preserved.] V.: “and to be observed.”

Fear a fall.] In accordance with 1 Corinthians 10: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.”

Likewise Psalm 101.] C. and M. are defective by one line through [Col. 0391B] “Likewise the same.”

The exaltation of pride.] M.: “the elation of pride.”

By the bestowal of glory.] Or, as C. has it, “by the bestowal of rewards.”

367 First Kings, chapter XV.] V. and M. specify chapter XXVI.

Second Kings, chapter VI.] Three: LXV.

Today and yesterday.] C. alone has “and yesterday,” and it is not in the scriptural text.

From behind those giving birth.] I did not see this in the text of St Gregory or in V.

Equalling himself with the least.] C.: “performing the least.” V.: “performing less.” M.: “performing the least.” In the text I followed the text of St Gregory.

Weak and lowest things.] St Gregory: “He did base and lowest things, so that those,” etc. C.: “he did very weak and lowest things.” By these is signified David’s profound humility and condescension.

He despised the humbled.] Thus far St Gregory.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0391C]

Ash and dust.] That is, as the margins M. and C. say, “They confess themselves to be base.” See St Gregory, *Morals*, XXVII, chapter 27.

They confess themselves to be.] C. is mistaken: “They do not confess themselves to be.”

In the eyes of the heart.] V.: “in my eyes.”

For there is a twofold humility of fault.] I acknowledge that I restored these four words to the context; only the margins C. and M. contained them.

From servile fear.] The Cambron fragment says: “And akin to humility is the humility of servile fear; for some humble themselves through fear alone, since they do not dare rage against others, though they desire to do so.”

The poet says.] Claudian, *Against Eutropius*, II.

He shall be humbled, by confusion.] Psalm 118: “Let the proud be confounded,” etc. C. incorrectly reads “confession” for “confusion.”

Proverbs, chapter XXIX.] Three: LIV, at the end.

[Col. 0391D] But Esau hunting.] Genesis 25. V. and M.: “a hunter.”

From behind the asses.] C.: “asses [masculine].” Sacred Scripture has “asses [feminine].”

Against the Apostle.] Or, as V. and C. have it, “against the disciple.”

The weak things of the world.] That is, the humble things. Hence M. and V.: “the lowest things of the world.”

And that it may confound.] V.: “and that it might break.”

When at Rome.] From here through “the son of the craftsman,” I restored the text from the margin of C. and the Cambron fragment alone.

Successor.] V.: “successors.”

Because of its four-sidedness.] Of these virtues, the four horns of the altar, Wisdom 8 says: “She teaches sobriety and prudence, justice and virtue, than which nothing in human life is more useful.” Do you want more? Read through the Gloss on Exodus 27, verse 1.

Gainful.] As in Proverbs 31: “She sought wool and flax,” etc. Far be it from you, therefore, to call the Mother of God “mercenary,” as C. does. Yet I think that this crept in through a copyist’s error. For below, in chapter XVI, it has “gainful.” Thus St Jerome calls her at the end of the epistle to Heliodorus, “With how great love.”

368 Spending nights awake.] The margin C. adds: “Whence visions appear to shepherds, and through the simplicity of little children enchantments, swords, and such things have effect.”

The secrets of the Nativity.] V.: “The secret mysteries of the Nativity.” I removed “mysteries” because I judged it superfluous. For here it has the same meaning as “secret” and “mystery,” as in Tobit 12: “It is good to conceal the mystery of a king.”

With little milk.] From the hymn on the Nativity of the Lord.

Humble things and hum—.] C.: “Because he preached humble things to the humble.”

In another’s tomb.] Which was Joseph of Arimathea’s, Matthew 27.

The responsory of humility.] That is, a shield and antidote.

With hyssop.] Cambron fragment: “With hyssop, that is, [Col. 0392B] humility throughout the whole body.”

We are admonished in the Psalm.] V.: “For this reason boys too are admonished in the Psalms to praise: ‘Praise, boys’”; M. has “are moved” for “are admonished.” It makes no sense.

A humble animal.] St John Chrysostom on Matthew 21: “For this animal is unclean and, more than almost all other beasts of burden, irrational, foolish, weak, ignoble, and especially burden-bearing.”

Our works.] C.: “our times.”

Catholic Epistle, chapter IV.] Three: chapter VIII. Why it is called Catholic we said in the notes to chapter XII.

But fear the more.] C. omits “the more,” incorrectly.

Pride there, ruin.] Thus Jeremiah threatens in chapter 50: “The proud man shall fall and collapse, and there shall be none to raise him.” Cambron fragment: “Where pride is, there is insult.”

To be humbled with the humble.] St Jerome’s version: “To be humbled with the meek”; but the Septuagint: “Better one meek in heart with humility.” The translation of the Chaldean paraphrase reads: “Better is one humble in spirit and meek,” etc. Had three witnesses agreed in the reading, I would have retained St Jerome’s version. Finally, the Cambron fragment read: “It is better to be humbled with the rich,” but incorrectly.

Likewise Gregory.] C. omits these two words. Gregory treats hypocrites in many places, especially *Morals*, book 18, chapter VII, and book XV, chapters 2, 3, and 4.

He who does not have humility.] M. contradicts this as follows: “He who does not have humility is not a hypocrite.” It may be tolerated in this sense: he who does not have humility—that is, who does not know how outwardly to feign humility—cannot be called a pretender to virtue or a hypocrite.

Job says.] Three, both in text and margin: chapter XV. Formerly the chapters of Job were fewer in number than today.

If he ascends into heaven.] The two margins add: “You are there,” from Psalm 138.

To seek the priesthood.] C.: “to take.”

On the desire for praise.] The margins C. and M. annotate [Col. 0392D] from Philippians 3: “I counted all these things as dung, that I might gain Christ.”

And as though concerning.] These were added by the author to St Jerome’s text through “we interpret.”

369 They turn [these things] into glory.] The aforesaid margins: “Rebuking glory.” How finely Seneca says, Epistle 113, at the end: “He who wishes his virtue to be made public labours not for virtue, but for glory.” Therefore those who make their writings public through their own study and industry should look to God’s honour and their neighbour’s benefit, not to the favour of popular applause. Let them say with the Lord: “I do not seek my own glory” [Isa. 8], etc. If detractors survive, scorning and demeaning their works, let them answer humbly and kindly: “Make known your right hand thus, and [make] those wise in heart instructed in wisdom” [Psalm 89].

And reputation among peoples.] The two margins: “A reputation is useful to one’s neighbour.” So it is. For “A good reputation fattens the bones” [Prov. 15].

A clanging cymbal.] These are St Jerome’s words; 1 Corinthians 13 has “a sounding [cymbal].”

[Col. 0393A] Athletic mockery.] Thus I restored it; otherwise Three has “Atlantic arena.” *Athletikē* (ἀθλητική) is understood as the art of contesting; hence *athlētēs* (ἀθλητής), athlete, wrestler. But *skōmma* (σκῶμμα) is mockery, calumny; *sophisma* (σόφισμα), a captious argument. Such persons mock and hurl insults adorned and shaded with seductive embellishments. And in the margin of C. I read on this: “They provoke one another to laughter by the word of God.”

Desirous of glory.] Does not the same margin cry out justly and truly:

> Why is man proud, whose conception is guilt,  
> Whose birth is punishment, life labour, and whose necessity is death?

Philippians II.] Three: III.

Second Corinthians IV.] Three: XI.

So that loftiness.] C.: “So that subtlety may be loftiness.”

And corruptible.] C. joins it to what immediately follows: “And the corruptible sack of dung.”

Recognize [your] dignity.] C. states eloquently in the side margin: “Man would have been great and happy if he had remained in that in which he was created; but greater and happier if he had remained in that for which he was created.” And again it adds: “And, O Christian, in that in which you have been restored.”

For how glorious.] C.: “For how glorious a tree of martyrdom was in him,” etc. Sigebert of Gembloux treats of Maurice and the Thebans in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 159; Marbod, bishop of Rennes, wrote the passion of the Thebans in verse. See further Surius, tome V.

Rebuking, he says, chapter XIII.] Three: XL.

Titus II.] Three: IV.

Jerome says.] Thus I restored it, as it is cited in VIII, question 1.

For what kind.] Three: “Augustine says.”

Rebuking, chapter XIX.] Three: LIV.

That saying of Gregory.] In the explanation of the third penitential Psalm, at the words, “There is no health in my flesh.” Three: “That saying of Jerome.”

The seven-runged ladder.] C.: “The seven utterances,” that is, the Beatitudes.

Humility as a foundation.] You will find this in the Gloss on Matthew 5: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

370 ## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0393C]

Concerning which it is good.] V.: “concerning which, namely humility”; acceptable.

Bordering and neighbouring.] V.: “continuous or adjoining, and neighbouring.”

Meek.] V.: “accustomed to the hand.”

Even one’s own injuries.] After this should be read the example which I gathered from the margin of C. alone. It is as follows: When inquiry was made about a certain religious man who possessed many graces, why he was not promoted, the monks answered: “Because in graces he is not gracious.” For he is not meek; he is not sufficiently tractable.

By the example of Andrew.] Of whom the Church sings thus: “This man appeared most gentle among his people,” etc.

The meek [in] his ways.] V. adds: “And Psalm 75:5, 9 [now 10]: ‘When God arose for judgment, to save all the meek of the earth.’ And the Apostle: ‘Rebuke with meekness.’ And shortly afterwards the Psalmist [Psalm 44]: ‘For truth and meekness,’ [Col. 0393D] etc. ‘For meekness came upon us, and we shall be corrected’ [Psalm 89]. The poet too approves this:

> Unlovely fierceness does not enter these characters,  
> Nor does it less depart from pursuits suited to itself.”  
> —Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, I

The Apostle’s words, “Rebuke,” etc., are gathered from 1 Corinthians 4 or 1 Timothy 6. C. also adds in the side margin: “And he exalted the meek unto salvation” [Psalm 149].

From the pursuits of a Gentile.] V.: “If it departs from a Gentile nature.”

1 Chronicles, chapter XVIII.] M.: “Likewise Chronicles LXVI, at the end.” V.: “Chronicles, book II, chapter XVI, at the end.”

## CHAPTER XVI

The governance of the heavenly [doctrine].] In this chapter V. differs greatly from the others, and thus begins: “To the ordering of his heavenly teaching, on Jacob’s ladder, after humility and meekness, the Lord added a third—not a virtue, [Col. 0394A] but the preservation and increase of virtues—poverty. By word and example he governs schools concerning it, because,” etc. M. begins the chapter thus: “To the ordering of his heavenly teaching concerning humility,” etc.

Which can save.] M. omits this sentence.

Is said to have been.] This is read in C. alone.

Blessed are the poor.] According to Luke, “in spirit” is not added.

But by example.] V.: “But he also commended it by example, that he might invite the people to desire it, and [might] himself,” etc.

Poor and gainful.] I added “poor” from V. to Lyra. At the end of his epistle to Heliodorus, “With how great love,” St Jerome calls the Virgin Mother of God “gainful.”

Little manger.] Not “little stable,” as M. has it.

371 To a certain young man.] This is the sound reading. C. and M.: “To a certain man possessing riches.”

Whether nevertheless.] V.: “Whether indeed.”

[Col. 0394B] A word of possibility.] C.: “Words of possibility.”

With the negative.] C.: “With the negative particle *not*.”

Or facility.] V. and M.: “Or capability.”

Or because, incorrectly.] From here through “Likewise Jerome,” V. alone has this in the text; the other two have it in the margin. Here *thus* seems to be required instead of “again,” although St Jerome adduces only the first reason why riches are called the mammon of iniquity.

They make [men] proud.] After this the margins C. and M. add: “The Apostle was not alarmed to say, namely, ‘death from—’”

Small and narrow homes.] Printed Lucan:

> The homes of the poor and cramped.

O gifts.] V. and M.: “O gods.”

God understood.] C.: “God understood.”

This could happen to walls.] The printed text:

> … This could happen to temples  
> Or walls.

A prey to citizens.] This half-line, together with the following one, is taken from the same Lucan and immediately precedes the preceding passage, thus:

> Secure from war, he knows that huts are not spoils  
> In civil arms. O safe means of life, etc.

Likewise in the same.] Namely, Lucan, though not in book V but in book I of the *Pharsalian War*.

Not men.] V. omits this. I add verses of Juvenal, Satire VI, written in the side margin of C. in a very faint hand:

> Foul money first brought foreign morals,  
> And ages were broken by shameful luxury.

Likewise Jerome, secondly.] Consult Epistle 146 to Damasus, “To Your Blessedness,” and the other to Demetrias.

Verses of poets.] M.: only “verses of poems.” V.: only “of poets.” In the notes to chapter 1 you will find more on this matter.

The Egyptians despoiled and the Hebrews enriched.] These words perhaps should have been deleted from the text as added notes, since C. alone reads them in the margin and V. in [Col. 0394D] the context. Let the reader judge from what is contained in the notes to chapter 97. They are taken from the blessing of the Paschal candle.

The hair of a girl.] An allusion to the woman seen among captives, concerning whom Deuteronomy 21 speaks.

Juvenal: “He will sing.”] Satire X. From here through “Likewise Jerome,” M. and C. are defective.

Claudian.] *Against Rufinus*, book I. The first verse differs from the printed editions of Claudian. For they read:

> … Nature gave to all  
> The power to be blessed, etc.

Cato: “Poverty.”] Why not cite the preceding verse of the same poem? It serves the purpose, and should therefore be repeated:

> When nature created you a naked infant,  
> Poverty, etc.

Likewise Seneca, to commend [poverty].] I restored “Seneca” from Epistle 42, which the margin C. also cited. Three had “Jerome” in place of Seneca.

[Col. 0395A] Therefore this.] V.: “Therefore indeed.”

To which [we attain] with great labour.] V.: “and with great labour.” It omits the rest.

With great labour.] Namely riches and revenues, say the two marginal annotations.

We ought to examine [them].] “When they are offered to us,” say the same margins and V.

We do not foresee.] This is Seneca’s genuine reading, Epistle 42. V., however, agrees with M.: “We do not perceive thoroughly.”

We call [them] gratuitous.] V.: “We deem [them] gratuitous.”

At what price it is conveyed.] V.: “is deferred.” It omits the following word, “of price.”

Often of the greatest price.] M. and C. here observe “although V., with the printed Seneca, reads, ‘Often the price is greatest.’”

The text’s author asserts that Lipsius’s reading was accepted by certain persons.

What is more foolish?] From here through “Likewise: Tobias’s wife,” two read this in the side margin, whereas V. has it in the text thus: “Jerome: What is more foolish?” etc.

[Col. 0395B] Likewise Jerome.] “In his short commentary on the Psalms,” say the two margins with V. Yet these words are not found in the commentary extant under his name.

According to the word of Wisdom.] I saw similar things in Ecclesiastes 5 and Job 20.

More often more sincerely.] V.: “more often more securely.” Certainly the former is preferable.

That he might sleep deeply.] The two margins with V.: “securely.” That is, he slept in deep, untroubled, rather than laborious, sleep.

Here, reader, you should be warned that V. differs greatly from the other two exemplars, not only in transposed word order but also in extent. Therefore I judged it advisable to transcribe it word for word from this place—“Likewise Jerome: For this reason, with ampler,” etc.—through Seneca’s words, “I remember Attalus”; but first the variation of C. and M. through the said words of Seneca must be noted.
