Naked, [following] the naked.] See St Jerome, at the end of the epistle to Rusticus, “Nothing [is] to a Christian.”

[Col. 0395C] Abundance of bread.] The margins C. and M.: “By bread all necessary goods are understood.” St Jerome on Eusebius 16: “‘Abundance of bread,’” he says, “the Septuagint rendered ‘the wealth of pleasures and luxury.’ It is right that pleasures are understood by bread; for bread is always fit and useful with every dish.”

373 Likewise Jerome.] After Seneca, Epistle 20, in the middle.

Likewise the same: This one thing.] Tome IV, on Ezekiel 34, at the beginning; and again after Seneca, *On Benefits*, VI.30.

Or in giving counsel.] M.: “or in counselling him.”

The fruits of repentance.] M. omits “of repentance,” incorrectly.

By the example of Xerxes.] On this, Seneca, *On Benefits*, VI.31.

Demaratus.] Not “Demoratus,” as M. has it. St Jerome mentions him in *Apology against Rufinus*, chapter 2.

You are conquered by yourself.] M. adds in the margin: “When the army has been seen, the enemies will flee in fear,” and such things. Likewise: “You will be conquered before you realize it.” V. reads these and the following marginal notes in the text, as you will see below.

And it will overwhelm [us].] C.: “It will envelop us and wrap us round.”

Likewise Jeremiah: Nabuzardan, chief of the cooks.] This Nabuzardan was commander of the soldiery or army of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Jeremiah 52 and 2 Kings 25 say of him in the same place: “The whole army of the Chaldeans which was with the chief of the army destroyed the walls of Jerusalem round about.” The same is repeated in Jeremiah 52:14. In these places the Septuagint translators always call him “chief of the cooks,” as four or five times in the said chapter 25 of book IV Kings. And in Jeremiah 52 the Septuagint reads: “Nabuzardan, chief of the cooks, who stood before the face of the king of Babylon,” etc.; “the force of the Chaldeans which was with the chief of the cooks destroyed every wall of Jerusalem.” Citing this passage, St Gregory explains it beautifully in a mystical sense, *Pastoral Care*, part III, Admonition 20, as follows: “Because luxury follows those devoted to gluttony, the prophet testifies, who, while narrating open things, announces hidden things, saying: ‘The chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem.’ For the chief of the cooks is the belly, to whose service cooks devote great care, that it may be pleasantly filled with food. But the walls of Jerusalem are the virtues of the soul raised to the desire of heavenly peace. Therefore the chief of the cooks casts down the walls of Jerusalem, because, while the belly is extended through gluttony, the virtues of the soul are destroyed through luxury.” Thus he.

[Col. 0396A] Jerome: “In this.”] See the Gloss on this passage of the Psalm.

His chosen ones.] Three read thus. Psalm 68: “His bound ones,” etc.

The fetters of nature.] “By which,” say the margins C. and M., “the rich too are bound, whether they wish it or not, such as thirst, hunger, and the like.” For more, see St Augustine on Psalm 68, after the middle, tome VIII.

The fetters of grace.] C., in the margin: “But these are twofold. Some are fetters of commandment. Hence: ‘My son, put your foot into her fetters’ [Ecclus. 6]. The Lord hears those bound in these fetters [Psalm 68].”

He burdens these too much.] M.: “He honours these too much.”

Likewise the philosopher: “I remember.”] Seneca, Epistle 110, near the end. I shall now transcribe from V. (as I said above) from the point at which I stopped annotating. This comes from Juvenal: “That he might sleep deeply.” After these words V. continues:

374 To this applies what the Lord says: that voluntary poor persons will sit with him in judgment: “You who have left all things and followed me shall sit” [Matt. 19], etc. For there they will oppress their oppressors and will judge them with the Lord. For the Lord consecrated poverty in his own house. Yet it must not be denied that the rich—that is, those who are poor amid riches—exist.

To the same purpose applies the fact that the fishermen, leaving their nets and boat and every wish to possess, naked followed the naked crucified one [Matt. 4]. To this applies [Col. 0396C] the fact that the young man, leaving his linen cloth, fled naked [Mark 14]. This is what Joseph [did] to the Egyptian harlot [Gen. 39], that is, worldly luxury: escaping from her, he left behind the cloak by which he was being dragged by her. This is what the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 9 [or chapter 10]: “Run so that you may obtain.” For everyone who contends in the contest abstains from all things, from obstacles and little burdens. Poverty is to be commended by its contrary. For abundance of bread brought forth the vice of the Sodomites [Ezek. 26], that is, the abundance of riches of every kind and pride of life. Idleness also followed from it, an idleness which displeases nature itself and turns into disgust. Hence the saying: “See what idleness and another’s food can do.” Juvenal, Satire VI:

> A humble estate better preserved Latin women chaste.

Gregory commends poverty, saying: “Those whom weakness of character wounds, the medicine of poverty often heals.” St Bernard asked an abbot subject to him how his house was doing. He replied: “We are still doing very well, because we are still poor.” Jerome (after Seneca, Epistle 20, book VII): “For this reason poverty is to be loved: because it shows by whom you are loved.” This one thing is lacking to a man who possesses everything: that there is no one to tell him the truth. All flatter him: confessors, courtiers, secretaries too. Nor is a rich man loved by anyone. Hence Lucan:

> The happy man does not know that he is loved.

(Seneca, *On Benefits*, VI.31): “How will one who loves no one believe that he is loved?” That one who has [much] lacks someone to tell him the truth is evident from Xerxes. After accomplishing so many and such great things—walking dry-shod over the sea and sailing by ship over land—he assembled an immense army against the Lacedaemonians and Athenians, with thirty thousand cavalry and an innumerable multitude of infantry. When he asked whether these would suffice to defeat the enemy, everyone answered with one voice that even the air would not suffice to contain the multitude of missiles; and, on hearing the king’s name, all cried that the enemy would turn to flight. But Demaratus, a foreigner and exile, while all the others lied in flattery, alone told him the truth: “You will be defeated,” he said, “before you perceive it. For this unwieldy mass is discordant and unfit for war; it will easily collapse and crush itself through its very multitude.” And so it happened.

To the same purpose belongs the fact that Nebuchadnezzar, through the prince Nebuzaradan, left poor farmers and vinedressers in the land of promise, set Gedaliah over them, and carried the rich and powerful away with him into captivity (Jer. LII). David, commending poverty, says: “The Lord has heard the poor and has not despised his prisoners” (Ps. LXVIII). Jerome: Poverty is greatly to be commended in this respect: the Lord heard its prisoners and set them free. Now there are shackles of nature, such as thirst, hunger, and the like. There are also shackles of fortune—namely poverty [Col. 0397B] and things attached to it. There are also shackles of grace, but these are twofold. Some belong to commandment: hence, “My son, put your foot into her fetters” (Ecclus. VII). Others belong to a more perfect grace and to counsel, as among cloistered religious; hence such men are called “fettered men.” The shackles of nature, however, are today burdened too heavily. Of these Augustine says: “He burdens them excessively who heaps up more than necessities require.” The Lord hears those bound by such fetters. There are also shackles of sin. Hence: “The cords of sinners have encompassed me” (Ps. CXIII). Likewise the philosopher [Seneca, *Letters*, CX]: “I remember Attalus,” etc.

The notes, interrupted for a while, follow.

**“Riches imposed.”** M., between the lines, means: “they deceived.”

**“But in a certain display.”** “Of high rank, perhaps where it stood,” say the margins of M. and C. On the word *display*, C. notes in the side margin: “perhaps games.” This spectacle, as appears, was a Circus spectacle. Seneca describes its procession [Col. 0397C] and arrangement. Tertullian treats it extensively in *On Spectacles*, book 7, chapter 7. The textual variation is as follows. C. read: “If in a certain display”; M.: “But in a certain display.” I restored the passage from Seneca.

**“The chased riches of the city.”** That is, of the city of Rome. I have written *caelatas* (“chased, engraved”) with a diphthong in accordance with Seneca’s text. M. indicates that it ought to be absent, for between the lines it explains *caelatas* by “hidden.” V., instead of *caelatas*, has *collatas* (“collected”).

**“Among things which have value.”** Such as spoils of war and all precious booty. So the margins of M. and C.

**“And other things which.”** V.: “and other [feminine plural things].”

**“Excited.”** V.: “corrupted.”

**“From this I carry off.”** Not “I offer,” as in V.

**“From the effect.”** I have seen this neither in Seneca nor in V.

**“Slowly.”** C., between the lines: “gently.” Seneca has *lentus*, “slow.” Hear the margins of C. and M.: When wares are displayed for sale slowly, they are arranged in order so that they shine more brilliantly through one another; but when they are gathered together all at once, their elegance and beauty pass away. So too with riches.

[Col. 0397D]

**“This [will occupy] the whole of life.”** “This [will occupy] the whole life.” V. is unsatisfactory.

**“Will occupy.”** Thus Seneca. The three manuscripts have *occupavit* (“occupied”), even with the question-mark excluded, at the end of the sentence.

**“Attendants.”** M. and V.: “colours.” Incorrect.

**“Let us have water.”** Words of Epicurus.

**“The remedy for want?”** M. and C. put the question-mark before the very word *want*: thus, “Do you ask what the remedy is? For want: hunger,” etc.

**“Take away complaints.”** This half-line, together with the following verses, is from Horace, *Epistles*, I.12. From the lower margin of M.: I note these words from Seneca: “And what difference does it make who said it? He said it to everyone. He who needs riches fears for them. No one enjoys an anxious good. He strives to add something to them; while he thinks of increase, he has forgotten their use; he receives account-books, wears out the forum, turns over the calendar, and from a master becomes a steward,” *Letter* 14, at the end. On these words see Lipsius’s notes.

[Col. 0398A]

**“And in other men’s little gardens.”** Namely, Epicurus’s.

**“To endure human limitations.”** Not “humility,” as V.

**“They wear out the toga.”** Again V. departs from the sense: “They wear out their whole life.”

**“Likewise the same author.”** Before these words of Seneca, M. and C. read: “He to whom poverty agrees well is rich.” But since the same words were repeated a little later, I judged them incongruous, warned by the reading of V., which here pleased me. See Seneca, *Letter* 2.

**“What is necessary.”** What nature demands, and what enables you to live. Lipsius.

**“What is enough.”** V. adds, “namely, satiety.” Lipsius: What human nature requires, and what enables you to live comfortably. Likewise: “For him to whom what is enough is not enough, nothing will be enough.”

**“He has satiety.”** Consult Seneca, *Letters* 60 and 119.

**“Necessity is content with a penny.”** M.: “It is content with an obol.” Conversely: “The faithless man needs even an obol.” Blessed Jerome, [Col. 0398B] *Letter to Paulinus*, beginning “Brother Ambrose.”

## CHAPTER XVII

**Augustine.** Tome X, book L, homily 13, in the middle.

**Likewise Jerome.** Tome IX, in the Rule for Monks, under the heading “On Poverty.” See further tome III, *Letter to Hedibia*, Question 1, near the end. St Gregory has something similar in *Morals*, XV.12. Finally, I shall cite the words of St Fulgentius on Matthew’s words, “Every tree”: “What will he receive who took another’s goods, if he who did not give his own will burn forever?”

**Augustine.** Tome X, homily 8; tome L, homily [unspecified]. Likewise Sermon 205, *On Time*.

**“But on the contrary.”** This, down to “Riches,” is absent from M.

**“But the occasion.”** V. states more clearly: “But its occasion, namely theft.” It continues: “For on the occasion of poverty someone begins to steal.”

**“But the disease.”** V.: “Indeed, only their disease.” This is more restricted.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0398C]

**The title.** “On Moderation” I took from V. alone and separated it as a new chapter.

**Augustine says.** Tome VIII, exposition of Psalm XXIX, exposition 2, at the end.

**Seneca says.** *Letters* 95, 98, and 104; after Valerius Maximus, VII.5; and after Cicero, *For Murena*.

**“To dinner-guests.”** Thus Seneca, *Letter* 95, at the end. The three manuscripts, meanwhile: “at banquets.”

**377. “What else except?”** V. alone adds “except.” This saying departs from Seneca. See him.

**“That no deed.”** Supply “except this,” as the margins of C. and M. seem to suggest: “That he might be counted among the gods; on the contrary, through this deed she was regarded and consecrated among the goddesses.” V., for “That no deed,” reads “even if no deed.”

**“Of one man only.”** The margins: namely, Tubero’s.

**“The gold of the others.”** Seneca, *Letter* 95: “Their gold.”

**“And silver.”** V.: “Silver because it has been broken.”

[Col. 0398D]

**“And to be handled.”** C. omits this.

**“Likewise the same author.”** In V. *idem* (“the same”) is absent, but Seneca is named below.

**“Which Augustine.”** C.: “which Augustine says, in whose,” etc.

**“According to the measure of the person.”** C. otherwise: “It seems to lie hidden, but then according to the measure of the person.”

**“One must live.”** V.: “In which you must live”; but Seneca speaks more precisely: “That,” etc. Here he cites Seneca by name, whereas the other two cite him silently and by implication, as “Likewise the same author.”

**“I admonish you of this.”** Words of Seneca, *Letter* 5; it is useful to consult Justus Lipsius’s scholia on them.

**“Perverted ambition.”** C. varies greatly: “And whatever else follows a short path through perverted ambition.”

**“Human custom.”** C.: “custom”; V.: “by custom.” On this the margins of C. and M. say: We ought neither to conform ourselves wholly to this age [Col. 0399A] nor to differ altogether from men in our manner of life (Rom. XII).

**“Human limitations.”** Not “humility,” as V.

**“Crude and harsh.”** C. and M.: “certain and harsh.” Seneca: “gloomy and harsh.”

**“Delicate things.”** C., absolutely: “luxuries.”

**“Not obtainable at great cost.”** “Let your service be reasonable,” say the margins of C. and M., from Romans XII.

**“Not unkempt.”** C.: “not disorderly.”

**“Our life.”** C. and M.: “your life.”

**“But let them not recognize [it].”** The three have this reading, and I explain it thus. Let all accept our life—that is, our outward actions—as good and exemplary; but let them not “recognize” it, that is, by scrutinizing inward things, namely the disposition in which these acts are done; rather, let them interpret everything in the better sense. Seneca has affirmatively: “But let them also recognize [it],” or, as our manuscript of Seneca has it, “But let them recognize [it].”

**“Of the great Attalus.”** Seneca, *Letter* 110, near the end. By no means read “Demetrius” in place of Attalus, as V. does.

[Col. 0399B]

**“He permitted [them] to be possessed.”** The two conclude the chapter thus. V., however, adds to the text what C. and M. place in the margin: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI).

## 378. CHAPTER XIX

**“Just as the spiritual.”** The two begin the chapter thus; but V. repeats what occurs at the end of chapter 14: “The Lord, having gathered the disciples,” down to “just as the spiritual.”

**I Timothy, chapter VI.** The two: chapter 8; V.: chapter 10.

**“He does not say, ‘they are.’”** V. also pleases here: “Not those who are, but those who wish.”

**“To become rich.”** “By will,” says the margin of M.

**“Unto destruction.”** The very faint interlinear characters of M. explain thus: “‘Unto destruction,’ temporal; ‘and perdition,’ eternal.”

## CHAPTER XX

From V. I added to the chapter summary the word: “and avarice.”

[Col. 0399C]

**“Which is the desire of having more.”** Words of St Augustine, tome I, book III, *On Free Will*, chapter 17.

**“Anything whatsoever.”** Namely, as the margins of C. and M. say: money, honour, high position, knowledge, food, clothing, and the like. More in St Augustine on Psalm CXVIII, discourse 11.

**“Therefore covetousness.”** M.: “Therefore this sin, namely covetousness.” Against this covetousness, St Jerome’s exhortatory letter to Pammachius and Oceanus, beginning “He who invites the Ethiopian.”

**“According to this.”** M. omits it.

**“Which specifically.”** Not “spiritually,” as M.

**“Love of money.”** That is the sense of the Syriac translation of I Timothy VI.10. Meanwhile hear the margins of C. and M.: By “money” I mean any temporal goods short of rank, honours, and such matters.

**“Of covetousness, Gregory.”** V. inserts between “covetousness” and “Gregory” the words: “By money I mean,” etc., as I collected in the preceding note from the margins; but [Col. 0399D] after “such matters” it adds: “II Book of Sentences,” distinction 42, near the end. But, to state my judgment, V. wrongly transfers this marginal note into the text, because it, like very many others, was added by the scholastics to the side of the text for explanatory purposes, as is clear from the notes on chapter 97, at the words: “Not of grace, but of vanity.”

**“Between these.”** Namely covetousness and avarice, concerning which Horace, *Epistles*, I.1:

> Avarice and wretched desire make the heart boil.

**“He does not distinguish.”** Here V. and C. strongly disagree, reading: “Between these he seems to distinguish, saying,” etc.—but wrongly. For at the beginning of the following chapter the contrary is plainly clear in these words: “Avarice [is] a species of covetousness, although Gregory does not distinguish between species and genus,” etc. Here, however, the three copies agree. Meanwhile, to understand this more easily, consult St Augustine on Psalm CXVIII, discourse 11.

**“On the day you eat.”** After these words, V. adds to the text what the other two place in the margin: “But how, when they had no itching in taste before sin? Perhaps only in the offering of food.” M. has “forgetfulness” for “offering.”

[Col. 0400A]

**“And also of high station.”** C.: “And also of lofty knowledge.” This does not please, because it departs from St Gregory, Homily 16 on the Gospels.

**“Indeed, and any thing whatsoever.”** This is taken from St Augustine, tome I, book III, *On Free Will*, chapter 17. Therefore the same author is cited below at the end of the period: “According to Augustine.” V. differs especially here. First, for “according to” it reads “But Augustine”; and having ended and punctuated the preceding period, it begins the next thus: “But Augustine resolves this difficulty of contradiction: the Gloss on Ecclesiasticus chapter X [otherwise XXXV], whose conclusion is: ‘Let us beware covetousness and pride, which are one evil, from which all evils arise.’” C. likewise has these things in the margin: “Augustine resolves this difficulty and contradiction, the Gloss,” etc., as above. The Gloss is on Ecclesiasticus X, verse [Col. 0400B] 15, and likewise reflects the teaching of St Augustine, tome IX, tractate 8 on I John IV.

**“Likewise the philosopher.”** V. somewhat more fully: “To slay covetousness, what the philosopher says ought to suffice.” *Letter* 16.

**“Let [riches] be heaped upon you.”** This is the genuine reading and Seneca’s as well. But V.: “Let all Croesus’s riches be gathered upon you.” I approve it, because it is a well-known note which M. reads in the margin.

**“So that [you cover] the earth with marble.”** Thus Seneca. The three meanwhile: “And [you cover] the earth,” etc.

**“Art [is] beyond luxury.”** Here *ultra* means “excess.” Seneca, however, reads not *ultra* but *ulla luxuriae*: “any art of luxury.”

**“The road for one going.”** M., from Seneca. The two: “the road for one going.” From *Letter* 16.

**“Blind covetousness.”** Here observe Lipsius’s notes.

**Proverbs, chapter XXX.** M. and C.: chapter LVI. V. omits it. You should know that *Parables* means Solomon’s Proverbs.

**“Of the leech.”** Leeches are scarcely content when their belly is not merely full but swollen. Horace, in the last verse of *The Art of Poetry*:

[Col. 0400C]

> The leech will not release the skin unless full of blood.

**“And while it seeks to satisfy thirst.”** The same author, *Metamorphoses*, III, fable 6. “O insatiable covetousness, whose desire extends to infinity,” as Aristotle says in *Politics* I. Hence Seneca plainly says in *Hercules on Oeta*:

> Here a man desires to fill his hunger with treasures;  
> Yet not every region of gem-bearing Ister is enough,  
> Nor all Lydia satisfies his thirst, nor the land  
> Subject to the west wind, where golden Tagus  
> Gleams in radiant stream;  
> Nor even if the whole River Hebrus served him,  
> And rich Hydaspes enclosed his fields,  
> And, within his own bounds, he saw the Ganges  
> Run in its entire flood.

## CHAPTER XXI

V. begins a new chapter here and prefixes the title [Col. 0400D] “On Avarice,” while the other two continue the preceding chapter.

**“Avarice [as] a species.”** See St Augustine, tome VIII, on Psalm CXVIII, discourse 11.

**Ecclesiasticus, chapter X.** C.: chapter XXXIV. The two have nothing.

**“He holds [it] for sale.”** C. and M. note in the margin: “To the devil in a just cause if he needs [something], and in an unjust cause even if he does not need it.”

**“Envy.”** V. omits it.

**“Active at the farthest limits.”** Horace, *Epistles*, I.1. Wadræus directs a similar epigram against Perus, mentioned in the notes to chapter 11:

> Fortune gives work to him to whom it gives wealth, as those who possess it admit.  
> Whoever seeks wealth through wealth seeks work through work.  
> Seek, Perus: let no one seek [the text is uncertain] through wealth, wealth, or work.  
> Work is sought by a sound mind through labour.

**“Likewise Jerome.”** See him in the letter to Paulinus beginning “Brother Ambrose,” a little before the end.

**“Rather than by what he has.”** The same author after Quintilian, book 7.

[Col. 0401A]

**“Nothing is more sordid.”** It will, I think, be useful here to bring forward Horace, *Satires*, I.1:

> But a good part of mankind, deceived by false desire,  
> Says, “Nothing is enough, because you are worth as much as you possess.”  
> What can you do with such a man? Tell him to be miserable gladly,  
> Since he does so—as a certain rich miser of Athens is remembered to have done—  
> Being accustomed thus to despise the people’s words:  
> “The people hiss, but I applaud myself at home  
> Whenever I clasp my coins in their chest.”

**“Whence Juvenal.”** I have not found in Juvenal, “Sordid down to the ankle”; perhaps it is: “White down to the ankle.”

**“A hundredfold.”** M. and C.: “a hundredfold.”

**“I have and behold them.”** V.: “I have my own [things],” etc.

**“What is kept for me.”** V. alone; but the two have: “Whence without anxiety.”

**“A guardian of what is put before [him].”** M.: “a guardian placed before.”

**“I shall feed upon the sight of it.”** M.: “From the sight I shall feed.”

[Col. 0401B]

**“They have been bestowed upon you.”** Not “placed upon you,” as V.

**“If you wish to lend at interest.”** This refers to Proverbs XIX: “He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord.”

**“Those which you have given alone.”** V. alone.

**“He says in chapter 14.”** M. and C.: 41. The preceding words, namely “rebuking the vice of [381] avarice,” occur only in V.

**“For a covetous and grasping man.”** There is great textual variation here. C. and M. agree thus: “For a covetous and grasping man, without reason, through right and wrong—if you can, rightly; if not, by whatever means [gain] wealth” (Horace, *Epistles*, I.1). The substance, therefore, is: “What use is gold to an envious man?”

**“And not therefore.”** *Therefore* is absent from V. and M.

**David: “He lays up treasure.”** This passage down to “his riches” is omitted in the text. C. and M. have it; but “And they shall leave,” etc., is in the margin.

**“Why does he begrudge himself?”** Down to and including “his own malice,” V. does not read it; in its place it has: “Ecclesiasticus below [chapter XIV]: ‘Even if he does good,’” etc. To these words must be appended the margin of C. and M.: “Because through [Col. 0401C] avarice he cannot bear to spend his possessions on necessary uses.” This is the Gloss on Ecclesiasticus XIV: “He who begrudges himself,” etc.

**“Drying himself up.”** The notes of C. and M. say: “Always thirsty.”

**“Likewise: according to someone.”** Since it is laborious here to compare with one another all the sayings and words arranged in a disordered sequence, I shall note word for word the divergence of V. Thus, first it omits “Likewise: according to someone,” and immediately after the words “drying up his own soul,” it reads: “But this may [be] … An enemy may pray that he may live long, and while living may torment and torture himself by greater desire and envy. The Apostle likewise detests this vice in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter I [otherwise V]: ‘Filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, avarice,’ etc.; concerning whom he says at the end of the same [chapter]: ‘Since those who do such things are worthy of death, not only those who do them but also those who consent to those who do them.’ Gloss: ‘To consent is to be silent when one can rebuke, or to foster error.’ To the Galatians V [otherwise X]:

> But the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, luxury, service of idols, etc.; those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.

He calls avarice everywhere “service of idols.” To the Ephesians V [otherwise 21]: “But let fornication, or all uncleanness, or avarice not even be named among you.” And later in the same [chapter V]: “Every fornicator, or unclean person, or avaricious person—which is service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” To the Colossians III [otherwise VIII]: “Therefore mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence, and avarice, which is the service of images.” Jerome, to the monk Heliodorus [otherwise Rusticus]: “He errs who judges that man an idolater who, through fear or compulsion or perhaps another cause, burns incense to an idol, rather than the man who is devoted to riches, who adores lord Money as God, who renders to a creature the honour due to the Creator.” Hence:

[Col. 0402A]

> O money, money, this man pays you such honour.  
> (*Juvenal*, *Satires* 5)

And elsewhere:

> Queenly money bestows both birth and character.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, I.6)

[382] Hence you have:

> “He does not ask about me, but it is necessary to have [wealth].”

Likewise the Lord in the Gospel, etc.; here V. agrees with the others.

**Augustine also.** Consult book IV of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 4, and the exposition of Psalm XCVI.

**“Jerome to Heliodorus.”** I restored the reference. For the three copies have “to Rusticus”; but the letter to Heliodorus begins “With how great love.” V.’s text certainly reflects the teaching of St Jerome’s letter, but more especially his Commentary on Ephesians V.

**“They produce and foster.”** Therefore certainly not “they destroy,” as C. has.

[Col. 0402B]

**“Riches wrongly acquired.”** V.: “worldly riches.” You have this in St Jerome’s letter to Eustochium, *On the Keeping of Virginity*, chapter 14.

**I Corinthians V.** C.: chapter XXXV; M.: 25.

**“If anyone called a brother.”** “By judicial sentence or a mark of infamy,” say the margins of C. and M. It continues: “Burial, the body of Christ, and the like”—that is, it is not lawful to share in these things, as they silently indicate.

**“Therefore they must be avoided.”** V. omits these words and instead has: “And similarly, such impenitent persons should not be granted common burial at life’s end, as happened to a certain usurer near St Denis. (C. and M. do not have this example in the text, but appropriately in the margin; hence I think it was added by the scholastics as a note. Meanwhile, since V. varies it, I reproduce it thus.) When a priest came to him as he lay dying, bearing the Eucharist, he found him powerless. The man thus signified that a familiar demon was constricting him [Col. 0402C] by the throat and did not permit him to restore what he had stolen, distribute what he had shamefully amassed, confess his sins, or receive the Eucharist. And so the wretch was snatched from this miserable life into misery without end. Yet he was secretly buried by certain monks. When this was discovered, the stinking corpse was removed from the tomb and, as a warning and terror to others, publicly cast back upon the dungheap. Perhaps this appears to happen to all who die impenitent, as to soldiers who confess that they publicly withhold tithes. How then will the Eucharist, or common burial in death, be given to them? In the same [epistle]: ‘Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers shall possess the kingdom of God’ (I Cor. V). In Luke’s Gospel (chapter XII): ‘Beware of all avarice,’ etc.”

**“From what he possesses.”** I restored “from what”; for the three omitted it.

[Col. 0402D]

**“For his possession.”** V. reads thus: “There is some possession; there is loss of grace and glory.” M. and C. note in the margin: “Life does not come from possession, but often its loss.” After “there is loss,” V. adds: “But to him who thus lays up treasure and is not rich toward God, the Lord says: ‘Fool, this night I shall demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose shall they be?’” (Luke XII.) In Proverbs: “He troubles his household,” etc. (Prov. XV).

**“But the man who hastens.”** The preceding words occur in V., but in disordered sequence; the following words [383] down to “Likewise Jerome” are absent.

**Ecclesiastes V.** C. and M.: 12.

**“The avaricious man shall not be filled.”** C. and M. have in the margin, from Claudian the poet, *Against Rufinus*, I:

> … And, lifted too high,  
> He feeds himself on the sight with an avaricious gaze.

Or, more freely, Horace:

> … So that the avaricious man may be freer.

[Col. 0403A]

**“I do not see.”** These words follow the preceding poem only indirectly, because another is inserted.

**Likewise Jerome.** Consult the Commentary on Proverbs XXX.

**“For he is insatiable.”** The margin of C. and M., after Claudian, *Against Rufinus*, I:

> Whoever desires is always poor; Fabricius, content with modest means, despised the gifts of kings.

I add from Horace, *Satires*, II.3:

> What of the miser?  
> A fool and madman. What if someone is not avaricious?  
> At once he is sane.

Why should I not also bring forward Cornelius Gallus, describing an avaricious man no less eloquently? Hear him, Elegy 1:

> What use are riches to me, if you take away their use?  
> Though rich in possessions, I shall always be poor.  
> Indeed, it is a punishment to devote oneself to goods  
> Which, though you possess them, it is forbidden to use.  
> No otherwise does thirsty Tantalus reach for neighbouring waters  
> And hold his mouth back from food set before him.  
> I become more the guardian of my own goods,  
> Preserving for others what has perished for me.

And a little later:

> I toil always to retain what I cannot obtain;  
> And always retaining, I think that I have held nothing.

[Col. 0403B]

**“Likewise the same author.”** Horace, *Epistles*, I.2. And in I.1 he says: “Avarice and miserable covetousness make the heart boil.”

**“Likewise the same author: ‘When.’”** Here understand that St Jerome is cited, Commentary on Proverbs XXX and book I *Against Jovinian*, chapter 15.

**“Why [do you cut] sinews?”** V.: “Why [do you cut] coins?” This verse is out of order. See Claudian.

**“Generosity.”** Absent from V.’s text.

**“Avarice accompanies [it].”** Seneca affirms in *On Benefits*, IV.27: “We do not free even the prodigal from avarice.” And St Jerome, in the Rule for Monks, under “On Poverty,” says: “And after they have attained this”—namely riches—“you see them give themselves over to luxury, pleasures, and every iniquity, so that what avarice gathers, luxury consumes.”

**“The poet Claudian.”** *On the War against Gildo.*

**“How then are they opposites?”** M., in the margin, has “common” for “opposites.”

**“Likewise Genesis XXXI.”** V. otherwise: “Likewise, to condemn avarice, as Jerome says, is useful the history in Genesis concerning Jacob: how he fled from Laban’s presence with wives, children, and many possessions. Among these Rachel had stolen her father’s golden and silver idols. When her father pursued them and searched, Rachel hid them in dung and under the camels’ bedding; pretending to be menstruating, she sat upon them, and thus, not rising before her father while he searched for his gods, deceived him. Later, when Jacob and Laban had made a covenant, Jacob, by the Lord’s command, ordered the strange gods to be cast away, and hid Laban’s idols—that is, the golden ones—with all their phylacteries under the terebinth tree” (Gen. XXXV).

[Col. 0403D]

By Laban is meant the world; by the idols, avarice; by Rachel, whose name means “sheep,” the gently repentant person, who hides idols—that is, avarice—under dung, but does not wholly abandon them; rather, she sits upon them, according to Horace (*Epistles*, I.1):

> I strive to make things subject to me, not myself subject to things.

Jacob is the wrestler, who hides avarice and its appendages beneath the fragrant terebinth with its phylacteries and appendages—that is, beneath the wood of the Lord’s cross—according to the Apostle: “I have counted all things as dung, that I might gain Christ and follow naked the naked Crucified One” (Phil. III).

Agatha and Agnes did likewise, rejecting for the Crucified One gifts offered by their lovers. The Lord likewise condemned this vice in the Gospel: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me, because he sought nothing worldly, nothing transient between us” (John XIV). Joseph likewise detested [Col. 0404A] the vice of avarice. When he was drawn by the cloak by the Egyptian harlot—that is, worldly desire—he did not wait until she broke or tore off a fragment, but immediately fled, leaving cloak and fragments behind, according to the Apostle: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from all things” (I Cor. IX). Likewise the young man who left behind his linen cloth and fled naked. Likewise Jerome: “To rebuke avarice, the history in Exodus, chapter XXXII, concerning the molten golden calf ought to suffice: Moses burned and crushed it, scattered its powder in water, and gave it to the children of Israel to drink, that they might thus detest idolatry, signified by avarice, as the end [read: dung] of the vilest excrement.” Likewise the example of a pagan should move us, cited by Jerome, Causa 12, Question 2: “The glory of a bishop [otherwise: of Christ] is to provide for all the poor.” Concerning Socrates [Note: “Concerning Crates of Thebes, not Socrates,” as St Jerome has it in his letter to Paulinus, *On the Instruction of a Monk*.] who, when he was going to Athens to study philosophy and to unlearn [otherwise: learn] the vice of avarice, [Col. 0404B] threw away a great weight of gold, believing that he could not possess riches and virtues at the same time.

Diogenes likewise applies: as empty of hope as he was free of fear, he passed through a secure poverty, content with a tub. When Aristippus, courtier of a certain prince, saw him washing vegetables, he is said to have told him: “If you had trusted me, you would not now be washing vegetables, but would remain at the court of the highest prince.” Diogenes replied: “If you had trusted me, you would not be a flatterer and toady at a prince’s court.” This man too, when he saw someone drinking with his hand at a spring, said: “I did not know that nature had given me a cup.” Immediately he smashed upon a stone the small cup from which he used to drink. These things are from the Vedastine manuscript codex.

**“Rachel fleeing.”** St Gregory explains this history in *Morals*, book XXX, chapter 16. I have not seen whether St Jerome explained it anywhere, though V. confidently asserts this. Caesarius, book IV, chapter 57 of his *History*, applies these matters to the avarice of religious persons.

[Col. 0404C]

**“When uncleanness.”** I have found a double “G.” in C. I think it means Gregory: “When uncleanness,” etc. I cited the passage in the preceding note.

**“I strive to make [things] subject.”** V. and M.: “I strive to make [myself] subject”; but Horace, whose verse it is, has *submittere*, “to subject.” *Epistles*, I.1, at the beginning.

**“A fragment.”** By no means “licentiousness,” as M. and C. have.

**“Worldly pleasure.”** C.: “will.”

**“Dung of the most unclean.”** M. and V.: “end” for “dung.”

**“Likewise Jerome.”** After Laertius, in the letter to Paulinus *On the Instruction of a Monk*, beginning “A good man.” He recounts the same things in book II *Against Jovinian*, chapter 7, and in the letter to Julian, “My son.” See further Causa 12, Question 2: “The glory of a bishop.”

**“Loaded with gold.”** St Jerome’s text: “Overloaded with gold.”

**“Diogenes in the tub.”** On this, see the same author, tome II, *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 9. The margins of C. and M. note: “He hoped for no one’s favour and feared no worldly person.”

[Col. 0404D]

**“When he cleaned and washed [vegetables].”** M.: “When he commended and praised his vegetables.” This does not agree with what Valerius Maximus writes, book IV, chapter 3, at the end.

**“You would not wash.”** M. consequently reads: “You would not praise.”

**“He who identifies me.”** C., in the lower margin, has: “He who calls me [by name], you are Diogenes.” But in the side margin at the beginning of the following chapter it retracts this thus: “He who identifies me, that is, Diogenes.”

## CHAPTER XXII

**“Not only by examples.”** V. begins this chapter differently; it breaks off in the middle at the Scriptural passages, but abounds in examples, one of which C. and M. restore in their margins. I shall now transcribe from V. as far as it agrees with the others; afterward I shall reproduce the notes of C. and M. deferred here.

Thus V. reads for the title: “Against the Acceptance of Gifts.” It begins: “Having set forth examples of pagans who condemn avarice, examples of the elders of the Old and New Testament, who likewise denounce it, must be presented. In Genesis, chapter XIV: [376] When the king of Sodom offered gifts to Abraham returning from his victory over the enemy—that is, the five kings who had laid waste Lot’s homeland—Abraham answered: ‘I lift up my hand to God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, that from a thread of the warp even to a sandal-strap I shall take nothing of all that is yours, lest you say: “I have enriched Abraham.”’ For the king said to him: ‘Give me the persons; take the rest for yourself.’” (These things are absent from C. and M.)

St Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, likewise condemned this vice. When he had given the chancellorship to someone, he forbade him to sell an image or accept even a secret object or little knife, lest gold or silver should be mixed into the handle under any pretext [otherwise: *protextu*, “covering”]. Note, however, that those who receive gifts are made reprobate; this is evident from Ephron, whose name was changed as a sign of spiritual [Col. 0405B] transformation, because he accepted money from Abraham for his field in which Sarah was to be buried, although under compulsion. Abraham did not wish to receive the field for free; and in this deed Abraham is excused and Ephron accused (Gen. XXIII). But if I compelled a moneylender or simoniac to accept [add: money], when he wished to give me a church benefice or a loan for free, would I sin more than he, or he than I? Thus Abraham appears to have sinned more than Ephron. Yet Abraham is excused by the saints; but Ephron’s name was changed because he accepted a gift, and he was called Ephrem. The rest is found in the other two, but in a disordered sequence. I return to the deferred notes.

**“Acceptance of gifts.”** C.: “acceptance of coins.” This does not please, because it limits “acceptance,” which should be understood of any gift, present, or thing of monetary value.

**“The king of Sodom.”** In the margin of C. and M.: Genesis XXII. C. adds at the end: “Today, Genesis XIV.”

[Col. 0405C]

**“Take the rest for yourself.”** The margins of C. and M.: “All the spoils except the people. See the Gloss at this place.”

**“Except those things which.”** Hear what I saw there: “He could renounce his own right and share, but not those of his companions.”

**Likewise Genesis XXIII.** C. and M.: Genesis XLIII.

**“Abraham weighed out the money.”** To this I add what I found in the margins of C. and M.: “But if I compelled a simoniac or moneylender to accept money when he wished to give me a church benefice or a loan freely, would I sin more than he or he than I? Thus Abram appears to have sinned more than Ephron. Yet Abram is excused by the saints; but Ephron’s name was changed because he accepted a gift and he was called Effrem—better, Ephrem.”

**Likewise Genesis XXXIII.** C. and M. in the margin: Genesis LVIII.

**“As though I saw the face of God.”** The aforesaid margins read here: “Because he feared him greatly.”

**“With devout intention.”** The same margins have: “So also for constructing the Temple.”

[Col. 0405D]

**Likewise Numbers, chapter XVI.** M. and C.: XLI.

**387. “To give you.”** The biblical text: “I shall give you.”

**“Balak offering.”** C. and M.: “Balak present and offering.” I restored the reading from the biblical text.

**“Yet, going on.”** Opposite this, I found in the margin of C. and M., and place it here: “They are like Balak, who give certain gifts so that others may bless or curse; their blessing is changed into a curse, and conversely.” Another marginal note follows on the immediately following words: “By conferring a spiritual benefit.” Likewise, on the same words, “I shall give you counsel,” I read what the Gloss has at this place: “Also by giving them beautiful women”—that is, to the children of Israel. Hence the saying from Revelation immediately follows.

**“In Revelation.”** M. and C. note chapter IX; today II.

**I Kings XII.** C. and M.: chapter LXXIII.

**“Speak concerning me.”** The aforesaid margins say: [Col. 0406A] “By excusing me, if I have failed or committed anything wrong.”

**“Namely Saul.”** M. alone reads this.

**“And I shall despise it.”** M., between the lines: “That is, I shall restore it.”

**“Likewise by David’s example, II Kings.”** These words are absent in C. down to: “Likewise by David’s example, III Kings XIII.”

**“Freewill burnt offerings.”** After these words, M. proposes a doubt in the margin and resolves it: “It is asked why Ephron is accused for taking a price (Gen. XXIII), selling a burial-place—that is, a place assigned for burials, where Adam and Eve were buried—and not Ornan the Jebusite, selling the place where a house was to be built for the Lord (I Chron. XXI). Answer: Because Ephron sold a burial-place, namely a place appointed for tombs, where Adam and Eve were buried.”

**“Likewise by the example of the prophet Addo.”** I restored *Addo* in place of David from M.

**“Nor shall I drink water.”** The genuine Scriptural reading. Therefore I greatly wonder why C. omitted “water” and why M. struck it out with a line and mutilated it with an obelus.

[Col. 0406B]

**II Esdras V.** M. and C.: II Esdras XXI. M. adds in the margin “Nehemiah”—correctly. For there he assembles “a great assembly,” in his own words, against them.

**Likewise Acts of the Apostles XX.** M.: chapter XLVIII; C.: the last chapter. In calling it the last, C. is mistaken.

**Epistle of Jude.** The two: chapter II.

**II Corinthians XI.** The two: II Corinthians XXV.

**“I preached the Gospel without charge.”** The two margins: “Although I could have received wages, because ‘the labourer is worthy of his hire’” (Luke X).

**“Boasting.”** The two have “glorification”; but V. is better, and thus: “boasting,” adding: “of not receiving,” which I also restored to the text; it reflects the Gloss at this place.

**“An opportunity to preach to them.”** The margins of C. and M. seem to express this: “On account of the curious, and for other reasons.”

**Ezekiel, chapter XXII.** M. and C.: chapter LIII.

Over your avarice.] The aforesaid marginal notes explain it thus [Col. 0406C]: “Of the priests,” as though: “I can scarcely believe such great avarice on your part; but I shall go down and see whether they have carried it out in deed.”

Acts of the Apostles XX.] C. and M.: XLII.

Up to the *canipulum*.] A *canipulus*, as though *canicapulus*, is a sword, dagger, or knife, bearing on its hilt the figure of a dog’s head. Hence the French *bracquemar*, which takes its name from the appearance of a dog. C. read: “Up to the *clipunum*”; M., *clinipulum*. In French we call such a little knife a *canivet*. Cantipratanus uses this word in *The Book of Bees*, book I, ch. 16, no. 2, and book II, ch. 29, no. 21.

Ecclesiasticus XX. Gifts.] M. and C.: Ecclesiasticus LVII.

And like a mute man.] It is useful here to consult the Gloss.

Their reproofs.] C.: “corrections.” But the former reading agrees with the scriptural text.

They fall silent.] I do not reject this altogether. C.: “They become silent.”

Likewise Isaiah.] C. notes chapter XCIV; M., XCIII.

[Col. 0406D] Note the word “shakes out.”] V. is lacking as far as “Likewise Strabus.”

But a small thing.] Margin of M.: “Such as a ring and the like.”

It is a little frog.] The same is to be seen in Ecclesiasticus chapter XX, at the words: “And like a mute man.”

But if they have seen him beforehand.] Thus St. Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book VI, ch. 4. The common saying, derived from this resemblance, is “the wolf in the tale,” when unexpectedly a third person arrives and stands beside two who are speaking ill of him. They immediately fall silent, or turn their conversation to whatever first comes into their mouths, in order to deceive the third person by this cover, unwilling to expose themselves as detractors or as thinking ill of him.

Likewise Job XV.] M. and C.: XIV. No wonder, since formerly Job had fewer chapters than it has today.

Likewise IV Kings V.] M. and C.: chapter LXVII. Our old Bibles read chapter XXIV. This chapter contains only four lines. It begins: “Now therefore you have received,” etc. [Col. 0407A] It ends, inclusively: “Leprous as snow.”

May you receive a blessing.] M. adds between the lines above “blessing”: namely, “a gift.” C., in the margin: “His gift.”

As the Lord lives.] He was, as it were, compelled by necessity to swear, so that by his oath he might more emphatically execrate avarice. Thus M. and C. in the margin; V. in the text.

He wrapped his head in wool.] Two marginal notes: “Pretending to be ill.” These remarks about Demosthenes are absent from V.

For *synanche*.] The Latins refer to this ailment by other names, calling it *angina* and *argentangina*.

But those are said to suffer from *argyranche*, or *argentangina*, who have been made mute by money and suppress those things which they know to be in the public interest.

By the example of Cyriacus.] I refer the reader to the *Life of St. Marcellus, Pope*, where this example occurs; Surius, vol. I.

Of Sapor, king of the Persians.] M. and C.: “of Sapon.”

389 Nor is a matron chaste.] This saying of [Col. 0407B] St. Jerome is absent from V., together with what follows down to “Likewise Jerome, writing.” On this word “chaste,” the margins say: “She is chaste whom no one has asked.”

The signs are corrupt.] See II, question 3, *Pauper*, and *Qui rector*.

Likewise Jeremiah chapter VI.] M. and C.: chapter XXV.

From prophet onward.] C., in the margin: “From the sole of the foot,” etc., Isaiah I.

Likewise Exodus XXIII.] Two copies read the same: LXXXI.

Concerning a certain orator.] Something similar is read in Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book V, ch. 10.

To a wealthy matron.] C.: “To the wealthy in common.”

On ingratitude.] The two margins likewise say: “Roman laws punished the ungrateful.” This is clear from Valerius Maximus, book V, ch. 3.

The intimacy of princes.] C.: “the reputation of princes.”

Of begging, intimacy.] Again C., in the margin: “acquiring the reputation of the powerful” [Col. 0407C].

## CHAPTER XXIII

V. gives another title: “Against the manifold acceptance of gifts, especially by spiritual judges.”

Accepted for an unjust cause.] Thus C. Two other copies: “accepted when no impending cause exists.”

Yet dangerous.] M.: “yet destructive.”

Without payment.] C. read *circa* (“about”), but this was corrected to *contra* (“against”). Neither pleases me.

When someone worthy proposes.] V.: “When, with others, he has worthily proposed to give an ecclesiastical benefice, it is an even greater cruelty,” etc.

Even for pious causes.] Because a good use does not justify what has been wrongly acquired. 14, question 5, *Neque enim*.

Granges.] This is the French word *granges*. Caesarius says that these are estates, villages, and so forth.

Done for justice.] Note the variation. I have taken from V. and [Col. 0407D] C. the reading restored in the text. M.: “done and omitted for justice,” or “for injustice to be committed.”

These are not shepherds.] V. and C. continue the period: “who are not shepherds,” etc.

But shearers.] C. once read: “but torturers.” Shame upon such men: no longer shepherds, but wolves.

Flayers.] That great emperor Tiberius used to say: “It is the part of a good shepherd to shear, not to skin.”

In the first book of Kings XXV.] M.: XLI.

As though about to take vengeance upon him.] C. incorrectly: “about to judge him.”

Go in peace.] C.: “Go in peace.”

They are pluckers.] In the margins of M. and C.: “You shall not shear,” etc., Deuteronomy chapter XV.

390 Venal through pandering.] In C., “venal” is absent. Around this I note marginal remarks touching the judges themselves: “Judges ought to be moderate—not gods, not men, nor [Col. 0408A] ‘conco’ [uncertain], just as the mass of affairs does not permit the wealthy to be moderately good or bad. Therefore let them be perfect, and:

> Among Socratics the pit is very well known to the catamites.”

“That is, of avarice,” says M. between the lines.

Those, namely, who—and because.] I was unwilling to omit the causal conjunction “and because,” even though M. and V. omit it; for it has force.

Daily plunder.] “Daily bread” (M. in the margin): supply, “they devour.”

So that they swallow up simple Christians.] V.: “by daily plunder they swallow up simple Christians.”

Existing.] V. and C.: *entes*, as I have already noted above.

With Aod.] Three copies: “with Aioth.”

Through avarice.] C.: “for avarice.”

But his left hand.] This, down to “who do not have,” is absent from V.

With lambs on the right.] C.: “with right-hand lambs.”

[Col. 0408B] Zechariah V.] M. and C.: VIII. From here to “Therefore Jerome: ‘A judge,’” etc., is absent from V.

He cast a mass of lead.] “Every avaricious man is impious”; as though to say: “You thirsted for gold; drink gold.” Thus M. and C. as a note.

Now truly golden.] From Propertius, book III, elegy 11. I append the preceding verse:

> Now, with piety conquered, all worship gold.

Honor comes.] Lest it be unwelcome if I add from the same source verses following and bearing upon the subject:

> … Love is won by gold.  
> By gold faith is driven out; by gold laws are for sale;  
> Law follows gold, and soon modesty is without law.

Likewise Arator.] The Venerable Bede used this author’s authority in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter IV, 5, and elsewhere. C., instead of Arator, reads Aratus, but wrongly, because they are different persons.

Where may the avaricious man halt?] The margins of C. [Col. 0408C] and M. say: “An avaricious judge is like a schoolmaster loudly threatening children until they offer him a small present. When he sees it, he lowers his voice and threatens them more gently. Although he first rejects the gift verbally, he afterwards receives it as though unwillingly, remits his anger, and leaves the children unpunished.”

The angel of the guardian.] “Like Laban’s idols.” Two margins, from Genesis XXXI.

Therefore Jerome.] This saying resembles his exposition of Proverbs XI; but the copies vary greatly here. For C. and M. omit the negation *non* in: “A judge ought not to be,” etc.

Less justly.] “That is, unjustly,” says M. between the lines.

Therefore Solomon.] C. at the side: Proverbs XXV; M.: XXXV.

391 And by appendages.] The appendages of a judgment are a grave brow, delay of the case, provision of an advocate, and the like. Margins of C. and M.

[Col. 0408D] Likewise Deuteronomy, chapter XXV.] Two copies: chapter XXXVI.

Augustine says.] Gregory, however, has almost the same things in *Morals*, book IX, ch. 17, in the middle. See further I, question I, *Sunt nulli*. V. omits “Augustine” in the text.

Having pity on him.] V. and M.: “merciful toward him.”

He strikes the heart.] C.: “he strikes the breast.”

They hate him.] After these words V. had: “Likewise in Proverbs: ‘Neither a just judge nor a judge recognizing.’” But because that sentence made no sense, I restored it to the notes as I had found it in the margins of C. and M. It reads: “A just judge, neither seeing nor recognizing”; or, more correctly, V. in the upper margin: “A judge—not seeing a gift nor recognizing a person—is just.” Rightly so, that justice may be blind.

Jeremiah XLVIII.] M. and C.: 57.

Gregory: “For.”] For brevity’s sake, reader, I refer you to *Morals*, book IX, ch. 17, where gifts are fully distinguished, as also by St. Jerome, vol. VII, on Psalm XXV, at: “Their right hand is full of gifts.”

[Col. 0409A] So that he cannot discern the truth.] Thus Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, book I: “Love, hatred, and personal advantage often cause a judge not to recognize the truth.”

Likewise Exodus XVIII.] Two copies: XXXIII. These and what follows down to “Likewise in Sallust, Cato,” are absent in V.

A multitude of affairs.] Margins: “Even useful and honorable affairs.” For Juvenal, *Satires* 6:

> A wise man sets a limit even to honorable affairs.

Noble men.] “For the very terror inspired by the rich claims honor for itself,” says St. Benedict, *Rule*, ch. LIII. In the margins of C. and M. I saw: Deuteronomy II. For there the same thing is repeated. I noted the place in the text.

Oil is added to the furnace.] This is a proverb used by Horace, *Satires*, book II, satire 3, at the end. It means supplying encouragement and fuel to an evil so that it grows more and more. Jerome also uses it in his letter to Eustochium: “Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure. Why do we add oil to the flame?”

[Col. 0409B] And deans.] The avarice of prelates has brought it about that one priest is now set over only a few, to judge among them. Thus the two margins.

Hear them.] Namely, the people. C. between the lines of the text.

Distinction of persons.] “Partiality.” Margins.

You shall hear the small.] The same margins: “The poor man”; as “the great”: “the rich man.”

Deuteronomy chapter XVI: C., LXXIV; M., LXXII.

Immovable.] The interlinear Gloss has this. But the margins ask: “Why then, through avarice, are leaseholders, who are to be removed every year, placed over the people?”

In all your gates.] That is, in every one, as M. gives between the lines. But again the question: 392 “Why then does one man usurp for himself two bishoprics and the judgment of two cities, so that, blind himself, he may through avarice swallow the sea?” Let such men be moved by Caesarius’s remarkable examples, book II, chs. 28–29 and the following chapters.

With just judgment.] “Of the divine law,” C. between the lines; M., however, “according to the order of the law.”

[Col. 0409C] You shall turn aside neither part.] Namely, through prayer or price, private affection or hatred. C. at the side; M. between the lines.

They blind the eyes.] M. there: “They turn authority aside.” This comes from St. Ambrose, on II Corinthians, chapter VIII, near the beginning. For there: “They bend the force of authority.”

Of the wise.] Namely, wise in the world, not in God. C. in the margin; M. between the lines.

The words of the just.] “Formerly,” says M. there.

You shall pursue.] Bible of St. [uncertain]: “You shall persecute.” C.: “you shall execute.” On this the margins say: “Neither through entreaty, nor price, nor more harshly than is fair, nor more leniently.”

In Sallust, Cato.] You will see the same in Cicero, *On the Orator*, and St. Anselm, *On the Likeness of the World*. The latter says: “Judgment is perverted in four ways: by fear, greed, hatred, and love.”

Cicero in *On Duties*.] Book III, before the middle.

And not to grant.] C.: “and not yet to grant”; M. adds: “truly.”

[Col. 0409D] These things belong to friendship.] Thus Cicero. C.: “Or to friendship.”

For he lays aside the person.] Cicero: “He puts on,” etc. V.: “For he lays aside the person of a friend, because he puts on the person of a judge.”

And for the soliciting of a suit.] Cicero: “Time for pleading the case.” C. has this, but in an inverted order: “for the pleading of a case as to time,” although he adapts it to the law.

I do not know you.] Here V. is silent down to: “Likewise: Hear this word.”

Likewise Amos.] Margins: chapter XIX.

Into wormwood.] Margins: “into bitterness.”

And the devastator, or.] C. omits these three words.

He brings it upon the powerful.] “He has stretched out his hand in repaying, and they shall repay abundantly those who do [so] above.” Margins from Psalm XXX.

They have utterly abominated.] Margins: “Of such a man it was said: when he rebuked the vicious, he made a satire, not a sermon.”

Just and unjust enemies.] A recent hand wrote [Col. 0410A] in C.: “unjust and unjust enemies.”

Judgment in the gate.] The margins supply: “just.” For judgment is nothing unless it is just. “If we are unfair to ourselves, let us at least be fair to our neighbors. Judge justly, O sons of men.” This “justly” is an interlinear Gloss in Leviticus chapter IX.

Who crush.] In the Bibles, concerning unjust men: “Who crush.”

Having taken pledges.] M.: *pigneratis*.

Likewise the same, chapter III.] Two copies: XII.

The same, chapter IV.] The same copies: XV.

Fat cows.] Margins: “By the feminine gender he expresses their effeminacy and wantonness.”

393 Who are on the mountain.] C.: “Who are effeminate on Mount Samaria.”

Of Samaria.] M. between the lines: “That is, of pride.”

To your officials.] In the Bibles: “To your lords.”

And we shall drink.] “From plunder taken from the poor.” Margins.

[Col. 0410B] Into Arnon.] C.: Vernon; M.: Ernon. C. and M. between the lines: “That is, into exile.” From this point V. is deficient down to “Likewise Amos.”

Likewise the same, chapter VI.] C.: 25.

Heads of the people.] C.: “philosophers.”

In Chalanne.] Two copies: “in Calagne.”

Criminal.] C.: “crimes.”

Among idolaters.] I note that in nearly all manuscripts *idolaters* should be corrected wherever it appears.

Likewise Joel chapter III.] Two copies: IX.

Into a brothel.] In the Bibles: “into a brothel.”

Destroying.] The interlinear Gloss is V.: “caressing.”

Likewise Hosea.] M.: II; today IV.

Forgetful of the law.] Two copies: “having forgotten.”

Offerings for sins.] This is an interlinear Gloss chiefly directed toward priests.

Likewise the same: Hear.] Two copies, both in text and margin: chapter 14.

And the king’s house, hear.] So that no one may be excepted. Margins.

[Col. 0410C] And a net spread out.] Or “extended,” as C.

Upon Tabor.] “The mountain,” says M. between the lines.

Likewise Amos.] Two copies at the side: chapter XXVII.

Into nothing.] C.: “You rejoice in nothing.”

Who say.] C. and M.: “What do you say?”

In strength.] Margins of C. and M.: “In nobility of birth and power.”

For ourselves horns.] Again V. is deficient down to that passage of Micah VI: “Shall I justify?”

Likewise Hosea: If you commit fornication.] M. and C. note chapter XIII in the margin.

Likewise Malachi.] Two copies: II. For brevity, I refer the reader to the Gloss on these passages of Holy Scripture.

Is not that evil in me?] C.: “evil is in me.”

I have no will.] M.: “There is no will except in these things.”

But I blew it away.] The biblical text of Malachi I reads otherwise.

Likewise the same, chapter 2.] C.: chapter 4; M.: 3.

[Col. 0410D] And the right shoulder.] Perhaps, as the Gloss has it, that is, the right shoulder of the animal.

The altar of the Lord with tears.] Not tears of penitence, but tears of stolen money, acquired by the tears of the poor. Thus the two margins.

Likewise Micah II.] M.: VII; C.: VI.

394 In the morning light.] That is: “In the morning you carry out what you discussed in words during the night.” Consult the interlinear Gloss at this place.

The hand is against God.] C.: “a contrary comparison,” but awkwardly; therefore M. better reads: “a contrary action, namely against God,” and this is taken from the interlinear Gloss.

Likewise the same: Is it not?] C. in the text and M. in the margin: chapter 7.

He has risen up as an enemy.] Two margins: “He has risen against me with my adversaries”; C.: “his adversaries.”

You have taken away my praise.] “Since through you my name [Col. 0411A] is continually blasphemed.” Marginal notes from Isaiah chapter LII.

Likewise chapter 3: Hear.] Two copies: chapter 9. “Hear, namely, you bishops, priests, and deacons,” say the same notes.

You strip off their skins.] “That is, their outward parts,” says C.’s margin; this is an interlinear Gloss. But M., in inverse order, reads the Gloss in the text—“that is, their outward parts”—and the text between the lines, namely “their skins.” It follows there: “And their flesh,” that is, “their inward parts,” C. there.

In the midst of the pot.] Margins: “Thus they afflict the wretched people in the Church.”

Likewise the same: Thus says the Lord.] C. and M.: chapter IX, today III.

They sanctify over him.] By their authority, because they affirm and command sacred things. Side margins of C. and M.

Likewise the same: Hear.] Two copies note chapter 2, today 3.

Because you build.] Biblical text: “Who build.”

[Col. 0411B] With bloods.] Margins add: “Of sin and carnal affection.”

Is he in our midst?] As though to say: “Because we have authority to bind and loose and to confer the sacraments.” Thus the margins.

Likewise chapter 6: Hear.] Two copies: chapter 17.

And who shall approve?] C.: “shall call.”

There is still fire.] M. between the lines: “Of concupiscence and pride.”

A smaller measure.] Two copies: “The vengeance of God,” for “measure,” etc.

Likewise chapter 7.] Two copies: 18.

There is no upright man among men.] “Through avarice and lust,” say two copies.

They lie in wait for blood.] “So that by fraud and sin they may compel their subjects to give to them.” Thus the two margins.

The judge is in giving.] The same notes: “They will defend one another by mutual favor, services, and remissions; for as they wish to be judged by [Col. 0411C] others, so they judge others.”

Amos chapter VIII.] Three copies: XXXII.

Malachi chapter II.] Three copies: IV.

To the Laodiceans chapter I.] V.: 3; C.: 4. “This epistle,” says Bellarmine, “is rejected among the apocrypha.” *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. It may be seen in book II of Sixtus of Siena’s *Sacred Library*, under the entry “Paul the Apostle,” and elsewhere.

395 ## CHAPTER XXIV

Little charms, doors.] Three copies have *hostia* (“victim”), incorrectly.

Fishers for money.] “Reapers—indeed, razors—of the purses of the poor.” C. at the side.

I Kings chapter II.] C.: chapter VI. Two copies omit the number.

There are three kinds of officials.] Three copies have this in the margins: “An official, confessor, collector, or—V. omits ‘or’—torturer, provost.” I scarcely dared write the word “torturer,” because it sounds ill and discordant among a bishop’s [Col. 0411D] subjects; hence today he is called a “promoter,” which sounds sweeter. On officials, ecclesiastical as well as secular, see what St. Augustine says, vol. II, letter 54 to Macedonius, near the end.

Confessor.] This is the penitentiary.

By right and wrong alike.] Not so today, at least in our Belgium.

Rural provost.] This is the dean of Christendom.

Rare consultation.] C.: “Rarely consultation.” Yet, as the two margins say, “In healing, the disclosure of diseases is necessary, so that they may be cured.” Thus Hippocrates: “A disease is not cured unless known.”

The purses of the poor.] V. alone adds “of the poor.”

Of money, of plunder.] The word “money” is absent in V. and M.

Of his own money.] V.: “of his own substance.”

To profit from everywhere.] C., at the side, thought that “for each person” should be read instead of “from everywhere.”

He began to curse himself.] Namely, to utter curses in rage [Col. 0412A] and to take devotion away from the saints. Hence Proverbs XX: “It is ruin to a man to curse saints.” C. wrongly: “to denounce.”

Over every sinner.] Trembling, I wrote this example in the text, fearing that certain scoundrels might turn it against the episcopal officials of our own time, although all these things are said of evil ministers. M.: “against every sinner.”

King Cyrus killed.] I restored this from the end of Daniel chapter XIV. For V. has “King Darius”; C. and M., “King Nebuchadnezzar.”

Augustine: Crime.] Consider the passage and it will be useful: vol. X, appendix, sermon 3 among the miscellaneous sermons, at the end.

Likewise Jerome.] Nor have I dared here to accuse the author of an error. Meanwhile I shall say that I have not yet read this saying in St. Jerome, but in St. Augustine at the place cited in the immediately preceding note, and in the Venerable Bede on Luke chapter III.

[Col. 0412B] A robber ranges abroad.] Here V. is silent down to: “Likewise—and what is more execrable.”

His payment.] M.: “his food,” as in Matthew X.

Through a vicar.] What is this in M.: *Privicarnium*?

The Jerichontine anathema.] M.: “The Jerichontine anathemas.”

In Joshua, chapter VI.] Two copies: chapter XIII.

396 On account of Achan.] Not on account of Achor, as M. and C. have it. For Achor is the name of a valley, Joshua VII.

It is spiritual.] M.: “It is special.” It makes no sense. Therefore, to sell absolution, since it is something spiritual, is simony. The same must be said concerning the administration of sacraments, as is clear from I, question 1, *Nullus episcopus*, and *Quidquid invisibilis*.

As a monetary penalty.] Or fine. M.: “as a penalty for sin.”

As regards the imposition of a penalty.] For it is simony to demand something for absolution from excommunication as though it were the price of absolution, but not as though it were a penalty [Col. 0412C] or fine for guilt. Thus St. Thomas judges, II–II, question 110, articles 2 and 3.

To some commune.] That is, community.

Which today is openly for sale.] “This evil,” says St. Augustine, “has grown so deep-rooted that laws are now, as it were by custom, sold, rights are corrupted, judgment itself is for sale, and no case can now exist without a cause [i.e. a payment]?” Vol. X, appendix, *Miscellaneous Sermons*, sermon 3, after the middle. Caesarius, almost our author’s contemporary, confirms this with many examples. Moreover Peter of Blois, detesting such things, cries out: “The office of officials today is to confuse laws, rescind settlements, suppress truth, pursue profit, sell equity,” etc. Do you seek more? See St. Bernard, sermon 6 on Psalm *Qui habitat*, where he says: “Even the offices of ecclesiastical dignity have passed into shameful profit and a business of darkness; in them the salvation of souls is not sought, but the luxury of riches. For this reason they are tonsured; for this reason they frequent churches, celebrate Masses, chant psalms. For bishoprics, archdeaconries, and abbeys men contend shamelessly today, so that the revenues of churches may be dissipated on superfluity and vanity.” These are his words on the venality of the administration of ecclesiastical offices in his time.

Fear of the archdeacon.] Truly, if I had not foreseen that the vices of predecessors reported here would serve as a warning to posterity, I should have passed over in silence what I found in the side margins of C. and M. beside the word “archdeacon.” What are they? Hear: “Bearing discord in the Church, not peace.”

The water ordeal.] Today no one is condemned to the water ordeal in a monetary case, because many other means have arisen for demanding and extorting money. The following remarks seem, however, to refer to the ordeal of casting into water, which belongs to the vulgar ordeal. This has been condemned and prohibited by canon law, because God is tested therein: II, question 5, chapter [Col. 0413A] *Mennam*; chapter *Consuluisti*; chapter *Monomachiam*; and in the Decretals, title *On the Vulgar Ordeal*, chapter *Dilecti filii*, of Honorius III.

I shall undergo the ordeal.] M. omits certain words here. It therefore says: “But I shall undergo the ordeal, and, if found just, I shall give the poor fifty solidi”—which would have been demanded for the blessing of the water—“for food.” He was mocked by all, including the collector of the palace.

397 Five solidi from a priest.] “As though under the pretext of religious punishment for crimes,” say the two margins, “whereas this is done in order to squeeze purses dry.”

From greed.] M. omits this.

Priests of Baal.] Not Balak, as C. has it.

They will conceal nothing.] M. does not read this.

They have delayed the summons.] M.: “They have delayed the provocation.” This is a minor corruption.

Since this Church.] M. and C.: “since this, for the greater part, [is] Church,” etc. *Pro* is placed in the wrong position.

[Col. 0413B] Is such an oath valid?] “I,” says C. at the side, “would neither swear nor keep an oath of this kind if I had made it; rather, I would annul it, since it is indiscreet, hostile to peace, and against God.”

At these little doors.] M., omitting these words, says: “Likewise: Certain canons,” etc.

In the second or third degree.] This occurs in *Extra*, *On Consanguinity and Affinity*, chapter *Non debet irreprehensibile*. The Council of Trent, session 24, chapter 4, *On the Reform of Marriage*, limited the impediment of affinity arising from illicit intercourse to the first and second degree only, decreeing that marriages contracted thereafter in other degrees should not be dissolved.

At our own pleasure.] Yet by means of that money. Therefore do dispensations obey money in this way?

Two-headed Decree.] See 30, question 4, *Qui spiritualem*.

Likewise: these little doors.] Here V. is silent down to: “These are flies.”

They are divers.] The Gloss on Leviticus chapter XI says: “The diver is a bird with a long neck, drawing food or prey from the depth of earth or water; it is not to be imitated,” etc.

It is forbidden in the law.] Leviticus XI. On the hawk, hear the two margins:

> The *nisus* and the hawk, for whom predation is life,  
> cause the common multitude of the other birds to spend their lives [sense uncertain].

The *nisus* is also called *haliaeetus*, as in Leviticus XI. See the story of King Nisus in the eighth book of the *Metamorphoses*.

Into the nets of others.] Namely, into the purses of the lords whose officials they are.

If we have sown.] M. varies thus: “If we have sown, namely, sowing is the cause of our harvest,” as though this sowing claims that harvest as its due.

In the account of what is given.] Thus M. and C. But V.: “In the account of what is given and received, since the peace of the Church gives spiritual things and receives temporal things?”

You give spiritual things.] M.: “If you give spiritual things duly, [Col. 0413D] you receive temporal things.” Correctly. Therefore some people wrongly—indeed impiously—censure the reverend religious fathers of the mendicant, or, as I prefer, fruitful orders because they receive food and other necessities of life from pagans, that is, peasants. Yet, I attest, they have deserved these things by right, because amid the sweat of their faces, nakedness, cold, and similar harshness of weather, they disseminate the word of God, thirsting eagerly for the salvation of souls.

From the unrebuked.] M.: “from the uncorrected.”

398 It is received from the wicked.] V. here added a question mark, but I placed it afterwards, at “calumny?”

Of administration due to himself.] V.: “of administration due to himself.”

Retinues of *garciones*.] *Garciones* are boys or servants, or sometimes, in a bad sense, petty scoundrels. St. Bernard uses this word in his *Apology to William*, and likewise Caesarius and Cantipratanus in many places in *The Book of Bees*.

From your hands.] V.: “from your gifts”; C.: “from your souls.”

Because such is due.] V.: “Because such food is due”; C.: “as though such food were due.”

But would that God.] C. and M.: “But would that someone.”

And they would devour.] Not “and they would name,” as C. once read.

Likewise: It is preached.] Here M. and V. are deficient down to: “Likewise: Officials.”

That they may subside.] C. omits this. Does not that saying of Horace’s *Art of Poetry* fit?

> The leech will not leave the skin until it is full of blood.

And the filth of sin upon themselves.] C.: “And thus the filth,” etc.

Job, chapter XXXI.] C. and M.: Job XXV, at the end. Formerly, as I said above, Job had fewer chapters.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0414B]

In C.’s summary, “ecclesiastical” is omitted. In V. the title varies as follows: “That spiritual things should be conferred and handled without gain and vainglory, and against hourly coins; but concerning these in the following chapter.”

But also.] The reading is sound and clear. Therefore M. incorrectly omits these words and reads in their place: “that, in the celebration.”

A profit-making commonwealth.] C.: “a public money-making enterprise.” On this I offer the words of the Wise Man, Proverbs XXIX: “A just king establishes the land; an avaricious man destroys it.” “For it is ruinous in a ruler,” says Peter of Blois, “either to worship the breeze of gifts or to seek the favor of persons. ‘In whose hands,’ says the Prophet, Psalm XXV, ‘are iniquities, and their right hand is full of gifts.’ Iniquities will pass into punishment, and gifts into sorrow.” These are his words.

Pythian Apollo.] Three copies: *Phitius*. *Pythius* is an epithet of Apollo, derived, according to some, from the serpent Python [Col. 0414C].

But also all.] On these words of Cicero, C.’s margin together with V. notes: “But also the Church”—which he had evidently mentioned before—“which today has fallen from religion and holiness through wealth and avarice, especially of prelates” (C. adds), “not only for food but also for gifts.”

They were born.] C.: “They were born,” feminine.

As though, left.] M. omits “as though.”

Left for right.] V. and C.: “Let the left be left, never the right for the left.” 399 Better in the text, as is gathered from the Gloss on this passage.

Because this [promised] eternal things.] This, namely the New Testament, promised eternal things; that, namely the Old, temporal things.

The sandals of the Apostles.] M.: “apostolic [sandals].” That sandals are footwear is clear from Isaiah chapter XX according to the Septuagint.

Under the ground in a vessel.] V. and M.: “In the ground under a vessel.”

And the censer.] A recent hand, in lead stylus, adds in V. [Col. 0414D] “is perforated,” so that it reads: “The sandals are overturned and the censer is perforated.”

The reason for which.] Note the variation. M.: “The reason for which”—here “which” is lacking—“ought to be God alone,” etc., as in the text. C.: “The reason for which, which ought to be God alone, and the cause without which they could not be done”—the rest is lacking—“if a spiritual act be for temporal gain alone,” etc. C. adds at the side, on “without which they could not be done”: “Otherwise he would do it.”

Without which they would not be done.] V. and M.: “Without which it would not be done although it can be.”

My cloak is too short.] Supply what is found in the text of Isaiah: “It cannot cover both.” Likewise in the next passage: “My bed is too narrow; it cannot receive both.”

Augustine: For gain.] I refer the reader to the Gloss on II Corinthians II.

But from simplicity.] Text and interlinear Gloss: “from sincerity.”

[Col. 0415A] There are two ends.] M. omits “two.” Distinguish these two ends from St. Augustine, vol. VIII, on Psalm CXVIII, discourse 12, before the middle.

Fear of punishment.] C.: “Fear of money and air?” V.: “Fear of punishment *ens*,” that is, existing or continually present. This fear excuses from sin, as appears below. Hence Horace:

> The wicked hate to sin from fear of punishment.

And love of God.] Again from the same author:

> The good hate to sin from love of virtue.

Namely, the right eye.] C. is mutilated here. It reads: “And the love of God, namely, the eye of the right hand for loving God. Where then is,” etc. The rest is absent.

These are the ends.] C.: “ropes.”

In place of a pledge.] M., in very thin characters, has *pigneris*, but here the words are synonymous, although someone would have it:

> The pledges of children are called *pignora*; those of things, *pignera*.

The one or the other millstone.] Since it would take too long here to recount many expositions, I direct the reader to the Gloss on this passage and to St. Gregory, vol. I, *Morals*, book XXIII, ch. 11, at the beginning.

But especially.] V. lacks “but.”

Therefore, since the first is not.] The first millstone, namely, that of fear. C.: “Therefore, since the first is meritorious.” It contradicts wrongly.

Without the second.] Namely, love of God. Therefore God alone is to be feared as Lord and loved, or honored, as Father.

400 The millstone of concupiscence.] Or “of covetousness,” as V. has it.

Or the fourth, of vainglory.] M. and C. incorrectly omit “vain.” For all glory, especially the popular breeze of applause, is vain—indeed vanity itself. The case differs with glory as the testimony of a serene conscience, of which II Corinthians I speaks.

So that not even the third.] M.: “So that this third.” Meaninglessly.

A divided mind does not.] “Take heed to yourself,” says St. Ephrem, *On Virginity*, near the end, “lest at any time in prayer your mind wander here and there.” And below: “Cut away from your heart, on every side, whatever thoughts and concerns of earthly things,” etc.

Amram, a man of the house.] Or Ammiramis, as Josephus calls him, begot Aaron and Moses by his wife Jochabed, also called Jochobet; *Antiquities*, book II, ch. 9.

Pray by working well.] C. at the side has: “Hosanna in the highest, not for the lowest.”
