When a double [invitation] is read.] M.: “When a double invitatory is read, and a third bell-call is also sounded in the Church, we find the denarius more effective than the rest.” V. likewise: “the denarius.” By *classicum* understand the ringing by which clerics are called to the Hours. I infer this from the following chapter. By Psalm XCIV is meant: “Come, let us exult in the Lord.”

The third in church is more effective.] Namely, because it more strongly invites mercenary clerics.

Augustine: not for.] C. alone has “Augustine.”

[Col. 0415D] Without all corruption.] This is both an interlinear and an ordinary Gloss.

The cross and martyrdom.] C.: “The cross, and especially that,” etc.

Therefore the Lord did not wish.] C. incorrectly: “wished.” For below he contradicts this with the words: “By the prompting of the removal of punishment.”

The punishment to be removed.] V.: “that is, our mortality.”

## CHAPTER XXVI

The title prefixed here was taken from M. For V. and C. do not divide the preceding chapter, though in C.’s side margin I read: “Against hourly denarii.”

Alluring things in spiritual matters.] That is, says V., hourly denarii for the clock, so that they may be made, etc. On this it says in the margin: “A Mass instituted, which otherwise would not be instituted, except that the poor may be supported through offerings made at it, produces simony.”

Better than one speaking.] M. and V.: “and better speaking.”

The blood of Christ.] V.: “By the blood of Christ.” Incorrectly.

Because unto the age.] This is Psalm CXXXV, although there we read not “unto the age” but “for ever.” St. Augustine says that the Greek expression can be translated either “for ever” or “unto the age.” It reads: *εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα*—“unto the age.” See vol. VIII, exposition of Psalm CXXXV, at the beginning.

For a hireling.] Thus St. Augustine, vol. IX, tractate 46 on the Gospel of John.

401 In the gambling of players.] Hear, clerics, St. Basil describing gambling: “If I dismiss you,” he says, “there are those who immediately betake themselves to dice and gambling. There are oaths there, most serious quarrels, and the offspring of avarice. An evil spirit stands by, adding frenzy and madness to players at those pips and bones,” etc. *Hexameron*, homily [Col. 0416B] 8, near the end. Long ago Wibold, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, constructed a notable game for his clerics, which Balderic describes fully in his *Chronicle of Cambrai and Arras*, book I, ch. 88. This spiritual game, or carefully divided and drawn board, is preserved among us; by it, apparently, our men played together.

Evening coins.] V.: “hourly coins for chanting Vespers,” etc.

And first in church.] V.: “And after them”—that is, after Vespers—“they are to be distributed in church.” Certainly this pleases.

To be distributed.] Margin of C., together with V.: “Yet often [they are given] first to those sitting”—V.: “seated”—“until the final bell should sound, that is, the last ringing.”

Likewise: the example of the prelate.] Supply: “serves for detestation,” as above. C.: “the example of a prelate giving, begging in church,” etc.

In silks.] Namely, with the altar frontal changed according to feast day and suitable color.

Of male and female mourners.] As is read of the *praefica*, a woman hired to lament the dead. Thus Horace in the *Art of Poetry*:

> Those hired to weep at a funeral say  
> And do almost more than those who grieve from the heart;  
> Thus a mocker moves more than a praiser.

For Gentiles are accustomed to sing dirges and mournful songs at the death of the departed and to induce others to weep. The same custom also existed among the Jews, as is clear from the Gospels, Matthew IX. There flute-players are recorded as having been present when the daughter of Jairus, the ruler, had died.

O money, money.] M. omits this verse of Juvenal, *Satires* 5.

“What are idolaters?”] Blessed Jerome proves it in chapter 5 of Ephesians, in these words: “Because he worships the engraving on the coin itself and venerates the idols stamped upon them. As the belly is the god of gluttons, so money may most justly be called the god of the greedy also, especially since elsewhere [Col. 0416D] the Apostle calls greed idolatry.” Formerly they wrote *idololatrae* for *idolatrae*.

I Thess., ch. V.] V. and C.: II Thess. C. also adds ch. IX.

“From every appearance.”] C., in the margin, from Ovid’s *Heroides*, epistle 16:

> It is a virtue to have refrained from pleasures that please.

“Because it gives scandal.”] V. and C.: “Because they give scandal to their neighbor by the left hand, enticing (C.: *to entice*) someone by the right.” Blessed Augustine, in the book *On the Sheep*: “Let us take care,” he says, “to do nothing that may give rise to evil suspicion in a weak brother.”

“But a shameful appearance.”] Does shaking out purses, like filling them, produce simony? Thus C. in the margin.

402 “Money-making hours”] V.: “The ninth-hour offices of St. Mary.”

“And with a barrier.”] A *repagulum* is a bar placed against a door to resist force. In French: *barrière*, or *barre*.

“And like old women.”] M., omitting this, says: “The clerics ran [Col. 0417A] as though to a solemnity. Some, etc.” C., however: “Like old women to a votive observance at a solemnity.” V., in my opinion, better: “And like old women to the anointing.” For there is a French proverb, *Courir à l’oinct*, or *au gras boudin* [“to run to the grease,” or “to the fat pudding”], by which clerics are mocked who run to church solely for gain and, having remained in choir for a short time (yet enough, as they say, to receive the distributions), immediately depart. Hence the poet:

> Cats, fat with love of profit, lick the candlesticks.

Thus it is said of advocates and others like them: *Engraisser les mains* [“to fatten the hands”].

“Was marked as touched.”] C.: “was seen.”

“A certain prebendary.”] C. and M.: *praebendatus* [a holder of a prebend].

“While Oliver ran.”] V.: Oliver. C., wrongly: *obliviorio*.

“He murmured and grieved.”] The two margins say: because they did not play dice and such games.

“Because they were constant.”] C.: “Because they were continually present”; perhaps it intended *assidui*.

[Col. 0417B] “Noble Church.”] The author alludes to Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book II, elegy 3: “That holy and venerable name of friendship,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXVII

V. here anticipates the title of the following chapter: “On venality,” etc.

“And damnable.”] “The contagion of the heresy of simony,” says Hugh, *On the Sacraments*, book II, part X, “long ago sprang up in Balaam, who, when payment for divination was offered, went to curse the people of God; thereafter two founders of this error are said to have arisen, one under prophetic teaching, the other under apostolic teaching. The first, Gehazi, appears to have been the teacher of sellers; then Simon, the buyer. Their followers, moreover, just as they are not diverse in error, are not divided in condemnation either.”

“For Christ entire.”] V., omitting the question mark, reads: “Especially in the Eucharist, where Christ entire, [Col. 0417C] etc.”

“May be distributed as graces.”] V. has *Ecclesiae* (“of churches”) instead of *gratiae* (“as graces”).

“Which nevertheless [they] put off.”] V. and M. omit this parenthetical clause.

“He calls them altars of God.”] More on this subject may be seen in Blessed Jerome’s commentary on Matthew 21.

“Giving nothing, and.”] C.: “Giving nowhere anything, and offering nothing.”

“Augustine: ‘The house.’”] In C. and V., “Augustine” is absent.

“No one in the oratory.”] We have the same words in the Rule of our Holy Father Benedict, chapter 52.

403 “In this, giving to all.”] “Of every sex and condition.” C. in the margin.

“It is said that he drove them out twice.”] “John alone,” says the same author in the same place, “speaks of the first expulsion; the others, of the last,” Matthew 21.

“The doves of venality.”] By the dove, understand the Holy Spirit to be figured, as Blessed Augustine teaches, tome IX, tractate 10 on the Gospel of John, before the middle.

[Col. 0417D] “Other things of neighbors.”] C., between the lines, suggested correcting *alia* (“other things”) to *similia* (“similar things”).

“Let us not accuse; let us not make public.”] C.: “Let us not accuse in order that we may make public.”

“Thus more ready.”] This is in Blessed Jerome on Matthew 21.

“Facility.”] C.: “The capacity for receiving.”

“Which, as though blind.”] M.: “Which, because the blind suffer the Lord himself.”

“A certain mass.”] I report what V. and C. read in the lower margins: “Against the venality and plurality of Masses; against the plurality of forms in a single Mass; and against their novelty.” These matters will be addressed below in their proper place. Moreover, another passage is found in the same margin of V.: “Impunity, mother of obstinacy, daughter of negligence, root of sin, nurse of adultery and incest, forerunner of eternal death, preparer of hell.”

“Let them make double entire [Masses] in a day.”] That is, celebrate two complete Masses in one day, or, in common speech, “binating.” C. [Col. 0418A] reads thus: “The one making double on an entire day”; M. does not add “and let them double.” M.: “They make double entirely in a day.”

“And out of fear.”] C.: “Instead of shame and terror.”

“Let them make one double.”] “Not daring,” says C., “to complete two [Masses], they would celebrate doubles, triples, and multiples—that is, [Masses] of many forms.” M. reads less well: “Not daring, etc., let them make one double, triple, and multiple—that is, etc.,” as in the text.

“And the first introit.”] Someone wished to correct the triple text by his note added in the margin of C., in this manner: “At the first office let there not be offered,” etc.

“Those singing tales.”] C. added: “Singers or those singing,” etc.

“Of Landric.”] M.: Landeric.

“Narcissus.”] Perhaps Narcisso.

“The offering which is for this.”] Namely, which is the cause, as stated above. M. and C.: “It is established that the offering is made for this,” omitting *which*.

[Col. 0418B] “At the root, that is, greed.”] M.: “Of madness (good God, what simony!) and simoniacal greed.”

“But of the Lord.”] These words appear in C. The margins prove that “the priest seeks the glory of the Lord and not of the world.” C., M.: Augustine: “This is signified by the many extensions of priests’ arms during Mass.” Consult Blessed Augustine, tome VIII, on Psalm 62.

“I shall raise [them] to another.”] V.: “to another thing.” C. seems here to err through an unsuitable punctuation. For it places the question there: “What [will I raise] to you?” and continues: “How [shall I raise] the price of the world,” etc.

“As though united.”] C.: “uniting.” V.: “helping.”

404 “Indeed, with my.”] V. and C.: “with the minister of the altar and mine,” namely my simoniacal minister, who will minister only for money, just as I celebrate only for the same.

“Greed rules.”] C. does not interrupt the period by punctuation, but continues it thus: “For a price [Col. 0418C] I shall perform [it], greed prevailing.” V. similarly, with a few omissions: “For a price I shall perform that which nevertheless is beyond price.”

“Less, but more.”] M. and C.: “not therefore less simoniacal,” etc.

“My daughter.”] M.: “The daughter of mine.” Here the author continues the words of Simon Magus, introduced on stage.

“It will break in.”] M.: “will creep in.” V.: “creeps in.” Choose whichever you please; both are acceptable.

“Offering things for sale.”] V.: “arranging things for sale.”

“From those offerings.”] “Greedily acquired and thus shamefully,” say both margins.

“Altars are erected.”] “This does not please God, because a good use does not justify things acquired badly and shamefully.” 14, question 5, *Neque enim*.

“With his household also.”] V.: “With servants,” etc. M. omits these words through “sold,” inclusive. Thus it has: “The man whom he believed pure, he sold.”

“He, repenting.”] Led by repentance—not genuine repentance: [Col. 0418D] Matthew 27.

“Though not truly.”] M.: “Though not rightly.”

“But in the Church.”] C.: “in the Church,” and thus begins another period: “But among us,” etc. Incorrectly.

“Shamefully acquired.”] V. and M.: “shamefully acquired [coins],” namely silver coins. But C. pleased me more than the others, because it refers to all things acquired for a price and capable of valuation.

“From more shamefully offered [things].”] V.: “from shamefully offered [things].”

“Churches are built.”] “That Zion may be built from blood,” say both margins, from Micah 3.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

V. continues the preceding chapter.

“The sacrifice was sufficient.”] From Blessed John Chrysostom, homily 17 on the Epistle to the Hebrews. The same is found in chapter 1, homily 4, book II, of *The Widow of Zarephath*, first brought to light by us in former years.

“Once in a day.”] M. lacks these words. Thus: “To represent Him who suffered once, [as] sacrificed.”

[Col. 0419A] “They are crucified again.”] This has been sufficiently discussed in the same *Widow of Zarephath*, book II, homily 5, chapter 1.

“Likewise Augustine.”] His words here have been altered somewhat. See the passage in tome III, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 53. Also Blessed Chrysostom, in the passage cited above in this chapter.

“If therefore Augustine.”] M.: “If according to Augustine [one can] scarcely [avoid] one suspicion in a day,” etc. It is mistaken.

“Too much in a day.”] C. and M.: “To repeat less in a day.”

“Then because of the mystery.”] Not “ministry,” as in C. “The mystery is such,” says the margin. C.: “The first Mass signifies the prophets; the second, the Fathers nearer to grace; the third, 405 apostolic teaching. Pope Telesphorus IX instituted these three Masses. If you desire more on them, see William Durandus of Ravenna, *On Offices*, book VI, ‘On the Office of the Nativity of the Lord.’”

“To the rural priest.”] To the pastor of country people, and dean of Christendom.

“But the greater prelate.”] A bishop or a dean.

[Col. 0419B] “But it becomes cheap.”] For, say the margins of C. and M., “frequency produces cheapness and carelessness, and removes devotion and reverence.”

“Because [it is] rare.”] “For what is rare is dear,” or, as Blessed Jerome says, “whatever is rarer is desired more ardently.” Letter against Vigilantius, after the middle.

“Because [it is] rare.”] Not “because [it is] dear,” as M.

“With incense among the holy things.”] V. alone added: “Because holy legal rites are to be venerated.”

“With wild lettuces.”] Let us hear here Blessed Gregory, speaking in the middle of homily 22 on the Gospels: “The flesh of the lamb is to be eaten with wild lettuces, so that, when we receive the body of the Redeemer, we may afflict ourselves with tears for our sins, in order that the very bitterness of penitence may wipe away from the stomach of the mind the corrupt humors of life.”

The Carthusian Order. The two orders of Cistercians. I consulted tested men on this matter, and none of them had ever heard of such a thing in his own order.

[Col. 0419C] “Here also of the offerings.”] M.: “This also, an offertory holocaust to God.” It certainly makes sense in its own way. But how is it that a priest—alas, I first of all—so confidently dares approach not merely to celebrate twice, but even only once daily, when Blessed Jerome, an exemplar of penitence, entered churches of martyrs only with the greatest and most fearful reverence, not to celebrate Mass but for the sake of devout veneration? “I confess,” he says, “my fear lest perhaps it arise from superstition. Whenever I have been angry, thought something evil in my mind, or been deceived by a nocturnal phantom, I do not dare enter the basilicas of martyrs; thus I tremble wholly, both in body and in mind.” Letter against Vigilantius, beginning: “Many monsters are in the world.”

“A sinful priest.”] C. adds “priest,” correctly: for the discourse is directed to him.

“On the sixth feria.”] Here clerics are taught not to number the days of the week by the names of planets or [Col. 0419D] pagan gods, as secular people do—Monday, Tuesday, and so forth—but, according to the rite of holy Mother Church, by the terms second feria, third, fourth, and so on.

“One day, as it were.”] V.: “as it were, with rest.” M.: “with one day, namely, intervening.”

“If then one food.”] C. and M.: “But then one spiritual food, not spiritually,” etc. Incorrectly.

“The seasonings of the introit.”] Repeated more often according to the wish of the payer and offerer. These words, from “Introit,” etc. through “Likewise: Certain,” are read in the margin of C.; V. and M. have them in the text.

“Some interpret badly.”] C.: “Likewise: Such persons badly,” etc.

406 “Mark [calls it] peculiar.”] Although three copies read thus, I shall nevertheless state my view. In place of Mark, Symmachus should be read. For he, as Blessed Jerome testifies, translated it “peculiar bread.” Moreover, the Lord’s Prayer, “Our Father,” is not found in Mark’s Gospel. I forbear saying more, intending to abbreviate the notes, in accordance with the author’s advice at the end of chapter 9; meanwhile, the [Col. 0420A] reader may consult Blessed Jerome’s commentary on Matthew 6.

“Which [he calls] not supersubstantial.”] V. and C.: “Which [he calls] not substantial.”

“So far as lies in itself.”] M.: “so far as lies in them.” It is the same.

## CHAPTER XXIX

“Falsehood seeks corners.”] “Truth does not love corners and does not seek whisperers,” says Blessed Jerome in his letter to Rusticus, beginning: “Nothing is happier than a Christian.”

“While fools avoid.”] A verse of Horace, *Satires*, book I, satire 2. M. reads: “and while they avoid the pursuits of vices, they run into their opposites.”

“To its own greed.”] C.: “of greed.”

“They fall into a monster.”] C.: “They monstrously fall into a monster, making Masses two-faced,” etc. There is a transposition of words.

[Col. 0420B] “Two-headed Janus.”] Of whom Ovid says, *Fasti* II:

> Truly, two-headed origin of the silently passing year.

“Seven-headed Hydra.”] Or, as V. and C. have it, “of seven heads.” Mantuan:

> And wars into the savage wrath of the sevenfold Hydra.

“Hundred-handed Briareus.”] Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> And double Briareus with his hundred hands, and the beast of Lerna.

Horace, *Odes* II, ode 17:

> Not even if the hundred-handed giant should rise again.

“Geryon.”] *Aeneid* VI:

> Gorgons and Harpies, and the shades in the form of a three-bodied monster.

And in book VIII:

> Proud in the death of three-bodied Geryon and his spoils.

On these and similar matters, see Blessed Jerome’s letter against Vigilantius, beginning: “Many monsters are in the world.”

“Two-headed Mass.”] C. adds: “twofold, or two-formed, many-formed.” That is, of manifold face and form.

[Col. 0420C] “They oppose the mystery.”] Not “ministry,” as C.

“Because [it must] be expressed.”] C.: “they express.” M.: “Because the office expresses,” etc. Margin on these words: “It expresses the order and groans of the prophets desiring Christ’s coming.” C. and V.

407 “Seven times or more.”] C. lacks the word “seven times.”

“And the mystery.”] Again C.: “the ministry.”

“Of the two introits.”] Not “of each of the two,” as M.

“From which of those two.”] M. and V.: “from both.” Here the question mark has been restored.

“If from cutting.”] Namely, from the introit.

“Or tricenary.”] Or “thirtyfold,” as V. A *tricenale* of Masses, lasting from the day of a believer’s death through thirty continuous days, seems to have originated with Pope St. Gregory, as may be gathered from his *Life*. Surius, tome II.

“Mass of the catechumens.”] Some divide Mass into four parts. First (Dominic Soto, *On the Sentences*, IV, [Col. 0420D] distinction 13, question 2, article 4): from the beginning to the Offertory, and it is called the Mass of the Catechumens; second, from the Offertory to the consecration, called by the Greeks *ἀναφορά* [anaphora, “offering”], and by the Latins the lesser canon; third, from the consecration to communion, called the greater canon; fourth, from communion to the end. If you desire more, consult Bellarmine’s *Controversies*, tome V, *On the Mass*, chapter 16. It was formerly called the Mass of the Catechumens because such persons were permitted to be present until the Offertory.

“It seems because.”] V. omits “it seems.”

“[It is] not yet the sacrifice.”] That is, consecration has not yet occurred.

“They oppose the institution.”] Except on the day of the Lord’s Nativity—unless necessity advises otherwise—it is sufficient for a priest to celebrate only one Mass once a day. *Extra*, “On the Celebration of Masses,” chapter *Consuluisti*. Likewise, *On Consecration*, distinction I, *Sufficit*. Alexander II.

“Masses were made two-formed.”] That is, introits and the rest were made of double form.

[Col. 0421A] “One and another.”] Namely, introit. C.: “one and another case as they please,” etc.

“Usefully approved.”] V.: “universally approved.”

“The right [hand] and for himself.”] “The right [hand]” is absent in M.

“To the Gentiles.”] C.: “Gentiles,” with this margin: “Because you have made yourselves unworthy and rejected the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.” These are the words of Blessed Paul and Barnabas to the Jews, Acts XII. For it was especially to be preached to the Jews, who were the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Hence the Savior: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, but go rather to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel” (Matthew XX). But when they saw that the Jews made light of the word of God, they turned to the Gentiles so that they would not be idle.

“Which it anticipates.”] C.: “Which it anticipates and hastens; indeed” (note here the variation in the reading), “it signifies the end of the Church, thus returning” (*frequenter*, “frequently,” is absent) “from horn to horn,” etc.

“It does not yet signify.”] M.: “Yet it has not represented the sacrifice to be,” etc. V.: “Since it has not yet represented [Col. 0421B] the sacrifice to be,” etc.

“Since from horn to.”] “Why do they return from horn to horn,” say the margins of C. and M., “when their hour has not yet come?” This alludes to the aforesaid words concerning Christ the Lord: “When His hour came.” From John XV.

“Or insertions of Masses.”] V. omits “visitations,” etc., in place of “insertions.” 408 V. has “graftings.” This may be accepted, since they are the same thing.

“More favored.”] V.: “favored.” M.: “more praiseworthy.” They are called “more favored” because they are retained from frequent recitation by memory, or because they are short and therefore completed more quickly. Hence C. in the margin and M. in the text: “As *Salve, sancta Parens* [Hail, holy Mother], *Spiritus Domini* [The Spirit of the Lord], *Requiem* [Rest], which are common introits.” M. wholly omits: “As the Mass of Blessed Linus,” etc., through “Likewise,” replacing it with the foregoing.

“Likewise, by the example of.”] This example, through the following one concerning the matron, is absent in M.

“Due to certain monks.”] V. elegantly reads it. But [Col. 0421C] C. is more obscure and feeble: “From the income of the first Mass due to the monks.” The Mass is not due to the monks, but the income or offering. Here I suggest one correction, especially in rural churches, which edifies neither parishioners nor parish priests. In certain parish churches one may see, as soon as the Offertory of the solemn Mass has ended, the steward or farmer of the patron of the place immediately approach the altar and receive from the minister’s hand, in everyone’s sight, the offerings devoutly made by the people, which he delivers to his patron and lord. I know that the patron rightly receives the offerings; but this would be done more discreetly and far more decently if the patron made an agreement with the parish priest and pastor that, in return for the offerings made at Mass, he should receive annually a respectable sum of money or some equivalent.

“Since authority holds.”] Blessed Gregory proves this by examples in *Dialogues*, book IV. After our author’s age, St. Thomas, *Supplement*, question 71, articles 12 and 13. In the former, he teaches that suffrages made for one deceased person [Col. 0421D] benefit the one for whom they are made more than others, namely by reason of their particular intention and application. In the latter, that suffrages made for many do not avail each individual as much as if they were made specially for each one. From this, as he says in the body of the article, it is clear why special suffrages were instituted in the Church. Finally, at the Council of Constance, session 8, two hundred years ago, the nineteenth article of John Wyclif was condemned, in which he said that special prayers applied to one person benefited him no more than general prayers.

“More often and more specially.”] Thus V. Not “more often and more spiritually,” as two persons wish.

“If the tricenale of one.”] C.: “If the tricenary.” Likewise below: “in the tricenary.”

“Let it be counted.”] M. wrongly: “Let it be counted.” This is practiced today. For, since certain churches are burdened with many anniversaries and their revenues are insufficient to support the priest and clerics, two or three anniversaries are combined into [Col. 0422A] one with the consent of the diocesan authorities. Note, however, that in former times these were celebrated for an honorarium of only four or five solidi, which today cannot be done except for a more respectable sum, because food is more expensive, and otherwise the ministers of the Church could not live from the altar.

“Yet he did not wish them.”] C.: “He wished,” by no means.

“I shall make a tricenale.”] C.: “tricenalia,” unless special ones.

“An insertion of this kind.”] Or “grafting,” as C. and V.

“When requested.”] M. is silent from here through “Likewise: Apart from doubleness.”

409 “Through an insertion of this kind.”] V.: “for an insertion of this kind.”

“Dry Mass.”] See William Estius, a man most learned and equally devout, in the discourse delivered at Douai from the public theological lectern, *On Dry Masses*, which is the thirteenth among his nineteen printed orations.

“Of consecration.”] V. omits this word.

“It will help equally afterward.”] V.: “equally helpful afterward.”

[Col. 0422B] “And the sacrifice previously set forth.”] Thus C. and V.: “Just as the sacrifice previously set forth.” The sense is excellent and easy to understand if *previously set forth* is referred to the dry Mass.

“Why therefore?”] C.: “Why therefore is the sacrifice inserted into the Mass set before it, through greed and to deceive souls,” without a question mark at the end.

“Apart from doubleness.”] V. and M.: “Because of,” etc., but it makes no sense.

“Likewise, the Mass.”] Supply here, as before: “Greed has found.”

“Decently allotted.”] The copyist of M. conjectured *on his day* in place of S. and D. There is indeed some sense, but it is alien to verse or poetry.

“And of sameness.”] C.: “And sameness removes weariness.”

“What I say weeping.”] O piety! O the author’s love! O devotion toward the venerable sacrament of the altar!

[Col. 0422C] “This sacrament alone.”] Well said. C.: “But this sacrament,” not so well.

“Waxen images.”] The sound and genuine reading. Through a scribe’s error, M. seems once to have read *caesareas* (“imperial”) for *cereas* (“waxen”); but, after the removal of two dots cancelling *sa*, it leaves *cereas*. V. similarly had *aereas* (“bronze”), but adding c made *cereas*.

“For slaughter.”] M.: “for the signification of the slain.”

“Of lesser superiors.”] No comma should be placed between these two words, although C. and M. do so. For here “superior” denotes one who has charge of lesser priests, as their instructor and superintendent.

“Even under the open sky.”] Or “under the sky.”

“Under Gregory VIII.”] He was elected in 1187 and reigned only fifty-seven days. Three of his letters survive in Roger of Howden’s *Annals*, part II.

“Except three times.”] V.: “except insofar as.” It makes no sense.

[Col. 0422D] “Hosea says, chapter VIII.”] C.: chapter XXV.

“The people multiplied.”] The biblical text: “Ephraim multiplied.”

“Altars for sinning.”] By no means “for preaching,” as V.

“So nevertheless that.”] C. does not admit these words through “plurality.”

“It produced ministries.”] V.: “it produced merchandise.” C.: “it produced gifts.”

## CHAPTER XXX

The three vary in the summary. C.: “Against those who unworthily communicate in the Eucharist”; M.: “the Eucharist,” while in the margin it has: “On those who consecrate unworthily.” 410 The Cambron fragment, discussed above at chapter 11, reads: “On those who unworthily receive the body of Christ.”

“In the first Epistle to the Corinthians, II.”] C. notes chapter LVIII.

[Col. 0423A] “But let a man examine himself.”] C. says in the margin: “Let him examine in many ways whether he is without mortal sin.”

“Eats judgment to himself.”] “Whence he is judged.” Margin of C.

“Not discerning.”] “From the custom of consecrating or receiving.” These margins are drawn from the Gloss on I Corinthians 11.

“That is, due.”] These too reflect the teaching of Blessed Augustine, tome II, letter 118 to Januarius, chapters 3 and 2. I once read things not unlike them in Blessed Gregory, tome II, on I Kings, chapter I, before the middle.

“He presumes to violate.”] “Because he celebrates for profit.” Side margin of C.

“Not according to the rite.”] Restored from V. M. omits it entirely, C. in part, as follows: “He presumes to violate. According to the rite, he sells who,” etc.

“Of unbelief.”] This is the Gloss on John 15:22, which V. alone has.

“But these through ignorance.”] C. adds in the margin: “Some, not all.” This is correct. For some knowingly crucified God, [Col. 0423B] or should have known Him, obstinately.

“If from childhood.”] Words of Blessed Augustine, also cited by Caesarius in *Book of Examples*, book IX, chapter 53.

“If Mary in so great.”] That is, Mary Magdalene, who, because of the ardor and diligence of her faith, claimed for herself the name of the tower, says Blessed Jerome in the epitaph of Marcella, near the beginning in the middle.

“How [do you], a sinner.”] V. is silent through “How hither, that is,” etc.

“II Kings, chapter VI.”] C.: chapter LXXII.

“And he was also a priest.”] It is certain that Uzzah was of the tribe of Levi, since he was the son of Abinadab along with Abiah; but Josephus denies that he himself was a priest, in these words: “Wishing to hold it [the ark], though he was not a priest.” *Jewish Antiquities*, book VII, chapter 4.

“It was said to the catechumens.”] I have spoken of this above at chapter 28.

“Namely, those possessing charity.”] I have taken these three words from C. alone, where charity is understood as love, which precedes the habit of charity.

“Concerning this.”] C.: “short of this.”

[Col. 0423C] “In the suburb.”] By “suburb” I understand the nave, or the forepart of the church.

“I do not define.”] The author calls the matter into doubt. From this the reader may easily gather how exactly the author weighs and how highly he values irreverence committed concerning this most holy sacrament of the Eucharist; and surely he should not be thought to have practiced anything other than what he taught and judged.

“Sanctified.”] M. and C.: “Even holy [persons].”

“Likewise he ordained.”] V. lacks this through “Likewise Exodus XII.”

411 “And solemn.”] M.: “Into solemn” (here it jumps two lines), “in the condensed sum of all the articles of faith.”

“Of tears.”] M. again skips, through “as far as the horn.”

“Exodus XII.”] C.: XVIII.

“With loins girded.”] An exposition of this history is found in Blessed Gregory, homily 22 on the Gospels.

[Col. 0423D] “Baked also.”] C.: “Taught also in an oven.” This is tolerable if *taught* is understood as *proved*, like gold in the furnace—that is, in every tribulation, etc., Wisdom 3.

“Entire in virtues.”] C.: “with all strength.”

“Whence, shod.”] V. is silent from here through “Likewise, for terror.”

“The pouring forth of the eyes.”] “With all the aforesaid things condensed,” says C. in the side margin.

“To the chalice of devotion.”] The verses of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, on this same Mary of Egypt have not yet been printed, as Molanus noted in his notes on Usuard, 2 April.

“He sacrifices.”] M.: “He mortifies.”

“With the bitterness of depravity.”] M.: “Of impiety.” It certainly works.

“But not by deity.”] The Cambron fragment: “But not by gift.” M.: “And not by number.”

[Col. 0424A] “To flesh, [and] the world.”] V.: “Renouncing the world and its desires.”

“Mark cut off [his thumb].”] If, for the reason alleged in the text, St. Mark cut off his own thumb, he did not sin, because he is believed to have done this by divine prompting, as St. Thomas says, II–II, question 185, article 2, objection 3. This was probably taken from the prologue attributed to Jerome, prefixed to the Gospel of Mark, where it reads—though it is not asserted: “Finally, he is said to have cut off his thumb for himself, so that he might be deemed unfit for the priesthood.” This prologue is found in the gilt English Bibles written in the time of Pope Gregory I or Charlemagne; likewise in the Royal Bibles, under the title: “Prologue of St. Jerome according to Mark.” But the Louvain Bibles corrected by the doctors of Louvain and published in 1547 omit it; nor is it believed to be by Blessed Jerome, but by some Greek, says Molanus, *On Images*, chapter 38—or, in the second edition, book II, chapter 47—and he adds: “The same author prefaces John thus: ‘This is John the Evangelist, whom God called from a wedding when he wished to marry.’ But I suspect that he took these things from apocryphal writings of heretics who condemned marriage, and of those who defended the lawfulness of self-mutilation. For among other historians or ancient writers you will scarcely find either account.” Nicholas Zeger says, moreover, in the preface to the New Testament which he corrected, that he found these prefaces written in very ancient Bibles inscribed a thousand years ago, even though their author is uncertain. Thus far Molanus, in the cited chapter 38, whom Peter Galesius follows in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 25 April, when the feast of St. Mark is celebrated.

Baronius also calls and rejects as a fable 412 what is said in the mentioned prologue about Mark, *Annals*, tome I, in the year of Christ 45. James of Vitry, who is not much later than Peter the Chanter, author of the *Abbreviated Word*, reports the same story as true in his *Western History*, chapter 30; so too St. Thomas in the passage cited above, citing the prologue attributed to Blessed Jerome.

[Col. 0424C] Lucas Pinellus, in his *Dialogue on Communion*, relates it of Mark the Anchorite; so does John de la Haye, S.J., in *Gospel Apparatus*, chapter LIV, where he says concerning the author of the aforesaid prologue: “It is established that that prologue is by an uncertain author, not by St. Jerome, and that what is said in it has no great authority unless supported by the testimony of another approved author.” Peter de Natalibus describes the same story in the *Catalogue of Saints*, book IV, chapter 86, as does Claudius de Rota; but it has little probability. Thus he says. The man whom he calls Claudius de Rota is James of Voragine, whose work commonly called the *Golden Legend*—which Melchior Canus, in his book *On Theological Authorities*, calls “leaden”—was published by that Claudius de Rota, as is clear from the preface.

Our distinguished lord and master Franciscus Sylvius, commenting learnedly on the cited passage of St. Thomas, refutes the same fable in these words: “What is objected in argument 3 concerning St. Mark the Evangelist, as though he cut off his own thumb [Col. 0424D] to render himself unfit for the priesthood, is fabulous. For it is clear from the histories that he founded and governed the Church of Alexandria, which he could not have done without priesthood. A certain Mark the Anchorite is recorded to have done this; and, because they shared a name, what this other man did was ascribed to St. Mark the Evangelist.” Thus he says.

Earlier, in the same cited year, Baronius had written: “And that little tale, rather sung by popular report than established by the authority of the ancients, is rejected: that Mark resisted becoming bishop so strongly, however much Peter requested it, that for this reason he cut off his own thumb. For this act, which is known to have been performed by a certain Anchorite, is most imprudently ascribed to Mark the Evangelist.”

Certainly, the natural law teaches that it is unlawful to mutilate oneself in any member, as does St. Thomas, II–II, question 65, article 1; and it was expressly forbidden in the First Council of Nicaea, canon 1. That Anchorite [Col. 0425A] is not to be praised for the act, unless he did it by divine inspiration. But who that Mark the Anchorite was, I have not found in the *Lives of the Fathers*.

“But sacramentally.”] M. errs: “But he had understood otherwise.”

“They bring unlawful things.”] V.: “They offer.”

“In the *Lives of the Fathers*.”] Omitting this, V. and M. read: “Likewise: Certain,” etc. This book called *Lives of the Fathers* has little authority among some; indeed, it is rejected as apocryphal. Thus Matthias Felisius, a Minorite, in his *Elucidation of Christian Instruction*, distinction 11, chapter 1.

“I shall not consecrate.”] “Out of reverence,” says the margin of C.

“By the bishop of Egypt.”] V. omits *Egypt*.

“That is, joyful youth.”] V. varies thus: “To God who makes my youth glad. He has already granted me youth—namely, of grace—in actuality, and youth of glory in hope. Youth,” etc.

413 “Those standing against you.”] C.: “before you.”

“Ready to avenge.”] C., reversing the order: “To prepare avengers.”

“At the time when the suppliant.”] A verse of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, on the mystery of the Mass. I have read an entirely similar thought in Blessed Gregory, *Dialogues*, IV, chapter 58, at the end.

“In Exodus.”] C., in the margin: chapter 5.

“For the place in which.”] “It is understood one way above and another way here,” says C. in the margin. I explain: above, from Joshua 5; here, from Exodus 3.

“Stained.”] M.: “Unstained from the unstained,” corruptly.

“At the kiss of the head.”] Three [types] in the margin: “There is a kiss of the feet, of the hands, and of the head.”

“And his own steps.”] “It is not an ascent but an intrusion, or an inrush,” says the margin of C.

“You sat at table.”] Blessed Augustine cites this passage in these words in his seventy-first exposition of Proverbs 23. See tome IX, tractates 47 and 84 on John, and tome X, Sermon 45 *On the Saints*, which in the new edition is 122.

[Col. 0425C] “He set forth innumerable.”] C.: “He set forth [them] upon the table,” perhaps “an immense [table].”

“Dishes and gifts.”] “Because he gave gifts to men, he received gifts in men.” Thus C. in the margin. Here gifts are the diversely bestowed talents of Matthew 25 and Ephesians 4:8, 11.

“A price for us.”] Blessed Thomas, the torch of theologians, says:

> By being born, He gave Himself as companion;  
> By eating with us, as food;  
> By dying, as price;  
> By reigning, He gives Himself as reward.

“If [you bear] the Lord’s stigmata.”] “Not those of the devil, not the splendor of garments.” Margin of C.

“Likewise Psalm CXVII.”] V. and the Cambron fragment are silent through the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER XXXI

V. has for the summary: “Against beasts with many [Col. 0425D] heads.” Besides the text’s heading, M. reads in the margin: “On the plurality of personates,” perhaps *personatuum*. Geryons were discussed at chapter 29.

“Not dissimilar.”] C.: “Not absurd, not discordant.”

“Of personates.”] M.: “Of personalities.” C.: “Of persons.” The subject is the plurality of *personatus*; see *Extra, On Prebends and Dignities*, *Ad haec licet*.

In certain churches, however, a *personatus* truly is a benefice, as at Oudenaarde in Flanders, where there are four pastors in the same church and each performs the office in his assigned weeks. The more distinguished among them is called the *persona*. Sometimes it is not a benefice, because a *personatus* can also be possessed by laymen; just as being the church’s custodian is not a benefice but an office. Thus the king of France is custodian of the church of St. Quentin; the bishop of Liège is custodian at Halle, which is also expressed in his titles.

“In personates.”] M.: “in personalities,” as above.

[Col. 0426A] 414 “The Church is a place.”] Not, as M. has it, “A place in the Church,” because the discussion concerns the Church, not a place.

“Against which.”] V.: “against whom,” namely the place. Let it pass.

“Primipilus.”] One who bears the spear before a king or military commander. A *pilum* is a weapon hurled before the defensive sword is drawn.

“Armiger.”] One who bears the arms of a military commander.

Constable.] Or *conestable*. In French, *connétable*: that is, “count of the stable” (*comte de l’étable*), the official responsible for the king’s horses; otherwise *écuyer* or *esquier*, “squire.” See the French booklet printed at Paris in 1600 under the title *Origines des dignitez et magistrats de France, recueillis par Claude Franchet*, book II, chapter 7. Gregory of Tours uses the word *connestabuli* in book III, chapter 32 of his history, where, speaking of the emperor Justinian, he says: “When the emperor saw that Belisarius was being defeated rather often, he removed him and appointed Narses in his place. Belisarius, however, he made count of the stable—apparently as a humiliation—an office which he had formerly held.” Aimoin likewise uses the word in his *History of the Deeds of the Franks*, book III, chapters 42 and 70; he says: “Laudegisil, overseer of the royal horses, whom the common people call *comistabilis*,” etc. But Jacques du Breul, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés—also mentioned by the aforesaid Franchet, chapter 7—gives another derivation of this name in his index to Aimoin, where one reads: “Count of the stable, also called count of the keepers of the royal horses.” Again: “The overseer of the royal horses is commonly called *comistabilis*, as though ‘the steadfast count’ (*comes stabilis*).” (Because he was never changed, as Franchet explains.) Montmorency alluded to this when, invested with this most exalted dignity, he adopted as his motto *Aplanos*, a Greek word meaning “firm,” “steadfast,” “not wandering.”

Francis Ragueau follows the former derivation in his book *Indices des droits royaux*, saying: “The constable was the grand equerry, *protostrator* [πρωτοστράτωρ], and had the superintendence of the prince’s stable or equerry [*escuerie*]. And the marshals were the squires. And below: After the office of Mayor”—that is, major-domo of the royal household—“of the palace had been abolished, officers for the conduct of war were created: one called constable, and lesser ones called marshals, ‘horses’ being used figuratively for horsemen. And below: The Constable of France is chief after the King.”

Seneschal.] M. and V. omit this term. The same Franchet cited above, book I, chapter 10, says that *seneschal* means the overseer of the king’s table, citing several verses from the romance of Raoul of Cambrai:

> They called his seneschal Raoul,  
> Who served him at the meal most pleasingly.

Likewise:

> And the barons are seated at the tables;  
> The seneschals have busied themselves well there.  
> Each had been well trained to serve properly, etc.

Concerning the same word, the said Francis Ragueau writes in his [Col. 0426D] index: “This word, he says, appears English or Germanic, as though it were an officer charged with the household, and it seems to belong to the same language as *marshal*. *Scal* and *scabin* mean judge, examiner, and reformer; hence *Eschevin*, *Scabinus*. The *dapifer* was called seneschal, and the overseer of the table, *siniscalchus*, etc. Today he is a count of a province.” So he writes.

Right wing of the battle-line.] By these the author means marquesses. Those entrusted in war with guarding the *march*—that is, a frontier, boundary, or limit—are called marquesses or border-counts. See George Colvenerius, notes on Balderic, book II, chapter 26, at the end.

It becomes fuller thereby.] C. and M. read “may it become fuller thereby,” but they are mistaken, as is clear from the gloss of St Augustine on this passage.

Attentive to many things.] M. and V. omit this.

Commanders of thousands.] These are drawn from the Greek paraphrase and are the same as the preceding material; I have therefore almost omitted them as superfluous.

[Col. 0427A]

Why then?] C.: “Because then.”

The same dean and archdeacon.] That is, one person simultaneously holds the office of dean and archdeacon.

The same person, two archdeacons.] That is, one and the same person possesses two archdeaconries.

Or another office.] C. distorts the sense, for it says: “Or another official who would have authority by his office to judge these matters.”

And several offices.] C. [lacuna]: “And popular offices.”

A concubinary priest.] Oh, scandals!

A man from his own tribe.] That is, from his own congregation and brotherhood, not from another. C. incorrectly reads “from the tribe of Judah.”

Lest the minister of one.] M., in the margin: “But lest one person hold different offices in the same place,” that is, under the same roof.

And he who was useful.] For one who embraces many things binds them together with greater difficulty; or: “Divided among many things, he is less suited [Col. 0427B] to each individually.”

A beautiful house.] Namely, the Church. This is Cassiodorus’s view.

Of the house’s splendid spoils.] C.: “This division of the spoils of the house.” M.: “This also, the division of the beautiful house.” Both are incomplete.

In the Gospel, chapter XI.] C.: chapter XXIX.

Likewise Isaiah.] C. notes chapter XXVIII.

Gathering in the morning.] The biblical text has: “devouring prey in the morning.”

Variety of chants.] “It makes commendable”—M. omits the rest—“the variety for the sake of lessons, responsories, etc.”

Antiphonaries, ornaments.] Between the words “antiphonaries and ornaments,” C. inserts: “Which are not mixed together, so that a chapter may be an antiphon.” But, warned by the dots placed beneath them, which themselves expunge these words from V.’s text as superfluous, I have restored them to the notes.

Consonant.] M. and V. lack this word.

James, chapter III.] C.: VI.

[Col. 0427C]

The interlinear gloss says.] That is, the gloss. C. has only this.

If it is forbidden.] This occurs in the appendix to the Third Lateran Council, under Alexander III, in many canons, under the title: “Several ecclesiastical benefices are not to be entrusted to one person, nor one benefice divided among several,” etc.

Not several to one.] This is the interlinear gloss on James 3:1.

He who serves at the altars.] These words are absent from C. and M.

In proportion to the time.] Or to absence. C.’s “in proportion to the time” is certainly acceptable. For the time during which clerics are absent from, or present in, choir is reckoned, so that distributions may be made to them equivalently.

The device of the young man.] Of Papirius Praetextatus. He acquired this name because, while still wearing the bordered toga and in youth, he seemed remarkably wise. V. recounted the whole story in the margin in Macrobius’s words from the *Saturnalia*, but I have omitted it, referring the reader there. A similar [Col. 0427D] example concerning Titus Veturius, son of Veturius, is related by Valerius Maximus, book VI, chapter 1.

At the gate of the Capitol.] C. incorrectly has: “At the lodging of the Capitol.”

Secular jurisdictions.] These are distinguished from ecclesiastical jurisdictions.

In the Church of St Medericus.] C. has this in the margin, whereas V. has it in the text. I nearly removed it from the text. For I cannot bring myself to believe that our author, a holy man, expressly censured the chapter or church of St Medericus built in Paris, since I have noticed nothing similar in the whole work. I therefore think that V.’s copyist here inserted a marginal note into the text, as he did in many other places, as he himself also reports in his note to chapter 97. The saint’s feast is marked in the Roman Martyrology on 29 August.

To make two legions.] Tria: “embassies.”

Concerning *marrantiae*.] Perhaps *morantiae*, from delay or [Col. 0428A] slowness; for the slow are said to “weave delays.” It is not merely absentees but also those who arrive late for the divine office who are rebuked.

1 Corinthians, chapter XII.] C.: chapter LVIII; V.: LIX.

Of human necessity.] V. and M. do not admit these words.

417 CHAPTER XXXII.

V. and M. do not divide the preceding chapter here.

Caesar was everything.] Lucan, *The Civil War* (*Pharsalia*), book III, not far from the beginning. M.: “Caesar possesses everything.” This hemistich is also found in the poet Alan, book X.

Gaul alone lacks monsters.] Though it may lack bodily monsters, it does not lack spiritual ones: namely, those who arrogate and establish for themselves several ecclesiastical benefices or dignities as though they were different heads. St Jerome complains of Vigilantius in this way in his letter to him. The letter begins, “Many monsters [exist] in the world,” which, as appears, the author has used here. Ecclesiastical monsters arose chiefly in the time of Charles Martel, around the year 720. Therefore he deservedly paid eternal penalties, as appears from the Life of Saints Rigobert, Archbishop of Rheims, and Eucherius of Orléans, and also from the annotation in the body of canon law, 16, question 1, *Quia*.

Or with the name of a dignity.] C.: “Or the name of a dignity”; it comes to the same thing.

Perhaps he would be offended.] On account of ambition and pride. He should not be entirely eliminated, as M. has, in place of “he would be held up to ridicule,” or, as they say, “pointed at with a finger.”

To be appropriated to him.] Correct. Not “to be approved,” as M. has.

With what knot may I hold.] N. S., our manuscript, with the printed editions of Horace, book I, epistle 1:

> With what knot may I hold Proteus, who changes his face?

The rustic of Sancerre.] V.: “Of Sancerre,” and adds: “the proper name of a town, which in Latin is called *Sanctum Caesaris*, ‘Caesar’s Saint,’ because Caesar built it very strongly [Col. 0428C] to defend Gaul.”

This person also.] V. seemed to wish to begin a new chapter here, but later silently corrected himself by placing four red dots in the margin.

Many breviaries.] This is the sound reading. What is M.’s “many pairs” (*multos binarios*)?

Let the little crow move.] Two hemistichs of Horace, book I, epistle 3.

For it is theft.] Thus 1, question 2, *Clericos*, after St Jerome’s letter to Pope Damasus, whose words are: “Those who can be supported by the property and resources of their parents, if they receive what belongs to the poor, undoubtedly commit sacrilege and, through the abuse of such things, eat and drink judgment upon themselves. But those clerics ought to be supported by the Church’s stipends for whom no resources of parents or relatives are available.” But what of the rich as well? “Thus securely,” says C. in the margin, “they hold thirty churches, or prebends, or dignities, just as they would twenty arpents of vineyard [Col. 0428D] or land.”

I shall briefly explain what an *arpent* or *arpenna* of land is. *Arpina*, French *arpent*, is also called in Latin *aripennis*. Gregory of Tours uses the term in *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 28. Writing that King Chilperic had burdened his people with taxes, he says: “He decreed that every landholder should pay one amphora of wine from his own land for every 418 *aripennis*.” The word also occurs in the Chronicles of Regino, and in book X, title X, chapter 14 of the Visigothic Code. It is the same as a *jugerum*, as Ragueau—mentioned in the notes to the preceding chapter—writes; it is named as though from *arvipendium* or *arvipennium*. Thus the ancients called the rope with which they measured fields, or the measuring rods. An *arvipennis*, he says, contains one hundred rods, and a rod twenty-six feet, though it is sometimes less according to local variation. Hence, in certain villages, the measure or length of the rod is hung upon, or inserted into, the wall of the local church or bell tower.

CHAPTER XXXIII.

[Col. 0429A]

And holy uniqueness.] *Unicitas* (“uniqueness”) is derived from *unicus* (“only one”); *unitas* (“unity”) from *unus* (“one”).

M., in place of *unicitas*, everywhere has *unitas*. “One” is said of one among many, but “only one” means alone.

Only one and poor.] In unity of faith, actions, and revenues. C. in the margin.

Of faith, sacraments.] V.: “of faith and of the sacrament and of morals”—an abuse by the notary.

Share the burden.] This is absent from C.

CHAPTER XXXIV.

M. continues the preceding chapter.

By which anyone [seeks] singularity.] Like the Jews and Pharisees, C. in the margin.

A double marriage.] Not a double number of wives, as M. and C. have.

They may be induced.] M.: “They may be enclosed.”

For begetting offspring. Nothing is better. Therefore exclude “for obtaining,” as M. wishes.

[Col. 0429B]

If they undertake these things.] C., omitting what immediately follows, says: “If they undertake these things in order to multiply children.”

Because Rachel.] C. varies: “because Rachel—that is, a certain Church—more fruitful in temporal revenues and fruits is preferred to Leah, though Leah is more fruitful in spiritual fruit.” But in the margin it appears corrected as a note: “In temporal revenues she is preferred to Leah, who is more fruitful.” M. has the same in the text as C., except for “and temporal fruits.”

Two churches.] Yet this is forbidden by 21, question 1, *Clericus*.

But not even to one physician.] M. is blank until “Likewise: In such persons.”

Where it is turned.] C.: “There it is turned.”

Deuteronomy, C. XXVIII.] C.: LXIII; V.: LXVII; M.: XLIII.

Let him minister.] C.: “Let him minister in it.”

But the contrary is the case.] M.: “But in the contrary [case].” This too is acceptable. C. makes no sense: “But it is continuous to them.”

419 They do not dig.] They do not dig with a hoe. What is C.’s “they do not *plastinate*”?

They do not stake.] They do not surround or fence with stakes. From *paxilli*, stakes are called *pali* by abbreviation, just as from *axilla*, armpit, comes *ala*, wing. Cicero says so in the *Orator*.

Concerning *marrantia*.] We explained this in the notes to chapter 31.

When in them, on one day.] M. omits this down to “But in one particular [case].”

First, bigamy.] M.: “Earlier, bigamy.” The sense is equivalent.

And thereafter.] M. is silent here down to “Likewise: Isaiah.”

Leaves an heir.] V.: “They leave an heir of all that has been gathered,” etc. It errs in number, because it previously reads “Such a person,” etc.

Isaiah, chapter V.] V. and C.: chapter XIII.

Woe to those who join.] “Even if he himself is a monk,” I shall disclose the marginal notes of C. and M., which say: “Against uncircumcised monks who are masters.” See more in the Moral Gloss on this passage of Isaiah.

[Col. 0429D]

Field to field.] I can scarcely make out C.’s “argument to argument.”

Of the greater place.] M.’s “of the sea-place” is not wrong either.

CHAPTER XXXV.

In the Gospel of John, chapter X.] V. and C.: chapter LXXXIX. This exposition of the scriptural passage is taken from both the interlinear and the ordinary Gloss.

Through the door, Christ.] V.: “Through the door—that is, through humble Christ—namely, lest he enter arrogantly,” etc. The former two readings please me more, although V.’s makes sense in its own way. C., in the margin: “On the false door by which one enters the Church.” I have also placed this in the margin of the text.

In whatever manner.] C. notes in the margin: “By a threefold gift of any kind, or by carnal affection.” By the threefold gift understand a gift from the tongue, the hand, and service; 1, question 1, *Sunt nonnulli*.

Pseudo-[shepherd] and hireling.] M. omits “and,” though it separates the terms with a comma.

If not: what is not his own.] C.: “If the governance of souls [Col. 0430A] has been entrusted to him; if it is not his own, such as patrimony,” etc.

Like a hidden robber.] “This hidden robber is worse than a violent one,” says C. in the margin.

The hidden things of Scripture.] Supply “he discloses.” M. varies considerably here: “He opens a broader way to blessedness by seeking the hidden things of Scripture, not confessions and counsels.” Perhaps the copyist wrote *quaerendo non* (“by seeking, not”) for *quaestionum* (“of questions”).

Of ignorance or sin.] This is the interlinear gloss.

Of which names.] V.: “It is said of which four names.”

As of a genus.] Absent from M. and V.

From Egypt.] C. omits down to “and the sheep follow him.”

By merit and example of life.] V. adds “and example,” from the Gloss on John 10.

420 Truth in the promise.] Gloss on this passage.

[Col. 0430B]

The burning of rivals.] Interlinear gloss on this passage: “the burning of the envious.”

The fruitfulness of the rod.] V.: “fruit-bearing of the rod.”

In Numbers, chapters XVII and XVIII.] Tria: chapters XLIII and XLIV.

Hebrews V.] C. and M.: Hebrews VII.

And no one.] Two marginal readings: “In whatever way, except”—M.: “through Christ’s power”—“according to Christ, can [one enter].”

They chose only two.] Barsabbas and Matthias, Acts 1.

Through foreign and blind [ways].] V.: *per ex solo* [uncertain reading].

CHAPTER XXXVI.

V. continues the preceding chapter without any break.

Corites.] V.: *Coreites*. C., I can scarcely say, has *Corinthians*. Who the Corites are, and how grave an evil their intrusion into ecclesiastical benefices is, will be explained [Col. 0430C] below in chapter 41.

And of superiors.] By “superiors” understand powerful men who, by their authority, intrude clerics into ecclesiastical benefices. C. reads “of others” for “of superiors.”

Jerome in his letter.] In place of this I would say: Jerome, in his commentary on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus, as quoted in 8, question 1, *Moyses*.

So that they may not seek.] I restored this from the original and from Gratian, 8, question 1, *Moyses*. Tria: “So that they may be unable.”

They love with private affection.] This refers to *sanguinitates*, kinship appointees. They are called *sanguinitae* because they are introduced by parents and relatives by reason of blood. Corites are those intruded through the power and authority of a superior. Simoniacs are those admitted by money or another thing, or by service, at an assessable price. To this is added a marginal note: “Cato loved or hated no one from private love or hatred, but according to the merit of life:

> … This house has nothing private.

Yet the words “private affection” are not in Jerome [Col. 0430D] or Gratian.

As though for an hour.] For, as the same margin says: “Taken captive and crucified, he was unarmed.” The same is found in chapter 27.

But with swords and poles.] Warned by Boethius, I judged that this should be restored thus from *The Consolation of Philosophy*. For he has: “You who now anxiously fear spear and sword,” etc. A *contus* is a slender pole, pointed with iron, suitable for defence. Besides a point, it sometimes also has a hooked iron. Sailors use such a pole to detect places dangerous to a ship. Hence, according to Donatus, *percontor*—“I inquire”; today, *percunctor*. V. reads: “But with swords joined together”; C.: “But with bloodstained swords”; M.: “But girded with swords.” What disagreement!

The three ways of choosing.] M.: “Of choosing the aforesaid three men.”

Let him preside by uprightness of morals.] See 1, question 1, *Hi quoscunque*, and *Vilissimus*.

It was simony.] Because it was the sale of a sacred thing.

421 If the priesthood of idols.] Strictly speaking, it was not simony, since an idol is not a sacred thing. Yet because idolaters regarded it as such, it was simony—just as Antiochus, wishing to despoil the temple at Persepolis, was guilty of sacrilege. 2 Maccabees, chapter IX.

Priests of the high places.] C. and M.: “That priests of the high places had the duty of preaching moral uprightness and a rule of life.”

In Luke, chapter II.] M.: chapter LXII; C.: LVII.

So that he may give them.] V. adds “food”: “So that he may give them food.” It is indeed from Psalm 144, but irrelevant.

*Amurca*.] Olive-oil dregs.

The priests of Bel.] C.: *Beli*.

In the Holy of Holies.] V. and M.: “Into the assembly of the saints.”

Deuteronomy, chapter XX.] Tria: LXXXVIII.

Let another dedicate it.] M., between the lines above “dedicate,” reads “enter it.”

Let him perform its office.] C. has instead: “And let another receive it.” It is mistaken.

[Col. 0431B]

They need pedagogues.] I recall that comic saying: “For one who needs a patron, they provide me with a defender; and for one who needs a pedagogue, they appoint me a teacher.” “Does he not fear to become the leader of religious persons,” says St Gregory, “who has never been a soldier?” *Register*, book IV, chapter 95.

Prelates mature in age.] In *Extra, De electione*, thirty years is fixed as the age for a bishop, twenty-five for a curate, and twenty-four for a simple beneficiary: *Cum in cunctis*. Otherwise, those elected beneath the fixed age must be deprived of the benefice: ibid., paragraph *Inferiora*; *Clerici*, Council of Trent, session 23, chapter 6.

Who in virtue.] Of deeds, examples, and instruction in the virtues. Two marginal notes.

From among good things, better things.] M., in the margin, proves by a similar case: “As when a maidservant chooses peas for eating.”

To be made known.] M., in the margin: “And discovered.”

Whenever by a man.] C.: “Whenever ever by a man.” M.: “Whenever ever by a man.”

[Col. 0431C]

Flesh and blood.] That is, the consideration of kinship, not learning, moral character, or another prerogative required in one holding or about to hold a benefice.

A sin of another kind.] Namely, respect of persons. For a person sins gravely who confers an ecclesiastical benefice even upon someone worthy, if he passes over one more worthy. St Thomas teaches this, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 73, article 2. How much more does one sin who confers it upon an unworthy person? Such a person is unworthy with respect to necessary learning, composure of morals, or fitness to exercise the office. Whoever fails in even one of these three is convicted of injustice committed through respect of persons. It is not simony, however, unless the giver intends some personal advantage. The same author, ibid., question 63, article 1, corpus, and article 2, reply to objection 3; likewise question 110, article 5, reply to objection 2.

And mortal.] Lest I render the Word prolonged rather than abbreviated in examining this chapter, I deliberately refrain, referring the reader to St Thomas, II–II, [Col. 0431D] 422 question 63, article 2; Alexander of Hales, part II, question 136, member 2; and Francis Sylvius, doctor of sacred theology of the University of Douai, on this passage of St Thomas, where cases are listed in which it is lawful to confer an ecclesiastical benefice upon a relative. Today young men receive benefices though they are capable neither through learning nor sufficient competence of performing the office. They excuse this on the ground that they will probably become worthy when they mature in age. But let benefice-givers note that a benefice is given for the sake of an office.

I do not define.] Today countless beneficiaries will define it, and indeed without the least scruple.

Base service.] Flattery and such things. So say two marginal notes. By “base service,” understand service improperly rendered, as St Jerome says, volume VII, on Psalm 25, at “Their right hand is full of gifts,” where he distinguishes a threefold gift.

For the bishop’s expenses.] M. read in the text “having been taken on,” but corrected it thus in the margin: “One’s own expenses, with some [uncertain: *mi…*], for an ecclesiastical benefice, are his own.”

I would rather be a thief.] Of two evils the lesser must be chosen. A thief is ordered to be flogged; a robber to be killed, as chapter 41 will show. A thief breaks into houses in order to plunder; a robber despoils people on the road and not seldom kills those whom he has despoiled. Hence Horace: “Robbers rise by night in order to slaughter men.”

Than a Corite.] The reason is given below in chapter 41.

CHAPTER XXXVII.

That ecclesiastical sacraments, except marriage.] Since the Councils of Trent and Florence defined that all sacraments confer grace, this must not be denied of marriage. But the author seems to have followed the Master of the Sentences, book IV, distinction 2, where he distinguishes the sacraments thus: some are remedies against sin and confer assisting grace, such as baptism; others are remedies only, such as marriage. Hence the marginal note justly says: “Here the Master does not think correctly.” Yet St Thomas, writing on the same distinction, defends the Master from error, saying that when he calls marriage a remedy only, he speaks of the end or effect for which it was principally and directly instituted. For although all sacraments avail against sin and give help toward right living, they are nevertheless properly distinguished thus: some were instituted principally to assist a person in good, such as confirmation, the Eucharist, and orders; some as remedies against sin, either to remove it, as penance and extreme unction, or to prevent it, as marriage. Hence St Thomas says: “Marriage is directly ordered to restraining the concupiscence which accompanies marital intercourse; and therefore,” he says, “the Master calls marriage only a remedy, but this is through the grace conferred in it.” Thus he. Baptism, however, is for both effects: through it the old person dies and the [Col. 0432C] new is born.

423 Consecrated to the Church.] V.: “vessels and vestments, the church consecrated.”

The first things are beyond price.] Namely, virtues and miracles, as stated above.

All wrought objects may be sold.] The vessels and vestments of the Church may be sold on account of their material—provided nothing is received for their consecration—and converted to profane uses, provided their form has first been removed; likewise broken vessels. For after being shattered, they are regarded as pure metal. See St Thomas, II–II, question 100, article 4, reply to objection 2.

Once dedicated to God.] *De consecratione*, distinction 5, *Nemo*; Archdeacon, likewise cause 1, question 3, *Si quis objecerit*; *Extra, De religiosis domibus*, chapter *Ad haec*; and in the *Sixth Book*, rule 51: “What has once been dedicated to God is not thereafter to be transferred to human uses.”

In Numbers, chapter XXXI.] M. and V.: chapter LXVI at the end.

Therefore for tricenaries.] St Thomas answers this, II–II, question 100, article 3, reply to objection 2.

[Col. 0432D]

Thus he who [receives] a dignity.] M.: “But he who [receives] a dignity.”

Not about to submit his neck.] M. and C.: “about to submit.”

I designate and indicate.] He calls *indicam* a sign. C.: “I indicate.”

A spoken agreement.] M.: “a voluntary agreement.” It makes no sense.

It has been indicated.] Tria reads thus.

Effective of simony.] Not “affective,” as M. has.

But to give is.] C.: “But to give is, whenever to give that or receive.” M.: “But to give is whenever thus, and to receive.”

By conjectures.] For example, if he says: “That man to whom I did a kindness is ungrateful to me.” So say two marginal notes.

His entry into it.] C.: “his entry to such a thing,” etc.

Or a small piece.] A little fragment. M. expresses this in the margin: *Trunçun* in French, “a slice.”

Conferred by the priest.] No: “inflicted by the priest,” as M. and C. have.

It is not thereby bound.] V. read in the text what the two marginal readings have: “It is not thereby assigned a title; bound,” etc.

CHAPTER XXXVIII.

Breaking of the door.] V.: *fractiva* (“breaking”), but below *fractura* (“fracture”).

Who is Christ.] M.: “Who is Christ.”

From service.] Or, as V. has, “from office.” See I, question 1, *Sunt nonnulli*.

From the *Morals* of St Gregory.] Book IX, chapter 17. But whether these are not rather St Jerome’s words, volume VII, on Psalm 25, at “Their right hand is full of gifts,” let the impartial reader judge.

For a bodily thing.] These are St Gregory’s words in the place cited above.

Of base service.] On this, see St Thomas, II–II, question 100, article 5, reply to objection 1.

But he seems to speak.] V.: “or he seems to speak.”

424 With a corrupt hope.] C.: “with a slight appearance on the part of giver and receiver.”

[Col. 0433B]

Of expectation and conception.] I restored these to the text, as V. advised, although M. and C. read them only in the margin.

Therefore interest and money.] Supply “produce.” I copied this from V. For M. has: “Therefore interest and the money of service without an agreement; thus indeed the service rendered would not be base if it were honorable. For example, etc.” C.: “Therefore the money of service, with execration concerning an agreement; thus indeed the service rendered would not be base if it were honorable—for example, if the giver,” etc.

He has pledged.] M.: “he attacked.” Incorrectly.

Because not immediately.] M.: “That not immediately.”

Of three years.] V. and M.: “of thirty years.”

They will withdraw.] M.: “They are withdrawn from the Church.”

He should assign.] V. added in the text what M. alone has in the margin: “As Pope Alexander.”

Alms.] C.: “Bishop.”

On the part of each.] Namely, giver and receiver. V. and M.: “from the hope of each.” If this is correct, supply “of receiving something.”

[Col. 0433C]

By himself or another.] I do not think the material I found in C.’s lower margin should be omitted. It is as follows: “It is the custom of certain churches that, when a person is instituted in an ecclesiastical benefice, he swears that he has neither given, promised, nor lent money, nor—so far as he knows—has another person given money or service for him under an agreement, so that this benefice may the more readily be conferred. M.”—perhaps the master, author of this work—“But it seems to me that this should be added: neither without an agreement nor with an agreement.” Correctly, because money could be given to that end even when no agreement intervened.

Secretly, he must resign.] By no means “secretly, he must reserve,” as M. has.

This is simony.] V.: “This man is a simoniac unless he is guilty,” etc.

If without distinction.] C.: “If with the least distinction.” Obscurely expressed.

More than offerings.] C.: “More than things brought.” This is certainly preferable, since this manner of speaking is frequent and customary today. Girls entering monasteries are said not to offer, [Col. 0433D] but to bring with them annual revenues or a sum of money.

Or if it is distinguished.] C.: “Or if he is judged among his own, or set apart.”

Temporal revenues.] M.: “Bodily revenues.”

But if perpetual [revenues].] How will abbesses or women superiors of nuns excuse themselves, when with the parents of a girl about to enter a monastery they do not merely negotiate but, like petty women in a marketplace, bargain for two thousand florins or more? Shame! Then will the door of the monastery be closed to poor girls—yet girls of the highest respectability, commendable alike in morals and piety? Today it seems to be according to the poet’s line:

> If you bring nothing, Homer, you will go outside.

Would that such persons carefully heard the warnings of St Jerome, who in chapter 5 of the Rule compiled from his works says: “May your community shrink even from hearing of the detestable heresy of simony, which nuns, through the devil’s widespread perversity, habitually commit.” And below: “Receive sisters who come to you freely for the holy marriage of Christ. Let holiness be preferred to money; let goodness of life be sought, not nobility of flesh or worldly advantage. Let absolutely no bargain, no expectation that disturbs purity of mind, precede.” Moreover, at 1, question 2, near the end: “From the authorities of many it is clearer than light that money may not be demanded from persons entering a monastery, lest both the person who demands it and the person who pays it incur the crime of simony.”

That increase.] M.: “For thus an increase.”

Not well-disposed toward me.] M.: “Not well-disposed toward me.”

What if they are not servants?] These words down to “but surely?” are absent from M.

Where I am to be ordained.] C. and V.: “That I may be ordained.”

Even if it has not preceded.] M. omits this down to “But he extends”; V., however, differs: “Even if, before reception and examination, I give something to one whom I am nevertheless worthy to have examine me, the entry will not be defective, since responsibility for ordination does not rest with him.” V. here observes the contemporary rite and custom. A doorkeeper stands at the door of the room in which candidates for ordination are examined and guards it carefully, lest they enter confusedly all at once. A small coin may be given to him for his service, but not for receiving orders. Nor ought the doorkeeper demand or extort anything from entrants, since he receives wages from his lord the bishop.

[Col. 0434B]

The ordainer’s chaplain.] M. and V.: “the chaplain of those ordained.” He says “of the ordainer,” not “of the bishop,” because there are also abbots who confer orders, though not beyond priestly orders.

Hand-towel.] A cloth with which hands are wiped; see distinction 25, chapter 1, paragraph *Ad subdiaconum*.

The widow received.] The mother of the person being ordained.

Archigallus.] Perhaps this is “archdeacon.”

On account of presentation.] M. omits the word “presentation.”

Canipulum.] M.: *quinipulum*; V.: *kenipulum*. We explained this word above in the notes to chapter 22.

Whence Gregory.] He is Homily 39 on the Gospels. Tria read “Augustine.”

Acceptance.] Why not “acceptation,” with St Gregory?

A reward given to patrons.] Correct according to the teaching of St Gregory; but some pedant wished to correct M.’s text by adding *portionis* (“of a portion”) for *patronis* (“to patrons”) in the margin.

He buys sin.] V.: “They buy sin.”

We do not define.] It is a very slight simony, if it is simony. Margins of C. and M.

426 For you, paradise.] C.: “For you, peace.”

Master Arnulph.] C.: Hervulph.

Canipulum.] I spoke of this a little above.

CHAPTER XXXIX.

M. does not divide the chapter by a new title or by any interval.

The Church to be redeemed.] *Ly redimenda* is absent from M.

Whence Cyriacus.] This occurs in volume I of Surius, in the Life of St Marcellus.

[Col. 0434D]

King Sapor.] Not “Sapon,” as M. and C. have.

Gifts from offerers.] These words down to “grace” were absent from M. and C.

Grievously by God.] Again those three words were omitted. On the punishment of simoniacs, see 1, question 1, *Quidquid invisibilis*.

CHAPTER XL.

For this reason.] M. and V. join this to the preceding material thus: “And what makes exchange simony for this reason: agreement,” etc. V., however, corrects this by a line drawn beneath it in a later hand, so that “exchange” and “agreement” are not separated by a full stop. C.: “And what makes simony. For this reason, by commerce, agreement,” etc.

Of this exchange.] C.: “Of a condition of this sort.”

He will acquire it simoniacally.] M. incorrectly repeats what occurred earlier: “Nevertheless, he will give simoniacally to his nephew.”

And revenues from little purses.] M., at *reddituum*, reads in the side margin: *Trunsum*. I discussed this word in the notes to chapter 37.

[Col. 0435A]

Of some church.] M.: “all the prebends of some person,” omitting “church.”

To have a blemish.] C.: “To have poison.” A *naevus* is a bodily spot. St Bernard, sermon 71 on the Song of Songs: “If there is a blemish in the conscience, neither will that which has proceeded from it lack a blemish.”

Unless it is given freely.] See 1, question 1, *Gratia*.

For not from God.] V. and M.: “Unless you are called by God, unless you ascend through him”—M.: “approach”—“unless you receive freely, namely, by introducing nothing of your own, you take honor to yourself.”

Entering by another way.] M. and V.: “You enter by another way than through the door; you ascend”—M.: “descend”—“by another,” etc.

Although with consent.] M.: “Although in evil consent.”

Concerning an increased pension.] M.: “Concerning a pension to be undertaken.”

Especially held.] M.: “held, especially among cloistered persons.”

427 If between a cleric.] C.: “But between a cleric.”

And a temporary vicar.] C.: “And a perpetual vicar.” Incorrectly.

[Col. 0435B]

CHAPTER XLI.

Into the Church.] V. alone reads this.

Those intruded in this way.] C.: “Now those intruded.”

For just as a robber.] M.: “For if a robber,” etc.

But a Chorite.] Or “but he,” as M. and C. have.

Exceptions.] M. omits this word.

Holiness or sincerity.] V. and M. lack “holiness or.”

From which it will be forged.] V. fails here to the end of the chapter.

CHAPTER XLII.

Uzziah also.] M., omitting the example of Uzziah, mentions Uzzah in this way: “Uzzah also, because he improperly touched the ark of the Lord.” A copyist could easily err in writing this: the two names and the histories are very similar. C. reads Uzzah for Uzziah.

As though if a priest.] These words through “struck with leprosy” I have drawn from V. alone. Consider whether this is not rightly taken from 2 Chronicles [Col. 0435C] 26.

And so Uzzah.] V. fails to the end of the chapter.

CHAPTER XLIII.

V., for the title: “Against kinship appointees.” The summary of this chapter is taken from Micah 3.

To be an impediment.] C.: “to be an impediment,” as above.

About to defraud and despoil.] C. and V.: “We defraud and despoil.”

And with his goods.] C.: “and with his gifts.”

Concerning those entering through flesh.] From here down to “in orders and benefices,” C. and M. fail.

Micah says.] I restored this in place of “Isaiah.” See Micah, chapter 3, and St Jerome’s commentary on this passage. There he explicitly discusses the present subject.

Likewise Jerome.] This passage was cited above at the beginning of chapter XXXVI from 8, question 1, *Moyses*.

Ananias and Sapphira.] Not “Obadiah and Sapphira,” as C. has.

Yet ecclesiastical.] V.: “But ecclesiastical,” etc.; M.: “That ecclesiastical.”

His merit requires it.] V.: “His merit extinguishes and excludes it.” M.: “His property extinguishes,” but in the margin, “excludes.”

428 As though by prescription.] There can be no prescription. What has no legal standing from the beginning is not established by passage of time. Thus Rule XVIII in the Sixth Book.

CHAPTER XLIV.

In 1 Corinthians, chapter XII.] Duo: chapter LX; M.: XL. See also St Gregory, *Morals*, book XXX, chapter VI, in the middle.

Exemption and withdrawal.] C.: “exception or withdrawal”; this is certainly acceptable.

And in usefulness.] V and M: “in the authority of a superior”; the rest is absent.

On *Consideration*.] This work of St Bernard is divided into five books. The passages cited here are therefore found in Book III, a little before the end; from it much else relevant to the present subject may also be gathered [Col. 0436A].

In the delights of paradise.] These are words of Ezekiel, ch. XXVIII.
