Consult also St Jerome’s commentary on this passage, or on Psalm LXXXI: “And like one of the princes you shall fall”; for there he reads not “the seal of likeness” (*signaculum similitudinis*) but “the unsealing” (*resignaculum*).

Captains of fifty.] Three copies add from the Greek: πεντηκοντάρχους, “commanders of fifty.” But why did they repeat the same thing twice?

Captains of a thousand.] From the Septuagint translation; for the Hebrew does not have this.

If he had disturbed.] C: *turpasset*, wrongly. For below follows: “Lest disturbance and division,” etc.

Unless when something.] M is lacking here down to: “Or to Hur.”

Romans XIII.] Three, XLII.

Hebrews XIII.] Three, XXII.

To inferiors or a superior.] C and M have *et* (“and”) in place of *vel* (“or”).

Nor ecclesiastical.] Two copies alike: “Nor ecclesiastical.”

Fief or homage.] Some use *homagium* for *hominium*, as Caesarius and others do. Homage is [Col. 0436B] the bond of service made to a lord by agreement, when a free man promises fidelity and makes himself that lord’s man or vassal. C read in the text “to a lord for homage,” but wrongly.

Nor is the Church a person.] That is, a congregation or community is not a person, to be punished in the manner of a person. For what is done sinfully by a multitude, or by one who has the multitude as his accomplice, is not punished by the Church but bewailed. Thus 23, question 4, *Non potest*. V varies here as follows: “But neither is the Church a person, so that it may be punished personally.”

Personally.] “Like sons,” says M in the margin.

Be bound by homage.] Not “by dominion,” as C again has.

And by a lesser person from whom.] C dislikes the same phrase being repeated twice. Hear it: “And by a successor, by whom he can be absolved; and by an inferior, by whom he cannot be absolved through a superior.”

And this man is bound.] M: “as that man is bound.” Add to this the margins of C and M, describing the custom of certain churches when clerics are instituted there as beneficed clergy: “I swear that I shall render reverence and obedience to you, your successors, and this Church” (C: “obedience reverently,” but corruptly).

By sacramental collation.] M is mistaken: “by the conclusion of the sacraments.”

Therefore not by jurisdiction either.] Supply, as above, “to deprive.” C varies thus: “Therefore neither the jurisdiction of the collation of orders.”

Justly excommunicated.] V has *jure* (“by right”) for *juste* (“justly”); the sense is equivalent. M corruptly has *iste* (“this man”) for *juste*.

He who has bound.] M is silent here down to: “By authority of a superior.”

Love justice.] The margins of two copies also suggest this authority from Psalm II: “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth.” To this may be added from Psalm XCVIII: “The honour of the king loves judgment.”

In which you have been set over others.] Restored from V. For the other two read very obscurely: “In which you who have been appointed [Col. 0436D] judges and superiors, offending subjects and inferiors” (what sense is this?).

But not even then.] Rule of law 76, in the *Sixth Book*.

II Corinthians XIII.] Three, XXVIII.

To have been or to be.] V and M omit the particle “or to be.”

Judges VIII.] Two copies, apart from V, have Judges X, at the end.

Against the altar of the Lord.] C: “against the Lord.”

A thing sacrificed.] C: “of those sacrificing.”

And concerning the bishopric.] Omitting this, C reads: “In his bishopric, and not under a bishop.”

And in the bishopric.] C: “concerning his bishopric” (the rest omitted), “of himself.” To this is added the example of Abbot Suger, recorded in the margins of C and M. It is as follows: “Abbot Suger, when labouring at the point of death, summoned the lord bishop of Paris and, like a son to his father, confessed to him, declaring that he had not procured the emancipation of his monastery from the power (C: ‘as from the power’) of the Church of Paris, but [had done so through] a certain deacon.”

If the horns of the mitre.] By the horns of the mitre the New [Col. 0437A] and Old Testaments are signified, as is clear from the Gloss on Matthew V: “You are the salt of the earth.” Hence St Benedict, in ch. 64 of his Rule: “A superior ought to be learned in the divine law, so that he may know and have from where to bring forth things new and old; and he should know that it is more fitting for him to benefit others by spiritual teaching and example than to preside by bodily presence or care of temporal things.”

From a little paper.] That is, from a small slip or piece of paper folded into the shape or appearance of a mitre. Idle little boys in elementary schools are accustomed to make similar objects. V and M: “from a note”; C: “from a diligent [thing].” They make no sense.

If his ring.] Namely, the boys just mentioned.

And if it can be repeated.] Or, “if it can be reiterated.”

Bishop Gilbert.] Surnamed de la Porée, or Porretanus. He was the sixty-first bishop of Poitiers, as appears from the catalogue in Claude Robert’s *Gallia Christiana*. He wrote much, and in the presence of St Bernard he abjured his errors before Pope Eugenius III in the year 1148. Baronius, under the year stated.

[Col. 0437B] With imposition of hands.] That is, it does not imprint a character.

Which has already been done in part.] After this V continues: “of which the Apostle,” etc.; the other copies omit it.

From the Roman empire.] The margins of two copies: “From which Greece has now withdrawn.” Here I bring back a double example which I gathered from those margins. “Having been absolved by Pope Alexander” (M adds between the lines: “through favouritism”), “whom St Luke of Hungary had excommunicated because he had not made satisfaction to St Luke, he was excommunicated by him again and again; and therefore Luke himself was suspended by Alexander, then excommunicated, and thus died. For him God worked many miracles after his death.”

“A certain count, excommunicated by his ordinary bishop and afterwards absolved by papal authority, still believed himself bound by two other bishops. Therefore he fled to his own bishop, confessed to him, and made satisfaction. Thus he departed absolved and without scruple.”

By objecting, I introduce.] C: “I object, I judge.”

[Col. 0437C] And led by private law.] C reads, not badly, “led,” if an appeal is made to the pope.

Consuls and proconsuls.] M, in the outer margin: “Bishops and archbishops.”

Let Caesar be everything.] From Lucan, Book II, or Alan, Book I, at the end.

## CHAPTER XLV

Or of execution.] Thus C. The other two have only “of base compliance.”

For a gift freely.] M and C: “For a gift less freely.” They do not understand.

Oil in the bones.] C: “in his mouth.”

Augustine: Oil.] The same author on Psalm CXL: “When men have mocked someone with false praise, they also say this of him: ‘I anointed his head.’”

Sellers of oil.] Words of St Jerome on Matthew XXV.

Frogs are flatterers.] On them see St Augustine, vol. X, Sermon 87 *On Time*; and St Jerome on Psalm CIV.

The crowd of greeters.] A verse of Claudian, *Against Rufinus*, Book I [Col. 0437D]. Thus the margin of C explains the words “crowd of greeters”: “Of applauding flatterers,” it says, “or rather secret detractors.” I recall that couplet of Peter of Riga in his *Aurora*, not yet published but soon, God granting strength, to be published. Thus in Exodus VIII:

> The dog-fly, staining food, stinging gluttons,  
> And biting, may be marked by its savage tooth.

Gnats.] M, in the margin: “Tiny flies.” On them the same Peter of Riga, in the same place:

> The talkative frog signifies heresy: this one croaks, that one croaks;  
> This or that swells with clamorous sounds.  
> Gnats dart about, disturbing human rest,  
> And signify wanderers who remain without peace.

Dog-fly.] “Dog-fly.” Both margins.

[lacuna] “Good, good!”] The first is mocking, the second flattering. The same authorities.

He comes out whole.] V: “he will be whole.”

[Col. 0438A] He who flatteringly.] This has the smell of the interlinear Gloss on this passage.

And the heads of the Church.] M: “and its heads.”

Whose head is sick.] C: “whose head is weak.” This too is acceptable.

For the error of a prince.] C is silent here down to: “Likewise.”

So severe.] C: “so followed.” The Cameron fragment: “No one is so rigid, and severe or followed.”

By which you fall when you climb.] Thus V; but the other two, with the Cameron fragment, read: “By which you fall”; supply “with the tongue,” and the reading is tolerable.

And preserved for you.] Restored from Juvenal, *Satires* IV, from the manuscript and printed copies, thus with the Cameron fragment; otherwise the three ordinary copies have:

> A turbot is kept, to consume ages, for you.

He receives an *endromis*.] Restored from our manuscript of Juvenal. The three copies have *endromadem*. An *endromis* is a thick garment (or, as the margin of C says, a fox-fur garment), very suitable for warding off winter’s injuries.

[Col. 0438B] For this reason they are to be feared.] Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book VI, ch. 30. See things not unlike this in St Jerome on Ezekiel XXXIV, on “You killed what was fat.”

As his companion.] C rejects “to entrust to him.”

Demaratus alone.] Not *Demoratus*, as M has. Consult Seneca, *On Benefits*, VI.31.

These are sirens.] Words of Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I, prose 1.

With Ulysses.] This recalls Seneca, Epistle 56, in its final period; from that place I restored *Ulysse* for *Ulixe*.

Whence Jerome.] Book I against the Pelagians, ch. 9. Also vol. IX, *To Demetrias, On Virginity*, after the middle.

Amasa’s chin.] By no means “Amaziah’s,” as C has.

In the groin.] The three copies read thus. But if you consider the history in II Kings XX, you will find that Amasa was not struck in the groin, but in the side. Abner, however, who was likewise treacherously slain by the same Joab, received a blow in the groin. St Gregory explains this treacherous betrayal by Joab in the *Morals*, XV.5, at the end.

The sword is the eye.] V: “the sword is sharp.”

[Col. 0438C] Jeremiah XXXVIII.] C and V: CXXXV.

Peaceful prophets.] Although M reads only “prophets,” it correctly recalls the Gloss. For the Gloss on this passage, “Men at peace,” says: “False prophets announcing peace to you.”

And nurse of pride.] The margins of C and M: “For,

> . . . . . . . . . . . Yet those men  
> Rose in their crests.” — Juvenal, *Satires* IV.

When we speak with God, [we use] the singular.] As there: “Give me, Lord, the seat of your wisdom,” etc., Wisdom IX. Likewise David: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments,” Psalm CXVIII.

We address a human being in the plural.] Caesarius very frequently employs this mode of speech in his books of memorable examples: “Thus, Lord, you have given me,” etc. This usage has also become established among the French: they never, or at least very rarely, use the singular pronoun *tu*, but use the plural even when speaking to one person only: “You have given” for “you have given,” and so in other cases.

You wish to name her.] M: “To name them.”

Carthage IV, distinction 56.] Two copies: distinction (or chapter) 46; M: 14.

Jerome in the letter.] To Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*. You will find nearly the same material in the letter to Celantia beginning, “The celebrated Old Scripture.” Besides, I ask you to consult Seneca, Epistle 123, in the middle.

Ecclesiasticus XIII.] Three: XL.

Deuteronomy XIV.] V: XCIII; M: LXV; C: XLV.

Song of Love I.] M and C: II.

In falsehood.] There is variation here. C: “because, being unaware, you delighted yourself in meditation and flattery”; the other two: “because you are unaware.”

Isaiah III.] V and C: VIII; M: VII.

## CHAPTER XLVI

The summary of this chapter in V is as follows: “Against those who accept as though lawfully even things acquired from others unlawfully, or even lawfully, while knowing this, and without inquiry” [Col. 0439A].

And even of things lawfully acquired.] This passage down to “There remains” is absent from V.

It seems to be sold.] C uses “world” in place of “sold,” etc.

For in things in which.] There is variation here. C says: “For in things in which we thus do not have a right of ownership, we cannot transfer it to others.” M: “For in things in which we do not have a right, we could not transfer a right of ownership to others.”

The sin is not forgiven.] Rule of law 4 in the *Sixth Book*.

For pious causes.] The margins of C and M: “From things found, acquired by use, and prescribed, alms may perhaps be made, while the owner is ignorant (C: ‘being ignorant’) and if conscience does not reproach one. See 14, question 5 throughout.”

The possessor’s part is the stronger.] Rule 65 in the *Sixth Book*.

If someone has received ten.] Namely, ten solidi.

By that rule.] Mentioned above: namely, Rule 65 in the *Sixth Book*.

433 A receiver from secondary recipients.] V: “receipts” [Col. 0439B] for “receivers.”

Of Abbot Stephen, the second.] Some make this Stephen the third abbot of Cîteaux. Among them are the most deserving Jean d’Assignies, abbot of Nizelles, in his French book entitled *The Cabinet of the Most Notable Things of the Sacred Order of Cîteaux*; and Chrysostomus Henriquez in the *Menologium of the Cistercian Order*, for 28 March and 17 April, where he treats him at length. Yet Peter the Chanter, below in ch. 105 as well, calls him the second.

Separately to beggars.] M: “to beggars divided”; C: “a divided beggar.”

They gave a cask of wine.] By *cadus* we should not understand a large jar, or what the common people call a “little daughter,” but a portable vessel holding five or six Belgian *loten*. In French, *cacque* or *barrile*. Thus Budé, *On the As*, Book V, before the middle: “From Pliny we learn that casks had a conical, that is, pine-cone-shaped form; for in Book XVII, speaking of aloe, he called them ‘cask-cones.’” The ancients also used them for preserving salted provisions. So he writes.

He distributed all those things.] M: “He distributed them to everyone.” I think these were only the things he had received from that simoniacal shepherd.

A cooked dish.] Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XX, ch. 2: “A *pulmentum* is derived from *puls* [porridge]. For whether porridge or anything else is taken mixed with something, it is properly called a *pulmentum*.”

I would call every relish eaten with bread a *pulmentum*, whether seasoned or prepared from herbs, fish, or another edible material. This seems to be implied by the blessed Father Benedict in his Rule: “We believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for the daily meal, whether at the sixth or ninth hour, on all tables, because of differing infirmities, so that perhaps one who cannot eat of one may be restored by the other.”

Religious people everywhere.] Here, I think, should be brought back an example [Col. 0439D] which I saw written in the lower margin of C and M: “By the example also of a knight meeting the corpse of his moneylender, carried to its burial by a crowd of monks. To them he said: ‘You leave me my flies and spiders’ webs; but you have the corpse of a spider, while hell has his soul. Why did you not order him to restore what he had taken?’” This example seems to have belonged in the text, as may be inferred from ch. 50.

He says in ch. 3, “To tax collectors.”] M and C: ch. 19.

Ambrose and Bede.] V corruptly omits “and Bede.” For the Venerable Bede and St Ambrose read in Luke at this place: “That they should exact nothing beyond what is prescribed.”

Or by forced service.] These words are absent from V.

Or what has been fixed.] C, omitting “or,” reads: “What has been prescribed and fixed.”

A written judgment.] The margins of C and M: “For judgment must be made according to the laws prescribed by the Lord (M wrongly: ‘vindicated’), not according to Justinian laws”—C: “justices,” also wrongly.

[Col. 0440A] You who are able to do this.] V reads this parenthetical expression in the text; M in the outer margin. On John’s words, “Extort from no one,” see St Augustine, Sermon 3 in the Appendix *On Various Subjects*, vol. X.

A rule for discernment.] V: “A rule for learning.”

Beyond what is prescribed.] Not “above what is written,” as M and C have.

St Fursey.] On him see the Venerable Bede, *History*, III.19, where he tacitly reports what is said here; it is stated openly in Fursey’s Life in Surius, vol. I, 16 January, and below in the notes copied from the margin of V for ch. 50.

St Launomarus.] His deeds appear in Surius, vol. I, 19 January.

An immense vicious giver.] C: “an immense giver,” excluding “vicious”; M: “a vicious giver,” omitting “immense”; V retains both.

In a small offering.] C adds in the outer margin: “Not of one denarius.” M, in the same place: “A coin of one denarius”—wrongly.

Private communion.] C alone accepts this.

But if not even money.] C: “If not money.” To the words “a large sum of money” it adds in the margin: “Such as one denarius.”

Like an infamous person.] M: “Although also infamous and notorious.” But in the margin: “To be prescribed by the Church.”

Scandal would arise.] M: “The scandal would wonder.” It has gone wrong.

Peter Abelard.] C and M: Abaelis. St Bernard convicted him of error; he is an author of the first class in the Index of Prohibited Books, but he repented of his errors and recanted them.

Count Theobald.] Perhaps the count of Champagne, of whom Caesarius writes in VIII.31; or Theobald, count of Chartres and Blois, of whom Cantimpratensis writes in *The Universal Good of Bees*, II.25, nos. 14 and 15.

He refused to accept.] V and C: “He wished to accept.” Absurdly.

Likewise Ecclesiasticus XXXIV.] M and C: XXII.

Into offerings.] Restored from Ecclesiasticus XXXIV. For the other two have “in offerings,” M “in prayers.”

[Col. 0440C] Gloss: “Which.”] This is the interlinear Gloss. M, omitting the word “Gloss,” read *quorum* (“of whom”) for *quam* (“which”).

They receive gifts.] Not “they deceive gifts,” as M has.

Achan and his companions.] The name has been restored. The three copies have Achor, which is the name of a valley.

Jerome.] M omits the name.

Through that many are lost.] For the author says below, *On Property*, ch. 153: “It is scarcely found that a multitude has been punished for certain sins, except for a sin of sacrilege of this kind.”

Ephod and teraphim.] M, in the margin: “Images.” C: “Seraphim,” wrongly; see Judges XVII and XVIII, likewise Hosea III.

435 Gideon and his whole house.] Because he had previously followed (C: “obtained by lot”) foreign gods. Thus the margins of C and M.

King Agag.] The three copies read Eglon for Agag, wrongly. I have therefore restored the name. In Judges III it is indeed said [Col. 0440D] that Eglon was exceedingly fat and obese, but he was not spared as Agag was; rather, he was killed by Ehud.

Therefore the rule is that a thing unlawfully acquired is never, etc.] That is, it is universally true because something unlawfully acquired is theft.

For the sake of preaching.] The margins: “For example, if a preacher eats with him for this reason.”

But not even what has been lawfully acquired.] M must by no means be heeded: “But it seems lawfully acquired.”

Safe and remaining.] V, omitting these words, reads: “Unless he has from where,” etc.

I think, from him.] M: “Against this rule also, things received when I give,” reading *cum do* (“when I give”) for *credo* (“I think”). The rest as in the text.

Concerning things sacrificed to idols.] M corruptly reads: “Because it is not to be understood concerning things sacrificed to idols.” For the interlinear Gloss on “Asking no questions” says: “Whether it is a thing sacrificed to an idol or not.” An *idolothytum* is something sacrificed to an idol. C had in the text *idolathycis* for *idolothytis*.

Those seated and eating in an idol-temple.] Thus *in idolio* has been restored for [Col. 0441A] *idolo*, from I Corinthians VIII, where one reads: “One reclining in an idol-temple.”

Those not corrected.] C: “the uncorrected,” perhaps “those not corrected.” In the margin there I see added: “For wealthy persons it should be put in a bag, not distributed, until they restore what they have taken.”

Likewise Ephesians IV.] M is lacking here to the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER XLVII

V has this summary: “Against those who give to persons not in need: for one who is not in need sins if he accepts gifts, and likewise the one who gives to such a person.”

Not to parasites.] Γνάθων, *gnatho*, a hanger-on for food. Hence Terence: “Gnatho the parasite.” That is, one wholly dependent on food. M and C read: “Not to nathonibus.”

Not to *permenones*.] Μενοινή is used for desire, from the verbs μενοινάω and μενοινέω, meaning “I wish” or “I desire.” C wished *permetionibus* to be read; V has *permenunibus*; both are wrong.

[Col. 0441B] And the Blessed Virgin.] V is silent down to: “Likewise, by the example of Elisha.”

Filled, we fill.] Or, as M and C have, “Having been filled, we fill,” when the measure is overflowing.

Luke XIV.] C and M: ch. LXXX.

Or a supper.] The two margins: “A modest provision of food.” But why? Because less should be eaten at supper than at dinner. Hence the School of Salerno:

> From a great supper comes the stomach’s greatest pain;  
> To be light at night, let your supper be short.

Some physicians maintain, from Hippocrates (*On Diet*, II) and Galen (*Method*, VII.6, and *On Diet in Acute Diseases*, I.18), that stronger food should be given to the body at supper than at midday; but experience is contrary. For everyone is generally readier for work through a light supper than through abundance. And someone aptly said: “What you subtract from supper, you add to life.”

And you shall be blessed.] M: “And you shall be freed,” contrary to the text [Col. 0441C] of the Gospel.

In the same chapter XIV.] Two copies: in the same Luke, ch. LXXXI.

In the third canonical epistle.] Two add the chapter number: ch. II. But today it is not divided into chapters.

Of a very wealthy monastery.] “By the example of a rich monk,” C says, “who in the monastery advised someone wishing to enter his cloister,” etc.—obscurely. Here C notes in the margin what I found in other copies at the end of the preceding chapter: namely, “For wealthy persons it should be put into a bag, not distributed, until they restore what they have taken.”

Those dwelling there.] “So that they might have needy poor of Christ to feed,” says M.

So greatly.] M makes one adverb from these two syllables and separates it from the preceding sentence, thus: “He received pardon. So no one is,” etc.

Isaiah I.] M: ch. II.

By delivering.] C: “by excepting”; M omits the words “By delivering them from their oppression,” and has instead: “By distributing his own goods.”

[Col. 0441D] The orphan and the needy.] “Cursed is he who perverts the judgment of the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow,” Deuteronomy XXVII.

May they help by patronage.] M: “May they assist the patron”; V: “May they help” only.

If she is useful to someone.] The margins of C and M: “That is, if she can work to seek her livelihood. There is a book entitled *The Widow of Zarephath*, recently brought by us out of obscurity, in which these matters and what follows concerning widows are explained more fully.”

Sixty years of age.] C alone has this. Consult cause 1, question 2, *Honour Widows*. And the explicit wording is I Timothy V: “Let a widow be chosen not less than sixty years old.”

Interlinear.] This is the ordinary Gloss, also that of St Augustine on this verse of Psalm CII.

Ecclesiasticus XII.] M and C: ch. XXXVIII.

And you shall give to kinsfolk.] M: “And you shall give with blood-relations”; *dabis* (“you shall give”) would have to be repeated: “from your own goods,” etc. C: “and to blood-relations.”

[Col. 0442A] It has been entrusted.] C quite properly: “It has been handed over,” that is, entrusted. St Jerome says in the letter to Paulinus beginning “A good man”: “The things you possess are no longer yours, but their stewardship has been entrusted to you,” at the end of the letter.

A pillar in the Church.] C: “A pillar of the Church.”

From the patrimony of the Crucified One.] Hear the margins of M and C: “Some, from this patrimony, namely, improperly marry off their nieces.”

And rather grace.] The same margins: “Grace is given when it is given to a needy, righteous, wise person, even to a prelate set over you, because of some grace belonging to him.”

Lives of the Fathers.] A book containing examples of the holy Fathers, hermits, though not accepted by everyone.

To a parent, a son.] C: “to a perishing son,” etc. It makes no sense.

In which you may understand.] V, after “Their revenues,” has: “In which [consider] what you intend and how much care ought to be taken,” etc. C omits “Because it must be given also”; the remainder [Col. 0442B] as in the text.

A certain man approaching another.] The former was called the Cynic Thrasyllus; the latter whom he approached was King Antigonus, of whom Plutarch writes in the *Apophthegms*, and after him Seneca in the marginally cited place. V says instead of the marginal note: “See how corruptly these two examples are introduced (or ‘clothed’) here. For in Book II of Seneca’s *On Benefits* it is read thus.” He cites Seneca’s words, which I omit for brevity. See Book II, chs. 16 and 17.

See to whom you give.] Or: “Trust, but see to whom.”

It is no less shameful.] This is gathered from St Augustine on Psalm CII, verse 6: “He who gives to actors, he who gives to soothsayers, he who gives to prostitutes—why does he give? Do they not also give to human beings? Yet in this they do not regard the nature of God’s work, but the wickedness of human work.” And below: “For if he were only a man and were not a hunter, soothsayer, or prostitute, you would not give. You honour in him the vice, not the nature.” Again I refer the reader to cause 23, question 4, *Duo ista*.

When they cannot.] C and M: “When it cannot be removed.”

Who [gives] not according to how much.] M: “who [gives] not so much.”

Give, therefore, because [he is] a prophet.] I have seen similar remarks in St Augustine, vol. VIII, on Psalm CII, verse 6.

The sinner and the actor.] It is an enormous sin to give one’s goods to actors. See distinction 86, *Donare*.

How without murmuring.] C: “How much without murmuring.” Wrongly.

Do not increase what has been increased.] This was proverbial. M: “Do not increase what has been done,” incorrectly.

Do not enrich the rich.] M: “Do not imitate the rich.” Cicero: “How unfairly arranged it is that something is always added to those who are richer.”

Jerome in that letter.] Cited at 8, question 1, *Moses the Friend of God*.

Just as not the seven.] C reads: “Just as not the seven deacons ordained by St Peter would have preferred [Col. 0442D] their own kinsmen to others for this office.” According to Rabanus, this order must be observed: the people choose and the bishop ordains. See him on this passage. Acts VI does not state by which Apostle they were ordained, but says they were ordained by the Apostles; and it is altogether likely that the other Apostles yielded that honour to St Peter as their head, just as the more worthy bishop usually ordains another and becomes his consecrator.

438 They change their condition.] That is, they enrich their relatives so as to make them, from poor people and servants, rich people and masters. Yet this may not be done from Church goods, though it may rightly be done from one’s own patrimony, or, as the margins of C and M say, “unless it comes from landed property and from things which fall to you by hereditary right.” Nevertheless, a bishop or other prelate may advance a relative to a financial office or another post according to his capacity; nor will such a person be judged to have profited from spiritual goods if he becomes wealthy or a knight from the income of his office. In [Col. 0443A] similar cases, one must avoid in one’s neighbour matter for envy and another evil appearance, and in the promoted person, pride. There is an example on this matter in Cantimpratensis, *On the Universal Good of Wealth*, I.18.

To have abandoned humility.] The lower margins of C and M continue this example—which V has in the text—as follows: “At whose feet Master Anselm fell, with his head covered and wrapped, asking that he would grant him his single request, worthy of being heard. For at that time, on account of the killing (V: ‘occasion’) of the bishop of Laon (C: Langdon), the judgment of the said seneschal had involved the just with the unjust, and he had imprisoned Master Anselm’s nephews along with others. Seeing that he had been heard, and recognizing him as Master Anselm when his venerable head was uncovered, he said: ‘Wretched and unhappy man that I am, I am nothing, since so great a man as Master Anselm, the mirror of the Church and light of Holy Scripture, has today fallen at my feet. Whereas until now I could avenge myself for every injury inflicted upon me by any powerful person whatever, I shall not be able to avenge this affront’ (M: ‘this injury’) ‘inflicted on me by so great a man. For it cannot but happen that he has fallen at my feet: he who, when there was once discussion of his promotion, said that he was the son of a deacon who, however, before becoming a subdeacon, had been in lawful marriage. He even showed a blemish on his thumb, saying that, if he were crucified’ (M and V: ‘when he had been crucified’) ‘at the altar, the people would be scandalized by it, and that for this reason he could not be chosen.’ Yet he was afterwards elected [Col. 0443B] archbishop of Canterbury.” C ends thus: “Yet after the election he was imprisoned.” Return to the text: “Likewise, some things are,” etc.

That [you give] to kinsfolk.] St Jerome in the letter to Demetrias beginning “Among all subjects,” says: “Give to the poor, not to the rich, not to relatives, not for luxury but for necessity. Whether he is a priest, kinsman, or relation by marriage, consider nothing else in him except poverty.” Besides this, see cause 8, question 1, *Moses*.

Isaiah III.] M in the margin, C in the text: ch. VIII.

Nor defend.] M, between the lines: “Unless he ought to give the exacted tithes.”

To those sinning more grievously.] M also admits between the lines “even worse”; but St Jerome on that passage of Isaiah has “to those sinning more grievously.” You will see similar material in his letter against Vigilantius, before the end, beginning “Many in the world.”

Likewise Jerome.] Besides the end of the letter to Nepotianus beginning “You ask of me,” see cause 12, question 2, *The Glory of a Bishop*, and his Commentary on Ezekiel XLVI, verse 18: “And the prince shall not take,” etc.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

V has as its summary: “Against those who improperly receive gifts when they are not in need.”

Clerics who [live] from goods.] In the rule under the title *On Poverty* [Col. 0443D]. It is also cited at 1, question 2, *Clerics*, and 16, question 1, final chapter.

The wealth of parents.] Not “the works,” as M has.

O monk.] See the aforesaid rule of the same St Jerome under *On Poverty*, vol. IX. Then read through his commentary on Psalm CXLV, “He gives food to the hungry,” vol. VII.

You give rather than.] C: “Rather than giving, you do not receive.” It makes no sense.

They make people liars.] They make [people] deceitful, so that even those speaking the truth are not believed; or, as Cicero says in *On Divination*, II: “We are accustomed not to believe a lying man even when he tells the truth.”

The true poor person is believed.] M: “Which does not suit the true poor.”

But it should be noted that.] These words down to “For certain persons” are absent from C.

In time of famine.] C: “in the sluggishness of famine.” It is mistaken.

This care.] M: “This indulgence is not applied.” I do not understand it.

[Col. 0444A] In the common way.] Correctly. Therefore not “tribally,” as M and C have.

Like Proteus.] From Horace, Book I, Epistle 1:

> With what knot may I hold Proteus, who changes his face?

What [is] a poor man? etc.

Trickery.] A *trutannus*, according to John of Genoa in his dictionary entitled *Catholicon*, that is, “universal,” derives from *trudo* (“I thrust”), because he thrusts with his words in order to deceive; for he makes one believe what is not true. *Trutannia* is such deception.

And this is twofold.] C: “And this is twofold.”

For they defraud.] V and M: “They have defrauded.”

Once dedicated to God.] Thus Rule 51 in the *Sixth Book* defines it.

From this rule.] Rule 66 there.

By analogy.] Here may be brought back the marginal note of C and M: “So it is with an error as to the person introduced in marriage”; M: “introduced in number,” absurdly.

[Col. 0444B] Deceit is owed to no one.] Rule 59 in the *Sixth Book*: “He acts deceitfully who demands what he himself ought to restore.”

Thus received.] V: “thus received” in the singular.

Let them be distributed.] V consequently: “let it be distributed.”

440 ## CHAPTER XLIX

Gamblers.] C omits this.

Thessalonians V.] M: ch. IX. The other two do not note a chapter.

That is, busybodies.] This is the interlinear Gloss, which also adds “wanderers.”

From which, he who ceases.] “From which,” that is, from correction, “he who ceases.” M: “From which, when he ceases.” V: “Those whom he therefore ceases to correct lest he lose,” etc. This indeed seems clearer, but we did not judge it should be restored to the text. Why? Because the words of the interlinear Gloss on this passage—which are St Augustine’s—are preferable.

II Thessalonians III.] M: ch. IV. See the Glosses on these Apostolic passages.

[Col. 0444C] But if anyone should not wish.] V: “Those who should not wish.”

The same Epistle, ch. III.] Three: ch. V.

Through Jesus Christ.] V omits this down to: “To whom be honour.” This is the interlinear Gloss with what follows.

That you withdraw yourselves.] V likewise omits this from the text but restores it in the upper margin.

Withdraw yourselves, namely.] C: “Withdraw yourselves thus from every,” etc.

Augustine: He wishes.] You have this first in the ordinary Gloss; then, if you desire the source, see St Augustine, vol. III, *On the Work of Monks*, ch. II. C reads *velut* (“as if”) for *vult* (“he wishes”).

Should preach the Gospel.] C has—painful to say—“should scandalize.”

Not rumour-mongers.] This is the interlinear Gloss. V: “Rumour-mongers”; C and M: “ruminating people.” A rumour-monger is one who carries rumours, whence *rumigerulus*.

Let him be ashamed when cast down.] Margin of C: “From the sentence issued.”

[Col. 0444D] False [brethren] are to be repelled.] See the Gloss on this passage. C: “Because of false repellers.”

Preaching.] V alone accepts this single word.

I Thessalonians IV.] C and V: ch. VI; M: ch. VII.

Leaving other people’s affairs.] The margins of M and C add a verse of Horace:

> . . . Such men attend to other people’s affairs.

Ecclesiasticus XII.] V: ch. XXXVIII; M: ch. XXXIV; C: ch. XXXIII.

To him [it is] to be given.] C: “For him to give.”

And to actors.] V omits this.

Because they are sinners.] This recalls St Augustine’s teaching, vol. VIII, on Psalm CII, verse 6. The same author elsewhere on actors: “To give to actors is an enormous vice,” vol. IX, Tractate 100 on the Gospel of John.

With whom you eat.] These are Seneca’s words, Epistle 19, after Epicurus. To this may be referred the margin of C and M [Col. 0445A]: “For example, if you eat with an actor.”

Unless you withdraw.] Again the same margin: “That you may depart as a poor man from fellowship with such people.”

441 Nomenclator.] C and M: “a giver of names.” V: *nomenculator*, and adds: “That is, a giver of names.” Restored from Seneca. If you desire a fuller explanation, consult Lipsius, the glory of the Belgians, on that author. Do you further seek the etymology of *nomenclator*? Here V gives it in the margin: “*Nomenculator*,” it says, “is the name of a lowly office, namely, of one who calls guests by name, derived from *nomen* and the Greek *kalo* (καλέω or καλῶ), meaning ‘I call’; from this also the Kalends are so named.”

Efficacy judges.] M: “indicates” for “judges.”

Friends to be won.] C: “minds” for “friends.”

A serious enemy.] C is mistaken: “a weighty enemy,” as is clear from the original.

If bestowed.] Thus V and C in the text. But C has “if placed” in the margin; M has “if placed” in the text, and “if bestowed” between the lines [Col. 0445B]. Justus Lipsius, on “If bestowed,” says: “Given with judgment; though some books have ‘if placed,’ which also suits this sense.”

Who, than.] V: “whoever.”

Likewise Jerome: Equal things.] Hear St Augustine: “To give one’s goods to actors is an enormous vice, not a virtue. And you know how common is the report concerning such people, accompanied by praise; because, as it is written: ‘The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who does iniquity is blessed’ [Psalm IX]. These praisers are not mistaken about the persons, but about the things. For what they believe to be good is evil.” Vol. IX, Tractate 100 on the Gospel of John. The same author says on Psalm CII, verse 6: “He who gives to an actor loves in him that in which he is most wicked.” Distinction 86, *Donare*, and *Qui venatoribus*.

By no virtue.] V puts “from vices” first, which the other two place later. Thus: “Redeemed from vices by no virtue, [he gives] out of necessity,” etc.

[Col. 0445C] If you say what is fitting.] C: “what is accepted.”

He declared war.] Not “he brought in war,” as C has.

Likewise Jerome: “Not only …”] See the letter to Oceanus, which begins: “Never, my son Oceanus,” before the end of vol. II.

Indeed today.] C. omits this passage down to: “Likewise these by their account.”

Because to the worst.] C.: “because from the worst.”

Had favoured.] M. and C.: “because from the worst.”

Had favoured.] M. and C.: “had suggested” for “had favoured.”

And by not correcting him.] But by keeping him from repentance. C., however: “and by not correcting him, by withdrawing or keeping [him] from childhood.” M.: “by keeping [him] from repentance.”

Namely, from another’s property.] V. has only “namely.”

Glutton and licker. [Note: [Col. 0445] A *lecator* is called a glutton; in French, *un lichard*.]] Just as *popinones* are named from taverns (*popinae*), so *ganeones* are named from *ganeae*. A *ganea* is a secluded, as it were underground, place frequented by gluttons and those devoted to sexual indulgence. *Leccatores* are so called from *lingo*, “I lick,” because they eat up and virtually devour whatever is set before them; and they lick and lap dishes so elegantly that you would say they had not yet been soiled by sauce or stew. [Col. 0445D] For more on the *ganea*, see the commentary of Libertus Fromondus on Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, book VII, chapter XXXII and the final chapter.

442 Had imitated.] By no means “had invited,” as C. has it.

Sixty solidi.] C.: forty.

Whence Virgil.] *Georgics* IV.

## CHAPTER L

The talent of nature.] The Cambron fragment, after the words “their souls,” says: “But it should be noted that there is a talent of nature, of grace, of fortune or money, of punishment, and of fault. But the talent of nature and grace commands,” etc. These additions are highly pleasing; had I found them in even one of the three exemplars, I would have restored them to the text. M. has this marginal note: “God, in giving [Col. 0446A] nature and grace, so that with ap . . . or gain re . . . A person may receive, with a manifold talent, a golden [thing] and a . . .”

Augustine: Usury.] Although C. alone has this, Augustine is rightly cited, for it is in vol. VIII, on Psalm LIV, verse 12. Verse 14 is noted in the margins of M. and C.

“Which the field will repay with manifold interest.” Ovid has otherwise in *Fasti* I:

> “And may the field repay its barley with vast interest.”

Faults inflicted.] Not “removed,” as M. has it.

Lending at interest.] C. has “giving interest,” wrongly omitting “at.”

Author of every evil.] V.: “agent of all wickedness.”

Strangers shall consume.] The passage in Isaiah is at chapter V, verse 17; the word “strangers” here has the flavour of the Ordinary Gloss on this place.

Which [is] to the serpent and the crab.] C.: “who [is] to the serpent and the crab.” It could be tolerated if referred back to “stranger.”

[Col. 0446B] Hence devouring usury.] Not “to this,” as C. has it. Above *usura*, M. reads between the lines: “Because it creeps.”

Interest in due time.] Not “into times,” as the same manuscript has it. See Lucan, book I.

Sacred fire.] In Greek, *erysipelas* (Ἐρυσίπελας).

Cancerous and pestilential.] C. has not “cancerous,” but “so confused and pestilential.”

In the whole city.] That is, Paris, where the author lived and was then cantor at the church of Blessed Mary, as is inferred from Caesarius, first part, book II, *On Contrition*, chapter 34. See the eulogies prefixed by us to the work. M. omits some words here. Compare its reading: “For in the whole city scarcely one moneylender was found, except among the poor, and not even then,” etc.

If perhaps there arose from it.] M. does not admit “perhaps.”

Evil suspicion.] C. rejects “evil.”

Vineyard, well.] In C., “vineyard” is absent.

And each of the two.] Correctly so. Not “either one,” as V. has it.

Whose sons.] M.: “Sons whose or money.” Perhaps it intended *quorum*, “whose,” as C. has it: 443 “whose sons [Col. 0446C] [and] money,” etc.

They vomit into the treasury.] Hear what Blessed Augustine thinks about the fisc: “Our forefathers therefore abounded in every kind of money because they gave tithes to God and paid tax to Caesar; now, because devotion to God has departed, the exaction of the fisc has arrived.” And below: “The fisc takes away what Christ does not receive.” Vol. X of his works, *Fifty Homilies*, Homily 48.

Lean, you will return to the hollow …] I restored this from Horace, book I, epistle 7. For C. read *arcum*, “bow,” in place of *arctum*, “narrow.” M. and V. omitted it, thus:

> “Lean, you will revisit the hollow which once, lean, you entered.”

V.: “which formerly.”

Indeed worse.] C. lacked this through “Because [he is] a Jew.”

By the prescription of the law.] C.: “by the command.” Deuteronomy XXIII.19.

So that in them no …] M.: “So that with them no …” Such persons may also be struck, and no excommunication is incurred, [Col. 0446D] because they are deprived of clerical privileges.

Or they themselves, even if …] M.: “or even they themselves, if they should be unwilling to make a will.” The other two: “should be willing.”

It is clear above under the heading.] From this it is inferred that the author wrote many things in his autograph which, through copyists, were relegated to the margins in the copies. For here he refers the reader to chapter 46, “On receivers of unlawfully acquired gifts,” though this example is not read in the text of the manuscripts but in the outer or marginal space. See the notes on chapter 46.

In the Lateran Council.] Under Alexander III, in the year 1180, in which there is much concerning usury. In the appendix to that council there is a title on usuries containing ten chapters; and in the council itself, title I, chapter 25, manifest usurers are excommunicated.

By some known sign.] See chapter 68 of the First Lateran Council.

[Col. 0447A] You shall eat your own bread.] C.: “your bread.” This too is valid.

You shall eat another’s bread.] The margins of C. and M.: “Strangers shall plunder his labours,” Psalm CVIII. “Others have laboured, and you have entered into their labours.”

Jeremiah, chapter XVII.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter XVIII.

The thing by whatever means.] From Horace’s verse, book I, epistle 1:

> “If you can, rightly; if not, by whatever means, [get] the thing [*rem*].”

It does not meet the outcome.] A verse of Ovid, elegy 1.

They will scarcely be able to restore what they have taken.] A Parisian usurer named Theobald made restitution in the time of King Philip. By the advice of Master Peter the Chanter, author of this work, the *Verbum Abbreviatum*, he ordered it to be proclaimed throughout the city by the voice of a herald that he was ready to restore to everyone from whom he had received anything above the principal. After making solemn restitution, he gave alms. See this example in Caesarius, *On Contrition*, book II, chapter 34, first part.

444 From the authority of Blessed Jerome.] See more in vol. IV, [Col. 0447B] on Isaiah chapter 58; on Jeremiah chapter XVIII; and on Amos chapter V.

Also from the example of Blessed Fursa.] I append here what I found in the margin of V. And again observe how corruptly this example concerning Blessed Fursa is introduced. For his *Legend* reads thus: “When the devil, after he had been snatched from the body, accused him of his crimes and offences, he objected among other things this: ‘The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes’ (Luke XII). When the holy angel answered on behalf of the soul of Blessed Fursa, ‘What part of his Lord’s will did he fail to fulfil?’ the devil replied, ‘He received the gifts of the wicked.’ The angel said to him, ‘He believed that he had done penance.’ The devil replied, ‘He ought first to have tested the repentance and perseverance, and then accepted [them].’” And below: “A man leapt out from the fire in which he was burning; the demons cast him upon Blessed Fursa’s shoulder, and, pressing his jaw against Fursa’s jaw, burned him. This was the man who, when dying, had given him his garment.” [Col. 0447C] Then the angel said to him: “What you set on fire, that has burned in you.” Surius, vol. I, *Life of the Same*, 16 January.

Or morphoea.] V. omits this. *Morphoea* means a change of face or complexion due to illness. Hence Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II:

> “It summons Morpheus, the craftsman and imitator of forms.”

## CHAPTER LI

Situated in dampness.] That is, in moisture. Virgil, *Eclogue* 10:

> “Beneath whose damp palate only a black tongue lies.”

Augustine testifies.] Consult vol. II, letter 54 to Macedonius, after the middle; then Cause 14, Question 5, *Non sane*; likewise Question 11, Question 3, *Non licet*. Blessed Augustine’s words are cited in these places.

You are not permitted to sell.] M. reads: “or if you do not need [it], if you are permitted to sell patronage,” etc. It makes no sense.

On account of the baseness of the office.] This is the sound reading, as is clear [Col. 0447D] from what immediately precedes and follows at a distance. Therefore do not say “for the usefulness of the office,” as C. wishes.

And they may beg for profit.] V.: “claim [profit].”

I Corinthians, chapter VI.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter XXVI.

And base.] This is the interlinear gloss, which says: “indiscreet, base,” etc.

But the more prudent.] C.: “prudent.”

And of subtle vein.] V. omits this, reading: “But the more prudent [are suited] to preaching,” etc.

Was despaired of.] C. and V.: “despaired.”

He was suitable.] Margin of M.: “of prosperous talent.”

Likewise Sidonius.] In the letter concerning judges.

445 Those who are sound.] M.: “those who are anxious.”

To take away possessions.] M.: “opinions.”

They disdain admonitions.] M., between the lines: “Without payment.”

They dictate matters to be judged.] M.: “enrich.”

They overturn dictated decisions.] Margin of M.: “where they have received [something].”

They draw back those making settlements.] M.: “those passing by.” Incorrectly.

[Col. 0448A] Reverence for clerics.] Cassiodorus speaks. See him on Psalm LXXIII.

Granted to predecessors.] Not “agreed to,” as M. has it.

Honorarium.] C.: *orarium*.

In deliberations, statues.] V.: “in conversations, statues.”

The claws of sphinxes.] Of which the poet Ausonius says:

> “The sphinx is a bird in wings, a beast in feet, a maiden in face.”

The cleverness of Ulysses.] C.: “cunning.” This too is good, in accordance with the verse of the poet Faustus Andrelini:

> “No greater constancy belonged to crafty Ulysses.”

Of Polymnestor.] V.: *Palinestor*. M.: *Pallinestor*. Propertius, book III:

> “And the crime of the Thracian Polymnestor, for gold received.”

Here, for metrical reasons, the letter *m* is elided.

Achitophel.] M. and C.: Architophel.

## CHAPTER LII

C. alone separates this chapter, adding in the margin a summary or heading in red letters.

[Col. 0448B] Proverbs, chapter XXIII.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter XLV.

As proud faith.] To be brief, I refer the reader to Blessed Augustine, who treats this matter more fully: vol. II, letter 46 to Valentinus, *On Free Will*; likewise in the same volume, letter 105 against the Pelagians; and finally vol. VIII, in the preface to Psalm XXXI.

That the tongue is for sale.] Two margins note Lucan’s verse on Curio, reconciled to Caesar, whom he had formerly opposed:

> “Bold Curio attends [him], with tongue for sale.”  
> Book I.

Who [are] little-brained.] Men of small brains and slight keenness of mind. V. and M. have *coterellos* for *cerebellos*.

From the coterel advocates.] The name *coterelli* seems derived from a whetstone (*cos*). For, like a knife upon a whetstone, such men sharpen cases and lend them an appearance of truth, though in themselves they are false and unjust.

Crocodiles.] The three [other witnesses]: *cocodrili*. Of all animals the crocodile alone lacks a tongue; likewise, in chewing it alone moves its upper part. Blessed Augustine, vol. I, book II, [Col. 0448C] *Soliloquies*, chapter 8.

Since you are not for me.] C. incorrectly: “since you are for me,” etc.

I investigated diligently.] Why not “most diligently,” in accordance with the biblical text, Job XXIX?

446 But the rich [bring] a lawsuit.] This is precisely so. The rich come into a suit and controversy, and over the slightest matter or a sour little word, or the lightest insult thrown at them, though they could endure and suppress it patiently and without damage to their reputation. It is no wonder that councils, courts, or provincial chambers today are overburdened with the decision of countless lawsuits. How praiseworthy was the action of Thomas More, martyr and most equitable judge. By his skill, diligence, and fairness, he freed the English Chancery, heavily burdened with lawsuits, from every case in his time. So Stapleton states in the life of Blessed Thomas More, martyr and Chancellor of England.

Commands [him] to defend.] M.: “to look upon.”

May I urge [him] toward peace.] M.: “May I move [him] toward peace.”

[Col. 0448D] Therefore you exhort him.] M.: “Therefore, exhorting him.”

If [he is] a hired man.] V. omits “if.” M.: “if hired.”

A certain just and prudent man.] M.: “just and provident.” The marginal note of V. should be brought here: “This same R., when he was bishop of Amiens—and compelled advocates and judges to make restitution for the harm which they had inflicted upon defendants and clients through unjust advocacy and judgments—was asked why he applied so much effort in such matters. He replied: ‘Because, unless I did this, I would be bound to make restitution from my own resources to those who had suffered injury.’”

Proverbs, chapter XXIII.] The three [other witnesses]: XLV.

## CHAPTER LIII

M. here reads, immediately, the heading of the preceding chapter, namely: “Concerning divine laws,” etc.

The summary reads: “That positive justice has no firmness, that is, whatever can be changed at the will of man.”

[Col. 0449A] Deuteronomy, chapter XVI.] V.: chapter LXXIV; C.: LXXXIII; M.: LXXXIV.

Justinian laws.] M., in the margin: “Human justice.” Laws are called Justinian laws because they were established and explained by the emperor Justinian. “Such [laws],” says the margin of C., “would punish rather in the arena than in the church.”

Numbers, chapter XXVII.] The three [other witnesses]: LIX.

Of these things, which according to the letter.] These are words of the same Origen, Homily 11. C. here adds in the side margin: “Against [this], Leviticus LXIII; Origen, what was said above,” etc., where it is said: “Among Christians there is no command that punishment be inflicted bodily; but the Gospel preserves the mercy of the law and rejects the severity of legal right.”

Not their own.] Thus reads Origen’s text. C.: “not its own.”

It is not enough [to fulfil] a part.] I append from the Gloss on Leviticus XVIII, verse 5: “For the Law does not give life unless the Gospel supervenes.”

But that nothing is firm.] M. only begins the chapter here, prefacing the summary: “That nothing is firm,” etc.

[Col. 0449B] 447 It is clear [that] decrees.] “As the bishop of Lyons says,” margin of M.

One rationale after another reforms [them].] Hence appeals are made from one judge to a higher judge. Thus Blessed Augustine, vol. I, *On Free Will*, book I, chapter 6, about the middle: “Although temporal law is just, it can nevertheless justly be changed with the times.”

Which in it.] M.: “which in him.”

Agellius.] C.: Augellius. By some he is called Aulus Gellius, whose twenty books of *Attic Nights* survive.

The laws of cities.] C. and M.: “Your laws are.”

And by comparisons.] “Like a blind man who, while pasturing another,” say the margins of M. and C., “pulls out his eye instead of his mouth”; M. adds: “his bleary eye.”

And by examples of saints.] V. omits this.

Establishing.] C.: “establishes.”

And other things of this sort.] Said of such men above in chapter 47.

Which seems.] C.: “But if it is not enough, it seems that the cleric,” etc.

[Col. 0449C] Established as transgressors.] “Therefore [this applies] also to you, who possess several churches without the knowledge and permission of the pope.” Thus the margins of C. and M.

## CHAPTER LIV

Greatest and foremost.] C.: “most greatly and most especially.”

Ecclesiasticus, chapter VII.] M. and C.: 19; V.: 29.

You should be exceedingly afraid.] Cyprian: “If a cleric or layman is afraid, he is near pardon; but when a bishop is afraid, it is all over with him.” Margins of C. and M.

And you shall gather.] V. omits this.

The scapegoat.] Not “emissory,” as C. has it. See Leviticus XVI and Origen’s Homily 9 on this place.

Ordained afterwards.] It appears that Nicholas of Lyra once saw this author of ours, for his Gloss has the flavour of what appears here in the text. Thus, on I Timothy V, “Neither share,” etc.: “Some explain this of the overly hasty ordination of an unsuitable person; and thus the bishop shares in the sins [Col. 0449D] of one who ministers unworthily.”

In the seat of scoffers.] This is Blessed Jerome’s Hebrew translation. The Chaldean version reads, for “in the seat,” “in the company of scoffers.”

And temporal.] V. omits “and.”

Bishop of Le Mans.] His name was Hildebert, and he published various verses. I saw these among our manuscripts. Under the title “On the mystery of the Mass,” they begin:

> “We are all carried away from our midst by pressing fates,  
> And drawn where our completed life summons us.”

Besides these, [I saw] others under this title, “The Sacraments of the Bishop of Le Mans.” They begin:

> “I have proposed to write what the mystical rites of the ancients  
> The Mass represents, and what the minister does.”

Then others, truly ingenious, having at their head this summary title: “On the equivalence of the virginity of holy Mary: How fire comes from the sun.” Their beginning is:

[Col. 0450A]

> “The sun, crystal, and water give some sort of image  
> Of virginal birth and instruct faith.”

Unhappy is he whom things …] M. and C. prefix: “Likewise the poet.”

I John II.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter IV.

II Corinthians XIII.] The three [other witnesses]: LXI.

And thus sometimes.] Above “and thus,” M. has “M.,” meaning *Magister*, “Master.”

And delight.] Not “pleasure,” as V. has it, nor “love,” as M. has it.

To the oar.] By no means “remedy,” as the margin of M. corrected it. For the same author says elsewhere: “He ought not to be chosen for episcopal dignity who has not learned to govern lesser offices; for the care of a ship ought not to be entrusted to one who does not know how to hold an oar.”

To the stern-ornament.] Or *aplustrum*, as I said above at chapter 1.

The danger is graver.] C.: “the danger is more difficult.” Juvenal, Satire 8:

> “Every fault of the mind bears a crime so much more conspicuous in itself  
> As the person who sins is considered greater.”

The papacy was vacant for so long.] For thirty-five days, as Baronius has in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*; and he is speaking of Sixtus II. It was vacant longer after Fabian.

Worldly pomp.] M. notes this in the side margin: “Gold embroidery on a mitre and things of that kind.” Gold embroidery is an elaborate ornament first invented in Phrygia, as Isidore says of the dalmatic, because it was first woven in Dalmatia of Greece.

He who is greater.] “In virtues,” says C. in the margin.

Let him become as the lesser.] The same [margin]: “In humility.”

But whether powerful.] V.: “But whether powerful m.”; perhaps *minus*, “less.”

Against conscience.] M.: “against knowledge.”

For conscience.] The same: “for knowledge.”

Whence he should not even wish to be.] Blessed Gregory has similar things in Homily 17 on the Gospels.

Life, knowledge.] This is the Gloss on II Timothy II.

[Col. 0450C] Geoffrey of Péronne.] V.: Gaufridus Paronensis. He was called Peronensis because he came from Péronne, a city of France. Caesarius, *Memorable Examples*, book II, chapter 29, and the Cistercian Menology for 15 January mention him without naming him. See the notes there. He is there called Godfrey of Péronne. Cantimpratanus tells not dissimilar things in *The Bees*, I.20, where he says of Hugh, dean of Cambrai, that he preferred to remain hidden in monastic habit under a rule at Vaucelles rather than be adorned with the episcopal mitre. There is also there an entirely similar account of a Regular Canon of Saint Victor at Paris.

449 Made guardian.] M. and C.: “Holy guardian.”

In an oratory.] That is, a private chapel.

## CHAPTER LV

Leviticus, chapter XXI.] The three [other witnesses]: LXXI.

In evangelical ministry.] C.: “in ecclesiastical ministry?”

Southernwood for the sick.] Thus the three exemplars and the original. In Greek, *abrotonon* (Ἀβρότονον). It is a plant, in French *aurosne*.

[Col. 0450D] But of this unworthy [person].] Above “of this,” M. reads “M.”, perhaps *Magister*, “Master.”

The lineage of birth.] Or, as the two margins have it: “nobility of blood.”

How great therefore [is] maturity …] V. omits this through “Therefore if.” C. has it in the margin.

And prudence.] C. there: “and every kind of prudence.”

That which is precious.] V. has this parenthesis in the text; C. in the margin.

To govern and reveal.] M.: “to veil and reveal.”

Let them beware.] M.: “Whence those promoting such persons must beware lest they be struck with a similar punishment, as the Philistines were,” etc.

Likewise it must be feared.] M. lacks this through “For thus.”

But also a whistle.] For oxen are driven by a driver’s whistle.

Namely students.] M. and C.: “namely poetic students.”

[Col. 0451A] Masters of schools.] M. omits this.

But why do I raise these objections?] M. abridges and leaps over the text thus: “But such men are not chosen as craftsmen, nor have they a place in the Church. Where there is no one seeing, we are deprived of those who see, as by the prophets there seemed to be an approaching captivity. Belshazzar abused the figurative vessels of the Lord, and therefore was slain that very night. How much more will those be punished who entrust living vessels—that is, souls—and ecclesiastical sacraments to unworthy persons?” etc.

Likewise Ecclesiastes.] V. alone has this in the text through “Likewise: How.” C. has it in the lower margin and notes chapter 21, though today it is chapter 10.

Matthew, chapter XXIV.] M.: chapter 68; V. and C.: 247. Formerly Matthew’s Gospel was divided into 355 chapters, according to Suidas, Ammonius, and Eusebius.

And honours.] M.: “from ambition alone.” C.: “from ambition for dignities.” V. adds “and honours.”

In those dregs of the times.] C., in the margin: “A saying of the Wise Man.” V. likewise has in the margin: “That is, the middle time between the decline of the Law and the beginning [Col. 0451B] of the Gospel; namely the time of the Lord’s preaching, when the Law was already failing and the Gospel had not yet shone forth fully. This time is called a perverse middle because of the perversity of the Jews who then existed, who were already beginning to destroy Moses’ Law and were unwilling to receive Christ’s Gospel.”

They sat everywhere.] C. and V.: “Each and every one sat everywhere upon the chair,” etc. Incorrectly, because “each and every one” is affirmative, whereas it follows, “but only the scribes,” etc. See the Gloss on this place.

450 The sign of religious life.] C.: “separated from others by the sign of religious life.”

Mature in age.] Words of the Ordinary Gloss on Matthew XXIII, verse 2.

If he is converted and repents.] M.: “If he is converted and leaves a blessing after him.” It wrongly omits “and repents,” as is clear from what immediately follows: “As concerning the sinner repenting,” etc.

And one promoted unknowingly.] M. lacks this. Its reading is: [Col. 0451C] “But for the fool there is no hope; just as”—here too it omits some things—“concerning the sinner repenting,” etc.

Hence, Augustine says.] Consult the Gloss on Leviticus IV; then return to vol. IV of his works, part II, *Questions from Both Testaments*, question 4.

Who will heal him?] The Holy Bible has: “Who will have mercy upon him?”

Gather the fragments.] V.: “Gather the grains,” and, for “of fragments,” “of grains.”

The hands of those dining.] C.: “of the prudent.”

Like baskets.] V. omits this through “For the time.” C. has it in the margin; M. in the text.

A substantial difference.] C.: “a substantial drachma.”

Jerome on Helvidius.] Blessed Jerome’s letter against the same man is in vol. II, beginning: “Recently asked by the brethren.” Gennadius mentions Helvidius in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*. C.: “Jerome on Edulius,” [Col. 0451D] for Helvidius. After “concerning faith and hope,” M. omits “and the Church’s good morals,” and continues thus: “Helvidius, a unique and horrible monster in Gaul, a priest [or] layman—though Gaul alone lacks monsters—was nevertheless learned, but wrote impiously concerning the Blessed Virgin. If by the Lord’s command,” etc. Blessed Jerome writes something similar concerning Vigilantius in the letter beginning: “Many monsters are in the world.”

## CHAPTER LVI

Against the unworthy.] M. abbreviates thus: “To repel the unworthy intrusion of unworthy persons, it is fitting to consider the office of prelates and priests. May the Lord provide,” etc.

Numbers, chapter XXVII.] V. and C.: 59. Consult Origen’s Gloss on this passage.

The Lord God of spirits.] Not “spirit,” as C. has it. The margin of V. sharply rebukes this: “Observe,” it says, “that the glossator did not understand this wording, glossing ‘spirit’ [Col. 0452A] for ‘spirits.’ For the codices which have ‘spirit’ for ‘spirits,’ found here for the first time, are corrupt. Yet nothing is so false that it does not admit some explanation. For every text is a prostitute and suffers a corrupter.”

Likewise in the same place.] I added “in the same place” because it is the same chapter. The three [other witnesses], meanwhile, read: “Likewise 60”—that is, the chapter—“Take,” etc.

Genesis, chapter XLVI.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter LXXV.

451 It is all over with him.] A saying of Blessed Cyprian.

Office and burden.] M. omits “office,” but incorrectly. For the Ordinary Gloss on Jeremiah I says: “Jeremiah abhors an office which, because of his age, he cannot bear.” Blessed Jerome, in his commentary.

Elementary in life.] Above, in chapter 7, he calls [such a man] “abecedarian.” It is worthwhile here to note what Alan has at the beginning of his *Penitential Book*, not yet printed, I think. He begins: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, for I am a child and do not know how to speak. If Jeremiah, sanctified from the womb, chosen by the Lord as prophet, free from criminal stain, [Col. 0452B] taught by divine inspiration, feared to undertake the office of preaching, feared to proclaim the words of God, and confessed himself a child, confessed himself tongue-tied: how do men of our time, unclean from the womb, rejected by the Lord, entangled in crimes, abandoned by divine visitation, dare to ascend the summit of the priesthood and stammer heavenly mysteries? They are not infants in childhood but boys [printed *puri*, perhaps *pueri*] in wisdom; they are not children in being wise but old men in being foolish; they are not merely tongue-tied in preaching but mute in speaking. If Jeremiah, who was eloquent in preaching God, confesses himself mute, how does a mute priest profess himself eloquent in speaking about God?” etc.—most worthy of reading.

But ineloquent.] M. varies, reading: “An innocent [perhaps *ineloquens*, ‘ineloquent’] and speechless manner of life, as much as it benefits by example, so much harms by silence.”

For by the barking of a dog.] M. alone admits this through “and said.”

For easily indeed.] M. omits quite a few words. After “make [them] audible,” it says: “By doing what you preach; otherwise you cause your words not to be believed. Therefore gird yourself,” etc.

Jeremiah, chapter I.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter III.

As Ezekiel, chapter III.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter V.

What Job [did], Elijah [did].] On Job see the same author, chapter XXXVIII, verse 3; on Elijah, III Kings XVIII.46; on Jeremiah, chapter I.17 of his book; on John, Matthew III.4. The author enumerates them in chronological order. For Job precedes Elijah—and indeed Moses—by time.

One who advances.] V.: “one who ceases.”

Likewise, approaching.] M. restricts this sentence thus: “Let the future judge consider that none of judges,” etc.

The spirit of Othniel.] M. compresses this into a few words: “The spirit of Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, before,” [Col. 0452D] etc.

Delbora.] The three [other witnesses] likewise have *Delbora* for Deborah. In antiquity Deborah was called Delbora, as I discovered from various codices.

Likewise Exodus III.] The three [other witnesses], not III but V.

The transformation of the rod.] M. and C., in the margin: “An iron rod is necessary for a prelate: so judges Blessed Gregory, *Morals*, book XX, chapter 8.”

Of a resonant voice.] These are words of Origen, Homily 3 on Exodus, at the beginning.

II Timothy II.] The three [other witnesses]: II Timothy IV.

452 In Acts of the Apostles, chapter XX.] V. and C.: chapter XLVIII; M.: LX.

To govern bishops.] Understand priests by this, though the term has been contracted, says C. in the side margin. In the primitive Church presbyters too were understood by the name “bishop,” and conversely. See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 184, article 6, reply to objection 1.

As far as the armpits.] After this the Cambron fragment continues: [Col. 0453A] “Concerning this mystery the Apostle says in II Timothy IV: ‘But you, be watchful.’ Gloss: ‘Labour in all things,’ teaching both the perverse and the good. ‘Do the work of an evangelist’: fulfil in deed what you preach with your mouth. ‘Be sober’: discreet in every work of yours, free from every excess.” It then adds: “‘I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of you all. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God’ (Acts XX). Therefore, if I had shrunk from declaring it, I would be guilty of their souls. For if a brother is bound to be his brother’s keeper, and a neighbour his neighbour’s keeper—otherwise the voice of blood will cry to God from the earth (Genesis IV)—how much more is a prelate bound to be the keeper of those for whom he pledged himself, that he would bring even the weak sheep into the heavenly fold upon his shoulders, setting all things aside and exposing his own body to death for their sake? Likewise, then let Jacob weep for Joseph,” etc. This is found there. But the same fragment omits what the text has in this place. [Col. 0453B]

Because preaching.] C. reads this in the margin, enclosed in parentheses; V. nowhere has it.

Or of each individual.] C. alone adds this.

Augustine: “What is for him …?”] Vol. IV, in the unfinished book *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, before the middle.

And strength.] M. omits this.

Is entrusted to the unworthy.] M. also has acceptably: “is entrusted to an unworthy person.”

The fish of sorrow.] V. wrongly omits this. It is the interpretation of the name Dagon.

To effeminate eunuchs.] M. lacks “eunuchs,” not “effeminate.”

Of the devil driving them away.] These words are absent.

Guardians of souls.] C.: “custodies.”

Romans I.] V. and C.: Romans II.

Your [faith] and mine.] C.: “your [faith] and mercy.”

In the same chapter I.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter III.

[Col. 0453C] That I may have some fruit.] M., in the margin: “Or, that you may bear fruit, or that I may obtain a reward on your behalf.” This is the interlinear Gloss on Romans I, verse 13.

In you, among your subjects.] M.: “in you and [your] subjects.” M. then continues: “an eternal and lasting reward,” etc.

The Apostle was ready to evangelize.] C. omits these words.

They must be applied.] C.: “they must be amplified.” It is mistaken.

Likewise IV Kings XI.] M. does not cite the passage. V. and C.: chapter 78. The same is read in Jeremiah XXIX and II Chronicles XXIII.

453 That he might be the Lord’s people.] C.: “that the people might be after God, obedient to God and the king.”

But who is the mediator?] M.: “But who is the mediator—not man but God—if he has been changed into a wolf or hireling, but without a guardian.” It omits: “It is not read, as is clear from the text.”

The sprouting of the word.] M. lacks this through: [Col. 0453D] “For he ought.” In a not dissimilar sense, Blessed Jerome, on the parable of the ten virgins and the words “Lord, Lord, open to us,” says: “Excellent is the confession in the address ‘Lord,’ and its repetition is an indication of faith.”

By the word of preaching.] M. and C., in the margin: “You, though a Jew, compel the Gentiles to Judaize,” Galatians II. It adds the Ordinary Gloss: “Not by the authority of teaching, but by the example of conduct.”

His spirit.] V.: “the Holy Spirit.”

But now.] V. omits this through “Whence a certain man.”

The shepherd cares for the sheep.] V. and M., omitting the first verse, begin with the second: “Draw,” etc. These verses occur in the Gloss on the chapter *Cum venisset*, *Extra*, *On Sacred Unction*. There the first verse is:

> “In the form of a staff this rule is given to you, O prelate.”

“Draw,” etc. St Thomas also has the third little verse in the *Supplement*, question 40, article 7, but reads *collige*, “gather,” for *attrahe*, “draw,” as does [Col. 0454A] Durandus, book III of the *Rationale*, chapter 15. The same verses are indicated in the Pontifical when the pastoral staff is given to a bishop.

Ezekiel, chapter III.] C. wrongly read Hezekiah for Ezekiel.

And chapter XIII.] V.: chapter XXVII.

And chapter XXII.] The three [other witnesses]: LIV, at the end.

And chapter XLIV.] Two [witnesses]: chapter CVIII. V. does not note the chapter.

And chapter XLIV: “Son …”] The three [other witnesses]: chapter CV.

## CHAPTER LVII

I Timothy IV.] The three [other witnesses]: I Timothy VII. M. begins thus: “Attend to reading, and then to exhortation, G. [that is, the Gloss]: ‘of those willing’; T. [the text]: ‘and to doctrine’; G.: ‘[of] ignorance.’”

Canonical election.] M. does not read “canonical.”

In the same epistle.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter II, whereas it is chapter I.

That is, according to.] These are interlinear glosses.

Which are called prophecies.] From here through “the grace [Col. 0454B] of expounding,” V. is silent.

I Maccabees, chapter V.] V.: chapter XVI; M.: XV.

IV Kings XXII.] C. and M.: IV Kings LXXXVII; V.: IV Kings XXXIII.

454 How much more carefully.] M. briefly: “The prelate of the Church ought to keep more careful watch for the thunderclaps of the Lord’s words. The flock [is] lost.” It omits the intervening remainder.

Their shepherds led [them] astray.] M. and C., in the margin: “By example. For the error of leaders is drawn into example.”

> “. . . . . Not so much can edicts overthrow human minds  
> As the life of a ruler [can].”

These verses are Claudian’s, in the book on the fourth consulship of the emperor Honorius, but differ somewhat from the printed text, which is:

> “. . . . . Edicts cannot so much bend human dispositions  
> As the life of a ruler [can].”

Of his bed.] C.: “of his chamber.”

[Col. 0454C] And contentious.] V. lacks this and has in its place: “and evil.”

Isaiah, chapter LII.] V. and M.: chapter 157; C.: 167.

Because the people today.] Note this carefully. V.: “Because the people today [are] not as the priest, and the priest less [is] not as the people.” C.: “Because the people today [are] more than the priest, and the priest less are not more.”

I Timothy, chapter IV.] C. and M.: V; V.: VII.

For there is nothing.] Blessed Jerome so judges in vol. VI, commentary at the end of chapter II of the Epistle to Titus.

Likewise Isaiah, chapter XXVII.] V.: chapter LXXIV; C.: LXXV.

They shall come upon them or upon us.] V. and M.: “They shall come upon us.” C. adds in the margin: “We are the Lord’s temple, the peculiar people.”

With the dung of temporal things.] M. corrected this in the adjacent margin. Earlier the text had: “With the stench of temporal things.”

You who have entered into counsel.] C. is mistaken here. For it reads: “You who did not enter into counsel.” The text of Isaiah chapter XXX—C.’s margin: chapter LXX; M.: LXXIX—reads: “that you might make [Col. 0454D] counsel.”

Amos, chapter VI.] The three [other witnesses]: chapter XXV.

On account of which I shall send forth.] M.: “On account of whom I shall send forth.” Certainly well.

He who does not burn does not kindle.] For just as a candle is not kindled except from a burning flame, so a hearer is not kindled unless the preacher first burns. Therefore let him teach first by example rather than by word.

Also Basil.] These examples, both of Blessed Basil and of St Sebastian, occur above in chapter VII. Therefore see the notes there.

Fiery tongue.] M.: “flame.”

Acts of the Apostles, chapter 20.] The three [other witnesses]: XLVIII. M. here omits quite a few words from “Likewise Luke” through “the Apostle hastened to keep Pentecost”—these are M.’s words—“at Jerusalem.”

Greater solemnities.] M.: “solemnities” simply, omitting “greater.”

455 The older men, elders.] M. adds “not young men.” C., in the margin: “Not boys, not young men.”

[Col. 0455A] Unknown things of salvation.] M. omits this.

And through houses.] C., in the margin: “Where now is preaching of this sort? For a prelate is not his own man.”

I go to Jerusalem.] M., in the margin: “Not to demand gifts, not to indulge myself”—C. adds, “not to feast and declaim”—“but to suffering”; M.: “to endure”; C.: “to be feared.”

Tribulations await me.] C. there: “In the world [you shall have] afflictions,” etc., John XVI.

Or my life.] C. alone has this. M., however, says in the margin at “my soul”: “That is, my life.” I would say that “or my life” was wrongly absent from the text because the Syriac translation appears to admit it.

Provided that I may finish.] The three [other witnesses]: “Provided that I may finish.” This was restored from the Holy Bible. Yet I have meanwhile also read: “Provided that I myself may finish.” See the text of the printed Gloss under the typeface of St Peter, as it is commonly called.

II Timothy, chapter IV.] C. and M.: chapter VI.

[Col. 0455B] Some discourse.] This is how it should be read, as I gathered from the interlinear Gloss. Therefore not “sometimes,” as M. and C. have it. Here I append C.’s marginal note: “Fathers about to be succeeded by their sons then give more useful counsels. For this is natural.”

For whom he pledged himself.] C.: “For whom he pledged himself that he must answer.” M. abbreviates thus: “Much more [is] the prelate a guardian of souls”—here words are absent—“who is bound to carry the weak sheep upon his shoulders,” etc.

On the same subject, Jeremiah chapter XLVIII.] This passage through “Attend,” M., C., and V.: chapter LVII.

Likewise III Kings, chapter XX.] V.: chapter LIV. The other two do not specify.

My departure.] M.: “departure.”

Ravening wolves.] M.: “grave wolves,” for “ravening.”

Holding in memory.] M.: “The remembrance of the divine command is no small safeguard.” The biblical text has “holding in memory,” not “memorably.” What I noted here from M. is the Ordinary Gloss, and also Rabanus.

[Col. 0455C] I coveted no man’s [property].] C. and V.: “I did not covet.”

And they are distinguished.] M. and V.: “and they are discerned.”

That they are not true prelates.] M.: “That they are not prelates.”

These hands.] M. has *my* for “these.” Incorrectly.

By wolves.] M. in the text; C. in the margin: “Lest the weak be scandalized or burdened.”

Commending them to God.] This is absent from M. and [lacuna].

A good ruler.] C. and V. incorrectly read “the ruler alone.”

And they weep especially.] M. omits this through to the end.

456 CHAPTER LVIII.

It should be noted that M. separated this chapter from the preceding one by a space, as it usually does; nevertheless, in the margin it indicates that this new heading should begin: “On the patience and impatience of prelates.”

Chief virtue.] M. omits this. Thus: “Patience is the prelate’s chief ornament,” etc.

It is patience.] C. explains in the margin: “And abundant [Col. 0455D] beyond the ordinary.” Why so? Because a prelate is a lamp set upon a lampstand, shining before other subjects by example, charity, patience, and so forth.

On I Corinthians, chapter XII.] The Three: chapter XXVII.

And when the horse was taken away.] M.: “Thus, when a beast of burden was being taken from someone, he said: ‘Indeed, take the whip as well.’ For the measure of a man is proved by an insult done to him. Likewise, IV Kings,” etc.

IV Kings II.] C.: IV Kings IX.

And in Homily 21, book II.] The Three: “in Homily 9 of the second part.” Certainly correctly. For by “the second part,” Book II is meant. In this Book II ten homilies were formerly counted, and the one under discussion is the ninth; today, however, it is the twenty-first, because modern editors join the twelve homilies of Book I to the homilies of Book II.

In the words of sacred utterance.] Thus C., following the text of St. Gregory, Homily 21 on Ezekiel. V., however: “He teaches the words of sacred utterance.”

CHAPTER LIX.

[Col. 0456A]

V. reads the following heading for this chapter: “That one charged with pastoral care ought to be free from secular concerns.” But since M. continually varies in its reading, we shall deliberately set it out in full after the notes. This chapter contains certain rather forceful statements against bishops who are not religious, as the apostles were. It is not sinful to possess riches, but to set one’s heart upon them.

Declaring this.] C.: “announcing this.”

Even the desire to possess.] See St. Jerome’s commentary on Matthew, chapter IX.

John, leaving the linen cloth, fled from them.] It is not likely that this young man was John the Apostle, because John entered the high priest’s courtyard: John XVIII, vv. 15–16.

Successor of the apostles.] V. omits these two words.
