Horses and trappings.] C., in the margin, on the words [Col. 0456B] “We have followed thee,” says: “How? Surely not amid the trappings and pomp of the world; with horses and chariots which not only carry but drag gold and silver behind them?” etc.

457 Luke, chapter XXII.] C.: chapter CLXX; M.: CCLXX. Nor should you wonder, reader, that so many chapters are counted. For in antiquity Oecumenius and Euthymius divide Luke’s Gospel into LXXXIII chapters; Ammonius and Eusebius into CCCXLIII; Ambrose into CLXIV titles; more recent Latin writers divide it into XXIV chapters.

Which prelates of the Church.] C., in the margin: “Those who are even carried in chairs upon the shoulders of leaders, amid a tumultuous crowd and flute-playing.”

The rich of the world.] V. has, not badly, “leaders of the world.”

Do they not serve as soldiers?] “I do not know how to resolve these,” says C. in the margin. As I promised, I transcribe the aforementioned chapter 59 word for word, as they say, from M. It begins thus:

“Someone added this: ‘What is added might be beneficial, and what is neglected harmful.’ It was said to the apostles, and consequently [Col. 0456C] to men who are successors of the apostles: ‘Do not possess gold or silver, nor money in your belts; nor a bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff; for the labourer is worthy of his food’ (Matthew X). Luke: ‘Eating and drinking such things as they have. Eat what is set before you, healing the sick who are in the house’ (Luke X). Modern preachers mutilate part of the authority: they wish to be supported, not to heal or preach. The labourer ought to work beforehand. The Lord says: “labourer,” and “food,” not “foods,” not delicacies; and “his own,” that which is due to him after his service, in return for spiritual service rendered beforehand. “Such things as they have”: not more delicate things sought by land and sea outside the house. Nor should a prelate seek to have a luxurious house and more sumptuous fare set before him; rather, he should be content with what is set before him. Hence: “Eat what is set before you,” that is, without selectiveness or murmuring. But now, they say, these commands had no place, but only in the primitive Church. They were said to peasants and fishermen; [Col. 0456D] today it is permissible for them to possess towns, slaves, trappings, riches, horses, changes of garments, and such things. For today the Church is nursed at the breast of kings; the bishop possesses royal rights; the count moves camps, has soldiers and attendants, and multiplies treasures and horses for himself. Yet this was forbidden to kings; much more strongly, then, to spiritual kings. David observed it, having only a mule, and Solomon was consecrated upon it (Deuteronomy XVII). Thus, according to them, the new Gospel—“the shortened word which God sent upon the earth” (Romans IX)—must be erased as though it were ceremonial law; although the saints say that such Gospel commands belong to morals, and are not to be blown away on grounds of place, time, or person, nor because of a contrary custom and practice of those who use them. For the Lord says: ‘What I say to you, I say to all’ (Mark XIII). And: ‘From the beginning I have known from thy testimonies’ (Psalm CXVIII),” etc. And: “The beginning of thy words is truth” (ibid.), etc. “Behold, we have left all things,” even the desire to possess. [Col. 0457A] A person who desires riches is counted among the rich, even if he does not have them. And: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle,” etc. “And we have followed thee” (Matthew XIX), not amid pomp and trappings, etc. “In the regeneration,” etc. The abandonment of all things confers this judicial power: namely, that naked men may follow the naked Lord and his disciples. Every preacher is bound to this by office. Hence John, leaving the linen cloth, fled naked; 458 Joseph, leaving his cloak; Matthew, his tax-office (Matthew IX); the Samaritan woman, her water-jar. And the man wishing to bury his father hears from the Lord: “Let the dead bury [their] dead,” etc.; “and follow me” (Matthew VIII). Since even the duty of burial toward one’s father is pious, he thereby signified that all other burdens were still more to be forbidden, and likewise the tumults of war to prelates, etc. For these are the things the Gentiles seek. The kings of Israel were forbidden to return into Egypt. If they say that they have left all things because they have no patrimony or private property, but only [Col. 0457B] stewardship entrusted to them over the possessions of the poor, then emperors too, who succeed by election, have left all things in this manner. What follows embraces two further points.”

CHAPTER LX.

V. gives this heading: “On the rank and dignity of deacons.”

And if he is wise.] The interlinear gloss, with what follows.

The subdiaconate.] Urban II expressly stated this, as is read in *On the Age and Qualification for Orders*, many times in many places.

Of another diocese.] V.: “of another bishop,” many times.

They should be appointed.] M.: “They should be instituted.”

To preach the Gospel.] C., at the side: “This seems appropriate only to archdeacons.”

“To whom thou hast entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood,” etc.] Both in the *Life of St. Lawrence* found in Surius and in Ambrose himself, *On Duties*, Book I, chapter 41, the reading is, omitting *body*, “the consecration of the Lord’s [Col. 0457C] blood” (as also in the Paris edition made from the Roman one): that is, the Lord’s consecrated blood, to be distributed to the people, as there is in the Mass: “This mingling and consecration.” But because this seemed offensive if not rightly understood, it was changed in the Roman Breviary to “for dispensation,” as St. Thomas reads it in the third part, question eighty-two, article three, and Baronius in volume two of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, year 261.

Not because he receives it.] M.: “Not because he consecrates it, or always receives it.”

The body is consecrated.] M.: “He consecrates it. And with greater reverence it is consecrated in the presence, ministry, and testimony of the deacon.”

Among the greater [orders].] This is absent from M.

And in rural places.] This too is omitted.

To preach by authority.] M.: “By office.” I once read in St. Jerome what I note here: [Col. 0457D] “Finally, that we may have ears for the Lord, the deacon cries aloud; he himself preaches, he himself exhorts,” etc.—words which we omit for brevity. Consult volume VIII, *On the Seven Orders of the Church*, on the fifth degree. Further, on the office of the deacon see distinction 25, chapter 1, paragraph “To the deacon.”

By the example of St. Vincent.] Surius, following Metaphrastes, relates the *Life of St. Vincent*, volume I, under 22 January.

459 Life, knowledge.] This is the interlinear gloss which the author frequently employs in the preceding material, in order to establish the fitness and sufficiency of clerics.

CHAPTER LXI.

V. has, in place of the summary: “On reverence for the priestly office.” M. omits it: “Or novices.”

Whence the bishop of Le Mans.] C. incorrectly has: “Whence Viocenomanensis writes to someone.” M. in the text: “To a certain man chosen.”

For in the high priests.] St. Gregory says, in Book II of his *Exposition* [Col. 0458A] on 1 Kings, chapter 3, after the middle: “Manhood is the time for administering the priesthood.” But all that follows, down to “But an objection is raised,” is Hildebert’s language.

The age of the prophet.] This and what follows have the flavour of St. Gregory’s teaching at the beginning of Homily 2 on Ezekiel.

He deferred, therefore, to age.] Margin of C.: “What greater thing is shown than that a boy is raised above old men?”

A fixed limit.] Formerly, assumption of a bishopric, as likewise of sacred orders, was more readily permitted at a younger age than today. The Council of Trent fixes the age of a bishop.

But an objection is raised concerning Solomon.] M. varies thus: “If Solomon was anointed king at twelve years of age, perhaps for this reason he did not have a good outcome. Jeremiah, Daniel, and Timothy were made prophets and teachers before the proper age; but the privileges of a few do not establish a consequence. Hence this should not be drawn into a general conclusion; if it is drawn, men similar to those mentioned should be chosen. Likewise [Col. 0458B] Isaiah,” etc. Resolve these objections with St. Jerome, volume IV, on Isaiah III, verse 4.

The privileges of a few.] Rule of Law 74 in the *Sext*. What is graciously granted to one person ought not to be drawn by others into precedent. Sometimes men young in age are ordained, whether priests or bishops, under pressure of necessity; nor should this be drawn into an argument, as is clear from Rule 78. Moreover, if the privilege appears personal, it follows that person alone and is extinguished with him, as Rule 7 there indicates.

Likewise Isaiah, chapter II.] M.: chapter IV; C. and V.: chapter VII. At the beginning I noted the number of chapters observed by the ancients.

A boy against an old man.] Margin of M.: “Conduct.”

A low-born man against a noble.] The same: “By birth.” From here to “Therefore the Apostle,” C. and V. are silent.

And he shall say.] Margin of M., namely: “Those who, from carnal affection, thrust forward their own people.” See St. Jerome’s commentary on this passage in Isaiah, volume IV.

[Col. 0458C] Ecclesiastes, chapter I.] M.: chapter XXVIII.

And pleasure.] C.: “will.” I note the same in Psalm XXVI: “That I may see the will,” for “pleasure”; Psalm IV: “To God, the living fountain,” for “the strong, living [God].”

To barren women.] This is absent from C. and V.

He eats in the morning.] M. omits this through “Likewise Jerome.” C., however, reads it only in the side margin; therefore I think this was noted by scholastics.

What art thou doing here?] Thus the biblical text. V.: “Why art thou here?”

For he thought.] This is a gloss on this passage, as C. indicates; but I have not yet read it.

Thou hast clothing.] M., in the margin: “All necessities.” This is the interlinear gloss.

Not immediately by the judgement of the multitude.] The margin of M. and C. refers here and runs thus: “Not now of a multitude, but of one man in a chamber.”

A similar thing is read.] V.: “A similar thing [is in] Jerome, cause 1.” See him [Col. 0458D] on Micah III.

He presumptuously suggests.] M.: “They presumptuously boast that they possess an old age of character,” etc.

As though he were saying.] M. omits this and says: “As though another Daniel, by reason of life and merits, had deserved a spiritual right, and the general law of the canons were infringed.”

Because he is lax.] M.: “more lax,” and notes in the margin: “1 Kings X.”

I Timothy, chapter V.] The Three: chapter VI.

Twenty-five years old.] C.: twenty years old. It is mistaken.

Lest those who need [a defender].] M. abbreviates: “Lest those who need a defender become administrators of others’ property.”

That comic saying.] C.: “that canonical saying.” This is an error.

And he who needs a pedagogue.] Absent from M. through “the Apostle only.”

A woman of sixty years.] Supply: “widow.” V. moreover adds: “Where, namely, he says to Timothy: ‘Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old.’” I noted the passage in the margin.

[Col. 0459A] Will he break bread for others?] It alludes to Lamentations IV: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them.”

To be a disciple.] M. adds: “Who was not even a novice,” etc.

For it is slippery.] M. omits this through “Likewise Moses.”

By the moving of human affection.] M.: “By moving affection,” and adds: “in comedies and tragedies, and still more in the serious and real matter of choosing pastors for the Church.”

Thresholds.] M. immediately adds: “The pastor who has not frequented this, with Paul, [is] not from man,” etc.

If among the Hebrews.] St. Jerome, in the preface to the first book of his commentaries on Ezekiel addressed to Eustochium, volume IV, spoke of this matter, chapter 4.

Wooden soldiers of Ogier.] This is absent from V.

To the theatre and spectacle.] M.: “To the spectacle of the theatre.”

I Kings, chapter I.] The Three: chapter III.

Anna does not wish.] M. omits this through “Because the Church.”

[Col. 0459B] Job, chapter XXXII.] The Three: chapter XXV.

461 CHAPTER LXII.

V.’s heading, with the addition “especially,” pleased [the editor] more than the others.

Not opposing.] The genuine reading, as is clear from Ezekiel XIII. V. and C., according to their own sense, have indeed well: “Unable to bark, but opposing themselves,” etc.

Isaiah, chapter LXII.] C. and M.: chapter CLXXXIV.

I will not rest.] After this M. continues: “The watchmen of the Church are all blind; they all lack knowledge. Upon the walls,” etc.

To him, the Lord.] C. alone: “the Lord.”

I see it portrayed.] M. continues: “For the Church does not yet seem established,” etc., which I deliberately enclosed in parentheses. V. and C. simply read: “In Holy Scripture I see it portrayed; I do not perceive it in practice.”

I see, I do not perceive.] M.: “I see it portrayed as I perceive it in practice.”

[Col. 0459C] And again, chapter XL.] V.: chapter CVIII; M. and C.: chapter CX.

Likewise the same, chapter VI.] The Three: chapter XVII.

Defiled not by lies.] M. prefixes the word *G.* to “defiled,” which is a gloss. I have not read it, either in the interlinear or the ordinary gloss. Yet Nicholas of Lyra seems to have seen it, for in this sense he says: “For just as lips are defiled by speaking what is unfitting, so also by keeping silent about what is fitting.” On Isaiah VI.

A burning coal.] I believe it was burning; otherwise there would have been no need of tongs. C. omits “burning.”

It burned my lip.] Note C.’s margin: “This appeared so to him imaginatively. For it must not be understood that his lips were actually burned.”

Iod: Alas, alas.] The Three manuscripts read: *Ioth*.

A suckling child.] The Three: “a nursing woman.” Incorrectly. For *lacteo* means “I suck milk,” which belongs to little children; but *lacto* means “I give milk,” which belongs to nurses.

Acts, chapter I.] V. and C.: chapter XLVIII.

And they were multiplied.] V.: “Even if they were multiplied [Col. 0459D] beyond number.” On “multiplied,” C. says at the side: “My adversaries [are] against me.”

Proverbs, chapter I.] The Three: chapter IV.

That is, among prelates.] V. mistakenly: “That is, in the streets.”

Jeremiah, chapter XXVI.] V. and M.: chapter XLIV.

And chapter III.] The Three: “and chapter XII.”

Acts XX.] The Three: Acts XCVIII.

They should detest.] C. and M.: “he should detest.” In St. Jerome may be found what is stated below concerning St. John the Baptist, volume VI, on Matthew I.

In Ecclesiastical History.] V.: “In the Lives of the Fathers.” Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X; Nicephorus, Book VIII.

While Athanasius was in exile.] C.: Anastasius—incorrectly.

462 Pope.] Not necessarily the Roman pope. For all bishops for many centuries were called *papae*, as may be seen in many places in St. Jerome writing to his contemporary St. Augustine. V. reads “bishop of Alexandria” for “pope,” also correctly.

[Col. 0460A] I eat bread idly.] V. and C.: “I eat idle bread.”

With Athanasius.] C. again: Anastasius. Incorrectly.

Why not rather?] M. omits this through “and going out.”

Enjoining this upon himself.] V. lacks this through “the righteous.”

And he is holy.] C.: “He is true,” perhaps “He is truthful.”

Athanasius.] C., as above and below: Anastasius.

In the Socratic decree.] Thus Boethius speaks in *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I, prose 4.

He is like a Cathar.] V. explains in the margin who this Cathar is. It says: “That is, a Montanist heretic or Cataphrygian, called Cataphrygians from the place Phrygia, where they first arose under their founder Montanus. They are called Cathars from cleanliness, because they considered themselves alone clean among men. Such heretics—namely Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla—asserted that the coming of the Holy Spirit was transmitted, not in the apostles, but in themselves.” St. Jerome, the letter to Marcella against Montanus, beginning *Testimonia*, at the end; likewise the letter against Vigilantius beginning *Multa in orbe*, volume II. In many other places he pursues and condemns the heresy of Montanus and his Cataphrygian followers. See volume VII, on Psalm CVII, at “And thy truth unto the clouds”; St. Gregory, volume II, *Register*, Book IX, indiction 4, chapter 61.

Do not reveal.] V.: “Do not betray.”

Jeremiah, chapter LI.] V.: chapter CLIX; M. and C.: chapter CLXIX.

And Anna and Mo.] I think “and Mo.” indicates Moses, who is likewise said to have cried out in prayer, as in Exodus VIII: “And Moses cried,” etc. V. and C. have only: “And Susanna, silent, cried out”; I added the remainder from M.

For confessing sins.] St. Jerome rightly indicates this, volume VI, on Matthew IX, verse 33.

Augustine.] Volume II, Letter XIX to St. Jerome, chapter 4 at the end.

[Col. 0460C] For disputation.] M. differs: “For disputation, it is good to be silent for litigation.” There follows: “Unless disputation becomes a conference such as befits saints.”

Befits saints.] C.: “Befits a priest.”

Of the worst silence.] C.: “But the causes of the worst silence are worldly or human fear.”

Except one who desires.] Thus Seneca: “No one fears except one who hopes.”

Into the mouth of Demosthenes.] Above I noted the source of the story.

With the Athenians.] M. and C.: “Against the Athenians. Hence also someone,” etc. The rest is absent.

Not *squinance*.] Better *synance*. For the other is French: *esquinancie*.

463 And the force of authority.] This is a saying of St. Ambrose, on 2 Corinthians, chapter VIII, near the beginning.

Paul abstained.] M. varies thus: “Paul, seeking his livelihood with his hands, did not receive necessities from his subjects.”

[Col. 0460D] Ah, ah, ah.] M.: “Ah, ah, ah.”

But no prelate.] M.: “But now prudence in prelates excuses age, which is false,” etc.

But this vice.] M. lacks this through “Quintilian.”

Whence Jerome.] See the letter against Helvidius, volume II, beginning *Nuper rogatus*.

Which is comparable.] Supply “is” or “seems,” to make the sense clearer. M. expresses the same in different words: “Since Gaul alone is free from monsters, Helvidius alone in it is both priest and layman—not because he lacked letters, but because, ignorant of figures of speech and of the various senses of this term *firstborn*, he erred in speaking against the Blessed Virgin. And [there is] the voice of repentance.”

And tears.] A half-line from Ovid, *Pontic Letters*, Book III, elegy X.

There is also the voice of confession.] See above, chapter 6, with the notes.

[Col. 0461A] In the voice of exultation.] C.: “In the voice of exultation and salvation in the tents of the righteous.” In all these matters silence is dangerous.

The second.] Namely, voice. V. adds: “That is, of confession.”

The third.] V. again adds: “Of prayer.”

The fourth.] V.: “Namely, of praise, that is, preaching.”

Of instruction.] Above, in the notes to chapter 6, I gathered that the word “instruction” is omitted and that, among these five kinds, the word “support,” or “mutual support,” is substituted.

CHAPTER LXIII.

Having censured the vice.] The beginning through “Let him open” is absent from M. It therefore begins as follows:

“Let the prelate open his mouth”—which the other two manuscripts omit through “For there is a time.”

For I know thee.] This is absent from M., which says: “The holy thing of God is not to be given to dogs,” etc.

The evil of detraction.] V. and C. lack this through “Whence Ezekiel.”

[Col. 0461B] Concerning the preacher.] V.: “preaching.”

And incapacity.] M.: “and incapacity.”

Which is done against a private person.] C. and M.: “Which arises from the vice of the tongue against a private person.”

Where sometimes.] M. omits “where.”

To strive in vain.] After Terence, St. Jerome, Letter to Domnion and Rogatian, beginning *Utrum difficilius*.

464 Jeremiah, chapter XXV.] V.: chapter III.

If a bad example.] C.: “If an example is feared by the wicked.”

CHAPTER LXIV.

Not the Lord.] V.: “Like a stranger and a traveller, and never”—the rest is absent. C.: “Like a stranger and be silent much, and never,” etc. I omitted “and be silent much,” because it is repeated shortly afterward.

If you wish to be loved.] C., in the margin: “He sets down charity.” But M. at the side has: “He notes rarity.” Refer this to [Col. 0461C] “Be silent much,” that is, speak rarely.

He was always silent.] M.: “He was silent for a long time.” I spoke of Lanfranc above, chapter 10, after the middle. Cantipratensis reports a remarkable example of a monk of Affligem in Brabant, who, because of his continual observance of silence, was called Ralph the Silent. When he saw a great fire in his aforesaid monastery, trusting in God’s goodness, he uttered these words: “Fire, stand at this hour; flame, wholly cease!” He had previously not uttered even a syllable for sixteen years. Book II of *The Bees*, chapter 13, no. 4.

Like a bridle.] M. omits it.

Since it is safer.] M.: “Since it is less.”

Of mercy.] Absent from M.

It is more safely heard.] M. alone reads this saying.

That his words may have.] M. immediately adds: “Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke II).

Not from the tip.] C. and V.: “Not from the tips of the lips.”

[Col. 0461D] But that they may be distinguished.] M. is silent through “Double.”

Using evil.] C.: “The ancients [use] evil.” It makes no sense.

But that the vice.] M. again omits this, and there begins a new period: “Note that [it occurs] in three ways.”

My son, do not let them praise thee.] V. omits this proverb.

Of every idle [word].] Only M. has this through “In Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXVIII.”

Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXVIII.] V.: chapter LXXV; C.: LXXXIII.

James, chapter III.] C. and V.: chapter VI. In C.’s margin I observed this: “How certain saints—undoubtedly St. Lawrence—provoked their torturers to anger, saying, ‘Turn me over and eat.’ He who is tortured can do more than the torturer himself, perhaps by inward revelation and the familiar counsel of the Holy Spirit.”

CHAPTER LXV.

That we may pursue the office of the prelate.] M. reads twice: “That we may more fully pursue the office of the prelate, and also more fully set forth his heedless [Col. 0462A] loquacity.” 465 etc. C. again reads *pursue* for “set forth.” V. has, better, “examine.”

And moderation.] V.: “and self-restraint.”

But to carnal persons.] M. is partly silent: “To carnal persons the preacher ought to announce historical matters.”

Apostolic men.] C. and V. omit this and substitute other matter. What? Listen: “Mountains rise and valleys descend—the same [waters] to the place which thou hast founded for them” (Psalm CIII).

To the Corinthians, chapter II.] The Three: chapter VII.

Sublimity.] V. rightly has this because it corresponds to the biblical text: “Not in sublimity of speech,” or “through sublimity of speech,” as the Greek texts and two Leuven manuscripts have. M. and C.: “subtlety.”

The same, chapter III.] The Three: chapter XIV.

The same, chapter IX.] The Three: XLI.

To the Romans, chapter I.] The Three: chapter III.

I Corinthians, chapter IX.] The same: chapter XLI.

[Col. 0462B] II Corinthians V.] Likewise the same: chapter XV.

It urges us.] C.: “It admonishes us.”

For this reason also.] M. omits it, reading: “Hence it is that saliva, spittle, and childish words,” etc.

And manly words to the greater.] C.: “For the prelate ought to have both manly and childish words for lesser persons.” M., however: “Thus the prelate [should speak] lesser things to lesser persons. Jacob saw angels,” etc. To this I refer C.’s margin: “Lest they say things too subtle and profound.”

Hortensius.] M. makes no mention of him in the text. Cicero treats of Hortensius in the *Brutus*.

Capitol.] C.: “chapter”; I admit this also. For it belongs to prelates to exhort and admonish their subjects in chapter.

Let him mingle with divine utterances.] Margin of C.: “From ignorance and display of learning.” M. in the same place: “Experience or display.”

Seeking rather.] M. omits this through “in the temple.”

[Col. 0462C] Concerning the Samaritan woman.] V. omits this through “basket.”

He sets down four words.] M. varies thus: “He says three things for uprooting vices,” omitting “you shall scatter,” “and two for planting virtues. ‘You shall pluck up’: by contrition, which he infuses into the minds of hearers. ‘You shall destroy’: by confession; ‘you shall scatter’: by satisfaction; ‘you shall build’: by preaching; and ‘you shall plant’: by consoling.”

Which occurs through [the removal] of vices.] C.: “which occurs through judgement, rebuke, hearing confession,” etc.

Therefore prelates are baskets.] M. reads as follows: “And it should be noted that the confessor ought to be a basket in which the filth of the city of God is carried and cleansed, as is said of Joseph: ‘His hands served in the basket.’ He ought to apply to his confessing subject first the wine of compunction and afterwards the oil of sweetness and consolation, 466 after the example of the Samaritan, who poured wine and oil into the wounds of the injured man. [Col. 0462D] He ought also to sympathize with his penitent and promise to share the burden of the penance imposed. (From St. Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, II, part [chapter] 6.) And above all the confessor ought to exhort his penitent to three things: namely, that he flee the occasion of sin, etc. (Likewise, *Morals*, Book 20, chapter 8.)”

And that he may [have] diligence.] C. and V.: “And that he may have diligence in making satisfaction for sins.” It then follows: “Likewise, on Esther, chapter I,” which M. omits. I have collected the rest of this chapter from M. alone.

One must immediately run to the confessor.] And this is for greater good; a person does not newly sin by postponing confession until the first opportunity. In the meantime, after sin it is safe and praiseworthy to have contrition, with the purpose of amendment and of making confession at the first opportunity given.

The obligation of satisfaction is incurred.] I corrected M., which read: “is not incurred.”

*Bien jujar.*] Perhaps, according to the Spaniards, *juzgar*: “to judge.”

The entire office of a prelate.] C. and V. end thus; but M. [Col. 0463A] adds: “Namely, to judge well, to preach, and to impose penance. And it must be known,” etc., which belongs to the following chapter.

CHAPTER LXVI.

There is variety in the summaries or headings of the three exemplars. C. has: “On the office of the prelate in three parts.” V., however: “Against respect of persons.” M. does not separate the present chapter from the preceding one, but notes this in the side margin: “On respect of persons.”

Before I add any notes here, reader, I wish you to be advised that, from this chapter 66 to the words in chapter 80, “The interjection expressing indignation of mind,” etc., I have transcribed exemplar M. word for word, as they say, in order to avoid continual labour. For since the Marchian manuscript differs greatly from the other two, both by its many variants in reading and by its disordered arrangement of sentences, it could with great difficulty be compared, sentence by sentence or clause by clause, [Col. 0463B] with the other two exemplars, much less reduced to common notes. What I transcribed from M. I placed immediately after our notes at the final chapter of the work.

I now continue my annotations from C. and V.

Augustine.] In place of Augustine, some might say Ambrose on Romans II; but it is more likely to be falsely attributed to Ambrose, even though it is not established that the saying belongs to Augustine.

I think because of religion.] C.: “suppose because of religion and uprightness of life.” In the margin, on “uprightness of life,” it notes: “Which alone God regards, namely the merit of one’s life.”

It is the rejection of a person.] Margin of C.: “The rejection of honour is a crime, just as its abuse is; this is called rejection of a person.”

But there are certain intermediate cases.] C. likewise in the margin: “On account of which of these is respect of persons a venial sin or a criminal one, and when is it more criminal? This is uncertain.”

Of Abelard.] V.: Abelard.

Of the pimp.] C.: “of Leo.”

James, chapter II.] The Two: chapter IV.

He judges thus inwardly.] C., in the margin: “This seems to be what this text means: ‘Do you not judge among yourselves?’ etc.” These matters are also gathered from the Gloss on this passage in James, though in different words.

But through conscience.] Margin of C.: “For he knows him to be righteous.” V.: “But through knowledge.”

Deuteronomy, chapter I.] C.: chapter II; V.: chapters 70 and 29. This is not right, because it is repeated also in chapter XVI, verses 19 and 20.

Likewise Job XXXII.] C.: Job XXIII; V.: 13.

It is said in Ecclesiasticus.] In the manuscripts it is marked chapter XXII.

The Catholic Epistle of Jude.] The Two—that is, C. and V.: chapter 3. Formerly the epistle of St. Jude the Apostle was divided into more chapters.

Admiring persons.] C. explains at the side: “Accepting [persons].” [Col. 0463D] M., however: “praising.”

Phinehas, with zeal for God.] V.: “Phinehas, with the dart of God”—incorrectly.

Bohemond.] V. correctly has this, as is clear from Baronius, volume XII, under the year 1100, folio 12. C.: Boimundus.

Mohammedan.] V.: Machometan; C.: Macometan. Such was the ancient spelling, just as Germans even today pronounce *nichil* for *nihil*.

I Kings, chapter XIV.] The Two: chapter XXV.

Jonathan against the decree.] Hear C.’s margin: “From this, however, one argues that such is the people’s fitting relation and power—not, I say, against the king, but toward him—and that of the clergy toward their prelate and bishop.” In the text M. says after this example of Jonathan: “And here you have an argument that a ruler ought not do anything without the consent of the people, nor a prelate without the counsel of the clergy.”

Likewise Exodus XXXII.] V.: 123; C.: 122.

With such equity.] St. Gregory’s text: “With such equality.”

[Col. 0464A] To live within the Church.] C. omits the single word “to live.”

He denies that he is of God.] On this exposition of St. Gregory, C.’s margin says: “Let this saying especially terrify the prelate.”

The life of carnal people.] The same margin: “As though neither because of carnal affection nor for any other cause.”

Likewise Haman.] V. notes Esther VII. Today it is chapter V.

And he was not moved from his place.] “But how could he not be?” says C.’s margin, “when the Apostle commands that authorities be honoured, and this man was second to the king?” Romans XIII.

John, chapter IV.] The Two: chapter XXXVIII.

468 CHAPTER LXVII.

Procrustes.] A notorious robber in Attica, concerning whom Plutarch writes in his *Theseus*.

The highest law, the highest.] V.: “The highest law is the highest [Col. 0464B] injustice.” From Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I.

To sin in remitting.] That is, by acting too leniently, or by mitigating punishment that is due.

In every work.] C.: “at every time.”

He considered [it] most prudent.] Cato says:

> To feign folly at the fitting time is the height of prudence.

Proverbs, chapter XV.] The Two: chapter XXXII.

On St. Malachy.] His life was written by the honey-tongued doctor, St. Bernard.

On the abbot of Igny.] His name was Humbert; St. Bernard discusses him in Letter 141 and in a sermon. I have seen a French-written life of Blessed Humbert of Igny among several other lives of holy Cistercian abbots, published by the Reverend Lord Jean d’Assignies, monk of Cambron and now most worthy abbot of Nizelles. Concerning the same Humbert, see the Cistercian Menology under 7 September and others cited by Chrysostom Henriquez in his notes for that same day.

He is recorded to have wept three times.] Namely, at the raising of [Col. 0464C] Lazarus, John XI; over the city, Luke XIX; and in prayer, as is gathered from Hebrews V.

Especially when all defects.] C., at the side for clarification, reads the verses of Juvenal, *Satires* 9:

> In the sick body you may discern the torments of the hidden mind;  
> you may discern its joys as well; the face takes its expression from both.

But could God have laughed rightly?] On this question, see John Nider, *Formicarius*, Book I, chapter 11.

Let him be suspect to you.] After quarrelling, laughter is a sign of dissimulation. Thus C. in the side margin.

CHAPTER LXVIII.

Modes of living.] C.: “modes of seeing.”

It produces a mark.] Quite so: for excessive familiarity produces contempt, while rarity wins admiration.

They suit a Christian.] Thus reads the text of St. Jerome, Letter to Eustochium *On the Guardianship of Virginity*, beginning *Audi filia*, at the end of chapter 12, volume I. C. has: “Or [Col. 0464D] they produce praise in dress.” Likewise Augustine.

Likewise Augustine.] Something similar occurs in volume III, Book I, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 4.

Or signify something.] C.’s margin says: “Such a person is directed to taste something of everything, lest he be suspected.”

Likewise the same.] Augustine, volume VI, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 31.

469 Provided that in these.] C., in the margin: “Lest compliance be made; lest we be conformed to the world.”

And may you deserve to be called.] It refers to the verse of Persius, *Satires* I:

> But it is fine to be pointed out with the finger and called: “There he is!”

But they desire to be seen.] C.’s margin adds: “As a cleric, or a layman, and things of that sort.”

Common sense.] C. divides it: “Sense, communion, humanity.” We are of Seneca’s age.

Thus customary.] M. reads “unaccustomed,” contrary to the original and the other exemplars.

[Col. 0465A] Not unkempt.] C.: “not unarranged.”

Not punishment.] C.’s margin adds: “And unsuitable sobriety.”

But let them not recognize.] Seneca’s text: “But let them also recognize.”

Just as with silver.] Thus the original; ours: “Just as with earthenware and silver.” But we added “just as with earthenware” at the end of the sentence from that same original.

CHAPTER LXIX.

Which more familiarly.] C.: “which to familiars”; M.: “which is more properly called solitude.”

Or commends.] By example, says Lipsius on this passage.

Or impresses.] By speech.

Smears on.] By association.

I was among men.] Margin of C.: “In a crowd.” For a crowd is always troubled, according to the etymology of its name.

Therefore one must withdraw.] The same Seneca, later in the same letter. M. often varies in this letter of Seneca. See [Col. 0465B] after our notes to the final chapter of this work.

With so great a retinue.] V.: “with a great retinue”; C.: “with great striving.” I have observed Seneca’s text.

One example.] Thus M. with Seneca. The Two: “Whence [an] example.” There follows: “With a simple mind.” Seneca omits “mind.”

If you conform yourself to them.] This is absent from Seneca’s text.

Likewise Jerome.] C., at the side: “In the Life of St. Paul, namely the hermit.” But it is not found there.

Jeremiah, chapter XV.] V. and C.: chapter 62.

Thou hast filled me with bitterness.] Thus St. Jerome’s translation in his commentary, and the Septuagint; today, however, it reads: “Thou hast filled me with threatening.”

CHAPTER LXX.

C., as heading: “On avoiding bad company.”

From association, morals.] Seneca: “Character is acquired from those with whom one associates,” *On Anger*, Book III, chapter 8.

470 Evil conversations.] A verse of the poet Menander. C.: “corrupt hearts.”

[Col. 0465C] Ecclesiasticus, chapter IX.] C.: 31; V.: 32.

And the philosopher.] Seneca, *Letters* 19, after Epicurus.

And Augustine.] Perhaps Gregory, book IX, letter 49, or the general synod over which he presided, chapter 2. Likewise 2, question 7, *Cum Pastoris*.

Nature is with the good.] That is, “will,” says V. between the lines.

For such as the judge is.] “Let the king desire honourable things; surely everyone else will desire the same.” Or:

> The whole world is fashioned after the example of its king.

Ecclesiasticus, chapter XIII.] V. and C.: chapter 40.

He loves his like.] C. at the side: “With the holy you will be holy” (Psalm XVII).

It must especially be avoided.] Because it is destructive, as Seneca attests, *Letter* 7.

Proverbs, chapter XIII.] C. and V.: chapter 29.

Scylla is described.] You have this in St Jerome, book IV, in the preface to the third book of the *Commentaries on Jeremiah*, and in the letter to Heliodorus, *On the Praise of the Solitary Life*, vol. I.

[Col. 0465D] Like Harpies.] On the Harpy-bird, see Virgil, *Aeneid* III, and Cantipratanus, book I, *On Bees*, chapter 25.

The affairs of the rich.] Margin C.: “The condition of the rich.”

Frogs in the inner chambers.] St Jerome speaks explicitly on this passage: “By frogs,” he says, “the poems of poets are indicated—poets who, departing from the Catholic rule, fill the hearts of earthly kings with fabulous deceptions.”

The condition of the powerful is perilous.] Margin C.: “The affairs of the poor are safe.”

I Kings XIV.] Two manuscripts: XXV.

I Kings XIX.] Elsewhere: XXXII.

## CHAPTER LXXI

V. reads for the title: “Against fleshly affections.”

Works from the flesh.] C. in the margin: “Under the title on consanguinity, and under the title on the promotion of the unworthy.”

He has not preferred.] Margin C.: “Things more useful must always be preferred to less useful, according to time and place.”

It ought to be moderated.] V.: “It ought to be restrained.”

But though they bellow.] C. incorrectly: “But not though they bellow.” For this is disproved by St Gregory in the passage cited in the margin [Col. 0466A]. He says: “They utter bellows from their inmost parts, yet their steps do not turn aside from the road.” V. reads: “But bellowing”; wrongly, because it errs in case.

Especially in spiritual matters.] C.: “Especially not in spiritual matters.”

For whom.] Namely, his wife. V.: “For this reason.”

Leviticus XXI.] C.: Leviticus LXX; V.: 71.

At the Saviour’s call.] C. at the side: “Lazarus, come forth,” John XI.

471 Let us repay our parents.] Margin C.: namely, with the necessities of life.

This, as regards necessi—.] C.: “That which concerns necessity.” Likewise below: “That which concerns precaution,” etc.

For this reason Benedict.] The blessed Gregory, pope, wrote the life and miracles of our holy father Benedict, *Dialogues*, book II, vol. I.

Aegidius.] See his life in Surius, vol. V, 1 September.

[Col. 0466B] They entered.] V.: “She entered.”

Judges 9.] V.: Judges XV; C.: Judges XI.

Joathae.] “Two Jonathans,” but corruptly.

They had advanced.] Margin C.: “And the deeds of Gideon in part.”

Where Augustine says.] Vol. X, sermon 6, *On the Words of the Apostle*.

Those descending from the side.] C. in the margin: “Namely, our nephews.”

Of military service.] C. in the margin: “Of a new soldiery. A sacrament is a kind of military service. See Erasmus’s notes on this passage.”

It is not iron for us.] C. in the same place: “Nor for you either.”

Not born from flint.] C. and V.: “not born from flint.” I restored this according to Jerome’s text.

To babble for the breast.] Two manuscripts, instead of *lallare* (“to babble”), read “to give milk.” I likewise restored the former. Persius says, *Satires* III:

> And, like children of kings, you ask for a little *pappare*,  
> and angrily refuse to babble for the breast?

*Pappare* means “to eat”; hence we call children’s food *pappa*.

It must be beaten back with the sword-point.] Thus I read in two manuscripts, although St Jerome’s text has *muro* (“wall”) for *mucrone* (“sword-point”).

To some relative.] V.: “To some one of his parents.”

Likewise, the example of the Templars.] V., after “to entrust,” adds: “But neither may a Templar have a kinsman as a servant. The example of the bishop also bears upon this,” etc. On the Templars at greater length, see text C.

When I was raised to the summit.] C.: “Since I was raised to the summit.”

Likewise, IV Kings IV, ‘Send.’] C., after “you advanced,” adds: “Likewise III Kings at the end; and 10 and 16 in the middle; and III Kings IX and 23 in the middle. Likewise IV Kings LXIII, ‘Send.’” Here V. and C. agree. I restored the chapter according to the present biblical numbering: IV Kings IV, otherwise 63.

[Col. 0466D] Woe to those who build Zion in—.] Habakkuk is cited, although his text has “the city” instead of “Zion.” Micah III reads “Zion in blood.”

## CHAPTER LXXII

The solitude of work.] Two manuscripts read *temporis* (“of time”) for *operis* (“of work”), but I restored the latter from what was said above. For at the end of chapter 69, where solitude is divided threefold, it reads: “solitude of place, of heart, and of work.”

472 There are, indeed, two kinds.] See the kinds of monks in St Jerome, vol. I, letter to Eustochium *On the Guarding of Virginity*, chapter 15; and after him our holy father Benedict, chapter 1 of his Rule.

The second, loftier.] V. omits *loftier*.

Your Bonosus.] M. wrongly: “Your Onesimus.”

Let them yield to this truth.] I restored this from Jerome’s text down to the words “despising his mother.” C. and V. omitted these.

Onesimus.] C. is mistaken: *honestissimus* (“most honourable”), not *Onesimus*.

[Col. 0467A] Made by census.] V.: “He gave his name for the census.” It suppresses the rest.

Limbs deformed.] Two manuscripts: “deformed limbs.” Restored from Jerome.

By no south wind of Euripus.] Certain printed editions of Jerome, though not those edited by Erasmus, read: “By no pleasantness of riverbanks.” See Erasmus’s notes on this passage.

Or prays to the Lord.] Printed editions: “When he prays to the Lord.”

There provisions of bread.] I recall that M. reads *cribrarios* (“sieve-makers” or “of sieves”).

The secrecy of the tree.] C. and V.: “the secrecy of the air.”

He shows.] This is tolerable. Printed editions: “they show.”

Complaining—or chattering, as M. has it.

I shall not buy wood.] Printed Jerome: “I shall not buy together.”

I shall keep watch warmly.] Printed editions: “more warmly.”

It is more useful: I shall not be cold.] Printed editions: “more cheaply, I shall not,” etc.

Likewise, Maximinus.] Bishop of Trier, concerning whom see Usuard’s martyrology, 29 May. C.: “Likewise, Maximianus.” Margin C. adds: “In the *Legend of All Saints*.” Surius has his life, vol. III.

Whence Stilpon.] Consult Seneca, *Letter* 10, at the beginning; but first read through the end of Letter 9. V. and C.: “Stilbon.”

So that you may see what judgment.] C. varies here: “and see what judgment I have of you—namely, I dare,” etc. I followed Seneca, *Letter* 10.

Let him depart.] V. incorrectly: “let him have.” See Seneca, *Letter* 10.

Angry and furious.] Seneca’s text does not contain these two words.

Explains.] Seneca’s text: “brings forth.”

I would rather that you be.] From Seneca I restored *you*, whose omission was greatly harmful.

Who not only in appearance.] I restored this from the same Seneca. For two manuscripts have, instead of *aspectus* (“appearance”): “Who not merely in presence,” as some advise. Lipsius says that he has read this in his books, and himself testifies that all manuscripts of Seneca have: “Who not merely in action.”

[Col. 0467C] Always show yourself to yourself.] Thus Seneca. C., for “show yourself,” has “make yourself.”

The Egyptian woman.] The life of this Mary of Egypt was written by Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, according to Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 5; Surius has it, vol. II, 9 April. I saw another life, written in Sapphic verse by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, in the celebrated monastery of Bonne-Espérance of the Premonstratensian Order.

Likewise, chapter XLIX.] C.: chapter 73; V.: 63.

473 Hazor.] Margin C. says: “Hazor is interpreted ‘an arrow.’ But the world is full of arrows and snares, and for that reason must be fled.”

Martin, still twelve years old.] See his life, published by Sulpicius Severus, in Surius, vol. VI.

St Germanus.] You have his life in Surius, vol. IV (31 July).

Remigius of Rheims.] There is a life composed by Hincmar. Surius, vols. I and V. M. adds after “Remigius”: “son of the count of Laon.”

[Col. 0467D] The second, more temperate.] V.: “The second, more temperate, the last and more desirable.”

The danger of the first.] C.: “The danger of the people which is in the city; the first, which is in singularity: Woe to the solitary,” etc. What I restored from V. is clearer.

By the small number of the circumcised.] C. says at the side: “For in the perfect, smallness of number, as a middle road, must be chosen.”

He offends and is offended.] C.: “He shows and is shown.”

It rebounds upon individuals.] “When he reports to his brothers what he has seen outside” (*Rule*, chapter LXVII), because, as St Benedict says, “it is a very great destruction.”

## CHAPTER LXXIII

When Achan sinned.] Two manuscripts: “Achor.”

He consents.] Perhaps a distinction should be made between greater and lesser consent, says C. in the margin.

Nothing perishes thereby.] A half-line of Ovid’s *Amores*.

The sign alone.] In singing. Margin C.

Through the multitude.] V.: “for the multitude.”

[Col. 0468A] On the Second Book of Kings.] C. and V. corruptly read: “On the Third Book of Kings.” I have seen similar things in St Augustine, vol. III, book II, *On the Wonders of Holy Scripture*, chapter 13. Moreover, these sayings are cited in *On Penance*, distinction 3, “But this”; likewise 1, question 4, “The Church which.”

Seventy thousand.] Not eighty thousand, as C. has.

Eli because of iniquity.] I changed nothing, although these words are not Josephus’s but rather St Jerome’s, vol. II, *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 20; they are also recorded in the Gloss on I Kings II.

With severe punishment.] V.: “with savage punishment.”

I Kings, chapter XXVIII.] V.: chapter XLV; C.: chapter XLVI. Regarding this, C.’s margin should be noted: “He extinguishes the Holy Spirit who does not freely—being, for example, constrained by fear or another improper cause—speak the truth, or who conceals it.”

474 ## CHAPTER LXXIV

V. varies in the summary: “That, on a slight occasion, saints declare themselves guilty of some sin, even a very grave one.”

He considers himself guilty of sin.] C. repeats this sentence in the margin with slight alterations: “A holy man, for a slight occasion, considers himself guilty of a sin which he does not commit by deed or express word.”

II Kings XXIII.] V.: II Kings XLIX; C.: II Kings XXVI.

Concerning the danger.] Because they had exposed their lives in order to draw water and carry it to David.

Acts of the Apostles, chapter XX.] V.: chapter XLVIII; C.: chapter LXIX.

Deuteronomy, chapter XIX.] V.: chapter LXXXV; C.: chapter LXXXIV.

You shall have guarded the church.] V., instead of “church,” reads “person.”

Little grates and supports.] V. omits these. It reads: “You shall make a wall around the roof, even if it is flat.” M., for *ruticulas*, has *luticulas*. Perhaps *reticula* (“grates”) or *retinacula* (“rails”). *Apodiationes* are supports or rails on which those wishing to rest after walking on a roof-platform may lean; in French, *apuys*.

A wall around the roof, even if it is flat.] C.: “A sloping wall, even if it is flat.” C.’s margin says of this: “Why, then, are churches built with towers and so high?”

Likewise an advocate.] See below in M., for it varies here.

Across the Apennines.] V.: *appenninum*; C.: *alpenninum*. Pliny writes on the Apennine mountains, III.12; Virgil on the Apennine dwellers, *Aeneid* XI:

> … the Apennine-dweller, warrior son of Annius.

Likewise Job, chapter IX.] C.: chapter XI; V.: chapter XL.

In Numbers, chapter XXXII.] C. and V.: chapter LXVII.

Likewise Exodus XXI.] V.: Exodus LIII; C.: LII.

Robert, bishop of Amiens.] He appears to be the one listed as the fortieth in Claude Robert’s *Gallia Christiana*, in the year 1166.

St Maurilius of Angers.] C.: Maurilius of Le Mans, but wrongly. In Claude Robert’s catalogue he is the thirtieth and is called Mauriolus. Usuard, in the martyrology for 13 September, calls him Maurilio. [Col. 0468D] There is a life in Vincent of Beauvais, book XXI of the *Speculum historiale*, chapter CXXVI, written by Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers.

To baptize a boy.] From the life of St Maurilius himself it follows that the matter should be not of baptizing a boy, but of confirming him. See Surius, vol. V, 13 September. A similar example occurs in manuscript M., concerning a certain bishop of Cambrai. See it below, after the notes on the final chapter of this work.

475 ## CHAPTER LXXV

C., for summary or title, has: “Against the superstitious,” wrongly.

What is done in himself.] St Augustine, Psalm CXVIII, exposition 12: “What is done in himself.” C. is mistaken: “What is stirred up in himself.” V. may be tolerated: “What he does in himself.”

Outward matters.] That is, matters of mere appearance. C.: “eyebrows,” through a copyist’s error.

Or on account of praises.] This is the interlinear and ordinary Gloss on Matthew VI [Col. 0469A], though I think the author drew it directly from St Augustine, vol. VIII, Psalm CXVIII, exposition 12.

But the judgment of matters.] V. alone adds: “made manifest.” On this point see St Thomas’s teaching, II–II, question 60, article 4.

Doubtful matters in the better sense.] The same author clearly resolves this in the same passage.

Romans XIV.] Two manuscripts: 45.

Galatians, chapter VI.] V.: chapter XII; C.: Ephesians, chapter XII.

Recklessly assailing.] He drew this from St Augustine, vol. IV, book of exposition on this passage.

Of cutting off communion.] St Augustine’s text reads *praecidendae* (“to be cut off”), but the variation is one of word, not meaning; therefore I retained the reading found in the manuscript(s). C. wrongly has not “communion” but “admonition.”

A bed of ash.] You have an example of this matter in manuscript M. below, after all the notes.

Sardanapalus.] Sardanapalus was the last king of the Assyrians, “a man more corrupted than a woman,” says Justin, book I. Hence arose the proverb, “more effeminate than Sardanapalus.” Tertullian uses this proverb, vol. I, *On the Pallium*, chapter IV, no. 79.

The Lord’s anointed.] Namely, a priest. This is M.’s opinion—or certainly a bishop.

James, chapter IV.] V. and C.: chapter 9.

Ecclesiasticus, chapter XI.] The same passage, chapter XXXVI.

476 ## CHAPTER LXXVI

[Col. 0469C] V. reads for the title: “On the noisy and the gossiping.”

II Thessalonians III.] V. and C.: II Thessalonians V.

And we beseech.] C.: “And we rebuke.”

And gossip.] This has the flavour of the interlinear Gloss on this passage. Thus: “Not gossiping.”

And Quintus Curtius.] The manuscripts have this in the text. But C. corrects in the margin: “Read Mutius.” Cicero discusses him in *Against Verres*.

Rumour, an evil.] A line from Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, to be read parenthetically.

And uttering with unwashed—.] C.: “immediately.”

Such bibulous persons.] From St Bernard’s *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius.

It ought to be certain.] Yet not in a judicial proceeding, says C.’s margin.

His little matter.] *Recula* is a diminutive of *res* (“thing”). C. reads “rule.”

Socrates commanded.] Aristotle observed this precept of Socrates, as is shown above at the end of chapter 5 and in the notes.

And Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXXII.] C.: chapter 85; V.: 86.

Makes known.] That is, “he may wish to explain it,” says C. in the margin. You will find more on this in chapter 5 of this work.

Likewise Ecclesiasticus XXIX.] C.: 65.

In Proverbs, chapter IV.] C.: chapter 14.

It will be unlike.] That is, difficult. Thus C. at the side.

Words unutterable.] Margin C. incorrectly corrects this to “utterable.” For the biblical text contradicts it.

The sum of sums.] Is this Seneca, *Letter* 40, at the end?

And the philosopher.] Who is this philosopher? Is he Seneca? I have not yet found this sentence in him. Meanwhile I would call Plautus, at the beginning of Act I, scene 1 of the *Mostellaria*, the principal author of this saying.

Nor to dispel fears.] C. omits the latter two half-lines, which are from Statius, *Thebaid* XI. V., for “to dispel,” has “to balance.” Here I follow the printed editions.

The emperor Augustus.] Besides this example, manuscript M. has another. See it below, after the notes.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

[Col. 0470A]

V. lacks a title and does not separate this chapter from the preceding one by a break.

Inconstancy accompanies it.] C.: “is communicated.”

Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXXIII.] C.: LXXXVI; V.: 87.

It belongs to women to be inconstant.] The interlinear Gloss on this passage.

477 The trembling head.] We spoke above, in chapter II, of the sign placed upon Cain.

And Isaiah III.] V. and C.: Isaiah VIII.

And Proverbs, chapter IV.] V.: chapter 13; C.: 14.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

C. completes the title with a few words: “Against foreign judgments.”

He consults diviners.] C. says at the side: “Read ‘he raises up’ or ‘is raised up.’ What is this? Is the text of Holy Scripture, then, mistaken?”

By sword or battle.] This certainly pleased them. V.: “or a basin.”

Or of an enchanter.] C. here has “enchanter,” but below [Col. 0470B] “enchantments.” In French, *charmes*.

But how shall I understand?] I restored this from the Holy Scriptures. Otherwise the two manuscripts read: “But how shall I understand that the Lord has spoken through him? You shall have this sign: if what that prophet predicted has not happened, then this the Lord has spoken” (V.: “and this the Lord has not spoken”), “but the prophet has invented it through pride of heart,” etc.

But foreign judgments.] Margin C.: “As ecclesiastical sacraments do.”

For these.] V.: “For those.”

But if it happens.] Same margin: “By the devil’s agency, with God’s permission.”

Likewise, chapter XVII.] V.: chapter 86; C.: 76.

Gloss: ‘Only.’] C.: “He who shall be killed by the sword. Only,” etc. The copyist wrote *gladio* (“sword”) for *Glossa* (“Gloss”). Thus the ordinary Gloss: “Namely, the testimonies of the Law, Prophets, and Gospel, according to John XI: ‘The word which I have spoken, that shall judge him on the last day.’”

Hebrews VI.] Two manuscripts: 9.

Scripture records.] Numbers, chapter V. This chapter too is cited in Cause 2, question 4, *Consuluisti*.

Because of excessive humility (ταπείνωσις).] Because of this same cause, says V.’s margin, it was forbidden at the general chapter at Cîteaux for Gratian’s *Decree* to be kept in our cloisters, since certain less discerning abbots abused their authority to investigate thefts from the monastery. Read through the text of M. at this point, because it recounts many examples.

Therefore, not even in the matter in which less—.] Likewise because of the uncertainty of a foreign judgment, says C. at the side.

Privileges of the few.] Rule of Law 74 in the *Sext* has: “What is granted graciously to one person ought not to be drawn by others into a precedent.” Or: “Things sometimes granted because of necessity cannot be drawn into an argument.” Rule 78 in the *Sext*, and 2, question 2, “Not immediately.”

478 In these matters judgment is made concerning—.] C. says in the margin [Col. 0470D]: “So that they may secretly reject the accused, or admit the innocent.”

They attain their effect.] The same writer says there: “Yet because several people were thereby saved, certain malicious persons transferred the practice to the judgment of fire, by which they perished all the more.”

Rather than by miracles.] Why is this? Because daily miracles, through their frequency, become cheap, says St Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels* 26, near the end. Moreover, he says, those bodily miracles sometimes show holiness but do not create it. But these spiritual miracles, performed in the mind, do not show the virtue of life but create it. The wicked too can possess the former; but none except the good can enjoy the latter. Homily 29, middle.

Those things which concern salvation.] “I do not mean adjuncts,” says C. at the side, “such as the grace of preaching and the like.”

Found by Solomon.] This book is condemned in the decree of Pope Gelasius, distinction 15, chapter *The Holy Roman Church*. Sixtus of Siena, book II of the *Sacred Library*, under “Solomon,” says: “In the Decree of Pope Gelasius there is also counted among condemned writings a certain book most falsely ascribed to Solomon, entitled the *Key of Solomon*.” On these exorcisms, see more fully Michael Glykas, part II of the *Annals*, p. 255.

But the author is unknown.] “Unless perhaps it is the devil,” says C.’s margin. Take what I found in V.’s margins at this point.

St Gengulf [Note: [Col. 0471D] Surius, vol. III, calls him Gangulphus.] was Burgundian by origin and very dear to King Pippin. Once, while returning and passing through Champagne, he came to a certain spring. As he was taking breakfast beside it, the owner of that small estate came up. Inviting him to dinner, Gengulf asked him to sell him the spring. The man, thinking privately to himself, began to mock him, believing that he could retain both things, namely the price and the spring; and he sold it for one hundred solidi. Therefore Gengulf, having paid the price and mounted his horses, returned and told his wife, who had committed adultery during his absence, what he had done. She, being proud and wanton, mocked him for wasting his property so lightly by buying useless things.

[Col. 0471B] After this St Gengulf, making a circuit of places adjoining his house, thrust into the ground the staff which he carried and, leaving it there, returned. On the following day, when he rose in the morning and asked for water to wash his hands and face, there was none. He ordered one of his servants to go to the place marked by the staff, draw out the staff, and bring the water which would follow it. As soon as the staff was withdrawn, the spring which he had bought in Champagne burst forth there; thus the greedy seller was deprived of his spring. It is whitish in colour and, even to this day, is said to heal the sick through the merits of St Gengulf.

The saint’s wife loved a certain cleric. When report of this disgrace reached the saint, he took his wife to the aforesaid spring as though for a walk, and said to her: “I hear many shameful things about you, but I offer you an easy test of purification. Here is a very cold spring: put your hand into it and bring up a hair from the bottom. If you suffer no harm, you are innocent.” Immediately, when she touched the hair and drew her hand back [Col. 0471C], whatever the water had touched was stripped bare of skin, as if she had put her hand into fire; so that flesh hung from the tips of her fingers, with the skin drawn off.

Then the saint said: “You deserved death indeed, but you shall not die by my hands. I reserve you for God’s judgment; yet if you repent, you will obtain forgiveness. But know this: you shall no longer be in my company. I leave you everything which I gave as dowry, so that you may have the means to live.”

Then St Gengulf went to his estates far away in the district of Avallon. But she, fearing that he would kill both her and her lover, spoke to the cleric. He came to the house in which the saint was sleeping and drew the sword that was at his head. The saint awoke, rose, and, while turning aside the blow aimed at his head, fell upon the sword-point and was mortally wounded in the thigh. The cleric fled to his mistress. After they had rejoiced together over what had happened—because the saint died a few days later—the cleric, intending to relieve his bowels, discharged all his entrails into the privy, and thus perished.

Meanwhile the saint was carried to burial and performed many miracles along the way. When one of his maidservants told his wife of this, she replied madly: “Gengulf performs miracles just as my anus does.” At these words, an obscene sound immediately came from the hidden part of her body. It was Friday. Thereafter she suffered such disgrace that throughout the rest of her life, as many words as she uttered on that day, so many shameful sounds issued from that part of her body. The report of this event became so widespread that King Pippin, passing through those places, sent messengers to investigate its truth and found it to be so.

This is what appears there; but C.’s margin recounts it much more briefly as follows: “It should be noted that Duke Ganculf, in order to test whether his wife had committed adultery, said to her: ‘If you draw a stone from the bottom of this spring without being burned, you are innocent.’ When she put her hand into the spring of cold water, she drew out a stone, and her hand was burned by the stone.” See more in the life of St Gangulphus in Surius, vol. III, 11 May.

He establishes the case.] C. corrects the text in the margin: for “establishes,” read “makes known.”

There is another manifest [case].] “Public and evident,” says St Augustine, vol. VIII, in his exposition of Psalm LXVIII.

Mammotrects.] Thus two manuscripts; a third, *mammotrepti*, Greek Μαμμότρεπτοι, meaning “those long suckled” or “brought up by a nurse.” St Augustine uses this word in sermon 2 on Psalm XXX. There is a biblical dictionary explaining obscure words, printed at Metz, called the *Mammotrectus*, because a certain member of the Order of Minors offered, as it were, a breast to suck to persons untrained in Latin (1509). The name appears to be of German origin: in that language *trecken* means “to draw,” as if one said “one who draws or sucks the breast.”

480 To the just under the New Testament.] C.: “To those sworn under the New [Testament],” etc.

[Col. 0472B] How then can the detestable form of the enchantment of iron be tolerated, etc.?] Not “in the incantations of iron,” as C. has. In the *Capitularies* of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious there is an edict on the use of boiling water, book IV, chapter 13. But in the fourth addition, chapter 81, use of cold water is forbidden in these words: “That the ordeal of cold water, which they have hitherto practised, be forbidden by all missi [that is, envoys], so that it may no longer take place.” Peter Pithou published these capitularies and added a glossary containing the exorcism of water used to reveal God’s judgment. Then comes a complete Mass for the same matter, called the *Mass of Judgment*. Thirdly, there are three adjurations of the water; fourthly, the same number of adjurations of the iron. He drew all these from the rite of Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury. These are the things which Peter the Chanter refutes throughout this whole chapter.

In boiling oil.] Prochorus, in the life of St John the Evangelist; likewise Tertullian, *On Prescription against Heretics*, no. 215.

St Marcellus of Paris.] A bishop, ninth in order. His life, by Fortunatus, is in Surius, vol. VI, 1 November. Note that these deeds of St Marcellus occurred before he was bishop, as is clear from M. See it after the notes, and you will find other examples that V. and C. omit.

On the heat of fire.] Ly omits “fire”; I supplied it from M.

And nine weights.] M.: “But nine,” etc.

O you, sinner.] V. between the lines: that is, “O you sinner.”

To Pope Eugenius.] M. adds: “In the presence of cardinals, archbishops, bishops,” etc. This is Eugenius III, to whom St Bernard sent the books *On Consideration*.

A certain Manichaean.] M. adds: “of Steila, a Briton,” perhaps from Britain. See the varying chapters of M. after all the notes.

Of the same city.] Namely, Rheims, no. 49, otherwise 50.

The blessing of water.] V. corruptly has “the cursing of water,” as is clear from what immediately follows.

By a convicted person.] V. also wrongly: “by a joined person.”

[Col. 0472D] Of acquitting Cathars.] The Cathars are heretics who follow Novatus, whence they are also called Novatians. St Jerome, vol. V, on Hosea XIV, says: “The interpretation concerning heretics is easy: they are called Samaria because they boast that they keep God’s commandments—not because they are guardians of his law, but because they say that they are so—in likeness of the schism of the Novatians, who also call themselves καθαρούς, that is, ‘pure,’ although they are the most unclean of all, denying repentance,” etc.

St Augustine likewise describes them in nearly these words: “The Cathars, who call themselves by this name, as though because of purity, most proudly and odiously, do not admit second marriages and deny repentance. They follow the heretic Novatus and are therefore also called Novatians.” Thus he, vol. VI, *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus*, heresy 38. On the Cathar heretics see more in Gabriel Prateolus, under “Cathari.” Under another name, Paterines or Patareni, they were condemned at the Third Lateran Council under Alexander III, chapter 27.

Of priests descended from the seed of Canaan.] Who wished to put Susanna to death. Margin C.: from Daniel XIII.

Hebrews, chapter XI.] V. and C.: chapter XVIII.

Sometimes victory is hidden.] Hidden victory belongs to the soul; manifest victory, to the body. St Augustine on Psalm LXVIII: “Attend to my soul and deliver it.”

Another confessed.] Accordingly, that sacristan of Compiègne was wrongly burned, once the truth of the matter had been discovered by the confession of the thief and culprit himself. M. recounts these examples more clearly below, after the notes.

A Cathars’ associate.] V. here reads “of gadflies,” but not well, as is evident from what follows, where the Cathar heresy is mentioned.

Therefore, in doubtful matters one must hold to—.] A saying of Seneca, *On the Four Virtues*, chapter 1.

By whose authority it is done.] Because one who acts through another acts just as though he did it himself. Rule of Law 72 in the *Sext*.

[Col. 0473B] Isidore says.] Perhaps St Gregory, as I infer from *Morals*, book III, and from the Gloss on II Kings XX.

II Corinthians IV.] V. and C.: XI.

But life works.] Namely, that life in which you delight in earthly things works eternal death in us.

I Corinthians, chapter XII.] C. and V.: chapter 60.

The analogy requires.] A sound reading, as found in Cause 2, question 8, *Whoever*. Therefore not “the analogy awaits,” as C. has.

Isaiah XLIV.] C. and V.: CXXIX.

An occasion for shedding blood.] “How much more do those sin who supply weapons to such people, so that they may unjustly shed blood!” Margin C. It is read in Cause 14, question I: “He who gives protection to evil men in an evil matter is a partner in the crime.” Moreover, one consents or gives protection when he joins to the deeds of evil men the fellowship of approval.

According to the saying: ‘A multitude.’] C. omits this through “therefore.” The proverb is commonly stated thus: “A multitude of persons in error does not provide error with a defence.”

Through violence into a tub.] C.: “Or if, compelled by violence, into care [or ‘cure’], he will be,” etc. V. reads correctly. Here *cuppa* or *cupa* means a cask used by sailors to support ships needing repair. Hence Lucan, *Civil War* IV:

> For empty casks support the vessel on every side.

When this is retained.] C.: “when this retains.”

It will be committed.] C.: “Or it will be committed.” I deleted *or*, which seemed superfluous.

The hand is calloused.] That is, hardened by continual practice. Thus in ironworks one may see smiths walk over almost glowing iron with calloused soles, without injury or burning of their feet.

482 That these foreign judgments of red-hot iron and water are forbidden in the Church is clear from Cause 2, question 5, *Consuluisti*; and from Ivo’s letter to Hildebert, beginning: “Ivo, by God’s grace minister of the Church of Chartres, to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans: patience in tribulation, endurance in patience.” There he warns Hildebert not, on any account, to seek to prove his innocence by the ordeal of fire which the king demanded of him, because it had been forbidden in God’s Church by many canons and decrees of pontiffs. I saw the letter, numbered 14 in our manuscripts and 91 in the printed editions. Moreover, Pope St Gregory I severely forbids these things in his letter to Brunhild, queen of the Franks, book XI, letter 8; it is cited in 2, question 5, chapter *Mennam*. They are likewise forbidden in book V, *On Popular Purgation*, in three chapters of Celestine III, Innocent III, and Honorius III.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

C. omits “and the multitude” in the title.

Those obeying.] C.: “testifying.” It makes no sense.

And disobedient.] C. varies greatly here: “Making those disobedient to them transgressors (there is no ‘unless’) in parsimony and in smallness.”

To divine commandments. These.] V.: “To divine commandments these,” and “to evacuate,” etc.

[Col. 0474A] Namely, silence.] V. admits only *namely*.

In more grievous matters.] “Read ‘in more restrictive matters,’” says C.’s margin; but what I retained in the text is better, as M. shows. For it says: “Concerning more grievous and enormous sins.”

If your right hand.] Understand by the right hand the contemplative life; by the left, the active life.

Return to the active life.] How is this? May one leave Mary in order to cling to Martha? Listen. The contemplative life is twofold. One kind is higher, simple, and pure, by which a person is carried into God, converses with him, or in mind takes part in the choirs of heaven. The other is inferior to the first and may be called the active life of contemplatives: by it one applies himself to honourable exercises, lest the mind’s vision, constantly fixed on contemplation, be impaired.

These exercises are various: devoting oneself to sacred reading; writing books, or copying them by hand, for one’s neighbour’s benefit. For St Jerome says in his letter to Rusticus: “Let books be written, so that the hand may earn food and the mind be satisfied with reading.” And in the same place: “To avoid idleness, let nets be woven for catching fish.” Likewise: “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.” More on this subject occurs in the Gloss on Matthew V, “If your right hand,” etc.; see also the relevant matter in manuscript M. after all the notes.

For married persons it is a remedy.] V.: “married persons.” M. more clearly: “The first is for abundant reward; the second is a compensatory remedy.” Likewise the active life is twofold: that of prelates, worthier in merit; and that of married persons, less worthy, a remedy for weakness, etc.—matters most worthy of reading and most conducive to a fuller understanding of these points.

To the evangelical abbot.] That is, Christ, says V.

Of the honey-flowing deed.] From the Office of the Nativity of the Lord.

What he should do.] C.: “what he does.”

Christian burial.] Perhaps monks would give such a person burial. Thus C. in the side margin.

With her head veiled.] C.: “With her body veiled.” How great today is the extravagance of girls, both noble and wealthy. Not only do they fail to veil the crown of the head, but—what is more detestable [Col. 0474C]—they bare their swelling breasts, spreading before young men and their suitors a hook of eternal damnation. One might now cry out, indeed mournfully, with Boethius:

> Alas, how the mind, sunk in a precipitate depth,  
> abandoning its own light,  
> tends onward into everlasting darkness.

Against this baring of girls’ breasts, not long ago introduced and accepted in our Belgium, a certain most chaste and learned canon of the metropolitan church of Cambrai inveighs sharply, learnedly, and, I hope, not fruitlessly. See his French printed booklets: *Le couvre-chef féminin* [“Women’s Head-covering”]; likewise *Le chancre, ou couvre-sein féminin* [“The Canker, or Women’s Breast-covering”].

Since authority says.] “Authority” is understood, as above, indefinitely to mean ancient authors. The matter cited here must be sought from the acts of the Lateran council under Alexander III, which have not yet appeared.

That the Gospel may be observed.] C. wrongly: “Lest the Gospel,” etc.

Decree of Gregory.] Of Gregory VII, whose eleven books of letters are contained in volume III of the councils. Gerard I, bishop of Cambrai, admirably teaches that such fasts ought not to be generally established, as the bishops of Gaul had done; see the chronicle of Cambrai by Baldwin, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, book III, chapter 52.

On recalling tithes.] On this matter there is a special title in the appendix to the Lateran council under Alexander III, part V; and on observing tithes, part XIII of the same.

Those relying upon.] C.: “those fortifying.”

Laymen.] “Saying,” says C.’s margin: “I shall marry this woman and become rich, because I shall leave her when I please, since she is related to me in the third degree of affinity.”

Protracting advocates.] Advocates have been discussed sufficiently above, chapter 51.

“While they are at work,”] Not *molliuntur* (“they are softened”), as V. has it. The words are Terence’s: “And you know women’s ways: while they are busy, while they are dressing their hair, a year passes.” In the *Heautontimorumenos*, [Col. 0475A] Act II, scene II, at the end; where old copies also read *molliuntur*.

Count Theobald.] Perhaps the Count of Champagne mentioned by Caesarius, *Memorable Examples*, book VIII, ch. 31, and by Cantimpré, book II of *The Universal Good of Bees*, ch. 25, nos. 14 and 15.

484 “But that it may be clearer”] V.: “but that it may be more extensive.”

Of Grandmont.] The Order of Grandmont, in the diocese of Limoges in France, was founded about A.D. 1080 and follows the Rule of our holy father Benedict. James of Vitry discusses it in his *Western History*, ch. 19.

On not confessing.] These words, down to “sinning,” are absent from C. The author rightly censures such traditions and enactments, because they cause all sins not to be disclosed in confession.

“By a bearded messenger.”] V.: “By a barbarian,” etc. See M. after the notes for a fuller treatment.

And Jerome.] Consult his commentary on Psalm 146, vol. VII; likewise his commentary on Ephesians, ch. V, vol. VI.

[Col. 0475B] “And of a canticle-psalm.”] A comparison between psalms and canticles occurs in Homily 1 on the *Song of Songs*, ch. VIII, of Blessed Jerome after Origen. The difference between a psalm and a canticle is this: a psalm pertains to the hands, that is, to actions; a canticle, however, to contemplation. The same Blessed Jerome says on Psalm 91, concerning the words “Upon the ten-stringed psaltery”: “I say simply: whenever we raise our hands without thoughts and disputes, we sing psalms to the Lord upon the ten-stringed instrument. ‘Upon the ten-stringed psaltery with the lyre.’ In our lyre, body, soul, and spirit are fitted with all the strings.” More on this matter may be found in the same author, vol. VI, in the commentary on Ephesians, ch. V, on the words: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.”

With Nicholas.] His life is found in Surius, vol. VI, for 6 December.

On one hundred pounds.] Budé recounts the distinctions and [Col. 0475C] origin of pounds in his books *On the As and Its Parts*.

“Why, etc., if.”] I have restored this passage from M.: 1 Corinthians 6, “Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” etc. V.: “Why, even if it be lawfully sworn.” The passage of the Apostle was not divided, and thus it is corrupt.

Likewise: “In another.”] Supply “church,” as above.

“And this sacrament.”] Here the word *sacrament* is used analogically for an oath, as in 22, question 5, “Little children who.” Consider attentively M.’s text on this subject, below after the notes.

“A purse to be squeezed dry.”] Archdeacons suffer the same treatment from bishops; they are now punished by the very instrument of their offense. Thus C. in the margin.

“The knowledge of greater prelates.”] C. is mistaken: “evil prelates.”

According to the laws.] An accusation against pastors of this kind does not proceed from charity and therefore ought not to be admitted: 4, question 4, *Let no one be introduced*. Moreover, charitable [Col. 0475D] admonition must come first: 2, question 1, *If he shall sin*, and 2, question 7, *Likewise concerning accusation*.

The example of the boys.] M. recounts this example more fully in its proper place.

“Beyond what is necessary.”] Duo: “beyond what is most necessary.”

2 Corinthians 8.] C. and V.: 2 Corinthians 22.

485 “From you.”] C.: “from us.”

On receiving legates.] This is inferred from Cause 10, question 3, near the end.

“In the house.”] That is, says V. in the margin, things which should be sought even far away, contrary to the poetic saying:

> What is not at home, but your neighbor has, let it be bought.

It does not say “your overseas neighbor,” nor one in another region or town, but “your neighbor.” Yet this should not be understood of costly things, but of things easily found. Hence it is clear that the man of Chartres wrongly censures the Cistercians in his trifles because they do not set meat before guests, using against them this poetic verse—whereas they dwell in forests and deserts, and it is the height of [Col. 0476A] luxury to demand flesh-pots from hermits, as from the Egyptians. Exodus 16.

Note that “the plunderer.”] Only V. read these words through the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER LXXX

“To sound absurd.”] V.: “to sound harsh.”

Mahomet.] I have restored this, for three copies have *Machometus*; everyone knows who he was.

“Adding no qualification concerning.”] Like those of whom Blessed Jerome says: “Whatever they have said, they regard as God’s law; nor do they deign to know what the prophets or apostles thought. Instead they adapt unsuitable testimonies to their own opinion, as though it were something great, rather than the most defective kind of teaching, to corrupt meanings and drag resistant Scripture toward their own will.” So he writes in his letter to Paulinus, beginning “Brother Ambrose.”

“The way of the commandments.”] C.: “the way of the world,” corruptly.

“The secret of Scripture.”] These words suggest Saint Augustine’s exposition of this passage.

[Col. 0476B] “Your tavern-keepers.”] From the interpretation of the Seventy, or the Greek version.

“And sincere truth.”] I have restored this from Blessed Jerome. V. and C.: “and sincere will.”

“Contained.”] C. has *contempta* (“despised”) in the margin. Meanwhile I shall say what I think. If the preceding phrase, “and sincere will,” is considered, *contempta* might be tolerated in some sense—namely, the will despised in Holy Scripture, because there we are taught to abandon our own will. “I came not to do my own will,” says the Lord, “but the will of him who sent me.” John 6.

Martin, seeing.] His life, written by Sulpicius Severus, is found in Surius, vol. VI, 11 November.

“Not soundly and sincerely.”] M. says: “And therefore the children of Israel perished, because they did not inquire of the mouth of the Lord,” that is, of Holy Scripture.

“They are unwilling to fulfill it in deed.”] C.: “They are willing to fulfill it.” What variation! Blessed Gregory says: “God grants the word of truth to those who do it, and takes it away from those who do not.” *Morals*, [Col. 0476C] book XI, ch. 9.

486 “For holy men indeed.”] Indeed, also unbelievers skilled in human learning. Of these I mention Seneca alone. He says in Letter 115: “I do not wish you, my Lucilius, to be excessively anxious about words and composition: I have greater matters for you to attend to.” Do you seek more? Read also his Letter 45.
