“By contrast, the philosopher.”] V. varies insolently here. It says: “By contrast, to the philosopher the integrity and composition of words are a greater concern than the truth of meanings.” Where, I ask, does Seneca say this?

“Men of this sort.”] That is, those departing from the surface of the evangelical letter, says C. in the margin.

In Matthew, ch. V.] V. and C.: ch. 33.

“In the phrase ‘in me, the head.’”] This is the interlinear gloss on this passage. Saint Jerome may also be consulted, vol. VI, on Matthew, for our author derived no little from him.

“Greatest, does not abolish.”] The words “does not abolish” are absent from V.

[Col. 0476D] “Also added in the Gospel.”] C. in the margin: “For example, not looking at a woman in order to lust after her, not being angry with one’s brother, and such things. Matthew 5.”

“An interjection.”] M. read in the text, “an inward indignation,” but corrected it in the margin, rightly. For the interlinear gloss has: “An interjection expressing indignation.” Here M. again agrees with the other two copies down to the end of the work; therefore in what follows the three will be compared with one another, as above before chapter 66: “On the threefold office of a prelate, and against respect of persons.”

“Special.”] C. and M.: “spiritual.”

“And other things determined.”] M.: “and [the process] has proceeded weakened.”

“Up to ‘fool.’”] Thus V. in the text; C. in the margin refers it back to “Fool.”

In John, ch. V.] The three copies: ch. 43.

Hence Augustine.] Vol. VI, *Against Faustus*, book XVI, chs. 22 and 26; likewise vol. X, *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*, sermon 46.

[Col. 0477A] “Since faith also.”] M.: “Yet faith too is drawn forth from certain small places, that is, from Holy Scripture, and from somewhat obscure cells. In which,” etc.

“I and the Father.”] In C.’s margin, “Church or cell” is added to the word “I.”

Augustine: “See.”] Only M. reads “Augustine,” who speaks thus in vol. IX, Tractate 36 on the Gospel of John.

“Do not depart.”] M. omitted *not*. The copyist’s negligence deserves blame.

“What faith requires.”] “The articles of faith,” says C. in the margin.

“Ought to await.”] C.: “ought to know.” V. omits it.

*Gastrimargia.*] The three copies have *castrimargia*.

“An opportunity for stealing.”] C. says in the upper margin: “One runs with a thief in nine ways: by not restoring; by commanding, as the lord who orders servants to steal; by silence; by advising; by consenting; by flattering; by not reporting; by recovering stolen goods, as an abbot; and by sharing.”

487 “Lest others do greater things.”] C. and V.: “Lest others not [Col. 0477B] do greater things.” Someone, by placing two dots beneath it, indicated that the negative particle should be removed in V.

2 Corinthians 10.] The three copies: 2 Corinthians 23. See the interlinear gloss on this passage.

“And sprinkle you harshly.”] M.: “And I sprinkle you.”

Isaiah, ch. III.] The three copies: ch. VII.

“I will remove from you.”] Or, as the text has it: “I will remove from Jerusalem.”

“They bring balances.”] Absurdly. C.: “they remove.”

Proverbs, ch. XX.] C. and M.: ch. XLI.

“Glutted sons of Romulus.”] C.: “Satyrs.” A verse of Persius, Satire X:

> Behold, amid their cups, the glutted sons of Romulus ask  
> what divine poems may relate.

“All dignities.”] M.: “all dominions.”

“To prefer himself a hundred times.”] C.: “a hundredfold.”

“What the corpse-bearer does, the physician too had done.”] Thus. V. and M.: *vispillo*. But C.: *vispilio*. On this word John of Genoa, in the dictionary entitled *Catholicon*, says: “*Vispilio*, or *vespilio*: a robber, thief, or plunderer, as though ‘one who despoils by force.’” [Col. 0477C] Peter the Chanter appears to use it here in that sense, perhaps as it was then employed. Otherwise, *vespillo* seems to be the reading. Nicolaus Perottus derives this word from evening, writing on Martial’s third epigram: “A *vespillo* is a lowly disposer of corpses, who used to carry out in the evening those who, because of poverty, could not be conducted with a funeral procession.” Martial says:

> Diaulus, once a physician, is now a corpse-bearer.

So Perottus, who mentions the same word in Epigram 59:

> Diaulus had been a surgeon; now he is a corpse-bearer:  
> he began to be what he could only now be as a clinician.

Ambrosius Calepinus and Adrianus Junius in his *Nomenclator* follow this spelling and meaning.

Isaiah, ch. V.] The three copies: ch. XV.

“Let us follow falsehood.”] M.: “Let us follow deceit.”

“Or a lesser good, a greater good.”] The words “a greater good” are absent from M.

[Col. 0477D] “And the worthier.”] V. and C. omit it.

Deuteronomy, ch. XXXI.] The three copies: ch. 143 and ch. XII.

And Acts of the Apostles, ch. III.] M. and C.: ch. 6; V.: ch. 12.

Ezekiel, ch. XXXIII.] The three copies: ch. 154. The prophecy of Ezekiel, as noted in the manuscripts, has 3,340 verses.

Proverbs, ch. XXX.] The three copies: 56.

To the Galatians.] I noted ch. I, at the words: “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you,” etc.

Ecclesiastes, ch. XII.] The three copies: 31, at the end.

488 ## CHAPTER LXXXI

In Proverbs, ch. VI.] The three copies: ch. 16.

The same, ch. XII.] V. and C.: ch. 27; M.: ch. 28.

The same, ch. XII: “The hand.”] The three copies: ch. 28. Therefore the preceding chapter-number is erroneous.

The same, ch. XIII.] The three copies: ch. 29.

The same, ch. XV: “The way of the slothful.”] I wonder how the error crept into certain printed Bibles whereby “the wicked” is read in place of “the slothful,” since Jerome’s translation and the Seventy, together with the Chaldean paraphrase, unanimously [Col. 0478A] contradict it. The three copies have ch. 33.

The same, ch. XVIII.] The three copies: ch. 37.

“From a good work.”] Correctly, according to the interlinear gloss; but C.: “from every work.”

“He is like.”] The interlinear gloss. The biblical text is: “He is a brother,” etc.

“Sloth casts into.”] Not “fatness,” as M. and C. have it.

“He shall hunger for pleasures.”] V. omits “pleasures,” wrongly. For this is the interlinear gloss. But why is he said to hunger for pleasures? Because, as Seneca says: “The idle man does not live for himself, but, what is most shameful, for his belly and sleep,” Letter 55.

Likewise, ch. XX.] The three copies: ch. 39.

“That is, to serve God.”] M. alone has this.

Likewise, ch. XXI.] V.: ch. 63; C. and M.: ch. 42.

“Desires kill.”] C. and M.: “Idleness kills the slothful man.”

Proverbs, ch. XXIV.] C. and M.: ch. 48; V.: ch. 47.

“Or drunkards.”] This is absent from V.

[Col. 0478B] The same, ch. XXVI.] V.: ch. 51; C. and M.: ch. 50.

In Ecclesiastes, ch. IV.] The three copies: ch. 7.

“A fomentation.”] C.: “a firebrand.”

Ecclesiasticus, ch. XXII.] V.: ch. 61; C. and M.: ch. 41.

“Abundance of bread.”] The Septuagint reads thus: “The wealth of delights and luxury was the origin of the sins of Sodom.” See Blessed Jerome on Ezekiel, ch. XVI.

“To be thought.”] Absent from C.

“Unless, namely, as much as.”] V.: “Where, namely, as much as.”

“And whenever you have given.”] Supply “to eat,” as C. indicates in the side margin.

“In not distributing.”] C. omits the word “in.”

“Not merely one who does.”] This reading pleases me. M.: “For not one who does,” obscurely.

“Of servants therefore.”] C.’s margin says: “For example, of grooms and nail-makers.”

“The Lord also promised.”] This is the invitatory for the nocturnal office on the first Sunday of Lent.

489 “At cockcrow.”] C. in the margin: “In the sleep-bringing night.”

[Col. 0478C] “The dead of night.”] Macrobius, book I, ch. 3, clearly sets forth these divisions of the day; likewise Honorius of Autun, vol. XII (*Library of the Fathers*, folio edition, p. 948).

“In necessary things.”] “For salvation,” says C. in the margin.

“Chosen strongly.”] M.: “elective.”

“Foreign.”] This is C.’s reading. Excellent.

“They sleep a second time.”] V.: “they sleep.”

“In Genesis, threatening.”] C.: “threatening destruction,” and adds in the margin: “And they try to make him a liar.”

“Since he is displeased.”] V. and C.: “Since these are displeased.”

Count Palatine.] Not the Count Palatine of the Rhine, but the count of the palace.

“For some time I kept silence.”] M.: “For a long time I kept silent from evil.”

Isaiah, ch. LVI.] The three copies: ch. 68.

“The human race.”] C. and V.: “the race of men.” M. added after “human”: “through human sloth,” but I removed it as almost superfluous.

[Col. 0478D] “By bread, every necessity.”] Because bread tastes good with every relish. “Bread is the first food,” says the *Widow of Zarephath*, recently first published by us, book III, homily 8, ch. 1; “bread is the middle food; bread is the final food. Bread is eaten with every dish.”

“But in clothing.”] Hence the marginal notes in M. and C.

> The diligent merchant hastens to furthest India.

C. adds: “Through the sea, fleeing poverty.”

Note that C. has *institor* (“trader”) instead of “diligent.” The verse is from Horace, book I, Epistle 1, before the middle.

“Both bodily and spiritual.”] C.: “both bodily and natural,” corruptly.

“Spiritual in thought.”] V. repeats only the word “spiritual”; and in my opinion this makes good sense, so that the latter is separated from the former for clearer understanding.

“Bodily [labor is] manifold.”] I do not reject C.’s “the body’s [labor is] manifold.”

“According to anxiety.”] Thus the interlinear gloss says: “Labor and foresight are not condemned, but anxiety that chokes the mind.” Therefore I rightly restored *according to* [Col. 0479A] in place of *namely*, which C. and V. admitted.

“The labor of grace.”] M. wrongly omits “of grace.”

“I will drench my bed.”] After this V. adds: “Likewise: ‘See my humility and my labor,’ Psalm 24.”

“Consists in.”] C.: “consists.” Seneca says at the beginning of Letter 120: “But it has consisted in one thing.”

“Provision for one’s neighbor.”] C.: “a promise to one’s neighbor.”

“More like a channel than a shell.”] I have restored the passage. The three copies have “carnal,” which is plainly an error from the following words in V.: after “than a shell,” “that is, flowing over to another rather than retaining for himself.”

“Even a certain laboring.”] V. and M.: “even by a certain labor, as envying,” etc.

490 “It itself is a fault.”] C. also properly has: “the fault itself is.”

“Yet the labor of nature.”] M.: “Yet the good of natural good, as often,” etc.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

[Col. 0479B] M. does not divide the chapter here, but only later at the words which begin chapter 83: “But how far it has departed.”

“And how?”] This question, notwithstanding the division of chapters, must be referred to the concluding words of the preceding chapter. This should not seem incongruous, since the same thing is found more than once even in the sacred Bible.

“More quickly and more elegantly.”] V.: “more vainly and more elegantly.”

“Of the most vast.”] Thus Seneca in the cited passage. C. and M.: “of your estates.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

“Even to birds’ feathers.”] Hence Horace in an epistle:

> Let a little crow, stripped of stolen colors, provoke laughter.

“Under the color of clothing.”] M. and C. cite in the margin a verse of Juvenal, Satire 6:

> Silken cloth burns up their luxuries.

“The eyes of those looking at us.”] C.: “the lights of those looking at us.” On a similar superfluity of dress, see Seneca, Letter 5; Blessed Jerome, *To Demetrias on Virginity*, ch. 10, vol. I, beginning “Among all materials”; likewise *To Fabiola*, vol. III, beginning “Until today.” The same author says: “If a man or woman adorns himself or herself and draws the eyes of men toward himself or herself, even if no harm results from it, yet he or she will suffer eternal judgment, because he or she brought poison, if there had been someone to drink it.”

“Therefore, tell me, pontiffs.”] Words of Blessed Bernard in the *Apology to Abbot William*, near the end, apparently echoing Persius the poet, Satire 2.

“For usury.”] C.: “for selling, which the poor.” M.: “for usury rather than suffer the rain.” What discordance.

“Judaizing.”] C. absurdly: “judging.”

“Sacrificial blood.”] I have restored this. M.: “the blood of those sacrificing.” One does not speak of “the blood of sacrificers,” but rather of their cruelty. C.: *immolaticensium*; V.: *immolatitum*.

“Others, [use] little mats.”] Thus, I think, it ought to be read, since it appears to be a diminutive of *matta*. Thus Blessed Benedict, in the Rule, ch. 55: “For bedding, a mat, blanket, woolen coverlet, and pillow shall suffice.” [Col. 0479D] C.: “others, little boats”; French *nattes*, that is, mats woven from straw. M.: “others, stains.” Perhaps here *maculae* means the square openings of a net, as in Varro, book II.

491 “Naked in the wood.”] V.: “Naked in the desert.”

“Very grammatical.”] Said ironically. Otherwise C.: “Less grammatical.”

“As if a transition.”] C.: “A transaction.”

Tubal-cain is reproved.] Perhaps Jubal should be read, who, Genesis 4 says, was the father of those who played the lyre. Yet Tubal-cain is supported by the mention of hammers. The interlinear gloss on this place also says: “He was the inventor,” namely, “of music, which belongs to the pleasure of the ears.” Tubal-cain, however, was a smith; hence the gloss there says: “He stirred up the lust of the eyes through the works,” namely, “of bronze.”

“For there is sin in adornment.”] It is shameful that so many and such varied fashions of clothing should be devised daily among Catholics. “This finery is not the Lord’s; [Col. 0480A] this veil is Antichrist’s,” says Blessed Jerome to the widow Furia. Why is this? Because girls offer poisons to chastity in their dress and bodily adornment and inflame young men with incentives to lust. The poet rejects them in his epistle to Hippolytus:

> Far from us be young men dressed like women.

Holy men detest such women. “Avoid the wantonness of girls,” says Blessed Jerome to Demetrias, *On Preserving Virginity*, ch. X, “who adorn their heads, let their hair fall over their foreheads, polish their skin, use cosmetics, wear tight sleeves, wrinkleless garments, and curling slippers, so that under the name of virginity they may perish more profitably.” Blessed Cyprian, in *On the Dress of Virgins*, says: “Women lay hands upon God when they strive to remake what he formed.”

“They have *syrmata*.”] A *syrma* (Greek: **σύρμα**) is a kind of tragic actor’s garment, or the train or trailing part of women’s dress. Marcellus, in his notes on Dioscorides, observes that **σύρμα** is used for sweepings, as though for that which is swept away with brooms. According to Aristotle, *syrmata* are bedding-straws.

[Col. 0480B] “Darians and Byrrhians.”] These seem to be names of peoples.

Milo of Thérouanne.] Or of Morini. There were two men of this name. The first was consecrated on 15 February 1131 and died in 1159. Milo II succeeded his uncle, having been a monk of Saint Mary of Bostho [otherwise Russiauville], and died on 14 September 1169. Thus the manuscript catalogue of the bishops of Morini. Claude Robert agrees in his catalogue of the bishops of Boulogne. At that time the following proverb was current: “In Bernard, charity; in Norbert, faith [see the *Life of Saint Norbert*, shortly after its beginning, in Surius, vol. III]; in Milo, humility.” He was also distinguished in religion and learning, according to Baronius under the year 1148. These details concern Milo I, a Premonstratensian, made bishop from being abbot of Saint Josse. I have nowhere read of his writings. On him see Miraeus, *Chronicle of the Premonstratensians* and *Belgian Feasts*, 13 November; likewise Raissius, *Supplement to the Saints of Belgium*, 16 July; [Col. 0480C] and, most fully, John le Paige, *Library of the Premonstratensian Order*, book II.

“Your foot.”] C. and M.: “Your foot now.” From Ovid, *The Art of Love*.

492 ## CHAPTER LXXXIV

Only V. begins a new chapter.

Furriers.] Those who prepare the skins of animals for human use. In French: *pelletiers*.

“Not Daedalian.”] From Daedalus of Athens, the most ingenious craftsman of his age.

“Not costly.”] M. omits this.

“Who [make] saddles and spurs.”] What is the use of this waste of gold? “Golden reins do not make a horse better,” says Seneca.

“Of dice.”] This is the French word, in Latin *alea*.

“I do not speak of chessmen.”] Polydore mentions them: “There is another kind of game, in which counters are played on a gaming-board—that is, in little boxes and trays—allegedly invented about the year 3635 from the creation of the world by a man named Xerxes.” And below: “Today they call these counters *schaci*, perhaps from climbing, because the [Col. 0480D] counters, when moved, seem to climb toward the opposing side.” So he writes in *On the Invention of Things*, book II, ch. 13.

“And when [there is] a judge.”] A sword is necessary to a secular judge, so that he may punish evil men as an example to others. The reading of V. and M., “and when necessary to judgment,” etc., is not satisfactory.

“And a spear.”] A *pilum* was a kind of Roman missile. Thus Lucan, book I:

> Standards confront standards, eagle matched with eagle, and threatening spears with spears.

M. reads: “And doubled projectiles piercing a cuirass.” If artillery had been in use in our author’s time, M.’s reading might be tolerated. For when this device is loaded, contrary to custom, with a double quantity or supply of powder, it more easily pierces and perforates cuirasses.

Poison.] *Toxicum* is poison produced by the tree called yew.

To the Corinthians, ch. IX.] The three copies: ch. 42.

“Lest anything by threats.”] Terence.

“To you, if you have.”] Supply: “He gives back to you what is yours, if you have,” etc. M., however, omits “to you.”

[Col. 0481A] “Travelers to Dothain.”] Thus C. But the other two have “travelers to Idithun.” Dothain is a place in Genesis 37, where it is said: “Let us go to Dothain.” The Hebrew means “passing,” or “beyond the river.” Idithun is the name of a singer in the titles of Psalms 38, 61, and 76, and is interpreted “his law,” or “lawful,” or “giving praise and confession.”

## CHAPTER LXXXV

Neither C. nor M. divides the chapter here. The division is pleasing because it is more agreeable to the reader.

“As Gregory says.”] And what does he say? I shall relate it: “Let no one suppose that sin is absent from the excess and pursuit of costly garments. For if this were not a fault, the Lord would by no means have praised John for the roughness of his clothing. If this were not a fault, [Col. 0481B] the Apostle Paul would certainly not, in an epistle, have restrained women from the desire for costly clothing, saying: ‘Not in costly apparel.’ Consider therefore how great a fault it is for men also to seek what the shepherd of the Church took care to forbid even to women.” So he writes, vol. II, Homily 6 on the Gospels. And from Blessed Bernard’s *Apology* I have learned this: “Soft garments indicate softness of soul. The care of the body would not be so great unless the mind, uncultivated in virtues, had first been neglected.”

“The vice of inconstancy.”] This is expressed by a reed shaken by the wind. Blessed Gregory says again in the same place: “Let us learn, dearest brothers, not to be reeds shaken by the wind. Let us strengthen the mind placed amid the breezes of speech; let the condition of the mind stand inflexible. Let no detraction,” etc.

“For religious persons to use splendid things.”] “But if you wish to be a monk,” says Blessed Jerome, “do not give attention to adornment. Let soiled clothing be an indication of a pure mind; let a cheap tunic demonstrate contempt for the world—provided only that the mind does not swell with pride and that attire and speech do not disagree.”

But lest this exhortation of Blessed Jerome seem to some too hard to observe, I offer another from Seneca, gentler and more favorable. Thus he writes in Letter 5 to Lucilius: “I warn you not to do anything, after the manner of those who desire [Col. 0481C] not to improve but to be noticed, that would be remarkable in your dress or mode of life. Avoid rough clothing, untrimmed hair, a more neglected beard, and anything else that ambition pursues by a perverse path.” And, to be briefer, he says below: “Let your toga not shine, yet let it not be filthy either. Let us see that the things by which we wish to procure admiration are not ridiculous and hateful,” etc.

“Therefore Bernard.”] C.: “Bernard.”

“Chisimus rises.”] M.: “Cifimus burst forth.”

“Marten and beaver, of no slight spoil.”] M.: “Marten and beaver, of no slight price.”

“These pelts.”] C.: “Sable pelts, and others.”

“Like masked persons.”] Or, through art, like goats, say C. and M. in the side margin.

“On account of softness, effeminacy.”] M.: “On account of soft effeminacy.” Nature taught various arts for necessity, as Seneca discusses in Letter 90, but not for misuse or softness.

[Col. 0481D] “This ambitious.”] M. changes the adjective into a substantive thus: “This ambition, furniture,” etc.

“You pursue with hatred.”] C.: “You should pursue with hatred.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

“And of provisions.”] Yet I do not reject M.’s “and of foods.”

“A thing [falls] into vice.”] Gallus says, Elegy 1: “It is not things but evil deeds that fall into vice.”

494 “From the simplicity of the ancients.”] The holy anchorites did not even dare to build cells, reasoning that whatever exceeded the necessity of sustenance pertained to care of the flesh. Hence someone said that he had seen a demon lifting a hammer with his companion while he used a hammer in making needless repairs. This example is cited in the book called *The Widow of Zarephath*, recently published by us, book I, homily 1, ch. 10.

“In little huts.”] That is, small cottages.

[Col. 0482A] “Roofs of straw.”] M.: “Roofs in straw.”

“Certain men of old.”] Blessed Jerome relates that Blessed Hilarion had a cell four feet wide and five feet high—that is, lower than his own stature. “You would have thought this cell,” he says, “a tomb rather than a house.” The caves and bark dwellings of anchorites are frequently mentioned in the book *Lives of the Fathers*.

“There, a little table.”] C.’s margin: “A three-legged table.” Likewise there: “Pure salt.”

“To be so anxious.”] Blessed John Chrysostom says at the end of Homily 23 on Matthew: “How do we differ from children playing and building houses—we who build splendid houses—except that we do this with punishment, they with joy?”

“Hence a certain man.”] Only V. adds in the text, “a cleric of Rheims”; C. has it in the margin.

“Of walls.”] M. alone has this.

Isaiah, ch. LXVI.] Only V. notes: ch. 98.

[Col. 0482B] “The Megarians, namely.”] Not “Megalensians,” as C. has it. See Blessed Jerome, vol. I, Letter 2 to the widow Ageruchia, *On Monogamy*, ch. 5 near the end.

Paul the first hermit.] These details are gathered from his life written by Blessed Jerome.

“In an underground chamber.”] In a subterranean place. Greek **ὑπόγαιος**, **ὑπογαίδιος**, or **ὑπόγαιος**: subterranean, below ground.

“Opposite.”] V. and C. say: “They ate opposite him”; the rest is absent.

“To be erected.”] C.: “to be chosen.”

“The remainder.”] C. and M.: “I leave.”

“Nature buries those left behind.”] Another half-line of Maecenas, to which I would gladly add a saying from Seneca and verses from Lucan. The former says, Letter 92 to Lucilius: “I ask no one to perform the final office; I entrust my remains to no one. Nature has provided that no one should be unburied. Whomever cruelty has cast out, time will cover.” The latter, in the cited passage, book VII, says:

> You accomplish nothing by this anger: whether decay consume the corpse  
> or a pyre, it makes no difference. Nature receives  
> all things into her peaceful bosom.

I have put the half-lines found in the text into order; otherwise C. and M. arranged the prose thus: “The loss of a tomb is easy, because nature buries those left behind.”

Gregory.] *Morals*, book XV, ch. 37. [Col. 0482D] Moreover, see Blessed Augustine’s book to Paulinus, *On Care for the Dead*.

Likewise, Psalm 73.] The three copies wrongly read Psalm 72.

Likewise, Jeremiah, ch. XXII.] C. and M.: ch. 80; V.: ch. 25.

“To avarice.”] M.: “to boldness.”

“To completion.”] Here the three agree, although the sacred Bible has: “To the course of evil work.”

Likewise Juvenal.] Satire 14.

And below:

“Contronius.”] M. and C.: “Centonius.”

Likewise Jerome.] See his letter to Heliodorus in praise of the solitary life, beginning “With how great love.”

“In hair-shirts.”] M.: “in counsels.”

“Mindful of the womb.”] C.: “Greater than the womb.”

“Or among ruins.”] The gloss on this passage, which is also Augustine’s.

Isaiah, ch. V.] C. and V.: ch. 13; M.: ch. 14.

Leviticus, ch. XXVI.] V. and M.: ch. 78; C.: ch. 79.

“Prodigal Paul.”] “They explain it of the proconsul; we, of Paul,” say two margins.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

[Col. 0483D] In the chapter summary M. has “thrusting in” in place of “plunging in.” Both make sense.

“That they may be light.”] C.: “That, just as they are light,” etc.

“Like a reed.”] M.: “Like a reed [moved] by every wind of doctrine.”

“By the gadfly of temporal things.”] Greek **οἷστρος** means a fly that stings oxen and horses in summer, called by some an asilus or horsefly. Virgil, *Georgics*, III:

> . . . whose name in Roman speech is *asilus*,  
> which the Greeks, calling it *oestrus*, have rendered.

Quintus Serenus says:

> Is he not like one whose mind is seized by the swift gadfly?

497 Epileptics.] Those afflicted with epilepsy, or the “comitial disease,” concerning which Serenus says:

> There is a kind of sudden illness, whose name derives from this,  
> because it prevents our public assemblies from taking place.  
> For often a dreadful seizure, with limbs falling in sharp sickness,  
> interrupted the people’s deliberation.  
> God himself mentions one conceived under the uncertain phases of the moon,  
> whom such a fall has often cast down.

[Col. 0484A] Proverbs, ch. XX.] M. and V.: ch. 41; C.: ch. 40.

“Of winnowers.”] The modern biblical reading is: “A wise king scatters the wicked,” etc. But the commentary attributed to Jerome, which is Bede’s, says on this passage: “The old translation has this verse: ‘A wise king, the winnower of the ungodly, will send upon them the wheel of evils,’ that is, punishment never ending. Opposed to this wheel is the crown of eternal life, which God has promised to those who love him (James 1).”

“Never to perfection.”] V. has this more briefly: “and never knowing: Always,” etc.

“They do not walk.”] C.’s margin adds: “For necessary things.”

“Unsearchable.”] V.: “unstable.”

Isaiah, ch. XIX.] V. and C.: ch. 52.

“The tail.”] C. says between the lines: “the end.”

The same, ch. LVII.] M. and C.: ch. 171; V.: ch. 172.

[Col. 0484B] “That alone, superficially.”] M. and C.: “Yet that, superficially.”

“Through worldly desire.”] M. and V.: “through worldly concupiscence.”

“Just as the Jews do not.”] These words through “But they rotted” are admitted only by M.

“A spider is a worm.”] Cassian on Psalm 38.

“Those *garciones*.”] *Garciones* sometimes means little boys and sometimes rascals. Blessed Bernard uses this name in the *Apology to Abbot William*.

“The foot of the world.”] M.: “The feet of the world.”

[Col. 0484C] “This is, those licking.”] Or “licking the ground.” For Blessed Jerome interprets the name Amalek as “licking the ground.”

498 ## CHAPTER XC

Hence Augustine.] On Psalm 7, vol. VIII, where he adds: “The Lord shall be known when he executes judgments; the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands.” From Psalm 9.

Augustine: “He who wishes.”] The three copies all read thus. Meanwhile I shall say that this exposition smells more of Blessed Ambrose’s teaching on Psalm 36 than of Augustine’s.

Proverbs, ch. XXVI.] The three copies: ch. 51.

Ecclesiasticus, ch. XXVII.] The three copies: ch. 72.

Fraud turned back upon itself.] A saying of St. Severian in his sermon On the Holy Innocents. St. Augustine has a not dissimilar statement in his exposition of Psalm 72, on the words: “Because of deceitfulness thou hast set them [in slippery places].” “The deceitful,” he says, “suffer deceit.”

[Col. 0484D] Likewise, by examples.] Besides the examples of Holy Scripture, there is also the well-known case of Euthymius, who was placed in the very cart and wagon which he had prepared for St. Ambrose, and was sent into exile; and thus his iniquity “came down upon his own head” (Psalm 9). From the Life of St. Ambrose in Surius, 4 April.

A certain courtier also.] His name was Perillus, at the court of King Phalaris. Concerning him Orosius, book I, chapter 22, relates a similar example; margin V. gives the following words: “In the Chronicles (Diodorus, book V; Strabo, book VII) and in Orosius (book I, chapter 11), it is read that Busiris exercised tyranny in Egypt, which he could not have done unless he had been king. He sacrificed strangers as though in the name of religion; Hercules afterwards killed him. Hence Boethius: ‘Busiris, sacrificing strangers, was killed by the stranger Hercules.’ But who taught Busiris such a religion is uncertain. Claudian, however, says that the very man who taught him was the first sacrificed at Busiris’s altar—that is, at the altar which Busiris had established. For he says:

[Col. 0485A]

> He who, when a guest was slain, taught how to appease the Thunderer,  
> Was himself the first to stain the altars devised by Busiris.

Moreover, Virgil, Georgics III:

> Who does not know harsh Eurystheus,  
> Or the altars of infamous Busiris?

Statius, Thebaid XII:

> You did not give us Busiris and his unspeakable, cruel monsters.

After the example of Busiris, Boethius adds another concerning Regulus. “Regulus,” he says, “had cast many Carthaginians captured in war into chains; but soon he himself offered his hands to the chains of the conquerors.” On the Consolation of Philosophy, book II, prose 6.

Drunkenness.] Seneca elegantly describes the madness of drunkenness in Epistle 83, from the middle to the end.

Counsels also of perfection.] M. in the text, and C. in the margin, read: “Counsels also of preaching.”

Of recompense.] M. and V.: “Of retribution.”

499 CHAPTER XCI

[Col. 0485B]

In the title V. alone reads: “Of man.”

Especially of benefits.] C.: “Especially of benefactors.”

To the love of God.] Not “to the delight of God,” as C. has it.

Into the form of four-footed creatures.] “That the outcomes of pleasure are sorrowful,” says Boethius, “anyone who wishes to recall his lusts will understand. If these can make men happy, there is no reason why beasts too should not be called happy.” On the Consolation of Philosophy, book III, prose 7.

Fellowship.] C. and M.: “Society.”

At the root of charity.] From St. Gregory, Homily 27 on the Gospels. “The Lord’s commandments,” he says, “are many and one: many by diversity of works, one in the root of love.”

Soldiers in clerical dress.] Clerics are so called because they belong to the Lord’s lot: for κλῆρος, *klēros*, is called *sors*, “lot,” in Latin. St. Jerome, Letter to Nepotian, On the Life of Clerics, beginning: “You ask me.” Clerical dress is treated in the Clementines, book III, title 1, chapter 2, where it is read thus: “Any cleric”—by *cleric* here understand one “who has received first tonsure,” as the Gloss says on this passage—“who publicly wears striped or parti-coloured clothing”—that is, clothing of different colours or sections, or adorned with silk weaving—“unless a reasonable cause exists, if he holds a benefice, shall by that very fact be suspended for six months from receiving the fruits of the benefices which he possesses. But if he does not hold a benefice, yet is constituted in holy orders below the priesthood, he shall by that very fact be rendered incapable for the same period of obtaining an ecclesiastical benefice. We decree the same also concerning other clerics”—that is, those who neither hold benefices nor are in holy orders—“who publicly wear such striped and parti-coloured dress together with the clerical tonsure.”

Actors by their speech.] Causing their hearers to laugh, and thus making themselves, in their eyes, contemptible in every respect. Hence Horace, Satires I.4, elegantly says:

> He who bites an absent friend;  
> Who does not defend him when another blames him; who hunts  
> For loose laughter among men and the reputation of a wit;  
> [Col. 0485D] Who can invent what he has not seen, who cannot keep entrusted matters silent:  
> He is a black-hearted man—Roman, beware of him.

Harlots by their gesture.] It is shameful to speak of this here.

Through the occupation of cares.] “I beseech you,” says blessed Jerome to Nepotian, “and, repeating the warning again and again, I shall urge you: do not think the office of a cleric is a kind of ancient military service; that is, do not seek worldly gain in Christ’s service. Do not have more than you possessed when you began to be a cleric, lest this be said to you: ‘Their clergy shall not profit them.’” And below: “Flee a cleric who trades, one who becomes rich from poverty, or glorious from obscurity, as though from a certain plague.”

But for glory.] Though tonsure and the crown in themselves signify renunciation of all riches and possession of the kingdom in God. Thus in 12, question 1, *Duo*: “These clerics are kings,” that is, ruling themselves and others in virtues; and so they possess a kingdom in God, and this is denoted by the crown on the head. They have this crown from the institution of the Roman Church as a sign of the kingdom [Col. 0486A] expected in Christ. The shaving of the head, however, signifies the laying aside of all temporal things.

Since that Psalm is divided according to the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, each letter containing eight verses, I count from the first letter, called Aleph, or from the first octave, which begins, “Blessed are the undefiled,” to the thirteenth octave, which begins, “How I have loved thy law”; and there I find the required letter Mem. 503 According to St. Jerome’s interpretation, this means “my inward parts,” or “from my very inmost depths.” We Benedictines, according to the statutes of our Rule, divide all the octaves of the aforesaid Psalm in the daytime hours, both canonical and Marian, by the recitation of the verse “Glory be to the Father.”

CHAPTER XCVI

M., for the title: “On good and evil weeping.” The other two: “On mourning,” etc.

And the eighth which returns.] These are the words of St. Augustine, vol. IV, book I, On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, chapter III.

[Col. 0488B] Many kinds of tears.] “I shall speak of tears. There are the tears of the wicked: namely, tears of weakness; hence, when a child is first born, it cries, so that it may be a prophet of its own misery. There are tears of adversity; hence, good things are possessed with love, and lost with mourning and grief. There are tears of pretence; hence: ‘Nothing dries more quickly than a tear’ (To Herennius, book II). There are tears of eternal damnation; hence: ‘Mourning occupies the end of joy’ (Proverbs 14). There are the tears of good people caused by compunction for sin; hence: ‘Thou hast set my tears,’ etc. Psalm 55. There are tears caused by a neighbour’s misery; hence: ‘Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep’ (Romans 12). There are tears caused by delay of the kingdom; hence: ‘Blessed are those who mourn,’ etc. Matthew 5.” I excerpted these from a manuscript codex.

Nothing dries more quickly.] Cicero, To Herennius, book II.

For we cannot.] Seneca says similar things in Epistles 63 and 99.

[Col. 0488C] Tears of the body.] V. omits the words “of body and heart.”

The sins of neighbours, *frix*.[Materially uncertain.] *Frixorium*, etc. See the Gloss on II Corinthians 11.

Diogenes also.] The three copies read thus, but I think it should be Heraclitus, who wept whenever he went out in public; Democritus, on the contrary, laughed. To the former everything appeared misery, to the latter folly. Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind, chapter 15; likewise, On Anger, book II, chapter 10.

“Axa,” he says.] V. omits this through the end of the chapter.

504 CHAPTER XCVII

Isaiah, chapter LV.] C.: chapter CLXIII; V. and M.: chapter CLXIV.

To mighty God.] *Fortis*, “Mighty,” is one of the names of God among the Hebrews. One should not read *fontem*, “fountain,” instead of *fortem*, “mighty,” as V. and certain other printed Bibles do. The most recent editions of the Bibles of Pope Sixtus V, compared with manuscript copies, correct this. Likewise also [they correct] “that I may see the will of God” in place of “pleasure”—namely, heavenly pleasure.

By the ministry of the body.] M.: “By the mystery he shows.”

With seeing faith.] Not “with hidden [faith],” as C. has it.

Neither grace, but vanity.] V.’s margin rightly asks: “How desire for temporal things may be vanity but not fault, I do not see how it can be understood, unless this is said of mortal sin and of necessary things. For to desire unnecessary things cannot fail to be both vanity and fault, since even to desire necessary things too greatly is sin, according to Gregory’s saying: ‘To ask temporal things from Jesus is not sin, provided they are not asked too greatly.’ Therefore to ask them too greatly is sin. But ‘too greatly’ is whatever is beyond necessity. Therefore whatever unnecessary thing is desired is desired culpably, and such desire is frivolous and foolish. But if foolish, how is it not culpable, since folly itself is never without fault? Therefore, as I have said, this distinction which says that desire is neither of nature nor of grace nor of fault, but of vanity, is frivolous—unless it is understood of mortal fault. But to desire temporal things for necessity is neither frivolous nor foolish, neither vanity nor fault. This whole member of the distinction must therefore be marked for deletion—that is, abolished. Nor should it be believed that the Parisian cantor, who is the author of this work, inserted this defect and the other defects found in this book; rather, the scholastics who copied him and added their notes at will corrupted the whole.” Correct. But the harm is that in V. those notes are very often placed in the text, as I gathered from M. and C.

CHAPTER XCVIII

Then in Christ the head.] Not “then in Christ the body,” as M. has it.

Our reading.] Or “instruction.”

First, from yourself.] “Have mercy upon your soul, pleasing God,” says C.’s margin, from Ecclesiasticus 30.

505 Above the works of others.] The same margin says: “Yet true mercy is not without the other virtues, nor is it rewarded [without them].”

Luke, chapter III.] The three copies: chapter VIII.

Bede: John.] Correctly Bede, on Luke 3; and these words occur in the Ordinary Gloss under the same cited author.

Let the robber plunder.] M.: “Let the soldier plunder.” The text of St. Augustine, whom Venerable Bede seems to have followed, reads this saying, but uses *praeda grassetur*, “let plunder range abroad,” instead of *praedo grassetur*, “let the robber plunder.” Vol. X, Appendix of Sermons, Sermon 3, at the beginning. St. Ambrose, in his exposition of Luke 3, likewise using this saying, writes: “Let the robber plunder.”

Namely, for “without.”] M. omits “namely.”

CHAPTER C

I gathered the summary from V. C. wished: “On spiritual [Col. 0490B] clemency.” M.: “On special mercy.”

The common form.] V.: “Beyond all this hope of mercy.” A scribe’s error.

Of the special [mercy] of the judge and the powerful.] This reading pleases me. For why “of the spiritual judge,” as V. and C. wish, rather than “of the secular”? *Specialis* means that which pertains especially to judges and the powerful.

It is among the powerful.] M.: “among princes.” But the original has *potentes*, “powerful persons.”

Or by the benefit of election.] V. omits “or”; the rest is as in the text.

You strike the other [cheek].] Seneca holds this view, On Clemency, book I, chapter 24, where one reads: “Punishments are no less shameful to a ruler than many deaths to a physician. The more gently a ruler governs, the better he is obeyed. The human mind is naturally stubborn, striving toward what is contrary and difficult; it follows more readily than it is led. And just as spirited and noble horses are better governed with a light rein, so voluntary innocence follows clemency by its own impulse, and the state considers it worthy to preserve for itself. Thus more is accomplished by this course. Cruelty is a thoroughly inhuman evil, unworthy of so gentle a spirit. It is a beastly frenzy to delight in blood and wounds and, casting aside humanity, to pass over into a wild animal,” etc.

It has established this.] M.: “It openly makes men,” etc. But the text agrees with the original.

More glorious in a prince.] Seneca, On Clemency, book I, chapter 3, says: “Of all men, clemency befits none more than a king and prince.”

But glorious.] C.: “More glorious.” The original: “Glorious.”

It belongs to the enemy.] Namely, blood, says V. between the lines. M., however, varies utterly: “He is an enemy, but [the enemy] of one who cannot become a friend.” I placed this in the text from the original.

He thinks he removes guilt.] “A good prince,” says V. between the lines.

Therefore, whenever it is shed.] Namely, blood, says the same gloss in the same place. M. wrongly reads *item*, “likewise,” for *ideo*, “therefore.”

Augustine.] C. cites the name alone.

508 CHAPTER CII

From M. I added “for enemies” in the title.

From Dan to Beersheba.] These words occur in I Kings 3. But Samuel neither interceded for Saul then nor did Saul wish to kill him, because he had not yet been chosen king. He did intercede for him in the same book, chapter 15, at the end, and at the beginning of chapter 16. Nor is it explicitly found in Scripture that Saul wished to kill Samuel; yet this can reasonably be inferred from chapter 19, when he persecuted David, who was with Samuel at Ramah. Hence Samuel says at the beginning of chapter 16: “Saul will hear, and he will kill me.”

CHAPTER CIV

Its effect.] C. wrongly: “Its affection.”

CHAPTER CVI

[Col. 0492C]

M. in the title: “On the manner of giving alms.” The other two: “On the order,” etc.

In creation.] M.: “with creation.”

510 And re-creation.] Absent in C.

Still His enemies.] M. also approves: “For us, His friends,” because immediately afterward there follows John 15: “Greater love,” etc., “than that a man lay down [his life] for his friends.” But I shall state [my view]. The words restored in the text please me more, because, although [Christ suffered] for enemies who were still enemies, nevertheless He offered Himself as a living sacrifice for those whom He knew would become friends. These may rightly be understood in a divided sense. But if they are expressed in a composite sense: is it not greater to suffer for enemies than for friends?

In the rebuke of a brother.] M. and V.: “in the correction of a brother.” We rebuke with words; we correct with lashes.

In the giving of holy counsel.] C.: “in the giving of sound counsel.”

Not another’s.] This is absent in V.

Ephesians, chapter IV.] V. and C.: chapter XIX; M.: XVIII.

As testamentary executors.] M.: “Of whose will we are indeed stewards.”

They have been reduced to poverty.] They become poor because they lavishly squander goods entrusted to them for the poor. Hence Seneca: “I forbid liberality to become *nepotari*”—that is, to imitate spendthrifts, to squander, as Lipsius says in On Benefits, book I, chapter 15. *Aporiati* is Latin, from the verb *aporior*, derived from Greek ἀπορέω, *aporeō*, used by the Apostle in II Corinthians 4; among other things it means to be reduced to extreme distress and to be in need. Hence Tertullian, in Scorpiace, chapter 13, renders the Apostle’s passage in Latin: “We are in need, but not utterly in need.” V. has here a marginal note containing what stands at the end of chapter 104, from the words “The Apostle to the Philippians: ‘No Church,’” etc., through chapter 105.

V. continues the preceding chapter and does not divide it with a new title.

As a general virtue.] C.: “As a virtue generally.”

CHAPTER CX

But sons universally.] M.: “But a son succeeds by hereditary right to all his father’s goods.” St. Augustine, near the end of his exposition of Psalm 124, says: “Peace is the possession of the godly, the possession of heirs. And who are the heirs? Sons.”

It is virtue and merit.] C. says in the margin: “Read: ‘of merits.’”

Whence He does not add.] That is, in the first statement, when He says: “Peace I leave to you,” He did not add: “My peace I leave to you,” as is clear from John 14:27. M. and C. wrongly omit *nec*, “does not,” in “Whence He does not add.”

Afterward.] Namely, peace of heart. M.: “More afterward.”

For it rages.] St. Bernard uses these words in the ninth sermon on Psalm 90, “He who dwells.”

You shall have peace.] M.: “Tranquillity” for “peace.”

In the Mass.] M.: “That he may announce it to him as Mass.”

The lowest things [are joined] to the highest.] Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, in his work On the Canon of the Mass, says:

> At the time when the priest stands suppliant at the altars,  
> And the Son Himself, remaining [what He is], is sacrificed to the Father,  
> The heavens stand open, the heavenly choir is present, the lowest things are joined to the highest,  
> And the agent and the thing done become one.

But is not St. Gregory the chief author of all these statements? Certainly believe it. For these are his words at the end of chapter 58, book IV of the Dialogues, vol. I.

We were enemies of God.] “We were by nature children of wrath; but God, because of the exceeding charity with which he loved us, when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ” (Eph. 2).

[Col. 0494C] To the Romans, chapter V.] The three [copies read] chapter XI.

And tractable.] C.: “and contractible.”
