513 Effective electrum.] Peace is rightly compared with electrum. For, as Tertullian testifies, electrum is an alloy of gold and silver; so peace is the bond of charity uniting humanity and God.

Therefore, for this as though.] M.: “Therefore the prophet, as though not sufficient for salvation. The same prophet,” etc. As appears, this is a copyist’s error.

“Give peace to those who endure.”] The three copies have it thus; but the Sacred Bible, Ecclesiasticus 26, has: “Give a reward to those who endure,” etc.

To the Philippians, chapter IV.] The three [copies read] chapter VII. Note, however, that C. and M. err here by reading “to the Colossians” instead of “to the Philippians.”

“And the peace of God.”] “By which he is at peace,” says the margin of C.

## CHAPTER CXI

“We are excessively devoted.”] C.: “devoted to many things,” etc.

[Col. 0494D] “With foolish labour,” he says.] The Bible printed at Basel in 1591 reads *multo* (“much”) for *stulto* (“foolish”), but incorrectly, as is clear from the Royal Bibles in St Jerome’s version.

“It is evident that the mind.”] Blessed Cyprian likewise proves this in *On the Twelve Abuses*: “Love of the world and of God cannot dwell together in one heart, just as the eyes cannot at once look upon heaven and earth.”

“To be free for the Lord.”] M.: “Not to be free for God, so that it may be fuller, insofar as it is stretched toward things above and eternal. They are darkness.”

“Without the cloudiness of allegory.”] For brevity’s sake I omit what the holy Fathers say on this matter. Meanwhile see Blessed Jerome, vol. IX, sermon for the Easter Vigil, *On Eating the Lamb*; Blessed Augustine, Tractate 18 on John; and Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 37.

## CHAPTER CXII

“If therefore from the aforesaid things.”] V. argues against this as follows: “This contradicts the Apostle, who says: ‘Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood’ [Col. 0495A]—understand, merely—‘but also against principalities and powers’ (Eph. 6),” etc. We cannot have peace from the devil, because God placed enmity between man and that serpent (Gen. 3). Nor from the flesh, because, by its original curse, it naturally brings forth thorns and thistles for us (ibid.), even when we cultivate it through the discipline of training. Nor can we have peace from the world, because the Lord says to his disciples: “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16). On account of these three, the Apostle says: “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Therefore he wrongly says here that we ought to have peace from them, since this is impossible in this life, where the flesh always desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5). For whoever has peace from them, and peace with them, acts against the counsel of the Wise Man, who says: “Never trust your enemy” (Ecclus. 12). And again: 514 “You shall love your friend [Col. 0495B] and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5). But when we sleep together in peace and begin to rest alone, established in hope (Ps. 4), then at last we shall have peace from those three. But now, in the meantime, Christ did not come to bring peace on earth, but a sword (Matt. 10); and, when he himself is about to suffer, he commands the one who has a tunic to sell it and buy a sword (Luke 22). For now is a time of war. The time of peace begins with death. “For the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). Hence it is said to all of us: “Be strong in war and fight against the ancient serpent, whose constant allies are the world and the flesh. No one shall be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2). But in a contest, what peace can there be? Thus V. in the margin.

Yet it is briefly answered that those who wage just wars—as is the war against the devil, the flesh, and the world—aim at peace; and therefore such a war does not oppose peace, except evil peace, concerning which the Lord says in Matthew 10: “I did not come to bring peace, but a sword.” “War,” Augustine says (*Letter* 205 to Boniface), “is waged in order that peace may be acquired.” The end is more excellent than the means. Therefore our author rightly commends peace above all things.

“The Lord [upon] the flood.”] C., at the side: “Of blows and afflictions.”

“Against this flood.”] An exposition of Blessed Augustine on this Psalm, vol. VIII.

“To his people in peace.”] That is, “for eternity,” says the margin of C., following the Gloss.

“In this work of peace.”] M. blunders in saying: “In the time of peace,” etc.

## CHAPTER CXIII

M. alone divides the chapter, adding the fixed title: “On the Twofold Peace.”

“And the peace of eternity.”] This seems the proper reading from ch. 110, where he makes this distinction of peace. V.: “Eternal peace.”

[Col. 0495D] Jeremiah, chapter XXXVIII.] The three [copies read] chapter CXXXV.

“From false brethren.”] C.: “from feigned brethren.”

“In peace, behold bitterness.”] These are words of Isaiah. V. reads *Ecclesiae* (“of the Church”) instead of *ecce* (“behold”).

“Therefore neither is there peace.”] Namely, that peace for the sake of which liberty is lost. For, as Cicero testifies in the *Philippics* (book II), “the name of peace is sweet, and the thing itself salutary. Peace is tranquil liberty.”

“Through which no other virtue.”] M.: “Through which not even virtue.” The ordinary Gloss on this passage puts it thus: “First indeed, she is chaste. Unless chastity first takes its seat in the mind, no perfection will follow in action.”

“Then peaceable.”] Margin of C.: “So that liberty too may not perish.”

“Not judging, without pretence.”] I have restored this passage. The three copies read it with “not judging, without pretence” omitted. I found the same omission in a text printed with the Gloss of Lyra in an old typeface, or, as is commonly said, of St Peter; but it is an error, as is evident from the Syriac paraphrase, which has: “Without judging, and accepting no face,” that is, no persons. Moreover, from the said paraphrase it is plainly established that these words, “Not judging, [Col. 0496A] without pretence,” must be set off by a comma or a double point, because of the intervening conjunction *and*.

“Caesar was everything.”] A hemistich from Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, book III, also used by Alanus at the end of chapter I.

“The liberty of the Romans.”] Valerius Maximus, in his account of Cato’s freely spoken and no less praiseworthy saying, uses this epiphonema: “What, then, is liberty without Cato? And no more is Cato without liberty.” Book VI, ch. 2.

“Hezekiah [spoke] a most gentle word.”] I think this should be read thus, rather than “Hezekiah, most evil,” as M. has it, as though he were evil in the superlative degree. For he, as is read in 4 Kings 21, destroyed the high places which Manasseh his son afterwards rebuilt. Further, since the word *mallissimus* lies outside the commonwealth of Latin and should therefore be banished to the Augean stable rather than followed, I shall say that the copyist, in place of *mollissimum* (“most gentle”), as two manuscripts read, mistakenly wrote *mallissimus*.

“A most evil word.”] V. omits *verbum* (“word”), retaining *pessimum* (“most evil”).

“Not guarding liberty beforehand.”] “Thomas of Canterbury did not act thus,” say the margins of C. and M.

“In my days.”] After these words C. adds: “Likewise Proverbs 28 [perhaps 13] according to the modern reckoning.”

## CHAPTER CXIV

To the Romans, chapter II.] The three [copies read] chapter VI.

Isaiah, chapter XLIII.] V.: chapter CXXXIV. C.: CXXV and CXXVII.

“Labour from iniquities.”] M. has *pro iniquitatibus* (“for iniquities”). The biblical text reads: *in iniquitatibus* (“in iniquities”).

Isaiah, chapter L.] V.: chapter CXLIX. M. and C.: CL.

And chapter LIII.] C. and M.: chapter CXL. V.: CLIX. There appears to have been a scribe’s error here in calculating the chapters: M. and C. count fewer than above, whereas the number necessarily ought here to increase.

2 Corinthians, chapter XII.] The three [copies read] chapter XXVII.

[Col. 0496C] “Thus the sign more clearly.”] V. and C.: “But the sign more clearly.”

“He placed ‘necessary’ before.”] C. and V. read *proposuit* (“proposed”), but incorrectly, as the following words show. Meanwhile hear what I found here in the lower margin of C.: “There is no patience unless equanimity of mind is maintained. For out of patience one man laughs, and another, though silent, smirks in his mind—which is worse—because they continue their deceits.” For fuller treatment see Seneca, *On Providence*, and Cicero, *On Duties*.

He says, chapter 8: “But that which.”] The three [copies read] chapter LXXVIII.

“It is sweeter whenever.”] C.: “It is sweeter, or more pleasant.” In the margin: “As prison and scourging are to a righteous man.” Hear also from Isidore, *Soliloquies*, book II: “It is a great virtue not to injure one by whom you have been injured. It is great strength, even when injured, to forgive. It is great glory to spare one whom you could have harmed.” 516

“The endurance of Job.”] Since the three differed greatly among themselves, I deliberately restored the passage in accordance with the new and accepted edition of the Bible, that of Pope Sixtus V. V. and M.: “the endurance of Job.” C. in the text: “the support of Job,” but in the margin corrects it thus: “I read ‘the sufficiency of Job.’”

“Crowned without patience.”] This and the preceding words are taken from Blessed Jerome’s letter to Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*, near its end. There it reads: “Was he crowned without contest?”

“Pressing iniquity.”] These are words of Blessed Augustine on Psalm 56, verse 2.

To the Romans, chapter III.] The three [copies read] chapter XI.

And chapter VIII.] The three [copies read] XXI.

“For the winepresses.”] These words are not found in the Psalms and must therefore be sought elsewhere. Where? In the titles prefixed by the prophet David to the Psalms, one of which, in Psalm 8, is as follows: “Unto the end, for the winepresses: a psalm of David.” See Blessed Jerome, vol. IV (vol. VIII), at the end of his commentary on Isaiah 10.

[Col. 0497A] “That is, the Churches.”] A sound reading. If you seek a fuller understanding of it, consult Blessed Augustine on the title of Psalm 8; there he clearly explains the matter. M.: “That is, those who are in the present,” etc.

“My hidden mouth.”] Some printed editions, as does C. here, read *cor meum* (“my heart”) instead of *os meum* (“my mouth”). I do not know whence this error crept in; but I know that Blessed Jerome, with the Septuagint interpreters, translated *os meum* (“my mouth”), or *ossa mea* (“my bones”).

“The possessed man triumphed.”] M. alone adds these two words. A possessed person is one seized by a demon.

“The demon coming out of whom.”] M.: “out of which,” namely, out of the jaw, “the demon coming out,” etc.

“It swells and bursts.”] M.: “it swells and strives.”

“And with an arched wound.”] M.: “it pricks as though with a wound,” omitting “arched.”

Job, chapter II.] The three [copies read] chapter V.

“In the face.”] M.: “At the end, may he bless you.”

“Nor he himself ever.”] M. omits these words through “injury to the body.” [Col. 0497B]

“It is given and increases.”] M.: “It is given and does not succumb.”

“He is the first of penitents.”] M.: “of penitence.”

“The compassion of one’s neighbour.”] By no means “the compassion of Christ,” as M. and C. wish. For the truth is clear from Blessed Gregory’s Homily 32 on the Gospels.

“Burn here, cut here.”] Words of Blessed Augustine in the *Confessions*.

“A heap of testimony.”] An allusion to the words concerning Jacob in Genesis 31: “A heap of testimony.” On these see Blessed Jerome, vol. IV, on Jeremiah 22.

“For a testimony of patience.”] V. and C.: “Into patience” only.

“For shame.”] C., from Amos 2, notes in the margin: “The wheel of a cart continually turns” (M. better has “continually creaks,” because it is closer to the word *stridet*, “it creaks,” as is read there in Amos), “and carries hay.” This prophetic passage is expounded by Blessed Gregory, *Morals* XXXII, ch. 6.

[Col. 0497C] 517 “Threefold persecution.”] V.: “Threefold injury.”

“Words of abuse.”] V.: “Words of insult.” Seneca distinguishes insult from injury thus, *On the Constancy of the Wise Man*, ch. 4: “Let us, if you please, Serenus, distinguish injury from insult. The former is naturally more serious; the latter lighter, and grievous only to the over-sensitive: by it they are not harmed, but offended.” I omit the rest for brevity. C., at the side, says for “insult”: “Read ‘of a spouse,’ perhaps, as M. [reads] ‘of abuse.’”

“Where contempt helps.”] A hemistich from Claudian’s *Against Eutropius*, book I.

“Are these servants?”] This term is sometimes used for a youth, and sometimes for a rogue. It is familiar to the French. Blessed Bernard uses this word in his *Apology to William*. But I would say that the text should read *gnatones* (“parasites”) rather than *garciones* (“boys, servants”). For these seem to be words of Seneca, who never used the term *garciones*. M. suggests this, because it reads *natones* in the text, intending *gnatones*, that is, parasites.

“To be despised through patience.”] Seneca excuses boys and youths from insult and injury, and therefore says that their taunts and reproaches should be patiently endured. For he says, book II of *On the Tranquillity of Life*, or the book *On the Constancy of the Wise Man*, ch. 11: “They actually purchase insolence in boys for this purpose, sharpen their impudence, and keep a teacher under whom they may practise pouring out reproaches; nor do we call these insults, but witticisms. But how great is the madness of sometimes taking pleasure, sometimes taking offence, in the same things—and calling a word spoken by a friend abuse, but one spoken by a little slave a joking taunt? The attitude we have toward boys, the wise man has toward all those in whom childishness remains even after youth and grey hairs. And below: “Not undeservedly, then, the wise man accepts the insults [of boys] and their jokes; and sometimes he admonishes and punishes them as bad boys—not because he has received an injury, but because they have done wrong, and so that he may make them cease.”

The same author, *On Anger* III, ch. 24: “Who am I, whose ears it is a crime to hurt? Many have forgiven enemies; shall I not forgive the lazy, the negligent, and the garrulous? Let age excuse a boy, sex a woman, freedom a stranger, familiarity a member of the household.”

“Custom also especially.”] “Count as belonging to this class the wise men,” says Seneca, *On the Constancy of the Wise Man*, ch. 9, “who by long and faithful exercise have acquired the strength to endure and wear down every hostile force. Many are gentle, indeed very gentle, while everything succeeds according to their wishes. But if they hear even the slightest word—not, I say, of reproach or insult, but of contradiction—directed against them, immediately they angrily attack and lavishly repay ten words for one. Why is this? I shall tell you. Such men, cherished beneath their mothers’ wings, nourished only on milk and honey, never given gall to drink, never provoked by injuries or blows—indeed, not even offended by words.” I repeat what I once heard at school:

> You cannot be happy unless you have first drunk some gall.

[Col. 0498B] “Whence what you bear badly.”] From Seneca, *On the Constancy of the Wise Man*.

“Tully in *On Duties*.”] Is it not book IV of the *New Rhetoric*, or book II of the *Tusculan Questions*?

“Custom will make it sweeter.”] Let no passion arise from things to which one is accustomed.

518 “He refused Sulla.”] The three [copies have] *Sillae*. Incorrectly, as is clear from Seneca, *On Providence*, ch. 3. But the edition made by Erasmus has *Syllae*.

“Of death and prison.”] C. in the margin: “As Socrates—and therefore patient.”

“Which did not kill.”] V. adds after these words: “Saying to Porsenna himself: ‘Let the hand which erred burn.’” But since these words are absent from Seneca’s text and two of our witnesses do not have them, I judged it more fitting to relegate them to the notes.

“In the legend of Blessed Vincent.”] See Blessed Augustine’s sermon on the same saint.

He says, chapter XX.] V. and M.: chapters LXXV and LXXXV.

“In my heart.”] I have restored this; otherwise the three [read], “In my mouth.”

“Ready to retaliate.”] That is, to take vengeance, as is gathered from 2 Corinthians 10:6. C.: “to reject.”

“And in Ecclesiasticus, chapter II.”] I have taken these words through the end of the chapter from V. M. notes the scriptural passages but does not give the words.

## CHAPTER CXV

Augustine to Macedonius.] Vol. II, Letter 52, in the middle. Moreover, he discusses the four cardinal virtues at length in vol. I, book I, *On Free Will*, ch. 13; likewise vol. IV, book LXXXIII of the *Questions*, ch. 31.

“What is to be chosen.”] M. alone adds these words. For the other two have: “But to choose this is prudence,” as Augustine has it.

“By these few things it has been shown.”] The margin of C. wants “it has been offended” in place of “it has been shown.” But why?

“Blessed indeed is the chariot.”] That is, the spiritual chariot, says the margin of C., which he prefigured. But I would say: was not Ezekiel’s chariot of four living creatures also a figure of these four virtues? I would assign to prudence the first wheel, bearing the image of a man; for prudence depends upon reason, and man is rational. I would give the second wheel, namely the calf, to temperance. A calf is slain in sacrifice. Are not the disordered desires of sensuality likewise slain by temperance when they are restrained? Strength has been bestowed by nature itself upon the lion. Finally, I would represent justice by the eagle; for with unblinking eyes it looks toward the sun. Justice is not broken by gifts or bent by bribes so as to depart from rendering to each his due; it continually sets before itself law that is just and stable, from which it in no way turns aside. Therefore Blessed Gregory says of the blessed Evangelist John, in his fourth Homily on Ezekiel: “While he fixed his attention on the very substance of divinity, like an eagle he fixed his eyes upon the sun of justice.”

Concerning this Ezekielian quadriga, which figures the Evangelists, I saw in our library elegant manuscript verses by Peter of Riga, a cleric of Rheims. His works on Holy Scripture, written in verse under an allegorical sense, have not yet been seen; but, God willing, they will soon be seen and published. From the verses written below, judge the author’s excellence and learning—as one recognizes the lion from its claw—concerning whom see Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

[Col. 0499A] 519 From the prologue to the Gospels.

> A divided lot draws the wheels: the first wheel goes;  
> The second hastens, the third runs, the fourth flies.  
>   
> The man marks Matthew, the ox Luke, the lion Mark,  
> The bird the disciple who was without blemish.

And below:

> Matthew’s page is milk; Luke’s letter, blood;  
> Mark’s writing, unmixed wine; John’s work, honey.  
>   
> Consult the Scriptures: this style is iron, that bronze;  
> This is silver, that golden.

“Figurative.”] M. alone adds this word. C. reads here: “That fire also, unless first,” etc.

“Unless first this.”] Namely, this chariot of the four cardinal virtues.

“He ascended this.”] C.: “He kindled this.”

## CHAPTER CXVI

[Col. 0499B] “And foot.”] M.: “And appearance.”

“Among the seven gifts.”] C. and M.: “Whence [come] the seven gifts.” There is no sense. St Thomas carefully teaches the distinction of all these matters in the First–Second and Second–Second parts of his *Summa Theologiae*.

Leviticus, chapter II.] The three [copies read] chapter I.

Peter, First Epistle, chapter IV.] The three [copies read] chapter X.

“Also in the council of the holy Pallid Ones.”] These are treated in the book *Lives of the Fathers*. They were called Pallid Ones because mortification of the body produced pallor in their faces. On this council, or conference, see Cassian, *Conferences of the Fathers*, Conference 2, ch. 2.

## CHAPTER CXVII

“To be chosen through prudence.”] Or, to make the sense clearer: “through prudence they had chosen what was to be chosen.” M., instead of *eligendum* (“what was to be chosen”), has *eligendos* (“those to be chosen”).

“To have failed in adversities.”] V.: “adversity.” On this V. has a large and lengthy marginal note which substantially illuminates this chapter on fortitude; below, after the notes to this chapter, we shall transcribe it.

“Most cloistered persons.”] V. omits *claustrales* (“cloistered”), incorrectly, as will be clear from what follows.

“How great [things] for those abandoned.”] M.: “Which [things] for those abandoned.”

“In prisons.”] M.: “In contradictions.”

“Whom he begot by Bathsheba.”] M. and C. rightly add these words. For the little child whom David had begotten by Bathsheba was his firstborn, and he too died, as is clear from 2 Kings, at the end of ch. 11 and in ch. 12. 520

1 Peter, chapter V.] V. and M.: chapter XII. C. does not note the chapter.

Proverbs, chapter X.] V.: chapter XXV. C. and M.: XXXVII. Incorrectly.

And chapter XII.] C. and M.: chapter XXVIII. This is an error, as is clear from the preceding note.

And chapter X.] The three [copies read] chapter XXV. Note that M. and C. calculated incorrectly as 37 in the preceding note, because here the chapter is the same, namely 10; and all three agree here, whereas there they disagree.

[Col. 0499D] Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXX.] M. and C.: LXXX. V.: LXXXI. I saw this margin in C.: “For fuller treatment of these things see Seneca, *On the Four Cardinal Virtues*, and Cicero, *On Duties*.” This is recited by the margin of V. mentioned above. It begins as follows:

“Tully, in the book *On Duties*: Prudence is knowledge of things good and evil, and discrimination between both. For this virtue distinguishes good from evil, goods from one another, and evils from one another. Its duties are to weigh future events from present circumstances and to fortify oneself by counsel against coming calamity. It belongs to intelligence, indeed, to consider beforehand what may happen in either direction and what should be done when something occurs, and not to do anything such that one might someday say, ‘I had not thought of that.’

“The parts of prudence are foresight, circumspection, caution, and teachableness. Foresight is present knowledge considering the outcome of future events. Circumspection is guarding against contrary vices: that is, avoiding one vice in such a way as not to fall into its opposite. [Col. 0500A] Caution is distinguishing vices, which bear the appearance of virtues, from virtues. Teachableness is the knowledge of instructing the ignorant. Cicero, book II of *On Invention*; book I of *On Duties*; Boethius, book IV, prose 6; Seneca, *On the Four Virtues* and Letter 5; Blessed Augustine, vol. III, *On Spirit and Soul*; Cicero, book IV of the *Academics*; the same author, book IV of the *Tusculans*; Blessed Augustine, book XIV, ch. 8, of *The City of God*, vol. V.

“Everything that Blessed Bernard, in *On Consideration* addressed to Pope Eugenius, says belongs to consideration belongs to prudence. Seneca, *On the Four Virtues*, in the chapter ‘On Prudence,’ sets down these highly useful maxims: ‘Determine the value of things not from the opinion of the multitude but from their nature’ [variant: ‘things determined’]. Again: ‘Do not value highly what is fleeting. You will be the same everywhere, and, as the variety of circumstances requires, adapt yourself to the time; do not change yourself in certain matters, but rather adjust yourself, like a hand which remains the same whether extended into the palm [variant: *palmum*] or clenched into a fist’ [Seneca: ‘drawn tight’; variant: ‘moves’]. Again: ‘Know that in some matters [Col. 0500B] you must persist because you have begun them; but do not even begin certain matters in which persistence would be harmful.’ Again: ‘Do not entertain wandering thoughts, as though like dreams.’ Again: ‘Let your speech not be empty, but let it either persuade, warn, console, or command. Praise sparingly; blame more sparingly. For excessive praise is reprehensible, as is immoderate blame. The former is suspected of flattery, the latter of malice,’ etc.

“Fortitude is the virtue which repels the onset of adversity. Its parts are magnanimity, confidence, security, magnificence, constancy, and patience.

“Magnanimity is the willing and rational undertaking of difficult things. For this virtue, as Tully says (*On Duties* I, after Plato), when it makes one ready to undertake hardships, looks rather to the common good than to private advantage. For just as knowledge separated from justice should be called cunning rather than wisdom, so a spirit prepared for danger, if it is impelled by its own desire rather than by the common [variant: ‘every’] good, deserves the name of rashness [Cicero has ‘audacity’] rather than fortitude. Those are to be considered magnanimous not who inflict, but who repel injury.

“Therefore, the first precaution in this virtue is against avarice. For it is not consistent with reason that one whom fear does not break should be broken by desire, nor that one who has made himself invincible against toil should be conquered by pleasure. The second precaution is against ambition. For distinction is sought through difficulties; for what is harder is thought more distinguished. The third precaution is against rashness. To expose oneself rashly in battle and fight the enemy hand-to-hand is something monstrous and beast-like. Nevertheless, if necessity demands it, one must fight, and death must be preferred to disgrace. Above all, however, we must avoid offering ourselves to dangers without cause. In encountering them, we should imitate the practice of physicians, who treat slight illnesses lightly, but are compelled to employ hazardous remedies for graver diseases. [Col. 0500D] But it belongs to the wise man to meet the storm by whatever means, and he more readily attains the good, once the matter is explained, than [he avoids] the feared [Cicero: ‘doubted’] evil.

“Confidence is the assured hope of the mind that it will bring a thing begun to its end. Security is not fearing impending hardships and those allied to the undertaking begun.

“Magnificence is the completion of difficult and splendid deeds. Its duties are partly peaceful and partly military (*On Duties* I). In peaceful affairs, two rules of leadership must be observed by rulers. First, they must so protect the advantage of citizens that, whatever they do, they refer it to that advantage, forgetting their own interests. Second, they must care for the whole body of the state, lest, while protecting some parts, they abandon the rest.

“In military duties, the first point is to undertake wars with the intention that one may live in peace without injury. The second is, before attacking, to make careful preparation. The equipment of war consists of four things: retainers, municipalities, funds, and arms.

“The third duty is neither to despair rashly through cowardice nor to be overconfident through desire.

“The fourth is to dread disgrace more than death, to look more to honour than to safety or other advantages, yet not to prefer popular rumours to safety.

“The fifth is to exercise one’s forces through frequent labours.

“The sixth is, once war has begun, to raise good natural disposition by exhortation: now to lift spirits by praise, now to shake off idleness by admonition.

“The seventh is to meet the first assaults in battle.

“The eighth is to bring aid to those who are wavering, and to support those who are faltering.

[Col. 0501B] “The ninth is, after victory, to spare those who have not been cruel or savage.

“The tenth is to keep treaties and promises made to enemies. But although most people think military affairs greater than civic ones, this opinion should be diminished. For many have sought wars from a desire for glory or money. Thus, if we wish to judge rightly, arms abroad are of little value if there is no counsel at home. It is more fitting, however, to seek glory through the resources of intellect rather than strength. For all that honourable excellence which we seek with lofty spirit is achieved by the powers of the mind, not the body. Yet the body must be trained so that it may obey counsel and reason.

“Constancy is firm stability of mind, persevering in its purpose. In evils this is called obstinacy and stubbornness. Its opposite is inconstancy, which is movement of mind among diverse occupations. The duty of constancy, as Tully says, is to maintain dignity in either fortune. For, as he also says, there are those [Col. 0501C] who are too little consistent with themselves in contrary circumstances: they most severely despise pleasure, but are weaker in pain; they neglect favour, but are broken by ill repute.

“Patience is the virtue that bears with equanimity the blows of insults and every adversity. Seneca [perhaps Tully], in the book *On Duties*—if Seneca, perhaps in the book *On Morals*, which begins, ‘Every sin is an action’—speaking of the four virtues in the chapter ‘On Magnanimity,’ by which title he denotes fortitude, says: ‘If you are magnanimous, you will never judge that an insult has been done to you.’ Again: ‘Know that forgiveness is an honourable and greater kind of vengeance.’

“Again (Seneca, *On the Four Virtues*): ‘Do not engage in a conflict unless you have declared it. Neither seek dangers like a rash man nor fear them like a coward. Nothing makes the mind cowardly except consciousness of a blameworthy life. The measure of magnanimity is to be neither timid nor daring.’”

## CHAPTER CXVIII

[Col. 0501D] “About to preserve virtue.”] M.: “About to serve virtue.”

“Opposes enticements.”] C. and V.: “Opposes enticements” [with the accusative *illecebras* instead of the dative].

“In the aforesaid chariot.”] Concerning which, ch. 115.

“While for you among others.”] C.: “While among others for himself,” or “from others among you.”

“Wounds minds.”] C.: “souls.” M. carries *animorum* (“of minds”) back to the following sentence, thus: “It wounds integrity. The use of minds is scarcely,” etc.

“To be torn away.”] M.: “to return.” On this I would say with Blessed Jerome: “What unformed minds have imbibed is eradicated with difficulty.”

“Pleasures frequented from the cradle.”] M.: “pleasures frequented more keenly.”

“When a man begins.”] M.: “A man conceives.”

“What pride.”] M. and C.: “which he restrains.” *Superbiam* (“pride”) is missing.

“A measure [is set] by a certain wise man.”] By Solomon, Proverbs 23: “Set a limit to your prudence.” Moreover Cicero, *On Duties* I: “By applying a certain measure and order to the matters handled in life, we shall preserve honourableness and propriety.” Horace:

> There is a measure in things; finally, there are fixed bounds.

[Col. 0502A] “By a philosopher.”] For the little book *On the Four Virtues*, ascribed to Seneca, has the heading “On Magnanimity.” Magnanimity is also called fortitude. V., in this chapter on temperance, reads this marginal note:

“Tully, in the book *On Duties*: Temperance is the rule of reason over desire and other unruly motions. This virtue is the ornament of the whole of life and the calming of every disturbance. The parts of this virtue are all those things which rule unfaithful motions. There are eight: modesty, shame, abstinence, honourableness, moderation, frugality, sobriety, and chastity.

“Modesty is to keep our dress, movement, and every occupation between deficiency and excess. In dress it must be observed that every ornament unworthy of a man be removed from a man. As Tully says, cleanliness should be employed which is neither offensive nor overly elaborate, and which avoids only rustic and uncivil negligence. The same author: ‘One kind of movement belongs to the body, another to the mind.’ In bodily movement we must take care not to use a gait so soft in walking slowly that we seem like the bearers of procession-platforms, nor in haste to adopt excessive speed. When this happens, breathing is disturbed, faces change, mouths are twisted; from these signs it is strongly indicated that constancy is absent.

“Now the motions of the mind are twofold: the thought of reason and the appetite of the will. Thought is exercised in seeking truth; appetite impels to action. We must therefore take care that reason governs and appetite obeys. For if appetites do not obey reason, to which they are subject, the laws of nature are disturbed—not only in minds, but also in bodies. One may see even in their faces those who are angry, or who are stirred by fear, [Col. 0502C] or exult in excessive pleasure. Their expressions, voices, movements, and postures all change. From this it is understood that all appetites must be restrained and calmed.

“Occupations, however, vary according to the variety of times, characters, and business. Just as there are great dissimilarities in bodies—some have speed for running, others strength for wrestling—so there are greater varieties in minds. Some possess a graceful manner of speaking, that is, urbanity; these, cheerfulness; those, seriousness. You see others skilful at concealing and dissembling. Others are simple and open; lovers of truth and enemies of fraud, they think that nothing ought to be done secretly or by deception. Therefore let us occupy ourselves in those matters for which we are suited [the text appears to lack *si*, “if”]. But if necessity drives us into things unsuited to our natural ability, every care must be taken that we perform them, if not becomingly, at least not very unbecomingly. Nor should we strive so hard to pursue goods not granted to us as to avoid vices.

“With these matters thus ordered, the duty of a young man is to respect his elders and to choose from among them the most approved men, on whose counsel he may rely. For the justice of one entering upon life must be guided by the prudence of the old. At the beginning of youth there is the greatest weakness of judgment; yet each person settles upon the mode of life which he has loved most. Thus he becomes entangled in a fixed course of living before he has been able to judge what is best. Therefore, as Terence says, the duty of a young man is to look into the lives of men as into a mirror and to take an example for himself from others. Above all, this age must be kept from lusts. Yet if they wish to relax their minds and give themselves to pleasure, let them beware of intemperance and remember shame. For what could be easier, if elders wish to participate in their sport? For recreation and jesting are permitted, but like sleep and other rest: namely, when we have satisfied the demands of serious matters.

[Col. 0503A] “There are two kinds of amusement for the mind. One is illiberal, wanton, shameful, obscene; the other elegant, urbane, ingenious, and witty. In old age bodily labours should be diminished and exercises of the mind increased. One should also devote effort to helping friends and young people by counsel. Nothing, however, must be more carefully avoided by old age than trusting itself to idleness. Luxury, though shameful at every age, is most foul in old age. For if intemperance is added to old age, the evil is doubled: old age itself incurs disgrace, and it makes the intemperance of the young more shameless.

“Duties also differ according to one’s affairs. The duty of a ruler is to judge that he bears the person of the state, preserve its dignity, keep its laws, and remember that they have been entrusted to his fidelity. The duty of a private citizen is to live with fellow citizens under equal law, and neither wish to abase himself excessively nor to exalt himself excessively in a tranquil and honourable commonwealth. The duty of a traveller (*peregrini*; variant *peregrinum*) is to do nothing beyond his own business and inquire into no one else’s.

[Col. 0503B] “The employment of those who buy from merchants what they immediately sell is base. For they make no profit except by lying a great deal. And nothing is more disgraceful than false pretence. A household’s resources should therefore be acquired by gains free from disgrace and preserved by frugality. For no gain is as great as keeping off expense from what one possesses. Medicine and architecture are honourable professions for those whose social rank they suit. Trade, if petty, must be judged base; but if great and abundant, bringing in much from every quarter and distributing generously to many without false pretence, it is not greatly blameworthy. Nothing is better, more productive, or more worthy of a free man than agriculture.

“So much for modesty. We must now speak of shame, which is nothing other than preserving propriety in bearing and speech.”

Tully (*On Duties*, I): In the structure of our body, nature seems to have exercised great care. For she placed our form, in which there is a becoming appearance, openly; but she concealed the parts given for nature’s necessity, because they would have had an unsightly appearance. Modesty has imitated this careful workmanship of nature. For all sound-minded persons remove from sight what nature concealed; they also take pains to satisfy necessity as secretly as possible. Modesty must likewise be preserved in speech. Since the uses of those parts are necessary, they do not call either the parts themselves or their uses by their proper names. Even in a serious matter it is faulty to introduce delicate language. When Pericles and Sophocles, colleagues in the praetorship, had met to discuss their common duty, Sophocles said concerning a boy passing by: “O Pericles, what a handsome boy!”

Pericles replied [the text has “Sophocles”]: “A praetor ought to have self-controlled not only hands but also eyes.” [Col. 0503D] If Sophocles had said the same thing at a banquet, perhaps he would justly have escaped reproof. It also belongs to modesty to avoid loquacity, not to pry into another’s secret, and to avoid contention. For to contend with an equal is hazardous, with a superior is madness, and with an inferior is degrading. Indeed, one who quarrels with a drunkard injures one who is absent.

It belongs to abstinence not to anticipate the appointed hour of dining, and this too is a matter of propriety; but it belongs to moderation to recall an excessive appetite for food under the rule of reason. Frugality is not to exceed the measure of one’s refreshment. Sobriety is to restrain excess by a sudden check. Its duty is to ward off the evil of drunkenness. Chastity is to tame wantonness by the governance of reason. Therefore, as Tully says, a brave man should always keep before him how far human nature surpasses beasts. For they perceive nothing but pleasure; toward it they rush with all their force. But the human mind is nourished by learning, reflection, and action. If anyone is somewhat inclined to pleasures, [Col. 0504A] provided he is not of the class of cattle, he understands from this that pleasure is unworthy of human excellence, because it seeks hiding places. For if anyone is caught by any pleasure somewhat too uprightly, he conceals his appetite for pleasure out of modesty. Let us therefore flee the most flattering dominion of pleasures. For most-flattering pleasures, as mistresses, turn the greatest portions away from virtue. One must never act against temperance out of love for other virtues. For some things are so foul that a wise man would not do them even for the preservation of his country, though they seem obscene even to mention.

Seneca, in *On the Four Virtues*, calls temperance self-control, concerning which, among other things, he says: “If you love self-control, cut off superfluities.” Likewise: “If you are self-controlled, you will reach the point of being content with yourself.” Likewise: “Reject everything that flatters.” Likewise: “You will neither cling to present pleasures nor long for absent ones. Let hunger stimulate your palate, [Col. 0504B] not flavours. Redeem your desires with little, because you ought to care only that they cease.” Likewise: “As far as you can, draw yourself away from the body to the spirit” [Seneca: “hasten to bring yourself back”]. Likewise: “Let neither poverty be filthy to you, nor frugality mean, nor simplicity neglected, nor lightness a subject for mockery.” Likewise: “Neither bewail what is yours nor marvel at what belongs to another.” Likewise: “Flee disgraceful things before they happen. Reverence no one more than yourself. Believe all things bearable except disgrace; abstain also from disgraceful words. For license in them nourishes shamelessness. Love useful conversations more than witty and agreeable ones, straightforward ones rather than compliant ones. Sometimes you will mix jokes with serious matters, but restrained jokes, without injury to dignity and modesty. For laughter is blameworthy if it is boyishly unrestrained or womanishly affected. A laugh also makes a person hateful when it is proud and loud, malicious and furtive, or provoked by others’ misfortunes.” Likewise: “Your urbanity shall not be buffoonish, but agreeable.”

[Col. 0504C] “Let your wit be without a sting; your jokes without baseness; your laughter without cackling; your voice without shouting; your gait without commotion; your rest without idleness. Let it grieve you as much to be praised by disgraceful persons as to be praised for disgraceful things. Likewise” (Seneca, *On the Four Virtues*): “You will not be bold or arrogant; you will humble yourself, not cast yourself down, preserving dignity. You will gladly accept admonition and patiently endure rebuke. If someone rebukes you deservedly, know that he has benefited you; if undeservedly, know that he wished to benefit you. Likewise: Do not exalt or humiliate anyone. Be yourself a fugitive from vices, but do not be an inquisitive examiner of others’ faults or a bitter reprover; rather, correct without reproach, so that you anticipate admonition with cheerfulness and readily grant pardon to error. Answer readily one who asks; yield readily to one who contends. Be adaptable, not fickle; steadfast, not stubborn. Be kind to all, flattering to none, intimate with few, fair to all; neither a sower of your own good reputation nor [Col. 0504D] envious of another’s; not at all credulous toward rumours, accusations, or suspicions. Be firm in adversity, cautious and humble in prosperity; conceal your virtues as others conceal their vices; despise empty glory. Let your knowledge of some subject neither be unknown nor burdensome. Despise no one’s ignorance. Be sparing of speech yourself, yet patient with talkative people; serious, not savage [or: “and more serious”], but cheerful and not contemptuous. Desire wisdom and be teachable; share without arrogance what you know with one who asks. Ask without concealing your ignorance to be taught what you do not know. You will make all equal to yourself if you do not disdain inferiors through pride or fear superiors while living rightly.” These are the notes found in the margin of V. on this Chapter 118.

## CHAPTER 119

“You boast of victory.”] M.: “You believe in victory.”

“You dream of health.”] Reading uncertain: “Far be it; M. has *Seminas valet ut habet*.”

“Swelling of pride.”] Not “fears,” as C.

“Has infected men.”] C.: “has slain.”

[Col. 0505A] “This first and last.”] M.: “first and last.”

“Has overcome vices.”] C. says in the margin:

> When you have fought well, when you think all things accomplished,  
> Pride remains to be conquered—the thing that most assails you.

“Into confusion.”] V.: “in confusion.”

“You boast of victory.”] C.: “boasting, or lying, victory.”

“Supported by good will.”] C.: “good will, or the building of each person, supported,” etc.

“Remember the scourge.”] C.: “remember the scourge, or fan,” etc.

Here I shall transcribe what I found in the margin of V. as notes on Chapter 119, *On Justice*.

Tully, in Book I of *On Duties*, sets forth these points concerning justice separately; we have collected them thence and set them together. “The foundation,” he says, “of justice is good faith, that is, constancy and truth in what has been said and agreed. Likewise: The parts of justice are not to injure human beings; of modesty, not to offend them. Every action [Col. 0505B] ought to be free from rashness and negligence. In every action to be undertaken, three things must be observed. First, that appetite obey reason; next, that attention be paid to the magnitude of the thing which we intend to accomplish, so that neither greater nor less care be undertaken than the matter requires. Third, we must take care that matters pertaining to a liberal appearance are regulated. Of these three, the most excellent is for appetite to obey reason. Likewise: Faults which seem small, and which cannot be understood by many, must be avoided with greater diligence. Just as, in strings or pipes, however slightly they differ, the difference is usually noticed by a knowledgeable person, so we must see in life lest anything perhaps differ—indeed, much more so, because the harmony of actions is greater and better than that of sounds. Thus, as musicians’ ears perceive even the slightest variations in strings, so, if we wish to be keen and diligent observers of vices, we often understand great matters from small ones: from the look of the eyes, the relaxing or contracting of the eyebrows, sadness, cheerfulness, laughter, speech, silence, raising or lowering the voice, and other things like these.”

Likewise: “The first duties are owed to God, the second to one’s country, the third to parents; then, by degrees, the remaining duties to the rest.” Likewise (for an explanation of these, see Peter Marsus’s commentary on *On Duties*, II): “The force of justice is so great that not even those who live by crime and wickedness can live without some share of justice. Unless an arch-pirate distributes his booty equally, he will either be killed by his companions or deserted; even robbers are said to have laws which they obey and observe. Thus, because of an equal division of booty, both Bargulus, the Illyrian robber mentioned by Theopompus, acquired great wealth, and Viriathus the Lusitanian acquired much greater wealth. Even for a solitary person living in the countryside, a reputation for justice is necessary; and all the more so because, if they do not possess it, [Col. 0505D] they will be judged unjust and, being surrounded by no safeguards, will suffer many injuries. Likewise: For the sake of preserving [variant: ardently practising] justice, kings of good character seem formerly to have been established; and the same was the reason for establishing laws as for establishing kings. For equal justice has always been sought; if people obtained it from one just and good man, they were content with him. When this occurred less often, laws were invented, which would always speak to all with one and the same voice.”

Justice, therefore, is the virtue which preserves human society and communal life. This virtue rises above every hardship. For no one can be just who fears death, exile, pain, or poverty, or who prefers to equity things contrary to these. Justice is divided into severity and liberality. Severity is the virtue which restrains injury by deserved punishment. Its first duty is that no one should harm another unless provoked by injury. The second is that he should use common things as common, [Col. 0506A] private things as private. Private things are those possessed not by nature, but either by prior occupation—such as the possessions of those who formerly came into empty places—or by victory, as those acquired in war, or by law, as those who became heirs through their fathers’ wills. And since what was common by nature becomes the property of a person, let each retain what is his. But whoever desires more will violate the law of human society.

The third duty is to remove from human society the pestilential class of human beings. For just as certain limbs are amputated if they have begun to lack blood and life and to harm the rest, so this savagery and bestial brutality in human form must be separated from common life. For what difference is there whether someone turns himself from a human being into a beast, or bears the brutality of a beast under a human appearance?

Liberality is the virtue that dispenses benefits. With reference to its disposition we call it kindness or goodwill; with reference to its effect, beneficence. It consists in giving [Col. 0506B] and repaying. Since human beings can both harm and help other human beings exceedingly, I judge it the peculiar office of this virtue to win human affections and join them to one’s own purposes. It is better for a ruler to be loved than feared; the power of goodwill is great, that of fear weak. No force of authority is so great that it can endure long when minds are oppressed by fear. Seven things must be avoided concerning liberality. First, do not be harsh; second, do not delay; third, do not plunder; fourth, do not be prodigal; fifth, do not reproach others; sixth, do not refuse maliciously; seventh, do not complain of an ungrateful person. For, as Ennius says, “I consider benefits badly bestowed to be wrongs.” In giving a benefit, a choice according to worth must be made, and one must consider the character of the recipient, his disposition toward us, companionship, partnership in life, and contribution to our interests; also benefits previously bestowed—even if we do not live with perfect people, but with people who possess only images of virtue. I think no one should be neglected in whom some indication [Col. 0506C] of virtue appears. Each person ought especially to be honoured insofar as he is more adorned with the gentler virtues, namely modesty and temperance. This is a most important duty: to the person by whom we are most loved, let us give most. But the case is different, says Seneca, for the person oppressed by misfortune and for the person who seeks better circumstances while none of his own affairs are adverse. For kindness is more readily owed to the unfortunate, unless perhaps they deserve their misfortune. I think a benefit is better placed among good people than among rich ones. For the wealthy, when they have received a benefit, think that they themselves have given it, or suspect that something is expected from them. Likewise: If you do good to a wealthy wicked person, gratitude remains in that one person, or perhaps in his household. But if you do good to a poor and good person, all poor and good people see a safeguard prepared for themselves.

Likewise: “One kind of beneficence is by service, another by money. The one by money is easier, especially for a rich person; the first is more splendid and more worthy of a good man. [Col. 0506D] For beneficence by money exhausts its own material. Thus kindness is destroyed by kindness. The more persons you assist in this way, the fewer you can assist thereafter; but the other kind, through the habit of doing good, makes people readier and more practised. Yet that kind of beneficence should not be rejected altogether. For one must often share one’s property with suitable persons in need, but carefully and moderately. For many have squandered their inheritances by inconsiderate generosity. Nothing, however, is more foolish than to arrange matters so that you cannot long continue doing what you gladly do.”

Likewise: “There are two kinds of generous people: some are called squanderers, others liberal. Squanderers are those who pour out money on banquets and gifts for actors and pimps. Such people will leave behind a memory either brief or none at all. Liberal people are those who use their resources either to ransom captives from pirates, to assist friends by contributing to their children, or in some other necessary undertaking to obtain or increase something. [Col. 0507A] Beneficence is exercised in deed by helping with counsel and defending cases by eloquence. For since a legal case consists of accusation and defence, defence is more praiseworthy. Yet accusation is very often approved, though it should be undertaken once rather than often. For it seems the mark of a harsh person—or rather scarcely of a human being—to bring capital danger upon many people. It is also shameful to jeopardize one’s reputation in order to be called an accuser. One must carefully avoid summoning an innocent person to a capital trial, which cannot be done without wickedness. For what is more inhuman than to turn eloquence, given for the safety of humankind, to the destruction of good people? The beginning of justice proceeds from nature. Then certain things came into custom by the reasoning of utility; afterwards fear of laws and religion sanctioned customs proceeding from nature and already approved by use.

Natural law is that which opinion did not produce, but a certain inborn force: it is devoted to religion, filial devotion, gratitude, vindication, reverence, and truth. [Col. 0507B] Likewise: The parts of justice are all the virtues by which good people render what is due. Religion renders God his due; filial devotion renders it to parents; innocence to inferiors; friendship to equals; concord to fellow citizens; mercy to the needy.

Religion is the virtue that brings care and ceremonial observance to divinity. Its duty is threefold (*On Invention*, II): to repent of sin committed, to esteem lightly the mutability of temporal things, and to commit one’s whole life to God. Its fourth duty is also to preserve truth.

Filial devotion is that through which dutiful and diligent reverence is rendered to those joined by blood and to one’s country. For, as Tully says (*Tusculan Disputations*, III), “He who is the enemy of his own people is the common enemy of all.” Innocence is purity of mind that abhors every infliction of injury. For, as Seneca says: “He threatens many who injures one.” Friendship, as Tully says, is good will toward someone for the sake of the person loved. [Col. 0507C] “This,” he says, “is the law of friendship: that we neither ask shameful things nor do them when asked.”

Reverence is the virtue that renders the observance of due honour to persons of dignity or exalted by some preeminence. Concord is the virtue that voluntarily binds citizens and compatriots in the same law and common dwelling. Mercy is the virtue through which the mind is moved by the calamity of the afflicted. This virtue, as Terence says, considers nothing human foreign to itself.

To the two aforementioned kinds of justice are opposed two kinds of injustice: truculence and negligence. Truculence is a readiness to inflict injury. It has three causes: fear, greed, and ambition. Truculence is divided into force and fraud. Fraud seems to belong to a little fox, violence to a lion. Both are utterly alien to humanity, but fraud deserves greater hatred. For no part of all justice is more pernicious than that of those who, especially when they deceive, [Col. 0507D] act in order to seem good men. Negligence is failure to repel injury when one can and ought to do so. Its causes are these: people either are unwilling to undertake enmities, labour, or expense; or they are detained by their own occupations; or they are so far removed by indifference that they allow those whom they ought to protect to remain deserted. In every injustice, moreover, it matters greatly whether the injury is done through disturbance of mind or deliberately. For disturbance is usually brief and temporary. Therefore, things occurring through a sudden impulse are lighter than those inflicted with forethought. Seneca, in *On the Four Virtues*: “Justice is a silent compact of nature, discovered for the assistance of many. Whoever desires to pursue it, first fear and love God, that you may be loved by God. You will love God if you imitate him, so as to wish to benefit all and harm no one. But if you are to be just, you will not merely do no harm, but will also prevent those who harm others. For doing no harm is not [Col. 0508A] justice, but abstaining from what belongs to another. If you are just, it will make no difference whether you affirm simply or swear.” Thus far the margin of V. on justice.

St Jerome says of the same Julian, vol. ## CHAPTER 125

[Col. 0511D]

V. is condemned by the following text in the title, because instead of “On the effect of prayer,” it has:

“On the affection [or disposition],” etc.

“The same, Chapter 18.”] Three copies: Chapter 50.

“Do not be hindered.”] C. in the margin: “By another work.” Likewise in the same place: “It is also understood of vocal prayer.”

“Luke, Chapter 3.”] Three copies: 14.

“Hilarion disputing.”] Consult the life found in Surius, vol. I.

“Likewise Luke, Chapter 9.”] V. and C.: Chapter 98. Nor should it seem surprising that I report so high a number of chapters. For Ammonius and Eusebius divided the Gospel of Luke into 343 chapters; Bede into 93 chapters; Oecumenius and Euthymius into 83; St Ambrose into 64 titles; while more recent Latin writers make 24 chapters.

“The same, Chapter 11.”] Three copies: Chapter 125.

[Col. 0512A] “Ambrose.”] Book VII on Luke 11, first title: “On the example that leads the disciples to insistence and perseverance in prayer.”

“Praying while awake.”] St Ambrose’s text has “striking while awake.” It is remarkable whence this variation arose. Not only here, but elsewhere in manuscripts I have read *orare* (“to pray”) for *vibrare* (“to strike”), as the recent edition of St Ambrose’s works, made and printed at Paris by Guillaume Merlin in 1569, notes in the margin.

“And Bede says: ‘If a friend.’”] Book IV on Luke, Chapter 27; but after St Augustine, vol. X, *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*, Sermon 36.

“In Luke, Chapter 18.”] V. and M.: Chapter 214.

“They seek by prayers.”] V.: “They strike by prayers”; C.: “they stretch [themselves] by prayers.”

> Things which do not help singly help greatly when many.

“And thus the prayer of many.” This leads me to believe that *multorum* (“of many”) is a better reading in the text than *minorum* (“of lesser persons”). Thus Proverbs 18: “A brother aided by a brother is like a strong city.” And James 5: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved.” And Homer, prince of Greek poets, says:

> United, even the utterly feeble are mighty.

“Jerome to Paula.”] I have not yet seen or read this in the letters to Paula, but it is indeed in the letter to Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*, Chapter 16, vol. I. Yet I will say this one thing. In the epitaph of her mother Paula addressed to Eustochium, I find something similar in these words: “And when she made the sign [of the cross] over her mouth and stomach, and endeavoured to soothe her mother’s pain by the impress of the cross,” etc. The same material found in the letter to Eustochium occurs in vol. IX, in the Rule under the title “On Contemplation.”

“Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 11.”] Three copies: Chapter 24.

“In what hour.”] These are the words of the interlinear gloss on this passage.

“Likewise, Chapter 12: Peter.”] Three copies: Chapter 27.

“Likewise, Chapter 9.”] Three copies: Chapter 20.

“Likewise, Chapter 5.”] C. and M.: Chapter 12.

“Peter, First Epistle, Chapter 3.”] Three copies: Chapter 8.

“Likewise, Chapter 4.”] C.: Chapter 10.

“Jesus son of Nave.”] Or son of Nun, Ecclesiasticus 46: “Mighty in war, Jesus son of Nave, successor of Moses among the prophets.”

For it is most often simian, because through habit the lips move without the heart’s attention.” This is true. For it often happens that such persons, after long movement or trembling of their lips, can scarcely say what they uttered in prayer.

Therefore, as St Augustine says, prayer should be brief and frequent. “For many words are one thing, and a prolonged affection another. The brethren in Egypt are said indeed to have frequent prayers, but very brief ones, launched forth, as it were, like darts, lest that watchfully raised attention, necessary to one praying, should fade and grow dull through longer delays.” And below: “For this business is most often carried on more by groans than by words, more by tears than by speech.” Vol. II, Epistle 121 to Proba, *On Prayer to God*, chapter 10. V.’s summary is as follows: “On the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh works of mercy.” M.: “On burial.”

Here, by grace, Antony.] C. has “Jerome” instead of “Antony”; hence, I think, arose the error that St Jerome wrote these things in the *Life of St Paul the Hermit*.

Leaning upon.] That is, supported, as I said above at chapter 124.

Mary the Egyptian.] See the Life written by Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, as Nicephorus testifies, book XVII, chapter 5. It appears in Surius, volume II.

That versifier.] “Who is he?” you ask. He is Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans and later archbishop of Tours. I do not think these verses have yet been printed.

Many pleased God.] Among them Tobias is especially famous.

Rather, we help ourselves.] Because we earn merit through a work of mercy.

Let it not be costly.] “The care of the funeral,” says St Augustine, “the condition of burial, and the pomp of obsequies are comforts for the living rather than aids to the dead.” *City of God*, book I, chapter 12. It is nevertheless useful to attach some memorial at the place of burial, by which mortals—and especially friends—may be reminded to pray for the soul of the deceased. Monuments exist in order to remind the mind. For the Greeks call it *μνεημεῖον* [probably *μνημεῖον*], what we call a remembrance and monument; and in their language the memory by which we remember is called *μνήμη* (*mnēmē*).

For remedies.] What benefit is it to a man sent into exile if the walls of his house are richly adorned? So what benefit is it to a spirit that its corpse has been decorated?

[Col. 0516A]

> Let dirges be absent from my empty funeral,  
> and shameful mourning and lamentations.  
> Restrain the cry, and send  
> no superfluous honours upon my tomb.

543 He is covered by heaven.] Thus Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book VII, concerning Caesar’s forbidding the slain bodies to be burned or buried:

> or a pyre, it makes no difference. Nature receives all things  
> into her willing bosom.

And afterwards: “Earth holds all things that it has produced; he who has no urn is covered by heaven.” And in Seneca: “Nature has given burial to all.”

Nature buries.] A verse of Maecenas:

> I care not for a tomb; nature buries those left behind.

In the Epistle to Marcella beginning “Ambrose,” [Col. 0516C] appears “coarse bread,” etc.; likewise in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book V, chapter 13.

He surpasses Christ’s sobriety.] For Surius, in his commentary on events in the world from 1500 to 1566, admiring the Turks’ frugality in food, attacks Christians as follows: “When King Ferdinand learned by reliable messengers of his own men’s slaughter and the Turks’ victory, he sent new and splendid gifts to Suleiman in order to win his favour. His ambassadors were honourably received by the Turks; on the following day they dined with the pashas and saw rice and mutton, and nothing else edible, set before them. That temperance of the barbarians undoubtedly severely rebukes the luxury of our people, since they satisfy not so much the desire of the throat as nature’s necessity. But our countrymen think they have furnished their banquets splendidly when there is no limit to drenching the throat and stuffing the belly, so that it may most truly be said of our people that more perish through drunken excess than through the sword. And indeed among most people that detestable [Col. 0516D] custom prevails, of prolonging banquets for many hours, although it is exceedingly harmful not only to the soul but also to the body. But, of course, one must do what is commonly said:

> Eat, drink, play: after death there is no pleasure.”

So he. More on this subject is found in Wiringus, canon of Arras, in his book *On Fasting and Abstinence*.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI

Incest and disgrace.] V.: “Incest, and the disgraceful foulness of the vice of the Sodomites.”

Joel says.] Three: “David says.”

The desire for fornication.] Bede, *On Solomon’s Temple*: “The pleasure of fornication is brief, but its punishment everlasting.” Hence Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, metre 7:

> Every pleasure has this:  
> it stirs those enjoying it  
> with goads; like a swarm of flying bees,  
> when it has poured forth pleasant honey,  
> it flees, and with a too-clinging bite  
> wounds the hearts it has struck.

The same occurs in prose 7 of the same work. From this point almost to the end of the chapter, V. differs and varies greatly in its reading; I have not restored those readings to the text for sound reasons. [Col. 0517D] They are as follows: “Boethius says in the book *Consolations*: ‘The appetite of pleasure is full of anxiety; satiety, of repentance.’ And, unless I am mistaken, Macrobius in the *Saturnalia*, and likewise Flavianus, *On the Traces of the Philosophers*, speaking of pleasure, say: ‘The end of pleasure is repentance.’ Hence, when Demosthenes, laying his hand upon the belly of the most famous courtesan Lais, asked, ‘How much is this?’ and she said, ‘A thousand denarii,’ he replied: ‘I do not buy repentance at that price.’ Jerome, indeed, in the *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, gives the example of a martyr who bit off his own tongue and threw it into the mouth of a courtesan lying bound upon him and touching his genitals, so that pain might overcome the pleasure that he unwillingly felt. The Lord forbids this not only in deed but also in intention: ‘Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,’ etc. (Matthew V). And likewise will and consent themselves, without the deed, are mortal sin. Nor is mere will alone, but even lingering delight, mortal [Col. 0518A] sin. Hence David: ‘Blessed is he who holds and dashes his little ones’—that is, who restrains the first motions of lust, lest they come to consent or lingering delight, because delay brings danger with it—‘against the rock’ (Psalm CXXXVI), that is, Christ. Hence Solomon in the Song of Songs, chapter II: ‘Catch for us the little foxes while they are little’; that is, restrain the small motions while they are first and without consent or lingering delight, lest they grow wild and large and thus demolish the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts—that is, kill the soul. Hence the prophet Daniel,” etc.

Because it is sticky.] Let us hear St Gregory here in the *Morals*, book XXI, chapter 2. “Once lust has occupied a person’s mind, it scarcely permits him to think good thoughts. Desires are sticky: from suggestion comes thought; from thought, affection; from affection, delight; from delight, consent; from consent, action; from action, habit; from [Col. 0518B] habit, despair; from despair, defense of sin; from its defense, boasting; from boasting, damnation.” V. reads “vicious” for “sticky.”

## CHAPTER CXXXVII

The measure of sins.] V.: “of crimes.” St Benedict, in his Rule, after the passage from Deuteronomy XXV, says: “According to the measure of the fault, the measure of discipline must be extended,” chapter 24. And Revelation XVIII: “As much as she lived in delights, give her so much torment and mourning.”

Likewise Augustine.] How finely he treats this matter in volume X, sermons 247, 243, and 244 *On Time*, where he rebukes adulterers for disfiguring God’s image in themselves. Therefore C. says in the margin regarding this: Ovid, at the beginning of the *Metamorphoses*:

> Though all other animals look down upon the earth,  
> he gave humankind an uplifted face.

In the fourth degree of affinity.] The Council of Trent, session 24, chapter 4, reduced the impediment of affinity arising from unlawful intercourse to the first and second degrees only, establishing that in more remote degrees a marriage thereafter contracted should not be dissolved. Pius V, to give greater liberty in marriage, declared in the extravangant *Ad Romanum* of 1566 that affinity of the third and fourth degrees neither dissolves nor impedes. Navarrus, chapter 22, no. 42. From these things one may infer, 547 as our author judges, that adultery is a graver crime than incest in the fourth degree. Concerning the children of adulterers, distinction 56, chapter *Si gens Anglorum*, says that they are neither steadfast in faith, nor constant in secular war, nor honourable among men, nor loved by God.

Proverbs, chapter VII.] Three, XIX.

In the legend of St Marcellus.] He was bishop of the city of Paris, as is clear from Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 89. His Life was written by Bishop Fortunatus; Surius has it in volume VI, on 1 November.

Had taken away.] Here I think the following material should be inserted, which I found in V. on an added leaf of parchment. Thus:

“Incest is a very unlawful and especially detestable intercourse of someone with a blood relative, with consanguinity understood broadly so as to include mother, maternal aunt, sister, female kinswoman, daughter, granddaughter, paternal aunt, and every blood relative up to the fourth degree; or with one related by affinity, such as a stepmother, sister-in-law, daughter-in-law, and so on. Incest is also the most detestable intercourse with Christ’s bride—that is, a nun—or with one anointed with sacred oil—that is, a queen—when she is known by someone other than her own husband, and conversely. To eradicate such a crime, the Apostle commanded that the Corinthian fornicator and incestuous man, who had known his father’s wife, his stepmother, be excommunicated, removed from the fellowship of the faithful, and handed over to Satan’s angels, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord (I Corinthians V). God deservedly often inflicts vengeance in the present life for this offence, as a foretaste of eternal punishment. Thus it is read in II Kings, chapter XIII, that Amnon, who had violated his sister, was slain by his brother Absalom. [Col. 0519A] Herod the Tetrarch also, defiled by this crime—namely, because he unlawfully used his brother’s wife—deserved to become a murderer, that is, to behead John; and afterwards he was banished into exile by the Roman emperor, where he and his wife died of hunger. God also often exercises present vengeance upon those who violate enclosed nuns, Christ’s brides, and other women consecrated to God. Some guilty of this crime often become mad and mute; some are struck with paralysis; others are overtaken by sudden death, and their souls are miserably tormented in hell.”

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII

And the pride of life.] “And superfluity of wine,” omitted by V. M., however, wished the addition, after “wine,” “or of anything whatever.” C. says at the side: “Gluttons” [in the manuscript *castrimargi*] “are like Esau, who sold his birthright for red lentils and lost his father’s blessing” (Genesis XXV). This had been omitted above at the end of chapter 135.

[Col. 0519B] Therefore concerning only those two sins, etc., a cry ascended.] Four sins are commonly reckoned as crying out to heaven: deliberate homicide; the sin of Sodom, of which this passage speaks; third, oppression of the poor; fourth, the wages of labourers fraudulently withheld. The third is treated in Exodus XXII, verses 22–23; the fourth in James V.4. But of the latter two it is not said so clearly that their cry ascended to the Lord from the earth.

The Lord is read to complain.] St Augustine treats this matter lucidly in volume X, sermon 247 *On Time*, and in 32, question 7: *Adulterii et Flagitia*.

In the field of Damascus.] I have read the same in the *Genealogy of Christ through the Levitical and Royal Tribe*, which I do not think has yet been seen by Trithemius, who calls it the *Breviary of the Bible*, written by Peter Berchorius. Its prologue begins: “Considering the length of Sacred History.” After the prologue the author begins the history thus: “Adam was formed in the field of Damascus,” etc., which I omit for brevity. It is an elegant work in which the succession of the Fathers is very finely outlined, their names being contained according to order and descent in circles carefully drawn and laboriously set out with compasses. The Abulensian also reports in his questions on Genesis I, question 22, that Adam was formed in the field of Damascus.

That they were to be androgynous.] This should be read thus, as I infer from St Augustine, volume III, book III, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter XXII; and I judge that these words were excerpted from there. Three has *Androgeos*. Androgeus was the son of Minos, king of Crete, concerning whom Virgil, book VI:

> At the gates there too hangs death, Androgeus’ punishment,  
> imposed upon the Cecropidae, etc.

Androgynes, or hermaphrodites, are called those who possess the sexual organs of both sexes. Such persons are reckoned among the legally disgraced and cannot be advocates. 3, question 7, *Infamis*, paragraph *In digestis*: *Infames*, etc.

A human androgyne.] Again, Three has *androgeo*.

Permits one to use.] V. and C.: “is permitted to use.”

As a man, they permit.] I would say here, as also in the following “permits,” that the reference is to the Church, of whom the preceding passage speaks. M.: “As a man they permit.” But what if the Church, says M.’s margin, has been deceived concerning the proximity of the sex and cannot remain continent?

What is abhorred by God.] This reading should be tolerated. For *detestor* is sometimes used passively, as in Horace, book I, *Odes*: “Wars abhorred by mothers.” M.: “What he so greatly abhors.”

Romans, chapter I.] Three, CIV and V.

Epistle of Jude.] Three, chapter II; and M. read *exfornicante* instead of *exfornicatae*, as in the biblical text. By that compound word he intended to signify fornication committed outside and beyond the order of nature.

Sardanapalus.] The proverb concerning him is: “More effeminate than Sardanapalus.” Tertullian, volume I, *On the Pallium*, chapter 4, no. 79; Justin, book I, says that he was more corrupt than a woman.

In crushing.] Not “In converting,” as V has in the text and C in the margin.

For, says St. Jerome, “what tender minds have absorbed is not easily uprooted.” These bonds are: first, the tickling of pleasure; second, consent; third, the deed; fourth, the depth of evils, or abyss of habit. For testimony concerning this sticky evil, consult St. Augustine, vol. X, Sermon 44, *On the Words of the Lord*, chapter 6.

Concerning Gregory’s monk.] This history is found in his Life. See Surius, vol. II; also St. Augustine, Sermon 62, *To the Brothers in the Desert*, or 12, question 1, “I do not wish.”

Even a layman is sacrilegious.] 17, question 4, “Whoever”; and 12, question 2, “Estates.”

He has gold coins.] How beautifully St. Jerome describes such people in his letter to Heliodorus, beginning “Great subjects”: “Let monks be richer than they were as secular men; let them possess under the poor Christ the riches which they possessed under the wealthy devil; let the Church sigh over those whom the world formerly possessed as beggars, now rich.”

Pittances.] Or *pitantiae*. Caesarius frequently uses this word for a larger portion of wine or a more lavish dish.

Tobias the exile.] C: “If Tobias is hungry, though he could have had possessions of his own.” The rest is lacking.

Certain religious.] Besides St. Paul’s statement, 2 Timothy 2, “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs,” I shall adduce another point from Boniface’s decrees, by which he determines that monks may hear confessions: “For Blessed Benedict, the bountiful instructor of monks, was in no manner an interdictor of this matter; rather, he decreed only that they were to be free from secular business.” And 16, question 1, “Monks,” reads thus: “Let no monk become an undertaker or executor of business before a secular court, except where the usefulness of the monastery requires it, and then only by command of his abbot.”

Depositaries.] C: “Depositories.” Their role is to receive money as security, a thing especially unbecoming to a monk. St. Jerome, to Paulinus, *On the Instruction of a Monk*, says: “Whomever you find always or frequently speaking to you of money, regard as a businessman rather than a monk,” 16, question 1, “If you desire.” See also St. Jerome’s rule, under the title *On Poverty*.

For this man, by many [means].] M omits this parenthesis.

Taken away.] Immediately after this C reads: “Likewise Leviticus 81,” that is, chapter 24, where restitution is discussed.

A certain prior to a certain [person].] C: “The prior of M. D., wishing to do [something].”

Likewise, the hermit.] From the book called *Lives of the Fathers*.

Likewise Jerome.] In the rule, *On Poverty*. You will also find similar statements in the Rule of Monks, “On Simony in Receiving Sisters.”

So much in Martin.] From the Life written by Severus Sulpicius.

As St. Benedict says.] Chapter 49 of his Rule.

Likewise Jerome.] In the letter to the monk Heliodorus, as I said above at chapter 21.

[Col. 0527]

# THE ABBREVIATED WORD, SECOND TEXT: FROM CHAPTER SIXTY-SIX THROUGH EIGHTY

> [Note: Since the Marchian manuscript differed from the other two in an almost continuous variation of readings, namely from chapter 66 through chapter 80, we transcribed it word for word, as they say, and have deliberately inserted the transcription here.]

## CHAPTER LXVI. On Respect of Persons

[Col. 0527B]

And it must be known that nothing more offends this threefold office of a prelate than respect of persons, “which is not with God,” as the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans (chapter 2). On this passage Augustine [in fact Ambrose] says: “There would be respect of persons with the Lord if, because of the dignity of their fathers, He had received the Jews, and because of the unworthiness of their fathers had despised the Gentiles.” See the notes to chapter 66. Peter says the same in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 10), when he was commanded to go to Cornelius: “Now in truth I have learned that God is not a respecter of persons; but in every nation, whoever fears God is acceptable to Him.”

It must be understood, however, that respect of persons is one thing, and honorific regard another. Honorific regard is reverence shown to someone in consideration of the rank and dignity of the person to whom reverence is shown and of the person who shows it. But the abuse of this reverence is respect of persons. This is not with God.

Note that when reverence is not shown to one to whom it is due, there is rejection of a person; but when it is shown to one to whom it is not due, there is properly respect of a person. Thus respect of a person, rejection of persons, and honorific regard for persons are distinct. It should therefore be noted that, with respect to this kind of honorific regard, some causes are wholly lawful and honorable; some are less honorable; some are intermediate, neither wholly lawful nor wholly unlawful; and some are wholly unlawful.

The causes wholly lawful and honorable are those in which reverence is shown to someone because of the holiness of his religious life; and this alone is with God. Less honorable are those in which reverence is shown to a prelate, prince, son of a nobleman, or learned man.
