Intermediate—neither wholly lawful nor wholly unlawful—are those in which reverence is shown to someone out of a particular association or indiscriminate goodwill; for example, when needy poor persons are passed over and persons not in need are received as guests. Wholly unlawful are those in which reverence is shown to someone because of some shameful quality or solely for money, so that one may say:

> O money, money, to you he gives honor here;  
> you are his brothers.  
> —Juvenal, *Satire* 5

The Lord utterly rejects this. Of this James says in the Catholic Epistle (chapter 2): “My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with respect of persons. For if a man wearing a gold ring comes into your presence, and you say to him, ‘Sit here comfortably’; but if a poor man comes in dirty clothing, and you say to him, ‘Stand there,’ have you not become a respecter of persons? Are you not a judge of wicked thoughts?”

Augustine says there—according to a second recension from Bede, who drew his material from Augustine—that, if this is applied to ecclesiastical offices, it is no light sin. For who could bear it if, when an upright and more learned poor man were rejected, a rich man were elevated to an ecclesiastical dignity? Likewise, if this is said of daily grants—other manuscripts have “consents”—who does not sin here? Yet he does not sin unless he judges within himself that, if a man is richer, he is therefore better.

Against respect of persons, the Lord says through Moses in Deuteronomy (chapter 1): “Hear all alike, and judge what is just. You shall not respect the person of a man, for judgment belongs to the Lord.” Therefore a human being who imitates God ought not to respect the person of a man. And Job says (chapter 32): “I will not respect the person of a man, nor will I make a man equal to the Lord. For I do not know how long I shall endure, and when my Savior may come to take away my spirit.” As though to say: If I respected the person of a man, that would be to make a man equal to the Lord.

And Ecclesiasticus says (chapter 35): “You shall not respect the person of a poor man,” that is, against the poor man, “and you shall hear the supplication of the injured.” And the Catholic Epistle of Jude says (verse 16): “Certain men are garrulous and murmurers, admiring persons for the sake of gain,” that is, praising them.

After adducing authorities against respect of persons, let us introduce examples. We read that Phinehas pierced through the genitals, with his dagger, a Jew having intercourse with a Midianite woman, although he knew that the man was a leader in the tribe of Simeon and she the daughter of a most noble prince of the Midianites (Num. 25). And in this deed he pleased the Lord, “and the shaking ceased” (Ps. 105). And the Lord said to Moses: “Hang the leaders on the gallows, that my wrath may be turned away from them” (Num. 25). Behold: not even leaders are to be spared in wickedness.

Moses himself, hearing that the people had sinned by making a molten calf, said: “Let him who belongs to the Lord gird himself with the sword beside me.” And, passing through the midst of the camp, he spared none who had participated in that crime; and Moses said: “Today you have consecrated your hands to the Lord, for you did not spare brother, father, or mother in the crime” (Exod. 32). And the Gloss says there: that man is to be chosen priest and Levite “who says to father and mother, ‘I do not know you’” (Deut. 33).

And it is written of the Lord that He was unwilling to turn aside to the house of the royal official (John 4), lest He should seem to honor riches. Again: in the Book of Kings we read that Jonathan, being hungry as he went, found honey and ate it, and his eyes were brightened and he pursued the enemies more vigorously (1 Sam. 14). When his father Saul heard that he had acted contrary to his command, he wished to kill him. He would have done so had not the people snatched him from his hands. Behold how paternal affection was unwilling to spare a son in transgressing a command.

And here you have an argument that a ruler ought not do anything without the consent of the people, nor a prelate without the counsel of the clergy. Again, on the aforementioned words, “Moses passed through the midst of the camp” (Exod. 32), Gregory says (*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, Admonition 26): “To pass through the midst of the camp is to live in the Church of the Lord with impartiality: to rebuke, preach, and judge, so that one rests in no one’s favor, and so that he spares no one from the sword of sentence on account of blood relationship or private affection. And if he is a man of God, girded by divine love to avenge sins, it is evident that he is not a man of God who refuses to avenge the sins of others.”

Nevertheless, action against respect of persons must be moderated. For some, while avoiding respect of persons, fall into the vice of a certain ingratitude and of a sober lack of civility, so that it may truly be said:

> While fools avoid vices, they rush into the opposite ones;  
> [lacuna]  
> but the blessed have held the mean.  
> —Horace, *Satires* I

For the strictest law is the greatest injustice (Cicero, *On Duties* I). Hence it is also said elsewhere: “There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness” (Eccles. 7); and elsewhere: “He who squeezes too hard draws blood” (Prov. 30); and elsewhere: “Do not turn aside, either to the right or to the left” (Deut. 17)—to the right through excessive relaxation of justice, to the left through excessive severity of the same. Hence the poet:

> There is a measure in things; there are, in short, fixed limits,  
> within and beyond which the right cannot stand.  
> —Horace, *Satires* I.1

For it is a fault to pursue every fault to the utmost.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On Moderation in Laughter

To the foregoing remarks against lack of composure, we must add something concerning moderation, especially in laughter, by which a wise person is readily recognized. Hence Ecclesiasticus says (chapter 25): “A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will laugh quietly.” And St. Bernard says of a most devout abbot, St. Malachy, that for fourteen years he did not laugh so that his teeth could be seen; but, for the sake of those present, he made his face cheerful. Yet, if we recall correctly, he did not permit himself full laughter.

Let us therefore pursue cheerfulness devoid of wantonness, and, to express it in a single phrase, let us rejoice according to the countenance of the saints (Judith 16). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke 6). Thus He Himself is recorded to have wept three times: at the raising of Lazarus (John 11), over the city (Luke 19), and in prayer, as is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews (chapter 5); but He is never recorded as having laughed. This raises a question. For He assumed our defects—those which it befitted Him to assume—and He truly had inner laughter, namely joy of mind; therefore it appears that He had outer laughter also, which He could have had, although it is not recorded.

It should be noted that, in order to maintain the moderation and temperance just mentioned, singularity must especially be avoided. There is a twofold singularity, evil and good. Let us speak first of the evil kind, so that, when the vice has been expelled, virtue may shine forth more clearly.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On Evil Singularity

Concerning evil singularity, the philosopher says: “Every singularity produces a mark.” He who does not avoid it is suspect, or suspicious. Thus he marks himself or signifies something. See the note to chapter 68. Perhaps this is why it was said: “Let him taste this little thing.” Avoiding this singularity, the Apostle said: “I became all things to all people” (1 Cor. 9). Therefore he also “shaved himself at Cenchreae” (Acts 18), and circumcised Timothy, that he might conform him to the Jews (Acts 16).

Thus Augustine says (Letters 86 and 110): “You ought to live according to the custom of your country and of the Church in which you must live. For a part that does not fit its body is ugly.” Hence perhaps it was said: “Woe to him who is alone, for if he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Eccles. 4): alone, that is, one who through a kind of presumption invents a new manner of life. Such a person is “a solitary wild beast which grazes upon the vineyard” (Ps. 79), that is, destroys and kills his own soul.

And Seneca says in his fifth letter to Lucilius: “I warn you not to do, in the manner of those who wish not to make progress but to be noticed, anything remarkable in your dress or way of life. Avoid rough clothing, uncut hair, a rather neglected beard, a proclaimed hatred of silver, a bed placed upon the ground, and whatever else follows an ambitiously perverse path. The very name of philosophy, even if practiced modestly, is sufficiently unpopular. Let everything within be different; let our outward appearance accord with the people. Let the toga neither shine nor yet be dirty. Let us not think that having no gold or silver is a mark of frugality. Let us aim to follow a better life than the crowd’s, but not a contrary one. Otherwise we drive away and turn aside from ourselves those whom we wish to reform. We also bring it about that our people are unwilling to imitate anything, while they fear that everything must be imitated.

“This is the first thing philosophy imparts: a more common feeling, humanity, and fellowship; dissimilarity will separate us from this profession. Let us see that the things by which we wish to gain admiration are not ridiculous and hateful. Our purpose is to live according to nature. To torture one’s body, hate easy cleanliness, seek filthiness, and use foods not merely cheap but raw and disgusting—this is contrary to nature. For just as desiring delicate things belongs to luxury, so avoiding unusual things that can be procured without great expense belongs to madness. Philosophy demands frugality, not punishment. This balance pleases it. Let our life be tempered between good customs and public ones; let all admire our life but not recognize it. Let us do the same things as others. There will be nothing between us and them. Whoever looks more closely will know that we differ greatly from the crowd. Whoever enters our house should admire us rather than our furnishings. Great is the person who uses earthenware as he uses silver; nor is he less great who uses silver as he uses earthenware. For it belongs to a weak person not to be able to endure riches.”

## CHAPTERS LXIX–LXXII. On Good Singularity

We must now speak of good singularity, which is more properly called solitude. Of this Anna [read: Sarah], daughter of Raguel, says, as is read in Tobit (chapter 3): “I have never mingled with those who play, nor have I made myself a participant with those who walk in vanity.” Of this the Wise Man says: “Rare in public, honorable at home.” Of this Jeremiah says (chapter 3): “I sat solitary and was silent.” And Seneca says in his letter to Lucilius: “What do you ask should especially be avoided? A crowd. You do not yet safely entrust yourself to it.”

“I certainly confess my weakness: I never return with the morals that I brought out. The company of many is hostile. What do you think I mean? I return more avaricious, more ambitious, more luxurious—indeed more cruel and inhuman—whenever I have been among people. A tender spirit, not yet firmly holding to the right, must be withdrawn from the crowd; it easily passes over to the many. A dissimilar multitude could have shaken Socrates’, Cato’s, and Laelius’s integrity. One example of avarice and luxury does much harm. A luxurious table-companion [perhaps *convictor*, ‘table-companion,’ as Seneca and other copies have] gradually weakens and softens one; a wealthy neighbor excites desire; a malicious companion rubs his rust upon one of bright and simple mind. What do you think happens when you approach such customs? You must either imitate or hate those customs upon which the multitude has made an assault. But both must be avoided: lest you become like bad people because they are many, or become an enemy to many because they are unlike you.

“Retire into yourself as much as you can. Associate with those who can make you better. Admit those whom you can make better. These things occur mutually: while people teach, they learn.”

This solitude depends especially upon good company. Hence Cato says (Book I): “Walk with the good.” Elsewhere it is said: “Character is formed from companionship.” And the Apostle says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). And the philosopher says—Seneca, Letter 19—“You should rather consider with whom you eat than what you eat.” And the poet says:

> The greatest virtue of a ruler is to know his own people.  
> —Martial, Book VIII, Epigram 15

St. Thomas of Canterbury approved this verse above many other verses. This especially pertains to prelates of the Church: they should have such chamberlains and table-companions that they may not seem to approve the life of those with whom they associate. Thus Abraham, when commanded to circumcise his household, immediately circumcised all his home-born servants, himself, and his whole household (Gen. 17). Therefore every Christian ought spiritually to circumcise his household, so that no one in his house may be disordered.

Likewise Solomon: “He who walks with the wise is wise; the friend of fools becomes like them” (Prov. 13). Hence a certain wise man says: “Similarity of character produces fellowship, and kindred pursuits are easily joined.” The Psalms also frequently speak of fleeing evil association and acquiring good association. Thus, in the first psalm: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners” (Ps. 17). And elsewhere: “With the holy you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen you will be chosen; and with the perverse you will be perverted” (ibid.).

For it is difficult to touch pitch and not be defiled by it (Ecclus. 13). Therefore a certain wise man says that Scripture compares good rulers who have wicked subordinates to Scyllas and Harpies. Scylla has a human face, but is described as girded with dogs’ heads. The Harpies have a maiden’s face but most rapacious claws. Similarly, rulers are good outwardly, but their ministers are evil. At the scent of prey, Scyllas prepare themselves for plunder.

Likewise, it should be noted that good companionship is most greatly impeded by excessive carnal affection. Against this we have especially examples from the Lord himself, the teacher of all good things. For when he was preaching, someone from the crowd said to him: “Master, behold, your brothers and sisters are waiting for you outside” (Matt. 12). And looking at his disciples, he said: “These are my brothers.” And, to conclude generally, he added: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and mother, and sister” (Luke 2). As though he said: Spiritual persons must always be preferred to carnal ones.

Likewise, it is read of him that, when he was twelve years old, he remained in Jerusalem. When he was not found among relatives, friends, and acquaintances, after three days his mother returned to Jerusalem and found him in the midst of the teachers, questioning them and answering them. And his mother said to him: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have been looking for you in sorrow.” But he said: “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in those things which are my Father’s?” (ibid.). That is: I always prefer spiritual things to carnal things.

He says the same thing at the wedding, when the wine of the master of the feast had failed, to his mother inviting him to perform a miracle: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John 2). Certainly, there was much between her and him, since he loved her most affectionately. Hence from the cross he said to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (John 19). But in these words—“What is there between me and you?”—he provided us with a greater example of preferring spiritual to carnal things: so that every prelate, and even a lesser priest, in every spiritual benefit may say to father and mother: “What is there between me and you, mother? What is there between me and you, father?” We are priests according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109), who is read as having had neither father nor mother. And he is a figure of Christ and of ourselves, who ought not to have father or mother in spiritual matters, but to say to them: “I am a priest according to the order of Melchizedek; I do not know you.”

Hence it is said (Gloss on chapter 25): “Let that man be chosen priest and Levite who says to father and mother: ‘I do not know you’” (Deut. 33). Thus under the Law a priest was forbidden to attend the funerals even of dead parents, lest he contract some impurity (Lev. 21); indeed, a priest may not withdraw from holy things. Hence the Lord said to the man wishing to bury his father: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but go and preach the kingdom of God” (Matt. 8).

On this saying Jerome states: “For Christ’s love, he ought to leave one unburied; and for his love, he ought to leave no one unburied”—that is, according to place and time. Nevertheless, it is brutish to hate one’s parents.

Thus the passage concerning the Philistines should be noted. They captured the ark of the Lord, and because of it were punished in their hinder parts. Seeing this, they placed the ark upon a new cart and yoked to the cart two cows that had calved (1 Sam. 6), that is, had been delivered of offspring. For *fetus* or *feta* is a word of many meanings [*polysenium*, that is, of varied signification]: it denotes both one having offspring and one delivered of offspring. Hence the two cows themselves had calves shut up at home. And they brought the ark of the Lord to Beth-shemesh, lowing after their calves but not turning their horns from the straight path. Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.” Therefore, whoever wishes to bring the ark of the Lord to Beth-shemesh—that is, to attain eternal life through receiving Christ’s body—must be inwardly *fetus*, fruitful, through good intention, and outwardly through good work.

For Gregory says (Homily 37 on the Gospels): “The cows lowed after their calves, but did not turn their horns from the straight way. So also the saints low after their parents in compassion, but do not turn their horns from the straight way through neglect of good work.” Therefore let us so feel compassion for parents that we do not omit good works on their account. Let us not be like Lot’s wife, who, looking back toward Sodom, was turned into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19).

Likewise Jerome, on Leviticus, says (chapter 21): “The high priest ought not to attend the funerals of the dead, even of rulers, lest he be polluted by the touch or sight of the dead.” But our high priest, Christ, raised Lazarus (John 11); and many monks and clerics today see bodies, and dine and feast with the body—that is, by seeing it.

Likewise, on that passage of Matthew (chapter 17) concerning the coin in the fish’s mouth, which the Lord paid as tribute for himself and Peter, the Gloss says: “Wonderful is the Lord’s poverty, which had nothing from which to pay the tribute.” Augustine objects here: “Did the Lord not have the money that Judas carried?” He certainly did; but he regarded it as wrong to divert to his own uses what belonged to the poor. This is directed against prelates who spend the patrimony of the Crucified One—which properly belongs to the poor—on their own uses.

Likewise: Against excessive affection for the flesh is what is read in the book of Judges (chapter 9). There it is read that Abimelech, Gideon’s son by a concubine, after Gideon’s death went to Shechem to his mother’s relatives. They made him king; and with their assistance he killed Gideon’s seventy sons, his brothers. He also killed the Shechemites, his relatives, who had made him king. Behold: we ought to kill carnal affections.

We should also be warned by the example of brute animals not to love friends excessively. They love their young while they are small and unable to provide for themselves; once they have grown somewhat larger, they immediately cast them off and take no care of them. Similarly, while our parents cannot provide for themselves, we ought to support them—not unto superfluity, but unto necessity. But if they can provide for themselves, we need not concern ourselves with them.

Likewise, Abraham was told: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12). And the Psalm says: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44). As though it said: You could not hear unless you forgot your father’s house.

Likewise, prelates ought to be instructed by the example of the Templars not to have their friends as close associates. For the Templars never have a blood relative serving them, lest they distribute to him the brothers’ common goods.

And especially what Jerome said in his letter to Heliodorus (*On the Praise of the Solitary Life*) makes against carnal affection. For he says:

> Hear the king’s decree: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11). Remember the day of your enlistment, when, buried with Christ in baptism, you swore in the words of the sacrament that for his name you would spare neither father nor mother. Behold, your adversary is striving to kill Christ in your breast. Behold, the military bounty which you received when about to serve: the hostile camp longs for it. Though a little grandson hang from your neck; though your mother, with dishevelled hair and torn garments, display the breasts with which she nourished you; though your father lie upon the threshold—go on over your father’s body; with dry eyes fly to the banner of the cross. The only kind of piety in this matter is to be cruel.
>
> A day will later come when you return victorious to your homeland, when, crowned, you walk through the heavenly Jerusalem. We do not have breasts of iron, nor savage hearts; Hyrcanian tigresses did not nurse us from rock. We too have passed through such things. Now a widowed sister clings to your arms with blandishments; now the household slaves with whom you grew up say: “To whose service do you leave us?” Now your former nurse, now an old woman, and your foster-father—second only to your natural father in affection—cry out: “Wait a little, and bury one who is about to die.” Perhaps your mother too, with the skin of her limbs grown slack, her brow furrowed with wrinkles, recalling her old breast, may seek to give you milk. Let grammarians say, if they wish (Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.59):
>
> > Upon you the whole household leans and rests.
>
> The love of Christ and fear of Gehenna easily break these bonds. Yet Scripture commands obedience to parents (Exod. 70 [an erroneous reference]). But whoever loves them above Christ loses his soul (Matt. 16). The enemy holds a sword to kill me, and shall I think of my mother’s tears? For my father’s sake shall I desert Christ’s military service, to whom I do not owe burial on Christ’s account—though on his account I owe it even to all others?
>
> Peter, timidly counselling the Lord who was about to suffer, became a stumbling-block. To brothers who sought to hold him back from going to Jerusalem, Paul replied: “What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 21). This battering-ram of piety, by which faith is shaken, must be blunted by the sword-point of the Gospel. “My mother and my brothers are” (Matt. 12) whoever support me as I fight for his name. If they do not believe, let the dead bury their own dead (Matt. 8). You are mistaken, brother—you are mistaken—if you think that a Christian never suffers persecution. And you are attacked most of all when you do not know that you are being attacked.

Let these things suffice against carnal affection (see notes on chapter 72).

We have spoken above about good singularity; to it must be added good solitude. But solitude is twofold: that of monks and that of anchorites. The former is in the cloister, the latter in the wilderness. The former is safer, the latter more perfect. Therefore Saint Benedict, in the Rule for Monks (chapter 1), says that a monk well tested in the cloister may pass into the wilderness.

This life is greatly commendable. In it Jerome subdued his flesh for four years. Inviting a fellow student to this life, he says (letter to Heliodorus, *On the Solitary Life*):

> O wilderness flowering with Christ’s flowers! O solitude in which are born those stones from which the city of the great King is built in the Apocalypse (chapter 21)! O desert enjoying God more intimately! What are you doing, brother, in the world—you who are greater than the world? How long will the shadows of roofs oppress you? How long will the stench [perhaps *nitor*, “brightness,” but likely *nidor*, “stench”] of smoky cities confine you? Believe me: I know not what greater light I behold in the wilderness.
>
> It delights me, casting off the burden of the flesh, to fly to the pure brightness of the ether. Do you fear poverty? Yet Christ calls the poor blessed (Matt. 5). Are you frightened by labour? No athlete is crowned without sweat. Do you think about food? Faith does not fear hunger. Do you fear to cast limbs worn by fasting upon bare ground? Yet the Lord lies with you. Does the uncultivated hair of your filthy head trouble you? Yet Christ is your head. Does the boundless expanse of the desert terrify you? Then walk in paradise with your mind. Whenever you ascend there, you are not in the wilderness. Does your rough skin, unsoftened by baths, trouble you? Yet he who has once been washed in Christ has no need to be washed again. And, that you may hear the Apostle answering all these things in brief: “The sufferings of this present world are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).
>
> You are a delicate soldier, my dearest, if you wish to rejoice with the world and afterwards reign with Christ. We shall point out to you, so that, if you do not know, you may learn; but if you have known, you may rejoice with us. Your Bonosus—indeed mine, and, more truly, ours—already climbs the prophetic ladder of Jacob’s dream (Gen. 28), bears the cross (Matt. 16), does not look back (Luke 9), sows in tears and shall reap in joy (Ps. 125). And, in the mystery of Moses, he raises the serpent in the wilderness (Num. 21).
>
> Behold, my boy, educated with us in the honourable pursuits of the world, who had wealth in abundance and outstanding rank among his peers, has despised mother, sisters, and his brother most dear to him; he walks, like a new settler of Paradise, upon an island wrecked by the sounding sea, whose harsh cliffs, bare rocks, and solitude inspire terror. There is no farmer there, no monk, not even a child. Onesimus, whom he enjoyed as a brother in the world, clings to his side as companion in so great a wilderness. Alone for you—or rather, not alone, with Christ as companion—he sees the glory of God which the apostles would not see except in the wilderness. He does not indeed look upon towered cities, but has enrolled his name in the register of the new city. Are his limbs made hideous by a rough sackcloth? Yet thus he will better be caught up to meet Christ in the air (1 Thess. 4). Does he enjoy no south wind from the Euripus? Yet from the Lord’s side he drinks the water of life.

Brother, in the wilderness, sifted bread and vegetables watered by our own hands, milk—the rustic luxury—provide cheap indeed but innocent foods (letter to Marcella, beginning *Ambrosius*). Living thus, sleep will not call us away from prayer, nor fullness from reading. If it is hot, the shade of a secluded tree will provide shelter. If it is autumn, the temperateness of the air itself and leaves spread upon the ground show a resting-place. In spring, the field is painted with flowers, and amid the chattering birds psalms will be sung more sweetly. If there is cold and winter snow, I shall not buy firewood: I shall keep watch and sleep warmly.

Let Rome keep its tumults, let the arena rage, the circus go mad, and the theatres indulge in excess. But for us it is good to cleave to God and to place our hope in the Lord (Ps. 7), so that, when we have exchanged this poverty for the kingdoms of heaven, we may burst into the words: “For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (ibid.). That is: when we find such great things in our homeland, we shall grieve that we sought petty and perishable things upon earth.

The lives of all holy anchorites are likewise commended. We are confident that the distinctive purpose of anchorites has not been separated from the solemnity of this day: they dwelt throughout the various places of the wilderness, in caves and the small huts of cells, content with scant food. Some had beasts as companions; others were supplied by birds. Hoping for the riches or delights of food, they trampled underfoot worldly luxury, did not love temporal praise, fled human eyes, grew accustomed to the speech of angels, and shone with many virtues; and the rest that is read there.

The Lord seems to have consecrated this life when, after casting out the tempter, he remained alone in the wilderness: “And he was with the beasts, and angels ministered to him” (Matt. 4). Some say that this life began with John the Baptist, who from his tender years sought the caves of the desert. Hence the Carthusian order solemnly celebrates his feast as that of its patron. Others say that it began with Elijah; others, with the Rechabites.

Martin desired this life when he was twelve years old (see notes on chapter 72). He would have fulfilled that desire had not weakness of body and age hindered him. Saint Remigius of Rheims commended this life: from boyhood he entered a reclusion, and from reclusion was chosen bishop.

This solitary life should especially be desired for two reasons: to avoid envy and to flee participation in sin. For where many are in a cenobium, one envies another because of precedence or something of the kind. And when many assent in chapter to something less lawful, all the others seem to have sinned in this. For to consent is not to object when one can do so. The sin of the whole body is dispersed among individuals, and one person’s sin redounds upon many. Hence the Apostle says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5).

Thus they wrongly invoke the common proverb of Lucan: “What is sinned by many goes unpunished.” It may indeed go unpunished in the world, but not with God; for they will not sin less because they sin with more people, nor burn less because they burn with more people.

This anchoritic life is more perfect than the cenobitic life. But between these two lives, the Carthusian life is safer [alternatively, Caturcensian]: they possess everything in number, weight, and measure—namely, a fixed number of livestock, fields, and persons. The Lord consecrated it when, tempted by the devil, he remained in the wilderness and angels ministered to him (Matt. 4). The Baptist likewise chose this life, remaining in seclusion and sustained by locusts and wild honey. Of him someone said: “Horns-nakes and vipers dare not touch him, yet a harlot and a dancer touch, without reverence, that head worthy of all reverence.”

The Carthusians have him as patron and advocate. They each lead an eremitic life in individual cells. Yet they stand midway between anchorites, who retain little or no property for themselves, and cenobites, who possess much in the person of the poor and live in common. The Carthusians, however, hold everything in common, in number, weight, and measure: thirteen persons, and likewise lay brothers, livestock, fields, books, and such things, desiring to imitate the Lord, who made all things in number, weight, and measure.

Some say this life began with the Lord’s forerunner, others with Elijah, others with Jonadab or the Rechabites, who drank neither wine nor strong drink (Jer. 35). Martin greatly desired this life when he was twelve years old, but weakness of age and constitution hindered his purpose. Once he had attained the episcopate, however, he chose a desert place in which to devote himself to prayer; and there is now the abbey of Marmoutier. Yet he performed more miracles before becoming bishop than after. That magnificent raiser of three dead persons raised two before, but one after.

Blessed Germanus likewise, while bishop, chose a solitary place in which, secluded, he conversed with God and his angels. Likewise Blessed Remigius of Rheims, son of the count of Laon, entered reclusion, but was carried off from it to become archbishop.

The prophet Jeremiah invites us to this desert solitude: “Flee, save your souls, and you shall be like tamarisks in the wilderness; and rise up, go up from Kedar. Flee from the midst of the habitation” (Jer. 48)—that is, depart vigorously; “sit in the deep places, you inhabitants of Hazor,” which is interpreted “arrow,” and by which the world is understood, since it shoots and wounds everyone with vices. “Withdraw from the midst of Babylon, and go out from the land of the Chaldeans, and be like kids before the flocks.” And elsewhere: “I sat and kept silence” (Lam. 3). And elsewhere: “Wait in silence for the saving help of your God” (ibid.).

This life is more perfect than the fellowship of cenobites, because those who dwell in it have neither gates nor bars. The others, however, join field to field and possess property, however sparingly, for their own use; yet these are provocations to plundering critics. Nor is every communal order wholly commendable in which some cannot be saved—or at least not easily—as converts.

## Chapter 73. On light involvement in sin

Merchants, whose sin is dispersed through the whole flock, as is found in the case of Achan [alternatively, Achor] and of the Corinthian fornicator; and the sin of several, or of the whole multitude, is conveyed to individuals, as the crucifixion by the Jews was conveyed to the people of Jerusalem. Hence: “Rescue the poor and needy; deliver him from the hand of the sinner” (Ps. 81).

Likewise: It is remarkable that sin or fault is not felt in a plurality, though it is very perceptible in an individual. The sin of many contaminates individuals; likewise, the sins or faults of individuals affect all, because:

> Though a thousand take, nothing is thereby diminished  
> (see note on chapter 73): all possess the whole.

Everyone who can do so ought to resist, object, or prevent it. Moreover, one who excuses and exempts himself from the sin or fault of the multitude is like Pilate, who, having an unclean conscience, washed his hands, saying: “I am innocent and free from the blood of this just man” (Matt. 27); or like the first parent, who cast back his sin upon the Lord, saying: “Lord, the woman whom you gave me gave me the fruit, and I ate.” And Eve said: “The serpent deceived me” (Gen. 3).

Likewise: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5). They will not burn less because they burn with more people, but more.

And that we may be instructed by some example in this matter: a certain man had a scrupulous conscience because he presided over many to whom he was of no benefit; he held many churches and many prebends, reaping where he had not sown, eating and drinking where he had not laboured, withholding milk and wool, taking no care, but assigning them to hired servants for years (Matt. 25). While trying to avoid Scylla, he fell into Charybdis: he entered a cenobium of regular canons and found that, in proportion to the number of persons, the cenobium possessed a number of churches and prebends. Since he was not permitted to leave, he grieved that he had found in a community the condition he had fled in private life.

What, then, ought he to do, when he has no free exit, nor freedom to object, as in secular chapters? Let whoever can solve this solve it.

But what Lucan says—“What is sinned by many goes unpunished”—is not true. Though it may be left unpunished by man, it is not left unpunished by God; for either God or man punishes sin.

Returning to solitude, we say that certain perfect persons, namely contemplatives, ought to pursue solitude of place and of time [alternatively, “of the breast,” i.e. inward solitude]. But certain other perfect persons, namely active persons and preachers, ought now to follow the crowd, because a tender mind is not to be entrusted to wine and beauty. Nor is it safe to devote oneself to solitude because of unlawful and very evil thoughts, which then especially creep in.

But you who are weak and imperfect “will go safest in the middle” (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 2.136): so that you are neither in a crowd nor in solitude, but among a few good people whom you have chosen, from whom you can receive instruction and whom, in turn, you can instruct.

But concerning the perfect person who can safely be entrusted to himself, Seneca says (Letter 10): “I change my opinion: flee the multitude, flee the few, flee even one person. I have no one with whom I would wish you to associate, but I dare to entrust you to yourself.” Socrates [Crates], seeing a young man walking privately, asked what he was doing there alone. “I am talking with myself,” he said. Socrates [the same passage attributes this to Crates] said: “Take care, I beg you, and pay close attention not to be talking with a bad man.”

We are accustomed to guard a grieving or fearful person lest he misuse solitude. For there is no one among the imprudent who ought to be left to himself. Then they devise evil counsels; then they construct future dangers either for others or for themselves; then they arrange improper desires; then whatever fear or shame concealed [perhaps “in the mind,” as Seneca has it] he exposes with less restraint; then he sharpens boldness, excites lust, and stirs anger. Finally—this being the one advantage boldness [Seneca: solitude] has—he entrusts nothing to anyone, has no informer or judge, spares the fool [Seneca: “sets him down”], and betrays himself. I find no one with whom I would rather have you be than with yourself. Live thus with people, as though God sees; speak thus with God, as though people hear.

It should be noted that Blessed Thomas of Canterbury instructed his household for this reason, saying: “Who would lie in his bed unless he wished to sleep or were hindered by sickness?”

Likewise Seneca (Letter 11): “A good man should be chosen for us and always kept before our eyes, that we may live as though he watched us and do all things as though he saw us. Let us appoint for ourselves a guardian and tutor. For a great part of sins is removed if a witness stands beside the sinner. Let the mind have someone whom it reveres, by whose authority it makes even its private life more sacred. Happy is he whom such a person corrects not only in action when present, but even in thought. Happy is he who can so revere someone that he composes and orders himself even at that person’s memory. Whoever can so revere someone will soon himself be worthy of reverence. Choose Cato for yourself; if he seems too stern, choose a man of gentler disposition—Laelius. Choose the one whose life and speech please you; keeping before you his spirit and countenance [the text is uncertain: “but you will have made before yourself also his countenance”], always set him before yourself as either an example or a guardian. We need, I say, someone to whom our character may raise itself; unless by a rule you will not correct what is crooked, unless by a rule you will not straighten what is bent.”

You, prelate, always choose Paul for yourself. But if he seems too strict, choose the gentler Nicholas or Augustine.

## Chapter 74. That sin is contracted on a slight occasion

Likewise, we must return to what was said above: that one person’s sin redounds upon the multitude, and the multitude’s sin upon individuals. The common saying is untrue: “Let all sins be turned upon the abbot,” so that he may be like the scapegoat which carries or bears away all the sins or faults of people outside the camp [the text perhaps reads *auferat*, “carry away,” rather than *afferat*, “bring”].

That someone may contract sin or fault easily, on a slight occasion, is shown by David in chapter 76, when Saul ordered Doeg the Edomite at Nob—after the executioners or officers refused to attack the priests of the Lord—to fall upon the eighty-five wearers of the ephod. He slaughtered them all because they had given David, whom Saul pursued, the loaves of offering and Goliath’s sword. Abiathar alone escaped this slaughter and fled to David. When David heard of the slaughter brought about because of him, he said: “I am guilty concerning all the lives of your father’s house” (1 Sam. 22), and of the others.

Therefore David says that he was saved from murdering Nabal, a foolish man who refused to send him in the camp the blessing due to the king. Nabal’s wife Abigail persuaded him not to kill the foolish man, lest, if he shed innocent blood, this very thing should always come upon him as a groan and scruple of heart (1 Sam. 25).

Then, thirsty in the army, he said: “O that someone would give me a drink of water from the cistern that is in Bethlehem!” Therefore three mighty men broke through the midst of the enemy army and brought David water drawn from the cistern. He refused to drink it; pouring it out as an offering to the Lord, he said: “May the Lord be gracious to me: shall I drink the blood of these men who went at the peril of their lives?” (2 Sam. 23).

Likewise, in Deuteronomy chapter 19 [alternatively, chapter 20], the Lord commanded that six cities of refuge be set apart in the midst of the promised land, situated at equal distances from one another, and that a direct road to them be carefully made, so that from every part of the promised land the man who had unwittingly shed his neighbour’s blood could reach them without hindrance. Otherwise, unless you exercise diligence in this, you will be guilty of blood.

Likewise, in Deuteronomy chapter 22 [alternatively, 21]: “When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you be guilty because another has slipped and fallen headlong” [perhaps *praeceps*, “headlong,” rather than *praecipitem*].

Likewise, it was commanded in the Law that whoever builds a house or temple must make small walls around it and projecting supports or walkways, lest a carpenter or mason fall. And yet the roof of every house in the Palestinian region is flat.

Here, therefore, those are touched who do not believe that they shed blood unless with their own hands: for example, prelates who, for an unjust cause, send agents to Rome or compel to go the opponents whom they harass. Those also strike who send people to sail or trade, and meanwhile they die or are drowned. Advocates, physicians, rulers who unjustly initiate wars, and many others in this manner are likewise touched.

Likewise Job says (chapter 9): “I feared all my works.” For everyone ought to fear lest his work be of the kind of evil works; and even if it is good, lest he sin in some circumstance, lest dust, chaff, or mud cling to it. For, as Job himself says, our works, even good ones, are in the sight of the Lord like the cloth of a menstruous woman (Isa. 64), than which nothing is more abominable. And as Gregory says: “Our good deeds are not pure good, but our evil deeds are pure evil.” Elsewhere: “A change of order changes the form of merits.”

Therefore say with Job: “I feared all my works”; for it belongs to good minds to recognize fault where there is no fault. Proverbs 18: “The just man is the first accuser of himself.”

Likewise, in Numbers 32 [alternatively, 46], the sons of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh say to Moses: “We pray you, give us this pastureland on this side of the Jordan, to feed our livestock and to settle our wives and little ones there.” Moses says to them: “If you refuse to follow Israel into the wilderness, the Lord will abandon the people, and you will be the cause of the death of all.” And they say: “We shall not return to our homes until the children of Israel possess their inheritance, but we shall go before them into battle.” Moses replies: “If you do what you promise, then you shall be blameless before the Lord, before the world, and before Israel. But if you do not do what you say, there is no doubt that you sin against the Lord; and know that your sin will find you out.”

Likewise, in Exodus chapter 21 [alternatively, 33]: “If an ox has been accustomed to gore yesterday or the day before, and its owner has been warned and has not confined it, and it kills a man or woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner shall be killed.”

Likewise, it is read in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7 [alternatively, 15], that the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of Paul, who consented to Stephen’s death; by keeping the garments of all those who stoned him, he had him, as it were, in his own hands.

What then should be said of the bishop who kept a stag with branching antlers, which attacked a certain woman with its horns, crushed her, and killed her? Did he not give an occasion of death? What of another prelate to whom a lion was given, who released it hungry from its cage, its foot armed with claws, and it wounded a woman on the head and, sucking her blood, killed her? Why do ecclesiastical men feed untamed beasts from the patrimony of the Crucified One, especially when they yield no benefit? Rather, domestic animals should be fattened, since they are suited to nourishment and human uses. Let those things that provide spectacles be removed—amusements which you are not permitted to watch or maintain, such as mimes and actors.

Therefore those who do not reckon themselves guilty of blood even when it has been shed, as far as they are concerned, on a slight occasion, are like Pilate washing his hands; like Judas the traitor, saying: “I have betrayed innocent blood”; like the Jews saying: “What is that to us? See to it yourself” (Matt. 27); and like the Pharisees, to whom it is said in Acts of the Apostles chapter 3 [alternatively, 6]: “You denied the Holy and Just One; you killed the author of life, whom the Lord raised from the dead.”

Recall the example of the man who committed sins with a lax hand through his satraps and attendants, compelled them by an oath publicly to confess, attributed everything to himself, and afterwards confessed the things he had perpetrated in his own person.

Gather together the examples of Master Robert of Cambrai. While teaching at Rheims, he supported in a case an innocent servant of one of his friends. The servant undertook single combat against a counterfeiter who had passed him false money, and thus defeated him. But because Master Robert had supported him, innocent though he was, in a case involving bloodshed, he always carried that sin as a groan in his conscience and thereafter refused to take part in cases of that sort.

Likewise Saint Robert (see note on chapter 74), bishop of Amiens, on the advice of his officials ordered ditches to be made for receiving fish. When a boy fell into them, there was a cry in the city: “This boy is drowned—come quickly!” At last he was pulled out. When the bishop heard of the accident, he first grieved inconsolably, saying that he was guilty of the boy’s blood because he had given occasion for the drowning. Afterwards he rejoiced wonderfully at the boy’s deliverance, because he escaped alive.

Recall the third example: how, by his permission, one of his officials hanged a man. That hanging continually saddened his mind and countenance and hastened the hour of his death.

We have said, and have adduced authorities to show, that by a slight occasion or cause someone contracts—or ought to consider himself to have contracted—sin or fault not perpetrated with his own hand.

## Chapters 75–78

It follows that we should show that one ought not, from slight suspicion, to defame another or rush into rash judgment. For we ought to regard our own good things as little or nothing, but to make the evils of others our own and regard them as our own. The Prophet asked that this be cut away from him in the fifth octonary: “Cut off my reproach” (Ps. 118), and so forth. Gregory: “‘Take away from me the reproach,’ that is, the sin, ‘which I have suspected’” (ibid.). He calls his own the reproach which he suspects concerning others, because he more readily supposes in another what he feels in himself; because the eye that sees vanity suspects it also of others, so that it believes another does something for the good for which it itself acts.

Since human secrets are not seen, a place has been given to suspicions. Therefore, when the Lord had commanded concerning the end or purpose of works that people should not do their righteousness for human praise (Matt. 6), or for money, or even food and clothing, because we could suspect others of doing good works for these things, he added: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” (Luke 6).

It belongs to the envious gladly to suspect another’s reproach, since they cannot gnaw away what rises above them. Suspicion is the greatest vice of human nature: it thinks otherwise than truth is, so that we speak good things of evil persons, or evil things of good persons.

Likewise, Romans chapter 2 [alternatively, 3]: “You are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge. For in judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge,” and so forth. And in the same epistle, chapter 14 [alternatively, 22]: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? By the Lord’s grace he stands or falls—and he shall stand; for God is able to establish him.”

Gregory [perhaps Augustine, vol. IV, book II, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 18]: “We ought to interpret ambiguous matters in the better sense, to desire their salvation rather than their death, and to retain hope for future good, even if another is presently otherwise.”

Who is evil today will be best tomorrow. Matthew, chapter VII [otherwise X]: “Do not judge,” namely concerning hidden and suspected matters, “that you may not be judged. For with whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged; and with whatever measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you,” and so forth.

[Col. 0540C] Again: It is the greatest presumption to attribute to oneself a prophetic spirit, as Elisha did, who foresaw by the Spirit that his servant Gehazi had received the silver, garments, money, and other things offered to Elisha by Naaman the Syrian, whom he had cured of leprosy (IV Kings 5). Or it is to take away from the Lord power, judgment, or office, and to usurp knowledge—he “who alone sees in secret” (Matt. 6), “who alone searches hearts and reins” (Ps. LXLIII), “who alone knows the thoughts of men, because they are vain” (Ps. VII). He also said: “Let him who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8). Likewise, let him who is without sin judge another concerning hidden things.

Again, on that passage of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, “This is my glorying: the testimony of my conscience” (II Cor. 1), Gregory says (Gloss on this passage): Let no one presume, against conscience, either to pronounce or even to entertain a judgment, saying: Who keeps chastity, or any other commandment? For if he thinks that no one does, he himself is no one.

Again: Some inquisitive, trifling, gossiping grammarians entered an hermit’s little room. They saw his bed, between two small beams, filled with ashes and haircloth, like the couch of blessed Germanus. Then they said freely and openly among themselves: “This man is a showman; he ought not display such things.” When the man of God heard this, he shut the little door again, and thereafter the secret of his religious life was disclosed to no one. Hence more suspicions than before arose concerning the bed. For they said: “Now he eats meat; now he lies on the feathers of Sardanapalus,” and thus they took scandal.

Whether in such matters he should follow counsel, while preserving the threefold truth—or rather, whether he should not abandon the threefold truth of life, doctrine, and justice: let that which puffs up perish rather than that which builds up be lost (I Cor. 8). Do not take upon yourself the office of the supreme Judge, who, as Isaiah says in chapter XI [otherwise XVII], possessing the fullness of gifts, “shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor rebuke according to the hearing of his ears; but [Col. 0541A] shall judge the poor in justice, and rebuke with equity for the meek of the earth.”

Again: The Lord alone, who is the supreme goldsmith or craftsman, knows who is a hypocrite—that is, one merely gilded or covered with gold—and who is golden. For *hypocrite* is said to derive from *hypo*, “under,” and *chrysos* [χρύσος, “gold”]. It belongs to God himself to give the gold of wisdom or the silver of eloquence.

Again, in Proverbs: “In doubtful matters do not decide quickly, but keep your judgment suspended” (Seneca, *On Prudence*).

Again, Jerome: “If you see the Christ of the Lord—that is, an angel—or a priest stroking a woman’s head, do not suspect evil, because evil matters must be interpreted favorably” (see note to ch. 75).

Again: Consider, if you sat as a judge, with how much deliberation, under what established judicial procedure, with what solemnity, you would pronounce sentence—yet now you pronounce judgment upon your neighbor so lightly, although you are not a judge (*Against Rumormongers*, ch. 76). Therefore, that you may have an antidote against this plague of rushing into rash judgment:

[Col. 0541B]

> Flee rumors, lest you begin to be thought their novel author.  
> —Cato, *Distichs*, book I

> Avoid the questioner; for he is a chatterer.  
> —Horace, book I, epistle 18

For he is the man who, “leaving his own affairs, attends to those of others.” Of him it is said in the book *On Consideration*: “Good brother, do not have ears that drink greedily, nor an itching tongue.” And Quintus Curtius says: “Let the rumor and vice of the idle soldier perish.”

The Apostle commands such idle, rumormongering, inquisitive, restless persons to be excommunicated in the final chapter of the First Epistle to the Thessalonians and in the Second Epistle to the same persons (II Thess. 3), because they are reporters of lies and cause their hearers to sin. For Virgil, *Aeneid* IV:

> Rumor is an evil than which none is swifter.  
> It flourishes by movement and gains strength as it goes.

Yet three reports are good; the rest are not to be heeded: namely, “The Lord has taken away your sin” [Col. 0541C] (II Kings 12), or “Your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9). The second is: “The Lord has risen” (Mark 16). The third: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth (Matt. 15).

Against trifling gossips and those who quickly rush into rash judgment—who utter what they do not know, who do not investigate their judgments more carefully, who slip with a slippery tongue, which is on wet [otherwise, bare] ground, whose words hasten to the tongue before the file: they speak in error, because they do not know that a judgment is a fixed and undoubting answer of the mind, first conceived and nourished in the mind and then brought forth into the light.

Hence Ecclesiasticus (ch. 33): “He who makes inquiry will prepare his answer; and thus, having prayed, he shall be heard, shall preserve discipline, and then shall answer.” And again below (ch. 37): “Before all works let a true word go before you, and before every act let settled counsel stand. For an evil word will change the heart.” Again (Ecclus. 32): “My son, do nothing without counsel, and after the deed you will not repent”—nor after speaking, if you speak after forethought.

Again (Ecclus. 21): “The lips of the imprudent tell foolish things; the words of the prudent shall be weighed in a balance. The heart of fools is in their mouth; the mouth of the wise is in their heart.” Again (Ecclus. 19): “He who believes quickly is light of heart and shall be diminished [the lesser text: ‘will be diminished’]; and he who hates talkativeness fears [variant: ‘extinguishes’] malice. Have you heard a word against your neighbor? Let it die [variant: ‘let it die with you’] within you; be confident, for God will not abandon you.”

The Apostle says (I Tim. 5): “Do nothing without prejudice,” that is, without prior deliberation. Look also to Aristotle, who taught that time should be granted for resolving a proposed question; to his two disciples, one of whom needed a bridle and the other spurs (see ch. V); to the most prudent Emperor Augustus, who was slow in all his actions and in giving judgments; and to the deed of Emperor Theodosius during his exile at Thessalonica. Hence it was afterward established that sentence should not be pronounced against anyone [Col. 0542A] before the thirtieth day.

Thus a certain wise man said: “I am angry; I will not strike you now.” For anger is this madness:

> Anger hinders the mind, so that it cannot discern the truth.  
> —Cato, *Distichs*, book II

> Grant time and a brief delay: impulse supplies all things for evil.  
> —Statius, *Thebaid*, book XI

Until anger has departed, do not pronounce judgment. Seneca (*Epistle* 40): “I command you to be slow of speech.” Hence, concerning such rumormongers (ch. LXXVII), unstable, frivolous, and inconstant persons [something is lacking here from Seneca, *Epistle* 2]: “I consider the first sign of a composed mind to be the ability to stand firm and delay judgment.” Seneca, *Epistle* 2; and Ecclesiasticus (Ecclus. 33): “The inner parts of a fool are like a cartwheel, and his thought like a turning axle.” Elsewhere (Prov. 15): “The heart of fools is unlike itself.”

[Col. 0542B]

> No one will agree with him who is himself at variance with himself.

In the First Epistle to the Corinthians, in the final chapter: “Watch; stand firm in the faith,” and so forth. Elsewhere (II Chron. 20): “Be steadfast, and you shall see the Lord’s help upon you.” As though he said: If you are inconstant, you shall not see it. “Upon you,” not below you, for earthly things, but above: “Hosanna in the highest” (Mark 11).

> Be steadfast and gentle, as the matter requires;  
> so good a cause will give steadfastness to the mind.  
> —Cato, *Distichs*

Again: Such inconstant people share in the curse of Judas, of whom David the Psalmist says (Ps. 108): “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned,” etc.; “Let his children be driven to and fro and beg; let them be cast out of their dwellings,” etc. (ibid.).

“Against foreign judgments” (ch. 18). We have spoken of those who judge perversely upon slight suspicion. Now let us say something against those who procure diabolical inventions—namely, foreign judgments, such as by red-hot iron, cold water, or boiling water.

First: That commandment of the Law is directed against them: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God, but shall serve him alone” (Deut. 6). Again, when the Lord was tempted by the devil saying (Matt. 4), “Command that these stones become bread; cast yourself down,” etc., he refused to work miracles for display. But now that the faith has been spread abroad, he wills that his people be afflicted here; nor does he always perform miracles. Hence the Psalmist says (Ps. 43): “But now you have cast us off and put us to shame, and, O God, you do not go forth in our powers.”

Again, against perverse judgments (distinctions 12, 13): “Do only this for the Lord: add nothing and take nothing away. If a prophet or dreamer arises in your midst, predicts a sign and wonder, and what he has said comes to pass, and says to you, ‘Let us go and follow strange gods,’ you shall not listen, because the Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him or not. That prophet or false dreamer [Col. 0542D] shall be put to death” (Deut. 12, 13).

Again, in Deuteronomy (ch. 18): “When you have entered the land which the Lord your God will give you, beware lest you wish to imitate the abominations of those nations. Let there not be found among you one who passes his son or daughter through fire, one who consults soothsayers, observes dreams and omens, a sorcerer or enchanter, one who consults spirits or diviners, or seeks truth from the dead. But the prophet who, corrupted by arrogance, wishes to speak in my name what I have not commanded him to say, or in the name of foreign gods, shall be put to death. And if you answer in silent thought, ‘How can I recognize words which the Lord has not spoken?’ you shall have this sign: what that prophet has foretold in the Lord’s name, if it does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it.”

Again: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses, he who is to be put to death shall perish” (Deut. 17). Again, Hebrews 6: “The end of every controversy shall be an oath.” Again elsewhere: Grieve whenever you shed blood which the Law commands to be shed. Therefore one must grieve much more whenever one sheds blood which the Law does not command to be shed.

Again, the Master [Peter the Chanter, as is evident from the text of ch. 78]: “If the universal Church commanded me, a priest, under penalty of anathema, to chant over that iron or bless that water, I would sooner undergo everlasting punishment than obey it.” Again [from this infer that this Marchian text is not the autograph]: “If diviners, soothsayers, and lot-casters are excommunicated in the decrees, how much more those who tempt the Lord through miracles, tempt the Lord to perform miracles, or seem to compel him by sacred words?”

It is indeed true that sacramental forms always have their effect, if pronounced by a priest, seriously, and in the proper manner. But incantations do not, except when the Lord permits and the devil procures it.

Again (see note to ch. 78): If curses were to be received, proofs ought rather to be received than curses—the proofs retained in the Law, as is read in the Book of Numbers concerning the adulterous woman tested by the water of cursing (ch. 5).

Again (ch. 26, distinction 5, “If anyone against clerics”; and ch. “On Divinations”; and ch. “Somewhat”): Even if persons were convicted by such diabolical tests, they ought not to be put to death, but endured and preached to. Prayer should be made for them, that God might rather enlighten them and pour grace into them. For faith belongs not to necessity but to the will. For if one said, “The Lord has not yet given me faith; he does not wish to visit me. Make me have it; I cannot believe by myself”—what then should be done?

Again (see II, question 2, ch. “The Lot,” and the following chapters): Foreign judgments seem to be rejected because they do not descend from between the two mountains, nor have their origin in the Old or New [Testament].

Again: Even things approved, permitted, or indulged by the Lord have now been removed from the midst of the Church because of their proximity to evil; thus the casting of lots in large or small groups long prevailed. But, as is read in the decrees, because lots bordered upon divination (26, question 5), they are today forbidden by the Church:

[Col. 0543C]

> For evils are neighbors to good things.  
> —Ovid

Much more strongly should such judgments be blown away, since they result in the shedding of blood.

Again (see note to ch. 78): In electing a pontiff you would not dare cast lots among a multitude—though perhaps it would be allowed between two, as happened at Lyons with two little slips—because, on account of the people’s sins, the lot might fall upon the most unworthy man. Yet the salvation or ruin of the entire diocese would depend on that election.

How much more, then, ought incantations or tests to cease here, when they shed blood and yield no benefit to the soul? Again: “The privileges of a few do not make a common law.” For if one reads of the three boys who were brought out unburned from the fiery furnace, and that even their *saraballa* were not changed (Dan. 3); if one also supposes that Jonah came out unharmed from the belly of the whale (Jonah 2), Daniel from the lions’ den (Dan. 6), John from the vessel of boiling oil, and many others of this kind: nevertheless, you cannot perform miracles by your blessing over water or iron, because here there is no Daniel, no three innocent boys, and no such persons.

Therefore you, sinful priest, must not rely today on miracles but on good works, because no one is found worthy for whose merit the Lord works miracles. Again: Even now the promises of God in the Gospel fail, impeded by our sins, or because the Lord alone knows the reason—namely these: “In my name they shall cast out demons, they shall speak with new tongues, they shall take up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly it shall not harm them; they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be well,” etc. (Mark 16).

[Col. 0544A] But you, wretched priest, always wish your curses to be fulfilled in effect. Again: In this promise of the Lord, “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he shall give you” (John 16), it must be understood of things pertaining to salvation—that is, things without which there is no salvation; asked worthily and perseveringly; for you, not for those for whom you ask or against whom you ask. Unless you add or understand qualifications of this kind, this promise of the Lord will not be effective.

But you, wretch, wish your incantations never to be false or deceptive, although you ask unworthily, not perseveringly, not even for yourself but for the condemnation or salvation of others; not for things belonging to eternal salvation, or things without which salvation cannot exist. For miracles are sometimes performed through the merit of the person to whom they are done, or of the person for whom they are done, or through the merit of the person who prays that they be done, or through the merits of the saints who are invoked. Sometimes the merits of all these cooperate jointly; sometimes the will of God alone; sometimes the merits of several but not all. [Col. 0544B] Why then do you wish always to work miracles?

Again: Such things are discordant and contradictory. For the accused is judged guilty when the nature of fire harms him, innocent when the nature of water receives him; yet, since nature in two things established for the same purpose seems bound to observe neither outcome. But if the nature of fire and water rejected the accused—if fire disdained to exercise its nature upon him so as not to burn tender flesh, and the nature of water refused to receive a heavy body—then the miracle would be more evident and the institution more fitting. Or if cold iron burned, or cold water did so, it would be clearer.

Again (see note to ch. 78): It is asked who invented and arranged the words used there, and whence they have authority. Solomon did not institute them as he did exorcisms. Again: When is this power given? Is it given when a man is made exorcist, deacon, or priest? From whom does he have this office? What is conferred upon him? Does he sin if he changes, shortens, or prolongs it?

[Col. 0544C] Again: Our exorcisms today have no efficacy except when the Lord wills it. For an exorcist today cannot cast out demons as in the primitive Church; nor could all the priests of one kingdom, with all Solomon’s exorcisms or even ours, by their power free one demoniac.

But who are you, wretched priest, who presume by your incantations to make fire not burn a hand capable of being burned? There is no Bricius there, who carried burning coals unburned in his cloak before the people, yet did not thereby put an end to the wickedly conceived suspicion of fornication. Therefore the man upon whom the necessity of carrying red-hot iron in his hand is imposed may say: “I am not another John, whole in mind and body, who deserved to emerge unharmed from a vessel of boiling oil. I am not the boy Marcellus, afterward bishop of Paris, upon whose tender hand a blacksmith placed a glowing mass of iron when he was seeking coals to kindle the altar incense.”

But the tender boy Marcellus is said to have said of the glowing iron: “It is hot from the heat of fire, but it weighs nine pounds.” Let that wretched, unlearned man say: “I will not be a balance for iron: ‘I will not tempt the Lord’” (Matt. 4).

Again, Psalm 68: “Attend to my soul and deliver it; rescue me because of my enemies.” This Christ says to the Father for himself and for his members: “because of my enemies,” Gregory explains, “who are to be converted.” But one deliverance is hidden, occurring for holy bishops, as for the seven Maccabean brothers, who were consumed by fire with their mother rather than consent to men against God’s law (II Macc. 7). Another deliverance is manifest, occurring for enemies either to punish or to free them, as the three boys were delivered bodily from fire. Thus Nebuchadnezzar himself was converted and proclaimed the Lord (Dan. 7).

For Christians, the hidden deliverance is that which occurs in the soul. An open deliverance is not now necessary, because all are believers. It belongs to few, and the Lord performs it rarely. “The Lord will not today go forth in our powers” [Col. 0545A] (Ps. 59), namely in works done through us; but in his own powers, when he wills and sees it expedient. He delivers thus rarely, but secretly, as he delivered blessed Lawrence by a hidden deliverance: when he was burned, he was not scorched in his soul.

Again: Even the sacramental form of baptism, instituted by the Lord, has no effect in this person because of one stain of sin. Yet will this human—or rather diabolical—invention never fail?

Again: Note that while Pope Eugenius presided at the council of Rheims, with cardinals, archbishops, bishops, learned men, and authoritative persons present (see note to ch. 78), Evus of Steila, a Breton, was corrupted by a certain foolish heresy. In confession he said that he was the one who lives and reigns for ever and ever, and, like a brute, spoke and asserted various other brutish things. Yet he was not there condemned to death; rather, Archbishop Samson held him in chains, where he ended his life on bread and [Col. 0545B] water, and thus corrupted no one afterward.

Again: Samson, Archbishop of Rheims, permitted no priest to perform such consecrations—or rather execrations—over that water unless the princes and magistrates had first given an undertaking that no blood would be shed if the accused were proved guilty in that foreign judgment. He never allowed a judgment by red-hot iron to be performed.

Again: In the lives of the saints it is read concerning pagans that, although they were zealous for their errors and for whatever law they had, they did not immediately sentence those joined to and confessing the law of Christ. Instead, they gave them thirty days’ reprieve, imprisoned them, and threatened them with bodily punishment and tortures. Sometimes they invited them to their error with promises, persuasion, and flattery. They did not require them to believe in their gods in their heart, but only not to blaspheme and to offer incense outwardly.

But our princes and prelates do not believe an oral confession. Rather, hastening to judgment, they assign the ordeal of fiery iron to one who confesses the Catholic faith even with his mouth; and one who refuses thus to tempt the Lord and undergo a diabolical judgment they cast into the pyre. Such men would likewise burn blessed Peter and all the men of Clairvaux.

Such a hasty sentence was once given in Flanders, when bishops, priests, and officials of princes and prelates called whomever they wished heretics and wrote them in the book of death. Thus they killed many matrons, who, as is read in Daniel, would not consent to them, under the charge of heresy; they extorted ransom from many [that is, townsmen] burghers; and they involved many innocent persons together with the guilty.

Again: A certain wretched and emaciated man was brought with others to Paris, in the presence of the kings, prelates, and princes of France. They asked whether he believed. He answered: “I believe in the Lord and in the articles of faith.” This did not suffice them. But when he was asked whether he would carry red-hot iron, he answered: [Col. 0545D] “No—not until these learned men and leading bishops first judge whether doing this is a sin or not, and whether it is tempting the Lord.” Then all fell silent.

Only the man of Bourges [perhaps Gerard], a Cistercian monk, dared open his mouth, saying: “We ought no longer take part; for, once an examination has been held, it is yours either to punish with shedding of blood or to spare.” And the accused man himself was marked out because he had dared to mutter. But that wretched man cried: “You carry the red-hot iron first; certainly I would carry it now.” At last, while he hesitated, a certain prince threw him into the fire, and he was burned.

Again: A certain matron escaped by God’s grace and asked the Master what she should do thereafter because of shame, since she had incurred that stigma, although falsely; she wished the earth would swallow her. The Master consoled her in a remarkable way, saying that henceforth she was bound to be regarded as holy and, if she died, to be placed among relics, because fire had not exercised its nature upon her and the Lord had worked a miracle in her and through [Col. 0546A] her.

Again: The best test would condemn these judgments. Today the universal Church would not dare stake and expose, as though upon a single hazard, its own head—that is, the Catholic faith—by arranging such a contest between Catholics, pagans, and Jews: if red-hot iron did not exercise its nature upon a Catholic’s hand, all Judaism and all paganism would be converted to the Christian faith; if the hand were burned, Christ’s faith would be endangered, and everyone would turn to Judaism or paganism.

If, therefore, for so great a gain you do not dare subject a hand to red-hot iron, on what grounds do you, priest, bless iron or water and grant authority to this detestable act, from which comes not only no gain but danger to souls, shedding of blood, or mutilation of limbs?

Again, note another example. There occurred at Rheims drought and harsh, harmful weather. Having brought out relics and reliquary chests, believers of every [Col. 0546B] sex and office performed for three days the arval rites (*arvalia*) and the city-circling rites (*amburbalia*), but not even a small cloud appeared. Seeing such distress, a Jewish archisynagogue said: “I grant that we shall all become Christians if, within three days, I do not give rain, provided you allow a scroll and the Torah to be carried about.” Most of the faithful said: “It is good, it is good.”

At last Master Alberic said: “Far be it that Christ’s faith be put in danger if a Jew should draw waters from heaven by magical art, with the Lord permitting it because of our sins or the devil procuring it. For evil men also are often read to have worked miracles. Thus Christ’s faith might altogether be blown away, and all would wish to convert to Judaism.” They therefore did not dare expose our faith to danger for the gain of so many Jews.

Again, Hebrews, chapter 11: “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions, extinguished the force of fire,” etc., as did the three boys (Dan. 5). The time for such things is not in the New Testament. Previously he gave such things, so that it might be clear that no other giver is understood even of earthly happiness, which belongs to the old man; but to Christ, the new man, he promises new things—that is, eternal things. Hence he dies mocked.

Therefore James says (ch. 5): “You have heard of Job’s endurance and seen Christ’s end. Suffer as Job did, but do not hope for his end—that is, the temporal goods which returned to him increased—but for eternal things, which came first in Christ.” As though he said: Do not rely today on miracles, but on faith working through love. If you rely on those things, you seem to presume the holiness of the three boys and other saints, who by their holiness changed the nature of fire.

Again, to proceed by examples: It happened at Orléans, in the church of blessed Samson, that a thief stole the church’s relics. A certain sacristan of that church was held suspect. As innocent, he offered to clear himself by ordeal. He was bound [perhaps “overcome”] as guilty outwardly and was immediately hanged. A month later, the man who had stolen the relics was caught in another theft. When hanging threatened him, he confessed that he had committed the earlier theft. He showed where the relics were; they were restored. He said that the sacristan had not been guilty. Thus those who had procured that judgment grieved until death.

Again, at Compiègne it happened that a certain recluse, defamed among many persons concerning relics stolen by theft, trusting in his innocence, first offered himself for the ordeal. He had a dwelling beside the church, and his hand was burned. Again, a certain recluse woman had her cell outside the town, and she was accused of having frequently received certain Cathars there. Feeling herself defamed and despised by people, she consulted a certain dean, a master and discerning man, saying: “Lord, among all these citizens I have become so despised that no one offers me bread because of this suspicion; they believe me to be a Cathar. What must I do to appear innocent, as I truly am? [Col. 0547A] I wish to clear myself by ordeal.” And he said: “You may do so very well, since you have such confidence in your innocence.” On his advice she underwent the ordeal of red-hot iron; her hand was burned by the iron, and afterwards she herself was entirely burned at the stake.

Again: Two Englishmen went abroad, and on their return one turned aside to Saint James while the other returned home. The latter was accused of having killed his companion and retained his possessions. He offered himself for this diabolical ordeal; he failed and was hanged. Shortly afterwards that companion returned sound and unharmed. Thus the judicial officials and those who had procured the hanging were put to shame. And the companion, on whose account his companion had been put to death, grieved especially and grieved until his own death.

Again: It is not found even in human laws that, if someone is found guilty in such a judgment, he should immediately be handed over for the shedding of blood. For he has not been convicted before a secular judge; indeed priests and clerics are present, and nothing could be done without them. Yet they immediately hand the accused over to death in judgment, which is exceedingly dreadful.

Again: Blessed Thomas of Canterbury incurred the king’s hatred for this reason: he did not permit a cleric, convicted before the Church, to be handed over to the secular court. Rather, he first degraded him, and thereafter did not immediately permit him to be given to torturers, saying that he had punished the sin when he degraded him. “For the Lord does not punish twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1, from the interpretation of the Septuagint).
