But if, after becoming a non-cleric, he sinned, it was fitting that he be punished by the lay hand. He was subject to the justice of the secular, not ecclesiastical, court.

Again: “Avoid a heretic after the third admonition or correction,” says the Apostle in the final chapter of Titus. He does not say: Kill him or hand him over for punishment. Again: “I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas” (I Cor. 1)—“Is Christ divided?” says the Apostle to the Corinthians in the first chapter. This is a kind of idolatry. Yet it is not read that Paul punished them or caused them to be punished; rather, he wrote to them kindly and corrected the erring in his Epistle.

Again: It is read that Absalom, having driven David away, came to his father’s concubines in Jerusalem and defiled them (II Kings 16). It is also read that, when David returned to Jerusalem, “he did not punish the ten concubines whom Absalom had defiled, but entrusted them to custody, providing them food; and he did not go in to them, but they remained shut up, living in widowhood until the day of their death” (II Kings 20).

By them are understood the false teachers who, cleaving to Absalom—that is, the devil—and being caught in this by David, are handed over to the court and prison lest they corrupt others. They are not slaughtered or subjected to the penalty of blood. For they must be endured and admonished until God pours faith into them, because the Lord sometimes melts crystal, though hardened; loosens those who are bound; and melts ice, however hardened, into water. “Let both, therefore, grow until the harvest, lest, while the tares are gathered, the wheat also be rooted up” (Matt. 13).

Again, to the Corinthians (ch. 12): “To another is given the grace [Col. 0547D] of healings in the same Spirit; to another the working of powers”—the Gloss says, that is, miracles contrary to nature. Therefore, since every priest may bless iron or water, it appears that every priest is holy, or usurps the grace of working miracles, or says that he himself is a person of many faces. The same seems true of one who dares undergo the ordeal.

That it is a miracle is proved by this: no inferior nature seems able to act there, but a superior one. For fire’s not burning a hand occurs through higher causes, as does water’s not receiving a heavy body. It is therefore madness to usurp such a thing for oneself and thus tempt the Lord.

Against such persons Isaiah says in chapter 44 [otherwise 75]: “I am the Lord, making the signs of diviners void and turning soothsayers to madness.” Elsewhere: So long as a man has something he can reasonably do, he does not tempt the Lord. Thus it would be foolish if someone, able to do so, refused to leave a burning, blazing house and instead awaited deliverance by a miracle. But if he could not leave, then he would entrust himself to the Lord: if he did not wish his body to be saved, he would take up his soul, saying, “Into your hands I commend my spirit,” etc. (Ps. 30).

But one who consecrates iron or water, or who wishes to undergo the ordeal, does not seem placed in such an extremity that he is compelled to tempt God by a miracle.

Again: Ask whether it is miracle alone. Why do priests act deceitfully, tempering the iron as though they were strong for one man and making it hotter for another? It happened that there were three men who had to undergo the ordeal. To the first, whom they did not much love, they gave red-hot iron; to the second, whom they loved more, they gave it already cooled; and finally to the third, whom they loved most. Thus it appears that they do not trust in miracles but rather in their fraud.

Likewise in water: sometimes they save whomever they wish and make whomever they wish guilty, because they deceive in submerging or drawing out. Thus they kill a person for whom Christ [Col. 0548B] died and lightly shed his blood. Again, if they trusted in the miracle, why should the person be bound? They ought rather to put him in upright and naked.

Again: They instruct such persons not to hold in the breath from mouth and nostrils, nor to descend with force; and physicians say that bodily constitution also cooperates. Again: They dispute concerning the immersed body. Some say that a man is not saved unless he strikes the bottom of the vat; others, unless he immerses his whole body, including his hair. Some say that hairs are not part of the truth of human nature, and so it does not matter if they float, nor is he any less saved; others say the contrary. Thus such judgments are ridiculous and provoke laughter.

Again: In single combat, why does a person who is neither sickly nor sixty years old appoint a champion in his place, if the Lord is there to show miracles?

Again: A certain old soldier was about to lose his inheritance unless he had a son or kinsman to undergo the ordeal of cold water for him. Having many sons, he tested which of them would descend most lightly and quickly to the bottom of the vat. The first two whom he sent into the water were found floating; the third, lowered for the third time, struck the bottom of the vat and cried out for joy: “Blessed be the hour in which I begot you, my son, because ‘you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me’” (Ps. 15). Behold, this man was now [perhaps: not] placing much trust in miracles, but rather in natural bodily constitution.

Again: The Master [Peter the Chanter] thus proved before the cardinals that these judgments are criminal sins and that one sins even more [from this passage and others it may be inferred that this is not the author’s genuine text]: if you provide a place, time, cause, or your servant to someone seeking to commit fornication, you sin criminally, even if you give any consent; if you can prevent it and do not, you sin gravely. How much more, priest, do you sin when you provide the entire cause, not merely the occasion; procure the whole homicide—[Col. 0548D] by blessing, binding, holding, sending into and drawing out of the water, or handing over the iron. Without you, even in your absence, nothing could be done by them.

## Chapters LXXIX–LXXX
Likewise, the Church sins very gravely (see ch. 78) when it supplies to men about to fight in single combat sacred things, hires out armour, gauntlets, and many such things, without which the combat would not take place. So much for that detestable and reprehensible supplying, which consists in foreign ordeals and diabolical inventions.

There are, however, three kinds of traditions (ch. 79). Some are unlawful and invented rather by the devil than by man, as has already been said—altogether contrary to the law of God. Some are lawful and useful, yet seem to place an obstacle in the way of divine commandments, such as certain traditions [contrary to traditions] of cloistered religious; and these are doubtful. Some truly do obstruct God’s law and, by their multitude, make it burdensome, and therefore must be avoided more carefully.

First, the Gospel commands concerning cloistered religious: “If he shall sin,” etc. (Matt. 18). You therefore, being cloistered, either cannot fulfil this commandment—for, according to some, it is universal—since you have no permission to speak with your fellow; or you cannot observe that evangelical order in the cloister. Therefore cloistered tradition obstructs the Lord’s commandment. Some say that the Gospel commandment was given concerning more atrocious and enormous sins; but in lesser matters one fellow accuses another in the cloister. Yet if he sees him committing fornication, it is doubtful to us whether he should disclose his shame before all, or only to the abbot. But it is evident that neither in middling nor in the greatest vices, nor in the least mortal sins, can he observe the order of that commandment; therefore he is disobedient to God.

Again, cloistered tradition seems to conflict with this commandment: “If your eye or your right hand causes you to stumble, cast it, or it, away from you” (Matt. 5). By the eye or the right hand is understood the contemplative life; by the left, the active life. But if the contemplative life burdens a cloistered religious, he will not be allowed to depart or return to the active life. Once he has ascended to Mary, he does not descend to Martha (Luke 10).

We say that a distinction is needed here. There is a twofold contemplative life: one simple and sincere, when someone, choosing suspension for his soul, rapt into deification (*apotheosis*), speaks with the Lord, takes part in the choirs of angels and the assemblies of saints; and thus:

> At the sound of the lyre the flock forgets its food.

And this belongs to few. From this kind of contemplation Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux also recalled one of his cloistered religious somewhat to the active life, because he had already wholly immersed himself in those theological persons and was beginning to suffer stupors of the head.

There is another contemplative life, lower than that supreme one, which may be called the active life of contemplatives. It consists in reading histories and the Acts of the Apostles, in making spoons, and in doing little works of this sort. Saint Bernard ordered the cloistered religious to come to such an active-contemplative life. And the Gospel may be understood to mean that every burdened cloistered religious should descend to this from the former. The first is for an abundant reward; the second is a compensatory remedy.

Likewise, the active life is twofold: that of prelates, more worthy for merit; and that of married persons, less worthy, a remedy for weakness. Again Augustine: “So long as a person has something that he may reasonably do, he does not tempt the Lord.”

Again, the commandment “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20) means: neither yourself nor another. This is what traditions given to cloistered religious seem to cause: that they may not lie down without a cowl, so that they may always be readier; for Saint Benedict commands in the Rule (ch. 22) “that they lie down clothed and girded, that they may be more prompt.” But by the same reasoning they are bound to lie down shod, because more time is spent in putting shoes into shape and tying them than in putting on cowls. Some say [Col. 0549D] that thus they imitate the Crucified One. And whoever takes off his cowl takes off his monkhood.

Thus one man, when others were escaping naked from a shipwreck, refused to remove his cowl; though he knew how to swim, he was drowned because the cowl impeded him, while the others were saved. Likewise, many are forced to die in summer while afflicted with some illness, such as an acute fever and the like; while in winter many die of cold because they do not dare put a hood over their heads on account of these traditions. Thus they have hoods on their garments in vain. They prefer, therefore, to be disobedient to God rather than to their traditions.

But it is asked what judgment should be made concerning the man who drowned himself. Did he not lay hands—indeed, mind and body—upon himself? Therefore he ought to have been denied common burial.

Likewise, no one receives to confession a person guilty, namely, of fornication or ownership of property, without sending him back to the Lord and master of the house—that is, to a layman. What then is this priest to do? The man who confesses to the priest says that he will not go to that lay master; he would sooner die without confession. But you, priest, would be lost if you did not send him. Yet by sending him, you in some measure disclose his confession; and, without hearing the confession, you dare not impose on an unwilling man satisfaction without the permission of the superior layman. Thus many are compelled to die without confession, concealing enormous sins.

The same is established in the Order of Grandmont (see ch. 70). When the priest of a lesser house hears of fornication or theft by a lay brother or cleric, he is to say to the lay master, according to their tradition: “Lord, these brothers need to be sent to Grandmont.” The provost immediately curses him; he is placed on a beast and sent from cell to cell, everywhere shamed by grievous disgrace, until he comes to the great prior. Thus, wherever he comes, his crime is as though made public. For all say: “This man has acted wickedly.” And so, because of these traditions, they are hindered in the way of God and remain unconfessed.

Other traditions produce suspicion [Col. 0550B] or scrupulosity, as happens among cloistered religious. They ask certain masters: “If new traditions are made every year in a Cistercian cloister, are we bound,” they say, “to all of them? Do I sin mortally whenever I knowingly transgress one of them? For instance, when I speak some word at an hour not fixed for this, or the like?”

Again, others produce weariness and sloth because they are numerous: for example, the singing of many psalms and the manifold Matins of the Black Monks (Order of Saint Benedict). Jeremiah says (ch. 48): “Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently.” And the Apostle: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14). And Jerome: “One psalm sung with gladness of heart is better than the whole Psalter with sloth and torpor.”

Other traditions (see note on ch. 79) produce schism and division. Thus, if you were the best singer or psalmist in the Church of Reims, once you became a monk you would know little or nothing among them, because of the diversity of offices and chant. Even secular churches have diversified the divine office, contrary to the decree requiring one manner of psalmody; and suffragan churches ought to have the same usage as the metropolitan church.

Other traditions produce a dangerous security, as happens to us clerics who safely continue the Song of Songs, or conversely, after completing the vocal hours, even though not attentively or devoutly, while giving no attention to the real hours: “I was naked, I was a stranger, I was in prison, I was sick,” etc. (Matt. 25). The seventh hour in Tobit concerns burying the dead (Tob. 2). “These things ought you to have done, and not to have left the others undone” (Matt. 23). Or, if something had to be omitted, the vocal hours ought rather to be omitted. Therefore these are the hours: real ones by day, vocal ones by night. Hence: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy,” that is, works of mercy, “and by night his song” (Ps. 41): namely, returning to one’s heart and praising the Lord. And elsewhere: “Sing to the Lord on the ten-stringed psaltery” (Ps. 32), that is, in the works of the law.

A certain wise man said that ten canons should be established in a church to visit the poor; another ten should be assigned to works of mercy; another ten to cleanse and investigate the vices of the city; and others should be appointed in the church to sing the vocal hours. Thus the Church would be “like an army in battle array” (Song 6), “clothed about with varieties” (Ps. 44).

We must return further to those traditions which obstruct the law of God, such as traditions concerning oaths that are required today in many places upon canonization. First, in a certain church the person about to be made a canon is required to swear that, to the best of his ability, he will observe the customs of the church; nor is he allowed to specify the good customs, or those agreeing with the Gospel, or at least not opposing the holy canons.

Again, in a certain church it has been instituted that the person about to be enthroned swear that, to the best of his ability, he will maintain the church’s rights and avenge injuries done to it or to those who belong to it. When Pope Alexander III was consulted as to whether this oath was reasonable, he said: “Then let one of them always be a booted man [perhaps: equipped with boots], with horses ready and saddled, so that they may seek what has been taken from them and never cease riding.” For nothing can be done “to the best of one’s ability” if such an oath is taken. You could not serve God to the best of your ability if you had sworn it. Yet it is found that one stretches out his hands to the Lord in prayer in vain who does not, to the best of his ability, stretch them out to the needy.

That expression, therefore—“to the best of one’s ability”—is difficult to interpret; and such an oath is rash in advance and should not be made indiscriminately, because it is indiscreet.

Again, in the same church it is sworn that, of property taken worth one hundred pounds, no more than one hundred shillings will be remitted; and of one hundred shillings, no more than five shillings. This seems contrary to the Gospel: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” [Col. 0551B] (Luke 6); and also contrary to the Apostle’s counsel: “Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded? Why do you not rather accept injury?” (1 Cor. 6). Those who have thus sworn are compelled to contend, and cannot renounce their right or lawsuits. Yet it would be a lesser evil had they sworn for the restoration of losses suffered by their people, rather than their own.

Again, in another church it is sworn that pledges for losses or debts owing to it shall not be received unless they are gold or silver. Accordingly, they accepted a ring from a noble and trustworthy man for a large sum, were deceived, and perhaps became perjurers.

Again, in some churches it is sworn that no one shall be made a canon unless he is freeborn. This was first introduced because of the prince’s serfs, who, on account of their parents, would not dare oppose matters with such free countenance. But today the sons of serfs are admitted into churches—scarcely or never anyone else—and those who are distant are not permitted to enter, however worthy they may be.

Again, it has been instituted in a church—and sworn—that whoever among the church’s people is suspected of homicide in town or house, and refuses to clear himself by the ordeal of red-hot iron or cold water, shall not be permitted in its territory but shall be wholly exiled. When the pope was consulted about this, he thought it extraordinary that decretists and learned men had ever established it; and a legate should be sent from the pope’s side to purge such harmful oaths and traditions. For just as “in much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Prov. 10), so in much swearing perjury will not be lacking.

That we may trust, not traditions, but rebukes of traditions, another customarily required oath must be noted and avoided (22, q. 1, *Non est contra*). Every priest swears to his prelates that he will observe their commands and not conceal the offences of subjects. This has been discussed above in connection with barbers and plunderers. Thus the priest is not peace; he is not “a tower abounding in peace”; he has not been made “a reconciliation in the time of wrath” (Ecclus. 44), since he cannot reconcile persons at variance with one another, though this belongs to his office.

They lose the freedom of the evangelical commandment, “If he sins against you,” etc., through “tell it to the Church” (Matt. 18), inclusive; for as soon as people commit an offence, they must report it to the Church—that is, the prelate—not so that he may exhort them to peace. Moses did not exact this oath from the captains of ten (Exod. 18), captains of fifty, and the like, whom he appointed under himself: that they should refer every case to him, but only the most difficult cases, which they were not sufficient to resolve.

Again, it happened that two boys were playing in a cemetery, shooting little arrows, and one carelessly wounded the other; the wounded boy died as a result of the injury. The boys’ parents became enemies. But the priest did not dare reconcile them, because the father of the boy who struck the blow was wealthier; and if it were heard that peace and a pact had arisen between them after the dispute, the matter would be reopened before the prelate, or the great Pilate. The priest asked the master to put an end to the discord. But he himself did not dare, because of that execrable oath, saying: “I am perplexed: if I report it to the prelate, I shall stir up quarrels between myself and those who will be fined by the prelates. If I keep silent, woe to me from the prelates.”

Again, it seems that they ought not to be spared, because the pastoral care entrusted to him by the prelate calls him back to this; and thus he does not sin if he discloses to the prelate the offences of subjects. Again, as archdeacons exact this oath, so prelates exact from them that they retain two parts of the fines for themselves and a third for the archdeacon. Yet the archdeacons cry out that they are treated unjustly in this, because bishops do not swear to them that they will reserve for them a third part of all fines, should they receive a vacancy.

Again, another pernicious oath is sworn in the Church: that if for seven or eight months—[Here ch. 80 is defective.]

Just as some inventions of traditions produce a certain presumption and foolish security against God’s commandments, so those must be accused of presumption and rash security who slacken the string of Sacred Scripture’s rigor—the bow, that is—and by foolish interpretation soften certain commandments of the Gospel into being ceremonial, given to the apostles and not to modern persons; others into counsels; others into things proposed to the perfect, according to place, time, person, and the like; others into mere threats.

Hence David says against them: “Unless you turn, he will whet his sword,” etc. (Ps. 7). Thus perverse interpreters bend and unstring this bow as they please, wishing God’s law to follow their perverse wills rather than directing and regulating themselves according to the boundary and rule of Sacred Scripture; nor do they consult it as it is written. The children of Israel perished because they “did not inquire of the mouth of the Lord,” that is, Sacred Scripture (Josh. 9). And Paul says: “I commend you to God and to the word of his grace” (Acts 20), that is, to Sacred Scripture. But instead they follow and consult the customs and examples of others. Against them the philosopher Seneca says: “The height of evils is that we live by the examples of the wicked.”

Yet it must not be denied [not Peter the Chanter commending himself here, but another scholiast] that custom and human interpretation are to be imitated when difficult cases arise, when reason must be consulted, where laws and canons—as well as God’s law—make nothing expressly clear. I therefore consult the Word made brief and plain, for acquiring faith and knowledge of morals.

Hence Augustine, on that verse (vol. VIII, on Ps. 118): “Great peace have they who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them,” whether acting or suffering. G.: “The law itself is the stumbling-block.” He who loves the law, if he does not understand something in it, worships it; and what seems to speak absurdly he judges to be profound, while judging himself ignorant. Therefore “the law is not a stumbling-block to him,” because his faith depends upon it, not upon human customs; nor, if any persons fall into stumbling, does he himself perish through the stumbling.

Let him therefore love the law confidently: it brings him peace, and no stumbling-block. Though many sin against it, he does not sin: “The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord,” etc., through “enlightening the eyes.” “All his commandments are faithful, confirmed for ever and ever,” etc. (Ps. 115); and elsewhere: “Your testimonies have been made exceedingly trustworthy” (Ps. 92).

On this passage Augustine says: Some heretics say that the Lord spoke more terribly than truly; indeed, he spoke more truly than terribly. And elsewhere: “You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly. I have cleaved to your testimonies, O Lord; do not put me to shame,” because “I shall not be put to shame when I have looked to all your commandments” (Ps. 118).

Blessed Martin clung well to these words when, meeting a shorn little sheep, he said: “It has been a long time since I saw one who fulfilled the Gospel like this little sheep, which gave its tunic—that is, its wool—while reserving the skin for one tunic.” He also divided his cloak with a poor man.

Do not, therefore, set a nut against a leaf by perverse exposition. Do not put a second shell over the kernel extracted from its shell, when Christ has been born. First cling to the simplicity of the Gospel. “Do not set the juice against yourself”: the Prophet says in the person of the Lord, “My heart”—that is, the secrets of my heart, namely Sacred Scripture—“has become like wax melting in the midst of my belly” (Ps. 21); that is, these frail persons, through their excessive softness, have melted and annihilated the simplicity and solidity of my Scripture.

Again, Isaiah says against such persons (1:70): “Your silver has become dross; your wine has been mixed with water; your tavern-keepers mix water with wine; the finest colour has been changed.” Thus those silver-workers, goldsmiths, or painters are perverse who corrupt pure wine, through the variety of their expositions, and disfigure its most unmixed, vivid colour with artificial dye or vermilion—that is, with fermented or superfluous interpretation.

Again, Matthew 5: “Be quickly agreeing with your adversary while you are on the way”; that is, agree with Sacred Scripture, which opposes you while you live carnally, “while you are on the way of the commandments.” For “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5).

Again (Jerome; see note on ch. 80): “He who speaks truth does not labour. For truth has no corners.” We labour in expounding Sacred Scripture because we are unwilling to act; and therefore we say: “This is for a place, a time, a person,” or “it is a counsel,” and the like. Philosophers and frogs cared more for correctness of words and elegant ornament than for integrity of things and meanings; but the saints, contrariwise.

Again: Be ashamed that your exposition, which you make as you please, is more discordant and at variance with the life-giving letter of the Gospel than the allegorical exposition of the ancients was from the killing letter (2 Cor. 3). This is what a learned Jew objected to a master at Reims: “You Christians say that everything in the Old Law was to be understood allegorically, because ‘all things happened to the ancients in figure’ (1 Cor. 10); but you burden the simplicity of the Gospel with allegorical and manifold exposition. Thus you dishonour your law, given by the divine mouth. For each of you makes his own exposition, saying:

> Thus I will; thus I command, etc. (Juvenal VI.223.)

And because none of you observes his own law, I do not wish to be a Christian; rather, I persist, and I am not the one corrupting it.”

Again: We have become like Muhammad. Seeing the law of the Gospel, he said to certain unruly people: “This is Christ’s law; but because it is too burdensome and severe, follow me and I shall temper it for you.” Thus, allowing them several concubines and loosening the reins with respect to food, drink, and care of the body, he led them into the error still called the error of the Muhammadans. They seem to have fallen into this error, softening the solidity of the Gospel to suit their customs.

[Col. 0553D] Note what a young man of good character and great promise said when dying at Reims: “I have not yet restored everything. I had a certain administrator; he gave me two tavern-keepers, and another gave me two cheeses. Restore everything equally.” His companions and priests said: “Such things need not be restored. You laboured excessively over those claims.” “I was bound to this very thing. I ought to have done justice to them. I never wish to dispute with the Lord over these matters. I fear him greatly, lest he condemn me, he who knows all things.”

Again, Augustine is against these perverse tavern-keepers (book 6, ch. 3). Origen, as is read in Ecclesiastical History, fulfilled the Gospel literally: content with one tunic, “ready, when struck, to offer the other cheek” (Luke 6). Of him it was said: “This is the man who lives as he speaks and speaks as he lives.” Likewise, when the Commonwealth decreed that a certain disciple, namely Basilides, should swear in a certain case, he replied that he would never swear. When they thought he had said this seriously, he affirmed it again, saying: “I am a Christian; I shall never swear.” Therefore he immediately underwent martyrdom.

Again, we make the Lord a liar, who says: “Narrow and strait is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7). But we make smooth that way of the Lord’s commandments by interpreting it according to our will, although it cannot be lightened except through love. For the love of God alone makes the narrow and difficult commandments of God light, and almost nothing.

Again, this may greatly terrify such perverse interpreters: the Lord says in the Gospel, Matthew 5, “Do not think that I have come to destroy the law or the prophets. I have not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil it”—as it were, perfectly or fully: according to the signification of the figures, the form of things foretold, and the moral sense.

What follows is indeed more terrible: “Amen I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, one iota”—that is, the least commandment, because iota is the smallest letter—“or one apex”—that is, the tiniest commandment, or a part of the tiniest commandment, because an apex is a title or upper part of a letter projecting above it for the letter’s ornament, or in charters and apostolic letters—“shall not pass from the law until all things are fulfilled” (ibid.). Hence elsewhere: “Cursed is everyone who does not fulfil whatever is written in this book” (Gal. 3): cursed with the curse both of punishment and of guilt. And at the end of Matthew: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (ch. 28).

Again, hear something more terrible: “Whoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and teach men”—namely, that even some least commandment should be broken—“shall be called least,” that is, worst, “in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5): that is, by those who will be in the kingdom of heaven, whether the Church militant or triumphant. “But whoever shall do and teach”—namely, that it should be done so—“shall be called great,” even greatest, “in the kingdom of heaven,” in merit and reward.

From these two I infer the other two cases: whoever breaks but does not teach; conversely, whoever does but does not teach; and conversely, what kind of person, or how great a person, ought to be called in the kingdom of heaven.

Again, hear what follows: “I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). He does not speak of their simulated or merely figurative righteousness, but of the moral and spiritual righteousness by which they were justified; unless you fulfil it, with the Gospel’s additions toward perfection, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.

For example: You have heard that “it was said to the ancients,” and the like: “Whoever kills shall be liable to judgment” according to the Law; “but I say to you,” adding more, namely, “do not be angry; for everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (ibid.). Therefore, if you are angry at his sin or at him through perverse impulses, beware lest, by being angrier than is fitting, you incur a greater judgment.

He adds also: “Whoever says to his brother, *raca*”—G.: an interjection [or an inward expression] expressing indignation of mind, etc.

Now let the reader return to the author’s genuine text (to ch. 80). For three manuscripts agree here and thereafter.

[Col. 0555]

## Letter of William, Archbishop of Reims, to Peter the Chanter, concerning his election as dean of the chapter of Reims

[Note: [Col. 0555] It is doubtful that Peter the Chanter accepted this dignity, since in the following year he became a monk at the Abbey of Longpont.]

(Year 1196.)

(*Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims*, II, 326.)

[Col. 0555A] William, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, cardinal of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved son M. P., Chanter of Paris—indeed, Dean of Reims—greeting and affection.

We rise to render due thanksgivings to God and to our Church of Reims, because, by the inspiration of the Most High, that church has elected you dean. We also considered that you should be congratulated because you accepted so humbly the burden offered you by God; neither an unworthy eye fixed upon the church’s richer revenues nor the spirit of avarice turned you aside.

We hold that election ratified and welcome. For previously, when the whole chapter had referred the matter of that same deanery to our decision, we first offered it to you, if you should wish it. But then, using sounder counsel and tending toward the end which, thank God, you have now attained, you wished first to distribute beneficially to many, in the place of more crowded studies and schools, the talent entrusted to you by God.

But now it is time that, from the seeds you have sown, you bring home to your own people other sheaves of rejoicing. Let the bread of doctrinal nourishment therefore be broken for our hungry little ones, and let the ample breasts of their mother, whose milk of teaching you yourselves once sucked as little children, be replenished through you in a pious exchange.

It was fitting and just that our mother Church of origin, which had for some time lent you to meet the needs of others, should call back her son in her own necessities and retain him, once recalled, for her own service. Therefore, with all the force of obedience that we can employ, we enjoin this upon you, counselling you with a conscience secure in the Lord not to believe anyone suggesting otherwise, so that you may persevere in this purpose steadfast and unmoved. For we trust in the Lord that you ought to produce fruit pleasing to God both in us and, with us, among others; since we believe that you have been provided not only for the Church of Reims but for the whole province—indeed, for the entire kingdom—and reserved even for these times. For we have resolved to make special use of the counsel of your circumspection in our private and common affairs. [Col. 0556B] And that you may stand still firmer in this purpose, whenever it pleases you to receive from us, or from our venerable brother and kinsman, the reverend Bishop of Paris, both the title of our church and the office of this dignity, by being promoted to the priesthood, it will be welcome to us, etc.

## In the Year of the Lord 1198: Garnier, Bishop of Langres

[Col. 0555]

## Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IV, col. 591.)

[Col. 0555C] Garnier, or Garner of Rochefort, brother of Simon of Rochefort and nephew of another Simon, formerly a monk of Longuay, first abbot of Auberive and then ninth abbot of Clairvaux, succeeded Manasses. But in what year? The Cistercian annals say 1195. For the catalogue of the abbots of Clairvaux states: “Garnier, abbot of Auberive, was made abbot here, that is, at Clairvaux, for nine years. Afterwards he was made Bishop of Langres.”

But he was elected in 1187, as the same catalogue notes; and thus, at the least, his administration of his monastery extended to 1195. This is indeed weighty evidence, but against the catalogue we set the chronicle, in which both the death of Manasses and the election of Garnier are assigned to 1193; and we set against it also the documents to be reported immediately, from which it is manifest that he bore the pastoral staff before 1195.

In 1193 he “grants to his beloved sons, the chapter of Langres, that the tithes which they possess at their village of Périgny may be reckoned to them by cartload, or by any other vehicle, at harvest time.” In 1194, 1195, and 1196 he approved gifts made to Grosbois. Thus his letter of 1194 begins: “I, Garnier, by the divine mercy minister of the Church of Langres, make known,” etc.

He, together with Renaud, Archbishop of Lyons, and G., bishop of Autun, subscribed certain privileges granted by Odo, Duke of Burgundy, to the city of Dijon. In the following year, 1195, these same men confirmed the foundation of the Chapel of the Rich at Dijon, which Garnier also blessed on 26 November; and an issued charter testifies that the canons of this chapel swore before him upon the holy Gospels that they would receive absolutely no parishioners of Saint Stephen.

In this same year Pope Celestine, by a diploma, confirmed a statute of the chapter forbidding any canon to presume to receive the income of a prebend unless annually he had remained in the church for sixteen weeks, continuously or intermittently, in such a way that he attended the office of one of the principal hours—Matins, High Mass, or Vespers.

It is evident from a charter of Renaud, Bishop of Lyons, that “our lord Garnier gave freely and wholly to Abbot Milo and to the Church of Saint Stephen the church of Til-Châtel,” which he confirmed in that same year. At about the same time he made many grants to the priory of Val-des-Choues, as a charter of that monastery testifies, in which he is called bishop and duke. He also ratified, in 1197, the foundation of secular canons of Blessed Mary of Sâlon [Sauz], made by the nobleman Guy, lord of that castle.

We also have another document recording an agreement between him and the chapter “concerning certain matters belonging to the Church of the Holy Twins . . . [lacuna] . . . causing no prejudice or impediment to the chapter in making an appeal or otherwise, if that agreement should not stand; all matters concerning which the settlement had been made were to return to their former state. Done at Langres, 18 Kalends of September, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1197, Pope Celestine being seated.”

A written charter declares that he approves, ratifies, and confirms by the attachment of his seal the donation of the churches of Saint John and Saint Philibert at Dijon, which Robert, of good memory, his predecessor, had made to Saint Bénigne; and commands that the abbot of Saint-Bénigne possess them with the freedom with which they were granted by the aforesaid Robert. “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1198, in the month of May, during the reign of Philip, King of the French.”

His end was disastrous, as three letters of Pope Innocent III make clear. The first, number 182 of the first book in Baluze’s edition, dated 16 May 1198, in the first year of the pontificate, reports that such discord had arisen between him and the dean and chapter of Langres that, when the canons accused him before the archbishop of Lyons of dilapidation and incompetence, he appealed to a hearing before the Apostolic See. The pope therefore orders him to present himself before the apostolic presence between then and the coming feast of St Michael the Archangel, to answer the accusations and to bring whatever charges he wished against them [Col. 0558B]. In the meantime he sternly forbids him, on the pretext of this dispute, to presume to squander the goods of his church.

The second letter, number 504 of the same book, first declares in anger that he cannot write to him without grief and shame, since the Apostolic See, which had once been known to approve what was in him, is now, sins demanding it, compelled to disapprove it. Secondly, from the very beginning of his promotion, many disputes had sprung up between him and the canons of Langres, and after the church of Langres had been committed to his government it had never possessed peace: “As public report relates,” he says, “and as has been brought to our Apostolic office by letters from very many prelates and religious persons of those regions.” Thirdly, not merely its movable [Col. 0558C] goods but even the immovable property of his church had been so dispersed by him that she who had formerly been noble and famous among the churches of Gaul was now regarded by those around her with reproach and contempt. Fourthly, he says that he took it exceedingly ill that, although the canons of Langres—especially those whom, at his request, he had caused to be summoned by apostolic letters—had appeared at Rome, he had not appeared. Instead, after a long delay, he had sent two messengers and stated by letter that, in the Cistercian chapter and in the presence of many religious and other persons, he had received the cross which was being preached and had vowed, for love of Jesus Christ, to go to the lands overseas.

He therefore concludes thus: “However distressing it may be to us to trouble you in any respect, nevertheless, since it is incumbent upon us to correct what needs correction and to reform for the better those things which are known to have been unlawfully undertaken concerning the condition of churches, having taken counsel with our brethren on this affair, we suspend you altogether, on account of manifest contumacy and notorious dilapidation, from the administration of the whole bishopric of Langres, both in spirituals and temporals. By the authority of these presents we strictly enjoin upon you to ensure that this suspension is inviolably observed.” Finally, he declares that he wishes—“unless perhaps,” he says, “you should prefer rather to resign, which we believe more conducive to your salvation”—that the case between him and the dean of Langres concerning the church, over dilapidation and incompetence and many other injuries and burdens [Col. 0559A] inflicted by him upon that church, should be investigated promptly and decided by a canonical conclusion, lest, if it were prolonged any longer, the church of Langres should fall beyond repair; it already seemed for the greater part to have fallen. He entrusts the bishop of Paris to receive the allegations of both parties and either to settle the case between them or, after giving judgment, to decide it canonically; otherwise, he was to send to the pope the proceedings of both parties, written down and confirmed under his seal, and send the parties to Rome within the appointed term to receive papal judgment. Meanwhile he orders the aforesaid bishop of Paris to provide the church of Langres with a suitable procurator.

From the third letter, number 553 of the same book, it is evident that he had, among so many adversaries, persons who pleaded his cause. For when, says the pope, the dean and his associates had left Rome with the letters of commission granted to the bishop of Paris, E., archdeacon of Langres, arrived and urgently requested that Peter of Corbeil—then a canon of Paris, soon to become archbishop of Sens, a very celebrated man—be given to the bishop of Paris as colleague; and he readily obtained this. Therefore in this letter he names him and commands them both that, if they find Garnier innocent, they are to absolve him completely, setting aside any appeal, not only from the sentence of interdict but also from the prosecution of the dean and chapter concerning the charges made [Col. 0560A]. They are also to hear and, with the obstacle of appeal removed, take care to settle any personal disputes which the same bishop and the archdeacon-major may have against the dean or any of the canons, etc.

Following the supreme pontiff’s counsel, Garnier appears to have resigned and, perhaps after completing his overseas journey, to have sought Clairvaux, where he both died and lies buried, with this brief inscription: “Here lies Lord Garnier, first abbot of La Rive, then ninth abbot of this monastery, afterwards bishop of Langres.” He also appears to be the man of whom Innocent, in the third year of his pontificate, on 14 May, says in a letter to the chapter of Langres: “Since your bishop resigned the bishopric itself into our hands, we made provision for his support from certain possessions of that church. Yet by the authority of these presents we forbid him to presume to enfeoff, alienate, or in any manner dispose of anything assigned to him, etc.; otherwise, we decree the act null.” The chronicle of Langres reports that after his suspension Hugh of Nuceries or Noeries (de Noyers), bishop of Auxerre, administered in the meantime the entire business, sacred as well as secular, belonging to the bishop; at his instigation Hilduin was nominated in the suspended bishop’s place, later rejected, and then admitted again.

[Col. 0559]

## Sermons of Lord Garnier, Former Abbot of Clairvaux, Afterwards Bishop of Langres, for the Feasts of the Lord and of the Saints

(Dom Tissier, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, Bonofonte, 1660, vol. III, p. 75.)

### First Sermon: On the Advent of the Lord

[Col. 0559C]

“The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. 8:22).

Beloved, we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be (1 John 3:2). For when that which is partial is done away and that which is perfect has come (1 Cor. 13:10), the eye that gives offence will be plucked out; and, having been made like him, we shall know as we ourselves are known (ibid.), because with one eye of love we shall behold him in the brightness of a sun sevenfold brighter [Col. 0560C] (Isa. 30:26). That eye cannot become dim, for neither the stain of sin nor the whiteness of filthy pleasure will cloud it.

For the present, as long as the cloud of flesh and the tears of bitter afflictions that come upon us darken not only the outer but also the inner eyes of reason, we must contemplate “through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12), making for him “little chains of gold, marked out with silver” (Cant. 1:10); that is, likenesses of wisdom distinguished by speech. For this purpose God the Father created his Wisdom—that is, his only-begotten Son—as “the beginning of his ways” [Col. 0561A] and before his works from of old: that he might be a way for those who stray, a guide for those who go, swiftness of course for those who hasten, security for the ignorant, and in some measure a teacher of unknown and desired things.

Thus he is said to have been created at the beginning of the ways from of old, because the Son of God, created in time but begotten of God before the ages, assumed, through a visible appearance subject to creation, the condition of creation. For the mystery of this dispensation and the sacrament of creation appeared from the beginning of the world and of God’s ways in the guise of diverse creation, for the knowledge of God and the advancement of our eternity. Indeed, in all things either brought forth from eternity or referred to eternity, whatever has been done either displays the dispensation of this creation [Col. 0561B] or is itself that creation. It is fitting that every creature should bear witness to the creation of him through whom every creature was made, when he was made a creature.

At the beginning of God’s ways, therefore—that is, at the beginning of the ways by which one returns to God—God revealed the mystery of creation, or, to speak more expressly, of incarnation; and this from of old, that is, from the beginning of the age. For no fitter way of returning to God has been found than the creation of the Creator—that is, the incarnation of the Saviour. Hence the Apostle says of this creation: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son upon earth, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4). And elsewhere more explicitly: “Put on the new man,” that is, Christ, “who according to God [Col. 0561C] was created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:24).

For the salvation of the lost mass, God began from the beginning of the age to reveal this mystery, as in the voice of one walking in Paradise, in the angel who spoke to Hagar, in the man who came to Abraham, and in the fire which appeared to Moses in the bush. Not that that voice, angel, man, or fire was God; rather, he appeared in creatures for this reason: that, when you heard that he appeared in a human creature which he assumed, you might believe him to be none other than he who, before assuming humanity, had appeared to humankind also in other creatures. And the nearer the fullness of time approached, the more perfect and, so to speak, the more rounded stood forth the crown of this year of kindness.

And because he who is is the same selfsame one [Col. 0561D] and is not changed by times, since he is eternal; nor can he be deceived, since he is wisdom; but is as certain of future things as of past, he spoke of the future as past because he holds the future as past. Hence: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21[22]:17). And elsewhere: “This is the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. 13:8). Thus the one created is the one slain. As the Lamb slain—that is, to be slain—was foretold from the foundation of the world, so Wisdom created—that is, to be created—was proclaimed at the beginning of God’s ways. And just as the mystery of the Lamb’s slaughter was prefigured in the death of righteous Abel, so the sacrament of creation was signified not only in Abel himself, but also in the other patriarchs and prophets, in whom it pleased him well to fashion it.

From the beginning of God’s ways, therefore—that is, from the age and origin of the world—let us run through the ages and seek out those mysteries which were then pre-signified for the advancement of our salvation and the increase of faith, and at last were delivered in fulfilment of promise at the end.

Adam went down from Eden into the field of Damascus; Abel went out into the field, where his brother killed him; Noah entered the ark; Abraham went down into Egypt; Isaac into the field to meditate; Jacob into Mesopotamia for Laban’s daughters; Moses entered a little basket of rushes; Samson went down to Timnah because of Delilah; David changed his appearance before Achish; Elijah went down to the widow at Zarephath; Elisha entered the upper room of the Shunammite woman; Tobit went down to Rages, a city [Col. 0562B] of the Medes; Ezekiel into a field full of dead bones; Joseph was clothed in a long tunic; Solomon was crowned with a diadem by his mother; Jonah was hidden beneath an ivy plant; Amos came to gather sycomore fruit; Jeremiah was sent to build and plant; a soldier is armed for single combat; the heavenly teacher opens the book sealed with seven seals; the good shepherd comes to carry the lost sheep on his shoulders back to the flock; the heavenly farmer comes to hide a grain of wheat in the earth; the wise architect applies the axe to the root of the tree; the smith’s son comes to soften the iron of human obstinacy in the furnace of wondrous love; with the cornerstone rejected by the builders, the new builder joined the two walls [Col. 0562C] together; the marvellous weaver wove for us the wedding garment, which he completed between two pieces of wood; the heavenly and new Adam sewed the new and heavenly garment of skins; the shod Majesty came to stretch into Idumea the sandal whose strap John was unworthy to untie; the doorkeepers receive the key which opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens; the new exorcist came to cleanse the house of God with brooms and command those possessed; the readers of the Church receive the book of life; the acolytes, the new candle; the subdeacons, a clean vessel prepared for our sacrifice; the deacons, the tabernacle to carry and the Word of God for the office of preaching; the priests, from the hand of the high priest, the burnt offering.

[Col. 0562D] Therefore let men rejoice, because God has become man; let virgins rejoice, because a virgin bore God; let widows rejoice, because the widow Anna recognized him; let old men rejoice, because Simeon received him; let children rejoice, because “a child has been born to us,” and the Word, made an infant, dwelt among us (John 1:14); let the nobles of the Church rejoice, because “her husband is noble in the gates, sitting with the senators of the land” (Prov. 31:23); let servants rejoice, because the Son of God, though he was in the form of God, taking the form of a servant, emptied himself (Phil. 2:6–7); let sinners rejoice, because he who knew no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22), was made an offering for sin on behalf of sinners (2 Cor. 5:21), to blot out the sins of all; let the righteous rejoice, because the Lord is righteous and loves righteousness [Col. 0563A] (Ps. 10[11]:7): in the power of his death, rendering a good judgment, he redeemed by judging justly; let the living rejoice, because they shall live with heavenly life and shall not die; let the dead rejoice, because immortal Life came to die for the dead; let every creature rejoice, because the Creator of all became a creature, that he might be all things in all.

You see how the Wisdom of God plays among ranks, ages, offices, occupations, every condition and profession. Thus he binds the whole world to himself as debtor; thus he summons all to praise, thanksgiving, and devotion. Although those things which are sacraments among rational beings ought to have sufficed to strengthen faith, nevertheless, in order that the form and observance of faith may endure in possession [variant: profession] of its freedom, let us seek the secrets of this mercy among irrational things [Col. 0563B], beginning with the four elements and investigating the creation of God’s Wisdom—that is, the incarnation of the Son—from the beginning of God’s ways.

For God first made the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire. Since we have found the sacrament in them, let us contemplate the same thing also in their adornment. Thus the Psalmist says: “Indeed, the Lord will give kindness, and our earth shall give her fruit” (Ps. 84[85]:13). This is “the crown of the year of kindness” (Ps. 64[65]:12): that our earth, namely the earth of our race and human nature, gave and brought forth the grain of wheat of which we read in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). On this Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 0563D] *Tractate 51 on John*.] “He was speaking of himself. He himself was the grain.”

This grain hidden in the earth—that is, in the earthly womb of the Virgin—the earth gave, that is, the Virgin herself brought forth. Hence, when the Jews brought before him the woman caught in adultery, setting before him the severity of the Law and saying that Moses commanded such women to be stoned, Jesus wrote with his finger upon the ground (John 8:6).

What is writing except that the inward and invisible Word becomes visible through writing? The Word of life was invisible, but was made visible through the character of servile form. He wrote with his finger—that is, with the Holy Spirit—showing that this sacrament was fulfilled through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0563D] For the Holy Spirit overshadowed the earth—that is, the Virgin (Luke 1:35)—and through the assumption of the servile character made the Word of life visible. O how worthy a deliverance for the sinful woman! How unworthy a confusion for her enemies! For the woman could not otherwise be delivered.

Yet what did he write? “Earth, earth, earth, judge these rejected men” (Jer. 22:29). Though he was equal to the Father in the form of God, by taking the form of a servant he became obedient to him. Hence: “He exalted him,” that is, the man assumed, “so that at his name every knee should bend, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal” (Phil. 2:9–10). “Of things heavenly,” he says, means those who are in the land of the living; “of things earthly,” those who are in the land of mourning; “of things infernal,” those who are in the land of the dying. Therefore, “Earth, earth, earth, judge these rejected men,” because while the earth of the living, mourning, and dying—that is, heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings—bends the knee and adores the footstool of his feet, that is, his incarnation, they alone, who were under the greatest obligation to believe, were scandalized.

The fact that the Lord anointed the eyes of the man born blind with mud also alludes to this sacrament (John 9:6). For as spittle and dust make one mud, so God and man are one Christ. Through this mixture the man born blind was enlightened, because the spittle of the head—that is, the wisdom of the Father—mixed with our dust, that is, united to our humanity, enlightened by faith the human race blinded by original sin, washed it by baptism, and cleansed it by confession [Col. 0564B].

There follows the second element, water.

The Psalmist says: “He shall come down like rain upon the fleece” (Ps. 71[72]:6). The book of Wisdom explains what this rain is when it says: “The water of saving wisdom shall give him drink” (Ecclus. 15:3). Therefore the water of the Father’s Wisdom is the Son, because he himself is the Father’s Wisdom. Hence Isaiah prays: “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the righteous one” (Isa. 45:8). This rain came down upon the fleece of a sheep. Of what sheep? Of the mother of the Lamb—of that Lamb, I mean, of whom Isaiah says: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth” (Isa. 16:1), and John says: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:29).

This sacrament is also approached by the fact that, when the waters of Jericho were barren, Elisha put salt into them [Col. 0564C] (4 Kings 2:19–21). But since it is written, “Many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 17:15), the waters of Jericho signify human deficiencies. Yet when Elisha—that is, Christ—mixed the salt of saving Wisdom with human deficiencies, the Son of God, by the will of God the Father, as saving Wisdom assumed the human deficiencies which he ought to assume. The barrenness of the waters—that is, the uselessness of the peoples—was healed.

This sacrament is also approached by the account that, when the ancient fathers had preserved fire in a well, their descendants, digging out the well and seeking fire, found thick water. Who were these fathers? The ancient patriarchs and prophets. They hid fire—that is, the light of faith—in the well, that is, in the obscure depth of the Scriptures. Their descendants, the apostles, seeking this fire, that is, this light of faith, found thick water: in the well of the Scriptures they found Christ hidden in figures. He is called water because of the deficiencies he assumed, and thick because of the richness of charity, by which alone he assumed those deficiencies. From this water so great a fire was kindled that that solemnity was called the Feast of Lights. For Christ’s Advent so illuminated the whole world by faith that his festival rightly ought to be called the Feast of Lights. Hence he himself says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Likewise: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9:2).

There follows the third element, air.

[Col. 0565A] It is read that after Adam’s sin the Lord walked “at the breeze after noon” in Paradise (Gen. 3:8): that is, when charity was growing cold and light was declining, as darkness approached, Adam and Eve heard the voice of God walking. This happened only through a creature, for the invisible substance wholly present everywhere—the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—must not be believed to have appeared to bodily senses by local and temporal movement. But in the creature then heard, he displayed the mystery of the dispensation to come.

For he was walking not only in foreknowledge or prescience, but by predestination and a loving will which nothing can resist; for, as Gregory says, to will something is to go in the mind. “At the breeze”: Elijah shows what this breeze is. When, from the entrance of his tent, he had seen a wind overthrowing mountains and breaking rocks, and after the wind an earthquake, and after the earthquake a fire, and the Lord had not appeared in these, at last there appeared the whisper of a gentle breeze, and there he recognized the Lord [Col. 0565B] (3 Kings 19:11–12).

And fittingly, because nothing more expressive could be said about God. It is called a whisper, to show that he is gentle, sweet, and rich in mercy. And since “his mercy is over all his works,” to mark the soothing sweetness of it, the whisper is placed first, by which he mercifully inspires one to do good. Hence in Isaiah: “The Lord will whistle for the fly” (Isa. 7:18), because he inspires the unclean sinner to come to him. Divine admonitions are likewise whistles, as in the book of Judges: “that you may hear the whistles of the flocks” (Judg. 5:16), that is, that the mind may receive the admonitions of the righteous.

It is called a breeze on account of its invisible nature, unweighed by any burden of corruption; and gentle because its nature is subtle, incomprehensible, and imperceptible. First Elijah had seen a wind overthrowing mountains and breaking rocks; but the whisper removes the hardness and severity of this wind. Secondly, he saw an earthquake; but the breeze removes this grave and visible disturbance. Thirdly, he saw fire; but gentleness removes this consuming and sensible fire.

God walked “at the breeze,” then—that is, at the whisper of a gentle breeze—to show in a subject creature the purpose of his mercy: he who was already calling the condemned person to judgment had determined that the one condemned should be recalled through the human creature [Col. 0565C] assumed and made subject at the beginning of his ways. Or he walked at the breeze for this purpose: since the serpent’s hiss had inflamed the hearts of both parents with the heat of desire, he might cool them by the whisper of a gentle breeze after noon, so that humanity might be restored at the same hour at which it was expelled from Paradise—after noon, namely at the ninth hour, when he gave up the spirit and said, “It is finished” (John 19:30). This, then, is his walking at the breeze: he was disposing and, as it were, considering in his mind how to call forth and lead into refreshment minds inflamed by the serpent’s hiss.

There follows the fourth element, fire.

“We read: ‘Our God is a consuming fire’” (Deut. 4:24) [Col. 0566A]. Whether he is called “consuming” or “perfecting,” both are true. For he is a consuming fire, boiling away our dross until it is pure and drying up the lees. He is also a perfecting fire, bringing virtues to completion and strengthening them. This fire appeared to Moses in the bush: he saw that the bush both burned and was not consumed (Exod. 3:2). What is understood here except the sacrament of our salvation? Fire in the bush signifies God in flesh; and this was the first sign of Israel’s deliverance, because, as has been said, the beginning of God’s ways was the mystery of the incarnation.

Let us now seek the secrets of this dispensation among the adornments of the elements. Earth is adorned either by things that exist, live, and sense, such as animals, worms, and serpents; or by things that exist and live but do not sense, such as vines, trees, and flowers; or by things that indeed exist but neither live nor sense, such as stones. What, then, is signified by the lamb except Christ? “Behold,” John says, “the Lamb of God” (John 1:29). What is signified by the fatted calf, killed for the prodigal son, except Christ? What is understood by the lion except Christ? Yet he is called lamb for one reason, calf for another, lion for another: lamb in his birth, calf in his Passion, lion in his resurrection. Hence in the Apocalypse: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:5).

So too he is called the tender little worm of the wood. Hence: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21[22]:7). For as a worm is born from earth or wood without seed, so the Son of God deigned to be born without seed from the virgin earth. For this reason he is also compared to a serpent, because he was clothed in mortal flesh. Hence in the Gospel: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). The serpent was upon the pole, Christ upon the cross. People were bitten by serpents in the desert; they looked upon the serpent on the pole and were healed from the bites [Col. 0566C].

Let us now seek the sacraments in things which exist, live, and do not sense. Thus the Psalmist says: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters” (Ps. 1:3). Christ himself testifies in another psalm that this was said concerning him, where he says: “At the head of the book it is written of me” (Ps. 39[40]:8). Therefore the tree was planted in earth, that is, hidden in the womb of the Virgin, beside streams of waters, that is, alongside the mortality of peoples. He also compares himself to the vine, saying: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). So too to the flower: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Cant. 2:1). And again Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). The rod—that is, the Virgin born from Jesse—brought forth Christ as a flower. Hence Aaron’s rod suddenly flowered as a type of this mystery; for he deigned to be born from both lines, priestly and royal. For this reason the mystery is declared in both lines. He is the flower by whose fragrance the dead revive. Hence the Apostle: “We are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15). For this reason he was also called Nazarene, that is, “flowery.” Hence the bride says: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Cant. 5:10), because among his flowers neither the rose of passion nor the lily of virginity was lacking [Col. 0567A].

There follows the consideration of things which exist but neither live nor sense.

The Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). And fittingly he is the rock which, struck, brought forth water. For when struck in the side, he poured forth for us the washing of regeneration, effected through the sacrament of water. He is the stone of circumcision, because unless the circumcision of vices is in Christ, it has become uncircumcision. He is a stone for striking and joining: for striking the statue, for joining the two walls. He is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, because he was born, without human works, from the height of the virginal womb and from the substance of her flesh. This is the stone of which we read in Zechariah: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” [Col. 0567B] (Zech. 3:9), because in Christ alone was the fullness of graces, as it is written: “Seven women shall lay hold of one man” (Isa. 4:1). And he grew into a great mountain, of which Isaiah says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2:3). The Psalmist also says of him: “A curdled mountain, a rich mountain; why do you look askance, you mountains curdled with cheese?” (Ps. 67[68]:16–17). For he is the mountain “curdled with cheese,” that is, made flesh (*incarnatus*). Hence Job says: “You curdled me like cheese” (Job 10:10).

Let us now see what should be considered concerning the adornment of the second element.

It is read that, as Tobit washed his feet in the Tigris, a great fish came out to devour him; and, terrified, he cried out: “Lord, it is attacking me.” The angel said: “Seize its gill and gut it; keep for yourself its heart, gall, and liver, for they are useful for healing.” And Tobit said: “Brother Azariah, what remedy do the things which you commanded to be kept from the fish possess?” He replied: “A piece of the heart placed upon coals, by its smoke drives out every kind of demon” (Tob. 6:2–8).

On this passage Bede says that, when Christ, on the cross [perhaps *in the flesh*], washed his feet which walked upon earth, the devil came seeking whether there was any sin in him; and by the fish he signifies the devil [Col. 0567D]. But I do not see how these meanings fit all the parts. For if the fish’s heart drives out every kind of demon, and even its smoke casts out Asmodeus, the Saviour’s saying appears weak: “If Satan casts out Satan, his kingdom is divided” [Col. 0567D] (cf. Matt. 12:26). Therefore, without prejudice to a better interpretation, it seems to me that it should be explained otherwise.

Tobit, whose name is interpreted “good of the Lord,” represents the good man in the Lord. He washes his feet—that is, cleanses his affections—because it does not suffice for a good man to cleanse his actions unless he cleanses his inward affections too. He shows how they ought to be cleansed when he says: “In the Tigris.” As water washes external stains, so confession washes internal ones. Confession, therefore, is compared to water—and not to just any water, but to the Tigris, which is called Tigris because of its speed: confession ought to be swift after sin.

Then the great fish attacks him, in order to devour him. This fish swam peacefully amid the storms of this great and spacious sea, as it is written: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119[120]:7). In his Passion he shattered the swelling waves with the scales of patience, and, as it were, lifted himself with little fins by hope of resurrection. Hence after the resurrection the disciples ate a portion of broiled fish. For there are two natures in Christ, divinity and humanity: one impassible, the other passible. The passible nature is called broiled because it suffered; and “portion” is used for “nature,” since God ought not be called a part of anything—unless perhaps in a causal sense, as in “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 118[119]:57) and Jeremiah, “The Lord is my portion, says my soul” (Lam. 3:24). For he is wholly God and wholly man, but not “the whole,” because he is not wholly God nor wholly man; nor is he God in part or man in part, because God is one nature and man another [Col. 0568B].

This portion—that is, the suffering flesh—he gave his disciples to eat, saying: “Take and eat of this, all of you; this is my body” (Matt. 26:26). But when the good man, knowing that none is worthy of these things, fears with filial fear—that is, reverently says, “Lord, it is attacking me” (Tob. 6:3)—who am I, that it should attack me, that is, enter into me, and devour me, that is, incorporate me into itself with eagerness? You have something similar in the eating of the paschal lamb: “The head—so Scripture [says]—with the entrails, you shall devour” (Exod. 12:9), that is, you shall incorporate it into yourselves with eagerness.

The angel shows, however, that fitness is produced partly by merit and partly by grace: merit, when he says, “Seize its gill” (Tob. 6:3). Seize with your hands—that is, with works—its gill, that is, its words: fulfil the commandments by works; this is merit. And lest you despair as though they were burdensome and unbearable, know that they consist solely in the affection of charity. “Gut the fish” and consider the inward parts of mercy by which he visited us; and “keep for yourself”—that is, keep stored in your mind for your own benefit—its heart, that is, the affection of love, because he gave himself for us; its gall, that is, the bitterness of the Passion—how he was struck with fists, mocked with words, covered with spittle, crucified, pierced with a lance; and its liver, that is, the shedding of blood (for the liver is the source of blood): how, in circumcision, sweat, scourging, crucifixion, and piercing with the lance, he poured out his blood for you [Col. 0568D]. If you place all these things upon burning coals—that is, upon the affections of a heart glowing with devotion—the smoke, that is, the report and fragrance of memory, drives out every kind of demon.

There follows the adornment of the third element, air.

Air is adorned with birds. Job says: “The bird did not know the path, nor did the eye of the vulture behold it” (Job 28:7). By these words he rebukes the Jewish people, who refused to believe that the Lord ascended to heaven and did not approve his commandments by obedience. Christ is fittingly compared with the vulture because, as Ambrose says:

> [Note: [Col. 0567D] *Hexameron*, book V, ch. 26.] The mother vulture becomes pregnant without intercourse with a male, and the vulture is conceived and born without an infusion of seed.

O unbelieving race, brazen brow! Could God give birds what he could not give himself? He who made nature and gave it even to vultures—what wonder if he reserved it for himself? A vulture can be born from a female without a male, and could Christ not be born from a Virgin without a father?

Because there are many clear correspondences of mysteries in the nature of birds, we wish, in passing briefly, to give the wise an occasion to gather from books the natures of birds and draw from those natures the hidden sacraments. Thus, as has been said, Christ was a vulture in being born; a pelican in compassion; a *pophinellus* in obedience; a kingfisher when he broke “the wondrous swellings of the sea” (Ps. 92[93]:4) [Col. 0569B] and its swelling waves, namely when he commanded the winds and the sea; a turtledove in feeding himself; a dove in feeding others; a hen in prayer; a *pelargus*, that is, a stork, in love; a heron in preaching; a night-raven in his Passion; a solitary sparrow when, abandoned in the Passion, he “trod the winepress alone” (Isa. 63:3); a phoenix in the Resurrection; and an eagle in the Ascension.

There follows the adornment of fire:

Because the nature of fire always tends upward, it is necessary that the things above—that is, those in the firmament, namely the sun, moon, and stars—should be fiery in light or heat, with which they are adorned. In these, therefore, Christ is figured in many ways.

In the sun, because it is written: “But for you who fear God, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. IV). Of him it is also said to Mary:

> [Col. 0569C] “Blessed indeed are you, holy Virgin Mary, and most worthy of all praise, because from you has arisen the Sun of righteousness, Christ our God” (Office of the Church).

And rightly is he called the sun: he illuminates, dries out, and strengthens. By faith he illuminates, he dries up impurities, he strengthens virtues. Or because he shone in darkness, as it is written: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. IX).

The moon also—that is, “one of the lights,” that is, the first—is called the wisdom of God. Hence it is written: “For sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot the upright in heart in the dark moon” (Ps. X). For where our translation has “in darkness,” another reads “in the dark moon.” Sinners therefore shoot at the upright in heart, taking their cause for harm from the dark [Col. 0569D] moon—that is, from divine wisdom and light hidden beneath the cloud of flesh. From the quiver of their own heart they indeed discharge such arrows in order to shoot the upright in heart: “How can the impassible become passible, the immortal mortal, the Creator a creature?” For this is what they say in the dark moon, not knowing that “the Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven” (ibid.); “his eyes thus look upon the poor” (ibid.). But they, constraining the infinity of divine power within the measure of human nature, do not understand that the operation of infinite eternity demands an infinite conception for its measure; so that, when God became man, and the immortal one died, and the eternal one was buried, this is not a matter for rational comprehension but an exception received by piety. So likewise, conversely, it is not understanding but power that is the measure [Col. 0570A]: that God should be from man, the immortal from the dead, the eternal from the buried.

Or Christ is compared to a star, as Balaam says: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Num. XXIV): that man, I say, of whom elsewhere it is said: “Will Zion say: ‘A man, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’?” (Ps. LXXXVI). And elsewhere: “He is a man; and who has known him?” Hence the Lord says through John: “To him who conquers I shall give the morning star” (Apoc. II), that is, Christ.

Therefore let all your works confess you, Lord (Ps. CXLIV), you who alone have performed these wonders in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths (Ps. CXXXIV), so that every unbeliever is without excuse, while the believer is certain of a worthy recompense, when you come to judge the living and the dead, and the world [Col. 0570B] through fire. Amen.

## SERMON II. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

“Gather up the fragments left over, lest they perish” (John VI). For many crumbs fall from the table of our masters; may we be worthy to gather them like little dogs. I say this, brothers, because if fragments were gathered from bodily food, they seem much more rightly to be gathered from spiritual food.

For your charity ought to remember how, in the preceding sermon, I have preached, through whatever comparisons I could, some very slight knowledge of the Savior. But why should this be given to me? Who am I, or what am I? How shall an inferior nature understand the cause of a superior nature, or how shall heavenly reason be subject to the human condition? For God’s power surpasses the human mind; if weakness stretches itself toward it, it is rendered weaker still, since whatever can be subjected to a weak consciousness lies within the awareness of weakness.

Moses, indeed, who by the merit of his holiness spoke to God as a friend is accustomed to speak to his friend (Exod. XXXIII), did not deserve to see God’s face. When he earnestly asked, he heard from the Lord: “You cannot see my face and live. For man shall not see my face and live. But there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock. As soon as my majesty passes by, I shall place you in a lookout and cover you with my hand until I pass; and then you shall see my back; for my face shall not appear [Col. 0570D] to you” (ibid.).

By the face is signified that form of God in which he “did not deem equality with God the Father a thing to be seized” (Phil. II), a form which no one can see and live. By the back, however, his humanity is understood: either because it is called “back” on account of the extremity of mortality, or because he assumed it near the end of the age.

That face, then, which ravishes the soul by desire for itself—the more ardently as the soul is purer, the purer as it rises to spiritual things, and the more it rises to spiritual things as it dies to carnal things—no one can see so long as we are away from the Lord and walk by faith, not by sight. But those who stand upon the solid foundation of faith [Col. 0571A], signified by the rock, can somehow see—that is, understand—his back, that is, his incarnation.

And because the merit of our faith lies in the resurrection of his body, as the Apostle says: “If you believe,” he says, “that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved” (Rom. X). For even his enemies believe that his flesh died on the cross; but they do not believe that he rose again. We, believing most firmly, are made certain as though by the solidity of the rock. Therefore he does not will that his back be seen except after he has passed by, so that faith may rest upon his resurrection. Hence John says: “Before the feast-day of Passover, Jesus knew that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father,” etc. (John XIII).

But what is this that he says: “There is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exod. XXXIII)? For what place is beside God, who “reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. VIII)?
