The place beside him, however, is understood to be the Catholic Church itself, where one beneficially sees the Lord’s Passover—that is, the Lord’s passing—and his back, that is, his body: whoever believes in his resurrection.

No one can see—that is, understand—in this life the face of God, that is, the majesty of divinity, where the body, dead because of sin, decays and weighs down the soul. But how can his back be seen amid the winepresses of afflictions? Because above all those who stand within God’s Church understand his incarnation in the solidity of faith.

Hence also that man according to God’s heart, King and Prophet David, when he wished to explore in thought the joy of heavenly blessedness but could not, placed for the sons of Korah—that is, for the Church—the psalm “For the winepresses,” so that they might know how to endure their pressures by patience, despise them by fortitude, or avoid them by love. Thus he says: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs for and fails away in the courts of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII).

You see how quickly this explorer returns to Jericho. Jericho, indeed, which is interpreted “moon,” signifies failure. He says: “My soul longs for and fails away in the courts of the Lord.” He who confesses that he has failed in the courts cannot arrive at the bridal chamber or the palace. And what wonder is that? For who can grasp, I do not say the bridal chamber of the divine secret, but even the common promise of heavenly blessedness? Scripture says: “No eye has seen, O God, apart from you, the things you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. LXIV). And again: “Neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II).

Whatever delight, then, whatever blessedness can be subject to human minds, all belongs to the courts of the Lord; but beyond this lies the palace. Beyond comparison, however, lies what is called the secret of the bridal chamber, of which it is written: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. XVIII), that is, from the secret of his divinity. Therefore he who has failed in the court does not reach the bridal chamber. Yet by so failing he has progressed, because to fail in this way is to progress. For the more anyone thinks that he progresses in reflections of this kind, the more he fails; and the more he fails, the more he progresses.

Elijah, who was taken up (IV Kings XIII), “lest wickedness should alter his understanding” (Wis. IV), or deceit deceive his soul—when he thought that he could understand the Lord either in a mighty wind, or in an earthquake, or in fire—immediately recognized his imperfection, saying that the Lord appeared neither in wind, nor earthquake, nor fire (III Kings XIX). But when his thought vanished and failed like the whisper of a gentle breeze, then he recognized that the Lord was in it (ibid.). Thus he progressed as he failed: he who had thought himself progressing understood his own failure.

Thus Rahab the harlot hid such great explorers of the land of promise beneath stalks of flax, and no way of deliverance is open to them except by a scarlet cord in the window (Josh. II). Who, then, is there whose ships, going to Tarshish, bring back nothing but apes and peacocks? (III Kings X). Ivory indeed is rare, silver rarer, gold rarest. I say “rarest,” because if, to discover whether the waters of the flood have diminished, I send out from the ark of my heart a dove (Gen. VIII), it is much if its back-parts are “in the pallor of gold” (Ps. LXVII).

And what is Rahab the harlot but the flesh of sin? What are stalks of flax but the corruption of earthly dwelling? What, then, does it mean that Rahab the harlot hid the explorers beneath stalks of flax, except what is written elsewhere: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. IX)? [Col. 0572C] For often, when holy men themselves wish to explore heavenly joy in their thoughts, they cannot accomplish as much as they wish because of the oppressive troubles of carnal things. At last, for a sign of deliverance and freedom, scarlet in the window suffices: that is, the understanding of the Passion retained in memory. For Christ’s Passion is the occasion of our freedom and deliverance. For it is written: “If the Son sets you free, you shall truly be free” (John VIII).

To contemplate freedom through scarlet in the window—that is, to think of the passible and human things concerning God’s Son—is to fail in the courts. But the gold, silver, and ivory which the ships of the saints bring back when they go to Tarshish—for ships are thoughts [Col. 0572D], and they are sent to Tarshish when they direct themselves toward an exploration of joy; for Tarshish is interpreted “exploration of joy”—are these: when thoughts bring back nothing except heavenly brilliance as gold, what the divine discourse can grasp as silver, or the strength of faith as ivory, then ships bring gold, silver, and ivory from Tarshish.

Yet it scarcely happens that these are brought without apes and peacocks. For apes or peacocks are more often carried without those things than those things without apes and peacocks. What is the ape of Tarshish? False and deceitful joy, such as belongs to those of whom it is written: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. II). But because all the beauty or usefulness of peacocks lies in their feathers, the peacock of Tarshish fittingly signifies [Col. 0573A] vain joy, such as belongs to those of whom it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII).

Yet the saints themselves often think of these things in order to despise them more strongly, adhere more devoutly to the divine commands, and desire heavenly things more and more. For the more they reflect upon the vanities and deceits of temporal joys, the more devoutly they love heavenly things and the more firmly they despise these earthly things. We never read that Solomon’s ships brought apes and peacocks without gold, silver, or ivory. But woe to me whose ships know how to carry nothing but peacocks or apes!

For if I send out from the ark of my heart a dove—that is, a spiritual thought—as a sign of the diminishing of the waters which more often enter [Col. 0573B] into my soul, I think it much if the back-parts of its back are in the pallor of gold (Ps. LXVII). What are the back-parts of doves? The remnants of spiritual thoughts.

When, therefore, the remnants of thoughts wish to celebrate a feast-day for God, they appoint for him a solemn day “among thickly interwoven things” (Ps. LXXV), because the back-parts of the dove’s back are in the pallor of gold. For scarcely anything concerning God is thought anagogically; rather, almost entirely, it is thought amid the dense enigmas of phantasms. I confess: my ship knows how to bring back from Tarshish nothing besides vain and deceptive phantasms, though it brings them back in great density.

Therefore, when Rachel saw that Leah was fruitful and that Zilpah had borne upon her mistress’s knees, she seemed to have conceived much matter for indignation [Col. 0573C]. First, because she was deprived of her husband’s embraces in exchange for Reuben’s mandrakes; second, because the idols which she had hidden beneath the camel’s saddle-cloth were discovered; third, because Jacob had not yet at least received her maid Bilhah in a husband’s embrace (Gen. XXX).

Leah, indeed, who was weak-eyed and is called laborious, represents the active life; Rachel, however, who was beautiful in appearance and is interpreted “sheep,” represents the simplicity of the contemplative life. Augustine divides these lives into knowledge and wisdom. Hence Job says: “Behold, piety is wisdom; to abstain from evil is knowledge” (Job XXVIII). “In this distinction,” Augustine says, “we must understand wisdom as belonging to contemplation and knowledge to action.”

Wisdom, however, is twofold, because wisdom is named either from taste (*sapere*) [Note: [Col. 0573D] It seems necessary to add: “or from sleep (*sopor*).”] or from sleep (*sopor*). Meditation serves the first part; contemplation, the second. For thought is accustomed to serve the active life—that is, Leah.

There are, then, three things: thought, meditation, contemplation. Although they are sometimes used indiscriminately, they are nevertheless known to differ greatly. The mind that thinks is like a traveler hurrying to go to an appointed place, yet seeking among the byways of error the straightness of paths which he does not know.

The office of meditation, however, is that, after many byways and dangers of error, the traveler should enter that road [Col. 0574A] which leads to Beth-shemesh, understanding the road, covered with conspicuous whiteness, to be the Milky Way. Therefore, running straight ahead, he turns neither right nor left until he finds and reaches the appointed place.

But one who contemplates, already near the place he has sought, stands astonished in mind, wholly carried outside himself; set above himself, he raises his ears to hear the harmony and choir; he opens his eyes to marvel at the useful and pleasant place. He is astonished at the King’s wisdom, the teaching of the law, the site of the dwelling, and the conduct of its inhabitants. He cries with his mouth; he cries with his heart: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end?” (Ps. XII). “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Cant. I).

Therefore, because thought labors after the manner of wanderers, and, weak-eyed like Leah, seeks through the nights the one whom it desires, it is said to serve the active life [Col. 0574B]. But what does the bride say? “By nights I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and did not find him” (Cant. III). And rightly he is not found by thought, since he is not attained even by contemplation. He who cannot be comprehended by any likeness cannot be found through nights. For phantasms of likenesses are drops of night.

These are Reuben’s mandrakes (Gen. XXX). Mandrakes indeed possess the likeness of a human body, but not its reality. They are aptly called Reuben’s—that is, “of one seeing in the middle.” For as heaven is above, hell below, and the world in the middle, so servile fear bends the eyes toward lower things, filial fear raises them toward higher things, and initial fear raises them toward things in the middle. For initial fear is love mingled with dread.

When, then, someone strives through certain worldly likenesses to apprehend the Creator, Leah is indeed made fruitful, but Rachel is deprived of her husband’s embrace. Thus it was that, when philosophers perceived God’s invisible things through the things made from the creation of the world (Rom. I), they made Leah fruitful but left Rachel barren: “they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened,” changing “the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and serpents” (ibid.).

Thus the divine word not unfittingly compares them to camels, which know how to chew the cud but do not divide the hoof: for they too chewed over matters in their thoughts, [Col. 0574D] but did not attend to what ought to be said, or why it ought to be said. For this reason they fell into these fictions, which Scripture compares to straw. For Rachel hid the idols beneath the camel’s saddle-cloth (Gen. XXXI), because heavenly wisdom does not ascribe truth to worldly likenesses compared with divine exemplars, but places them beneath the fictions of philosophers.

Let Leah, therefore, wipe away the blearedness of her eyes and the vexation of her rheum, so that Jacob may enjoy the desired embraces of his Rachel, until she gives birth, in the savor of wisdom, to Joseph, or, in wisdom made wise, to Benjamin. For when Benjamin was born, his mother gave him the name [Col. 0575A] Benoni; but his father changed the name to Benjamin (Gen. XXXV). Benoni means “son of sorrow,” but Benjamin is interpreted “son of the right hand.”

This is the teaching of wisdom of which the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “All discipline indeed at the present time is not a matter of joy but of sorrow; but afterward it will yield to those exercised by it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness” (Heb. XII). Wisdom, therefore, gives birth to teaching which at present is not of joy but of sorrow—that is, Rachel gives birth to Benoni—but afterward it yields to those exercised by it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness, just as afterward his name was changed to Benjamin.

She also bore Joseph, a son increasing and beautiful in appearance (Gen. XXXV), against whom his brothers quarreled and envied him, having arrows. This is indeed that teaching of which the Lord says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. II). What is sweeter or more beloved than this saying? And yet his brothers envied and quarreled with him, because this teaching is “a stumbling-block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to us the power and wisdom of God” (I Cor. I).

The divine word set before you at the beginning sends us to both teachings. “Behold,” Scripture says, “Adam as one of us” (Gen. III). This can be the voice of God the Father speaking in Moses; or the voice of an angel speaking to Moses; or even that of Moses himself. If it is understood as God the Father’s voice, it can be ironic or anagogical. It is ironic if understood of the first Adam, of whom it was said: “The first Adam, earthly, from the earth” (I Cor. XV); it is anagogical [Col. 0575C] if of the second, concerning whom it follows: “The second, heavenly, from heaven” (ibid.).

If the first Adam is meant, the word “as” will express resemblance; if the second, it will express the truth itself, just as in the passage: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John I). If the letter is understood of the first Adam, it is to be punctuated thus: “Behold, Adam, made as one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III).

And note that when Adam sinned, he blasphemed against three persons. For the serpent promised him three things, saying: “You shall not die at all” (ibid.). By assenting to this statement he blasphemed against the Holy Spirit. For, though he had been made a living soul, he believed that he could become a life-giving spirit. Again: “You shall be like gods” (ibid.). By assenting to this statement he blasphemed against the Father. For God is a name of power; and power is customarily attributed to the Father in name, not in reality. Then it added: “Knowing good and evil.” In this he blasphemed against the Son, because wisdom is customarily attributed to the Son—in name, I say, not in reality.

Therefore he who dwells in heaven laughs at him and mocks him, saying: “Behold, Adam as one of us.” He wished to be immortal and died because of sin. He wished to be almighty, and lost power even over himself. He wished to be wise; but when his eyes were opened, he knew nothing except that he was naked of virtues and stripped of gifts freely given. O truly a wisdom of sorrow, not joy: for by what reasoning will he spare the children who did not spare the father of all?

If the inhabitant of paradise was thus cast out of paradise because of disobedience [Col. 0576A], what will become of us who are disobedient, whose sojourn has been prolonged because of sins and who do not deserve to dwell except with the inhabitants of Kedar? (Ps. CXIX.) Yet through this it will yield to those exercised by it the most peaceful fruit (Heb. XII), when we are made more fearful and cautious by this example, and readier for obedience.

> I fear the neighboring house already ablaze:
>
> Your own affair is at stake when the wall next door is burning.  
> (HORACE, *Epistles* I.18.84)

But if the saying concerns the second Adam, nothing is sweeter than to hear: “Behold, Adam as one of us.” For this is what the Apostle says: “Who was predestined Son of God in power” (Rom. I); that is, it was predestined that, being man, he should be Son of God in power. It is a great mystery of piety that one and the same should be both Son of God and son of man. Hence Adam is interpreted “man.”

I say one, but not one; I say the same, but not the same. I say the same in person, but not the same in nature. For God and man are not one nature, because nature is not mutually convertible into nature; but God and man are one person. “Behold,” he says, “Adam,” that is, man, “as one of us.”

In the assumed nature he did not cease to be one of us. He did not cease to be what he was, but began to be what he was not: one of us. What is said here in the type of truth, the Lord says elsewhere in the truth of the type: “I and the Father are one” (John X). Just as “we are” and “from us” remove solitude, so “one” (*unum*) and “one” (*unus*) remove diversity. For neither “we are” nor “from us” suits one who is solitary; nor, conversely, do “one” (*unum*) and “one” (*unus*) suit one different from himself. Thus, by saying “one” (*unus*), he removes diversity from nature; by adding “from us,” he removes solitude from the persons.

Similar is the statement elsewhere: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). By saying “let us make” in the plural, he removes solitude; by saying “image” in the singular, he removes diversity.

The whole assertion of theological truth therefore depends upon this: in confessing the one and only God, it removes solitude from the persons; and when it confesses three persons, it removes diversity from the nature. For this reason the minds of heretics, reckless in impiety, despairing in themselves and savage toward all, imposed an interpretation upon the words rather than awaiting it from the words; they brought a meaning to the words rather than drew it from the words.

Thus, constraining God’s mighty nature by the weakness of their own nature, and enclosing the unlimited within the bounds of their own understanding, from these two poisonous roots—diversity and solitude—they poured forth the venom of diverse heresies.

Sabellius therefore wished to preach solitude in such a way that he preached no plurality of persons. Thus, just as he said that the Son was what the Father was, so he said that the Son himself was the same one as the Father. Arius, conversely, preached diversity in such a way that, just as he affirmed another Father and another Son, so he affirmed something different.

Manichaeus, however, preached that what was in the Virgin was a portion of the divine substance, and wished it to be the Son of God—something drawn from God’s substance in some part and appearing in flesh. Thus he imagined in the Son a portion of the divine substance as though divided and cut off.

Valentinus likewise, devising certain ridiculous and foul notions in order to separate the Son’s nature from the Father’s nature, introduced, besides God the ruler, a family of gods and numerous powers of vanities. He asserted that the Word of God—that is, the Son of God—was born as nothing other than an utterance produced by the mystery of the divine will.

Hierarchas also, ignorant of the only-begotten’s birth, preached the Father and Son as two lights of one lamp. He said that, as a lamp burns at both ends with the same papyrus wick, and the oil, as a middle material, extends from itself both lights, so the same substance of Father and Son contains the nature of both lights.

Photinus, however, imagined the Son of God to be a creature made perfect by God—not made as other creatures are, but created from nothing and from non-existent things before the ages, in order that God might make all things through him. He affirmed him to be the Son of God for the same reason that we too are called sons of God by grace, and for the same reason as it was said: “I said, You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI).

Thus, amid the gravel of Cocytus, the sweet-voiced, many-headed Cerberus barks and pours out venom.

But we confess the Son to have been born from the Father in such a way that we do not divide the unity of divinity. The Son is from the Father so as to be other in person, the same in nature; and he is one in nature, though not the same in person. Nor, as Manichaeus lied, is there in the Son some portion of the divine substance; rather, whole God from whole God, one from one, true from true, he was born—not cut off.

Nor, as Valentinus asserted in his lie, do we confess an utterance produced by the frenzy of a reckless actor to remain [as the Son]; rather, the Son, born from the Father by his birth, does not lose being what God is, nor is he himself not God in his birth; and he did not begin to be God, yet is so brought forth from the Father that this very bringing forth is believed to be birth.

Nor, as Hierarchas lied, are Father and Son from the same substance as two lights kindled from the same oil. Rather, he is God born from God, light from light, who grants his own nature without loss to himself, so that he gives what he has and retains what he has given; and that which is may be born, since nothing other than what is has been born; and both may be one, since what is born is born from that which is, and what is born is neither from elsewhere nor something else. For light is from light.

Nor, as Photinus says, is he a creature or a thing made, because “in the beginning was the Word” (John I). It is not said, “In the beginning God made the Word,” as it is said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I). What is created is made in the beginning, and did not exist when it was being created. Therefore that which was made in the beginning was not in the beginning. Therefore what was in the beginning was not made in the beginning.

Set down, then, whatever beginning you wish according to your opinion: you do not contain him within a beginning. “In the beginning was the Word.” Therefore the Word which was in the beginning precedes every beginning of making [Col. 0578A]. He is not, therefore, a thing made, since he precedes every beginning of all making.

For this reason, to cut off the roots of error mentioned above—diversity and solitude—the divine word meets them in four ways: by distinction of names, generation by birth, power of might, and equality of honor.

There are certain names of God which are said in relation to one another—that is, relatively—and these remove solitude: Father, Son, begetter, begotten; sender, sent; and the like. The Father is other, the Son other; the begetter other, the begotten other; the sender other, the sent other. This is known in many ways from the divine word: when it testifies concerning the Son, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III); when the Son professes concerning the Father, saying, “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. XV); when the angel proclaims that the Son of the Most High will be born, saying: “Do not fear, Mary; you have found favor with the Lord. Behold, you shall conceive and bear, and he shall be called Son of the Most High” (Luke I).

Hosea also testifies to this same thing, the Lord saying in Hosea: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos. XI). The Apostle likewise says the same thing: “Because of his exceeding love with which God the Father loved us, he sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Eph. II). Caiaphas too testifies to this: “Are you,” he says, “the Son of the blessed God?” (Mark XIV). By these words he does not deny that he is the Son of God, but asks concerning the person whether that man is the Son of God.

A Gentile also testifies to it. Hence the centurion says: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII). The devil himself further testifies: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Luke IV).

By these names, then, solitude is removed; but diversity is removed by names said of themselves. The names said of themselves are these: nature, essence, and, according to the Latins, substance. For according to the Greeks, substance is nothing other than person. They are called names said of themselves because they are not relative. Thus by these names this unity is preached in God: just as they are said in the singular of each individual person, so also they are said not in the plural but in the singular of all the persons together. The Father is God, nature, essence, substance; likewise the Son; and likewise Father and Son are one God, one nature, one essence, one substance.

God the Father makes us certain through Isaiah concerning the Son’s divinity, saying: “The labor of Egypt, the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the men of lofty Saba shall pass over to you and shall be your servants; they shall worship you and pray to you, because God is in you and there is no God besides you. Truly you are a hidden God” (Isa. XLV). For who is the God in whom God is, except he who said of himself: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”? (John XIV).

Jeremiah also testifies to this, saying: “This is our God; no other shall be accounted beside him. He found out all the way of instruction and gave it to Jacob his servant and Israel his beloved. After this he was seen on earth and conversed with men” (Baruch III). Who is the God seen on earth except he who, invisible in the form of God, was made in the form of a servant?

Hence also the Psalmist says: “Your throne, O God, is for age upon age; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Ps. XLIV). And Moses: “The Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah fire and brimstone from the Lord” (Gen. XIX). “The Lord,” he says, “rained fire from the Lord.” And who except the Father rains from the Son—that is, through the Son?

Hence also the Apostle says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ, who is God over all” (Rom. IX). Since, then, Moses says, “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI), and the Apostle says, “One God, and one mediator between God and men” (I Tim. II), and since from the authorities set forth above the Father is God and the Son is God, it necessarily follows that Father and Son are one God. Otherwise, either the authorities stated above or those cited below would have to be proved false.

Diversity and solitude are also simultaneously removed by generation through birth. For although the one born is other than the one from whom he is born—for nothing generates itself—yet the birth cannot fail to possess the nature from which it proceeded. For nothing exists as God except what subsists from God and not from elsewhere. I mean the same nature, in such a way that the one who begot is not himself the one born. The property of birth, therefore, by itself embraces name, nature, power, and confession.

By the power of might, too, not one but both of the two errors mentioned above are removed, when it is said: “Whatever the Son does, the Father likewise does” (John V). For “all things” and “the same things” show the truth of the same nature; “likewise” shows the signification of birth. So also is this: “As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills” (ibid.). Equal power is shown through the unity of undissimilar nature.

But the other error—that is, solitude—is removed where it is said: “He cannot do anything from himself except what he sees the Father doing” (ibid.). So that that equality might not remove faith in the birth, he says: “The Son cannot do anything from himself.” For he can do it from him from whom he is, because his being is nothing other than being from him. And in order to show that he has this ability by the power of might and nature, he added: “Except what he sees the Father doing.” For he does not see in bodily modes, but his whole seeing lies in the power of his nature.

Thus what he says—“The Son cannot do anything from himself except what he sees the Father doing”—means: the Son cannot do anything except what he has from the nature of his birth in order to do it. “For the Son,” says Hilary, “has nothing except what is born.”

Diversity is also removed by equality of honor, where it says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (ibid.).

What room remains here for an occasion of impiety? How can the nature of the birth be understood to differ, or any inequality be conceived? For it follows: “He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father” (ibid.); and, in order that solitude might be removed, he adds: “Him who sent [Col. 0580A] him.” For the sender is one, and he who is sent another, because the Father who sent him is one, and the Son who was sent by him another. Thus, through this firmness of faith, that confession of truth is made complete, in the figure of which it seemed to be said: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. III).

Yet, as was said above, this may be the voice of the angel speaking to Moses, and may nevertheless be understood of both Adams. To understand it of the first Adam, one must know that God made two rational creatures in the beginning: one spiritual, that is, angelic; the other bodily, that is, human. Among the angels, however, he made one singular and pre-eminent being, of whom it was said: “You are the seal of the likeness of God,” etc. (Ezek. XXVIII). He, then, is the one who said: “I will ascend into heaven,” that is, to equality with the [Col. 0580B] Father, “and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). Therefore he rightly fell, because he wished to be exalted and made equal to the divine majesty.

Among bodily creatures God willed the first man to be pre-eminent and singular, of whom it was said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). But he likewise wished to make himself equal to majesty when he gave consent to the serpent saying: “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (ibid.). For this reason he too fell. Thus the angel rightly says: “Adam has become as one of us” (ibid.), because as he was one with the angel in guilt, so he was one with him in punishment.

Yet in this likeness a dissimilarity must be noted. Although each fell through pride, they fell differently: man fell from a different place, into a different place, and in a different manner from the angel. From a different place: the angel from the empyrean heaven, man from the garden of Eden. Into a different place: the falling angel fell into this dark air, while man fell lower still, onto the earth. In a different manner: man, falling, was damaged in more respects than the angel. For man was damaged in body and spirit, whereas the angel was damaged in spirit alone. Yet the angel was more grievously harmed by falling than man, because man can rise from his fall, whereas the angel fell and will not rise again. Therefore the angel was damaged more than man, but man in more respects.

But if the angel intended this to be said of the second Adam, it is a voice of exultation. For what is more joyful than that the Lord of angels became an angel—that is, the messenger—of servants? [Col. 0580D] For he is “the Angel of great counsel” (Isa. IX, according to the Septuagint), of whom Malachi says: “And immediately the Lord whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the Angel of the covenant, whom you desire” (Mal. III). He is the Angel who said to Abraham: “I cannot hide from Abraham my servant what I am about to do” (Gen. XVIII). That this Angel was the Son of God is shown by Abraham when, concerned for the righteous together with the unrighteous, he said: “This is not fitting for you, who judge the whole earth” (ibid.). Hence it is fittingly proved that he who spoke to Abraham was the Son of God.

Therefore the angel rightly says: “Behold, Adam as one of us,” sent from the bosom of the Father into the world, to those and for those “who shall receive the inheritance of salvation” (Heb. I). Or, as has been said, this may be the voice of Moses himself, and again be understood of both Adams: “Behold, Adam as one of us.”

Behold him who had been made by God good, just, perfect, mortal and immortal—that is, able to die and able not to die. Though he was not blessed, he was not miserable. He became as one of us: evil, unjust, harmful to himself and his own; after sin, dead and unable not to die; miserable through sin, necessity, and misery. Adam was indeed made good because he was made by God, “who saw all that he had made, and behold it was very good” (Gen. I). But through sin free will in him was depressed, so that he remains powerless for good and free for evil. For, contrary to the lie of the Pelagian heresy, a human being cannot by free choice alone, without grace, do good or rise again if he falls; but by free choice alone he can do evil—and is free precisely for that purpose. [Col. 0581B]

He was also made just, that is, innocent and without guilt; but he did not possess meritorious righteousness. He was also perfect, insofar as was suitable to that time—that is, according to the perfection of created nature, not of glorified nature. What he had received was sufficient for attaining greater merits. He was mortal because he could die; and immortal, that is, not mortal, because he could avoid dying—not immortal as though he could not die. He was not blessed, because he did not know his fall; or, if he knew it and did not guard himself, he was outside blessedness. Yet he was not miserable, because he had not yet committed sin, was not subject to human necessities, and had not yet endured afflictions of body or mind.

But behold: through Adam’s sin human nature is ready for evil, unjust, corrupt, dead, because it cannot avoid dying, and given over to human miseries. We experience all this through Adam, who was the first, singular, and one of us. But if this is understood of the second Adam, Moses rightly says: “Behold, Adam, as one of us,” a passible and mortal man, who assumed our infirmities which he willed, which he ought to assume, and to the extent that he willed and ought. Hence Jesus, wearied by the journey, sat thus by the well (John IV). And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry (Matt. IV). At death he began to be afraid and distressed (Mark XIV).

Nor should the heresy of Marcion deceive anyone through the word *as*, for it imagined that Christ assumed phantom flesh, so that it confessed neither a real birth nor a real death. For, as Isaiah says: “Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. LIII). Nevertheless, he assumed these same affections to the degree that he willed. For he who is read to have wept over Lazarus’ death said to the apostles: “Lazarus is dead, and I am glad for your sakes that I was not there” (John XI). He is said to have feared, yet he went out to meet those armed to seize him (John XVIII). He was sorrowful unto death, yet at the moment of death said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John XIII). And he who said: “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you; take this cup away from me” (Mark XIV), himself said to Peter: “Put the sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (John [Col. 0582A] XVIII). And he who said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII), at that same time also said: “Amen I say to you, from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God” (Matt. XXVI). And he who descended into hell said to the thief on the cross: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke XXIII). The hand which a nail fastened to the cross healed Malchus’ ear by touch alone (Luke XXII). And when at last, dying, he hung upon the wood, he darkened the sun, shook the earth, split rocks, and opened tombs (Matt. XXVII). Thus in every respect he tempered the infirmities he had assumed according to the requirement of the dispensation, so that whoever considered him human because of weakness might also understand him to be God because of power, and might know that he became one of us by will, not [Col. 0582B] necessity.

Therefore, whenever divine discourse instructs us concerning the Son of God, it makes us certain either of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father, or of his assumed humanity, by which he is less than the Father. When it instructs us concerning divinity, it intends either to show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have the same nature, or that the Son is a person other than the Father and the Holy Spirit. Hence divine discourse now speaks of the Father, now of the Son, now of the Holy Spirit; sometimes, however, of only two persons, without mention of the third, in order to show the distinction of persons. More often it speaks without distinction of persons, in order to show one and the same nature.

For in the voice heard when Jesus appeared on the mountain before Peter, James, and John; in the voice heard when the dove descended upon him after baptism; and when, crying to the Father concerning his own glorification, he heard, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII), no person but that of the Father can be understood. But when the Son says, “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Ps. II); or, “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John XVI); or, “Father, glorify your Son” (John XVII), and similar sayings, no voice but the Son’s can be understood. When the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove at the baptism (Matt. III), or in fiery tongues to the disciples in the upper room (Acts II), no person but the Holy Spirit’s must be understood.

When Daniel saw the Ancient of Days, seated upon a throne, and the Son of Man presented to him (Dan. VII), the Father as well as the Son, but not the Holy Spirit, must be understood in this vision. But whenever the Son or the Holy Spirit is read to be sent, while the Father never is, whenever there is speech of a mission it must be understood of the Son or Holy Spirit, never of the Father. When it is read, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established; and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII); or, “Go, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII), the whole Trinity is understood. But when it is said, “Hear, Israel: your God is one God” (Deut. VI), and similar discourse is made indiscriminately about the Trinity as though about no individual person, this is usually done so that the one nature of Father, Son, [Col. 0583A] and Holy Spirit may be known.

When discourse concerns humanity, it speaks either of the Son according as he is in the form of God—whence he says, “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII), and “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John X), and similar sayings—or according as he took the form of a servant. Hence: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV), and “My flesh shall rest in hope” (ibid.), and similar passages. Sometimes, to show the union of the two natures, what belongs to God is attributed to man and what belongs to man to God. What belongs to God is attributed to man when it is said, “that child created the stars”; and what belongs to man is attributed to God when it is said, “the Son of God died.”

But when divine discourse speaks of him without distinction in order to show the unity of person, it says: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven. He who descended is the same one who ascended above all the heavens” (John III). And since three substances—God, soul, and flesh—are united in one person by the grace of union, what belongs to one substance is customarily attributed to the whole person. Hence during those three days of his death he is said to have descended into hell, on account of the soul; to have lain in the tomb, on account of the flesh; and to reign in heaven, on account of the divinity. Faith must therefore attend to what is said and on what account it is said; for unless anyone understands this faithfully and firmly, and believes what he understands, he cannot be saved. But “the just lives by faith” (Heb. X), because this is eternal life: that we may know God the Father and [Col. 0583C] him whom he sent to us and for us, our Lord Jesus Christ his Son (John XVII), who with him and with the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages.

## SERMON III. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

“I looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen,” etc. (Dan. X).

The words proposed are Daniel’s words, so that from the very name *Daniel* it may be understood how trustworthy have become for us these testimonies (Ps. XCII) which the Prophet, summoned from the third heaven, teaches us. For, on the witness of sacred Scripture, we learn that there are three kinds of visions: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual.

A bodily vision is perceived through the body and presented to the bodily senses. “Spiritual” is said in many ways. The Apostle calls the body which we shall have in the resurrection spiritual: “It is sown,” he says, “a natural body; it shall rise a spiritual body” (I Cor. XV). It is called spiritual because, in marvellous ways, it will be subject to the spirit in every ease and incorruptibility, and will be enlivened by the spirit alone without any need of bodily food—not because it will pass into an incorporeal substance, just as the body we now have does not possess the substance of a soul although it is called natural.

The air, too, is called spirit. Hence: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, spirit of storms” (Ps. CXLVIII). The soul, whether of a human or a beast, is also called spirit, as in: “Who knows whether the spirit of man rises upward, and whether the spirit of the beast itself descends downward?” (Eccli. XII). The rational mind is also called spirit: it is as a certain eye of the soul, to which belong the image and knowledge of God. Hence the Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. IV). And elsewhere: “The flesh lusts against the spirit” (Gal. V). The mind which he calls mind, he also called spirit. God is also called Spirit, as in the Gospel: “God is Spirit” (John IV).

We do not call this kind of vision spiritual according to all these meanings, but according to the one sense of which the Apostle speaks to the Corinthians, where he distinguishes spirit from mind: “If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful” (I Cor. XIV). By “tongue” he means obscure and mystical significations; if the understanding of the mind is removed from them, no one is edified. Therefore, when they are not understood, he says they are in spirit, not in mind. Hence elsewhere more plainly: “If you bless in spirit, who shall fill the place of the unlearned?” (ibid.). Thus by a transferred use of language he calls “tongue” or “spirit” any utterance of signs before they are understood. When understanding, which belongs to the mind, is added, there is revelation, knowledge, prophecy, or teaching. Then one ascends to the third kind of vision, which is intellectual. Thus the Apostle says: “If I come to you speaking in tongues, what shall I profit you unless I speak to you in revelation, or knowledge, or prophecy?” (ibid.). That is: if I speak through verbal signs—that is, in a tongue—and understanding does not follow, so that what is done is done only in spirit and not in mind, what good is it? [Col. 0584C]

There is, then, bodily vision, to which the bodily senses pertain in relation to visible bodies. The Apostle calls this the first heaven, since from the seat of the liver fire flashes upward to the lofty place of the brain, as though to the heaven of the body. From the middle of the brain, as from a centre, slender channels are led not only to the eyes but also to the other senses: namely, to the ears, nostrils, and palate, for hearing, smelling, and tasting. The sense of touch itself, which is throughout the whole body, is directed from that same brain through the marrow of the neck and that enclosed by the bones from which the spine of the back is joined, so that from there certain extremely slender streams, which produce the sense of touch, are spread through all the limbs.

Thus, when heat is restrained, the light of fire alone first shines from the brain in the rays of the eyes for beholding visible things. It then descends to the ears, which are as it were nearer to the brain after the eyes, mingled first with pure air; secondly, to the nostrils with misty air, setting moist exhalations in motion; thirdly, with a more substantial moisture, as far as taste; and finally it descends to earthly thickness, in order to produce touch. For bodily vision is known to belong not only to the eyes but to all bodily senses. It is called bodily not because it is from a body, but because through it bodily things are perceived.

Spiritual vision, however, is that by which we behold not bodies but likenesses of bodies, whether the body is present or absent, whether the thing which occurs is as it appears in the mind or not. For varied forms of bodily likenesses are altered in the mind when we plan in thought something to be done or omitted; when dreams, signifying nothing or something, appear to sleepers; when bodily illness disturbs the inward pathways of sensation and mixes images of bodies with real bodies so that they can scarcely, or not at all, be distinguished, whether they signify something or do not; when some illness or bodily pain grows severe and blocks the inward paths by which the soul’s attention senses through the flesh, so that, with the spirit more deeply withdrawn than in sleep, images of things are shown, whether signifying something or not; or when, with no bodily cause, some spirit takes up and carries away the soul into such visions of bodily likenesses, even mingling bodily sights with them; or when, through the spirit’s taking possession, it is so alienated from every bodily sense that it is held only by likenesses of bodies in spiritual vision. Because of these varied illuminations, the Apostle calls this vision the second heaven. [Col. 0585B]

The third kind is what is conceived by the mind, so secret, remote, wholly withdrawn from the senses of the flesh, and purified, that it can ineffably see and hear the things in that heaven, the very substance of God, and God the Word through whom all things were made, in the love of the Holy Spirit. We rightly suppose that this was what the Apostle reached (II Cor. XII), and what the prophets reached when they were caught up. For signs displayed in the spirit through certain likenesses of things are not prophecy unless the office of the mind is added, by which what has been seen is understood. For the one who understood what another saw was more a prophet than the one who saw it. Joseph, who understood what the seven ears of grain and seven cows signified, should more properly have been called a prophet than Pharaoh, who saw them (Gen. XLI).

Although intellectual vision, like spiritual vision, is customarily produced in many ways—now by the Creator himself, not through bodily sight or an audible sound but by inspiration alone; now by a likeness of a thing brought before the mind as a sign; now through some higher rational creature, as through angels, or a lower one, as through human beings; now through a higher irrational creature, as through a cloud, or a lower one, as happened in the bush; whether during sleep or waking while the inward pathways of sensation are disturbed; or by another mode mentioned above—yet spiritual and intellectual vision differ in this: things seen through spiritual vision are not judged, whereas things seen through intellectual vision are understood.

Likewise, what is seen in bodily vision can deceive the observer, when one supposes that what occurs in bodily sensations occurs in the bodies themselves: as sailors see things on land moving, see the stars moving in heaven as though fixed, and see a stick broken in water. Similarly, spiritual vision can deceive the observer when likenesses of bodies occur in the mind of one thinking otherwise than they are. But in intellectual vision the mind is not deceived, because either it understands, and the thing is true, or, if it is not true, it does not understand.

Thus spiritual vision is nobler than bodily vision, but intellectual vision far surpasses spiritual vision. Spiritual vision is, as it were, a middle between the two; for that which is not a body but resembles a body is rightly called a middle between that which is truly body and that which is neither body nor like a body. Therefore, because the prophet understood from the proposed vision—which he saw intellectually, otherwise he should not have been called a prophet—the judgment of God by which the prince of this world was to be cast out, as it is written: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John XII), there is no doubt that he is rightly designated by the name Daniel from him whom he saw clothed in linen, when he says: “I Daniel mourned greatly,” etc. (Dan. X). For Daniel means “judgment of God.”

But it must be noted that he first sets forth penitential mourning and the fitting fruit of abstinence, because just as outward eyes, clouded by the fatness of flesh, cannot clearly behold what they desire, so inward eyes cannot see the true sun unless the mind grows lean from excess. Therefore he says: “I Daniel mourned greatly.” From this it is clear that it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting (Eccl. VII).

For Job’s sons also, while they were feasting, were crushed when a wind from the wilderness struck the four corners of [Col. 0586C] the house (Job I). For a banquet of diners can scarcely take place without unrestrained merriment. Scripture says: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII). Yet there is a feast of those who live together, and a feast of those who banquet. A feast of those who live together is dwelling in one house with one manner of life, if they live well together; for if they live badly, they do not live at all. Perhaps they are half-alive, but not alive, because though they live in body, they are dead in soul. But a feast of banqueters is sitting in the company of diners and, for that reason, of those at play. Hence Jeremiah says: “I did not sit in the company of those at play” (Jer. XV), but rather in that of mourners, because through mourning the head is troubled, the face grows thin, and sorrow is assuaged. The head is troubled by bitterness; the face grows thin from loss of fatness; sorrow is assuaged by the consolation of hope.

See how effective are the tears of mourners for obtaining God’s mercy: they were able to defer the years of Hezekiah, years merited and belonging to the lower cause (Isa. XXXVIII), and deserved to bring those predestined and belonging to the higher cause to their desired end. For the end of mourning is occupied by joy, just as the end of joy is customarily occupied by mourning (Prov. XIV). The unhappy Zoroaster, reported to be the inventor of magical art, is said to have laughed alone at the beginning of his birth. For who laughs when he is to be imprisoned or is imprisoned? And what shall I call prison but flesh or the world, into which Eve’s children have been thrust? For what else is the world but a prison? What is a human being but one imprisoned? Who is the torturer of the prison but the ancient enemy, who never ceases to torment?

These are the general causes of mourning, besides those special or particular causes which each of us has. For not only the general misery of the whole world, but also the particular misery of the Jewish people and, beyond that, the individual misery of his own captivity, moved the prophet when he said: “I Daniel mourned greatly for three weeks of days” (Dan. X). He sets down a fitting time for mourning when he says, “for three weeks of days.” For the Christian religion itself, on the authority of this saying concerning three weeks, consecrated before the day of Christ’s Nativity—which the prophet saw clothed in linen—a period of mourning and penitence, so that, when the mourning of three weeks has passed, we may deserve to see—that is, to understand with the eyes of the heart—him who came clothed in linen for us. [Col. 0587B]

For this reason also the Church yearly observes three penitential periods of seven days, of which I recall having spoken elsewhere and therefore do not think should be repeated. Since there are seven principal vices committed in heart, speech, or deed, the perfection of penitence is fittingly completed under three sevens; and for this purpose also the seven penitential psalms were appointed. Therefore through this fruit of penitence the prophet not only weakened the arm of the prince of the Persian kingdom, but deserved to see the man clothed in linen. “Behold, you are a man of desires,” the angel speaking to him says, “I came to help you, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days” (ibid.). Since, then, the Jewish people had deserved by their sins to be subject to the Persian kingdom, the prince of the Persian kingdom is rightly said to have resisted Daniel’s angel, Daniel being one of the children of the captivity; for one angel does not resist another except insofar as he is aided by human merits.

But after penitential mourning he saw the Saviour and guardian of the people of Israel. Hence he adds: “On the twenty-fourth day a man clothed in linen appeared.” Note that this number is evenly even and abundant. Every evenly even number is diminished by one less than itself. Likewise, an evenly odd number is either perfect or deficient, unless it descends to the second and composite [number], and then it is abundant. This number exceeds twelve when divided by its aliquot parts, so that the sum increases to the first cyclical number derived from the root of six. [Col. 0587D]

Since, therefore, it contains two twelves in itself and gains a third in the sum of its parts, let us see these three twelves commended by the testimony of sacred Scripture. The first was commendable in the patriarchs, who under the law of nature planted for us the root of faith. The second was commendable in the prophets, through whom faith, once planted, flowered and through the written law imparted to us, in hope and expectation of the Redeemer, an invigorating fragrance. The third was commendable in the apostles, through whom faith, sprouted and flowering, bore fruit through the law of grace. For the six of good work, begun by the patriarchs, was brought by the teaching of the prophets to the completed end of apostolic truth; and the apostles, through faith working by love, completed the perfect work.

Therefore, on the twenty-fourth day the man clothed in linen appeared: when the time of the patriarchs, by which faith first illuminated the world, had been completed, and also the number of prophets, by whose oracles the world was strengthened, the man clothed in linen came, by the aids of whose grace apostolic teaching bore the fruit of good work.

But what does he mean when he says: “I was sitting beside the great river Tigris” (ibid.)? Great is the flow of our mortality, great and like a torrent flowing more swiftly than cloth is cut down from the weaver’s loom. “And who shall deliver us from this body of death? The grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ” [Col. 0588B] (Rom. VII), who alone is the deliverer from our mortality. Therefore, to one sitting—that is, attentively considering the flow of his mortality—there appeared the one man clothed in linen who alone could deliver him. Having already passed through winter, he laid aside Adam’s garment of skins and wished to be clothed in linen alone, like a bridegroom coming to his bride, clothed in a wedding garment. For winter has now passed and gone away, and the whole world appears in flower—and truly the whole world, because there the flower of flowers appears where the dung of beasts is usually found.

Or, he is one man clothed in linen because, coming to us as a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, “entering into the Holy of Holies not through the blood of goats or bulls but through his own blood” (Heb. IX), he wished to wear a linen ephod in good works and a tight linen garment in the mortification of the flesh.

It follows:

“And his loins were girded with fine gold.”

Awake, righteous ones: behold, the hour in which your Lord comes. “Blessed are those servants whom he finds watching” (Luke XII). Amen, I say to you: he girded himself like a giant to run his course (Ps. XVIII), like an almighty warrior (Exod. III), to execute vengeance. Hence, he says, “with fine gold.” John and Elijah had their loins girded with a leather belt (Mark I; IV Kings I), because, although they were righteous and holy and had laid aside Adam’s garment of skins, they at least retained a belt of skin—that is, they felt the stirring of the flesh descending from transgression. But this one was girded with fine gold, for he felt nothing of the flesh’s stirring. Though he is read to have been tempted in likeness, that temptation was without sin (Heb. IV).

Or, because the loins signify the weakness of frailty and gold signifies power, he fittingly had his loins girded with gold: in the weakness of our flesh he did not lose power. Paul was bound with this gold when he said: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (II Cor. XII). Yet Paul was not girded with fine gold, since he was powerful in weakness not from himself but from God. But this one is rightly said to have been girded with fine gold, since he possessed power from himself.

Or, because gold signifies angelic nature, as in: “Fine gold shall not be given for it” (Job XXVIII)—as if he said openly, “Angelic nature cannot be compared with it.” He had fine gold around his loins, he to whom angelic nature ministered in temptation. Hence it is said: “And angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. IV). For the loins, being the part of the body more frail and inclined to pleasure, signify temptation. [Col. 0589A]

Or indeed, because gold is understood as the brightness of holiness. Hence Jeremiah says: “How has the gold become darkened?” (Lam. IV). He fittingly had not merely gold but fine gold around his loins, because in that very humanity, both through the display of signs and through the radiance of virtues, he appeared among the holy not merely holy but the Holy of Holies.

Note that Ezekiel saw at this man’s loins not gold but a writer’s inkhorn (Ezek. IX); John saw him girded at the breasts with a golden belt (Rev. I); but Daniel saw fine gold at the loins, and not at the breasts (Dan. X). For thus the Holy Spirit apportioned to each as he willed. The inkhorn at the back signifies the bond of death, which Christ himself fastened to the cross in the Passion. He saw gold at the breasts who acknowledged in the word of preaching the wisdom of God and the power of God. He saw gold at the loins who recognized him lying in the tomb through the frailty of our flesh and shining in the resurrection through the power of divinity. He had gold at the breasts in preaching, the writer’s inkhorn at the loins in the Passion, and fine gold at the loins in the Resurrection.

It follows:

“And his body was like chrysolite.”

The body of Christ is understood in two ways, because by “body” either the Church is sometimes signified, or the flesh assumed from the Virgin. [Col. 0589C] That flesh is rightly compared to chrysolite. Chrysolite is a precious stone, produced in Ethiopia, effective against serpents and nighttime terrors; it is green in colour, like the sea, gleaming with gold, and sparkling like fire. Therefore Christ’s body is fittingly compared to chrysolite: as chrysolite is in Ethiopia and light is in darkness, so Christ is in the world. He is the cornerstone, for joining the two walls and striking the erected statue. He prevailed against serpents when he overcame the devil and his thoughts. Hence Moses raised up the serpent on a pole in the wilderness, as a sign of Christ hanging on the cross (Num. XXI), so that through it the people of God might escape the bites of serpents.

Christ was fittingly compared to green chrysolite in preaching, for he was like a cut tree that became green and whose leaf did not fall. He was like the sea in the Passion, when, sweating blood, his soul was sorrowful unto death. He also sparkled like fire through the miracles outwardly displayed to the peoples. He was like gold when he shone in the Resurrection through the power of divinity. Thus he was green in preaching, sparkling like fire in the display of miracles, like the sea in the Passion, and gleaming with gold in the Resurrection.

But if by this man’s body you understand the Church, it is compared to green chrysolite in virgins, like the sea [Col. 0590A] in martyrs, sparkling like fire in preachers, and gleaming with gold in the citizens above.

It follows:

“And his face was like the appearance of lightning.”

Knowledge is in the face, as in: “You shall see his face in joy” (Job XXXIII). This will indeed be then, when what the Apostle preaches is fulfilled: “Then I shall know as I also am known” (I Cor. XIII). The nature of lightning and fire is to illuminate, dry, enliven, kindle, and strengthen. Thus his face is rightly said to be like lightning, because knowledge of God illuminates through faith, dries through the exclusion of evils, enlivens through hope, kindles through fervour, and strengthens through charity.

It follows: “And his eyes were like a burning lamp.” By Christ’s eyes are signified either wisdom itself, by which he searches hearts and reins, or the order of those who shine in the Church with the light of truth. Hence Wisdom itself says: “My eye has grown dim through indignation” (Job XVII). Christ’s eyes are fittingly compared to a burning lamp, because just as the glass visibly appearing on the outside of a lamp cannot resist the brightness of the fire burning within, so the glass of our frailty cannot withstand the wisdom of God, which foreknows all things.

It searches the reins and hearts, for it knows all things before they come to pass. But if holy preachers are denoted by the eyes of Christ, they are rightly compared to a burning lamp: although outwardly, through the glass of frailty, they appear corruptible, inwardly they are nevertheless enriched with the oil of charity and burn with the fire of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0590C] It follows: “And his arms, and what is below down to his feet, were like the appearance of glowing bronze.” Observe the mystery of the cross according to the simple sense of the letter. Christ’s arms, and what was below them down to the feet, had the appearance of glowing bronze when, fastened to the cross, he chose rather to die than to bend: for glowing bronze can sooner be broken than bent. So also one who is fastened to a cross, though he moves his head, cannot move his arms or what is below them. Or indeed, the arms signify whatever faithful persons in the Church are active or subject to authority. They rightly bear the appearance of glowing bronze, because they preserve the faith not so much with the mouth as with the heart. For faith is effective through love. Bronze, inasmuch as it is resonant, signifies confession [Col. 0590D] by the mouth; inasmuch as it glows, it shows fervour of heart. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom. 10). It follows:

“And his voice was like the voice of a multitude.” Christ’s voice signifies preaching. [Note: [Col. 0589D] This alludes to 2 Kings [4 Kings] 13.] For he is the one who, slaying the wicked with the rod of his mouth, struck the ground five times—or, rather, six times—in order to destroy Syria. He struck five times when he gave the Law; but six times when he divided the Law into six distinctions. For in the Law one utterance of God is contained in justifications, such as that by which a leper or a menstruous woman is cleansed; another in judgments, by which we are commanded to exact eye for eye, [Col. 0591A] tooth for tooth; another, content with the plainness of the letter, is set down as a kind of interruption, so that the coverings of the sacraments may be concealed by it; another in counsels, whence the Lord Jesus answered the young man asking about salvation: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor” (Matt. 19). This was a counsel, not a commandment. Another is in prohibitions, as there: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20); another, again, in commandments. Thus you have: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6).

Or certainly, he struck the earth six times with the dart of his mouth when his voice thundered over the waters; when his voice was in power, in magnificence, in the breaking of cedars, in cutting off the flame of fire, in shaking [Col. 0591B] the wilderness, and in unveiling the thickets (Ps. 28). For he is the one upon whom the sevenfold Spirit rested. By the spirit of fear he subdued the flood of our frailty as waters; by the spirit of piety his voice was in power; by the spirit of knowledge his voice was in magnificence, because through teaching he shone forth gloriously among the nations; by the spirit of fortitude his voice broke the cedars, when by the power of his divinity he humbled the glorious ones of the earth; by the spirit of counsel he cut off the flame of fire, when by the counsel of his consolation he interrupted the heat of temptation; by the spirit of understanding he shook the wilderness, when he converted the Gentiles to faith through the compunction of devotion; by the spirit of wisdom he unveiled the thickets, when through wisdom [Col. 0591C] he opened to us the mysteries of the sacraments. Therefore his voice was like the voice of a multitude when he subdued the flux of the flesh and opened to us the inward parts of his mercy; when he appeared glorious through teaching, humbled the proud, called the Gentiles, overcame temptations, and revealed the sacraments of the Church. These are the wings of the cherubim, which the holy man heard striking one against another (Ezek. 1).

## SERMON IV. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

“Lift yourself up; arise; sit down, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. 52). “For now it is the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13): from that sleep, I mean, in which one who sleeps neither sees nor feels anything; or, if he sees, does not understand what he sees; [Col. 0591D] or certainly, if he understands, forgets and neglects it. When the Lord said, “Lazarus our friend sleeps” (John 11), this was said of that sleep in which nothing is seen or felt. The Apostle exhorts us to rise from this sleep when he says: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5).

The second kind of sleep is figured in Nebuchadnezzar’s sleep: having seen the statue, he neither remembered nor understood it (Dan. 2). The third is figured in the sleep by which the disciples were weighed down, when the Lord, drawing near to his passion, said to them: “Could you not watch with me for one hour?” (Matt. 26). They saw what Jesus had foretold them, saying: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man [Col. 0592A] will be delivered over” (Matt. 16), and they understood it. Thus Peter answered: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen” (ibid.). Yet when the passion was imminent, oppressed by the sleep of sloth, they did not remember his word. Hence, when during the passion the Lord had said to Peter, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matt. 26), and Peter, understanding the word, replied, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (ibid.), he is questioned, denies him, and the cock crows. Then the Lord looked upon Peter, and Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken to him (Luke 22). Had he not understood, he would not have answered; and had he not forgotten, he would not have remembered.

Thus the pagan is benumbed by the first sleep, the Jew by the second, the false Christian by the third. For the pagan neither sees by reading, nor understands, nor [Col. 0592B] recalls the power of God’s word. The Jew sees by reading, but does not understand or recall; the false Christian sees and understands, but forgets and neglects. The first sleep benumbs the person who believes neither God, nor that God exists, nor in God; the second, the person who believes that God exists, but believes neither God nor in God; the third, the person who believes both God and that God exists, but does not believe in God. The first sleep, therefore, is ignorance; the second, unbelief; the third, dullness and sloth.

If, then, you wish to dwell in the vision of peace—for Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace”—and to see good days (Ps. 33), lift yourself from the sleep of ignorance, you pagan; lift yourself from the sleep of unbelief, you Jew; arise from the sleep of dullness and sloth, you false Christian. For one who lies down, prostrate in the depths, cannot [Col. 0592C] behold things far off, but looks only upon things near at hand. Hence those who performed abominations in the midst of Jerusalem—when they set up at the door of the tabernacle the idol of jealousy to provoke jealousy, when they worshipped images, mourned Adonis, and, with their backs turned toward the Temple, worshipped toward the rising of the sun—are said each to lie in the secret place of his chamber (Ezek. 8). Thus the Lord says to the prophet: “Surely you have seen, son of man, what these men do in darkness, each in the secret place of his chamber” (ibid.).

Because they lay down, therefore, they opened their eyes to things that were near. For what can be more present and, so to speak, nearer [Col. 0592D] than popular favour, love of the world, love of carnal desire, contempt of God, and the beginning of unbelief? He sets up the idol of jealousy at the door of the tabernacle who outwardly, in the sight of men, displays an appearance of zeal; and this appearance indeed provokes God to anger. For by the door of the tabernacle is figured the sight of the people; by the idol of jealousy, the appearance of zeal. He worships images who desires the things that are in the world; for the things that are in the world are like pictures, because they appear to be something when they are nothing. There are certain things which appear to be, yet are not—for example, present things. Thus Paul, arguing from the greater, says: “If anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. 6). Since he said that a human being is nothing, he plainly showed [Col. 0593A] that other things made for humankind are nothing. Hence Isaiah also says: “All things are before him as though they were not” (Isa. 40). But certain things are and do not appear to be, namely eternal things.

Those mourn Adonis who grieve because they cannot fulfil the desires of the flesh. For there are some who, though crucified to the world, do not wish the world to be crucified to them. These seek the pleasures of the world; but when they cannot have them, they grieve and groan, and then, as it were, mourn Adonis. For Adonis, Venus’s lover and the tinder of pleasure, signifies pleasure itself. Those have their backs turned toward the Temple who, despising the Creator, render undue honour to the creature. Since, therefore, these are the deeds of those who lie in the secret place of their chamber, you who lie [Col. 0593B] in the depths, lift yourself up.

For as long as the living creatures lower their wings, the wheels must also be lowered; because as long as the motions of the soul are bent toward earthly things, thought must be lowered and reflection must turn about in the depths. We appropriately compare the motions of the soul to the living creatures, and thought to the wheels.

For just as there were four living creatures—of which the first was like a human being, the second an ox, the third a lion, and the fourth an eagle (Ezek. 1)—so too in the soul there are four motions which prefigure the appearance of the four living creatures. The first is the motion of reason, rightly attributed to the human being, because reason properly belongs to the human being alone. The second motion is that of sense-perception, which we rightly compare to the ox. For just as the ox is slower among those four living creatures, so among the motions of the soul [Col. 0593C] sense-perception is found slower in considering. Through the other motions, indeed, both things not present and things present are seen; but sense-perception considers only those things which lie before bodily eyes. The third motion of the soul is avidity, which we rightly compare to the lion, because the lion is a ravenous animal. The fourth motion of the soul is devotion of heart, which we rightly assign to the eagle: for just as the eagle is found swifter than the other animals and can proceed higher, so devotion can fly higher than the other motions of the soul; and just as the eagle has clearer eyes than the other animals, so through devotion we discover more clearly the things we seek.

And indeed, wherever reason is directed, [Col. 0593D] sense-perception is fixed, avidity snatches away the mind, or devotion flies, there reflection must direct itself and thought must turn. Since thought, or reflection, is never stable but always turns, it is rightly compared to a turning wheel. Thus the prophet says of those wheels: “And, while I heard, he called them ‘the turning ones’” (Ezek. 10). If, therefore, reason or sense-perception or avidity or devotion is lifted on high, thought also must be lifted on high, because when the living creatures are lifted from the earth, the wheels are lifted with them; and when they lower their wings, the wheels following them are lowered. For they lower them when they attend to earthly things.

Therefore, you who lie down and are placed in the depths, lift yourself up. Lift yourself through reflection; lift yourself through thought; lift yourself through [Col. 0594A] the practice of the active life; lift yourself also through the height of the contemplative life. For truly he is in the depths who is placed below himself. Some lie below themselves, others beside themselves, while still others are raised above themselves. Below themselves are those who in all things obey the flesh, the world, and every passing thought. Beside themselves are those who cut off pleasures and every superfluity, yet refuse to relinquish anything among necessities. Above themselves are those who abandon for God not only pleasures but often even necessities themselves. Therefore lift yourself to your own level, you who are situated below yourself, by relinquishing at least pleasures, even if you do not yet wish to relinquish necessities. Raise yourself also above yourself, so that, laying aside even necessities, you may look with thought and avidity toward him who comes to you from afar and is above you. [Col. 0594B] For one who looks from afar sees God’s power, as he says: “Looking from afar, behold, I see the power of God coming.” For the name of the Lord comes from afar, and rightly so.

Thus Abraham went out from his land and his kindred, that he might become rich among the Canaanites. Thus Elijah went out, that he might be sustained, however scantily, by a widow. Thus Jacob went out from his father’s house, that he might enjoy the inheritance of Laban’s daughters. Thus Tobit sent his son abroad, that he might be joined to Raguel’s daughter. Thus Jesus himself went forth, “for his going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18), in order that the captive daughter of Zion might be recalled to the liberty of the glory of the children of God.

“Loose, therefore, the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion.” For unless the bond of the neck is loosed, neither can the hand be put into the bosom [Col. 0594C] nor words be drawn forth outside. But when the time for the redemption of the children of Israel drew near, that they might be called from captivity in Egypt, from Pharaoh’s bondage, into the freedom and fertility of a land flowing with milk and honey, the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to Pharaoh, that he may let my people go” (Exod. 6). “But you shall speak with this sign: Put your hand into your bosom” (ibid.). This is the sign of our redemption. Unless we put our hand into our bosom, we cannot shake the neck free from beneath the yoke of the prince of darkness. For one puts his hand into his bosom who, in his deeds, has recourse to conscience. The hand signifies deeds; the bosom, conscience. No one can be freed from the bondage [Col. 0594D] of the devil who does not examine his conscience in all his deeds.

The breasts must also be drawn outward if this daughter of Zion is to be found faithful in her promises. What, then, is the daughter of Zion? The Church. And what does the Church say and promise to her bridegroom? “Let us go out into the field,” she says, “let us lodge in the villages; and there I will give you my breasts” (Song 7).

Behold, the bridegroom has gone out into the field. But for what purpose? To meditate and to give life: to meditate with Isaac—that is, to meditate thoughts of peace and not of affliction (Jer. 29)—so that there Rebecca may descend from her camel before him; or that the captive daughter of Zion may be delivered from the captivity of sins. Isaac signifies Christ, and the field the world. For the Lord went out into this field [Col. 0595A] to devise good things for us and to give life to dead bones: those bones, I mean, of which the Lord says to blessed Job in his description of Leviathan: “His bones are like pipes of bronze” (Job 40). The bones like pipes are the wise people of this age: although they have the skill of speaking well, they do not have the skill of living well. Or certainly, the dead bones are those of which the Lord says, when describing the rich man: “His bones are full of fat” (Job 21). For the rich are like bones full of fat when, fattened by riches, they oppress the poor by their strength. These bones were dead when the life of which it was said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), was not in them.

And the Lord came into the world to give life to these bones [Col. 0595B] when, by the example of his works and the teaching of his words, he called the rich and the wise to eternal life, instilling in them patience in temptation, harmony in conduct, true knowledge in teaching, restraint in religion, and devotion in the heart. For temptation is figured in the shaking; harmony in the joining of the joints; knowledge in the stretching of the skin; the principle of restraint in the binding together of the sinews; and devotion of heart in the flesh. For thus it is written in Ezekiel, that the Lord led him into a field full of dead bones, and it was said to him: “Do you think, son of man, that these bones will live?” (Ezek. 37). And behold, a shaking occurred. Afterwards each thing began to return to its own joint. Then they began to have sinews, flesh, and skin; [Col. 0595C] and then, when the spirit had been summoned from the four winds, they lived (ibid.).
