For the principle of restraint is rightly understood by the sinews. Job had placed his foot in such a sinew when he said: “You have put my foot in the sinew” (Job 3). The Lord put Job’s foot in a sinew when he bound him with the principle of his strict discipline. Devotion of heart is figured by flesh, as there: “I will take away from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11). For God gives a heart of flesh in place of a stony one when, in place of obstinacy, he bestows devotion of heart. The name “skin” signifies attention to sacred reading, as there: “Stretching out heaven like a skin” (Ps. 103).

Thus the Lord went out [Col. 0595D] into the field to give life to dead bones when he came into the world in order to summon the wise of this world and the rich to poverty of spirit. Likewise, he came to lodge in the villages when he descended into the broad expanse of this world. For when the Lord came, the world was both a field and a village: a field because of labour; a village because in it a human being could find no fortified defence against his enemy. But the Lord came and made himself a wall in the house of Israel; then Zion became the city of our strength, because our Saviour was set in her as a wall (Isa. 26). “Loose, therefore, the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion,” so that, according to your promise, you may give him your breasts. For thus you had said: “Let us go out into the field, let us lodge in the villages, and there I will give you my breasts” (Song 7).

What are [Col. 0596A] these breasts? Judaea and the Gentile world summoned together to faith. For these are the breasts of which the bridegroom says: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among the lilies” (Song 4). When Jews and Gentiles both offer the milk of sacred teaching to others and drink it themselves, they can be called the bride’s breasts. They are rightly fawns by humility, gazelles by the height of devotion, and twins by charity. They feed among the lilies by the brightness of life. Therefore, that these breasts may be drawn forth—that is, that Judaea and the Gentile world may be converted to confession of the true faith—“loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion.”

For if by the daughter of Zion we understand the Church, we rightly understand the Church’s prelates by her neck. The neck is that part of the body through which [Col. 0596B] food is conveyed from the head into the body. The food of the soul is the word of life; Christ is the head; the Church is the body. Since through prelates the word of preaching, insofar as they are divinely inspired, is spread through the body of the Church, the Church’s prelates are rightly signified by the neck of the daughter of Zion. The bonds of the neck may be called those hindrances by which prelates are prevented from profiting themselves or others as much as they wish: namely, the bitterness of temptation, the frailty of the flesh, temporal persecution, and secular occupation.

The bitterness of temptation is plainly figured in those bonds with which Joseph threatened to bind his brothers, when he said: “By Pharaoh’s life, you shall not depart; but send one of yourselves, while [Col. 0596C] you remain in bonds, until Benjamin, your youngest brother, comes; and we shall test whether what you say is true” (Gen. 42). For Joseph wished to test his brothers, not persecute them. Joseph is rightly said to bind his brothers with the bonds of temptation while they await Benjamin. For the faithful, signified by Jacob’s sons, are bound by the bitterness of sorrow—through an increase of virtues—while awaiting true hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God (Titus 2). For the more the faithful advance, the more they grieve that they cannot yet be with Christ.

Joseph signifies progress in virtues; Benjamin signifies Christ, because he is the son of the right hand, being the natural Son, while we are, as it were, of the left hand, because we are adopted sons. He is the son of the right hand because [Col. 0596D] he sits at the Father’s right hand, to whom the Father said: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). Although he is our Father through the gift of human nature, he became our brother through participation in that nature. He is rightly the youngest, because through assuming flesh he was made a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8 [citation printed as Ps. 2]). He is rightly the youngest: in whose type God raised to kingship the youngest of Jesse’s sons, namely David, from whose lineage the Lord himself chose to be born. He is rightly the youngest, who, though great, became little for us, as it is written: “A little child is born to us” (Isa. 9). Although he was the Word of the Father, he became an infant, as it is written: “You will find an infant” (Luke 2), and so forth. Although he was first of all, he became last of all. Thus Isaiah says: “And we considered him the last of men, a man of sorrows” [Col. 0597A] (Isa. 53). Likewise the Psalmist, in his person: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21).

The frailty of the flesh is quite plainly figured in those cords of sinew with which Delilah wished to bind Samson (Judg. 16). For a sinew comes from flesh and therefore signifies the hindrances of the flesh, by which one is bound as by chains, so as not to advance as much as one can, wishes, or ought. Temporal persecution is figured in those bonds with which the Lord commands Ezekiel to be bound, saying: “But you, son of man, behold, I have placed bonds upon you, and they shall bind you with them” (Ezek. 3). For the words of the prophets, and likewise their deeds, were often set before the people of Israel as an example. Thus, as a sign of the persecution by which they were to be bound and led captive in Babylon, [Col. 0597B] the prophet was bound before them, as it was said: “You are a sign to the house of Israel.”

Occupation is signified by the cord which that same Delilah braided into Samson’s hair, in order to fasten it to the ground (Judg. 16). For the hair of the head signifies the thoughts of the mind; the cord braided into the hair, the occupations of thoughts. These are fastened by a cord to the earth when, through some occupation, thoughts become entangled in earthly things. Or certainly, occupation, as blessed Gregory says in the *Moralia*, may be figured by the millstone which must be fastened to the neck of the person who causes one of God’s little ones to stumble. Let it therefore be said to the Church concerning her prelates: “Loose the bonds from your neck.” For if the Church is to be able to follow Christ, her prelates must make light both of the bitterness of temptation and the frailty [Col. 0597C] of the flesh, and also of persecution; and they must sometimes set aside temporal occupation in order to devote themselves to prayer, as it is written: “Be still, and see” (Ps. 33).

Or certainly, the neck signifies sacred utterance, as there: “Your neck is like the tower of David” (Song 4). Sacred utterance is like the tower of David when in it are found the defensive works of fortification against the fiery darts of temptations. The bonds of this neck may therefore be called those impediments which hinder the preacher of sacred utterance in speech: this is commonly caused by obscurity of words, unbelief in the hearers, fear, and the prohibition of the powerful.

Obscurity of words is signified by those bonds of which Belshazzar speaks [Col. 0597D] to Daniel, saying: “I know that you have power to interpret obscure things and to loose things bound” (Dan. 5). This is a repetition: what he first called “obscure things” he repeats when he says “things bound,” and what he first called “interpret” he repeats when he says “loose.” Unbelief in the hearers is signified in the bond by which Zechariah’s mouth was bound. Since he refused to believe the angel’s word concerning John’s birth, he heard: “You shall be silent and unable to speak” (Luke 1). But after John’s birth he believed, and at once the bond of his mouth was loosed; and he prophesied, saying, “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (ibid.), and so forth. Prohibition is signified by the bond of which it is written: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain” (1 Cor. 9), that is, you shall not forbid the word of one who works well. Let it therefore be said [Col. 0598A] to the Church’s preachers: “Loose the bonds from your neck.” As though it were plainly said: Since the things spoken concerning the Son of Man are now naked and open, let obscurity be removed, let unbelief be removed from the heart, let not the prohibition of the powerful frighten you; but “lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58), and say to the cities of Judah: “Behold your God.”

Or, because the height of pride is signified by the neck—hence the daughters of Zion were reproved by God because they walked with outstretched necks—the bonds of the neck may rightly be called those things which bind pride upon the heart so that they cannot be loosed.

There are, then, three things that bind pride upon the heart: ignorance of truth, the affection for sinning, and obstinacy of mind. A person becomes proud when he knows neither God nor himself, [Col. 0598B] when he loves to sin, and when he disregards the voice that admonishes him. Ignorance of truth is signified by the bond with which the she-ass was tied in the Temple, concerning which the Lord commanded his disciples: “Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a she-ass and a colt with her. Loose them and bring them to me” (Matt. 21). For what do we understand by the she-ass except the Gentile world, of which Isaiah says: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass the manger of its lord” (Isa. 1)? By the ox he signified the Jews; by the ass, the Gentiles. Bound by the chains of ignorance, this people did not wish to submit to God’s yoke until, loosed from the bond of ignorance through the apostles’ preaching, it was placed beneath the divine yoke.

The affection for sinning is quite plainly figured in the bonds by which Lazarus [Col. 0598C] was kept bound in the tomb. Of him the Lord also said: “Loose him and let him go” (John 11). For if Lazarus signifies the sinner, the sinner’s bond rightly signifies the affection for sinning. Through the affection for sinning, indeed, the sinner is bound by sin. We say that obstinacy of mind is figured by the bonds in which we read that four angels were bound in the great river Euphrates, as John heard one voice from the horns of the altar. For he says: “And I heard one voice from the horns of the altar crying: ‘Loose the four angels who are bound in the great river Euphrates’” (Rev. 9). What do we understand by the four angels but four kinds of temptation? We rightly say that temptations are signified by angels, [Col. 0598D] because, just as ministering spirits are sent into the world to announce the Lord’s will, so temptation is sent by the devil in order that the devil’s will may be communicated by it.

There are, therefore, four kinds of temptation. One is light and hidden, as “the terror by night”; another light and open, as “the arrow that flies by day”; another heavy and hidden, as “the business that walks in darkness”; another heavy and open, as “the noonday demon” (Ps. 90). Therefore, just as those who announce good things are called angels, temptations also can be called angels because they announce evils to us. For *angelus* means “messenger.” But those who announce good things are called *calodaemones* [good demons], whereas those who announce evil things are called *cacodaemones* [evil demons]. These angels are bound in the great river Euphrates when, in the unstable [Col. 0599A] mind, they are bound by obstinacy and hardness of mind.

Therefore let it be said: “Loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion.” For if you wish to attain the summit of contemplation—for Zion means “watching” or “contemplation”—you must first know God and then yourself; you must abandon the will to sin and soften your heart toward heavenly desire. Thus, without any hindrance, you will be able to meet him with her who cries: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1), ascending, that is, from virtue to virtue, until we see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83), that is, in the height of contemplation, aided by the grace of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0599B]

“The Word was made flesh” (John 1). We have heard a shortened word about the shortened Word. But:

> While I labour to be brief,  
> I become obscure.  
> —Horace, *Art of Poetry*, vv. 25–26

For we speak an abbreviated and obscure word concerning the abbreviated and obscure Word. But my word is obscure because it is abbreviated; that Word, however, is abbreviated because it is obscure. For it was obscure before it was abbreviated, and it was abbreviated so that it might become manifest. Before it was abbreviated, it could not be seen by the eyes of the mind; once abbreviated, it could be seen by the eyes of flesh. The Word was unshortened and could not be spoken; the abbreviated Word was, and could be spoken. Perhaps it could be said not what it was, but that it was; but it could be said not what it was, but what it was not. For God was the Word. No one can state what God is; but one can state what he is not. For negative propositions concerning God are compact [compactae]; affirmative ones are non-compact [incompactae].

Therefore, in that the Word was, no human being could utter him; but the Word was made flesh, and then became an infant. Thus he was the Word, whom no human being could utter; he was an infant, whom a human being could utter. He was the Word, whom one could not utter. These are Isaiah’s words: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). He was an infant, whom Matthew could utter when he said: “The book of the generation [Col. 0599D] of Jesus Christ” (Matt. 1). O ineffable Word and utterable infant! O ineffable Word with the Father, and utterable infant with the mother! Why is this so? Because the heavenly jubilation, the Father’s Word, can neither wholly be uttered nor wholly be kept silent. It could not be uttered because it is the Word; it ought not be silent because it is an infant.

Do you see? By proper words he is signified improperly, and by improper words properly. And because we have no proper words, let us ascend, insofar as he grants it, to knowledge of him through improper words. He is the Father’s Word; and, to speak in human usage, he is the Father’s substantial Word, the Word eternal with the Father, the indeclinable Word, of simple form, present tense, singular number, infinitive mood. Do you read and understand these things? Perhaps you say: “We read them, and we pass over not one iota [Col. 0600A] of the entire lesson; we understand them, but we have not been taught thus from Priscian’s grammatical rules.” Very well. Your reading and mine are one; but yours is learned, mine unlearned.

Although the reading is one and the same, you derive a human meaning from human words, whereas I derive a spiritual one. Therefore attend to the spiritual meaning, so that we may have one and the same understanding: mine spiritual and yours human. At the beginning I said that the Father’s Word is substantial because his Word is consubstantial with the Father. For if it were accidental, it could both be present and absent. But perhaps you say: “The Father could be absent from the Word, because the Word said, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’” (Ps. 21). We cannot deny that these words were spoken in the person of the Son. [Col. 0600B] For in the Gospel he says: “Eli, Eli, lamma sabactani?” (Matt. 27), that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Hence the Psalmist adds, in order to reinforce the argument: “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear” (Ps. 21). The Son cries that he has been forsaken by God and is not heard; therefore he has been forsaken.

You consider what was said, but not why it was said. For these are the words of the son of man who is the Son of God, who was predestined Son of God in power, so that he might be son of man and Son of God. The son of man therefore cries out that, in the passion, he was forsaken with respect to the protection of divinity, not with respect to a division of the union; for then not only did the Father forsake him, but the Son himself forsook himself. For if he had wished to defend himself as he was able, who would have accomplished our salvation? Evil will might perhaps have belonged to the devil or to the Jew, but power could not have belonged to anyone except God (Rom. 13). Hence the Son says: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19). And elsewhere: “No one takes my life from me; rather, I lay it down and take it up again” (John 10). Again, that the Word is substantial to the Father can be proved.

Therefore, from all things that were made, the Lord said, “and they were made” (John 1). Therefore he made all things through the Word. Either, then, there were two omnipotent beings, or the Father and the Word are the same. But there cannot be two omnipotent beings, because for one to be omnipotent he would necessarily have to be able to restrain the power of the other; otherwise something would be lacking to his power, and thus he would not be omnipotent. Since, therefore, there is one omnipotent being, and the Father is omnipotent, and the Word is omnipotent, the Father and the Word must be one and the same. And because they are altogether one, beyond doubt they are one God, one substance.

The Word, then, is active—not only in the things that have been made, but in the things that were to be made, before anything came to be. For just as the will of a craftsman, having before its eyes all the material of the house to be built, is directed over it and in a sense already makes it in the mind, while it determines what it will make from what; so, in the supreme craftsman, all things that were made were present, so that, just as a house to be built is first made in the craftsman’s knowledge, is made materially when stones and timbers are smoothed, and is made essentially when the smoothed materials are arranged in the structure, [Col. 0601A] so also the supreme craftsman, through the omnipotent Word, made all things: in foreknowledge he brooded over the things to be made; in matter, over things made; and in essence, over things ordered. Hence it was said, “Let it be,” and he made, and they were made (Gen. 1).

For what is it to say, “Let there be light,” except that he begot the Word in whom was the coming-to-be of light—and the Word was before anything whatever was made? Therefore, “let it be” refers to the work in foreknowledge; “he made,” to the work in matter; and “it was made,” to the work in essence. Thus what he first made, what he arranged when made, and what he set forth for human benefit—all of it existed in foreknowledge; and that foreknowledge was from eternity. From eternity, therefore, he foreknew that he would make, arrange, and set forth. Thus making, arranging, and setting forth existed eternally in God.

And just as we see that the things which are made are first made, then arranged, and finally set forth—so that the kindly presentation of things is, as it were, the beginning of human benefit; the wise ordering, the beginning of that presentation and benefit; and the composition of things, the beginning of the ordering, presentation, and benefit—so the whole flowed from the craftsman’s foreknowledge, when he proposed to compose, arrange, and set forth in this manner. Thus kindness, setting things forth, was the principle with respect to all made things; wisdom ordered those things kindly set forth; power acted through wisdom and kindness. In this way wisdom had all from power, while kindness had from both wisdom and power together. Yet although diversity appears in the operations, there was no diversity in the agent. For no craftsman differs from himself when he thinks to compose, arrange, and set forth something, although composing, arranging, and setting forth are different things. [Col. 0601C] Thus God was one before the ages: he powerfully composed all things, wisely ordered them, and kindly set them forth. Nor was power composing, wisdom ordering, and kindness setting forth anything other than the one God, who cannot be divided into parts because he is simple and is not a body; nor is anything in him imperfect, because he is wholly good.

You see, therefore, from what has been said that wisdom, power, and kindness are the same in God. Yet wisdom is from power, and kindness from both. And since we call nothing other than the Father “power,” the Son “wisdom,” and the Holy Spirit “kindness,” it can be argued from created things that [Col. 0601D] the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same—yet the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both. Although they are one, they are nevertheless distinguished by certain properties, just as it was proper to power to act, to wisdom to order, and to kindness to set forth. Yet what powerfully made was also the work of wisdom and kindness; and what kindly set forth was also the work of power and wisdom.

Hence also, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same, it was proper to the Father to be heard in the voice, proper to the Son to be baptized, and proper to the Holy Spirit to be seen in the dove (Matt. 3). Yet for the Father to be heard, the Son and Holy Spirit acted; for the Son to be baptized, the Father and Holy Spirit acted; and for the Holy Spirit to be seen [Col. 0602A] in the dove, the Father and Son acted, because the works of the Trinity are certainly inseparable.

Since, therefore, the Word is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, it is rightly called indeclinable, because it is the selfsame reality. “But you,” says the Psalmist, “are the same” (Ps. 101). Hence James says: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 1). And elsewhere:

> …Remaining steadfast, you grant all things to be moved.  
> (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, III, metrum 9)

For he who is everywhere does not change from place to place; he who always is does not change through the succession of times; he who is from eternity does not change through the varieties of ages; he who is not a body does not change through divisions of parts; he who is God does not change through alterations of rank; and he who is always [Col. 0602B] the same does not change through diversities of affections. For if he is said to have been angry (Exod. 4), or to have repented (Gen. 6), this is said figuratively, because no passion can befall God. Thus he is called angry because he punishes; he is said to repent if he destroys what he made, as one who repents is accustomed to do.

And because the one who is from the Father is one with the Father, he is rightly said to be of simple form, since he is “the brightness of glory and the figure of the Father’s substance” (Heb. 1). He is not the Father’s figure as though formed by the Father, nor a figure corresponding to the Father’s figure, as a human being is God’s image; rather, humanity is made according to God’s image. Nor is he the Father’s figure in the sense of being according to the Father’s likeness. For he does not share some likeness with the Father, because there is no participation where there is totality, nor likeness where there is identity. There is no diversity in him who says of himself: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John [Col. 0602C] 14). Therefore Father and Son are one substance, altogether one, giving form to all things; neither is formed by the other.

Consider an evident argument for this. The brightness of the sun is from the sun, not the sun from its brightness; yet the sun and the sun’s brightness emit one brightness. Is the emitted brightness different from itself? If someone asked you what shines in a house, would you not rightly answer, “the sun”? Or, if he asked again, could you not rightly say, “the brightness of the sun”? Did you speak of two brightnesses when you said “the sun” and “the brightness of the sun”? Certainly not; rather, you answered in both ways because the sun and the sun’s brightness are one brightness. Yet, as was said, the sun’s brightness is from the sun. And although it is from the sun, they are coeternal, because [Col. 0602D] brightness is never without the sun, nor the sun without brightness.

Thus, although the Son is from the Father, they are nevertheless coeternal. For this reason the present tense is also used: for with him that eternal “today” is present, knowing neither past nor future. Hence the Father says to the Son: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). This is expounded in another Psalm, where it says: “In the splendours of the saints, from the womb”—that is, from the secret place of divinity—“before the morning star I have begotten you” (Ps. 109). With him, “will be” does not exist, because he is from eternity. With him, “was” does not exist, because he cannot have an end. With him, therefore, “is” is always. For what was or will be does not exist with him, because whatever was or will be is in him.

And although unity or singularity belongs to the substance, plurality belongs to the persons, so that singularity does not confound plurality, nor does plurality render singularity separable. They are many, and not one; they are one, and not many. I say “one” from unity, not “one” from union. Three persons are one. The Trinity is worshipped; yet, because they are not different, there is no triplicity there. There is absolutely no diversity, because there is absolute unity; yet there is plurality, because the Trinity is distinct. Therefore one must not apply a division of difference, but a discrimination of distinction. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one. Yet the Father is distinguished from the Son because the Father is begetter, or unbegotten, while the Son is begotten. The Father and Son are one and the same wisdom, yet the Son is begotten wisdom and the Father unbegotten wisdom. [Col. 0603B] Begotten wisdom is not unbegotten wisdom; nevertheless, they are one wisdom.

Likewise the Holy Spirit, although he is the same wisdom as the Father and Son, is neither unbegotten wisdom nor begotten wisdom, but proceeding wisdom. Nor should we call it unbegotten, lest it seem to be the Father; nor begotten, lest it be believed to be the Son; but more safely, proceeding, so that it may be distinguished from both.

Consider, brethren, why Isaiah said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). For who can define the manner of this generation? It is without measure because it is infinite. Yet understand in human things what is hidden in divine things. Understand through something similar what is hidden in the reality itself.

Jesus said to his disciples: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have abiding life in yourselves” (John 6). This was great and salutary wisdom; and who taught Christ this? “For who has been his counsellor, and who taught him knowledge?” (Isa. 40). It was altogether untaught. John, however, bears witness to this teaching and wrote these things, insofar as he had been taught by Christ. Therefore Christ’s and John’s wisdom was one wisdom; but in Christ it was untaught, and in John taught. We see written, read, and understand what John wrote. Who taught me that wisdom? Not John, because I have never seen John, nor anyone else from John. Therefore my wisdom is not taught. Yet if Christ had not taught this wisdom to John, neither would I have possessed it. Thus, although my wisdom is not taught to me, it is nevertheless not untaught: [Col. 0603D] it was taught to John. Christ’s wisdom, John’s wisdom, and mine are one and the same wisdom; but in Christ it is untaught, in John taught, and in me in a sense neither, but proceeding, because I received this wisdom from Christ, who taught John, and from John, who wrote it.

My wisdom had its beginning from Christ and John; John’s wisdom had its beginning from Christ; Christ’s wisdom had its beginning from no one. Yet this wisdom is one and the same. Thus John’s discourse is, as it were, begotten from Christ’s discourse; Christ’s discourse is, as it were, the begetter of John’s discourse; and my discourse is, as it were, proceeding from Christ’s and John’s discourse. Yet Christ’s, John’s, and my discourse are one discourse.

You see, therefore, that some word is one and the same; and yet in one respect it is untaught, such that it cannot be called either taught [Col. 0604A] or proceeding; in another respect it is so taught that it ought not to be called untaught, because what is taught is not untaught, nor proceeding by that procession through which it proceeds in the reader. For it proceeded from Christ into John through the instruction of teaching, and from John into me through the effort of reading.

Thus Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are altogether one and the same; and yet the Father is begetter, such that he can be neither begotten nor proceeding; the Son is so begotten that he is neither begetter nor proceeding from the Father by the procession by which the Holy Spirit proceeds. For in a certain respect the Son can also be said to proceed from the Father. Hence he says: “I proceeded from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). The Son proceeds by generation; the Holy Spirit by mission. And the Father is the principle of the Son and Holy Spirit; the Son is the principle of the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit is the principle with respect to all creatures. [Col. 0604B] As if I were first to make known to you the aforesaid discourse, which John wrote and heard from Christ: my discourse would be the principle of your instruction; John’s discourse, of mine; and Christ’s discourse, of both John’s and mine—yet throughout it is one discourse.

And the Word was made flesh. The Father was not made flesh, nor was the Holy Spirit made flesh; although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, the Son alone assumed flesh. For when Christ said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” and so forth, some understood carnally; hence, scandalized, they wished to go back (John 6). They thought that they ought to eat him in the bodily form in which he was crucified, rather than in the sacrament of bread and wine. Jesus therefore said to them: “Does this scandalize you? The words that I speak to you are spirit and life” (ibid.); and he opened their understanding.

In Christ there was understanding, not carnal but spiritual; in those disciples there was both carnal and spiritual understanding. Since it was carnal, they were scandalized; and since it finally became spiritual, Peter said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6). In Christ the Word was not flesh, because flesh and blood did not reveal it to him. In the disciples the Word was, as it were, flesh. The disciple and the master were the same: but in the master it was divine only, whereas in the disciple it was both human and divine. But what was human in the disciple was from weakness; [Col. 0604D] and what was divine in him was not from himself, but from divine power. Why marvel in the Son of God, why marvel in the Word of God, when you do not marvel in this person?

For the Father and the Word are one: one God, one omnipotent being. And the Word was made flesh, but the Father was not made flesh. The Word assumed flesh and did not cease to be God, because he remained what he was and assumed what he was not. But that he assumed flesh he received from the weakness contracted from the Virgin; that he remained God he had from the same divinity of the Father, which he himself was. He himself was his own divinity, and he himself was the Father’s divinity.

Therefore, the Word, which was substantive, became adjectival by assuming flesh, because it so united flesh to itself that the union endured neither mixture [Col. 0605A] nor division. For divinity was not changed into flesh, nor flesh into divinity; nor could they be separated after the union. Yet the Son of Man was in his mother’s bosom, and the Son of God in the Father’s bosom. For although at death the soul was separated from the flesh, neither flesh nor soul could be separated from divinity, because he was wholly in hell with respect to the soul, wholly in the tomb with respect to the flesh, and wholly in heaven with respect to divinity.

When you read a book, do you not see both the parchment and the writing? There is one parchment, one writing, and one understanding arising from writing and parchment. The writing can be separated from the parchment, but the understanding cannot be erased. Such is the Word made flesh. The parchment is the flesh; the writing, the soul; the understanding, as it were, the inner word, [Col. 0605B] the Word of the Father. The soul could be separated from the flesh without the understanding of the Word departing. And this is “the Word was made flesh”: that is, God was made man. For “flesh” signifies a human being, as in: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. 52).

Moreover, in being made flesh he was abbreviated. “The Lord made an abbreviated Word upon the earth.” For he had made a lengthy discourse, burdensome and full of weariness to its hearers, in the word of the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa—“God, who spoke to the fathers in the Prophets of old in many portions and in many ways” (Heb. 1). For those then living had said: “There is no lack of one who fulfils; but there is a lack of one who commands.” Accordingly, one who commanded was not lacking, but one who fulfilled was lacking. For, in order that their pride of this kind might be rebuked, there was imposed upon them, as Peter testifies, such a yoke that neither they nor their fathers could bear (Acts 15). Therefore, at the word of one commanding, they were neither well-disposed, nor teachable, nor attentive: indeed, they were people stiff-necked, with unconquerable brow and stony heart, as the Prophet says: “They stopped their ears like deaf asps” (Ps. 57); and, murmuring against Moses, they longed for the flesh-pots which they had left in Egypt (Exod. 16).

Therefore, in order to make his hearers teachable, well-disposed, and attentive, the Lord made an abbreviated Word upon the earth. Abbreviated in the world, indeed; abbreviated in the womb; abbreviated on the cross. And, what is more wonderful, the more abbreviated the more he was extended upon the cross. He was stretched out and abbreviated; [Col. 0605D] and the more he was seen, the more he was hidden.

Therefore, from many words, whose knowledge was lengthy and incomprehensible, the wisdom of the Father selected the abbreviated Word, whose teaching is salutary and concise. For among words, one is substantive, another adjectival; one active, another passive; one deponent, another neuter. All were restored in the one Word, deponent and abbreviated. For the substantive Word is God in the Father; the adjectival Word, God in flesh; the active Word, in the creation of things; the passive Word, in the Passion; the deponent Word, in the laying down of the soul, when it was separated from the body. Hence he says: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down, and take it again” [Col. 0606A] (John 10).

Therefore that which, as we said above, was indeclinable and immovable—as it is written, “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101), and again:

> …Remaining steadfast, you grant all things to be moved.  
> (Boethius)

For he who could not be moved either in time or place nevertheless moved all things: according to time and place, in the case of bodily things; according to time but not place, in the case of spiritual things. In his abbreviation he became mobile according to distinctions of times, moods, or persons.

The present tense of his abbreviation was that fullness of time in which he made himself present to humankind. Under the time of the Law, under which he foretold the time of his coming, there was not fullness of time but imperfect time—especially because the Law brought nothing to perfection. The sacraments of the Law did not effect what they signified; they were signs of a reality, not the reality of the sign; not things signified, but signifying things. Under grace, however, the sacraments effect what they signify; all prophecy has been fulfilled; and those things said to Mary by the Lord have been perfected.

Hence this perfection was completed under the time of the sixth age, so that he might restore humanity in the sixth age, he who made it on the sixth day; and so that he who, under the perfection of the number six, completed the whole work of the first creation might show that the perfect time of human restoration had come under the perfection of the number six. [Col. 0606C] The fullness of the perfect time was completed then, when on the cross he said: “It is finished” (John 19). And just as, in the first creation, after the sixth day, he rested on the Sabbath day from all the work he had accomplished (Gen. 2), so, after this perfection of his abbreviation and our redemption, on the day of his Ascension, lifting up the eternal gates (Ps. 23), he opened for his own the entrance into an eternity more than perfect, because uncreated.

The glory of this opening will then be revealed to those set at the right hand, when the future time of the Judge arrives. From that time there will be time without end, infinite time, because it will remain without end.

Therefore, in the days of his abbreviation he chose to employ the indicative mood when he instructed his disciples; and he indicated by words and works what was useful, salutary, and necessary; the imperative mood in commands and miracles; and the optative mood in the devotion of prayer and in the desire for our salvation. He used the subjunctive mood in the union of soul and body, in the joining together of the two walls, in the bond by which he joins the lowest to the highest; and also the infinitive mood in the distribution of glory, which is bounded by no end.

But when he prepares this glory for all who follow him unto life, he uses the impersonal mood, because, whatever their sex, age, or condition, he calls all to himself, since God is no respecter of persons (Acts 10). He used the gerundive mood as a merciful physician when he himself bore our pains and carried our sicknesses (Isa. 53); and when he supports us amid harsh misfortunes and grants the grace to bear them. [Col. 0607A] He used the supine mood when he subjected himself to Mary and Joseph. Hence you have: “And he was subject to them” (Luke 2).

With regard to the person of the Word, this must be understood: just as in the doctrine of philosophical grammar we are taught that there are three persons and one verb, so in the doctrine of faith we confess three persons and one God. The incarnate and abbreviated Word did not cease to be what it was, but began to be what it was not. It did not cease to be God and one substance with the Father; nor did it cease to be a person other than the Father. But in its abbreviation it was the same God, the same substance which then was a person not altered, but other than the Father. Hence the Apostle says: “Who was predestined Son of God in power” (Rom. 1). He was predestined in the power [Col. 0607B] of God so that, being Son of God, he might be Son of Man.

And although in his majesty he was, as has been said, of simple form—for even if someone is called the figure of God because he was made according to God’s figure, this one is uniquely the figure of the Father, as the Apostle says: “Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. 1)—yet he is not figure in the sense of corresponding to a figure, because he wholly fills the Father’s figure; but he is in no respect dissimilar or unequal. Nor is he similar by participation in likeness or equality, but is that very thing which the Father is, by reason of identity. In the abbreviated Word, however, the figure of man was outwardly manifest; but the figure of God—neither other than God—lay hidden within. And there was one person: man manifest, God hidden.

[Col. 0607C] What then? Shall we say that this abbreviated Word was of composite form? But on this point we reserve a definitive judgment for those who, relying on the authority of John Chrysostom, say that this man consists not only of a rational soul and flesh, but of human and divine nature—that is, of three substances: divinity, flesh, and soul. They confess this Christ to be only one person: before the Incarnation simply one, but by the Incarnation made composite from divinity and humanity; and therefore not a different person from what he was before. Hence John says: “In our Lord Jesus Christ we acknowledge two natures, but one hypostasis composed from both.”

We reserve this judgment for them because others [Col. 0607D] contradict them. In the Incarnation of the Word they deny not only that a person is composed from natures, but even deny that any human being or any substance composed or made from soul and flesh exists there. Rather, they say that those two things, soul and flesh, are one with the person or nature of the Word in such a way that no soul, substance, or person is made or composed from those two or from those three—rather, that the Word of God is clothed in those two as if in a garment, so as to appear suitably to mortal eyes; not that those two, or anything composed from them, are one person with the Word. Hence the Apostle says: “And, found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2).

In discussing this apostolic expression, Augustine plainly shows that God is said to have been made man, or to be man, according to appearance. On account of matters of this kind, our blindness does not presume to enter so difficult a path without a guide. Yet this we can say: when he had neither form nor beauty, but appeared as a leper and as one struck by God and humbled (Isa. 53), the figure of God seemed emptied, and the figure of man appeared misshapen and disfigured—bloodied, smeared with spittle, made pale by blows, blackened by death. [Col. 0608A]

But because he deigned to endure all these things for us—he who so abbreviated himself, so inclined himself, and, if I may say so, disfigured himself, indeed even emptied himself (Phil. 2)—let us, dearest brethren, after his example abbreviate the pride of our arrogance; turn aside from the counsel of those at play; disfigure with the pallor of fasting our wanton comeliness; and empty the wantonness of flesh and manners, so that, conformed in all things to the abbreviated Word, we may preserve the outwardly deformed form of man and the inwardly beautiful form of God. Yet this is by his help, without which we can do nothing, nor ought to do anything—indeed, through whom all things are and do not cease to be made.

For although he was abbreviated in the world, he nevertheless reigned in heaven ever measureless without measure, and great without magnitude; for his power was not diminished when he suffered, nor his greatness when he was abbreviated. Subject in the form of a servant, he reigned as God in the form of God, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0608C]

“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). Because, brethren, today we have seen wonders: he who is measureless without measure lies small in a manger; he who is the Word has become an infant, and the Wonderful Counsellor is without speech; the uncontainable one, enclosed within a small place in the womb. Therefore we have not judged it unfitting to speak small things concerning the great, human things concerning God; to be still and see how wonderful God is in his work.

For God, mindful of ancient wonders and neither less powerful in the truth of the sign nor in the thing signified, revealed in the true sign and in the signifying reality what he had prefigured. The rod blossomed without a root (Num. 17); the fleece became wet while the ground was dry with drought (Judg. 6); the bush shone with fire without being consumed (Exod. 3): thus the Virgin gave birth without seed. The heavens dropped dew upon the fleece of flesh; the bush of mortality shone with the immortality of God.

Be still, therefore, and see how wonderful God is. Be still from servile work, and see the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. 8). For unless you remove the blearedness from your eyes, you cannot behold the true sun; unless you close the eyes of the flesh, you cannot open the eyes of the mind. God closed Paul’s outer eyes, which were open, in order to open his inner eyes, which were closed (Acts 4). Thus Job, in order to keep the eyes of his heart open, made a covenant with his eyes not even to think of a virgin (Job 31).

Be still, therefore, from transient things and see eternal things; be still from [Col. 0609A] low things and see the things above; be still from the world and be still for God; be still through the leisure of reading, and see with the eyes of attention; be still by reading, and see by understanding. For the *Book of the Generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham* is openly set before us for understanding.

And rightly so: for the walls of Jerusalem have been restored, the strength of its enemies has ceased, its gates have been built, and the bars of its gates strengthened (Ps. 147); and in the seed of Abraham her children have been blessed within her. Certainly her walls have been rightly restored, because the Saviour has been placed in her as a wall (Isa. 26). The strength of the enemies ought rightly to cease, because David has entered into single combat against the Philistine (1 Sam. 17).

Therefore, just as those who lived under Nehemiah and Ezra did, so let us do, my brethren, who are children of the heavenly Jerusalem. For all these things were written for our instruction and done for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10). We read that, after Jerusalem had been rebuilt and the enemies’ destruction had ceased, Ezra took the book of the Law and read from it before the children of Israel for open understanding (2 Esdr. 8).

Thus God the Father, in the rebuilding of the Jerusalem above, which is our mother (Gal. 4), opened for us that book which Isaiah saw sealed (Isa. 29). John also saw in this same book seven seals, which no one could loose until the Lamb who was slain was found worthy to open it (Rev. 5). Therefore, since that Lamb who was silent before the one shearing him and did not [Col. 0609C] open his mouth (Isa. 53) came to remove the seven seals from the book—when, that is, he chose to be born, to be subject, to suffer our passions without sin, to be tempted, to fast, to die, and to bite hell—we ought not without reason to devote ourselves to reading, since we see all these things naked and open.

Formerly Isaiah saw him, but the ancients could not yet be still. For the book was offered both to one who knew letters and to one who did not, and they could not read it (Isa. 29), for it was sealed with seven seals (Rev. 5). Today, however, we see the book so open that both one who knows letters and one who does not can find and understand what is useful, honourable, and necessary. “Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of this book, and keeps the things written in it” (Rev. 1).

For nothing superfluous is written in it that might be cut away; nothing is said too little that ought to be added; nothing is ill said that ought to be corrected. Rather, all is useful, so that hearers may be well-disposed; all is brief, so that they may become more attentive. “The Lord has made for us an abbreviated Word upon the earth” (Isa. 10). Formerly God wrote us a book in which, under many words, he comprehended one thing; today he opened us a book in which, under one Word, he enclosed many things. For whatever had been written concerning the Son of God in the ancient books beneath the coverings of words has been explained entirely in the Word of this book. “God, who spoke to the fathers of old in many portions and in many ways through the Prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1), that is, in his Word.

[Col. 0610A] This scroll, then, is that scroll which became sweet as honey in the prophet’s mouth; for he says: “And he fed me with that scroll, and it became sweet as honey in my mouth” (Ezek. 3). But what is this book? There is a book great in its outward surface but small in meaning, because the Law brought nothing to perfection (Heb. 7). There is a book that has nothing burdensome on its outward surface but is great in meaning. And there is a book greatest in its outward surface and incomprehensible in understanding. “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11).

He himself is the book that has flesh in place of parchment and the Word of the Father in place of writing. Therefore, the book great in its outward surface and small in meaning is the Law, or this world, which is written outwardly through the forms of things and inwardly through their natures. It is like a book unrolled by the revolution of times and days. The book that has nothing burdensome upon its surface and is great in meaning is the human conscience—a great book, I say, written by the stylus of humanity. The stylus of humanity is the defectibility of human nature. This book is written outwardly by considering visible things, inwardly by considering eternal things. This book is greater than the first, for it can comprehend both the things that are in the world and those that are outside the world.

But above all is that book which comprehends both what is in the world and what can exist in conscience. Hence it is said: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book” (Ps. 138). Yet the Word comprehends other things also, [Col. 0610C] things that do not rise into the human heart. “Eye has not seen, nor has it risen into the human heart, the things which those who study in him will know” (1 Cor. 2).

To explain briefly, the greatest book is the incarnate Son, because just as, through writing, a word is united with parchment, so through the assumption of humanity the Word of the Father is united with flesh. Since, therefore, he is the one who received from the Father all authority of judgment—for “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5)—he is fittingly figured in that scroll in which lamentations, a song, and woe are written (Ezek. 2).

And because of the two things that the prophet David heard, namely power and mercy (Ps. 61), by which he renders to each according to his works (Rom. 2), this scroll became sweet as honey in the mouth of this prophet (Rev. 10). For in this scroll are written lamentations for those placed in the world; songs for those raised to heaven; and woe for those condemned in hell. Or, lamentations for those who advance in the active life; song for those who advance in the contemplative life; and woe for those who advance in neither.

Just as a cup is said to be in his hand, full of mixed wine and dregs, because its dregs have not been emptied out (Ps. 74), so we say that a scroll is in his bosom, in which lamentations, a song, and woe are written. These correspond in the lamentation to the mixed wine; in the song to the wine; and in the woe to the loss occasioned by the dregs. And we rightly say that this book is in the Father’s bosom, because we know that the Son descended into the Virgin’s womb. [Col. 0611A]

Let us therefore apply ourselves to the lamentations through the observance of commandments, endurance of temptations, and exercise of labours; to the songs through the grace of devotion and the joy of promise; and to the woe through fear of human failure and grief at the divine threat. For if we fear because of the threat in such a way that we rejoice because of the promise, we shall not fail amid labour or temptation. Let us therefore apply ourselves to the book in which lamentations, songs, and woe are written, first considering what is the matter of this book, what its intention is, what is the cause of that intention, what its usefulness is, what its mode of treatment is, and what its title is.

Matter is matter that gives material form to all things, or matter that is given form, or that which is one thing composed of formed matter and formative matter. Formed matter is the flesh assumed from the [Col. 0611B] Virgin; formative matter is the divinity that assumes it; the matter composed of the formed and the formative is the one person constituted from flesh and God. Hence in the book of the Law or the Prophets the Son sometimes speaks insofar as he is man, sometimes insofar as he is God; very often the whole Christ speaks.

The intention, moreover, is to enrich the poor, to lead the exiled back to their homeland; to bring slaves to freedom, sinners to pardon, and the condemned to everlasting glory. For like a wise woman he lights a lamp, that he may illumine those in darkness and recover the lost drachma (Luke 15). Like the angel of Tobit, he comes to offer himself as companion to one journeying (Job 5), and descends with the three youths into the furnace of the world (Dan. 3). Like the Samaritan, he poured heavenly ointment in the manger upon the half-dead man [Col. 0611C] whom the Levite and priest had despised (Luke 10); and like Elisha he bent himself over the son of the Shunammite, whom the staff sent by Gehazi had been unable to help (4 Kings 4). O merciful intention, not cruel; voluntary, not compelled by necessity. He who thus intends has not been disappointed of his hope, he who waited in expectation. “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me” (Ps. 39). Let us hope in him, brothers, and wait, because he who attends to us, when he comes to us, will also attend to us when he saves us. For in all these things his love has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out (Isa. 9). He attends to us by coming to us in grace and humility; he will attend to us by coming to us in glory and majesty. He attends to [Col. 0611D] us by promising glory; he will attend to us by bestowing it.

The cause of so great and such an intention was, on the one hand, the fall of the wretch; on the other, the misery of the fallen; on the one hand, the singular love bestowed upon the miserable in heart; on the other, the manifold misery in the lover; on the one hand, the omnipotence of the giver; on the other, the generosity of the Omnipotent One. By these six steps Solomon ascended to the ivory throne, because for these six reasons Christ willed to be incarnate of the Virgin, whose womb, by reason of her virginity, became an ivory throne. For our true Solomon came to sit upon this throne when his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal (Song 3). For as a crown befits a king, so too does a throne. The crown is upon the head: an ordered union of affections in [Col. 0612A] the mind; the throne is the virginal womb. He came to sit upon the throne on the day of his espousal when he united divinity to flesh. Of this throne we read that King Solomon made for himself a great throne of ivory, and that it was approached by six steps (3 Kings 10). In the throne, as I have said, the Virgin’s womb is signified; in Solomon, Christ; and in the six steps, the six causes of the Incarnation. And rightly we say that Christ is figured by Solomon, because he is the one who made peace for those far off and for those near (Eph. 2): peace for Jews and peace for Gentiles, peace for angels and human beings, because he is the one who joined the two together, dividing the wall of partition (ibid.); at whose death the veil was torn, so that the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies might be one. Hence he is compared with Solomon, because Solomon [Col. 0612B] means “peaceful.” The discussion of the usefulness follows.

Wonderful and admirable is the benefit by which eternal delight and delightful eternity will be restored to us: there joy without sorrow, rest without labor; there no fear in the lesser, no exaction in the greater, no rancor of envy in peace. There all shall possess Solomon in wisdom, Moses in gentleness, Asahel in swiftness, Samson in strength, Caesar in power, Absalom in beauty, Noah in justice. There the lame shall leap like a stag (Isa. 35); there the blind shall see like a panther. There the slave shall possess nothing apart from freedom, nor the minor heir anything in common with a slave (Gal. 4); but there shall be free and slave, small and great, lion and lamb (Isa. 2), and this little child, who is born today, shall feed [Col. 0612C] them as the good shepherd (Isa. 9).

I have said much, and said nothing: I have spoken as if stammering, like a child striving to speak and unable. For what comparison is there between temporal glory and everlasting glory? They do not share the same kind of excellence. These things are transitory; those eternal. These are earthly; those heavenly. These may be present and absent; but those, since they are all things to all, can never be lacking. For just as there can be no agreement of Christ with Belial, or of light with darkness (2 Cor. 6), so there is no comparison between present justice, wisdom, gentleness, swiftness, strength, power, and beauty, and those to come. In comparison with that, all our justices are as though they did not exist, and are like the cloth of a menstruous woman (Isa. 64), so are they before [Col. 0612D] God. Likewise, wisdom compared with that wisdom is madness; gentleness is the cruelty of Herod; swiftness is what an eagle is to a tortoise, and the swiftness of the moon compared with the sluggishness of Saturn. Strength is the utmost weakness, power poverty, beauty the ugliness of an ape. I have said much, and said nothing. And how could I say what I did not know? And how could I know what cannot enter the human heart? “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2). But I have said these things in order to give you an occasion for reflection, so that by means of them you might believe in things much better.

The manner of treating so great and such a mystery was as follows:

First of all, the angel Gabriel was sent by God [Col. 0613A] into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the Virgin’s name was Mary (Luke 1:2). But the Virgin, when greeted, is troubled; being troubled, she conceives, becomes pregnant, and gives birth. Thus the heavenly physician healed the disease inflicted on us by the ancient enemy, partly through likenesses and partly through unlikenesses. For at the beginning of our condemnation the serpent was sent by the devil into the place called Paradise, to a woman betrothed to a man whose name was Adam, of the house of God; and the woman’s name was Eve. But the woman, deceived, rejoices; rejoicing, consents; consenting, acts (Gen. 3). Thus the former was the beginning of our salvation, when she was greeted by an angel; the latter, of condemnation, when she was deceived by a serpent. The former, troubled, conceived the common joy; the latter, rejoicing, consented—not, I say, to her own disturbance, but rather to ours. The former gave birth to the author of life; the latter to the fuel of eternal death.

Therefore God willed to become Son of Man, that human beings might be sons of God; he willed to labor and suffer, that human beings might enjoy rest; he willed to be mortal, that mortals might be unable to die. He gave us what was his, that we might give him what was ours. That human beings might be with God, Emmanuel came. For what is Emmanuel? “God with us.” God came among human beings, that human beings might be with God, as Jeremiah testifies when he says: “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He showed all his way to Jacob, and to Israel his servant. After these things he was seen upon earth and conversed [Col. 0613C] with human beings” (Baruch 3). Therefore, because he came to human beings in order to save Jews and Gentiles, and those who are from Jews and Gentiles; to cleanse the defiled; to separate sheep from goats; rejecting the goats and ruling the faithful—rightly the title of the cause was written in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19). Jesus means “Savior”; Nazarene, “one who cleanses” or “separates”; Jew, “confession” or “one confessing.” And he is rightly called Savior, because although we read of many saviors—as in the book of Judges, where we read that the Lord sent them a savior (Judg. 3), and as the Egyptians said to Joseph, “Our salvation is in your hand” (Gen. 47)—yet he could be called Savior in the preeminent sense, since he supplied salvation not so much for beasts as for human beings, not so much gracious as glorious. They could save beasts, not human beings, and therefore supplied temporal, not eternal, salvation. But he bestowed salvation not so much upon bodies, which are like beasts, as upon souls, which we compare with human beings; not so much the favor of this time as the glory of eternal salvation. For he will conform not only souls, but also the body of our humiliation to the body of his glory.

Let us therefore, brothers, apply ourselves to this book, possessing the same matter that is in the book; having no other intention, nor another cause of intention; seeking the same benefit; and let us maintain in our study the method which he kept, that we may rejoice in him who was written for us. For all labor of study [Col. 0614A] is carried on by thinking, speaking, or acting. If, therefore, you think, speak, or do anything that differs from the law of the Lord, you have gone beyond the matter of this book. Likewise, if in your work, thought, or speech you aim at anything other than refreshing the poor, clothing the naked, showing compassion to travelers, and suffering for the brethren, you have departed from the intention of the book. But if, in this good intention itself, you have some cause of intention other than piety and love of the Omnipotent, you are removed from the cause of the intention. For it often happens that the intention of a good act is good, while the cause of the intention is not good. If someone zealously intends to conduct the just cause of a widow, not indeed from the affection of piety or compassion, but for the sake of some temporal gain, his intention is good, [Col. 0614B] but the cause of his intention is not good.

Likewise, you must imitate the same cause of usefulness that is found here. When you intend to do something well from the affection of piety, seek no other benefit than to obtain thereby everlasting glory. For it often happens that human favor or temporal recompense is sought for a good deed. You must also imitate the manner of acting, so that you may not be proud of a good deed, but rather be humbled. For everyone who rightly considers his own frailty ought to wonder how he can do good even for a moment. He ought likewise to be troubled lest perhaps the power to do good has been granted for this reason: that, when he has become less cautious, he may be attacked more fiercely by the enemy. For the devil often ceases from his vexation [Col. 0614C] in order to render unwary the person he seeks to overthrow. You must therefore be troubled in such a way that you do not cease doing good. Fear is never evil except when it is excessive. The Virgin, troubled, conceived, became pregnant, and gave birth. She gave you an example, that you should be troubled by fear, yet conceive in thought, become pregnant in love, and give birth in delight through the working of salvation. But of what salvation? Not of the body, but of the soul. For one ought not to work out the salvation of the body, because “he who hates his soul,” that is, his life, “in this world, keeps it unto eternal life” (John 12).

Behold, brothers, the teaching of heaven; behold, the school of the Savior; the study of the sons of God. These things are written in the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, and must be written for us [Col. 0614D] in the great book. For it is written: “Let these things be written for another generation” (Ps. 101). Which other generation? What is the first, of which this is the other? The first generation is the generation of the first Adam, who is earthly, from the earth: that is, the generation of Cain, the generation of Esau, the seed of Canaan and not of Judah, the brood of vipers (Matt. 3), a perverse and provoking generation, a generation that did not direct its heart aright, and whose spirit was not faithful with God (Ps. 77). It studies and aims always, not in the book in which the generation of Christ studies, which is the book of the generation of Jesus. For this generation too has its own book: it has wickedness for its matter, blasphemy for its word, evil will for its intention, the vanity of the world for the cause of its intention, and momentary pleasure of the flesh for its usefulness. Concerning the manner of that pleasure, we have judged it both useful for ourselves and fitting for you to pass over in silence. For the Apostle says that such things should not even be named among us (Eph. 5), and blessed Benedict does not permit the mouth of a disciple to open to such speech (Rule, ch. 6).

But the other generation is the generation of the second Adam, who is heavenly, from heaven (1 Cor. 15): the generation of those who seek the Lord; which is innocent and clean of heart (Ps. 17), meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. 1), studies and aims at the exercise of righteousness, the salvation of the soul, the ordering of the mind, contempt of the world, and the praise of God. His praise and the honor of his dominion remain without end, unto age upon age. Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON THE SAME FEAST

[Col. 0615B]

“In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne; and the whole earth was full of his majesty,” etc. Blessed are the eyes that see what you see (Isa. 6). For many prophets rejoiced in the shadow of the thing whose fulfillment in truth you see. Hence the Lord, speaking to the Jews, says: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and rejoiced” (Luke 10). When did he see it? When he saw three angels in the figure of the Trinity (Gen. 18). Therefore he saw not the thing itself, but a figure of the thing, and rejoiced. Likewise Isaiah saw in figure the day of the Lord’s Incarnation, and rejoiced when he said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (John 8). And lest he should doubt the vision, the fullness of time in which the vision was to be fulfilled was likewise shown to him in a figure. Hence he says: “In the year in which King Uzziah died.”

For Uzziah was king of the Jewish people. He therefore saw a figure of that time in which the Jewish kingdom came to an end, since all these things were shown to him in figure. For when the kingdom of Judaea finally took its leave, the Messiah who was to be sent arrived, according to the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 40); and this came to pass. For about four hundred and seventy-five years and three months elapsed from the return from Babylonian captivity, during which the Jewish kingdom had been interrupted, until Aristobulus, surnamed John, son of Hyrcanus, placed the diadem upon himself. He had no sons, but brothers; one of these, Antigonus, he killed, while he committed the others to prison. After him his elder brother, the most wicked Alexander, was raised to power by Aristobulus’s wife, because in six years he killed fifty thousand elders for detesting his crimes. But when he was struck by fever and died, his son Hyrcanus succeeded to the substance, though not to the name, of the kingdom; Pompey declared him high priest. Later Pachorus, king of the Parthians, handed him over to Antigonus, who mutilated his ears, and was raised to the kingdom through Pachorus. But when Pachorus had seized Hyrcanus together with Phasael, Herod’s brother, Herod fled to his fellow-tribesmen, the Idumaeans [Col. 0616A]—that Herod the Idumaean who was called the Ascalonite—who succeeded Antigonus in the kingdom. For after Antigonus, who during Herod’s lifetime had been raised to the kingdom by Pachorus, no Jew reigned.

Hence Josephus (*Antiquities*, XVIII, ch. e), a trustworthy historian of that period, gives this testimony concerning Christ:

> “At the same time there was Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is lawful to call him a man; for he was a worker of marvelous deeds and a teacher of those who gladly hear what is true. He joined to himself many Jews and many from among the Gentiles. He was the Christ. When Pilate, at the accusation of the leading men of our nation, had decreed that he should be put to death on the cross, those who had loved him from the beginning did not abandon him. For he appeared to them alive again, as the prophets had foretold these and other things that were to happen concerning him. And to this day both the name and the race of Christians, who are named from him, endure.”

Since, therefore, the anointing ceased, let them say with us that the Messiah came, and that he came at the time when, after the kingdom of Antigonus, who was of the Jewish race, had ended, the kingdom was transferred to Herod, a foreigner. In the anguish attending the Lord’s birth, he killed all the boys in Jewish Bethlehem who were two years old and under (Matt. 2).

Although what was said, “In the year in which King Uzziah died,” may be understood otherwise. For this Uzziah, at the beginning of his reign, did what was pleasing before the Lord: he defeated enemies, made the Ammonites tributary to himself, and rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem which Joash king of Israel had destroyed. But when he had become rich in mortal possessions, he grew proud against the immortal God. For on the feast of propitiation, clothed in a high-priestly robe, he entered the temple to offer incense, though the high priest Azariah, with eighty priests, forbade him. Therefore an earthquake occurred, the brightness of the sun shining more than usual struck the king’s face, and he was smitten with leprosy in his face (2 Chron. 26).

While the proud and impious king lived, Isaiah did not deserve to see the vision of Israelite freedom, because good subjects are sometimes deprived of God’s grace on account of evil prelates, and good prelates through evil subjects. Thus the Lord says to Ezekiel [Col. 0616D]: “Behold, I shall make your tongue cleave to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, and shall not be one reproving them, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. 3). Therefore, because the impious king was not worthy of so great a vision, the prophet through whom it ought to have been revealed was not to see it while he lived. Yet after he died, the prophet saw the vision, in order that it might thereby be understood that the Lord withdrew from Isaiah the spirit of prophecy not by Isaiah’s own departure, but by the king’s removal.

Consider, beloved, how dangerous it is to depart from humility when we perceive ourselves to excel in gratuitous gifts. Since the face is the most prominent part of the body, Uzziah was deservedly struck with leprosy in the face, because he wished to appear more eminent than others. He rightly received leprosy as the reward due to his merits, since with the leprosy of pride he had defiled the freely given gifts of virtues. Unless one has washed the stain of pride from the eyes of the heart and died to vices, no reasoning can support even a pious will in discerning visions of God.

He says, therefore: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord,” etc. He who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer; but not a seer because he has the eyes of the flesh open, since these are customarily open alike to either object, namely good and evil. Adam’s eyes were opened after the fall (Gen. 3); the eyes of the disciples journeying to Emmaus were opened in the breaking of bread (Luke 24): Adam’s for evil, theirs for good; Adam’s for desire, theirs for faith in the Resurrection.

Nor should we trust the robbers of the heart [Col. 0617B], who, when they have subjected the heart to their own will, make it a den of thieves (Matt. 21), especially because they can be deceived, so that what is seen is not what it seems to be. The firmament seems to stand still, though it is always moving; to a sailor the shore seems to move, though it remains fixed. A stick appears broken in water, though it is whole; sight is deceived. Nor is he called prophet because he opens the spiritual eyes of the heart to see. “Do not believe every spirit,” says the Apostle, “but test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4). For the eyes of the heart are deceived through images of things when they are conceived otherwise than they are. But the prophet was called a seer because with the intellectual eye he saw what, by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, he understood could not come about otherwise: whether what was seen was given to be understood through an enigmatic or an anagogical vision.

Such was the vision of Isaiah son of Amos, who says: “I saw the Lord sitting” (Isa. 6). Adam saw the Lord walking (Gen. 3), Stephen standing (Acts 7), Isaiah sitting. Thus, while remaining stable, he seems to move, though he moves neither in disposition, place, nor time. Adam saw him walking because, in that Adam sinned, he knew that it was not so much the Lord who had departed from him as Adam himself who had departed from the Lord. Stephen, however, saw him standing because, when he saw him standing, he was given a sign of standing bravely with him in the struggle of tribulation. But Isaiah saw him sitting upon a high and exalted throne, because he recognized him either as at rest [Col. 0617D] or humbled among mortals. For sitting is a sign either of humility or of rest.

Yet sacred discourse presents us with many varieties of seats upon which it declares that the Lord sits. For the Psalmist says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). Hence in the angelic hymn we sing: “You who sit at the right hand of the Father, have mercy on us.” Elsewhere, however, the same Psalmist says: “You who sit upon the cherubim, show yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” (Ps. 79). And again: “I saw a man sitting upon a high throne.” Elsewhere the Lord himself says: “Heaven is my seat” (Isa. 66). And again: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Gregory, Homily 33). And there, whether the same thing or something else is signified: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and [Col. 0618A] exalted throne.” In all these passages he is proclaimed to us whose birth Isaiah celebrates when he says: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9). For he is God who sits at the right hand of the Father; Counselor, who sits upon the cherubim—for *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge”; Wonderful, sitting upon the throne, for a throne is the king’s, and he appears wonderful in governing the firmament and the whole structure of the world, which he governs wondrously. In that heaven is his seat, he is shown to be Father of the age to come. In that he sits upon a high throne—that is, in that he transcends angelic nature—he is understood to be strong and mighty.

Hence, when the angels to whom it is said, “Lift up your gates,” etc., reply, “Who is this King of Glory?” they are answered: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23). And in that he is said to sit in the soul of the righteous, or upon an exalted throne—which is the same thing—he is shown to be Prince of Peace, because peace can never be in the soul without him, nor can there be peace except with him. Or, alternatively, we may distinguish the varieties of seats by their proper names. One seat is called a throne, another a litter or seat, another a chair, [addition: another a synhedrion], another a tribunal, another an *exhedra*. A throne belongs to kings; a litter or seat, to the poor; a teacher’s chair, to teachers; a synhedrion, to hearers; a tribunal, to judges; an *exhedra*, to the assessors of a judge.

Therefore from eternity the Son of God has a throne at [Col. 0618C] the right hand of the Father; but he made for himself a litter in his mother’s womb. He does not cease to make a teacher’s chair in the hearts of faithful teachers, synhedria in devout hearers, a tribunal in just judges, and exhedrae in faithful counselors, judging together with judges. For the Psalmist calls such people seats when he says: “There seats sat for judgment, seats over the house of David” (Ps. 121). There—that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem—shall sit those in whom the Lord now sits through teaching, obedience, justice, or faith.

And although he is said to sit in so many ways, Isaiah nevertheless says, with especial propriety, that he sits upon a high and exalted throne. For he made two rational creatures, namely angel and human being. In these the Lord rests, because if it is his delight to be with the children of human beings (Prov. 8), much more is it so with angels, who did not depart from the state of their good creation. Isaiah calls this angelic nature a high throne, because they did not fall from the height in which they were first created. He calls human nature an exalted throne, because it fell from the state in which it was created but was afterward raised through the outpouring of the blood of Jesus Christ. Hence the Lord himself says: “When I am lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). Or he calls the soul a high throne, because it is high in that it was made in the image and likeness of God. He calls human flesh an exalted throne, because, made from a lowly form—namely the clay of the earth—it is now raised above the choirs of angels [Col. 0619A]. Thus he who humbled himself in order to assume soul and flesh sat upon the high and exalted throne.

And lest the prophet should lose confidence through the miracle of so great a vision, he adduces a clear example of it in created things. For he continues:

“And the whole earth was full of his majesty.” The whole earth, I say: that of which it is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1); or that of which it is said, “The Lord will give goodness, and our earth will yield her fruit” (Ps. 84); or even that of which it is written, “My soul is before you like earth without water” (Ps. 142). For when God disposed the adornment of the earth, he said: “Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” And it was so. And God said: “Let the earth bring forth green grass,” etc. (Gen. 1).

Let us consider how living and effective is the word of God (Heb. 4), how useful and swift this voice: “Let the earth bring forth green grass,” and immediately, without the benefit of moisture, without the heat of the sun, without the exertion of human labor, it brought forth.
