For many are accustomed to say that unless the mildness of the air has moistened the herbs, or a more moderate heat of the sun has warmed them, or they have been cultivated by the exertion of human labor, they cannot sprout. For that reason some people bestowed, and still bestow, divine worship upon Maia, as upon a goddess of moisture, at the beginning of May; dedicating that month also to her, they called May from Maia. This error cannot even to the present day be dissuaded from certain persons who bear the marks of the Christian religion—which we say with grief. [Col. 0619C] Others assigned divine honors to the sun because by its power it penetrates the bosoms of the earth, cherishes scattered seeds, and loosens the frost-stiffened veins of trees. Still others assigned various honors, as to gods, to human beings for their various benefits.

But let this vain opinion depart. For without moisture—not soil, but dry land—sprouted, before it received the sun’s cherishing warmth, indeed before the sun itself was made. With no human labor, but by divine gift, crops without sowing and fruits without seed—so necessary, pleasing, and useful—sprang forth at that word of God, so that, when they are abundant, they serve not only use but delight. For whether in roots, bark, marrow, leaves, fruits, or seeds, whatever was made, God made it all so that the weak nature of the human being might be sustained by them, or, when weakened, restored, or, while healthy, preserved, or healed when not duly preserved. Therefore people should not render to the creature the honor they owe to the Creator; let not the creature glory in itself, nor glory in the creature, but rather in the Creator. For neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but the one who makes the earth sprout and gives growth to its shoots (1 Cor. 3).

All things he made were born either for food or for human use. For whatever does not help as food is useful for medicine; and if any things seem harmful to you, yet they provide harmless fodder for beasts or birds [Col. 0620A], and thus return to human benefit. For starlings use hemlock, and human beings use starlings; deer use snakes, and human beings use deer. And if perhaps there are things which benefit no one, indeed harm them, yet they were made for this purpose: that in them a human being may be punished, exercised, instructed, or humbled. Thus all things return to human usefulness, and the earth is full of his majesty.

But if the divine word was so powerful and effective in the creation of things, by what presumption do heretics wish to confine the power or mercy of the Word within the limits of weakness, so as to deny that for the salvation of the soul—which is much worthier than the body—he can do what he did for the body’s necessity? The earth sprouted without moisture, heat, or labor, when it was still a virgin, that is, uncorrupted, undefiled, and not slain in blood. What wonder, then, if the earth of our nature, uncorrupted and virgin, without the moisture of seed, without the heat of lust, without the work of a man, conceived and bore the seed which, unless the Lord had left it to us, we should have been like Sodom (Isa. 1)? For he himself is our life, and even the dead revive at his fragrance. Can the Word of God do what the nature of the vulture possesses? A vulture conceives and gives birth without intercourse; and could a woman not conceive through the Word of God by whom that occurs?

But you say: “You declare Father and Son to be one. Therefore, if the Son assumed flesh, so did the Father.” It is not so. For though fire is heat and brightness, brightness was in the bush but heat was not. And though the liver is the seat of fire, it rises to the brain, and, the heat being restrained through the veins, brightness reaches the eyes and is united to that bodily member; yet heat does not adhere to the eye, though the heat of fire is in the brain, and there is nevertheless one fire which affects both brain and eye—hot in the brain, bright in the eye. So God the Father and Son are one God; and the Father did not assume flesh, as heat is not in the eye, while the Son assumed flesh as brightness affects the eye [Col. 0620C].

Therefore let heretics confess the earth to be full of God’s majesty in this: that the whole majesty of the Son willed to be united, and was united, to human nature. And if they refuse to believe us or our authorities, since all the prophets bear witness to him, let our enemies at least be judges, because, in order to tell us the truth, iniquity lied to itself (Ps. 26). For Porphyry, the fiercest opponent of the Christian religion, gives Christ this testimony: “The gods declared Christ most pious and immortal, and recalled him with commendation.” And a certain Sibyl is reported by Augustine [Note: [Col. 0619D] *The City of God*, book XVIII, ch. 23.] to have given the following testimony concerning Christ:

> “He shall come into the hands of unbelievers; but with unclean hands they shall strike God, and with an impure mouth spit venomous spittle. He shall simply give his holy back to blows, and, receiving buffets, shall be silent, lest anyone recognize what the Word is, or whence he came, that he may speak to those below; and he shall be crowned with a crown of thorns. For food they gave him gall, and for thirst vinegar; this table did they provide in their inhospitality. For you yourself, foolish race, did not understand your God playing with the minds of mortals; but you crowned him with thorns and mixed bitter gall. The veil of the temple shall be torn, and at midday there shall be a most dark night for three hours; and he shall die by death; and then, entering the underworld, he shall come first to the light, showing the beginning of resurrection to those recalled.”

Behold, what could be said more explicitly concerning Christ? And what could be more exalted than he? At his birth the temple of peace at Rome fell, and a fountain of oil burst forth as far as the Tiber. And fittingly: for the fountain of mercy was bursting forth from the earth of our nature, through which not only did every cult of idolatry come to an end, but every practice of religion began, because it mercifully gathered together the temple of true peace, as it is written: “Let the waters be gathered into one place” (Gen. 1). “Many waters” are many peoples (Rev. 17). These waters were scattered according to the various wills of human beings and the various errors of unbelief; but they were gathered into one place, into that place of which the Lord says to Moses: “There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exod. 33). But what place is there with him who reaches mightily from end to end? (Wis. 8). It is the Church, where he dwells, feeds, and rests at noon (Song 1). This is the place, the womb, in which he gathers the waters of the sea (Ps. 32). This place is Rebecca’s water jar, from whose fullness Eliezer and the camels were given to drink (Gen. [Col. 0621C] 24). It is the Samaritan woman’s water jar (John 4), which the Lord made fruitful from the well of water springing up to eternal life (ibid.). By it are also figured the six water jars found at the wedding feast, according to the purification of the Jews (John 2), that is, according to the cleansing of the continent. For by one place both a single water jar and six water jars are fittingly figured: because, though the universal Church is one, there are nevertheless many particular churches, which are figured by six water jars on account of the number six, which is perfect. “They held,” says the Evangelist, “two or three measures apiece” (ibid.). Hence Noah’s ark, which in the same manner prefigured the Church, is said to have been two-storied and three-storied (Gen. 6).

For the Church has been gathered from patriarchs and prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, and perhaps for that reason is compared to six water jars. There are three kinds of goods: temporal, natural, and gratuitous. In the patriarchs and prophets, therefore, the water jars held three measures, for they abounded in temporal, natural, and gratuitous goods. But in the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, they held only two, because, renouncing temporal goods, they abounded in natural and gratuitous goods. The waters were gathered into one place, moreover, so that they might be fit for fishing:

For the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind (Matt. 13). Thus Peter’s net enclosed a very great multitude of fish, both good and bad. The good are to be put into vessels, but the bad cast out, when the shore is reached. Do you not see, most beloved, Peter drawing his net full of crabs—that is, plotters; octopuses—that is, flatterers; and sea-urchins—that is, sinners, who impede a ship’s course and force it to halt rather than make progress? Are there not, as it were, crabs in the Church: those who, envying the simplicity of others, deceive by plots those whom they cannot overcome openly or by force, casting the stumbling-stones of deceivers at the innocent? I should rightly call flatterers octopuses: they change according to people’s faces; just as they do not fear to speak good things of the good or evil things of the evil, so also they do not fear, in order to please people, to speak good of the evil or evil of the good—like octopuses, which take on the colour of whatever rock they approach. Such persons are enclosed in Peter’s net together with dolphins and seals, which, as a sign of extraordinary affection, when they fear attacks by enemies, take their tender young back again into their bellies through their mouths. They offer an example to prelates: by a word of compassion they should receive their children into the bowels of charity, especially when they see danger of mind or body impending.

The waters were gathered together, and dry land appeared. The first virtue is *Gnōthi seauton* [Γνῶθι σεαυτόν], that is, “Know yourself.” For this purpose the fluid minds of human beings have been gathered and constrained in the wineskin of discipline: that each might know how great is the dryness of human weakness. This also he knew who said: “My soul is like earth without water before God” (Ps. 142), so that, once the dryness of his own lack is known, he may await the command of him who said, “Let the earth bring forth green grass” (Gen. 1). This is customarily brought about miraculously at first, because without any labour, without any preceding moisture of devotion, without any warmth of charity, the soul sprouts by the infusion of the Holy Spirit alone: now roots of thoughts, now seeds of affections, now fruits of works. Thus the earth is full of the majesty of the Holy Spirit. Let us therefore bless the Father, by whose majesty the earth is full in the creation of things; let us bless also the Son, by whose majesty the earth is full in our restoration; and let us bless the Holy Spirit, by whose majesty the earth is full in the sanctification of humankind. Let us therefore bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit, to whom be praise and glory through endless ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE APPEARING OF THE LORD

“When Jesus had been born,” etc. (Matt. 2). “Let the islands be silent before you, O God, and let the nations renew their strength. Who raised up the righteous man from the East, called him that he might follow him?” (Isa. 41). Who, I say, except he who raised up children of Abraham from stones? (Luke 3). For when the nations worshipped stones and wood, they were like stones, according to the saying: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113). Like stones, they had neither eyes for understanding, nor ears for obeying, nor nostrils for discerning, nor a mouth for confessing, nor hands for doing good. Accordingly, in this respect they were stones, and like images comparable to stones, because although they had eyes, they did not see. Their wickedness had blinded them. And though they had ears, like deaf asps they stopped up their ears (Ps. 57). You may understand the same concerning the other senses, if you consider their folly, their unbelief, and the abomination found in obscene acts. Since, therefore, they neither saw, heard, perceived, spoke, nor acted as they ought, in one respect they were dead. Who raised them up? Their eyes were opened, and they saw the star; they understood that it was the sign of a great King; they set out on their journey, and they came to confess at Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” (Matt. 2).

Who then raised them up from the East? Who but he who was little in the manger and great in the East; who became pitiable in the West and worked wonders in the East; who lay hidden from those near at hand and appeared to those far away; who made Isaac ignorant of things close at hand and know things far in the future; who appeared as a wonderful counsellor to Easterners and Westerners; who—[Note: Col. 0623D: A word such as “despised,” “mute,” or something similar is missing.]—was the Word in the bosom of the Father and an infant in the lap of his mother; who was governed by human beings in the world and governed the elements in heaven; who was silent among the Jews and called the Chaldeans? God was already known in Chaldea, while his name was small in Israel [Col. 0623C]. He came into his own, and his own did not know him (John 1). He did not come to strangers; yet as soon as he was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East (Matt. 2).

Since, therefore, he was both God and man, Word and infant, governed and governing, speaking and silent, it was not unfitting that the Reason of his birth should be known through the intelligible meaning recognized in an irrational thing. For when the Magi came, a star was their guide on the journey; it spoke, as it were, while remaining silent. It was silent because it was an irrational thing; it spoke because it showed the Magi the King who had been born. Although it did not utter an external word accessible to bodily ears, nevertheless it spoke through that inward word by which we are accustomed to be taught inwardly in the mind. And rightly so: it indicated the Word that lay hidden within flesh, not the word outwardly manifest in the mouth. Therefore, so to speak, it taught the Magi by an inward word, because it indicated the inward Word lying hidden in flesh. Nor was it fitting that the incarnate Word should be manifested through some other rational thing, because as a star is in the night, so God is in the flesh; as light shining in darkness, so is the Son of God in the gloom of our mortality.

Thus raised up, thus called, the Magi followed Christ. How did they follow? Attend here, my brothers—you to whom it was said: “Whoever does not carry his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). You know that Christ, rich in heaven, became poor in the world; though above humankind, he became subject to humankind; though Lord of all, he became servant of all; though seated at the Father’s right hand in his kingdom, he set out into a far country, to receive a kingdom for himself and return (Luke 19). So too the Magi followed. Leaving their occupations, abandoning royal dignity and homeland, they wished to be subject to him who had subjected himself to others; they became servants of him who had come freely to offer himself as a servant to others; they wished to journey abroad with him who had descended into a distant country because of the hundredth sheep (Luke 15). “Blush, O Sidon,” says the sea (Isa. 23): at the showing of one small sign, these men, who had heard no word of life and seen none of Christ’s miracles, came. Yet we, to whom apostles cry out daily, evangelists cry out, prophets cry out, the examples of saints, Christ’s deeds, signs, and words cry out, stop up our ears like deaf asps (Ps. 57).

We see God’s tabernacle covered with so many and such coverings, yet we remain out in the open; still we expose ourselves to winds and rains. The charity of the saints, like scarlet twice dyed, guards the truth of the Incarnation on one side; the teaching of sacred discourse, like hyacinth-blue cloth, on another; the affliction of penitents, like a sackcloth garment, on another; the passion of the Saviour, like purple, on another; the purity of chastity, like twisted fine linen, on another; abstinence of the flesh, like a ram’s skin dyed red, on another. Why then do we not rest in Christ? Why are we still given over to the wind of vanity and the rains of occupations? Why do we not hear the voice that exhorts and says: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11)? They despised their wealth and homeland for Christ’s sake; do we, who have nothing, fear to lose our nothing? If, then, we can leave many things behind with a wealthy king, at least let us leave our net with poor Peter. For, as Jerome says, “He leaves everything who abandons his own will.” [Note: Col. 0624D, Commentary on Matthew, ch. 19.] The kingdom of God is acquired not with money but with the mind—not by the giver, but by the lover. The widow acquired it with two small coins (Mark 12), Zacchaeus with half of his goods (Luke 19). Finally, the kingdom of God can be acquired with a cup of cold water, though Simon Magus or Ananias could not acquire it with all their possessions. Let us therefore follow with the Magi, for they have now been raised up and called. We have been raised from the destructive death by the glorious death of the Saviour: raised in baptism, but still to be raised at the judgement.

Therefore the wicked do not rise again in the judgement (Ps. 1), because they have not been raised from destructive death in baptism. They will rise, then, but not rise again; they will rise in order to die the worst death, because they were not raised by the glorious death. But we shall rise again from precious death, in order to live gloriously, because we have been raised from destructive death so that we may die precious death. For just as “the death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33), so “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115). Nor can one die a precious death unless one has first been raised from destructive death. Therefore we shall rise again in the judgement, because in this world we have been raised from a threefold death: destructive, propitious, and precious. From destructive death we are raised to propitious death; from propitious death to precious death; from precious death to glorious death. For the death of sinners is destructive; the death of penitents, propitious; the death of saints, precious; the death of the Saviour of all, glorious.

Thus, that blessed Job might be raised from destructive death, he desired to die a precious death. Considering the deeds by which he believed that he had incurred God’s wrath, he said: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish as soon as I came from the womb? Why was I received upon knees? Why was I suckled at breasts?” (Job 3). He would die in the womb if he dismissed the sin that is in thought; he would perish upon leaving the womb if he did not display the thought in action; he would not be received upon knees if the fault displeased him in the act itself. For necessity excuses many whom the will cannot excuse. And he would not be suckled at breasts if, after taking delight in fault, he did not seek grounds of excuse in sin when admonition speaks. Thus, when he said, “Why did I not die in the womb?” etc., the meaning is: Why have I not died a propitious death, when I am dying a destructive one? Why have I not been raised into precious death, when I have fallen into destructive death?

For he raises a human being from this fourfold kind of death who raised the only son of his mother at the gate (Luke 7), the synagogue-ruler’s daughter in the house (Mark 5), the son of the Shunammite through Elisha in the chamber (4 Kings 4), and Lazarus by himself from the tomb (John 11). He, then, is the one who raises some from the east, others from the north, others from the south, and others from the west. Since every sin is ordinarily committed either in thought, deliberation, delight, or action, when sin is, as it were, at the doors, a person perceives the thought and comes to his senses in thought. The sinner is raised from destructive death, as it were from the east or at the gate; and sin dies a precious death, as it were in the womb. But when, after thought, he begins to deliberate sin and comes to his senses in that deliberation, the sinner is raised from destructive death, as it were from the north or in the house; and sin dies a precious death after it has come out from the womb. If, after deliberation, he begins to take delight and is then corrected, the sinner is raised from destructive death, as it were from the south or in the chamber; and sin dies a precious death after it has been received on the knees. But if, after delight, sin is brought into action and he is then amended, the sinner is raised from destructive death as it were in the tomb, or from the west; and sin dies a precious death after it has been suckled at the breasts.

Therefore, recalled from the very intention of wickedness and called to faith, the Magi came from the East: “When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod” [Col. 0626A]. Herod, because his name is said to mean “glory of skin,” fittingly signifies for us the one who glories in our flesh. For God has glory in a human being; the human being also has glory; and the devil has glory. At times God glories in us when he finds us humble in subjection, strong in penitence, vigorous in labour, prompt in obedience, and devout in prayer. Human glory, however, is the testimony of one’s conscience (2 Cor. 1). The devil’s glory is to corrupt flesh by pleasures and indulge the body. Since, therefore, he customarily corrupts a person—first by making sin known through suggestion; then by causing the mind to turn in different directions through thought; afterward by making the mind acquiesce in thought through desire; then by adding swiftness in consent after desire; afterward by adding consummation in action after consent, and delight also in the consummation of the act; finally, by adding the boldness of self-defence in delight—we may appropriately call the impulses of the mind by which the devil corrupts us, in order to glory in the flesh, “the days of Herod.”

For Herod makes the first day in us, which the nations used to call the day of the sun, when, as though the sun enters the hemisphere of the heart, he first makes sin known by suggestion. For the name of the sun often signifies manifestation, as in: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18), that is, in the open. He makes the second day in us, called the day of the moon, when the moon enters the hemisphere of the heart as the mind is changed in many directions. He makes the third day in us, which the ancients called Mars’s day, when Mars enters the hemisphere of the heart as the mind is inflamed by thought. For Mars was called *Pyron* [Πυρόν], that is, “fiery.” Likewise, he advances to the fourth day in us, which they used to call Mercury’s day, when Mercury, as it were, inflames the hemisphere of the heart as swiftness enters consent after desire. For the ancients called Mercury *Stilboute* [Στίλβουτα], that is, “swift.” He makes the fifth day in us, which people call Jupiter’s day, when the flame of ardour burns the soul in the consummation of an act, because then Jupiter enters the mind; philosophers call him *Phaetonta* [Φαέθοντα], that is, “burning.” When, however, after consummation the mind begins to rejoice in the pleasure of the act, Herod makes the sixth day in us, which we are accustomed to call Venus’s day, because Venus then shines in the mind when the work of transgression is pleasing and makes the mind bright. Hence the ancients called Venus *Phosphoron* [Φωσφόρον], that is, “bright.” To make the seventh day in us, which we call the Sabbath day but the ancients called Saturn’s day, Saturn enters the hemisphere of the heart when a person makes light of what has been wickedly done, grows angry at the voice of admonition, and, swollen with pride, even threatens the one who corrects him. Hence the ancients called Saturn *Pheuma* [φευμα], that is, “threatening.”

On these days, then, Jesus was born: not only by that birth through which he formed us, according to which he was eternally born of the Father without a mother; but by that through which he re-formed us, according to which he was temporally born of a mother without a father; or by that through which he is customarily formed in us by inspiring devotion; or by that through which he sanctified us in baptism; or by that through which he redeemed us on the cross. Of the first it was said: “This day I have begotten you” (Ps. 2); of the second: “A child is born to us” (Isa. 9); of the third the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4); of the fourth the Lord himself says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3); and of the fifth we say that we celebrate the birthday feast of saints when we celebrate their death. Hence, fittingly, when we commemorate the death of Christ, who was the Holy of holies, we should believe that his birthday feast is celebrated.

For the Lord was born to us in order that we might be born to him in the same number of ways. Yet his first birth was the cause of our fifth; his second, of our first; his third, of our second; his fourth, of our third; and his fifth, of our fourth. By the power through which he was eternally born of the Father, we were born temporally. By the birth through which he was temporally born of a mother, we too were made children of God. For the Son of God made human beings, the children of men, into human beings; but the Son of Man made those same human beings children of God. He who was Son of God so that we might be human became Son of Man so that we might be called children of God. “But as many,” says the Evangelist, “as believed in him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1).

Likewise, his third birth was the cause of our second. For he was baptized in order to sanctify the waters for us, and that we might be born anew to him through water. Likewise, everything he did in the world was done wholly as an example for us, that we might be his workmanship, created in him for good works. “For,” he says, “I have given you an example, that you also may do likewise” (John 13). He also died for us, that we too might die to him by a precious death. For, as it is written, “We have been buried with Christ through his death” (Rom. 6). “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3).

First, then, he was born of the Father without a mother; second, of a mother without a father; third, he is formed in us daily through the devotion of works; fourth, he was born from the waters of the Jordan; fifth, when his mortal nature put on immortality through the wood of the cross. Hence he is rightly said to have been born in Bethlehem of Judaea. Bethlehem is interpreted “house of bread.” What, then, is Bethlehem of Judaea but the synagogue of the Jews, or the Church, or each faithful soul, or indeed the glorious Virgin, or the heavenly and eternal homeland? When the sayings of God were first entrusted to the synagogue, it was a house of bread, because the Word of life is as bread to the soul. But after those same words had been transferred to the children of the Church through faith and the preaching of teachers, the Church began to be a house of bread. When each faithful person either chews this bread for himself or breaks it for others, he too may fittingly be called a house of bread. The glorious Virgin likewise became a house of bread when she bore in her womb him who says of himself: “I am the living bread, who came down from heaven” (John 6). That heavenly homeland also can be called a house of bread, because there is the bread of angels, with which alone the Psalmist testifies that he can be satisfied, saying: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16).

But the first house was, so to speak, a house of barley bread; the second, of fine wheat bread; the third, of a cake spread with oil; the fourth, of bread baked under ashes; the fifth, of bread turned over. When God spoke through the coverings of the synagogue’s words and commanded harsh and severe things in them—for example, “Whoever does this or that shall surely die”—he served, as it were, the kernel amid the chaff. But when, through the teachers of the Church, the bark of the letter was removed and the kernel of understanding was disclosed to those beneath, he broke fine wheat bread for the children of the Church. When, moreover, someone chews this word of life with charity and devotion, it is swallowed down as a cake enriched by the fatness of charity and spread with the oil of devotion. But when the Son of God, taking flesh, lay hidden in the Virgin’s womb, her womb was like a house of bread baked beneath ashes, because there, under the ashes of our mortality, he hid for us the bread of life. But at the Ascension, when he sat at the Father’s right hand, and after every corruption of mortality had been removed from him he received from the Father the fullness of power, the bread baked beneath ashes was turned over.

Therefore, because he was born of the Virgin; made the bridegroom of the Church through baptism; formed daily in the faithful heart through devotion; suffered on the cross through the synagogue; and raised to heavenly majesty through the power of divinity, he is rightly declared to have been born in Bethlehem of Judaea. Therefore, brothers, since the bread baked beneath ashes became turned bread in ascending; a cake spread with oil in showing charity and mercy; bread, so to speak, to be swallowed in baptism; and bread baked in an oven in dying for us, let us receive this bread, and, giving thanks to God the Father, eat the food that does not perish but endures to eternal life (John 6). Amen.

## SERMON IX. ON THE DAY OF EPIPHANY

“Let there be light” (Gen. 1). It was the same one. It was true light, but it had not been made. Before it was made, it existed; for it existed from eternity, because it was from eternal light. For light from light, the Son from the Father. “And light was made” (ibid.), because he was made of a woman, made of the seed of David according to the flesh (Gal. 4). “And God saw”—that is, the Father made visible—“the light, that it was good” (Gen. 1). It was good not from elsewhere but from itself; good not through participation in good but through all fullness; and for that reason uniquely good, because nothing else is good in that way. “And he divided the light from the darkness” (ibid.), because there was no fellowship of light with darkness—that is, of Christ with Belial (2 Cor. 6). “And evening and morning were made one day” (Gen. 1), because one Christ was made both man and God. He is one because he is unique, because singular. This is the Lord’s day, which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it (Ps. 117), because the people who walked in darkness saw this light (Isa. 9).

For he ascended upon a light and white cloud and entered Egypt (Isa. 19), and he illuminated the hidden things of darkness (1 Cor. 4), so that, casting off the works of darkness, people might put on the armour of light (Rom. 13). For when light ceases, darkness succeeds; and in darkness the works of darkness succeed. “Those who sleep sleep by night, and those who are drunk are drunk by night” (1 Thess. 5). They sleep through ignorance, negligence, or sloth. But those are drunk who live without the restraint of reason, without the balance of justice, without the measure of law. They are drunk who, having neither bridle nor measure, do not know how to give place to anger (Rom. 12), but are cruel, covetous, quarrelsome, returning evil for evil or curse for curse in unwarranted retaliation (1 Pet. 3). These are the works of darkness which follow upon departing light. When light ceases, darkness comes, in which the beasts of the forest pass about (Ps. 103), owls fly, and night-ravens come forth from their dwellings to perform works of darkness.

Hence this is read quite mystically: “Nahor begot Tabee and Gaham, and Thahas and Maacha. These are the sons of Nahor by his concubine Roma” (Gen. 22). Nahor is interpreted “light at rest,” while Roma means “high” or “sublime.” From light at rest—that is, from the cessation of light’s brightness—the lofty mind, that is, the sublime and proud mind, bears adulterous rather than legitimate children: works of darkness, namely the work of cruelty, covetousness, unwarranted retaliation, and contention. Scripture says that he begot Tabee, interpreted “killing,” in whom cruelty is represented. He also begot Gaham, called “valley of heat,” through whom worldly covetousness is understood. He also begot Thahas, interpreted “retaliation,” by which evil is returned for evil, tooth for tooth, eye for eye, and curse for curse (Exod. 21). Such people always have before their eyes a punitive judgement, never a forgiving one—the latter requiring a Catholic to surrender his tunic to one who takes his cloak (Matt. 5), and to offer the other cheek to one who strikes a cheek (ibid.). He also begot Maacha, called “consent,” because, without doubt, once the light of truth has ceased, contentions, anger, quarrels, and discords follow—works of darkness.

[Col. 0629D] Therefore, lest the children of the slave woman—namely, the works of darkness—be heirs with the children of the free woman, that is, with the works of light (Gal. 4), put on the armour of light (Rom. 13), that the former may be powerfully cast off. We understand the armour of light from the power and nature of light. For light comes from fire, and this light from that fire of which it is written: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4). Consequently, it is by nature ascending, discriminating, restraining, strengthening, kindling, and illuminating. For it does not depart from the nature of the fire from which it was born.

By its ascending power a person orders ascents in his heart (Ps. 83), beginning with servile fear and, advancing through initial fear to filial fear, runs in the way of God’s commandments (Ps. 118), led by straight paths, until, brought into all truth, he arrives at the more excellent way of charity (1 Cor. 12). Thus, with the mind cleansed and clarified, he contemplates with thought and eager desire, either enigmatically or anagogically, the supercelestial and superessential Theophany—that is, the manifestation of God. The discriminating power advances reason toward Epiphany; and Epiphany is said to be from *epi*, meaning “above,” and *phanes*, “manifestation.” For by the discriminating power of light reason ardently desires to examine carefully and discern by the balance of judgement not only the caution required regarding opposed vices—lest, fleeing avarice, you fall into prodigality—but also carefully to distinguish vices from virtues that bear the appearance of virtues, lest cruelty be concealed under the pretext of justice or sloth under gentleness. It therefore takes care not to love things that ought not be loved, and takes thought to love what ought to be loved; or not to love equally what ought to be loved less or more, nor to love less or more what ought to be loved equally.

The restraining power advances the mind to Hyperphany; and Hyperphany is said to derive from *hyper*, meaning “middle,” and *phanes*. For it restrains the mind with the bonds of religion and obedience, teaching the degrees of obedience and the practice of work; and through its observance it endures and wards off adversities. The strengthening power also advances the mind to Hypophany. Hypophany is said to derive from *hypo*, meaning “below,” and *phanes*. For it strengthens and confirms the mind by the power of its virtue and by the hidden meanings of words through which it visits each person according to that person’s capacity. The drawing power advances us to Bethphany. Bethphany is said to derive from *beth*, meaning “house,” and *phanes*. It is this power that drew those far away with the cords of charity. The kindling power advances the mind to Phagiphany; and Phagiphany is said to derive from *phagin*, meaning “to eat,” and *phanes*. For from the dishes of xerophagy and sariphagy it kindles five thousand people to mercy and compassion (Matt. 16). Hence the Lord says: “I have compassion on the crowd” (Mark 7). *Xerophagy* is said to derive from *xero*, “dry,” and *phagein*, “to eat.” *Sariphagy* derives from *sario*, “fish.” For in distributing five barley loaves and two fish to five thousand people (ibid.), he kindled in their hearts the flame of charity. The illuminating power likewise illumines minds toward Sepherphany; and Sepherphany is said to derive from *sepher*, meaning “letter,” and *phanes*. This is the key and bolt of the storehouse of physics, logic, ethics, and theory. For through the Scriptures the mind is enlightened, God is manifested, and it is the key to all the other manifestations. It unlocks every manifestation and enlightens our reason toward the natural, rational, moral, and divine.

These are the manifestations of God, of which nevertheless we commemorate four in particular today with the honour of remembrance: Epiphany, Theophany, Bethphany, and Phagiphany—according as Sepherphany, the key-bearer of all manifestations, enlightens the minds of believers. The first occurred through the star on the thirteenth day after the Lord’s birth. It is therefore called Bethphany, because the star led the Magi to the lodging where the child was (Matt. 2). The second occurred in the thirtieth year through the Father’s voice at the baptism; it is therefore called Theophany (Matt. 3). The third occurred on the same day in the following year, at the feast, through the changing of water into wine (John 2). It is called Epiphany from *epi*, meaning “above,” because there he first manifested himself as God. A fourth is said—[Note: Col. 0631D, Bede, *On Luke*.]—in the commentary on Luke to have occurred on the same day in yet another following year, namely the feeding by the five loaves.

Thus almighty God, who wished first to manifest himself to angels and second, through angels, to human beings, also wished to manifest himself to human beings in this way. For this purpose he made two rational creatures, angels and human beings: so that he who was incomprehensible in his own nature might somehow be manifested from his works, both to them and by them, and, being known in them and through them, might be praised; and so that he might be believed to be the author and creator of heaven and earth, appearing venerable to angels in heaven and to human beings on earth. For just as John, surnamed Scotus, describes in heaven four manifestations—Theophany, Epiphany, Hyperphany, and Hypophany, of which I remember having discoursed elsewhere—through which he manifests himself to angels, so he willed to appear wondrously to human beings on earth through four manifestations corresponding in equal balance to those mentioned above; and these indeed after his birth and before his Passion.

For after the Resurrection also he deigned to appear through four other manifestations, not very unlike those mentioned above. One was when he was recognized in the breaking of bread by the two disciples going to Emmaus (Luke 24). Another was when Jesus stood on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias: the disciples came down onto land and saw coals laid out, fish placed upon them, and bread; then Jesus came, took the bread and gave it to them, and likewise the fish. When they had eaten breakfast, the Lord said to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” When he answered a third time, “Lord, you know that I love you,” Jesus said: “Feed my lambs” (John 21). The third was when he appeared to the eleven disciples as they reclined and said to them: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature, baptizing them,” etc. (Mark 16). The fourth was when, shortly afterward, while eating with them, he was lifted up and, as they watched, a cloud received him from their eyes.

From these things, surely, it may be known that he appeared manifest by many proofs. Since a proof gives assurance concerning a doubtful matter, the appearances that occurred on earth became plausible proofs of those things that were hidden from human beings in heaven: so that the one and same Lord might be shown to have appeared to angels in heaven and to human beings on earth, appearing in the Passion as mortal man and in the Resurrection as immortal God. For Theophany is nothing other than the manifestation of God. But when the Lord was baptized, the Son was baptized in the Jordan, the Father was known in the voice, and the Holy Spirit appeared in the dove. Yet John’s mind, cleansed from images, confessed the Son of God in flesh, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1); and the Holy Spirit in the dove, saying: “He who sent me to baptize, he said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Spirit’” (ibid.).

Therefore, theophany is the manifestation of God; its type was Christ’s baptism, where the whole Trinity, one God, was manifested. A confirmation of this type was that after the Resurrection he said to his disciples: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature, baptizing them,” etc. (Mark 16). By the type of epiphany, however, we mean that manifestation of which Bede speaks in his Commentary on Luke: it took place in the wilderness, on this same calendar day, in the year following [Col. 0632B] the miracle by which he changed water into wine, and by which, that is, he distributed five loaves and two fishes to five thousand men (Luke 9). This is plainly shown if we recall the definition of epiphany given above. For, as John Scotus says, Epiphany is “the distributed result of a warming affection and of the balance of a higher insight and judgment.”

Jesus therefore said: “I have compassion on the crowd” (Mark 8). Behold the warming affection. Moreover, the breaking of the five loaves itself directs us to a higher insight, because those five loaves signify nothing other than the five books of Moses, which the boy—that is, the Jewish people in the childishness of its understanding—carried, as it were, whole. But Jesus broke those loaves, because he opened the mystical meaning hidden in the Scriptures; and, by the balance of judgment, he commanded the fragments to be gathered lest they perish, because he wished the sacraments still hidden in the Law to be retained in memory, so that the hungry might be satisfied through the apostles. A confirmation of this type is that, after his Resurrection, he was recognized by the two disciples going to Emmaus in the breaking of bread. Hence they showed both warming affection and higher insight when they said: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, while he spoke and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24); and, by the balance of judgment, they returned to Jerusalem saying that the Lord had risen (ibid.).

The type of hyperphany, moreover, is that manifestation in which, led by a star, the three Magi come; for then the heavenly hyperphany marked its participants—that is, the Magi—with reverence according to the scale [Col. 0632D], taught them its use, and restrained its opposite, when, refusing to obey Herod who contradicted it, they returned to their own country by another way (Matt. 2). By this same reverence according to the scale, after his Resurrection the Lord marked his disciples when he led them out to Bethany (Luke 24). Thus Bethany is interpreted “house of obedience.” For, instructed in its use, they returned to Jerusalem worshipping, with great joy; and, restraining the contrary, they grew stronger and stronger and confounded the Jews who opposed them, preaching what they had learned from the mouth of Truth: that Christ thus had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day (ibid.).

The type of hypophany [Col. 0633A] is expressed by the changing of water into wine (John 2). For by this the laws of nature are overridden and hidden mysteries are disclosed. In those wedding-feast rites, indeed, nothing other is figured than the union of Christ and the Church. The change of water into wine signifies nothing other than that the tradition of the old Law, sufficiently tasteless in respect to the letter, in the union of Christ and the Church intoxicates the feasters with the spiritual savor of charity. But the type of hypophany is also expressed for us in this: wine mixed with water is substantially changed into Christ’s blood; the secrets are disclosed, because the sacraments bring about what they signify. Hence the Lord entrusted to Peter, prince of the apostles, once he had been satisfied with roasted fish and bread, the feeding of his sheep (John 21): because Peter, after incorporating into himself by the devotion of faith both the true bread which came down from heaven (John 6) and, in the Passion, the roasted fish, deservedly undertook the general care of the Church. You see, then, how great must be the dignity of these manifestations, by which heavenly manifestations are made known and again confirmed by testimonies of such a kind: so that not only the man born of the Virgin, but also the only-begotten Son of God and firstborn of the dead (Rev. 1), may be believed, and the Prince of the kings of the earth may without doubt be worshipped by unbelievers.

## SERMON X. ON THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED MARY

“They excavated the well and found pieces of wood, coals, and thick water; and, when these were placed upon a pile [Col. 0633C] of wood, fire burst forth” (2 Macc. 1).

That sacred fire, I say—the fire which Moses obtained from on high by his prayers; which was commanded continually to burn upon the altar, because no sacrifice could be consumed without it; which for a thousand years and more, partly in the tabernacle and partly in the Temple, had kindled the legal sacrifices down to the deportation of Judah. For when the deportation was imminent, Jeremiah secured the pieces of this fire in a well in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, where they lay hidden throughout the seventy years of captivity, until Artaxerxes, surnamed Longimanus, granted Ezra first, and afterward Nehemiah, permission to return and rebuild Jerusalem. When the walls had therefore been repaired by the work and labor of these two, they offered saving sacrifices to the Lord, but complained [Col. 0633D] that they did not have fire from on high. Then there were present persons who told of Jeremiah’s deed. Accordingly, in order to find the wood and coals, they excavated the aforesaid well. Thus they named the day Nephar, that is, “Purification,” because fire burst forth from the discovered pieces of wood; afterward it kindled the Temple’s sacrifices for seventy years, until at last Antiochus Epiphanes sold the high priesthood to Jason. On account of this, the sacred fire was wholly extinguished, and God’s Temple had no holy fire until Judas Maccabaeus, after purifying the Temple, again celebrated Nephar. At this feast, fire burst forth from the stones of the old Temple; hence it was called the Feast of Lights, and, because of its dignity, it alone in the whole Old Testament was celebrated with an octave.

And since today, dearest brethren, we celebrate the day Nephar and the Feast of Lights, let us derive an understanding of these sayings from the occasions on which they are spoken, comparing signs of things with the things signified by the signs. For today that unique Temple was purified, in whose Holy of Holies the Son of the living God came to sit above the propitiatory of mercy, humbling himself and taking the form of a servant. Today that well was excavated, in praise of which you sing: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters” (Song 4). Today those ancient pieces of wood, kindled by sacred fire, were found: namely Joseph and Mary, Jesus, Anna, and Simeon, by whose example every class of human being is kindled. Mary gives an example of devotion [Col. 0634B] to virgins; Simeon to the infirm; Joseph to married persons; Anna to widows; Jesus to children. No condition has been omitted to which these five have not given an example of devotion.

The coals of charity were also found with and in the pieces of wood: namely, Joseph’s service, Mary’s humility, the graciousness of Jesus’ humanity, Anna’s religious devotion, and Simeon’s devotion. With all these water was found: namely, the water of tears, washing away defilements in devotion. [Note: [Col. 0633D] Augustine, in a Sermon on the Purification.] For who, recalling Simeon’s devotion, with which he said in tears, “Do you think I shall see? Do you think I shall endure?” etc., would not kindle within himself the fire of which it is said: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4)? And again he himself says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8). Therefore Simeon says: “A light for revelation to the Gentiles,” etc. [Col. 0634C] (Luke 2). Thus Mary’s purification, of which it is written, “After the days of Mary’s purification were fulfilled” (ibid.), was made a sign of our purification.

Therefore, what is first read as the excavation of the well and the purification of the Temple is shown as accomplished in Mary and as needing to be accomplished in us. Let us consider, if you please, the ministers of the purifications. Judas Maccabaeus was minister of the Temple’s purification; Ezra and Nehemiah of the excavation of the well; and Anna and Simeon of Mary’s purification. And fittingly so. For the first of our purifications is confession, since all things are washed in confession; and Judas is interpreted “confession.” Since, however, that confession alone washes which is preceded by the consolation of hope, as by grace at work, and is completed by the discipline of penitence, as by grace cooperating, Ezra and Nehemiah, Simeon and Anna, are fittingly joined to these [Col. 0634D] purifications. You know that no one repents who does not hope; yet one hopes in vain who does not repent. As has been said, those four joined together demonstrate this.

For, according to their office and the interpretation of their names, Nehemiah and Anna, Simeon and Ezra, signify one and the same thing. Nehemiah and Anna were present at the purifications as helpers; Simeon and Ezra as priests. Nehemiah is interpreted “the Lord, the Comforter.” But the Lord, the Comforter, is the Paraclete; the Paraclete is [Col. 0635A] the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is grace; grace is Anna. Anna, therefore, is Nehemiah. You see how they are joined. Nor should the difference of sex trouble you, because the Holy Spirit, masculine in Latin, is feminine in Hebrew and neuter in Greek.

The same must be said of the other two, because Ezra is interpreted “discipline,” and Simeon “hearing sorrow.” The Apostle says of discipline that it is not of joy but of sorrow (Heb. 12). Through discipline, then, we are accustomed to hear sorrow, being made sorrowful unto repentance, as the Apostle says: “If I made you sorrowful for a time, I do not regret it—not because you were made sorrowful, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance” (2 Cor. 7). There is, then, a sorrow that makes us sorrowful unto repentance. It is necessary, therefore, that everyone confessing, like Judas, should join to himself in every purification Ezra with Simeon—that is, the discipline of laborious penitence—so that by this he may prove himself a Maccabee, a fighter and strong in the contest.

For that ancient patriarch Judah also fruitlessly spilled seed so long as he was with Shuah; but he produced useful fruit when he joined Tamar to himself. Shuah, indeed, is interpreted “song.” Confession joined with song is unfruitful. Tamar, however, is interpreted “bitterness,” and confession becomes fruitful when it is uttered with bitterness. Yet a person ought to be made sorrowful by penitence in such a way that he does not cease to be consoled by hope of pardon. Let him therefore join to himself Anna and Nehemiah—that is, grace that consoles concerning forgiveness. For Judas Iscariot burst open in the middle [Col. 0635C] because he did not take Anna and Nehemiah to himself. He refused consolation; despairing, he hanged himself with a noose.

With these aids and examples, therefore, let us strive not merely to cleanse defilements, but also to refine the virtues themselves; for no one is so holy that he cannot be holier. Let us cleanse not only the defilements of deeds but also those of thoughts. Let us cleanse not merely evil, so that it may be good, but also good, so that it may be better. For first a grain of wheat must be purified from straw, second from chaff, third from bran. After this flour is drawn out; but it too must be divided little by little in offerings. These are the three purifications: bodily cleanness [Col. 0635D], signified in the purification of the Temple accomplished through Judas; purification of conscience, figured in the excavation of the well accomplished through Ezra and Nehemiah; and refinement of the virtues, prefigured in the Purification of the immaculate Virgin, first celebrated through Anna and Simeon.

How difficult it is to cleanse consciences is shown by the troublesome harassment of the Philistines, who filled Isaac’s wells with earth. Others conceal their consciences as a well of Hilkiah filled with mud, whose dregs often boil up to Jeremiah’s throat. Others remove defilements and, as though digging wells, examine their consciences; but they are neither cold nor hot, but rather lukewarm. Like a well in the wilderness, dried of every spiritual moisture, such a conscience often imprisons Joseph himself [Col. 0636A] captive. Others, digging their consciences as cisterns, find them filled with adulterous waters; and there, once the two tails of firebrands have been found—namely Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, that is, worldly knowledge and a mouth speaking lofty things—they draw out the fire which, coming down from heaven, consumed Job’s sheep and servants; or else the fire which never says, “Enough.” Others, as has been said, while digging wells could find living waters if they wished courageously to resist the Philistines. Others, digging out the well, happily find with Isaac living waters of abundance or breadth. Thus different persons dig wells differently, and kindle fire from excavated wells.

For some, having wicked people as logs—the examples of depravity—and examples of vices as coals, kindle or place upon the altar strange fire: namely, unlawful ardor, by which they become estranged from God. They do not celebrate Nephar, but rush into wickedness. Others, keeping the life of the saints before their eyes, and cleansing their lips by means of logs and coals taken from among the wheels of the cherubim, kindle the sparks of their reed-bed according as the Father of lights kindles them: Jesus Christ, light from light, brightness from brightness, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY

“Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the hollow of the pit from which you were hewn” (Isa. 51).

If it is true—indeed, because it is true—that there is no work, [Col. 0636C] no reason, no counsel against the Lord, then from the destruction of the consequent it may rightly be inferred that with the Lord there can be nothing but work, nothing but reason, nothing but counsel. For in him and through him the idle find an example of work, the faithless a reason for understanding, and the simple and deceived counsel. Through him the wild olive and the olive have together been grafted in, so as to produce the fruit of work; the simple and the shrewd become wise; Jews and Greeks have received the counsel of salvation. For with him there is no respect of persons: whatever their condition, race, dignity, or age, all are one in Christ—those who are not overcome by evil but overcome evil with good.

Therefore, brethren, considering Isaiah’s concise counsel, let us all look to him and await salvation from him who saves all those hoping in him. “Look,” says Isaiah, “to the rock” (Isa. 31 [perhaps an erroneous reference for Isa. 51]). Now the rock was Christ. The prophet speaks to all, because all find refuge in it. Consider the nature of things themselves. Does not the dove flee to the rock so as to be safe, and likewise the hedgehog? For the dove nests in the holes of the rock; and the rock is also made the hedgehog’s refuge.

Let the dove, therefore, look to the rock in which it gathers its labors, rests, nests, and rears its young. Whether it gathers grain or thorns, all benefits itself and its own if it is in the rock. It places all things in the rock: thorns, namely, so that it may have a bed of necessity rather than pleasure; grain, so that it may refresh both itself and its own. But if it proposes to rest from labor, it flees to the rock so as to be secure. And even if, resting, it puts its head out from the hole of the rock in order to look outside, it nevertheless does not withdraw its body from the rock; but while looking outside, it grieves and groans. If, however, a fledgling, before it can raise itself in flight into the heights, rashly leaps out beyond the rock, the dove rebukes it with the sound of its voice and calls it back to the rock. Thus it feeds its young in the rock, but sparingly, from time to time, and in measure, lest perhaps the liver burst and even the wheat’s kernel, through excess of food and corruption of the flesh, be expelled with the bran as dung. It does all things in measure, so that food may be desired more eagerly, the appetite restrained, food digested, incorporated, [Col. 0637B] or expelled. Bran, indeed, ought to be expelled, but the kernel incorporated.

Such is the dove of which it is written: “My dove in the holes of the rock, in the hollows of the wall” (Song 2). But what is this dove? The person who has no gall of bitterness by which to grow angry, no beak with which to bite by detraction, and no feet swift to shed blood by action, knows by experience. Rather, whoever is devout in thought, truthful in speech, and simple in deed is a dove.

This dove, therefore, nests in the holes of the rock. The rock is one, but its holes are many. The Church’s house is one, but the house has many windows and many doors. The rock is Christ; the house is the Church; while the holes or doors are the diverse entrances to salvation opened through the exercise of diverse religious observances [Col. 0637C]. For just as one enters through a hole in the rock or a door in the house, so through the manifold holiness of religious life we have access to the Church or to Christ. The door of the Church, or the hole of the rock, is the order of married persons, of the continent, and likewise of virgins. The holes of the rock are the Cistercian, Premonstratensian, and Cluniac religious orders. The doves nesting in these holes gather now grain, now thorns.

Let the prelates hear the proposed example, and let subjects hear it also. Let them observe the example of the dove nesting in the rock, so that they may become like doves in their windows. Both must labor: for grain and for thorns. Thorns are for supplying necessity; grain for refreshing the hungry soul. In the thorn is figured worldly care; in the grain, he who compares himself to a grain of wheat (John 12). Since both what belongs to God and what belongs to the world are necessary for the children of the Church, we must labor as far as possible; but in matters of the active life, for the sake of necessity rather than pleasure, and in matters of the contemplative life, solely for the sake of devotion. Jacob the patriarch also joined both Leah and Rachel to himself; Judah begot both Perez and Zerah; Christ likewise loved both Martha and Mary. Whatever, therefore, one does and labors at, let him place it all in the rock, whether it concerns the world or God [Col. 0638A]. For some perform one kind of work, others both, out of love for God; while others do so out of love for the world.

But if at some time one rests from labor for the sake of contemplation, let him flee to the rock in order to be safe, since it is very dangerous to think anything apart from God, to consider transient things by thinking upon them. “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” said Ecclesiastes (Eccl. 1). But if he puts his head outside the rock in order to look outward, let him nevertheless not depart bodily from the rock. If perhaps through a sudden temptation he fixes his mind upon low and perishable things, let him not stray from the purpose of good action; rather, amid temptations, let him place hope in Christ, who makes a way out in temptation. While thinking on transient things, let him, after the manner of the dove, grieve and groan, because in the world there is absolutely nothing but pain and groaning. For all things are perishable and transient.

He nourishes fledglings in the hole of the rock when, under some strictness of religious observance, he refreshes those subject to him with the grain of God’s word. But there are certain persons who, in the novice fervor of religion, amid the bitterness of temptations and without the wings of devotion or contemplation, wish to know more than is fitting and to walk in things great and wonderful above themselves; they seek lofty things with elevated thought while knowing nothing but low things. They banish their misery from the sight of their heart, wish to become investigators of majesty, and, desiring to know things above them, do not yet know themselves; they do not yet know how to suck milk, yet already gnaw bread. Therefore, crushed by glory, they often fall into unbelief itself, because the investigator [Col. 0638C] of majesty will deservedly be crushed by glory. The higher he raises himself, the more heavily he falls from on high. For where the worm of blasphemy gnaws at the root of faith, all branches of the virtues must necessarily wither; where the spirit of blasphemy damages the foundation of a building not yet firmly established, the building itself must also collapse.

For it is against the Law to plough with a firstborn ox, to keep the first fruits of the crops, to retain the firstborn, and not to circumcise the foreskins of trees (Deut. 15). Such persons must be rebuked by prelates, because they eat the fruit of an uncircumcised tree when they apply themselves to the works of an unclean mind. One ploughs with a firstborn ox when a mind still wanton in its newness investigates the depths. They retain the first fruits of crops and firstborn offspring when, at the beginning of conversion, they approve their own thoughts or works; but these should instead be committed and, according to the Law’s decree, offered to God. Let them therefore hold and dash their little ones against the rock, and, like the dove’s fledglings in their nest, restrain them, lest perhaps, wishing to fly without wings, they fall from the rock and lie exposed to the kite’s claws. There indeed they are to be nourished, but from time to time and in measure, lest perhaps the liver burst and the very kernel of wheat be cast out as dung in vomit.

Hence it is that, at the gate of Samaria during the famine, a fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung was sold for a high price (2 Kings [4 Kings] 6). Thus it sometimes happens that the very abundance of food and its delights are turned into disgust. But [Col. 0639A] for subjects to desire the food of the word by hearing, retain it by understanding, digest it by reflection, incorporate the kernel by acting, and expel bran by cutting away superfluities and correcting evil speech, prelates must distribute to their subjects a measure of wheat according to manner, time, and person. Hence that dove of doves, who had no beak with which to bite when he was slandered, no claws with which to wound when he was killed, and no gall when provoked to bitterness, said while feeding his young: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16), lest the liver perhaps burst through an unconsidered distribution of foods.

When, therefore, a prelate about to speak to subjects considers what word of God to distribute, to whom, how much, and how, so that he may assign carnal things to the carnal and spiritual things to the spiritual according to their capacity of mind and devotion, he feeds fledglings like a dove in the hole of the rock. You yourselves, my children, who receive grain from my mouth quite unconsideringly, I confess, bear witness and examine your consciences. We speak to you almost every day; every day we admonish you. Yet through daily familiarity itself the word of God has become a weariness to very many. Certainly, if those unaccustomed to hearing God’s word heard the things which you reject as dung, they would obtain them for themselves with great devotion and many tears.

Hear an example. Is it not reported that, during the famine, at the gate of Samaria an ass’s head and a fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung were bought for a high price? (4 Kings 6.) Who are the hungry? Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. Hungry were the little children asking for bread, and there was no one to break it for them. These are at the gate of Samaria when, anxious about themselves, they begin to guard the mind. For by “gate” is figured a beginning, and by “Samaria” guarding, since Samaria is called “guarding.” At the gate of Samaria, then, the person sells an ass’s head who, in the guarding of the mind, amid the burdens of labor, the curses of people, the pricks of temptations, and threats of power, outwardly displays an example of patience, knowing that from this he will obtain the worthy fruit of penitence. For the example of patience is figured by the ass’s head. And the person buys the ass’s head who, for the sake of penitence, begins to possess his mind in patience [Col. 0639D].

The hungry person also buys dove’s dung when what he who is accustomed to be fed, like a dove, with the grain of the word, lightly esteems as dung through familiarity. Since God’s word is customarily divided into historical, moral, allegorical, and anagogical senses, the person who strives and labors to be corrected through one of these four rightly buys a fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung.

Therefore, looking to the rock after the manner of the dove, whatever you think, do not labor for empty glory or human praise; do all things instead for love of God. But if you think anything apart from God or against God, grieve and groan; retain and do the grain of God’s word, seeking or thinking nothing beyond what God inspires. And if you wish, in thought, to comprehend anything of the sublimity of the divine majesty [Col. 0640A], cleanse the eyes of your mind from unclean desires, knowing that he who is clean does not dwell in an unclean mind. Thus the dove looks to the rock.

But what of the hedgehog? For the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs. The hedgehogs, however, are sinners. A hedgehog is an animal full of spines; when caught by an enemy, it hides its head among its spines and, as though safe among them, awaits its pursuer. But does it escape? Is it not captured? Unless it flees to the rock, it does not escape. There indeed it is secure. Let sinners full of the spines of temptations hear this example, those who walk the broad way leading to death. For the sinner follows the hedgehog’s habit: he hides his head among the spines when his pursuer seizes him, because, when the ancient enemy tempts the sinner, he consents in mind to his sins and suggestions. He waits securely among the spines on the road when, among the evils he does, he does not fear the evil hearing by which the Judge will say: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). But will he escape? He will not escape—indeed, he will be captured—unless he flees to the hole of the rock. The hedgehog too has its hole in the rock, as does the dove. The hedgehog’s holes are the wounds of the Lord’s Passion. Therefore, when the ancient enemy pursues the sinner, let him flee to the wounds of the Lord’s Passion, committing his hope to him and saying: “Have mercy on me, [Col. 0640C] you who suffered for me.”

Therefore let the hedgehog and the dove, the righteous person and the sinner, look to the rock; for he who redeemed sinners by his Passion will sanctify those cleansed by the strictness of religious observance. The dove’s hole is the strictness of regular discipline; the hedgehog’s is the wound of the Lord’s Passion. Therefore, dearest brethren, whoever you are that are children of Mother Church, look to the rock, lest the building fall when its foundation slips. For when Christ withdraws from the mind of the faithful through the prompting of some diabolical suggestion, a part of the Church falls, because it was not founded upon the rock.

There are some in the Church only in body, separated in mind and deed. Others, although they confess with the mouth and believe with the heart, nevertheless bear the foreskin of the flesh in transgression. Others desire doctrine, but being faint-hearted and timid are afraid to undertake the religious life of doctrine, because they find another law in their members resisting the law of their mind. Others undertake what they desire, but, impatient and soft in the face of temptation, when they put their hand to the plough look back and return. Others, as they advance in virtues and religious life, become proud and puffed up, taking material for pride from that from which they should instead have been humbled. Others, in order to advance more and more, put on the religious life of innocence and holiness. The first, indeed, are heretics or schismatics; the second sinners and uncircumcised persons; the third thirsting for righteousness but faint-hearted [Col. 0641A] and timid; the fourth soft; the fifth timid; the sixth simple and religious persons.

Therefore let schismatics look to the rock which joined the two walls. Let sinners look to the rock by which they must be circumcised from the foreskin of transgression. Let those who desire the doctrine of salvation look to the rock which brought forth water. Let the swollen look to the rock which cast down Goliath. Let the soft look to the rock which Jacob placed beneath his head. Let the proud look to the rock which shattered the statue. Let the simple look to the rock in whose hole the dove nests. Look to the Rock. Now the rock was Christ. Look to power in his divinity; submission in his humility; discipline in his conduct; knowledge in his doctrine; charity in all things [Col. 0641B]: the power by which he subjected you to himself; the submission by which he raised you on high; the discipline by which he wonderfully taught you; the knowledge by which he instructed you through the word; the charity by which he loved you.

Look to him in adversity; look to him in prosperity. In prosperity, look to justice, lest you become proud; in adversity, to mercy, lest you despair. “Look to the rock from which you were cut.” Cut—not cut away from him, but cut from him and through him: because you were both circumcised from sin and divided from unbelievers. “From which you were cut.” For Christians are derived from Christ, as streams from a fountain, branches from a trunk, sons from a father. For he was established the father of many nations. Through him we received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father.” Hence the prophet made clear what he had stated obscurely when he added: “Look to Abraham your father” (Isa. 51). Abraham is called father of many nations. It follows:

“And to the hollow of the pit from which you were hewn” (ibid.). What is this hollow but Eve, from whose wombs we were born and, as though coming out of a hollow, descended into this pit of misery? Therefore, since when one of two contraries is known the other is known also, look to this hollow of the pit, so that through the misery which Eve brought upon us you may consider the mercy by which Christ delivered you. For from the magnitude of the disease the usefulness of the physician is proved; from the wisdom of the disciple the teacher’s instruction is praised. Weigh, then, with equal balance in the scale of the mind the evils you endure through Eve and the goods you have received through Christ, so that the small weight of justice may be brought back to the center of justice.

Or certainly, by the hollow of the pit we ought to signify the Church still dwelling as a pilgrim upon earth. From her, the children of the Church have been propagated far and wide as from a mother’s womb. For Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, begot us from her womb by the word of truth; and through her, grace going before us, we were divided from unbelievers. Thus it was said: “From which you were hewn.” “Hewn,” that is, through prevenient grace; “cut through her,” that is, divided. Therefore look to the Church, considering with what ornaments of virtues her Bridegroom adorned her, with what dignity he exalted her, with what ring of perfection he pledged her, with what staff of strength he supported her, and with what bracelets of works [Col. 0642A] he completed her. Look and praise; give thanks to her through whom you have deserved to be daughters of so great a Bride.

Or certainly, by the hollow of the pit we may signify her of whom the Prophet, almost by way of explaining what he had previously said, added: “And to Sarah, who bore you.” For when he had said, “Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the hollow of the pit from which you were hewn,” he added: “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah, who bore you.” The subsequent statement is indeed a confirmation of the preceding one.

For since Sarah is interpreted “princess,” what can we understand by Sarah except her who obtained sovereignty over herself, sovereignty over the world, and sovereignty over heaven? Sovereignty over herself, indeed, because she did not consent to pleasures; sovereignty over the world, because the vanity of the world did not seduce her; sovereignty over heaven, because she has now ascended to the right hand of her Son above the choirs of angels. This, then, is the Sarah who bore us. For she was made our mother in him who is not ashamed to call us brethren, as in the passage: “I will declare thy name unto my brethren” (Ps. 21).

Therefore the hollow of the pit, which sent forth to us the Lamb, is the blessed womb of Mary, which bore the Son of the eternal Father. It is called a pit because, although she was outside the world by grace and devotion, she was nevertheless of the world by nature. Thus, because of the height of her virtues, her patience in tribulations, her strength of mind, and her perseverance in religious devotion, the glorious Virgin is compared, according to the prophets, either with the high mountain from which the stone was cut without hands, or with the rock of the desert, from whose hollow the Lamb was sent forth to us [Col. 0642C].

Let those who lie in the depths of the abyss—who quickly consent to the world or to the flesh, who are exposed to the devil’s will—look to the high mountain, the rock of the desert, and the hollow of the pit, so that they may become lofty in thought, strong in temptation, and find hiding-places of refuge when some evil suggestion arises. For in the mountain we find height, in the rock strength, and in the hollow refuge. Let us therefore look more attentively at both: at the rock and the hollow, at Christ and Mary, lest, recognizing what each has bestowed upon us, we be charged with the fault of ingratitude.

For as there are two things that harmed us unto condemnation—the guilt of transgression and the punishment of recompense—and these two were wrought by a man and a woman, Adam and Eve; so two things benefited us unto salvation—the purification of the mind and the passion of redemption—and these likewise came through a man and a woman, Christ and Mary [Col. 0642D]. Let us therefore look to Christ and Mary: to the desert rock and the deserted rock. One of these sent forth to us the Lamb; the other nourishes for us the young doves. For these accord, according to the Law of Moses, with our purification.

For it is written: “A woman who, having received seed, bears a son shall be unclean seven days” (Lev. 12). *Woman* (*mulier*) is so called from softness (*mollities*): for because she is soft and fragile, she is called *mulier*. What, then, do we understand by the woman except the soft—those, that is, who readily consent to the devil’s suggestion? A woman receives seed, as it were, when a soft and fragile soul consents to a perverse suggestion [Col. 0643A]; she conceives when she deliberates; she gives birth when she acts.

And it should be noted that she sometimes gives birth to a male and sometimes to a female. She gives birth to a male if, in committing the sin, some element of manliness is mixed in. For when someone determines to sin, yet avoids a sacred place or a sacred time, or alleges necessity as a pretext, or even observes a natural measure: he indeed gives birth, because he does not resist; but he gives birth to a male because, in the act itself, some element of manliness has been mixed in. But when neither time nor place is considered, and pleasure alone is regarded in the matter, and a mode is sought that is contrary to nature, she gives birth to a female, because she has left nothing praiseworthy in the commission of sin. Hence it is quite clearly commanded that she who gives birth to a female be punished with double penance [Col. 0643B].

“A woman,” he says, “who, having received seed, bears a male shall be unclean seven days.” “She shall be unclean,” that is, she shall judge herself unclean. For she ought to judge herself guilty and unclean before God because she rejoiced in committing the sin. A day signifies exultation of mind, because just as daylight makes the world bright, so the exultation and gladness of the heart renders the mind lucid. As one who sins is accustomed first to rejoice in suggestion, delight, consent, deliberation, action, and pleasure in the action, so, when he repents, he ought to judge himself unclean for all these things, and nevertheless grieve that he rejoiced in them.

But because contrition of heart avails nothing unless confession of the mouth follows, Moses immediately adds and says: “On the eighth day he shall be circumcised” (Lev. 12) [Col. 0643C]. What is the circumcision of sin but confession? For when, after contrition and confession of the mouth, we cheerfully cut off, all around, the members of our body, so that we may rise from the death of the soul, we circumcise our male child, as it were, on the eighth day. For the eighth day signifies the illumination of the mind, through which we rise from the night of sin and from the death of hell.

Yet there are many who, after confession, do not humble themselves, but act more negligently because they know it is written: “Everything is washed away in confession.” Therefore they more readily fall into sins and suffer relapse. They ought also, in good works, to declare themselves unprofitable servants, knowing that they will come before the judgment of him [Col. 0643D] who will even count the hairs of their head.
