They ought also to fear if they believe that they have acted well, or that they have fully stated what they committed. For who does not hold his own frailty in suspicion? Who ought not to fear the lethargy of human negligence? Who ought not diligently to confess every circumstance [or surrounding condition] that attends sin? Or, even if he confesses, how does he know whether his confession was acceptable to God? “For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?”

Abel offered, and Cain also offered; but he accepted the sacrifice of the former and rejected that of the latter. Jacob and Esau were brothers from the same womb; but the one was chosen by God, the other rejected. Likewise, two are in a house, two in a field, and two at one mill; but one shall be taken and the other left. Yet I do not say these things [Col. 0644A] as though I were uncertain whether a simple, pure, and devout confession washes away sin. I say them because, when we confess, we do not know whether, in the sight of him who searches hearts and reins, our confession possesses the simplicity, purity, and devotion that it ought necessarily to possess.

Fear, then, is always necessary in such matters. Yet let the sinner fear after confession without despairing; and let him hope in such a way that he fears. Let him become more attentive to the ordering of his actions. For he who rejected Cain’s sacrifice received Mary’s repentance; he who rejected the words of the Pharisee did not despise the publican’s prayer; he who sanctified Jeremiah and John in the womb hated Esau in his mother’s womb; and he who did not receive Judas’s confession washed away David’s sin by confession after adultery and homicide [Col. 0644B]. Let him fear on account of justice, rejoice on account of mercy, exult so as to fear, fear so as to exult, dread lest he become proud, and rejoice lest he despair.

Hence follows the statement: “For thirty-three days she shall remain in the blood of purification” (ibid.). Although this number is counted among the odd numbers, it is nevertheless said by arithmeticians to be secondary and composite. There are also other odd numbers which are primary and non-composite.

Who, then, is figured by an odd, primary, and non-composite number except one who, through the disorder of his actions, departing from the rule of equality and justice, cleaves through the presumption of disobedience to him who is earthly from the earth? “The first Adam,” says the Apostle, “is of the earth, earthly; the second is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15) [Col. 0644C]. Unequal, primary, and non-composite are those who put on the old man with his deeds through inequality, injustice of heart, and disorder of themselves.

But by an unequal secondary and composite number are figured those who, although they have departed from the rule of equality through the fault of injustice, are nevertheless, from fear of sin itself, attentive to the ordering of their actions, so that they may deserve to put on him who is heavenly from heaven. For the second is heavenly from heaven. Thus for thirty-three days one remains in the blood of purification who, through illumination of heart and orderliness of action, is purified from the inequality of transgression, putting on [Col. 0644D] the new man, who was created according to God in justice and holiness of truth.

But because the mind is illuminated by faith, and true religious devotion is ordered by contrition of heart, it is quite plainly added: “And a lamb, or two young doves, shall be offered for him” (ibid.). In this lamb is figured he who was silent before the one shearing him and, when he suffered on the cross, did not open his mouth: first offered in the hands of Simeon, and secondly on the summit of the cross for the salvation of the world. It should be noted that he is offered daily through the hands of the priest in the sacrament of the altar in a manner far different.

But because the whole purpose of our salvation depends upon him and through him, he is offered for us and by us through the sacrament of the altar; and we incorporate him into ourselves, so that we may be one body with him [Col. 0645A] and be conformed through him to the example of his simplicity. For he gave us an example through the innocence of his life, so that we too might act in like manner. For if you are not simple and innocent, it does not benefit you, but harms you, that Christ was offered for you. With the lamb, indeed, you must offer young doves, in which a twofold simplicity is signified: namely, that of actions and of thoughts.

Therefore, dearest ones, if we wish to be purified and cleansed, let us look to Christ and to Christ’s mother; to the rock and the hollow of the pit; to the deserted rock and the rock of the desert. For the rock of the desert was the Virgin Mary, who sprang from the tribe of Naomi. Hence it was said: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert unto the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16) [Col. 0645B]. But Christ is called the deserted rock, of whom it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117).

Let us therefore look to Mary, confessing her blessed among women. Let us look also to Christ, giving thanks to him who, offered for us according to his humanity, according to his divinity offered us to God the Father, who lives and reigns through ages without end. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON THE SAME FEAST

“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man, finding, hides; and for joy thereof goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field” (Matt. 13) [Col. 0645C].

Beloved, as Truth testifies, “one thing is necessary” (Luke 10). But human covetousness—blind, cruel, and the dropsy of all vices—divides the human mind into many things and distracts it in different directions whenever it withdraws from unity. What unity? “Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God” (Deut. 6). He is one because he cannot be divided into parts, for he is not a body; nor can he be divided by affections, because he is not a soul; nor is he called one from union, because he is not a collection or mass of many things.

Yet many things divide us from this unity, while they do not divide unity itself. Many things divide us from unity because many things do not agree with unity. For a thing divided into many cannot be one; but unity is not divided, because, being simple and one, it has no division [Col. 0645D]. From this unity, therefore, the mind is first divided by covetousness, the mother of divisions, which tears the mind into as many parts as it multiplies it through the varying diversity of affections. Now by desires for pleasure, now for honour, now for riches, it moves the mind from the stability of unity. Covetousness alone, indeed, invented the two words of division: “mine” and “yours”; and charity, in that it “seeketh not her own,” utterly detests them.

When this affects the mind, it thirsts, after the manner of dropsy, all the more the more it drinks. Increase of money brings increase of wickedness. The greater the wealth acquired, the greater the desire to possess it.

> Love of money grows in proportion as money itself grows.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* 14.138

[Col. 0646A] But it is called blind in this respect: it desires what should not be desired and does not desire what should be desired. For if it either desired what should be desired or did not desire what should be avoided, it ought not to be called covetousness but charity. Thus it rages more cruelly in the mind, and more abominably lays waste and burns its own dwelling, in proportion as a person embraces or receives its tyranny more affectionately.

For this reason, beloved brethren, Isaiah rightly rebukes this detestable poison of death, saying: “Woe unto you that join field to field unto the end of the place” (Isa. 5). What is “unto the end of the place”? Unto the field bounded by the limit of a place. “Unto the end of the place” is said so as to exclude that field which is neither enclosed, circumscribed, nor bounded by any limit of place.

For this is the field which Solomon mentions in praise of the bride, saying: “She considered a field and bought it” (Prov. 31) [Col. 0646B]. This is that full field of which Isaac speaks in praise of his son: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field, which the Lord hath blessed” (Gen. 27). This is the field in which Isaac himself sowed and found a hundredfold. This is the field of lentils in which Shammah the Hararite stood bravely when the people of Israel fled, and he, standing bravely, defeated the Philistines (2 Sam. 23). This is the field which Hanameel, son of Shallum, offered for sale to his cousin Jeremiah (Jer. 32). Though Jeremiah was in danger of death, being in the mire of prison up to his throat, and knew that he could not become the possessor of the field until seventy years had passed, he nevertheless desired the field so greatly that he bought it, knowing that he could not be disappointed in his hope.

Thus either the kingdom of heaven, which is purchased by the exertion of labour, or the flesh in which Christ wrought the salvation of the human race through the labour of his passion, is signified. For it is called a field (*ager*) from acting (*agere*); it is called a field of lentils because it was capable of suffering. In it Shammah the Hararite stood when Christ became obedient to the Father unto death. Hence Shammah is interpreted “obedient,” and he is aptly called Hararite, that is, “mountain-dweller,” because in his assumed flesh the Father glorified him with the glory which he had before the world was made. Hence the Apostle: “Wherefore God also hath exalted him and given him a name which is above every name” (Phil. 2) [Col. 0646C].

When the people fled because there was none that did good, he alone trod the winepress and struck down the Philistines, because he alone overthrew spiritual enemies. Hanameel—that is, the grace of God, namely the mercy of Jesus—offered this field for sale to Jeremiah, because anyone who is exercised in the height of the spiritual life becomes a participant in so great a benefit when the grace, or mercy, of God goes before and the exertion of labour follows.

Blessed is the one who joins his own field to this field, so that he may be one in Christ and Christ one in him; thus joining field to field that is bounded by no place. For Solomon says of this field: “Prepare thy work, and diligently cultivate thy field” (Prov. 24). But woe, Isaiah says, to him who joins field to field unto the limit of a place—that is, unto the field bounded by a limit of place [Col. 0647A]. This field is shown in the parable of the sower and the seed, because “the field is the world.” Whoever joins the world to himself, or himself to the world, by love—woe to him, because, as authority says, “whosoever will be a friend of the world is made the enemy of God” (Jas. 4).

From the authorities already cited, then, divine discourse has set before us three kinds of fields: the world, the human being, and Christ. They are aptly compared with fields, because no one can possess either the world, or Christ, or even himself, except by labouring and acting. But one who uses the world misuses it; one who uses Christ enjoys him; one who uses himself does indeed use himself, but neither enjoys nor misuses himself.

For a person ought to love himself in God and for God; God, however, for God’s own sake; and he ought not to love the world except perhaps for God’s sake in some respect [Col. 0647B]—that is, when God’s power is commended in its immensity, his wisdom in its beauty, or his goodness in its usefulness. Otherwise, we must use the world as though not using it, as possessing nothing and yet possessing all things. If you wish to use the world otherwise, you misuse it. For what greater misuse can there be than to serve that which was made to serve you?

For the world was made to serve humanity, but humanity to serve the Creator—yet so that whatever the world bestowed upon humanity, or humanity offered to the Creator, should all serve human benefit. For God does not need our good things. Again, from the beginning God gave humanity two goods: one visible and the other invisible; one freely, the other by merits. Freely, the world; by merits, heaven. For Adam had done neither good nor evil when the Lord gave him the world and all things that he had made in the world. Hence, once fish, birds, and beasts had been made, he brought them to Adam to see what he would call them, so that he might know how to distinguish them by names as his own possessions [Col. 0647C]. He also willed that, through the merit of obedience, Adam should acquire for himself the invisible good.

But what a strange thing—indeed, a miserable one! Man willingly buys what is given freely, but wants to have freely what can be acquired only by buying. But what do we wish to buy, brethren? Do you see in it the field of the slothful man, which nettles entirely filled? Do you see thorns or stones, or seeds trodden under the feet of those walking on the roads? Do you consider the mountains of Gilboa, on which neither dew nor rain comes? Do you not see souls like earth without water, before God? Do you behold earth that is not satisfied with waters—indeed, earth that does not receive the rain coming upon it?

But now inspect the innate possessions of fields, and then the things brought into them. The earth is infected with corruptions. A man sows good seed, and, through the defect of the soil, tares spring up along with the good seed. It sometimes has this defect within, sometimes without, sometimes both within and without. Sometimes it infects the seed at the root; sometimes it infects the thorns with barrenness; sometimes the sprouting of tares comes not from a defect of the soil but from an affliction introduced from elsewhere. For an enemy is accustomed to do this: to sow tares over the field while the owner of the field sleeps (Matt. 13) [Col. 0647D].

Even if, perhaps, the field answers its owner well according to what was sown, those who reap another’s field at night do not know how to sleep. Therefore they imitate Cain, who urged his brother to go into the field; and I see them, in their children, offering what they gather through avarice and robbery.

Therefore what the caterpillar has left the locust eats; what the locust has left the grub eats; and what the grub has left the mildew eats (Joel 1). How detestable is the labour, how scant the fruit, how brief the gain, when in all things man destroys and consumes himself as uselessly as he does marvellously. If you open your bodily eyes, you will see these things; if your spiritual eyes, you will behold them more detestably. Is not idleness a provoker of bloodshed? This is the sluggard’s field, full of nettles. Do not riches produce the thorns of cares, hardness and obstinacy stones, instability roads? [Col. 0648B]

There are also proud persons in the world who disdain to receive the rain of preaching, like the mountains of Gilboa. There are avaricious persons who, like earth not satisfied with water, are not satisfied with riches. There are also those who are infected inwardly in their intention while their outward action is good. There are those who are corrupt in action while their intention is good. There are also those who are infected outwardly in action. Very often, when a person sleeps through negligence, the ancient enemy sows the tares of vices after the seed of faith or some other good has been received.

The elder brother also envies the younger—that is, the flesh envies the spirit—either because of the fatted calf or because the younger works in the field. For because the flesh loves the world, it places the salvation of the soul second [Col. 0648C]. I have called flesh and spirit brothers because they are brothers from the same womb, not drawing their origin from one father or one mother. For when flesh is infused and coagulated from seed, the spirit, formed by God from nothing, is without delay infused into unformed flesh in order to form it, and is formed in being infused. Once the outlines of the limbs have been formed, after the space of forty-six days, the soul is formed in being infused and, once formed, is immediately infused. For the soul is not transmitted by propagation, but the flesh is.

Hence the Prophet: “He who fashions their hearts one by one” (Ps. 32). And elsewhere: “Dust shall return to dust, and the spirit shall return unto God who made it” (Eccl. 12). And again Moses: “If anyone strikes a pregnant woman and causes miscarriage: if it was not formed, he shall be fined money; but if it was formed, he shall render life for life” (Exod. 21) [Col. 0648D]. Yet both come forth into the light from one womb and emerge together, as it were, from one womb in a fraternal fellowship.

But I call the flesh older in birth because it is first infused into liquid and formed with the outlines of limbs; then the soul, made from nothing by God alone the Creator, is joined to the formed flesh into one human being. The elder therefore envies the younger, because, when the flesh directs itself to the delights of this world, it makes little of the soul’s good.

Moreover, there are four kinds of temptations, compared with the caterpillar, locust, grub, and mildew: temptation long deliberated and hidden; sudden and open; long deliberated and open; sudden and hidden [Col. 0649A]. For if the enemy cannot suddenly overthrow the mind, he does not on that account press less strongly; rather, he gradually inclines the mind like a wall and pushes it down like a rampart. What he cannot openly seize, he steals secretly, so that he is now a serpent *vectis* [uncertain reading], now tortuous, now may be called *antemos*, now *diclux*, and shows himself to be the beast whose number is six hundred and sixty-six.

Therefore, since, as has been said, the earth is not only infected but also slain in bloodshed and defiled by works of oldness, casting away the old things when new things come, “renew for yourselves a new field, and sow not among thorns.” People call a new field (*novale*) a field which, after weeds have been uprooted, stubble burned, manure spread, ploughing, sowing, and harrowing completed, has been cleansed of every harmful old condition and yields its owner’s seed manifold increase in profit [Col. 0649B]. Such is our field of lentils, the field of Hanameel, of which I spoke.

But since weeding is nothing other than the uprooting of briars or thorns, it appears that there were briars or thorns there which were uprooted. For what was not there could not be uprooted. But if, as has been said, we understand Christ’s flesh by the field and sin by the thorn, it appears that that flesh was at some time bound by sin which was afterwards uprooted. What then is the meaning of what we read: that “he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2)? Was it not bound by actual sin, but perhaps by original sin?

But if this is so, how was he not tithed in Abraham’s loins, as Levi was tithed, if his flesh was liable to sin there as Levi’s flesh was? Therefore some have thought that the flesh assumed by the Word had been free from every sin from the first parent down to its assumption by the Word, and had been transmitted pure, so that it had never been under sin but was not merely liberated from sin, but free from it. Yet I do not discover through what channels it could have descended in this way, since it descended only through those born in concupiscence [Col. 0649C].

For this reason the affirmation of Catholic truth maintains that the Son of God, who was born for sinners, assumed flesh from flesh liable to sin. That flesh was indeed free from sin; but free because it had been liberated: free not because it had never been under sin, but because it had at some time ceased to be under it. But when? After the Virgin’s conception. For she herself, because she was conceived in concupiscence through the union of man and woman, was conceived in sins by her mother. But after conception she was cleansed and sanctified in her mother’s womb, so that she who had been conceived in sins might be born holy.

For if we believe this to be true of Jeremiah or John the Baptist because they were to be vessels of election, in whom God was to be hidden through indwelling grace, much more ought that unique vessel to have been cleansed in which the Son of God willed to dwell, not only through indwelling grace but through union of flesh; in which God assumed a human being—by “human being” I mean human nature, not a human person, but humanity into his person [Col. 0650A]—so that humanity passed into God, not through mutability of nature but through God’s gracious condescension. For neither was God changed into human substance by assuming humanity, nor was humanity changed into divine substance when it was glorified in God.

Therefore she was cleansed so that he who intended to wipe away the filth of the world might assume pure flesh for himself from pure flesh. Thus the assumed flesh required no cleansing either in conception or in birth, because from the mother’s womb it was pure in the Virgin mother. Since in Levi’s case there was in Abraham only what was afterwards to be his, Levi ought to be tithed; but Christ ought not, because Levi had both nature and guilt in Abraham’s loins through propagation of origin, whereas Christ had nature alone, which did not need tithing (Heb. 7) [Col. 0650B]. For an offering is made not for nature but for guilt; if guilt did not exist, nature would have no need of an offering.

This is the weeding of the field: namely, the cleansing and sanctification of the Virgin, who at birth received free choice, like every rational creature. And because she had free choice and it was not yet liberated, she could incline in either direction. Because she was mortal by nature, she had weakness toward evil; and because she was cleansed by grace, she had aid toward good. Thus she could sin through weakness and, through grace, could avoid sin. Hence she was all the more graced when holier: she could transgress because of weakness, yet did not transgress because grace aided her.

Therefore, as the Virgin was cleansed from original sin in her mother’s womb through operative grace [Col. 0650C], so, having been born clean, she was free from actual sin through cooperative grace. By actual sin I mean criminal sin, or perhaps venial sin—wood, hay, and stubble. Perhaps there were in her light thoughts or suggestions without consent, with which charity does not disdain to dwell. Indeed, just as straw or a drop of water is added to a furnace, so charity is joined to such venial sin.

But after the Holy Spirit, who is the ardour of the Father and the Son, came upon her and overshadowed her, and the Son of God, who is a consuming fire, made her fruitful within, he utterly burned away every straw of venial sin. Thus, while free choice remained—indeed, was rather liberated and confirmed—she was able not to sin, and she was unable to sin. For just as angels or saints already confirmed do not lack free choice and yet cannot sin, because no one compels them to do this, but by bare freedom, made firm and confirmed, they do it; so also the blessed Virgin, because of the singular privilege of grace, was so blessed in this frailty of flesh that, following the spontaneous motion of her mind, she neither wished to sin nor could sin [Col. 0650D]. This is the burning of the field’s stubble.

The angel therefore greeted one so cleansed and so gloriously purified, saying: “Hail, full of grace.” And shortly afterward: “Behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb” (Luke 1), etc. But the Virgin, not distrusting the angel’s words but asking about the manner of the event, answered: “How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?” (ibid.). As though she said in other words: How can a field be fertile unless it is first opened, unless the debt of nature is first rendered to it? How then shall this be, seeing I know not a man?

But what do you ask, Virgin? Do you ask the manner of grace in this event, or a miracle, or customary occurrence, or nature? If you ask the manner of grace: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee” (ibid.), who will burn all the field’s stubble and renew his new field, “making a new thing upon the earth, because thou shalt encompass a man.” If you ask for a miracle, dew shall descend upon the fleece of flesh and the threshing-floor remain dry. A rod shall produce a nut without a root; a bush shall be set alight by heavenly fire and shall not be consumed.

If you seek such a customary occurrence in created things, the sun of justice shall penetrate the glass of flesh without injury to the glass: neither shall the glass be corrupted nor the sun’s brightness diminished. If you seek a similar instance in nature [Col. 0651B], just as gnats arise from wine, butterflies from water, birds from trees, bees from honeycomb, woodworms from wood, and even as vultures become pregnant and conceive without intercourse with a male or infusion of seed, so you too shall conceive and be pregnant without union with a male or infusion of seed.

Nothing, therefore, can oppose this event. For it would be exceedingly absurd that he who could grant this to others could not confer it upon himself. Only open your heart to obedience, and you shall become fruitful, so that the field may be fertile. For the word of God, living and effective and sharper than every two-edged sword, shall open your heart, so that the ploughing of the field may be the opening of the heart; and you shall be made fruitful by that seed promised to Abraham: “In thy seed shall all nations inherit” (Gen. 22) [Col. 0651C]. And Isaiah again: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa. 1).

Therefore the sowing of the field was the sending, or incarnation, of the Son. What then did the Virgin answer the angel? “Behold,” she said, “the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). How fittingly and truly she might have said: Behold the queen of the world—indeed, the queen of heaven—who said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” But thus she sprinkled her field with the manure of humility, concerning which we read in the Gospel: “Leave it this year also, until I dig around it”—that is, around the fig tree—“and put manure upon it” (Luke 13).

For *stercus*, *laetamen*, and *fimus* are the same thing. It is called *stercus* because it is spread out (*sternitur*); *fimus* because it becomes low (*fit imus*); *laetamen* because it makes shoots joyful (*laeta*). Under this manure, therefore, the seed was harrowed in. The harrowing of the seed is the hiding of the Word. The seed is the Word of God, and to harrow is to cover. The harrowed seed is the hidden Word [Col. 0651D]. This seed, then, is the treasure of which it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field” (Matt. 13). For it is written: “Desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21). And elsewhere: “The Word is near thee, in thy mouth” (Rom. 10).

There is, then, no word in the mouth of the wise other than “the desirable treasure in the mouth of the wise.” The treasure, therefore, is the Word. But the word in the mouth of the flesh is one thing; the word in the mouth of the heart another. There the word is inward and hidden; here it is outward and manifest. For of the mouth of the heart it is written: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom” (Ps. 36 [37]). From the mouth of the supreme Father—that is, from the mouth of the heart—this Word was brought forth: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44 [45]). What is the Father’s heart? That which elsewhere is called the Father’s womb. In this womb the hidden Word of the Father was brought forth into the Virgin’s womb, and was again hidden there.

But in the Father’s womb it was hidden because the Father’s wisdom is incomprehensible. For the Father’s wisdom is the Father’s Word. Yet it was hidden in the mother’s womb lest it be recognized by the faithless Jews. “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” Yet, just as he did not will to be wholly manifest, so neither did he will to be altogether hidden: he willed in some measure to be made manifest, lest unbelief find an opening, and yet to be hidden, so that faith might have merit. Therefore wisdom, which was immutable in its own nature, willed to be hidden beneath our mutability, [Col. 0652B] so that through assumed mutability we might be changed to immutability—or, better, might be made immutable. For the faithless will be changed, but will not be made immutable, because they will not be changed in him. Hence the Apostle says: “We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15).

But then we shall be made immutable, not only when our corruptible nature puts on incorruption, or our mortal nature immortality, but when death is swallowed up in victory. Therefore, as has been said, the Father’s wisdom, immutable in its divinity, willed to be mutable in our humanity. Thus immutable in what is its own, mutable in what is ours. It is immutable in what is its own because it could neither be increased nor diminished nor changed. It could not be increased because it is immeasurable; nor diminished, because [Col. 0652C] it is simple and one. Nor could it be changed in place, because it is everywhere; nor in time, because it is eternal; nor in thought, because it is most wise; nor in affection, because it is supremely good.

For although, because of the diversity of names, it appears to change in human affairs—being called now knowledge because of present things, now foreknowledge because of future things, now disposition because of things to be done, now predestination because of those to be saved, and now providence because of things subject to it—this does not mean that it itself changes among things, but that things change their mode of being in it, or at least beneath it. Yet it was made mutable in our humanity, either according to the mutability of coherence or separation, of attachment or inherence.

The mutability of coherence is when one thing coheres with another thing of a different kind in such a way that it changes it and is itself changed: as when food is incorporated, the food is changed into flesh, and the flesh is made stronger. Or when one thing so coheres with another that it is not itself changed but changes the other, as wisdom, when it comes to the soul, changes the soul for the better, making it wiser, while it itself is not changed. Or again, when one thing coheres with another such that it is itself changed but does not change the other: as humanity cohering with divinity; divinity changed humanity because it made it worthier and better, while it itself was not changed.

The mutability of separation, however, is when a thing that is one is changed into another such that both accident and subject are changed together; this occurred when water was changed into wine. There [Col. 0653A] wine so passed into another thing that both the color and taste of water passed into the color and taste of wine, and the very substance of water into the substance of wine. Or when one thing passes into another so that, while the subject remains, the accidents change—as happens when hay is changed into glass: there only the accidents are changed, namely hayness, if one may put it so, into glassness, while the same substance of the hay remains. Or when one thing so passes into another that the subject itself changes but not the accidents: as when bread becomes, or passes into, Christ’s body. The substance of bread passes into the substance of Christ’s body, but the accidents—that is, the roundness of the bread and the taste of the wine—do not change. These accidents are not in a subject, because they are one set of accidents and the accidents of the subject another. For there is not breadness, but, if one may put it so, fleshness.

The mutability of inherence is when the soul is changed by diverse affections, so that it now rejoices, now grieves; now is affected by fear, now by love.

According to these affections the wisdom of God was made mutable in our humanity. For it is written: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18 [19]). And in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26). Again: “Jesus began to be afraid and weary” (Mark 14). And elsewhere: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22). Thus the assumed man is variously affected through changes of inherence.

The mutability of attachment is when the outward man is variously affected through different sufferings. [Col. 0653C] Hence it is written of that assumed man: “Jesus, after fasting forty days and forty nights, afterward hungered” (Matt. 4). And again: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, sat thus beside the well” (John 4). And Isaiah says: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53). Behold how mutable he was. In all these things the Son of God was hidden. For this reason the Psalmist says: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 29 [31]). And Isaiah: “Truly you are a hidden God” (Isa. 45). Therefore, “the kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field” (Matt. 13), etc.

He was hidden, as has been said, either because he is incomprehensible in divinity, or because he was found mutable in humanity by the faithful. [Col. 0653D] But who are they who found him? Those who today came to meet Christ. This feast is called the *Hypapante* of the Lord, that is, the Meeting of the Lord, because today the solemn commemoration of Simeon and Anna is celebrated: they met Christ in the Temple when his parents brought him in order to set him before the Lord—that is, to present him to the Lord by offering him.

And this is most fitting. For Simeon is interpreted “obedient,” Anna “grace.” Grace moves the mind to faith; obedience advances the mind once moved to action. Grace moves the mind so that it may will; obedience advances it through cooperating grace. Grace gives the light of faith; obedience gives an increase of virtue. Thus, advancing honorably in this procession—the men apart, Simeon and Joseph, and the women, Anna and Mary—they deserved to receive mercy in the midst of the Temple.

[Col. 0654A] For, as has been said, Anna means grace; Mary, illuminating; Simeon, obedient; Joseph, increase. And because one faith is great in knowledge but small in affection, another great in affection but small in knowledge, while another is great both in knowledge and in affection, God approves that faith which weds affection to knowledge. The first is the faith of the wise, namely, from *sapere*, “to know”; the second is the faith of the wise, namely, from *sapor*, “taste”; the third is the faith of those wise persons in whose hearts the knowledge and affection of faith make sweet what they know.

The first belonged to the philosophers, who, “when they had known God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts; and, professing themselves to be wise, became fools.” The second belonged to the Canaanite woman and the centurion. Of the one it was said: “O woman, great is your faith” (Matt. 15); of the other: “I have not found so great a faith in Israel” (Matt. 8). The third belonged to Anna and Simeon, who are shown to have possessed faith in both ways, since it is written: Simeon received weakness in his hands, but inwardly recognized majesty. Behold the greatness of knowledge. Seeing him, he blessed God and said: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace” (Luke 2). Behold affection. Likewise Anna the prophetess, coming upon them, spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel.

Accordingly, affection is also indicated in the finding of the treasure, when it is said: “And for joy he goes and sells” (Matt. 13), etc. Love’s affection does not know how to be idle, [Col. 0654C] but goes forth into effect. Therefore he goes, either by the way of the commandments, or by the way of truth, or by the more excellent way of charity. For one must go first by the way of truth, through which the beginner is led into all truth; secondly by the way of the commandments, through which one advancing is guided along straight paths; finally by the way of charity, through which the perfect person is brought to God, who is charity. Thus the beginner, the advancing person, and the perfect person, going by the way of truth, the way of the commandments, and the way of charity, are led in, guided onward, and brought through.

Therefore he goes and sells his possessions. He sells them in order that he may be freer to run. For who can run while burdened? Therefore he sells what is his, that he may buy that field.

What does he sell? Temporal things, natural things, and gratuitous gifts. By temporal things I mean himself together with his possessions: first himself, and afterward what is his. He must deny himself to himself: the Lord says, “He who loves his life shall lose it; and he who hates his life in this world shall keep it unto eternal life” (John 12). And concerning possessions it is written: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses is not worthy of me” (Luke 14).

Natural things are memory, will, reason, and understanding; and these must be expended in order to possess the field. For whatever you have of memory, will, reason, or finally understanding, you must spend in obtaining the field. Gratuitous gifts are faith, hope, and charity; all these must be offered in purchasing the field. Whatever you are and whatever you have, give it all. What are these worth? [Col. 0655A] In comparison with the field, all must be reckoned as a drop from a bucket and as the weight of a balance. Therefore the wise man goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.

A man buys the field in order to possess the treasure, because unless the field stands between, man does not come to the treasure. So great a possession would not fittingly belong to one so small, unless through the price of the field, proportioned to our poverty. You should remember that I said above that divinity is signified by the treasure and humanity by the field. By humanity I mean the body and soul assumed by the Word.

There are, therefore, two extremes, diametrically opposed: God and man. God in his own nature is immortal, impassible, and just; man, in his nature infected and corrupted by sin, is passible, mortal, and unjust. Therefore, in order that these two extremes, so utterly contrary to one another, might be united, two middle terms were interposed: Christ’s flesh and soul. It is like the four elements, in which the two extremes, earth and fire, are greatly opposed to one another—for fire is subtle, sharp, and mobile, while earth is tangible, blunt, and immobile—and are mediated by the other two elements: air, which has much in common with fire because it is subtle and mobile, though not sharp; and much also with earth because it is blunt; and water, which agrees with air because it is mobile, and with earth because it is blunt and intangible. These are bound together by certain numbers, as it is written (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, metrum 9, line 10):

> He binds the elements by numbers.

[Col. 0655C] Thus too those two extremes, God and man, are united by two middle terms, bound by the same numbers, and figured in the same elements. For what prevents us from figuring God by fire? “For our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4). By earth, then, is figured man made from earth; by air, the soul, because philosophers called air the soul of the world. By water Christ’s flesh is not unfittingly figured. For it too is denoted by the thick water found in the well.

God, then, as has been said, in his own nature impassible, immortal, and just, assumed a soul that was indeed immortal and just but passible; and he willed it to be a middle term between the assumed flesh and God, because it possessed something befitting God—namely immortality and justice—and something shared with flesh, namely passibility. He assumed flesh that was passible, mortal, and just; and he willed it to be a middle term between man and the soul, because it possessed something in common with the soul, namely passibility and justice, and something in common with man, passibility and mortality. For man, as has been said, is passible, mortal, and unjust.

Hence the Church, whose head is said to be Christ and whose body is man, is compared to a tabernacle. Christ indeed is the head of the Church—I mean Christ entire, in two natures and three substances. His Holy of Holies is divinity; the holy place, the soul; the inner court, the assumed flesh; and the outer court, the mass of penitents. [Col. 0656A] The veil between the holy place and the inner court is mortality; between the inner court and the outer court, injustice.

For passibility separated the immortal, just, and passible soul from the immortal, just, and impassible one. Mortality separated the passible, just, and mortal body from the just, passible, and immortal soul. Injustice separated sinful, passible, mortal, and unjust man from the mortal, passible, and just flesh. But Christ suffered, and the veils of the tabernacle were torn from top to bottom. Then that soul ceased to be passible, the flesh to be mortal, and man to be unjust. For through Christ’s passion man acquired the merit of impassibility, immortality, and justice, so that through the shedding of his blood [Col. 0656B] he might be united with the immortal, impassible, and just One.

Thus, in the creation of things, the sacrament of so great a reality came first; in the Church came the reality and the sacrament; in man and Christ, the reality without sacrament. In creation, the figure came first; in the Church, the image followed; in man and Christ, truth was fulfilled. In order that the extremes may thus be joined, it is necessary to devote attention to how the middle terms are joined. This will fittingly occur if our soul is like the kingdom of heaven, and that kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden and found.

It must therefore be known that when the soul is variously affected by diverse affections, it takes on diverse forms within itself—or rather transforms itself into diverse forms. For when through bestial motions it conforms itself to beasts, it is “compared to senseless cattle and made like them.” When it deforms itself in the filth of vices, lingering and dwelling where Satan’s seat is, it is compared to the gravel-banks of Cocytus. But when it frees itself from slavery to sin, rules itself through wisdom, reigns through fortitude, and becomes the seat of Wisdom, then it is like the kingdom of heaven. For authority says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” And Wisdom says: “Heaven is my seat” (Isa. 66), from which Gregory proves that heaven is the soul of the righteous.

For heaven is called, as it were, *caelum*, that is, *casa helios*, “house of the sun,” because through the indwelling grace of the Sun of righteousness the soul becomes a house, as it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14). It is therefore not unfittingly compared with heaven. And because there are diverse degrees and varied advances in virtues, it is made like not the kingdom of heaven, but the kingdom of the heavens.

[Col. 0656D] For when it is troubled by diverse tribulations or temptations, it is like the clouded heaven, called aerial. Hence, because of the clouding brought by rains, the Apostle compares it to darkness when he says: “We do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness” (Eph. 6). But because the Lord says: “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. 90 [91]), in that clouding of tribulations it becomes like a hidden treasure, not yet found.

But when, after temptations, it begins to clear through devotion, it is compared to the heaven of serenity, called ethereal. In this too it is like a treasure not hidden but found. When it is strengthened by stability, so that it always strives to divide the waters from the waters—that is, care for the spirit from care for the flesh—then it is compared to the crystalline heaven, called the firmament. Then too it is made like the man who sells his possessions to buy the treasure, because he despises lower things in order to possess higher, and counts temporal things as little in order to acquire heavenly things.

But when it grows ever more ardent through desire, so that, though placed in this pilgrimage only in body, it dwells in thought and longing in that eternal homeland, it is made like the uranian heaven, called the empyrean. And through this it is also made like him who [Col. 0657B] buys the treasure he has found through labors, desires, and sighs. Finally, when after passing struggles it is raised to the prize of the heavenly calling, that is, as far as the heaven of the three hierarchies, then it enjoys the treasure it has bought, because it shall be one in God and God one in it: immortal, impassible, and just with the immortal, impassible, and just One, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. FOR SEPTUAGESIMA SUNDAY

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Rather for Quinquagesima Sunday, or for Lent, as is clear from the entire course of the discourse.]

“I repent that I made man” (Gen. 6). It must not be supposed, dearly beloved, that any mutability or injury can befall him with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration. He judges all things indeed with tranquillity, yet Scripture often declares him angry. But this itself is said on account of its effect, so that it may show us to be worthy of his anger. Hence it is said: “I repent that I made man.”

Yet in this expression, according to two modes of understanding, justice and peace have kissed. Justice, if it is understood thus: “I repent that I made man,” as though he said, “I shall do what a repentant man is accustomed to do, because he destroys what he has made.” Peace, if it is taken thus: “I repent that I made man,” that is, punishment holds me on account of the man whom I made; as though he said: guilt holds man liable to punishment, but punishment for guilt will hold me. He acted, and I shall bear it; he seized, and I shall pay. Therefore I shall bear what he did, because I shall bear it for him whom I made. For who would think little of what is his own?

“What woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one of them, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and diligently seek until she finds it? Or what man, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost?” (Luke 15). “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock” (Ezek. 34). This does not rest upon man or angel, because perversity was found in each. Therefore “my soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26), since if a man was angry over an ivy plant for which he had not labored, our Jonah should much more justly be [Col. 0658A] sorrowful over the ivy plant which he made.

And rightly we compare the Son of God to Jonah, because just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so the Son of Man was in the heart of the earth. Hence, when a wicked and adulterous generation sought a sign, no sign was given it except the sign of Jonah. This Jonah, therefore, planted the ivy when he made man; sustaining him with the fork of discernment and the staff of reason, he raised him from the earth, because he gave man an exalted countenance. Giving him also the greenness of understanding, he found the shade of love. Hence it is written: “His delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8).

But at length a worm gnawed the ivy’s root, and, as the burning hot wind blew, it withered. Who, do you think, is this worm? It is he of whom Isaiah speaks: “Their worm shall not die” (Isa. 66). That horrible worm is the ancient serpent, who clearly gnawed the root of the ivy when he deceived the first man by fraud. For from him, as from a root, all human beings have sprung as branches.

But how did this occur? “At the rising,” he says, “of dawn” (Jonah 4). The name “day” sometimes signifies the perverse delight of action, as in: “Let the day perish on which I was born” (Job 3). The twilight of this day is negligence of mind; its night, the darkening of the heart; its dawn, consent to suggestion; the brightness of its day, delight in the deed. Therefore at the rising of dawn the worm corrupted the root of the ivy, when the ancient enemy infected the first parent through consent to suggestion.

Or, because hairs are customarily signified by the root of man, and thoughts of the mind by hairs, it struck the ivy at the rising of dawn when, through consent to thought, it alienated human beings from their Creator. And then it made the ivy wither, because, its moisture withdrawn, charity made man like land without water.

Rightly, therefore, both Jonahs—the spiritual and the material—grieved when touched by one sorrow. For the loss of each, of the one through the sacrament of the reality, of the other through the reality of the sacrament, was one and the same. Let us therefore see with what grief each grieves. Tell us, Jonah, tell us: “Do you think you are rightly angry?” “I am angry,” he says, “unto death” (Jonah 4). And you, Lord Jesus, are you rightly angry? “My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26). Certainly you are rightly angry, because good is the anger that is relieved by such great mercy. You are rightly angry, I say, because when you are angry, you remember mercy.

Therefore be angry unto death, good Jesus, and repent—you whom, if I grieved you for an hour, I no longer regret. For we have no salvation apart from your precious death: by your saving death you slew death.

[Note: [Col. 0658D] Words of the Church in the blessing of the Paschal candle.]

> “O happy fault, which deserved to have so great and such a Redeemer. O necessary sin of Adam, which obtained mercy instead of the punishment it deserved.”

O blessed anger, through which the Son of God so endured death as to render grace in place of punishment and, through grace, to increase glory for us.

[Col. 0659A] Therefore, touched inwardly by this grief of heart, God, showing us the tender affection of a father rather than the dreadful disposition of a master, says: “I repent that I made man” (Gen. 6). As though he said: “I see every man has corrupted his way and become subject to the devil’s will; nor can he be rescued unless I repent—that is, unless punishment falls upon me. Therefore I repent, and rightly so: for I made him.”

But let us see what punishment falls upon him: the punishment of birth, the punishment of labor, and the punishment of death. For through sin man had deserved these three things: to be born with labor, to labor, and to die. And in these three things the Son of Man conquered the devil, because in order to give what was his, he assumed what was ours. O repentance, merciful and not cruel; fruitful and not barren; voluntary and not imposed by necessity. It was cruel in Judas Iscariot, barren in Esau and Saul, but necessary in every sinner. The Savior’s punishment, however, belonged to his will alone, he who “committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth.”

This, then, is the anger of Jonah—indeed, of the dove. For Jonah is interpreted “dove.” Since the dove has no gall in its heart, nor teeth in its beak, nor claws on its feet with which to harm, it reveals its anger only by the sound of its voice and outwits the enemy by its threat. This is the anger of Jonah, which proclaims that Nineveh is to be overthrown; or the anger of the dove, which presents an olive branch to those shut in the ark. The words may seem discordant, but the meaning of both is one.

For what is it for Nineveh to be overthrown? To cease to be what it was. And what was it? A city of blood, full of vices, utterly unworthy of divine consolation. It ceased to be this because Jonah—or rather the dove—presented them with an olive branch. What is the olive branch? It is the abundance of divine mercy: when it turned away from the evil which it had done, and did the good from which it had turned aside.

But when? After forty days. For it is written: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3). But how after forty days? After repentance. For after forty days the dove presented the olive branch, and Jonah proclaimed that Nineveh was to be overthrown. For we cannot turn away from evil or share in divine mercy unless we first grieve over past sins through repentance.

And repentance is fittingly signified by the number forty, because just as the fiftieth is obtained from forty, and through repentance remission of sins is acquired, so remission of sins is signified by fifty; hence the jubilee is also called “remissive.” The children of Israel did not receive the promised land unless they first suffered in the wilderness for forty years. Thus Elijah fasted forty days before coming to the mountain of God.

Moses too abstained forty days in order to receive the Law a second time; and the Lord Jesus fasted forty days and as many nights in order to show that no one ought to be excluded from the penitence of Lent (Matt. 4). Therefore, if we wish, like the Ninevites, to turn from evil to good; if we wish to share in divine mercy; if, with Elijah, we wish to ascend the mountain [Col. 0660A] of divine contemplation; if, with Moses, to know God’s mysteries; if finally, with the Savior himself, to receive the fellowship of angels, we must offer ourselves as a tithe through Lenten repentance. For in these sacred times, since they make up the tenth part of the year, we ought, as if in payment of tithes, to give ourselves to God.

Let us therefore fast from vices and worldly business; let us fast from food and from impure desires. For in these four things the whole affliction of repentance consists. Fasting is the common satisfaction of all the members, so that the members may make satisfaction according to the sins they have committed. And fasting (*jejunium*) is said to derive from *jejunum*, a certain human intestine which is found empty after its owner’s death. Likewise we ought to be found empty of vices both in body and in soul.

There is a threefold authority for fasting: from the antiquity of time, the quality of the place, and the institution of the teacher. It comes from the institution of the teacher because it came from God; from the quality of the place because it was in Paradise; from antiquity of time because it was from the beginning of the world. Hence it was said: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat” (Gen. 2). So long as Eve abstained, she was a virgin and remained in Paradise; but once the fast was violated, she felt the lust of the flesh and did not remain in Paradise. Adam likewise, after violating the fast, fell into the misery of the world.

Again, the authority of fasting is shown by periods and persons: before the Law, by Moses; under the Law, by Elijah; under grace, by Christ. Moses indeed spoke with God after fasting (Exod. 25); Elijah, after fasting, was carried up into heaven in a fiery chariot (4 Kings [2 Kings] 2). Thus Jerusalem, in the time of King Hezekiah, was delivered through fasting, when one hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain in one night. Unable to endure the stench of the dead, King Sennacherib fled with only ten soldiers to Nineveh, where on the fortieth day he was killed by his own sons (4 Kings [2 Kings] 10). Again, when Jonah preached, pardon was granted to the Ninevites through fasting. Joshua son of Nun likewise, through fasting, checked the course of sun and moon and overcame the Gibeonites.

It should be noted that one kind of fasting belongs to the body or flesh, another to the mind. Bodily fasting is when someone abstains from food so that the flesh may not grow overly fat; but this is not virtue. Mental fasting is when someone fasts from vices, lest the flesh grow fat through lusts. Again, one fasting is of institution, another of devotion; one of frugality, another of dispensation. Again, one fasting is rational, another irrational. Again, one fasting concerns quality, another number; one is of strict exactitude, another of alternation. One is solely from charity, another solely from necessity, another from vanity or pretense.

Institutional fasting is such as Lent and the other fasts instituted by the holy Fathers. Under the old Law, indeed, the holy Fathers offered the Lord tithes and firstfruits from all their possessions. Likewise we ought to offer tithes to God, not only from our possessions but also from ourselves, by fasting. Hence Lent was instituted as a tithe of days, [Col. 0661A] so that out of the three hundred and sixty-six days in the yearly cycle we may render not merely a tenth, but a tenth of a tenth; and, to make up for the two days not tithed, as Augustine held, Mass should be celebrated at night on the vigil of Easter. Hence it is said in the collect: “O God, who hast made this most holy night …”

There are also the institutional fasts of the four seasons, which Pope Callixtus instituted.

[Note: [Col. 0661D] Epistle 1, Decree.]

Writing in this manner: “To the blessed brother and fellow bishop: the fast which you have learned is observed among us three times in the year, we now decree should more fittingly be observed at the four seasons, so that as the year revolves through four seasons, so we too may celebrate a fourfold solemn fast through the four seasons of the year, according to the words of the prophet Zechariah, who says.”

“The fast of the fourth [month]” (Zech. 7), etc.

[Col. 0661B] For the Jews fast four times in the year: before Passover, before Pentecost, before the Feast of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*), and before the Feast of Dedication (*Encaenia*). Or this is because the ancients fasted forty days four times a year, so that in place of one forty-day fast we may at least fast three days. Or these fasts occur four times in the year to signify the four events occurring in the four seasons: the Lord’s conception in spring, his Nativity in winter; John’s conception in autumn, his Nativity in summer. Or because they signify the four *tessaredecads*, that is, the four generations of the Lord. For *tessare* means four and *deca* ten. Thus there are fourteen generations from Abraham to Moses; likewise there are fourteen weeks from the first day of March to the second of June; and so proceed through each interval.

For the ancients customarily fasted as follows. The spring fasts occur in March, so that vices may wither in us. The summer fasts, namely in the week of Pentecost when the Holy Spirit came, occur so that the Holy Spirit may come upon us. The September fasts, when the fruits of the earth are gathered, occur so that in thanksgiving we may render the fruits of good works. The December fasts, when plants die, occur so that we may die to the world and deserve to be reborn to God.

The spring fasts are called the first because they occur in the first month; the summer fasts are called the fourth because they occur in the fourth month, that is, June; the August fasts, the seventh, because they occur in the seventh month, that is, September; the winter fasts, the tenth, because they occur in the tenth month, that is, December.

Or rather, according to Zechariah’s prophecy, we ought to observe these distinctions of fasts for as long as we are in mourning and, as it were, exiles. For Sarazar and Rogummelech had inquired through envoys whether they ought to fast in the fifth and seventh months; finally the prophet answered in the Lord’s person: “The fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid solemnities” (ibid.).

The prophet’s mention of the fast of the fourth was based on history, because the Hebrews relate that in the fourth month, namely July, Moses came down from the mountain [Col. 0662A] and broke the tablets (Exod. 32); and according to Jeremiah, at that time the city walls were first breached. In the fifth, that is, August, a sedition arose among the people because of the scouts of the Holy Land; they were commanded not to ascend the mountain, but wandered in the wilderness for forty years, so that all died there except two, Caleb and Joshua. In this month too, first Nebuchadnezzar and later Titus destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem and captured the city of Bethel, to which many thousands of Jews had fled; and the Temple itself was ploughed over.

In the seventh month Gedaliah was killed, together with the tribe of Judah, and the remnant of Jerusalem was scattered (Jer. 41). In the tenth, Ezekiel in captivity and the people of the captives heard that the Temple had been overthrown. These are the reasons for mourning and fasting. By such fasts, therefore, the Church imitates the holy Fathers.

But the Church’s substitution of the fast of the first for that of the fifth is done for symbolic reasons. First, it is necessary for us to restrain our sensuality, which subsists through the five senses; next, the licentiousness of our flesh, which consists of four elements; thirdly, we must restrain the spiritual affections that flow from the seven spiritual vices. We must also restrain ourselves from the vanities of the world, through which we have disobeyed the commandments contained under the number ten of the Decalogue.

## SERMON XIV. FOR LENT
“Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit” (Matt. 4), etc. So long as we contend in the struggle and suffer shipwreck amid dangers, my brothers, we need great vigilance. For who would not fear amid so many dangers from men, dangers from demons, dangers from the flesh, dangers from the world, dangers from thought—the strength, multitude, cunning of our enemies, and their sleepless watchfulness? They are many; we are few. We are unarmed; they are armed. They are already trained by an ancient campaign; we, newly kindled with religious zeal, need much training. Therefore let not the soldier who is girded boast equally with the ungirded, because, as long as we live, we cannot be without danger. “For the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7).

The Canaanite could never be driven out from among the children of Israel; it was much if he could be made tributary. For the ancient enemy, although he sometimes yields to us, nevertheless never withdraws from us, but always walks with us. If he does not go before us so that he may be seen, he becomes a deceitful spirit at our side, that he may pursue a person more cautiously; or indeed he follows behind, that he may not be recognized at all. He goes before us when he corrupts us through open and violent wickedness. This is well prefigured in Zedekiah, before whose eyes the Babylonians slew his sons (4 Kings 25). The Babylonians are evil spirits, sons of confusion, because they commonly so confuse us that, while we see and know it, they destroy and extinguish the virtues which ought, as it were sons, to be begotten from their mother, reason. [Col. 0663A]

For often you know that you are sinning, that you are acting wrongly, that you are offending the Lord; yet you are so transgressive that you can no longer restrain yourself. Thus Adam sinned, because, as the Apostle says, “Adam was not deceived, but Eve was deceived” (1 Tim. 2). Eve believed to be true what the wily serpent had promised her: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). But Adam knew this to be false; yet, lest he offend Eve, he took the forbidden fruit from her hand and ate it. Hence, since sin is customarily committed in three ways—through weakness, as Peter’s sin; through ignorance, as Paul’s; through deliberate purpose, as this sin—Adam deserved punishment so much the graver as his fault before God was graver. “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who does not know shall be beaten with few” (Luke 12).

He accompanies us at the side when he persecutes a person through a collateral vice. Every virtue is confined between two vices: one opposed to the virtue, and the other collateral to it. Mercy, for example, is placed between cruelty and sluggishness: cruelty is its opposite, while sluggishness is collateral to it. Likewise courage stands between faintheartedness and obstinacy: faintheartedness opposes it, while obstinacy accompanies it collaterally. The same may readily be recognized concerning all virtues. Therefore, when the ancient enemy seeks to afflict someone endowed with virtue and sees that his effort can accomplish nothing through the opposing vice—but recognizes that he has been detected and expelled—he does not therefore retreat or press less hard. Rather, he turns himself to the more cunning weapons of the collateral vice. [Col. 0663C]

This is well figured in Paul’s zeal, which he certainly possessed, though not according to knowledge, when, having received letters, he came to Damascus in order to kill any men whom he found belonging to the way of truth (Acts 9). For he judged the persecution of God’s Church to be the height of religion; and thus he obtained mercy because he acted in ignorance. Behold how the devil walked at his side, for he concealed cruelty beneath zeal for justice. But if he perceives that he cannot prevail even thus, then he rises as though from behind, when, in the very exercise of virtue, he deceitfully causes the person whom he persecutes to exceed due bounds with regard to manner, place, time, or person. For virtue itself must be accounted a vice if manner, place, time, or person is not carefully considered.

Hence the Law commands that the members of the sacrifice be arranged upon the pile of wood. “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” If you offer your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you (Matt. 5), yet do not reconcile yourself to him, then your offering profits you nothing, although it is good to offer to God. For you ought to have left your gift and been reconciled to your brother. Therefore, because you did not observe the proper time, you sinned. [Col. 0664A]

See how great a capacity for prudent foresight, circumspection, and caution we need. We must forestall manifest evils by the virtue of foresight; collateral evils by circumspection; and the very exercise of virtues by the caution of discernment. For often, when we labor to search the conscience and examine the mind in order to separate virtues from vices, unless we are very cautious, the very labor of examination corrupts the examiner’s conscience.

Dinah went out to see the foreign women; and Shechem corrupted her, soothing the virgin with blandishments, as Scripture says (Gen. 34). For what is represented in Dinah but conscience? She is rightly called Jacob’s daughter when she struggles to examine vices, for “Jacob” is interpreted “wrestler.” She goes out to see foreign women when, in order to recognize the evils she has done, she wanders outside herself in thought. But when vainglory steals in through the very labor of examination, because she recognizes herself as cautious, Shechem corrupts the virgin with blandishments. For what is represented in Shechem, whose name is interpreted “shoulder,” except labor? And what in the blandishments except vainglory? She is rightly called a virgin, because she is barren and, through vainglory, deprived of the reward of her labor.

Hence blessed Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0663D] Homily 12 on the Gospels], explaining the parable of the ten virgins, says: “From today’s reading of the holy Gospel I am compelled to say that you must perform the good deeds you do with great caution, lest, through what is rightly done by you, you seek favor or human approval.” [Col. 0664C] For five of them were foolish, because through desire for praise they became barren of the reward of virginity. Therefore I say to you, brothers: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Luke 22). Watch with vigilance; pray with devotion.

For who can be secure from temptation when Christ himself is led by the devil to be tempted? Where the Lord is struck, will the servant be safe? The elephant swims: how shall the lamb cross over? The waters overflow up to the head: who can ford them? Perhaps these are the waters which the prophet feared to cross, although he had crossed those reaching to the ankles, loins, and knees (Ezek. 47). For it is not to be feared if we must cross waters overflowing to the ankles, loins, or knees; but we cannot enter without fear and danger those which we see rising above the head. The waters are certainly temptations, of which the Prophet says: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. 68).

They overflow to the ankles of the Church when evil spirits hasten to tempt those who are lower and subject within the Church. “The saints experienced mockings and scourges, moreover bonds and imprisonment; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted” (Heb. 11). They come to the knees when they bring troubles upon those who know, through discipline, how to stretch themselves out and, through compassion for a brother’s suffering, how to bend down. They rise to the loins when they constantly afflict with troubles the teachers of the Church, who beget children from her through the word of preaching. [Col. 0665A]

Therefore, when the prophet foresaw that all these things would happen in the Church—that subjects, teachers, prelates, and all who wish to live piously in God would be tempted and suffer persecution—he did not for that reason abandon the Law of the Lord or fear to fall into human hands. Rather, with the children of Israel he passed through the persecution of the Babylonian captivity. For he knew that the children of Israel had sinned and ought to wash away their committed guilt by a worthy fruit of repentance. But when he saw the waters growing up to the head of the Church, he could not ford them, because by human reasoning he could not discover beforehand why Christ, who was God and “did no sin,” was tempted. Perhaps he knew that this had to happen; and this is what it means that he came to the water. But, marveling and greatly afraid concerning these things of God, he entrusted nothing to himself but everything to the will of God. Therefore it is said that he did not ford the waters. Those three matters were perhaps difficult to him; but the fourth was most difficult for his mind to comprehend at all. [Col. 0665B]

Since, then, we cannot be without temptations, because Christ himself was tempted (Matt. 3), we must keep watch concerning temptations, because there is nothing that can save us if vigilance is absent. Who will heal the half-dead man if the Samaritan passes by? Who will resist the sons of the Berothite if the doorkeeper who cleans the wheat is asleep? For what is signified by the doorkeeper or the Samaritan except the watchful care of the mind? “Samaritan” is interpreted “guardian.” Nothing can resist the ancient enemy if the guard of the mind sleeps through negligence. This is the doorkeeper who cleans the wheat when, by discernment, she examines virtues and vices as grains from chaff.

Therefore, lest we die with Ish-bosheth in our bed (2 Kings 4), let the doorkeeper of the house keep watch in cleansing the wheat. If we are negligent in examining virtues and vices, the ancient enemy must kill the soul through thought. Yet even in this vigilance we must be careful: through thoughtless vigilance, an excessive conflict makes the vigilant person fainthearted and fearful; or a victory over temptation obtained through vigilance makes him presumptuous. How could Peter resist when Caiaphas’s doorkeeper ensnared him as he warmed himself at the coals? For fear is figured in the cold, and thoughtless vigilance in Caiaphas’s doorkeeper. Thus, when thoughtless vigilance makes the mind founded upon the rock of faith fearful concerning its sins, so that it despairs through thought, Caiaphas’s doorkeeper indeed ensnares Peter as he grows cold (John 18). [Col. 0665D]

But if through vigilance you conquer in conflict and become presumptuous through victory, you will be slain, like Eleazar son of Mattathias, by the elephant which you kill (1 Macc. 6). You kill the enemy when, not sluggish in vigilance, you overcome an evil thought. But when you grow proud of victory, you fall, as it were, beneath what is falling. I say, indeed, that it is often better to succumb to a vice and thereby be humbled than to perform a virtue and thereby become proud. For when you succumb to the devil through an act of vice and are afterward humbled, you kill enemies like blind Samson as he dies. Hence it is said: “The iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42).

O happy Samaritan woman, I say, who found the Lord Jesus seated above the well, and made the barren water-jar fruitful with the water springing up from the well into eternal life (John 4). For “Samaritan woman” means “guardianship,” “Jesus” means “Savior,” and “Jacob” means “wrestler.” [Col. 0666A]

Jacob’s well, therefore, indicates the wellspring of our conflict and temptation. For since desire is occupied with riches, honors, and pleasures, and these three flow, as streams, from the fountain of desire, when you are tempted and struggle concerning one of these three, you have arrived not at a stream but at Jacob’s well. But if you struggle against desire as a whole, you come to carry in the water-jar of your heart the water of devotion from Jacob’s well. Therefore, when you guard your mind, you are like the Samaritan woman. When you fight and conquer, you find Jesus at the well. And when spiritual grace makes the soul fruitful, it fills the water-jar with the water of saving wisdom.

Therefore, that you may be more cautious through such vigilance, watch and pray lest you enter into temptation. For, as we said above, the waters have reached up to the head and cannot be forded unless he divides them who divided the river Jordan with Elijah’s cloak (4 Kings 2), and the Red Sea with Moses’ rod; for by these two means the entire water of temptation is divided and dispersed (Exod. 14). You know that a cloak is customarily made for exposure to winds and rains. Therefore patience is rightly understood by the cloak, and the undefiled law of the Lord by Moses’ rod. Thus the waters are divided by rod and cloak because, when the undefiled law of the Lord converts souls and through patience we possess those who have been converted, all streams of temptation are dried up.

Therefore pray that you may not enter, that you may not be led into temptation. For thus the teacher of wisdom taught us to pray: “And lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6). “Lead us into,” not merely “lead.” For it is dangerous to be led into, but not dangerous to be led. For Jesus “was led into the wilderness by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil” (Matt. 4). He was led, not led into. Some are led, others are led into, others are led all the way through. They are led through suggestion; led into through consent and deliberation; led all the way through by committing the act. Therefore, one tempted by suggestion alone, not by consent or action, is rightly said to be led, not led into or led all the way through. [Col. 0666D]

Jesus, therefore, was led into the wilderness; but why? Because he came to die for us and concealed from the one who intended to arrange his death through Jewish hands the mystery of his power. Thus Tobias dipped his foot in the Tigris so that the fish might approach more quickly (Tob. 6). Thus David changed his appearance before Achish that he might crush his enemies more cautiously (1 Kings 21). Thus Samson joined himself to one of the daughters of the Philistines that he might seize the Philistines themselves more safely (Judg. 16).

For Christ uncovered his foot in the Tigris when he showed the reality of his humanity in temptation. David changed his appearance before Achish when Christ concealed from the devil the power of his divinity. Samson joined one of the daughters of the Philistines to himself when, in the sun of righteousness, the misery of our humanity was made known through the sign of temptation. But why? That the fish, the enemies, and the Philistines might be seized. Therefore, in order that the cunning of the devil, the ancient enemy, might be caught, Christ showed in temptation the reality of his humanity, concealed his divinity, and assumed the misery of our humanity. Therefore Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit (Matt. 4). [Col. 0667B]

Here it must be asked, as Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0667D] Homily 16 on the Gospels], by which spirit Jesus was led into the wilderness. And rightly so, for there are four kinds of spirits: the spirit of the world, the Spirit of God, the spirit of man, and the spirit of the devil. The Spirit of God is the graciousness of devotion; the spirit of the world, the wind of vanity; the spirit of man, the understanding of reason; the spirit of the devil, the intention of an evil will. These four spirits therefore differ in some respect and agree in some respect. The wind of vanity and the understanding of reason differ, because where one breathes in, the other breathes out. But the spirit of the world and the spirit of the devil agree, because where one breathes toward, the other sighs along; and likewise the understanding of reason and the graciousness of devotion. [Col. 0667C]

By this fourfold kind of spirits, then, we are customarily led into four kinds of wildernesses. The first is the heavenly homeland: thus the Good Shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, descended to the one that had strayed. The second is the religious life, concerning which it is written: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” (Song 3). The third is the world, concerning which it is said: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness?” (Song 8). The fourth wilderness is hell. Thus, according to the Law of Moses, the scapegoat is commanded to be sent into the wilderness.

Wherever, then, you go, you are led by one of the spirits mentioned above. If you tend toward heaven, the graciousness of devotion breathes in and the intention of evil will breathes out. If you tend toward hell, the intention of evil will breathes in. If you desire a religious place, the understanding of reason sighs and the graciousness of devotion breathes in. If you tend toward the world, the wind of vanity breathes toward you and the intention of evil will breathes in.

Since they partly agree and partly differ, it must be known that these spirits, compared with one another, stand in different logical relations: one is contrary to another, one subordinate, another contradictorily opposed. The graciousness of devotion, compared with the wind of vanity, is contrary to it. This we can recognize from universal propositions contrary to one another: in the former there is true blessedness; in the latter there is no true blessedness. The understanding of reason, compared with the intention of evil will, is subcontrary. [Col. 0668A] For when we are led through the understanding of reason into religious life, we arrive at true blessedness, though not at a certain or complete blessedness.
