For as long as we are in the struggle, it is uncertain whether we can attain the prize. Thus, though true blessedness is in religion, it is not yet certain. Again, while we are in religious life, we are continually wearied by troubles and temptations. Thus we lack complete blessedness, since complete blessedness will be where every misery ceases.

But when we are led by the intention of evil will into hell, we must believe ourselves in every respect miserable and unhappy. Therefore there is some blessedness in the one case, but not all blessedness; in the other there is not even some blessedness. The graciousness of devotion, compared with the understanding of reason—or, conversely, the wind of vanity compared with the intention of evil will—is subordinate. For in the graciousness of devotion which leads to heaven there is all blessedness; in the understanding of reason which makes one religious there is some blessedness. Likewise, in the wind of vanity there is no blessedness; in the intention of evil will there is not even some blessedness. But the graciousness of devotion, by which we are led to heaven, compared with the intention of evil will, by which we are led to hell, is contradictory: there is all blessedness there, but here there is not even some blessedness.

From the differences and agreements of these propositions, then, a certain ambiguity customarily arises in our hearts when we are led by one of the spirits into one of the wildernesses. This ambiguity is like a crossroads at which the king of Babylon sits, seeking divinations and mingling arrows (Ezek. 21). For when the Spirit of God raises you on high so that you may ascend from virtue to virtue, the king of Babylon shoots at you an arrow flying by day, when you are raised up in your progress through vainglory. When you desire religious life through the understanding of reason, the danger of terror by night threatens you through the vice of faintheartedness. If, through the wind of vanity, you desire this world’s glory, the devil shoots at you by the thing that walks in darkness. But when, through the intention of evil will, you do not fear to undertake the misery of Gehenna’s punishment, you are undoubtedly troubled by the noonday demon. [Col. 0668C]

Therefore, because the Lord Jesus was God and man, he was led by a twofold spirit into a twofold wilderness: by the Spirit of God and the spirit of man; by the understanding of reason and the affection of graciousness. Hence Elisha said to Elijah: “I pray that your spirit may become double in me” (4 Kings 2): that is, that I may abound in such graciousness of devotion and so great an affection of reason as you do. Led by this twofold spirit, Jesus came to the perfection of religious life and the height of heaven.

Therefore, when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, the devil tempted him with terror by night and said: “Command that these stones become bread” (Matt. 4). Again, showing him the glory of the world, he said: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (ibid.). But if, through the thought of graciousness and desire for the height of heaven, he sought that height, the arrow flying by day persecuted him when it said: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down” (ibid.). But the Lord, leaving an example for posterity, conquered temptation in all things and prevailed in all things, so that through him and in him those who wish to follow him to glory may be conquerors.

## SERMON XV. ON PALM BRANCHES

“The children of the Hebrews, taking branches of olive trees, went to meet the Lord, saying: Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21), etc. Not all who are of Israel are Israelites, because among those who are of Israel some came to meet the Lord with swords and clubs, while others came with palms and flowers. Some came to laugh, others to mock; some crying, “Crucify, crucify,” while others cried, “Hosanna in the highest.” Of these it is said: “The children of the Hebrews,” etc.

“Hebrews” is interpreted “those who cross over.” Therefore Hebrews are those who do not have here an abiding city but seek the one to come. Hebrews are those who, whether by sacrificing a lamb or offering a kid, make the *phase*, that is, the crossing. Hebrews are those who celebrate Passover, that is, the crossing of this life, in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. A Hebrew is one who, in confession of praise, crossing from Adam’s old language to the apostles’ new language, becomes *Idithun*, that is, “one who leaps over.” A Hebrew is one who, established in this pilgrimage only in body, makes a crossing in thought and desire to the heavenly homeland and becomes a Galilean, that is, “one who migrates across.” [Col. 0669B]

These Hebrews have children—not by birth, not by thought, but by preaching, concerning whom the Apostle says: “For through the Gospel I have begotten you” (1 Cor. 4); or by imitation, concerning whom it is said: “Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (Ezek. 18). It belongs to these to take up olive branches. “Olive” in Greek is called “mercy” in Latin. The olive branches, then, are the diverse kinds of mercies; we take them up when we gather in our mind examples of God’s manifold mercies. God’s mercy is great in that he made us; greater in that he governs us; greatest in that he redeemed us; overflowing in that he calls back the unworthy; superabundant in that he saves the unjust. The more devoutly every person remembers God’s mercy, the more confidently he cries, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” that is, he cries to Christ: “Save, I beseech you.”

Therefore the privileges of today’s feast invite us to gather these olive branches. First, because on that day the children of Israel entered the land of promise and crossed the Jordan with dry feet. For it so happened that that year there were as many days until Passover as there are from this Sunday onward; and the moon was on its tenth day, as it was on the day when the Lord came to Jerusalem to suffer. Concerning this day the Lord had commanded in the Law: “On the tenth day of the first month let each take a lamb according to their families and houses; and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening” (Exod. 12). [Col. 0669D]

It should be noted that after the ten plagues which Moses and Aaron performed before Pharaoh, the commandment was given—and with good reason. Pharaoh could be afflicted by ten plagues, but he was not conquered until the lamb was sacrificed. Pharaoh signifies the devil; Egypt, the world; the children of Israel, those predestined to life; the Egyptian captivity and the servitude of the children of Israel, the misery of this world, in which the chaff of vanity, the mud of pleasure, and the bricks of desire blind human eyes. Moses’ rod signifies the discipline of the Law; Aaron, the priesthood of the same Law; and the ten plagues, the ten commandments. Hence they correspond one to another.

The first commandment concerns the worship of one God (Exod. 20); the first plague is water turned into blood. To turn water into blood is to change spiritual teaching into carnal teaching. They turned water into blood who “changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man” (Rom. 1). [Col. 0670B]

The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 20). The second plague is the bubbling up of frogs, in which the chatter of vanity is figured. One takes God’s name in vain who changes truth, which is God, into the vanity of chatter.

The third commandment is the sanctification of the Sabbath, in which is figured the rest of the mind produced by a good conscience. The third plague was gnats (*sciniphes*) (Exod. 8). Gnats are very tiny flies, flying about disorderly and most restlessly. Such are the phantoms of temptations, which remove the mind from rest.

The fourth commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20). The fourth plague is the sending forth of dog-flies (*coenomyiae*). The *coenomyia* is a dog-fly; it is characteristic of dogs not to recognize their parents. Hence they are born blind.

The fifth commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20). The fifth plague is death among the cattle. Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0669D] *Morals*, book 24, chapter 8]: “The beasts rotted in their dung” (Joel 1). For beasts to rot in dung is to end life in the stench of lust. Therefore death among cattle is the stench of lust in those people who “are compared with senseless beasts and made like them.”

The sixth commandment is: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20). The sixth plague is swollen blisters raised from the furnace, in which is figured inflated pride arising from the fires of envy. It is written: “Anger kills the little one, and pride the fool” (Job 5). Therefore the swollen blister is the death of the soul. [Col. 0670D]

The seventh commandment is: “You shall not steal” (Exod. 20). The seventh plague is hail upon the crops. No one has illicit gain without just loss. While you steal, you acquire a garment but lose faith: visible gain, invisible loss. Therefore, those who outwardly steal through evil desire are inwardly struck by hail through just desire. And while money is multiplied through theft, spiritual riches are diminished.

The eighth commandment is: “You shall not bear false witness” (ibid.); the eighth plague is the sending forth of locusts. A locust is an animal harmful by its bite; a false witness harms by biting and consumes by lying. [Col. 0671A]

The ninth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; the ninth plague is thick darkness. And truly darkness is thick when one especially desires another’s fury who has suffered injury. Truly, one who undergoes this is blinded by rage, because nothing hurts so much when suffered, and nothing would be so unwelcome to suffer, as the very thing one does oneself.

The tenth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s goods” (ibid.); the tenth plague is the death of the firstborn. Those who covet others’ goods wish to be heirs of those who are dying. And whoever wishes to become an heir in someone’s case does not wish that the person whose goods he covets should have heirs, among whom nothing is dearer than firstborn children.

Therefore one who, by coveting others’ goods, seeks a shadow of legal right is rightly punished in the firstborn; and he loses the better firstborn of the heart, namely faith. [Col. 0671B] Thus, as was said, the ten plagues correspond to the ten commandments. But just as Pharaoh was not so overcome by the ten plagues as to let the people go, so that Law could not so overcome the devil as to make humanity return to paradise. But after the lamb was sacrificed, Pharaoh let the people go; all Egypt’s firstborn died; indeed, the Egyptians also perished in the Red Sea, while the children of Israel crossed over (Exod. 12).

After the shedding of Christ’s blood, original sin, as it were the firstborn, was erased; and baptism received efficacy so that through it those predestined to life—that is, the children of Israel—might escape Pharaoh, that is, the devil; and the Egyptians, that is, actual sins, might come to an end in baptism. This is also why he came to Jerusalem on the tenth moon, for the moon signifies defect. He rightly came on the tenth moon who came, amid the defect of the Decalogue, to accomplish our salvation in the midst of the earth.

But the children of the Hebrews, the common people of Jerusalem, and the great multitude who had come for the feast, taking olive branches, went out to meet him. And those going before and those following cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David.” *Osanna* is a Hebrew word, formed from a corrupt and a complete element. *Osy* means “save,” while *anna* is an interjection of entreaty, like *pape* as an interjection of amazement. Because this expression does not exist in Latin, Jerome rendered it by *obsecro*, “I beseech you.” The sense is: they cried, “Hosanna to the Son of David”; that is, they cried out, saying to the Son of David: “Hosanna—that is, save, I beseech you.” [Col. 0671C]

That procession signifies that we, who are children of the Hebrews—that is, of those who cross over, namely those who do not have here an abiding city but seek the future one—of whom was the Apostle who said: “Through the Gospel I have begotten you all” (1 Cor. 4), and elsewhere, “We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. 2): some of these are fathers of the Old Law, going before as it were; others belong to the New Testament, following as it were. With works of mercy, as with olive branches, let us bear in our bodies the marks of Jesus through compassion for our neighbors and suffering in our own bodies.

Why the verses beginning “Glory, praise,” etc., are sung in that procession should also be known. A certain Theodulf, abbot of Fleury and bishop of Orléans, lived in the time of Louis the Pious. When he had been falsely accused before Emperor Louis of many crimes, he was banished into exile at Angers. While he was held there in custody, it happened that the aforesaid emperor came there on Palm Sunday. As the procession passed beside the house in which Theodulf himself was confined, silence was made in the emperor’s presence, and Theodulf sang those verses through the window. Moved by these words, the emperor ordered him freed from his bonds and restored him to his former favor.

For this reason the Gallican Church adopted the custom that those verses, composed by Theodulf, should be sung each year in that procession with the doors closed as a sign of his prison. Nor is it devoid of mystery. The priest’s going outside the town figures Christ ascending to the place of Calvary; the people accompanying him signifies those who bear Christ’s reproach outside the camp. The two clerics singing the hymn signify the triumphant Church, consisting of angels and human beings, which praises God and glorifies the Son in his Passion. The people responding outside figures the Church militant, which agrees in the praise of the same Son by reason of that same Passion. The closing of the doors prefigures the time before the shedding of Christ’s blood, for Christ’s blood alone opened for us the gates of heaven. They are therefore rightly closed then, because Christ’s blood was shed on the Friday after that Sunday. [Col. 0672B]

When the procession of which we have spoken—that is, the one in which the children of the Hebrews went out to meet Christ—was completed, Jesus entered the Temple. He showed that the ruin of the city, for which he had wept, would arise especially through the fault of the priests. For the priests, serving their own greed, sold sacrifices in the porticoes of the Temple so that those who came from far away and wished to offer might find them ready. They also stationed money-changers there, from whom people might receive money on loan at interest if they lacked it.

And lest arrivals perhaps excuse themselves on grounds of poverty, or because the Law commanded that they should not take interest from their brethren, they devised the *collybistae*. For among them *collybia* are called small gifts of little value, such as chickpeas, raisins, and fruits of various kinds. [Col. 0672D]

But Ezekiel also forbids this, saying: “You shall not take interest or any excess” (Ezek. 18). For this reason Jesus, having made a whip of cords, drove out those who were selling and buying, and overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves (John 2; Matt. 21). He had performed this sign similarly on another occasion before Passover—namely, in the year in which he was baptized and John was imprisoned. Therefore the chief priests questioned him and, in astonishment, said: “What sign do you show us, that you do these things?” (John 2). As if to say: “Do you signify something by this unprecedented action?” Truly, what he does is a sign.

Oh, if the pontiffs of the present time knew the sign which Jesus performs, how greatly they would fear what has been done! For who are the buyers [Col. 0673A] and sellers of doves except Gehazi-like persons and Simoniacs, who wish to acquire spiritual things for a price? The Gehazi-like are sellers, who, since they sell spiritual things as though they were doves, deservedly incur, like Gehazi, leprosy of the mind. The Simoniacs are buyers, whose money, like Simon’s, is with them unto destruction. But those who sell and those who buy are one and the same. All are money-changers; all are worthy of expulsion. Let the pontiffs, therefore, who say, “What sign do you show?” understand the sign: he excludes them from the Church. And what is exclusion from the Church? It is the same as excommunication.

He did this on this day, and he did it on the other occasion as well. Repetition is confirmation, as when we excommunicate and say at the end, “Let it be so, let it be so.” Therefore, not through a vicar but in his own person, [Col. 0673B] that great High Priest and Priest according to the order of Melchizedek drives them from the Temple—that is, from the fellowship of the faithful. And the whip made of cords shows that he does this justly. For in return for the cords of sins with which they are entangled, their scourges are many.

Nor should we pass over this admirable point: on Sunday, the first day on which the Father began the work of creating the world, the Son undertakes the labor of the Passion; and throughout this entire week he worked our salvation, and on the seventh day he ceased and rested in the tomb. Thus the entire week is called painful, because throughout it the Lord labored in restoring creation, just as throughout the first week of the world he labored in creating it. For on this first day he begins the work [Col. 0673C] of the saving Passion with such great splendor as corresponds to the dignity of that day on which he said, “Let there be light,” and light was made (Gen. 1).

Some relate that, when he drove out the sellers and buyers, a radiant flash issued from his eyes; terrified by it, the priests and Levites could not withstand him. For he was the light shining in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it; rather, those who could not endure the splendor of the light—that is, the terror of the divinity which is in Christ Jesus our Lord—were overcome by the light and vanished away. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Col. 0673D] “A certain man made a great supper,” etc. (Luke 14). That man, I say, of whom it is written: “He is a man—and who shall know him?” That man, therefore, God and man, today prepared both a midday meal and a supper for his disciples. But because the supper was worthier than the midday meal, the whole solemnity deserved to be called the Lord’s Supper.

By the midday meal I mean that at which he ate the typical Passover, saying: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you that I shall not now eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” And, having received the cup, he gave thanks and said: “Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you, I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes” (Luke 22). And thus, after the typical Passover had ended, he rose and washed the disciples’ feet. [Col. 0674A] Having done this, he reclined again and gave them the sacrament of his body and blood, which he showed to be worthier than the typical Passover when he said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 2). That was the midday meal; this is the supper.

These are the privileges of today’s solemnity; nor are they the only ones, but there are many others. We believe that some of these, which are necessary for salvation, should be made known to your charity. Today, indeed, the Church receives back penitents whom it expelled on the first day of the fast. Today, the Old Testament having been brought to completion, the New began. Today oil is consecrated, not only for healing the sick or enlightening catechumens and neophytes, but also for confirming and strengthening the baptized.

Therefore, on this day the disciples said to Jesus: “Where do you wish [Col. 0674B] us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” And he answered: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him; and wherever he enters, ask the master of the house for a place to prepare it; and he will show you a large upper room, and prepare it there” (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22). In the upper part of a house the Palestinians made dining rooms, while below they made bedchambers. What Mark calls a *lagena* [flask], Luke calls an *amphora* [jar]: one specified the kind of vessel, the other its size.

Thus, on the evening of this day he reclined with his disciples; and for this reason we call this day the Lord’s Supper. After supper he washed his disciples’ feet, in memory of which washing we customarily wash the feet of the poor. Having done this, he reclined again and taught that he had given them an example by this deed: [Col. 0674C] namely, that they should serve one another, forgive one another’s injuries, and assist one another when they sin. Note that it follows from what he said—“He who has bathed does not need except to wash his feet; and you are clean, but not all” (John 13)—that the apostles had already been baptized.

Then troubled in spirit, he said: “One of you will betray me” (ibid.). He was troubled—that is, he compassionately suffered with Judas. When the disciples asked which one it was, he said: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me” (Mark 14).

Another Evangelist says “in the *paropsis*” (Matt. 26). But the term “dish” (*catinus*) shows that it was an earthen vessel; the term *paropsis* shows that this vessel had equal sides. For *apsis* means an extremity; whence *parapsis* is a vessel having equal extremities. Or, as some say, the name *parapsis* indicates the squareness of its sides. [Col. 0674D] This vessel was set there in order that the juice of wild lettuces, necessary for eating the lamb, might be placed in it. Therefore he said, “dips.”

But although all twelve dipped in that vessel, Peter was not made certain by what Jesus had said as to who it was. So he indicated to John, who is said to have reclined upon his breast—though he is said to have reclined upon his breast in no other sense than that, leaning back, he reclined before Jesus’ breast—that he should ask him secretly who it was. In a low voice the Lord said to him: “He to whom I shall hand the dipped bread”; and he gave Judas a dipped morsel (John 15). Hence the Eucharist is not [Col. 0675A] given dipped; and this is also intended to remove the heresy of those who teach that Christ is wholly present simultaneously under both species and not under only one species.

Then Satan entered Judas’s heart—not for the first time, but so as to possess him as his own. And he immediately went out in order to fulfill what he had agreed with the chief priests. Then, after he had gone out, Christ gave his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood. Hence on that day it is said in the Canon: “Who, on the day before he suffered for our salvation and that of all”—that is, today—etc.

But in saying that Judas went out before receiving the Eucharist, we seem to contradict Luke, who mentions the traitor after the cup. Perhaps, however, Luke recapitulates the betrayal. For Hilary, in his commentary on Matthew, proves that Judas was not present. [Col. 0675B] For Jesus said that those who drank the cup with him would also drink with him in his Father’s kingdom (Matt. 26), of which Judas was unworthy. Nor did he exempt anyone among those drinking when he said, “It shall be poured out for you.” For he made an exception concerning others when he said, “for many.”

But if it is said that Judas received it, Hilary’s words must be qualified, because things which cannot be said together may nevertheless have occurred together. For the order of the Gospel does not conflict with the Lord’s having distributed the sacrament of his body and blood before he identified his betrayer by the dipped morsel. Note also that some hold that a meal was eaten after the washing of feet, which took place between the typical Passover and the new one; and thus they call that meal itself the Lord’s Supper.

For clarity on this matter, it must be known that the Lord’s Supper was partly old and partly new. For after his disciples had prepared the Passover and the Lord reclined with them, he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22). According to the authority, he desired first to eat the typical Passover and then to disclose to the world the mysteries of his Passion, teaching that now that the reality had come, the shadow must cease. Hence it follows: “For I tell you, from this time I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God” (ibid.). [Col. 0675C] As though he said: “I shall no longer celebrate the Mosaic Passover until the Church, which is the kingdom of God, is fulfilled.”

It follows: “And having received the cup, he gave thanks and said: ‘Take this and divide it among yourselves.’” This cup also belongs to the old Passover, concerning which it is further said: “For I tell you, I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes” (ibid.). Thus, just as he said that he would not drink the typical Passover food of lamb and unleavened bread until the glory of the Resurrection had been revealed and the kingdom of God—that is, faith throughout the world—had come, so too he said that he would not drink the typical Passover drink.

Therefore let no one restore the Lord’s Supper in wine or unleavened bread, any more than in the eating of the lamb, which the Lord here ended; otherwise, he Judaizes. The final part of the supper, which belongs to the new man as the first part belongs to the old, in which the Lord distributed the sacraments of his body and blood, must itself be frequently performed or repeated, by the Lord’s authority, who said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11). And who would dare to represent it otherwise than as the Lord himself [Col. 0676A] handed it down? If, therefore, antiquity is repeated, why is it not repeated completely, so that lamb too may be joined with unleavened bread and wine? Yet you shrink from eating meat during fasts. Why, then, if you are going to fast, do you not shrink from eating twice? Thus you make yourself a transgressor in two ways, since you do not observe the appointed time of fasting.

Therefore, when the Lord said, “Do this in remembrance of me,” he instituted this sacrament. Hence, although all the hours of this day are mournful, the Mass alone is solemn, in chant and ornament. And just as on the fifth day in the week of the world’s creation, the kind produced from the waters was partly returned to the deep and partly raised into the air, so that, though their stock was one, they might occupy different places; so on the fifth feria of this week, in which we were restored, the sacraments [Col. 0676B] of one and the same salvation partly cast us down into sorrow and partly raise us into joy.

Thus this Mass is to be celebrated with such solemnity of spiritual joy that every pontiff ought on this day to carry out in full every duty of his office: that is, to restore penitents to the Church, bless oil, prepare chrism, and sing “Glory in the highest.” Now *chrisma* is Greek, and *unctio* is Latin: thus Christ is “Anointed,” and chrism is called “ointment.” It is made from the fruit and fatness of the olive mixed with balsam, whose tree is fragrant and chief among aromatic trees.

Chrism is a sign of the Holy Spirit and contains his power. For the Holy Spirit is the fatness of the divine substance, so that whoever has been refreshed by it may say: “You have made my head rich with oil” (Ps. 22 [23]). The scent of balsam in the oil signifies the sweetness of the same Holy Spirit; whoever receives it is drawn by the good scent of discernment and may say with the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2).

Therefore, this anointing with chrismal oil is called the principal anointing because, at its anointing, the principal Spirit is bestowed—that is, the sevenfold Paraclete. This day, the fourteenth moon, is fittingly chosen for its consecration, because on this day the lamb was commanded to be sacrificed in the evening, and both doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which the lamb was to be eaten were to be smeared with its blood, so that, on seeing that sign, the Egyptian destroyer would pass by the houses untouched (Exod. 12). [Col. 0676D] Likewise, the sign of Christ’s cross is made from this chrism, so that the destroyer, the devil, may have no right to harm in the dwelling-places of souls and bodies; and this was prefigured by the blood of that typical lamb, with which the doorposts were marked.

But since this anointing of the baptized is deferred until Holy Saturday, the question is asked why, on the very night in which the lamb was to be eaten, this anointing with sacred chrism is not placed upon the foreheads of the baptized, when on that night—the fourteenth day of the first month, that is, today—the lamb ought to be sacrificed and the doorposts and lintel of houses smeared by the Lord’s command. For that anointing, as has been said, was a sign of this chrismal anointing.

We answer that this would indeed be fitting if the Church celebrated the Paschal feast on this day. But because it has determined to defer the joy of the Paschal solemnity until the third day, on which the Lord rose, and meanwhile to devote itself to mourning on the day on which he suffered, it has also judged that the chrismal anointing of baptism should be deferred until Saturday, which for us is the evening of the Paschal feast. [Col. 0677A] Then, with their foreheads marked, let the baptized hasten toward God, fleeing Pharaoh—that is, the devil—through the Red Sea of baptism, so that the baptismal anointing and the feast of the Paschal lamb may be celebrated together, as was prefigured in the ancient Law, when the doorposts were smeared with the lamb’s blood.

If you ask why the consecration itself has not been deferred, we answer: because from this Thursday until the evening of Saturday, the hour when chrism is to be used, we are without the solemnities of Mass. But chrism itself may lawfully be consecrated only amid the solemnities of Mass and at the place where we receive the peace.

It should be noted that oil is consecrated for three reasons: either for the healing of the sick—healing, I mean, both of bodies and souls—for enlightening catechumens and neophytes, or for confirming and strengthening the baptized. Hence there is called the oil of the sick, the oil of catechumens, and the oil of chrism. And fittingly, with great mystery: for these three kinds of oil were prefigured in those spices which the three women—Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome—bought, that they might come and anoint Jesus (Mark 16); or in sign of that threefold anointing by which Christ’s body [Col. 0677C] was anointed.

First, while still mortal, it was anointed by Mary Magdalene six days before Passover in the house of Simon the leper, when she opened an alabaster vessel of ointment of spikenard (*nardus pisticus*) (John 12). Second, when his body was already dead, Joseph, a councillor from Arimathea—that is, Ramah, which was the city of Elkanah, Samuel’s father (1 Sam. 1)—who was a secret disciple of Jesus, and Nicodemus, who had come to him by night, anointed it, bringing with them about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes (John 19). Third, it was in sign of that unique and invisible anointing by which the Father anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions. Hence he says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61).

For since he is the one of whom it was said to David: “Of the fruit of your womb I shall place [Col. 0677D] upon your throne” (Ps. 131 [132]), this third anointing of his was fittingly prefigured in David’s threefold anointing. David’s first anointing was in the house of his father Jesse, by Samuel; second, the men of Judah anointed him king only over the tribe of Judah; third, he was anointed over all Israel. He received the first anointing as a sign of kingship, not as the reality signified; the second as the reality signified, but only with a portion of its responsibility; the third in the fullness of power. Thus the first anointing was for one beginning, the second for one advancing, and the third for one reigning fully and established in the kingdom.

According to these three states, the heavenly physician prepares medicine for human beings. For it was necessary that, corresponding to the state in which the body was dead because of sin—in which a person could sin and could not but sin, the state after sin and before restoration, for which Christ died for sins—there should be prepared the oil of the sick, namely penitential contrition, like myrrh and aloes, [Col. 0678A] with which Christ’s dead body was anointed. For just as myrrh and aloes by their bitterness drive away worms, so contrition and repentance, though bitter, drive away the worms of vices and free one from dead works.

Again, because after restoration and before confirmation the human body is, as it were, mortal, no longer dead but partially raised, though not wholly—for it is subject to death in that it can sin, but raised in that the inward person can, through grace, refrain from sin—it is necessary that the anointing of spikenard, with which Christ’s body while still mortal was anointed, should anoint the Christian’s head, that is, his mind: namely, initial love, prefigured by *nardus pisticus*. For initial love is affection mingled with fear, since *pistis* is said to mean “mixed.” Thus *nardus pisticus* is a mixed anointing—that is, love mixed with fear.

It is initial love, in which there is indeed a beginning of virtue but not perfection. It fittingly belongs to catechumens, who have been enlightened through faith but not yet reborn through baptism. Faith is the beginning of virtues; baptism is the drowning of vices and the cleansing of virtues.

Again, for the strength and confirmation of the baptized, chrismal anointing is necessary: namely, filial love, with which the body of the Son of God was anointed. This Spirit too is given as consoler and guardian, as it were, to children, that he may preserve the inheritance bestowed by the Father; for it profits little or nothing if a parent grants a great inheritance to a little child unless he also provides a guardian. [Col. 0678C] For the very manner and order of consecration indicates, in that threefold consecration, the dignity of this threefold progress.

When the oil of the sick is blessed, neither the words of greeting at the beginning—namely, “The Lord be with you”—nor “Let us pray” are used; nor is it concluded at the end as other prayers are, at whose end is said, “Through the Lord,” etc. Rather, it is concluded within that prayer in which it is said: “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things,” etc. For finally, before this is said, the pontiff, in a low voice and with only those standing around hearing, should first exorcize the oil fittingly offered by the acolyte, then bless it, and end his blessing: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Then he begins: “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things,” etc.

But the consecration of the oil of catechumens and of chrism has an office of its own. First it is exorcized; then, at “The Lord be with you” and “Lift up your hearts,” the blessing of the chrism begins. Two acolytes, taking two flasks containing the oil for chrism and the oil of catechumens, wrapped in cloths of white silk so that they may be visible from the middle onward, should fittingly carry them before the bishop. The cloths are cast over the left shoulder [Col. 0679A] so that they return to the right shoulder and their hanging ends may be held at the right. The procession is then made in this order.

First go two acolytes with candlesticks and burning candles. Two crosses are carried, and between them the chrismal oil. Then two censers are carried, and between them the oil of catechumens. Then the Gospel is carried, so that every good thing may be fulfilled. Next follow twelve priests, proceeding two by two. Finally, two boys follow, singing the hymn “O Redeemer.” All this is a sign of a great mystery.

For the flask containing chrism in a certain manner figures the body taken from the Virgin, containing in itself bodily the fullness of the Holy Spirit. Before it passed to the altar of the cross, it was for a time covered and for a time uncovered. When it was carried into Egypt as though it were not a king, when it was carried into the Temple, when it was subject to Mary and Joseph, it lay hidden as though covered. But in miracles, preaching, and the display of its majesty, it was in a certain manner uncovered.

Thus it is suitably carried between two crosses, because Christ is upheld as mediator of God and men both through the Passion of his own body and through compassion for his neighbor. But the other flask is carried between two censers, because reason, as though in the middle, is nourished through devotion and contrition of spirit. Once it has been blessed and returned from the altar, it is visibly and openly saluted by the pontiff and the ministers of the altar. [Col. 0679C] This signifies that, after Christ passed from the altar of the cross, he showed his bodily presence to his disciples, whom the twelve priests standing by represent, and wished them to be witnesses of his resurrection.

But its being carried to others for salutation invisibly and covered signifies that Christ, returning to heaven, became invisible to human beings. We said that the cloth covering the flask is white and silk because silk comes to us from worms. It also signifies the flesh of Christ, beneath which divinity lay hidden; in this respect it possessed the nature of a worm, since he was born of the Virgin both without the contagion of sin and without the corruption of lust. Hence he says in the psalm: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21 [22]).

This worm is also fittingly figured in the one whom the Jews call *Rhamis*, saying that stones were easily cut with its blood when they were to be placed in Solomon’s Temple, and that therefore the stone-cutters did not need a hammer. If this is true, the mystery greatly favors our faith. For by the blood of this worm living stones were cut from the corruptible mass for the holy Temple, which is the Church. Nor was it afterwards necessary for the severity of the Law, like a hammer, to be heard, because by the shedding of his own blood he raised up children of Abraham from stones upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone (Eph. 2).

The cloth’s transfer from the left to the right signifies that through the cloud of his uncontaminated flesh there occurred the change of the right hand [Col. 0680A] of the Most High, prefigured by our patriarch Jacob, who changed his son’s name from Benoni to Benjamin (Gen. 35). For Benoni is interpreted “son of sorrow,” but Benjamin “son of the right hand.” Christ’s humanity, therefore, brought this about: that the son of sorrow—that is, the son of wrath—through the struggle of his Passion (for Jacob is interpreted “wrestler”) should become a son of the right hand—that is, a son of grace—so that we, who by the merit of our perversity deserved that terrible voice which will be spoken to those placed on the left, namely, “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25), may, with those to be placed on the right, hear: “Come, you blessed,” etc. (ibid.).

Therefore, fittingly, on this same day on which Jesus was betrayed, the pontiff, with the doors opened, meets penitents before the doors of the church, who had through sin become children of wrath, saying: “Come, come, come, children; hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33 [34]). That this utterance of the pontiff is spoken in the person of the Lord is shown by the psalm title, which is inscribed thus: “A psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and was carried in his own hands, and dismissed him and went away” (ibid.).

For David, whose name is interpreted either “strong in hand” or “desirable in countenance,” signifies the Lord Jesus. Before Abimelech, interpreted “the kingdom of my Father”—that is, before the Jews—he changed his countenance today, that is, the rite of sacrifice, when, after the lamb of the old Passover had already been sacrificed, taking bread and wine, he was carried in his own hands, saying: “This is my body, and this is my blood” (Matt. 26). [Col. 0680C] Thus the pontiff’s voice is the voice of an inviting friend—the voice, I say, of Christ—who invites us to the banquet of his body and blood, saying, “Come, children.” And in order that the ample and capacious bosom of the receiver may be opened, all the doors of the church stand open, as though the pontiff said to the north: “Give,” and to the south: “Do not withhold” (Isa. 43).

Jesus’ rising from supper and washing his disciples’ feet is not without mystery, although the example of humility displayed in that action might seem sufficient. He rose from supper, that is, from the banquet of paternal glory; and he laid aside his garments because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Girded with our earthly flesh as with a linen cloth, whose material grows from the earth, he poured his blood, shed like water, into a basin (John 13), and with it washed our feet, that is, our actions. Thus it is written of some: “They washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7). He gave us an example that we too should do likewise, because, as he laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for our brethren.

Because the Lord was betrayed in the evening, and in that seizure he had neither appearance nor beauty, but was reckoned a despised man and the lowest of men, the altars are stripped in the evening and despoiled of their furnishings and adornment. They are washed with wine and water, in sign that in his Passion he washed us by the blood of redemption and the water of baptism. They are struck with whips, in sign that he himself was scourged for us. Bells are not rung, [Col. 0681A] because the heralds of faith—that is, the apostles—not only fell silent, but all fled after abandoning him. Thus Peter, prince of the apostles, from whose mouth first came the proclamation of truth, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16), suppressed that voice, fell silent, abandoned Christ, and denied him three times.

## SERMON XVII. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER

“Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wondrous things” (Ps. 97 [98]). A psalm of David. This psalm is attributed to David because he performed wondrous deeds: for he was desirable in countenance and strong in hand—such is the interpretation of David’s name—he who killed Goliath, defeated the lion, and struck down the bear; when before Abimelech he changed his countenance; when before his servants [Col. 0681B] he struck against the doors of the gate, carried himself in his own hands, and saliva ran down over his beard; or when, stripped of his garments, he danced before the ark of God. In all these things he truly did wondrous deeds.

For he is that David who is “fair in beauty beyond the sons of men,” desirable in countenance, upon whom the angels themselves desire to look. He fittingly changed his countenance when he was reckoned a leper, smitten by God and humbled, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people, because he had neither appearance nor beauty. He beat the drum when the skin of his flesh was stretched upon the wood of the cross as upon a drum, so that all his bones could be numbered, as he says: “They numbered all my bones” (Ps. 21 [22])—that is, they made them capable of being numbered.

He struck against the doors of the gate when he shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars, and, like another Samson, carried the gates of Gaza to the brow of the mountain (Judg. 16). He also carried himself in his own hands when, holding his body in his hands, he said to his disciples: “Take and eat of this, all of you” (Matt. 26). Saliva also ran down over his beard when the Wisdom of the head seemed to flow down, as it were, in the manner of a little child speaking, when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). He also danced stripped of his garments before the ark when, deprived of the company of his disciples, he trod the winepress alone and humbled himself before God so as to seem viler than he had become.

[Col. 0681D] Therefore, although Michal—that is, the Synagogue—mocks him (2 Sam. 6), and although Achish—that is, the Gentile people—despises him (1 Sam. 21), since Christ was a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, you, most beloved, who believe that all these things were done by the power and wisdom of God, “sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wondrous things.” For what is more wondrous than that the King of kings and Lord of lords was willing, under an accusation of injured majesty, to receive purple for a garment, thorns for a crown, a reed for a scepter, myrrh for an anointing, and a cross for a throne?

But all these things were done as an argument and testimony of Jewish condemnation, and for the glory of our salvation. For all these were, as it were, testimonies of our salvation, because by being clothed in purple [Col. 0682A] he openly showed that he is the one who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah. Edom is interpreted “son of my people”; Bozrah, “tribulation.” Hence Bozrah, which is in Edom, signifies the tribulations of the son of his people—that is, the affliction which the sons of his people, the Jews, inflicted upon him.

They clothe him in purple and say: “Why is your garment red?” (Isa. 63). And when he had disclosed the reason to them, saying, “I have trodden the winepress alone” (ibid.), they wished to understand; yet, in contempt of his treading, they clothed him in purple. Wretched nation, nation worn down by the fountain: was it not necessary that Joseph’s blood-dyed tunic should be presented to his father? How could you be delivered from the Egyptians unless both doorposts were smeared with blood?

You gave thorns for a crown. Your land fittingly gave what it possessed, not yet cleansed from the curse. It had thorns and thistles; it gave thorns. Wretches, was it not necessary that God should appear in the bush? Was it not necessary that the ram should be caught by its horns among brambles? You gave a reed for a scepter, most plainly showing that the work which was in Jesus’ hands made the scepter of your kingdom reed-like and fragile; and, in order to write your condemnation so that it could not be erased, you prepared a reed for the scribe who had an inkhorn at his loins (Ezek. 9).

For an anointing you gave myrrh, not understanding that Mordecai ought thus to introduce Hadassah into the house of Ahasuerus. For Mordecai is interpreted “pure myrrh,” Hadassah “mercy,” and Ahasuerus “blessedness.”

[Col. 0682C] Therefore the myrrh with which you anointed him brought mercy into the house of blessedness, so that not justice—namely Vashti, “laying waste all things”—but mercy might exercise royal dignity. Hence elsewhere he says: “My hands dripped with myrrh” (Song 5).

You gave a cross for a throne, because it was necessary that wood should be put into the bread. For this is the wood which sweetened the bitterness of Marah (Exod. 15), through which the iron of your hardness floated (2 Kgs. 6), and because of which an angel descended into the pool in order to raise it up. When the angel stirred the water with the wood, whoever first descended was healed of whatever infirmity held him (John 5).

For the Queen of Sheba had foreseen that the kingdom of the Jews was to be destroyed by this wood, and she told Solomon this. Therefore Solomon hid this wood beneath the pool of Siloam; and when the time of the Passion drew near, the angel of the Lord began gradually to move the wood. At its motion the pool was stirred, and whoever descended into the pool was healed through the power and motion of the wood. Thus the angel moved this wood so that on the very day of the Passion it floated to the surface. Therefore, as Jesus was being led to death, the people removed the wood from the pool as useless and harmful to those drawing water, and prepared it for the gibbet of the cross. For what Nichaula had said was fulfilled: that this wood would destroy the kingdom of the Jews.

Therefore, beloved, “sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done these wondrous things.” For what is more wondrous [Col. 0683A] than that the impassible should suffer, the immortal die, the just one for the unjust, the friend for enemies, the Lord for servants, and one so great should deign to be crucified for such insignificant beings? He underwent the deficiencies of our mortality, yet in such a way that one who saw him to be human from weakness might believe him to be God from power, so that we might understand that he assumed such deficiencies voluntarily, not of necessity.

For he who is recorded to have been afraid offered himself willingly to armed men, saying: “I am he. If you seek me, let these go” (John 18). He who said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26), also said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John 13). He who said, “Abba, Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Mark 14), said also to Peter: “Put your sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (John 18). He who descended into the underworld said to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). And he who said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27), also said: “From now on you shall see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Matt. 26).

The hand, too, which had been fastened with a nail healed Malchus’s ear by touch alone. And while he hung ignominiously on the cross, he shook the earth, darkened the sun, broke rocks, opened tombs, and raised the dead. And quite fittingly, because he is the one who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble. It ought especially to have been shaken then, when, bowing his head, he looked upon it. Therefore he moved and disturbed the earth, because by a miraculous deed he shook earthly hearts with terror. He darkened the sun, because it gave brightness and, when the conjunction of the moon approached, suffered an eclipse. For the moon is the Church, which he joined to himself by the covenant of blood and water flowing from his side. Earthly people, not knowing the cause of this, wondered that the sun had been darkened at midday, not knowing that the sun of righteousness stood, in direct alignment, at the conjunction of the moon, namely his Church. He broke the rocks, because he moved even the hard hearts of unbelievers to repentance. Hence the centurion said: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII). He opened the tombs, because the uncleannesses of the Pharisees were exposed, of whom it was said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly are beautiful but within are full of every uncleanness” (Matt. XXIII). He raised the dead, because by his death he killed death, not so much that of the body as that of the soul: bodily death indeed, in hope as regards all and in fact as regards many; death of the soul, as regards sufficiency, though not as regards efficacy. Yet the victim was sufficient, since it could free all, although not all have received its effect.

Let Mary therefore take up the tambourine, and let her joyfully meet our David as he plays the tambourine, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honoured, because he has worked wonders: he has cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. XV). For it is fitting that Mary—whose name is interpreted “enlightened”—should take up the tambourine of mortification when Christ dies, because by his death he destroyed the dominion of death. For when he himself was cast into the sea, he cast horse and rider into the sea. Christ indeed, like another Jonah, wishing to flee to Tarshish, entered a ship and fell asleep; but the sea is disturbed, a storm arises, the ship rocks, the sailors grumble, and, having awakened Jonah, they say to him: “What have you done?” Jonah says to them: “If this storm has arisen because of me, cast me into the sea” (Jonah I). He was cast into the sea, and there was a great calm; he who was cast into the sea cast horse and rider down into the sea.

For Jonah, whose name is interpreted “sorrowing” or “dove,” signifies Christ, who, while bearing our sorrows, had neither a beak with which to curse when cursed, nor claws with which to harm when harmed, nor a voice of bitterness when provoked to anger. Therefore, after he had experienced the many tribulations of the world and the time had now come when he ought to pass from this world to the Father, he hastened as though fleeing toward an exploration of heavenly joy. This is what it means that Jonah wished to flee to Tarshish; but he entered a ship because he came to preach to the Synagogue. Yet when he had assumed human weaknesses there, he slept as if in a ship. Hence the Jews, attending to the weaknesses of his humanity and not to the glory of his divinity, disturb the sea and stir up the world. Thus they say: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs, and the whole world goes after him” (John VI). A storm is raised, both when they seek to catch him in his words and when they disparage his works, saying: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons.” The ship rocks: the Synagogue wavers. Some said that he was good; others, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (John VII). The sailors grumble, namely the scribes and Pharisees, saying: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX). For they say: “What have you done? Are you the Word made flesh? How long do you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John X).

Jonah says to them: “If this storm has arisen because of me,” that is, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, “cast me into the sea,” that is, cast me into the bitterness of death. He was cast into the sea, because he became, with a certain abasement, “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.” He was cast into the sea: he who endured for us the bitternesses of death—yet of a passing death—by which he cast the devil and his followers into the bitterness of death, but everlasting death. These are the wonders which he performed in laying down his life—he who had power to lay down his life and to take it up again. But since we have learned the wonders which he performed in laying down his life, let us now see those which he performed in taking it up again.

“I have power,” he says, “to lay down my life, and to take it up again” (ibid.). A marvellous and unheard-of thing: for from the beginning of the age it has not been heard that anyone raised himself. Elijah raised the son of the widow of Zarephath (III Kings XVII); Elisha, the son of the Shunammite woman (IV Kings IV); others raised others, but none raised themselves. But the signs of his appearances, by which he showed himself plainly to his disciples, demonstrate what benefit there is in this resurrection of Christ.

For, rising early on the first day of the Sabbath, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene (Mark XVI), as to one greatly weak, as to one more seriously sick. And lest she return to her vomit and to her former contempt for God, lest she look back after having already put her hand to the plough, he visited her in the spirit of fear when an angel appeared to her, whose appearance was like lightning and whose garments were like snow. And because fear is never evil except when excessive, he tempered it by the spirit of piety, when he appeared to her again in the garden and, looking upon her with an eye of compassion, said: “Mary” (John XX).

He visited Cleophas and his companion in the spirit of knowledge, when, beginning with Moses and the prophets, he began to preach to them that thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to enter into his glory (Luke XXIV). He visited the eleven disciples gathered in a house in the spirit of fortitude, when, although the doors were shut, he came in among them and said: “Peace to you” (John XX). “Take courage, for I have overcome the world.” He visited Peter and John by the Sea of Tiberias in the spirit of counsel, when, as they had laboured all night to no purpose, he said: “Cast [the net] on the right side of the boat, and you will find [fish]” (John XXI). He visited Thomas, who had said, “Unless I see the marks of the nails,” and so forth, in the spirit of understanding, when after eight days he again came to the disciples while the doors were shut, and said to Thomas: “Put your finger into my side; put your hand into the places of the nails; and do not be unbelieving, but believing” (ibid.). In the spirit of wisdom he appeared to the disciples reclining at table, reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, and said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Mark XVI).

These are the wonders which he performed in taking up his life. Therefore sing a new song, because he has worked wonders. But what is a song? A song is the exultation of the mind bursting forth into voice. Therefore, because in the voice of exultation and confession there is the sound of one feasting, let us sing a song, we to whom it has been granted to feast today. For Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover, as the Apostle says: “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast” (I Cor. V). Our Passover is Christ, namely the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, whom we ought to incorporate into ourselves—or rather, labour and pray that he may incorporate us into himself. Scripture says: “You shall consume the head with the entrails and the feet” (Exod. XII). The head signifies divinity; the feet, humanity; and the entrails, those things pertaining to the soul.

For there were heretics who confessed that Christ was the Son of God, but did not believe that he became man. These ate the lamb’s head without its feet and entrails. Others said that he was merely a man because they saw him die; but they believed neither that he rose again nor that he was God. These consumed the feet and entrails, but omitted the head. Others believed that he was God and man, but falsely asserted that he had divinity in place of a soul. These consumed the head and feet, but left out the entrails. But we, who confess him to be true God and true man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh, ought to consume the head with the entrails and feet; that is, we should strive eagerly to convey our Passover not into the belly but into the mind.

Or, because *Pascha* is interpreted “passage,” let us, as though invited to heavenly nuptials, pass from darkness to light, from unbelief to faith, from vices to virtue, from death to life, or from the world to the Father; so that in the voice of exultation and confession we may celebrate the historical Passover in the first sense, the allegorical in the second, the tropological in the third, and the anagogical in the fourth. Therefore let us sing a song—and a new song—on account of the promise, the sign, and the commandment. On account of the promise, because “the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new.”

Hence it is no longer old or temporal things, but new and spiritual things, that are promised to us. Put off therefore the old man, dearest brothers, and put on the new man, who was created according to God. “Make new ground for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.” Sing also a new song because of the new sign. For the Lord has made a new thing upon the earth: not only that a woman encompassed a man, but that this man raised himself. Sing also a new song because of the new commandment: “A new commandment,” he says, “I give you, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XIII). How greatly did he love us? Even unto death—indeed, death upon a cross.

The very sign of the cross invites us to this love. For the cross has two outstretched arms. Let us therefore extend both arms, the right and the left, to love of friends and enemies; let us have length in perseverance unto death; let us love with height, looking only to God; and let us have depth in humility with all people. Thus let us bear the Lord’s cross and die with him, so that we may deserve to rise from the death both of soul and body, with his help, his protection, and his supplying aid—he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER

“You shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. XXXIV).

As the Apostle bears witness, the law brought nothing to perfection (Heb. VII), but was given because of transgressions, until the fullness of the law should be given in the fullness of time—not through the word of the law, but through the law of the Word. Behold: at Israel’s departure from Egypt the paschal lamb is commanded to be sacrificed, and in this manner: “You shall not eat of it anything raw or boiled in water, but roasted only with fire. You shall consume the head with the entrails and feet, and you shall smear its blood upon the lintel of the house and upon both doorposts. And according to this rite you shall also take the kid” (Exod. XII).

But one rite belongs equally to lamb and kid; one rite, one ordinance of the law, one faith concerning him who came in the likeness of sinful flesh, and who “committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth.” One faith concerning him who came to associate with sinners, and yet confidently said: “Who will convict me of sin?” (John VIII). One rite belongs to him who, as the Apostle testifies, “was made sin for us” (II Cor. V), in order that he might condemn sin through sin; and to him who was the Lamb without blemish, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

Therefore, when we receive his body, we ought to eat nothing raw of the paschal lamb or kid. Rather, in the sacraments of things let us recognize the reality of the sacraments. For there are two sacraments and two realities there. The sacrament is the visible form of bread and wine, [the sacrament] of that invisible sacred reality, namely the body of the immaculate Lamb, who chose to become a victim for our sins when he hung upon the cross. And that same body, born of the Virgin, is, in the truth of the sign—which is also a sign of truth—the sacrament of that body of Christ which is the Church.

Therefore the visible form of bread and wine is sacrament but not reality; the body born of the Virgin is sacrament and reality; his body which is the Church is reality but not sacrament. Whoever therefore believes that the sacrament exists there without the reality eats it raw, because he believes that there is nothing spiritual there; for spirit is fire. Whoever believes that there are reality and sacrament, yet believes that, while the substance of bread and wine remains, the true body of Christ is present—as certain heretics falsely asserted—does receive the body, but half-raw. But whoever by receiving the reality and sacrament makes himself a member of the Church receives Christ’s body, cooked by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

It follows: “Not boiled in water.” Things roasted by fire are more firmly bound together, but things boiled in water are more easily dissolved. Therefore he eats it boiled in water who supposes that, on receiving Christ’s body, it can be dissolved and divided into parts, or who judges that the union of God and man was dissolved in the Passion. And because we ought to believe nothing phantasmal in that sacrament, it must be known that what is seen, and is not, is truly broken; not what is, and is not seen. The visible form is broken, not the invisible reality. It is not substance that is broken, but accident, which neither exists in a subject nor serves as a subject.

It is a wondrous thing, yet true; nor is it very wondrous if we attend to whose [body] it is. When you consider this and wonder, consider whose body it is and you will not wonder. For it is that very body which came forth from the Virgin’s womb through the closed gate. It is that body which entered among the disciples when the doors were shut. It walked upon the sea with dry footsteps; against nature, clouds received it and lifted it up. Do you marvel that this species of bread and wine is transubstantiated into Christ’s body? Is it not he who was transfigured before Peter, James, and John? Is it not he who, walking with two disciples to Emmaus, took the form of a stranger? You do not marvel at those transformations, yet are astonished at this one? Can the Word through whom all things were made, and who can do all things, not do this? By the Word by which he spoke and they were made, did he say this and will it not be done?

He is truth; his words are spirit and life (John VI). If you understand these things spiritually and with charity, his words are spirit and life and are so for you. If you understand them not charitably but carnally, his words are nonetheless spirit and life, but they are not so for you; rather, they are for you a foment of condemnation and death. Prepare therefore your mind, not your tooth: believe, and you have eaten.

Therefore Christ is received whole and entire: whole in person, entire in nature. Scripture says: “You shall consume the head with the feet and entrails.” It did not say, “the feet with the head or entrails”; nor did it say, “you shall consume the entrails with the feet or head.” For by saying what is, it excludes what is not. Since, then, the head of Christ is God, the head denotes the sublimity of divinity; but the feet signify the humanity of humility. Hence John did not think himself worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal (John I); that is, he did not think himself worthy to disclose the mysteries of Christ’s humanity. The entrails are the soul and the soul’s powers and capacities, which Christ possessed as was fitting and necessary.

There were therefore heretics who asserted that he was merely a man, while denying that he was God. These consumed the feet and entrails but omitted the head. There were others who believed that he was God but denied that he had taken true flesh, asserting instead that it was as though phantasmal, so that he merely appeared thus to human beings. These consumed the head and entrails, but not the feet. There were others who confessed that he was God and had assumed true flesh, but denied that he had a soul, claiming instead that his divinity itself was his soul. These consumed the head and feet, but not the entrails. But we who confess him to be true God and true man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh, are bound to consume the head with the feet and entrails—to consume, that is, to receive with all eagerness. For whatever belongs to God must be done eagerly. For this reason the Psalmist says: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII).

Observe the order of the words: “the head with the feet.” It does not say, “the feet with the entrails,” or “the entrails with the feet”; for we confess the separation of flesh and soul when he was dead in the tomb. Yet such was the union of God and man that he could be separated neither from the flesh in the tomb nor from the soul in hell. He was whole in the tomb, but by reason of the flesh; whole in hell, but by reason of the soul; whole everywhere, but by reason of the divinity. Whole, I say, but not entire.

But did he speak truth when he said: “Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani”—that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII). For Ambrose says concerning this: “The man cried out, being about to die through separation from divinity.”” Hence Hesychius, speaking on Leviticus (book V) about the two goats, one of which was sacrificed and the other permitted by the people to depart into the wilderness, said: “Humanity was sacrificed as the goat; but divinity, as the other goat, departed into the wilderness, that is, into heaven, in order to bear our sins—not in order to possess them, but in order to consume them.”

But this must be understood with respect to defence and protection, not with respect to a dissolution of the union. For in this respect divinity forsook him: it withheld protection, so that the enemy might have the power by which to bring the Passion to completion. For if divinity had wished to defend him, the enemy would not have had the power to kill him. And if he had not died, he would not have accomplished our salvation. Therefore, in order that man might be saved, Christ had to die. But he could not die unless the enemy had the power to kill him. The enemy could not have this power if divinity had wished to defend him. Therefore divinity forsook him in this: that it did not protect him, but it did not dissolve the union.

The words must indeed be noted. For he did not say, “You will forsake,” but “You have forsaken.” He said this while alive; therefore divinity had already forsaken him while he was alive. Therefore he was not God even then—which it is impious to believe or say. Rather, it had forsaken him in this respect: Pilate and the Jew had received from God power to kill that man. For although evil will comes from man or from the devil, every power, whether good or evil, cannot exist except from God. Hence the Lord says: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX).

It follows: “And you shall smear the blood of the lamb upon the lintel and upon both doorposts.” Hence the Lord said to the angel who had the writer’s inkhorn at his loins: “Mark *thau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan over all the abominations done in Jerusalem” (Ezek. IX). What the Lord said by the prophet concerning the forehead, the same Lord said through the lawgiver concerning the lintel; and Boethius himself recognized this same sign depicted on the lower border of Philosophy’s garment.

> [Note: Col. 0689D, *De consolatione philosophiae*, book I, prose 1.]

For the blood placed on the lintel and the theta [Θ] depicted below are the same thing. Gideon too stationed and selected at the right hand the three hundred soldiers who were to go out to battle (Judg. VII), signifying that the blood of the lamb is to be placed, and *thau* depicted, upon the right-hand doorpost. For that number, represented by the figure theta, is the strongest protection of conscience both against all adversities when they terrify and against prosperities when they flatter. If the little stage-harlots of vices call you back to temporal things; if the false presumption of disordered hope makes you secure in sins: mark *thau*, place the blood of the Passion in your conscience, since Samson also conquered with the jawbone of an ass. For there is nothing which frequent meditation upon Christ’s Passion and patience does not conquer.

It follows: “And you shall eat unleavened bread with wild lettuces.” Not every leaven is to be cast away, for the wise woman put leaven into three measures of flour; but from the spiritual food of the soul both manifest malice and feigned religion must be cast away. Of the first the Apostle says: “Purge out the old leaven” (I Cor. V); of the second, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (Matt. XVI). For this reason the Apostle sets forth the unleavened bread of sincerity against malice, and of truth against feigned religion.

We are also bound to eat wild lettuces, not cultivated ones. For just as one lettuce is cultivated and another wild, so one bitterness is wild and another cultivated; for lettuce, because it is bitter, signifies bitterness. But just as John used wild honey in the wilderness (Mark I), so we are commanded by the law to feed upon wild lettuce. John did not use cultivated honey, nor does the lawgiver command us to eat cultivated lettuce, because both are abominable to God. For cultivated sweetness is to rejoice amid prosperities; cultivated lettuce is to become bitter amid adversities. But wild honey is to rejoice when adversities sting; wild lettuce is to be bitter when prosperities seek to deceive. Therefore Jeremiah says: “Set bitterness before yourself” (Jer. XXXI). The prophet ate this lettuce when he said: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. XXXVIII). And again another prophet says: “Let rottenness enter into my bones and bubble up beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation” (Hab. III).

It follows: “You shall gird your loins.” It is necessary that either virginity gird the itch of human flesh beforehand, so as to empty it; or continence gird it, so as to restrain it; or the married state bind it in an ordered way. For it is not a sin if the bridegroom knows the bride in due order, not for intercourse’s sake but for offspring’s sake, so that from that union a child may be sought who may later be regenerated to God through the water of baptism.

We are commanded also to hold staffs in our hands, that is, to show discipline in our works. This discipline should not be a rod for us but a staff, so that the thickness of the staff may be represented in the strictness of discipline. We ought also to have sandals on our feet, lest earthly mud defile our affections; but the examples of teachers should so protect us that their intercessions also defend us from mud.

Behold, beloved, if all the things said concerning the lamb or kid suffice for healing, why was it necessary to add to such perfection what you have heard: “You shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk”? It must therefore be observed that the Father handed over the Son, and the Jew handed over the son. The Jew did the same thing as God. But God acted with good will, whereas the Jew acted with evil will. Therefore the Jew’s will was evil, though he did the same thing as God. Thus the will of Jew and God was the same [in its object], but evil in the Jew and good in God, because it was necessary for God to will what the Jew did not will to will [rightly].

Conversely, a human being may have a good will and yet will something other than God wills. But if the human will differs from God’s will, it is not thereby alienated from God, because God wills that a human being should will what God himself does not will. For the will of the judge ought to be one thing, and that of the person under judgment another. The judge wills to exercise justice; the person to be judged awaits mercy. The judge intends to condemn him. Yet “who has ever hated his own flesh?” Therefore the wills of judge and judged are contrary; indeed, perhaps the person should be condemned more severely if he wished harm for himself, because “if he is evil to himself, to whom is he good?”

Therefore the will of the judge, who does not will what the person to be judged wills, is good; and the will of the judged person, who wills something other than the judge, is good. For it is not opposed to that will even if it is beside it. Nor is it surprising if two people have different wills which are not adverse, when even in each individual person there are different wills, by one of which he does not will something that by another he wills. For according to the lower power of the soul, called sensuality, he wills something which, according to the higher power of the soul, called reason, he does not will to will. Yet these two are in the soul, and the soul is one. Is the soul divided? Is one thing contrary to itself? Therefore the Apostle says: “I find in my members a law resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive to the law of sin. To will is present with me; to accomplish [it] I do not find” (Rom. VII).

But because in this diversity there seems to be a certain opposition, since the law of the members and the law of the mind do not appear to agree well, let us raise our eyes and consider in the head what we do not see clearly in the members. Let us consider in Christ both wills: one and another; different, yet not different; the other, yet not another; and both good. “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI): the Son of Man spoke. But what did the Son of God answer? “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (ibid.). Therefore the Son of Man spoke one way, the Son of God another; man one way, God another—yet the whole is Christ himself.

What the Son of Man spoke as man, the Son of God spoke as God; but the same God—indeed, absolutely the same Father and Son. Therefore the will of Father and Son is the same, because for them willing and being are the same; for will is essence. Thus what the Son says, “Not what I will, but what you [will],” is the same as though he said, “Not what I will, but what I [will].” “I do not will” and “I will” are very different; yet both wills are in Christ, and both are good. For who, unless mad in mind, would dare confess that there was an evil will in Christ?

Therefore, insofar as he was man, he willed what, insofar as he was God, he did not will; nevertheless, he subjected the human will to the divine will. But I say further: not only does he, insofar as he is man, will what he does not will insofar as he is God; God also sometimes commands what he does not will to be done, and often prohibits what he wills to be done. For commanding is more than willing. He commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac (Gen. XXII); but did he will that this be done? If he did, why did he send a ram caught by its horns in the thicket? Therefore he commanded it, yet did not will it to be done. But he commanded it in order to prove Abraham’s faith and obedience.

Again, when he had healed a certain sick man, he said: “See that you tell no one” (Mark I). Did he will so great a miracle to pass by in silence? Certainly not; rather, he was setting forth an example of humility. Behold: it was God’s good will that he willed the Passion of the Son; and what he willed is good, because he cannot will except what is good. For he cannot will evil, though omnipotent. But the Jew willed that same thing with evil will, and what is good became evil to him: it became poison to him, which is antidote to me.

For although our outward person often indicates the inward person, and works disclose goodness or will, nevertheless will must not be judged from works; rather, works must be judged from will. For it is written: “Your disposition gives your work its name”; and every sin, as Augustine says,

> [Note: Col. 0691D, *On True Religion*, ch. 14.]

is so voluntary that it is not sin if involuntary; nor is anything criminal if it displeases, nor anything venial if it pleases.
