Therefore what the Jew did with evil will, although in itself it was simply good, nevertheless became for him an occasion of stumbling and evil, and was reckoned as injustice. Through the prophet the Lord condemns both the work of evil will and the evil will of the agent, both the author of the work and of the will together. For he says: “You shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk.”

The cooking of the kid is Christ’s Passion. But what does the addition “in its mother’s milk” mean? His mother was Mary. His mother’s milk was the tenderest little portion of flesh which, formed and coagulated by the Holy Spirit for the assumption of human flesh, passed into Christ’s body. For that flesh was not from heaven, as some believed, but from the substance of his mother’s flesh. Job says in the person of Christ: “Did you not milk me like milk and curdle me like cheese?” (Job X). From where did you milk me? From the substance of my mother. For he is the stone cut without hands from the mountain, which grew into a great mountain, into a mountain curdled and made like cheese, concerning which the Psalmist sang: “The mountain of God is a rich mountain; why do you look with suspicion upon the mountains made like cheese? It is the mountain in which God has been pleased to dwell” (Ps. LXVII).

Therefore the coagulating of this milk, the binding cement of this mountain made like cheese, was the Holy Spirit, by whom, contrary to the nature of others, the limbs were formed in the mother’s womb. For the limbs of others take their natural form from the seed of both parents over intervals of time and days. Thus after the forty-sixth day they receive a soul; but it happened otherwise in Christ. For on the very day of conception, in that very milk of his mother, all the limbs were formed together, a soul was infused, and on that same day it was made of such wisdom that God could add nothing to it. For on that day, according to his soul, he knew all that God knew, though not so clearly or distinctly.

Otherwise, there was some day on which the Son of God had flesh and was not man. The formed limbs could therefore increase with age and receive a greater quantity; but wisdom, or infused grace, could not receive a greater quantity, because he was begotten, not created, Wisdom; and he was made wise by unbegotten, uncreated Wisdom, which is one with begotten Wisdom, by whose benefit created, not begotten, wisdom, though joined [to it], could not be increased. For unbegotten, uncreated Wisdom united created, not begotten, wisdom to begotten, uncreated Wisdom; and an inseparable union was made, so that what belonged to God might belong to man, and the Son of Man might be the very Son of God.

Therefore the intended sense of the saying is this: “You shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk,” that is, you shall not afflict Christ with the Passion on the day of his conception. On the sixth day Adam was made; on the sixth day he fell; and on the same day, as some hand down, Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit, and on the same day he suffered. And fittingly: so that he might restore to incorruption the corruption of nature brought about through Adam by the incorruption of his own conception; and so that he who had fallen by chance might, through the setting of the Rising One, ascend—setting beyond setting [an uncertain wordplay].

Yet if Christ is signified by the kid because he came in the likeness of sinful flesh, then sinful flesh is signified by the kid. But why? Because of the sin of the flesh. Therefore by the kid is understood not only sinful flesh, but more properly the sin of the flesh. What then is meant by “You shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk,” unless it is plainly said: “You shall not cherish sin in the sweetness of thought”? The Lord says: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, and these are what defile a person” (Matt. XV). Therefore thought takes the place of a mother as the foment of wickedness.

For it is in this mother’s womb when it is suggested; but it comes out of her womb when it is deliberated. When, however, it sets confidence before itself through false hope, the mother receives it upon her knees. And when through the examples of elders it induces one to act, it draws forth from her breasts the milk of false consolation. When sin is committed but the mind is still blinded through ignorance and false consolations, the son is brought up to infancy. But when, through excessive habit of sinning, knowingly and deliberately he puts his hand into the flame and cannot restrain himself, so that he sins no longer from ignorance but rather from weakness, he grows from infancy into adolescence. For infants are naturally ignorant, and adolescence is weak.

But when afterward, from that same weakness, sin is so cherished that the person who sins not only wishes to commit it but also to defend what has been done, he has, as it were, grown from infancy into adolescence. For young men are those who, from twenty years old and above, are able to go out to war; concerning them it was said:

> At last, when his guardian has been removed, the beardless youth  
> Delights in horses, dogs, and the grass of the sunlit field;  
> Wax to be bent toward vice, harsh toward his advisers.  
> *(Horace, Art of Poetry, v. 160.)*
When, through the habit of self-defence, the sinner begins to be contemptuous and obstinate, he slips from youth into old age and is near destruction; for this is sin against the Holy Spirit, who is the ardour of the Father and the Son, [Col. 0694A] and he is as far from warmth as he is far from charity and from the ardour of the Holy Spirit. Since old men are naturally cold, he falls into the old age of sin, in which no spiritual sweetness is found. When it is added, “in its mother’s milk,” the sign of the accursed is set before us; for “the child of a hundred years shall be accursed.” Indeed, the obstinate sinner, in the sweetness of his own thought, is a child of a hundred years, and a kid boiled in its mother’s milk. Therefore Job said: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why, when I came out of the womb, did I not perish at once? Why was I received upon the knees? Why was I suckled at the breasts?” (Job 3). For the holy man transfers to himself not what was done to him, but what he did.

Blessed, however, is he who deserved to be raised in the house; but far more blessed is he who deserved to be raised [Col. 0694B] outside the gate, inasmuch as he was nearer to the funeral and the grave. Most blessed is he who, already buried, had been four days dead and stank in the tomb—by which the sin of obstinacy is signified—the harder to heal in proportion as he is more tightly bound by the cords of vices.

Or, he boils the kid who puts fire and wood beneath it. The kid is guilt; the wood, the cause; the fire, the punishment. Thus there is sin which is guilt, and sin which is not guilt. There is a cause of sin which is not sin; and there is a punishment of sin which is not sin. There is also sin which is guilt, but neither cause nor punishment. There is sin which is guilt and punishment, but not cause; and there is sin which is sin, guilt, cause, and punishment. Sin and guilt: the act of sin and its liability; sin and not guilt: the sacrifice for sin. Hence the Apostle says of Christ: “He was made [Col. 0694C] sin for us, that he might condemn sin through sin” (2 Cor. 5).

A cause of sin and not sin: the preaching of truth, from which vain glory arises. A punishment of sin and not sin: contrition of heart, even after penance has been performed, because it is written: “Do not be secure concerning a sin that has been forgiven” (Ecclus. 5). Sin which is guilt, neither cause nor punishment: that which, immediately after being committed, is washed away by repentance and is not repeated. Sin which is guilt and cause, but not punishment: liability which by its own weight draws on another sin; and then it is washed away by repentance, just as theft commonly proceeds from prodigality, and perjury from theft. Sin which is guilt and punishment, but not cause: that which immediately, through obstinacy, draws one unto death. Sin, guilt, cause, and punishment: liability [Col. 0694D] which draws on another sin and persists through obstinacy. In so many ways is sin inflamed; in so many ways is the kid boiled.

## SERMON XIX. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER

“On the sixth day, the prince of the sons of Gad, Eliasaph son of Deuel, offered a dish full of fine flour as a sacrifice” (Num. 7).

The sequence and power of our discourse consist in gifts given and received. For by the favour of receiving and giving, even mother and daughter are bound together in mutual love. But an empty hand makes the prayers of the poor empty. And although Isaiah says that he who shakes his hands free from every gift will dwell on high, because gifts blind even the wise, yet this authority is not so universal [Col. 0695A] as to admit no exception.

For there are certain benefits conferred by gifts: some diminish one’s wealth but not one’s understanding; others diminish understanding but not wealth; some diminish both. There are also gifts which do not diminish but protect: some indeed protect wealth but not understanding, others protect both. God bestowed many benefits upon blessed Job and took them away. His wealth was diminished, but not his understanding. For he said: “The Lord gave, the Lord took away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

Many benefits are commonly given to the usurer: wealth increases, understanding diminishes; for thereby he is blinded by greater greed, as it is written:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 14.138.)

[Col. 0695B] There are also others who are tortured by excessive grief over the loss of temporal things, and often hang themselves with a noose. These are diminished both in understanding and in wealth. But the Lord enriches others with gifts of grace; and the more they abound in spiritual things, the more lightly they value temporal things. Hence they choose rather to be lowly in the house of God than to dwell in the tents of sinners. These diminish wealth and protect understanding.

Those, however, who bestow the gift of alms upon the poor: when that benefit is carried into heavenly treasures through the hands of those who receive it, the giver of the benefit lays up treasure where neither rust nor moth exists, and where thieves do not break in or steal. Their wealth is kept, to be returned on the day of judgment with interest. For he gives what is temporal, but will receive what is eternal. He gives what he cannot keep; [Col. 0695C] he will receive a reward of which he cannot be deprived. Rightly, therefore, are both the understanding and wealth of such persons protected.

For such a reason Moses the lawgiver—or rather, the Lord through the lawgiver—commands: “You shall not appear empty before the presence of your God” (Exod. 23). For who would appear empty at the judgment? “For he gave gifts to men,” as he says: “Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me” (Rev. 22). Hence it is that the divine discourse speaks quite figuratively of the gift which he bestowed upon us and for us, when it says: “On the sixth day,” etc.

When, therefore, it says, “On the sixth day,” it sets before us a fitting time of mercy and one profitable for our deliverance. For there is no doubt that he was crucified on the sixth day, so that on the same day on which he formed humanity he might reform it, and so that on that same day humanity might rise again through him, on which it fell. Or “on the sixth day,” that is, in the sixth age. For just as the world proceeds through seven days, so it is distinguished by seven ages.

The first extends from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to Moses; the fourth, from Moses to David; the fifth, from David to the Babylonian deportation; the sixth, from the Babylonian deportation to Christ; the seventh, from Christ to that time when the Spirit will say to the blessed dead who die in the Lord that they may rest from their labours. Hence the Church distinguishes these seven ages by seven Sundays. And although every Sunday ought to be venerable [Col. 0696A] and joyful in honour and reverence of the Lord’s resurrection, nevertheless she rightly judged that these seven Sundays should be counted with a black stone, because in them she describes the miseries of the whole age.

For the more affectingly the misery of the sufferer is recalled to memory, the more earnestly is the mercy of the one who spares desired. For a great illness there is a great remedy; for great misery, great mercy is necessary to us. Therefore, that we may await God’s mercy more devoutly, we must more often recall our misery to mind.

The first age, then, begins with Adam. Accordingly, on the first Sunday the benefit bestowed upon Adam and his descendants is recalled to memory. But because he did not answer his Maker and benefactor either in words or deeds—indeed, when humankind had multiplied, the evils of Adam’s children multiplied also—so that the Lord, inwardly touched with sorrow of heart, was compelled to say: “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. 6), that is, “I shall do what a penitent man commonly does: he destroys what he has made.” And this indeed occurred. For that whole generation, except Noah and his household, perished in the waters of the flood. Therefore the Church groans, saying: “The groans of death surrounded me” (Ps. 17). Hence also, at the Easter vigil, no responsory follows this first reading, because Adam did not respond to the Lord’s divine benefits.

The second age begins with Noah. From him the whole human race was propagated. Hence, by analogy, on the following Sunday this is read in the Gospel: “He who sows went forth” (Luke 8). He who sows—that is, he from whom the whole human race was propagated—went out from the ark, that there might be fulfilled what the Lord said to him: “Increase” (Gen. 8), etc. He therefore went forth to sow his seed.

But when the earth was filled with his seed, that is, with a multitude of people, they gathered in the land of Shinar to build a tower whose top should touch the heavens (Gen. 11). Some were led to this because, having hearts hard and stony, they had no moisture of devotion toward God: this is the seed that fell upon the rock. Others, led solely by vanity, consented to the wicked work, so that it might be said of them in later time that they made a work which had no like before them [Col. 0696D] and could have none after them: this is the seed that fell by the way. Others, deceived by greed, consented to this evil desire; for they believed that the top of that tower could reach the heavenly treasures: this is the seed that fell among thorns.

Therefore the Lord confused their languages. Yet the Hebrew language, then common to all, remained in Peleg, because he was the seed that fell into good soil and yielded fruit a hundredfold. For from this Peleg was propagated the race of Abraham our father. But since we confess that we are Abraham’s children, why do we not praise God in the language that remained among Abraham’s children, but rather in that which the children of unbelief spoke because of their offence?

Accordingly, it should be observed that among all languages three became pre-eminent: Greek, Latin, and Hebrew. Hence Pilate wrote the title over the cross in these three languages as though they were the chief ones (John 19). Greek indeed sounds on the lips, Hebrew in the throat, Latin in the middle—that is, on the palate. Therefore, because the Mediator between God and human beings came to unite circumcision and uncircumcision, namely Greeks and Jews, in the unity of faith, it was fitting that he should be made in the Latin language, which, as was said, is intermediate between Greek and Hebrew.

The third age began with Abraham and ended with Moses. From Abraham came the first path of faith, and he first enlightened the world by faith, because he first preached one God. Before Abraham, each person claimed a god as his own, and in this changeableness and instability sought him who, remaining stable, gives all things motion. This man first freed the world from that error, preaching one God, the maker of all, remaining immovably in himself but moving all things; and Moses afterwards confirmed this by writings, words, and miracles.

Hence the blind man begging beside the road (Luke 18) is presented as an example in the office of the third Sunday. Who is that blind man but the human race, not yet enlightened by faith? He was begging by the road because amid this mutability it claimed a god for itself. One made a stone his god, another wood, another moles, and the like. But under this generation it first began to be enlightened through Abraham and Moses; yet finally, through him who is the end of the law unto righteousness for everyone who believes, namely Jesus Christ, the world, still dim-sighted in faith but no longer blind, was fully enlightened.

The fourth age began with Moses and ended with David. Consider the valiant men in war of this generation, and how at that time the land did not cease from battles. See with what strength of spirit Moses led the people of Israel out of Egypt, and how much he suffered in the wilderness. Joshua succeeded him and courageously defeated his enemies. After them came the judges Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, Jephthah, Manoah, and Samson. None of these was ever without wars. At last came the priest Eli, in whose time the ark of God was captured. After him came the kings, namely Saul and David. Nor did the land rest from wars in that time.

The divine discourse sets before us the bravery of all these so that, after their example, we may resist our enemies courageously, since we can never be without war in this world. For all who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution. Hence he himself says: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). For the world fights unceasingly against us; the flesh fights; the devil fights. Hence Peter says: “Your adversary the devil,” etc. (1 Pet. 5). For no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully.

Hence on the fourth Sunday it instructs us concerning these battles both by word and by example: by word, where it says, “Through the weapons of righteousness,” etc. (2 Cor. 6); by example, when it teaches how Christ overcame the evil one in his temptations. [Col. 0698A] And who is secure from temptations when Christ himself was tempted? Where the elephant swims, how shall the lamb cross over? But what is the end? “Behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. 4). Thus, if we courageously resist the devil, we shall deserve to obtain the ministry of angels.

The fifth age began with David and ended in the Babylonian captivity, that is, at the time when the children of Israel were led captive to Babylon. Of this captivity, as is read in the Psalm, the captives said: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Ps. 136). Hence on the fifth Sunday the chant is omitted, though not the prose. For whatever is read in prose, such as the Epistle and Gospel, has its place in the Mass; but it has no chants—namely the introit, gradual, offertory, and postcommunion. All these are borrowed from the preceding Wednesday, in which it implores deliverance from captivity: “Remember thy mercies, O Lord” (Ps. 24).

The sixth age, beginning with the Babylonian captivity, ended in Christ’s coming. For he is the Word of the Father, who came to break the silence of despair, of whom it is written: “While all things held the middle of silence,” etc., “thy almighty word came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18). The first silence was that of ignorance. For people ceased from crying out because they did not know to whom [Col. 0698C] they should cry. The second was that of despair: when the voice of the prophets had ceased, people were led into despair because their promise was deferred. The third will be in rest, where there will be neither groaning nor crying, nor any pain.

Therefore, while all things held the middle of silence, the Word of the Father came into the world to open the mouths of the mute, to break the silence of despair, and to make eloquent the tongues of infants. Hence on the sixth Sunday this is read in the Gospel: “Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute. And when he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke” (Luke 11). And because the Lord himself came to bind the strong man and distribute his goods, the Gospel continues: “When a strong man armed,” etc. (ibid.). Therefore, because of such benefits, at the end of the Gospel a certain woman from the crowd raised [Col. 0698D] her voice and said: “Blessed is the womb that bore thee and the breasts which thou didst suck” (ibid.).

The seventh age, which begins with Christ’s coming, will end in the joy of rest—that is, in the sabbath-rest left for the people of God—when that heavenly Jerusalem receives its citizens. Hence, on the seventh Sunday, the children of Zion, awaiting such joy with all confidence, exult and say: “Rejoice, Jerusalem.”

Rightly, therefore, on the sixth day—that is, in the sixth age in which Christ came—the prince of the sons of Gad offered, etc. But what have we to do with a prince, when Scripture says: “Put not your trust in princes” (Ps. 145)? Hence the Lord says in the Psalm: “Princes persecuted me without cause” (Ps. 118). And again: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together [Col. 0699A] against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

But it should be observed that the name *prince* is understood in four ways. A prince may be called so from *principium*, “beginning,” because he holds the first place in dignity and rank. He is also called *princeps* from *praecipio*, “I command,” a term fitting both bad and good men; for bad princes often command good disciples. He is also called *princeps* because he ought to be pre-eminent among disciples. He may also be called *princeps* from *praecipitium*, “a precipice”; hence the devil is called the prince of this world because he casts people down into the abyss. The Apostles, however, are called princes because they were pre-eminent among others. Hence the Prophet says: “Thou shalt set them as princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44).

The princes called from *praecipio* are those who sat upon the tribunal to order the deaths of martyrs. But Christ, who is called prince from *principium*, is “the Prince of the kings of the earth,” and says of himself: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8). Therefore he is the prince, and especially the prince of the sons of Gad.

Now “son” may be said either by generation or by imitation; here it is understood in the latter sense. He is therefore prince of the sons of Gad. *Gad* is interpreted “girded.” Those are girded who have either their loins girded about or are belted up. Virgins have their loins girded; those continent after sexual pleasure are belted up. Christ girded himself with a linen cloth at the supper, for he was a virgin. Peter girded himself with a tunic, because after marriage he was continent. Whether, therefore, they are girded about or belted up, all are girded. For everyone who contends in the arena is girded. Scripture says: “Let not the girded man boast himself as the ungirded” (3 Kings 20).

Eliphas is the prince of such persons. *Eliphas* is interpreted “the watchtower of my God.” There is a watchtower of contemplation, of which Isaiah says to Belshazzar: “Set the table; contemplate from the watchtower” (Isa. 21); a watchtower of prelation, of which Ezekiel is told: “I have made thee a watchman over the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3); and a watchtower of circumspection, whence the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Set up for thyself a watchtower; set up for thyself bitter things” (Jer. 31). It is also used for a guard-post. Hence Isaiah says: “Set a watchman; and whatever thou seest, announce” (Isa. 22).

Christ, then, is the Watchman; unless he guards [Col. 0699D] the city, the one who guards it watches in vain. Hence he is called Samaritan, that is, “guardian.” For this reason he is also called “the Watcher” in Daniel. Therefore the flesh assumed by the Word was, as it were, a watchtower, because through the windows of this watchtower God mercifully looked upon the world. And because through him we have full knowledge of the Father, he is rightly called the son of Duel. For *Duel* is interpreted “knowledge of God.” Since he made known to us whatever he heard from the Father, he is rightly called the son of Duel.

Therefore the prince of the sons of Gad, Eliphas son of Duel, offered a dish (Num. 7). In him there was no necessity, but only will. By will alone, not necessity, he bestowed this benefit upon us. Thus it is said, “he offered,” lest he seem to have offered under compulsion. He offered a dish. A dish is called the vessel in which vinegar is put. I have read that a dish was among the vessels of the Temple; but I do not remember having read for what purpose it was there.

But because vinegar was offered to the Lord Jesus Christ in his Passion, of which it is written: “When he had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished’” (John 19), his body was fittingly a dish, that is, a vessel serving as a receptacle for vinegar. Therefore he offered it not empty, but full of fine flour. He offered a dish full of fine flour because his conscience was without the bran of malice and wickedness. For unleavened bread of sincerity and truth is made from such fine flour. Therefore Christ our Passover has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5). In these unleavened breads—that is, without the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with unleavened bread of the fine flour of sincerity and truth—he offered [Col. 0700B] sacrifice.

“Sacrifice” is so called, as it were, from “making sacred.” Truly, neither true faith, nor holy life, nor a work of charity could have made us holy unless the Lord had offered this dish full of fine flour. But because in suffering he passed from life to death, and in rising passed from death to life, therefore if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him. If through patience we have been imitators of his death, we shall likewise be imitators of his resurrection. For as all die in Christ, so all shall be made alive in Christ. Let us therefore die, and let our life be hidden in Christ, so that when our life appears, then we too may appear with him in glory—he who is our leader and forerunner, and who lives and is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XX. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0700C]

“Who is this leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills?” Is he not the son of leaping, whom Achish despised the day before, when he danced, when he played the tambourine, when he struck against the doors of the gate? Is he not the son of leaping whom Michal, daughter of Saul, mocked when he played and uncovered himself before the ark of God? For he is Adeodatus, the most tender little worm of wood, the Bethlehemite (2 Kings 21), the worker in many colours, strong of hand, desirable in countenance, “fairer in form than the children of men,” and “beautiful in his robe, advancing in the multitude of his strength.”

He is therefore called the son of leaping because from the bosom of the Father into the womb of the Virgin, [Col. 0700D] from there into the world, from there to the gibbet, from there to the tomb, and from there even into hell, he made a leap and ran, that he might attain the prize. For it is written: “All indeed run, but one receives the prize” (1 Cor. 9). Who is the one? He of whom it is written: “There is none that does good, not even one” (Ps. 13). For although others had run in the way of God’s commandments, as Abraham, obedient to God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness; others in the way of justifications, as righteous Noah; others in the way of truth, as Moses led into all truth—yet they had not reached the prize. But he, walking in the shorter and more excellent way of charity, reached mightily from end to end and ran swiftly.

For it is written: “No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven” (John 3). Thus he alone descended, but he ascended wholly. Therefore, when the Jews placed him upon the brow of the mountain on which their city was built, so as to cast him down, the rock gave him a hiding place, which to this day is called “the Leap of the Lord.” But, as was said, Achish and Michal mocked him in the aforesaid leaps, because it is written: “We preach Jesus Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). For in Achish the Gentile world is figured; in Michal, circumcision.

For what Gentile would believe God confined in a virgin’s womb? Who would not blush at one hungry, thirsty, wearied by labour, as though playing the tambourine? Who, finally, would believe him striking against the doors of the gate when he cried to the Father: “Eli, Eli, [Col. 0701B] lamma sabacthani?” (“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”) And likewise: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 27). In all these things our faith appears folly to the Gentile world.

But Michal herself mocks him as he plays, because she knew only how to play the game of vanity, of which it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32). She knew only the game of wickedness, with which the boys of Abner played with the boys of Joab, and with which the son of the slave woman played with the son of the free woman. For she did not consider that the wisdom of God the Father, which was playing with him at the beginning of the first creation, came through humility also to play at the end of our re-creation. Hence it is written: “I will play and become more lowly” (2 Kings 6).

Likewise, he was stripped for us before John [Col. 0701C] in the Jordan, that he might give the waters the power of regeneration, through which those who have put off the old man may put on the new man, who is created according to God. A second time he was stripped by the man whose name means “glory of skin,” so that, laying aside the glory of the flesh, he might show that Adam’s tunic of skins and fig-leaf coverings had been put off. A third time he was stripped by the soldiers, when they divided his garments, that he might more fully make known to us the excessive love with which he loved us. A fourth time, rising again, he was stripped when he laid aside his grave-cloths, that he might thus prepare himself for heavenly leaps, made a Bethlehemite and worker in many colours—he who in his first leaps had been made Adeodatus and the most tender little worm of wood, in all things and through all things the son of leaping.

For, descending from above, he is declared to us as Adeodatus, “given by God.” “A child,” it says, “is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9). He is called the most tender little worm of wood because he himself says: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21). Like a little worm hidden in wood, he concealed his strength in the wood of the cross. For it is written: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Hab. 3). He is called most tender for this reason: feeling the touch of the Syrophoenician woman, he said, “Who touched me? Someone touched me” (Mark 5). Truly most tender: showing compassion to Mary Magdalene because she had not yet received the Holy Spirit unto strength, he said: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20). As though he said: Do not touch me—that is, do not imitate me—because I have not yet ascended to my Father, who will send the Spirit unto strength, through whom you will be able to bear your cross and touch me, that is, imitate me.

Truly he is most tender, because in common speech what is sweetest is called “most tender.” Do you wish to hear specifically what worm he is? He is *Thamir*, by whose blood the ostrich broke glass, so that, when the glass was broken, it might joyfully receive its young. He is Thamir, by whose blood Solomon taught that the hardness of stones could be cut and polished. For how great is the hardness of a human being whose heart is not softened by remembrance of this blood? Who, pondering the remembrance of the Passion, does not overcome spiritual enemies?

For in the jawbone of an ass our Samson overcame his enemies. The ass was he who bore the cross upon his shoulders, who bore the burdens of our sins. Its jawbone is the remembrance of the Passion; this not only conquers enemies but also leads all our wills into all truth. Hence Samuel said to Saul: “When you depart from me today, you will find two men beside Rachel’s tomb, leaping great pits, and saying: ‘The asses have been found’” (1 Kings 10).

Who are these two men? The first Adam with his body; the second Adam with his body. The first, who is from the earth, is earthly; the second, from heaven, heavenly. The first pit is the depth of guilt; the second, the abyss of punishment. Of the first it is read: “Let not the tempest of water overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me, nor let the pit press its mouth over me” (Ps. 68). Of the second: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole which he made” (Ps. 7). The first Adam made a leap into the pit of guilt; the second, into the pit [Col. 0702C] of punishment.

Therefore the two men leap great pits beside Rachel’s tomb: namely, when charity grew cold and iniquity abounded, falsehood counterfeited its appearance and innocence was buried. These two men found the asses of Kish because they changed the hardness of the human heart into the sweetness of charity. For *Kish* is interpreted “hard,” and his ass is, as it were, a certain sluggishness of heart. The human heart resembles an ass: it never does good unless compelled; released from the bond of subjection, it raves playfully; it scarcely thinks rightly unless pricked by the goad of fear. If it loses fear, it raves through its thoughts as though wanton.

Therefore it is written:

> Rule your mind, which, unless it obeys, commands;  
> restrain it with reins, restrain it with chains.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* 1.62–63.)

There are some who subject their own will to God’s will and, as though setting Christ upon their ass—their will—intend to visit Jerusalem. They imitate him who said: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matt. 26). This ass is guided by a bit, not driven by spurs.

There are others who set Balaam upon their ass because, greedy and avaricious, they subject their wills not only to cursing the people of God but also to doing them harm. This ass is driven by spurs, not governed by bridle or bit.

There are others who have the will to do good, but, faint-hearted, fear to undertake the good they desire. Hence they can say: “My soul has desired to long for thy ordinances at all times” (Ps. 118). These set their ass beneath Achsah, daughter of Caleb, who, sighing because of dry land, sought from her father an upper spring and a lower spring (Judg. 1). He sought them in Shalishah, in case perhaps he might find Achsah’s ass there; he also sought in Shaalim, where perhaps Balaam’s ass might be found; and he sought in Zuph, a place most suitable for finding Christ’s ass. For *Zuph* is interpreted “watching.” And what is watching but contemplation? For through contemplation the human will is subjected to Christ.

The ass, therefore, is sought in Zuph but is not found. For we see in one way through a mirror and in an enigma, and in another face to face. Rachel does not depart from Laban without idols. Rachel signifies the contemplative life; Laban, the world; the idol, imagination. For the mind scarcely ascends to contemplation without images of the world. Yet when it examines itself, what does it say? “It has happened to me according to the custom of women” (Gen. 31). As though it said: Whatever the mind comprehends concerning God is nothing true, but wholly frail and imaginary.

Hence, when Elijah at the entrance of his little tent first beheld a wind overturning mountains and breaking rocks, then an earthquake, and thirdly fire, he knew that the Lord was in none of these, because he understood them to be not the truth of the image but the image of truth. But at last he perceived him to be in the whisper of a gentle breeze, because no image followed that whisper (3 Kings 19). For the more the mind fails in contemplation, the more it advances in faith; because concerning God all negations are true, and affirmations are inadequate. For I cannot know what God is, but I can know what he is not.

Thus the ass is sought in Zuph and is not found: that is, the mind subjected to God is sought in contemplation and is by no means discovered. Balaam’s ass, however, must be sought in Shaalim, which means “fox.” For the fox is a crafty and malicious animal. Whoever subjects his will to avarice seeks to increase money by craft and malice, but does not find it, because:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 14.138.)

[Col. 0703D] The ass of Achsah, daughter of Caleb, must be sought in Shalishah. For *Shalishah* is interpreted “third” or “three-year-old.” Whoever strives to subject his will to God, when faint-heartedness or lethargy drives the mind from its purpose, must always raise the eyes of the mind to him of whom it is written: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 3). For when the mind is raised to devotion, God is raised in the mind, as it is written: “A person shall come to a deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63).

Or, because it is interpreted “three-year-old,” it is sought in Shalishah when, through a word sown in the heart by preachers or through a thought arising spontaneously, God is sought in the mind through thought; yet he is not found, because in this life, as has been said, God is not comprehended by thought. We must therefore come to those who leap the pits. For Samuel says: “You will find two men beside Rachel’s tomb, leaping great pits” (1 Kings 10).

The remainder is lacking.

## SERMON XXI. ON THE HOLY DAY OF PENTECOST

“And I saw in the midst of the seven lampstands one like a son of man” (Rev. 1).

Whoever wishes to remain in Christ ought himself also to walk as Christ walked. For he says: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John 12). Therefore, whoever does not follow him does not serve him. But how can one who is in darkness and does not know where he is going follow him who dwells in inaccessible light?

For thick darkness lies over the face of the abyss, that is, of the world; concerning it Wisdom says: “The abyss says, ‘He is not in me’” (Job 28). This is the abyss of misery, which calls upon the abyss of mercy. It calls—that is, it summons it to itself—that it may be one within it. It calls inwardly, because through the infusion of grace it calls in the voice of its cataracts—that is, through the voice and preaching of its apostles, who, like the cataracts of heaven, poured forth the rains of doctrine.

Yet the cloud of darkness, the shadow of death, the blindness of original or actual sin, has not yet departed. For although the laver of regeneration washes away the filth of the liability of original corruption, it does not erase the film of actual sin. For through baptism the burden of liability is removed, but concupiscence is not.

This blindness, then, is rightly figured in the darkness of the man born blind, because the divine discourse calls those who have not been reborn through baptism “dogs,” for the reason that they are born naturally blind and do not recognize their parents. Actual sin, however, sometimes remains in guilt but not in act, sometimes both in guilt and in act: in guilt but not in act, because, although the act for the most part ceases, the guilt nevertheless does not. Often indeed the eye of the mind is darkened both in act and in guilt. And this affliction commonly arises from various causes: sometimes through ignorance, sometimes through neglect of a mind badly guarded, sometimes through an obstinate will toward evil; at times through desire for temporal things; not infrequently through fleshly pleasure; very often through contempt for salvation.

Paul persecuted the Church of God; but at the preaching of Ananias scales as it were fell from his eyes (Acts 9), and, having received his sight, he obtained God’s mercy, because he acted in ignorance. Zedekiah was led captive and bound by the king of Babylon, who, after killing his sons before him, blinded him and ended his life by making him drink a laxative draught (4 Kings 25). Thus, through neglect of the mind, the devil, king of confusion, often so draws the mind with the cords of sins that, while it knows and understands, he kills its virtues by violent temptation. After this he so blinds the eyes of reason that the captive willingly follows his captor; nor would he wish to be released even if the devil himself withdrew his hand. At last it receives a laxative drink, because he pours into the mind [Col. 0705A] every overflow of dissimulation, so that whatever enters the mind, as into a belly, it casts out, and is loosened toward every stench of sin.

Moses too, when he had performed many signs before Pharaoh and Pharaoh would not accept correction by dismissing his people according to God’s command, brought darkness over the land of Egypt, so dense that it could be felt by touch (Exod. 10). This was a sign of their obstinacy. Truly, those deserved to be blinded, and were blinded, who remained stubborn against so many and such great signs. Tobit also, we read, was blinded by the hot dung of a swallow (Tobit 2). Swallows are holy men, who gain life by the flight of contemplation; their dung is temporal things, which, in order to gain Christ, they reckon as dung. This hot dung [Col. 0705B] of the swallow blinded Tobit’s eyes when, touched by an ardent desire for temporal things, he sent his son to travel abroad to Rages, a city of the Medes. Hence his wife said: “Would that money had never existed,” etc. (Tobit 5).

Samson, however, who formerly could not be held even by sinew-cords, was afterward so enfeebled by fleshly pleasure that, held fast by a little woman, he was blinded. That blood also which washes the garments of sinners, adorns the cheeks, and restores the whiteness of snow to scarlet, and the whiteness of wool to crimson—when in its outpouring it split rocks, shook the earth, opened tombs, and convulsed the elements of heaven—became black like a sackcloth of hair, because the sack of the Sun of righteousness was being torn. The visible sun hid its illuminated brightness, because the Sun of righteousness concealed the Illuminator. For the children of men, loving vanity and seeking falsehood, alienated from truth, lied to the Son of God when, opening and digging the pit of death, they fell into the pit which they had made. Seeking to destroy life, they lost life; seeking to extinguish light, they became blind. Therefore darkness came to be, because they despised the light of truth and being in the light of truth, as it is written: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1). Behold, by so many causes this abyss of misery is darkened.

For this reason the lawgiver—or rather the Lord through the lawgiver—commanded that seven lamps should be lit in the tabernacle of God and placed upon the seven branches of one lampstand. “You shall make,” says the Lord, “a lampstand wrought of the purest gold: its shaft, and branches, cups, and spheres. Six branches shall come forth from its sides, three on this side and three on that” (Exod. 25). For what is figured by the lampstand but the universal Church, whose universality is expressed through the number seven of the branches? For what the Law prefigures through seven branches, John prefigures through seven lampstands. He says: “And turning, I saw seven golden lampstands” (Rev. 1). And shortly afterward: “The seven lampstands are the seven Churches” (ibid.). Yet he treats of them by name under the seven Churches which are in Asia: Ephesus, Pergamum, Thyatira, Smyrna, Philadelphia, Laodicea, and Sardis. The universal Church is one indeed, but its particular churches are many; its head is the finest gold. For [Col. 0706A] the head of the Church is Christ, who is called the purest gold because he is the wisdom of the Father, who assumed our nature without sin. It was wrought, because both in its head and in its members—that is, in martyrs through the outrages of sufferings, and in confessors through the distresses of temptations—it advanced to immortality.

The lampstand had spheres, cups, and lilies: cups in preachers, because it belongs to them to make the hearts of the faithful drunk with wine which either brings forth virgins or gladdens the heart of man; spheres in contemplatives; lilies in those who are pure and undefiled. But since the cups are said to have been shaped like a nut, those who seem to preside over others in word and example ought to bear something of the nut’s likeness. In their outer shell they have something which must be broken through abstinence; outside, the bitterness of the rind, which must be endured through patience; and the sweetness of the kernel, the hope of salvation, which sweetens the soul through devotion.

That three cups, three spheres, and three lilies are said to have stood upon each branch signifies that preachers, who intoxicate others by word and example, must possess such discernment as to know what they ought to preach to whom.

For some are content with the bare text of history; others must be instructed in faith through allegory; others must be built up in morals through tropology. Thus spiritual things are to be compared with spiritual people, fleshly things with fleshly people. Spheres likewise are placed at three points on the branches so that contemplatives may know which things are to be considered as according to reason; which as beyond reason but not contrary to reason; and which as beyond reason and contrary to reason. Those things are called according to reason which are simply possible; those things are beyond reason but not contrary to reason which are called possible to God; those things beyond reason and contrary to reason are impossible.

For just as there are three kinds of possible things, so there are three kinds of impossible things. One thing is possible according to lower causes and the course of nature, as when a human being is born from a human being, an ox from an ox. Another is possible according to custom and higher causes, as souls being infused into bodies. Another is possible according to higher causes and through grace, not according to nature or custom, as first grace being infused and a person without merits being cleansed from sin. This is not called simply possible, but possible to God.

Likewise, one kind of impossibility is beyond reason but not contrary to reason, as certain cases in which there is a return from privation to possession, such as health restored to the sick or sight restored to the blind. Another is beyond nature and contrary to nature, where divine grace does not supply for nature’s incapacity, as that a log should become a calf. Another is contrary to nature, in respect of which divine authority has supplied what is impossible to nature, as that a virgin should have given birth, Lazarus should be raised, and the like. Likewise lilies were at three points on the branches, because the brightness of purity is considered not only in regard to virginal integrity or widowed continence, but also in regard to marital chastity. That all these things were contained in four places on the branch which held the middle position signifies that he who is the head of the Church, the Mediator of God and men, possessed all these things beyond the measure of others: to him was given the fullness of grace beyond the measure of all mortals. This is what the fourfold squareness signifies.

Above these seven branches, in order that the Church of God might be illuminated, Moses commanded seven lamps to be lit. The first of these is the Word of God, the lamp which darkness could not comprehend, of which it is said: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. 118 [119]). A lamp is called light in an earthen vessel; and light in an earthen vessel is God in flesh. Therefore the very Word of God is the true light, “a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.” The prophetic word also is a lamp which illumines the Church; of it Peter says: “You have the prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1). Spiritual understanding beneath the vessel of the letter is also called a lamp.

There are also the examples of the saints, which illuminate the Church in different ways. Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “So let your light shine before men, that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.). Hence John, than whom none greater arose among those born of women, was called “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5). The preaching of truth also illumines God’s Church, because it is the lamp which the wise woman lights in order to find the lost drachma. The lost drachma is the loss of spiritual grace; the lit lamp is the preaching of truth. For through the preaching of truth spiritual grace which was not possessed is given, and grace which was lost is found. The eye of reason is also illumined, of which it is said: “The lamp of your body is your eye.” Therefore reason is compared to the ethereal heaven in which the luminaries are found.

There are also miracles of the saints, which illuminate the minds of believers, especially when mortification of the flesh and a holy confession of faith accompany the miracles. These are the lamps of Gideon, which appeared in the breaking of the jars and the sounding of trumpets. The trumpet’s sound is an open confession of truth; the breaking of the jar is mortification of the flesh; the manifestation of the lamps is the flashing forth of miracles. And who is not illumined by the example of one who mortifies the flesh, strengthens the spirit, and flashes with miracles? Above all, however, and before all else, the wisdom of the Judge and the severity of the future judgment ought to open sinners’ eyes and remove all blindness of negligence. It will neither be deceived, nor wish to deceive, nor be able to deceive, when it searches Jerusalem with lamps. These lamps ought to be lit and set upon lampstands by the angels of the seven Churches, which, as has been said, are figured either in the lampstands or in the branches.

By the seven angels I understand the prelates of the seven Churches, appointed to govern the Church according to the ranks of seven orders. Since Ephesus is interpreted “will” or “counsel,” the angel of Ephesus figures the messenger of the divine will or counsel—that is, the order of readers. They are ordained in the Church so that, by reading and expounding the Law, they may disclose to us the divine counsel and will. Hence, when they are ordained, it is said to them: “Receive and be proclaimers of the word of God, and, if you faithfully and profitably fulfill your office, you shall have a share with those who have ministered the word of God.”

In the angel of Pergamum the order of exorcists is figured. For Pergamum is interpreted “scattering horns.” When they are ordained, they receive authority to scatter the horns of sins, of which it is said: “I will break all the horns of sinners” (Ps. 74 [75]). Hence, when they are ordained, the exorcism is given to them and it is said: “Receive this and commit it to memory, and have authority to lay hands upon the possessed, whether baptized persons or catechumens.”

By the angel of Thyatira, moreover, the order of acolytes is figured: those who have first been illuminated are bound to illuminate others. Hence they are also called candle-bearers; for Thyatira is interpreted “illuminated.” When these men are ordained, it is said to them: “Receive the candlestick with the candle, that you may know that you are assigned to kindle the lights of the church.”

The subdeacons, also called Nathinaeans, from that Nathanael of whom it is written, “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John 1), are figured in the angel of Laodicea, because Laodicea is interpreted “the tribe beloved of the Lord.” Indeed the Nathinaean is beloved of the Lord and without deceit if [Col. 0708C] he faithfully fulfills what is enjoined upon him by the bishop, when it is said to him: “See what kind of ministry is entrusted to you; and therefore, if until now you have been slow in coming to church, from now on you ought to be assiduous,” etc.; and at last, in conclusion: “Therefore I admonish you to conduct yourselves in such a way that you may be able to please God.” As if the bishop said: “Therefore I admonish you to conduct yourselves in such a way that you may be angels of Laodicea.”

Since the office of deacons is to proclaim the Gospel of God in church, their order is well figured by the angel of Smyrna, because Smyrna is interpreted “song.” For although we read of many songs, that should especially be called *the* Song by which the heavenly bridegroom kissed his bride with the kiss of his mouth. Priests, however, are ordained to be spiritual physicians of souls, because they are bound to heal with spiritual remedies those who wish to cling to the Lord: some through the sweet draught of exhortation, others through the bitter potion of penance. Therefore the rank of priesthood is rightly figured by the angel of Philadelphia, which Philadelphia is interpreted “saving one who clings to the Lord.”

In these six ranks, the order of office, not of dignity, is considered; in the seventh, both office and dignity are commended. This is the order of bishops, who, in the place of the apostles, have been appointed rulers over all the earth—that is, over the universal Church. Hence their order is aptly designated by the angel of Sardis, since Sardis is interpreted “prince.” These are the angels who are said to have sounded the trumpets which they held in their hands.

[Col. 0709A] To hold trumpets in their hands is to demonstrate the word of preaching more by the example of one’s works than by the word of doctrine, lest they be among those who say and do not do; rather, as it is written: “The word which came in the hand of Haggai the prophet” (Hag. 1). For the word of God was in Haggai’s hand, since he fulfilled God’s command in deed. He sounds trumpets who preaches with his mouth what he fulfills in his works, as it is written: “My son, drink water from your own cistern, and let the streams of your well flow abroad” (Prov. 5).

Preaching is aptly figured by a trumpet, because as the sound of a trumpet in war compels enemies to flee and urges friends to battle, making timid enemies afraid but faithful friends courageous, so the preaching of God’s word ought both to frighten sinners with threats and to exhort the well-disposed with promises. And as a trumpet is usually broad at its mouth, broader in the hand, and broadest beyond the hand, so preaching ought to be clear in word, clearer in deed, and clearest in affection before God.

Because preaching must be supported either by manifest reasons or by the testimonies of Scripture—for otherwise it ought to be rejected as readily as it is offered—the angels must sound different trumpets according to differing arguments or differing scriptural authorities. The trumpet of bark is the enigmatic voice of the prophets; the stripped trumpet is the open truth of the evangelists; the horn trumpet is the preaching of teachers; the fleshly trumpet is the preaching made through the incarnate Son, as it is written: “God, who at many times and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1). The golden trumpet is the voice of the Father himself, who says: “This is my Son,” etc. (Matt. 3); and again: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (John 12). The silver trumpet is the voice of angels; the bronze trumpet, which the Apostle calls the last, signifies the final trumpet. It is called bronze because the definitive sentence will be inflexible and irrevocable, by which it will be said either to the good, “Come, blessed ones,” or to the wicked, “Go, accursed ones” (Matt. 25).

For this reason the many voices of preachers draw the Holy Spirit through devotion and open the mouth in preaching. Hence the Psalmist says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit, because I desired your commandments” (Ps. 118 [119]). For the preacher sometimes draws to himself, by prayer, devotion, and good merits, the spirit of fear, and opens his mouth to the voice of God’s judgments, which will come upon the waters—that is, upon those who, in the manner of flowing water, run down toward the precipices of pleasure. Sometimes he draws to himself the spirit of piety and opens his mouth to the voice of mighty works; and this in power—that is, through the power of miracles—lest those whom he rebuked through fear of judgments should despair, since the hand of him who raised Lazarus and looked upon weeping Peter is not shortened. Often he draws to himself the spirit of knowledge and opens his mouth to the voice of commandments; and this in magnificence, because he teaches how we may nobly know how to keep ourselves upright according to God’s commandments amid this crooked and perverse generation.

Very often he draws to himself the spirit of fortitude and opens his mouth [Col. 0710A] to the voice of threats, which breaks the cedars—and not merely cedars, but the cedars of Lebanon. For he boldly preaches the threats of him who will destroy by the breath of his mouth either those who, when they have come into the depths of evils, are contemptuous, or those who are proud and glory in their own merits. The former are simply cedars; the latter, cedars of Lebanon. At times he draws to himself the spirit of counsel, in order to open his mouth to spiritual counsel, by which the flame of fire—that is, the consent, act, and habit of sin—is cut off. The Lord does not extinguish it but interrupts it, that is, cuts it short, lest the fire, namely the tinder of sin, reach consent.

Sometimes he draws to himself the spirit of understanding and opens his mouth to the voice of justifications, so that he may shake the wilderness, even the wilderness of Kadesh. According to the gift of the spirit of understanding, he preaches how souls are justified by contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and the labor of penance: souls which sins had made deserted by God, whether they had never been good or had departed from the holy law after observing the commandments. The first are called simply wildernesses; the second, wildernesses of Kadesh. For Kadesh is interpreted “holy of the law.” Sometimes he draws to himself the spirit of wisdom and opens his mouth to the voice of promises, in order to prepare the stags for the revelation of dense thickets. For stags are holy men, who repel and overcome the poisonous assaults of malignant spirits. The dense thickets are the heavenly abundance of sweetness, of which it is said: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30 [31]). And again: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64). He prepares God’s stags for this abundance of sweetness through the voice of promises when he sets before them rest without labor, joy without sorrow, victory without conflict, and everlasting glory without failure. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE MOST HOLY TRINITY

When I saw the inflated words of philosophers and the empty verbal finery of those who speak grandly about trifles knocking at the hearts of certain believers, wishing by a shake of head and a wrinkling of the nose, along with the rest, to console my own ignorance, I lived, I confess, as a Pharisee, saying within myself: “If these men had not invalidated faith’s promise, they would surely know whose and what kind of learning it is that touches them, because it belongs to a sinner.” But what displeased me in this except Christ speaking to the Samaritan woman? For he did not thirst for the woman’s water in order to lack it himself, but in order to refresh his water-carrier from a better spring—she who had previously burdened the shoulders of her bearer. Therefore the righteous person ought to set forth the living image of God’s wonders in himself, as in a mirror, so that he may make water-pots full of water bring forth wine for those at table. For this purpose Elijah accepted food from the widow of Zarephath: that she whose hand had scarcely found a handful of flour might afterward possess oil in the flask and flour in the jar without ceasing (3 Kings 17).

Thus the city of the sun speaks the language of Canaan (Isa. 19), and Abraham becomes rich among the Canaanites (Gen. 13). Thus Ezekiel goes out into the plain so that he may see as he had seen beside the river Chebar; and the wild olive, grafted among olive trees, buds, bears fruit, and becomes fertile (Ezek. 3). Thus we steal golden vessels from the Egyptians; thus the proselyte, his nails cut and his hair shaved, serves the Hebrew. Thus Moses takes an Ethiopian woman to himself; Hosea, a prostitute. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy:

> “If you go out to battle against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hands, and you lead captives away, and among the number of captives see a beautiful woman, and love her and wish to have her as your wife, you shall bring her into your house. She shall shave her head, trim her nails, and put off the garment in which she was captured; and, sitting in your house, she shall mourn for her father and mother for one month; afterward you shall go in to her and sleep with her, and she shall be your wife” (Deut. 21).

For ecclesiastical teachers went out to battle against their enemies when, armed with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, they advanced to overthrow the doctrines of worldly wisdom. The Apostle says: “The weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds: destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity for the obedience of Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Since, therefore, the Lord has delivered these enemies of ours into the hands of his servants and made a way in the sea for his horses, in the mire of many waters, a beautiful woman among the captives is loved when some useful doctrine which pleases is found in foreign writings. If any of us wishes to take her as a wife and make her his household companion, he is not forbidden, provided that the maiden, her hair shaved and nails cut, puts off the garment in which she was captured and, sitting among us, mourns her father and mother for one month. Her hair is shaved and her nails trimmed when whatever is superfluous in her is cut away. She puts off the garment in which she was captured when she is stripped of the outward surface of pride with which she was wholly clothed among her parents—who, calling themselves wise, thought themselves great in their teachings and did not know how to speak humbly, even concerning what they rightly understood.

Therefore this woman is brought among us in another habit when we read their useful sayings without haughtiness and express them with sober gravity. Yet she sits among us and mourns for her father and mother when, as we read, she moves us to pity by making us grieve over the destruction of such great men. For a letter is commonly called joyful because it makes people joyful, and a pit blind because it takes sight from those caught inside it. The Holy Spirit too is said to intercede for the saints because he makes those whom he fills become intercessors. So also this woman mourns her parents among us when she compels us to mourn; and, prompted by her, we grieve for the ruin of those whose genius we admire.

The month, in which the moon’s course is completed by waxing and waning, signifies the changeability of human life. They are mourned for an entire month because, having never done anything by which they might escape everlasting wrath, they are mourned as barren throughout their whole life. I shall not pass over how blessed Augustine, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, agrees with our meaning, teaching that the woman captured from the enemy may be received in marriage, yet that the salvation of her parents cannot be presumed:

> “Whoever,” he says, “is a good and true Christian should understand that, wherever he finds truth, it belongs to his Lord; and, by comparing and recognizing it even in sacred writings, he should reject superstitious fictions and mourn for those people who, though they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. For, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.”

I think these words sufficiently show, concerning the captive woman—that is, philosophical teaching—when she passes into our marriage, what the trimming of the nails and shaving of the hair are, when superstitious fictions are rejected; and what the mourning for the parents is, when we grieve for people who, though raised by a divine gift to knowledge of God’s very divinity, were nevertheless reduced to folly through pride.

What else, then, does God’s servant do when he draws mystical meanings [Col. 0712C] from the books of his fellow-servants, the philosophers, than offer us water from the rock and oil from the hardest stone? If, then, he wishes to use these arts without enjoying them, he cannot be confounded in his labor, because so great was the glory of the cherub that the sound of its wings could be heard even in the outer court. They ought not to be loved for their own sake, because it is not fitting to enjoy them; but authority proves, reason teaches, work counsels, and necessity compels that it is good to use them. We must, as far as we can, imitate the works of Christ and use well not only good things but even evil things. For all things are ours; we are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s.

And, to say something about necessity, we should know that no one can be a perfect theologian without the significance of things and words. Theology surpasses the other arts in this respect: words without things, or things without words, signify. In theology, however, not words alone but things too are significant. The property of words consists in two things: utterance and signification. Utterance belongs to grammar; signification to dialectic; both, however, concern rhetoric. Likewise, the signification of things consists in two things: form and nature—form in respect of external arrangement, nature in respect of internal quality. Form is recognized in four things: number, measure, proportion, and motion. Number belongs to arithmetic, measure to geometry, proportion to music, motion to astronomy; nature belongs to physics.

Since God deigned openly to make known to the world that he was, and what he was or was not, he first gave a foretaste of the beginnings of his knowledge in the arts, so that through reason they might know him in these disciplines who had not yet deserved to know him through inspiration. For God gave reason to all. But let us see how he was known through reason in these disciplines.

Philosophers knew God through reason in two ways: either in things which were within themselves, or in things which were outside themselves. Hence the Apostle says concerning that knowledge by which they knew God within themselves: “What is known of God is manifest in them, for God revealed it to them” (Rom. 1). “What is known,” he says, “of God.” For God was not known fully, just as he was not wholly unknown. He did not will to be known fully, so that faith might have merit; nor to be wholly hidden, lest unbelief find a place. And thus it is manifest *in* them. He does not say *to* them, as he does concerning the knowledge by which they knew God outside themselves: “The invisible things of the world are clearly seen, being understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made” (ibid.). But because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, they became vain in their thoughts; and, professing themselves wise, they became fools.

Thus in the things outside themselves they knew God through certain probable and necessary arguments, in which the trace of the supreme Trinity appears, not merely probably but necessarily demonstrated, as is openly shown in that geometrical proposition which is put forward for those who claim this art for themselves:

> From a given straight line, construct an equilateral triangle.

[Col. 0713C] In this proposition we must first consider what it seeks to prove, and how, and from what premises it infers what is proved. From the proposed line—which no process of argument had demonstrated, but which had perhaps come into being from the middle without a means, as though subsisting through itself—it requires lines to be arranged for itself of such a kind and in such a way that they do not differ from the equality of the first and constitute the mother of all figures, namely the triangle. For among all figures the triangle is found more excellent, since it proves the rationale of the square, the circle, and every figure whatsoever. In the proposition set forth, however, it is not the triangle but the equality of a triangle’s lines that is demonstrated in the circles, so that the difference of the right, acute, or obtuse angle of any proposed triangle may be discerned. For the equilateral triangle displays equal angles just as it displays equal sides.

But now let us consider the mystery of the triangle. In a triangle three lines so imitate unity, are so joined to one another, and so draw near to each other, that they become alike. Hence there is in it such singleness that nothing can be added to it, increased in it, diminished from it, or removed from it. Otherwise, if something is increased, it exceeds the circles by which it is demonstrated; if something is diminished, it will not reach the circumferences of the circles; if something is removed, it is destroyed altogether.

Yet such plurality is demonstrated in the lines that this line is not that or the third, nor conversely; otherwise it would not be equilateral, since there would be nothing to which it was equal. But that triangle is plainly one, without division of the Trinity, and threefold without confusion of unity. There is in it neither imperfect singleness nor superfluous plurality, because it shows no imperfection in the lines, since none individually has less; nor superfluous duplication in the whole, since none there is imperfect. Hence it is clear that there is no dissimilarity of parts there. Nor is there a collection of different things there, because it is not a crowd. For the term “triangle” is not a collective noun; otherwise grammatically one would say, “triangle are.” Nor is there bodily composition of members there, because it is not a body. For if it were a body, it would consist of surfaces.

The equality of the lines is proved in this way. Around the proposed line, called *a*, a circle is drawn such that its circumference touches the end and places its center at the endpoint. A second circle, in which the reversed relation is discerned, is also added and called *b*. From the endpoint of the given line a second line is drawn to the point at which the circles meet, and this is called *c*. The second is proved from the first in this way: *a* and *b* extend from center to circumference; therefore *b* is equal to *a*. The third, namely *c*, is proved from the first and second by an argument which logicians call “from the first to the last,” in this way: *a* is equal to *b*, because this has already been proved. But *a* is equal to *c*, because they go from center to circumference. Therefore *b* is equal to *c*.

I have said all this so that you may know that the first line is proved by none; the second by the first; and the third by both. But when one figure is proved from another, what else does it do but derive its being from that by which it is demonstrated to be as it is? It remains, then, that we compare the truth of the sign with the sign of truth. As in the triangle we confess plurality in the lines and singleness in the figure, so in the supreme Trinity we confess unity in substance and Trinity in persons. As we said that nothing ought to be added to, increased in, or diminished from the triangle, so neither ought anything be added to, increased in, or diminished from the supreme Trinity. We increase it if we say that the Father is greater than the Son or the Holy Spirit. We diminish it if we say that the Son is less than the Father or the Holy Spirit. We remove something if we believe in only one person and not three persons.

We assign plurality in the persons just as in the lines. For as *a* is not *b* or *c*, nor *b* *a* or *c*, nor *c* *a* or *b*, so the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor is the Son the Father or the Holy Spirit; nor is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son.

And just as the lines are equal to one another, so also are the persons. For as the Father is, so are the Son and the Holy Spirit, and conversely. But just as we have demonstrated that there is there neither a bodily composition of members, nor dissimilarity of parts, nor an aggregate of different things, so assuredly there is there neither—because the Holy Trinity is neither a crowd nor a body—any imperfection in the persons, nor any superfluous duplication in the whole; rather, God is one without division of the Trinity, three without confusion of the unity. And as the first of the lines is from none, the second from the first, and the third from both, so the first of the persons—that is, the Father—is from no one; the second—that is, the Son—is from the Father; and the third—that is, the Holy Spirit—is from both.

And as the equality of the triangle is established from two circles so arranged in relation to each other that one is placed in the middle of the other, so also the truth of the Holy Trinity is established from the two Testaments—of which one is understood in the other—namely, the New and the Old. Ezekiel, contemplating their arrangement, says: “And there was a wheel within a wheel” (Ezek. 1). For a wheel being within a wheel means that one Testament is understood in the other.

Therefore, to establish the Trinity from the first Testament, as from the first circle, this argument may be brought forward, as the Psalmist teaches: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). By “Word” we must understand the Son; by “Lord,” the Father; and by “the Spirit of his mouth,” the Holy Spirit. But since the heavens and all their power were established through the Son and the Holy Spirit just as through the Father, equality in the persons is evident.

The Lord who gave that Testament proves the singleness of the substance: “Hear, Israel: your God is one God” (Deut. 6). From the second Testament, as from the second circle, Truth itself establishes the same plurality, commanding the disciples and saying: “Go, baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). He says “in the name,” not “in the names,” in order to show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one name.

But the plurality of the persons was shown still more plainly when, after the Lord had been baptized, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the likeness of a dove and the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3). Truth itself also establishes the singleness of the substance, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 20).

This assertion of ours seems to be supported most clearly by that ineffable name called the Tetragrammaton, because it consists of four characters: namely *jod*, *he*, *van*, *he*. For when these letters are joined together, they make one name, signifying the divine essence: namely, *je ve*. But when divided by three separations, they make three names, signifying the three hypostases: the first division being *je*, the second *eu*, and the third *ve*.

That the letters when joined signify the divine essence, and when divided the hypostases, may be inferred from the interpretations of the letters. *Jod* is interpreted “beginning”; *he*, “life”; *vau*, “itself”; and *heth*, “vitality.” Let *je ve*, then, be understood as “the vitality itself, the beginning of life,” so that the meaning is: the vitality itself of all things is the beginning of temporal and eternal life. For all things live through him who is the vitality itself of things; and this is the one divine essence.

The first division of the letters, namely *je*, is interpreted “beginning of life.” This properly belongs to the Father, because in every way the term “beginning” is fitting for the Father. For the Father is the beginning of the whole Trinity: the beginning of the Son, because the Son is from the Father by generation; the beginning of the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit is from him by procession or breathing forth.

[Col. 0716A] He is also a beginning in relation to creatures. This cannot be said of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. For the Son is not the beginning of the Father, but of the Holy Spirit and of creatures. The Holy Spirit, however, is the beginning neither of the Father nor of the Son, but is called a beginning in relation to creatures. Therefore, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one beginning, yet “beginning” belongs antonomastically—that is, by special appropriation—to the Father, because it is predicated of him in every respect, but not of the Son or of the Holy Spirit.

The second division, that is, *eu*, is interpreted “life itself”; and this properly belongs to the Son, because he singularly appropriates to himself this term “life” when he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Hence the Apostle says: “When Christ, your life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3).

For although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one life, the Son, by the union of divinity with soul and flesh, became in another and in a certain more beneficial manner the life of all. In that he was God, he gave temporal life to man, because he himself is life; but through the union of which we have spoken, he gave man eternal life, because he is blessed without end. Thus, in every way the term “life” is predicated of the Son.

The third division, namely *ve*, is interpreted “vitality itself,” and this properly belongs to the Holy Spirit, by whom all things are quickened and cherished so that they live by his warmth. For he is the ardour of the Father and the Son. Hence it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1); or, as another translation has it, “was brooding over the waters,” as a mother bird broods over eggs in order to give them life.
