[Col. 0716C] Hence Ezekiel also says: “Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I shall send into you a spirit, and you shall live” (Ezek. 37). And a little later: “Come, spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, and they shall live again” (ibid.). Thus, just as in the first creation of man God breathed into his face and man became a living soul, so in the second creation—the resurrection of the dead—it may be given life by the Spirit as he breathes. Therefore the Holy Spirit is rightly called “vitality itself”; for as in the first creation, so in the second, all things are made alive by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, because he is the vitality itself of all.

Since, then, there are ten names, some signifying the divine essence and others the plurality of persons, as Hebrew truth attests, this name is found more worthy than the others, so worthy indeed that it was to be worn on the golden plate on the priest’s forehead; for it signifies both, as was said, the unity of essence and the Trinity of persons.

These are the names that represent the essence: *Saddai*, which we may take to mean “mighty” and sufficient for all things; secondly, *El*, which is interpreted “God” or “strong”; then *Eloi* and *Eloe*, which likewise mean “God”; fifth, *Sabaoth*, which the Septuagint translated “of powers” or “of hosts”; sixth, *Je, je*, which in Exodus is rendered, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3); seventh, *Iah*, which forms the final syllable in *Halleluiah* and is called “invisible.” Hence *Halleluiah* is interpreted “Praise the Invisible One.”

[Col. 0717A] The eighth, *Elohim*, is as if I were to say “our Gods,” its singular being *Eloah*. Likewise, when I say *Adonai*, it is as if I said “Lords,” its singular being *Adon*. Hence where we say in the Psalm, “I said: You are gods” (Ps. 81), the Hebrew has *Elohim maten*, that is, “You are gods.” So too Laban says to Jacob: “Why have you stolen *elohim*?” (Gen. 31), that is, “my gods.” And Moses: “You shall not have *elohim elim*” (Exod. 20), that is, “foreign gods.” Lot likewise called the two angels speaking with him *Adonai*, that is, “my lords.”

Yet because these names are very often joined with a singular verb, we believe this is done in order that one God may be shown in three persons, while the plurality of persons is also indicated by these names. In Hebrew they are also often openly used with a plural verb. Thus, when the Lord said to Jacob, “Rise and go up to Bethel, and dwell there; and make an altar to God who appeared to you” (Gen. 35), the Hebrew here uses the singular, *Eloe nigla*, that is, “God appeared.” But later, when Scripture says that Jacob built an altar there and called the name of the place Bethel because the Lord appeared to him there when he was fleeing from his brother, this is expressed in the Hebrew in the plural. For it has *Elohim niglam*, which means in the plural, “they appeared.” For if it had wished to say it in the singular, it would have used *nigla*, that is, “appeared.”

Similarly, when David, praising God, says: “What nation on earth is like your people, for whom God went to redeem it as a people for himself?” (2 Sam. 7), both “God” and “went” are here plural in Hebrew: namely, *Elohim alchu*, which means “they went,” its singular being *halac*, “he went.”

[Col. 0717C] It has therefore been clearly shown that some Hebrew names signify unity of essence and others plurality of persons. But this name, Tetragrammaton, is found more worthy than the others because it prefigures both, as was said. What we said concerning the triangle is found most fully in the signification of this name.

But now let such a triangle be set between the same circles, with only its second line, *b*, overlaid in red. I ask the geometer whether the same singleness in the figure and plurality in the lines remain in the triangle; whether its quantity or ratio has been changed; whether it has received an increase or a diminution. For if its singleness is no longer the same as before, there are several figures; if its plurality is greater, it is not a triangle. If it exceeds in size, it exceeds the circles; if it has suffered diminution, it does not reach them.

[Col. 0717D] Hence it is evident that the same singleness, plurality, and quantity have not been altered. This triangle reveals to us no slight mysteries of our faith: although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in essence, the Son alone could be overlaid with the redness of flesh, in such a way that the Trinity suffered no diminution, the unity of the essence was not divided, it received no superfluity of increase, and no loss of perfection.

[Col. 0718A] And just as this trace of the Holy Trinity, this mystery of the true faith, necessarily confirmed the argument that was outside itself, so it could confirm it through the argument that was within itself, by considering the threefold faculty in the soul and not doubting that it had received them not from itself but from God: namely, reason, wisdom, and love.

For it considered that wisdom was born from reason. Brute animals are not capable of instruction because they are not rational. It was pleased with its wisdom, which distinguished it from brute animals; it loved this wisdom; and it considered whence came that love by which it loved its wisdom. It saw that it proceeded from reason and wisdom themselves. For it is rational, and characteristic of a wise man, to love his own wisdom.

[Col. 0718B] It therefore considered three things in itself: reason, which was a certain power of the soul, as though subsisting from no one; wisdom, which was born from reason; and love, which proceeded from both. It contemplated these same things in God. For it was not fitting that God should be called powerless, when he had given it the power of reason; nor foolish, when he had so orderly and wisely instilled wisdom from reason; nor one who hated his own wisdom, since that proceeds from human folly. Rather, knowledge plainly declares power, wisdom, and goodness in God.

And because it dared not confess—and it would not have been true—that anything in God was diverse, but all that belongs to his essence is one, it was compelled by reason to worship unity in that Trinity. Again, since nothing in God was imperfect and he had no superfluous duplication in himself, it dared not worship in him any dissimilarity of parts. Rather, it believed without doubt that the person who was from no one, as also the Son who is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit who is from both, is God. Yet because those three persons were one in themselves, it had to believe not that they were three gods, but one God.

Having learned these things, no less devout than faithful, it sought names by which it might more easily recall those three persons to mind and worship them devoutly. And since it saw among human beings that he from whom a son came was called father, while he who came from a father was called son, it named them Father and Son. It did not wish to call him mother or daughter, in whom it recognized nothing feminine.

[Col. 0718D] But the Holy Spirit, who was from both, it designated by a name belonging to both, so that from this very fact he might be recognized as proceeding from both. For the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit; the Father is holy and the Son is holy. Therefore it wished to call him the Holy Spirit.

Yet the difference between these things which it recognized in itself and the three persons which it contemplated outside itself must be noted. Those things which are in a human being can be present and absent without corruption of the subject—some of them, I mean, if not all—and they affect the soul more or less. But in God whatever is, truly is and exists essentially; and all that he is is one. Hence it is evident that in the argument of the triangle you will find the mystery of the Trinity more familiarly.

Thus we are confirmed in faith through the triangle; but, if you examine closely, we are no less instructed in morals. Since we believe and confess not only that we glory in the soul, but also that the body of our humility shall be conformed to the body of Christ’s glory, we must commend our whole human being to God: the outward person through works, the inward through affections. This will fittingly happen if we join different actions to different virtues in such a way that, once certain circles of perfection have been impressed upon us, we may know that we are striving for the everlasting crown.

[Col. 0719A] For it is evident that there are four affections of the mind. If you join to them the four principal virtues, they will form a certain circle of perfection in life, which the Lord will transform into a crown for your inward person. Those four virtues ought indeed to be joined to one another, because the true perfection of human affairs is that which knows the light of prudence, the beauty of temperance, the strength of fortitude, and the holiness of justice.

For as James says in his Epistle: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2). Prudence without fortitude is like a sword in the hand of a cripple; fortitude without prudence, like a sword in the hand of a madman. Again, a person cannot long stand without fortitude, since for a human being to be justified is to mortify the flesh. Nor can justice stand without temperance, since it is written: “My son, do not be excessively just” (Ecclus. 7). Moreover, prudence does not remain without temperance, because it is written: “Do not be wise beyond what you ought to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. 12).

[Col. 0719C] But when a person knows what ought to be done and does what he knows, he is truly just, provided that justice is regulated by temperance. Prudence, therefore, must be just, strong, and temperate. Likewise justice must be strong, prudent, and temperate; fortitude, prudent, just, and temperate; and temperance, prudent, strong, and just.

Therefore, if these virtues are to complete the circle of perfection, they must be bound together in you with the four affections, as with a certain bitumen: namely, sorrow, desire, joy, and fear. Sorrow binds prudence to temperance. For the wise person loves the house of mourning more than the house of rejoicing, knowing that “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” as it is written: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1).

And that sorrow itself belongs to temperance is taught by the mortification of the flesh. For if gluttony produces luxury and joy, according to the text, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32), sorrow is not unfittingly joined to temperance, which is opposed to gluttony. Desire joins prudence to fortitude. A person readily listens to and does what he loves; nothing is difficult to one who loves. Whatever one does seems burdensome if it displeases, and conversely light if it pleases. But in vain does one lend the ears of the flesh to receive instruction who closes the ear of the heart.

Joy binds fortitude to justice. For from strength of mind proceeds that cheerfulness in action which works justice, as it is written: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9).

[Col. 0720A] Fear joins justice to temperance: the fear, I mean, which we call filial, not servile. For perfect virtue drives out servile fear, as it is written: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4). But it always kindles and increases filial fear, as it is written of that same fear: “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” (Prov. 28). Yet this fear too must be regulated by the rule of justice, lest we fall into faintheartedness or despair, because it is written: “Fear is never evil except when excessive.” If justice is thus moderated by temperance, fear will undoubtedly join justice to temperance.

To summarize these matters briefly, we have said that the first circle of perfection is completed by temperance joined to prudence through sorrow, prudence to fortitude through desire, fortitude to justice through joy, and justice to temperance secured through fear.

[Col. 0720B] Likewise, we may discover the circle that makes our outward person perfect if we join the four kinds of good works to the same virtues. Whoever desires to be perfect in his deeds ought to be wholly devoted to counsels, remedies, services, and assistance: to counsels, if he pours out his knowledge for his neighbours’ benefit; to services, if he anticipates them with benefactions; to assistance, if he does not fear the terror of the wealthy when their affairs are to be managed; and to remedies, if in their needs he also puts his own hands to work.

For it is necessary to pour out completely for one’s neighbours not only one’s words but also oneself. Prudence therefore joins counsels to assistance; for it belongs to a wise person both to know and give counsel, and to conduct the causes of others. Fortitude joins assistance to services; for it belongs to the magnanimous not to fear the faces of the powerful and to share their own goods with others. Justice joins services to remedies, because it belongs to the just person alone to expend himself and his possessions for his neighbours. Temperance joins remedies to counsels; for a person ought so to moderate through temperance the counsels and remedies by which he anticipates others that he neither undervalues his neighbours for his own sake nor himself for theirs.

[Col. 0720D] Behold, unless I am mistaken, you have two circles, neither of which is found wholly within or wholly outside the other. For in part they agree and in part they differ. In that part in which they agree—that is, in the four virtues—one is contained within the other; but in that part in which they differ, each is found as though outside the other. And such they had to be.

From these two circles you can discern the threefold usefulness of human life, through which a person ought to be useful to God, to himself, and to his neighbour. To God, through simplicity or innocence, which commends both persons to God and, as it were, touches the circumferences of both circles, especially because it is possessed from the four virtues which we assign in each circle. To oneself, through sobriety, which weakens the outward person and strengthens the inward, and, arising from fear and desire, as it were touches the circumference of the nearer circle. To one’s neighbour, through piety, from which proceed counsels, services, assistance, and remedies.

[Col. 0721A] Hence piety, as it were, touches the circumference of the second circle; and simplicity is like the given line, for the sake of possessing which you have drawn the two circles. But because simplicity alone does not make perfection—for it is written, “Ephraim is a deceived dove, having no heart” (Hos. 7), plainly signifying simplicity by the dove—the triangle of perfection had to be completed through piety and sobriety.

If, then, all these things, which could scarcely be grasped in simple speech, are reconsidered by means of the example set forth—not once but often, not with the mouth but by ruminating on them in the heart—what else follows but that the perfection of this triangle is formed in the finest powder? For reflection upon our works is customarily signified by powder, as we read in Exodus, where the Lord says to Moses: “Take for yourself spices—stacte, onycha, sweet-smelling galbanum, and most pure frankincense; all shall be of equal weight. And you shall make incense, compounded by the work of the perfumer, carefully mixed, pure, and most worthy of consecration. When you have crushed all these into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the tabernacle of testimony” (Exod. 30).

Gregory says: “We make incense composed of spices when, on the altar of the heart, we give forth fragrance through a multitude of virtues. We crush all the spices into the finest powder when we reconsider our good deeds by hidden examination in the mortar of the heart. For to reduce spices to powder is to grind virtues by recollection.” [Note: [Col. 0721D] *Morals*, book 1, chapter 39.]

[Col. 0721C] He depicts virtues in powder who does not doubt that he himself is dust. He depicted piety in dust who, moved by compassion for the Sodomites and Gomorrhites, humbly said to the Lord: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). And the prophet says: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. 102). For in vain does one exercise oneself in virtues who, still puffed up with pride, does not remember that one is dust.

May God the Father grant that we may so reduce all virtues to powder that, having had the circles of perfection impressed upon us, we may deserve to possess the everlasting crown, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with God the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON THE NATIVITY OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Col. 0721D]

“The Lord blessed Isaac, and he dwelt by the well of vision” (Gen. 25). A faithful saying, worthy of all acceptance: for Isaac, unto reward; for us, unto merit; for all, unto example. For if it were granted us by God to understand what is the vision of Isaiah son of Amos (Isa. 1), what is the book of visions of Nahum (Nah. 1), what are those wonderful visions of God which Ezekiel saw (Ezek. 1), and finally what are all the oracles of the prophets, who of old were called “Seers,” then perhaps it would also be granted us to understand of what blessing one is worthy who dwells by the well of vision.

The visions of the prophets are compared to wells because of the depth of their mysteries. But when I carry my vessel to the waters of vision, I seem to renew that ancient proverb: “Behold Saul among the prophets.” For who will grant me even to pass beside the well of vision? I fear the Philistines who come upon me, who are accustomed to fill up wells with earth (1 Sam. 11). Moreover, the water fails from my skin, because I carry an earthen and broken vessel, without fastening or cover; I have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep.

[Col. 0722A] For this reason my soul has become like land without water before God; and, like Hagar fleeing and thirsty in the wilderness, it has become as far removed and alien from Abraham as one who went down into a far country to feed swine. Alas for me, because my exile has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been long a sojourner (Ps. 119), or, what is the same thing, has become so.

But this is too little for me. For in Kedar I dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar: indeed, I lingered in the darkness of sins, I whom the scales of Paul have so often blinded through ignorance, the hot dung of swallows through desire, Delilah through pleasure. Along with the people who dwell in darkness and inhabit the region of the shadow of death, light could not arise for me, nor could the Sun of righteousness; nor could I dwell by the well of vision.

Yet, trusting in him who opened the eyes of thirsty Hagar so that she saw the well of vision of living water, he will open my eyes so that I may draw water from the well of vision and give drink from it alike to us and to you—indeed, to our camels also. For in order that our eyes may be opened, the Lord placed a lamp upon a lampstand, that he might enlighten the blind, overturn houses, and find the lost drachma. Hence it is written: “John was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5): burning for himself, but shining for his neighbour.

[Col. 0722C] And he was brighter in proportion as the Lord declared to us through him every path of righteousness. For although one path of righteousness was proclaimed to the patriarchs, another to the prophets, another to the apostles, another to the martyrs, another to the confessors, another to virgins, and another to hermits, the Lord made John a brief compendium of all the paths of righteousness.

Therefore, with this lamp going before and leading the way, I shall open my eyes, that I may see the well of vision and draw water for you—if he who said, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80), deigns to fill my vessel.

Indeed, from the sacred Scriptures we gather many mysteries of wells, some worthy of blessing, others of admiration. We read that Jeremiah, lowered into a well by ropes, was at last drawn out by other ropes made of old rags. A marvelous thing, worthy of all admiration! If an elephant swims in this way, how will a lamb cross over? If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear? For if the waters reach even to the height of the Lord—for that is how “Jeremiah” is interpreted—who smaller than he can be safe?

[Col. 0723A] This is set before us as an example, because the ropes of sins often entangle us and lower us into so great an abyss of sins that we must rightly cry with the Psalmist: “Let not the storm of waters overwhelm me; let not the deep swallow me up; and let not the well press its mouth upon me” (Ps. 68). But those are let down by old rags who imitate, after the example of the ancients, the humility of poverty.

Hence Moses, considering and recognizing together that one who walks in darkness does not know where he is going and therefore falls into a well, when he fled from Egypt and came into the wilderness, lifted up his eyes and saw a well, beside which were the seven daughters of Raguel, priest of Midian, to water sheep. But when the shepherds of that land prevented the sheep from drinking, Moses drove out the shepherds, watered the sheep, and betrothed one of the daughters of the priest of Midian, named Zipporah.

This is what is written: “Moses was instructed in all the learning of the Egyptians” (Acts 7). For the well signifies doctrine. The seven daughters, I think, are the seven liberal arts, in which Egyptian learning is signified; their sheep are the philosophers, their shepherds the natural philosophers and teachers, and the priest of Midian their inventor, a gentile and therefore a son of iniquity, because *Madian* is interpreted “iniquity.”

[Col. 0723B] But when those shepherds hindered the sheep, just as teachers of philosophy today hinder those subject to them, bringing them to no perfection, Moses first watered the daughters and then the sheep, when he first recognized the mysteries of divinity in the arts and offered the Egyptians themselves an example of learning. For the liberal arts were devised in order to serve theology.

For in some of them either things exist without words or words are significant without things; and theology needs their service in proportion as things and words signify within it. Where do we have greater need of a word than when we speak of the Word? Where greater need of ornament of speech than when we speak of the Word, “beautiful in form above the sons of men,” who is the splendour of the Father and the image of his substance? Hence very often the figure of both [Note: [Col. 0723D] Something is missing.]. Where do we have greater need of rational discourse than when we speak of wisdom?

Thus grammar, like a handmaid, should serve the Word; rhetoric, the adornment of words; and logic, reason. The signification of things, however, concerns either form or nature. A wolf, by the rapacity it has by nature, signifies the devil; a lamb, by its simplicity, signifies Christ. And in this respect natural philosophy, like a handmaid to her mistress, serves theology. Form, moreover, consists in number, measure, proportion, and motion.

[Col. 0723D] Accordingly, arithmetic serves theology in numbers, geometry in measures, music in proportion, and astronomy in motion. For from the rising and motion of a new star the Magi recognized the birth of the new King. Yet from writings of this kind we must preserve for ourselves those things which ought, through contemplation, to lift us on the wings of reason to the heights.

“And Moses took Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian,” says Scripture (Exod. 2). *Sephora* is interpreted “bird”; she is the daughter of a priest. Midian means “iniquity”; the priest of Midian is a teacher of iniquity. For although he is a teacher of iniquity, his teaching, if it forms morals, is not to be rejected.

Hence also the Egyptian midwives, one of whom was called Sephora and the other Phua, preserved the male children although Pharaoh had commanded the opposite, for they feared the Lord. For whatever ought to be manly in you may be preserved through a twofold doctrine: one that forms morals and another that builds faith, even though they are Egyptian, even though they have been devised by teachers of darkness—that is, of unbelief.

[Col. 0724B] Phua, who is called “reddish” or “modest,” signifies that doctrine which forms bodily morals through the active life. But Sephora, who, as was said, is interpreted “bird,” signifies that doctrine which lifts the mind through contemplation. Hence it is read that Ahithophel’s counsel was made foolish by the counsel of Hushai. Ahithophel had given Absalom counsel against David. And Hushai said: “This time Ahithophel has not given good counsel” (2 Sam. 17).

Then Hushai, employing the counsel of Nathan and Zadok, sent Ahimaaz and Jonathan to David, saying: “Do not remain in the plains, but go up to the mountain.” As they went away, a boy saw them and reported them to Absalom, who sent messengers to seize them. But a certain man had a well in the entrance-court of his house, in which they hid themselves in fear. And behold, a certain woman placed a covering over the mouth of the well. Thus Absalom’s deceived messengers returned. But the two men, reporting Hushai’s counsel to David, delivered him from Absalom’s hand.

[Col. 0724C] Absalom, whose name is interpreted “peace of the father,” represents the heretic who says that he proclaims the peace of the heavenly Father and promises it to others. But although he says this, he persecutes his father David. His counsellor Ahithophel, whose name means “the ruin of a brother,” signifies the heresiarch, because through him falls that brother whose Father is Christ, from whom he is also called Christian. For we are all brothers in Christ. As the Apostle says: “You have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father” (Rom. 8).

But Hushai frustrates his counsel. Hushai is interpreted “Ethiopian.”

Therefore Ahithophel’s counsel is frustrated by Hushai’s counsel, because the authority of the gentiles commonly condemns the counsel of the heresiarch—provided, however, that their authority agrees with the Law and the Prophets. For Hushai himself used the counsel of Nathan and Zadok. Nathan signifies prophecy; Zadok the priest signifies the Law. Employing their counsel, Hushai sent Ahimaaz and Jonathan to David.

[Col. 0725A] What I first called Phua, I now call Ahimaaz. For Ahimaaz is interpreted “the beauty of my brother.” Two brothers are born from one father and one mother, namely the outward and the inward person. The inward person is always beauty. For this is what the inward person always strives for: that the outward person may be made beautiful through purity. Thus Ahimaaz signifies the active life, which forms morals.

Jonathan, however, whose name means “gift of the dove,” signifies the same thing as Sephora: namely, that doctrine which raises us by the wings of reason through contemplation. Yet with this difference: there the bird was named generally, here the dove specifically—a bird, namely, that mourns. And rightly so, because the doctrine necessary to us is that which teaches sorrows and groanings, as it is written: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1). And again: “I shall recount to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38).

The boy who saw them and reported them to Absalom is the faithful person who, through purity of mind, understands and discerns the Scriptures. He reports them to Absalom because he convicts the heretic. But the heretic sends after them the missiles of Scriptures which he perverts and which seem to support his heresy.

[Col. 0725B] But behold, there is a man whose name is “Rising,” whose house is the Church. He had a well in the entrance-court: that is, the profound mysteries of Scripture, where matters suited to the active and contemplative life are hidden beneath the covering of the letter. For that woman who lit the lamp—namely, the wisdom of the highest Father—spread out the covering. Thus those who persecuted David were deceived by the covering of the letter.

But those two counsel David to leave the broad way of vices and ascend the mountain of virtues: Ahimaaz, “strong of hand”; Jonathan, “desirable in countenance”; and each is David. Do you wish to hear Ahimaaz’s counsel, and this very counsel by the counsel of Nathan and Zadok?

> Since nature created you a naked infant,  
> Remember patiently to bear the burden of poverty.

Hence it was said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, because the kingdom of heaven is yours” (Luke 6). And again:

> Rule your spirit, which, unless it obeys,  
> Commands; restrain it with reins, restrain it with chains.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.60–61

Hence also in sacred Scripture: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4). Do you wish to hear Jonathan’s counsel?

[Col. 0725D] “Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.” (VIRGIL, *Eclogue* 4, v. 7.) Hence Isaiah also: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc. (Isa. VII). Thus we steal the golden vessels from the Egyptians; thus we beget children from concubines. Thus the proselyte serves the Hebrew, his nails cut and his hair shaved, because so great is the glory of the cherub that its voice is heard in the outer court. Therefore, although the writings of philosophers instruct us either in matters that build character or contain a testimony to faith, since they are not wells of visions, nor wells beside which Isaac dwells, it is not safe for us to linger there too long or dwell there more persistently; rather, having tasted a little water, we should pass on.

For this reason the woman said to those seeking Achimaas and Jonathan: “Having tasted a little water, they passed on” [Col. 0726A] (II Kings XVII). For we ought briefly, as by way of introduction, to taste such waters, so that afterward we may draw more deeply the water of saving wisdom from the wells of the Saviour. We should know that philosophical teaching is like a harlot, a foreign woman, a concubine; but theology is to be loved as the one wife, the woman of the household, the queen. Hence Abraham said to his servant: “Swear that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell; but that you will go to my land and to my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son” (Gen. XXIV). Thus he regarded the daughters of the Canaanites, whether for himself or for his son, as attendants and strangers, not as mistresses or members of the household.

The servant therefore went away; and, taking [Col. 0726B] ten camels with him, he came to a spring of water and said within himself: “The maiden to whom I shall say, ‘Give me water,’ and who shall say, ‘I will provide drink for you and your camels also’—she is the one whom Thou, O Lord, hast prepared for the son of my master.” He had scarcely finished speaking when, behold, Rebekah appeared. Returning to the well, she gave water to both the servant and the camels. Taking her with him, they found Isaac at the well of living water.

Behold again, dearest brethren, I open my eyes and behold two wells of living water. At one Isaac’s servant finds Rebekah; at the other Rebekah finds Isaac when he goes out to meditate. In these two wells is signified that twofold teaching, one part of which builds character and the other faith. Yet theology excels the other arts as much more eminently and clearly as the art of arts and the governance [Col. 0726C] of souls excel all other arts.

For Abraham, whose name is interpreted “father of many nations,” bears the image of human understanding. Just as Abraham begot Ishmael by Hagar—the concubine—a bastard son, hateful; by Sarah—the wife—a son of promise and legitimacy, Isaac; and by Keturah, his second wife, a son of iniquity, as Midian is interpreted: so human understanding, from conscience when it is estranged from its God, produces a will most evil and hateful to God. But sometimes conscience, when it holds the primacy of the virtues, when the feminine qualities begin to fail in it, when it feels in itself nothing womanly but all manly, brings forth the fruit of the Spirit: joy, peace, patience, [Col. 0726D] and so forth.

Very often, from Keturah, whose name means incense or frankincense, while the body is almost dead, it begets Midian—that is, a son of iniquity. Although carnal temptation is dead in it and conscience breathes forth a sweet fragrance in every place, nevertheless it begets from this very circumstance a son of iniquity when conscience conceives thereby either vain glory, pride, or contempt. Yet it has a faithful servant, the eldest of its household—namely reason—which saddles ten camels for it when it subjects all sensuousness to itself. Thus this servant first approaches the spring of water when he approaches the beginning of wisdom. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” For when reason instils fear into the mind, the servant comes to the spring of water.

Accordingly, the servant seeks such a maiden as will give drink both to him and to the camels: that is, one who refreshes reason and sensuousness itself with the water [Col. 0727A] of saving wisdom, which flows from filial fear. And behold Rebekah, whose name is interpreted “patience.” For patience meets reason and refreshes it with filial fear when conscience fills the jar with the water of saving wisdom. The servant therefore leads Rebekah upon a camel. The servant leads Rebekah when patience proceeds rationally along the way of truth. But she is still upon a camel, because she does not seek vengeance against an adversary either in God or for God’s sake, but for some sensuous motive: either because she fears greater losses or because the time or place for taking vengeance is unavailable.

But when Isaac meets her at the well, where he had gone out to meditate, Rebekah descends from the camel [Col. 0727B] (Gen. XXIV), when she possesses nothing of sensuousness. This fittingly happens when in her meditations she draws the water of devotion from the well. And she is joined to Isaac when she is united with joy, when she becomes voluntary. Hence Isaac is interpreted “joy.” But for human understanding to acquire this voluntary patience through reason, it is necessary above all things first to set before the eyes of the mind Him who, because of His excessive charity whereby He loved us, safeguarded the fire of His divinity beneath the ashes of our mortality; who, for the unjust, willed unjustly to be held by the unjust; and who willed voluntarily to suffer through patience, that He might offer sacrifice to God the Father for us. Thus the Sun of righteousness, which first appeared darkened because of wrath, might afterward appear not so much burning as shining [Col. 0727C] through love.

We must therefore return to the well in which our fathers—that is, the prophets—hid the fire of divinity under a covering of mysteries; but their descendants—that is, the apostles—under those mysteries recognized thick water, that is, Christ made man (II Macc. I). Water, because of His humanity; thick, because of the richness of His charity. Having become both priest and victim, He offered a whole burnt-offering for us, and thereby reconciled the lowly with the highest things. Then He removed the veil from Moses, opened the sealed books, and lifted the stone from the mouth of the well, so that, like Jacob, He might water Rachel’s sheep—that is, satisfy the children of the Synagogue with the spiritual word—and might betroth Rachel herself to Himself, that is, unite to Himself [Col. 0727D] the Church gathered from the Jews.

But this was little for His mercy: He also satisfied the Church of the Gentiles with the word of life, when He filled with the fountain of baptism the Samaritan woman’s jar which He found at Jacob’s well (John IV). Thus, instructed in all these matters and consequently worthy of every blessing, Isaac not only dwelt by, but also dug, wells of vision. For every kind of teaching mentioned above is contained under a fourfold teaching: logic, ethics, physics, and theology. Logic is rational knowledge, ethics moral knowledge, physics natural knowledge, theology spiritual knowledge.

Isaac dug the first well and called it “Enmities” (Gen. XXVI), because when a man begins or desires to live according to reason, the world becomes hostile to him, the flesh becomes hostile, and the devil opposes him. [Col. 0728A] But if he attends to the ordering of morals, the shepherds slander this by their actions: having drunk this most clear water through teaching, they muddy it for the sheep by their works, as though with their feet. For this reason that well was called “Slander,” the shepherds saying, “The water is ours” (ibid.). When shepherds are customarily reproved and reply to the reprover, “It is not yours to reprove, for making laws is ours,” they seem to say: “The water is ours.”

The third well, which he called “Abundance” (ibid.), is natural knowledge. It abounds all the more fruitfully because it gives drink not only to human beings but even to brute animals themselves. For there is no brute animal that does not keep its own nature. The fourth well, called “Oath” or “Satiety” (ibid.), is spiritual [Col. 0728B] knowledge. It is called satiety because through it the thirsty soul is satisfied by the Word of God. It is called oath because, according to both the historical and spiritual sense, Abimelech, Ochozar, and Phicol make a covenant there (Gen. XXVI). For, according to Origen’s testimony, Phicol, whose name means “mouth of all,” signifies moral knowledge; Ochozar, who is said to mean “holding,” natural knowledge; and Abimelech, whose name means “my father is righteous,” rational knowledge.

Therefore, these make a covenant with Isaac at the well when those three kinds of knowledge agree with spiritual knowledge. For spiritual wisdom teaches whatever belongs to nature, to reason, and to morals. Therefore this well is called the well of vision. [Col. 0728C] The servant of Isaac found the water of this well breaking forth with great force, and announced the discovery to the Lord. For he first drank the water of this well and led its fountain outward. But who, do you think, is this servant? “For the hand of the Lord was with him” (Luke I). He is the one of whom his father Zacharias said: “And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Most High” (ibid.). He drank that water from the well of which it is written: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John VII).

Would you notice how he first refreshes himself with these waters, and then how he refreshes us? Let us lay down the foundation of the history: “In the days of Herod the king there was a priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia; and his wife was of the family of Aaron, named Elizabeth” (Luke I). Elizabeth, moreover, is interpreted “the oath of my God” or “the satiety of my God.” [Col. 0728D] Already in the name Elizabeth we possess the well of Oath or Satiety. But what is “the oath of my God”? “I have sworn,” says the Lord, “that I will not again bring the waters of the flood upon the earth” (Gen. IX). Again: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). And again to Abraham: “By myself have I sworn, because thou hast not spared thy son Isaac, I will make thee a great nation” (Gen. XXII). And again Zacharias says: “The oath which He swore to Abraham our father, that He would give to us.”

God had sworn all these things, but had fulfilled none of them, because water had not yet been found in the well of oath; Elizabeth was barren—that is, the oath of my God was without the fruit of accomplishment—because He Himself says in the Gospel: “My food [Col. 0729A] is to do the will of my Father who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him may have eternal life” (John IV). Since He had not yet fulfilled even this, no water had been found in the well of satiety; Elizabeth was barren, because the satiety of my God had not yet come to accomplishment. But the child entered the well of Oath—that is, Elizabeth’s womb—and rivers of living water flowed from her belly.

Would you hear how rivers of living water flowed from the womb? “Whence is this to me,” says Elizabeth, “that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke I). Behold, that child who dug the well of the womb leaped for joy because he had found the water of saving wisdom. But He also poured out upon us the fullness of this water, He who, by being born, living, [Col. 0729B] and dying, furnished us with an example of perfection and grace.

“In the days of Herod the king there was a certain priest named Zacharias” (ibid.). Zacharias is interpreted “memory of the Lord.” But what does Solomon say? “In the day of evils, do not be unmindful of good things” (Ecclus. XI). The day of evils is that of which Jeremiah says: “I have not desired the day of man, Lord, Thou knowest” (Jer. XVII). Therefore the day of evils and the day of man are the days of Herod. Herod is interpreted “glory of skin.” Therefore their days are the days of Herod who glory not in the soul but in the skin. “All the glory of the King’s children is within”; but the glory of sinners is outward. For that son of Judah who was called Her—that is, “skin”—was cursed. Nor is a sacrifice acceptable to God unless the skin has been removed from the victim.

Thus, in the days of Herod, Zacharias enters the Temple when, amid prosperity and the glory of the flesh, he remembers the righteousness of his Lord; when, despising the things of the flesh, he wills through devotion to cling to Him alone and offers Him through prayer the incense of a sweet fragrance. For whoever, when the prosperity or joy of the world smiles upon him, despises it for the Lord’s sake, he is the one who ascends with Abraham to the mountain of devotion to sacrifice Isaac. He is visited by an angel and made mute when he meditates upon that heavenly, supercelestial, and incomprehensible hierarchy of divinity. [Col. 0729C]

For the mind, accustomed to its own darkness, when it strives to contemplate the inward brightness of divinity, cannot bear the force of an unfamiliar splendour with lights that tremble and grope, and is driven back by the very rays of its first gaze. Hence it is written: “He who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. XXV). Thus Solomon also says: “I said, ‘I will become wise’; and wisdom itself withdrew farther from me” (Ecclus. VII). For this reason Moses himself, though instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, when he had directed the eyes of his mind toward the inaccessible light, confessed himself feeble of voice and ineloquent. Elijah too, at the entrance of his cave, did not see God in the great and mighty wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire; yet he recognized Him in the whisper of a gentle breeze (III Kings XIX). For indeed the Lord is rightly known there where human understanding fails. Therefore the Psalmist also says: “How beloved are Thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and fails [Col. 0730A] for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Therefore, when the mind is carried on high in contemplation, in some respects it becomes not only mute but blind; in others it becomes seeing and eloquent. For when, according to contemplation, it chooses to investigate the true in all that is and all that is not, it ascends by certain degrees of contemplation to the summit. It either contemplates mathematically the visible forms of visible things; physically, the invisible causes of visible things; symbolically, collects and joins visible forms for a demonstration of invisible things; or theologically contemplates invisible substances and the invisible natures of invisible substances.

Yet by all these modes the principal and super-principal blessed hierarchy of the divine Father may in some measure be made manifest in figurative [Col. 0730B] symbols, so that afterward the human mind, ascending by fixed degrees of contemplation to the heights, may also contemplate the heavenly mysteries anagogically by holy inspection of the divine utterance. Thus from two kinds of visions it ascends to all perfection, which has been infused by the grace of divine revelation into the minds of theologians and prophets.

One kind is that by which the truth of hidden things is shadowed forth in forms, figures, and likenesses of things; this kind of vision they call in Greek *theophanies*—that is, divine manifestations. The other is that by which the mind, by ascent and ecstasy, strives nakedly and purely, and without covering, to contemplate that heavenly most sacred principality as it is; this is called anagogical.

But in this latter kind of vision the human mind trembles and quivers so greatly that, wrapped in the darkness of its ignorance, it cannot go out toward that brightness and light of truth unless it is guided. Rather, like a blind person using a guide’s hand, it proceeds where it does not see; and it begins to melt away through the vision and visitation of the Beloved, so that it can neither conceive concerning God what it ought or wills, nor speak what it conceives, while it still strives to investigate the realm beyond the veil of the heavenly kingdom and the uncircumscribed divine light, and fails in investigating. [Col. 0730C] The astonished mind clings fast in contemplation, trembling it is stupefied, and, though speaking, it becomes utterly mute; abundance renders it poor, though poverty had made it rich. In a wonderful manner, by advancing it fails; and then it advances more when it has come to failure.

For when the ray of its mind flees before the light of that heavenly ray, which is most subtle and most piercing, the ray of the mind itself must be most subtle, piercing, and bright. For dense things do not accord with the most subtle, blunt things with the sharp, or dark things with the bright. Therefore it is necessary all the more to illuminate, direct, and sharpen it toward that light, so that it may be made fine by the finest light, as by the whisper of a gentle breeze. Yet whatever it can think concerning God and recall to memory, it should recognize as proceeding not from the subtlety of its own intellect or the perspicacity of a subtle memory, but attribute it all to the grace of God, who wills neither to be wholly known, so that faith may have merit, nor wholly hidden, lest unbelief find a place.

What is generated from memory’s knowledge of God through faith [Col. 0731A] receives the name not of Zacharias but of John—that is, the grace of God. Thus in all these things is figured the birth of John, that is, the rising of grace, without which no one comes to the Father, nor can anyone contemplate that glory which Jesus Christ our Lord promised to those who love Him; He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

“Behold, I John saw an angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God.” The authority of the seer, the usefulness of the vision, and the revealed truth of both show how credible these testimonies have become for us. For this is the water of saving wisdom [Col. 0731B] distilling from the fountains of the Saviour. This is the faithful word, poured forth from the breast of truth. This is the sunbeam which strikes the eyes of the spiritual eagle with all the brighter brilliance because it has flown higher.

According to his name, therefore, so also is his praise in the grace of the Word which was in the beginning; which he saw, which he heard, and which his hands handled concerning the Word of life; and he proclaimed it, saying: “Behold, I John,” etc. Brethren, we should not suppose that this vision was bodily, imaginative, or animal, but rather spiritual; not sensuous or fantastic, but rather intellectual. Let him therefore say: “Behold, I John saw an angel.” Observe that he had already seen the angel descending, who had a rainbow on his head—the seal [Col. 0731C] of the living God. And fittingly so: for He who descends is the same who ascends, and no one ascends except He who descends. Therefore Christ alone descends and Christ alone ascends. He descends alone, but He ascends entire; He descends alone, because the head comes to the body; He ascends entire, because He is head and body. Hence He says: “Sacrifice and offering Thou didst not desire, but Thou hast prepared a body for me” (Ps. XXX; Heb. X).

“I saw,” he says, “an angel ascending from the rising of the sun.” What is meant by the addition, “from the rising of the sun”? Is ascending always from the rising of the sun? No. For the seeds withered when the sun rose. “For the sun rose with heat and withered the grass” (Jas. I). Jechoniah son of Saphan also, with twenty-five men, worshipped toward the east, and the Lord said to the prophet: [Col. 0731D] “Surely thou hast seen, son of man, the abominations which these do” (Ezek. VIII). Were those who worshipped in that manner ascending from the rising of the sun? Therefore ascending is not always from the rising of the sun, and yet without the rising of the sun there is no ascending.

Before the rising of the sun there was night, in which the beasts of the forest, the lion cubs, roamed. But the sun rose, they gathered together, and man was able to go out to his work, advance by working, and by advancing ascend from virtue to virtue. Learn, then, a parable from the sun’s rising. For just as the sun traverses the zodiac, circles the firmament, and illumines the sphere of the macrocosm, so in the microcosm the Sun of righteousness raises the affection of the mind, kindles the heart toward the firmament of virtue, and illumines the sphere of thoughts.

For man is called a microcosm—that is, a lesser world—because of the likeness he bears to the macrocosm, that is, the greater world. Hence in the Gospel man is called “world,” in the words: “The world knew Him not” (John I). Thus the first man was called Adam, that by the name itself he might know that he was a microcosm. For the macrocosm has four regions: east, west, north, and south. These four are indicated by his name. For the name is composed from four letters: *anatole*, which means east; *dysis* or *delta*, west; *arctos*, north; and *mesēmbrion*, south. Hence the whole succession of his progeny seems able to derive an explanation from this name, so that they ought rightly to be called not merely sons of Adam, but all of them Adams. [Col. 0732A]

For all are formed in the wombs of their mothers in the lineaments of their members during the forty-six days from the day of conception, so that, formation having been fully completed on the forty-sixth day, spirit is infused into the living soul. The letters of that name represent the number of this formation. For it is made up of α, δ, α, μ: α signifies 1, δ 4, again α 1, and μ 40. If you join these together, you complete both the name Adam and the fullness of human formation. Hence the Saviour foretold that the Temple built by the Jews in forty-six years would be destroyed (John II), in order that through this the perfect man might be shown. For if the first perfect number, six, multiplies the aforesaid number, it completes the number of days from the day of his conception to the day of his birth: namely, nine months and six days; for six times forty-six makes two hundred and seventy-six.

You will find precisely this number of days if they are counted from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which He is believed to have been conceived by the Holy Spirit, to the eighth day before the Kalends of January. Just as the greater world is said to have a sphere, so the lesser world has a little sphere. Hence Moses commanded that a little sphere be placed on the tabernacle’s lampstand among bowls and lilies (Exod. XV), so that whoever has the light of faith in the Church of God must, together with the lily of purity and the teaching of wisdom, turn over in thought the course of his life.

For Solomon says: “The sun rises and sets, returns to its place, circles [Col. 0732D] through the south, and turns toward the north” (Ecclus. I). Thus the sun rises when the Sun of righteousness illumines the mind through faith, but it sets when, after faith, the mind slips into sin. The sun rises when He visits a man in the early morning, but it sets when He suddenly tests him. Again, it circles through the south when through knowledge He restores him to devotion; it turns back toward the north when, through the mind’s consent, he bends toward temptation. It circles through the south when the fire burns in meditation; it turns toward the north when charity grows cold through an unjust suggestion.

Already, unless I am mistaken, the two colures of the spiritual little sphere appear with their distinctions. A *colure* is said to derive from *colon*, meaning “limb,” and *urus*, meaning “wild ox.” One is the colure of ascent, *anabibazōn*, that is, “ascending upward”; the other of descent, *katabibazōn*, that is, “hidden.” The first distinction of the former is that the sun rises; the first of the latter that the sun sets. The second of the former is that it circles through the south; the second of the latter that it turns toward the north.

But what do these things contribute to the mind? It rises so that you may hope; it sets so that you may grieve; it circles through the south so that you may love; it turns toward the north so that you may fear. You now discern five parallels joined to the two colures. If, therefore, when persecution arises, you fear in such a way that you neither feel devotion present nor believe it will be present, you will fall into worldly fear. But if, because of the setting of guilt or punishment, touched inwardly by sorrow of heart, you reflect upon your years in the bitterness of your soul, yet in such a way that sorrow is relieved neither by the consolation of hope nor by the joy of devotion, you will grieve servilely, [Col. 0733B] and grief will produce servile fear; and if you then do good, you will do it servilely.

But if you rejoice in fervour in such a way that you neither grieve over past things nor fear future temptations, you must become proud, because such joy will produce presumption in you. But if through the light of faith the Sun of righteousness rises for you, so that you grieve over past sins and fear the recurrence of temptation, the beginning of wisdom—initial fear of the Lord—will immediately come to you. If, however, you rejoice in the fervour of charity, yet always grieve that you are a sinner, so that you are not secure because sin has been forgiven but always fear, filial fear will immediately come to you: the chaste fear which remains for ever and ever.

Thus from this you can distinguish the regions of the spiritual little sphere, like the five zones of the greater sphere, three uninhabitable and two inhabitable. Of the uninhabitable, two are cold and one is torrid. For what is colder than worldly fear, by which divine charity is driven away? Fear is likewise cold when charity is absent from it. But disordered fervour is torrid, against which the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “He ordered charity within me” (Cant. II). Therefore these regions are uninhabitable for every righteous person. The temperate region is initial fear, with which charity begins. Filial fear is also temperate, and charity perfects it. The names of the zones themselves seem to support our assertion.

We call fear worldly when, upon the arrival of fear of persecution, we do not dare to do good. [Col. 0733C] Hence it is aptly called Arctic. For *Arctic* is named from *arctos*, that is, from the north, where the north wind rises. Thus, because we do not dare to do good, iniquity abounds and charity grows cold. Servile fear, however, is when we do good solely from fear of punishment, not from love; nor is charity possessed in this. Yet doing good from fear and failing to do good from fear are opposites. Therefore, if worldly fear is rightly called Arctic, servile fear is rightly called Antarctic.

Again, one who becomes proud because of his fervour is first burdensome to others and finally to himself, when he despises others as it were and is himself despised. And when without discernment he undertakes the burden of labour, he makes himself a burden to others. Because a burden is carried on the shoulders, this zone is not improperly called the shoulder-zone (*humerinus*) from its producing cause. But because through initial fear charity is gradually kindled and rises, it is rightly called the summer tropic (*therinos tropicos*). For philosophers call that circle the summer tropic in which the sun, from the lower sign, namely Capricorn, grows warmer and rises ever more. Since it has nowhere lower to descend, it is called *tropic*, that is, “turning.” And because summer grows hotter and hotter through such an ascent, it is called from *theros*, meaning “summer.” [Col. 0734A]

And because filial fear stands at the higher degree of virtues—for it differs in nothing from charity—it is rightly called the winter tropic (*chimerinos tropicos*). For that circle is called the winter tropic in which the sun, from the higher sign, namely Cancer, turns through the wintry zone toward Capricorn. Since it cannot rise higher, it is called tropic. And because it returns toward winter, it is rightly called wintery, *chimerinos*. Nothing, then, is higher than filial fear, which is proved perfect when a man always humbles himself more and more and judges himself, as it were, a bad and unworthy labourer, according to the saying: “When you have done all these things, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke XVII). And again: “The greater thou art, humble thyself in all things” (Ecclus. III).

Having gathered and considered all these things together, we must consider how the sun ascends the circle of the solar sphere through twelve degrees. This is the crown of twelve stars of which John says: “A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, [Col. 0734C] and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars” (Apoc. XII). A sign—that is, the figure of a great reality—appeared in heaven, that is, in the heavenly mind, when the woman, that is, the soul, is protected and the affection rules over every defect; and upon her head, that is, in her mind, is a crown, that is, the perfection of twelve stars, which are called twelve signs.

For the things that are truly stars are called signs because they are one thing and signify another. For one should not believe that this actual sun, as it completes its circuit, enters horned goats, fishes, rams, or anything of that sort. Rather, in these things one thing is said and another is signified. For what is signified in Capricorn, which is called a horned goat, except the stench of sin? Its horns are those of which it is said: “I will break all the horns [Col. 0734D] of sinners” (Ps. LXXIV). Hence John is commanded to write to the angel of Pergamum—that is, “scattering horns.”

Therefore the sun enters Capricorn when knowledge of truth begins to possess a mind made foul by sin; when the mind begins to know itself defiled by sin, because the first virtue is *Gnōthi seauton* [Γνῶθι σεαυτόν], that is, “know thyself.” After this it rises into Aquarius, when, reflecting upon its years in the bitterness of its soul, it washes its bed each night with tears, so that its eyes may be pools in Heshbon and its face like a cloud pouring forth rains of tears. After this it rises into Pisces, when among the waters of tears it lifts itself by the little wings of hope and protects itself with the scales of patience, lest either the multitude of its crimes or the greatness of its griefs sink it into the deep through impatience, that is, into despair.

From there it rises into Aries, so that now, governing itself through reason, it may show itself to possess the serpent’s shrewdness in its horns and the sheep’s simplicity in its fleece, as it is written: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X). Then it rises into Taurus, when by this simple shrewdness or shrewd simplicity it offers itself as a sacrifice to God for an odour of sweetness, either outwardly by mortification of the flesh or inwardly through a contrite spirit. For the bull bears the type of the sacrifice of a contrite spirit, as in the Gospel: “My oxen and my fatlings are slain” (Matt. XXII), that is, those who pleased me either through bodily martyrdom or through the devotion of the mind. [Col. 0735A]

After this it rises into Gemini, the sign of twofold charity. Here it should be noted that some people, just as they wish to be indulged in pleasures themselves, so wish the same for others. Others, just as they are strict with themselves through abstinence, are strict with others also. Others again spare themselves by living luxuriously and are harsh with those subject to them. There are also those who are hard and strict with themselves through mortification of the flesh and yet, kindled by the ardour of charity, are benevolent toward the needs of their neighbours.

In these, therefore, the emblem of twofold charity—toward God and toward neighbour—shines forth: they burn inwardly through devotion and shine outwardly through compassion. Thus the Sun of righteousness ought to enter Taurus through suffering, so that it may pass into Gemini through compassion. Then [Col. 0735C] it enters Cancer, where the summer tropic occurs, namely the summer solstice, at which the sun cannot ascend higher. By this, as has been said, filial fear is signified, when that which is the beginning of wisdom gives place—namely initial fear, signified by the winter tropic, that is, the winter solstice. This happens when the sun enters Capricorn and from the opposite position looks toward the summer solstice, which occurs when the sun enters Cancer, the sign of humility. Hence:

> Cancer, withdrawing backward, bears its footsteps curved behind.

For humility is the guardian of all virtues. Since the greater a man is, the more he ought to humble himself in all things, so that, when he has done everything, he may say: “I am an unprofitable servant.” And the Prophet says: “I was reduced to nothing and did not know it; I became as a beast before Thee, and I am always with Thee” (Ps. LXXII). But because excessive humility commonly so casts down the simple that they fail through excessive self-abasement, a man ought to be humble in such a way that he acts manfully and his heart is strengthened; he should be like Cancer in humility and like the Lion in magnanimity. Humility, therefore, should be strengthened by fortitude, and fortitude strengthened by humility. The strength of action guards the outer person; humility preserves the inner person from every corruption of vices.

As a sign of incorruption the sun enters Virgo; under that sign it reaps with joy, from the seed of humility, the fruit of good action. But since it is no lesser virtue to preserve what has been gained than to seek it—especially since nothing in the world is stable, but all things change beneath the sun—it is necessary for the mind to set itself in the upright Balance, [Col. 0736A] and make, as it were, a spiritual equinox of the mind; it must know how to make days equal to nights and nights to days. This fittingly happens when neither adversity depresses the mind beyond due measure nor prosperity exalts it too high. This is commonly effected in two ways: by fear and by love.

If fear produces it—namely initial fear, which perfect charity casts out—the equinox takes place, but it is the vernal equinox, which occurs under Aries, because the person is watchful and humble under fear. For he defends himself with horns through watchfulness and is warmed with sheep’s fleece through humility. But if love produces it, the equinox is autumnal; and, established in the Balance of uprightness, he walks by the more excellent way of charity, lest he turn aside to the right hand or to the left.

[Col. 0736B] For he does not turn aside to the left if, reflecting on his last things, he fears an evil report and the end. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. Terrible will be the day of darkness and gloom, when the sun shall be like a sackcloth of hair, and the Scorpion’s tail shall be darkened; when he who, like a lamb before its shearer, was silent, shall roar like a lion at the last judgment, and shall hiss like a serpent at the flies of Egypt, reproving in wrath and saying: “You did these things, and I kept silence” (Ps. 49 [50]). And: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). Therefore it is written: “My son, remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7).

Then also the sun of righteousness, entering Sagittarius from the tail of Scorpius and [Col. 0736C] sending forth the sharp arrows of the Mighty One, will render to each according to his merits: wounding the enemy unto eternal death, and the friend unto love, when love in the blessed soul will then be as strong as death, so that it may say: “I am wounded by love.” Then the sun will enter Sagittarius when it bears in its hand the rainbow which it now has upon its head: it will manifest in deed the judgment hidden in foreknowledge.

For this is the heavenly sphere which opens to us the Galaxy—that is, the Milky Way, alike white and sweet. Therefore, having set the gnomon of reason beneath such circles over nothingness, let the wise and understanding man hang the earth of his own body upon nothingness, saying with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). [Col. 0736D] “When shall my pitcher be broken at the fountain? When shall the wheel be crushed at the cistern?” (Eccles. 12). When shall dust return to dust? When shall rest come after labour, freedom after servitude? May the grace of God the Father grant us these things, brothers, and add them to us through our Lord Jesus Christ.

## SERMON XXV. ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

“John was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5): burning in devotion, shining in deed; burning in words, shining in examples; burning for himself, shining for his neighbours. He was not the light, but a lamp—and this because of the lamp’s small measure of light. Hence it is written: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3): because of weakness, since he was a mere man; because of obscurity, [Col. 0737A] since he hid the treasure of light in an earthen vessel.

This is the lamp which the woman in the Gospel lit and turned the house upside down in order to find the tenth drachma. The woman, indeed, is the wisdom of the Father. She lit this lamp in the very womb of his mother, in order to find the tenth drachma that had been lost—that is, in order to make up, from humankind, the dignity lost by the fallen angels. For when nine orders were created, enough fell from each order to make a tenth order; and their places are to be filled by human beings. Therefore the nine orders of angels are compared to nine drachmas, while the human race is compared to the tenth drachma. For its sake she also overturned the house, namely the Synagogue, of which it was said: “My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you [Col. 0737B] have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. 21).

For it is written: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16). She overturned it so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved. Therefore, since the lamp of which it is written, “You have the prophetic word, to which you do well to give heed as to a burning lamp in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1), had now been extinguished, the Lord lit this lamp: lit in the womb, displayed in the wilderness, trimmed at the Jordan, extinguished in prison.

Thus it is rightly said: “John was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5). A lamp is burning but not shining when one benefits oneself but not others. A lamp is shining but not burning when one benefits others but not oneself. A lamp is neither burning nor shining, but [Col. 0737C] extinguished, when one occupies the place of a prelate yet benefits neither oneself nor others. But John was a burning and shining lamp, benefiting both himself and others.

For this reason his sublimity is commended in many ways. First, by Christ’s testimony: that among those born of women there had not arisen one greater than John the Baptist (Matt. 11). Second, because wherever mention of John occurs in the Gospel, he is commended by Christ. Therefore one who is praised by God does not beg for the support of human praise, since he can say: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord” (Ps. 33 [34]). Third, because his birth was announced by the archangel Gabriel and within the Holy of Holies. Fourth, because he leapt in the womb when the Lord’s mother came, and Elizabeth prophesied: [Col. 0737D] “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as soon as the sound of your greeting came into my ears, the child leapt for joy in my womb” (Luke 1). Thus, sanctified in the womb, he was holy before he was born.

Fifth, because whatever holiness God bestowed upon others in portions, he fused in its entirety into John. For he was a prophet—indeed, more than a prophet—because the one of whom he had prophesied, saying, “One stronger than I comes after me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loosen” (Mark 1), he pointed out with his finger and said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). He was also an apostle, as it is written: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.” *Apostle* means “one sent.” He was likewise a martyr, whom Herod [Col. 0738A] ordered to be beheaded in prison. He was also a confessor, because he confessed and did not deny; and he confessed: “I am not the Christ” (ibid.). Nor did he lack the honour of virginity, since he was not defiled with women, but followed the Lamb wherever he went. He was also a hermit, who prepared the way of the Lord in the wilderness.

Thus he was a lamp which, like another pillar of fire, provided light to those travelling through the desert. The miracle of his conception shines; the joy of his birth shines; holiness in his manner of life, humility in exaltation, truth in preaching, zeal in correction, constancy in suffering, all shine. Thus he shone by the merit of his life, he shone by word, he shone by example. He gave us light in his entrance, in his progress, and in his departure. His entrance [Col. 0738B] illumines our first and initial works; his progress, our middle and advancing works; his departure, our final and consummated works. In his entrance operative grace is commended; in his progress, cooperating grace; in his departure, consummating grace. For *John* means “grace.”

John’s birth—that is, his entrance into the world—therefore represents for us the rising of grace. Many privileges commend this rising of grace to us: namely, the time of his birth, the names of both parents, nobility of lineage, holiness of life, and dignity of office. Luke records the time of his birth where he says: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judaea” (Luke 1). As light to the blind, medicine to the sick, freedom to slaves, and rest to the weary, so welcome was the rising of grace in the days of Herod.

Gentleness had already ceased to reign in Judaea—the gentleness of David, the wisdom of Solomon, the piety of Hezekiah, the simplicity of Josiah—and Herod’s cruelty reigned. For at the coming of the Holy of Holies, anointing had already ceased; and the children of Israel had begun to sit without king, without prince, and without teraphim. The glory of the king’s daughter was not within, because the glory of skin now reigned: for this is the meaning of *Herod*. Judaea’s glory lay in outward things, while within it was full of shame. But in evil days the lily grew among thorns, and the apple-tree among the trees of the forest.

“There was a certain priest named Zacharias” (Luke 1). *Zacharias* means “the Lord’s remembrance.” “In the days of evils,” says the wise man, “do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclus. 2). In the days of Herod, do not forget your [Col. 0738D] Creator. “I have not desired the day of man,” says Jeremiah (Jer. 17). What is the day of man? The prosperity of the world. “Let that day,” says Job, “be turned into darkness; let it not be counted among the days of the year” (Job 3). But worldly prosperity is the glory of skin. Therefore the day of man is Herod’s day. Yet Zacharias was in Herod’s days. This is the first rising of grace: when remembrance of God occurs amid worldly prosperities and the pleasures of sin.

But such remembrance should not be brief or passing; it should be constant and abiding, until the soul is satisfied in its thoughts by the sweetness of good thoughts concerning creation or re-creation, as by richer foods. Thus it was not just any Zacharias, but one whose wife was Elizabeth. Zacharias means “the Lord’s remembrance,” while Elizabeth means “the satisfaction of my God.” [Col. 0739A] Yet sometimes gifts are from the Spirit and in the Spirit; sometimes, however, they are from the Spirit but not in the Spirit. For to some the Spirit is given both personally and through gifts, as to those living chastely and religiously in cloisters. But scholars who sin mortally have gifts from the Spirit, though not in the Holy Spirit personally inspiring them: they have remembrance of God, but not in God or for God, but so that people may call them Rabbi.

For this reason such remembrance must be directed solely by the regard of God, so that Zacharias and Elizabeth may both be righteous before God and without reproach. Some are without reproach in their neighbours’ eyes but are not righteous before God. Others devote themselves to works of righteousness and are without reproach, but not before God, because they occupy themselves in such matters for human favour. Others are righteous before God but are not without the reproach of the envious, because one kind of righteousness is tainted, such as that of the Sadducees—hence *Sadducees* means “the righteous”; another is insufficient, such as that of the Scribes and Pharisees. Thus it is said: “Unless your righteousness shall abound more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

Another righteousness is sufficient in a qualified sense, that is, for a particular time. Thus Adam and Eve were made righteous insofar as was suitable to that time: innocent, yet bearing no sign of righteousness. Or the Mosaic law is called sufficient for the time in which it was given. For it was given to beginners and neophytes, for whom that law sufficed temporarily, though it does not suffice for the perfect. [Col. 0739C] “For the law brought nothing to perfection.” Or righteousness is called sufficient in relation to that of which it was said: “Noah was a righteous man in his generations” (Gen. 6). Or, simply, natural righteousness is sufficient: namely, “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4), and “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7). But consummating righteousness is evangelical righteousness, of which it is said: “Whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5). Yet this is commonly endured neither without reproach nor without murmuring.

Therefore perfect righteousness before God and without reproach is that which renders to each what is due. This is fittingly done when religion renders God his due; filial devotion, one’s parents theirs; innocence, those beneath one; friendship, equals; reverence, superiors; concord, neighbours; and mercy, the needy. Thus these two were righteous before God and without reproach.

Or Zacharias is called righteous and without reproach when remembrance of God contains no admixture of unbelief, so that it is righteous; nor hatred or rancour toward one’s neighbour, so that it is without reproach—so that it is directed to God, whether it arises from God or not. For there are some movements from God but not toward God, as when we blaspheme. Some are toward God but not from God, when we have compassion on our neighbours. Some are neither from God nor toward God, when we are moved to adultery. Some are from God and toward God, when we love him perfectly. This is righteousness before God and without reproach.

Therefore Zacharias entered the temple at the hour of incense (Luke 1). Incense signifies [Col. 0740A] prayer. Thus David says: “Let my prayer be set before you as incense” (Ps. 140 [141]). The hour of incense, therefore, is the hour of prayer. But what is the hour of prayer, when Tobias says, “Bless God at every time” (Tob. 4), and the Psalmist says, “I will bless the Lord at every time” (Ps. 33 [34])?

It should therefore be noted that we are bound to God by a threefold service: obligatory, devout, and instituted. Obligatory service is that of *latria*, worship due to God; devout service is that of works of mercy; instituted service arises from human ordinance. For it has been instituted that at the canonical hours we praise God more than at other times; hence, by instituted service we are more bound to serve at one hour than another. But by obligatory or devout service, no one is more bound to serve at one hour than at another.

There are eight instituted hours, which Ezra first established; but the Lord later confirmed the same number by his deeds. Of such hours the Psalmist says: “Seven times in the day I have given praise to you” (Ps. 118 [119]), and: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (ibid.). This sacred number is fulfilled if at [matins], prime, terce, sext, none, vespers, compline, and midnight we rise to give thanks to God for the judgments of his righteousness.

At prime, Christ was handed over to Pilate by the Jews, already spat upon, mocked, struck with blows, bound, and filled with insults. At this hour also he rose from the dead, appeared to Mary Magdalene, and was seen on the shore by the seven disciples, to whom he said: “Children, have you anything to eat?” (John 21). At the third hour he was crowned with thorns, crucified by the tongues of the Jews, and the Holy Spirit was given to the disciples on the day of Pentecost. At the sixth hour he was fixed to the cross with nails, and at that same hour ascended before the disciples’ eyes. At the ninth hour he gave up his spirit; pierced with a lance, he sent forth from his side two sacraments for us: the water of baptism and the blood of redemption.

At vespers he was taken down from the cross; at that same hour he gave his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood. At the same hour he was recognized in the breaking of bread by the two disciples going to Emmaus. At compline, after Judas the betrayer had gone out to the Jews, Jesus began to fear and be distressed; being in agony, he prayed more earnestly and, with his body prostrate, sweated drops of blood.
