At midnight, when the Lord was born, shepherds keeping the watches of the night over their flock heard angels crying: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2). At this hour also the cry will be made: “Behold, the bridegroom comes” (Matt. 25). At the same hour Samson broke the gates of the Philistines with their bars, as a sign of Christ, who then opened for us the gates of hell. Hence we sing: “Let them confess the mercies of the Lord, and his wonders to the children of men, for he has broken the gates of bronze and shattered the bars of iron.”

These are the hours of incense. Zacharias therefore enters the temple at the hour of incense when remembrance of God enters the heart so that we may praise God. And this satisfaction of the remembrance of God begets grace that cleanses filth and prepares the Lord’s ways in the wilderness of this world, since Elizabeth bore a great man, [Col. 0741A] John the Baptist, the forerunner of the Lord.

## SERMON XXVI. ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

“When you have departed from me today, you will find two men beside Rachel’s tomb in the territory of Benjamin at noon, leaping over great pits; and they will say to you: ‘The asses have been found’” (1 Sam. 10).

See, beloved, why Caleb’s daughter sighed; how justly she complained of the barrenness of Debir, which was also called Kiriath-sepher; and why she wished to have joined to herself the upper and lower springs (Judg. 1). For the divine discourse is found very barren if one attends to the surface of the letter. This is what the barrenness of Debir signifies; *Debir* means “eloquence,” and it was also called Kiriath-sepher, that is, “city of letters.” [Col. 0741B] Therefore the Psalmist says: “Because I have not known learning”—that is, because I have not clung to the letter—“I will enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 70 [71]).

It is necessary, then, that the upper and lower spring be joined to it: namely, that the moisture of spiritual grace should water the affections, by which the mind is moved to love God, as toward the upper spring, and to love one’s neighbour, as toward the lower. For what does it matter to us through what negligence the asses of Kish were lost, through what care they were sought, or with what benefit they were found? Debir is plainly barren in this respect unless both springs are joined to it.

It should therefore be noted that in sacred discourse asses signify, allegorically, the simple and unlearned; tropologically, movements of the soul, as it is written: “The oxen were ploughing, and the asses were feeding beside them” (Job 1). “The asses,” says Gregory [Note: [Col. 0741D] *Commentary on Job*], “feed beside the oxen when the simple are nourished by the understanding of the prudent.”

But asses often perish through the negligence of shepherds, while some, wishing to avoid the labours, enmities, or hatreds of their subjects, under the appearance of freedom permit them, like wild asses, to go freely through the precipices of vices. How evil this is, the negligence of the priest Eli shows us. God rejected his tabernacle because he was lax and indulgent toward his subjects.

Others, putting on savagery under the appearance of severity, oppress their subjects with discipline, hunger, and labours, not merely to press them down but to crush them. Kish, whose asses were lost, represents these persons. For *Kish* means “hard”; and by his very name is signified the harshness of those who impose heavy and unbearable burdens upon their subjects. They resemble not the ministers of Christ but the king of Egypt, who afflicted the children of Israel with labour and did not give them straw. What does it mean that they gave no straw? They did not apply moderation to burdens. For straw signifies moderation, as in: “They themselves were plastering the wall with mud without straw,” that is, without moderation (Ezek. 13). Hence it follows: “Say to those who plaster the wall without moderation that it shall fall” (ibid.).

Emmanuel did not, no, did not feed on cheese and gall, but on butter and honey, in order that he might know to reject evil [Col. 0742A] and choose good. For in order to discern evil from good, and good from evil, he used honey and butter, not gall and cheese. And what is Emmanuel’s food? He himself explains it in the Gospel, where he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). Therefore, in the judgments by which he distinguishes the good from the evil, he uses honey of sweetness, the moisture of compassion, and the richness of love. For butter is naturally rich and moist. These are the means used by the wisdom of God the Father, namely Emmanuel, to whom the Father gave all judgment: so that he might always be inclined to distributive and remissive judgments, not punitive ones—toward love, compassion, and sweetness; not toward the gall of bitterness, the dryness of inhumanity, or the hardness of cruelty, like those persons who in their judgments are always found bitter, inhuman, [Col. 0742B] and hard, as though using gall, which is bitter, and cheese, which is hard and dry, rather than honey, which is sweet, and butter, which is moist and rich.

Therefore, when they afflict subjects with heavy burdens—subjects who, as God’s beasts of burden, willingly bow themselves to receive burdens—do they not act like the Chaldeans who formed three companies to carry off blessed Job’s camels or to kindle the furnace for the children? *Chaldeans* means “fierce”; and when by their fierceness they oppress their subjects, they show themselves persecutors not of their own household but of God. As Job signifies Christ, so the Chaldeans signify his persecutors. And when the Herodians, Sadducees, and Pharisees gathered together for Christ’s passion, the Chaldeans formed, as it were, three companies.

Thus, when these persons press their subjects with burdens, they become Herodians in cruelty, Sadducees in false righteousness, and Pharisees in simulated religion; but in all things they are Chaldeans. Or rather, when with the zeal of bitterness they burn the souls of their subjects by their cruelty, they kindle the furnace for the children as Chaldeans did—the children, I mean, of whom it was said: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isa. 8).

These men, deaf hearers of the words of the apostle Peter, prefer to lord it over the clergy rather than become an example to the clergy (1 Pet. 5). They do not consider that one is our master and that we are all brothers. And that they may learn humility, let them consider the place which they prefigure, whether in Noah’s ark or in Moses’ tabernacle; for in both the Church of God was prefigured.

Scripture says that in the ark were made upper rooms and three stories (Gen. 6), that is, divisions which another translation calls two-storeyed and three-storeyed: namely, five chambers. The first was called the dung-chamber; the second, the store-chamber; the third, that of untamed animals; the fourth, that of tame animals; the fifth, that of human beings and birds. In the first is figured the order of those who have care of souls: while they receive confessions, those confessing discharge among them sins as though the dregs of filth. The second represents the order of teachers, who prepare the spices of salvation from the sayings of Scripture. The third represents those who are in God’s Church in name, [Col. 0743A] not in spiritual power; in number, not in merit; from whom the threshing floor cannot be cleansed until it is winnowed. The fourth represents gentle and obedient subjects; the fifth, rational and contemplative human beings.

Moses’ tabernacle was also covered with four coverings: first, coverings of goat’s hair or haircloth; second, skins of rams dyed red; third, twice-dyed scarlet; fourth, likewise skins of blue rams. In these are figured those who protect the Church of God. In the first are prelates, exposed to winds and rains; in the second, active persons, who, afflicted by labours, are reddened like rams’ skins; in the third, charitable persons, who, even if unable to labour, bestow benefits from their own resources for God’s honour and their neighbour’s benefit; in the fourth, contemplatives, who, like heaven and like blue skins, contemplate heavenly things.

Behold: those of whom we speak are compared to dung-chambers and haircloth coverings. Whence, then, comes such arrogant pride in them, if their place in the Church is so lowly? How, then, do they wish to lord it over the clergy, when Christ alone is our master and we are all brothers? Or how do those who wish to remove the speck from their brothers’ eyes fail to cast the beam out of their own?

For, as Augustine says, the priest to whom every sinner is brought and before whom every infirmity is set must not himself be liable to judgment for any of the things which he is ready to judge in another. For one who judges another while himself liable to judgment condemns himself. Let him therefore know himself, and cleanse in himself what he sees others bring before him. Let him beware of, and cast away from himself, whatever he finds harmful in others. Let him consider that whoever is without sin should be the first to cast a stone at the woman (John 8). For Christ delivered the sinful woman because there was no one who could justly cast a stone at her.

But now let us hear what a good subject merits under such a prelate. For it follows:

“But Saul had a son, chosen and good, who stood taller than all others from the shoulders upward; nor was there a better man than he among the children of Israel” (1 Sam. 9). It is not praiseworthy to live well when no one urges one to live badly; rather, it is glorious not to consent to one who urges evil, and still more glorious to resist temptation than to be unable to be tempted. For who deserved greater merit: Peter, [Col. 0743D] who, girded with his tunic, came to Christ over the sea, or those who came by boat? What does the swelling of the sea signify except the swelling of temptation? And what is it to come to Christ over the sea except, in coming to Christ, to tread upon the swells of temptation? And what is it to come by boat except to approach Christ without the hardship of temptation—indeed, with the remedy of consolation?

Therefore, since a prelate’s austerity is to a good subject nothing other than a file to iron, a furnace to gold, a flail to grain, and a winepress to wine, a subject is proved praiseworthy in proportion as he patiently endures the blows by whose beating virtue is purified. Kish’s son indicates such persons; and thus he is called good and chosen. Rightly, therefore, is care of the lost asses—or, better said, souls—committed to him, because [Col. 0744A] a person worthy of pre-eminence is one who through patience has learned to suffer with the sufferings of subjects, and who is watchfully concerned to seek what was lost, to restore what was broken, to support what was weak, and to guard what was strong and fat.

For concern in seeking souls is commended when it is said: “And he sought them through the mountains of Ephraim” (1 Sam. 9). A prelate ought to be concerned with the care of souls in two ways: by example and by teaching. For he must offer his subjects an example of labour, chastise his body and reduce it to servitude, lest, after preaching to others, idleness condemn him. The mountains of Ephraim signify the heaviness of labour in the fruitful work of good action. For *Ephraim* is interpreted “fruitful.”

But since the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us, he must seek, as though passing through the mountains of Ephraim, until he comes to the land of Salisha. For earth alone is a solid element, and solidity is fittingly signified by earth. *Salisha* means “three-year-old.” The land of Salisha, therefore, is a three-year land, of which Isaiah speaks when he says: “Eat what you find this year; in the second year, what grows of itself; in the third, sow and plant vineyards; eat and drink” (Isa. 37). It should therefore be understood that from the time we are born, we find natural gifts bestowed upon us by God. We are born with them and cannot exist without them. To eat in the first year what we find is to use worthily our natural gifts: memory, [Col. 0744C] intelligence, reason, and free choice.

Gratuitous gifts, however, grow of themselves—of themselves, because no preceding merits exist; otherwise they would not be gratuitous, that is, freely given. To eat in the second year what grows of itself is to use gratuitous gifts worthily. Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 6). But in the third year we must sow and eat: joining free choice to gratuitous gifts, we must freely perform what is good according to the grace bestowed upon us by God.

Therefore one who knows how to use natural and gratuitous gifts in this way, so as to merit worthily by their use [Col. 0744D] and exercise, instructs simple subjects by examples, or restrains foolish movements within himself. Yet in all that he does, let not his left hand know what his right hand does, so that he acts not for temporal and perishable things but for heavenly and eternal things.

Let this traveller pass from the land of Salisha through the land of Jemini. For *Jemini* means “right hand.” Therefore let him pass through the land of Jemini, so that he may always seek nothing of the left hand, but what belongs to the right. But since fear of persecutions draws many back from a good purpose and pulls them toward unlawful things, he must fortify himself in this respect. He must not recoil from a good purpose through fear of persecution, but must also pass through the land of Salim in seeking out simple movements. For *Salim* means “fox”; persecutors are signified by foxes. Hence Samson made foxes, with burning torches, run through [Col. 0745A] the fields of the Philistines (Judg. 15), because Christ sometimes permits cruel persecutors to destroy the goods of the ungodly.

Let him therefore be watchful and provident in all things, that he may arrive at the land of Suph. For *Suph* means “watchtower.” There is a threefold watchtower: that of preaching, of which it is said, “I have made you a watchman over the children of Israel” (Ezek. 3); that of contemplation, of which it is said, “Set a table for yourself, and contemplate upon the watchtower” (Isa. 21); and that of circumspection, of which it is said, “Set up for yourself a watchtower, place bitterness before yourself, and direct your heart into straight ways” (Jer. 31). Therefore let him approach the watchtower of circumspection—that is, the land of Suph. For it is written: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4).

For Ish-bosheth [Col. 0745B] is recorded to have been killed by an unexpected death; Scripture testifies that he had a female doorkeeper, not a male doorkeeper. While this female doorkeeper, cleansing wheat, fell asleep, his enemies secretly entered, taking ears of wheat, and struck him in the groin. The female doorkeeper cleanses wheat when the mind separates virtues from vices. If she falls asleep through negligence, she opens a way for malignant spirits to kill the soul. Once entered, they carry off the ears, because they remove the shoots of good thoughts; and they strike in the groin, because through carnal pleasure they kill the strength of the heart.

Whence Ish-bosheth is called “a man of confusion,” because anyone not fortified by manly vigilance is worthy of every confusion. Let him direct the perseverance of his solicitude and the final end of his work toward Him who is the end of those who work well, without whom he can do nothing, and through whom he can accomplish even impossible things. He promises those who ask and seek, saying: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find” (Luke 11). Therefore let God be the ultimate object of his petition. Thus we read of this chosen son of Kish that he eventually came to Samuel at Ramah. For Samuel is interpreted “God is my petition.” He therefore comes to God, who ought to be the end of all our petition, at Ramah, when, inflamed with heavenly desire, he runs in the way of His commandments. For Ramah is interpreted “the high place.” And what is higher than heaven? Samuel is found at Ramah, because through just petitions to God one arrives at Him, in this life by merit and after this life by reward. Hence Samuel says: “When you depart from me today,” etc. [Col. 0745D] He goes wrongly who does not go forth from God, whom the way of righteousness does not instruct, whom it does not lead into truth. But he goes forth from God who runs in the way of His commandments, whom He leads by straight paths and finally brings through the way of charity.

“When you depart,” he says, “from me today, you will find two men” (1 Kings 10). For what purpose will you find them? That they may offer you guidance if you desire to go from God and are in darkness. If you are blind and do not know where to go, yet desire to go, Paul can offer you guidance on the way, he who was caught up to the third heaven. Peter too will open for you the entrance to the kingdom of heaven, he who received the keys alike for opening and shutting. And who, contending in the contest, would not now run toward the prize of the heavenly calling, when he finds one man changed from a persecutor [Col. 0746A] into a vessel of election, and another, after denying at the voice of a serving-girl, made chief in apostolic rank?

Scripture says: “You will find two men.” Two, because of the mystery of the twofold charity; men, because by teaching they are men of truth, and by example men of virtue. For *vir* (“man”) is said to derive from *veritas* (“truth”) or *virtus* (“virtue”). You will indeed find such men on the way. But what will they be like in their homeland? “You will find them beside Rachel’s tomb.”

Observe that the Church is one, general and universal, but divided into three particular states: the Church militant, the Church awaiting, and the Church triumphant. The first is figured by the earthen altar, concerning which it was said: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20). An altar of earth is made for the Lord when the corruptible, earthly Church serves God. Hence the priest prays in the Canon: “We humbly beseech you, almighty God, command that these things be carried by the hands of your holy angels to your high altar, so that all who receive from this participation at the altar,” etc. [Col. 0746B] For the priest prays that, through the power of the sacrament, the whole Church militant and triumphant together may be united into the one body of Christ: that is, that the Church militant, which is represented in the present sacrament and is, as it were, offered upon the lower altar, may be carried to the high altar, which is the Church triumphant, and joined to its head, namely Christ, whose body it is.

For, as Pope Sergius says, the body of Christ is threefold. Accordingly, three fractions are customarily made in the form of bread. The portion consumed signifies the body of Christ still walking upon earth, that is, the Church militant—the lower altar [Col. 0746C], still corruptible and earthly. Hence it is commanded to be made of earth. The portion placed in the chalice signifies the body of Christ already risen, namely the Church triumphant, which is also figured by the golden altar that stood in the Holy of Holies. But the portion reserved upon the altar until the end of Mass signifies the body lying in the tomb, that is, the Church awaiting the resurrection of bodies. This altar is commanded to be made of stones untouched by iron, because, already endowed with assured blessedness, it fears no cutting either of heresy or schism. It is also figured by the altar beneath which John heard the voice of the slain crying: “Avenge, Lord, the blood of your servants that has been shed” (Rev. 6).

For this reason the Church that awaits is compared with Rachel’s tomb [Col. 0746D]: there “a voice was heard in Ramah,” that is, on high—Rachel, that is, the Church, weeping for her children—and there she refuses consolation until the number of her brethren is fulfilled. Rachel’s tomb, therefore, is the hidden place of the Church awaiting the resurrection of bodies lying concealed in tombs. These two men await beside this tomb, because although, as regards the glorification of their souls, they are members of the Church triumphant, yet, as regards the reception of their bodies, they are members of the Church awaiting.

O how glorious is this tomb! Isaiah says: “There shall be a root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples; him the nations shall entreat, and his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. 11). From the root of Jesse there rises a flower, that is, Christ, who was also called a Nazarene [Col. 0747A]. This is His tomb, because, just as He is head of the Church militant and triumphant, so He is head of the Church awaiting. For the Church awaiting and triumphant is one. It is glorious because there the wicked cease from their tumult, and the voice of the taskmaster is not heard. There the kings and counsellors of the earth sleep in silence and rest in their sleep. Therefore those who dig for treasure rejoice exceedingly when they find this tomb. It follows:

“In the borders of Benjamin.” Benjamin is interpreted “son of the right hand.” The sons of the right hand are those to whom, when they have been set at the right hand, the Judge will say: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25). This Benjamin has many boundaries: perseverance in the fear of the Lord; observance of the commandments; affection [Col. 0747B] of charity; and the vision of God, which alone is the final end.

There is a first end, the end by means of which. Of this you have: “Let us hear together the end of the discourse: Fear God and keep His commandments” (Eccl. 12). The second is the end toward which one tends. Thus you read: “The end of the law is charity” (1 Tim. 1). The third is the end for the sake of which one acts. Thus the Psalms are directed “unto the end”; and the Lord says in the Apocalypse: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1). Through fear of the Lord and observance of the commandments we attain charity, in which we must persevere for the sole sake of the vision of the Lord. These two men were found within the borders of Benjamin, for in their lives they possessed faith working through love, persevering in it until the vision of God.

They were found, therefore, in the borders of Benjamin and at noon. [Col. 0747C] For they found where the Bridegroom feeds and where He rests at noon. Not in the mournful day in which men grope as in the night—the day of this age, and the dawn of that great day which will be one of calamity and misery—but at noon, that is, in the pure day which knows no setting, which no night interrupts and which possesses no darkness. It follows:

“Leaping over great pits.” By a pit earthly cupidity is signified, as in Job: “Cast their faces down into the pit” (Job 40), because the reprobate bend their entire gaze toward earthly desire. Or by a pit the sentence of death is understood, as in the Psalm: “They dug a pit before my face, and fell into it” (Ps. 56): that is, they killed themselves in what they thought would kill me. These pits are great and open, but those who despised earthly desires and escaped the sentence of eternal death leapt beyond them. These men therefore give assurance concerning the finding of the asses: they know how to regulate the simple movements of the soul and have brought their simple subjects back, by writings and example, to the stable of the Samaritan.

## SERMON XXVII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

“Who is this who ascends,” etc. (Song 8). On God’s way some are driven, as though compelled, concerning whom it is written: “When He slew them, they sought Him” (Ps. 77). Others are drawn, those who grow strong amid temptations. Hence the Lord says: “I will draw them with cords of charity” (Hos. 11). Others walk, those who with untiring step proceed through the path [Col. 0748A] of justice amid difficulties. Of them it is sung: “As they went, they went and wept, casting their seed” (Ps. 125). Others run, those who strive, through fervent desire, to exceed their strength. Hence David says: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118). Others ascend, those who, ascending, dispose the steps of merits in their hearts. Hence it is said: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has disposed ascents in his heart in the valley of tears, in the place which He has appointed” (Ps. 83).

Among those who ascend, some ascend in order to fall; some fall for this purpose, that afterwards they may ascend more strongly; others ascend in such a way that they cannot fall; while others fall in such a way that they can no longer ascend. Those ascend in order to fall who become proud because of their virtues, who live falsely in religion, who are unstable in temptation, who retain youthful dispositions even as they grow old. Of these Solomon says: “Three things are difficult for me, and a fourth I wholly do not know: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the way of a ship in the sea, and the way of a man in his youth” (Prov. 30).

The way of the eagle in the sky is the way of one who walks amid things great and wonderful beyond himself. For the eagle has great wings, and comes to Lebanon when it approaches the gleaming mountain of virtues. Yet it takes away the pith of the cedar when, through contempt and pride, it disparages even religious persons. The way of the serpent upon the rock is the life of those who outwardly show that they adhere to Christ in a religious manner, [Col. 0748C] while inwardly concealing the poison of malice. In carrying the poison of malice, they are serpents; in living religiously, they go upon the rock. I say upon the rock, not in the rock, because neither are they in Christ nor Christ in them—just as the Scribes and Pharisees are said to sit upon, not in, the chair of Moses.

The way of the ship in the sea is the life of those who, amid the bitterness of temptations, stagger and sink when some wind of vanity blows. The way of a man in youth is the life of those who, though old and advanced in years, nevertheless retain youthfulness in their manners, not in their age. Isaiah curses them when he says: “Accursed is the child of a hundred years” (Isa. 65).

Those fall in order to ascend who humble themselves that they may be exalted. Of them Solomon says: “Four things are least upon earth, yet are wiser than the wise: the ant, which prepares food for itself in summer; the coney, a feeble people; the locust has no king, yet goes forth in companies; the lizard supports itself with its hands and dwells in kings’ houses” (Prov. 30). [Col. 0748D] In these are signified the industrious, the timid, the humble, and the subject.

Those fall and cannot ascend whom the storm of water has submerged, whom the deep has already swallowed, upon whom the pit is now pressing its mouth: so that they fall into the depth either of guilt or of punishment. Of these Solomon says: “Three things are insatiable, and a fourth never says, ‘Enough’: hell, and the mouth of the womb; the earth which is not satisfied with water; and the fire which never says, ‘Enough’” (ibid.). In the first is shown the depth of punishment; in the other [Col. 0749A] three, lust, cupidity, and avarice—the depth of guilt.

Those ascend and cannot fall who cannot be bent either by temptations or adversities, but confidently say with the Apostle: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. 8). Or certainly, they are those who fulfil in deed what they preach by word; or who preserve prudence by innocence, so that they may be among those who slaughter the lamb “on the north side,” or who are “as doves to their windows.” Of them Solomon says: “There are three things that go well: the lion, strongest of beasts, which fears no encounter; the cock girded about the loins; and the ram—there is no king who can withstand him” (Prov. 30).

In the strong lion are signified those who cannot be bent by adversity in the world, weakness of the flesh, or temptation of the heart; for he fears no encounter. In the cock girded about the loins are signified preachers who demonstrate in deed what they preach in speech. They strike themselves before they crow, because they chastise their bodies and restrain their loins with the girdle of continence, lest, after preaching to others, they themselves be found reprobate. In the ram, whom no king can resist, are signified the simple, who nonetheless preserve such prudence in their simplicity that they need fear no assault from an adversary. For, like doves to their windows, they are prudent as serpents but simple as doves.

It should also be observed that among those ascending, some ascend in order to flee from the desert; some ascend from the desert; some ascend in the desert; some ascend through the desert; and some ascend to the desert. By the desert [Col. 0749C] are often figured either demons or hell. Demons, as in the Psalm: “Nor from the desert mountains” (Ps. 74), because even among the malignant spirits there is no place of escape from the divine majesty. Hell, as when the scapegoat, *apopompaeos* (ἀποπομπαῖος), was commanded to be sent into the desert, because Christ, in respect of His soul, descended into hell because of the people’s sins.

Or they ascend from the desert, that is, from the Mosaic law, concerning which it is written that Moses sweetened the bitter waters of Marah in the desert by placing wood upon them. Or they ascend from the barren rite of paganism. Hence: “He made the desert into pools of water” (Ps. 106). And again Isaiah says: “Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16).

Or they ascend from the desert, that is, from the world. Hence in the Song: “Who is this who ascends from the desert?”—that is, who is this who is lifted up from the world? For the world is compared to a desert for five reasons: because of pilgrimage—“We do not have here an abiding dwelling, but seek one to come” (Heb. 13); because of labour—“Man is born unto labour” (Job 5); because of need—“I am poor and sorrowful” (Ps. 68); because of the bites of serpents, that is, the suggestions of demons—“There are creeping things without number” (Ps. 103); and because the world is uncultivated, just as a desert is uncultivated.

Or they ascend in the desert, that is, in [Col. 0750A] cessation from vices, which is called the desert of the breast or the sabbath of the mind, without which there is no salvation. Woe to you, prelates of the Church, who abandon this desert when you build Zion in blood, boast of the horn of the altar, revel in the patrimony of the Crucified One, and disfigure holy Church through your relatives and kinsmen. For thus you build Zion in your blood, and, abandoning this desert, you also abandon the rights of the Church.

Or they ascend in the desert, that is, in a holy mind. Hence in Exodus: “When Moses had driven the flock to the inner parts of the desert, the Lord appeared to him” (Exod. 3), because the Lord then appears to us spiritually when we bring our thoughts into true unity in a devout mind devoted to holy solitude. Or they ascend in the desert, that is, in holy conduct. Hence in Exodus: “We shall sacrifice to the Lord in the desert” (ibid.), that is, we shall serve the Lord in holy conduct.

Or they ascend through the desert, that is, through contemplation, which is deserted by many and inhabited by few. Hence in the Song: “Who is this who ascends through the desert?” (Song 3). Or they ascend to the desert, that is, to heaven. Hence the Lord left the ninety-nine sheep in the desert, because He left angelic nature in heaven. It is called desert because it was abandoned by the angels who fell through pride. To this desert, as to the throne of the true Solomon, one ascends by the six works of mercy, as by six steps: if we give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, visit those [Col. 0750C] confined in prisons, receive strangers with hospitality, clothe the naked, and offer the sick the consolation of counsel or assistance. For because of these works they will hear words of consolation: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

Thus the glorious Virgin ascended from virtue to virtue: that she might flee the desert of hell; that she might ascend from the desert of the world to the desert of holy conduct; through the desert of devout contemplation; even to the desert of the heavenly calling.

## SERMON XXVIII. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY

> [Note: Col. 0749D. This is more fitting for the feast of the Assumption.]

“Raise your rod, stretch out your hand, and divide the sea, that the children of Israel may pass through the midst of the dry sea” (Exod. 14). What I say to one, I say to all: to all, I mean, who, like good advocates of the poor, have learned to argue spiritually against the frivolous excuses of those invited to the wedding feast. For we have all been invited to the wedding feast, but there is still someone who says: “I have bought a farm” (Luke 14). To buy a farm is to toil amid the vanities of the age. This is the man who serves Pharaoh in a basket of chaff.

There is also one who says: “I have bought five yoke of oxen” (ibid.). This is the carnal man who longs after the desires of the world and subjects himself to Pharaoh in a basket of bricks. For earthly [Col. 0751A] desire is like mud baked by the fire which never says, “Enough”; or indeed by the fire which consumed the sheep and the servants when it struck them, since:

> “The envious man wastes away at another’s abundant goods.”  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.57

There is besides one who says: “I have taken a wife” (ibid.). To take a wife is to soften the mud of the flesh through pleasure. This is the man who obeys Pharaoh in a basket of mud. Those, then, who repel vanities, pleasures, and desires, and reject frivolous excuses, shake their necks free from beneath Pharaoh’s yoke. But who is he? And we shall praise him? (Ecclus. 31). He is the one who urges and soothes; for this is the meaning of Moses, to whom it was said: “Raise your rod,” etc. He urged through the discipline of the active life and soothed through the discipline of the contemplative life. Therefore the prophet says: “I cut for myself two rods: one I called Cord, and the other Beauty” (Zech. 11). For from the root of the earth he cut a rod, as it were, of discipline: “Cord” in respect of the active life, “Beauty” in respect of the contemplative. The cord urges; beauty soothes. Nothing so calms and soothes the soul as the devotion of holy contemplation, as someone says: “In all things I sought rest” (Ecclus. 24), and nowhere found so great a rest as in holy reflection. But the active life urges the soul and constrains it, as it were, with a cord, while it pricks, solicits, and is troubled about many things.

Therefore the glorious Virgin is proclaimed as a rod [Col. 0751C] of the spices of myrrh and incense. A rod, I say, because she is light and flexible; a cord because, raising herself on high, she emitted an odour of sweetness. Light, because she lacks the weight of sins; flexible, because she is merciful. Of myrrh and incense, because she continually exercised herself in every discipline. She was a rod of myrrh because of the discipline of the active life, but of incense because of the discipline of the contemplative life.

Hence, on the feast of the present day, she is compared to the little town in which Mary and Martha lived: a town founded on firm rock, impregnable, incorrupt, filled with as many citizens as virtues, whose gate was always shut and opened only for the prince. It is, by antonomasia, the town of Jesus, in which Martha truly dwelt [Col. 0751D] in the solicitude of service, while Mary dwelt in the fervour of love, or the desire of charity (Luke 10). For in these two sisters the two lives are signified under the New Testament, just as Leah and Rachel signify them under the Old Testament. What Leah signifies in the Old Testament, Martha signifies in the New; and what Rachel signifies there, Mary signifies here—but for differing reasons.

Martha signifies the active life because of the office of charity; Leah because of the exercise of labour, whence she is interpreted “laborious.” Mary signifies the contemplative life because of the height of contemplation; Rachel because of simplicity of mind, whence she is interpreted “sheep.” Therefore Mary signifies the contemplative life because of the higher power of contemplation, Rachel because of its lower power; Martha the active life because of the higher power of activity, Leah because of its lower power. Though the higher power of contemplation and the lower power of activity differ greatly from one another, the higher power of activity and the lower power of contemplation do not seem to differ greatly. For the delight of devotion differs greatly from the affliction of labour, but the office of charity does not differ greatly from the simplicity of good will.

Hence, in the construction of the tabernacle, the court, the Holy Place, and the Holy of Holies seem to be built according to the office of these four sisters. In the court there were a bronze altar, a gridiron, a frying-pan, and an oven. There flesh was slaughtered for burnt offering and sin offering. In all these things the office of Leah is figured, namely labour and affliction. Behold the lower degree of the active [Col. 0752B] life. In the Holy Place, however, was the table of the offering, with warm loaves placed together upon it: namely, Martha’s office. At its side was the lampstand with lamps, in which Rachel’s office was figured. But in the Holy of Holies was the golden altar, on which incense was offered, according to Mary’s office.

For in Christ’s Church four kinds of rulers have been appointed: priests, who fulfil Mary’s office; kings, who fulfil Rachel’s office. Since these two kinds belong to the contemplative life, they receive the benefit of anointing. Pastors, however, fulfil Martha’s office; judges, Leah’s. Since these belong to the active life, they do not have the benefit of anointing, but rather the rod in their hands, for the preservation of discipline in works.

Hence, in the primitive Church, four persons were first ordained: Aaron, who fulfilled the priestly office; Jacob, the pastoral office; Moses, the judicial office; and David, the royal office. To these four the ordering of the Church was chiefly entrusted. But what then, brethren? The sons of Korah rose up against Aaron the high priest; Aaron’s rod blossomed and bore fruit as a sign of the priesthood and a rebuke to the sons of Korah. Jacob likewise placed rods of poplar, almond, and plane-tree in the channels, so that at their sight the sheep might conceive diverse offspring, and thus he might outwit Laban and multiply what was his own (Gen. 30). Moses, however, raised his rod against Pharaoh and performed signs and wonders with it [Col. 0752D], afflicting Egypt with ten plagues. David, although he often had Saul in his power, refused to lay his hand upon the Lord’s anointed; nevertheless his rod was raised and straight, as it is said: “The rod of rectitude is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44).

All these things, beloved, happened to them in figure and were done for us. A rod has been given us: the rod from the root of Jesse—the root, I say, of fire. For the Virgin is the root of all fervour and charity, and she is the rod. The rod has been exalted, the rod has been raised, so that she who has been exalted in herself may be exalted in you, exalted for you, exalted by you, exalted in you—she who has been exalted for you.

Therefore, whoever you are, shepherd of God; whoever fulfils Jacob’s office: if Laban confronts you, if the world oppresses you, if those whose iniquity comes forth from fatness mock your labours [Col. 0753A] and struggles, hold in the channels of your heart the rod that contains the almond of fruitfulness, the poplar of virginity, and the plane-tree of justice and holiness, or simplicity. Raise, then, the rod fruitful in offspring, virginal in body and mind, level in justice and simplicity. But observe what was said, and of whom: “Like a planting of roses in Jericho” (Ecclus. 24). What applies particularly to Mary ought to apply generally to all—and would that it might apply finally to me! For Jericho signifies the same as Laban, namely the world; and the just person is like a planting of roses in Jericho, that is, in the world, because he subjects to himself the thorns of temptation, while through outward mortification of the flesh and inward devotion of mind he emits in all things the fragrance of sweetness.

Take Jacob as your example; take as your example the wrestling man. If the world mocks, if the thorns of temptations rise up, let the greenness of the mind remain; be the sweet odour of Christian devotion. But if you are a priest and the sons of Korah rise up against you—the sons of Calvary, the sons of the cross—that is, hypocrites, who habitually envy others’ good deeds, or who habitually seek temporal gain from ecclesiastical benefices: do not, priest, seek what is eternal except for eternal things. Seek first the kingdom of God and His justice, and all these things shall be added to you.

Blessed is he for whom this utterance may be true: “Like a palm tree I have been exalted in Kadesh” (ibid.). The palm tree, those who described the natures of things say, bears fruit after a hundred years; Kadesh means “change” [Col. 0753C] or “holy.” In Scripture, too, one hundred signifies perfection. Therefore the just person is exalted like a palm tree in Kadesh when he is transferred from the left hand of this temporality to the right hand of blessed eternity, according to the saying: “When He gives sleep to His beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126); and Wisdom: “When a man has finished, then he begins” (Ecclus. 18). For then he will be in the womb of the right hand of the Most High, when he can say: “Now I have begun” (Ps. 76). Then indeed there will be a holy change, when this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body has put on immortality.

But if you are a judge, and the king of Egypt—that is, of these darknesses—rises up against you, so that you fail to discern the difference between good and evil, true and false, profane and holy, clean and unclean, consider the cypress exalted on Mount Zion. For Mount Zion signifies God’s Church, where the cypress of the cross was exalted, because the cross on which the Saviour hung is said to have been made of cypress. Long before, He foretold: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12); and: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (ibid.). Seek, then, no other judgment. Attend to Him who says: “Judge not, and you shall not be judged” (Luke 6). Open your eyes only to this: how the prince of this world may now be cast out, so that he may rule neither in you nor among your own. Let your struggle be not only against flesh and blood but also against the prince of these darknesses, against spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places (Eph. 6).

But if you desire to exercise the office of king, raise your mind to Him for whom to serve is to reign; desire to share in His kingdom, which is eternal. Consider, then, the cedar exalted in Lebanon. The cedar remains in Lebanon immense, fragrant, and incorruptible. Mount Lebanon is white, for Lebanon is interpreted “whiteness.” There are men outstanding in virtues, fragrant in reputation, incorruptible in eternity; and all who are there reign, because they are kings. There they receive the dignity of exaltation; there they are subject to no one—not to man, not to angel, but to God alone. It follows:

“Stretch out your hand and divide the sea.” Observe that Moses was told: “Stretch out your hand” (Exod. 14)—that is, he to whom it had been said: “You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5). He demands more from you, who stretched out both hands upon the cross. “Unless your justice exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). He therefore demands more because He says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you. If anyone strikes you on the cheek,” etc. (ibid.).

He who stretches out only one hand and divides the sea perhaps retains the upper waters and does not cast away the lower. This is a great mystery. There is an upper bitterness and a lower bitterness. For the sea signifies bitterness, because it is bitter. The upper bitterness must be retained; the lower removed. If you are bitter in spirit because you are long detained in this exile and do not enjoy the vision of God, you are bitter for higher things. Of such bitterness it is said: “Set bitterness before yourself, and direct your heart into the straight way” (Jer. 31); and elsewhere: “I shall call to mind all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38).

For this is Mordecai, the foster-father of Edissa, who was also called Esther (Esther 2). [Col. 0754C] Mordecai is interpreted “pure myrrh,” and myrrh signifies bitterness. This is the bitterness that must be retained, because it is pure. He is the foster-father of Edissa, that is, of mercy, because Edissa is interpreted “mercy,” while Esther means “hidden.” This is the hidden mercy of which it is said: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30). Therefore the bride says in the Song: “My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers are full of choicest myrrh” (Song 5): that is, myrrh which is pure and therefore must be retained.

The lower bitterness, however, is when someone is bitter because he cannot exercise against his enemy the malice he has conceived. Hence the Psalmist says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4). This lower bitterness must be rejected, because it is impure, because it nourishes God’s wrath more than mercy. In the first bitterness Christ’s cross is signified; in the second, Haman’s cross—Haman meaning “iniquity.” Stretch out your hands, then, and divide the sea, that you may know how to distinguish between the two bitternesses: lest you be troubled where you ought to rejoice, or rejoice where you ought to be troubled. Do not rejoice that you are in the world; do not [Col. 0755A] be troubled that you have been bound to God’s service.

Thus the children of Israel walk through the midst of the sea, that is, through the way of virtues, when vices have been dried up through bitterness. They walk as far as Horeb, the mountain of God. Horeb is interpreted “dryness.” Yet it should be observed that one dryness is commendable and another blameworthy, and both are figured in Horeb. Good and praiseworthy dryness is figured in Horeb, as in: “Even unto Horeb, the mountain of God” (3 Kings 19). That heavenly mountain is called Horeb because it is shown to be clean from every defilement. For defiling things, being harmful, flow down from mountains into valleys. Thus angel and man—the one through pride, the other through disobedience—fell from the mountain of heavenly glory into the valley of temporal misery. Hence it is written: “Nothing defiled shall dwell therein” (Rev. 21). And the Psalmist says: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Ps. 14). Here you have both dwelling and rest.

Praiseworthy dryness is that which, drinking up the harmful humours of bodily fatness, weakens the wanton motions of slippery frailty and renders the body less fit for them. There is also blameworthy dryness, which dries up the fountain of the heart and the veins through which the devotion of tears is accustomed to flow even to the eyes, thereby shutting off the grace of devotion. A twofold concupiscence both brings about and removes this twofold dryness. The concupiscence of the spirit against the flesh brings about commendable dryness and removes blameworthy dryness; but the concupiscence of the flesh against [Col. 0755C] the spirit brings about blameworthy dryness and removes commendable dryness. Through the first dryness a person has a heart of flesh; through the second, a heart of stone: fleshly through the abundance of devotion, stony through the hardness of obstinacy.

## SERMON XXIX. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BERNARD
When Jesus reclined in the house of Simon the leper, an alabaster flask of precious genuine nard ointment was broken, and the whole house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment (John 12). Although, beloved, the trustworthy and wholly credible account of blessed Luke records that the things we have set forth took place six days before Passover at Bethany, in the house of Simon, yet because we see these same things repeated in this spiritual Bethany—not historically, indeed, but mystically—we see these things repeated [Col. 0755D], and ought by vows and prayers to implore the wonderful mercy of God in this event, since his love has not turned away from his faithful ones, but his hand is still stretched out.

For what is this Bethany except this house of obedience, which gladly recognizes itself as the mother of so many sons, whom it has brought forth from the Holy Spirit, with the hand of obedience acting as midwife? Since it is known both by the brightness of its example and by the humility of its valley, it is not undeservedly called Clairvaux, “Bright Valley.” In this house, therefore, that Simon who became obedient to the Father unto death—whose spirit rests in the sons of obedience, as it is written, “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet man, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66)—sought rest and found it [Col. 0756A], because “his delights are to be with the children of men.”

Or, since in sacred discourse a house commonly figures the conscience, he built for himself a house of the precious stones of virtues and brought it to the cubit of perfection: that Simon, that is, the son of obedience, whose memory is in blessing. Following the Lamb wherever he went, at the command of obedience he went forth from his land and kindred, like another Abraham, in order that he might become a great nation; hence he was made father of many nations, and in him we cry, “Abba, Father.” Likewise, like another Isaac, in the field of this solitude, into which he went out to meditate, he joined Rebecca to himself, because he both learned and taught alike, from the things which he suffered, patience. He too, like another [Col. 0756B] Jacob, having gone out from his land and kindred, joined Rachel and Leah to himself: Leah in the duty of service, Rachel in the leisure of contemplation. God multiplied his seed upon the earth, so that from Leah he begot an innumerable multitude of those who labor actively, and from Rachel an abundant multitude of contemplatives.

Thus in all these respects he is deservedly compared with patriarchs and prophets; and not only with them, but with apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins. For, sent by God to you, though not an apostle to others, he was nevertheless made an apostle to you, because all of you in the Lord are the signs of his apostleship. Through the suffering of the flesh and compassion for his neighbor, he also ran farther in the contest than a martyr who endures the blow and sheds blood beneath the sword’s edge [Col. 0756C]. And, in confessing praise while worshipping the Lord, what the ark of his heart believed he also confessed before men. Never defiled with women, he followed the Lamb wherever he went. For, leaving the broad road and undertaking the steep one that leads to life, he became for you like a lamp burning and shining: burning in speech, shining in example; burning in the breaking of bread, shining in the paths of God’s ways. Thus, excellent in both goods—burning and arduous—he was not undeservedly called Bernard.

Consider how great this man was, who entered not merely for your salvation but for the correction of all: John for kings, Moses for Egyptians, Phinehas for fornicators, Elijah for idolaters, Elisha for the avaricious, [Col. 0756D] Peter for liars, Paul for blasphemers, Christ for merchants. A pattern of righteousness, mirror of holiness, example of piety, champion of truth, defender of faith, friend of the bridegroom, bridegroom’s attendant of the bride, organizer of the clergy, shepherd of peoples, teacher of the ignorant, refuge of the oppressed, advocate of the poor, hope of the wretched, guardian of orphans, judge of widows, eye of the blind, tongue of the mute, staff of the aged, avenger of crimes, terror of the wicked, glory of the good, salt of the earth, light of the world, priest of the Most High, vicar of Christ, the Lord’s anointed, God to Pharaoh: severe in deed, serene in countenance, serious in speech, made all things to all people—so that you might believe him called not to a share in pastoral care, but to the fullness of authority.

Therefore Jesus reclined in his house—he who [Col. 0757A] is in all things by his essence. For he who is absent nowhere is everywhere. Yet in some he passes through; in others he dwells; in others he reclines; in others he feeds and is refreshed. He passes through interrupted thoughts, as Eliphaz says: “When a spirit passed before me, all the hairs of my flesh stood up” (Job 4). A spirit passes before us when we think of invisible things, because we see them not steadily but fleetingly. The mind is not fixed long in contemplation, because, struck back by that very light, it is recalled to itself. But then the hairs of the flesh stand up, when we cut away from the mind the thoughts of the old life in such a way that we are wearied by that pain.

He dwells, however, through grace, now working so that a person may will what is good, now cooperating lest he will in vain [Col. 0757B]; yet grace is often veiled by temptation, as it is written: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30); and sometimes uncovered by devotion. But then he not only dwells, but reclines, because to recline is for the mind to dwell with devotion. He is refreshed in those, or by those, in whom or by whom the Son fulfills the Father’s will, as the same Son says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4).

Thus he reclines and feeds in the house of Simon, that is, in the conscience of one who obeys. “The leper” is added, however, for the safeguarding of humility, because humility is the guardian of obedience. Unless obedience is preserved through humility [Col. 0757C], it is quickly raised up into contempt. Therefore one who withdrew outside the camp through the leprosy of pride must return to God through the humility of obedience, because simple obedience is insufficient unless it is attended by its companions. For obedience to be full and perfect, it must itself be pure, voluntary, humble, patient, faithful, devout, strengthened by the might of divine love. Of this it is said: “Love is strong as death” (Song 8).

These qualities are figured in the seven persons who, as we gather from the divine words, are marked by one and the same name, namely Simon. For we read of Simon Magus, Simon of Cyrene, Simon the leper, Simon the Maccabee, Simon Peter, Simon the Canaanite [Col. 0757D], and Simon son of Onias. These seven figure the seven things we have mentioned—not all of them every quality, but some one quality and some another; certain ones negatively, certain ones positively.

There are those who obey the commands of prelates solely from ambition. These put on Simon Magus, who wished to obey apostolic commands solely out of greed. Therefore obedience must be pure, so that God alone—who is the most causal cause—may be its motive, and that he who is the final end may also be its end in perseverance. Others obey the commands of prelates, but always unwillingly, always with grumbling. These put on Simon of Cyrene, who carried the Lord’s cross under compulsory service (Mark 15). Therefore obedience must be voluntary, because forced services do not please God; rather, he loves a cheerful giver, because that sacrifice is acceptable to him upon whose head the hand of the offerer is laid [Col. 0758A].

Others, mindful of their former evils and therefore humble, humbly obey divine commands precisely because they trust that through the good of obedience they can return to God. These put on Simon the leper, who, when he invited God, was nevertheless called a leper. So too they retain for themselves the name of sinner, even though they do not know that they may be secure concerning a sin that has been forgiven.

Others obey concerning matters that seem lawful to them; but if something that is commanded seems less lawful, they believe that they may lawfully object, paying no heed to the obedience of Abraham, or of John, who watered a dry piece of wood and rolled an enormous stone, or of the man who threw his son into a burning furnace for obedience’s sake. For if we obey only in lawful matters [Col. 0758B], who will fulfill what our lawgiver—Benedict both in deed and name—says concerning that chapter: “If impossible things are enjoined upon a brother?” For what is so unlawful as the impossible?

Therefore let us put on Simon the Maccabee, who obeyed Tryphon, although he knew that what Tryphon asked was unlawful. When this Simon had risen up for his brother Jonathan, whom Tryphon had killed, though Simon was not unaware of it, Tryphon deceitfully sent envoys to him, saying: “We detained your brother because of the money which he owed in the king’s account; now send one hundred talents of silver and his sons as hostages, and we shall release him” (1 Macc. 13). Although Simon recognized his deception, he nevertheless sent the silver [Col. 0758C] and the boys, lest the people murmur and say, “He did not ransom his brother because he wished to reign.” By this example we must often be obedient in order to remove a greater scandal, even if perhaps unlawful things are commanded. This is patient obedience.

But since everything that is apart from faith, or not from faith, is unlawful (Heb. 11), we do not say generally that one must obey in every unlawful matter. For we are never bound to obey in matters in which faith is injured. Rather, in every act of obedience let us have faith beforehand. For we ought not so to put on Simon the Maccabee that we put off Simon Peter; because, however great obedience may be, it is nevertheless nothing unless founded upon the rock of faith. Nor do I mean any sort of faith, but that which is affectionate and emulous of all virtues. For what can harm us if we become emulators of the good? Therefore emulate divine gifts, so that your obedience may be both faithful and affectionate. Thus put on Simon Peter, and also put on the Canaanite. For “Canaanite” is interpreted “Zealot,” or “emulator,” which is the same thing, “imitator.”

Nor should the deficiency of human frailty frighten you if at times the burden of commands seems to exceed your strength. Know that those who trust in the Lord shall renew their strength. For your strength ought not to be in yourselves but in God, and in the strength of his obedience, who makes an outcome together with temptation.

When, therefore, something burdensome is commanded of a brother [Col. 0759A], let the useful brother say in his heart: “God is my strength; the Lord is my power; and therefore, despite human weakness, I shall undertake what divine strength will accomplish.” Thus Simon son of Onias was broken, that is, the imitator of him who always says in his mind: “My strength is not sufficient for me to endure; yet the Lord is my power, so that I may be able to accomplish it.” Hence Onias is interpreted, “The Lord is my strength.”

In the house of this Simon Jesus reclined; and while he was at table, the nard gave forth its fragrance, because the alabaster flask of precious genuine nard ointment was broken, and the whole house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. Alabaster is said to be a vessel of white, translucent marble, which preserves ointments unspoiled. Such an alabaster flask was this vessel of election: vessel of psalm, vessel of song, jar of flour [Col. 0759B], flask of oil, Pharaoh’s cup, turned bowl, intoxicating and splendid chalice. It was marble in perseverance, white in purity, translucent in reputation. It always preserved its ointments unspoiled, because neither infamy darkened it, nor an unlawful deed, nor consent to a thought corrupted the gift of graces bestowed upon it.

It is called an alabaster flask “of ointment,” just as we customarily say “a cup of wine”; and it is called “of ointment” because the words poured forth from the vessel were so medicinal that through them the sick were healed, the blind enlightened, and the strong anointed unto strength. For they were an antidote for the weak, an eye-salve for the dim-sighted, and chrism for the strong. Thus what Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome did [Col. 0759C] in order to anoint the head (Mark 16), he acquired for himself at the price of much labor, many vigils, and fasts: that he might anoint the members of the Head—or rather, the Head in the members.

Therefore this alabaster flask was broken today, dissolved by a precious death; but not like a potter’s vessel, rather like a vessel of gold which, released from the bonds of flesh, returned to the Lord with gain the talent entrusted to it. And the whole house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. For through his words the whole Church is a good fragrance to God in every place, because his fragrance is “like the fragrance of a full field, which the Lord has blessed.” Let us therefore run in the fragrance of his ointments: that is, in the fragrance of genuine (*pistici*), faithful and precious—and thereby good—nard ointment. For the alabaster flask of good nard ointment was broken [Col. 0759D], or, by syncope, of Bernard, whose words breathed the rose for martyrs and the lily for the chaste.

May the ordered disposition of his outward members, discipline of conduct, exercise of labor, adornment of virtues, example of deeds, and pharmaceutical healing of words draw Christ’s faithful after him. And may he draw them from exile to their homeland, from labor to rest, from death to life, from darkness to light that knows no setting: Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honor and glory through the endless ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

“If, walking along the way, you find on a tree or on the ground a bird’s nest, and the mother sitting above upon the young or the eggs, you shall not take the mother with the young, but shall let her go, keeping the young which you have captured, that it may go well with you and that you may live a long time” (Deut. 22).

Whenever, placed beneath the open sky and exposed to the winds, I diligently consider the beloved tabernacles of wisdom, I seem to myself necessarily to be building in Kiriath-sepher. But when, with Achsah’s sigh preceding mine, I inquire about or complain of the dryness of the place, I perceive that I must seek from the Father of lights—from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends from above (James 1:17)—both the lower and the upper watering, so that the city may deservedly be named Dabir. For “whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15). In them the Lord made us ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit; for the letter [Col. 0760B] kills. For this is the dryness of Kiriath-sepher, which is interpreted “city of letters.”

And what is the city of letters except that learning which defends from enemies and adorns with virtues? It is called a city in distinction from the learning that neither fortifies nor adorns. Hence the Psalmist says: “Because I have not known learning, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 70). But the dryness of this city is the surface of the letter, which seems to have no fruit in itself unless faith and understanding are watered by the lower irrigation of fear and the upper irrigation of love. For, in order to build gold in wisdom, silver in eloquence, precious stones—

> [Note: Col. 0759D: Some words are missing here.]

—silver in logic, and gold [Col. 0760C] in theology, fear and love must necessarily go before together, so that, just as those two men, Aaron and Hur, formerly supported Moses’ heavy hands, so they may uncover and cleanse his face.

Otherwise we must fear lest we build wood, which heretics are accustomed to put into the word “bread,” as it is written: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11); or lest we place beneath it the hay of human frailty, which the hungry ought to put beneath themselves, as those attached to the letter customarily do in songs; or lest we build stubble of some vanity—into which the dryness of the present theme would lead us unless it is made fruitful by the irrigation of fear and love. “If, walking along the way,” he says, and so forth. What is more vain than this, if one attends to the surface of the letter? For what if, after capturing the young, one lets the mother go? Has he possessed better things or lived a longer life? Yet if fear of God and love precede understanding, nothing is found more devout, truer, or more worthy of God. Then the city shall deservedly be called Dabir, because then the divine word will be approved, and the eloquence which Dabir signifies will be accepted.

For he says:

“If, walking along the way.” This “if” is used not conditionally but causally. For there is no human being upon earth who does not walk along the way until he reaches his homeland; for God, stable and unchangeable, gives all things to move and change. The sleeper does not differ from the wakeful person, nor the resting person from the laboring person. For we all travel onward to death; we all roll about the sphere of the world; and, with the living creatures, we walk about the circuit of the wheel. “The living creatures went and did not return; they went and returned” (Ezek. 1) [Col. 0761A]. Indeed, what is more marvelous, they returned by not returning, and by returning they did not return.

What is this instability of human life, that when it returns to that from which it was taken—as the Lord says, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3), and as Job also testifies: “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job 1)—it nevertheless does not return to the beginning of youth or infancy if it has reached old age and decrepitude? Just as you see movement in a choir of singers: they return to the place from which they began, yet they do not return, because they always go forward before their own face.

Whoever you are, then, who have not yet deserved to rest in your homeland, but are still a pilgrim and stranger: if you walk along the way in order to arrive at your homeland, you must seek and find the nest of a bird. Note that Scripture sets before you one bird’s single nest, in distinction from very many birds: some of them ate the seed that fell beside the way; others carried off the food prepared from the baker’s basket; others even flew toward the sacrifice of our father Abraham. For birds, because they are greedy, are demons: they often either take away or strive to take away thoughts as though seeds, actions as prepared food, or devotion itself dedicated to God as a sacrifice.

The nests of these birds, therefore, are the hearts of sinners [Col. 0761C]. The nests of divers are the covetous, of birds flying at night are heretics, of rapacious birds are the avaricious, and of raven-kind are diverse classes of sinners. For this reason the lawgiver judged such birds unclean. Their nests must not be sought; but if they are found without having been sought, they must either be driven away, or neither mother nor young must be taken.

The single bird is the unique phoenix, who came forth into the light from the spices of another phoenix—namely, the unique Virgin—through the mediating fire of the Holy Spirit, and made his nest in the hearts of the saints. Hence he compares himself with many kinds of birds, as in the words: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like a night-owl in its dwelling” (Ps. 101). Elsewhere the Psalmist says of his humanity: “Even the sparrow has found itself a house, and the turtledove a nest” (Ps. 83) [Col. 0761D]. He also compares himself to Jonah, whose name means “dove,” when he says: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days” (Matt. 12, 23 [sic]). He is compared to a hen when he says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23): that is, I did this despite your unwillingness. He is compared to an eagle where he says: “Like an eagle stirring her young to fly and hovering over them” (Deut. 32).

And rightly he was a pelican in compassion, a night-owl in suffering, a turtledove in making peace, a dove in feeding, a hen in pacifying, and an eagle in bringing peace. Hence it is written: “Man is born for labor, and a bird for flight” [Col. 0762A] (Job 5). Because he was man in the labor of his Passion, he became like a bird in the flight of his resurrection.

The nest of this bird is often found in trees: he nests as though in a cedar in the hearts of those who, by the fragrance of devotion, cast away evil suggestions like serpents; in a thornbush, in the hearts of penitents; in myrtle, in those of the continent; in olive, in the merciful; in fir, in contemplatives; in boxwood, in believers. He nested in cedar in the demoniac; in thornbush in the wilderness; in myrtle before Caiaphas and Pilate; in olive, in the woman caught in adultery; in fir before Peter, James, and John; in elm, when he bore our pains on the cross; in boxwood, when he endured the lot of death.

He is also found on the ground [Col. 0762B], because Christ nests not only in contemplatives but also in those active in good works. Zacchaeus came down from the tree in order to receive him as a guest; Peter went into the sea in order to reach him. The Samaritan visited the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho; and he permits the sinner to be carried captive even to Babylon, and delivers him there. Thus he also rebukes the presumption of Elijah, who said: “Lord, they have killed your prophets; they have dug down your altars; and I alone remain” (3 Kings 19). And the divine response says to him: “I have reserved for myself many thousands of men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (ibid.).

It follows:

“And the mother sitting above upon the young.” The mother of the nest is the Virgin Mary, because from the substance of her flesh the nest of humanity came forth [Col. 0762C]. Of this it is written: “In my little nest I shall die, and like the palm tree I shall multiply my days” (Job 29). She has therefore sat upon the young and eggs as often as she brought holy thoughts to action by the warmth of love: there are as many young as works, and as many eggs as thoughts.

If, therefore, you find such a mother sitting upon them, you shall not take her with the children, because “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of the winged creatures”; much more so before her wings, who “flew upon the wings of the winds”; much more before her power, which transcends the blessedness of all spirits, both human and angelic. For although likeness is promised, equality in reality is denied. For if a likeness of equality is promised you [Col. 0762D], the reality is nevertheless [lacuna] denied. For of her it is said: “You have been exalted, holy Mother of God, above the choirs of angels, into the heavenly kingdoms.” For other human beings, it is already much if they reach as far as the choirs of angels.

You shall not, therefore, take hold of her, because you cannot; because, even if you exerted yourself to breaking, you could not attain to her grace or glory, merit or reward, struggle or prize. Those who belong to her party do indeed imitate the perfect holiness of the Mother of God, and each does so more perfectly the more perfect he himself is. Yet although all strive to resemble her, none can equal her.

Hence it is written in the book of Joshua that, when the children of Israel were about to cross the Jordan, heralds passing through the midst of the camp began to cry: “When you see the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, and the priests of the Levitical stock carrying it, rise up also and follow those going before; and let there be between you and the ark a space of two thousand cubits, so that you may see from afar and know by what way you must go” (Josh. 3) [Col. 0763A]. The ark of the covenant, therefore, is she of whom it is written:

> Blessed Mother by her office,  
> Whose heavenly maker,  
> Holding the world in his fist,  
> Was enclosed beneath the ark of her womb.  
> *(Office of the Church)*

This ark went before the people, because she was higher both in gifts of virtues and in the excellence of rewards. A space is left between the ark and the people because no one is joined to her holiness. In that interval two thousand paces are counted, because her perfect sanctification, inwardly and outwardly, surpasses the grace of others. Thus all are commanded: “Beware lest you approach the ark” (Josh. 3).

Nevertheless, you shall keep the young when captured, because you shall imitate her virtues. Consider that she confesses herself a handmaid, though she knows herself to be a queen. She went with haste into the hill country, into the city of Judah, to minister to Elizabeth, who ought to have ministered to her. Learn patience from her example when the sword of suffering passed through her soul, since she is recorded neither to have murmured nor cursed. Learn devotion from her example when she kept all the words spoken concerning Christ, pondering them in her heart. These are the young [Col. 0763C] whom you are bound to keep when captured, so that it may go well with you.

For then you will keep them captured when you fulfill them in deed, because it is written: “Say to the righteous that it is well, because he shall eat the fruit of his devices” (Isa. 3). For one eats the fruit of his devices who thus seeks and finds, and fulfills in deed what is sufficient. “And may you live a long time”: nothing is longer than eternity. Thus it will go well with you when you receive a hundredfold in this life, and you will live a long time when you possess eternal life.

## SERMON XXXI. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

“Shallum son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, built the Fountain Gate” (2 Esdras 3). “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, is a thief and robber. But he who knocks at the door—to him the doorkeeper opens; and he shall enter and go out and find pasture” (John 10).

The sheepfold, beloved brothers, is that in which the good shepherd left the ninety-nine sheep and came to seek the hundredth which had perished. The door of this sheepfold is he who says of himself: “I am the door” (John 10). Let us therefore knock at this door, beloved; let us knock by prayers, let us knock by works. Let us enter in order to meditate well; let us go out in order to act well; and we shall find the pastures of heavenly teaching in order to live well. “Knock, and it shall be opened to you”; and “enter his gates with confession,” he who exalts you from the gates of death, “that you may proclaim all his praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.”

But before you knock at his gates [Col. 0764A], set a guard upon your own gates, lest perhaps the strong armed man or the sons of the Beerothite find the house of conscience empty and exposed to the passerby, enter in, and dwell there. Our gates are those concerning which Ezra commanded the children of Israel not to bring their burdens through their gates on the Sabbath day (2 Esdras 13). And rightly so: whoever desires to possess the rest of contemplation and inward brightness ought not to admit, through sight, vanity; through hearing, curiosity; through smell, pleasure; through taste, gluttony; or through touch, impurity. Unless they are diligently guarded, sin will immediately be present at the doors.

Therefore let us entrust them not to a negligent doorkeeper-woman, but to a diligent male doorkeeper, fearing and keeping before our eyes that the woman doorkeeper who was cleaning wheat fell asleep (2 Kings 4); or certainly that the doorkeeper of Caiaphas compelled Peter, warming himself at the coals, to deny [Col. 0764B] (John 18). The strong and faithful doorkeeper is the fear of the Lord, whose maturity does not permit wandering. Its steadfastness is commended when it is said: “The fear of the Lord remains for ever and ever.” Its vigilance is commended where it says: “He who fears God neglects nothing” (Ecclus. 7). And rightly, because from the beginning of temptation to its end it does not abandon the mind entrusted to it, but keeps watch over it continually. From the beginning, because it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110). To the end, because it is written: “Let us hear together the end of the discourse: Fear God and keep his commandments; this is the whole human being” (Eccl. 12).

It is therefore the proper task of this faithful doorkeeper to close our gates, or, if they are opened, to lift them up when closed; for the Lord entered to his disciples while the doors were shut. In Ezekiel the closed gate is called praiseworthy [Col. 0764C], through which no man entered, but the prince himself sat in it to eat his bread. If you stop your ears lest you hear bloodshed, and close your eyes lest they see evil, the fear of the Lord closes your gates well. Job closed his gates well when he said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think of a virgin” (Job 31). And the Psalmist: “I became mute, and did not open my mouth” (Ps. 38). For Phinehas, whose name means “mute mouth,” made atonement, and the plague ceased. “The cultivation of righteousness is silence”; and “in silence and hope shall be our strength.”

But if the gates are opened, let them be lifted up, as it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes” (Ps. 8 [sic]). He who lifts his eyes to the mountains, whence his help may come; who raises his hands in the sanctuary, as it is written, “I will lift my hand to heaven” (Deut. 32)—he is one who lifts up his gates.

It follows:

“And enter his gates with confession” (Ps. 99). With confession of heart, of which it is written: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart” (Ps. 109). With confession of mouth, of which it is said: “I will confess the Lord greatly with my mouth” (Ps. 108). With confession of deed, lest we be among those of whom it is said: “They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Tit. 1): “Enter his gates with confession.” He explains elsewhere what his gates are, when he says: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered them, I shall confess to the Lord” (Ps. 117).
