For the gates of righteousness are his gates [Col. 0765A]. Whatever belongs to moral conduct, virtues, or good works: these are his gates. Among them patience was a gate through which Job entered to God; faith, through which Abraham entered; gentleness, through which Moses entered; humility, through which David entered. Through such gates the saints deserved an entrance to God.

But some gates of righteousness are temporal, others eternal. Temporal are those which shall be made void and destroyed, such as faith and hope. Eternal are love and its exercise. For to love God with all the heart, all the soul, and all the strength begins in this life, but will be brought to perfection in eternal life. In this life it can indeed be begun, but cannot be perfected or completed. Of such gates, therefore, it is said: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23), he who exalts you from the gates of death.

Just as virtues are called gates of righteousness, so also vices are gates. Five principal ones, however, are gathered from sacred discourse: the gate of greed, of pleasure, of obstinacy, of reproach, and of rejection. Of the first, it is read in the book of Judges that Samson carried the gates of Gaza to the summit of the mountain (Judg. 16). Of the second, in Daniel, where the he-goat raged at the gate of Ulai against the ram (Dan. 8). For Ulai is called a marsh, not from a stake (*palus*), but from a swamp (*palus*). Ulai, therefore, is the gate [Col. 0765C] of the swamp, by which the mire of pleasure is understood. Of the third it is said in the Psalm: “Because he shattered gates of bronze and broke iron bars” (Ps. 106). For bronze is inflexible and for that reason signifies the hardness of obstinacy.

Of the last two it is read in Zephaniah: “From the first gate,” he says, “there shall be a cry, and a wailing from the second” (Zeph. 1). For when the Lord comes to judgment, he will say to the wicked: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” etc. (Matt. 25). Then they themselves will cry out and say: “Woe to us! We fools thought their life madness: behold how they have been counted among the children of God” (Wis. 5). And when the Lord adds: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire,” then there shall be wailing. They will utter a bestial cry, because they lived bestially. At the first gate there shall be reproach; at the second, rejection. Reproach, when the Lord says: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food”; rejection, when he says: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire.” Then there shall be wailing.

From gates such as these the Lord exalts you, that you may proclaim his praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion (Ps. 9). Zion is interpreted “contemplation.” Now contemplation is of one kind enigmatic, of another anagogical. Hence it is named either from a mirror (*speculum*) or from a watchtower (*specula*). For when someone contemplates God “through a mirror in an enigma,” that is, through likenesses and images of things, contemplation is named from the mirror and is called enigmatic. This occurs in three ways: through similar likenesses, through similar unlikenesses, or through dissimilar likenesses.

Through similar likenesses, when someone strives to comprehend God [Col. 0766A] by means of something very like him, as by an angel. For just as God is subtle, swift, invisible, and incorporeal, so too is an angel. Hence the angel who appeared to Hagar is called God, as she herself says: “You are the God who saw me” (Gen. 21).

Through a similar unlikeness, however, when comparison is made by antithesis, that is, by contraries. For it is written that, once one of two contraries is known, the other also is known. Thus, if I am about to speak of God’s goodness, I first describe the devil’s wickedness, so that God’s goodness may taste sweeter in my mouth and become more clearly known. Hence the saying in the Gospel: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16).

Through dissimilar likenesses, when by means of some base and contemptible thing [Col. 0766B] we strive to grasp the greatness of God, so exalted and so lofty. Hence he compares himself to a worm and to a serpent. And what is more lowly than a worm or a serpent? Yet in the Psalm he says: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21). And in the Gospel: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 12).

Contemplation is named from a watchtower when the mind is so raised upward that, with no preceding signs and no supporting causes, cleansed of every image, it is simply and reciprocally referred to the superessential and infinite source. This is treated in many places in the *Soliloquy* [lacuna]; it belongs indeed to very few, and is called anagogical, from *ana*, “upward,” and *agoge*, “leading.” It can scarcely happen that [Col. 0766C] Rachel, coming from her father’s house and hastening to the land of promise, can set out without the images of Laban.

The contemplative soul, therefore, is the daughter of Zion; she must enter by many gates into the degrees of contemplation. And unless through those gates she comes to the vision of peace, she will sing God’s praises in vain, for “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.”

Hence in Jerusalem, which is interpreted “vision of peace,” there was a multitude of gates: namely, the Old Gate, the Cloudy Gate, the Horse Gate, the Gate of the Shield-bearers, the Fish Gate, the Dung Gate, the Gate of the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and the Fountain Gate. Whoever wishes to contemplate God must enter toward God through one of these gates.

“Glorious things have been spoken of you, city [Col. 0766D] of God, because the Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tents of Jacob” (Ps. 85). Glorious things have been spoken of you, contemplative soul, who are full of virtues as though of citizens, surrounded by a wall of strength, and adorned with such gates.

The first gate was called Old. But in what sense old? “That which is becoming old and growing aged is near to destruction” (Heb. 8). The Savior came to baptism, renewing the old man. Such oldness is most evil: namely, original sin, which persists from the first human being to the last and is not removed in any person, even after baptism. In baptism, indeed, it cannot be removed so that it does not exist; rather, it is weakened so that it does no harm. After baptism it remains for punishment, not for guilt; it remains in act, not in liability. Actual [Col. 0767A] sins, if they are present in act, must necessarily be present in liability; but they can be present in liability even if they are not present in act. Original sin, however, can be present in act and not in liability; but if it is present in liability, it must necessarily be present in act.

Therefore in the prayer [Note: [Col. 0767D] In the Mass of the Nativity of the Lord.] we ask that the new birth of the incarnate Word may free those whom an old bondage holds beneath the yoke of sin.

But there is also a praiseworthy oldness, of which we read in the Song of Songs: “All fruits, new and old, I have kept for you, my beloved” (Song 8). And in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. 13).

The Old Gate, therefore, is the Church of God, which endures from the first righteous person to the last: militant, expectant, triumphant. Militant in the world, expectant in purgatory, triumphant in heaven. For it is the house [Col. 0767B] founded upon firm rock. The floods came and the winds blew, but it did not fall, because the wise man founded it upon rock. At this Old Gate the Ancient of Days sits with his elders: that is, God the Father rests there with his angels, who remained after the fall of the apostate.

There the very oldest things of the old are consumed, because the offering of bread and wine which the priest Melchizedek offered before the Law to our father Abraham is daily transubstantiated in the Church into the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence the same Lord who commanded these things to be done was called: “A priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

It is therefore necessary that we enter through this gate into the vision of peace, namely through the faith of the Church; for one who does not enter through it does not deserve to possess the riches of heavenly glory. For there silver has the sources of its veins, and there is a place for gold where it is refined.

The second gate was called Cloudy: namely, that gate of which it is said, “Let his children be far from safety, and be crushed at the gate” (Job 5). He calls Christ the gate, without whom there is no entrance to the vision of peace, or to the peaceful vision. Hence we end all prayers “through our Lord Jesus Christ,” because only through him is the entrance to the heavenly kingdom open.

It was called Cloudy for many reasons, since *nebulosa*, “cloudy,” is derived from cloud. It was called Cloudy either because of the profound secret of the divine counsel; or because of the obscurity of the prophets, who foretold what was to come concerning him; or because of the hidden and unexpected fruitfulness of the Virgin; or because of his ascent, which is naturally in the clouds; or because of the pouring forth of rain; or because of the swiftness of clouds.

Because of the profound secret of the divine counsel, as it is written: “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One” (Isa. 45): that is, let him of whom it is written descend from on high like rain, through the profound secret of the divine counsel: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17), that is, obscure knowledge in the prophets; because of the hidden fruitfulness of the Virgin. Hence it is written: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud” (Isa. 19). Because of [Col. 0768A] the ascent, moreover, since it is written: “Who makes the cloud his ascent, who walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103). Because of the outpouring of rain, because “he descended like rain upon the fleece.” Because of swiftness, because it is written: “Call his name: Hasten to take away the spoils, swiftly to plunder” (Isa. 8). Hence in the Gospel: “As lightning appears from the east unto the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be” (Matt. 24).

The third gate was called that of Horses. Horses are those who, by enduring, confessing, and preaching, bore the Lord throughout the whole world; they ran in the way of God’s commandments. “Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world,” because their word ran swiftly.

Job describes by the likeness of a strong horse the virtues of such persons [Col. 0768B], saying: “The glory of his nostrils is terror; he digs the earth with his hoof; he exults boldly. He goes to meet the armed men. Above him the quiver will sound; spear and shield will flash. He does not regard the trumpet’s sounding blast; but when he hears the horn, he says: Ha!” (Job 39).

Thus the glory of his nostrils is terror, because he glories in the terror of adversity which he foreknows will come upon him. He digs the earth with his hoof, because by the example of his works he shakes off earthly thoughts. He exults boldly, because he is worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus. He runs to meet the armed, because he manfully withstands the devices of spiritual enemies. Above him sounds the quiver, by which he preaches to us divine [Col. 0768C] mysteries. The spear flashes when he drives the devil from his borders; the shield too flashes when he protects himself from the devil’s snares. He does not regard the trumpet’s sounding blast, because he makes little of the threats of the powerful; but when he hears the horn, he says, “Ha!” because when he hears of tribulation prepared for him, he exults. “Ha!” is indeed a cry of exultation.

Zechariah saw such horses in the spirit, namely white, dappled, pale, and red (Zech. 6): by the white understanding virgins; by the red, martyrs; by the pale, the abstinent; and by the dappled, those who pleased God according to diverse virtues, as Abraham by faith and Job by patience. Blessed are those who have deserved to enter this gate, who have had such an entrance into the vision of peace.

The fourth was that of the shield-bearers. A shield-bearer is named from a shield. Shield-bearers are those who have been eternally predestined by God; or are protected by God; or temporally protect others; or who, with God’s aid, fight manfully against the ancient enemy. Of those eternally predestined the Psalmist says: “Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5). Of those protected in time he says elsewhere: “His truth shall surround you with a shield” (Ps. 90). Of a man’s battle elsewhere: “Take hold of weapons and shield, and rise up to help me” (Ps. 34). Hence in the Song of Songs: “A thousand shields hang upon it” (Song 4), that is, upon the Church: the whole armor of the strong.

Shield-bearers, therefore, are those who have been predestined by God, or deserve to be protected, or do not desist from spiritual warfare, [Col. 0769A] fortified by God’s help. O truly happy are those who enter Jerusalem through the gate of the shield-bearers, that is, into the vision of peace! Yet let the shield-bearer beware, while he is still girded for battle, lest by Nahash’s counsel he pluck out his right eye and hide it beneath the shield on his left (1 Sam. 2). For in battle such a one-eyed man differs in no respect from a blind man.

He who, at the prompting of the ancient serpent, plucks out his own right eye does not fight for a heavenly reward, but for temporal gain. For the right eye signifies the understanding of heavenly things, and the left that of earthly things.

There follows the Fish Gate. A fish is one who, among the waves of this great and wide sea, raises himself from the depth with the little wings of hope and defends himself from the waves with the scales of patience. The first and greatest of these was he whose heart, gall, and liver drive out every kind of demon. For who, considering the love and affection of Christ’s heart toward us—of whom it is written, “They offered him a piece of broiled fish” (Luke 24)—or the shedding of his blood as a liver, or the bitterness of his passion as gall, all of which were roasted over the coals of charity, would not repel every demon? Truly its smoke, that is, the report of his love, banishes all sophistries or phantasms of spiritual wickedness.

There follows the Dung Gate.

The Dung Gate was that through which the city’s refuse was carried outside. You know, brothers, that the saints account whatever is in the world as dung. Hence the Apostle: “I have accounted all things as dung, that I might gain Christ” (Phil. 3). What else, then, is an accumulation of riches, honors, or dignities, but as it were an accumulation of dung, a dung-heap? Hence Tobit is read to have been blinded by the warm dung of a swallow: by warm dung, that is, by an excessive passion of avarice. Therefore his wife complains, saying: “Would that that money had never existed, for which you sent our son to travel abroad—the light of our eyes, the staff of our old age!” (Tob. 5).

And it is rightly said to have been swallow’s dung, because the swallow acquires its living by flying. The swallow, then, rightly signifies those who, though established in this pilgrimage only in body, [Col. 0769D] acquire sustenance for themselves through the thought and eagerness of the soul. Hence John the Baptist also, who, though raised above bodily weight, was wholly journeying toward God, is signified by the swallow, as is read in Jeremiah: “The turtledove and swallow, kite and stork, have known the time of their coming; but Israel has not known me” (Jer. 8).

[Note: [Col. 0769D] Augustine, Sermon on the Purification.] By the turtledove, namely the groaning bird, Simeon is signified, who said: “Do you think I shall see? Do you think I shall endure?” He knew the time of the coming of grace when he said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2).

By the kite, which lives by snatching, is signified that greedy and avaricious Balaam, who, led by avarice alone, gave Balak counsel against Israel. Yet he knew the time of the coming of grace when he said: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel” (Num. 24).

The stork, which feeds upon poisonous creatures, signifies the poisonous and great Sibyl, who nevertheless foretold the Lord’s coming, saying:

> From heaven the King shall come, destined to be through the ages,
>
> Present, indeed, in the flesh, to judge the world.

For thus our enemies ought to have been judges of the faith; hence those who would not believe even their own witnesses deserved to be condemned by a just judgment among the faithful.

By the swallow John is signified, because he had a red neck in his beheading, a white belly in virginity, and a black back under the burden of labor. He therefore knew the time of the coming of grace when he said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

Thus the Lord bestowed the charisms of charity upon friends and enemies alike, so that no one can excuse himself from faith and love of him. The Dung Gate, therefore, is an entrance or exit to the dung-heap of temporal grace. At it the avaricious often sit when they consider how deceitful are worldly honors, how treacherous riches, how momentary pleasures, in order that they may thus scrape them from their consciences and remove them from their hearts.

Thus Job sat on the dung-heap, scraping away the discharge—that is, the rottenness of the dung-heap—with a potsherd—that is, with the stern discipline of penitence. Or vices are signified by the dung-heap, as is read of the sinner in Job: “And in the end he shall perish like dung” (Job 20). The Dung Gate, therefore, is the prelates to whom sinners confess their vices. For through them, as through a gate, the dung of sins is carried out.

See, most beloved, see what place they hold in God’s Church who today grow proud of the Crucified One’s patrimony. In the tabernacle there are goat-hair coverings; in Noah’s ark a dung-room; in Jerusalem, a Dung Gate. Why are you proud, furnace-sweep? Why are you proud, priest of the Old Testament? It was the priests’ task to offer sacrifice outside the camp; yet they themselves remained unclean until evening. Thus the furnace-sweep cleans the furnace, but becomes all the more unclean and filthy.

Such are those who consume the sins of the people and receive the confessions of others. Yet not all are such; for as neither winter harms the laurel nor the fire burns gold, so the infusion of vices does not touch the hearts of saints. They do not feel them by suffering when such things are told to them, but rather by compassion. Yet it is difficult to touch pitch and not be defiled by it.

There follows the Gate of the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Of it we read thus in Joel, where the Lord says: “I will gather all, and lead them out into the valley of Jehoshaphat, because there I shall sit to judge all the nations round about” (Joel 3). Some, understanding this saying childishly, falsely assert that the Lord’s judgment must take place on earth, namely in the valley of Jehoshaphat, which lies beside the Mount of Olives; whereas the Apostle says to the Thessalonians that it will occur in the expanse of this air.

For he says: “We who live, who remain unto the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep; for the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first. Then we who live, who remain, shall together with them be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thess. 4).

Behold, it is plainly said that judgment will occur in the air. Yet the Lord says that he will plead with the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat because Jehoshaphat is interpreted “judgment,” and it is called a valley. It is rightly called a valley because when or how it will occur is hidden from us. Hence it is written: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (Luke 12). Therefore he will plead with the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat because he will judge them with a hidden judgment.

[Col. 0771B] Hence it is written: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35). Judgment is therefore to be feared all the more because it is hidden. “The lion will roar: who will not fear?” Who will stand to behold him, before whose sight the stars are not clean, and in whose angels he finds perversity? How much more unclean and perverse are those who inhabit houses of clay and have an earthly foundation, whose righteousnesses shall appear like a drop from a bucket and like the cloth of a menstruous woman, when he speaks with enemies in the gate, when he comes to judgment with his elders, as it is written: “Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. 31).

And truly in the gates, because all people shall come forth from the gates: namely, the sons of men, fellow judges with the Son of Man, as it is written: “You who have left all things shall sit upon seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

From the Old Gate angels shall come forth, accusing sinners because they would not believe their admonitions. From the Cloudy Gate, prophets, accusing them because they would not assent to their prophecies. From the Horse Gate, apostles, accusing them because they did not assent to their preaching. From the Gate of the Shield-bearers, martyrs, accusing them because they would not suffer for the Lord according to their examples. From the Fish Gate, confessors, accusing them because by their examples they did not possess their souls amid the waves of this great and wide sea through patience. From the Gate [Col. 0771D] of the Valley of Jehoshaphat virgins shall come forth, accusing them because they corrupted their souls not only by bodily fornication but also by spiritual fornication.

Why then, miserable people, do you not fear with the foolish virgins that saying by which it shall be said: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25), and the door shall be shut? The door of heaven shall indeed be shut to you, who by iniquity, hypocrisy, and unbelief open for yourselves the gates of hell.

For your iniquity is an open and manifest gate of hell, as it is written: “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me” (Ps. 68). That this is a gate is made clear elsewhere when it is said: “Let the wicked be ashamed and be led down into hell” (Ps. 30), that is, they shall be ashamed and shall be led down into hell. For this must be understood not optatively but prophetically [as in the saying]: [Col. 0772A] “Let deceitful lips be made dumb, which speak iniquity against the righteous in pride and contempt” (ibid.).

Hypocrisy also is a gate of hell, as was prefigured in the gate where Absalom, a dissembler in speech, deceived by hypocrisy those coming for judgment. Unbelief likewise is a gate and entrance into hell. At it perished the ruler of Samaria, who would not believe Elisha when he promised abundance in time, but said: “Even if the Lord opened the floodgates of heaven, what you promise could not happen” (4 Kings 7).

What then must we do, brothers? Let us flee from corruption to correction, from direction to direction, through desire for heavenly life, to the refuge from the crime of our human [race], to the refuge of our aid against crime: namely, to the Fountain Gate, the harbor of salvation, the harbor of health.

What is this Fountain Gate? It is that gate which Sellum built—the glorious Virgin, whose nativity today is a memory in blessing. Of her it is said elsewhere:

> You are the gate of the high King,
>
> And the shining gate of light.

Of this gate we read thus in Ezekiel: “This gate shall be shut, and shall not be opened. No man shall enter through it; the prince shall sit in it, to eat his bread” (Ezek. 44). It is rightly shut, because she was not corrupted before giving birth, in giving birth, or after giving birth. It was not opened because she did not lose her virginity. No man entered through it because she conceived without male seed. The Prince sat in it because the Prince of kings humbled himself in her womb. There [Col. 0772C] he ate his bread, because he fulfilled his Father’s will, as it is written: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4).

It is rightly called the Fountain Gate because it was a gate of sacred instruction, a gate of charity, and a gate of life. Of instruction, concerning which it is written: “Let the fountains of your well be carried abroad” (Prov. 5). Of charity, of which we read: “A private fountain, in which a stranger has no share.” Of life, as we read in the Psalm: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35).

Hence the glorious Virgin herself is called a fountain of gardens, and rightly so; because she does not cease to water the garden of nuts, the garden of fruits, and the garden of spices: of nuts, because the sword of the Passion passed through her soul; of fruits, when [Col. 0772D] she went up into the hill country in haste and ministered to Elizabeth; of spices, when she kept in her heart, pondering them, all the words spoken concerning Christ.

This Fountain Gate, therefore, Sellum built. He built it, that is, he made it a temple, a dwelling and bridal chamber, because with love of God she kept the commandments, as it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). For Christ came forth from the Virgin’s womb like a bridegroom proceeding from his bridal chamber.

Sellum built her. Sellum is interpreted “peaceful.” And who is this peaceful one except he in whose type the Psalmist sings: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” [Col. 0773A] (Ps. 119)? For he is not only peaceful, but peace itself, as the Apostle says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2).

He left us the peace of the breast, which makes one patient, concerning which it is written: “Pursue holiness and peace, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12). This peace was left to those laboring in the world. Hence in the Mass for the Dead the peace is not given, because the dead have no need of peace of the breast but of the peace of eternity.

Hence it is written: “The bodies of the saints were buried in peace” (Ecclus. 39), that is, in the most certain hope of eternal peace. He left the one peace and gave the other, as it is written: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14).

But peace of the present age he neither left nor gave, as it is written: “I came not to send peace, but a sword.” Nor did he wish to give it, because that peace is always imperfect, feigned, defiled, criminal, or disordered. Imperfect, because the flesh always desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. Feigned, like that of those who love one another for the enticement of the flesh. Criminal, in those who are at peace with one another for theft, robbery, or another crime. Disordered, when we do not love those who love us, or do not love what ought to be loved, or love less-worthy things more, or more-worthy things less.

Who this Sellum is is shown when he is called “son of Cholhozai.” Cholhozai is interpreted “seeing all things” or “providing all things.” What, then, does he signify except God the Father? Hence Job says: “He is wise in heart and strong in might” (Job 9). For he sees all things who knows all things before they come to pass. He sees all things through wisdom; he defends all things through power. Knowledge and power, indeed, as with two keys, shut or open the treasure of the heavenly kingdom. “He shuts, and no one opens; he opens, and no one shuts.”

Hence he gave these keys to Peter and his successors, saying: “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16).

Hence Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, in a type of the Church killed Sisera with a nail and a hammer: with the nail of knowledge and the hammer of power. With the nail, I say, of knowledge, because it is written: “The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails driven deep” (Eccles. 12).

Both keys are necessary to Peter’s successors. Whoever has knowledge without power lacks a key, but not a nail; whoever has power without knowledge lacks a key, but not a hammer. For knowledge without power is a nail in a blind man’s eye; power without knowledge is a hammer in a madman’s hand.

Sellum, therefore, was rightly the son of Cholhozai: that is, he was the son of him who understands all things and is all-powerful—not by imitation, not by adoption, not by teaching, not by grace, but by nature. Although it was by grace that, being human, he was the Son of God, he was nevertheless not the Son of God by grace but by nature.

Yet the Apostle says: “Who was predestined Son of God in power” (Rom. 1). This must be understood in this sense: that it was predestined by God’s power that, being human, he should be the Son of God.

There follows the matter of dignity:

**Prince of the district of Maspha.** Note that “prince” is understood in many ways. It can be derived from *principium*, “beginning.” Hence Christ is called prince of the kings of the earth, and elsewhere says: “I am the beginning, I who also speak to you” (John 8). And in the Apocalypse: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1).

It can also be derived from *praecipio*, “I command.” Hence the apostles are called princes because they preached God’s commands. It can also be derived from *praecipitium*, “a precipice.” Hence the devil is called prince of the world because he hurls down those who love him. Therefore it is written: “The prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12).

Yet “prince” seems to be derived from “beginning,” because it is written: “He was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8). But “from the beginning” means “after the beginning,” as in [Note: [Col. 0773D] Aristotle, *Categories*.] “There is no predication from primary substance,” that is, after primary substance. And there:

> O Janus, whose back no stork has pecked,  
> Persius, *Satires* I.58,

that is, behind the back.

Sellum, therefore, was prince of the district of Maspha. A district (*pagus*) is named from *pege*, “spring.” Hence pagans are called, as it were, *pegeni*, because they used to establish villages near springs. Hence Isaac is read to have dug wells.

Sellum, then, was prince of the district of Maspha, that is, of the spring of Maspha. Maspha is interpreted “contemplation.” Hence it is said of Christ in the Psalm: “His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. [Col. 0774C] 75). Zion and Maspha have the same interpretation. The dwelling of Zion, the district of Maspha; the prince of the district of Maspha, the prince of the dwelling of Zion.

Whenever, therefore, you place Christ before all things in your heart, contemplate him with devotion, and faithfully and devoutly consider his deeds, you dwell in the habitation of Zion, or in the district of Maspha, and rest in peace.

For of the watchtower of prelacy it is written in Ezekiel: “I have appointed you a watchman over the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3); of contemplation, however, in Isaiah: “Set a table for yourself, and contemplate from the watchtower” (Isa. 21); and of circumspection in Jeremiah: “Set yourself a watchtower, place before yourself bitterness, and direct your heart in the straight way” (Jer. 31).

Therefore, most beloved, let us place Christ before all things; let us contemplate him; let us consider his power, his wisdom, and his goodness. Let us direct our way into the straight way, that we may dwell in Zion and in the district of Maspha, with the prince of the district, Jesus Christ our Lord, leading and going before us. He lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

“A star in the midst of a cloud” (Ecclus. 50). “Mary, sprung from royal stock, shines forth” (*Office of the Church*).

Whenever, most beloved brothers, you choose, in coming to hear the word of consolation, the consolation of God’s word, you ought not to consider who speaks, but what is spoken. For leprous men [Col. 0775A] preached a word of consolation at the gate of Samaria; but that ruler upon whose hand the king leaned incurred death because he would not believe. An Amalekite, too, weary on the journey, became commander of David’s army (4 Kings 7). That city also which used to speak the language of Canaan became a city of the sun: namely, the Gentile world, when a language that dries up, illumines, and kindles spoke to us—drying up our iniquity, illuminating truth, kindling charity.

And fittingly, because so great is the glory of the cherubim that its voice can often be heard in the outer court, according as the Lord sends his crystal like morsels, brings bread out of the earth, or out of the rock, and oil out of the hardest stone. Thus an ass often sees an angel whom a human being does not see; for just as the swallow and the turtledove knew the time of Christ’s coming, so too did the kite and the stork.

By the swallow I mean John the Baptist; by the turtledove, Simeon; by the kite, Balaam; and by the stork, the Sibyl. These preached wondrously concerning God: John, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1); Simeon, “Now dismiss [your servant]” (Luke 2); Balaam, “A star shall arise from Jacob”; the Sibyl:

> “From heaven the King shall come, destined to be through the ages.”

For it is commonly said: “The sluggish pig often finds a good root.” By these pigs I mean those who, not by chewing the cud but as though digging in the earth—that is, investigating earthly things—dug up for us the root of Jesse and showed us how Mary, sprung from the root [Col. 0775C] of Jesse, shines forth.

Hermes and Asterius, philosophers of the king of Persia, proclaimed this feast of the glorious Virgin with many worthy praises, whether from the greatness of their learning or from a spirit of prophecy which they might have received from the Spirit—and, if perhaps not in the Spirit, in many ways nevertheless they proclaimed: namely, concerning the Virgin’s birth, the fullness of time, the giving of the name, the nobility of her lineage, the pursuit of spiritual learning, the practice of temporal life, the place where the gold of her wisdom was refined, and finally the consummation of true, certain, and complete blessedness.

For Asterius says: “Under the decan of Virgo there shall arise a certain girl, who in the Persian tongue is called *Sedeozordama*, but in Arabic *Adrevedefa*, sitting upon a gilded throne, holding two ears of grain in her hand; and rightly feeding her son in the place called ‘Hail’; and they shall call the child Jesus.”

Hermes, with a few words changed, spoke thus concerning the same virgin: “Under Virgo there shall be born a certain girl, called *Corcisclastalis*, sitting upon the public road; bearing ears of grain in both hands; granting her son the right to feed in the land of the Hebrews; and they shall call the son Jesus.”

A third poet, whose name is Albumazar, agrees with them, saying: “Under the decan of Virgo there shall arise a virgin mother; she suckles her father and sits with him upon the same throne, no man touching her.”

Hear, most beloved brothers, leprous men proclaiming the praise of Christianity, Amalekites as leaders on the journey of Catholic faith, asses seeing angels [Col. 0776A] of God, storks crying out wondrously. Suck honey from the rock; anoint yourselves with oil from the hardest stone; break crystalline morsels and eat bread from the earth. For the truth of Catholic faith is so glorious that our enemies are its judges; and in the mouth of three witnesses stands the word of glory and the testimony to the glorious Virgin.

For where it says, “there shall arise,” her birth is commended; the fullness of time, where it adds, “under the decan of Virgo”; the giving of the name, where it adds, “Sedeozardama, etc.”; nobility of lineage, when it goes on, “sitting upon a gilded throne”; the pursuit of spiritual learning, where it adds, “holding two ears of grain in her hand”; temporal activity, where it says, “and rightly feeding her son”; the place of her wisdom, where “Hail” is placed; and the consummation of blessedness, where it says, “they shall call the child Jesus.”

Let us therefore hear and marvel at the stretching toward heaven of the stork’s neck, uttering this wondrous cry. It is certain that the sun rises in Virgo, namely in September, in which month the glorious Virgin was born. As to the phrase “the decan of Virgo,” I suppose that a decan is a tenth part of one of the degrees through which the sun rises in Virgo; for every sign has thirty degrees, and those degrees have their portions. Yet whether the poet meant degrees or portions of degrees, this is certain: Mary arose under Virgo.

You find something similar in the book of Kings, where it is said: “In the month Ethanim the ark of the covenant was placed in the house of the Lord” (3 Kings 8). I mean the ark of which it was said:

> Blessed mother in her privilege,
>
> Whose heavenly Maker,
>
> Holding the world in his fist,
>
> Was enclosed beneath the ark of her womb.

And it is called “of the covenant,” because in the secrecy of the virginal womb a covenant was made through the God-man, between God and man. For this ark was set in the temple of the Lord—that is, in the honour of God’s Church—when she was born and brought forth to the world. She herself was the king’s *Musac*, the priests’ *Corban*, the treasury of the poor, the ark of heavenly treasures. In the month *Bethanim*, that is, in the seventh month. Therefore, in the month Bethanim—that is, under Virgo—the glorious Virgin was born.

There shall therefore arise under Virgo a girl, or young maiden, concerning whom Solomon speaks thus in Proverbs: “Three things are difficult for me, and a fourth I wholly do not know: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the way of a ship in the midst of the sea” (Prov. XXX)—things which cannot without difficulty be discerned or discovered. But the fourth Solomon wholly did not know: namely, the way of a man in a young maiden. We are accustomed to say “in youth,” but the Hebrew corrects us more accurately: “in a young maiden.” For neither by nature, nor by Scripture, nor by reason could he understand that the Lord had made a new thing upon earth: namely, that a young maiden encompassed a man—the man, I mean, of whom it is written: “Behold the man; Orient is his name” [or “his name is the Rising”] [Col. 0777A] (Zech. VI). Hence Josephus: “In those days there was Jesus, a wise man—if indeed it is lawful to call him a man—and a teacher of those who gladly hear what is true; he was a worker of marvellous deeds.” And thus he concludes: “This was the Christ.”

This maiden, then, was called *Sedeozardima Adrevedefa*, or *Corcisclastalis*; for these three words are synonymous and have one interpretation. They mean “a pure and honourable virgin,” concerning whom Jeremiah gave the Egyptians a sign that their idols must be uprooted when a virgin should give birth. Hence the priests of Egypt set up and worshipped, in the inner places of the temple, an image of the Virgin and her Son. And when Ptolemy asked them why they did this, they replied: “It is the mystery of a paternal tradition, which we received [Col. 0777B] from a holy prophet, and we believe that it will come to pass in this manner.” Hence Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII); or, as the Hebrews correct us more accurately: “Behold, an *alma* shall conceive.” For among the Hebrews a virgin was called a young woman who could be given in marriage; but a *bethula* was called an older woman who had not known a man. An *alma*, that is, “hidden,” was called one so concealed from the sight of men that there could be no suspicion that she had been defiled. Hence she is also called “holy *alma*”; and “holy” means “firm,” because it was firm and certain that she was incorrupt.

She was therefore a pure and honourable virgin. When the Lord instructed his disciples, he said: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” [Col. 0777C] (Luke XII), because men’s lust is in the loins and women’s in the navel. But she was pure and honourable, whose navel was cut off; and her lamps were burning, because she was one—and a singular one—of the prudent virgins: without stain, without wrinkle, without cosmetic paint. Without the stain of sin; without the wrinkle of duplicity; without the paint of deception. Or she was pure and honourable because she is wholly beautiful: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved; wholly beautiful” (Song IV). For as a notorious and shameless woman is wholly ugly, from the sole of her foot to the crown of her head, so a holy woman is wholly beautiful, from the sole of her foot to the crown of her head.

For what is uglier than that monster, redeemed by no virtue, which represents a serpent in twisted hair, has the eyes of a basilisk, the cheeks of a *pharea* [uncertain term], the nostrils of a sow, canine teeth, the lips of a siren, the breasts of a lamia, the hands of a wolf, the belly of a goat, muddy shins, and the feet of a peacock? Conversely, she is wholly beautiful who wounded her bridegroom’s heart with one lock of her neck, having dove’s eyes, turtle-dove cheeks, a nose like the tower of David, teeth like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing, scarlet lips, breasts like two twin kids of a she-goat, rounded hands, an ivory belly, marble shins, and straight feet. Or indeed she is wholly beautiful because she was glorified in body and soul: as full of grace, so full of blessedness. Grace could not be full unless blessedness were full. For if her decaying body had remained in the tomb, neither grace nor blessedness would be full. Her blessedness might perhaps be true and certain, [Col. 0778A] but not full; for then blessedness will be full, when, according to merit, the double garment is restored to a human being, and one is glorified in body together with soul. It follows:

“Upon a gilded throne,” that is, a royal throne. This is nobility of lineage, because she was a rod from the root of Jesse. Jesse, moreover, begot King David, concerning whose throne Isaiah speaks thus: “Upon the throne of David and over his kingdom the Lord shall sit” (Isa. IX). Hence: “Mary, sprung from royal stock, shines forth.” Therefore Albomazar says: “And beside the same throne sits a man who does not touch her”—that is, Joseph, who was born of the same royal stock. Hermes’s statement that she sat upon a public street informs us of the place of birth: because when she bore her Son, there was no place for her in the inn; rather, she sat upon a public street to give birth.

It follows: “Holding two ears of grain in her hand.” The two ears are the two Testaments, because, just as in an ear or awn grain is joined with chaff, so the sacraments lie hidden beneath the letter. The apostles rubbed these ears; hence the Jews murmured, since they are accustomed to cling more to the letter than to mysteries. Or, certainly, by ears of grain are signified the teachings of Scripture and works: teachings of Scripture, as Job says of heretics: “They take away ears of grain from the hungry” (Job XXIV), because heretics take from the hungry for good the teachings of Scripture by which they ought to fight against and overcome them. Works, moreover: we read that the leaders of the robbers, Rechab and Baanah, entered Ish-bosheth’s house and, taking [Col. 0778C] ears of grain, struck him in the groin (II Sam. IV), because evil spirits take away whatever good works a negligent person possesses and kill him by delight of the flesh. Hence the sons of Benjamin pursued the Ephraimites because they did not know how to pronounce *Scibboleth*: they said *sibboleth*, being unable to articulate “ears of grain” (Judg. XII). The sons of Benjamin—that is, sons of the right hand—seeing the Ephraimites, that is, heretics, struck them with the teachings of Scripture. For some carry these ears in their mouths by preaching, and others in their hands by working. Hence it is written: “The word which came by the hand of Haggai the prophet” (Hag. I). This Virgin, therefore, held ears of grain in both hands, she who shone in life and doctrine. It follows:

[Col. 0778D] “And she fed her Son with broth.” Hear: *Sedeozardima*, the pure and honourable virgin, feeds her Son; a virgin feeds her Son; a virgin mother suckles her Father. She feeds him *jure*, that is, with fatness. Thus we read that Jerubbaal, placing a kid’s flesh in a basket and the broth of the flesh in a pot, placed both wholly upon a rock; and the angel touched them with a rod, and fire consumed the flesh and the broth itself (Judg. VI). It should be understood that there are three kinds of fatness: external, properly called fat; internal, called suet; and that in the bones, marrow. External fatness is the movement of charity in action; internal fatness is the movement of charity in effect; marrow is the affection of loving in both movements. For just as it is worse deliberately to turn one’s mind downward to earth, so it is better to have the affection of loving [Col. 0779A] than merely to love. For as a trumpet is broad at its mouth, broader in the hand, and broadest beyond the hand, so the love of God ought to be broad in the mouth through preaching, broader through action, and broadest through affection and good will.

But if *jus* is named from justice, because Seneca says: “Justice is the virtue that renders to each person his due,” she feeds her Son with justice who renders to each person what is due: namely, *latria*—worship—to the Creator; *dulia*—veneration—to the creature; reverence to superiors; harmony to equals; peace to all. It follows: “In the place where it was said, ‘Hail.’” Behold the place where the Virgin’s gold of wisdom was smelted: namely, in the land of the Hebrews, where the angel says to her: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” But she is astonished, saying: “How shall this be?” and so forth. And the angel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you,” and so forth. And the Virgin: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” And, like a glowing dawn, she announced the day to come, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke I).

And this is the consummation of her blessedness: that her Son’s name was called Jesus, and it was called so by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. In all these ways, therefore, “Mary, sprung from royal stock, shines forth.” Mary means “illuminating,” or “illuminated,” or “star of the sea.” A star of the sea is called *transmontana*, by which sailors observe the state of the sea or the course of a ship. And truly a star is said to derive its name from standing, because it is said to stand, as it were, at the centre of the Zodiac; it does not move retrograde, but is fixed regularly and uniformly. [Col. 0779C] It is called the morning star because, in the preceding night, through it the dawn of the Sun of righteousness shone forth. It shone in the midst of the cloud: namely, between ignorance and despair. For the Gentiles at first did not know of Christ’s coming before the prophets arrived. But after the preaching of the prophets, while he delayed, they despaired; and then suddenly the morning star shone forth, glowing as from Jesse’s root. And truly from Jesse’s root—that is, from the root of fire; for Jesse means “fire.” We are wondrously kindled by the fire of this new planting, which was devoid alike of wood, hay, and stubble; and it kindles all who trust in her and believe that they can be aided by her merits, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. AT THE GENERAL CHAPTER

[Col. 0779D]

“If you see the daughters of Shiloh come forth, according to custom, to lead the dances, come suddenly out of the vineyards, and each of you seize for himself one wife; and go to the land of Benjamin” (Judg. XXI).

According to Gregory’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0779D] Homily 34 on the Gospels], true justice has compassion, false justice indignation. Thus brutality is sometimes disguised under severity, and indolence under gentleness, so that severity may be harsh and gentleness lax—although severity ought to govern gentleness, and gentleness to adorn severity. Our watchmen, paying too little attention to this, dig through our walls where an opening is exposed: either to bend those who stand erect or to cast down those already bent; or indeed to plaster without tempering, namely, with mud without straw. In both respects they deserve rebuke: either because they cannot dig with the unjust steward; or because, while cutting wood with the foolish prophet, the iron slips from their handle. For a bruised reed should be gently bound so that it is not broken; smoking flax should be vigorously kindled so that it is not extinguished.

Hence the children of Israel vigorously afflict the stubborn children of Benjamin; they receive penitents mercifully and do not reproach them. Therefore, after vengeance had been taken on sinners, the penitents were told: “If you see the daughters of Shiloh.” And since we have all sinned and need repentance, let us listen carefully to the counsel of repentance. Since living reason is the life of the good, it is necessary that, as through wicked works [Col. 0780B] we have been deformed from the image of our Maker and likened to senseless beasts, becoming like them, so through the examples of the good we may be re-formed into the same image, likened to heavenly angels and made of like form with them.

He says, therefore, “If you see”: not with bodily eyes, but with the understanding of the mind; not in effect, but rather in affection, recognise and understand the daughters of Shiloh—that is, souls which the Son of God formed by nature and re-formed by the outpouring of his blood; souls which, as imitating their Father, have shaped themselves in conduct according to their Father’s admonitions and conformed themselves in works to his examples. For this reason they are called daughters of Shiloh. Shiloh, indeed, is interpreted “sent,” “dismissed,” “asked for,” or “seed.” But the seed is the word of God, and the word of God is the Son of God. Therefore the seed is the Son of God. Hence Isaiah says (ch. I): “Unless the Lord had left us seed, we should have been like Sodom.” Since, therefore, the Son of God was asked for by the patriarchs and prophets, dismissed by the Jews, and sent to faithful Christians, souls both brought forth through the Gospel and born again through baptism are rightly called daughters of Shiloh.

He says, therefore: “If you see the daughters of Shiloh come forth, according to custom, to lead the dances,” etc. (Judg. XXI). What is signified by the dance but the mutable life of this world? This is Ezekiel’s wheel, around which the holy living creatures moved, and which he describes pointedly when he says: “In the vision of God I saw, and behold, a whirlwind wind was coming from the north, and a great cloud, and enfolding fire, and brightness round about it” (Ezek. I). He proposed that he had seen four things in the vision of God, two set against two: cold wind against the heat of fire, and the density of cloud against brightness. Wind and cloud, lest prosperity raise us too high; fire and brightness, lest adversity oppress us. For the wind coming from the north is the storm of temptation proceeding from the mind’s coldness; and the cloud is the blindness of mind resulting from temptation. But the fervour of fire enfolds both, because it kindles the cold heart and illuminates blindness. Yet brightness surrounds all, because the cheerfulness of good will brings the mind to devotion in both prosperity and adversity.

God sets brightness before you, that you may hope; fervour, that you may rejoice; the wind of temptation, that you may fear; the cloud of sin, that you may remove. You lead this dance, therefore, by straight paths if you so fear on account of the past that you rejoice in God’s mercy and hope in his promises; if you so grieve also over present things that you hope and rejoice at the same time; if you so rejoice also in God’s mercy that you are troubled over your own deed and fear future threats; and if you so hope that fear and sorrow likewise do not depart. For often, after the north wind, we return to fire; from the cloud we press toward brightness, because where sin has abounded, grace also is accustomed to abound. Often too fire is scattered by the wind and brightness by the cloud, because gold is darkened, its finest colour is changed into earthen vessels, the work of a potter’s hands.

The dances of the daughters of Shiloh must therefore be led according to custom, so that amid this world’s mutability and unstable life neither fear in temptations makes one faint-hearted nor sorrow for sin leads to despair. So too rejoice in good things, lest you be lifted up into pride; so too hope in God’s promises, lest you fall into the presumption of sinning. Behold how the daughters of Shiloh go forth to lead the dances. But if, as has been said, you see this, come out of the vineyards. There are vineyards of Sodom, whose wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps (Deut. XXXII). There are also vineyards that yielded wild grapes instead of grapes; no one doubts that it is good to come out of these.

But there is also the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, whose cluster is of *Cyprus* (*cyprus*, henna), whose vine is true, whose branches are the faithful; yet among them unbelievers frequently lurk, all the more to be feared and hated because they shoot the upright of heart in darkness. Of them the Bridegroom says under the figure of foxes: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song II). Such persons must come out of the vineyards if they see the daughters of Shiloh proceeding according to custom to lead the dances. Or this is so because there are sinners in the Church who are ashamed to disclose their sins through confession; but just as Adam hid himself among the trees of Paradise after his sin, so they wish to lurk among the branches of this vineyard and appear otherwise than they are. Such people must come out of the vineyards and uncover themselves; and, though naked and without virtues, they must not be ashamed to be seen by him from whose heat they cannot hide. It follows:

“And each of you seize for himself one wife” (Judg. XXI). [Col. 0781D] Behold, one must come out suddenly; nor are the daughters of Shiloh merely to be taken, but seized. For it cannot happen without violence that you are joined in such a marriage, that you are united to the fellowship of the saints; for the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. But do so without delay and suddenly—not seeking postponements or reprieves, but breaking the bonds of your occupations, saying with the Prophet: “You have broken my bonds; I will offer you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXV). Therefore bring upon yourself not unwilling violence but willing violence, seizing for yourself a suitable daughter of Shiloh.

Now briefly consider which are suitable for particular persons. There are some in the world, simple as well as poor, who nevertheless are strong in body and have learned to live by the labour of their hands. Others are not much accustomed to labour and not greatly educated in wisdom, but are wealthy. Others are weak in body and poor in resources, yet rich in understanding. Others are poor, weak, and simple, yet live innocently by the example of others. Therefore let each offer in the tabernacle according as God has disposed in his heart, because God willed that purple and hyacinth, as well as red-dyed skins and goats’ hair, should be offered to him. Some please God through the active life; others through the contemplative life. Indeed, some please God through the lower power of the active life, others through the lower contemplative power; some through the higher active power, others through the higher contemplative power. The lower power of the active life is bodily labour; the higher is the office of charity. The lower power of the contemplative life [Col. 0782B] is simplicity of heart; the higher is the devotion of contemplation.

Behold four modes of life: the first in Leah, the second in Martha, the third in Rachel, the fourth in Mary. These are the daughters of Shiloh leading the dances when they proceed according to custom. They proceed according to custom if they do not throw the dance into confusion. For some labour in order to serve their avarice, not to assist the needy. In these, Leah confuses the dance because she has not kept Martha. Others assist the poor, not from their own labours but from goods which they steal: Martha confuses the dance because she has not kept Leah. There are others who give alms from the works of their hands, but perhaps do so that their hidden crimes may not become known, or to obtain some temporal profit thereby. In these Leah has indeed kept Martha, but both nevertheless confuse the dance because she has abandoned Rachel. There are others who have learned from childhood to live without grave transgressions. Therefore they refuse to sweat in labour because they do not believe themselves to need repentance; and when they see others who are sinners, they are indignant and do not know how to have compassion on others because they themselves have not known suffering.

In these, then, Rachel confuses the dance because she has scorned to keep Martha and Leah. There are perhaps others, simple persons, who both give attention to labour and know how to have compassion, but neglect to devote themselves to holy thoughts, prayers, and psalmody: then Rachel confuses the dance because she has not kept Mary. [Col. 0782D] There are also others, learned in sacred utterances, who give attention to them not in order to fulfil them in deed or to live simply, but in order to have the first seats in the marketplace and be called Rabbi by men. In these Mary confuses the dance, for she has abandoned Rachel. There are others who devote themselves to contemplation in order to live simply; but while the mind rests inwardly through study, the flesh grows fat outwardly, broken by no labour. Thus the fat person is lifted up and casts the mind down from the mirror of contemplation, so that she who lifted her eyes to God no longer sees herself; and she lies sluggishly depressed beneath herself, though she had raised herself above herself into heavenly things. Therefore Mary confuses the dance if she neglects to keep Leah. There are others who so immerse themselves in temporal supports and become entangled in worldly cares that they scarcely, or never, direct themselves to God in prayers or meditations. In them Leah confuses the dance because she has abandoned Mary.

Do you see how the daughters of Shiloh lead the dance? We cannot all do everything. You can labour; Leah pleases you: receive her while she keeps Martha. You have the means to distribute to the poor; you love Martha: receive her, but between Leah and Rachel. Simplicity of heart pleases you; you wish to live simply: let it be so. Receive Rachel, but between Martha and Mary. You desire to devote yourself to psalmody and prayer; you wish to seize Mary from the dance: but then come out of the vineyards when she holds Martha on this side and Leah on that. Therefore let the daughters of Shiloh lead the dance, to the song of our Cithara-player. For he says: “You shall eat the labours of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” [Col. 0783B] (Ps. CXXVII). What are you doing, Leah? Break stubbornness through bodily labour; break the body in leading the dance. He also says: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor” (Ps. XL). What are you doing, Martha? Strip yourself, that you may proceed more lightly to lead the dance. He says again: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy mountain? He who is innocent in hands and clean in heart” (Ps. XIV). What are you doing, Rachel? Lead the dance according to custom, drawing your sides in with your hands, in tranquillity. He also says: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he shall nourish you” (Ps. LIV). For he knows well how to weigh the mind of one who suffers. What are you doing, Mary? Make light leaps, and lift yourself from the earth in the progress of your dance.

It follows: “And go into the land of Benjamin.” [Col. 0783C] What profit is there in doing all these things unless it is for the contemplation of the heavenly kingdom? Otherwise the labour would be great and the fruit none. Therefore, that labour may be small and the fruit great, as it is written: “The days seemed few to him because of the greatness of his love” (Gen. XXIX), go into the land of Benjamin, because the land of Benjamin is called the land of the sons of the right hand. But the sons of the right hand are those whom the Lord shall place at his right hand; their land is the land of the living and the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world, which he will restore when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. AT THE GENERAL CHAPTER

[Col. 0783D] “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I).

Fearing and reverencing him to whom the Father gave all judgment, judge justly, children of men. Fear, I say, your judge, fellow judges, because his judgments are a great abyss. For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor? Who, I ask, comprehends what is hidden and immovable, manifest and movable, hidden and movable, or manifest and immovable?

Hidden and immovable is the judgment by which he judges the predestined. For according to this judgment of predestination, he judged Peter, even when he denied him, worthy of love; but Judas the betrayer, even while working miracles, worthy of hatred. Manifest and movable, however, is the judgment exercised through action; and then he judges through secondary causes, that is, according to the present state of the one acting. Hence it is said: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III); and likewise to Hezekiah: “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live” (Isa. XXXVIII). Note that whenever judgments of this kind are made by God, understand them to have been pronounced conditionally. Thus, when it is said, “Yet forty days,” etc., supply the condition: “if it does not turn.” Likewise, “Set your house in order,” etc.: supply, “if you do not correct yourself.” Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “Even if I say to the sinner, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he turns and does penance, I shall not remember any of his sins” (Ezek. XXXIII). Understand the condition when he says, “If I say.”

Hidden and mutable is the judgment exercised according to cause. It is hidden because he judges sometimes according to lower and sometimes according to higher causes: according to lower causes, things simply impossible; according to higher causes, things possible to God. Or “impossible” things which are beyond nature, though not against nature, such as infusing initial grace or freeing a person from sins. Or those impossible things which are both beyond nature and against nature, but where divine power nevertheless assists nature’s powerlessness: namely, that a Virgin gave birth, or that Lot’s wife was changed into a pillar of salt. But things impossible for which divine power does not supply nature’s powerlessness—such as making a calf from a tree trunk—he judges neither according to lower nor according to higher [Col. 0784C] causes.

We call simply possible those things which occur according to the course and custom of nature, such as a human being born from a human being and an ox from an ox. But possible to God are things that occur not according to nature, but according to custom, such as the infusion of a soul into a body; for he judges this to occur according to higher causes. Manifest and immutable, however, will be the judgment according to retribution, when he renders to each according to his works, saying to some, “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. XXV), and to others, “Go, accursed ones.” Because of so many diverse and hidden judgments it is said: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXVI).

Yet amid all these diversities one sentence has been given to you all: “With the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged” (Matt. VII). Hence your justice must abound more than that of the scribes or Pharisees. For their justice was shaped by severity; yours must be shaped by love. Theirs had punitive judgment; yours must have either, rarely, dispensatory judgment, or always remissive judgment, as: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Luke VI). Hence it was said: “Love justice” (Wis. I). And what justice except justice that is to be loved—that is, shaped by love—not justice to be feared and shaped by severity?

Yet severity and love ought to accompany justice in such a way that neither is severity without love, nor love without severity. For if you have severity without love, you will be like the man who, cutting wood with the prophets in the forest, had the iron slip from its handle and kill his brother (Deut. XIX). For we cut wood when we examine others’ deeds; but the iron escapes the handle when action exceeds reason. It kills a brother when it makes him worse by that through which he ought to have been corrected. But if you have love without severity, you will be like the man who, cutting wood, had the iron slip from its handle into the water. For when we examine others’ deeds in such a way that action exceeds reason and, in judging, love without severity is maintained, laxity must follow, and thus the iron of reason is lost in water. Severity without love, therefore, is a scourge in the hand of a madman; love without severity is in the hand of one whose hand is withered. Therefore severity with love is justice to be loved, because it is shaped by love. Now justice is shaped by charity.

Now justice shaped by charity is that covenant about which God makes us concerned when he says: “When I have covered the sky with clouds, my bow shall appear in the clouds, and I shall remember my covenant which I made with you” (Gen. IX). We confess God to be impassible and immutable. He cannot increase, because he is supreme; nor diminish, because he is one; nor change place, because he is everywhere; nor change in time, because he is eternal; nor in thought, because he is most wise; nor in affection, because he is best. Hence James says: “With him there is no change or shadow of variation” (Jas. I). Therefore let us not suppose that, after the vigilance of remembrance, he should fall sick with the lethargy of forgetfulness, or that, after the disease of forgetfulness, he should recover again by the antidote of remembrance.

Nevertheless, he is said to remember his covenant in order to awaken sluggish human nature, which is always weak toward good and free toward evil; whose understanding is dull and whose memory is sodden in thanksgiving, a memory which no stork has sharpened in *antipelargosis*, that is, in the repayment of benefits. For if he calls himself concerned with the covenant by which he is bound to us through liberality alone and bare will, how much more ought the covenant by which we are bound to him by necessity make us concerned? What he owes us by covenant is induced by his will; but what we owe him by covenant is compelled by necessity itself. What he owes us by covenant is permissive justice; but what we owe him by covenant is compelling justice.

They call that permissive justice by which something is done justly, though it would not be unjust if it were done otherwise. But they call that compelling justice by which something is done justly, and if it were done otherwise, it would not be just. Thus God saves a person justly, because of the justice of power; if he wished to condemn that person, he would condemn him justly, because of the debt owed to the sufferer. Therefore, whom he saves, he saves justly because of the obligation of the agent; whom he condemns, he condemns justly because of the merit of equity.

Thus, by permissive justice, he either saves or condemns, because of either the obligation of the agent or the merit of the sufferer. Hence the covenant by which we are saved, when it has been entered into by agreement, is first made compelling justice through ratification, though it was permissive justice; so that I do not say it may be violated, but it is not even lawful to defer it. For how can you [Col. 0786A] violate a covenant that is secured by such earnest-money and so great a pledge; that rests alike on natural and civil reasoning; that is confirmed by stipulation, oath, and final will; that is completed by prescription, good faith, and just titles; that is clothed, as every covenant ought to be, with cause, words, writings, form, content, and confirmation; and that is finally observed inviolably under *mundiburd* and the praetor’s protection? Let us run through each point and examine this inviolable covenant.

The covenant of the patriarch Judah instructs us concerning earnest-money and pledge. By such a covenant he agreed with Tamar that he would send her a kid; he promised it and sent what he promised. And, lest he break the covenant, he gave a ring, bracelet, and staff as a pledge (*arrhabon*) (Gen. XXXVIII). Thus that universal Father, to whom in the Lord’s Prayer we say, “Our Father”—that patriarch, I say, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father”—made a covenant of this sort with the Synagogue. He had planted her as a chosen vine, but afterwards she turned into the bitterness of an alien vine; therefore Tamar is called “bitterness.” He covenanted with her that he would send her, in the likeness of sinful flesh, the Messiah in particular, like a kid for making the Passover. Hence he himself says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). Of him the Apostle says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V).

Meanwhile, until he carried the promise into effect, he gave the ring of faith, the bracelet of works, and the staff of the Law: the Law as a pledge, but faith and works as earnest-money. The difference usually assigned between pledge and earnest-money is that a pledge does not leave the jurisdiction of its giver, while earnest-money passes into the right of its recipient. Therefore, it belonged to him who gave the Law to fulfil the Law, because after the Messiah’s coming the Synagogue was no longer subject to the Law. She ought to have renounced the pledge once the promise was fulfilled; but he gave faith and action as earnest-money because, even after his coming, she was not released from faith and action. But miserable woman that she was, she carried back the staff and retained the pledge against the Law, because she wished always to remain subject to the Law.

Reason itself instructs us about such matters. For what does a staff suit a woman? It seems madness for a woman to carry a staff; but it was fitting for her to be adorned with bracelet and ring. The covenant rests on natural and civil reason: on natural reason, because, as the law says, [Col. 0786D] “Nothing is more fitting than to keep a covenant.” Natural law cries out: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another”; or, “What you wish done to yourself, do to another.” Unless a covenant is violated, these two always agree among those who make peace; otherwise they cannot keep a covenant—that is, an act of peace. Therefore fear and love compel us to observe this covenant.

And because it rests on civil reason, the person who abuses the privilege of granted goodness is deservedly crushed in his nature and wounded in natural things. For it is written: “He deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power granted to him.” Love also compels us for this reason: one who is known not to have acted against the act of peace ought to enjoy perpetual peace. But it rests on civil reasoning in this respect: the praetor proclaims, “Keep the covenant.” Who, then, so rash a presumptuous person, would dare to violate it if the praetor himself promises to uphold the covenant?

It is confirmed by stipulation, because when the priest said to us in baptism, “Do you believe in God?” and the answer was, “I believe”; “Do you renounce Satan?” “I renounce him”; “Do you wish to be baptized?” “I wish”: by all these stipulations we transferred ourselves from the devil’s jurisdiction and subjected ourselves to the divine covenant. It has also been confirmed by an oath. For “the Lord has sworn and will not repent” (Ps. CIX): the oath that he swore to Abraham, that he would give to us (Luke I)—and this has been done. For “a child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us.” For we have sworn and decreed to keep the judgments of his justice whenever we bound ourselves to him in the words of the Psalmist: “I have sworn and decreed to keep the judgments of your justice” [Col. 0787B] (Ps. CXVIII).

Let the rash violator therefore see to it that he is not convicted of perjury. It has also been sanctioned by a last will, for the law says: “Nothing is more properly owed to human beings than that the expression of their final will, when they can will nothing else, should be free, and that what no longer returns to their discretion should be lawful.” But the Apostle says: “The testament of Christ was confirmed in death” (Heb. IX). Thus we also, all who have been baptized, have been baptized into His death. The threefold immersion in water is indeed a figure of the three-day death. Baptism, therefore, is a certain precious death, by which we have died, as the Apostle says: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III) [Col. 0787C]. Nor have we merely died: we have also been buried with Him through baptism into death. When, therefore, we were baptized—that is, when we thus deserved it—what was our final will except that which we confessed when we were asked, “Do you renounce Satan?” and said, “I renounce him”? This is the final will that we confessed; and immediately we were baptized—indeed, immediately we died. If, therefore, a testament is confirmed in death, it is permissible on no grounds to transgress this covenant; on no terms may this final will be violated.

It is also completed by prescription, because Peter of Ravenna says, as is written in the Decrees: “Thirty years silence all questions under human laws.” Yet is the ineffable generation of Christ still rashly debated after the course of so many years? The argument is from analogy. May a covenant that has been confirmed and observed for more than thirty-six times forty years be violated again? Far be it! It is also confirmed by good faith. For when we make a covenant with someone, we fear breach of the agreement because we see that he pursues his own advantage more than ours. But who would presume to violate this covenant, whose benefit is transferred not to Him with whom we contract, but is returned to us? For if God bestows upon you some service, will not the benefit be yours? And if you render Him some service, what benefit do you confer upon Him? Does not the whole benefit return to you?

[Col. 0788A] This is a contract of good faith, in which your advantage is considered in every respect. This covenant is also confirmed by lawful titles. What is acquired by title of heir, purchaser, gift, legacy, dowry, or by the title called *pro suo*—“as one’s own”—is confirmed to the possessor. Behold, He possesses us as heir, of whom the vine-growers say: “This is the heir” (Matt. XXI). Hence He says: “Israel is my inheritance” (Isa. XIX). Likewise, He possesses us as purchaser. Thus the Apostle says: “For you were bought with a great price” (I Cor. VI). He possesses us also as redeemer, who redeemed us by His precious blood. Hence we cry: “You have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth” (Office of the Church). Likewise, by title of gift, because He was given to us, or because we were given to Him. Of the first it was said: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. IX) [Col. 0788B]. Of the second He Himself says to the Father: “Sanctify in Your name those whom You have given me” (John XVII). Similarly, by title of envoy, of whom Sophonias says: “We have heard a report from the Lord, and He has sent an envoy to the nations” (Obad. I). And also by title of dowry. For He endowed and enriched His bride—that is, His Church—together with His faithful.

Finally, He possesses us by His own title. Of this the law says: “What is in no one’s goods is granted by natural reason to the occupier.” And they call this title *pro suo* when a thing that is of benefit to no one is transferred, by occupation and labor, to the occupier’s legal right and benefit. And what was more useless than man? Not merely useless, but harmful; harmful not merely to another, but to himself. But now [Col. 0788C] he has been made wholly useful, when he renders to God the service due to Him, fearing God and keeping His commandments: “this is the whole of man.” In what way, therefore, is a covenant to be violated which we see strengthened by such pillars of title?

It is also adorned by its cause. A *causa* [legal case] is called so from a *casus* [fall]. And by what fall is this case called so, except by the fall of man? For in the fall of man three parties enter into the case. One is plaintiff, and plaintiff only: namely, God. Another is defendant, and defendant only: namely, the devil. The third is both plaintiff and defendant: namely, man, but in different respects—defendant in relation to God, plaintiff in relation to the devil. God is plaintiff, and not defendant, in this case, because there is no one who ought or could complain of God, although He Himself has cause to complain both of man and of the devil [Col. 0788D]. He could complain of the devil because the devil dared to reap a field not his own and to cut down the Lord’s harvest with the sickle of deception, when he did not fear to subject God’s creature to his own lordship. He could summon man, as a runaway servant, for disobedience; accuse him of the vice of ingratitude; and proceed against him for the crime of injured majesty. By all these things man is proved a defendant.

For man is shown to be plaintiff in this respect: he could proceed against the devil for fraud, falsehood, and calumny, if a judge or advocate could be found who would compel him to obey the law. But no one could do this except God; and God did not will it, because He was angry with man. Therefore, in order that God might will it, man had both to pay the debt and make satisfaction for [Col. 0789A] contempt. But man could not accomplish this, even if he gave either an irrational or a rational creature in payment of the debt. For an irrational creature is far less worthy than a rational one; and an unjust rational creature is less worthy than a just rational one.
