Therefore among neither rational nor irrational creatures could anything be found worthy of such recompense.

For this reason God, pitying man, gave to man One far worthier than all that had been lost, so that He might be given for man; and thus mercy and truth met together: mercy, indeed, because He gave to man; justice and truth, because One was given for man. Thus sufficient payment was made for the debt; but satisfaction also had to be made for the contempt. Yet this, too, could be done only by one who owed no punishment. Therefore He underwent punishment who did not deserve to undergo punishment, so that He might both pay the debt and make satisfaction for the contempt [Col. 0789B]. This is the action of our peace; and therefore we call this covenant the transaction of peace, because it may on no grounds be violated, just as no one can otherwise be saved.

The covenant is also adorned with words, in many portions and in many ways: now by patriarchs, now by prophets, now by apostles, now by evangelists; but especially through the Word, in whom God the Father spoke to us. We know that that Word is truth, which confirms the covenant, and for this reason it cannot be violated.

It is also adorned with writings. For what theology or liberal discipline of the New and Old Testaments—indeed, even of the philosophers themselves—does not declare this: that beginnings of things obtain a good end? But the philosophers were deceived in this: some said that pleasure, others that virtue, was the end of things. Nor would these latter have been far from the truth if they had said that virtue was the final end. For God is the final end of all virtues. Hence Solomon: “Let us hear together the conclusion of the whole discourse: Fear God and keep His commandments; this is the whole of man” (Eccli. XII) [Col. 0789C]. Therefore God, not virtues of fear and commandment-keeping, ought to be the final cause of virtues. But the philosophers believed virtue to be God, rather than a gift of God, and for this reason they became vain in their thoughts.

Hence Moses, who is reported to have been most wise in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, is read to have watered at the well the flocks of the seven daughters of the priest of Midian, so that it might thereby be understood that he, who was the foremost preacher of theology, would imbue the lovers of the seven liberal arts with the deep mysteries of Holy Scripture, and would establish theological wisdom by means of the arts of philosophy themselves. For whereas among the seven liberal arts some instruct us concerning words and others concerning things: among those concerning words, one instructs concerning pronunciation, as grammar; another concerning signification, as dialectic; another concerning both, as rhetoric. Among those concerning things, one concerns nature, as physics; another form. And among those concerning form, one concerns measure, as geometry; another number, as arithmetic; another weight, as music; another movement, as astrology. Theology excels them all in this: all are servants to it [Col. 0790A].

For under that sense which proceeds from the signification of words to things is contained history, served by three disciplines: grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric. Under that sense which proceeds from things to mystical events is contained allegory. Under that sense which proceeds from the signification of things to things to be done mystically is contained tropology. Arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy, and physics serve these latter two. Whatever is taught under history, allegory, or tropology teaches the cause of this covenant—that is, our restoration. For although Moses treats, at the beginning of his narrative, of the works of creation, his principal intention was nevertheless to instruct the fallen concerning the works of restoration. For he could not fittingly show [Col. 0790B] how man was repaired unless he first showed how he fell. Nor could he fittingly show his fall unless he first explained how he was created. And in order to show the creation of man, it was necessary to show the creation of the whole world, because it was made for man. For spirit exists for God, flesh for spirit, and the world for the human body. He therefore treats matters in this order:

First, how the world was made for man; second, how man was endowed with natural and gratuitous goods; third, how he fell; finally, how he was repaired. Thus the covenant of our restoration is adorned by every kind of teaching. It is also adorned [Col. 0790C] with the form in which covenants were customarily made in antiquity. For of old, when the ancients entered into certain covenants, they poured out the blood of a foul sow in the place where they ratified the covenant. Hence a covenant, by another name derived from the foul sow, is called a *foedus* [compact]. But since the pig is an unclean animal in the Law, when Moses bound the people to the Lord by a covenant, he used not the blood of a sow but the blood of twelve bulls, received from the twelve leaders. With half of it he sprinkled the tabernacle, the vessels, and the people, as a sign that, if they served the Lord, the Lord was bound to them by covenant. He poured the other half at the base of the altar, as a sign that the people bound themselves to the Lord by covenant. Joshua, moreover, through the pouring out of water, bound the same people to the Lord, and the Lord to the people [Col. 0790D]. But our Savior, through the pouring out not of bulls’ blood but of His own blood and water, bound us to Himself all the more strongly because He imitated Moses in the shedding of blood and Joshua in the shedding of water. For when blood and water came forth from His side, He ministered to us two sacraments: one of our redemption, the other of regeneration. If, then, according to the ordinance of the ancients, men were bound by covenant through the blood of a foul sow; or through the shedding of bulls’ blood, as Moses willed; or through the pouring out of water, as Joshua ordained: how much more ought we to be bound to Him who by His own blood and by water poured out from His own side made us His covenant-partners?

It is likewise adorned by continuity. For the covenant continually precedes us when we are joined to it through the food of His body [Col. 0791A] and the drink of His blood. For just as the Church never ceases from the sacrament, so she never ceases from the covenant. The covenant is continued while the sacrament is continued. For we mean by this covenant nothing other than the communion and union effected through the sacrament of His body and blood. Finally, it is adorned by confirmation, because the law confirms the covenant, saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in yourselves” (John VI). And again: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (ibid.). Behold the obligation of the covenant through the bond of the sacrament. Behold why it must be more certain than certain that this covenant cannot be violated.

Yet you say: “What cannot be violated can be suspended.” In order that it may be suspended, age moves me, necessity compels me. Age indeed promises me hope of repentance, hope of pardon, hope of longer life. Necessity does so because I was born not for myself alone, but also for my friends, parents, and relatives, whom I am bound to benefit and assist; for, as Seneca says, “Our native land claims one part of our birth, our friends another.” Hence John says: “Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, and closes the bowels of mercy—how does the love of God abide in him?” (I John III). Therefore, in order that we may assist our friends, let us have a postponement. Very well. You think that the plaintiff of all should be constrained by a civil forum—perhaps because you say that the plaintiff ought to follow the defendant’s forum. Let it be so.

[Col. 0791C] I ask what postponement you wish granted you. There are five kinds of postponement: namely, those of summons, deliberation, appeal, preparation, and restitution. You say, therefore: “I seek postponement for restitution, because I have been despoiled.”

You have said this truly, because you have become like the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, who fell among robbers, and they stripped him, etc. (Luke X). You have therefore been stripped of gratuitous goods and wounded in natural ones. You possess free will, indeed, but depressed; intellect, but dull; memory, but sodden; reason, but as though bleary-eyed; and besides, you have been stripped of your gratuitous gifts. Therefore, because you have been despoiled, you seek restoration, since the law says that however criminal a person may be—thief, heretic, robber, schismatic—provided he denies being such and no alleged crime has been proved against him, he must be restored to the goods of which he has been deprived [Col. 0791D]. This is true indeed, but the vice of dissipation is excepted. For if anyone is disgraced for the vice of dissipation and on that account despoiled, he ought not be restored; rather, the things taken away must be kept in sequestration until he proves himself a faithful steward of the thing entrusted to him.

But you are judged guilty of the vice of dissipation. Are we not like that younger son who, having received the portion falling to him, went into a far country and squandered everything by living luxuriously with harlots, so that upon returning to his father he was compelled to say: “I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance” (Ps. LXVIII)? Temporal things are, as it were, accidental: they can be present or absent without corruption of the subject. But natural and gratuitous things are substantial: they cannot be absent without harm to the subject. We squander these goods by living voluptuously; hence we should not enjoy restoration until the contrary is proved.

Yet, lest any ground of complaint remain to you, restoration has been made to us not only in law, but in law and in fact [Col. 0792A]; and this abundantly and beyond merit. Restoration in law occurs when a sentence of restoration is pronounced; restoration in law and fact occurs when the sentence is pronounced and what was pronounced is put into execution. For we have been restored not only to possession, but to legal standing and reputation. We could not be restored for appeal, because there is no superior to whom we ought to appeal. Therefore we have been restored to possession. Our possession is paradise: Adam was expelled from this possession, and it was of this that he was stripped. But the blood of Christ removed the flaming and turning sword and opened the gates of heaven which the first-created man had closed. Thus, as a type of this restoration and peace restored, the veil of the temple was torn while the Lord suffered (Matt. XXVII) [Col. 0792B].

We have also been restored to reputation, because through the dishonor of the ancient sin we had lost the right to accuse, bear testimony, and judge. For by civil law alone the devil could have pleaded the criminal objection against us: when we charged him with the crime of lying and malice, he could also repel us from the case, saying: “You cannot bring a charge against me, because you are my servants.” But now, by God’s grace, we have been restored to both forms of reputation, ecclesiastical and civil, so that authority has been given us not only to accuse him, but even to judge him, as the Apostle says: “Do we not judge angels?” (I Cor. VI). This is so that no suspicion and no reproach from the old filth may remove us. We have therefore been restored to ecclesiastical reputation because the power to accuse or judge has been given to us; and to civil reputation because every suspicion of ancient infamy and every shameful reproach has been erased. And in the same way we have been restored to legal standing: for whereas before this covenant we had no power to make a claim against the devil, we have been granted not merely the right to plead against him but, as stated, even [Col. 0792D] the authority to pass sentence upon him.

Since, therefore, every excuse based on restitution is frivolous, perhaps you seek a postponement for preparation. A postponement for preparation is said to occur when someone denies that he has at hand the documents or witnesses by which he ought to strengthen his case against the plaintiff, and in this case seeks documents or witnesses. But since it almost always falls upon the plaintiff to prove the affirmative claim which he makes, and not upon the defendant to prove the negative—for if the plaintiff fails, the defendant prevails even if he has produced nothing (I said “almost,” because, as some maintain, there is an exception in a case of divorce)—it seems remarkable if the defendant wishes, contrary to laws and the privileges of freedom granted, to weaken himself against so many documents and witnesses of plaintiff and defendant. For there are as many instruments of our salvation as there are teachings of theology; and as many witnesses as there are martyrs, since *martyrs* in Greek are called *testes*, “witnesses,” in Latin [Col. 0793A].

For this reason you seek a postponement for appeal; but in vain, because it must be requested before the joinder of issue, unless the appeal is from an unjust sentence. But after the case has been joined and is still being argued, and no final sentence has yet been pronounced, but that critical day is still awaited on which the Judge will say to the good, “Come,” and to the wicked, “Go,” etc. (Matt. XXV), no appeal is to be made. But who would dare appeal from that sentence as unjust, or to whom, I ask, would he appeal? For an appeal is customarily made from a lesser to a greater. Since there is no one greater than that Judge, the sentence will undoubtedly stand, appeal being excluded [Col. 0793B].

You therefore demand delays for deliberation, but too late. For when you were asked, “Do you renounce Satan?” and you answered, “I renounce him,” this was afterward ratified by the sacrament of confirmation. With what face do you wish, as though anew, to deliberate about what you could have excused under slow deliberation? Yet because the law says that the plaintiff ought to follow the defendant’s forum, and God is plaintiff in this dispute while you are defendant, it appears that He ought to summon you by the law of the forum, not by the law of heaven. Let it be so. You are therefore not permitted to obtain a postponement for deliberation. For under the law of the forum, delays for deliberation are not granted; indeed, the accused person must answer at once or suffer capital punishment, especially if the case is criminal. Under the law of heaven, however, whether the case is criminal or civil, the defendant will have postponement for deliberation. Therefore, because you wish your plaintiff to proceed against you by the law of the forum, postponement for deliberation must be denied you; but unless, when accused, you answer adequately at once, you will deserve to suffer capital punishment [Col. 0793C].

I said “adequately,” lest you answer by calumniating, prevaricating, or evading. To calumniate is to make a false claim; to prevaricate is to truncate the truth; to evade is to depart from the issue. To suffer capital punishment is to be deprived of Christ, who is our head. There remain to you, therefore, postponements of summons: namely, delays of three times thirty days, specified by three edicts, or by one peremptory edict covering all, extended or shortened at the judge’s discretion. But since the Judge has already issued to us through His apparitors, the apostles, a summons and a warning, nothing remains but the peremptory edict. And who would demand or desire it? “Woe,” says the prophet, “to those who desire the day of the Lord.” For that day is a day of wrath, a day of cloud and darkness, a day of trumpet and alarm (Amos V; Zeph. I) [Col. 0793D]. Therefore delays of summons are not necessary.

## SERMON XXXV. AT THE GENERAL CHAPTER

“The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth; for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II). O how great is the mercy of the Creator! We were not worthy to be servants, yet we are called angels. Great is what is said of us, yet it is said truly. For He bears witness whose testimonies have been made exceedingly trustworthy: namely, the prophet Malachi, an angel in office and in name [Col. 0794A]. This is he of whom it is said that, while he prophesied, an angel appeared, bearing witness to his words. Therefore, according to the prophet’s testimony, the Lord established ranks of men on earth in accordance with the orders of angels, so that, as in heaven the character of the heavenly theophany is the uniform multitude of blessed spirits, so on earth the character of that same theophany might be the multiform union of spiritual men.

Therefore He not only makes His angels spirits and His ministers a flame of fire: those who are led by the Spirit of God are His angels; and those who shine with the splendor of charity are made His ministers. For just as the flame of fire is distinguished in three ways—by brightness, heat, and sparkling; [lacuna] and thereby, as has been said, they become characters of the heavenly theophany, which John, surnamed Scotus, defined thus: “Theophany is the simple and reciprocal manifestation of a superessential and defining origin, to minds purified from images, through consequent signs, not through substantifying principles.” Hence *theophany* is interpreted “manifestation of God,” from *Theos*, meaning “God,” and *phanes*, meaning “manifestation.” Since, then, it belongs both to angels and to you to make God’s glory manifest to the simple, let us briefly set forth for you, as an introduction and according to our capacity, some matters concerning the manifestation of God.

It must therefore be known that God is manifested in five ways: by word, thing, imagination, reason, and anagogical contemplation [Col. 0794C]. By word in three ways: according to the imposition of a word, its interpretation, or its signification. According to imposition, when it is said: “Behold the man: Branch is His name” (Zech. VI). By the giving of this name, “man,” I understand that He is truly a man whose leaf does not wither; and through this I understand Christ, because *vir* [man] is said to derive from thriving in strength or vigor. According to interpretation, as David signifies Christ because it is interpreted “strong of hand” or “desirable in countenance.” According to signification, as Christ is signified by a hand, because He is the hand through whom the Father works.

God is manifested by a thing in two ways: according to nature and form. According to nature, when I read, “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Apoc. V), I understand Christ. Likewise, when I read, “Behold the Lamb of God,” etc. (John I), I understand Christ through the nature of the lamb. Christ is called lion because of strength; lamb because of simplicity or meekness. God is also manifested through form in four ways. For form consists of number, weight, measure, and movement. God is designated by number, as by unity. For just as unity suffers neither mixture nor division, so in the union of God and man Christ suffered neither mixture nor division. He is also figured through measure, as in Ezekiel by the measuring reed with which the spiritual temple is measured (Ezek. XL). He is manifested also by weight. Hence, through the balance which the Father holds in His hand—that is, in the Son—the equity of divine judgment is figured, as John says: “These things says He who has a balance in His hand” (Apoc. VI) [Col. 0795A]. He is figured according to movement, and thus is signified by the morning star. Behold how God is manifested by a thing. We must now consider imagination.

The manifestation of God by imagination occurs in three ways: by a similar likeness, a dissimilar likeness, and a similar dissimilarity. By a similar likeness, as when I manifest God through comparison with an angel, because an angel, being spirit and invisible, is very like God, who is spirit and invisible. By a similar dissimilarity, as when I understand what belongs to God through its opposite: thus, on considering the misery of the devil, one recognizes what the blessedness of God is. For when one of two opposites is known, the other is known also. Such a similar dissimilarity is found in the Gospel, where we read: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke XVI). God is manifested by a dissimilar likeness when He is figured through some vile and lowly thing. Hence in the Psalm: “But I am a worm and no man” (Ps. XXI) [Col. 0795B]. For what is more vile than a worm, what more worthy than Christ? Yet Christ is figured through a worm.

God is manifested by reason. But here it should be noted that a thing is manifested by reason in three ways: through preceding, accompanying, and subsequent signs. Through preceding signs, as a physician recognizes from pulse or urine that a sick person is near death. Through accompanying signs, as wine for sale is indicated by a wreath. Through subsequent signs, as it is proved from ashes that there was fire in the furnace. It should therefore be known that God is always known through subsequent signs, because nothing precedes God. For this reason John says: “Theophany is [manifestation] through consequent signs,” etc.

There follows: “Not through substantifying principles.” Substantifying principles are subsistent causes; and no cause subsists by reason of which God is what He is. For if that were so, what is caused would have to precede its cause, which cannot happen—especially since God Himself is the cause of all things and the most causative cause. The following phrase, “to minds purified from images,” is said with reference to anagogical contemplation, by which God is contemplated properly, since He is manifested less properly through images. Hence Rachel, when she carried with her the idols of her father Laban, sat upon them when she was apprehended. When they were sought, she said: “I cannot rise before you, because the manner of women has befallen me” (Gen. XXXI) [Col. 0795D]. Rachel indeed signifies the contemplative soul, which carries Laban’s idols when it contemplates according to images. But afterward it sits upon them when it believes the things imagined to be greater than images—not equal to them, but very dissimilar. And it confesses that the manner of women has befallen it because it attributes wholly to human weakness its belief that it could attain, through certain likenesses, to that simple and divine nature.

This is also why Elijah, at the entrance of his cave, after the wind breaking rocks and overturning mountains, after the earthquake and fire, did not deny that God was in the whisper of a gentle breeze: for then the soul makes progress when it fails in contemplation, because it conceives nothing imaginary about God. Hence the Psalmist: “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII) [Col. 0796A].

For one is truly proved to love when one is proved to fail in contemplation. For this reason minds contemplating God must be purified—that is, cleansed—from every image. For theirs is the theophany, that is, manifestation of God, which John calls a superessential and defining origin. It is superessential because it surpasses every essence; defining, not in a destructive but in a constitutive sense. It is a defining origin because through it everything has the origin of its definition. For everything has its own definition, by which it differs specifically from other things. The manifestation of God must therefore be simple, because we ought not to conceive divisions of members, changes of places, varieties of times, or even varieties of spiritual affections.

The same John describes three characters of this supercelestial theophany in heaven, after whose likeness He also made priests angels on earth. He calls the first epiphany, the second hyperphany, and the third hypophany. He distinguishes each into three orders of angels. *Epi* means “above,” *hyper* “middle,” and *hypo* “below” [Col. 0796C]. Thus there is a higher, middle, and lower manifestation. He defines epiphany thus: “Epiphany is a distinct outpouring, through ministries, of warming affection, higher vision, and the balance of judgment.” He says “distinct,” that is, differentiated. For epiphany is expressed distinctly through the ministries of warming affection in the seraphim. The seraphim grow warm with the divine love in an affective manner; hence they are interpreted as “burning” or “warming.” Epiphany is also expressed through the ministries of higher vision in the cherubim, because they behold the divine majesty more highly and subtly than all those beneath them; hence *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” Epiphany is also expressed by the balance of judgment in the thrones, because in them God sits to judge, as a king upon a throne, so that through them He may judge the world in equity.

He defines hyperphany thus: “Hyperphany is that which marks its participant with graduated reverence, teaches its practice, and drives away what is contrary.” For hyperphany marks its participant through the ministry of dominions with graduated reverence. The office of dominions is to teach subjects reverence for prelates according to the different ranks of dignity; hence it is called graduated. For obedience is owed differently to a prior, differently to an abbot, differently to a bishop, and differently, finally, to the lord pope [Col. 0796D]. And since there are some who have the knowledge of obedience but not its practice—for what they possess in knowledge or habit, they do not possess in act—the office of principalities is to teach us the practice and exercise of this reverence. And because this is opposed by love, weakness of the flesh, and the devil’s suggestion, the office of powers is to drive away everything contrary.

He defines hypophany thus: “Hypophany meets the laws of nature and reveals hidden things according to its capacity.” The virtues indeed meet the laws of nature, because God frequently works miracles through them, according to higher causes and outside the usual course of nature. They also reveal hidden things, but according to their capacity, because angels and archangels reveal heavenly secrets to us differently. It belongs to archangels to announce the highest and greatest matters, but to angels the least.

You, most beloved fathers, are on earth the characters of such beings, whom Malachi calls angels. For when you grow warm with the ardor of divine love; when through contemplation you read and study with higher vision in the book of life [Col. 0797B]; when with the balance of judgment you judge your subjects justly, you put on the character of epiphany. But when, in your very prelacy, you recognize yourselves to be fellow-servants of your subjects; when you render to your prelates the practice of obedience that you wish rendered to yourselves; and when you courageously drive away everything contrary to these things, you are marked by participation in hypophany. But when you live in the flesh beyond the flesh and lead a heavenly life on earth, imitating what is written of a certain saint [Note: [Col. 0797D] St Bernard says this of St Victor in his sermon on the same Victor], “The first miracle that he performed was himself”; when you also reveal heavenly mysteries to each according to his capacity, comparing spiritual things with spiritual; when you have honey and milk beneath your tongue and prepare food [Col. 0797C] and drink for the heavenly banquets of the wedding feast, you perform on earth the office of hypophany.

Therefore it is necessary that your lips preserve knowledge: lips to which the utterances of God have been entrusted; lips to which it has been granted to pronounce that blessing which can transubstantiate bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ; lips to which has been committed the charge of praying for your own ignorance and that of the people; lips to which has been given the power of binding and loosing, since they have been made the keys of the kingdom of heaven. For because some men’s lips did not preserve knowledge, they perished through their folly. And those who ought to have been figures of angels standing firm became figures of angels who had fallen. For your prudence does not fail to know, dearest brethren [Col. 0797D], that some from every order of angels fell; imprisoned in this dark air, they corrupt humankind and make them, as it were, figures of themselves in their works.

For when I see some burning with the fire of greed, some abusing the gift of knowledge, some judging their subjects without discernment, I undoubtedly behold those who fell from the heavenly Epiphany. And when I see others who possess neither a knowledge of reverence nor render it to their superiors as they wish it rendered to themselves by subjects, nor desire to repel what is contrary to the virtues, but wallow in their own filth, I behold figures of the angels [Col. 0798A] who fell from heavenly hyperphania. But when certain people oppose the laws of nature, serving the laws of the flesh against nature, intent upon trickery and fraud, games and empty talk more than spiritual things, they become figures of those who fell from heavenly hypophania.

Therefore it is necessary that your lips preserve knowledge, because one key is not enough for binding or loosing: with the power to loose or bind there must also be the knowledge to discern. Therefore, since you have gathered to judge, you ought to keep before the eyes of your mind the judgment of three laws: namely, the natural law, whose judgment is: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another; and what you wish done to yourself, do to another.” Yet at times you must employ the judgment of the written law—rarely, however, and when an unavoidable case occurs [Col. 0798B]—whose judgment is: “A tooth for a tooth, an eye for an eye” (Deut. 19). But rarely, as has been said: as our lawgiver, blessed Benedict, says, namely when the ointments of exhortation avail nothing, when the punishment of blows and the prayer of himself and his brethren—if these have first been applied—avail nothing, then let him use the sword of excision, as it is written: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Cor. 7), lest one diseased sheep contaminate the whole flock.

More often, however—and almost always, unless a shameless and incorrigible man abuses your patience—you ought to use the judgment of the spiritual law, that is, the law which says: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5), so that, like wise and discerning men, you may know [Col. 0798C] in which cases you should exercise a lenient judgment and in which a punitive one, knowing that with whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged by that Judge who, when he comes to judge the world through fire, will render to each according to his works.

## SERMON XXXVI. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

“Gather to him his saints, who arrange his covenant above sacrifices” (Ps. 49).

Let no one think it strange that blessed Boniface, having obtained that ancient temple from the Emperor Phocas, wished it to be consecrated in honour of All Saints. For this is a commandment in Israel and a judgment [Col. 0798D] of the God of Jacob. That ancient herald, the leader among the singers, son of Barachiel, rebuking those fishermen whose nets were broken by the enclosing of their fish, exhorts other fishermen, whose nets were not broken by the enclosing of one hundred and fifty-three fish, saying: “Gather to him his saints.” For the psalm is entitled *Asaph*.

It will not be useless to learn who Asaph was: by family, by the rank of his office, and by the interpretation of his name. Asaph, as is read in Paralipomenon, was the son of Barachiel and became one among four masters of the singers. His name means “synagogue,” or, what is the same thing, “assembly” [Col. 0799A]. Yet although every gathering, whether of people or of cattle, could be called a synagogue, *synagogue* properly denotes the assembly of the people of Israel.

But whose Israel? For there is an Israel according to the flesh and an Israel according to the Spirit. “Not all,” says the Apostle, “who are descended from Israel are Israelites; but in Isaac”—that is, in the son of promise—“shall your seed be called” (Rom. 9): that seed, I say, of which it was said to Abraham: “In your seed shall all nations be blessed” (Gen. 22). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “He does not say, ‘in seeds,’ as of many, but ‘in your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3). Therefore those are Israelites who are blessed in Christ.

But who are these blessed ones? “All who see them shall recognize them, because [Col. 0799B] these are the seed whom the Lord has blessed” (Isa. 61). For who, seeing your obedience, your abstinence, your labour, and your devotion in vigils, fasts, and psalmody, would not recognize that you are the seed of the Lord of Hosts—the seed from the seed which the Lord left to us? “For unless,” Scripture says, “the Lord of Hosts had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1).

Nevertheless, dearest brethren, your assembly is Asaph, son of Barachiel; and it may truly be called Asaph—Asaph, because “many daughters have gathered riches, but you surpass them all.” For you are that heap of witness gathered at the covenant between Jacob and Laban [Col. 0799C]. For, by your patience and perseverance, you bear witness that the Lord himself has peace with the people of the land, as it were with Laban. As often as you show courage in labour, patience in temptation, and perseverance in good work, you gather stones into the heap of witness.

For from these a witness-mound is formed, in which Jacob first placed a stone, and after him his brethren. When the Lord, in the struggle of his Passion, showed patience like an invincible wrestler—for Jacob means “wrestler”—he placed a stone in the heap. Then, when his sons, or brethren, imitate him by accumulating diverse virtues, they heap stones in the mound. We are sons in respect of his being God; brethren in respect of his being man [Col. 0799D]. We are sons because he made us; brethren because, without sin, he shared with us the weakness of human nature. Thus we are sons through the gift of grace; brethren through participation in nature. Hence he is not ashamed to call us brethren, saying in one place: “I will declare your name to my brethren” (Ps. 21).

Therefore you whom Christ’s love has gathered into one from the north and the sea, to glorify himself; you who, with the true Jacob in the covenant of God and man, do not scatter but gather with him, as he says: “He who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11); you, I say, who by gathering virtues establish ascents in this valley of tears, so as to ascend the mountain of the Lord and receive mercy and blessing from God [Col. 0800A], may be called Asaph and sons of Barachiel: Asaph, because of the gathering of virtues; sons of Barachiel, because of the gift of blessing. For Barachiel means “the Lord’s blessing.” You are therefore Asaph by merit, sons of Barachiel by reward; Asaph through grace, sons of Barachiel through recompense.

You are Asaph, who holds the mastership among singers. For though sweet sound and pleasing harmony can be made on harps, timbrels, choirs, and various kinds of musical instruments, sweeter than all before God is that melodious man in whom the strings of the heart are touched and life answers to words: where the high string is touched by devotion, but the low string of the heart by patience and tribulation. How should he not hold first place among singers who knows how to sing through the trumpet by preaching [Col. 0800B]; through the psaltery, which sounds from above, by contemplation; through the harp, which returns sound from below, by examination of his own misery; through the timbrel, by mortification of the flesh; through the choir, by brotherly love; through strings, by the intention of the heart; through the organ, by devotion; through cymbals of jubilation and well-sounding cymbals, by cheerfulness and exultation? “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9).

Such singers are you, dearest brethren; and with such instruments you have learned to delight the ears of God. Let Asaph therefore cry out; let you too cry out. Let him cry to our fishermen, whose nets cannot be broken. Let him cry out against those in rebuke; let him cry out for these in exultation. Let him cry out against those to reprove; for these, to exhort. Let him cry out against those, that they may cast out the fish [Col. 0800C] which break the nets; for these, that they may gather them and rejoice in the catch.

Do you wish to hear, dearest brethren, what the ancient nets were that were broken, who the fishermen were, and who the fish? I understand the ancient nets to be that ancient Synagogue which you now see torn apart and scattered. In the making of these nets we may call the knots those signs by which the ancients adhered to God, or the deeds of those among them who were holy. For as a knot is formed from two cords, so from God’s miracles and the deeds of the patriarchs there was made in the nets a bond of love.

For God to love the ancients, there was, as it were, a knot in Abel’s innocence, Noah’s righteousness, Abraham’s faith, Isaac’s devotion, Jacob’s affliction, Moses’ gentleness, and David’s courage [Col. 0800D]. On the other side, so that they themselves might love God, he accepted Abel’s sacrifice; saved Noah from the waters of the flood; enriched Abraham in Canaan; fulfilled Isaac’s desire; delivered Jacob from Esau’s hands; brought Moses and his brethren, the children of Israel, out from under Pharaoh’s yoke; and raised David, taking him from behind the nursing ewes, to kingship.

In these and such things, therefore, he wove the ancient nets. But the fish gradually began to struggle in the nets, and they broke the nets. For what were that faintheartedness by which they murmured against God between the Egyptians and the Red Sea; that excess concerning the bitterness of the waters at Marah; that murmuring in disgust at the light food; that sensual desire in longing for the flesh-pots of Egypt [Col. 0801A] (Exod. 17)—what were these but breaches of rupture made by the fish gathered in the nets?

For from this point the bond of love, by which they had been tied to God, began to be loosened: ungrateful for his benefits, they desired Egypt; they made a molten calf; they murmured against Moses; they even blasphemed God himself (Exod. 32). Yet if any such persons were found among them, who offended God in blasphemies of this sort, still, for the sake of some among them who were holy, he spared the whole multitude and did not allow the nets to be entirely undone. For he is the one who, as he said to Abraham, would have spared all the Sodomites for the sake of ten righteous persons, if he had found them in Sodom (Gen. 18).

But because, as the love of the children of Israel gradually grew cold [Col. 0801B], such wickedness, pride, greed, and unbelief grew among them that they were not merely evil toward themselves or God’s saints, but were not afraid to rage against, seize, and kill the very Son of God, certainly no good person was found among them. As they were found equal to the Sodomites in transgression, so they were made equal to them in rejection.

This is why Asaph, rebuking that Synagogue, says there: “But God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” (Ps. 49). As we have already said, he invites to an abundant catch the fishermen whose nets were not broken, where he says: “Gather to him his saints” (ibid.). The nets that cannot be broken are the present Church, which [Col. 0801C] is the assembly of saints. Their knots are, on one side, religion, life, or conduct; on the other, the gift of nature, grace, and glory. The fish in these nets are the subjects; the fishermen, the prelates.

Therefore they are told: “Gather to him” the good fish—not those who confuse God’s law through barren observances and carnal sacrifices, but gather those saints who arrange his covenant above sacrifices. Therefore, brethren, gather them: by preaching, by pursuing them in your conduct, or by honouring them. Gather by preaching those who are to be sanctified; by imitating in conduct those whom you see should be imitated; by honouring those who have been rewarded or are to be rewarded. For, according to metonymy—the figure by which the container is denoted by what it contains—he gathers saints who heaps up the holiness of saints [Col. 0801D].

For if in contemplation of God you imitate the angels; in faith, the patriarchs; in hope, the prophets; in preaching, the evangelists; in religion, the apostles; in continence, the virgins; in patience, the martyrs; in abstinence, the confessors—you rightly gather all the saints.

“Gather to him.” To whom, “to him”? To him who said: “The God of gods has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Ps. 49). Of those who gather, however, some gather for the God of gods; others for gods—that is, human beings or demons. Of human beings it is said: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 31). But of demons: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95).

Therefore those gather for human beings who preserve holiness of life for the favour of the powerful or for earthly honour [Col. 0802A]. Hence a subject cries out to those in power: “Behold, I have served you all these years and have never transgressed one of your commands; yet you have never given me even one obedience.” And, speaking as though with the mouth of that son in the Gospel, he troubles his father by saying: “Look: this man who has now come from the world, who until now has squandered his portion by living extravagantly—once he came inside, he was immediately called to obedience. But I have conducted myself vigorously for all these years, and the abbot does not give me even one obedience.”

Others gather not for human beings but for demons, like those of whom it is said: “They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know” (Deut. 32). For the nations, in honour of their gods, diligently engaged themselves often in renouncing temporal property, often [Col. 0802B] in abstinences, and many times in carnal sacrifices. But the fathers of the Old Testament were devoted not to human beings or demons, but to God; they rendered him the worship of religion which those others offered to demons. And this was far better, for the latter had neither faith nor the worship of true religion. The former, though they did not yet know true religion, nevertheless already had faith.

But as faith grew, religion grew. For the fathers of the New Testament began to arrange God’s covenant above the commandment concerning sacrifices, which those others, attending to it carnally, confused with the intention of the giver. For God, when speaking to them concerning legal ceremonies, spoke not of the thing of the sacrament but of the sacrament of the thing; not of the sign of truth but of the truth of the sign; not of the signifier but of the thing signified [Col. 0802C]. Hence in this same psalm he says: “I will not rebuke you concerning your sacrifices” (Ps. 49). And: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 105). Hence he also says through Isaiah: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? I am full” (Isa. 1). And through Jeremiah: “Eat the flesh,” he says, “because I did not speak concerning these burnt offerings on the day when I brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. 7), signifying that he intended spiritual sacrifices, not carnal ones.

Hence, in contrast to those who, in zeal for God—which indeed they had, but not according to knowledge—confused God’s commandment with sacrifice, it is said: “Gather to him [Col. 0802D] his saints, who arrange his covenant above sacrifices.” Gather not those who confuse it, but those who, according to the commandment, put salt on their sacrifices, remove the skin, and, so that they may bear varied offspring, place in their troughs rods partly with bark and partly stripped.

What does it mean to put on salt? To understand the commandment concerning sacrifice according to the spiritual meaning of wisdom. What does it mean to remove the skin? To retain the meaning and remove the covering of the letter; this is also to strip the rods. For when prelates meditate upon the spiritual meaning in the letter of books, as in troughs, so that their subjects may acquire diverse virtues from it, they strip the rods so that the sheep may bring forth varied young. These, therefore, are those who arrange God’s covenant above sacrifices.

For in those sacrifices [Col. 0803A] the lawgiver intended nothing else than to show in them what he intended: how a person ought to conduct himself both in the good things customarily done freely and in the good things customarily done out of necessity. For the good which is done freely, because it is more worthy before God, he shows to be of the first order by first subdividing it into its kinds. Among freely performed good works, some are carried out with greater devotion, others with less. Those performed with greater devotion are therefore included under burnt offerings, while those performed with lesser devotion are mentioned under peace offerings.

Likewise, among the good works done with greater devotion, some belong to the active life and others to the contemplative life, since the active life comes first not in dignity but in practice. He divides the active life [Col. 0803B] into the burnt offerings of an ox, a sheep, and a goat. For there are some who commit themselves wholly to God, strong in bodily strength and energetic in labour, who, according to God’s commandment, leave all things and sustain both themselves and their brethren by the labour of their hands. These offer an ox as a burnt offering. When they seek no earthly reward in their labour, but do everything with regard to the supreme priest—that is, God—they bring the ox, as it were, to Aaron. And when they work cheerfully, because “God loves a cheerful giver,” they lay their hands upon the victim’s head.

When, amid their labours, they remove whatever pleasure or carnal affection may have been present, they take the fat from the sacrifice. When, in that labour itself, they know how to distinguish time and place, because they ought at times to be free for prayer, they arrange the limbs of the victim. But when, under the weight of labour, as commonly happens, they do not lose devotion but think upon the reward of recompense in their labour, then, laying beneath it the wood of their thoughts, they kindle the fire of the Holy Spirit upon the altar of the heart [Col. 0803C].

Others, weak in strength, old in age, simple in understanding, rich in possessions, when they make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity and commit themselves and their possessions to God in the monastery, like sheep feeding their owners with milk and wool, support those serving God from their patrimony and riches. Therefore, as the former are industrious, so these simple persons ought to live innocently, solely for the love of God, with cheerfulness and the devotion of the Holy Spirit.

Others, neither physically strong nor wealthy in goods, nevertheless, because for their sins they have a conscience branded by their deeds, devote themselves in every way to penance, to mortification of the flesh, fasting, and every form of submission [Col. 0803D]. Living as the Gospel tax collector, they do not dare lift their eyes to heaven (Luke 18), but, judging themselves guilty of their sins at every hour, they regard themselves as evil and unworthy labourers for everything imposed upon them. These offer a goat to God as a burnt offering. They observe the rite of the ox and sheep in sacrifice when, with cheerfulness, devotion, and hope of eternal salvation, they bring their undertaken penance to a blessed completion through perseverance.

Distinguishing the contemplative life under the kind of burnt offerings, the law subdivides its species under the type of the turtledove, the dove, or the offering of fine flour. Whoever desires to be contemplative must devote himself to purity of life, seek the teaching that teaches groaning, and by groaning and contemplation seek what is on high [Col. 0804A]. Such a person offers a turtledove as a burnt offering. He breaks its wing-bones when, for the sake of study, he rests from labour; removes its crop when he rejects pride; casts away its feathers when he abandons former vanity; and pours out its blood at the altar’s base when, for God’s sake, he despises every affection of carnality.

He likewise sacrifices a dove according to the same rite when he thinks simply in his heart, as it is written: “I will meditate like a dove” (Isa. 38). He offers fine flour from the oven through the observance of a pure conscience and contempt for secular life; from the griddle through mortification of the flesh; and from the frying pan [Col. 0804B] through the frying of the mind. When he suffers this with devotion, he anoints the fine flour with oil; and when he does not lose the devotion of prayer amid these things, he also admits incense into the sacrifice. Yet neither leaven nor honey ought to be mixed into this sacrifice, because neither wickedness nor the sweetness of carnal delight should be loved. Nevertheless, let him offer God the firstfruits of honey, because it is necessary that the beginning of religious life be undertaken with devotion.

But concerning those sacrifices that are performed with less devotion, he treats them under peace offerings, dividing them, as said above, according to the type of ox, sheep, or goat. For just as among those who commit themselves and their possessions there are some who are industrious and devote to God everything they earn by labour; others, weak in body, who relinquish what they possess so that they may live simply; and others who are poor and cannot work, yet for penance commit themselves to God in the monastery at their prelate’s discretion: so too among those living in the world, some can work, retain much from their labour for their descendants [Col. 0804C], and generously give much to the needy for God’s sake. These offer a peace offering from an ox.

Others, lacking bodily strength, live simply in the world; they do no evil to their neighbours, do not attempt to do it, and give from the things they have acquired since youth according to the measure of their means. These offer a peace offering from a sheep. Others, weak and poor, anxious concerning their consciences, confess the sins they have committed, and devoutly undertake and perform the penance imposed upon them. When these do penance, they sacrifice a goat as a peace offering.

Yet in all cases they ought to offer to God the tail and the fat: the tail in perseverance, the fat in affection. Every affection—for gluttonous enticements, like fat covering the belly; for worldly love, like fat covering the vital organs; for some evil will, like fat of the liver; or for pleasure, like fat covering the kidneys—together with the kidneys themselves, they ought entirely to abandon, even those who strive to live for God in the world, so that they may use this world as though not using it, as though possessing nothing and yet possessing all things. Nor are the kidneys alone to be relinquished in the act of pleasure, but also the fat of the kidneys [Col. 0805A], that is, the affection for pleasure itself, must be consecrated to God.

But the good done from necessity is also subdivided by the lawgiver under the types of sacrifices customarily made for sins. Whoever sins must correct himself by the good of penance. Therefore the Lord cries to the brood of vipers, as to sinners: “Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3). The fruits are worthy of repentance if you consider the person acting and the sinful act: whether, in accordance with each, you give the good of penance to others or undertake it yourself. Hence the sin offering also is divided in two ways: according to the person and the act. For one sin is individual, another universal; one occurs through ignorance, another through rashness; one [Col. 0805B] through contempt, another through deliberation.

Therefore he first discusses sin customarily committed through ignorance under the ignorance of the priest, the ignorance of the ruler, and that of a person. For every sin must be judged greater or lesser according to the differing persons. If the sinner is wise, or powerful enough to be able to avoid sin or know better, he ought to be punished much more severely than one who neither knows nor can avoid sin. The priest, whose sin of ignorance he discusses first, signifies the wise person; the ruler, whom he treats second, represents the powerful person; the individual signifies the foolish or weak person.

Since the sin of the wise or powerful is greater than that of the simple person, it needs a greater punishment for sin. Accordingly, when he discusses a priest’s sin committed through ignorance [Col. 0805C], he sets out his penance under the offering of a calf. But he divides the ruler’s penance under the type of a he-goat, because the sin of the powerful is greater than the sin of the poor, yet less than the sin of the wise; the he-goat is recognized as worthier than a she-goat but less worthy than a calf. He shows that the sin of the poor and unlearned is expiated through a she-goat.

Since, then, when the wise person sins, he must correct the pleasure of sin through the rigour of labour, his expiation is fittingly shown by a calf, an animal devoted to labour. When he displays cheerfulness of mind in penance, he lays his hands upon the victim’s head. When, by full confession of sin, he interrupts the discord which sin made between himself and God, he sprinkles seven times the veil between the holy place and the Holy of Holies with a finger dipped in blood [Col. 0805D].

For the discord of sin is represented in the veil. Just as that veil separated the holy place from the Holy of Holies, so the discord of sin separates a human being from God and God from a human being. Therefore we dip the index finger in blood when we point out sin in confession. We cast blood seven times against the veil when, through a sevenfold confession of sin, we show that that discord is being divided.

For every sin is recognized from seven circumstances: the act and the agent, the accomplices in sin, the place, the time, the cause, and the manner. We pour the remaining blood at the base of the altar [Col. 0806A] when we pour out before God, who is the altar’s base, the entire cruelty of sin. We dip the altar’s four horns when we grieve for sin in such a way that we do not lose hope, and grieve over the pain of punishment in such a way that we do not cease to rejoice in the fruit of penance. The altar represents the heart; the four horns, the heart’s affections.

We consecrate all the fat to God when, for God’s sake, we relinquish the richness of every pleasure. We carry the skin when we endure the outward act of penance; the dead flesh, when we endure the mortification of the flesh; the head, when we consecrate to God the beginning of penance; the feet, when we bring penance through to perseverance; the entrails, when, possessing our souls in patience, we endure contrition and bitterness of heart; and the dung, when we endure the disgrace of human nature.

But because some endure all these things not for God but to be seen by people, it was therefore commanded that they carry them outside the camp to a clean place. He carries the victim outside the camp who lives a religious life before God outside human notice. For that is the clean place where ashes are customarily poured out, because everyone who desires to be cleansed must complete there the perseverance of penance itself [Col. 0806B].

The same thing is shown concerning the ruler’s sin-offering, which is made under the type of a he-goat—or, to speak more spiritually, a *chymarrus*. A *chymarrus* is a winter he-goat; in the winter he-goat the bitterness of penance is signified. Yet this penance is less than the preceding one, because a calf is greater than a he-goat, and a ruler is inferior to a priest. We say the same of the she-goat, because it represents the penance of a simple person, being smaller than both he-goat and calf.

I have many similar things to say to you, my brethren. I have sampled for you abundant material, but lest it produce weariness, let these things suffice. For, in order to give you an opening, I have shown how the saints arrange God’s covenant above sacrifices. Gather them, therefore, into one, so that you may be able to reign together with them, with Christ, who is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 0806D]

“Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen,” etc. (Isa. 62).

It is no lesser virtue to preserve what has been gained than to seek it. For just as three things commonly attend temporal riches—the first preceding, namely labour in acquiring; the second accompanying, the anxiety of guarding; and the third following, namely grief in losing—so in spiritual riches the labour of acquiring must be the more arduous, and the concern of preserving them the more lasting, in proportion as the pain of not possessing or of losing them is more ruinous, and their acquisition more precious than the trade in silver and gold.

Therefore, mindful of the sons of Beeroth, who killed Ish-bosheth in his bed [Col. 0807A] because the gatekeeper had fallen asleep while cleaning wheat, let us entrust both ourselves and what is ours, not to a woman gatekeeper, but to a strong gatekeeper; for a thing that is loved after it has been acquired, and perishes through negligence, does not merely fail to give joy but afflicts the mind.

And because the Apostle says that we are God’s temple (1 Cor. 3), let us take our parable from the temple of testimony. Consider with how much labour the temple stones were cut from useless and confused material; how much labour afterwards polished them; how afterwards they were formed into members; and finally compacted into the one body of the Church. Consider also with what care, through what sprinklings, illuminations, anointings, incensings, the temple of God was dedicated. For all these things happened to us in a figure, who are living stones in God’s building.

When, therefore, the troublesome suggestion of demons or worthless people oppressed us, and their conversations or company corrupted our best morals, we were hardened in the manner of a stone, because we were made immovable as stone for the exercise of good work. But now, separated by God’s grace from that confused material and polished by many blows of temptations, we have been formed into members of the Church and united by the one cement of love into the one body of the Church [Col. 0807B].

Moreover, by the sprinkling of tears, the illumination of reading or preaching, the anointing of devotion or exhortation, and the frequent incensing of devout prayer, we have been dedicated to God alone for the merit of holiness, so that nothing is lacking for the building of the outer person and the sanctuary of the human being [Col. 0807C]. Such are the ordinances of religious life; but what use can they be if they are not guarded?

For this reason Solomon commanded thirty small houses to be made around the temple, to serve as sleeping-chambers and upper rooms for the weekly ministers and those who guarded the Lord’s temple or served that temple. Watchmen were likewise appointed upon Jerusalem’s walls, of whom the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The watchmen of the walls found me” (Song 1). Hence we cry in prayer: “You, Lord of all, who have no need, willed your temple to be made in us; preserve this house undefiled for ever” (Antiphon from 2 Macc. 14).

Thus Moses arranged watches around the tabernacle, not only outside but also inside [Col. 0807D], that is, not only around the court but around the sanctuary. I have said these things because, just as each of these terms has several meanings, so taken together they all signify one thing. For just as the tabernacle and temple, so also the house and Jerusalem, represent the Church, though under different aspects.

The Church is a tabernacle insofar as it is the rest of those who serve in warfare and fight; a house insofar as it is the rest of those who labour and live the active life; a temple because it is the rest of contemplatives; and the vision of peace—for that is the meaning of *Jerusalem*—because it is the rest of the blessed. For the Church is universal, though divided into parts.

As I said, each of these terms is also equivocal, that is, capable of several meanings [Col. 0808A]. For it is used sometimes emphatically, sometimes antonomastically, sometimes specifically, sometimes allegorically, sometimes anagogically, sometimes tropologically. Emphatically—that is, expressively—it is said of Christ, God and man. For just as in that tabernacle there were the court, the holy place, and the Holy of Holies, so too in that Christ who is God and man, the body, outwardly manifest, was as it were the court; the soul, the holy place; and the divinity, the Holy of Holies. Specifically, it is the Virgin Mary, who beneath the curtains of her white flesh enclosed God and man in three substances. Allegorically, it signifies the universal Church: its court, as it were, is the Church that labours openly; its holy place, the Church that waits in purgatory; its Holy of Holies, the Church that reigns [Col. 0808B] in heaven. Anagogically, too, that heavenly Church is represented, of which it is written: “Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle?” (Ps. XIV [15]). Its court is the ministering order of angels, sent into the world for those who receive the inheritance of salvation. Its holy place is the middle hierarchy, which receives from the higher and assigns to the lower hierarchy. Its Holy of Holies is the higher hierarchy, which stands before God, as it is written: “Thousands of thousands ministered unto him, and ten times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII [7:10]). Or we may assign the court to hypophany, the holy place to hyperphany, and the Holy of Holies to theophany. The ark is within the sanctuary: its rod is the power of the Father, its tablets the wisdom of the Son, and its manna the kindness of the Holy Spirit. Tropologically—that is, morally—it signifies the whole human being. By “whole” I mean both inner and outer: the outer human being is the open court, while the holy place, or Holy of Holies, is the human heart. And the four terms mentioned above are univocal with this designation. For of the tabernacle of the human body it is written: “We have an altar, whereof they have no right to eat who serve the tabernacle” (Heb. XIII [13:10]). The same is signified by “house,” as the Apostle says: “We know that if this earthly house is destroyed, we have a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V [5:1]). And again Job: “Behold, those who stand in his presence are not steadfast; and in his angels he finds perversity: how much more those who inhabit houses of clay and have an earthly foundation, who shall be consumed [Col. 0808D] as by a moth” (Job IV [4:18–19]). The Apostle likewise says of the temple: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (I Cor. III [3:17]). And in the book of Maccabees: “Thou, Lord of all, who hast no need, hast willed thy temple to be made in us” (II Macc. XIV [14:35]). And of Jerusalem, in the Psalm: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI [122]). In the Gospel: “Jesus entered into a certain little town” (Luke XI [likely 10:38]). The whole of that Gospel reading is understood and expounded allegorically concerning the glorious Virgin. For she was the little fortified town, enclosed by every defence of virtues.

Therefore, as a figure of this tropological tabernacle, Moses appointed watches in that emphatic tabernacle: some to guard the court and others the sanctuary; and, both outwardly [Col. 0809A] and inwardly, he stationed some guards in the east, others in the south, others in the north, and others in the west. This was done as a figure of the twofold human being: the outer person, whose actions must be examined and tested; and the inner person, whose thoughts require every care. For the outer person is, as it were, in the court, and the inner person in the sanctuary.

Since among human beings some begin good actions, others advance in the ardour of charity, others languish after beginning a good work, while still others fail utterly, it is necessary to apply diligent watchfulness to beginners, who are still camped in the east. The same I say of those who advance, as it were, from the south in the ardour of charity. Likewise, it applies to those whose charity grows cold because iniquity abounds [Col. 0809B], and who thus decline northward through failure; and to those upon whom the sun of righteousness no longer shines, because “he who does evil hates the light,” and who thus, through the fall of a wicked deed, slip westward. Therefore Moses says: “On the east they shall guard the tabernacle: Judah, Zebulun, and Issachar.” And fittingly: for a person to preserve the good work which he begins, he must imitate the good farmer, who labours in hope of a fruitful harvest: first uprooting thorns and briars from the field, then setting vigorously to his undertaking, and hastening to sow what he judges expedient. Whoever wishes to safeguard the beginning of a good work must attend to these three things. He must attend to the fruit of eternal reward; this reward is signified by Issachar, whose name is interpreted “reward.” He must also hoe out, by confession, the thorns [Col. 0809C] of sins and the briars of vices. For this reason Judah, interpreted “confessing,” is joined to him. He must also apply himself vigorously to his labour, lest he fail; and thus Zebulun, “dwelling-place of strength,” may preserve his works once begun.

Those who are ascending in fervour must be restrained, lest perhaps they grow proud because they appear better to themselves than others. It must be said that the good fortune of a sailor is to be praised—but when he has reached port; the boldness of a fighter is to be praised—but when he has attained triumph. Therefore let not one who has girded himself glory as one who has laid aside his belt; nor let him rejoice while sailing, until he reaches shore. Therefore let him not cease to obey or despise his superior.

[Col. 0809D] Yet let him judge himself with moderation: neither raised to the heights through pride nor cast down to the depths through despair. For this reason Moses commanded that Reuben, Simeon, and Gad should guard the southern side. Reuben means “seeing in the midst,” Simeon “obedient,” and Gad “girded,” so that one may see and know that one is in a world where nothing is stable; that one has not yet laid aside the belt of Christian warfare and has not yet been released from the servitude of obedience. But if he should contemplate turning aside from the good work he began and from his fervour, let him immediately consider how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God—the wise Judge and mighty King. One must fear that final, decisive sentence of the last judgment, by which he will say to his ministers: “Bind the hands [Col. 0810A] and feet, and cast such a one into outer darkness” (Matt. XXII [22:13]). There he will groan amid weeping and gnashing of teeth, imprisoned and bound again. Bound again, because his feet and hands are bound, since in his affections and actions he was unrestrained during life. For this reason Moses says: “On the north shall be Dan, Naphtali, and Asher” (Num. II [2]). Dan means “judgment,” Naphtali “bound again,” and Asher “imprisoned,” so that from the names themselves he may consider what awaits those who despise God’s commandments. But if he has fallen through the lapse of sin, despair must be restrained within him. For just as one must fear that those in fervour may grow proud, so one must fear that those who have fallen may despair. Let the sinner consider how great is the mercy of him who made an apostle out of a publican, the chief of the apostles out of a blasphemer, and a chosen vessel [Col. 0810B] out of a persecutor.

Strengthened, then, by these examples, let him regulate himself in regard to his actions so that, concerning what he has done, he may be, so to speak, Manasseh—that is, “forgetful”—as the Apostle says: “Forgetting those things which are behind, I stretch forth to those things which are before” (Phil. III [3:13]). Let him also, in what he is doing, be Ephraim—that is, fruitful, namely useful—so that, abandoning vanity, he may devote himself to matters conducive to usefulness; and through these labours may be transformed from a son of wrath into Benjamin, that is, a son of the right hand, and so may deserve to be set at the right hand by him who will say to the sheep placed at his right: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV [25:34]). Therefore Moses says quite fittingly: “On the west Manasseh, Ephraim, and Benjamin shall pitch camp.” This has been said concerning the guarding [Col. 0810C] of actions and the discipline of the outer human being (Num. II [2]).

For the guarding of knowledge—that is, the thoughts—of the inner human being, Moses appointed other guards: the sons of Levi, namely the Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites. And fittingly, because those should be appointed to guard the sanctuary who know how, in patience, to possess their souls; who have here no abiding city, but, knowing themselves to be strangers, seek the one to come; who also make bitterness for themselves in the valley of tears, because they are delayed from the kingdom and still labour in exile. Such is the meaning of these guardians of the sanctuary. For Kohath is interpreted “patience,” Gershon “stranger,” and Merari “bitter,” or “bitternesses.” He arranged them about [Col. 0810D] the sanctuary in this manner. He divided the Kohathites, because he entrusted the care of the sanctuary on the east to himself and to Aaron his brother. He placed the remaining Kohathites on the south under the authority of Eleazar, Aaron’s son; the Gershonites on the north; and the Merarites on the west; and over the last two he appointed Ithamar, Aaron’s son.

It must therefore be understood that a wicked thought arises in the heart in four ways: by suggestion, as it were conception, and as it were from the east; by delight, as it were already from the southern heat; by deliberation, as it were from the north, because, as charity grows cold, iniquity begins to abound; finally by contempt, as it were from the west, because when one has come to the depth of evils, one despises. Therefore a thought must be feared at its very rise in suggestion, because the foreskins of trees must be circumcised—that is, the beginnings of deeds must be cut off—for it is written:

> Resist beginnings . . . . .  
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, I.91.)

And because idle leisure, which is hostile to the soul, readily produces the beginnings of evil thoughts—for a field which the farmer does not cultivate produces thorns and briars, as Solomon testifies when he says: “I passed by the field of the slothful man, and by the vineyard of the foolish man; and nettles had filled it all” (Prov. XXIV [24:30–31])—therefore let Moses and Aaron guard the sanctuary from the east. Moses was the giver of the divine law; accordingly, divine law is signified through Moses, as the Apostle testifies: “So long as Moses is read,” that is, the law of Moses, “a veil is laid over their hearts” (II Cor. III [3:15]), namely, the hearts of the Jews. [Col. 0811B] Therefore the vigilance of Moses signifies application to divine reading. Aaron, however, whose duty it was to offer for his own and the people’s ignorance, signifies the fulfilment of God’s commandments. In these two things—assiduity in reading and fulfilment of the commandments—the first stirrings of a wicked thought are cut away. Thus it is written in the Psalm: “The mercy of the Lord is from everlasting and unto everlasting upon those who fear him; and his righteousness unto children’s children, to those who keep his covenant and remember his commandments to do them” (Ps. CII [103]).

If the thought rises as far as delight, then, by the strength of patience, even if it cannot control the mind, let it at least restrain the hand; for one who is patient is better than a strong man. Nor can the delight [Col. 0811C] of a thought be uprooted except through the strength of patience. For once evil circumstance has opened the door to the will, it can be uprooted by strength alone—and by no strength other than patience—because the Kohathites alone guard the sanctuary on the south. Therefore let him force himself and say to the overflowing sea: “Hitherto shalt thou come, and here shalt thou break thy swelling waves, and shalt proceed no farther” (Job XXXVIII [38:11]). Yet let him ascribe the strength of patience on which he relies wholly not to himself but to the help of him who says: “Without me ye can do nothing” (John XV [15:5]). For human patience can do whatever it can do not by human aid but only by divine aid. For the Kohathites are under the hand of Eleazar, that is, under the power of divine assistance; for Eleazar is interpreted “the help of my God.”

[Col. 0811D] But if the thought has declined as far as deliberation, let him not omit also to deliberate what end the offence, once committed, will receive. The act passes, but guilt remains. The pleasure of the deed passes away, but the calamity of affliction is eternal. Let him therefore consider the sojourning of his pilgrimage, since all of us are Gershonites—that is, strangers—and our sojourn will not be prolonged for long. But wretched that we are, what shall we do or say when we bring no good thing before the supreme Judge? Therefore let the Gershonites guard the sanctuary from the north.

And if one despises thoughts, however small, one falls into the depth of evils; for no sin is so venial that it cannot, through contempt, become mortal; just as, conversely, no sin is so mortal that it cannot, through contrition, [Col. 0812A] become venial. Contempt indeed merits punishment, but contrition merits pardon. Since contempt and contrition neither agree well nor remain in one heart, opposites must be cured by opposites: contempt by contrition. This is why they guard the sanctuary on the west—that is, those who are contrite in mind for every contempt, not only of a deed but even of a thought, however slight.

Nor do I think it should be passed over what burdens were distributed, to whom, and in what manner, for carrying when the tabernacle moved. Moses and Aaron entered the Holy of Holies and touched the Lord’s ark uncovered; having wrapped it in a covering of hyacinth-blue and purple, they handed it over to the remaining Kohathites to carry. The Gershonites had charge of safeguarding all the soft things [Col. 0812B], namely the curtains, coverings, and cords. The Merarites guarded all the hard things, namely forks, cauldrons, little mortars, boards, and pegs.

It must therefore be understood that the human mind is accustomed to be moved by different affections. Thus the movement of the tabernacle signifies movement of the heart. It is moved now toward lawful affections, now toward unlawful ones; but movement toward unlawful effects has no place in the tabernacle of God. When it is moved toward lawful affections, it is moved either toward the love of God, or toward love of neighbour, and thereby also toward love of itself. For as one who loves iniquity hates his own soul, so one who is moved toward charity loves his own soul. It is moved toward love of God by the practice of the contemplative life, and toward love of neighbour [Col. 0812C] by the exercise of the active life.

But those who are moved toward love of God through the practice of the contemplative life are moved in two ways: by affection and knowledge, or by affection without knowledge. Those who are moved by knowledge but not by affection have no place in the sanctuary of God. To them the Judge will say in the future: “Why dost thou declare my justices and take my covenant into thy mouth? But thou hast hated discipline” (Ps. XLIX [50:16–17]). And again through another prophet: “When you drank the clearest water, you fouled the rest with your feet” (Ezek. XLII [likely 34:18]). Still less are those known to belong to God’s sanctuary who are moved neither by knowledge nor affection. But those are moved by knowledge and affection who possess the gift of wisdom [Col. 0812D] and the merit of holiness. Thus it is said of Aaron: “And Aaron, the holy one of the Lord” (Ps. CV [106]). These deserve to possess an anagogical, comprehensive, and fully unfolded faith.

Therefore to such persons it was said in the Gospel: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke VIII [8:10]). Hence we read that Moses and Aaron touched the ark of the covenant uncovered, because by their deeds they fulfilled the sacraments which they understood nakedly and openly. Others, however, have a great faith in affection but a small one in knowledge; yet the Son of God himself approved their faith. Of the centurion he said: “I have not found so great faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII [8:10]); and to the Canaanite woman, who desired to be fed from the crumbs that fell from her masters’ table [Col. 0813A]: “O woman, great is thy faith” (Matt. XV [15:28]). These are therefore the simple persons in God’s Church, who indeed do not possess the gift of understanding but have the merit of holiness and life. They carry the Lord’s ark wrapped, because they do what is laid upon them with an enigmatic and veiled faith, even if perhaps they do not understand the mysteries. They carry it wrapped in a hyacinth-blue and purple covering: hyacinth-blue, when, although they do not understand the things of divinity, they nevertheless embrace them devoutly; purple, when, although they cannot investigate the mystery of humanity, they nevertheless are devoutly moved by it. Thus oxen plough and she-asses feed beside them. Such people are represented by those Kohathites who carried the Lord’s ark wrapped upon their shoulders.

But those who are moved toward the exercise of the active life [Col. 0813B] are moved in two ways: either to the office of charity or to the exercise of labour. These are the two grades of the active life, represented in the two women, one of whom was called Martha and the other Leah. For in each is represented the active life according to both grades: in Martha, those who hold the office of charity; in Leah, those who engage in labour. Those who hold the office of charity carry the soft things of the tabernacle, because whatever is bestowed through charity seems sweet and, as it were, soft to the doer.
