This is the work of those who count nothing dearer than God, who bear the Lord’s sweet and gentle yoke; who hasten to store up treasure where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal (Matt. VI [6:19–20]). Therefore, holding all worldly things cheap [Col. 0813C], they distribute, scatter abroad, and give to the poor. Thus this duty belongs to the Gershonites—that is, to those who know themselves strangers and sojourners in the world, and consequently despise every transitory thing for the sake of eternal things.

The Merarites carry the hard things, because the things pertaining to the exercise of labour are hard: through labour the body is afflicted, and for this reason the mind is weighed down. Therefore these works belong to the Merarites, because they are full of every bitterness. Yet such people also have a place in God’s sanctuary. For they are Levites, because they are worthy both of blessedness and of being taken up. Therefore they deserve to dwell in the courts of the Lord, that they may behold the Holy of Holies, the Lord of lords, King of kings, Jesus Christ our Lord.

## SERMON XXXVIII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 0813D]

“The rush of the river makes glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle” (Ps. XLV [46]). Not without reason does one rejoice whose joy is full, and whose joy no one shall take from him. And therefore you ought to rejoice, because “glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI [87]), things which no one shall take from you, because the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle in you (Ps. XLV [46]). He has sanctified—not with that sanctity which still needs sanctification, according to the saying: “He that is holy, let him be sanctified still” (Rev. XXII [22:11]). By this sanctification holy men are holy through merit; although renewed in righteousness and holiness of truth, they yet feel the assault of diabolical [Col. 0814A] suggestion and the weakness of the flesh, and need the reward of the divine promise, according to the saying: “Have mercy upon me, for I am holy” (Ps. LXXXV [86]). But in you the tabernacle of the Most High has been sanctified with a full, perfect, heavenly, and everlasting sanctity.

Therefore the joy of this holy city is full: from the rush of rivers; from the strength of its walls; from the kinds of weapons; from the watchfulness of guards; from the security of its inhabitants; from its common law; from its civil law; and from its mighty king. There, indeed, by the water of sweat, which heals the diseases of the sick; by the water of tears, which washes the face of mourners; and by the shedding of blood, which “has been poured out like water round about it” and makes white the robes of martyrs, the river of God is filled with waters. There is the deep well of humility, through which the vessel of the barren Samaritan woman is made pregnant (John IV [4]).

There, by the rushing streams of Elim, the bitterness of Marah is sweetened (Exod. XV [15]); there the water of saving wisdom is offered to drink; there, from the well of breadth, springs forth the loftier fountain of charity. Likewise, it must rejoice no less in the strength of its walls, because its foundations are upon the holy mountains; and in the foundations is laid the precious cornerstone: the stone, I say, that supports the stones built upon it with the bitumen of charity. For stones ought to be built upon it—not wood, hay, or stubble—lest they fall through the wind of vanity, the storm of disturbance [Col. 0814C], the battering ram of hypocrisy, or some trembling kind of punishment in Gehenna. Therefore the strength of the walls must be fortified with living stones: with sardius through humility, emerald through the greenness of faith, and topaz through the brightness of wisdom. For it is a bright stone and like gold; in it the brightness of wisdom is signified.

Thus the city of God is built: for from the unbreakable stone of patience, or perseverance, strength acts according as wisdom directs, temperance measures, and justice completes. The teachers of the Church, like wise architects, build in that edifice breadth of heart in charity, height in hope, and depth in humility. Next comes the kinds of weapons. There are the shield of good will, the breastplate of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word [Col. 0814D] of God. There are the sharp arrows of the Mighty One in the word of preaching; coals in examples; the stone in the sling of the Shepherd; the jawbone of an ass against Samson’s enemies; and the breaking of jars in accordance with Gideon’s victory. With these weapons the saints fight and conquer: by mortification of the flesh, signified by breaking the jar; by remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, represented by the jawbone of the ass; and by thought of divine strength, represented by the sling and stone.

Next comes the watchfulness of the guards. The Bride bears witness of them that they spare no one walking by night. For when she herself sought her beloved by night and did not find him, the guards of the walls found her, struck her, wounded her, and took away her cloak. The guards are the prelates, who by the word of preaching strike with compunction, wound with charity, and strip of the covering of error the soul that still wanders on the way of moral life and seeks God, as it were by night, through the bypaths of heretical depravity. Therefore the inhabitants, considering the abundance of waters, the strength of the walls, the kinds of weapons, and the vigilance of their prelates, enlarge the Church’s joy through their security and say: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. VIII [8:35]).

Likewise the Church of God ought to rejoice in the common law, because whatever is established in her is worthy and just, whether it be justification, judgment, prohibition, commandment, admonition, or counsel. There is no double standard there; rather, all is equitable and wholly perfect. We call a law “common” when it is imposed upon all alike, as in the words: “Thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not steal” (Exod. XX [20]). Besides these, according to the different professions of religious orders, there are diverse observances, as it were civil laws. The observances of the Cistercian order differ from those of the Premonstratensian, and those again from the Cluniac; nevertheless all is just, and is as it were the civil law of the city of God.

But although the Church of God rejoices in all these things, she must rejoice above all and before all in her mighty king. For “great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy in his city” (Ps. XLVII [48]). Great in dignity, praiseworthy in wisdom; great in the height of his power, praiseworthy in the ordering of his house. Who would not marvel at the preciousness of its garments, the variety of its furnishings, and the abundance [Col. 0815C] of its feasts? In the rational house, contemplatives are clothed in the breastplate (*rationale*); actives in the ephod; teachers in hyacinth-blue; virgins in linen; martyrs in purple; confessors in twisted fine linen. The variety of furnishings is likewise this: the gridiron in mortification of the flesh; cauldrons for receiving ashes, in remembrance of committed iniquity; tongs in the virtue of discernment; the turned cup in the love of reading; forks for fire-receptacles, in the illumination and ardour of the mind.

How great the abundance of the feast is, the man bears witness who, making a wedding for his son, summons the invited guests to the oxen, the fattened animals, and all that is prepared (Matt. XXII [22:4]). What are these “all things”? Those without which a supper could not be called a supper, and in which every dish of spiritual food is contained: namely, the marrow of wheat [Col. 0815D] and the purest blood of the grape. In spiritual food the Lord prepared the ox in his Passion; the fattened animals in his resurrection, or ascension; the marrow of wheat when he broke bread with the disciples, saying: “Take, this is my body” (Matt. XXVI [26:26]). Likewise, he provided the blood of the grape when, taking the excellent cup, he blessed and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and drink; this is the cup of my blood” (Luke XXII [22:20]). Thus the invited person eats the ox when, in imitation of Christ, he afflicts the flesh; the fattened animals when, while bodily situated in pilgrimage, he dwells in thought and desire in that eternal homeland; the marrow of wheat and the blood of the grape when he fortifies himself with the most sacred viaticum. Therefore he eats oxen through the exercise [Col. 0816A] of labour; fattened animals through the height of devotion; and the marrow of wheat and blood of the grape through the sacrament of the altar. Behold, brothers, in how many things and in what things the Church’s joy endures. Behold what makes glad the city of God. It follows:

“The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle” (Ps. XLV [46]). If by “tabernacle” you wish to understand the womb of the Virgin, the body of Christ, or finally the soul of any man, it will be sufficiently clear how no one can take from the city of God that joy which has plainly been shown to be full. For who can take from her the joy of her sanctification, which has been accomplished with such preparation, operation, and confirmation? For the saying, “The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle,” is a mystery. For the hidden mysteries of the sons of Korah—that is, for you, brothers, who are sons of Calvary, namely of him who was crucified at Golgotha, which is the place of Calvary—the Psalm is inscribed “concerning the matter of the sacrament,” that is, concerning the tabernacle made by hand and the sanctification of this creation. Let us see how great is the joy in the sanctity of those tabernacles—that is, in the sacrament of the thing itself. Sanctification is represented in the sacrament of dedication; and since its sanctification is completed in five things—sprinkling, anointing, illumination, blessing, and inscription—we should know that the first, sprinkling, belongs to the preparation for holiness; three—anointing, illumination, and blessing—to its working; and the fifth, inscription, to its confirmation. By these things it is sufficiently made clear that no one can become a holy temple of the Lord and a sanctified tabernacle of the Most High unless first sprinkled with water, wine, salt, ashes, and hyssop.

For at the dedication of a church, the bishop first blesses water, mixing in salt; then he goes around the church three times and sprinkles it externally, while twelve lamps are meanwhile lit within. As the bishop goes around the church, he strikes with his pastoral staff upon the lintel of the doors, which must be closed for the symbolic meaning of the sacrament, saying: “Lift up your gates,” etc. The deacon answers from within: “Who is this King of glory?” And the bishop answers: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII [24]). On the third occasion, when the door is opened, the bishop enters, saying: “Peace to this house,” and prostrates himself in prayer; rising from it, [Col. 0816D] he exhorts all to pray, saying, “The Lord be with you.” Afterwards he writes the Greek alphabet upon the pavement, beginning on the left side of the church in the east and proceeding to the right, which is in the west; afterwards the Latin alphabet, beginning on the right side of the church in the east and proceeding to the left, which is in the west. After this, coming into the middle of the church, he begins, “O God, come to my aid,” etc.; and does this three times, completing the verse with the *Gloria*, without *Alleluia*. Then he blesses the symbolic water, mixing in salt and ashes. When these have been mixed, wine is added to them. After this he dips his finger in the water, making a cross through the middle of the altar and at its four corners. Then he goes seven times around the altar [Col. 0817A], sprinkling water with an aspergillum made of hyssop; afterwards, he goes three times around the church, while the clergy sing the prescribed antiphons. Then, after a prayer has been said, the bishop wipes the altar with a linen cloth; afterwards he censes it with incense; then he makes a cross in the middle of the altar and at its four corners with consecrated oil, and does this twice. For the third time he does the same with chrism. Then twelve crosses are anointed with chrism on the walls; and finally, fire being kindled from incense, the middle of the altar and its four corners are lit. Thus the altar is covered with white veils. Since all these things require much exposition, let us nevertheless expound something briefly concerning them all.

The house to be dedicated is the soul to be sanctified; water is penitence cleansing from the filth of sins; salt, reason seasoning the tasteless mind; the twelve lamps, the teaching of the apostles enlightening the world; the bishop, Christ; the staff, power; the threefold striking of the lintel, dominion over heaven, earth, and hell; the question from within, the people’s ignorance; the opening of the door, removal of sin. The bishop entering the house prays for peace; and Christ, coming to us, has wrought the soul’s salvation. The writing of the alphabet signifies the simple teaching of faith. That both alphabets are inscribed in the form of a cross means that each people is fortified through Christ’s Passion. Then the church is sprinkled. Water signifies confession; salt, biting penitence; ashes, remembrance of mortality; wine, devotion; hyssop, humility. The church and altar are sprinkled with all these, because by them body and soul are cleansed [Col. 0817C].

Next the altar is wiped with linen. The altar is Christ, upon whom we offer the gifts of devotion; the linen is his flesh, which through the beatings of the Passion was brought to the brightness of incorruption. Incense signifies prayer; oil, the grace of the Holy Spirit. The altar is anointed twice with this oil because God and man is believed to be full of the Holy Spirit. Or, if the altar signifies the soul, it is anointed twice because the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out for remission both of sin and offence. Finally chrism is applied, because after cleansing it is given for the strength and perfection of the spirit. Twelve crosses are made with chrism because through apostolic teaching the Church rejoices in this perfection. The white veil by which the altar is covered after consecration signifies the glory of incorruption with which humanity, mortality having been consumed, was clothed after the Passion [Col. 0817D]. Hence it is written: “Thou hast rent my sackcloth and hast clothed me with gladness” (Ps. XXIX [30]).

Therefore you cannot become the sanctified tabernacle of God unless first you season yourselves with the salt of wisdom, wash yourselves with the water of purity, drink the wine of compunction, and sprinkle your heads with the ashes of penitence; unless also knowledge of truth illuminates the mind, the oil of charity anoints it, steadfast perseverance inscribes it, and finally divine recompense blesses it: through our Lord Jesus Christ.

## SERMON XXXIX. ON THE FEAST OF ST BENEDICT

“If I bring a sword upon a land, and its people choose one man from among their least; and he sees the sword coming, and sounds the trumpet, and gives warning; and anyone who hears does not guard himself, his blood shall be upon his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not guard himself” (Ezek. XXXIII [33:2–5]). “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves,” and his testimonies, made exceedingly trustworthy, rightly shake the ears of hearers, because they are neither deceived nor deceive. If we reflect, “Thou art earth, and unto earth thou shalt go”; if we fear, in the man according to God’s heart, “My soul before thee is as earth without water” (Ps. CXLII [143]), we understand that the words, “Land upon which I shall bring a sword,” are spoken pointedly of us and concerning us. A sword has been brought against us because we are earth. Hence the earth was slain amid the bloods by which it remains defiled to this day. For this reason the Psalmist cries: “Deliver me from bloods, O God” (Ps. L [51]). Therefore we endure the sword brought upon us not because we are soil, not because we are ground, not because we are land, but because we are earth.

I have named four terms that signify the same thing, but not for the same cause or on a similar rationale. For *humus* (“moist soil”) is named from moisture; and it was truly *humus* when, in primal matter, it was mingled together and confusedly whirled about with watery waters. But it was truly *terra* (“earth”) when the waters had been divided from the waters, dry land appeared, and it could be trodden, and it was more shapeless than the other elements. Hence, because of its deformity, earth was called terrible earth (*terra terribilis*). It was *tellus* when it could endure, or began to endure, human labours, as it is written: “When thou hast worked the earth, it shall not yield its fruits, but shall bring forth thorns and briars for thee” (Gen. III [3]). But it is called *solum* (“ground”) because it stands solid. For while the other three elements are movable, this remains solid and tangible. Hence it is written: “Thou hast founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved for ever and ever” (Ps. CIII [104]).

Therefore man, formed from the mud of the earth, as something material made from matter, has received from these diverse terms diverse meanings according to the different states of life. For he was truly *humus*, and therefore deserved to be called *homo* (“man”), when, compacted by spiritual moisture like clay of heavenly wisdom, in his first condition he was made in the image and likeness of God and became a living soul.

For just as, in the first condition of things, moisture without heat held sway in the soil, so that, since all things are quickened alike by heat and moisture, it was not so much enlivened as made to grow [Col. 0818D], it suffered some deficiency from the lack of heat and had some perfection from the abundance of moisture; so too, in his first condition, man had both a certain deficiency by which he could die and a certain perfection by which he could avoid dying. He possessed a certain perfection by which he could stand; but he also bore a certain deficiency, because he did not have the grace by which he could advance. For he was made mortal and immortal: mortal, because he could die; immortal, because he could avoid dying. He could die because he could sin, for sin is the sting of death; he could not die because he could not sin. This was granted him through free choice [Col. 0819A], which is a will free for evil and for good. And because he could have refrained from sinning, yet sinned, being deprived of the infusion of heavenly moisture, he could be called earth, as though worthy to be trodden underfoot. And it appeared dry, because the soul was toward God like earth without water. And because it was deformed by the deforming form, it appeared exceedingly deformed and dreadful, because “though he was in honour, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII). Hence he deserved to be called not only mortal but also dead, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Indeed, the body is dead because of sin” (Rom. VIII). And the Psalmist says: “The earth was slain in blood” (Ps. CV). For it has a necessity of dying because it had a will to sin.

And even now [Col. 0819B], although it does not have a necessity of sinning, it nevertheless has a necessity of sin. For it was defiled by Adam’s sin as necessarily as it was voluntarily—voluntarily for him, but necessarily for us. Yet not necessarily in the sense that sinning is necessary to man, that is, useful; rather, necessary in the sense that it is unavoidable. Hence it can die and cannot fail to die, because after the Fall it was restored by assisting grace, in the fullness of time, so that through the endurance of sufferings and labours it might be able to put down roots toward the waters; and, beneath the tree, might become a tree of life; because, once the turning sword—that is, temporal punishment—had been removed, it might deserve to eat of the tree of life. Thus it might repair the loss of immortality through labour, not only so that it could avoid dying, but so that it could be unable to die.

Meanwhile [Col. 0819C], during the intervening time of labour, it could die, because through weakness and weariness of life it could sin; and likewise it could avoid dying, because it could refrain from sinning, on account of original concupiscence weakened in baptism and assisting grace. By this grace that sole High Priest, entering once with his own blood into the Holy of Holies, made in himself alone the one man whole. I say “one” (*solum*) from solidity, because it was made firm, so that what is mortal might put on immortality and our corruptible nature might put on incorruption; in such a way that it is granted us to be able not to die, and not to be able to die. Free choice, however, is not removed, but made freer; for by will and assisting grace it will come about that we can refrain from sinning and cannot sin.

Therefore the saying, “A land upon which I shall bring a sword,” etc., can be understood not according to man’s first state, nor [Col. 0819D] according to the third or fourth, but according to the second, which is signified by earth. For, as has been said, man’s first state was after his creation and before the Fall; the second after the Fall and before restoration; the third after restoration but before confirmation; the fourth after confirmation, when our earth will be neither infected nor slain, but rather firm and perfect.

He said, then: “A land upon which I shall bring a sword” (Ezek. XXXIII). He said, “I shall bring,” not “I shall draw.” For now is the time for brandishing, the time for bringing in, but not yet the time for drawing out. He brandishes in order to terrify, as it is written: “He has brandished his sword” (Ps. VII). He brings it in so that it may prick the heart within; he draws it out so that [Col. 0820A] it may strike openly. This will happen when his sword is roused against those who hate him. Therefore he brings it in so as to pierce the affections of the heart and direct them toward what is right. For in piercing it moves the affections, and in moving them it pierces.

He therefore has the piercing sword of hope, concerning which it is written: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). And elsewhere: “The word of God is living and more penetrating than any two-edged sword” (Heb. IV). That it is piercing in respect of hope is shown when it is said: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. XV). He also has the piercing sword of human reason, which is called Solomon’s sword, by which the child said to be divided is restored alive to its mother. He also has the piercing sword of sorrow, by which temporal punishment and the endurance of sufferings are signified; without its piercing we cannot return to the tree of life. He also has the piercing sword of fear, by which the Lord will slay all sinners of the earth, as it is written: “My sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. XXXII), that is, carnal persons.

If, therefore, a man, pierced by fear, love, hope, desire, or sorrow—by the sword of God’s word, the sword of reason, the sword of temporal punishment, or of final vengeance—chooses one man from among his least, as has been done, because today you have chosen one man who was truly *vir unus* (“one man”), though not *vir unum* (“a single entity”). For he is truly both *vir unus* and *vir unum* [Col. 0820B–C] who alone was and is that which he is. But he alone is that which he is who is selfsame (*idipsum*): who is not composed of fathers, because he is not a body; nor of compounded elements, because he is simple; nor of obscurities, because he is light; nor of unlike things, because he is spirit.

Yet a man is one whose countenance does not change into different things, but who, necessarily hastening toward one other reality, confesses one faith and one baptism. For just as many men are said to be “of one face” according to the outward man, so also according to their inward affection, of whom it is written: “They had one heart and one soul in the Lord” (Acts IV); so likewise one man may be called “of many faces,” whose countenance changes into different things. Therefore that man was one who was one in Christ, and Christ was one in him.

But let not the phrase “from among the least” [Col. 0820D] be despised in the mind, because it is customarily a term of reproach, as it is written: “We considered him the least of men” (Isa. XLIII). Rather, he was least because, invited to the Lamb’s wedding-feast, he chose to hold the lowest place, so that he might deserve to hear: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke XIV), fearing and understanding that the last were first and the first last, because the Spirit of the Lord rests upon the humble and quiet.

You have therefore chosen this least one. For although you have imposed a certain necessity upon yourselves, you are subject to the necessities of the Rule by will, not by compulsion. Of your own accord you have put your foot into Peter’s net and Benedict’s fetter. And rightly so: for where necessity is, there is no freedom; and where freedom is not, there is no will. [Col. 0821A] Where there is no will, there is no merit. For the will alone earns merit, as authority says: punishment if it is evil, reward if it is good. Therefore, in order that a man may rejoice in necessary freedom, he must employ a free necessity in deed, so that by it he may be freed from sin: having the necessity of suffering, so that his will may be free for righteousness and freed from sin.

For this reason, then, you chose a watchman. I call him a watchman (*speculator*) from a mirror (*speculum*), not from a watchtower (*specula*). For what was Saint Benedict other than a kind of mirror? By his obedience our contempt is convicted; by his humility, our pride; by his most pure religious observance, the defect of our own observance. For from such mirrors of this holy, dried soul there has been made for us a basin of cleansing. A basin ought to be made from mirrors, so that by the examples of the saints sins may first be recognized and then, once recognized, washed away by contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and fitting satisfaction and cleansing.

And what else does this mirror and model of life, shown to us on the mountain of religious observance as an example, teach except this? Or he may be called a watchman from a watchtower: one who ascends for us the watchtower of contemplation, of which it is written, “Set a table for yourself, and look attentively from the watchtower” (Isa. XXI); or the watchtower of circumspection, of which Jeremiah says, “Set a watchtower for yourself; place bitter things before yourself” (Jer. XXXI); or indeed the watchtower of prelacy, of which Ezekiel says, “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III).

This is he whose memory is in blessing [Col. 0821B–C], made a watchman for us: ascending the watchtower of contemplation in matters belonging to wisdom; of circumspection in matters belonging to knowledge; and of prelacy with respect to his household Church. He therefore saw—that is, understood—by the way of truth the approaching sword of the word of God; by the way of ordinances, the sword of reason; by the arduous way, the sword of sorrow; by the way of justice and severity, the sword of fear; and he sounded the horn.

And would that he sounded it—that is, made it sound inwardly—so that the bodily sound might strike the outward ears in such a way as to touch the inner ones. For he sounded a horn, not a trumpet, because he gave sound to those who were in Gibeah, not in Ramah. For Benedict sounded the horn (but Basil the trumpet), who calls the Rule, as it were, a horn, when he says: “We have written this Rule” [Col. 0821D] (*Rule*, final chapter). In it he does not assert that all righteousness has been written down, but that they may show themselves to possess some beginning of monastic life. But, as he himself says: “Whoever wishes to attain the summit of perfection has the teachings of the holy Fathers, and also the Rule of our holy Father Basil” (*ibid.*).

Behold, the horn sounds for us while we are still in Gibeah, for Gibeah means “hill.” So long as we refuse to turn aside from the wickedness of the world, we do not attain the height of virtues. But Basil sounded the trumpet of a greater perfection for those who were in Ramah. Ramah indeed means “heights.” And because the loftiness of the perfect life is described in that Rule, he sounded his trumpet in Ramah.

Whoever, therefore, has heard the voice of the horn has placed his neck beneath the perpetual yoke of the Rule; but if he does not observe himself according to the form of the institution, the blood of transgression will be upon him, so that the Rule becomes for him a cause of perdition which ought to have been a cause of salvation. For just as the Rule has become a norm of righteousness for the obedient, so for the disobedient it becomes a snare and trap of punishment.

Let us therefore hear the sound of the horn, and not, like deaf adders, stop our ears; but let us guard ourselves with every vigilance, lest what was given for life become death to us; what was given as an antidote become poison; what was given for rest become toil. Rather, according to the form of the Rule, let us change ourselves [Col. 0822A–B] into other men, fleeing from fault to contrition of heart; from contrition of heart to confession; from confession to penance; from penance to pardon; from pardon to grace. This is the way by which Saint Benedict both ascended and furnished examples of ascent, our Lord Jesus Christ himself leading him, who lives and reigns with the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages.

## SERMON XL. ON THE SPIRITUAL ARK

> [Note: [Col. 0821D] Because the words of this theme are those of the Philistines, the author, taking this occasion, discusses from the very beginning those who preach [Col. 0822D] or preside but live badly.]

“Make a new cart, and yoke two milch-cows upon which no yoke has been laid, and place the ark of God upon it” (1 Sam. VI). The proposition is a faithful saying, and would be worthy of all acceptance if the merits of the speaker corresponded to his useful words. But the life of the speaker commonly weakens the force of his words to no small degree. For Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 0822D] Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 12.]

> “When a man’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching too is held in contempt.”

Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise [my body]” (1 Cor. IX), etc. Therefore the Lord rebukes such persons in the Gospel, saying: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye” (Luke VI), etc.

But if this is so, what does the same Apostle mean when elsewhere he says: “Whether through pretext or through truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice and shall rejoice” (Phil. I)? Since in the Church of God one man is a shepherd, another a hireling, another a thief, another a robber, will the Apostle rejoice at the preaching of the hireling, thief, and robber just as he rejoices at the shepherd’s preaching?

For the shepherd is one who speaks the truth for the sake of truth. The hireling is one who does so for temporal profit, not for truth itself. But the thief, for the occasion of falsehood, offers stolen waters and hidden bread. “For the thief comes only to steal, kill, and destroy.” By deceitful lips they are accustomed to seduce their hearers. The robber, however, openly rages against the sheep with unjust lips. “O Lord,” says the Prophet, “deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. CXIX). Why, then, would the Apostle rejoice at the preaching of such persons?

It should be noted that among the reprobate some are contemptible in life but not in reputation; others in reputation but not in life; and the worst are contemptible in both reputation [Col. 0823A] and life—as the best are so in neither reputation nor life. Those who have an evil reputation are such either because of a private sin or a public one. “Public” is understood in three ways.

A matter is called public, as though “of the people” (*populicum*), when anyone from among the people may accuse it, as in the crime of treason, heresy, or simony. Or a matter is called public when it is manifest and notorious; for “manifest” and “notorious” are not the same. Every notorious matter is manifest, but the converse does not hold, since something can be manifest to a judge but not to others, or to others but not to the judge. What is notorious is known both to the judge and to others. Yet it is difficult to discover what is notorious.

For the sins of the Sodomites were manifest to the Sodomites; nevertheless the Lord came down so that they might become more notorious [Col. 0823B] (Gen. XVIII). A person may be contemptible because of a public or notorious sin, but not because of a merely manifest one. Even if a sin is manifest to the judge but not to others, or indeed to others but not to the judge, the sinner does not thereby deserve condemnation until the truth of the allegation is established by lawful witnesses.

A private sin is one which private persons can testify to or accuse. Or “private” means hidden: what is known to no one, or to one person only. For even if it is known to one person, it is no less hidden, since the voice of one is the voice of none. A private sin, therefore, condemns no one until, through the matter of which he is convicted or which he freely confesses, he becomes as a heathen and publican. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you”—that is, if he sins with your knowledge—“rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. XVIII).

But if he denies it, even if it is manifest to you, cease accusing him, because you have delivered your soul: you saw the arrow that struck him, and he did not take heed when you warned him. But if he confesses and nevertheless does not amend his ways, then bring in two witnesses. And if, before them, he denies what he had confessed secretly before you, again cease, because you have delivered your soul.

Yet in this matter you must beware lest, by a gesture or by your words, it can be wholly detected what he confessed to you in secret. Rather, as if entirely unaware, say: “Brother, this and this are said of you; see that you have not done it.” [Col. 0823C–D] But if he confesses before two witnesses and still does not correct himself, pray the Lord to pour into him a penitent heart by which he may shake off his neck from the yoke of diabolical slavery. If even then he does not correct himself, avoid him as a heathen and publican; for he can no longer convict you of falsehood, since you could have overcome him through suitable witnesses.

Those who are contemptible in life are infamous in faith or morals. Those infamous in morals are so either through a sudden and hidden temptation, a sudden and manifest one, one long deliberated and hidden, or one long deliberated and manifest—as are those corrupt in morals and publicly defamed. Thus the Psalmist says: “You shall not fear the terror by night”—behold, a sudden and hidden temptation—“nor the arrow flying by day”—behold, sudden and manifest—“nor the business that walks in darkness”—behold, long deliberated and hidden—“nor the demon at noon” (Ps. XC)—behold, long deliberated and manifest. Those corrupt in morals through a long-deliberated and manifest temptation are contemptible before God.

Those who err in faith are either within the Church or outside the Church, for even though they are decayed members, they are not thereby separated from the body of the Church. Those within the Church who are corrupt in faith adulterate God’s word for three reasons: simplicity, weakness, or malice. But one kind of simplicity arises from vincible ignorance and another from invincible ignorance. Vincible ignorance [Col. 0824A–B] is when someone can know but does not wish to know; of this it is said: “The ignorant person shall be ignored” (1 Cor. XIV). Of the second the Apostle says: “I received mercy because I acted in ignorance” (1 Tim. I). The former deserves punishment; the latter, pardon.

Weakness sometimes arises from greed, sometimes from fear. Since people fear the countenance of the powerful, or covet riches or honours, they are accustomed to spare the powerful and to lick their wounds, which they ought to cut away with the sword of correction. Thus they become calumniators, prevaricators, and equivocators. A calumniator brings a false charge; a prevaricator conceals the truth; an equivocator grows weary of and abandons a truth once undertaken.

Therefore, those who sin through simplicity born of invincible ignorance or through weakness are to be admonished and corrected; for we ought not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more they can do, but rather him who, after killing the body, can destroy the soul in Gehenna. But those who sin through simplicity born of vincible ignorance, or through malice, rightly deserve contempt from God and men.

Those unbelievers outside the Church either have never been within the Church, or have been cut off from it. Those cut off either cut themselves off, or are cut off by a definitive sentence from a judge. Those cut off by a judge are cut off by excommunication, deposition, or degradation. Therefore, those who have cut themselves off [Col. 0824C–D], whether by deposition or degradation, are contemptible and to be condemned. But those cut off by excommunication are to be endured and awaited. Those who have never been within the Church, if they have mingled some truth into their writings, are not to be altogether despised, because they sinned through ignorance.

For they are channels of the Lord’s garden, a furnace-sweep, a dung-house of the ark, Elijah’s ravens, a priest cleansing others by truth while himself remaining in filth until evening. For often, as the turtledove and swallow, so the kite and stork have known the coming—not, I say, of their own [coming], but of Christ’s.

By the turtledove I mean Simeon, namely that groaning man who said:

> [Note: [Col. 0825D] St Augustine, in the sermon *On the Purification*.]

> “Do you think that I shall endure? Do you think that I shall see?” etc.

For this is he who said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II). We rightly compare John the Baptist to the swallow: martyrdom reddened his neck, virginity whitened his belly, and the burden of penitence darkened his back. Though placed in this pilgrimage in body alone, he was fed with spiritual food from the heavenly homeland. Thus, seeing Christ come to baptism, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

But the kite, because it is rapacious, aptly represents the rapacious Balaam, who, enticed by Balak’s promises, changed altars in order to look out from there [Col. 0825A–B] for the direction from which he might curse God’s people. Yet the Lord opened his mouth when he said: “A star shall rise out of Jacob,” etc. (Num. XXIII).

By the stork, which lives on venomous animals, we mean the Erythraean Sibyl, a poisoner and enchantress. Yet Augustine adduces this testimony of hers concerning Christ:

> [Note: [Col. 0826D] St Augustine, *The City of God*, ch. 23.]

> “He shall come into the hands of unbelievers; they shall give God slaps with unclean hands, and, receiving blows, he shall remain silent. He shall give his back to the scourges; they gave him gall for food and vinegar for thirst; they had set before him this table of inhospitality,” etc.

Therefore, because the Spirit breathes where he wills, attention should be paid not to who speaks, but to what is spoken. Thus an Amalekite, wearied on the journey, after receiving food became guide of David’s army; because those who lick the earth—that is, love the earth—and, satiated by temporal things, are as if wearied on the way, after receiving spiritual food often become leaders and teachers of the army of the true David.

Such are those of whom we proposed to speak at the beginning: those who bear in the Church the figure of persons who preach well but live badly. Hence they are aptly called Philistines, that is, “falling through drink.” And what is God’s word except a kind of drink against the devil’s poison? Yet those who preach well but live badly fall through this drink. For they will hear the Psalmist’s words: “Why do you recount my righteous ordinances? Yet you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you” (Ps. XLIX); and finally: “I shall rebuke you and set you before your face.” Therefore, because the good that is done is not good for the person through whom it is done, but for the person to whom it is done [Col. 0825C–D], let us attentively hear what was said: “Make a new cart,” etc. (1 Sam. VI).

It is called new in contrast to the old—that is, ancient—cart, which began to roll among four wheels at the beginning of the world. The first is the instability of time; the second, the changeability of age; the third, the alternation of affections; the fourth, the uncertainty of events. For nothing in the world is stable, because God,

> Remaining stable, gives all things motion.  
> (*Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy*)

For the sun rises and sets, circles through the south and turns toward the north, and again returns to its place. Behold the wheel of time. The wheel of age is that [Col. 0826A] man begins from earth and returns to earth; begins in infancy and returns to infancy; his life begins in weeping and ends in weeping. The events of the world are so unstable that adversities always follow prosperity, and prosperity adversities. Affections likewise are so unstable that love always follows hatred and hatred love.

Among these four wheels human life is loaded like a cart, now with hay, now with mire. “All flesh is hay,” and its burden does not cease to roll among the four wheels while life lasts. We compare sin to mire because, just as mire by its decay produces worms and by its drying sends forth smoky heat, so too does sin. Isaiah says: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI). Hence the Gospel says of such persons: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XIII): weeping from smoke, gnashing of teeth from the bite of worms. O wretched people who choose to load the cart of their life with such mire!

In contrast to this cart, then, the other is called new: namely, that which rolls among Ezekiel’s four wheels. The first concerns Christ’s humanity, the second his Passion, the third his Resurrection, and the fourth his Ascension. The four living creatures did not cease to turn these wheels. Hence it is written: “Wherever the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them” (Ezek. I). Accordingly they received their names from their office. The first had the face of a man as the sign of humanity; the second, the face of a calf as the sign of the Passion [Col. 0826B–C]; the third, the face of a lion as the sign of the Resurrection; the fourth, the face of a flying eagle as the sign of the Ascension. It follows:

“And yoke two cows.” Nature and usefulness disclose to us the mystery of so great a thing. Nature, because a cow chews the cud and divides the hoof. Its usefulness is found to be fourfold: with its hide it protects people’s feet; with its flesh it feeds its master; with its milk it nourishes the child; with its dung-smoke it enriches the field.

“Hear this, you fat cows who dwell on Mount Samaria” (Amos IV), who cast aside the sweet yoke, who have learned to love threshing, not farming: wanton cows, not lowing ones; who neither chew the cud in affection nor are useful in effect. Attend to how affection is adorned, and how effect advances. Chew the cud by meditating upon God’s word; distinguish what has been chewed, lest any falsehood be mixed with it. Adorn your souls with affections, but your bodies also with actions. For if you protect Christ’s poor, as though feet, with your outward possessions, as though hides; if through mortification of the flesh you do God’s will, which is to feed Christ; if by the milk of your teaching you refresh one subject to you; if finally you enrich the Lord’s field with dung—you yoke two cows, that is, soul and body, to the new cart. For in this way flesh is joined to spirit, and spirit to flesh.

“Yoke two cows upon which no yoke has been laid” (1 Sam. VI). He does not say “every yoke”; speaking indefinitely, he says “a yoke,” [Col. 0827A] and rightly. For there is the yoke of nature, of which it is written: “A heavy yoke lies upon the sons of Adam” (Ecclus. XL). There is the yoke of discipline: “My yoke is sweet” (Matt. XI); and beforehand he said, “Learn from me.” There is the yoke of guilt: “The yoke shall rot away because of the oil” (Ecclus. XL), that is, sin shall fail before the presence of the Holy Spirit. And there is the yoke of punishment. Hence Isaiah says: “The yoke of his burden” (Isa. X), etc. You have overcome the yoke of burden, that is, captivity to eternal punishment. Since we cannot avoid the yoke of nature and ought not avoid the yoke of discipline, if we wish to avoid the yoke of punishment, let us beware lest the yoke of guilt be laid upon us.

It follows: “And place the ark of God upon it.” Note that “ark of God” is said in four senses. There is an ark of preservation, an ark of religious life, an ark of signification, and an ark of sanctification. Of the first it is written: “Jehoiada the high priest made a treasury in the Temple and placed in it an ark, making in it an opening above, so that money might be stored in it for repairing the damaged roofs of the Temple” (4 Kings XII). Of the second, God said to Noah: “Make yourself an ark” (Gen. VI), etc. Of the third it was said to Moses: “Make yourself an ark of shittim wood” (Exod. XXV).

In all these the holy mind is figured, in which we store the treasure that we have in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge: wisdom through divinity, knowledge through humanity. It ought therefore to be made of wood smoothed by immunity from sin, polished by the splendour of virtues, coated with pitch through fullness of grace, and joined together through the union of concord. In such an ark the golden urn should be stored through faith in Christ’s humanity; the manna, through faith in his divinity. In it should be stored the tables of both Testaments and the Deuteronomy of evangelical truth.

This is the ark of sanctification [Col. 0827B–0828A], God’s rest and the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. Yet there is another, special and unique ark, which much more worthily and more sublimely than all others is to be placed upon the new cart. This is she in whose praise we sing:

> Blessed Mother by her gift,  
> Whose heavenly Maker,  
> Holding the world in his fist,  
> Was enclosed beneath the ark of her womb.  
> (*Office of the Church*)

This is the ark of preservation in which the heavenly treasure was uniquely enclosed—namely, the wisdom of God the Father. She was made of wood not so much smoothed as light, because, sanctified in her mother’s womb, she was born free from every sin; and she shone by the fullness of singular grace, as though made of polished wood. This is she who freed us from the floodwaters of which it is said: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. LXVIII). This is she in whom were enclosed the unique urn of Christ’s humanity, the manna of divinity, the words of discipline, and the tablets of the Testament—the Deuteronomy of the abbreviated Word. For she kept in her heart all the words spoken concerning Christ. Place her, therefore, upon it through love, veneration, praise, and prayer, that she may intercede for us with the Lord.

## ABOUT THE END OF THE TWELFTH CENTURY: LETTERS OF GAUFRID, SUBPRIOR OF THE REGULAR CANONS AT SAINTE-BARBE IN NEUSTRIA, AND VARIOUS LETTERS ADDRESSED TO HIM

[Col. 0827]

(*Dom Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 494, from a manuscript of the monastery of Lyre.)

## LETTER I. JOHN, ABBOT OF BAUGÉ, TO ABBOT GAUFRID

He laments the pastoral burden imposed upon him.

[Col. 0827C]

To the reverend lord G., to be honoured with every expression of veneration—formerly prior, but now co-abbot of Baugé—

> [Note: [Col. 0827] Baugé, commonly Baugercy, a Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Tours, three leagues distant from Villaloup.]

Brother J., the unworthy servant of Christ’s servants [Col. 0828C] dwelling in the same monastery, wishes whatever so small a man can pray for one so great.

For those who are in sorrow, it is usually a great remedy if they can have reciprocal conversation with someone in whose affection they have confidence. But because so great expanses of land separate and prevent us [Col. 0829A] from speaking together, it seemed to me a great consolation if at least through a letter I might disclose to you the anxiety of my heart.

I, who could scarcely govern myself, scarcely feed my kids, scarcely restrain the motions of the flesh and the irrational impulses of the mind, am now compelled to judge the innocence of others, serve the habits of others, order the lives of better men, and instruct those more learned than myself. And this is contrary to the Apostle’s judgment: “If anyone does not know how to govern his own household, how shall he have care for the Church of God?” (1 Tim. III).

The saying therefore may be applied to me: “They set me as a keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I have not kept” (Cant. I). I who was once nourished among crocuses now embrace dung, and things which my soul formerly refused to touch are now my food because of distress. For I who was formerly intent on spiritual studies am now compelled to hunger after temporal advantages and to attend to earthly cares.

These, dearest Father, are the things that sting my mind, torture it with continual sorrows, do not allow me to rest, and consume me without sleeping. Open therefore to me the bowels of your charity and be a companion in tribulation, that you may be a sharer in consolation. Farewell, and pray to God for me, who am yours. The bearer of this letter can make known to you our outward circumstances, lest I detain you with a lengthy discourse. Your people greet you; do not disdain to take the trouble of visiting them as soon as you can.

> Go, consoler, for grief and anger overcome me—  
> Anger, which I have often learned to overcome by the lyre.

To Timothy:

> You have a father’s blows; have a mother’s breasts.

To Titus:

> You have a mother’s breasts; have a father’s blows.

## LETTER II. GAUFRID TO JOHN

Reply to the preceding letter.

To his venerable father and lord J., his abbot, Gaufrid, wholly his own: the Spirit of counsel and consolation.

We received and read your letters, which poured forth tears instead of words. [Col. 0829D] For in it we saw a cloud flying aloft in its accustomed way, yet carrying a certain darkness of sorrow. Thus two different, indeed contrary, feelings suddenly arose together in our mind: compassion, namely, for your affliction, and joy for your advancement. But the greatness of our joy readily softened and tempered the pain of compassion.

Therefore I rejoice and congratulate our vineyard, over which, by God’s ordering, it has fallen to you both to preside and to be of service. For, with your fatherhood established there upon an exalted watchtower, it will be granted to it by the Lord, under your governance, both to spread its branches, to flower, and to bear fruit. From the very time of your youth you have been accustomed to stand upon your ways and inquire concerning the ancient paths. From the first bloom of youth, I say, you deserved to dwell in gardens, to be nourished among saffron, to live among vineyards; there you heard and saw, and by the teaching of experience learned [Col. 0830A] how you ought to work.

You know, therefore, how to prune useless branches, so that those which thrive may bear more abundant fruit. You know how to build a wall around the vineyard, dig a winepress in it, and build a tower in its midst; nor will the generous hand of the householder be lacking to supply the expense of completing it. Rightly, therefore, have they set you as keeper over vineyards—you who know so well what vineyards require. Be strengthened, then, in the Lord and in the might of his power.

But behold: you complain of labour as though you were already wearied; as though, exhausted by the tribulation of evils and groaning beneath the burden of governance, you allege causes of difficulty, saying: “These are the things, dearest one, which stir my mind, which torment me with continual sorrows, which [Col. 0830B] do not allow me to rest, and which consume me even while I do not sleep.” Yet it is fitting that you bear patiently the cares which Christ’s members require of you, since both his fear and his love compel you to serve them.

We therefore ask you to act in these matters with somewhat greater consolation and more watchful attention; for, as the Apostle says, “we are appointed for these things” (1 Thess. 3). He himself considers it a great gift of grace to share in Christ’s sufferings; therefore, instructing the Philippians, he says: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1). These and similar things we wish you to bring forth from the treasury of Scripture before the eyes of your mind whenever the sorrow of tribulation comes upon you. Let not the apostolic consolation slip from you: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared [Col. 0830C] with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). In that confident joy the Prophet, faithfully rejoicing, says: “We rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evils” (Ps. 89).

Thus the Apostle instils terror, but forearms the ignorant, removes sloth, and sets forth matter for victory, when he says: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Be of more even mind, therefore; make virtue out of necessity, and a crown out of tribulations. By enduring them with equanimity you can lighten them; by fleeing you cannot escape them. Therefore act manfully; let your heart be strengthened; and wait for the Lord.

But if you seek relief in dispatching the external occupations by which you are busied and burdened, custom and authority allow—as you know—the care and burdens of governance to be distributed among subordinate persons: the prior, subprior, and other officials; so that external affairs may in due order serve through the supports of common life, and internal matters may preserve spiritual fruits according to the Rule. In this way you will more often be able to find the free seclusion of contemplative repose, in which the brightness of the heavenly vision may smile upon you; and to fly back to those heights of peace, where you may touch heavenly secrets with the hand of the heart and behold supernal joys incorporeally.

Ever since I received your letter and learned that you had been appointed to this honour—indeed, this burden—whenever I approach to celebrate the sacred solemnities of the Mass, I always remember you [Col. 0831A] in my prayers, beseeching that you may shine forth in pursuits pleasing to God. May your fatherhood deign to return the same service to my littleness, by praying similarly for me and loving me, who love you as myself. Farewell.

> Honour serves those who do not serve honour;  
> He rightly holds the rod for whom the rod inspires no fear.  
> He loves Rachel, nor refuses to bear Leah;  
> Thus the new Jacob takes both as wives.

## LETTER III. GAUFRED TO THE MONKS OF BAUGÉ. He congratulates them upon having at last arrived at their newly founded monastery and praises their solitude.

To the beloved brethren in Christ of the monastery of Baugé, [Col. 0831B] G., servant of your holiness: one heart and one soul in the Lord.

Our mouth has been filled with joy and our tongue with exultation on hearing of the arrival of your holy community at the place which God prepared for you to serve him. Blessed be he who has caused you to dwell in a region sufficiently peaceful; for it befits the children of peace to inhabit a land of peace.

Behold, separated from the tumult of the world, you have gone far away in flight and remain in solitude. For you have fled, as Isaiah says, “from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the drawn bow, from the face of grievous battle.” This is a praiseworthy flight: thus Elijah fled from the face of Jezebel. Of flight it is said: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, my people” (Jer. 51).

You remain, therefore, with those who, according to Job, “build for themselves solitudes.” Your heart is a desert because it is far from the noise and tumult of vices, is not trodden down by the multitude of thoughts, but remains green and flowering; it will bring forth shoots of virtues, and within it the dove—the Holy Spirit—sings. There, you who love the law of God possess abundant peace: abundance, that is, in tranquillity of mind and joy of contemplation. God speaks of the former to his people, but of the latter to his saints. The former is within a human being; the latter is above the human being.

You have therefore chosen and loved solitude, so that the soul, free for God alone and with its affections purified, may fly to heavenly things and taste beforehand the sweetness of supernal delight. There may the way of the holy ants be fervent; there may the works of holy bees give forth fragrance; there may fruit be borne in patience, with the virtue of perseverance. There may that heavenly manna refresh your minds: it became the price upon the cross, the provision for the journey in pilgrimage, and will become the reward in the homeland. There may God write the words of the Law on the tablets of your hearts with the finger of his mercy. There may the tabernacle of the covenant and the ark of the Testament be constructed, so that whatever the veils of the material tabernacle signified in the splendour of gold, the brilliance of gems, and the diversity of manifold workmanship may shine forth in your morals and deeds.

There may luxury be slain and every lust struck down. Let the sacrifice of chastity be offered for the turtle-doves, and the purity of innocence for the young pigeons. There, with angelic aid attending, bring the fragrant offerings of prayers in the golden vessel of libation before the throne of the Father. There also pray for us, you who are worthy to be heard; for you approach God with the great sacrifice of sincere love and offer his praises in holy works.

But I beseech you, brethren, bear the word of consolation. For, to use the words of blessed Augustine, no discourse is more fruitfully given, returned, received, or accepted than that concerning the source of our goodness and blessedness. May God himself be your honour, your joy, your delight; consolation in sorrow, counsel in uncertainty, defence in injury, patience in tribulation, medicine in weakness. In him possess everything whom you desire to love above all things. And because you have assembled in that place with hearts devoted to serving him, may you carry away with you the gifts of spiritual joys and eternal rewards. Farewell.

> Happy in their lot are those whom a boundary restrains,  
> And for whom the deepest repose is welcome in return.

> *For modesty: Let your mind be a turtle-dove; for simplicity, a dove.  
> Thus acceptable to God, thus you will become a holy offering.*

## LETTER IV. TO JOHN, ABBOT. He urges him manfully to cut away vices in the monastery and punish offences.

To the venerable abbot JOHN, G., wholly his, wishes that he may correspond to the grace of his name.

We read that holy Moses received counsel concerning the ordering of authorities from an apostate man, namely a priest of idols; and thereafter, as Scripture says, “God spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Exod. 33). Yet this wise, discerning, and provident man did not despise a good word or good counsel, though it came from a Gentile, but did everything that he had suggested. Thus a faithful man faithfully accepted the faithful counsel of an unbelieving man; and so it came about that the unfruitful man made the barren fruitful, and the unjust man made the just man more just.

I have said this beforehand lest your holiness judge that what I am about to say ought to be rejected because of the unworthiness of its speaker or his less praiseworthy manner of life. Attend not to who speaks, but to what is said.

You stand upon the Lord’s watchtower. They have set you as keeper of vineyards, that you may consider diligently and with close attention what may harm and what may be of benefit, and that you may catch the little foxes which destroy them. I speak to one who knows. It is your office to prune useless branches so that those which are strong may bear more abundant fruit. At length, the season of pruning has come. You ought to take heed lest some solitary wild beast devour the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts over which you preside, and lest those who pass along the road harvest it.

Under your cultivation may the barren fig tree flower again and return into favour with its Lord, whose threats and axe it fears. It is yours to dig around it, lay dung upon it, and take careful care lest it become wild again. I do not assume the part of one teaching, but of one admonishing. For, as Jerome says to Eustochium, it is foolish to teach one whom you know already knows what you teach.

Your prudence knows that Eli [Col. 0833A] is condemned because of his sons’ iniquity. He knew that his sons behaved shamefully, and he did not correct them. Lest this should happen to you also—far be it!—may zeal for the Lord’s house healthfully consume your mind, zeal which threatens together with Moses and says: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32). Of this sword the Prophet says: “Cursed is he who keeps his sword from blood”—that is, his word from correcting sin.

But someone says: “If a prelate rebukes a delinquent subject, he often fears that the latter may become worse because of the correction and that he may incur his hatred.” God consoles this fear, for he himself says: “You have delivered your soul, and your good shall return to you” (Ezek. 3). Hence a certain wise man says: “To offend a man for God’s sake is to gain the favour of God.” The Apostle says to Titus: “Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority” (Tit. 2). Prelates must deal with delinquent subjects in such a manner that it may not be said of them: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56).

How many make their reputation stink—those upon whom their masters have imposed external affairs, yet who refuse to remove from them the occasion of wrongdoing! They become participants in evils because they make them a stumbling-block and rock of offence to others. “We provide things good,” says the Apostle, “not only before God, but also before men” (Rom. 12); and whoever neglects his reputation is cruel.

But, alas, how rare today is a Phinehas to pierce the shameless; how rare a Moses to kill the sacrilegious; how rare a Samuel to mourn the disobedient; how rare a Job to offer sacrifice for his children’s negligence; how rare an Aaron to proclaim divine threats before Pharaoh; how rare a Noah to provide a pitch-covered ark for those threatened with drowning. May God grant that the community of brethren entrusted to you may breathe the fragrance of divine sweetness, and that its fruits may become fruits of honour and integrity. May the north wind daily be regarded with suspicion, not only for the flowers but also for the fruit and leaves. Therefore may the south wind come and blow through your garden, so that its fragrance may become like the fragrance of a full field which God has blessed. Amen.

Do not be offended by the dry appearance of the page and the bloodless colour of its letters. Weigh the meaning, not the words; for, as that poet says:

> Everyone feeds on the fruit, not the leaves, of trees;  
> Meaning must be preferred to words.  
> Often virtue lies hidden beneath a cheap garment;  
> Often a humble house contains many good things.  
> It is mercy to punish crime; it is a crime to spare criminals:  
> Such mercy has nothing of mercy in it.

## LETTER V. TO THE SAME. He asks him to visit him at least by letter.

To his venerable abbot J., brother G. wishes always to have his eyes upon the Lord.

We learned from the report of the abbot of St Andrew of Gouffern—an eminent man of proven religious life—

> [Note: [Col. 0833] At Gouffern, in French *en Goufer*, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Séez; this monastery was subject to Savigny.]

—that, as you were returning from the Cistercian chapter, you had planned to come to us. This report indeed gave joy and gladness to my hearing, for I greatly desired to see your face and speak mouth to mouth. But, I suppose, the grievous disturbance of stormy weather impeded your journey. For contention has been poured out upon princes, and it causes many to wander in a trackless place and not on the way.

I beg you, however, if you learn that anyone from your region is coming to ours, grant us at least your presence through a letter. These are the words of Jerome, a man—as you know—approved by the merit of his life and most celebrated for the singular title of his wisdom. The comic poet Turpilius, treating of the interchange of letters, says: “It alone is the thing that makes absent people present.” Nor did he give a false judgment, one which he knew to be true from his own experience.

For what, so to speak, is as present as to address and hear through letters the person whom you love? Hence those uncultivated people of Italy, whom Ennius calls *Cassi*, and who, as Cicero says in his *Rhetorics*, procured their livelihood by the sword, before the use of paper and parchment, used to exchange letters on tablets hewn from wood or on the bark of trees [perhaps *missitabant*, “sent repeatedly,” rather than *musitabant*]; and from the bearers of these they called letter-carriers *tabellarii*, and writers *librarii*, from the bark-books of trees.

How much more, then, now that the world has been refined by the arts, ought we not omit what those possessed who lived amid crude rusticity and in some sense did not know civilization itself. Pope Innocent says in his decretal letter to Aurelius of Carthage: “Your love consists in familiar writings; for the offices of charity deserve to be rendered more securely in private.” Likewise Jerome, in his letter to Tranquillinus: “Truly,” he says, “and simply I speak to your most candid heart: the very little sheet and the many strokes of its letters breathe into us the affection of your mind.”

Thus I take up the words of blessed Jerome himself, addressed to a particular friend, and make them my own to you: “Whenever I am well, I present letters on my behalf to you; and, though absent in body, I come in love and spirit.” I earnestly ask that friendships newly born, which have adhered by the glue of Christ, may not be torn apart either by time or by the distance of places, but rather that we may bind them together by reciprocal letters. Let them run between us; let them meet one another; let them speak with us. Love will not lose much if it converses with itself in such discourse.

For the aforesaid doctor knew, and had often experienced, that devout conversation among friends is accustomed to stir a certain pleasantness, while a letter passing between them creates a marvellous kind of presence. For when it puts on the mind of the writer, it is not merely sent by the friend, but, indeed, wholly carries the friend himself across.

I say this, dearest Father, because I should like to be informed by the return of your letters concerning your welfare and the condition of your house, which I especially love and in which, though absent in body, I dwell in soul and spirit night and day—unless Normandy is so hateful to you that you fear even to let your letters come here. I have often challenged you to the duty of correspondence, and have scarcely obtained one little note from you. Awake; arise from sleep; render your little letters to love. It will be a great solace for my longing here if I receive your letters even once a year.

May God, opening his best treasury, make you abound in every good thing. We greet with united service the brethren who deign to know and love us. Farewell.

> Happy is he who abounds in gifts of such great virtue,  
> For scarcely any trouble disturbs his mind.

> *Live, I pray, but live for God; for to live for the world  
> Is the work of death; to live for God is living life.*

> *Would that I were as happy as you are pure in heart:  
> There is still no one wounded by my speech.*

## LETTER VI. JOHN TO GAUFRED. Reply to the preceding letter.

JOHN, by God’s permission abbot of St Mary of Baugé, to G., beloved above all and especially dear among those whom he loves most—namely the subprior of St Barbara—whatever is, and more if it were possible, in the Lord.

As often as the devout hearing of your letters strikes the ears of our bodily being, so often the sweet memory of you touches the inner love of our heart; so much so that, if it were possible, we should wish not merely that your inward love speak to us through letters, but that your bodily presence itself might continually be granted to us. But since, owing to the abounding discord of kings and the malice of men, free access is not presently allowed us, let us strive, where we cannot have bodily presence, to preserve with whole mind the love conceived in the bonds of charity.

Concerning the death of Lord N., which you asked us to make known to you: by this letter we direct that you endeavour to observe annually his anniversary on 10 September, with the due office of charity. May you always fare well in the Lord. Amen.

> If there is in him a fault which must be cleansed,  
> May he cleanse it, and may God grant the cleansed man eternal being.

## LETTER VII. GAUFRID TO JOHN, ABBOT. He complains of the brevity of the letter; mentions a library at Caen, should he wish to buy it; and announces the death of his cellarer.

To his venerable abbot J., G., servant of your holiness, greeting—that greeting which is true.

I received the writings of your love; seasoned with the honey of affection, they tasted sweet to my heart. I read them eagerly, gladly reread them, and they please me more when repeated. I complain only of this: that to one who loves you greatly, and whom you love greatly, you sent things so few and so brief. You speak to us rarely; we should have preferred a longer discourse. We should have wished to hear from you something that would instruct our morals, relieve the weariness of our pilgrimage, and kindle us in love for the heavenly homeland.

I make known to you that you may still find at Caen, if you wish, that excellent library about which I wrote to you long ago. Perhaps you would have bought it, but in your letter you sent us no word about it.

Our chief cellarer, who raised our walls and built our houses—a man of great reputation and much integrity—has put off the human being. We therefore beseech your fatherhood to pour out prayers to the Lord for him together with the brethren, especially during the solemnities of the sacred rites. For, as blessed Gregory says, the offering of the sacred altar, presented with tears and kindness of mind, especially aids our absolution.

Commend me to the holy prayers of the community of Baugé. Greet it first from me, the servant of all, if you judge me worthy. May God be gracious to me, that he may not remove your prayer and his mercy from me, but may mercifully correct my actions, amend my life, order my morals, and bring me together with you to the inheritance of the heavenly paradise. Amen. Rejoice always in the Lord.

> May God, who is rest, life, and day, grant him  
> Day without night, life without death, rest without end.

> *The offering is praise for the righteous,  
> A safeguard for those to be justified; for the rest  
> It pleads another’s cause.*

## LETTER VIII. TO RIC., A PRIEST. He gives him various counsels.

To his venerable friend and fellow-priest Ric., brother G. wishes the greeting he wishes for himself.

It has been reported to us that, having—as we believe—God’s fellowship, you withdrew from the bishop’s fellowship. The proud manners of his servants were burdensome to you, and you used to brand them with the severe cautery of rebuke. For you had read: “Those who rebuke shall be praised, and blessing shall come upon them” (Prov. 24); and: “To offend a man for God’s sake is to gain the favour of God.” We read that blessed Jerome was driven from the city of Rome by certain clerics and monks whose vices he had rebuked. For such a cause, as you know, the holy Baptist was beheaded, and many saints suffered many grievous things.

For the words of the wise are like goads and like nails driven deep. They do not know how to stroke vices, but how to prick them. To some, however, the words of the righteous are only piercing, not healing; to others they are at once piercing and healing. As good people become better, so evil people become worse through correction. But enough of this.

As for your request that we write what you ought to do: we approve, if it lies close to your heart, that you should again be with the bishop. Through the dean of Lisieux, or through other persons whom you know to be suitable for this purpose, approach him and promise that you will offer him more welcome and devoted services.

But if you seek counsel not about this but about the salvation of your soul, I shall answer you briefly in the Lord’s words: You know the commandments; you have the teaching of the holy Fathers; you have Moses and the prophets—listen to them. You also know the counsel which says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19). But if you cannot yet receive these things, use what is yours lawfully. You can remain in the world and yet not live worldly lives. Have freedom, but consider whether you can possess eternal blessedness.

In this great and wide sea may the breath of the Holy Spirit carry you onward and bring you to the harbour of the desired shore. Rejoice always in the Lord.

> May the wind be gentle, the sea calm, the air clear,  
> The sailor skilled, the anchor firm, the vessel sound.

## LETTER IX. TO G., CHAPLAIN OF THE BISHOP OF WORCESTER. He exhorts him to contempt of the world.

To his venerable friend G., chaplain of the lord bishop of Worcester, G., called subprior of St Barbara, wishes him always to fare well in the Lord.

I thank your kindness because, as you write, your mind has been stirred more than usual by a closer bond of charity to love me. My own soul has also grown warm toward you, nourished by the tenderness of your charity. I have now received with open hands what you were pleased to write, read it eagerly, gladly reread it, and find it more pleasing when repeated.

I also gratefully embrace your promise. For at the end of your letter you stated that, when one of your people comes again to us, if we have leisure, you will write more fully to your kindness, which is beloved to us in the Lord, employing at the end of the note the words of a certain religious man.

I presume to exhort you in charity: do not regard the falling glory of the world as though it stood firm and so lose that which truly stands; do not love your possessions more than yourself, and so lose both yourself and what is yours; do not let flattering present prosperity conceal its end from you, lest adversity without end follow; do not let temporal joy cover for you the eternal sorrow which it produces, and produce that sorrow which it covers; do not imagine death to be far off, lest—God forbid!—it overtake you unprepared, according to the saying: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them, and they shall not escape” (1 Thess. 5). May God grant you, after times happily prolonged, to receive everlasting joys.

## LETTER X. TO GAUFRID, HIS FRIEND. He announces that peace has been made between the king of England and his son.

To his beloved G., brother G. wishes delightful outcomes at morning and evening.

The letter which I had intended to send to your love had already been written, because I believed that your messenger would cross the sea more quickly, when behold: suddenly a new light seemed to arise in our regions, and divine clemency poured a most bright light into sorrowful hearts. For peace having been made between the king and his sons, peace, long a wanderer, entered our dwellings with a cheerful face.

They return to the native soil of your country; that noble castle of your birth is rebuilt, and new roofs rise everywhere within it. Thanks be to the just and merciful Creator, who wounds and heals, strikes [Col. 0838A] and whose hands restore health. Strive with all earnestness to please him, so that after the great perils of this great and wide sea you may deserve to enter the most secure harbour of heaven.

## LETTER XI. TO A BROTHER WEAK IN THE KNEES AND AT ODDS WITH HIM IN CERTAIN MATTERS. He consoles him and exhorts him to patience.

“If there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort of charity, any fellowship of the Spirit, any bowels of compassion, fulfil our joy: think the same thing, have the same love, being of one mind and agreeing in the same thing.”

Indeed, the arrows of the Lord are in you, and his hand is heavy upon you. But if you make your dwelling peaceful, store oil in your vessel, and season every sacrifice with salt, he who wounded you will heal you; he who struck you will cure you. Or else these very losses of your limbs will become increases of virtues for you. With Paul you will gladly glory in your infirmities, so that Christ’s power may dwell in you. You will doubt which is more expedient: to be healed or to remain infirm.

This infirmity is not unto death, unless—God forbid—you wish to bend the knee before Baal. We hope for your return, and that it may be swift. Return to us without hesitation; return, made like a roe or a young hart upon mountains of spices. Let weak knees be strengthened; leap upon the mountains; spring over the hills. Let it suffice that you have lived so long in that Babylon and have been a tenant of the purple-clad harlot.
