We do not wish our fellow-citizen to remain shut up so long within Babylon’s borders, but to go forth with Abraham from the land of the Chaldeans, with Lot from Sodom, and with Israel from Egypt; so that, for rebuilding the walls of the new Jerusalem—which Nebuzaradan and the whole army of the Chaldeans hoped by repeated blows to destroy utterly to the ground—he may show himself to us as Ezra and as Nehemiah, a helper and comforter. Fare well in the Lord and recover strength.

> Sometimes it goes well with the good, lest they be overcome by grievous affliction.  
> It goes ill, that they may wash away their stains and be purified by adversities.  
> Sometimes it goes well with the evil, that they may be struck more grievously.  
> It goes ill, that they may return—or that here they may already suffer both conditions.

## LETTER XII. TO BARTHOLOMEW. He teaches by what manner one must walk in the way of the Lord.

To Lord BARTHOLOMEW, brother G., called subprior of St Barbara, greeting and perseverance in good resolution.

We have heard, and rejoiced, concerning your conversion and manner of life, and we pray that our joy may be full through your advancement and perseverance. Grow warm, therefore, with God’s fire, and recover strength from weakness. Bloom anew in holy renewal. May the Holy Spirit be present to your heart, working subtly and changing it healthfully, who by his grace makes good people out of bad ones and better people out of good ones.

I confess that you have treated us well, nor are we ungrateful. While we lived in your land, we have therefore desired the more ardently to have you as a fellow-citizen in our own homeland. You have begun to enter the way that leads to life. See that you do not turn aside either to the right or the left. It is narrow and confined indeed, but as time goes on and the heart is enlarged, one runs along it in the ineffable sweetness of love; thus in a certain manner it appears broad: narrow at the entrance, broad in the progress. Yet only those who are unencumbered walk upon it.

There are, as has been said before us, three impediments to this journey: the swelling of pride, the weight of avarice, and the softness of luxury. Against these three steps are opposed: humility, patience, and poverty. Let poverty make us unencumbered, humility make us moderate, and patience make us strong; and so we shall sing in the ways of the Lord: “How great is the glory of the Lord!” (Ps. 137).

Let Christ’s cross no longer appear empty in us, as it does in many children of unbelief, who delay conversion from day to day, are suddenly taken away by unforeseen death, and descend in a moment to hell. Let present glory become contemptible. Let worldly wisdom—which has flourished in you exceedingly so far as the world is concerned—be judged folly. Renounce the affections of loved ones and relatives; do not comply with flesh and blood. Count favour, honours, and dignities as dung, that Christ may be your gain. This is the way: walk in it. You have minded things on earth; henceforth mind things above.

Formerly you used to say to us: “May God give you a better understanding.” And I say to you: May God increase in you the best understanding: namely, that you may think of the Lord in goodness and seek him in simplicity of heart. In these very few words, which I have drawn from the springs of the Fathers, I have presumed to exhort your love in charity, because I love you purely and simply.

But behold, while dictating, something perhaps came back to memory which I shall insert. Master W., surnamed Tuobe—of whom, I think, you have heard good reports, because the splendour of his work and the fragrance of his reputation, harmonizing in his renown, made him very widely known—dwelt not far from our house. When someone came to him saying that he wished to renounce the world and submit to the yoke of religion, he would say: “Good: in a few words I shall teach you your entire rule. Hear nothing; see nothing; behave like an ass: go this way, go that way; eat your fodder. Thus you will be able to sing: ‘I became like a beast before you’” (Ps. 72).

You understand what is being said; for God has given you understanding. Let not your love for the place of Baugé grow cold, but love it as you have always been accustomed to do. From now on we seek affection from you, not revenue. When you go there, I ask you to take care both to exhort and console the brethren whom I left there. I should wish, if it were possible, that you would come to us and spend a little time among us. You would hear many things and see many things by which you would profit. Farewell; and greet, in our place, the lord abbot and our other brethren, if you consider it fitting.

May the fervour of heavenly desire grow more ardently each day in your mind, and may your works be seasoned with the salt of devotion and the sweetness of spiritual grace. Amen. Farewell again.

> You rejoiced in delicacies, you rejoiced in a rich table;  
> Now a sober meal will provide sparse food.  
> Despise earth, you who seek to possess heaven;  
> If you wish what endures, flee what here is fleeting.

> **The glory of the heavenly kingdom shall not be given to the slothful,  
> Nor to the slow, but to the strong and the forceful.**

## LETTER XIII. TO PETER, HIS FRIEND. He exhorts him to continual reading of Holy Scripture.

To PETER—

> [Note: [Col. 0839D] Perhaps he is Peter of Buxières, to whom Letter XV is addressed later and whom the writer also calls his own; or Peter Mangot, to whom Letter XVIII below is addressed.]

—his G.

Having found an opportunity, and rendering the service of greeting due to your merits, I urge you to devote to Holy Scripture no less care than you customarily do. For, to use the words of blessed Augustine, it is a sincere and substantial thing: it does not seek access to the mind by artificial eloquence, nor does it make any empty and unstable clatter under any covering of language. It greatly moves one eager not for words but for things, and is greatly able to make one secure. In it crooked minds are corrected, small ones nourished, and great intellects exercised.

But if it would be welcome for me to write to you again, write, that I may write in reply. Yet perhaps you say: “I do not wish the dry appearance of your page and the bloodless colour of its letters to offend your sight. I do not wish ivy to creep for you among victorious laurels.” To this I reply:

> “We do not ask either to sport with Sidonius, hunt with Hortensius, or weave intricate constructions with Martianus. There are those who disguise eloquence eloquently, accumulating as much charm in their discourse as they deny that they are pursuing. Let none of these things please us as play, provided this alone suffices for your devotion: that a plain letter may run with festive simplicity.”

Farewell, and commend me to the Lord by your prayers. For these are saving victims, acceptable vows, rich burnt offerings, fat sacrifices, fragrant spices, which you offer upon the golden altar before the eyes of the Lord.

> As the vine is the ornament of trees, grapes of vines,  
> The bull of herds, and crops of fertile fields,  
> So you are the whole ornament of your own people.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE CHAPLAIN OF THE BISHOP OF WORCESTER. On familiar letter-writing and contempt of the world.

To his beloved lover—

> [Note: [Col. 0840D] The same person as above, Letter X.]

—G., chaplain of the lord bishop of Worcester, brother G., surnamed de Britolio, wishes that greeting which is true.

As Pope Innocent writes, true affection is found in familiar letters. You therefore do well in sending us friendly writings, in bestowing the gift of apostolic conversation, and in taking care to comfort the bodily absence between us by the spirit of your lips. For the duty of a letter, as blessed Jerome says, is to write something about familiar or daily intercourse, and in a manner to make those who are absent present to one another, while they mutually report what they wish or what has happened; though at times such a banquet of conversation is also seasoned with the salt of instruction. You seasoned your letter with this salt when you described how wholly to be despised are all temporal things. For all mortal things run like flowing water, nor can anything stable exist under the sun. Therefore happy are those who scorn the world’s happy fortunes, and whose desire is supremely to please God. These are the words of blessed Gregory: “Behold, the world which is loved is fleeing. Why then is that loved which is left behind? Why is neglected that to which we arrive? We follow what flees; we cling to what is slipping; and, since we cannot hold back what slips away, we slip with that very thing to which we cling.” And I say to you: one of two things will happen—either we shall leave it, and shall not fall with it; or we shall hold it, and shall fall with it. Farewell; and, that you may always fare well and always abide, ascend from the valley of vices to the mountains of virtues.

> Thus I compare the joys of this present life to winds:  
> Since neither lasts, let no one strive to grasp them firmly.

## LETTER XV. TO PETER DE BUXERIA

To Lord Peter, surnamed de Buxeria, his G. sends greetings and fullness of affection.

“I have earnestly desired to see your face and speak mouth to mouth”; but the places in which we dwell, separated by so many spaces, begrudge us this desire. Yet though you are absent, though you remain so far away, I nevertheless seem sweetly to kiss you and clasp you in the arms of sincere affection. My spirit is joined to your spirit; for you have refreshed my inmost being in Christ, pouring out upon me from the good treasure of your heart words of health, words living and efficacious, which, seasoned with the honey of love, tasted sweet to my mind. For just as a fragile little vessel recently steeped in another’s vinegar imparts the same flavour to one tasting from it, so indeed the vessel of the Holy Spirit—the vessel prepared for every good work, the vessel containing the word of life unto glory—pours forth from itself to those who taste it a most sweet and welcome savour.

But why say more? The messenger, on whose account I earnestly entreat your fatherhood, is in haste. He is in haste, I say; and therefore I say little to one whom I love greatly. Thus I put an end to my words, though by no means intending to put an end to affection. I ask, moreover, that you pray more earnestly for the weakness of my heart, so that almighty God, through your intercession, may defend my mind from every evil and swiftly bring me from the storms of this present life to the shores of eternal rest. Amen. May He also grant you what may bring glory today and answer with a crown tomorrow. Farewell, half of my soul.

> Those whom equal love binds, whom one ardour of mind unites,  
> Are not two because they dwell in different lands.

## LETTER XVI. JOHN, ABBOT OF BAUGEZEI, TO GAUFRID. He complains that Gaufrid has long failed to write, and asks him for letters of exhortation.

[Col. 0842A]

To G., beloved in Christ, venerable subprior of Saint Barbara’s, brother J., the useless servant of his household which serves Christ at Baugezei, wishes every good.

We wonder whether through forgetfulness we have been lost to you, or whether your affection toward us has again hardened, since for a long time now you have sent us no letter and conveyed to us no remembrance of yourself. It is indeed a worldly saying: “All things that are new always please.” But concerning one whom we know to have soared toward heavenly wisdom, we believe even this carnal proverb has vanished. Yet perhaps you plead as an excuse what, with your leave, we take as a divorce: namely, that because we delayed to write to you, you have withheld yourself from writing to us; so that, because our cistern is dry, you hold back your torrent from watering our little gardens—though the Wise Man has said: “Let your fountains be poured abroad, and divide your waters in the streets” (Prov. V). For then you will have them alone, if a friend does not share them with you. Hence the notable saying spoken of those two friends, that they were one soul in two bodies. For the differing forms of their bodies cannot divide those whom the equal unity of their minds joins.

But who am I to write to you, to console and instruct you, as you ask? For however greatly the mind may shine in learning, says Gregory, however greatly the tongue may excel in eloquence, it is nevertheless the height of ignorance to wish to teach one better than oneself. For you, to use the words of blessed Paul, know how to be brought low and how to abound; you know both how to have abundance and how to suffer want; everywhere and in all things, taught by grace, you have been instructed. Yet things do not go thus with me. But if you do not care for me, I must fear faintness of spirit and storm; and unless you lay upon me the hands of your prayers, I must succumb beneath the burden under which I have been placed amid the wickedness of this time and region. Farewell, and remember in the Lord one who remembers you.

The lord abbot of Oratory sends you greetings [Note: [Col. 0841] Oratory: a Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Angers, called in French Loroux, of which the abbey of Baugezei was a daughter-house.], as do the other brethren. Lord Peter Mangot sends greetings; we wish you to strengthen him in the Lord by letter, and among other things to urge him concerning the purchase of a library.

> Although men of the present age are commonly delighted by novelty,  
> Yet no novelty is without usefulness.

> Read sacred teachings with eager zeal, if you wish  
> To quench thirst with the gushing stream of sweet water.

## LETTER XVII. GAUFRID TO JOHN. Reply to the preceding letter.

To his venerable abbot J., brother G. sends greetings and fullness of affection.

What does not lie under one’s daily gaze, as has been said before us, soon slips from the mind. But according to that familiar popular proverb, one who loves well forgets slowly. How, then, can I forget those whom I delight always to behold with the sight of the inner person? How, therefore, can you be lost to me, whom I embrace with the single affection of sincere love? For what is our confidence, or what our hope of glory? Is it not you before God? Therefore my affection toward the place of Baugezei, Christ being gracious, shall never harden; for its advancement—for its elevation into an abbey—I often approached the king of England, and, as I say with less wisdom, repeatedly sought this from the king of England by devout prayers. Although this action displeased certain persons of less sound judgment, who in this affair sought their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, and although they brought certain grave reproaches to my ears, yet in this I rejoice and shall rejoice. For I trust that it shall turn to my salvation through your prayer and the God-pleasing conduct of many dwelling there.

Moreover, the reason why I have written to you less frequently has been the scarcity of your replies and of travellers. You certainly draw waters from the fountains of the Saviour; living waters flow from your belly; within you is a fountain of water springing up unto eternal life. Yet you complain that, your cistern being dry, you have nothing which you can offer us to drink. But I do not doubt that the ability is present if the will is not lacking. Would that we might be able as we perceive that you are able.

Further, you put us to shame when you say: “Who am I to write to you, to console and instruct you?” You further introduce the saying of Gregory, that it is the height of ignorance to wish to teach one better than oneself. But if it is not as is said—that I am better than you—let it be as is said, lest he who is not accustomed to lie should prove false. Yet even if I were in some respect better than you, I ought not for that reason to lack your consolation and admonition. For blessed Gregory’s meaning is not that those who are better ought ever to admonish (the text reads “ought,” but should read “ought not”), but that he may restrain the swollen will of the insolent—their audacity, rashness, and the presumption of a proud heart. For that an inferior ought sometimes to admonish a superior, he himself writes in the *Morals*: “When certain deeds of better persons displease inferior persons, what moves the mind must by no means be kept silent, but must be put forward with great humility, so that the intention of the pious speaker may all the more preserve the form of rectitude because it proceeds along the way of humility.”

Jethro gives Moses counsel concerning the appointment of authorities; it is not the presumption of an arrogant man, but the service of one not ungrateful. Lord Peter says: “A dumb beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness.” The philosopher says: “Attend not to who speaks, but to what is said.” It is said proverbially:

> What you do not know, perhaps a little ass knows.

Do not therefore seek an occasion for not writing back to us; rather, from your abundant treasure, pour out something to us from time to time [Col. 0844A]. If you do so, I too, though my cistern is dry, shall at least endeavour to patch together and compile a little something to offer you to drink. A king drinks from a wooden or even earthen vessel after golden cups. But enough of this.

I humbly entreat your graciousness to greet in our stead our brothers—your sons—whom I love in truth. We have sent to our new monastery relics of our new martyr [Note: [Col. 0843] Perhaps Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury?], and have added to them something greater, as you will be able to see. May your holiness live forever and flourish before the Lord.

> Happy are the waters by which the inner parts are washed  
> And the countenance of the mind is made brighter.

> There are two things on earth which do no good while concealed:  
> Wealth buried in the ground, and understanding shut within the breast.

## LETTER XVIII. TO PETER MANGOT. He congratulates him on having been granted authority to build a monastery, and discusses the necessity of acquiring a library for it.

[Col. 0844B]

To his dear friend Peter Mangot [Note: [Col. 0843] He was the monk of Baugezei mentioned above in Letter 16.], brother G. sends greetings and perseverance in the work undertaken.

God has fulfilled your desire. You have what you so ardently sought; from us indeed, from the king through us, from the Cistercian chapter through the king’s letters, and from other helpers, you have obtained what you wished. At first these matters appeared most difficult, and because of adverse events we almost fell into despair. But God Himself, looking upon us with a merciful eye, has by His strong hand levelled everything before us. Therefore carry out more devoutly the work first conceived in a devout mind and devoutly begun, and diligently provide what is necessary for it. Build a temple for the Lord out of living and chosen stones, which may receive you into everlasting tabernacles.

I give thanks to the grace of God Himself, who works in you, and to you who cooperate with that grace. For the grace of God which wrought good will in you without you now works through you. Rejoice, therefore, because He uses you as an instrument for a good work—He who did not use you for producing in yourselves the desire to work well. Consequently, you must strive in every way lest through your negligence the creation of so great a craftsman diminish within you; lest harmful repentance obstruct the growth of heavenly grace and your blessed purpose; lest distrust, instilled by evil angels, frustrate the end of completion sought through so many labours.

If a tower lacks defensive works, it is as easily attacked as it is difficult to defend; because of its imperfection it is judged neither fit for defence nor inaccessible to attack. And if it has no armoury, from which weapons are brought forth at the proper time to overcome enemies, it lacks both strength and weapons in itself. Your work, therefore, begun with such great zeal and such vigorous vitality of faith, is like a fortification against the devil. There the soldiery of Christ, gathered by your devotion and sustained at your expense, is trained day and night in the arms of righteousness against spiritual wickedness.

Since you are the steward and minister of this army, you must supply weapons to those who fight, presenting to God and His angels a pleasing spectacle as they stand firm in the defence of virtue. For they conduct your cause, whose soldiery you equip. A cloister without an *armarium* [Note: [Col. 0845D] In monasteries the *armarium* was the place where books were kept; its keeper was also commonly called the *armarius*.] is like a fortress without an armoury. Our very book-chest is an armoury. From it we bring forth the judgments of divine law, like sharp arrows, to assail our enemies. From it we take the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, the shield of faith, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Act, therefore, so that in the armoury of your fortification there may not be lacking the chief fortification of that fortification itself. This fortification is the instruction of the sacred library [Note: [Col. 0845D] Here, and below at the end of the letter, “library” seems to mean a copy of the Holy Bible, as the final two verses appended to the letter indicate.], in which there is praiseworthy instruction in life and morals. There every sex and every age finds what may advance its benefit. There spiritual infancy finds nourishment, youth finds strength, and old age finds support. Blessed is the hand which supplies all with that from which salvation comes to all. If, then, you supply arms to the aforesaid army, nothing remains but that you say to it: “Take hold of arms and shield, and rise up to help me.” Farewell; and take pains that the library itself—without which no monastery ought to exist—be acquired.

> You are called Peter: be steadfast;  
> Founded upon Christ the rock,  
> The wall rises by hope; love completes its heights.  
> Faith lives by acting; where there is no act of love,  
> Dying faith produces abortive hope.

> Though many books may please you, and many please you greatly,  
> Possess this one and be wise: it alone suffices you.

## LETTER XIX. TO MASTER R. He congratulates him on entering the Order and teaches what he ought to be within it.

[Col. 0845C]

To the venerable master, Lord R. [Note: [Col. 0846D] Perhaps Richard the priest, to whom Letter 8 above and Letter 34 below are addressed.], G. wishes that he may always set the Lord before his eyes.

A certain brother from the castles came to us and brought joy and gladness to my hearing. When I asked whether he knew you, he replied that he knew you very well and had stayed with you for several days. He also informed us that you and your companions had recently embraced the Order. Before undertaking the Order, indeed, you lived orderly according to your measure; but henceforth you will do so much more ardently, by the bounty of God’s grace. Apply yourselves to the Rules of the Fathers, and especially to those of blessed Augustine.

Order, as that doctor himself defines it, is an arrangement assigning to each of equal and unequal things its proper place. There is indeed order when

> Each individual thing occupies fittingly the place allotted to it.

It belongs especially to the order of regular clerics that they strive to possess nothing of their own, carefully preserve the integrity of heart and body undefiled, and humbly obey the commands of their elders. It belongs to that order, I say, that there be simplicity in the eyes, obedience in the ears, temperance in taste and smell, cleanliness in the hands, humility in the heart, and gravity in one’s walk.

But it belongs to the master of the order [Col. 0846A], to use the words of a certain wise man:

> When he rebukes anyone in words or with the stroke of a rod,  
> Let neither his tongue nor his hand exceed due measure.

He must also be such that:

> If anyone injures him, while wishing to injure the injurer,  
> He bears it more by compassion than by suffering.

Let sobriety flourish in him and gracefulness of manners,

> Piety with tears, vigour with piety;  
> Weightiness in counsel, custody of heart and mouth,  
> The grace of teaching, zeal, and love of the flock;  
> Care for the household, sure provision of goods,  
> Greater concern for honour, lesser for property.

For he must so order his house that charity may always appear at its door, purity around its altar, and discipline in its chapter-house. You have come together so as to dwell unanimously in the house: to have the same food, not unequal clothing; the same place for eating, the same for sleeping, the same discipline, the same prayer. For a community (*conventus*) is so called as if from a way (*via*): you have come together as companions on the road, so that the labour of the journey may be less through the pleasantness of fellowship. Stand therefore in your ways; hold fast the purpose of the holy Order, so that at last you may deserve to reach the fellowship of the saints. May God grant that your congregation may be terrible to evil spirits, like an army drawn up in battle order. Pray for us; let what we have written to you be attributed not to presumption but to charity. Farewell.

[Col. 0846C]

> Let neither hatred, price, nor entreaty make him blind:  
> Let the rigour of justice and the strength of faith be equal toward all.

## LETTER XX. TO W., FORMER PRIOR OF SAINT STEPHEN OF CAEN. On contemplation.

To his beloved W., formerly prior of Saint Stephen’s at Caen [Note: [Col. 0846D] Saint Stephen’s at Caen, a celebrated Benedictine monastery founded by William the Conqueror, king of England; its first abbot was Saint Lanfranc, later Archbishop of Canterbury.], may he always have his eyes toward the Lord.

As blessed Gregory exhorts us, let us seek from the Lord neither earthly gifts nor false riches nor fleeting honours, but light—not light confined by place, bounded by time, varied by the interruption of nights, and seen by us in common with cattle; but, if we seek light, let us seek that light which we may see with angels alone, which no beginning initiates and no end confines. The beauty of that inward and eternal light is so lovable and so wonderful that whoever contemplates it with the clear sight of the heart is immediately conformed to it by cleaving to it.

Though you lack the eye of flesh, you do not lack the eye of reason, nor the eye of contemplation. With the eye of flesh you have seen the world and the things in the world; with the eye of reason you see the mind and what is in the mind; with the eye of contemplation you see God [Col. 0847A] and what is in God. Contemplation is the keen and free gaze of the mind, diffused in every direction for discerning realities; or contemplation is the true and certain insight of the mind concerning any matter; or the undoubting apprehension of truth; or, more precisely, contemplation is an illumination of the mind which healthfully affects the soul with respect to invisible things.

There are, as you know, two elevations of good contemplation: one in understanding and the other in affection; one in light and the other in fervour; one in knowledge and the other in devotion. Didymus, that seeing man from whom Jerome learned the sacred Scriptures, flourished in these. “My Didymus,” he says, “having the eyes of the bride in the Song of Songs, and those eyes which Jesus commanded to be lifted up to the whitening harvest-fields, beholds something more sublime.” When blessed Antony came to Alexandria, he consoled him with magnificent words: “Let it not offend you, O Didymus, that you have been deprived of bodily eyes. For you lack the eyes possessed by mice, frogs, and lizards; but rejoice because you have the eyes possessed by angels, with which God is seen and through which a great light of knowledge is kindled for you.”

“The darkness to be feared,” says Augustine, “is not that of the eyes but of morals; and if it be that of eyes, it is not of the outer but of the inner eyes, by which not white and black but just and unjust are distinguished.” Indeed, the splendour of the day of brightness has shone upon you. For you have flown, like a most chaste dove, to those lands which the near sun of righteousness looks upon, lands abundant in the ripe fruits of virtues. Therefore we no longer fear for you that you may pass from light to darkness, from the bed of rest to the wallowing-place of mud, from the paradise of delight to the field of Damascus, where righteous Abel perished.

Speaking briefly to you, I have adorned myself, like the foolish little crow, with borrowed colours; yet I do not fear that, should the flock of birds someday return to reclaim its own feathers, I may provoke laughter as a little crow stripped of stolen colours. May grace and peace be multiplied to you. Amen.

> Fulfilling the office and restraining the privilege of the prior,  
> In life as in rank you were foremost.

> Mind, face, eye: pure, serene, chaste;  
> Right hand generous; tongue modest; feet grave.

## LETTER XXI. JOHN, ABBOT OF BAUGEZEI, TO GAUFRID. He asks Gaufrid to reserve a library for him.

[Col. 0847D]

To G., beloved in Christ, venerable subprior of Saint Barbara’s, J., minister of the brothers at Baugezei, wishes that he may always live in Christ.

On seeing your longed-for letter of affection, I burst forth, as though awakening from a heavy sleep, into the words of the patriarch Jacob: “It is enough for me; I shall come and see him before I die” (Gen. XLV). Believe me, I had fallen into grave anxiety of heart and spirit, fearing that because after a long period—not even after letters had been sent—I had heard nothing concerning you, death, which spares no one, had separated your beloved soul from the flesh. I would have hastened to see you, had not the urgency of the time compelled me to hasten my journey to the Cistercian chapter. On my way there I would also have passed through your place; but I feared that, while hurrying onward, I could not sufficiently see you or converse with you—which I ardently desire.

We now ask you, therefore, to keep that library, if it is as good—indeed, because it is as good—as you write, so that it may not be sold to another. For on our return from the chapter we shall come by way of your place and, God willing, shall purchase it with your counsel.

> What true love is, and what painted pretence in words,  
> Words denote; the face indicates; deeds prove.

## LETTER XXII. GAUFRID TO JOHN. He asks that John’s prayers obtain from God for him a happy death.

[Col. 0848B]

To his venerable abbot J., his wholly devoted G. sends greetings, not so much upon the way as in the homeland.

That I am still living in the flesh, you learn from the letters which I send to you. Thus likewise, God willing, you will learn from letters sent to you of the swift laying aside of my tabernacle. For I trust in the charity of the brethren that, after the funeral rites have been celebrated, the messenger travelling to you will not prolong his delay. Therefore, however long I may defer writing to you—for this delay, as with our letters, is caused by the scarcity of travellers—let every fear concerning my departure be removed.

Above all, and prostrate at the feet of your holiness with all devotion of mind, I ask that, when the aforesaid messenger comes to you, you endeavour to do for me what the fraternal letter shall request in the pursuit of piety. Pray to the Saviour, who does not will the death of a sinner, that meanwhile He may deign to grant me the strength by which I may so follow Him as to attain Him: that is, follow Him unto merit so as to attain unto reward. He has plainly shown the way by which we ought to follow Him, offering an example by living in innocence and dying in patience. If I hold to this way, Christ Himself is life to me, and death gain.

How great a gain, and how precious, to die by the death precious in the sight of the Lord; in few days to complete many ages, and to depart full of days! “He dies full of days,” as a certain saint says, “who in passing time accomplishes that which time does not touch.” Happy departure, which is the entrance into life and the reward of labour! Therefore I labour, I labour as one coming to the end; for I know that if I refuse to labour here, I shall come to the end of life but not to the end of labour. I know that earth is the place of merits and heaven of rewards, and that one does not ascend from the lowest to the highest unless the cause of salvation appears in the middle. I know that, by divine judgment, the final outcome of things always answers to their merits.

But how great, as blessed Cyprian says, is the dignity and holiness of departing hence joyfully; departing glorious amid anguish and pressure; closing in a moment the eyes by which men and the world were seen, and immediately opening those same eyes that God and Christ may be seen! With such ease of passing, with such speed, you are suddenly withdrawn from earth and placed in heavenly kingdoms. “These things,” he says, “must be embraced in mind and thought; these must be meditated by night and day.” But let it suffice that we have said this.

You confer welcome consolation upon us when you direct your letters to us. Nor do we do what some are accustomed to do—throw away a little sheet once it has been read. Rather, we eagerly preserve it and diligently copy it. I rejoice that this is added to your titles: that the memory of your name may remain among us; that the very remembrance of you may be sweetened in our mouth as honey; and that, like music at a wine-banquet, the Lord may be with your spirit. Amen. And may He grant you what may bring glory today and answer with a crown tomorrow.

> We live in service of death; death is the gate of life,  
> But for those for whom life prepares the road to life.

> By a little labour may you earn perpetual rest,  
> And by brief weeping, long joys weighed out.

## LETTER XXIII. JOHN TO GAUFRID. Reply to the preceding letter.

To G., beloved in Christ, his J. [Note: [Col. 0849D] John, abbot of Baugezei, calls himself Gaufrid’s vicar because Gaufrid yielded the monastery of Baugezei to the Cistercians, though, according to the original intention of Henry II, king of England, its founder, it ought to have belonged to the Order of regular canons of Saint Barbara’s in Augia [Col. 0850D].], sends due greeting.

Truly, as it is written, “Love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell” (Cant. VIII). For since my soul has been united to yours by the bond of mutual affection, the fire kindled from it exerts such force within me that, though disturbed and though wounded, I cannot banish the sweetness of your memory from my mind. Although I had earlier promised, and almost confirmed under oath, that I would receive no more letters from you until I received the gift of your bodily presence, as soon as I saw the bearer of your letter, I seized the little packet and not only eagerly read and reread it, but could not restrain my hand from writing.

Joining my voice, then, to the words I find in the present little sheet, I reverently exhort and desire that you may run with tireless foot in the way of God’s commandments, until you may happily attain Him whom from early youth you began courageously to follow. For it is certain that He must be followed through the bitterness and labours of the present life, since it is manifest to all that He passed through the same. But let the prophetic pot be sweetened by flour mingled with it, and let the remembrance of heavenly sweetness temper the harshness of present labours. “You are good, O Lord,” says the prophet (Lam. III), “to the soul that seeks You and longs for You.” If He is good to one who seeks and longs, how much more to one who finds and enjoys Him! If memory is so sweet, what will His presence be like? If honey and milk are under the tongue, what will be upon the tongue?

Now, therefore, dearest one, let us enjoy one another in the Lord until the time comes when we shall enjoy Him in ourselves. For in eternal blessedness, as a certain saint says, we shall enjoy God in three ways: seeing Him in creatures, possessing Him within ourselves, and—what is more delightful and blessed than these—knowing the Trinity itself in itself, and contemplating its glory without any enigma with the pure eye of the heart. For this shall be eternal life: that we may know the Father and the Son, and in both the Holy Spirit. This is the abundance of divine sweetness which He has hidden for those who fear Him; this is the good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, which shall be given into our bosoms. This is the fullness of our happiness, surpassing glory, overflowing blessedness, to which He will bring us who, though in differing habit, has nevertheless called us in one Spirit.

> But the way of virtue seeks the steep hill on the right,  
> And offers a difficult entrance to those who first behold it.

## LETTER XXIV. GAUFRID TO JOHN THE ABBOT. He grieves that, summoned to the council at Paris, he was absent when John, abbot of Baugezei, came to Saint Barbara’s.

To his venerable abbot J., G., a sinner.

I grieve, and have grieved greatly, that I was not in Normandy when you came into Normandy. Long had I awaited you; long had I thirsted for your presence. I had even hoped that I might put the finishing hand to the business for which you came, but my sins prevented me from attaining my wish. I was disappointed because you did not come with the abbots of Normandy returning from the chapter. When you turned aside to your own people, I thought you would remain there for some time before coming. Thus, deceived by this expectation, I was meanwhile drawn away to the council [Note: [Col. 0850D] Perhaps the Council of Paris held in 1170, at which Peter Lombard’s error concerning Christ’s humanity was condemned.] held at Paris by the urgent necessity of a certain abbot who was dear to me. Had I known things to come, I certainly would not have moved, but would rather have waited for the long-desired arrival of my friend.

But alas for me! I went where I wish I had not carried my foot. On returning, I groaned when I heard that you had been in Normandy but had departed from Normandy. I found tribulation and sorrow because I did not find you in Normandy. Farewell—but share my grief over this misfortune. We greet our brethren, asking them to remember us in prayer, so that the coldness brought on by the abundance of our iniquity, with charity frozen, may be thawed by the warmth of the Holy Spirit.

> Now, O king, be master of your mind; restrain your grief.  
> No one can lighten losses by the help of sorrow.

## LETTER XXV. TO THE SAME PERSON. Apparently on the same subject.

To his venerable abbot J., G., a suppliant, sends the small gift of himself.

Whatever the sincerity of conscience has that is excusable is pardonable with good minds. I sent you a brief apology through the very bearer by whom your letters were presented to me, in which you complain that you were offended and injured. But if you were offended, so was I; if you were injured, so was I; and, unless my conscience deceives me, I was more so. Believe me: I grieved enough, disappointed in my desire and expectation. If, having been deceived, I gave offence, forgive one who erred not from malice. Forgiveness should be granted to a fault not accompanied by malice.

We send what you commanded us to send. Let the object entrusted represent the countenance of its sender and suggest to the mind what forgetfulness denies. But we pray this: that you remember us, that you entreat the Lord for us, and that for our miseries you pour out inward tears in His presence. For prayer bends the judge; tears compel the merciful one. Know, moreover, that whatever may answer to your success contributes in every way to our state of well-being. For friendship between us is not held as merchandise, but is one born not from money but from favour; not from bargaining over prices but from rivalry in goodwill, especially since it is itself a virtue, not a profit. O virtue worthy of praise, which binds absent minds in the bond of affection, unites what is divided, joins unequal things, and perfects what is imperfect! O virtue truly worthy of praise, than which nothing in human affairs is more beautiful!

May your letter gladden my heart concerning the state of your welfare and give certainty concerning the progress of your house, for whose honour and usefulness you provide with watchful eye. May your health thrive and your holiness flourish forever before God.

> A thing, if it is given well, though given, is always retained:  
> No glory belongs to what is kept back; much to what is given.

## LETTER XXVI. ROGER, FORMER PRIOR OF SAINT ABRAHAM, TO GAUFRID. He rejoices in what Gaufrid wrote concerning the vision of God and exhorts him to humility.

You delight our ears by asserting in Augustinian fashion what you eloquently discuss concerning the vision of God. You utter words joyful and exact, refined and thoroughly examined, polished and adorned, upon the great balance of praise. Indeed, you declare that souls cleansed from every dreg of carnal sense, and affections of the heart purified from every attachment to earthly things, ought and can soar above every creature and, reaching the Creator with a pure heart and unobstructed, clear light, contemplate God. These things please us greatly, both because they are true and because we rejoice that you are an attainer and knower of this truth.

These are surely great matters, which humility alone can attain. Although humility is known to derive its name from the human, it nevertheless dwells in heavenly things with God; through its epithet the hostile angelic host is driven from heaven. Recall that Moses yielded to Jethro’s counsel through humility; and above all consider with utmost care the Head Himself together with His members. For gracious condescension always accompanies humility, while indignation is joined to pride. Therefore, if you desire to experience and ascertain our contemplations [Col. 0852A], seize humility, the preserver of all goodness, and do not disdain to know us through our writings. Nothing unknown to us ought to displease us. First understand; afterwards praise or despise. Reveal to me what you have written, and do not seek concealment: you will immediately find me a reader; you will be shown to be a despiser.

> I shall praise God as the author; openly He is injured  
> By whoever is envious in this work.

## LETTER XXVII. GAUFRID TO ROGER. Reply to the preceding letter.

You extol as worthy of the highest praise what is a monkey by calling it a lion, and an owl by calling it an eagle. Yet I fear [Col. 0852B] that if anyone acquainted with my ineptitudes should read that letter of yours, he would bend his hand behind my back into the sign of a stork. You also call polished and carefully weighed words those which have neither been sharpened on the whetstone of dialectic nor smoothed by the oil of rhetorical art—though this too is a fault, if discourse luxuriates in an excessive flowering of words. Yet, as Jerome says, though a talent be elegant and well-trained, and though speech run smoothly, worn by long practice, unless it has been tended and polished by the author’s hand, it smells of the grime of negligence and is either gaping in its vowels or harsh in its consonants. Hence, he says, it is also reported of Virgil that he fashioned his books like bear-cubs with his tongue, and by licking made them better, [Col. 0852C] so that they might endure in everlasting memory, supplying in free prose what metre required.

There are indeed some who employ a flood of eloquence and a torrent of words; twisting swollen whirlpools, they rush downhill amid the astonishment of their spectators. They rush downhill, certainly, who are not raised by the wing of heavenly intention but are shaken by the desire for earthly praise [sic]. But so long as we are in the valley of tears, in the place God has set for conflict, in order to give a crown to those who conquer, I greatly desire to set ascents in my heart and to go from strength to strength; to burn fervently in the reading of the Holy Scriptures; and to discover and examine both your interpretations and those of other teachers. Nor do I disdain to know you through your writings, especially since I have resolved to venerate, proclaim, and admire them as [Col. 0852D] words of the Lord.

For you desire to imitate that householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old; and the bride of the Song of Songs, who says: “New and old, my beloved, I have kept for you” (Song 7). Therefore we gladly receive your learning and urge you to run in the broad field of the Scriptures. Even if Victor does not cast forth firebrands, you should press on along the road you have begun. The evil of every vice returns upon its own author. But charity is kind; it is not jealous; it does not seek its own interests (1 Cor. 13); it loves another’s goods as its own. Therefore, with devout studies, spread the sails of your exposition to the Holy Spirit. May the breath of that Holy Spirit carry you forward and bring you safely to the harbor of the desired shore.

> Fame’s glory, applauding Jerome’s merits,  
> Raises the man in praise and makes him everlasting.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE BROTHERS OF BAUGÉ. He sends them the Life of Blessed Hamo.

To the beloved brothers in Christ of the monastery of Baugé, G., servant of your holiness: everlasting salvation in the Lord.

You have, dearest brothers, a memorial of blessed Hamo: namely, the stole which, out of affection, he had sent to us. How pious, religious, and pleasing to God his life was, the writing appended below declares. Read this for your edification, and reflect upon his virtues in his gifts.

In the *Life of Blessed Antony*, St Athanasius of Alexandria writes of himself as though of another [Col. 0853B]: “The legatee of blessed Antony, who by his command deserved to receive the worn cloak together with the sheepskin, embraces Antony in Antony’s gifts; and, enriched as by a great inheritance, he secretly recalls through the garment the image of his holiness.” In like manner, may grace and peace be multiplied to you as you act thus, recalling in his gifts the image of the holiness of Hamo, that man of God.

Before his death he also ordered that another part of his own clothing, an *orarium* [liturgical cloth or stole], be sent to me. I embrace and preserve it with such joy that I consider myself to possess the wealth of Croesus. When this blessed man heard that we had found a faithful and distinguished man who promised, at his own expense, to build a house of the Cistercian Order in the poor place where we were living, if we could obtain this from the king and from our own people, he encouraged us toward so pious a work by his counsels. He also earnestly asked the king himself—who held him dear and treated him familiarly because of the merit of his holiness—to grant it kindly, handing us most private tokens for presentation to him. [Col. 0853C] We also received from him relics of many saints, which we placed in the aforesaid location.

Therefore let the affection of your devotion toward him increase. Remember me, your servant, in praying to the Lord Jesus that he may swiftly crush Satan beneath our feet, and that, through your intercession, I may deserve to enjoy in the heavenly homeland the fellowship of that blessed man, by whose friendship and favor, through the Lord’s generosity, I deserved to be relieved in this pilgrimage. I desire that you be joined through everlasting fellowship to the citizens of heaven and the choirs of angels. Again, may your holiness, fruitful through the sprinkling of divine dew, grow day by day, green and flowering before the Lord.

> Always content with little, he loved poverty,  
> And, desiring nothing, was lord of all things.  
>
> Bright, he marvels at heaven’s unfamiliar light,  
> And sees beneath his feet the clouds and stars of heaven.

## LETTER XXIX. TO JOHN THE ABBOT. He sees presented to himself in the monastery of John, abbot of Baugé, an image of future blessedness.

To his venerable abbot JOHN, brother G.: may he imitate the virtue whose name he has received.

Those who maintain and faithfully keep the claims of friendship are gathered into one by the breadth of charity, although absence of place separates them. That charity itself, by whose gentle bond we are joined, commands me, whenever a suitable messenger can be found, to write to you—although my mind is no more eager than capable of writing, since my talent is slight and meagre.

I had indeed thought and hoped, if circumstances and the condition of the time permitted, to come to you in person. But because urgent affairs have detained us, I have meanwhile sent these letters as my representatives to you. I hope, however, if life remains with me and God permits, that I shall soon come to you; and the grace and mercy of the Redeemer will not fail to yield abundant fruit to one who comes.

For the beauty of God’s house will offer a lovely spectacle: an ordered battle-line of camps; the religious life of the brothers; the enlarged site; [Col. 0854B] running waters; wilderness turned into fertility; and every individual thing dedicated to divine worship. Living and effective speech will give joy and gladness to my hearing (Ps. 50): a good word above the best gift; faithful speech worthy of all acceptance; good utterance, fiery eloquence, thanksgiving, and the voice of praise with which that place resounds daily.

The good odor, an odor of life unto life, will breathe upon Christ’s nostrils when I enter your places, places fragrant with the finest ointments; when I enter beds of spices planted by perfumers; when I enter a garden flourishing in a blooming turf, a garden of delights, an enclosed garden, a garden producing rose blossoms and lilies of the valleys. There I shall feed among the lilies; I shall be nourished by the bread of life and understanding, and drink the water [Col. 0854C] of saving wisdom. I shall rejoice and be gladdened, fully satisfied from the breasts of your consolation. You will introduce me into the wine-cellar, and there drink will be given me, so that I may feed in the richest pastures.

We shall greet one another with a holy kiss, a dove-like kiss: not deceitful, not raven-like, not a kiss that falsely professes peace of hearts, but one that signifies the true union of souls. These things, therefore, which we have mentioned will present to you as it were an image for me of future blessedness, in which we shall see, gathered together at one and the same time, whatever delights the sight of the eyes.

So great and such, as blessed Augustine says, will be the beauty of the glorified body that it will delight the gaze and in no way bend the heart toward vice. “And such,” he says, “will be the delight of that beauty, that it will always be present to you and you will never be sated—indeed, you will always be sated. For if I say that you will not be sated, there will be hunger; if I say that you will be sated, I fear weariness. There will be neither weariness nor hunger. I do not know what to say; but God has what he may show to those who cannot find how to speak of it and who believe that they shall receive it.”

There, surely, we shall eternally perceive, in the same instant, every melody, every harmony whatsoever, and all that is harmonious and sweet to the ears. There we shall experience at once every kind of spice and the scents of all sweet-smelling things. We shall be able to taste everything which, tasted, gives sweetness; to touch whatever can suitably give delight when touched. To come to the kiss, [Col. 0855A] embrace, and sight of the saints is ineffable joy. What most perfect beauty! What most blessed delight! There, to use the words of the aforesaid teacher, shines that which does not occupy space; there sounds that which time does not snatch away; there smells that which no breath disperses; there tastes that which eating does not diminish; and there clings that from which satiety does not tear one away.

For the attainment of the glory of so great a blessedness, we trust that we shall be helped by your prayers and merits. Farewell, and frequently beseech the Lord for us. To refresh your mind, dearest friend, I have taken care to send you three spiritual games: concerning shepherds, fingers, and pictures. Looking upon and pondering these, learn delightfully to play in the field of Scripture, thinking sublime things from small ones. Even Wisdom herself plays before God; hence also that saying:

> Divine power plays amid human affairs;  
> Isaac plays with Rebecca; David dances with all his strength before the Lord,  
> Touches the lyre, sounds Christ upon the lyre,  
> And on the ten-stringed psaltery awakens the risen one from the dead.

But do not expect me to explain these to you orally, or to pour them forth in polished and eloquent speech. Elegance of style must be sought elsewhere.

> Sooner will light deer feed in the air  
> Than your face fade from my heart.  
>
> Brief saying: if you wish to live, be ashamed in secret, before the Judge as witness,  
> Of what is not fitting to be done openly.  
>
> When you lay aside the body, whenever you wish you will go to the heavens;  
> Having become a god of kindly heaven, you will escape being a man.

## LETTER XXX. TO R., PRECENTOR OF THE CHURCH OF TROARN. That he may visit him, at least by letter.

[Col. 0855C]

To his beloved brother in Christ and intimate friend R., precentor of the church of Troarn—[Note: [Col. 0855] Troarn, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Bayeux, between Caen and the monastery of Saint Barbara.]—G., unworthy assistant minister of Saint Barbara: “sing wisely.”

As that man says, it is the duty of good character to attend to the requests of friends, especially when the justice of the petitioner does not oppose the request. I had asked your affection that you would deign, by sending a letter, to exhort, visit, and console my littleness by singing to me something favorable from the songs of Zion. For we rarely behold one another with bodily eyes, rarely enjoy mutual conversation, and I fear lest the memory of friendship grow old through temporal silence.

Therefore I wanted to be able to look upon you in your letters as in a mirror; and I thirsted in a great heat of longing that the tongue might dip from the heart what the mind might hear resounding, at least on a page of writing. For I do not want letters dripping from the top of the mouth. I ask for those which, as a certain wise man says, do not know how to dry up, which are drawn from the innermost fountain of the breast. I do not say that they should have gaiety smeared upon them with Tully’s honey, or be sprinkled with Attic salt, or fragrant with thyme, or composed, so to speak, by a Nestor-like hand; but that they should be written by the pen of charity alone. This, as you know, is found in a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.

In letters of this kind, therefore, I desired somehow [Col. 0856A] to have my friend present; but because of your occupations I excuse you. For I attribute the cause of your silence neither to your will nor to idleness, but to those very occupations. Thus my speech has opened the first door toward you, while I am the first to cast the gifts of my mouth upon you. When you have opportunity, take care to show us your presence at least in a little note.

Turpilius, the comic poet, speaking about the exchange of letters, says: “This alone is the thing that makes absent persons present.” Cassiodorus writes—and the more common opinion hands down—that Mercury, discoverer of many arts, is remembered to have gathered letters from the flight of Strymonian birds. For even now, he says, cranes, which move together in a flock, trace the shapes of the alphabet under nature’s instruction. Arranging this into an orderly sequence, with vowels suitably mixed among consonants, he discovered a sensory path through which the mind, seeking high things, might very swiftly arrive at the inner chambers of prudence.

By this sensory path, with God’s grace cooperating, you have already arrived in part at the secrets of Wisdom herself. Hence it is that you read and understand the divine laws; hence it is that, according to that most beautiful and salutary exhortation of the Apostle, “in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs you sing and make melody to the Lord in your hearts” (Eph. 5). These are the things you think upon, savor, and weave again. Hence it is also that the writings of the Fathers and songs of many kinds delight your inner ears night and day. But allow a goose to make noise among the swans in your ears for a little while. Hear [Col. 0856C] and understand: especially when the goose is crying out, custom has it that those desiring help flee to tested aid.

Therefore, that the hoped-for result may smile upon us, take the hope of our petition into your care. Our petition is this: that you pray more earnestly that the Lord may grant us forgiveness of sins, the grace of merits, and the glory of rewards. As you pray more attentively for us, may the grace of the Lord Savior guard and cherish you. Our wish is that your holy congregation may prosper and be enriched with the everlasting endowment of merits. May the Holy Spirit, helping our weakness and inspiring reason into the understanding and devotion into the will, leave room neither for error nor for lukewarmness. Farewell; and when opportunity arises, let the friend who asks you hear from the instruments you have hung up the words of songs.

> Pleasant is the voice of the choir whenever heart accords with mouth,  
> And much sweetness comes from the sweet lyre-player.  
>
> The day when I may tell of your deeds—  
> Behold, then I shall be able to bear them throughout the whole world.

## LETTER XXXI. N. . . . TO GAUFRID. It appears to be a response to the preceding letter.

To the dearest father and friend in Christ, G., leader—by the preceding grace of God—of the canons of Saint Barbara: may he who was once yours, not the least among your friends, as I believe, hope, and rejoice, prosper in the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without complaint.

The day before yesterday, when my heart recalled the familiar remembrance of you—which, I confess, is sometimes not absent even while I sleep—I suddenly began to think of it, and to rebuke myself because I had not written back to you, especially since I feared that I had incurred the reproach of ingratitude or contempt. But let this be far from me, and far from the affection of everyone who truly loves; for this would indeed have been nothing other than returning evil for good.

Nevertheless, I cannot entirely excuse myself for any negligence or sluggishness of mine; but let this repayment of charity, though late, excuse me. Nor should I greatly seek elegance of speech; rather, desiring to draw forth from the poverty of my breast some sprinkling for your request, may I, through Christ’s generosity, satisfy your wish.

From what, then, shall I take the beginning of speech? If I begin to speak, my own mouth will condemn me—and rightly. For what in me is not worthy of rebuke? “Those who praised me swore against me” (Ps. 101) . . . their lie is called such; and those who call blessed are deceivers, and those who call blessed are cast down. For the children of men are liars in balances: they deceive, confessing that they know God while not knowing themselves; holding their own good deeds, if any, before their eyes, while concealing their evils—or, what is worse, defending them. This is the deceitful balance [Col. 0857C] and detestable measure: weighing one’s life with unequal judgment.

Therefore the meaning of your little verses moves me, for while they silently rebuked the idleness of my silence, they at the same time uncovered my shame. As I recall, they were written below in this manner:

> The day when I may tell of your deeds—  
> Behold, then I shall be able to bear them throughout the whole world.

What deeds, most beloved? A vain life, lukewarm conduct, cold love. I know this work of mine. Wretched me: I, who ought to be struck, am to receive praises? Are these those distinguished deeds which should be related throughout the whole world? Far be it, far be it! It is more tolerable that they should remain hidden within their walls, or—what is more desirable to me—that they be erased from the book [Col. 0857D] which will be opened on the day of judgment, that is, from my conscience, rather than corrupt followers by a wicked example.

But perhaps you may reasonably ask why, when you requested songs of Zion, I speak of the rivers of Babylon, though south seems to differ so greatly from north, Zion from Babylon, song from lamentation. But what have I to do with song? Would that, sitting alone and silent by these rivers of mine, I might prefer to weep rather than say anything, if perhaps I might deserve to be raised even a little above myself as though by the Spirit of the Lord, crying out in the longing of my soul through remembrance of Zion: “My soul will desire you in the night” (Isa. 26). What is this night except my wretched life, dark with the clouds of temptations, the shadows of vices, and the gloom of sins?

But why do I remain burdensome to you, when I have become burdensome to myself, pursuing mourning instead of song and unable, though requested, to bring my mind to sing? Yet not every weeping excludes song, because there is a certain pleasure in weeping when the soul feeds upon its own sorrow, delights in laments, and is strengthened by sighs, so that suddenly, bursting forth into a voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting may say with the Prophet: “My song is always in you” (Ps. 70); “I will sing to the Lord, who has bestowed good things on me” (Ps. 12); and “Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 119).

With what joyful bosom does that mother of ours receive and console those returning thus from battle—her children who refuse to be consoled in this age, daily bearing in sorrow the misery of their exile, who have not received their good things in their lifetime, waiting for the consolation promised by the Lord to those who mourn. The Father of mercies himself, and God of all consolation, comes to meet them and embraces with his right hand those who languish in love for his only-begotten Son and are wearied by desire; who have had his left hand under their head; who are irradiated by the brightness of that precious pearl, rooted in charity, and thirsting with panting spirit for the fountain of everlasting life.

Therefore kindly Jesus, now refreshing them as they sit beneath the shadow of him whom they had desired, leads them to drink from the torrent of his delight, to the springs of the waters of life, wiping every tear from their eyes and caressing them in festal joy. He places them in the pleasantness of paradise, [Col. 0858C] on the throne of the chosen Fathers, among the splendors of the saints, in the homeland of angels, in the city of God, in the land of the living.

To this happiest land, most beloved—ignorant of death and evils; to this kingdom of eternal gladness, from which pain, sorrow, and sighing flee—may our life, by God’s inspiration, sigh upward, until that day of eternity breathes upon us and the shadows of our mortality decline. Thus perhaps, seized among pious sobs of longing, even if we do not, like that young man of the tribe of Benjamin, go out of our minds into God as far as the third heaven, or even if our soul, turned in its distress for perhaps half an hour, begins to weep from love and, breathing again in grace, to sing, let us say to the Lord in our hearts: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments, because your scent has stirred eternal desires within me” (Song 1).

Let us therefore walk and sing, but unencumbered and unburdened, so that we may run our course more swiftly and securely, which robbers beset. Blessed and secure is poverty of spirit; but the mind of the greedy is not blessed, but always fearful; and woe to it, because it will be silent, having neither David’s nor Moses’ cry. On the contrary:

> The traveller, empty-handed, will sing before the robber.

Would that we were empty—not of truth, but of vanity; not of oil, but of wind; seeking testimony not of the mouth but of the heart; advancing not in words but in virtues—indeed, in the power of words, because by the strength of such food one reaches the mountain of God. “Your word,” says the saint, “is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 119). Divine utterances are sweeter than honey to the mouth, but wisdom tastes sweeter still to the heart. Yet the harmony of virtues renders to divine ears a most sweet concord, which I rejoice that our beloved has attained: he has joined God-given simplicity to the highest prudence, discretion to temperance, humility to fortitude, and mercy to justice. Thus, as he runs swiftly, the fifth wheel—which is accustomed to impede the spiritual cart—is crushed beneath his feet, and by day the chariot proceeds straight upon the royal road leading to Beth-shemesh, turning neither to the right of prosperity nor to the left of adversity. It carries the ark of sanctification: that is, a good conscience [Col. 0859B] containing manna, namely unfeigned faith, through which Christ dwells in our hearts, as the Apostle says.

I rejoice in you, therefore; but I do not want you to be forgetful of one who remembers you. I have become foolish; you compelled me to bring forth a song in the night, music in mourning, and, in the misery of my beloved, a jubilation of holiness. I beseech you, as one an alien and pilgrim: hold me, slippery and foolish as I am, with the hand of your prayer, and guide me carefully, so that I may reach with you where you are heading—to the house, namely, of the true Sun of Righteousness, the eternal house not made with hands in heaven—cleansed from sin and washed from my iniquity in the bronze basin made from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle.

May I pass into the wondrous dwelling-place, as far as the house of God in the Holy of Holies, into the most radiant light, the wondrous light, where the rose blossoms and lilies of the valleys do not wither; where is sung the ineffable and inimitable song of virginity; where a humble and blessed people, whom jubilation alone knows . . . of charity, are made to abound in delights and rejoice in the Lord. There are the beauty and glory of Lebanon, knowledge of Judaea, the vision of Israel, Jerusalem’s furnace, Sabbath rest, and jubilee remission. There is grace for grace, Sabbath after Sabbath, month after month.

Behold again: he who is of the earth speaks of heaven; night pours forth a word to day; and one unskilled strives to sing, though his voice reproves his life, his words scourge his conscience, and his deeds do not answer to his sayings. But what wonder if I, who am not good, speak of good? Wretched man that I am, of whom Balaam’s beast could not be silent! Greedy and avaricious, gaping after earthly things, he is deservedly compared to irrational beasts; departing from the dignity of his nature, or of human reason, he passes into brutish feeling. Indeed, in departing from God he is written in the earth: neglecting the desire for higher things, he goes away, digs, and hides in the earth the talent of understanding he had received. He is not to be hidden in an earthen pit from the face of the Lord’s terror and from the glory of his majesty when he rises to strike the earth, unless, coming to his senses in repentance, shaking off the dust from his feet, casting aside slavery to mud and brick, leaving the adulteress’s cloak, and more blessedly clothed in poverty, he may escape the contagion of worldly contact; and, withdrawing and fleeing into the wilderness which he had abandoned, may deserve to enter, from the foreign land in which he has grown old among all his enemies, [Col. 0860A] into the land of promise, and to be received into the number of the holy nation, the peculiar and acquired people, into the grace of adoption and the liberty of the glory of the children of God.

Therefore, dearest friend, having subdued and subjected to the spirit the beast of the flesh, let us look to heaven; with groaning and a sigh of piety, through holy desires let us pass from this world to the Father, seeking the things above, not those upon the earth. For this earth which we tread—and ought to tread—which he gave us under the curse of thorns and thistles, is thirsty and, as it is said, dry. But that land of promise, in which one truly lives, blooms in beauty as in spring days, puts forth leaves in grace, is fruitful in blessings, and is watered by the rushing stream, by the springs of the Savior, and by waters leaping up into eternal life.

Therefore, made a beast of burden, yet not like Balaam, who kicked against the divine goads and bent the back of his mind beneath those that passed over it; rather, bearing the Lord God in meekness and humility of heart, with him presiding and perfecting our steps in his paths, let us make for the heavenly Jerusalem. Thus may we deserve to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living: eternal and ineffable good things, which we cannot worthily estimate, desire, or merit, as it is written, “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), and your promises which surpass every desire, etc. “And the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us.” May Jesus Christ bring us to that glory. Amen.

Perhaps I have been somewhat troubled by remembrance of the dreadful judgment and fear of Gehenna, but I have not spoken without awareness: I know to whom I have spoken and in whom I have believed. I am certain that he has passed to a better disposition of heart not as a servant or hireling, but as a son abounding in bread in his father’s house, already led through fire and water—that is, through charity and wisdom—into refreshment. Hence I do not deny that I can be charged with vain presumption, since I, such as I am, have dared to admonish such a man—not him alone, but myself along with him. Yet let charity excuse what rashness accuses. Still, I understood the matter more as applying to myself, needy and poor, [Col. 0860D] than to him, who has no need of my words.

But now speech, demanding an end, must be closed. I desire most ardently to enjoy consolation not so much in papers as in conversation and the sight of your charity, that I may be refreshed with you, and that the scarlet cord and the sweet utterance of my heart may restrain its wanderings. Let those separated from one another in place at least be joined in prayers; let those absent be present, who in presence are absent.

Yet I fear lest your friendship, buried beneath so great an absence and so great a silence, fall asleep and sleep, like the bridegroom who delays. Let this rather happen to us: “New wine and a new friend will grow old, and you will drink it with sweetness.” Haimo of holy memory used to say that he was entirely renewed when, after much time, he himself visited a friend, or someone from among all his dear ones visited him.

The good shepherd has departed: Lord William, formerly prior of Caen, but now a new inhabitant of paradise, a fountain of living water. I beg you not to forget him; for his memory is sweet and pious, so that he too may not forget to have mercy upon us. It is a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead: both that we may pay them the debt of charity and that they may be saved from sins, and that, when it goes well with them, they may remember and turn to the Lord, interceding for us that he may bring us out of this prison and make us sharers in heavenly goods.

Lord Simon, monk of Saint-Sauveur, greets you through me, and truly, I believe, a monk of Jesus. Finally, the least of all, the writer of the present letter, greets you, [Col. 0861B] whose name I keep silent lest its disclosure be unwelcome—not from shame at the name, but from the lowliness of the person. Commend him to those of your household whom you know to live a heavenly life on earth, so that, through their intercession, his reward may be to have escaped punishment. Farewell always in the Lord; again I say, farewell. Do this rather: at some time forget me, rather than at any time remember me. May the God of peace always be with you. Amen.

## LETTER XXXII. GAUFRID TO A CERTAIN YOUNG HERMIT. He gives him salutary admonitions.

Your father earnestly and humbly asked me to write to you and, while you are set in the flower of youthful age, to make you more weighty by the gravity of maturer counsel. [Col. 0861C] For it belongs to a father to fear more serious dangers for a son in the springtime of life. As Jerome testifies, lust subdues iron minds; once it has passed, it always leaves repentance for itself, is never satisfied, and, when extinguished, is rekindled. This is a sulphurous coal, burning and stinking. This is a fire consuming unto destruction and uprooting every shoot of virtue. This is an enemy to God, an enemy to virtues; it is a mouse in the purse, fire in the bosom, a serpent in the lap, and it repays its hosts badly. Flee from the face of this most seductive pestilence, and strive to restrain your eye, mouth, hand, and every movement of the body from every appearance of frivolity. There is that familiar little verse:

> She smiled, and promised something with her bright little eye.

[Col. 0861D] An immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart. May love of chastity dwell more sweetly in your heart, clothing it in that affection for purity with which he was clothed who said: “I have made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not so much as think of a virgin” (Job 31). If temptation strikes you, then, after the temptation, return to yourself; blush before yourself because of yourself, and blaze up against yourself as a most severe avenger. Consider fleeting joys, the miseries of life, swift death, and the life after death, everlasting either in good or in evil. Have a pure heart and a dove-like eye. Gird yourself, like a new recruit, for spiritual combat; put on arms mighty through God: the humility of holy poverty, the rigor of discipline, perseverance in prayer; and let fervor of devotion accompany length of prayer.

[Col. 0862A] Remember how much God has done for you; do not be ungrateful for his gifts, but strive always in mind toward better things. Let every hypocrisy and every pretense be far from you, so that every good you do may always, through its intention, be raised toward heavenly things. Be watchful in deed, speech, and thought, so that you may utterly abandon what displeases God, and may display before God’s eyes in your conduct what you show to human eyes in your outward habit. What you wish your brothers to do to you, do also to them according to the Lord’s commandment; in this short and compact precept many counsels are contained at once. Do not be like a reed shaken by the wind, but keep the summit of your mind inflexible amid human praise and disparagement. Let plain furnishings and a humble cell suffice you, lest [Col. 0862B] what is said of the Megarians may also be applied to you: “They build as though they were always to live, and live as though they were to die the next day.” Do not forget that when a man’s life dies in sin, his death lives in punishment. “Though the draught is bitter,” Augustine says, “it must nevertheless be drunk, because the inward parts are in danger; and a little bitterness in the throat is far better than eternal torment in the inward parts.”

Indeed, Scripture supplies innumerable examples to teach you that avarice must be fled. Jerome to Eustochium: “Why should I recount what happened not many years ago in Nitria? One of the brothers, more sparing than avaricious, and not knowing that the Lord was sold for thirty pieces of silver, when dying left behind a hundred solidi which he had earned by weaving flax. A consultation was begun among the monks [Col. 0862C] (for in that place nearly five thousand dwell in separate cells) as to what ought to be done with this money. Some said it should be distributed to the poor, others given to the Church, some sent back to his parents; but Macarius, Pambo, Isidore, and the others whom they call Fathers, with the Holy Spirit speaking in them, decreed that it should be buried with its owner, saying: ‘Your money perish with you’” (Acts 8). “Let no one think this was done credulously. Such terror seized everyone throughout Egypt that leaving behind even one solidus was reckoned a crime.”

Therefore, renouncing this vice, set each day the steps of holy desire upon God’s way. Apply yourself especially to humility, and do not raise yourself through pride, so that you may keep in your mind the purple of the heavenly [Col. 0862D] kingdom. Go forth for your neighbor’s benefit; stand for your own guard; rise to the contemplation of God. That you may be able to do this, may the wings of virtues lift you toward heavenly desire. Yet put no confidence in any virtue; rather tremble in great fear, until your mind, warmed and vehemently kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, turns fear into love. Do not seek to please those whom you know displease God. “It is very foolish,” Gregory says, “if we seek to please those whom we know do not please God.” For he denies himself to be God’s friend who pleases God’s enemy; and he will oppose the enemies of truth who is subdued in heart to that same truth.

Gladly lend your ear to sound teaching. “The word of God,” says a saint, “is seed in the hearer’s heart; and a good hearer brings forth from it [Col. 0863A] a great harvest of knowledge, from the small seed of speech that he first received.” Moreover, as we read in the life of a certain saint, our conduct and life ought to show forth the beauty, strength, and purity of our inner person; we should bear the outward person always in one and the same manner, and that the most modest and becoming, so that nothing whatever may appear in it capable of offending attentive observers; we should not utter an idle word, nor make a gesture, nor move hand or foot without purpose. Let there be nothing unedifying in your walk, gaze, dress, or countenance. Finally, let grief not darken the cheerfulness of your face, nor laughter make it frivolous. Let everything in you be disciplined, everything marked by virtue, a pattern of perfection. Be relaxed at times, but never dissolute; neglect nothing, though for a time you may pass over many things; be often at rest, but never idle.

[Col. 0863B] I therefore urge you, observing these things, to cling to the footsteps of blessed Eligius, in whose place you live night and day. Using the words of the saints, I have wished, as on a small tablet, to set forth very broad matters briefly. Something appears to be missing here.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO HUGH, PRIOR OF SAINT MARTIN OF SÉES
