He praises Hugh, prior of Saint Martin of Sées, and teaches how they ought to prepare themselves for the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection.

To Hugh, venerable prior of Saint Martin of Sées, from his own G.: what he wishes for himself.

The bearer of this letter could, without a letter, have explained anything you might inquire concerning [Col. 0863C] me; but because, as someone says, “a greeting conveyed in bare speech is wearisome,” I have joined writing to my messages—especially so that our exchanges of words may serve as a consolation. It is fitting that by such a remedy we should ease the weariness of our pilgrimage and cultivate our mutual affection through religious greetings. I desire the debt of friendship between us to increase daily.

Thus I write to you, not in learned words of human wisdom, which God will destroy, but in simplicity of heart and sincerity of charity, which never fails. There will be no rhetorical magnificence of language here: I am not greatly trained in such matters, and religious ears ought not to take delight in the splendor of worldly eloquence. They have those who delight them spiritually: namely, the holy [Col. 0863D] doctors, flowing from the milky fountain of divine eloquence. Yet I trust in the Lord that, aided by your merits, he will quicken the barren and lifeless waters within me, season them with the salt of heavenly wisdom, and make them fruitful by the infusion of his grace. He himself waters parched fields, and sweetens the torrent of thorns and the Dead Sea.

Hence it is that, watered by divine dew and rooted and grounded in charity, you strive with supreme zeal, together with Elijah, to stand in the cleft of the rock, to pass through the eye of the needle, and to behold the Lord’s back. Hence indeed it is that you place the world beneath your feet, and strive here in order to be crowned elsewhere. And you plainly possess, after the example of [Col. 0864A] Elijah, a fiery chariot to raise you to the stars; whoever mounts it shall not taste death for ever. This is the four-horsed chariot of the virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

Prudence, as it is said, consists in despising this world and all that is in the world through the contemplation of divine things, and directing every thought of the soul toward God alone. Temperance consists in desiring nothing that one must repent, exceeding the rule of moderation in nothing, and taming desire under reason’s yoke. Fortitude consists in raising the mind above fear of danger, fearing nothing except what is shameful, and bearing adversity and prosperity alike with courage. Justice consists in preserving for each person what is his due. By these virtues, religious persons beloved of God joyfully join themselves, through a kind of flight from human things, to divine things alone.

[Col. 0864B] These are, as the Wise Man says, virtues of a soul already purified and clarified, wholly and completely cleansed from every defilement of this world. With these ornaments of virtue, through your prayers, may we be prepared worthily to celebrate the approaching day of the Lord’s Resurrection. Its most sweet fragrance has filled the world, so that no part of the earth, as Pope Alexander writes, feels itself alien to or deprived of this fragrance; rather, all rejoice that by this sweetest scent they have now conquered spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places.

Further, as another writer says, to signify Christ’s Resurrection spiritually, the holy women carried spices to the tomb, prefiguring his glory by the sweetness of fragrant ointments; this glory brought terror to hell, joy to heaven, and holiness to earth. I have ventured to write these things to you as one speaking to a friend. Although you have an anointing from the Holy One which teaches you about all things, nevertheless take away the holy thing given to dogs and pearls trampled by swine.

For you know that waters flow through stone channels to garden-beds; Moses, to whom God spoke face to face as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend, accepted the counsel of Jethro, a Gentile; and Elijah, mighty in fire and holding the keys of the clouds, patiently awaited food from a raven. May the Father of mercies soon grant us to see your face with joy.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO R., A PRIEST

What the priest’s position on the right during Mass signifies, and concerning certain other rites.

[Col. 0864D]

To his venerable friend and fellow priest R.  
[Note: [Col. 0863D] He seems to have written to the person named above in Letters 8 and 19, and below in Letter 38.]  
G., the least and refuse of all priests: may you be wise and understanding, and provide for your latter end.

I have been well pleased with myself insofar as I can do anything that may please your will. You ask me to set down in writing what the priest’s station on the right means in Mass, why the Gospel is read on the left, and, if I am not mistaken, you desire other matters of this kind to be explained to you. The desire is praiseworthy in a priest who fears that sentence of the Lord: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, that you may not serve me as priest” [Col. 0865A] (Hos. 4).

But do not suppose that I have handed down notions of my own, nor receive them as though they were mine. Rather, know that I have selected opinions from many discourses of the Fathers, whose praise is sufficiently worthy in the Church, insofar as they seemed suited to this matter. Understand, therefore, what I say; for God will give you understanding in all things.

The priest’s entrance to the altar signifies the entrance of the Son of God into this world. Burning tapers are present: signs, that is, of the joy which shone upon the whole world at the Savior’s birth, concerning which the angel said to the shepherds: “I announce to you great joy” (Luke 2), and so forth. He enters clothed in sacred vestments; whence that excellent versifier:

> He is covered in sacred garments; flesh clothed the Word,  
> Wholly without stain, wholly consecrated to God.

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours.]

[Col. 0865B] To speak briefly: the alb signifies purity; the girdle, continence; the shoulder-piece, justice; the maniple, discretion, which is the mother of all virtues; the stole, the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden; and the chasuble, worn over all the other ornaments, signifies the holiness and justice by which priestly glory ought to shine.

He goes to the right side of the altar because Christ always led a right-hand life: for by the right hand heavenly glory is attained. The aforementioned versifier says:

> “He stands at the right,” he says, “because the people, having cursed vain gods,  
> Sought their Creator, and were as it were on the right.”
>
> Hence, he says, the Lord’s sacred words are read on the left.  
> When Judaea rejected the faith, Christ’s grace  
> Passed to the nations; Israel still wanders.  
>
> Whenever the Gospel is recited, this passage  
> Comes before the mind and is expressed by its place.  
>
> It is read on the left because the people to whom it passed had gone astray,  
> And the idolatrous nation was, as it were, on the left.”

> [Judaea, destined to return to Christ’s faith, is signified,  
> When the Father sits at the right and completes the work.]

[Note: [Col. 0865D] These two poems are lacking from the printed editions of Hildebert and from a manuscript of Marmoutier written in Hildebert’s time [Col. 0866D].]

But I have not proposed to write you all that you can find in the writings of the Fathers. Some are quite puzzled that, once the sacraments have been completed, the sign of the cross is made. For where it is said, “A pure offering, a holy offering, an immaculate offering, the holy bread of eternal life and the chalice of everlasting salvation,” the fivefold sign of the cross, impressed upon the substance of bread and wine, sends the instructed contemplator of these realities—truly incorporated into Christ sitting at the Father’s right hand—to that blessed [Col. 0865D] Passion.

These, then, are the clefts of the living rock, in which the beautiful and immaculate dove—that is, the Church—is found; there she nests most surely when, amid the words just mentioned, faithful remembrance contemplates the five wounds of the Beloved through the five signs of the cross: namely, the two wounds of the hands, the same number of the feet, and one of the side. As remembrance of his Passion wounds the Church’s charity, so remembrance of the Resurrection strengthens faith, and contemplation of the Ascension gladdens hope.

Therefore, as we stand to make the offering, let us rightly divide—that is, first offering ourselves, let us kill and mortify the ram-like pride of a stubborn spirit, bull-like savagery, and goat-like lust—according to what we sing in the Psalm: “I will offer you sacrifices full of marrow, with incense of rams; I will offer you bulls with goats” (Ps. 66). Then God will deign to accept our sacrifices.

[Col. 0866A] Why three portions are made from the host, the same writer explains quite elegantly in verse:

> “The portion dipped in wine prays for the living, and flesh itself  
> Expiates by the work of blood and flesh.  
>
> For the blessed dead we offer you two portions, O Christ:  
> One, more purified, needs no such intervention; the other needs it.  
>
> Yet, for the same persons, the two offerings do not effect the same thing.  
> For one portion is for the righteous; the other is for those to be justified:  
> The former represents the nations; the latter pleads with God.”

[Note: [Col. 0866D] These verses differ somewhat in the printed editions.]

This most holy mystery of the altar is called *missa* (“Mass”) because it is the sole mission sufficient and fitting to bring about reconciliation and the removal of the enmities that existed between God and humanity. But let this suffice for what we have said about the Mass. If, however, you ask what the altar, chalice, paten, and corporal cloths signify, hear:

> The altar has the office of the cross; the chalice, of the tomb; the paten, of the stone;  
> The white linen cloth has the office of the shroud.  
>
> Further, in the censer  
> There are three things that you should signify: the vessel, the incense, and the fire.  
> The vessel is the heart; the incense, the psalm; the inward heat, the nourishing Spirit.

[Col. 0866B] But take care not to offer strange fire in your censer before the Lord. Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, did this and died. Sacred fire is the domestic fire of charity; hence the Prophet: “In my meditation fire shall blaze forth” (Ps. 38). The fire of greed and the fire of lust are strange fire; hence Job says: “It is a fire devouring unto destruction, and uprooting all offspring” (Job 31).

[Col. 0866C] You see that this fire has today blazed forth in many ways among many people. Though they serve the Author of purity in a pure heart and body, they do not fear to stand before the angel [perhaps: before the angel] of the Lord, who may cut them asunder and destroy them. Rather, they dare altogether to touch the sacred flesh of the immaculate Lamb, to dip their impious hands in the Savior’s blood—hands which, a little before, alas, handled the flesh of prostitutes—to walk thus around the altars and frequently recite psalms, although such praise is accursed and their prayer becomes sin.

[Col. 0866D] They sell the sacraments and betray justice—men whose throats no blasphemous word, sacrilegious voice, or wicked speech has yet drawn to the noose, and whose jaws it has not yet choked: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. 26). From their censers there rises before the Lord, instead of a sweet odor, a stench. “May my soul not come into their judgment, nor my glory be in their assembly”; for a fire has been kindled in the Lord’s wrath against them, and it will burn unto the lowest depths of hell (Deut. 32).

But we must now come to what you finally ask to have written: namely, what the priest owes the people, and what the people [Col. 0867A] owe the priest. To state it briefly, the priest’s part is to teach and intercede: to teach by word and example, and to appease God by prayer and sacrifice. These, then, are what he owes the people: the word of teaching, the example of life, and the offering of sacrifices and prayers on their behalf. Hence Peter was told: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21). Therefore it was repeated three times, and “Feed” was said three times; “Milk” or “shear” was not added even once.

The priest, therefore, should strive more to feed the Lord’s flock than to shear it, and to feed it in three ways: by the example of his conduct, by the word of preaching, and by the fruit of offerings and prayer. It is the priestly office to appease heavenly wrath by sacrifices. Yet not all who intercede for others obtain an answer from God, nor do all who sacrifice to God appease God. A criminal offers sacrifice, but through Isaiah God says: “The criminal who sacrifices to me is like one who kills a dog” (Isa. 66). And the Prophet says: “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, God will not hear” (Ps. 65). God is not appeased by such vows; indeed, God is provoked by the sacrifices of the wicked. “When one who displeases is sent to intercede,” Gregory says, “the judge’s mind is provoked to anger.”

[Col. 0867B] Thus your sacrifices provoke God if your life displeases him; but he will be appeased toward you, and toward others through you, if sacrifice is offered to him by you with a pure heart and body. But lest we prolong matters, let us say what we proposed: what the people owe the priest. For the honor of God, whose ministers priests are, the justice of the people ought to show priests humble submission and the devotion of charity, so that all their obedience may be both humble and devout.

Moreover, if you see paleness in the leaves, know that there is disease in the root; if you see crime among the people, know that there is fault in the priest. But now let us make an end of speaking. I desire that, in the receptacle of your heart, after the little thorns of vices have been removed, you may plant the heavenly virtues; and that, by their abundance, you may instruct the hearts of those subject to you, and, while teaching, never fail in good work.

> Either you will fear sweet loves, or you will experience them as bitter;  
> It is no small matter to set this before human perceptions.  
> No sap is withheld from cattle, nor milk from lambs,  
> Nor do the evil contagions of a neighboring flock harm them.

## LETTER XXXV. TO JOHN, ABBOT

He expresses sympathy for a misfortune that had happened to him.

[Col. 0867D]

To his venerable abbot J., Brother G.: act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord.

I had desired a letter from you when certain persons were coming, whom I presumed would convey your message to me. But when that hope disappointed my expectation, I took care to address you of my own accord, so that by the example of my service I might prompt you to like care. I therefore ask that you do not allow the offices of friendship, which I impatiently seek, to grow cold. Although I know your affection for me and am confident that, even while you refrain from writing, it is retained [Col. 0868A] in a faithful heart, I say this confidently.

For we know, as someone says, that trust springing from simple affection is a kind of virtue. I too confess that I have been silent for a long time, waiting for your letter to supply me with a fitting subject for reply. But when I saw that I had not yet been prompted by any inducement, I was the first to break out into words of greeting. For it is the nature of things that those who stammer speak more; they seek abundance to cover the shame of their deficiency. This example applies to me, who have a great impatience to write when speech fails me; but your love compels me to it, for it pierced my heart with the sharpness of compassion when, through the report of the travelers mentioned above, I learned how savagely fortune had dealt with you by depriving you of your most loving and excellent patron.

[Col. 0868B] Alas for me, for the fear that I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has happened (Job 3).

> There is a certain pleasure in weeping.  
> Pain is fulfilled in tears and driven out.

But the mournful pen and tragic stylus must be spared, lest I aggravate your mind’s wound, lest a late revisiting tear open the scar of past grief. Rather, the mind must be armed against these things with virtue and reason. A better hope must also be adopted. Often, as a certain wise man says, things that totter have been made firm. Nothing is eternal for human beings; frequent changes roll mortal affairs about.

> The passing years take individual things from us,  
> And truly unstable age is filled with many miseries.  
>
> Times slip away, and we grow old in silent years,  
> And the days flee, with no restraining rein.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti* 6.772.)

But every fortune must be overcome by endurance.

“Gold,” Job says, “has a place in which it is refined” (Job 28). Certainly, gold’s purity is proved in the furnace, a horse’s speed in the racecourse, and a soldier’s courage in the field. We know that the three children came out of the furnace purer than they entered it. Therefore, refined in the furnace of this figurative Babylon, let us be strong in battle; and let us run through the course of the sixth age in such a way that our perseverance, by the Lord’s grant, may attain through the common seventh the prize of the eighth.

[Col. 0868C] Rise up, then, like that old man Mattathias. For in your sons and brothers you possess Judah’s courage, Jonathan’s vigor, and Simon’s prudence. These indeed fight the Lord’s battles with you. We ask that you greet them in our stead. We also greet in the Lord that lady—namely, your dear sister—whom we desire to be untouched by every harmful sweetness, and to whose sweet joys one comes only through bitter tears. I beg that your prayer for me may flourish anew before God. May the charity of God thrive and ever burn fervently within you.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO SIMON, A FRIEND

Concerning the praise of a certain virgin.

To his venerable and dearest lord and friend Simon,  
[Note: [Col. 0867D] Perhaps Simon, monk of Saint-Sauveur, mentioned above in Letter 31.]  
[Col. 0869A] from his most devoted G.: greeting and his whole self.

I give thanks to your kindness, which, as I have heard and am certain, does not forget a friend far away; and, remembering me with pious affection, grants me a saving remedy by strengthening my weakness with holy prayers. By often imparting such a remedy to me, have mercy upon me—not because I am worthy, but because “I am poor and needy” (Ps. 85). Have mercy upon me, I say, not because I have deserved it, but because I am in need. Have mercy upon me, as one who has received mercy from the Lord, so that you may serve him in holiness and justice.

I entreat you, when a suitable opportunity is found, if it can be done, to gladden us with the consolation of your visit. This will benefit our salvation and will not harm the purpose of your holiness.

[Col. 0869B] Certainly, if I could, I would gladly come to you—not only because of you, but also because of your virgin, in whom God works so wonderfully that, contrary to nature—indeed almost above nature—she can subsist without human food. Wonderful to say! In these two respects she lives in an angelic manner: by not eating and by preserving virginity. It has been granted her by the Lord both to preserve the title of virginity and to attain its fruit.

She has left the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as demons, so that, forgetting worldly pomp and despising the flesh, she may be joined to the embraces of her bridegroom and, forgetting her people and her father’s house (Ps. 44), dwell in the land of the living. She saves herself not in the little city of Zoar, but, having climbed the summit of virtue, upon the mountain; nor does she descend from the roof after Christ’s tunic to take another garment.

[Col. 0869C] She is indeed the virtue of chastity, found on a land that brings forth thorns and thistles, and which the serpent eats: like gold in mud, a jewel in dung, a lily among thorns. Virginity itself is the virtue of the heavenly city and the glory of its heavenly citizens, where no one has integrity to lose or corruption to grieve over. Its praise and exultation are a song of virtue which widows do not know and married women do not understand. Let us therefore rejoice in the glory of her virtue, she who is reported to have rejected the deceptive glory of the world, and who chose to be married to God, a virgin in body and spirit.

Oh, with what becoming blush, to use that writer’s words, does the innate jewel of modesty suffuse her virgin cheeks! Discipline makes ordered every condition of her maidenly body and habit of mind: it lowers her neck, sets her brows, composes her countenance, restrains her eyes, checks laughter, governs her tongue, curbs her appetite, calms anger, and moderates her gait. It is fitting that the garment of chastity be adorned with such pearls. With such variety is virginity surrounded.

[Col. 0869D] Furthermore, you have told me many things about your aforementioned wonderful virgin. I do not disbelieve them, and ask that she pray to the Lord for us. Convey our prayers to her on our behalf.

Fare well, and keep continual remembrance of your servant.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO R., A PRIEST

He is troubled by the praises bestowed upon him.

[Col. 0870A]

To his beloved and ever-to-be-loved fellow priest R., Brother G.: be sparing in praise, still more sparing in blame.

There is no need to address you in many words, nor to distill the honey of rhetorical sweetness. The latter, indeed, my lack of skill denies me; while the former is permitted neither by the scarcity of time nor by the bearer’s haste. Yet you cover my cheeks with the deepest blush, since in praising me you employ an extravagant manner of writing. It is plain that you write to someone unknown, when you pour out things so foreign to me; for the beginning deserves little praise if an uncouth ending detracts from its savor.

To use the words of blessed Gregory, you surely call a monkey a lion; for we see you acting as we often do when we call mangy puppies leopards or tigers. This, too, has happened to increase the sum of my iniquities: when iniquity ought to have been avenged upon me, I receive praises instead of punishment. And indeed it is not as is said; but would that it were as is said, so that one who is not accustomed to lie would not be lying!

[Col. 0870B] To these things I reply with the words of a certain good woman: “Do not call me Naomi,” that is, “beautiful”; “but call me Mara, because I am filled with great bitterness” (Ruth 1). Yet I approve your writings in this: that they breathe of scholarly exercises and provide an abundance of polished discourse; the speech runs on cheerfully in a certain festive style. I therefore render you the thanks due for this, that your affection deigned to run first to me upon the vehicles of letters.

Farewell; remember me in the Lord. I speak with your mouth: I am yours; be mine.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO W., ABBOT OF SAINT ANDREW’S

He congratulates the abbot of Saint Andrew’s of the Cistercian order on his promotion.

To the beloved and venerable father W., abbot of Saint Andrew’s, from Brother G., humble assistant minister of Saint Barbara’s: may you defend your flock with the shield of good will.

My spirit rejoices at your promotion, accompanying it with thanksgiving to him who humbles the proud and exalts the humble. For we do not judge you to be of the lot of those of whom it is written: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72)—those who advance in honors but fall in character; who desire rather to rule than to benefit; who feed themselves, not the sheep; who seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ; who, when the wolf comes, do not defend the flock but flee; whom God sets as a wheel; who, in taking up authority, take up a greater judgment. Of them also the poet Claudian says:

> … I no longer complain that the unjust have risen  
> To the heights of the earth: they are lifted on high  
> That they may fall with a heavier ruin.

[Col. 0871A] But we trust that you belong to the number of those who govern with diligence, whom zeal for God’s house has consumed, and under whose cultivation the barren fig tree blooms anew and is restored to favor with its Lord, whose threats and axe it fears. You belong, I say, to the fellowship of those who, with Moses, kill the sacrilegious; with Phinehas, pierce the unchaste; with Samuel, mourn the disobedient; with Job, offer sacrifice for their children; with Aaron, proclaim divine accusations before Pharaoh; and with Noah, provide an ark smeared with pitch for those threatened with inundation.

For them there is a rod of correction for the sheep and a staff of defense against enemies; their mind is the little worm of humility in prosperity and the shield of constancy in adversity. You make flourish, by the sprinkling of divine dew, the planting which your heavenly Father planted amid the wild trees of that forest. For you grow rich through abundant reading of heavenly writings, and from your breast flows a fountain of water springing up to eternal life, a well of living waters.

[Col. 0871B] We have often seen many roots of a single wild trunk bear fruit happily through the grafting of one single shoot. Therefore, a shoot has been taken from the branches of a native and sweeter tree—a shoot known to belong to the aforesaid plantation, whose fruit gives off fragrance far and wide—and inserted into the trunk of a native tree, though one of lower rank. Yet it has been restored from there to the former tree from which it was taken, and grafted again into the crown of that tree, so that, by the Lord’s gift, greater fruit may result from it.

Since, therefore, from that new plantation of the district of Le Mans, to which you went to provide irrigation, you have returned to the earlier and aforementioned plantation, and there authority has been given you to say to one, “Go,” and he goes, and to another, “Come,” and he comes (Luke 7), we offer devout prayers to your fatherhood that you send your sacristan, Brother Robert, to us. Once he has completed the matter for which we have judged him necessary to you, we shall send him back after two or three days.

[Col. 0871C] May your fatherhood prosper and always advance in the Lord.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO PETER OF BUXERIA

He says that the vow of his profession and the office of provost prevent him from remaining in solitude.

To his most beloved father and lord P. of Buxeria,  
[Note: [Col. 0871D] Peter, to whom he wrote above in Letter 15.]  
from his son G.: greeting and the full affection of sincere love.

[Col. 0871D] To me, venerable Father, it would indeed be desirable to enjoy the blessedness of a more secluded life and to live in the company of such persons as those with whom I might frequently hold discourse upon the Scriptures. Therefore, having taken up the wings of a dove, I would desire to pass into a pure and free flight, to rest and remain in solitude. But in our church, in which I am not without such companions, I am bound by a twofold bond of necessity: namely, by the vow of my profession and by the office of provost in the order. How, then, I can fulfill what you so earnestly request, I do not see.

I know indeed, most blessed Father, that the very sweetness of your presence, for which I thirst ardently, and your voice [Col. 0872A] full of honeyed sweetness, would often restore me there. I know that, while living with you, the weariness of our pilgrimage would more frequently be relieved by speaking of the eternal homeland. I know that through your fiery speech the flame of charity, conceived from grace, would often kindle our affection toward the eternal joys of invisible things. For the Holy Spirit, who, as we believe, has prepared a pleasant dwelling for himself in your breast, through the intercession of your merits would sometimes raise our heart to that throng of heavenly joy.

For, aided by your words and examples, I would strive to recover the secret freedom of the contemplative life, in which the brightness of the heavenly vision smiles upon you, to fly back to those heights of rest where you touch the heavenly mysteries with the hand of the heart, where you seek to see incorporeally the joys above.

[Col. 0872B] May the charity of God thrive and ever burn fervently within you.

## LETTER XL. TO JOHN, ABBOT

He explains the rarity of his letters.

To his venerable abbot J., from Brother G.: what exceeds the merits and prayers of suppliants.

Love, the more simple it is, the more tender and vulnerable to injury: it advances by its very simplicity, and if it encounters anything clouded in a friend, it takes offence. For it demands from a friend what it itself offers. The mind of one who loves, as the poet says, is indeed tender and keenly sensitive to every feeling of pain. I shall briefly explain the point of this address. I am intensely impatient of your silence [Col. 0872C], a kind of complaint familiar to lovers. You have long postponed the task of writing, and I fear that perhaps your affection toward me has grown lame. The more tender the affection, the readier the complaint. Perhaps you plead occupations in excuse; but may that event never occur, that labour should diminish your talent, care bend your kindness, or practice exhaust your eloquence. Although I am conscious of my very poor ability, yet, prompted by love for you, I am not ashamed to disclose the meagreness of my childish speech, while you are silent as though the spring of your eloquence had run thin. But I beg that your affection may deign to visit me, and pour into my soul the eternal manna of life with the sweet dew of letters. May your gracious favour be present to us [Col. 0872D] in the affection of charity, by which souls are joined far better than bodies by places. This would indeed be sufficient for those whom the love of the Spirit has more perfectly raised from the earth; for us, however, exchanges of discourse must serve as consolation. Religious concern made you write first; you will not be so discourteous as, once invited, to refrain. It accords with nature that services begun by you and welcomed by me should grow together. Therefore, henceforth be liberal with your speech: my care shall not fail, which will requite you with a reciprocal interchange of writing. Moreover, I confess that for many reasons I am bound to you, so that whenever I conveniently can, I both ought and desire to visit you in person; but [Col. 0873A] at present opportunity does not answer my desires. Very many obstacles stand in the way; nevertheless, I thought it profitable to send you words of greeting and excuse, hoping that, once the necessity is understood by your prudence, charity will obtain pardon. God himself, who *is* charity, knows with what affection I embrace you; and would that you could see my heart with lynx-eyed vision, as they say! But now let my letter have its limit, though my affection for you never shall. I pray that the course of the office you undertook long ago may now smile upon you, although I cannot doubt that you are able to change your goodness, and to be more happily spurred on in virtue by the incentive of rewards. May our brothers prosper, those who, together with you, cherish us in their holy prayers.

[Col. 0873B] I truly love you. If you ask how: purely.

If you ask how much: according to the weight of friendship.

## LETTER XLI. TO HUGH, PRIOR OF SAINT MARTIN OF SÉES

He praises his virtues and exhorts him to write the Life of Walter.

To his beloved and venerable lord and friend [Note: [Col. 0873D] Hugh, monk and prior of Saint Martin of Sées, to whom Letters 33, 43, 46, and 49 are addressed.] H., brother G., greeting in God his saviour.

As Pope Innocent testifies in his familiar writings, true affection consists in this: therefore what I write to you is a sign of steadfast friendship. For the power of love draws me after you, because true love draws you after Christ. And we love you with so much the greater affection, and hold you dearer in our inmost heart, [Col. 0873C] as you more willingly and readily aspire to those things which you know belong to the honour and increase of religious life. For it is clear that in heart and deed you frequently cleave to divine services and devout acts. Hence, indeed, in our young man there is rougher clothing, more restricted food, and a spirit readier for every good work. Age does not hinder this where it has poured itself into heavenly power. Truly, as Scripture relates: “Venerable old age is not that which is prolonged, nor measured by the number of years; but the grey hairs of men are understanding, and a spotless life is old age” (Wisdom 4).

But the soul of this our young man, set among the maidens who run after the Bridegroom in the fragrance of ointments, reaching, as we believe, [Col. 0873D] perfect age and arriving, so to speak, at marriageable years—years, I say, of merits, not of time—has become fit for the nuptials of the heavenly Bridegroom. By desires that tend upward, it knows how to seek his absence with groaning, and to seek him by groaning. That simplicity, adorned with the jewels of heavenly wisdom, has recognized its Creator; it has recognized him, I say, and with all its strength *has loved* the Lord. The dove of Christ, washed with milk, dwelling beside waters very full, and emulous of angelic chastity, has devoted itself to his bridal chamber, to his bedchamber.

Hence, dearest brother, your mind burns with the flame of love amid tears of compunction [Col. 0874A], sets before its eyes the rewards of the heavenly homeland, and already longs to take its place among the citizens above. You give God the flower of your age, and, not estranged from the thresholds of wisdom, have wisely deliberated between life and death, spirit and flesh, Christ and the world. Deservedly, then, we receive such a man into the eager and open bosom of friendship. Deservedly we desire that we too may be received into the care of your holy and most faithful heart. With all our affection we earnestly desire that you may bear the sweetest fruits of good things—you who have flowered in abundant praise of virtues. I do not fear that your zeal will grow lukewarm under such praise; rather, I hope that your goodwill may be stirred by this as by a certain spur toward what is better. For, as a wise man says, it is characteristic of the good [Col. 0874B] not to grow lukewarm at their own praise, but to heap up good endeavours, whose reward they know does not perish. But enough of this.

Furthermore, do not be reluctant, if life accompanies you, to continue and complete what, by God’s inspiration, you have begun to write concerning the Life of the blessed man [Note: [Col. 0873D] Walter of Mauritania, whose letters are extant [Col. 0874D] in the *Spicilegium*, vol. II, and whose manuscript treatise *On Marriage* is in the library of Saint Martin of Sées.] Walter. He will not be without glory in God’s sight who has been the herald of such great merits. As my mind was swifter than my letter, so I loved you before I wrote to you. Let a return letter teach me of the things about you. Rejoice always in the Lord; may the breeze of the Holy Spirit speed you and bring you onward to the harbour of the desired shore. Farewell.

> If anyone loves truly, he does not know how to remove what he loves  
> From the chamber of his heart.

> There is a reason why love knows no use of reason.

[Col. 0874C]

> There is one measure in love: to have had no measure.

## LETTER XLII. HUGH, PRIOR OF SAINT MARTIN OF SÉES, TO GEOFFREY

A reply to the preceding letter.

To his beloved and venerable father and friend G., his H. sends such greeting as he would wish to possess.

I have received your letter, a letter of joy, which soothes a devout mind and awakens it to salvation. Would that the day of my departure from this Egypt might find me such as your letter now declares me to be! But, setting before my eyes the mirror of the Scriptures, I find my soul stained [Col. 0874D] with the blemishes of sins, wretched, empty, and unworthy of praise. Yet God’s grace does not permit me to be so blinded that I should entrust my soul’s salvation to human praises. For I return to conscience: if I find it weak, I condemn my weakness; if sound, I give thanks to the Healer.

You wrote that I should continue what I began concerning blessed W.; but now I advise and ask you to write, because, as I have heard, he stayed a long time with you, God’s grace giving him illness—on your account, I believe. For unless he had been ill, he would not have remained with you so long. Now therefore write in sequence what you heard from him, and [Col. 0875A] send it to me; and ask him, if he is still with you, to come safely for the feast of Saint Martin, since on that journey he will suffer no serious infirmity either in body or soul, and will confer much benefit upon many.

I have briefly replied to your letter. To the two commands which you sent me through Lord Ernald the canon—namely, that I should drink wine and eat fennel, of which the first is burdensome and the second easy—I do not wish to reply in writing; rather, I myself shall answer you sweetly. Know that what you gave me in writing on the roll, and your words, have greatly benefited me. Farewell; and pray for us more earnestly, that we may not fail but always advance on the way; and come to the Valley of God by way of us as soon as you can [Note: [Col. 0875D] A monastery of the Carthusian order in the diocese of Sées, not far from Mauritania and from [Col. 0876D] La Trappe.].

[Col. 0875B]

> Three enemies vex me with a threefold conflict:  
> The ancient serpent, slippery flesh, and an unrighteous brother.

## LETTER XLIII. GEOFFREY TO HUGH, PRIOR OF SAINT MARTIN OF SÉES

He urges him to write Walter’s life and praises his abstinence from wine.

To his beloved lover H., brother G. sends the putting on of a long tunic and the offering of the tail of the victim.

That most sweet and flowering breath of your speech, which you sent to me through a venerable man of approved religious life, delights me. I read it, read it again often, and it pleases me more when repeated. Whenever I take it up, some image of your presence comes before my eyes. Love has answered love, [Col. 0875C] letter letter. Therefore I rejoice that we are equals not only in mutual affection, but also in exchange of letters. Yet I shall take care that the balance and scale of my service outweigh yours. For, as the poet says, it seems a kind of collusion with sloth always to be reckoned on equal scales.

You desire, as your very letter declares, that the final day of your departure from this Egypt may find you such as our writing speaks of you. But you say that, holding the mirror of Scripture before yourself, you find your soul stained by sins, wretched, empty, and unworthy of praise. And indeed you rightly think this of yourselves; for no one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day old. Who will boast that he has a pure heart? [Col. 0875D] The stars are not clean in his sight. Certainly we all offend in many things; and if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. But there is a mercy-seat above the ark, and “his compassion is over all his works,” to whom we sing in the Psalm: “Your mercy, Lord, is great over me” (Psalm 85). For we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is propitiation for our sins, who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood (1 John 2:8). This is our hope; this is all our confidence.

But concerning what you ask and advise, namely that I should compose the Life of blessed W., which you [Col. 0876A] have already partly produced, I reply that it seems unfitting for me to confuse so illustrious a subject by a diversity of pens; moreover, I judge the undertaking to be beyond the powers of my weakness. Rather, complete what you have begun, and pray God that he may fill the outspread sails of your faith and devotion with the breath of his Spirit, drive you forward in the course of the work undertaken, grant you significance in your words, dignity in your utterances, the light of understanding, knowledge of truth, and defend you from the danger of falsehood. Thus, as Anastasius did in writing Antony’s deeds, Sulpicius Martin’s, Jerome Hilarion’s, and Gregory Benedict’s, so may you, in recording the acts of venerable W., spread all the sails of your talent to the Holy Spirit. May the breeze of that Holy Spirit speed [Col. 0876B] your little vessel and carry it to the harbour of the desired shore. Therefore do not seek to make our frail skiff fit for further turbulent waves, but scarcely even for pools and quiet waters.

I instructed you to use a little wine mixed with water, because of your stomach and especially because of your infirmity, in order to avoid consumption; Paul too writes this to Timothy, not as an apostolic command but as medical advice. But you say that this is burdensome to you, for you read that wine is not at all for monks [Note: [Col. 0876D] In the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 40.], and: “It is good for a man neither to eat flesh nor drink wine”; and of the Lord’s Baptist: “He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink” (Luke 1). Yet God is able to defend you from the infirmity, for whose love you abstain from such a cup. Would that I too had received from him such a grace of abstinence; but I am weak, weighed down by the burden of vices, and almost fail on the road. Groaning, I say this when I look upon my wormwood and observe your cups sweetened with honey. You ask that I come to the Valley of God through you as soon as I can; but many delays meet me. Still, if divine favour smiles upon my wishes, I shall do as you exhort. Farewell, and pray to the Lord for us more frequently. May the Lord himself grant that you may so run through the condition of the sixth age that, after the common seventh, you may attain the prize of the eighth. Amen.

> He shall receive God in life, and shall see heroes  
> Mingled with the gods; and he himself shall be seen by them.

[Col. 0876D]

> As the pliant willow yields to the pale olive,  
> As lowly saliunca (wild nard) yields to crimson rose-beds,  
> So much do I yield to you.

## LETTER XLIV. TO AUGUSTINE, HIS FRIEND

He praises Augustine and exhorts him to pursue spiritual things.

To AUGUSTINE, his venerable and sweetest friend in Christ, G., wholly his, sends greeting—and whatever may be better than greeting.

Truly, “a faithful friend is a strong protection; whoever finds one has found a treasure.” Therefore I rejoice and congratulate you, as one who has found a desirable treasure, because you received me into the grace of friendship with such festive beginnings and such joyful countenances. Nor will the happiness of that beginning turn to the contrary, but it will run its course in due order until, by God’s gift, it deserves to reach the desired goal. Yet I bear this grievous thing: after the kindly simplicity of your charity opened its inner chambers to me, you were not permitted to remain longer among us [Col. 0877A] or to relieve the distress of my mind by your sweet presence. What, then, you dealt with more gently in person, accomplish through the returning gift of your letters. My spirit will rise whenever a word of your affection is brought to me. For it will bring assurance of your health, show the advance of your ability, and, what is greater, shine forth in the service of charity.

Therefore I urge you to sprinkle me more frequently with such little flowers of your tongue. I might rightly call these flowers of speech sweet sounds of the Muses, for they delight the ear of the heart with the pleasing modulation of their composition. Yet when you write to us, you inflate, as it were, pastoral reeds; when you compose the sacred deeds you know, you begin your song as though upon sacred trumpets. Therefore sing as you have begun: sound the trumpet in Zion; blow the horn before the servants of God, who will gladly hear. For the more recent they are, the more welcome. Let them then be produced elegantly and poured forth splendidly upon beaten-metal trumpets and the sound of a horn trumpet. By beaten-metal trumpets I mean your very studies, produced by the gift of the Holy Spirit as by the blow of a hammer. By the horn trumpet, because horn surpasses flesh, [Col. 0877C] I mean the intention of one composing and contemplating heavenly things, looking to nothing other than God’s glory and honour and the edification of neighbours.

Thus indeed, according to the custom of the ancients, you mark the title of splendid testimony with a white pebble. For the praise granted to you has not come from an empty mouth, but good fruit has smiled from the good treasure of your heart and the abundant storehouse of your conscience. Hence we trust that the Lord will give you a white stone, and on the stone a new name written which no one knows save the one who receives it. Let the hope of reward therefore be the consolation of labour, until what we sigh for in hope we know in direct vision.

Furthermore, you say that those amorous, epithalamic songs, and songs exhorting to contemplation, which I dedicated to your [Col. 0877D] name, have benefited you. I wish you sometimes to sing them in the more secret hours within the inner bridal chamber of your heart, in order to stir your soul toward the kiss and chaste embraces of the sacred Bridegroom. For I pray—and from my heart’s deepest affection desire, using not my words but those of the saints—that you may strive by devotion to penetrate the heavens; that your mind may traverse the dwellings above; that you may greet the Fathers and apostles and companies of prophets; admire the triumphs of martyrs; marvel at the most beautiful ranks of angels; and, because you cannot yet taste perfectly the sweet food of the heavenly homeland, at least taste it by longing.

I pray, I say, I pray that you may strive every day to pass into that metropolis of angels, which is free, stained by no filth of pollution; and that, with every pleasure trodden down and the waves of luxury compressed—which, as the poet says, swell more frequently against us—we may be joined to the heavenly choirs, so that, already transported there in mind and contemplating the narrower places, we may be what we shall be. [Col. 0878A] May the Holy Spirit inspire holy desires in your heart, so that your works may be seasoned with the fervour of devotion and the sweetness of spiritual grace. Pray more earnestly, that the fervour of heavenly desire may daily grow more ardent in our mind, until, the burden of the body cast off, the soul returns to its Maker and ascends to its ancient possession after its long pilgrimage. Amen.

## LETTER XLV. TO GEOFFREY THE PRIEST

Small gifts ought not to be despised because they are small; one should consider the greatness of spirit with which they are given.

[Col. 0878B]

To the priest G., great and exalted in the word of glory, his brother of the same name sends joy, which he bears to be in harmony with the sound of his own name.

Thus we are admonished by saving precepts and formed by divine instruction: “Rejoice always; give thanks in all things.” You therefore ought not to be troubled by the small gift which a poor friend sent with joy—small indeed if valued by its own price, but devout if weighed by love; no, you ought to rejoice and give thanks for that small gift. For I have been told that you complained of it. Consider whether the Fathers in whose footsteps you ought to walk acted in that way.

The vessel of election, to speak first of him, the teacher of the nations in faith and truth, says to the Philippians: “I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that now at last your concern for me has revived, as you were concerned before; but you were occupied. I do not say this because of want, for I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be brought low, and I know also how to abound. Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to be full and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:10 ff.)—and the rest, which is burdensome for me to recite and perhaps unnecessary for you to hear.

Paulinus to Augustine: “We have sent you one loaf by the grace of unanimity.” This bread the said teacher certainly received with thanksgiving. Jerome to Eustochium [Col. 0878D] concerning gifts received: “Gifts received from a virgin—bracelets, letters, and doves—are small in appearance but great in charity. Yet, lest I seem to have diminished the gifts, we also received a basket full of cherries, so red with such maidenly modesty that I should now think them brought from Lucullus, since he first brought this kind of fruit from Cerasus to Rome after Pontus and Asia had been subdued; whence the tree too received its name from its native land.” Gregory to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch: “Thanks be to God, because what you say, do, and give is both fragrant and savoury.” And again: “I have received all the most abundant blessings which were sent to me, which you, a man of God poor in spirit, transmitted. Concerning them you say: ‘For what can a poor man give except poor things?’ But unless you were poor through the spirit of humility, your blessings would not have been rich.”

A holy man to a friend who had sent him a gift while he was sick: “I have received,” he says, “your charity in charity, not in pleasure.” Ildebert to Matilda, queen of the English: “I pursue your blessing with thanksgiving, and embrace your gift no otherwise than the incense of heaven or the rich libations of victims. For they consider not the sacrifice but the affection, and devotion, not expenditure, earns their favour: a pure and whole mind inclines them wherever it wishes, and appeases heavenly indignation no less by a farthing than by a talent. So too your spirit commends, magnifies, and adorns your gift in my eyes.”

A learned man playfully wrote in verse about a gift sent him by a friend:

> Abbot Fulcher repays me honey for honey:  
> I gave spiritual honey; he gave material honey.  
> The fruits of the fruit-tree, cooking pears, overflow with honey;  
> The sender’s kindness tastes sweeter to me than honey.  
> He repays gifts with gifts, which, sweet in themselves,  
> The honey from the old man’s tongue sweetens more fully.  
> Representing the Lord’s words and serene countenance,  
> The messenger himself commends the gifts to me.

Certainly those from whose writings we have woven the flowers of various testimonies, as it were, into one garland knew that, according to the common proverbial saying, in the matter of giving and receiving mothers and daughters become friends. [Col. 0879C] Thus love is nourished and harmony grows.

In my ignorance I rashly presume to teach one who is learned. Yet I rejoice that matter has been given me for play with you. I rejoice whenever a breeze reaches my ears that reports you safe. But I ask you to pray more earnestly for my heart’s infirmity, that strength may be given me by the Lord by which I may with all my love tend toward that end in which I may rejoice with you without end. Rejoice always in the Lord.

## LETTER XLVI. TO H., HIS FRIEND

He sympathizes with his friend’s adversities.

To his dearest H., brother G. sends a good life and a blessed end.

[Col. 0879D] A great path of love, as the poet says, is opened when, for the sake of heavenly sweetness, it passes into the delights of one who loves; and when that Spirit—that ruler of heaven and inhabitant of paradise—binds the minds of friends, whom true charity gathers together in one heart and one soul. We write this of the two of us because we feel it thus; and we especially rejoice in this, that this affection does not so much flower in a temporal service as germinate in spiritual progress.

And I, most beloved friend, in carrying out the business of friends which you entrusted through the bearer of your letter, visit my lord and friend; and since I have learned something of your adversity, I grieve with one whom I know. Nor is it surprising if a great storm has risen in the depth of a devout heart. Great God! How great is the deceitful cunning of the ancient adversary! When [Col. 0880A] he sees the limit of our life, he does not impose a limit on our adversity, but burns more fiercely against us, that he may seize our actions more tightly for himself.

But far be it, my lord—far be it, I say—that the enemy should disgrace you in the very labours in which God has hitherto honoured you. Rather, may the eternal husbandman reap your fruitful countenance in the flower of youth, and may your fragrance become like the fragrance of a full field which God has blessed: so that the flower of the vine may smell sweet in you through preaching; so that by the grace of a healing tongue you may cure the diseases of many souls in many persons; that the flower of the lily may smell sweet through chastity, the flower of the violet through humility, the flower of the ear of grain through the ripeness of good works, the flower of the olive through mercy, and the flower of the rose through patience. Through the virtue of that patience, with the Lord pouring patience into you, every adversity will wholly yield to you. For, according to Job, you have a song in the night, and amid present pressures you are comforted by future joys.

Be comforted and nourished also by the writings of the saints, sweet with God’s word and anointed with the oil of gladness, with which you gladly anoint your head. For in you there is no false working of the olive, in which charity dwells from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. You know well, as blessed Gregory writes, that no one is perfectly good unless he is good even with the wicked. Therefore let your mind, drawn away from the whirlwinds of this troubling world, serve as a station in the harbour of salvation; let it lift itself toward heaven, and, already near to its God, let it glory, as the most blessed martyr and most sweet teacher [Col. 0880C] Cyprian teaches, that whatever among others appears lofty and great in human affairs lies within its own conscience.

By experience, moreover, you are given, as we believe, to understand how affectionately the memory of you remains wakeful and devoted in us, and how the consolation of mutual conversation is not asleep. In this place we remember that sweet conversation which you had with us at Saint Barbara’s, when the discussion ranged over spiritual things. Our discourse overflowed with the heavenly Spirit; the words we spoke were spirit and life, and they have not departed from our memory, where they are inscribed in recollection in the book of life.

At the urging of certain great men, your friends, whose counsel to reject is to deceive oneself, we admonish you in this letter that your abstinence may be so prudent [Col. 0880D] that, while you intend to crush an enemy, you do not kill a fellow citizen. For the rest, we pray God that present action may be so ordered by wisdom that we who are separated on the way may be united in our homeland.

## LETTER XLVII. TO NICHOLAS, SUBPRIOR OF SAINT VICTOR

He gives thanks for friendship.

To the venerable father and lord NICHOLAS, subprior of Saint Victor in Paris, brother G., humble assistant-minister of Saint Barbara.

This sacrifice of thanksgiving is that of the poor, who have no gift from their hand. Although my spirit answers to both my nation and my place—for the Normans are said to be harsh [Col. 0881A] and savage, and the name Barbara suggests a certain natural harshness—I am nevertheless not so stony, alien from every moisture of affection, and dry that I can be ungrateful for your manifold kindness. For you have opened in our hearts a great path of love, by which, for the sake of heavenly sweetness, one passes into the delights of the lover.

The clerics through whom, in accordance with your merits, we sent the due service of greeting have experienced this; in a wonderful manner they found you kindly and generous toward them. It is indeed a beautiful and praiseworthy kindness, returned for no merits, bestowed by no claim of justice, acquired by no entreaties. It came at the name of a friend, not at prayers. Moreover, as the poet says, benefits which arise not through another’s intervention but from spontaneous affection are more welcome.

Therefore I do what I can, and shall do what I can; and I shall continually offer the sacrifice of praise in place of all the sacrifices of the Law. If fortune smiles on my wishes and God grants the kindness of grace, surely our land will yield its fruit, so that righteousness may thus walk before us and repay the debt of grace. Yet whatever I may do, he who is first in time is stronger in right. For you have gone before us in blessings of sweetness. As you promised us who still dwell among a barbarous people, pray that we may be bound in the charity of God by the bonds of longing, bind the first-fruits of our spirit in love for the heavenly homeland, and deserve to become fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household. The very house [Col. 0881C] of Jacob which is among the people of Barbara greets you . . . . You know well that holy Barbara seems by her name to denote not her own but a native barbarism. Peace be with you, and grace be multiplied.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO JOHN, ABBOT

He praises Abbot John for the grace of his speech.

To the venerable abbot J., brother G. sends glory and honour together with the adornment of virtues.

Love impels me to write to you; I hesitate whether I should entirely abandon toward you our accustomed practice. I should be thought to have grown cold toward you, or to have forgotten you altogether. I know that love is moved by spurs; therefore I would gladly stimulate your love if I could, but [Col. 0881D] the smallness of my talent bears exceedingly slender fruits. For it is not sharp, but weak and blunt. Would that I had received this gift from you instead! For you have received grace from the Lord, so that you know how and when you ought to utter speech.

For, to turn by comparison to the saints: you instruct like Jerome, establish arguments like Augustine, rise lofty like Hilary, lower yourself like John, correct like Basil, console like Gregory, are concise like Rufinus, exhort like Eucherius, provoke like Paulinus, and persevere like Ambrose. But perhaps you silently reply that a more careful concern for psalms and for things more suited to divine service and the provision of household affairs [Col. 0882A] has turned the ornaments of speech and refinements of letters into neglect for you. Yet I do not require from you Greek elegance, Italian rapidity, or Gallic abundance. Do not thunder at us from Quintilian’s throne; rather, be willing to exhort and console us in the manner of the saints. Let simple writing proceed only with festivity, so that the sweetest draught of great nectar may be drawn in with delight.

For you have urgency in examples, faithfulness in testimonies, weight in meanings, and refinement in figures. Or, if it pleases you more, let your words not be from yourselves but drawn from divine springs. We rejoice and are glad in the Lord that, under your governance, the house of the Lord is enlarged and prospers. Blessed indeed is he from whose summit joy is given to friends, punishment to the envious, glory to posterity, an example to the vigorous and eager, and encouragement to the sluggish and idle. We greet all your brothers and sons most affectionately. Pray more earnestly that God may give his grace and by his mercy make us heed the end of rewards, and run with all readiness and eagerness in the way of his commandments, through which he may lead and bring you onward—he who is the way of those who run and the prize of those who arrive. Amen.

## LETTER XLIX. TO HUGH, PRIOR OF SAINT MARTIN OF SÉES

He again urges him to write Walter’s life.

G. to his Hugh.

[Col. 0882C] It would have been fitting to restrain our talkativeness by retaliation for your silence. But because perfect love ought not so much to remember what service it renders as to remember what it owes, now, loosening the reins of modesty, I repeat the service of an importunate address—whose shamelessness is especially evident from this, that you are silent. I always regard your letters as great rewards. I should therefore wish you to feed the hungry appetite of our ignorance with the wholesome compunction of your discourse.

We exhort you in Christ’s charity to place your hitherto idle fingers upon the anvils of the old workshop: that is, to take up again the long-interrupted work concerning the *Life [Note: [Col. 0881D] Concerning whom, see above, Letters 41 and 43.] of the righteous man*, and complete for God’s praise what you began. The material is abundant, full of nectar, flowers, and pearls. It is pleasing and illustrious, [Col. 0882D] flaming with scarlet, gleaming with gold, milky with fine linen. But perhaps you fear that it may be attributed to boasting or vain glory. Let your charity remove from its brightness the blemish of such a miserable suspicion; despising human judgments, do not fear to do what it knows to be pleasing to God. The labour will lie in the study, but the rewarder of labour, who grants grace, will be present; in whose hand are both we and our words. For we are not sufficient to think anything from ourselves as though it came from ourselves; our sufficiency is from him.

Know well that I converse with you day and night. Blessed be the goodness of the Creator himself, who confines human habitation rather than charity within the narrow limits [Col. 0883A] of boundaries. I pray that you may prosper in him, dearest friend, and deign always to remember your Geoffrey.

> I judge him worthy of the praise of style whom the royal court of heaven  
> Receives and the stars inscribe with gleaming gems:  
> Whom exile changes into homeland, sea into harbour, struggle  
> Into peace, cross into palm, and faith into knowledge.

## LETTER L. TO ANDREW, ARCHDEACON OF TOURS

He gives him various counsels.

To his beloved and ever-beloved lord ANDREW, archdeacon of Tours, G., humble assistant-minister of Saint Barbara, eternal salvation in the Lord.

I did not further delay the discourse of my duties, lest your affection should attribute to my fault, as [Col. 0883B] to an unpolished sword, the rust arising from infrequent care. For I fear lest the love once granted me by you should be weakened either by the length of the intervening journey or by our long common absence. Therefore, since by your worth and affability you have drawn our affection more warmly toward you, we ask from you the assistance of your prayers, and gladly grant you in the Lord a share in ours. For you know, as the most learned philosopher among Christians and foremost of all scholars says, that by the recompense of righteous humility we earn the immeasurable return of divine grace—this, he says, being the only way by which men are thought able to converse with God and, even before they obtain what they seek, [Col. 0883C] to be joined to that inaccessible light by the very manner of their supplication.

O how sweet and fragrant is the sacrifice of pure prayer which, from the fatness of devotion and the fire of love, rises from the hearts of the saints to that lofty altar! Therefore, upon the very altar of your heart kindle incense of good fragrance with the fire of compunction and divine love. Let your chief concern be with letters, but especially sacred letters, in which the marrow of meanings should occupy you more than the froth of words. Do nothing idle; do nothing unpeaceful. I do not take the part of a teacher, but of one giving counsel. Let rather that man receive your bread often who will not repay it; being strangers to all popularity, do not seek the favor of everyone, but of the good: neither becoming cheap through indiscriminate familiarity, nor failing to be esteemed precious through tested solidity; [Col. 0883D] most to be sought because least ambitious. Do not strive to receive the honors of dignities, but to deserve them.

Seek friendships that have been tested; retain them steadfastly; preserve them enduringly. For you ought not to seek the friendships of those who, according to Sidonius—some of whose sayings we here excerpt—are:

> Stony in understanding, talkative in judging, fiery in being roused, iron in forgiving; leopards in friendship, bears in wit, foxes in deceiving, bulls in pride, Minotaurs in consumption. In their counsels one becomes bloodier than Phalaris, greedier than Midas, more boastful than Ancus, prouder than Tarquin, craftier than Tiberius, more dangerous than Gaius, more sluggish than Claudius, more impure than Nero, more avaricious than Galba, more extravagant than Vitellius, bolder than Otho, [Col. 0884A] more savage than Domitian.

But enough of this. We further ask Your Worthiness to greet in our name Master John, your fellow archpriest. As we rejoice that you correspond to the manliness of your name, so we rejoice that he corresponds to the grace of his own name. Many good qualities meet in his person. He has sternness joined with charm; when he receives counsel, he abounds in wit, and when he gives counsel, in honey. In church he preserves the dove’s simplicity; in the court, the serpent’s shrewdness.

Please make me known as a canon and fellow-member of the household to Lord Adam, librarian of Marmoutier, your intimate friend. Though he takes his name from the earth, he nevertheless savors the things above and dwells in heaven. Likewise may your own love, raised above earthly things, place its affection in heavenly sweetness.

> This corner and this most humble retreat please you.  
> A more burdensome honor has been bestowed upon you.

May the illumination of the Holy Spirit deign to visit you, raising you to higher advancement and turning both your purpose and your will toward better deeds.

## LETTER LI. TO R., HIS FRIEND

*He praises his friend R.’s ardor for contemplation.*

To his venerable and heart-beloved friend R., G., his own: to seek the things above, to set one’s mind on the things above.

By habit, the mind always seeks that from which it is accustomed to rejoice, as has been loved before us. [Col. 0884C] Hence your mind, burning with desire for heavenly rewards, asks that something favorable be sung to it from the songs of Zion; it asks that songs be given to it in the night; it asks for songs that summon it to divine contemplation. I confess that your request pleases me—if only it had seemed good to do this through someone richer and better instructed in spiritual music. Yet receive from my poverty what I have, lest by keeping silence I be thought a philosopher, or lest you wish to apply to me that saying of Horace:

> All singers have this fault among their friends:  
> When asked, they never make up their minds to sing;  
> Unasked, they never stop.  
> (Horace, *Satires*, book I, satire 3.)

I know well the ardor of your desire; I know that the labor of your warfare is directed toward the embraces of beautiful Rachel, to whom her own vision is most pleasing. [Col. 0884D] For your spirit ardently desires to keep sabbath, to gather the sweet fruits of contemplation, to taste beforehand the joys of that eighth day. Your soul longs to cleave to the immortal Bridegroom and devote all its love to him; thus, bound by a fixed covenant of love to the gifts of supreme joy, you offer the first fruits of your spirit.

For charity, poured into your heart through the Holy Spirit, teaches you as an inward mistress in the school of the breast to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones. In you she employs a friend for grace, an enemy for patience, those whom she can for beneficence, and all persons for goodwill. Dwelling at the center of the virtues, she, like queen and mistress, dispenses, adorns, and orders the outcomes of all things. And as root grows into shoot, shoot into bud, [Col. 0885A] bud into flower, and flower into fruit, so charity is strengthened by its beginnings and advances to the perfect state, to the measure of fullness.

It leads the mind into contemplation. For the contemplative life, as blessed Gregory writes, is indeed to retain with the whole mind charity itself—that is, love of God and neighbor—yet to rest from outward action, so that one no longer desires to do anything, but, all cares being trampled underfoot, the mind burns to behold the face of its Creator.

But here, as we read in the Conferences of the Fathers: “Our chief effort ought to be that the mind may always cling to divine things and to God. Whatever differs from this, however great it may be, must nevertheless be reckoned secondary, or even lowest, or certainly harmful.” Therefore, he says, when the mind can attain divine contemplation, let it rejoice; when distracted from it, let it grieve and sigh. Let it feel that it has departed from the highest good as often as it discovers itself separated from that vision, reckoning even a momentary departure from Christ’s contemplation to be fornication. Whenever your gaze has strayed from him even a little, let us turn the eyes of the heart back to him and, as by the straightest line, recall the mind’s sight.

On this sublime step of contemplation stood the most humble Father Gregory, when, still situated in the quiet of the monastery, he trod beneath him all transitory things; when he rose above the things that roll onward; when he thought of nothing but heavenly things; when, though still held in the body, he crossed by contemplation the barriers of the flesh; when he loved death—which is punishment to almost all—as the entrance [Col. 0885C] into life and the reward of his labor. Thus, in his letter to the emperor’s sister, having been torn away from such sweet quiet and placed in the burden of government, he complained:

> “I have lost the high joys of my repose; and, falling inwardly, I seem to have risen outwardly. Therefore I lament that I have been driven far from the face of my Creator. For daily I strove to be outside the world, to drive every bodily image from the eyes of my heart, to behold incorporeally the joys above; and, longing for God’s face before God, I cried not only with my voice but with all the marrow of my heart: ‘My heart said to you: I have sought your face; your face, Lord, will I seek.’ Desiring nothing in this world, fearing nothing, I seemed to myself [Col. 0885D] to stand on a certain summit of things, so that I believed fully fulfilled in me what I had learned from the prophet through the Lord’s promise: ‘I will raise you above the heights of the earth.’ For he is raised above the heights of the earth who tramples underfoot, by contempt of mind, even those things that seem lofty and glorious in this present age.”

But enough of this. We further ask the Lord to grant you to taste the sweetness of that heavenly contemplation itself. May he grant you to form your character and the whole ordering of your life after the pattern of the heavenly order. Amen.

## LETTER LI N . . . . TO N . . . .

To his most beloved father and lord, his son and his own—if he is anything, whatever he is.

[Col. 0886A] You ordered—or rather, imposed upon me—that, writing to you for the third time, I should for the third time display the boldness of audacious irreverence, piling up from the poverty of my own wallet, from the pierced pouch of vanity, the riches of Croesus. But I pondered long and deeply in my heart whence the urgency of so great a demand had arisen, considering this command laughable, unless I perceived in you the preeminence of true charity and sincere truth. For abundance banishes the subject matter of writing through lack; lack corrupts abundance of discourse through deficiency of sense and memory.

What then does my lord mean? Does he intend to drain my poverty even in a small matter, when not in one sending of literary friendship, not even in one single point, have you multiplied it so as to enrich it? What, I ask? Is it that the sluggishness of my intellect may be stirred, [Col. 0886B] or that the dryness of my mind may be wholly dried up? The first may indeed lawfully be said to a friend; the second, as the saying goes, is unlawful to think of a friend.

What then shall I do? I do not know. Seeing my poverty and the urgency of your command, I am hemmed in on every side: neither does ability supply matter to my tongue, nor does richness of thought redeem the leanness of my words—unless perhaps the obedience of a loving heart, pierced as it were by the violence of one commanding, may produce a thought which dares more readily to obey you than to command itself. Thus, while you command, you help. I therefore do what you lay upon me; I do what you require. Yet I do so on this condition: that you also make return, and repay the diligence and affection of the author of this letter with the corresponding [Col. 0886C] ardor of one who loves in return.

I do not therefore ask that you put these presents into your purse, but that you place me as a seal upon your heart. I ask something great, indeed something that ought almost deservedly to be refused to one unworthy—except that love freely bestowed more abundantly commends the grace of its giver, and, because of the greatness of gratuitous charity, does not so much earn a grateful recipient as make one worthy of love. I therefore exhort and desire that your heart may possess me; though I am ashamed to have said it, I do not regret it.

For in that heart, as in the ark of the law, hidden manna is contained—not manna swarming with worms, but manna giving birth to the spirit of salvation, crushing the injury and overturning the opposition of spiritual worms. And while it removes every uncleanness from your heart, as from a chamber of glory and a vessel of purity [Col. 0886D] and cleanness, it commends, raised up in a lofty but not proud dining room of the mind, the ordered storing-up of faith, hope, and charity.

But why should I, an animal man, why should I, a worm and son of man, dare to name such things, when I do not even name them as becomes a saint, as I ought to have done? For in saying these things I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal, which acts or resounds only through the work of another’s help. Likewise, I myself do not reap another’s harvest but beg for nourishment; and if I have gathered wages, I have gathered them only into a pierced pouch, in which love of virtues is not nourished but vanity of vanities is admitted.

But perhaps you will answer these things in your customary manner: “This is your humility.” Yet you know that false humility is not truth but a double vanity. This is the message of your son; this is also the message of your friend, long deprived of a friend, deprived of a companion, deprived also of consolation, deprived of his desire; seeking and not finding a man according to his heart, one who alone may people the vast solitude of his mind, with whom he may share his heart, upon whom he may lay his head. O happy me, if I find one! O if it be the very same man—he to whom our discourse is addressed!

But because flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, those who are led by the Spirit of God ought to walk and to love in spirit and truth, so that the spirit of one who loves may have and show spiritual affection, and the truth of one who loves in return may, according to the meaning of its own name, proceed and advance from unfeigned faith. And because I think that I know a man, whether in the body or outside the body, to stretch with all his strength his whole heart, soul, and power toward the things that are before him, and to direct toward them the whole diligence of both the inner and outer person, is wholly difficult for me—indeed, I fear that it is denied to my littleness and perversity—lest flesh and spirit, which do not agree, should fit ill together and depart from one [Col. 0888A] seat. Behold: although one rules under Moses, Pharaoh turns to a taste for garlic, he who has not tasted manna in its savor.

And because God is the avenger against everyone who does evil, I confess that I rejoice—and shall rejoice—in him who has not so much avenged himself as visited me, who made and created me. For the Lord’s hand struck me with a correcting blow, and did not hand me over to death. Willing or unwilling, I received the cleansing scourge; in the severity of the scourge I recognized my unexpiated wickedness. I fainted at the presence of his hand; for he visited me with his hard sword, with his strong sword—not raging against an enemy so much for vengeance as serving, fatherly and mercifully, the enemy’s good.

And because my iniquity surrounded [Col. 0888B] my walls day and night, his hand was heavy upon me day and night. Truly his wrath has not yet rested, his indignation has not yet been lulled, his vengeance has not yet been restrained; rather, his hand is still stretched out. Enough of this. Remember me. May kindly care correct into better form whatever I have spoken badly. Farewell.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1196: MAURICE OF SULLY, BISHOP OF PARIS

[Col. 0887]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, VII, 70, under the bishops of Paris.)

[Col. 0887D] Maurice was not born of the illustrious family of the lords of Sully, but of humble birth at the town of Sully on the Loire, his mother being Humberga; hence his surname “of Sully.” By industry and worthy accomplishments he rose to the height of the episcopate. The monk of Auxerre, William of Nangis, Vincent of Beauvais, and others report this remarkable fact about him: when he was young, poor, and a beggar, he refused to accept an alms offered on the condition that he should never become bishop.

Certainly, having first gone to Paris to devote himself to learning, he advanced so far in it that he not only taught theology publicly, but also delivered sacred sermons to the people. These are still preserved among the Victorine manuscripts; Trithemius reports that he showed outstanding zeal in delivering them. Trithemius mentions two books of his sermons and a short work written by him for priests, *On the Care of Souls*. He was first a canon of Bourges, as we learn from the records of that church, and afterward a canon of Paris. As to the manner in which he became bishop, Caesarius of Heisterbach, a Cistercian monk, writes as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 0887D] *Dialogues*, book VI, chapter 19.] “When in our time the bishopric was vacant and the electors could not agree among themselves, they entrusted their votes to three men. When these three could not agree upon one person, two gave their authority to Master Maurice, who was one of the three, so that whomever he named should be bishop. Since this Maurice, as the outcome proved, desired rather to be useful than to preside, he named himself, saying: ‘I do not know the consciences and intentions of the others; I propose, with God’s grace helping me, to govern this bishopric without reproach.’ And he did so. For he was holy in life, benefited very many both by word and example, and ended his days in that same bishopric.”
