A charter of his, issued at that time [Note: [Col. 0889D] *History of the Church of Paris*, vol. II, p. 149.] for Hérivaux, where he established regular canons, proves that Maurice had already been elected in 1160. In the same year he confirmed the donations made by his predecessors to the church of Saint-Victor.

In August 1162 he accompanied King Louis when the latter went to meet Emperor Frederick in the city of Saint John of Latona, for a conference concerning the two contenders for the papacy. He was sent by the king, with Joscius, archbishop of Tours, and William, abbot of Vézelay, to seek a truce with Count Henry of Troyes. When Maurice had accompanied Pope Alexander to the dedication of the church of Saint-Germain on 21 April 1163, the monks, disturbed by the bishop’s presence, obtained from the supreme pontiff that he should withdraw from the church. Indignant at this, Maurice brought his complaint before the pope at the Council of Tours, claiming jurisdiction over the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; this was denied him.

About that time he laid the first foundations of the new cathedral, the chief stone of which Alexander III laid, according to John, a Victorine canon. [Col. 0889C] His successor Odo completed the work for the most part. The monk of Auxerre says in his Chronicle that he also built two stone bridges, one over the Seine and the other over the Marne.

He had a dispute with Roger, abbot of Colombs, over the monastery of Saint-Germain-en-Laye and its parish; it was settled by arbitrators in 1163. A disagreement had arisen between Maurice and Odo, abbot of Saint-Denis, regarding the monastery of Argenteuil. The bishop maintained that either an abbess with a community of virgins ought to be installed there, or an abbot whom he himself should bless. This controversy was committed, by agreement of both parties, to the decision of judges in the Paris palace before Alexander III during Lent. They did not settle it in April 1164, but only quieted it for three years; it was not ended until the pontificate of Innocent III.

In the same year Maurice confirmed Hugh Capet’s donation to the monastery of Fossatus. In the same year he bought two houses situated before the parvis, in order to make a road before the church of Blessed Mary. [Note: [Col. 0890D] Sauval, vol. III, p. 8.]

He baptized the son of Louis VII—Philip, surnamed Augustus—on Sunday, 22 August 1165, in the church of Saint Michael of the Square. The sponsors were Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain; Hervis, abbot of Saint-Victor; Odo, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève; Constance, the king’s sister; [Col. 0890A] and two Parisian widows. In the same year he settled the lawsuit between Roger, abbot of Fossatus, and Ralph of Buxy. He attended the Council of Beauvais in 1166, where the monks of Resbach, rebellious against their bishop and abbot, were excommunicated. In 1167 he testified by charter to a vineyard granted by Guy of Mont-Gai to the monks of Charlelieu. With the chapter’s consent, in 1168 he assigned the bed of a deceased bishop to the poor of the House of God. On 22 December of the same year he consecrated William of Champagne as archbishop of Sens.

In the following year he approved the agreement made in 1169, the ninth year of his episcopate, between the abbess of Éder and Albert concerning the wood of Plaissy. In that same year he bought from Ledemal, a knight, possessions near Saint-Cloud, and from Theobald Cocherel everything he held near Viriacum, in the tenth year of his episcopate. In 1170, the tenth year of his episcopate, he bought land near Vitry from William of Mâchecourt, knight.

In the same year he had a dispute with his canons over the revenues of the deanery, each side maintaining that they became its own upon the dean’s death. The case was referred to Alexander, who delegated William, archbishop of Sens. Meanwhile the canons yielded, and the controversy was quieted with Archbishop William’s approval, expressed in letters which mention the new house of the bishop of Paris; Maurice had caused a new residence to be built for himself and his successors. Pope Clement confirmed those letters, which Maurice had presented to him, by other letters preserved in the royal library.

[Col. 0890C] In 1171 Maurice placed the body of Saint Landric, bishop of Paris, in a wooden shrine with Remigius, dean of Saint-Germain of Auxerre. In the same year he approved a house given to the nuns of Éder: “Done,” he says, “in our new house, in the eleventh year of our episcopate.” In 1172, the twelfth year of his episcopate, he ratified a gift made to the same nuns. When Garin was elected abbot of Saint-Victor, Maurice bestowed the blessing upon him in the same year. He attended the division of the city of Le Puy, made in 1173 between the bishop of Le Puy and the count of Polignac. In 1175 he received the homage of Anselm of Garlande and his son for the castle of Tournan, which King Philip confirmed in March 1185.

[Col. 0890D] On 8 August 1176 he consecrated John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres, at Sens. Persuaded by his counsels, King Louis gave his consent to a sale made that same year by the canons of Sainte-Opportune. In the following year, the seventeenth of his episcopate, he confirmed the gift of the tithe of Luabium made to the church of Blessed Mary of Pomponne by John and Maurice of Pomponne. In the same year he bought from Peter of Chanteloup half the mill of Canturana near Corbeil.

In 1178, the nineteenth year of his episcopate, he testified to the settlement of the dispute between the abbess of Éder and Peter of Canteloup. Early in the following year, namely on 19 March, he consecrated the altar of the abbey of Barbeau. [Col. 0891A] In 1179 a public assembly of bishops for the inauguration of Louis’s son Philip was held at Paris, in the palace of Bishop Maurice, by King Louis. In 1180, the twenty-first year of his episcopate, he bought, on the feast of Saint Agatha, one hundred solidi of annual revenue at Vitry from Lord Philip of Lévis. In the same year he gave Sancelina, a woman of servile status, permission to marry Drogo, a free man.

In 1181, the twenty-first year of his episcopate, in the new lower hall, he reconciled by apostolic authority the prior of Gisors and Romanus, priest of Saint-Gervais, who were in conflict. On the Wednesday of Pentecost in 1182, Henry the legate consecrated the altar of Saint Mary at Paris together with Bishop Maurice. [Note: [Col. 0891D] Labbé, *Bibliotheca*, vol. II, p. 330.] In the same year, the twenty-second of his episcopate, Maurice ratified the sale made to the monastery of Saint-Magloire by Robert, prior of the lepers of Givry.

He is still mentioned in that year in the cartulary of Reignac together with Stephen, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève; in letters of Guy, archbishop of Sens, concerning Saint-Denis; and in the records of Villeperreuse, where 1182 is called the twenty-third year of his episcopate. In 1183 he confirmed a grant made to the regular canons of Hérivaux. In the same year, the twenty-third of his episcopate, he confirmed some matters and decreed other statutes for the canons of Saint-Germain. [Note: [Col. 0891D] *History of Paris*, vol. III, p. 72.] In the same year he had a dispute with the monks of Marmoutier regarding the church of Saint Nomni, whose presentation he left to them.

In 1184 he confirmed the chaplain presented to the church of Saint Thomas of Montmagny by Hervé and Burchard of Montmorency. [Col. 0891C] He received a bull from Pope Lucius, issued at Anagni on 4 January, against priests who publicly kept concubines. [Note: [Col. 0891D] Sauval, vol. III, p. 50.] On 16 January of the following year he solemnly received the envoys sent by the king of Jerusalem, especially the patriarch. In that year they held a general council at Paris for defending the faith against the enemies of the Cross.

On 20 August 1186 he buried Geoffrey, count of Brittany, in the greater church, with Philip Augustus present. Philip founded four chaplaincies in that church, paved all the streets of Paris at royal expense with square stones because of the intolerable mud, and caused a public cemetery, enclosed by walls, to be built in the place called the Fields, later named that of the Holy Innocents; Alberic speaks in his Chronicle of its beginning. [Col. 0891D] In the same year Maurice confirmed the donation made to the church of Saint Lupus in the Montmorency valley. In 1187, the twenty-seventh year of his episcopate, he purchased from the knight Galeran a rent in the borough of Saint-Cloud.

A synod was held at Paris in mid-Lent 1188, at which tithes called the Saladin Tithe were granted to the king for the holy expedition. Peter of Blois strongly disapproved of this in Letter 112 to the bishop of Orléans: [Col. 0892A] “What reason is there,” he says, “that those who fight for the Church should despoil the Church?” He maintained that money was not to be demanded from clerics, but prayers alone.

In that same year, the twenty-eighth of his episcopate, Maurice confirmed a house given by the knight Theobald to the hospital of Sainte-Opportune, now Saint Catherine’s. [Note: [Col. 0891D] *History of Paris*, vol. III, p. 67.] He received a bull from Clement III, issued at the Lateran on 5 July in the first year of his pontificate, granting him authority to place under interdict regular canons who denied to him and his archdeacons procuration in parish churches. The same pope further confirmed to him the Parisian church’s free right of conferring prebends. In 1188, the twenty-ninth year of his episcopate, he approved a gift made by Elizabeth, wife of Anselm, to the nuns of Éder.

In the following year, the twenty-ninth year of his episcopate, he made the church of Bessancourt a parish church. In May 1190, for the soul of Elizabeth, wife of King Philip, who had been buried by him in the church of Paris, he erected an altar; the king established two priests to celebrate Masses there, according to Rigord. In the same year he obtained from King Philip II the Paris synagogue of the Jews in order to build a church there. In December he entered into an agreement with the canons of Corbeil concerning procuration owed to him; the abbots of Pontigny and Preuilly had been delegated by the supreme pontiff as arbitrators.

At Maurice’s request, Philip Augustus, in the eleventh year of his reign, confirmed the charters of his father Louis, who had remitted to Theobald, Maurice’s predecessor, the furnishings of a deceased bishop and the levy due from the men of a deceased bishop. [Col. 0892C] In the same year King Philip, in order to fortify Paris against enemies, began a new circuit of walls with ditches and ramparts opposite the University.

In 1191, the thirty-first year of his episcopate, Maurice established a chaplain in the church of Saint Leufroy from the alms of Robert Baldwin. [Note: [Col. 0892D] *Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 497.] On the feast of Saint John the Evangelist in the same year, he honorably received King Philip at Paris with a vast multitude of clergy and people as he returned from the siege of Acre. About that time, by order of Octavian, legate of the Apostolic See, he bestowed the blessing upon Herleva, abbot of Saint-Martin of Pontoise, without consulting and against the will of the archbishop of Rouen.

In 1192, the thirty-second year of his episcopate, he made the church of Le Plessis-Saint-Leu in the Montmorency valley a mother church. [Note: [Col. 0892D] *History of Paris*, vol. III, p. 73.] In the same year, the thirty-third of his episcopate, he confirmed the rights, churches, and presentations to churches belonging to the canons of Saint-Germain of Auxerre. [Note: [Col. 0892D] Ibid., p. 114.] He approved donations made to the monks of Blessed Mary of the Valley in 1193. In 1194, the thirty-fourth year of his episcopate, he confirmed the church of Saint-Germain to the monks dwelling at Pirose. [Note: [Col. 0892D] Ibid., p. 91.]

In the same year, the thirty-fifth of his episcopate, he approved the sale of a certain oven to the church of Blessed Mary [Col. 0893A] of Mont-Étif, and granted Hugh, abbot of Saint-Denis, authority to establish a parish church in the village of Villeneuve. In September 1195 he confirmed to the monastery of Fossatus the chapel of Saint Peter of Bobus, the church of Saint Eligius, the chapels of Saint Bonitus, Saint Peter of Assis, Holy Cross, and Saint Martial, and the church of Saint Paul with its courtyard, [Note: [Col. 0893D] *History of Paris*, vol. III, p. 23.] the great and small tithe, together with the presentations belonging to these churches.

So great a flood occurred in February at the beginning of 1196 that Maurice was compelled to take refuge at the monastery of Saint-Victor. In the same year he issued letters concerning the tithe of land near Châtenay, which Anselm sold to the church of Blessed Mary. In the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate he confirmed the gift of Guy of Lévis, knight, to Blessed Mary of La Roche. [Col. 0893B] At the beginning of that very year a council was held at Paris by legates of the Apostolic See to reform the marriage of Philip Augustus. On the pretext of consanguinity he had repudiated his wife Ingeborg, sister of Canute, king of the Danes, in order to take another wife; but nothing was accomplished in the matter.

Among the letters of Stephen of Tournai there is the fourth letter of Maurice, addressed to Pons, bishop of Clermont, who had asked him whether a baptism administered with the words “I baptize you” omitted was valid. Maurice replied that it was not baptism if anything were omitted from or altered in the form handed down by the Church. Shortly afterward Alexander III made the same decision. He delegated Maurice to hear the case between the church of Saint Evurtius at Orléans and Herbert of Gervais concerning certain tithes; Maurice adjudged these to the aforementioned church in the presence of Stephen, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, Peter, dean of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, and others.

In volume II of the *Amplissima Collectio* there survive two letters of Alexander III to Maurice. The first, issued at Tarragona on 23 December, entrusted to him the accusation against R., abbot of Flavigny, in civil and criminal matters; the other, issued at Genoa on 9 February, concerned the dispute between Hugh of Sens and the abbot of Ferrières. He also received a bull from Alexander III confirming the agreement made between bishops and archdeacons, and at the same time forbidding the latter to burden priests subject to them through excessive demands for hospitality. A second bull of Clement III accords with this.

He received bulls from Urban III, issued at Verona on 4 January, and from Clement III, issued at Pisa on 13 January, confirming the arrangement made by Pope Eugenius concerning the parish of John in the church of Sainte-Geneviève. The archbishop of Sens, presumptuously exercising unauthorized powers in the diocese of Paris, subject to him by metropolitan right, provoked the complaints of Bishop Maurice. Clement III judged them just in the decretal *Cum ex auctoritate canonum*.

Besides the privileges granted to his predecessors by the supreme pontiffs, the same pope, by the bull beginning *Justis petentium desideriis*, approved the abbeys of Hérivaux, Hermeray, [Col. 0894A] Mont-Étif, and Gif, which he himself had founded or had enlarged and endowed with estates. Celestine III adds to these the abbeys of Saint-Cyr and Vallis Profunda, now Val-de-Grâce near Paris.

Shortly before his death, according to the manuscript Chronicle of John of Saint-Victor, Maurice withdrew to Saint-Victor and became a canon there, that he might be freer to devote himself to God and prepare to render an account of his stewardship. Caesarius relates that, while then afflicted by a violent fever, he asked for the holy Eucharist. But because the priest feared to administer the sacred elements to a delirious man, he brought him an unconsecrated host. Perceiving this, Maurice cried out: “Take it away, take it away; it is not my Lord.” Astonished, the priest brought the true body of the Lord, [Col. 0894B] which Maurice received with the greatest faith, and shortly thereafter passed to the Lord.

As he lay dying, a slip bearing these words of Job was laid upon his breast:

> “I believe that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and in my flesh I shall see the Savior, whom I myself, and not another, shall see, and my eyes shall behold. This hope has been laid up in my bosom.”

He had so directed this in order that others might thereafter not hesitate to profess the resurrection of the dead, then attacked by many, which he himself had confidently professed while dying. At death he charged Robert, abbot of Saint-Victor, and Reginald, dean of Saint-Marcel, to make satisfaction to any persons whom he might perhaps have injured by occupying what was another’s right. [Col. 0894C] Shortly after his death they restored to Richard, prior of Marcoussis, what Maurice had unlawfully taken from him: the patronage and presentation of the church of that village.

After his death he was buried in the middle of the choir of the church of Saint-Victor. Four verses from the twelve inscribed upon his tomb were written by Stephen, bishop of Tournai, at the request of the Parisian canons, as is clear from his Letter 260:

> “We write a few elegiac verses, from which you may select two or four that please you best. We ask and beseech you in the Lord that they be recited without naming their author.”

These are the four selected verses, printed in Roman type:

> Cut off from the vale of tears in this wretched world,  
> A living stone is placed in the eternal city.  
>
> Teacher and bishop, worthy of both chairs,  
> From the first he deserved to continue the two.  
>
> Sound faith, abundant teaching, unceasing almsgiving,  
> Cry aloud that Paris had none his equal.  
>
> The magnificence of his house’s structure and his church’s fabric  
> Proclaim him generous to stranger, poor man, and needy alike.  
>
> Granaries open to the poor, coffers always open—  
> His hand stood always open to the wretched.  
>
> Virgin Mary, preserve your Maurice,  
> A bishop of such merit and a faithful servant.

Two further verses were added to these four, recording the day of his death:

> The day, third before the Ides  
> Of the virgin month, buries its brightness beneath a cloud.

Long afterward, when the choir tomb at Saint-Victor had been newly completed, this new inscription was placed upon it: “Here lies the reverend Father Maurice, bishop of Paris, who first began the basilica of Blessed Mary the Virgin. He died in the year of the Lord 1196, on the third day before the Ides of September.”

Nicholas Camuzat, canon of Troyes, had formerly supplied the Sammarthani with these verses, published from a manuscript codex and composed by a contemporary on Maurice’s death:

> Maurice, Paris’s father, departs for the fatherland of paradise:  
> Martha to the world, Mary to God.  
>
> This pilgrim dies fasting from the fifth dawn;  
> He hungers to behold God in true flesh.

The bread is offered, which the Spirit, within closed senses, inspires to be the food of the body;  
with word, mind, and hand he rejects cup and bread,  
and thus with a heavenly mouth rebukes the deception.

[Col. 0895B] “They mocked me as though I were a guest: I ask for the suffering One;  
under true flesh I ask for the suffering God.”

The hearer marvels at the matter; the venerable abbot offers  
what is asked; the father meets it with mind and hand.

He senses God present and burns with kisses; he holds the holy  
vessel, and thus adores the true body:

“Behold the salvation of the world: the Word of the Father, the sacred victim,  
living flesh, undivided Godhead, true man.

“I hunger for you, God, whom you do not permit the outward man to receive;  
may the inward man be able to receive you, God.

“May Christ’s flesh pass to the Father’s right hand—the Redeemer, man,  
who with the Father orders the Father’s kingdoms.”

Thus hope here deserved to foreknow the reality, and faith  
to know and see God—the man who is to be glorified.

Thus love flamed forth, thus hope foreknew, so that one  
faith both believed and knew the things believed to be certain.

A distinguished notice of Maurice occurs in the Paris Necrology [Col. 0895C]:

> “On the third day before the Ides of September died Maurice, bishop of Paris, of blessed memory. In his own lifetime he opened, before the gates of the church, a new street made at his own expense; he founded four new abbeys dependent upon the Church of Paris; he established bridges in the bishopric; he built new episcopal residences; and he increased the revenues of the bishopric in many ways.  
>
> He also gave us a house situated beside the gate of the cloister, for providing the allowance on the feast of Saint Maurice; likewise, a roadway from Castanet for providing the allowance on the day of his anniversary; and also the fief at Ivry for providing the allowance on the day of his election, namely, on the third day [Col. 0896A] after the feast of Saint Denis. Our canon John, his nephew, shall possess these things for as long as he lives; after his death they shall revert to our chapter. If, after the three allowances have been provided as stated above, anything remains, it shall go to the benefit of the canons’ morning-money.  
>
> Moreover, he gave us twenty marks of gold for making a golden frontal before the high altar; also a gold chalice of two and a half marks, a gold censer of four marks, and silver panels for adorning the altar; two copes, three mitres, one pallium, one dalmatic, one tunic, and two prepared albs with amices, and one stole. He likewise gave three hundred pounds to the church: one hundred, namely, for the canons’ morning-money [Col. 0896B]; one hundred for the morning-money of poor clerics; and one hundred for making the roof of the new building of lead.  
>
> Further, he gave us one hundred and ninety marks of silver, which were laid out in purchasing the lands, tenants, and vineyards formerly belonging to William de Bezon, knight, and his wife at Vitry. Master Philip shall hold all these during his lifetime and shall pay annually from them ten Parisian pounds; and whoever after him holds the said revenues shall likewise pay ten pounds. From these the canons and those serving the high altar who attend the vigil of the anniversary shall receive twelve denarii, the clerics four, and the boys two; and on the following day the distribution shall likewise be made at Mass. The lay matricularii [church officers] [Col. 0896C] shall receive two solidi.  
>
> It was decreed by the chapter that his anniversary should be observed solemnly, with the canons keeping choir both at Vespers and at Mass; and Mass shall be celebrated at the high altar.”

Rigord, chronicler of Philip Augustus, in his book *On the Deeds of the Same*; William of Nangis under the year 1196; Vincent of Beauvais, part III of the *Historical Mirror*; Robert in the *Supplement to Sigebert*; James of Vitry; Caesarius of Heisterbach; the *Great Belgian Chronicle*; Antoninus; Trithemius; and others speak extensively of Maurice’s death and deeds.

[Col. 0897]

# LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF MAURICE DE SULLY, BISHOP OF PARIS

## I.—LETTERS

### I–III. LETTERS TO POPE ALEXANDER III in the case of Saint Thomas of Canterbury. (1169–1170.)

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. Giles, II, 229.—See among the various letters to Alexander III, *Patrology*, vol. CC.]

## II.—DIPLOMAS

### I. Charter concerning the tithe of Campelles. (1164.)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame de Paris*, Paris, 1840, quarto, vol. I, p. 71.]

[Col. 0897A]

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God humble servant of the Church of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that John of Versailles and his wife Hermessendis have, through our hand, pledged to the canons of Saint Martin of Campelles the tithe of Felioc for four harvests, for sixty pounds in Parisian currency. The terms are that, should the said currency happen to fall in value or be debased, one mark of silver shall be paid for every forty solidi. Nevertheless, if the tithe is not redeemed after the four [Col. 0897B] harvests have been received, the canons shall peacefully possess it until the aforesaid money is paid.

The aforesaid John gave assurance in our hand that he would warrant this pledge of the tithe against the church of Campelles and would allow no loss to be suffered by the church on its account. William of Muret, brother of the said Hermessendis, from whose fief the aforesaid tithe came, granted and approved the same. Hermessendis herself, under whose protection the property was, likewise gave this assurance in our hand, as did her two sons Baldwin and Frederick.

Very many clerics and laymen were present as witnesses: Radulf, provost; Peter, canon of Campelles; Saanbert, priest; Isenbard; Walter, chaplain; Asselin, priest; Vitalis, dean of [Col. 0898A] Moisset; Odo, canon; Fulco, priest; Herbert of Villeneuve; Josbert of Moisset; Herbert of Ville-Crena; and very many laymen: Gilbert of Gueregnioc; Simon of Candor; Gocelin of Santeac; Robert of Attiliac; Hodius of Genuliac; Morel of Campelles; [lacuna] Richard the mason.

Done publicly in our presence at Moisset, in the octave of Saint Denis, in the year 1164 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and the fourth year of our episcopate. And lest this agreement be dissolved either by human litigation or by the fraud of evildoers, we have considered it fitting to confirm it with the seal of our authority.

### II. Concerning the property sold by the knight Ledemallus at the town of Saint-Cloud. (1169.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 50.]

[Col. 0898B]

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that Ledemallus, knight of Villes-Coblen, sold to us for forty pounds everything which his brother Thomas, a canon, possessed in the town of Saint-Cloud—whether in vineyards, dues of money and wine, pressing-dues, offerings, or corvées—in Ledemallus’s name. All these things were to revert to Ledemallus and belonged to our fief.

His brothers, namely Thomas the canon and Hungerius the knight, approved this sale, as did the sons of Ledemallus himself, Matthew, a knight, and Philip, not yet a knight, [Col. 0899A] who with their father bound themselves by pledge of faith as sureties for this sale and undertook to provide warranty. Philip likewise promised, under pledge of faith, that in the first year of his knighthood, within a month of being summoned, he would do the same.

There were also other sureties: Hugh of Plessis and Hugh of Saint-John.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] We have added the names of the witnesses and the dates and places from the Great Cartulary, fol. 102v, and the smaller one, fol. 220.]

The witnesses present were Walter the chaplain, Erchembald the dean, Bruno the canon, John the priest, Peter the knight, Matthew Panis, Seheric, Andrew of Tremblay, and Girbert the mayor. Present at Hugh of Plessis’s suretyship were our nephew John and John Rufus; present at Hugh of Saint-John’s suretyship were Thomas the marshal, and Guilert and Matthew, our servants.

[Col. 0899B] In order that this may remain valid and unshaken in future times, we have considered it fitting that it be recorded in writing and strengthened by the authority of our seal.

Done publicly at Saint-Cloud in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the ninth year of our episcopate.

### III. Concerning the property sold by William of Mâcy at Vitry. (1170.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 48.]

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that William, knight of Mâcy [variant: Mathiaco], sold to us for twenty-five pounds twenty arpents of land which he possessed at [Col. 0899C] Vitry and held from us at a rent of five solidi; and he constituted himself a surety for the warranty so given. Avelina, William’s wife, and Stephen Palmarius, his brother, approved the sale.

Present in Paris before us at this sale and at the approval of the aforesaid Stephen were very many persons: Asselin, dean of Saint-Marcel; Walter, our chaplain; [lacuna]. Laymen: Drogo, knight of Sainte-Croix; [lacuna]; Stephen the baker; Thomas the marshal; Hugh the *baticularius*; Matthew the pantler; Simon the carpenter; William the cook; Richard the chamberlain.

Present at the approval given at Cailly by William’s wife were [Col. 0899D] very many persons: Alberic, priest of Cailly; Walter, his chaplain; [lacuna]. Laymen: Brunel, mayor of Vitry; Helluin, dean; [lacuna]; Odo Censarius; [lacuna].

Done publicly at Paris in the year 1170 of the Incarnate Word, the tenth year of our episcopate.

### IV. Concerning the rent possessed by the canons of Saint-Victor at Saint-Marcel and Ivry. (1171.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, 245.]

Because many persons of perverse mind are especially intent on deceiving, it is our duty, for the good of peace, to transmit to posterity the memory of matters well conducted in our presence [Col. 0900A] and to confirm them in writing. I therefore, MAURICE, bishop of Paris, make known to present and future alike that Ferric of Gentilly seized a certain rent at Saint-Marcel and Ivry, which the church of Blessed Victor of Paris had long peacefully possessed through the gift of Brother Ferric, canon of that church. He asserted that this rent belonged to his fief and that of his predecessors.

The church of Saint-Victor brought a complaint against the said Ferric and pleaded the matter before our court. At last, after counsel had been taken with prudent men in the said church, it gave the aforesaid Ferric four pounds of money to confirm the peace; and he surrendered the prescribed [Col. 0900B] rent to the often-mentioned church, renounced it, and granted to that church, to possess perpetually in peace in our presence, whatever proprietary right he claimed in it. He promised to provide lawful warranty for it. Anselm of Brunoy, brother of the aforesaid Ferric, likewise granted and approved this, in the sight and hearing of those present with us, whose names and marks are set below.

The mark of Lord Anselm, dean of Saint-Marcel. The mark of Simon of Saint-Denis. The mark of Walter, our chaplain. The mark of Master Manerius. The mark of Marcel, our cleric. The mark of Theobert of Montlhéry. [Col. 0900C] The mark of Peter of Montreuil. The mark of Philip of Athis. The mark of Hugh the merchant. The mark of Drogo the butcher.

Lest creeping forgetfulness erase this, or an arising claim challenge it, we order it to be committed to writing and strengthen this present charter by the authority of our seal.

Done publicly at Paris in the year 1171 of the Incarnation of the Word, the eleventh year of our episcopate.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] This passage makes clear that the beginning of Bishop Maurice’s pontificate must be dated not to 1164, as the Sammarthani maintain, but to 1160.]

### V. Concerning the half of the mill of Chant de la Grenouille sold by Peter, knight of Chantelou, to the bishop of Paris. (1177.)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame de Paris*, I, 51.]

[Col. 0900D]

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that Peter of Chantelou and his wife Ermengardis sold us one half of a mill called Chant de la Grenouille, situated at Corbeil. This half belonged to the inheritance of the aforesaid Ermengardis. They also sold us their milling-right in the same mill which, in addition to the half-share, they held independently of their partner’s share.

Their son Geoffrey, [Col. 0901A] a knight; Odo, a cleric; Simon; Hugh; and their daughters Richeldis and Avelina approved this sale. The aforesaid Peter and Ermengardis, with their sons and daughters, promised under pledge of faith to uphold and warrant this sale; and they constituted themselves and many others whose names are written below as sureties: Hugh Pinel, Ranulf of Chantelou, Geoffrey of Solorra, Joscelin of Genartville, and Robert of La Bretesche. The prior of Saint John of Corbeil and the prior of Saint Guenael, within whose rent-district the said mill lies, approved and granted the sale.

Present were many clerics: Brother Daniel, our chaplain; Marcel, canon of Paris; Geisbert, dean of Moissy. Laymen: [Col. 0901B] Gosbert, knight of Porrigny; Adam the pepperer; the postellus of Moissy and his son John; Richard the chamberlain; Enjorran and Boson, our servants; [lacuna].

Lest it be erased through the harmful antiquity of time, or in any way weakened through the fraud of malicious persons, we have considered it fitting to safeguard it by the attestation of this document and the seal impressed upon it.

Done publicly at Moissy in the year 1177 of the Incarnate Word, the seventeenth year of our pontificate.

### VI. Concerning the property sold by Philip of Sevies and Galeran of Gallardon. (5 February 1181.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 45.]

[Col. 0901C]

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that Lord Philip of Sevies and his wife Elizabeth sold us, for eighty pounds, an annual rent of one hundred solidi, which Philip held in fief at Vitry from Lord Galeran of Gallardon. Under pledge of faith they promised to provide lawful warranty, and furnished as sureties for the warranty Guy of Palacel, Bartholomew of Carlertin, and Michael of Vileir, bound by pledge of faith.

The aforesaid Galeran and his wife Idonea approved this sale, as did Lord Becelin of Sinaiis, his wife Loherengia, and their son Hecelin [Col. 0901D]; and they constituted themselves hostages for the warranty under oath of faith. Furthermore, the said Galeran sold us for eighty pounds the remainder that he held from his wife’s share, with his wife Idonea approving and assenting; both he and his wife promised under pledge of faith to provide lawful warranty.

Lord Hecelin of Linays, from whom Galeran held this property, his wife Loherengia, their son Decelin, Rencia, wife of Guy of Palacel, and the other two younger daughters of the aforesaid Hecelin, likewise approved it, renounced any claim, and, after pledging faith, granted that they would provide lawful warranty. Galeran also supplied us as sureties for the warranty the aforesaid Geoffrey, Pocot, Guy [Col. 0902A] of Vaux, Garin of Malpertuis, and Guy of Vallée Grineuse, who undertook under oath of faith to warrant this.

These sales and the grants of approval by the persons named were witnessed by others, etc. For the greater security of the matter, Philip and his wife Elizabeth, Galeran and his wife Idonea, Hecelin and his wife Loherengia, offered the aforesaid land and rents upon the altar of Blessed Mary as alms to the Church of Paris.

Done publicly at Vitry in the year 1180 of the Incarnate Word, on the feast day of Saint Agatha, the twenty-first year of our episcopate.

### VII. Maurice, bishop of Paris, confirms the foundation of Hérivaux. (1183.)

[*Gallia Christiana Nova*, VII, 74.]

[Col. 0902B]

Whatever has been beneficially ordered for the increase of divine worship must be secured by perpetual stability. Therefore I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that the nobleman Guy, cup-bearer, with the assent of his wife Margaret and of his sons Guy the cup-bearer and William, for the salvation of his own soul and those of his ancestors, granted freely, absolutely, and peacefully [Col. 0902C] for perpetual possession to the canons who serve God there regularly under an abbot’s rule, the place of his property called Hérivaux, in which a church has been built in honour of Blessed Mary ever Virgin. Retaining there no right of power or lordship for himself or his heirs, he gave the same place, with every liberty so far as concerned him, through our hand. He granted also sixty arpents of land which they had purchased from Thierry des Fosses, and thirty arpents purchased from Hugh, mayor of Luzarches; a small wood adjoining the said house; half a modius of grain from the mill of Coye, given as alms by Count Reginald; and everything which they had acquired in his own property or fief, through his or another’s liberality or in any other manner—in tithes, woods, arable land, vineyards, pastures, wine-dues, and mills—to be held and possessed by the brothers under perpetual right and in full freedom [Col. 0902D] for God’s sake.

The witnesses to this gift were Peter our chaplain; Stephen, dean of Senlis; Theobald of Viri; Philip, canon of Paris; and many others.

Done at Hérivaux in the year 1183 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the twenty-second year of our episcopate.

### VIII. Concerning the property sold by Tiulf and Herbert of Moriana and their sister Avelina. (1187.)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame de Paris*, I, 52.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, [Col. 0903A] wish it to be known to all, present and future, that the brothers Tiulf and Herbert of Moriana and their sister Avelina sold us, for one hundred and ten solidi, six solidi and ten denarii of annual rent situated upon our land and payable yearly in the octave of Saint Denis. They transferred to our ownership, under a pledge of lawful warranty made in our hand, whatever right in the rent belonged to them.

Henry, John, and Milo, sons of Richard of Musterol, approved the sale and constituted themselves vendors and sureties for the warranty under pledge of faith. Present as witnesses were Brother Daniel, Nicholas, and Adam of Barris, canons of Paris; John of Chastres; Hervey, archpriest; Berner, dean of Musterol; [Col. 0903B] Andrew of Exona; Enard of Basneuil, priests; Hamelin, our provost and matricularius; Baldwin of the Place; Henry of Termes; Henry the Fleming; Emerbold of Vitry; William the cook; Albert the chamberlain; Gervase the cup-bearer; Thomas the marshal; Robert of Chavenois; and many others.

Done at Paris in the year 1187 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the twenty-seventh year of our episcopate.

In order that it may possess perpetual force, we have ordered it to be recorded in this document and confirmed by the authority of our seal.

### IX. Concerning the rent sold at Saint-Cloud by Galeran of Saint-Lieu and his wife. (1187.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 46.]

[Col. 0903C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that Galeran, knight of Saint-Lieu, and his wife Havis sold us, for twenty-five Parisian pounds, their entire rent situated in our borough of Saint-Cloud. They retained no power or lordship there, but transferred to our ownership everything that they had in it.

Since this Galeran held that feudal tenurial holding from Peter Latruge, knight, and Peter himself had rendered homage to us for that fief, Peter, appearing in our presence, approved this sale and surrendered into our hand the entire homage and fief. He too, with his brother John and mother Felicia, constituted himself under pledge of faith a surety of lawful warranty.

The witnesses to this sale made to us by Galeran and his aforesaid wife were Osmund, archdeacon; Peter, dean of Saint-Germain; Brother Daniel; Nicholas and Adam, canons of Paris; Matthew of Modum and Adam of Gif, [Col. 0904A] deans; Hervey, archpriest; Roger of Asnières; William of Palacel; Jordan of Celeuil [variant: Sarcuil]; Clement and Nicholas Becceriis, priests; John of Chastres; Theobald Veltro; Hugh Blondel; Theodinus of Vitry, knights; Floard; Odo of Saint-Médéric; Richard; Capicerius; Garner Andrew; Garner Vaalius; John of Tremblay; Reric of Saint-Marcel; Geoffrey of Solorre; and Robert, innkeeper of Moissy. Present at the approval and surrender of the fief performed by Peter La Truie were [lacuna] John the matricularius, Simon the carpenter, Albert the chamberlain, William and Herbert the cooks [lacuna], and John the porter.

Done at Paris in the lower new hall in the year 1187 of the Incarnate [Col. 0904B] Word, the twenty-seventh year of our episcopate.

In order that it may possess perpetual force, we have committed it to this document and confirm it by the authority of our seal.

### X. Concerning the mill of Chant de la Grenouille at Corbeil. (1190.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 49.]

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all that, whereas Guy of Moissy and we jointly possessed a mill called Chant de la Grenouille at Corbeil, the same Guy, for his own need, and his son Gerard, now made a knight, sold us for twenty-five Parisian pounds the share [Col. 0904C] which they held in the said mill, after giving into our hand a pledge of warranty. They constituted as sureties for this sale, under pledge of warranty, Hugh of Évry, knight; Henry of Luigny; Gillibert of Moissy; and Geoffrey of Solorre. Thus we made the whole mill ours.

We also take care to make known to present and future persons that the aforesaid Guy and his said son Gerard likewise sold us, for eighteen Parisian pounds, twelve arpents of arable land called Saint Peter’s land, beside our cultivated field. The daughters of the aforesaid Guy, Hildeburgis and Ermengardis, his sons-in-law Peter and Matthew, his sons Odo and Guy, and Guismund, brother of the latter and canon of Campelles, approved both sales, of the mill and of the land [Col. 0904D], and promised under pledge of faith to provide warranty.

Done—

[Note: [Col. 0903] We completed this charter of sale from copies of it contained in the Great Cartulary, fol. 134, and in the smaller cartulary, fol. 268 bis.]

—concerning the sale of the mill, indeed, at Paris; but concerning the sale of the land and the approvals of the relatives, at Moissy, with witnesses, etc., in the year 1190 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the thirty-first year of our episcopate. In order that it may possess perpetual force, we have ordered it to be recorded in writing and confirmed by the impression of our seal.

### XI. Charter of Maurice, bishop of Paris, granting to the abbot and monastery of Saint-Denis of Paris the right to establish a baptismal church, with right of patronage, in the estate of Neuville. (1194.)

[Doublet, *History of Saint-Denis*, 526.]

[Col. 0905A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that in the town of Saint Denis called Neuville, near the newly cleared land of Ternomium, we wish to establish, and have graciously granted the establishment of, a baptismal church. It shall pay to us and to our successors, the bishops, and likewise to the archdeacon, its parish-priest dues, synodal dues, and other parochial obligations [Col. 0905B]; it shall possess font, cemetery, bells, and the other parochial rights as a mother and baptismal church, and shall enjoy the presence of its own priest.

The right of presentation and of selecting for that church a priest to be instituted by the bishop shall belong to the abbot as patron, with the bishop’s and archdeacon’s right wholly preserved. That this may remain ratified and firm, we have ordered this charter to be written and secured by the authority of our seal.

Done in the year 1194 of the Incarnate Word.

### XII. Concerning the meadows of the Island of Mera. (1195.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 53.]

[Col. 0905C]

In the name of the Lord. Amen. I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, make known to all that Hugh, son of Ebrard, and his wife Ascelina, after providing a pledge of warranty in our hand, sold us for eight Parisian pounds two arpents of meadow situated on the island called Mera and adjoining our meadows. The sureties for this sale were Garner, the said Hugh’s son, Walter, his son-in-law, Garner Andrew, John Aldegundis, William of Moncel, and Matthew son of Joscelin; they undertook to provide warranty. Witnesses: [lacuna] Richard the capicer [Col. 0905D], Erchembald the provost, Guimbert the pantler [lacuna].

Done at Saint-Cloud in the year 1195 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the thirty-fifth year of our episcopate.

That it may remain ratified, we have committed it to writing and confirmed it with our seal.

### XIII. Charter of Maurice concerning Ansel of Châtenville and his wife Aalix. (1196.)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame de Paris*, II, 114.]

In the name of the Lord. Amen. I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, make known to all, present and future, that Ansel of Châtenville and his wife Aalix sold to the church of Blessed [Col. 0906A] Mary of Paris, for twenty pounds, their entire tithe at Châtenet, both from arable land and from land called Martanda. John of Bièvres, from whose fief that tithe came, granted and approved the sale, and, together with Ralph of Plessis and Walter of Châterun, constituted himself defender and surety for the warranty under a pledge of faith made in our hand.

The witnesses are Hugh the dean, Peter the cantor, Galo the subchanter, Matthew dean of Meudon, Nicholas dean of Vizeur, Guibert, Aubert, and Hunaud.

Done at Paris in the year 1196 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the thirty-sixth year of our episcopate.

### XIV. Concerning the tenants and rent sold at Vitry by Hugh Malvias and his wife Gondrea to the bishop of Paris. (1160–1196.)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame de Paris*, I, 52.]

[Col. 0906B]

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that Hugh Malvias and his wife Gondrea sold us for sixty pounds seven tenants, an annual rent of twenty-six and a half solidi, and everything which they possessed at Vitry. He and his wife renounced this in our hand, and each gave security for this sale and firmly promised under pledge of faith to warrant it forever. [Col. 0906C] The mother of the aforesaid Gondrea likewise granted this and gave security under pledge of faith. John of Courcelles, to whose fief it belonged, also granted and approved it.

### XV. Concerning the settlement made between Bishop Maurice and the canons of Saint-Marcel of Vitry. (1163–1196.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 53.]

I, MAURICE, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that a dispute arose between the canons [Col. 0906D] of Saint-Marcel and Girold of Vitry because he had married our female serf, although he belonged to the household of Saint-Marcel. Moreover, the said canons sought to claim a certain acquisition of land and vineyards which Girold had received from his father and mother.

At length, when this dispute had been brought before us, it was settled by an agreement on these terms: we shall have Girold’s first child; the canons the second; we the third; and they the fourth, both of those already born and those yet to be born. If one child remains unpaired, that child shall be given to the clergy. Girold’s and his wife’s inheritance shall be divided fairly between them as between siblings, etc.

[Col. 0907]

# CHARTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS CONCERNING THE CHURCH OF PARIS, ISSUED DURING MAURICE’S ADMINISTRATION

### I. Charter concerning land given by the chapter to the monks of Carolilocus on lease at Épiais. (1164.)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame de Paris*, II, 340.]

[Col. 0907A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. I, HUMBERT, called abbot of the monastery of Carolilocus, and the whole convent of brethren, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that, with Maurice bishop of Paris present and consenting, and with Eumauric, bishop of Senlis, also present, we have taken on rent from the canons of Blessed Mary of Paris sixty-seven arpents of land situated in the territory of Épiais, on this condition: every year, on the feast of Saint Martin, we shall pay the aforesaid canons eighteen sextarii of the best grain [Col. 0907B] grown on that land, by the Paris measure, according to the king’s mina, and convey it to Paris at our own cost.

The canons who receive that grain shall suitably lodge and provide for our six horses and four men for one day only, namely the day on which they arrive. But if the aforesaid grain comes into the common stock of their whole chapter, our horses and men, in the number stated above, shall be maintained from that common stock. That this may in no way be violated, etc. [lacuna] The mark of Abbot Humbert; the mark of Prior Humbert; the mark of Subprior Enjorran [lacuna]; the mark of Alfred, precentor and priest; the mark of Odo, subchanter and priest; the mark of Guarembold, cellarer [lacuna].

[Col. 0907C] Done publicly in the year 1164 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our glorious king Louis, and the fourth year of the pontificate of Maurice, bishop of Paris.

### II. Instrument of Milo, archpriest of Milan, and Osmund, canon of Paris, concerning the church of Argenteuil. (1164.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 43.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. Concerning the dispute between Lord Maurice, bishop of Paris, and, on the other side, Lord Odo, abbot of Saint-Denis, Milo, styled archpriest of the holy Church of Milan, and Osmund, canon of Saint Mary, together with Aymeric, brother of Saint-Denis—to whom each party committed itself by oath—made the following temporary settlement, without prejudice to either party.

The dispute was as follows. The lord bishop of Paris maintained that the church of Argenteuil ought to be restored to its former state, so that he might establish an abbess there, as formerly, and there might be a community of virgins; or, if this could not be granted him, he insisted that he ought there to confirm an abbot and confer benediction upon him. Upon this demand the aforesaid bishop lodged his complaint in consistory before Pope Alexander against the said abbot, during Lent in the Paris palace.

The lord abbot, on the contrary, replied that the bishop had no right whatever to establish an abbess or a community of nuns, or to confirm or bless an abbot, because he and his predecessors had long peacefully possessed the said church through the grant of the bishop of Paris and the confirmations of many popes, whose documents he produced in evidence.

After the joining of issue and the arguments advanced by both sides, the aforesaid bishop and lord abbot committed themselves by oath to the said mediators. The mediators decreed, and under the oath by which the parties were bound commanded each side, that the aforesaid claim should cease from the Resurrection of the Lord for three continuous years, without prejudice to either party; that meanwhile neither should in any way contrive against the other concerning this question; that the bishop should not through this settlement be deprived of his customary right; that the lord abbot should possess peacefully; and that, once the three years had elapsed, the lord [Col. 0908C] bishop should not be prevented from bringing an action against this abbot or his successor.

That these provisions might have greater force, the aforesaid arbitrators decreed that the settlement made by them should be confirmed in writing and secured by the subscriptions and seals of both parties.

Done in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in April.

I, Maurice, bishop of Paris, have granted and subscribed this settlement.

I, Odo, abbot of Saint-Denis, have granted and subscribed this settlement.

### III. Concerning the release of Garnier of Domibus to the bishop of Paris, made by the abbot and convent of the Church of Fossatus. (About 1165.)

[*Ibid.*, p. 54.]

[Col. 0908D]

I, ROGER [Note: [Col. 0907] This Roger, abbot of Fossatus, is mentioned in the years 1163, 1164, 1165, and 1168. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, *Inst.*, cols. 293–294.], by the grace of God abbot of the Church of Fossatus [Col. 0909A], and our whole convent, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that we have released Garnerius de Domibus, son of Dode, from the yoke of servitude by which he was bound to us; and we have granted him to the lord bishop of Paris, to possess him in perpetuity together with all his property and possessions, and his heirs, whether those he now has or those he may hereafter have, and under the same condition by which he was subject to us. This was done on the following terms: that the lord bishop of Paris has granted to us, to possess in like manner in future times, a certain man of his, namely Stephen de Domibus, son of Bernard. That this may be held inviolably hereafter, we have judged it fitting to secure it by the present writing and the authority of our seal.

IV. Instrument of Ralph, count of Clermont, concerning the renunciation of the prebend which Peter de Monciaco held in the church of Blessed Mary at Paris. (In the year 1169.)

[Ibid., 39.]

[Col. 0909B]

I, RALPH, count of Clermont, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that I had brought a claim against the lord Maurice, bishop of Paris, concerning a certain prebend which Peter de Monciaco had held, and which I asserted belonged to my right by reason of the fief of Luzarches; but the bishop wholly denied this. At last, at his request and entreaties, and out of the affection of love which [Col. 0909C] I wished to show to the Church of Paris, I granted to the aforesaid Church whatever right I had in that prebend. Upon the altar of Blessed Mary, through the bishop’s hand, I declared that prebend free and quit in perpetuity; and, recognizing the Church’s and bishop’s right by one ring, I surrendered it, on these terms: that none of my successors may in future claim any right in that prebend, but that it shall belong in future times to the right of the bishop of Paris, like the other prebends.

And lest this might be erased by forgetfulness or in any way weakened hereafter through human malice, I strengthened it by the authority of my seal. I also granted this in the presence of Lord King Louis, and requested that he confirm this same act with the protection of his seal. Present at the aforesaid grant [Col. 0909D] made to Blessed Mary were very many persons: namely, Lord Maurice, bishop of Paris; Albert, cantor of Paris; Peter, archdeacon of Soissons; Ascelin, priest; Guy of Issy, who was then celebrating Mass; Master Odo, deacon; Walter, subdeacon; and Master Hilduin, deacon. Present at the memorial and acknowledgment made before the lord king were several others: Count Theobald; Frederick of Paris; Buchard Veautrus; and others; and, among the canons of Paris, Barbedaurus, dean, and others.

Done at Paris in the year 1169 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

V. Charter of an agreement between the chapter of the Church of Paris and Henry the Great, Arnulf of Corberon, and Peter called Girbont. (In the year 1173.)

*Cartulary of Notre-Dame of Paris*, II, 175.

[Col. 0910A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, BARBEDAURUS, by the grace of God dean of the Church of Paris, and the whole chapter of that same church, wish it to be known to all that a certain controversy was pending between us and Henry the Great, Arnulf of Corberon, and Peter Girbont, concerning a certain tithe from the territory of Bonneuil (otherwise Bonueil), [Col. 0910B] which lies between Créteil and Sucy. Finally, this agreement was made between us and the aforesaid knights, in the presence of our venerable father Maurice, bishop of Paris: that we should have the tithe of all vineyards then existing in the same territory, and wherever vineyards should thereafter be planted in that land, even if the entire aforesaid territory should be occupied by vineyards.

Moreover, in the grange of the aforesaid knights, situated in the village of Bonneuil, we shall receive every year one muid of grain, half wheat and half oats. The aforesaid knights and their successors shall hold by hereditary right the whole tithe of crops gathered in the aforesaid territory; and this shall remain so even if the whole territory is brought under cultivation, as far as the Wood of Barez. [Col. 0910C] If it should happen that, after the aforesaid wood has been cleared, the land is brought under cultivation, they have peacefully and absolutely relinquished to us in perpetuity whatever right they had in that wood.

The above-named knights, together with their wives, sons, and daughters, have granted and confirmed by faith that this agreement is to remain valid and observed forever. If we are called upon by them to enforce justice, we shall cause ecclesiastical punishment to be carried out. Lest this be invalidated by any successor, we have decreed that it be secured by a chirograph, and strengthened by the testimony of the persons subscribed below and by the authority of our seal.

The mark of Barbedaurus, dean. The mark of Albert, precentor. The mark of Germund, archdeacon. [Col. 0910D] The mark of Simon, archdeacon. The mark of Gerard, archdeacon. The mark of Master Walter, priest. The mark of Jocelin, priest. The mark of Simon, deacon. The mark of Helduin, deacon. The mark of Baldwin, subdeacon. The mark of Hervey, subdeacon. The mark of John, boy. The mark of William, boy.

Done publicly at Paris, in the presence of Maurice, bishop of Paris, in the year 1173 of the Incarnate Word, and the thirteenth year of Lord Maurice’s episcopate.

Given by the hand of Master Peter, chancellor.

VI. Charter concerning Gunsanville. (In the year 1189.)

[Ibid., p. 197.]

[Col. 0911A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, amen. I, HERVEY, dean of Paris, and the whole chapter of that church, make known to future and present persons that Robert, son of William of Gunsanville, granted to our church, to possess in perpetuity, through the hand of our venerable bishop Maurice, that which his father and mother had acquired and had themselves given to our church as alms, for the salvation of the souls of his father, mother, predecessors, and himself. [Col. 0911B] His elder brother, named William, together with William’s wife, heirs, sisters, and nephews, consented to and ratified this gift.

Since, with respect to that share which we have from Robert, the tenth part of all portions, the entire *vicia* [sic; perhaps a local due], all forage, and all persons threshing and hauling belonged severally thereto, he quitclaimed half of these to us in perpetuity. But he assigned to his brother Robert, as his hereditary portion, nine muids of wheat in newly cleared land, payable by the tenants on the first Sunday after the feast of Saint Denis, at the measure of Gunsanville. This was on the following condition: regarding the first five muids assigned to Robert, jurisdiction in its entirety shall belong to Robert; but regarding the other four muids later granted to Robert, [Col. 0911C] the aforesaid William retained for himself sales rights and jurisdiction, except that, if the tenants do not pay Robert their rents annually on the appointed day, jurisdiction and amends in this matter shall belong to Robert.

It should be known that these nine muids shall revert to William and his heirs after Robert’s death. Robert has quitclaimed to William and his heirs in perpetuity whatever may descend, or may be able to descend, to William by hereditary right or by any revenue, except half a muid of wheat, which the aforesaid William and his mother shall pay Robert every year within the aforesaid term. After his mother’s death, however, William or his heirs shall be bound to pay the half-muid [Col. 0911D] in full. That this may remain ratified and firm, we have authenticated the present charter by the authority of our seal and confirmed it by the subscriptions of the witnesses.

The mark of Hervey, dean. The mark of Master Peter, precentor. The mark of Maurice, archdeacon. The mark of Hosmund, archdeacon. The mark of Gerard, archdeacon. The mark of Master Peter, the bishop’s chaplain. The mark of Galon, priest and succentor . . . . .

Done publicly at Paris, in our chapter, in the year 1189 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

Given by the hand of Hilduin, chancellor.

VII. Concerning meadows sold by the abbess of Saint Cyricus on the island of Mere. (In the year 1190.)

*Cartulary of Notre-Dame of Paris*, I, 55.

[Col. 0912A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, SOUCELINA, by the grace of God abbess of Saint Cyricus, wish it to be known to all that we, with the common consent of our entire convent, have granted to the venerable lord and father Maurice, bishop of Paris, and to his successors, to possess in perpetuity, two arpents of meadow on the island of Mere, from the alms of Gilo Pilosi, having received from the benefaction of that bishop four pounds of Parisian money. For the perpetual validity of this matter, we ordered the present charter [Col. 0912B] to be made and confirmed it under the impression of our seal.

The mark of Eugenia, prioress; the mark of Hildegard, subprioress; the mark of Mamiha, chantress; the mark of Odelina, cellarer; the mark of Agnes la Chevrelle; the mark of Hemeline, secretary. Witnesses: . . . . Hugh and Peter, chaplains of Saint Cyricus.

Done at Saint Cyricus, in the common chapter, in the year 1190 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

VIII. Concerning the bishop’s procuration at the church of Saint Exuperius of Corbeil. (1191, March 3.)

[Ibid., 44.]

In the name of the Lord, amen. ADELA, by the grace of God queen of the Franks, wishes it to be known to all who see or hear the present letters that, when the complaint brought by the venerable Maurice, bishop of Paris, against the church of Saint Exuperius at Corbeil concerning the procuration to be provided to him had, by the command of Lord Pope Clement III, been entrusted to Mainard, abbot of Pontigny, and Guy, abbot of Prully, it was brought into an amicable settlement in our presence through the mediation of the venerable men Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, and John, bishop of Nevers, in the following manner.

If the bishop of Paris comes to Corbeil, with the archdeacon of that castle or without the archdeacon, to celebrate divine service in that church on the feast day of Saint Exuperius—namely, the first day of August—[Col. 0912D] the canons of Saint Exuperius shall be obliged to pay him only fifty shillings for procuration. But if the archdeacon comes to that church on the said feast day without the bishop, the canons shall pay the archdeacon nothing for procuration. On any other day or at any other time when the bishop or archdeacon comes to the church of Saint Exuperius, they shall be obliged to provide no procuration either to the bishop or to the archdeacon.

Done at Melun, in the royal residence, in the first week of Lent, in the year 1190 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the presence of Hugh, abbot of Saint-Clement, etc.; Hugh, Enguerrand, and John of Perracheto, canons of Saint Exuperius; [Col. 0913A] Matthew, Nicholas, and John, canons of Paris; Brother Daniel; Master Albert Lombard; Peter of Lodeville; and very many others. For the perpetual remembrance of this matter, we ordered the present charter to be written and confirmed by our seal.

Given by the hand of Robert, our chaplain.

IX. Instrument of the chapter of Paris concerning the same procuration. (In the year 1191.)

[Ibid., p. 45.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, amen. I, MICHAEL, dean of Paris, and the whole chapter of that church, wish it to be known, etc., as in no. XXXIII . . . . . . .

[Col. 0913B]

Accordingly, we approved and ratified this agreement, brought before us under the testimony of the seals of the aforesaid abbots. We ordered the present charter to be drawn up under the division of a chirograph, and authenticated it under the impression of our seal.

Done publicly in our chapter in the year 1191 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the presence of those whose names are subscribed:

The mark of Michael, dean. The mark of Peter, precentor. The mark of Maurice, archdeacon. The mark of Osmond, archdeacon. The mark of Gerard, archdeacon. The mark of Galon, succentor. The mark of Stephen, priest. [Col. 0914A] The mark of Ralph, priest. The mark of Matthew, priest. The mark of William, deacon. The mark of Peter, deacon. The mark of Odo, deacon. The mark of Adam, subdeacon. The mark of Suger, subdeacon. The mark of Henry and William, boys.

Given by the hand of Hilduin, chancellor.

X. Concerning the relinquishment of Emelina, a Parisian woman, made by the abbot and convent of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. [Note: [Col. 0913] This charter was issued between 2 May 1194 and the date of the death of Fulco, abbot of Saint-Germain, and 11 September 1196, the day on which Bishop Maurice died.] (About the year 1194.)

[Ibid., p. 54.]

I, ROBERT, by the grace of God humble abbot of Blessed Germanus of the Meadows [Col. 0914B], greeting in the Lord to all who inspect the present letters.

Let all of you know that the venerable Maurice, bishop of Paris, gave us and our church his female slave Isabel as wife to Robert, our man, so that he may not hereafter claim anything in her or in the sons or daughters descended from her. In exchange for his aforesaid female slave, we likewise gave the lord bishop of Paris our female slave Emelia as wife to Guarin, his man, so that neither our church nor we may hereafter claim anything in her or in the sons or daughters descended from her. That this may remain ratified, we have ordered it to be strengthened by our seal.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1198: ODO, BISHOP OF TOUL

[Col. 0913]

NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. XIII, p. 1004.)

Odo, son of Count Hugh I of Vaudémont and his wife Agelina of Burgundy, and full brother of Count Gerard II, was educated in the Church of Toul under Henry of Lorraine. He first held the offices of archdeacon and then treasurer; he attained episcopal rank in 1192. At the beginning of his pontificate difficulties arose concerning the dignity of primicerius. Theodoric of Lorraine, son of Duke Matthew I, had procured his promotion to that dignity, although Bishop Riquin had united it to the chapter’s common fund. After Theodoric’s death, an archdeacon of Toul named Simon obtained bulls from the pope, on a false allegation, that he should succeed him. The canons opposed his taking possession and appealed to the Apostolic See. But Simon, supported by the influence of his powerful family, entered into possession. Unequal to resisting him, the canons fled to the supreme pontiff, who appointed as judges in this case the bishops of Châlons and Langres, and the abbots of Haute-Seille, Belle-Pré, and Clairvaux. They gave judgment in Simon’s favor. An appeal was made from this judgment to the supreme pontiff, who, after carefully considering the matter, pronounced according to the wishes of the chapter.

At that time the chapter consisted of sixty canons and one hundred clerics or vicars. Seeing that the revenues were insufficient to support so many people, Odo obtained from Celestine III a reduction of the number of canons to fifty, on condition that the revenues of the ten suppressed prebends should be distributed among both the canons and the vicars. Odo also established that each of the three masters of the schools should receive a canon’s prebend, while those teaching humane letters should hold vicars’ prebends. [Col. 0915]

He undertook a pilgrimage to Rome; in what year is unknown to us. But we know certainly that, during his absence, his nephew Gerard, treasurer and archdeacon, was appointed vicar-general of the diocese by the archbishop of Trier. He made another journey to the monastery of Cluny, in order to adopt and emulate the holy way of life and virtues of the monks living there. In the *Acts of the Bishops of Toul*, he is said to have bestowed many things on his church.

At a synod held on 8 May 1192, at the request of archdeacons and abbots, he promulgated statutes for pursuing robbers, heretics, and apostate monks. In that year, and again in 1196, he ratified donations granted to the monastery of Flavigny-sur-Moselle. He subscribed letters in favor of Saint Michael in 1194. In that same year he made peace between Duke Simon of Lorraine and the Church of Remiremont. He consecrated in 1195 the church of Éuville, founded by Herbert, son of Ralph of Apremont. In the same year he gave the cross to Simon of Parois, who was shortly to depart for Jerusalem, and carried out the will of Simon, who died during that pilgrimage and had entrusted it to him.

In 1196 he granted the altar of Midrevaux to the monastery of Murevaux. In the same year, together with his nephew, he attended the assembly summoned at Speyer by Emperor Henry VI; there he too received from the apostolic legate the cross for undertaking a journey to the Holy Land. In the following year he brought before the emperor a complaint against Count Theobald I of Bar, as an oppressor of the Church of Toul; and he granted to the canons of Saint-Leon the priory of Nas and the lepers’ house situated in the parish of Pierre-la-Treiche. On 25 May of that same year, he also confirmed to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, the church of Mosterol. He issued letters as well concerning the controversy that had arisen between Duke Simon of Lorraine and the Church of Remiremont [Note: [Col. 0915] Benedictine, *History of Toul*, proofs, p. 98.].

In this year or the next he set out for Jerusalem, as he had vowed, and died on the journey on 26 November, according to the necrology of Saint Mansuetus. His body was brought back to the city and buried in the middle of the nave of the cathedral; it was afterwards transferred to the tomb of Count Hugh II of Vaudémont, his nephew, buried in the same church.

[Col. 0915]

SYNODAL STATUTES OF ODO, ISSUED IN 1192.

(D. Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV, 1178, from the autograph of Belle-Pré.)

[Col. 0915A]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of the Leuci, to all ecclesiastical persons established in our bishopric, forever.

Let all persons hereafter know and keep in remembrance that our dearly beloved brothers and friends in the Lord, the archdeacons and abbots of our bishopric, came to us. Groaning together over the lamentable injuries by which our church and the ministers of the churches were daily, irremediably oppressed and afflicted, they unanimously asked us mercifully to furnish them, against the tyranny of robbers and of all malefactors raging against them, that counsel, protection, and safeguard which we were bound to give them paternally by the pastoral care and office laid upon us. Therefore, after taking counsel with them, as seemed reasonable to us and as their prudent judgment advised us, we have established what we ordered to be set down article by article in the present document.

I. Divine offices are not to be celebrated in places through which goods unjustly taken from churches pass.

We establish, therefore, and forbid under anathema, that whenever goods of our churches or of any of our clerics, carried off by unjust seizure, happen to pass through any castle or village situated in our bishopric, or perhaps to remain there overnight, so that none of them at all remains there afterwards, divine offices shall not be celebrated there in the meantime. Wherever, however, those goods happen to be stored, sold, or expended in any manner, whether wholly or in part, [Col. 0916A] we absolutely forbid divine offices to be performed there. We decree that buyers, together with plunderers, are bound by the same sentence of excommunication until full restitution and fitting satisfaction have been made.

We add this: if in the meantime any inhabitants there who neither consented to nor caused that injury are at the point of death, they may receive the aid of confession and viaticum; but they shall not have burial in the churchyard until the stolen goods have been restored in full, divine offices have been celebrated there, and those buried outside the churchyard are honored with the burial due to the churchyard without any further payment.

II.

We also establish that if any prince or nobleman of this land violently plunders in his own person any goods whatsoever belonging to our churches or clerics, and carries them into his own village, divine offices shall not be celebrated in that village or in all his other land until the stolen goods are restored in full. But if knights, or any members of the household of princes or nobles, likewise violently take any goods whatsoever belonging to our churches or clerics and carry them into their lord’s village, divine offices shall not be celebrated there at all until the stolen goods are fully restored with satisfaction.

When those who committed the crime have been individually excommunicated by us and this is known throughout our bishopric, they shall be named and excommunicated by all priests every Sunday wherever divine offices are celebrated. If the principal amounts have been restored in full under the strictness of justice, [Col. 0917A] they shall nevertheless not be absolved unless satisfaction has first been made to us. We now further add that whoever receives in his house any such malefactor individually excommunicated by us, or allows him to lodge overnight there, shall be excommunicated with him, unless he can prove that he did this through ignorance. If he wishes, he may make this proof by his own hand alone. But if he cannot clear himself in this matter and wishes to make amends for the offense, he shall pay ten shillings for that night, and ten shillings as many times as he received him for nights; then he shall be released from the bond of the sentence.

III. Those who transgress these statutes are deprived of office and benefice.

[Col. 0917B]

Since we have determined these things after careful and highly useful deliberation, and since we have decreed and commanded their observance by the common request and consent of all clerics subject to us, we establish that any cleric simply subject to us, or any monk, who transgresses this command of ours shall be deprived forever both of benefice, if he has one, and of office.

IV. Divine offices are to cease when anyone is buried in a cemetery during an interdict.

Furthermore, concerning those who violently bury the body of a deceased person in a cemetery at a time when that village has been suspended from the offices of Christian worship on account of justice, [Col. 0917C] we establish that, as long as the body remains buried there, divine offices shall not be celebrated there at all; and after it has been removed, it shall never thereafter be buried either in that cemetery or in another. If any of those who buried the body in this manner dies before reconciliation, he likewise shall be deprived forever of Christian burial.

V. Against those committing violence against religious houses.

And because a grave and intolerable affliction threatens religious houses from the fact that powerful men of the land violently seize their oxen, other animals, or carts for plowing on their own behalf, we establish by irrevocable determination that those who commit such violence shall at once be held under an excommunication interdict. Those who give or sell them what they will use for plowing, after learning of that violence, shall likewise be excommunicated; and the village to which what they have plowed with has been carried [Col. 0918A] shall be suspended from every office of Christian worship, until the damage inflicted on the religious houses has been fully repaired and proper satisfaction has thereafter been made to God and to us.

VI. Against fugitives.

Concerning fugitives who render their professions void and return from any religious order to secular life, we likewise establish that they shall be excommunicated every Sunday throughout all parishes. If they take wives, their wives likewise, their households, and all who knowingly provide them any communion of Christian fellowship shall be held under interdict with them.

VII. Concerning one who celebrates in the presence of an excommunicated person.

[Col. 0918B]

If any nobleman or powerful man of the land, while excommunicated by us, brings in a priest and has divine offices celebrated for himself contrary to our interdict, the person who presumes to celebrate in this manner shall be excommunicated and shall be deprived forever of ecclesiastical office and benefice in our bishopric.

VIII.

We also establish that if a priest excommunicated by us presumes to celebrate divine offices in our diocese, he shall be deprived forever of ecclesiastical benefice and office.

IX. Against the Waldensian heretics.

Concerning heretics called *Wadoys* [Waldensians], we command all faithful people, clerics as well as laypeople, for the remission of their sins, that whoever finds them shall keep them in chains and bring them to the see of Toul for punishment.

X.

This too is to be commended to memory: if any persons are, God forbid, driven from their own residences because of carrying out this justice, they shall unquestionably find with us, under our protection and at our disposal, provision of food and clothing as shall be fitting. May peace and joy be unto all who observe the tenor of this charter, through all ages of ages.

Lawfully enacted, publicly read, and canonically confirmed [Col. 0918D] in the holy synod of Toul, in the tenth indiction, on 8 May, in the year 1192 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

ABOUT THE YEAR 1200: ALEXANDER, ABBOT OF JUMIÈGES

[Col. 0919]

LETTER ON “THE SON OF MAN”

(D. Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. I, col. 777, from a manuscript of Jumièges.)

[Col. 0919A]

Brother ALEXANDER, to R., his beloved brother in the Lord: may you behold the will of the Lord.

As I was once seeking in secret meditation how I might explain to the simpler brethren in the French tongue that Gospel saying, “Whom do men say the Son of Man to be?”, such great difficulty presented itself that I would either have to use an interpretation too far removed, which would scarcely seem to approach the letter, or else, by satisfying people rather than the letter, say one thing for another in the manner of those who dispute sophistically and bring forward a solution not suited to the expression but to the person. For since this noun, *homo* (“human being, man”), does not determine sex, I could correctly render “Son of Man” neither as “son of a man” nor as “son of a woman.” Of these, one is altogether false, and neither can be maintained from the letter. For “Son of Man” does not expressly convey what “son of a woman” or “son of the Virgin” conveys, although “Son of Man” is wholly the same as “son of the Virgin”; nor did anything else readily occur by which this expression, “Son of Man,” might be expressly indicated.

Compelled, therefore, by this difficulty, I returned to the deeper aids of meditation; and, as it were chewing over what I had heard from others, I called back to mind whatever I could. All this, dearest brother, I pour out to you without pretence, so that, when you have examined our little paper, you may seem to have read what is in our heart.

They say, then, that there is one only son of earth, one only Son of Man; all the rest are sons of men. Adam alone [Col. 0919C] is the son of earth; all who are begotten through carnal desire are sons of men. Christ alone, begotten without it, is not the son of men but the Son of Man. Since this designation properly belongs to him—indeed, since he himself so willed—it was assigned to him as a description which belongs to him alone and always.

But if it is objected that this expression is also found written concerning Ezekiel, they think it is used improperly, so that he who is called “son of man” is to be understood as also “son of men.” This is the view held by almost everyone concerning the aforementioned appellation.
