You, however, who seek not to be falsely delighted by the surface of words but to be nourished by the inward marrow of truth, observe that the foregoing words are in part as though true, but in part offer an evasion. For that Christ is called the Son of Man by this expression is more certain than certain; but that it was said for the reason that he is the son of one human being and not of several, they do not explain from the words but impose upon the words.

It must be known, however, that in sacred Scripture “son” is understood in four ways: by reason of creation, as in Luke, “Adam, son of God”; by reason of succession and lineage, as there concerning Christ, “son of David, son of Abraham”; by reason of law, according to which Joseph is called the son of Heli. For according to the flesh he was the son of Jacob; and perhaps in this same sense, according to worldly law, adopted sons are called sons. In the fourth way, however, a son is so called according to a proper generation of substance from substance; in this sense Christ is called Son of God and Son of Man.

To believe both of these things concerning substance belongs to Christian faith; and therefore [Col. 0920B] Jesus Christ never used trope or figure when he named himself Son of God and Son of Man. It is the same in the other sacraments in which the substance of faith is involved, such as the Eucharist and baptism. For what could be more manifest than his saying that his flesh is to be eaten and his blood drunk? What could be clearer than his saying: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16)? Thus, clearer than light and without any obscurity, he calls himself Son of Man—not son of men, that is, of a man and a woman, but singularly son of a human being—so that we must understand not a male but a woman, whose natural property is to conceive and give birth.

Therefore, in order to show in himself the truth of human nature which we must believe, sincere Truth called himself Son of Man, and the son singularly of one person, so that by the singular number he might exclude the man and, by silent indication, intimate the Holy Spirit. Hence “Son of Man” is understood as though he had said, “son of that Blessed Virgin who from the beginning was found in the company of Christ.”

Perhaps another solution to this question may be inferred from the Apostle’s words, where he says that Christ was not at all tithed in Abraham’s loins, because he was born from Adam without Adam’s sin, in order that he might abolish that man’s sin. But blessed Jerome says that where we read “Son of Man” in the Gospel, the Hebrew has “son of Adam.” For *Adam* means the same as “human being.” Hence, because this name *homo*, “human being,” first belonged to the old Adam, and we derive from him by propagation of the flesh, we are also called from that old human being, according to the saying: “Put off the old man,” etc. (Ephesians 4).

Adam was rightly called old because he himself first grew old and gave others the cause of growing old. For when he had sinned and declined from his first state into a worse one, he was rightly called old and made old. Indeed, he had been blessed as new; but by growing old—that is, by losing the grace in which he had flourished, and with nature weakened through sin—he was found most miserable through failing in himself. This misery is marked by the name of oldness because it takes its beginning from that one who had grown old.

But newness is signified by the term “son,” because when “son” is heard, something new is indicated. Therefore Christ is called Son of Man, that is, new from old. For Christ is from man according to the flesh, which is to be from Adam, but contracts no contagion of oldness or sin. Although he is wholly son of the old human being, he is new because he is wholly without sin.

That Christ was truly Adam’s son, and so a son as also to be an heir, he himself plainly showed when, by ascending to heaven, he took possession of Adam’s inheritance. For by God’s decree, if Adam had not sinned, an inheritance in heaven was due to Adam and his seed, where the Church was to be built from two walls, namely, those of human beings and angels, corresponding to one another equally in number and dignity. But the first human being, by transgression, forfeited this inheritance for himself and his descendants; and because all human beings were then in him, all were deprived of the same inheritance, since they descended from him with the cause, or punishment, of sin for the same cause.

For all born into the world drew corruption from the corrupt first parent; and because, being corrupted, they could not resist their desires, all were disobedient to God, as was their father Adam. But it was God’s decree that no one should enter heaven until obedience as great should be found in one human being as the disobedience which had been in the first parent. Therefore none of the others was properly Son of Man—that is, Adam’s heir—because no one could obtain his inheritance except that one [Col. 0922A] alone who was conceived and born without every sin and cause of sin. He was obedient to God the Father in all things, because no desire resisted him; he was wholly mighty because he was God and God’s Son. When he reconciled God to us through the offering of his body, he had no need first to offer for his own sins and then for those of the people, but paid only what he had not taken.

Hence it is that he is named with such great proclamation, now heir and now son. Thus it is said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance” (Psalm 2). And elsewhere: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3). And again: “A little child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9). Finally, he himself is Abraham’s seed, in whom all nations are blessed.

Do not therefore suppose that I say [Col. 0922B] that he is Son of Man, or of Adam, only because he descends from him according to the flesh. Others had that as well; but he is so called because he is heir, which the others, conceived as it were illegitimately in sins, could by no means be. This is the male child whom the woman bore in the Apocalypse, whom the dragon could not harm, nor his mother, because he was caught up to God.

And because not Adam alone, but in him the entire human race, was deprived of the inheritance, a son was given also to the entire human race, according to the saying: “In him the nations shall hope” (Romans 15). Rightly, therefore, in his appellation this noun *homo*, “human being,” which does not distinguish sex, is used, because he was given not exclusively to any, but in common to all who should wish to cling to him. For in Christ Jesus, as the Apostle says, “there is neither male nor female; neither slave nor free; nor is there respect of persons; but whoever fears God is acceptable to him” (Galatians 3).

You should also remember that *Adam* and *homo* have the same etymology, for each is interpreted “earthly.” For *homo*, as was said, which was Adam’s proper name, was made common to us, in whom, as in Christ also, we all existed without distinction of sexes. But, lest this excessively wandering discourse further weary the eyes, we believe that “Son of Man” means “new from old,” or “son of Adam,” with reference to the state in which Adam had been before sin.

CIRCA THE YEAR 1200: GERALD, BISHOP OF CAHORS

[Col. 0923]

LETTER TO EMPEROR FREDERICK

He asks the emperor to command his release from imprisonment by soldiers.

(D. Dachery, *Spicilegium*, quarto, vol. II, p. 403.)

[Col. 0923A] To FREDERICK, by the grace of God triumphant and most glorious Emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, GERALD, called bishop of Cahors:

“To spare the subject peoples and subdue the proud.”

Since, most serene prince, at the feast of the Lord’s Nativity at Alba, your Highness wished me to take part in the joyous celebration of your coronation and honoured me; since your Excellence granted me this favour, that among the other proofs of your kindness you deigned to grant me letters of safe-conduct throughout your whole empire and to all your faithful subjects: I have conceived such fervour of loyalty toward your greatness that there can be nothing consonant with your honour and pleasure to which my littleness is not in every respect inclined and, in all purity of heart, most ready.

And since your Highness then enjoined upon me that I should obtain leave to return through you, when I presented myself before your sight at Piacenza on Palm Sunday, imperial magnificence received and dismissed me with such kindness of your grace that, as a faithful servant to his dearest lord, I became from that time bound to your honour and obligated according to my strength.

While established in this purpose of loyalty, it happened that I went into those regions to visit a kinsman of mine, the viscount named Eborus, who, while returning from Jerusalem, had fallen ill at Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino. When he had already died, since the lord king of France, your kinsman, had told me to come to the court to which the lord Pavembergensis had been sent by your command for the restoration of peace in the Church, and the lord of Mende had been sent by him with your approval, so that I might see what had been done about that peace, I passed through that court. I also wished to satisfy the lord marquis of Montferrat, who had entrusted certain business of his to me, his faithful man.

When I was returning from there, although I had absolutely no letters from Coitradus, your messenger, or from Guarnerius, marquis of the March, I was seized and held in custody with certain clerics and monks from the kingdoms of the French and English. They were not wealthy, indeed, but belonged to noble churches, and all had gone under hope of the Church’s peace, which they too had similarly heard had been made. Although some among them carried letters, these contained nothing against your honour, but only the legal claims of their churches.

Therefore, prostrate at the feet of imperial mercy, we humbly entreat your Majesty that the compassion of your graciousness may cause me, and a kinsman of mine, the viscount of Albucione, marquis of that land, and all the others, to be released with honour and with complete restoration of what has been taken away. For the monks and clerics are religious persons, travelling on this road without deceit or malice under hope of a peace which they had heard had been made. They desired nothing which they believed contrary to your interests; and if they could obtain justice from another concerning other grievances, they would certainly have gone to him more willingly.

Thus, with repeated and tearful prayers, we cast ourselves at the feet of your Serenity, humbly begging imperial mercy: for the love of God, and out of regard for the lord marquis of Montferrat and the lord count of Saint-Gilles, your faithful man, may your clemency open its eyes toward my release and that of my fellow captives. May God repay you for this, and may we—who shall cause abundant thanks to be rendered to you by all the princes of the kingdom of France—be bound always to pray for your welfare and to prove ourselves more faithful.

Moreover, most gracious of princes, I beseech your Highness to grant again and send me those letters of safe-conduct to all your faithful subjects which you once granted me, not temporary letters, but, as I believed, perpetual ones. By such a token of your grace I shall become not only most faithful to your empire, but also your most devoted servant. Your liberality will suffer no diminution through our release; rather, this may greatly contribute to the increase of your name and glory. For as soon as I was captured, I appealed to your Majesty, placing myself, my possessions, and my companions under your protection. I wished to pledge my faith that, before returning directly to my own country, I would present myself before you in order to obey your commands. For I trusted so greatly in the favour you had given me that your kindness would pardon me if I had unknowingly committed any fault.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1200: MATTHEW OF VENDÔME

[Col. 0925]

NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. V, p. 54.)

[Col. 0925A] Matthew, a native of the French town of Vendôme, and praised by Henry of Ghent, chapter 23, who dedicated to Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours from 1177 to 1206 [Note: [Col. 0925C] Sammarthani, vol. I, p. 770 ff.], his *Tobias*, or metaphrase of the Book of Tobit, written in elegiac verse, must necessarily be considered different from Matthew, guardian of the kingdom of France under Louis IX, Saint Louis, king of France, and abbot of Saint-Denis from 1260 [Note: [Col. 0925C] See Félibien, book V of the *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*; Sammarthani, vol. IV, p. 336; Sandius on Vossius, p. 508.]. An epitaph of 1286 was written for the latter, beginning:

> Here lies the specially approved mirror of abbots,  
> Who gave the Church great splendour by his virtue,  
> Who declined the honour of the archbishopric of Tours, etc.

What Oudinus argues, vol. III, p. 483—that the *Tobias* was dedicated to a Bartholomew long dead, and that Matthew, by poetic licence, honoured his shade as though he were living and breathing—is certainly scarcely credible. The words with which he addresses him say something very different:

> Summit of the Church of Tours, watcher over the sheep,  
> As a mirror, Bishop Bartholomew, be favourable.

And after speaking of Bishop Engelbald, who died in 1157 and was Bartholomew’s uncle, he says:

> Guilty death carried this man away; you, his most worthy heir,  
> Wield his paternal sceptres with a hand that has earned them.

Then he adds:

> Live and fare well, glory of the Church; grant to one who prays  
> A harbour; drive away shipwreck; heal the vessel.  
> Receive the titles of Tobit with your brother the dean,  
> That a double star may calm the fearful journey.  
> I rejoice that you shine forth with new light, etc.  
>
> Live happily, brothers, whom the same mind proves to be two,  
> Though in body alone you are two, etc.

Certainly, therefore, the abbot of Saint-Denis, Matthew, is different from the Matthew who composed the metaphrase of Tobit. To the former are addressed letters of Saint Louis IX, who died in 1270, and of his successor Philip III, as well as letters of the abbot to this Philip, king of France, who died one year before the abbot. Those letters are found in Dachery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 548 ff., and vol. III of the new edition, pp. 663, 664, 666, 669, 670; and there is a letter of Peter of Condé to the same Matthew, p. 667, concerning the peace made with the king of Tunis.

The author of the *Tobias*, which some wrongly called the *Thebaid*, declares that he composed this metaphrase of the Book of Tobit from Jerome’s Latin translation:

> As Jerome’s sacred translation hands it down,  
> The man of Vendôme tills prose in whatever metre.

And, after several intervening verses:

> Jerome translates, Bede explains, Matthew  
> Sets it in metre; envy rejects it, a friend possesses it.

And in the epilogue:

> . . . . . This present pitcher draws its waters  
> From the spring of blessed Jerome.

Matthew of Vendôme is mentioned by Henry of Ghent, in *On Illustrious Men*, p. 166, chapter 23. He is cited by Vincent of Beauvais in the *Moral Mirror*, and by his contemporary Thomas of Wales. He is cited several times by the author of the *Flowers of Poetry*—not Alan, as Barthius thought, but a certain younger writer—and likewise by Sparanus in the *Rosary*. He himself praises Walter, author of the *Alexandreis*, concerning whom see above, vol. III, p. 107 [Note: [Col. 0926C] See *Patrologia*, vol. CCIX. EDITOR.].

> Let the hexameter of Walter’s poem be wanting to you;  
> Matthew of Vendôme delights in elegiac pentameters.

Matthew’s *Poetics*, or *Poetria*, as it was then called, unknown to others and written partly in prose and partly in verse, is praised more than once by Jeremiah of Montagnone, a citizen of Padua, in his *Epitome of Wisdom*, as Daumius shows in his preface to Jerome the Greek’s *Philoponia* (Φιλοπονία, “Love of Toil”). For this *Poetria*, as well as another work by Matthew of Vendôme, *On Equivocal Terms*, in the Royal Library of France and in English manuscript libraries, see Oudinus, vol. III, p. 484.

Daumius, however, did not possess in manuscript a *Poetria* distinct from the *Tobias*, as is stated in the *Bibliotheca curiosa* of Hallervord; rather, he possessed the *Tobias* of the man of Vendôme, perhaps the very manuscript which Barthius received from Gevartius, from which he inserted about one hundred verses, corrected in several places, in book XXXI of his *Adversaria*, final chapter. There he promised to publish the whole work of the Vendômois in a corpus of all poets which, arranged by centuries, he declared himself to be preparing.

Although that corpus of poets did not appear, Johann Hering, Doctor of Civil Law and syndic of Bremen, published Matthew’s *Tobias* at Bremen in 1642, octavo, from two manuscripts. Nor was this the first edition of the Vendômois, as Hering thought; there is also a Lyons edition of 1505, in larger quarto, with commentary among the *Eight Moral Authors*, and a Strasbourg edition of 1510 from the same edition. Both are much fuller than Hering’s, especially toward the end. There is also another Lyons edition, by Johann Raenerius, 1538, octavo, published by Theobaldus Paganus, but without commentary. Finally, there is the Oporinus edition prepared by Johann Herold in 1563, quarto. [Note: [Col. 0926C] Fabricius did not know the first edition, which appeared at Lyons in 1489, printed by Jehan du Pré, small folio, with glosses. EDITOR.] I gladly acknowledge that I owe my knowledge of these editions to the diligence of the distinguished Daumius.

Moreover, the most illustrious and learned Joachim Feller, through his singular goodwill and kindness, by which while living he embraced all students of good letters, in 1690 gave me a copy of the Vendômois transcribed by a learned man, in whose manuscript various readings were noted here and there in the margin. That codex ends at verse 1510, that is, at the end of the tenth chapter of Tobit. Polycarp Leyser offers certain variant readings from the Wolfenbüttel manuscript in his *History of Medieval Poetry*, p. 766. Andreas Rivinus had written certain notes on that passage which I said above had been published by Barthius in his *Adversaria*, and I remember having examined them likewise in manuscript. You will also read several passages of Matthew of Vendôme elucidated in the letters of Reinesius to Daumius, p. 344, in which Bartholomew, to whom Matthew dedicated his *Tobias*, is also discussed here and there.

[Col. 0927]

MATTHEW OF VENDÔME’S METRICAL PARAPHRASE OF THE BOOK OF TOBIT

(From the edition entitled: *Sacred History of the Elder and Younger Tobit, elegantly illustrated several centuries ago, according to theological, ethical, and juridical subject matter, both by a paraphrase in elegiac verse and by a rhetorical exposition, by Matthew of Vendôme and Ambrose of Milan; the former, a poet, now for the first time restored to light from manuscripts, including parchment manuscripts; the latter, an orator and first a governor or judge and afterward a bishop, restored from ancient printed codices; with a letter, testimonies, variant readings, observations, and a dissertation variously added, by the editor and author Johann Hering, Doctor of Civil Law, of Oldenburg and syndic of the cathedral chapter in the bishopric of Verden. Bremen, printed by Wessel and at the expense of Hoismann, in the year of Christ 1642.*)

DEDICATORY LETTER

To the most reverend, very reverend, most noble, illustrious, venerable, and most learned lords of the chapters, monasteries, and archiepiscopal and episcopal sees of Bremen and Verden, close neighbours; to chief provosts, deans, archdeacons, canons, abbots, provosts, priors, etc.; to lords, patrons, and friends formerly and still to be dutifully and devotedly honoured: Johann HERING, Doctor of Civil Law and syndic, gives, declares, and dedicates this sacred history L. M. Q., with devoted and dutiful service.

Twenty-four years have elapsed since I published and prefaced works composed by me at different times, on individual subjects, in various ways, and inscribed to particular persons. In the meantime I have not abandoned my purpose of seeking out and setting forth more, although placed amid the various vicissitudes of these present times, summoned to and employed in diverse labours of office, and distracted by them; except that certain obstacles have repeatedly delayed the work and publication. Yet I have almost ready most of the things which, under the title of *Theoretical-Practical Observations*, drawn from public and private law and from the historical-political antiquities of various peoples, I promised, drawn from most recent annotations; together with certain other works, both discourses and treatises, and I gather more daily.

While these are being brought to completion and polish, and are also finding printers and patrons, I have thought it proper to commit to print, for the common good, after my own writings, other writings, whether foreign or adopted, new and old. The greatly desired and most eloquent Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam [Note: [Col. 0927] Erasmus, in the dedicatory letter preceding Ambrose’s works, Paris edition of 1539.] almost preferred this pursuit; and Johann Alexander Brassicanus, a man of our own profession and a diligent examiner and cultivator of ancient books, has illustrated the same subject more extensively [Note: [Col. 0927] Brassicanus, preface to Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, *On the Providence of God*, Rittershus edition.].

There now come before me two very ancient parchment codices, written by hand, at least from the year of Christ’s birth 1315, and thus copied or written three hundred and twenty-six years ago. Their author, a Frenchman by nation, has been placed neither by Abbot Trithemius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* nor by Gesner, theologian and philologist, in his *Library*. He is mentioned among later writers only by the most learned polymath Caspar Barthius in his richly furnished *Adversaria* as Matthew of Vendôme—whose native place is also mentioned several times by the very celebrated historian Jacques-Auguste de Thou—as I too think, and as both his prologue and epilogue indicate. Yet at the end of the other exemplar used by me are these words: “Here ends the book of Master Conrad”; perhaps they belong to some owner, copyist, or lecturer before whom the other lived and flourished. Barthius published only a portion of the work, namely, the preface and first chapter, scarcely reaching the second.

It is a metrical paraphrase, fairly polished in view of that age and in comparison with others, on the little sacred history of Tobit, which, according to certain chronologists, occurred in the year 740 before Christ’s birth. On the occasion of this work, though with another manner of speaking and aim, Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, expounded his subject in theological-juridical fashion among the Fathers of the Church. Likewise, in England the Venerable Bede, a priest, composed an allegorical exposition of the little Book of Tobit, inserted in volume IV of his works. Later Helmbold left monostichs, and Golthus rhythmic iambics, now appended together, to posterity.

I have not yet found older and shorter works; nor have I heard of authors of the immediately preceding and present centuries, partly seen by me and partly cited by others—writers of both kinds who wrote on the Book of Tobit and whom Barthius calls holy commentators [Note: [Col. 0927] Barthius, book XLIX of the *Adversaria*, chapter 10, fol. 2299.]—except the author of the Ordinary Gloss, Nicholas of Lyra, Cardinal Hugh, Denis the Carthusian, Peter Comestor, Sebastian Münster, Paul Fagius, Frederick Nausea, John Benedictine, Conrad Pellican of Rouffach, Johann Matthesius, Victorinus Strigel, N. Serarius, Michael Saxon, Andreas Schoppius, and Adam Kolbius. They have published explanations, translations, annotations, commentaries, sermons, and scholia on the often-praised biblical history of Tobit, which offers various domestic goods and evils as examples either for encouragement and imitation or for correction. The little Book of Esther and its supplement, concerning Mordecai and Haman, do no less: they display what a man and women who deserve well or ill commonly do and can accomplish in both Church and commonwealth, and particularly at court.

On this occasion, therefore—and, as we are now accustomed to speak, in this respect—I first bring again to light and restore to their former brightness these two ancient authors, the sacred-profane rhetorician [Note: [Col. 0929] Saint Ambrose’s book *On Tobit* is found in *Patrologia*, vol. XIV, col. 759, among the works of the holy bishop. EDITOR.] and poet. I do not think that either of them, according to my candid confession, is foreign even to the condition of the present age.

For who does not know what Moses, the first lawgiver and ocean of theology, said and wrote? Indeed, should anyone be considered a Christian who neither reads the canonical and apocryphal books of sacred Scripture in teaching and learning, nor expresses them in life? [Note: [Col. 0929] Deuteronomy ch. 6; ch. 16, v. 18; ch. 17, vv. 9, 12, 18, 19; Acts ch. 5, vv. 34–39, v. 8 with what follows; ch. 10 throughout; ch. 17, vv. 10–12; ch. 18, vv. 2, 4, 7, 8, 14, 15, 17; ch. 19, vv. 6, 7, 20, 35, 38, 39; ch. 21, vv. 8, 9, 16–20.]

Nor has it hitherto been held a fault in Ambrose that, having become bishop from being an orator and governor or judge, he mingled many secular, and indeed juridical, matters into his sacred exposition, now reprinted. [Note: [Col. 0929] Erasmus before Ambrose’s works; Herberger, part II, *Postilla cordial*, after the feast of the Annunciation of Mary, fol. 192, at the end.] And certainly the Book of Tobit itself contains various admonitions and examples. There the theologian finds much concerning religion, persecution, and the burial of the pious; concerning true marriage; likewise concerning the guardianship of angels, the malice of devils, the begetting and upbringing of children, long life, the art of dying, God’s providence, the efficacy of prayers, and similar matters.

The jurist too finds there a broad field: concerning the commands of princes, confiscation and recovery of property, loans and interest—these two matters especially illuminated by that bishop of Milan—also promissory notes, marriages, dowry agreements, one’s own goods and stolen goods, wedding feasts and other things, captivity, journeys, inheritances, migrations, divisions of property, lawful modes of acquisition, and so forth. The physician and natural philosopher likewise finds there certain matters concerning waters, fish, eyes, blindness, physiognomy, fumigations, the care of the sick, and the properties of things especially useful to medicine.

Nor is matter lacking for the ethical or political philosopher and other philosophers: hospitality, patience, constancy, chastity, generosity, reverence and obedience among rulers and subjects, parents and children; then thrift, poverty, riches, diversity of dispositions, fellow-feeling or sympathy, wages and salaries, and the reward of servants. Thus everyone will freely and rightly concede that the books of both Testaments are the rule of life, the sum of studies, and a compendium of the whole world: such a gift that nothing more wonderful, greater, or more health-giving has been given to humankind. Whoever possesses it is happy; whoever reads it, happier; whoever learns it thoroughly, happiest; whoever understands it becomes most like God—as Tobias Hessius said among jurists [Note: [Col. 0929] Hessius, *The Case of the Sword of the Spirit*, axioms 192 ff.], thereby expressing in deed and name our Tobit.

Indeed, even the definition of jurisprudence alone—that it is the knowledge of divine and human things—sufficiently indicates that men of this profession are accustomed, and ought, to treat such matters also. [Note: [Col. 0929] The common doctors, on the beginning of the *Institutes*, *On Justice and Law*, together with the title, chapter *On the Supreme Trinity*, and the following title.] And perhaps someone would call it paradoxical that Saint Chrysostom dared to affirm that reading and meditation upon sacred literature are more necessary for lay or secular people than for clerics and priests themselves. He gave this reason: the more occasions for sin are presented to laypersons in the management of human affairs, the more remedies against sin they need, and these are to be sought from the divine book. [Note: [Col. 0929] Chrysostom, Homily 3 on Lazarus, in Hutter, *Commonplaces of Theology*, fols. 38–39; Rittershus, *Exposition of the Novels*, part I, chapter 1, no. 9, together with words of the same Chrysostom in Jacob Heilbrun, *Bucathol. Pabsthumb.*, article XX, chapter 20, chapter 3, fol. 764.]

Hence, I think it came about that, in particular in the preceding age and in our own, the Syriac version of the New Testament reached Europe through envoys; and that they taught Syriac letters to Theseus Ambrosius, the Albanian petty ruler and jurist; likewise that Albert Wicmanstadt, jurist and chancellor of the eastern Austrian provinces in the time of the emperors Charles V and Ferdinand I, rendered many good services in advancing this sacred undertaking. [Note: [Col. 0929] Johann Balthasar Baumbach, *Treatise on Oriental Languages*, ch. XIII; Johann Gerhard, *Exegesis of Theological Commonplaces*, vol. I, locus 1, “On Sacred Scripture,” sect. 3, pp. 557–559.] Above all, John Reuchlin, commonly called Capnion, published his book *On the Miraculous Word* and performed other services concerning the Hebrew language—this jurist being exceptionally conversant with sacred matters. [Note: [Col. 0929] Reuchlin, *On the Kabbalah*, *On the Miraculous Word*, *Mirror for the Eye*, etc.] Appointed by Eberhard, surnamed the Upright, prince of Württemberg, as envoy to Emperor Frederick III, Reuchlin preferred to bring back with him certain exceedingly ancient and finely written Hebrew Bibles, given by the Emperor in place of an immense weight of gold, rather than receive richly equipped attendants, horses, golden bowls, and other gifts. [Note: [Col. 0929] Brassicanus, Preface to Salvianus, Rittershusius edition.]

I further think it followed from this that not only is it lawful, in controversies concerning divine, natural, international, canon, and civil law, and in the public and private decisions of forensic and political disputes, to cite and aptly apply sayings of both the Old and New Testament, in accordance with the opinion and praiseworthy examples of Joseph Mascardus, Tiberius Decianus, John Althusius, Henry Velstenius, and Jonas Fulevius, [Note: [Col. 0929] Mascardus, *On Proofs*, conclusion 191; Decianus, *Apology for Jurisprudence*, ch. XXII, nos. 92–93; Althusius, throughout the *Politics* and *Dicaeologica*; Velstenius, *Political Questions*, question I, thesis 7; Fulevius, dissertation *On Sacred Scripture*, ch. X, together with Sirach 40:11; 44:4.] and others; but also that jurists from various nations and offices have written and published the following works:

Augustine Callia, *The Work of the Mysteries of Jehovah*; Francis Galetius, James de Graffiis, Melchior Zambramus, Ludovicus Lopezius, and others, treatises *On Cases of Conscience*; Nicholas Mangeorgius, a code *On Elucidating Mosaic and Ancient Law*; Thomas Galletus, *The Religious Jurist*; Horace Lucius and Innocent Gentiletus, works on the traditions of the Council of Trent; Conrad Brunus, *On Ecclesiastical Ceremonies*; Henry Bottaeus, *On Episcopal Synods*; John Francis Pavus, *On the Visitation of Churches*; Francis Duarenus, a treatise *On the Sacred Ministries and Benefices of the Church*; John Corasius, a *Paraphrase on the Treatise on Priesthoods*; Ulrich Zasius, *On Baptizing the Children of Jews*, against Stella, and an apologetic defence, *Must Faith Be Kept with an Enemy?*, against the theologian Eck; Scipio Gentili, *On St. Paul’s Epistle to Philemon*; and his brother Alberico Gentili, dissertations *On the Book of Maccabees* and *On the Latin Version of the Bible*; George Ederus, *The Household-Ordering of the Bible*; John Baptist Ficklerus, *Juridical Theology*; Sylvius Tintus, *On the Ordination of Clergy*; Martin Anthony of Genoa, *Manual of Pastors* and *On the Church*; Sebastian Medices, *Sunday Homilies*; Marcus Antonius Natta, *On the Passion of Christ*; Isidore Masconius, short works *On the Majesty of the Church Militant*; Peter Asylus, Joachim Hopperus, and Conrad Heresbachius, paraphrases of the Davidic Psalms; Tobias Hessius, *The Sheath of the Spiritual Sword*; Joachim von Beust, *Orthodox Expositions*, together with Latin verse renderings of the Gospels; Joachim Mynsinger, Peter Heigius, and Rutger Rulandus—who also promised a *Postil for Jurists and Politicians*—various sacred prayers and meditations; Eberhard von Welhe, *Theological-Juridical-Political Probabilities* [Col. 0931] on Samuel’s chapter *On Royal Right*; John Alexander Brassicanus and Conrad Rittershusius, a preface and commentary on Bishop Salvian of Marseilles’s *On the Government, or Providence, of God* and other short works; George Remus, gleanings on Solomon’s Proverbs and Ecclesiastes; Andreas Alciatus, Antonius Faber, Ernest Cothmannus, Justus Mejerus, and others, lectures on the titles of the Code *On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith*, *On the Most Holy Churches, Bishops, and Clerics*, and *On Heretics*; Thomas Lansius, orations *On the Care of Religion* and *On Luther’s Jubilee Year*—Luther, who at first was devoted to the study of law, being a great theologian, as Wolfgang Crüger testifies in his *Catalogue of a Thousand Men*, p. 191; Christopher Besoldus, *Philosophical-Theological Axioms*, and dissertations *On the Conversion of the Jews* and *On Samuel’s Royal Right*; Henry Cranius, Justus Springerus, and the Dillingen professors, *On Religious Peace between Catholics and Evangelicals*; Henry Gebhardus, otherwise Wesenerus, treatises *On Ecclesiastical Power, Religion, and the Sacred Ministries and Orders*; Jonas Fulevius of Chur—who held out hope of a complete theological-juridical system—a juridical dissertation *On Sacred Scripture*; Ambrose Lobwasser, the Psalter of David rendered into songs by German rhythms; indeed, among my former countrymen and colleagues, Gerhard Gisekenius, *On the Truth of Christ’s Body in the Supper*, and John Tilingius, *Handbook of Theological Disputations*. Other members of the body of jurists have also composed and made public other complete books, both formerly and recently. To these have very lately been added Christopher Schwanmann, with his Latin-German epigrams on the Sunday Gospels and Epistles, likewise his brief ejaculatory prayers, sacred sighs, and rhythmic hymns; Henry Besselius, with *The Trumpet of Repentance*; and earlier myself, by the publication of my discourses *On the Appeal to God’s Judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat* and *On Wilful Murder*, from Moses’ account in Genesis of Cain the fratricide, and at various points in my treatise *On the Law of Mills*, and its supplement *On Boroughs or Castles, Hearths, Grain-Monopolists, Famine, and Wage-Labourers*.

I therefore hope that I shall now be all the more excused: not only because, following from afar in the footsteps of those most illustrious men who went before, I have composed writings of my own and have now faithfully brought to light writings by another which had not previously been seen, adding thereto various readings, notes, and observations; and because in due course I intend to add a separate dissertation on the difficulties in the little book of Tobias—concerning the source of the Hebrew language, the Greek-Latin translation, the history or chronology, and the analogy of faith, and thence the complete rejection of its canonical status. [Note: [Col. 0931] We omit Hering’s more extensive notes, which concern the Book of Tobit, not the paraphrase of Matthew of Vendôme. Let the reader consult the notes of the Benedictine Fathers on St Ambrose’s book *On Tobit*, *Patrologia*, I, XIV.] But I also hope to be excused because I had a grandfather who was a theologian, as well as kinsmen by blood and marriage in the same faculty, and a brother—who, alas, died last year. My father likewise practised as theologian, jurist, historian, and antiquary. Of these men I am heir, imitator, participant, and successor in studies, labours, and offices, as I am in goods, blood, and relationships; appointed in the place of a kinsman to an illustrious lord count and father of the country. According to the powers granted me by God, for seven years I was employed there in counsel and judgment, in the consistory, and also in the visitation of churches and schools; and again, successively performing the office of syndic in the chapters or ecclesiastical colleges of the neighbouring archbishoprics and bishoprics. Such transfers or repeated holding of offices is adequately defended by the distinguished John Dauthius. [Note: [Col. 0931] Dauthius, dedicatory epistle before the treatise *On the Testament*.] I have frequently treated subjects of this kind. Finally, after living so many years in this present age, full of warfare and wickedness, in which the mind ought to be strengthened by steadfast examples—not so much profane examples, as Tacitus said, [Note: [Col. 0931] Tacitus, *Annals*, book XVI, at the end.] but rather sacred ones—for which end Luther commended this little book of Tobias as if restored to life, [Note: [Col. 0931] Luther, Preface to Tobit.] while another has recently called those who value human history above divine history “pseudo-politicians.” [Note: [Col. 0931] Adam Contzen, *Politics*, book I, ch. 9.]

From these considerations it also becomes clearer in particular, most reverend, very reverend, most noble, most distinguished, venerable, and most learned men, why I have resolved to present and dedicate these sacred-profane labours to you. For among you are persons of like rank to whom our Vendômois inscribed his little work. You are regarded as successors of those whose forebears—and still some among those to whose fidelity things are entrusted—according to ancient custom mingle the reading of sacred literature with giving and drinking, as Albert Grotius [Note: [Col. 0931] Grotius, treatise *On the Perfect Cleric*, ch. LVIII, no. 9.] and Jonas Fulevius report. [Note: [Col. 0931] Fulevius, dissertation *On Sacred Scripture*, ch. I, no. 25.] It especially befits you to live by this divine canon or rule, whether one calls you spiritual or secular, according to Albert Krantz. [Note: [Col. 0931] In Gebhardus, cited treatise *On Ecclesiastical Power and Government*, on ch. XXII, no. 310, pp. 300–301, and elsewhere.] Thus the treatment *On the Canonical and Ecclesiastical Books of Sacred Scripture* pertains all the more to you; you who are called canons not so much from a region as from religion, and rather in accordance with the rule of life than with the annual payment commonly called a canon, as Francis Duarenus [Note: [Col. 0931] Duarenus, cited treatise *On Ecclesiastical Benefices*, book I, ch. 18.] and Matthias Martini record. [Note: [Col. 0931] Martini, *Philological Lexicon*, under “Canon,” folio.] You often examine major and minor causes concerning ecclesiastical colleges, persons, affairs, and goods. You have hitherto proved zealous defenders and propagators, to the extent of your knowledge and ability, of the religion admitted—indeed, divinely commanded—in the Holy Roman Empire in these regions. You are praiseworthy cultivators of libraries and antiquities. Amid these long-lasting disturbances of sacred-profane war, concerning both public and private affairs, you have suffered various things with me. You have again received me into honourable offices, encouraging me with an honourable salary and hope of further rewards. Among you I have thus far found steadfast lords, patrons, and friends. Finally, this offspring of my intellect, born and brought forth again among you, accepts no other patrons in return or by reciprocity.

Receive then this work, whatever it may be, with cheerful countenance; examine it with your eyes and handle these new-old little books with your hands, until a more favourable time and sweeter leisure provide greater works, if not better ones. Fare well and live long with me in the Lord.

Given from my study, now at Verda, on the feast-day of St Michael the Archangel, in the year 1641.

To your most reverend lordships, noble, distinguished, and venerable dignitaries,

Most devoted in all fidelity and duty,

John HERINGIUS, Jurisconsult and syndic.

# MATTHEW OF VENDÔME’S METRICAL PARAPHRASE OF TOBIT

[Note: [Col. 0933] This title is the editor’s, composed from what follows.]

[Col. 0933]

## PREFACE

To Bartholomew N., and his brother N., respectively bishop and dean of Tours.

[Col. 0933A]

From the ancient field the seeds of virtuous character—  
A rich crop of justice—sprouts as a tender plant. [Note: [Col. 0933] In Barth’s manuscript: “of love.”]

Lot proves the glory of hospitality; Job, patience;  
Solomon, doctrine; Abraham, faith; Simeon, hope.

Individual praises designate the rest; Tobias alone  
Has all things marked out beforehand. [Note: [Col. 0933] Or “prefigured,” there.]

Tobias is adorned by almsgiving, firm worship of God,  
Hope, uninjured faith, and honour in burial rites. [Note: [Col. 0933] That is, service of God, there.]

As Jerome’s sacred prose translation relates it,  
Vendôme ploughs it in verse, of whatever metre. [Note: [Col. 0933] “Describes” in place of “ploughs,” there.]

O crown of the church of Tours, watcher over the sheep  
And bishop Bartholomew, whom men look upon: grant favour.

Adorned with noble forebears, glory of the world, honourable  
In bearing, jewel of priests, lamp of the flock;

A sun whose rays the city of Martinopolis lends to the world,  
[Col. 0933B] And whose honour honours the whole through its part.

Defence of the clergy, path of peace, at whose honour  
And light the twice-repeated day stands amazed:

You are a ray of the sun, in whom rare but fitting  
Beauty of chastity abides as an honourable companion. [Note: [Col. 0933] The other manuscript: “agrees.” In Barth’s manuscript the whole couplet is transposed.]

You are a ray of the sun, whose bishop-uncle was  
A lamb as pastor, lesser as ruler. [Note: [Col. 0933] Barth: “to whom.”]

You are a ray of the sun through whom Vendôme hastens  
To the pole of Tours, whose citizen was a bishop. [Note: [Col. 0933] That is, the uncle, in the other manuscript.]

Pitiless death snatched him away; as his most worthy heir  
You wield your father’s earned sceptre with your hand.

God chose you that you might feed the sheepfolds by doctrine,  
[Col. 0934A] Foster them by example, aid them by beneficence;

God chose you that you might willingly dispense  
The talents entrusted to you with manifold diligence. [Note: [Col. 0933] Barth: “handed over.” These two couplets are absent from the other manuscript.]

God chose you, a noble vessel, a vessel unto honour,  
A vessel special to himself, general to his own.

Live and farewell, glory of the Church; for one who prays, provide  
A harbour; drive away shipwreck and heal the ship. [Note: [Col. 0933] Barth: “harbour.” There: “to be wet,” possibly for *medere*, “heal.”]

Receive the titles of Tobias with your brother the dean,  
That a double star may make the timid path serene.

I rejoice that you shine before us with new light—  
For the sun gleams in the Twins and the other signs are void. [Note: [Col. 0933] That is, you and your brother, in the margin of the other manuscript.]

The sun gleams in the Twins, because the grace of the true Sun  
Blesses, increases, and nourishes you by the lamp of virtues. [Note: [Col. 0933] Barth: “us.”]

Live happily, brothers whom only bodily form  
Shows to be two; one faith unites you in the same mind. [Note: [Col. 0933] Barth: “one love.”]

[Col. 0934B]

You two are one; I marvel that two bodies, in mind  
United as one, are divided in body. [Note: [Col. 0933] There: “body.”]

I pray you—you, your own planting, your Amiclas—  
That you may cherish my timid course. [Note: [Col. 0933] Barth: *Amiclus*, perhaps a flattering contracted diminutive. There: “Portus,” or, according to the manuscript gloss, “just servant”; thus the humble man’s former name, Amiclas, would remain. The other manuscript: “destitute.”]

Look upon the beggarly little vessel of our pen. [Note: [Col. 0933] Barth: “your.”]  
Trusting in your favour, it does not fear the shoals of the sea.

It is shameful to crave the husks of swine; it is shameful  
For a pen to have served the Pierian Muses. [Note: [Col. 0933] The other manuscript: “it is wearisome.”]

This new work is taken from an ancient law to be read,  
As the work of the ancient Fathers bears witness. [Note: [Col. 0933] There: “summit.”]

Jerome translates, Bede expounds, Matthew  
Puts it into metre; envy rejects it, a friend keeps it. [Note: [Col. 0933] That is, “keeps it with himself,” in the margin.]

# TEXT WITH METRICAL PARAPHRASE

[Col. 0933]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0933C]

Tobias’ native soil is Galilee; his will is sacred;  
Fear of the Lord and love of religion are his. [Note: [Col. 0933] Or “religious”; in Barth: “and religious.”]

In the boy mature gravity performs its service: few days  
Make the tender body an old man in mind.

A boy of the city and tribe of Naphtali, in mature years  
[Col. 0935A] He gives off the sober fragrance of a man beyond his tender age. [Note: [Col. 0933] Alternatively, “a Naphtalite”; Luther: “of Naphtali.” This couplet is omitted in Barth’s manuscript.]

Among his people he is lesser in years, but greater in honourable  
Purpose; he leads the way by meritorious simplicity. [Note: [Col. 0933] Alternatively, “wonderful”; Barth: *merito*. For similar thought, see below under chapter VII, no. 25.]

The little plant bears fruit; in tender grass the ripe  
Harvest grows grey; mature faith surpasses grey-haired years.

The hazard of fortune tests the strong; gold gleams  
In the furnace, faith amid anxiety. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “faith.” The same: “gleams.”]

In King Shalmaneser’s time he is taken captive; with honourable  
Mind he remembers God, fears him in gracious hope.

Virtue laughs amid adversities; the winter of submerged prosperity  
Does not break an honourable purpose. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “submerges.”]

Tribulation endured for God’s name gives forth fragrance; suffering nourishes;  
Injury delights; punishment tastes sweet.

He shares his wealth among captives, is pressed by the common  
Loss, yet does not grieve over his own ruin.

He visits the sick, consoles the sad, feels compassion for the needy,  
And lovingly rejoices in the members as does the head. [Note: [Col. 0935] The same: “in.”]

He suffers with them by a threefold aid: resources, doctrine, heart;  
In heart he groans, by doctrine forms them, with resources feeds them.

He is a worshipper of the faith which circumcision, precursor  
Of our baptism, strives to celebrate with it. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth and the other manuscript: “is accustomed.”]

He hastens on the road to Jerusalem; he rejects gentile  
Rites and strives to sacrifice himself to God. [Note: [Col. 0935] The other manuscript: “undertakes.”]

He shudders to go to the calves which King Jeroboam had made;  
He rebukes apostates and keeps away that path.

He prefers divine service to things of clay; idolatry is foul,  
Foul, so that the work may be set before its maker. [Note: [Col. 0935] That is, “divine worship.” Barth: “idolatry.” The other manuscript: “maker.”]

He denies that there are many gods; he proclaims one, praises one,  
[Col. 0935C] So that he may reap all things in praise of the One.

He hates, loves, condemns, approves, curses, worships—  
Crimes, laws, wickedness, right, idols, God;

Right, idols, God he approves, curses, worships;  
He hates, loves, condemns crimes, laws, wickedness.

He sows, increases, nourishes, exterminates, rebukes, wards off—  
Doctrines, laws, honour; he sows, increases, nourishes. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth’s manuscript: “schisms, reproaches, deceits.” This sort of verse, transposed and wholly or partly retrograde, sometimes delighted antiquity, as is evident from other examples and follows below.]

Lest the light lie hidden in darkness, a double lamp  
Causes Tobias’ renown to shine more brightly.

The first lamp is manifest in speech; the second gleams  
In example: what the tongue does, the deed confesses. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “says.”]

Teaching is read—that is, known—in example; what it teaches,  
The interpreting hand confirms in action. [Note: [Col. 0935] That is, “is known,” in the margin.]

Under this teacher Judah remembers God; worship  
[Col. 0936A] Of gods departs; right service is active; error goes away. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “dies.”]

When the third year returns, he gives God all the first fruits and tithes  
With a compassionate hand. [Note: [Col. 0935] There: “all.”]

He sustains proselytes and foreigners; for the present  
He sows and scatters so that he may reap without end. [Note: [Col. 0935] “That is, strangers,” in the manuscript margin.]

He shares the distress of the afflicted, is kind to the miserable;  
The wealth he bestows he thinks will be multiplied. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “consoles the miserable.” The other manuscript: “scatters”; Barth: “may scatter.”]

Now the honour of boyhood sighs;  
The adult crop grows and rises into harvest. [Note: [Col. 0935] The other manuscript and Barth: “breathes its last.” Barth: “harvest.”]

A rose disdaining to be held in its earliest tunic  
Emerges from its flowery covering; its fragrance breathes.

The rust of earliest age perishes; riper age  
Shines forth and refuses to conceal its fruit.

Adolescence is a more suspect age—an age  
[Col. 0936B] Slippery, drunk with pleasures, lacking law.

Lest he have many mates like a stallion, Tobias appoints  
Anna to be his partner in the marriage-bed. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: *admissarius*, that is, a stallion mounting every female; compare below, chapter VI after the middle. Luther: Hanna.]

Not through Venus’ incentive, but through love of offspring,  
He takes a wife and loves to bear fruit for God. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “having taken a wife.”]

The licence of adolescence is bridled; to the bridegroom  
A bride is given—sober, just, and equal to her equal.

Virtue rejoices to marry virtue; honour rejoices  
To become the companion of honour.

The union of good persons accords and gives a sweeter fragrance;  
Flower with flower, brightness with brightness, is more pleasing. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “gives a better fragrance.” The other manuscript: “colour with colour.”]

Thus, by mutual consent, the chamber of modesty  
Conceives and sends forth its earned burden from prison. [Note: [Col. 0935] B.: “necks.”]

The field enriches the farmer; the fruitful  
[Col. 0936C] Wife blesses her husband with more flourishing offspring. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “wife.”]

The birth is released into a boy; the offspring equals the father  
In name, and by the father’s diligence. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth and the other manuscript: “is given the same name.”]

A new ray proceeds from the sun, light from light;  
Sun worthy of ray, ray of sun, brightness of brightness.

The worthy father blossoms in his offspring, the offspring worthy of his father;  
The vessel of the potter, the potter of the vessel, the boy of his parent.

His father’s guardianship teaches him to keep the course  
Of the law and forbids him to luxuriate in excess. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “caution.”]

That he may fear the Lord: this is the first teaching, assured  
That fear of the Lord is the first good. [Note: [Col. 0935] Barth: “may fear the Lord”; “the first doctrines proved”; “the principal good.”]

Then he comes to Nineveh, son accompanying father,  
Wife accompanying husband, with kinsman and tribe.

He avoids sacrilegious companions, devotes to rejection  
Gentile foods, and refuses to defile his faith by them. [Note: [Col. 0937] “For them.”]

He does not join their assemblies; indeed, he shudders  
[Col. 0937A] At those whom he sees offering incense to idols.

But because the righteous man honours God in his heart,  
The highest one repays honour with the honour of the all-powerful Father. [Note: [Col. 0937] Or “because”; Barth: “and who.” Barth: “as.”]

Shalmaneser alone grants him by divine gift  
That he may enjoy freer choice at his own discretion. [Note: [Col. 0937] The other manuscript: “of offspring.”]

He is pleasing in the king’s sight; the king’s favour and honour  
Give him free rein, not the rest. [Note: [Col. 0937] Barth: “extends.” Barth: “before.” The other manuscript and Barth: “love.”]

He distributes wealth to kinsmen, proclaims precepts  
Of salvation, and doubles the aid owed to neighbours.

His hand is kindred to his tongue; he joins instruction  
To resources and joins the burden of speech to honour. [Note: [Col. 0937] The other manuscript: “words.” That is, “joins,” there. There and Barth: “resources.”]

[Col. 0937B]

Thus he refreshes minds and bodies: minds by doctrine,  
Bodies by relief; by both he nourishes God.

He buries the dead, sustains the living, and active  
Piety flourishes in every service.

He helps by a fourfold piety: the living with aid,  
The dead with tombs, souls with doctrine, bodies with food.

Grace increases Tobias’ four titles of virtue:  
Lilies mixed with roses have greater savour.

Tobias is steadfast, wise, prudent, honourable—  
In courageous spirit, doctrine, laws, and moderation. [Note: [Col. 0937] The verses have been published by Barth thus far; I have not yet seen the remainder. The other manuscript: “by law.”]

Laws make him just, moderation moderate, doctrine learned,  
And afflicted flesh strong.

Thinking a square stone can build Solomon’s square temple  
By fourfold piety,

[Col. 0937C] He then sets out for the city of Rages of the Medes, accompanied  
By man, wife, son, and tribe.

There the sight of his kinsman Gabael’s poverty admonishes Tobias;  
Kind faith shares the wretched man’s distress.

Fortune, powerful over nature, outweighs it; gain, sophistry,  
And favour follow nature—and he recoils.

The venal friend wavers toward wealth, away from the needy man;  
But true, unfeigned love restores him.

Tobias’ piety does not know how to waver: he feels compassion  
For Gabael and does not wish to dissemble faith. [Note: [Col. 0937] Alternatively, “refuses.”]

Under a written bond he hands over ten talents of silver;  
The deed bears witness to friendship.

The friendship of King Shalmaneser toward Tobias, friend of the king,  
Had given these things; the client flourishes in love of his lord.

When the course of a long time has run, Shalmaneser’s hour  
[Col. 0937D] Of death draws near, demanding tribute.

The king dies, removed from the midst; his most wicked offspring,  
Sennacherib, seeks to squander the kingdom.

Through fault in the root the little branch is foul; the wicked heir  
[Col. 0938A] Surpasses his father in harmfulness.

The stepmother-like power rejoices to rage against the afflicted;  
The path of crime, servant of injustice, grows hard. [Note: [Col. 0937] Alternatively, “the afflicted.”]

Under this king virtue lies prostrate; impiety prescribes to honour;  
Reason becomes foolish; honour grows cold.

The wicked, unjust, idle man oppresses, kills, and excludes  
The righteous, innocent, and dead—by prison, slaughter, and pyres. [Note: [Col. 0937] Perhaps “holy persons.”]

Tobias cherishes the afflicted; for piety’s use  
He strives to dispense the wealth of mind and speech.

By love of the heavenly Father he accomplishes what the law’s  
Honour commands; he consecrates himself to the Lord and fulfils his duties. [Note: [Col. 0937] Alternatively: “he accomplishes by love of the Father.”]

He fulfils his duties, consecrates himself to the Lord, accomplishes by love  
Of the heavenly Father what the law’s honour commands. [Note: [Col. 0937D] This couplet is not found in the other manuscript and perhaps intruded, because the verses are made wholly retrograde by accident or design: thus a hexameter is born from the pentameter. We had another kind of this in part above.]

The king, returning from Judah, lies struck by a grievous  
[Col. 0938B] Wound and streams with a rain of blood from his limbs.

He rages against Israel’s people; Tobias’ dutiful hand  
Strives to bury the slain.

King Sennacherib learns that Tobias buries the slain;  
His wrath roars, and the cruelest punishment pleases him.

He orders Tobias killed and condemns him for a benefaction;  
For merit he tortures him; for piety he oppresses him.

Tobias’ wealth is confiscated—the wealth which, as a stranger,  
He regarded as common rather than his own; now he knows poverty.

God does not know how to be absent from the just man: Tobias is saved  
From the enemy, with his only child, wife, and tribe.

They flee to the antidote against death, use a friend’s  
Protection; the honour of kinship covers them. [Note: [Col. 0937] Alternatively, “love.”]

Tobias hides naked; seeking an antidote  
[Col. 0938C] To fear, he lies hidden with the Lord’s help.

After lamentation joy returns; the king’s jurisdiction  
Expires, joy returns, grief dies. [Note: [Col. 0937] “For joy,” in the margin of the other manuscript. “For jurisdiction.”]

After forty-five days are spent,  
The king crushes the potter’s vessel, the father’s offspring.

Tobias returns to the light, compelled to hide;  
He emerges, and his possessions are restored by the ruler.

## CHAPTER II

A feast-day presses on; Tobias labours for the service  
Of joy, and the cheerful household smiles.

He calls kinsmen to a little banquet; when the food  
Is arranged, he summons his son and gives this command: [Note: [Col. 0937] The other manuscript has “adds.”]

“Go, call whatever good men our ancestry commends;  
Choose the God-fearing.” Commanded, he goes.

While the boy hastens, ready to obey his father,  
[Col. 0938D] A slain Israelite lies exposed before him, stripped naked. [Note: [Col. 0937] Alternatively, “street.”]

Mourning the slain man, he admonishes his father by piety,  
Striving to act like his father and refusing to degenerate. [Note: [Col. 0937] That is, by imitating or representing him in conduct; or *moneta* is made by an image and, as it were, admonition.]

[Col. 0939A]

He hastens back to his father and recounts individually  
What he has seen; the father’s concern is wet with tears.

He rises from the table, goes away fasting, invites  
Piety, and longs to bury the body.

He takes and hides the body, because, injured, he dreads  
Ambushes; he fears to make what he does known.

At nightfall he sighs; he chooses the dark time  
And timidly seeks the friendship of night’s aid. [Note: [Col. 0939] “Desires in a friendly manner,” or in the other manuscript “is put beneath.”]

He fears gentile ambushes pressing upon him, since, injured,  
He recoils from waters boiling over. [Note: [Col. 0939] “Boiling over,” there.]

While he buries the body, compassion of heart honours  
His acts; the holy work blossoms in tears with his wife.

Watering his face with tears, he is not unaware that whoever  
Sows in tears will reap in prosperity. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “is unaware.”]

Then he returns home, striving to recall what Amos  
[Col. 0939B] Sings with prophetic mouth—or rather, what God says:

“Festival days are turned into lamentations”; in events  
The proclaimed words of prophecy are manifest. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “in act.”]

His envious neighbours reproach Tobias, condemn  
His service, and suppress his merit with chatter:

“You mindless man, do you dare to bury corpses? Can you  
Remember Sennacherib’s swords?”

Tobias remains steadfast in the act of his righteous purpose  
And strives to bear the fruit of justice.

A good man first becomes better and then best; honour burns  
More richly under the harsher clamour of the populace.

For fear of the Lord outweighs reproaches; he recoils  
From depreciating faith because of popular murmuring.

For the man weary from exhausting labour, most welcome  
[Col. 0939C] Is sleep; rest invites his languid limbs. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “savour.”]

The man, his numbness broken, lays his limbs upon the bed;  
The weary swallow chirps round its home and warms its eggs. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “lies on his back.”]

Nearby is the wall where, as nature commands,  
The nest of its offspring, pleasingly made with mud, is found.

Its dregs blind his eyes when the swallow pays  
The tribute of its belly; his sight perishes through swallow-droppings.

Thus patience tests servants, in order that it may provide  
An example, as the sun gives its adjacent ray. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “that wisdom may provide.”]

The threshing-floor of the highest Judge separates chaff from grain,  
Purifies limbs, and chastises in love. [Note: [Col. 0939] “Purifies,” in the margin of the other manuscript.]

What the furnace is to gold, what the file is to iron, the scourge—  
The burden of adversity—is to righteous harvests.

Blind, the man gives thanks; he does not murmur in anger  
[Col. 0939D] Nor seek noisily to magnify God.

Patience makes harshness honey-sweet; whatever bitterness  
Presses in, Elisha’s flour makes it sweet.

Elisha directs that the wild herbs be ground;  
The assembly of Israelites obeys the command. [Note: [Col. 0939] “Multitude.”]

They grind them into the pots, preserve them for nourishment,  
And nevertheless thereafter strive to make peace. [Note: [Col. 0939] Omitted in the other manuscript.]

[Col. 0940A]

When they taste the exceedingly bitter food, they are astonished; they cry: “Father,  
There is death in the pot!” The father applies the honeyed flour. [Note: [Col. 0939] Perhaps “very bitter.”]

See what lies hidden: the kernel lies in the nut, the grain  
Is present if it is drawn out from the straw. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “look.” That is, “in this story,” in the manuscript margin. Alternatively: “if it pleases.”]

Let the cloistered assembly be for you, people of Israel; the herbs,  
Discipline; the pot, severity; the prophet, God.

The true Elisha sweetens bitter things, makes hemlock honey-sweet,  
Strengthens the frail, and gives help.

The welcome flour is humble patience, the kindly companion  
And nurse of a noble heart’s character.

If anything is bitter to you, if anger grows cold,  
Apply this flour: strife smiles, hemlock tastes sweet.

You may wish to restrain with a bit or rigid bridle  
[Col. 0940B] The jaws of the she-ass, the burden that kicks. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “with the rigid bridle.” “Of flesh,” there.]

The burden is a weighty order, yet an honour; the jaw is desire,  
The bridle severity, the bit sluggishness, the she-ass flesh.

Tobias’ tribe insults him: “Most wretched blind man,  
For your reward punishment is given; hemlock for honeycomb.

“These are the fruits yielded you by your abundant almsgiving,  
Your repeated service at burial, your persistent faith.”

The man rebukes them, judging by reason; gentle, he recoils  
From making evil reproaches equal to evil reproaches:

Striving to dash the first impulses against the rock,  
He forbids the first beginnings of anger to run wild. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “law.” Alternatively, “strike against.”]

Rejoicing on the Lord’s day, with sorrow buried in the Lord, he praises him  
Whose burden is light and whose yoke is sweet.

Unmoved and patient, he offers the reproachful few responses  
[Col. 0940C] Which active piety commands:

“Do not speak perverse things against the Lord. I judge nothing  
Troublesome that the highest, all-powerful one does.

“We ought to await that life whose joys whoever loves  
Receives by continuing in faith. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “may receive”; alternatively, “may love.”]

“This life is brief, dark, sophistical; the life to come  
Endures, bright and true in faith.” [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “day.”]

Whatever the Lord does, blessed be he reigning at every  
Time; his praise is ever in my mouth. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alternatively, “may reign.”]

Thus temptation did not prevail over righteous Job;  
The blow itself established the man in steadfastness.

Not merely as perverted nature commands, but beyond it,  
Hannah shares her husband’s distress in a womanly manner.

The medicine of frail nature’s character visits the sickbed,  
[Col. 0940D] And the shell of the kernel tastes by its savour.

Nature is astonished to lie when the angry wife  
Shows faith to her husband in prosperity.

She strives to keep intact the laws of marriage-bed, though this  
Crop is rare when the farmer fails.

She shares her spouse’s distress and with companionable mind  
[Col. 0941A] Supports, obeys, soothes, honours, and loves her husband.

She labours for food; what her weaving yields, she offers  
To her husband in small amounts with manifold diligence. [Note: [Col. 0941] “Labours,” in the margin.]

She brings sustenance for Tobias, earned by her hands;  
Her mind compensates for what her work has less of. [Note: [Col. 0941] Alternatively, “for life”; alternatively, “brings”; “fitting.”]

When, after Phoebus has retired—when the sun is hidden—she brings  
A kid, the diligent husband hears it and recognizes it. [Note: [Col. 0941] “For the hidden sun,” in the margin.]

Neither ear unwillingly announces this, and the other  
Sense is active through mutual disclosure—or loss. [Note: [Col. 0941] Or “destruction.”]

“Give it back!” Tobias cries. “See that it is not stolen  
Plunder; let people keep their own; thefts oppress.”

Hannah grieves; her feminine nature returns; she declares herself in speech  
And rebukes him in a harsher tone:

“Your vain hope has perished; what your almsgiving  
Can avail is manifest through the destruction of your sight.”

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0941B]

Tobias doubles his groans; the wave of tears, handmaid of grief,  
Waters his cheeks in a streaming shower.

The creature asks its father, the vessel its potter, the sick  
Rivulet its fountain, for a physician—in voice, fear, and faith.

You are just, and your judgments are just, supreme  
King, eternal, mighty, life, light, salvation;

King of kings, Lord of lords, whose words are friendly [Note: [Col. 0941] that is, affectionate; ibid. in the margin],

Punishment grows sweet and scourges are helpful.

Whom the mind cannot remember [Note: [Col. 0941] another manuscript inserts *nescio* (“I do not know”); perhaps *nescia* (“unknowing”) for the following *noscere* (“to know”).], know, exalt in praises, speak of,

No tongue can utter, no place contain.

You dispose all things by measure; with you as mediator no work

Loses its due effect.

Not the sinner’s death, but conversion; life,

Not vengeance: blood does not please you, but rather salvation.

[Col. 0941C] I give you thanks; though blinded, I worship you;

Though condemned, I fear you; though tortured, I love you.

Do not remember the offences of your servant; although the sins

Of my parents be many, forgive the guilty.

We have done wrong; we have transgressed your commands; but sick

Wounds need not the sword, but the physician’s help [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “help.”].

Do not enter into judgment with the poor man, you who are rich;

With the servant, you who are Lord; with the wavering, you who are mighty.

Do not enter into judgment [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “Enter into judgment.”] with dust, you who are strong;

With the exile, you who are king; with the guest, you who are established; with the harvest, you who are sower.

What potter takes arms against a vessel, what craftsman against his work,

What father against his offspring, what sower against straw?

Let vengeance not please you, but compassion; bend

Judgment, spare the wretched, heal their evils.

I have sinned, I return: have mercy, I pray; the time

[Col. 0941D] For mercy is here; it is fitting that you revive the miserable.

Alas, I suffer, in need of one to revive me: the people’s outcast,

A byword among neighbours, a laughable pest!

Alas, I seem a worm, not a man, born

To consume crops; life harms me, and I ask to enjoy death.

[Col. 0942A] Alas, my soul is weary of life [Note: [Col. 0941] perhaps “after I have become.”], having become

A public mockery: I ask to die; death alone is salvation to me.

I ask that you receive my soul; let your holy will

Be done, that I may enjoy the love of my desired death.

For me, to die is life, and death is to live; death is to me

Sweeter than life; the love of death has the scent of life.

I pray: breathe upon me; I suffer: help me; I am troubled:

Console me; I follow: look upon me; I ask: favour me.

Thus grief summons death; the sentence of death

Is plain upon his face; the burden of grief is read in his expression.

To these prayers corresponds the similar complaint of the city

Of the Medes: the places differ, the time is the same.

Fair Sarah, virgin daughter of Raguel and Hannah,

Rebukes the transgression of her maidservant.

In the fragile sex, beauty admires honourable character;

[Col. 0942B] As a bride, she weds riches to herself through the pattern of her morals.

This woman had been married to seven men, whom the rage

Of a demon crushed, while her chastity flourished in unharmed honour.

Punishment crushed the guilty while, through love of the flesh, they strive

To taste beforehand [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “to take first-fruits of.” The former truly means “to taste beforehand,” in the margin of another manuscript.] the rose of virgin modesty.

The demon’s name is Hasmo [Note: [Col. 0941] for *Asmo*.], with the last syllable of the word

Remaining, lest I seem to give a title to evil;

Let the name be divided for God’s honour [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “love.”] [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “mockery.”]: for it is the shame of God’s enemy

To make himself equal to God.

There is no union of the Lord with Belial, nor of light

With darkness. Themesis [Note: [Col. 0941] perhaps *Tmosis*.] is acceptable on this reasoning.

Let the account return from its digression to the virgin Sarah:

While she rules the maidservant, the woman’s anger is stiff;

The savage maidservant plots poison against her mistress

Of a natural kind [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “natural”; perhaps *natura*, with the ending omitted.]; being talkative, she brings forth and reports this:

[Col. 0942C] “Barren woman, I pray that you may live useless and deprived

Of marriage, overwhelmed by losses and without offspring.

May punishment restrain you, guilty woman; may divine pity refuse

To make fruitful the murderess of men.

Do you intend, perhaps, to kill an innocent man also, just as

In a prodigious night you destroyed your husbands?”

The devout virgin grieves upon hearing this; the prophetess of sorrow,

Her virginal tears spring forth and wet her face.

She groans at the destruction of her reputation, lest her wounded

Reputation suffer [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “suffer.”]; an impetuous longing for death pleases [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “lies hidden.”].

She lies [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “sits.”] alone in her chamber, sorrowful upon her bed,

And applies herself to an unbroken course of tears.

As she flows [Note: [Col. 0941] alternatively, “flows down.”] into tears, she repeats her laments; this three-day fast

Is her food; here she is content without food.

On the fourth day, sorrowful and anxious, she prays to the Lord and pours forth

[Col. 0942D] Such prayers, her sobbing impeding her:

God of our holy fathers [Note: [Col. 0941] “father of the saints.”], gracious one, blessed be

Your name; to you be praise, glory, kingdoms, and honour.

The way in exile, life in heaven, guide in the world, lamp

[Col. 0943A] In darkness, sailor upon the sea, rest in labour;

Beginning without beginning, prior to time without end,

The succession of time marvels that you are.

Hope without the obstacle of failure, sun without a cloud [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “stain.”],

Peace without sloth [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “distinction.”], day without night.

I worship, praise, invoke, entreat, love, and seek you—with fear,

Affection, prayers, hope, devotion, and faith—

Because judgment, mercy, and truth belong to you;

You are the true judge: have mercy, I pray [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “on me.”].

You delight in forgiveness, not judgment; in mercy,

Not killing: not the sword but healing pleases you.

Absolve me, I pray, innocent of the slaughter of men;

May you wish to cleanse this imputed [Note: [Col. 0943] *objecta*, and thus the preceding ending would need to be inserted here.] crime.

I married not from the sting of the flesh, nor from love of male

Embrace [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “contacts.”]; remove the charges, spare me, I pray.

Spare me, I pray, because I prefer to undergo the hardships of life

[Col. 0943B] Rather than endure [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “be oppressed by.”] the fouler disgrace of reputation.

Spare me, I pray, because I suffer so many hardships in life;

I desire to enjoy a more advantageous death.

You search hearts and reins, O God; every

Heart lies open to you, the mind speaks, the deed is made known.

You know, supreme Father, that I am free from blood and slaughter;

I neither wish nor have wished to stain my faith [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “hand.”].

Your judgments [Note: [Col. 0943] perhaps an “O” has been omitted.], most just ruler, are a deep

Abyss, not in need of the human condition.

After winter you grant flowers [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “winters.”], after wormwood honey, laughter

After tears, brightness after darkness.

Why the men fell, you know; I do not know: perhaps you wish

Her to enjoy another husband while her virginity remains safe.

I prefer that my state of life should perish rather than that my reputation should be sullied by the stain of guilt;

[Col. 0943C] Let punishment cease, and guilt will remain [Note: [Col. 0943] in the manuscript this verb is called archaic.].

Bestower of pardon, supreme King, lover and giver

Of salvation, command the imputed crime to be absent.

You are my sole salvation, my sole remedy: either take away

The disgrace of the accusation, or grant me death.

I am afflicted: have mercy, I pray; defend me, for I suffer;

Help me, for I am tormented; protect me, for I am wounded; will you be present?

God does not know how to be absent from those who hope in him:

He visits the sick, raises the crushed, and drives away burdens.

Devotion obtains help: the devout virgin and the old man pray,

And their prayers, fragrant in the mouth [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “in honour” or “in scent.”], rise.

The aforesaid complaint of the two is accepted by God;

Their vows are granted: one salvation, a twofold wound [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “punishment.”].

Raphael, sent from heaven, is present; he heals [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “may heal.”]

Both, redeems [Note: [Col. 0943] why not “redeems”?] their disgrace, and brings help.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0943D]

Tobias gives thanks to the Lord because he is about to die;

He believes his prayers have prevailed [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “recovered strength.”] with the Lord.

This welcome death displeases the father, because the fatal day

Of death will scatter the joys of his child.

For a father flourishes in devotion toward his child [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “flourishes through his child.”]; the glory and love

[Col. 0944A] Of his child makes his grief glad [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “honour.”].

[lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0943] Here there follows not only a lengthy excursus, but also, in another manuscript codex, there stood: “Second Book on the Instruction of the Son.”]

The younger Tobias strives to resemble his father; the fragrance of a little rose,

The garden’s delight, bears witness to this.

A crop scents the field, a shoot its root, a stream its spring;

The crop proves the field, the harvest proves the crop.

A lamp shines by its light, light by its lamp; a child

Outshines through the father’s honour, the father through the child’s honour.

The field is renewed into fruit; the first rose makes the thorn festive [Note: [Col. 0943] for “adorns.”];

The pleasant little plant crowns the old man.

As the father recalls his child and the sacred beginnings

Of his disposition, joys arise [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “glory.”], and life is pleasing.

As he recalls the reproaches of his wife, grief overwhelms his joy [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “grief.”];

Grief [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “overwhelms.”] makes his love of life languish; he longs to die.

Thus he hesitates; thus the love of death debates and struggles

With the love of his child, and grief with devotion.

[Col. 0944B] The father wishes to live not for himself but for his son, although

He denies that he should live longer, yet does not deny that he is a father.

Death and life please the father: to the grieving man life is pleasing,

Death is pleasing; death flees from the father, while life grieves.

Thus he approves and rejects life, denies it, desires it, dreads it,

Demands it, attacks it, chooses it, hates it, loves it.

Grief argues for death; nature pleads for the child:

Thus the father wavers between the two.

Yet death pleases him for this reason: he hopes, when his service is ended,

For rewards; he hopes for the heavenly kingdom of the Father.

A stranger in the world, he longs for his homeland, that he may exchange

Exile and lodging for his Father’s house.

Certain of the hoped-for reward, he rejects the contagions of the world

[Col. 0944C] And meditates beforehand upon the road to heaven.

Therefore he calls his son, who is his father’s glory,

His father’s mirror, his father’s frequent care.

Believing, as he thinks, that the desired death is at hand [Note: [Col. 0943] another manuscript: “certain of death.”], he speaks thus,

Having summoned his child, to make disposition for his household:

“Son, I pray, willingly understand my commands: it is fitting

That a father’s prayers bear fruit in deeds.

Son, beware what must be avoided; pursue what must be pursued; banish [Note: [Col. 0943] that is, expel; ibid.]

Crimes; strive to cleanse the vessel of your mind.

He who sows must clear a new field of thorns and thistles [Note: [Col. 0943] alternatively, “ought.”],

So that the seed may be able to bear fruit.

Cleanse the vessels: unless you cleanse them, all liquor poured in

Turns sour, the seed perishes, and the harvest dies.

Cut away evils; cultivate virtues: thus the garden will abound with flowers,

The threshing-floor with harvest, the thorn with roses.

[Col. 0944D] Let the strong thorn of windy pride be absent,

A spendthrift of morals, tinder of wickedness, origin of death.

Let there not be the dregs of greed, which is amazed that its own

Store should fail—drunken thirst, full hunger.

Flee envy, born to harm: glad in grief,

It grieves at the happy and suppresses advantages it sees.

[Col. 0945A] Reject Luxury, lavish of blood, enemy

Of the soul, harmful friend of frail flesh.
