Let anger, while still small, be dashed against the rock, that,

Anger lulled, schisms may perish and love reign.

Never trust Gluttony, which Drunkenness serves; taste obeys it,

And sweet flavour flatters in the mouth.

Escape the contagions of the greedy mind, the wearinesses

Of life; be mindful of the divine gift.

Be humble, generous, chaste, merciful, rich

In peace; rejoice in God by the gift of a temperate life.

Plant virtues: when the thorns have been cut down and the garden cleansed,

The roses will be able to bear fruit.

This I pray, this I command with all my strength, from my whole

Soul: love God with your whole heart,

That you may favour the law given to you; as you are loved, let your neighbour be loved;

[Col. 0945B] The second command depends upon the first love.

Devoutly remember [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “remember.”] the sabbaths, as the gracious

Law commands: let the feast-days banish [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “banish.”] servile work.

May you possess honour [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “love.”] for both father and mother; by this devotion God multiplies

The course of life.

Do not kill [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “you shall not kill.”]; never commit adultery; commit no theft

[Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “you shall not commit.”]; bear no false witness [Note: [Col. 0945] for “nothing”; as others too have written.].

Let another’s money not make you covetous; no one ought

To luxuriate in another’s losses.

Do not take [Note: [Col. 0945] perhaps “desire.”] the wife whom your neighbour has married; rather,

Let neighbourly love flourish unharmed.

These, unless I am mistaken, you may hold to be the ten precepts

Of the law, from the tradition of the ancient fathers.

Do to others what you know to be beneficial to yourself; do to no one

What, if done to you, you fear as harmful [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “avoid.”].

[Col. 0945C] I judge that there are three handmaids whose united action

Makes every work bear fruit [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “Each”; alternatively, “into deed.”].

If the third is absent, a work will either lack effectiveness,

Or remain unfinished and half-full.

Whatever people do, the first handmaid is the will

Of purpose, the path of the mind preceding the deed.

She is first among her companions, and dutifully sets

The first step before the works of her sisters.

Then comes a prudent permission, the second, which strives

To bring together whatever may lawfully be expedient.

The third is capacity, to bring purpose to completion [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “will.”];

It labours to bring the task to its final stroke.

Cultivate these three in whatever you do: when they concur,

Every human work will bear fruit.

Flee the three enemies of the soul, whose cunning

[Col. 0945D] Harms it with threefold destruction by perverse means.

The three enemies of humanity—devil, flesh, and world—corrupt [Note: [Col. 0945] that is, corrupt; ibid.]

By their snares: spiritual fruit dies [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “wealth.”].

The flesh is handmaid of failure; the world is a sophistical enemy;

The apostate wrath [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “of the apostate.”] of the devil is hard.

The world promises wealth; kindred pleasure rules

[Col. 0946A] In the flesh; superstition bears the devil’s weapons.

The world tempts by greed; the flesh rages with yawning appetite;

The devil’s anger restrains the barking of lust.

The devil betrays the soul; the world seduces the eyes;

Sick flesh flatters the reins.

Despise the wheel of the world; restrain the flesh; worship God with all

Your heart. There are three weapons, a threefold remedy:

Break the flesh—it is beneficial; indulge the flesh—it threatens;

Afflict it—it favours you; serve it—it kills.

There are three handmaids of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “the flesh’s handmaids.”]: a slippery tongue, unbridled

Reins, and the ambitious greed of the throat.

The reins seek vain things; the throat devours; the drunken tongue

Quivers and runs with freer course.

There are two motions in a human being: flesh and spirit; each

Strives to diminish the worth of the other.

[Col. 0946B] The spirit is the bridegroom, the flesh the bride—the domestic enemy;

The bride presses the bridegroom by nearer deceit.

Harmful flesh fights [Note: [Col. 0945] for “labours.” But another manuscript has *mulcitat*, “soothes.”] against the soul; the bride harms the bridegroom;

The bridegroom asks [Note: [Col. 0945] that is, implores; or invites as a friend.] help for the bride.

She harms, he teaches; she destroys, he builds; he

Rewards, she tortures; she presses, he groans.

If you look upon the light of things [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “truth.”; alternatively, “accomplish.”], Adam is spirit,

Eve is flesh, the destructive companion of her bridegroom.

Guilty Eve offers Adam an apple; she appeals

With blandishments, caresses with a gift, harms by deceit.

Thus [Note: [Col. 0945] here and above understand “thus.”] the flesh plays with the spirit, flatters, ensnares,

Caresses, fawns, and binds by promises.

The pleasure which the flesh gives the spirit

Can be an apple; greedy flesh bites the apple.

There are three things in the apple: scent [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “colour.”], taste [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “and scent.”], and colour [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “taste,” but the other order is immediately repeated.]; indeed,

[Col. 0946C] Ambitious flesh is allured by these three.

The scent of praise, the taste of touch, and the colour of the face

Are in the flesh, by which a human being is ensnared.

From the forbidden bite comes death, said to be “all-biting,”

Explaining [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “explains.”] the meanings of its own name.

“Set out pure wine [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “pure wine” or “fear.”] and dice,” the flesh cries; the spirit’s honour hears

And grieves that it is offended.

The spirit cries out: “Crucify the guilty woman! Crucify

The flesh! Sick flesh destroys God’s temples.”

The spirit attacks the flesh lest the bride injure

Her husband and inflict associated harm.

Venus, boasting, pride,

Ambition, envy, drunkenness, strife, and deceit are kin to flesh.

[Col. 0946D] With its belly stuffed, flesh, the friend of Venus,

Sighs for the use of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “of the belly.”], seeking carnal members.

The moderation of food provides a welcome remedy for excess

And Venus: use little, and excess dies [Note: [Col. 0945] alternatively, “departs.”].

The spirit excludes the carnal vice; mortified flesh offers

Life to the spirit.

As Solomon affirms, there are three things whose confusion

Drives frail persons from a more advantageous home.

[Col. 0947A] These three are: smoke, dripping water, and a harmful wife;

Spiritual grain lies hidden beneath straw.

Water is habitual sin; smoke is ignorance.

The flesh, born to harm, can be a wife [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “A wife can be.”].

Son, I pray, unlearn evils; cultivate doctrine; restrain the flesh:

There are three weapons; cure the three [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “harms; a threefold remedy.”].

Overthrow for God the seven things which he hates; the supreme [Note: [Col. 0947] for “last”; ibid.]

One detests them, as you have warrant from Solomon.

Namely these: lofty eyes, a deceitful tongue,

A hand bloody with the killing of innocent blood;

To these is added evil meditation of the heart [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “heart.”]; feet readily

Running [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “running.”] to evils;

A lying witness—which, clearly, is detestable

[Col. 0947B] To God—and one sowing [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “bearing.”] cruel schisms among brothers.

Put no confidence in flesh; restrain

The flesh, lest vicious flesh restrain you.

If anyone weighs the matter of this origin [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “whence.”],

Whence comes pride? Whence swelling?

The flesh is a clay vessel, a lamentable vessel, dry

Hay, a fragile little clod, a foul-smelling sack.

The life of flesh is toil, its conception corruption,

Its end menstrual putrefaction, its origin mud.

First semen, now a foul-smelling sack, afterwards food for worms

In the tomb [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “in the tomb.”], though man grows proud of his endowment.

You are wise: wisdom withers; wealth, overflowing in death,

Flows away in a more shifting fall [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “Riches”; alternatively, “more freely.”].

You are good: goodness expires; you are honourable: honour

[Col. 0947C] Falls; you are strong: strong things lie in death [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “are struck down in war.”].

Ash returns [Note: [Col. 0947] for “is reduced.”] to ash; the dissolution of flesh

Shows the material [Note: [Col. 0947] for “beginning.”] beginning: mud.

Do not fear enemies: you must circumcise your own

Members for God; strive to cleanse away what harms [Note: [Col. 0947] that is, cut away; in the manuscript margin.].

Lest you see an empty thing, turn your eyes away; lest, through open

Windows, the winter of death enter.

Drive deceit from your lips; let meditation of the heart

Keep watch over the sight; pray for the Judge’s [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “Avenger’s.”] help.

Turn your foot away from a fall [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “feet.”]; turn wandering eyes [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “turn.”]

Toward tears, lest your soul die; love.

O vessel, strive to praise the potter; let a mind matching the mouth

Accord with it, that the work may confess praise.

Let it conform to praise [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “confirm.”]; unless you fulfil [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “holy” or “sacred.”; that is, fulfil; ibid.]

Words with deeds, frivolous words harm and the fruit dies.

[Col. 0947D] The dove bends its beak toward its wings [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “armpits”; this stands for “wings.”] in action [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “in the act.”];

The wise man makes his words bear fruit.

God’s sacred praise is the way of life, the heavenly life,

The praiser’s honour, the burden of the creature’s enemy.

[Col. 0948A] Divine praise helps; let the labour of the lips be a guest [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “becomes.”];

In your other members [Note: [Col. 0947] namely, members; ibid.] strive to magnify God.

Let not the slippery chance of fortune oppress you; live

Greater amid adversity, smaller in prosperity.

The greater you are, live by descending amid evils;

In great things be least; under a ruler, a client [Note: [Col. 0947] this couplet is absent in another manuscript codex.].

Be inclined to your own interests, humbly toward the advantages of your neighbour [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “advantages close at hand.”];

Rejoice at another’s applause, grieve at another’s grief.

Despise the wicked, cultivate the prudent, restrain the rebellious;

Give to the wretched, look upon the guilty [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “rebuke.”], spare the accused [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “of the king.”].

Whatever you do, let honour never be submerged in vice.

Let honour be perfected by reputation and profit [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “let the work or honour be set before.”].

Let love of justice be yours, fear of . . . [Note: [Col. 0947] in another manuscript codex, “exile.”], gracious shame,

[Col. 0948B] The honour of innocence free from crime.

Let the law be your rest in the Lord; the flesh a victim; the world

Exile; heaven homeland; God life.

Thus good, and fragrant with the sweetness of reputation, life grieves

To die deprived of the lamp [Note: [Col. 0947] that is, charity; ibid.] of morals.

Be devout in obedience, eloquent in doctrine, pleasant

In speech, steadfast in mind, pleasing in favour.

Let peace restrain anger, patience pride, sobriety excess,

Grace hatred, honour disgrace.

If honour is sought, let a burden [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “burden.”] be joined [Note: [Col. 0947] that is, joined; ibid.] to honour;

If you seek wealth, they seek to bear fruit for work [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “burden.”].

If wealth is sought, give, as you ought, to the needy;

Rich in wealth, bring help: thus wealth works.

[Col. 0948C] If honour delights, its attendant burden requires that there be

The fruit of burden: honour [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “honour.”; alternatively, “of burden.” The initial letters are, as it were, interchanged; the same occurs in both the following lines.], the fruit of honour: burden.

If honour is sought, let honour’s burden restrain

Its pleasures; let honour suffer with its burden.

Let honour marry burden; let the burden not cast down [Note: [Col. 0947] that is, lay aside; ibid.] the protection

Of honour, nor let honour disown [Note: [Col. 0947] alternatively, “be distrusted.”] the burden.

You seek wealth: bring help to the needy; you hunt honour:

If honour is sought, let burden not be fled.

Let not an income torment you, drunken thirst whose

Multiplied hunger springs from taste [Note: [Col. 0947] These couplets are transposed in another codex, which has “May it torment.”].

Among the covetous, drunkenness thirsts; present goods are lacking;

Though possessing, it seeks; abundance gapes; the full man is in need.

Alas, why do you desire dung instead of saffron-coloured [Note: [Col. 0947] for “heavenly.”] goods of character [Note: [Col. 0947] that is, worldly things.]?

[Col. 0948D] Alas, why heap wealth upon wealth? Why seek what is your own,

When no one can make even himself his own?

The possessor has nothing, because whoever is possessed cannot possess

[Col. 0949A] Anything; he does not possess himself, therefore nothing.

He who possesses is slave to what he possesses [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “a man is the slave of ambition.”]; he does not possess but is possessed;

Wealth possesses the miser; riches lord it over their master.

By the law of heaven, not by the law of the court, all things remain

Common: one liberty and an equal condition.

By heaven’s law nothing is private [Note: [Col. 0949] for “nothing,” as often elsewhere, and in Leonardo Aretino’s letter, as I noted in the afterword to my discourse *On Homicide*, no. 10, p. 101.]; from civil law

There arises the wicked love of private property.

Wealth is acquired by ambition; original community

Expires; divided equality flees.

Since you cannot be your own, nothing is yours;

No one can be his own: therefore I judge that nothing is one’s own.

Private ownership excludes from human affairs, enclosing

Everything in the fist of the First-Mighty One’s honour.

O happy man—and happier than every happy man—

[Col. 0949B] Whom the First-Mighty One appoints to be his own!

O happy he whom the supreme possessor possesses: thus he can be possessed . . . [Note: [Col. 0949] a word is missing, so that the sense is: “Thus all can [possess].”] by the riches of ownership [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “prosperity.”].

Again, death’s winter, ending life, snatching away breath,

Allows man to possess nothing as his own [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “promises to love.”].

At death’s coming possession ceases; both the possessor

And what is possessed pass to masters and are absent.

The slave of greed does not rule himself; misusing

Free choice, he lacks ownership.

Thus divine power deprives you of your own possessions [Note: [Col. 0949] perhaps *te*, “you”; or *depropriant* for *destituunt*, “they deprive.”],

Enclosing all things: the bitter plague, the yoke of death.

Since you know that nothing is private, and that the faculty of giving

Benefits each person, whereas things kept back harm him.

Distribute what you have for use, as need advises;

Do not apply help [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “wealth.”] to feed greed.

[Col. 0949C] Give to the naked, give to the poor; it does not become you

To use abundance while God is hungry in his members [Note: [Col. 0949] another codex reads *dedecet* (“it disgraces”) for both words.].

Four related things belong to giving: the cause, the will

Of the giver, the person to whom you give, and the material of the gift.

Let the person to whom you give be needy; let your will, with your knowledge, be

Kindness; let the material be your own; let God be the cause.

Affection produces affection: do not consider how much,

But with how great a diligence it was given.

Understand not what will be given to you, but why: the form

Of the will alone marks [Note: [Col. 0949] that is, designates, indicates, shows, as above he spoke similarly concerning the son.] the work.

Love is nourished by service, because the true friend

Is shown by the giver’s act [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “affection”; perhaps *affectu*, “by affection.”], not by the gift.

Sometimes decline what is given: acceptance of a gift

[Col. 0949D] Sells the riches of freer choice.

Often refusal helps; obtaining harms; refusal

Frees the will, gifts accepted bind it.

Free choice is sold when one lives at another’s

Expense; eat your own bread and you will be safe [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “free.”].

If occasion permits, do not reject a gift when it is given [Note: [Col. 0949] perhaps “sometimes”; another codex has “usually.”],

For if you flee what is offered, you refuse to repay it.

A giver who asks for gifts in return adulterates them, insists,

And has the appearance either of usury or of sale.

Give quickly; give gladly and freely [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “freely, gladly.”], lest kindness become

For sale; by a welcome gift you will be welcome [Note: [Col. 0949] that is, accepted.].

Delay darkens the giver’s merit; gifts given promptly [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “the giver’s merit—delay; things done at once.”]

Have more praise and more favour.

What is given at once is more welcome; the slothful hand

Of the giver is commonly the stepmother of merit.

Give according to the measure of your means, lest a prodigal virtue

Of giving fall into the opposed [Note: [Col. 0949] that is, opposite, as it were “in the region facing.”] vice.

You will be generous in giving what is worthy to be given, and in giving what is worthy to be retained;

As a spendthrift, beware lest you receive welcome but harmful things.

You will be frugal in retaining what you judge worthy of retention

[Col. 0950B] For use; you will be miserly in holding what ought to be distributed.

Let your hand be generous [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “for you.”], not prodigal; beware of being frugal

Or miserly; when the husk is despised, you will harvest grain.

Let prudent foresight govern poverty; as a poor man,

Strive to be sustained by compact sobriety [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “patience.”].

Poor man, flee luxuries: humble simplicity is required

To be the resourceful companion of poverty.

Take counsel from the wrinkled purse [Note: [Col. 0949] that is, it needs to be empty; ibid., in another codex.],

Unacquainted with coin, asking for copper with fasting jaws.

Let these three things displease you: lascivious old age, forced

Worship [Note: [Col. 0949] that is, the worship of God; ibid.], and poverty seeking luxuries.

The burden of poverty is honour to those who endure it; indeed,

[Col. 0950C] It makes more advantageous seeds of virtues.

Not lack of wealth but despair makes

Poverty of spirit amid an impoverished condition.

Not an accumulation of things but sufficiency of mind

Makes rich: let a little suffice and you will be rich.

Give thanks to the Lord in poverty; if you lie upon a bed [Note: [Col. 0949] for “bed,” as above, joined with Psalm XLI, vv. 2–4.],

Praise God with a sound mind.

Do not pray to the Lord in hope of gain: grace seeking profit

Seems to be for sale.

As he loves and embraces us for our own sake, so the Lord wishes

To be loved for his own sake [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “for.”], not for love of gain.

Give thanks [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “praises.”] to the Lord in joyful times; praise

God in the more tearful storm of fortune.

Praise condemns delay; delay, the stepmother of favour,

[Col. 0950D] Is a postponement. Remove delay, lest love die.

If you have received good things by the Lord’s granting, do not, when evil comes,

Accuse [Note: [Col. 0949] alternatively, “conceal.” In the margin of such a manuscript, “to accuse.”] God.

Love those whom the fruits of love proclaim as friends; and let love be love

Worthy of the prize [Note: [Col. 0949] that is, reward; from the Greek **βραβεῖον** (*brabeion*), of which the present form is corrupt. Martinius, *Lexicon Philologicum*, s.v. “Brabeum.”].

[Col. 0951A] The fruit of friendship redeems the losses of sorrowful life

And makes exile more welcome.

Life lacking friendship’s union [Note: [Col. 0951] that is, coupling; ibid.] is a honeycomb without honey,

A field without harvest, a tree without fruit.

Sweet is the meeting of friends, flourishing; there can be no excess

Of an honourable bond.

Be gentle with the gentle; cherish those who remember you; faith rejoices

In a just honour rendered by one who will render what is just.

There are three stages in love, a threefold grace: the first

Founds, the second cherishes, the third strengthens the work.

Origin founds, progress cherishes; faith continued

In service makes the bond firm for a friend.

The first sows the bond, the second waters it, the third dries the harvest

[Col. 0951B] And strives to store it in a little granary [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “bring it together.”].

Let a threefold nourishment be given to tender love under your guidance;

Unless you cherish [Note: [Col. 0951] “you” or “unless.”] its seeds, the harvest goes [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “dies.”].

A bond is nourished by an equal grace of character, an equal

Pursuit of studies, and mutual faithfulness in services.

Rule, I pray, the five servants which accommodating Nature

Has given as ministers for human uses:

Sight, smell, hearing, touch, and taste—the friend

Of the belly—perform their natural [Note: [Col. 0951] that is, natural; ibid.] office.

If a sense flatters, do not trust the malicious servant:

Often a servant makes his master bitter by his service.

While sight keeps watch over the body, abusing

Its office, it wounds the mind and presses its master.

Sight harms; the eye, love’s envoy, adulterer

[Col. 0951C] Of the mind, strives to diminish the soul’s riches.

The open window [Note: [Col. 0951] namely, the eye; ibid.] announces inward Babylon’s [Note: [Col. 0951] that is, confusion; ibid.] riches—the world’s ornaments [Note: [Col. 0951] that is, adornments; ibid.]—unto death’s losses.

It corrupts the flesh with pleasures and intoxicates it; thence

Bitter love comes forth, bitter plague comes forth [Note: [Col. 0951] that is, perpetual death; ibid.].

Sometimes hearing harms when the ear receives

Things not to be believed; rash faith [Note: [Col. 0951] namely, of believing; ibid.] harms.

Touch flatters [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “a flatterer,” with the punctuation omitted.] and deceives while it sells to the lover

A smooth surface beneath which rough things lie hidden.

Taste, the belly’s gluttonous hunter, the purse’s robber,

Rebukes empty hands with angry mouth.

Smell, less harmful than these senses, can be

Without fault in comparison with its brothers.

Compel these servants to serve you; for ministers

To rule their lord is commonly disgraceful [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “possible.”].

[Col. 0951D] Let your life be becoming, your discrimination provident, your counsel

Just, your action steadfast, and your reputation shining.

A precious hunger belongs to reputation: if reputation suffers,

Life totters, worth falls, honour grows cold.

It is more pleasing to possess the merit of reputation than reputation itself;

It is less to possess power than to have deserved honour.

[Col. 0952A] The merit of punishment is more grievous than punishment; to be killed

On a cross, I believe, is less than to have deserved a cross.

Remember renowned morals [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “remember morals.”]; infamy is the appearance of death:

Buried reputation buries honour.

The burden of disgrace outweighs loss; every burden

Is less than the destruction of reputation.

Reputation does not trust titles: take counsel from yourself, trust

Your mind. A true mind speaks truly; reputation favours itself.

Reputation summons praise, praise rewards, rewards the mind,

Mind effort, effort doctrines, doctrine honour.

Besides the father of learning there is practice; learning confined

To school perishes, while continuous learning flourishes.

Natural ability, knowledge not yet in flower [Note: [Col. 0951] namely, branches of knowledge; ibid.], springs up with labour,

The servant of virtue; strengthened rest harms.

Labour is the cultivation of the soul; flesh without labour

[Col. 0952B] Is barren, overgrown with thorns, and without a harvest.

From rest creeps the most savage pest of luxury,

Armour-bearer of love and spendthrift of reputation.

Unjust love is a judge; joining contrary things [Note: [Col. 0951] for “joining.”],

It causes the natures of things to degenerate.

In love antithesis accords: knowledge does not know,

Anger plays, honour is foul, the needy man abounds [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, *habundat*, as elsewhere *honus* for *onus*.].

Disgraces approve [Note: [Col. 0951] that is, praise; ibid.], praise reproves; despair hopes,

Hope fears; harmful things benefit, profits harm.

Anxiety is savoury in love; bitter things grow sweet,

Winter flourishes, cold things sweat, sickness nourishes.

Lest it harm, restrain flesh by labour [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “grief.”]; labour [Note: [Col. 0951] but then a comma should be added, or perhaps *labore* repeated, as shortly below *patrum, patres*.],

Vice grows languid; do nothing, and disease is present.

Follow the footsteps of our fathers; cultivate what the fathers

Cultivated; teach what they taught.

[Col. 0952C] There are four assistants of learning, by whose

Union study is accustomed to bear fruit.

First comes nature, which nourishes talent and increases it;

The force of exercise completes the work.

Talent is an uncultivated but fertile field, lacking art

And the diligent application of study.

A field is barren though cultivated: such is labour in study without

Talent. Join these two and the harvest is present.

Consult teachers of the law; depart from the assemblies

Of evil men; keep company with the good.

As you harvest honey from the honeycomb, nectar from nectar,

A stream from a river, and a ray from what shines [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “you will set bounds.”],

So you will gather grain from the harvest, drink from a wholesome spring,

And doctrine from a learned mind [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “doctrines”; for “you will gather”; ibid.].

Rejoice in the good; flee the fellowship of the wicked. A diseased hand contracts a stain

[Col. 0952D] From touched pitch [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “contracted”; perhaps “touched.”].

That you may please the Lord, do not sin; banish

Sin, ask pardon, and you will be blessed.

Give to the wretched; pour drink for the thirsty; gladden the afflicted;

If you are sparing with seed [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “sparing seeds.”], you will reap little.

Simple [Note: [Col. 0951] alternatively, “supplicating”] almsgiving, the handmaid of God, is an antidote against death,

[Col. 0953A] the gate of forgiveness, the path of salvation. [Note: [Col. 0953D] But what is said concerning almsgiving, both in the text and in the gloss, must be understood soundly in accordance with the canonical books of Holy Scripture and the more reliable interpreters.]

It pleads against the sins of the giver, intercedes  
With its Maker, redeems reproaches, prays for help.

Sin is the death of the soul; death is the penalty due  
To sin. Heal the wounds, and the disease is absent.

The love of the heart outweighs the hands; a humble spirit  
Is an acceptable offering to the Lord, a pleasing altar.

Give what you love, if a friend asks anything of you; if you do not give,  
Though the gift be bitter, you will receive none of the things you request. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively: “Unless you give what is deserved.”]

“Give” is a word of joy, a noble word,  
A honey-sweet word, the giver’s glory and honour.

“I beg” is the voice of the needy, an importunate voice,  
Prodigal of shame, full of sorrow, lacking favour.

Pay what is owed, I beg; grant what is asked to the petitioner.  
If you can, the honour of a willing mind surpasses gifts.

[Col. 0953B] Give, and it shall be given; forgive, and the bountiful [Note: [Col. 0953] for “best.”]  
Judge will forgive you: you shall reap seed in a like balance.

Scatter food; clothe the naked; receive guests beneath your roof;  
Bury bodies; live for God.

Despise the malicious; consult the wise; do not  
[Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “lest.”] reject [Note: [Col. 0953] that is, despise.] the wicked, nor desire to magnify yourself.

Pay the labourer his wages: every hired worker  
Ought to enjoy the recompense earned by his contract.

Love only your sole bride; cherish her alone;  
With this companion alone desire to join yourself alone. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively: “alone love your sole bride.”]

Let not the sinner’s oil enrich your head; and if some flatterer  
Caresses your ears, [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “may soothe you.”] withhold belief. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “upon.”]

If anyone censures someone, you ought to discern whether  
He is an enemy, an envious person, or an ambitious person. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively: “whomever anyone.”]

Ambition, envy, and hatred are three evils, whose

[Col. 0953C] supporters [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “makers.”] harm through ready credulity.

If an enemy censures an enemy, do not believe him: he desires  
To exercise his rage through you. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “thirsts.”]

The envious man strives to harm others; but the ambitious man loves  
Either to benefit himself alone, or to benefit his own people.

Thus the servant’s hoped-for reward [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “minds.”] perishes; enduring trust  
Arms the powerful against their servants.

Willingly discharge death, lest despair of life,  
Prodigal in earned betrayal, oppress you.

Death hastens; no escape is open. By nature’s law,  
A human being is bound to pay the mortal tribute.

Accept the Lord’s judgment with simple prayer, with goods  
Distributed abroad, with a humble heart, fear, and faith. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “with what is ratified.”]

What wretched exile would flee his homeland? Heaven is the homeland;

[Col. 0953D] the world is exile; here is the sea, there the harbour.

From this heavy valley comes a hard course, a slippery road, continual [Note: [Col. 0953] for “unremitting,” likewise there]  
Anxiety, unstable time, and brief life.

[Col. 0954A] Death spares the reprobate and strips the blooming flowers; indeed,  
The thorn rises in the winds, while the rosebeds lie low. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “lie low.”]

[Note: [Col. 0954D] Here at last the author turns his digression back to the father’s admonitions found in the text, as the manuscript itself indicates in the margin.]

Strive to enjoy the honour of your mother; honour your mother: it is fitting  
For offspring to flourish to their mother’s glory.

After your father’s funeral, when your mother has died, strive  
To continue the maternal tomb beside the paternal.

It is fitting that those whom one faith and the integrity  
Of love unite should not be divided by separate tombs. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively, “should not divide.”]

Be peaceable; flee quarrels. The bonds of peace  
Are heavenly nourishment for the soul; they nourish the body.

Applause nourishes peoples; a people, joys; joys, peace;  
Peace, rest; rest, seed; seed, … [Note: [Col. 0953] A word is missing.]

Alas, we live a needy life. Let God be feared with a friendly  
Heart when abundance of prosperity is at hand.

[Col. 0954B] “To Gabael, your kinsman, ten talents of silver.

My son, I gave them by a written bond as witness.

He dwells in Rages of Media: go and demand  
The debt. Return the bond, and you will receive what is requested.

Add to these paternal admonitions the duty of entrusting yourself to your father’s  
Counsels; unblemished piety commands it. [Note: [Col. 0953] alternatively: “Approach these admonitions.”]

Live and farewell. May you fare well when you come before the tribunal  
Of the Judge [Note: [Col. 0953] namely, God] and possess in your homeland [Note: [Col. 0953] that is, heaven] your Father’s joys.

## Chapter V

Thus the father, whose devoted offspring shows him favour,  
Grants assent and says these things:

“According to the measure of my age, Father, I am ready  
To obey you. I approve what you advise; I follow your commands.

If you do not know, I do not know the roads; I do not know Gabael.  
He will scarcely give to an unknown person the wealth he holds for you.”

[Col. 0954C] To him the father: “Do not doubt what is certain. Let the worst fear  
Of a prophet depart in an uncertain lot.

Do not fear: the depositor [Note: [Col. 0953] rather, in fact and in law, the borrower or debtor, in accordance with the text and the following words] will repay you every  
Deposit; he will return what is owed. Go safely.

When he sees the bond, he will render what is sought.  
Lest you be led astray by a division [Note: [Col. 0953] that is, a separation] of the roads, seek a guide.”

Commanded, he departs and sees a young man, offered to him, distinguished  
By the gifts of beauty; rejoicing, he says:

“Whose are you, young man?” Raphael answers: “I am  
An Israelite.” The youth asks him: “Will you make known the road to Rages?”

Raphael replies: “The way is familiar and open to me; I have stayed  
In Gabael’s house. If you wish to go and return, come.

I know the road; Rages is a city situated on the mountain called  
Abathanus.” [Note: [Col. 0953] Luther calls it Ecbatana.] “I know whither you intend to hasten.”

[Col. 0954D] The youth sees him but does not know him; he does not know Raphael  
To be his companion on the journey, though he asks him to be so.

The angel conceals his angelic gifts; the likeness of a man overshadows

[Col. 0955A] the spiritual radiance.

Piety bends low one whom nature raises; the appearance  
Of humble service compensates for the riches of honour.

Thus a cloud darkens a ray, shadow a lamp;  
Thus the summit of angelic nobility lies hidden.

Thus the angel, not forgetful of his teacher, wishes  
To be lesser in service though greater in rank.

The youth hastens back to his father, recounts all he has seen;  
The father gladly commands the young man to be brought in.

Raphael, prepared for the journey, comes, enters the house, and as he goes forward greets  
The father and the humble dwelling, [Note: [Col. 0955] that is, the house, likewise there]

saying: “May the Lord be with you”—words of salvation.  
The darkened anxiety of the old man is astonished.

Blinded by darkness, languishing, wretched upon his bed, [Note: [Col. 0955] for “bed,” as above]  
The poor man does not know whence salvation springs.

[Col. 0955B] Anxious and asking for the swift means of death, wretched,  
He recoils from the gifts and help of life.

Thus he complains: “Whence may salvation flow to me, poor man, whose  
Rest is punishment, whose living is death and whose dying life?

Alas, slow death comes but does not arrive. To me  
Death is better than life; I mourn in darkness and seek to die.”

Raphael answers him: “Hope for the Lord’s aid; hope  
In the Lord; love the Lord, and you shall be well.

God’s most welcome piety is a most sweet scourge; [Note: [Col. 0955] perhaps, “welcome to God.”]  
A teaching rod, a useful wound, a pleasant yoke.

They are a father’s strokes, like welcome blows: he heals  
By wounding; with wounds [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “with blows.”] he softens, tames by love,

refines and reworks [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “and bakes anew.”] his vessels, as a potter does; he scourges

[Col. 0955C] those whom he receives, as a physician with a wound, a shepherd his sheep.”

Then the old man: “Good young man, tell me, I beg, what is the origin  
Of your blood? From what stock do you derive your lineage? Declare it.”

Raphael replies: “Do you ask whether a hired servant is available to you, [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, *assit* for *adsit*]  
Or whether it is enough to make known his lineage?

Do you wish to hear? I am called Azarias,  
Son of Ananias. Let this anxiety fall from your heart.”

The angel refuses to exalt his own gifts; rather,  
With provident cunning he conceals his lineage.

Then the old man, humbly: “Friend, you will not be angry [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “will I be angry”]  
That I wished to know the condition [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “edition.”] of your lineage.

If it pleases you to lead my son to Rages, offer  
Counsel [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “protection”]; advise the boy and give help.

Do not doubt: you shall receive worthy payment,  
An antidote for your labour; when I restore the sum, you shall receive it.

[Col. 0955D] I beseech you, lead the boy to the Medes and bring him back.  
I ask more: the return pleases me more than the outward journey.”

Raphael replies: “What you ask is at hand. Trusting in me as protector,  
Under my guidance he will be safe; with me as companion, safe.” [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “assured.”]

The father weeps at his child’s departure, [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “offspring’s”] but rejoices in so great a protector;

[Col. 0956A] hope of return causes joy to prevail.

Child and father exchange sighs; [Note: [Col. 0955] perhaps, *alternant*. German: “each sighs for the other, or both sigh against one another.”] the child groans from love for his father, the father from love for his child.

The father’s care therefore prepares fitting provisions for the journey  
And strives to multiply thanks to God.

At his departure the boy doubles his “Farewell”; the father doubles  
His kisses upon his son with more tearful groaning. [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “the old man.”]

In tears, the father’s sorrowful old age pours out its soul; [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “tears [and] spirit.”]  
For the father refuses [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “is unable.”] to prove unworthy.

He cries: “The Lord will be with you; may an angel accompany you  
And govern you with vigilant diligence.”

Father and mother lament; the son greets them both.  
Then they depart and set out upon the journey. [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “set out.”]

Hannah, [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, Anna] his mother, breaks into tears; she repeats

[Col. 0956B] lamentations and complaints and cannot disguise herself as a mother.

He who pleased her when present torments her when absent:  
What brought praise in his presence brings grief when he departs.

A mother’s love shows itself worthy of a mother; saddened, she quarrels  
With her husband, as dutiful piety commands.

“Alas, would that the money had never been sought, for whose  
Sake you, the father, are bereft of your child, and I lament as bereft.” [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “parent”—or “mother,” namely, I.]

Why has all my salvation gone away—my care,  
The support of my old age, my motherly joy and honour?

The grace [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “glory.”] of my child redeemed the poverty that was ours;  
With his flight, salvation fled.

When present, my son accumulated delights; every  
Anxiety tastes sweet when it beholds the honour of one’s child.

Thus the mother. The father restrains her tears, wins her over

[Col. 0956C] with gentle words, and forbids her groans to overflow.

“Do not fear; cease your complaint. I think an angel  
Of the high counsel accompanies the boy’s journey.

God will lead and bring him back. Our son will return safe  
And unharmed, with more prosperous steps.”

At these words the mother’s complaint ceases; she checks  
Her weeping, ends her tears, and closes her lips.

## Chapter VI

The companions proceed, the boy and the angel; happy with this guide,

This companion—Raphael as the youth’s guide. [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “Here”; perhaps it should be read: “Hence, companion.”]

The boy does not know that, with Raphael as his minister and so great a guide,  
He is diligently governed by the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “the Lord’s.”]

Both nourish the way with speech; the faithful companion  
And guardian hastens before as guide. [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “dog.”]

On the first day he leads them near the Tigris; Tobias hastens into the river

[Col. 0956D] to wash his feet.

A fish appears, presses upon his immersed feet, opens  
Its jaws wide, that with gaping mouth it may devour [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “may devour.”] his foot.

He cries: “A fish is devouring me—alas!” [Note: [Col. 0955] alternatively, “may devour.”] “Pull it out,”  
The angel counsels; once the fish is pulled out, a remedy is at hand.

He draws it out at the angel’s direction, disembowels it, and then  
Takes out the entrails according to the guide’s diligent instruction.

He chooses and examines the gall, heart, and liver;  
The provident angel indicates that these three are to be kept, and the boy complies.

What remains of the fish, seasoned with salt,  
Suffices for food until the journey to Rages is completed.

[Col. 0957A] On the following day, [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “day.”] they relieve weariness with alternate conversation.  
The boy asks Raphael:

“Tell us, Brother Azarias, [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “Brother Azarias, concerning.”] do the things you urge us to preserve from the fish  
Have any usefulness?” [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “advantage.”]

The angel replies: “You ask not vain but serious questions. I ordered  
Three things to be preserved which I know are very useful.

Apply a portion of the heart to coals: every  
Demon flees when aided by the smoke.

The gall benefits the eyes; by the medicine of the gall every disease,

[Col. 0957B] capable of darkening the eyes, is absent.” [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “you are able.”]

Gall heals the eyes; the shared power of heart  
And liver, after the demon is driven out, gives aid.

Then the boy says: “Where do you wish us to remain this  
Night? It is yours to say; I follow your commands.” [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “I shall follow your words.”]

The angel replies: “Raguel lives nearby, a just man, a cultivator  
Of honour [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “guardian”] and a kinsman by nearness of tribe.

Your father’s estate is preserved with him; one fair  
Daughter blossoms there for him—the glory and honour of her father [Note: [Col. 0957] perhaps, “mother,” as below in Chapter X].

She is owed to you; ask for her [Note: [Col. 0957] for both words alternatively, “demand her”], and her father will give her. Indeed,  
With her as wife you will acquire lands, fields, and houses.

Your father’s entire substance is owed to you. Take  
Her, I advise.” Amazed by this, the boy says:

“I have heard—so report goes—that she was given to seven

[Col. 0957C] husbands, and they lie dead, slain by a demon.

If I suffer like misfortunes, I, the only son of both my parents,  
It is certain that they will die when I die.”

The angel answers: “Accept the welcome remedies which are at hand,  
The fitting antidote; heed [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “warnings”; perhaps, “perform,” likewise there] my instructions and you shall be safe.

The demon kills those whom the pleasure of the flesh,  
Not the desire for children, moves to enjoy virginity.

Whoever, like a horse [Note: [Col. 0957] see above, Chapter I] or mule, delights to abuse  
Marriage, conquered by love of flesh, perishes.

Before touching the virgin, persist for three nights  
In vows upon vows; strive to heap up prayers. [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “I beg.”]

On the first night burn the fish’s liver;  
You will drive away the demon: the liver serves this purpose.

On the following night offer prayers for God’s aid, so that you may

[Col. 0957D] enjoy the religion of the patriarchs.

The third night will yield its fruit, so that, blessed with the honour  
Of abundant [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “multiple.”] offspring, you may flourish.

Keep these three night-watches, lest, conquered by lust of the flesh,  
You earn the death that you fear.

Act thus: the fruit is at hand; by divine [Note: [Col. 0957] the word, or one like it, should perhaps be present; it is difficult to read] love,  
Let your flesh, still virginal, refrain from flesh.” [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “virginal.”]

[Col. 0958A] The fourth night grants the marriage-bed [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “the marriage-bed”] in hope of offspring,  
Not for Venus. Trust the instructions: a remedy is given.

## Chapter VII

The angel says these things; the boy obeys. At the angel’s  
Diligent prompting they go into Raguel’s house. [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “to.”]

Raguel meets them, brightens the hospitality with a joyful expression;  
Honour flushes his face.

The favour of a host smiles upon the guest; the welcome  
Of the host makes the guest’s hospitality more pleasing. [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “service”; alternatively, “can.”]

He gazes [Note: [Col. 0957] that is, he hesitates, likewise there; or, “fixedly with his eyes.”] upon the boy’s appearance, judges the image of his face,  
And is amazed at so great a likeness.

Because [Note: [Col. 0957] At the end of the preceding line, with comma or full stop omitted; otherwise, “from.”] from the child’s face he foretells the parent, [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “father.”] as a tree  
Is revealed by its foliage, so the father is read—that is, known [Note: [Col. 0957] that is, “recognized,” likewise there]—in the child’s face.

Then he says: “This boy, how greatly he accords in similar countenance  
With his cousin, the Ninevite, my sister Hannah.”

[Col. 0958B] Then he says to the guests: “Please disclose to me  
What is your origin; make known [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “certify.”] your lineage.”

The angel replies: “We are Nephtalites [Note: [Col. 0957] *Nephtalici* for both words] from among the captive  
Ninevites. God willed us to survive.”

Raguel says: “Does your household happen to know Tobias?”  
The angel answers: “We both know the man.

Tobias is our neighbour in city and tribe; this is  
Tobias’s boy and son. Believe it.”

When this had been told him, Raguel marvels and gladly  
Kisses the boy, bathing his face with tender tears.

He testifies his joy in words: “My son, I pray  
That abundant blessing and perpetual honour be yours.

Born of the holy father whom you acknowledge in speech  
And countenance, you are pleasing in a like simplicity.”

[Col. 0958C] As the man says this, his wife Anna overflows with tears;  
The sacred daughter Sarah [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “Hannah”; alternatively, “Sarah”] is wet with weeping.

Then he commands them to see the house; famed Anna, the maiden, and the father  
Labour at the offices of hospitality.

They prepare festive dishes; a ram is sacrificed. The honour  
Of hospitality, overflowing from the heart, makes the meal abundant.

Raguel runs here and there and gladly urges both to recline.  
The boy refuses [Note: [Col. 0957] that is, “declines,” likewise there in the margin] and says:

“I shall take neither food nor meal [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “drinks”] until  
You give me in marriage the daughter whom I seek.”

Raguel marvels, recalling that seven have perished;  
He fears this man also may fall into similar destruction.

While he hesitates to give what is asked, the angel says: “Lay aside  
All fear: God will give you every good thing in these matters.

[Col. 0958D] Believe: your daughter is reserved for the boy; the height of virginity  
Is owed to him alone, and to him alone.” [Note: [Col. 0957] alternatively, “is owed to him alone”; alternatively, “wealth.”]

Then Raguel says: “The Lord, I think, has received my groaning,  
Lamentations, and complaints; my prayers have prevailed.

The Lord’s mercy has assented to my prayers. After seven have been laid low,  
God has willed this one to bear fruit.

[Col. 0959A] And, according to the law of Moses, when a kinswoman  
Is given to her kinsman as husband, she abounds in the aid of offspring.

I gladly give her to the young man’s right hand, then, joining them in marriage,  
Her virgin hand to his. The father weeps and says:

“May the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and Jacob, cherish  
And bless you at every time. Amen!

May he confirm your marriage, make you happy with offspring,  
Strengthen your covenant, and give you help.”

Then the father requests a pen and confirms the marriage covenant  
By a written record as witness.

Then [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “afterward”] they apply themselves to the meal, as sufficiency requires—  
Not gluttony, not the appetite of the belly, but hunger itself.

When these things are done, with darkness come and the sun asleep, at her father’s command  
Anna prepares the bridal bed.

Then the pious father brings his daughter in to serve

[Col. 0959B] her husband; the compelled maiden enters the bed.

The maiden fears; she overflows with tender tears and fears  
The first clod beneath an unfamiliar ploughshare.

Her father consoles her thus: “Daughter, having endured many  
Wearinesses and labours, pour forth prayers.

May the Almighty grant joy after tears, honey after wormwood;  
May he redeem the cross by prosperity.”

Then the pious father brings in the young man. Each lies down  
So that hand is joined beside hand.

Equal in mind, equal beauty delights them, equal grace of character,  
Harmonious vows [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “life.”] and love of equal [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “father’s.”] religion:

A happy marriage, an equal union in which are joined  
Those whose piety is equal, whose lineage is equal, whose faith is one.

Both equal: equality of face and age joins them; and

[Col. 0959C] equality of mind refuses to divide them.

The chaste maiden marries a man, devoted to the just man; [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “pious.”]  
The man is worthy of his wife, the maiden worthy of her husband.

For the boy, pure of deceit, [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “the pure boy.”] abhors  
Boyish excesses, and knows that an old man is discernible in a boy.

Reason precedes age; the ripe harvest outweighs the field,  
And the lesser field is astonished at its harvest.

Virtue, transcending years, refuses to wait for the sluggishness of time  
And continually reproves delay.

In a tender youth there is the wisdom of one who has finished his course;  
The greater tree marvels at its fruit, the threshing-floor complains that it is less than its harvest.

Wondrous things stand revealed: the novelty of age, forgetful of its days,  
Is astonished that an old man lay hidden in the boy. [Note: [Col. 0959] See also how he embellishes what has been stated here, under Chapter I after the beginning.]

The young maiden blooms in character beyond the female sex;  
Rare faith dwells in her frail breast.

[Col. 0959D] Her becoming beauty strives to be subject to chastity,  
And chastity strives to reconcile itself to beauty.

Sweet in conversation, elegant in speech, [Note: [Col. 0959] that is, charming, likewise there] modest  
In expression, free from deceit, and dutiful in what is given,

Sober in mind, free from wandering distraction,  
Unacquainted with pride, she leads by considered simplicity. [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “pleasing.”]

[Col. 0960A] Her brow bears arms that exclude unlawful favour;  
Her beauty refuses to lend support to Venus. [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “Venus’s.”]

Beauty makes a pact for the peace of chastity and strives  
To preserve fidelity, though it is usually an enemy. [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “which.”]

A woman—just, strong, pious, chaste, [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “beautiful.”] modest [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “restrained.”]—marries.  
Thus she binds fast the things which tend [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “are accustomed.”] to drift away.

How far the character of the marriage described above differs from modern  
Marriages! What marriage-bed is without stain?

How much does the faithful Synagogue [Note: [Col. 0959] namely, that of the Jews; here is a short digression or application concerning fallen ecclesiastical discipline, as also in the following chapter]  
Of ancient time surpass our Church? From what source comes shame,

that modern Judaea has surpassed the Church? The shell precedes  
The kernel, the figure the reality. [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “because.”]

Alas, how greatly abandoned faith begs, and from what height  
The summit of Catholic religion has fallen!

[Col. 0960B] What woman now marries, or what man takes a wife, for love  
Of offspring? Who refuses to be Venus’s armour-bearer?

## Chapter VIII

The pious maiden, brought in, fears—an omen [Note: [Col. 0959] as elsewhere, for an indication or sign] of fear.  
Blushing modesty pleads in her most simple face.

The untouched soil fears the ploughman; virginity’s honour  
Fears the approach of the male.

Tobias remembers the angel’s instructions and then brings out  
The helpful liver of the *cassidulus* fish. [Note: [Col. 0959] namely, the fish, likewise there and below in Chapter XI; but see Martin’s *Lexicon philologicum*, under *Cassidilis*, fol. 403.]

He burns a portion of the preserved liver upon coals; [Note: [Col. 0959] for “joined,” likewise there]  
The smell of smoke spreads, and the enemy departs. [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “goes away.”]

With Raphael as minister, that demon’s wickedness lies bound  
In the farthest parts of Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “perishes.”]

Tobias calls his wife and says to her: “Sarah,

[Col. 0960C] rise from the bed; it is an honour for us to keep vigil for God.

It is fitting that for three nights we join ourselves to the Lord,  
Praying and striving to magnify God.

We ought to imitate our fathers; born of a holy stock,  
We must equal the fathers in merits.

After three days the granted [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “it shall be granted to us”; for “conceded,” alternatively, “promised”] privilege  
Of marriage will be given us.” Commanded to rise, the maiden assents.

The maiden is modest; loosening the bonds of virginal  
Modesty, rosy blush pleads upon her face. [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “loosening.”]

Both rise and strive to pour out prayers, asking  
To enjoy sound life in greater prosperity. [Note: [Col. 0959] perhaps, “prosperity” or “advantage,” as in the other manuscript or as follows below.]

Tobias teaches by example what he proclaims with his mouth;  
He prays as dutiful piety commands:

“Almighty God, may all things bless you; [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “each single thing”] may fire, water, air, and earth  
Offer you praises.

[Col. 0960D] It pleased you to form the first parent from the clay  
Of the earth; [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “it pleased the earth.”] he was alone, lacking posterity. [Note: [Col. 0959] alternatively, “prosperity.”]

Your providence ordained that Eve, his companion, should be joined  
To him, whence our race springs.

Thus join us together; thus strengthen the covenant  
Of our marriage; thus will that we may be fruitful.

[Col. 0961A] The wantonness of Venus does not move us, [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “may not move us.”] but rather  
Offspring, indeed the honour of posterity.

Consent of mind joins us and lawfully makes us friends; it loves  
The prize of modesty, not that of Venus [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “of tenderness”] [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “robber”] [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “love.”]

Grant us offspring, I pray, which may strive through ages of ages  
Successively to magnify your glory.”

Sarah replies: “Have mercy, I beg, have mercy on us both,  
That we may be permitted [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “that noble [one] may be permitted”; alternatively, “God,” perhaps with a comma placed earlier] to grow old together.”

Then Raguel calls his servants, when [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “while”] the herald of day,  
The cock, sings the day with wakeful voice.

The anxious old man keeps watch, fearing that this husband  
May fall, as the seven are known to have fallen.

Therefore, in mournful thought, he prepares a pit, a grave  
For Tobias, fearing that his son-in-law lies dead.

Then he says to the bride: “Let one maidservant go and quickly report  
To your husband whether he lives or has died.

[Col. 0961B]

If the bridegroom has fallen like the rest, it is fitting that  
He be buried by night. I refuse to degenerate in regard to my son-in-law.”

The servant, commanded, hastens to the bedchamber; having seen them alive,  
She reports it.

Raguel rejoices; Anna [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, Hannah] celebrates with glad  
Heart and strives to multiply thanks to God:

“Let us bless you, God of Israel: salvation has been given us  
By your gift; favour comes through you.

You exchange weeping for gentleness, hemlock for honey; [Note: [Col. 0961] for “bitterness,” likewise there in the margin]  
By your favour you give straw in place of loss, harvest in place of fear.

Your mercy has looked upon us. May your grace, which binds us,  
Govern us with perpetual diligence,

so that we may be able to offer prayers and burnt offerings, confess  
You as Lord, and celebrate your praises together,

[Col. 0961C] so that it may be clear to all nations that you alone  
Possess the rights of supreme monarchy.”

Then Raguel commands the pit to be filled in [Note: [Col. 0961] for “filled,” likewise there];  
Hope returns from exile, joy rises, sorrow departs. [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “dies.”]

He then commands Anna [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “Hannah.”] to procure meals, [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “dishes.”] to obtain  
Everything suitable by which honour may be duly observed.

Then he orders two fat calves and four rams  
To be slaughtered; Anna complies.

Gladly he commands the feast to be served, [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “commands the feast.”] brings in neighbouring  
Friends, and rejoices in the honour of his house as master.

[Note: [Col. 0961] Again an invective against contemporary customs, as above at the end of Chapter VII.]

Alas, how greatly the measure of that table differs from modern  
Luxuries, how great the wealth that a buffoon devours!

What profit is there in serving the belly, so that the spoil of the meat-market  
May weigh down the limbs with the belly’s headlong burden?

The prudent eat [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “eat.”] in order to live; the actor lives

[Col. 0961D] in order to eat, selling estates and selling fields.

Food is given for bellies, and bellies for food; [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “the belly for foods.”] God destroys both  
Foods and bellies: thus [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “as.”] the sacred words sing.

For this little banquet, nourishment [Note: [Col. 0961] that is, sustenance, likewise there] is enough for life;

[Col. 0962A] all luxury and all drunken excess are absent; few things please.

No hunting is sought to please the palate, no fatted bird,  
Nor pepper’s anger upon dry flesh. [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “not.”]

No birds turn upon spits; no arbiter [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “judge.”] of taste  
Here busies himself to label wine.

No feeling [Note: [Col. 0961] namely, “sense,” likewise there] flatters; no judgment of the palate  
Is sought: here it is enough to appease hunger.

Any drink whatsoever and every food and meal suffice here,  
So long as every hunger is overcome, every thirst by liquid. [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “and.”]

Nothing is supplied for gluttony; a few things [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “cups.”] for nature, many for the poor,  
All for God’s service.

Honour surpasses food. Amid the cheerful banquet Raguel asks Tobias,  
And the latter [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “the former.”] requests:

“Your departure troubles me, I confess. I rejoiced  
When you were present; when you depart, I complain.

[Col. 0962B] This I ask, this I urge: at my request, let it please you to prolong  
Your stay by two weeks.

Let your favour uphold the feast with prayers; do not— [Note: [Col. 0961] perhaps, with the preceding comma omitted, “our”]  
Do not reject the first-fruits of our prayers. [Note: [Col. 0961] The Germans say: ‘Do not refuse, defer, or reject our first request.’]

Armed prayers prevail, because [Note: [Col. 0961] for “when,” in the margin of the manuscript]  
When friend asks friend, or lord asks servant, he bears arms.” [Note: [Col. 0961] that is, “asks,” likewise there. The Germans say: “When lords ask, it is commanding.”]

Then, with cheerful countenance, the father-in-law divides his property  
In half for Tobias, as the written record bears witness.

After his death, he grants Tobias the remaining half to possess.  
They confirm and establish their agreements and bind the compact.

## Chapter IX

Tobias’s piety delights Raphael and wins him over;  
He obeys and gladly complies with guileless simplicity.

Deceived by his appearance, Tobias judges him a man;  
The angel refuses to disclose his angelic dignity.

He does not know what lies hidden beneath a human image,

[Col. 0962C] what is covered by a frail rind: the fragrance of incense.

He gives him thanks, honours him, and, prompted by the herald of favour—  
Affection—asks him with faithful diligence:

“Brother Azarias, I confess that by no reward  
Can I prove equal to your services.

If I give myself to you as a servant, no recompense  
Corresponding to you can be given; no reward is worthy.

For sacred religion is yours; honourable  
Counsel blossoms in you, grace of manners, steadfast faith.

You surpass human excellence: you cause mind, speech, and hand  
To bear fruit for the practice of virtue.” [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “you do.”]

Such faith, such great merit [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “price.”] disdains to win its honour  
For itself among human minds

[Col. 0962D] by manner, carriage, and limbs [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “words”]—you who, wholly lifted toward heaven,  
Cast off the burden [Note: [Col. 0961] alternatively, “work”; that is, “you surpass human nature.”] of human condition.

This I pray, this I ask: may the Lord grant me honourably

[Col. 0963A] to answer your honour with a more prosperous hand.

If delay holds us when we return, grief, restrained,  
Oppresses each parent with manifest anxiety.

My companion adjures me; his entreaty  
Binds me, and shame forbids me to reject his prayers.

Go to Rages; take servants and animals; safely give  
The bond to Gabael, and you shall receive the talents.

Go, farewell; [Note: [Col. 0963] perhaps *valea*, “fare well”] bid Gabael, our kinsman, farewell for us.  
I pray that he may come when you return.”

Raphael obeys Tobias. He does not know that angelic dignity  
Is never absent from the righteous.

He lends support to the prayers, prepares to depart, chooses two camels  
And twice two servants, and takes the road.

Then he hastens swiftly to Rages; entering Gabael’s  
House, he explains the reasons for his journey and says these things:

[Col. 0963B] He gives the bond, receives the talents [Note: [Col. 0963] alternatively, “the things sought”]; at Tobias’s request [Note: [Col. 0963] that is, at his petition]  
Gabael returns with him.

They hasten back. Gabael enters Raguel’s house  
While the marriage rite is being celebrated. [Note: [Col. 0963] alternatively, “marital.”]

Tobias runs to meet him with hurried step; each calls out in friendly  
Voice, about to speak: “Farewell!”

Receiving that greeting, Gabael bathes his face in tender  
Tears and recognizes [Note: [Col. 0963] for “recognizes,” likewise there] the father in the son’s face.

Weeping, he asks: “May abundant blessing and great  
Prosperity be yours; may the Lord bless you. Amen.

Excellent is your father, whose almsgiving pities  
The needy, buries bodies, and gives aid.

May the Lord give you prosperity, and grant [Note: [Col. 0963] alternatively, “God both gives and may grant”] you to see the children

[Col. 0963C] of your children; may he grant your race to multiply.

May you see the third and fourth generation, I pray,  
In the prosperity of your offspring.”

Those standing by answer “Amen”; then he gives festive food and wine from a flask.

The sweet meeting of friends breathes forth affection. Friends rightly  
Exchange [Note: [Col. 0963] that is, give in turn, likewise there] their stories with one another.

They recount their experiences, and the festive meal does not exclude  
Fear of the Lord or lack piety.

## Chapter X

Father Tobias waits, wonders, and is distressed—  
Fear in uncertainty sings of worse things.

He reckons the loss of the time that has passed and sick at heart  
Complains of his son’s prolonged delay.

When he remembers the worth of his child, he who lacks his child

[Col. 0963D] complains that he is deprived of half himself.

Wretched in unkempt grey hair, he offers lamentations  
Which the piety of his mind bids him utter:

“Woe is me, for I have harmed you, my son! Woe is me! Can  
Treacherous divisions of the road be detaining you?

Tell me, sister Anna, do you suppose that that debtor  
Has died [Note: [Col. 0963] that is, is dead] and that the wealth is being withheld?”

Mother Anna falls into deepest tears, heaps  
Lament upon lament, and tears her cheeks with armed nails.

[Col. 0964A] The mother sighs for her child’s return; with loving  
Mind she acts as a mother and refuses to prove unworthy of one.

The old man and the old woman give groans; neither finds relief  
From continuous weeping. Anna says:

“Alas, my son, my salvation, my glory! Let  
This delay cease, lest the fixed delay compel us to die.” [Note: [Col. 0963] alternatively, “lest this delay compel our limbs to die.”]

We sent you travelling abroad—you, the sole  
Staff of our old age, the honour of our posterity.

With you present, nothing was lacking; your present grace  
Enlarges and redeems whatever can be deficient.

We wretches suffer deservedly, since the opportunity for your departure  
And the cause of your journey were furnished by our own effort.

Thus the mother; the father consoles her: “Put away complaints.  
In uncertainty it is fitting for us to speak more hopefully.

Be silent, Anna; do not be troubled. With your son safe,

[Col. 0964B] you will rejoice; tears lack advantage.

Do not fear: the man who guides the boy’s reins  
Will adorn his return with piety and faith.”

The mother accepts no consolation for tears; she keeps  
A mother’s watch with vigilant diligence.

She goes about in circles, searches the crossroads by which he went out,  
Investigates and searches; she cannot cease remembering her child.

As she recalls her offspring, lamentations seem sweet; complaints  
Grow sweet; grief is fragrant with love for her child.

Raguel besets Tobias with prayers, presses him,  
Argues, entreats, and refuses his journey.

Thus he discourages the return: “My son, I ask you, trust  
My counsel; refuse to hasten your return.

Do not let delay trouble you. Let us send a messenger, [Note: [Col. 0963] that is, a messenger, likewise there]

[Col. 0964C] through whom your safety may be made certain to your father.

Please stay; do not depart, do not—  
By returning—make your father-in-law’s house anxious.

The fruit of friendship bids me speak these private words,
To take counsel together, to mingle jests alternately. [Note: [Col. 0963] That is, to mix them in turn, as in the preceding chapter.]

Tobias refuses assent: thus the shore is ploughed,  
thus a brick is washed, thus pious words fall vainly.

While the son speaks of both parents [Note: [Col. 0963] Another reading: *memorat gemitus*, “recalls the groans.”], he longs [Note: [Col. 0963] For “hastens.”]  
for his homeland and plans a sudden journey.

For the dutiful offspring fears lest the sad old age  
of both be destroyed by an excessive delay. [Note: [Col. 0963] *Luxuriare*: “to abound,” ibid.]

Again and again he excuses himself thus: “Cease, dear father,  
from entreating me; spare your admonitions, withdraw your prayers.

“For father and little mother count the days; I do not wish—  
[Col. 0964D] nor is it fitting—to hurry old people toward death.

“The father weeps; the mother repeats her laments. Woe to me if,  
through a delay caused by me, they perish while I linger.

“I do not wish my father to die on my account; I prefer  
to hasten the delay rather than die a parricide.

“May there be for us an opportunity of return. No entreaty  
can obtain it; command us to go back.” [Note: [Col. 0963] Another reading: “may it be granted.”]

When Raguel perceived that neither prayers nor affection could hold them back  
[Note: [Col. 0963] Another reading: “turn them back.”]—he perceived them so [Note: [Col. 0963] Another reading: “perceived.”]—  
he sorrowfully grants his consent.

[Col. 0965A] He gives him Sarah, servants, herds, camels,  
maidservants, and the remaining wealth which is kept in store [Note: [Col. 0965] “retained” for *reticentur*, ibid.].

He divides among his son-in-law all that he possesses individually; he adorns him  
with attendance, loads [*honerat* for *onerat*, as above *honus* for *onus*] him with goods, and honours his wealth. [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “wealths.”]

The son-in-law’s departure afflicts the father-in-law [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “and the father-in-law”];  
when he sees his daughter [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0965] A word difficult to read in the parchment manuscript; perhaps *ire*, “to go.”], he cannot fail to be a father.

Thus he prays: “May the angel of the Lord direct you, stand beside you,  
breathe favour upon you, and assist you with a more prosperous step.” [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “cherish you.”]

“Oh, if my offspring should be revealed to me, may I enjoy  
the highest delights and the fullest prosperity.

“May the Lord govern you unharmed, make you blessed with offspring,  
and rule you in steadfast piety.” [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “rule.”]

The sorrowful parents both escort their daughter; they give loving  
kisses and are drenched in freer tears.

With such words they exhort her: “Honour your father-in-law; love your husband;  
[Col. 0965B] reject adultery; despise the wicked.

“Provide for the household; be kind to servants; correct the insolent;  
care for the poor; applaud the good.

“Let licence for roaming about be restrained [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “for running about”];  
cultivate your husband’s kinsfolk with humble diligence.

“Be devout, simple, gentle, modest, faithful,  
just, gracious, humble, religious, and pleasing.”

Having said this, they repeat their farewell, give kisses drenched  
with holy tears, and depart.

## Chapter XI

The returning party scarcely reaches Carran [Note: [Col. 0965] Luther: Haran.] in five days;  
here it completes half the journey begun.

Raphael advises Tobias thus: “Friend, remember your father;  
blind though he is, he needs the sight of your safe return.

[Col. 0965C] “Let us hasten our journey. Your wife, animals, and servants  
will be able to follow us at a slower [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “later.”] pace.”

Tobias agrees; the two proceed, leaving behind  
the rest, who follow at a more languid pace.

The angel says this: “Keep the portion of the fish’s gall given you;  
it will be of help to us.”

Tobias is pleased by this and desires, in his father’s welfare,  
the welfare that the son enjoys. [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “which the son enjoys.”]

They hasten and rejoice in the sweetness of their native soil [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “he rejoices”];  
Tobias and each parent add spurs to their pace.

Anna watches from a mountain height [Note: [Col. 0965] That is, its summit, ibid.], devotedly  
performing in turn the office of a watchman.

While her eyes serve longing, she catches sight  
of her son, and the grief that was before expires.

She announces to the father the joys she has seen; running to meet her child,  
[Col. 0965D] the old woman goes out, forgetful of age.

At the son’s return, no service of speech can fully express  
the father’s joy.

The angel repeats this: “Bow down in prayer and worship the Lord  
when you enter your father’s house.

“Give thanks to God, by whose aid you return joyfully,  
[Col. 0966A] safe and enjoying tranquil contentment.” [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “advantage.”]

“By whose protection, whose assistance, whose  
counsel, our journey has borne fruit.

“Multiply kisses for your father. With the remedy of gall  
which you carry, anoint your father’s eyes: the disease will depart.”

Redeeming nature’s defect, faithful in piety.  
The watchful dog vies to hasten ahead [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “to go before”];

It fawns upon the familiar household and insinuates  
greetings to its master [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “and speaking”], speaking with a more lively-moving tail. [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “by the movement of its tail,” or “with a more lively tail,” that is, otherwise than it was accustomed.]

Tobias’s dog foretells his arrival [Note: [Col. 0965] Above: “predicts.”], goes out;  
both parents run—the old woman on this side, the old man on that.

The blind father empties out the years; he presses kisses on his son  
and feels him with a hand that hesitates in uncertainty.

Their faces are wet with joyful tears, with kisses and applause;  
the father eagerly redoubles embraces.

[Col. 0966B] As the angel advises, Tobias enters, worships,  
and dutifully gives thanks to the Lord.

As piety dictates, he applies the medicinal gall  
of the little helmeted fish [Note: [Col. 0965] That is, the fish, ibid., as above in Chapter VIII; but see Martini cited there.]; his eyes are healed and sight is present.

A cataract, like the membrane of an egg, falls  
from [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “away from.”] his eyes; light is restored and shadow flees.

Sight cheers the blind man; the sweetness of health  
tastes more grateful after preceding illness.

The strength of vision breathes again; deprivation, driven off,  
yields; possession returns and gladdens the old man.

The forerunner is glad that his staff can cease; the hand  
which is wont to test the way rests.

The old man and aged woman glorify the Lord; joy overwhelms them.  
The old man prays; she says this:

[Col. 0966C] “Let us bless you, God of Israel: you are to me a welcome  
protection, the end of sickness, the way of health.

“You test in order to lift up; you press in order to heal; by scourges  
you cure; by wounds you know how to make the father fragrant again.

“I praise you, glorify you, proclaim you, by whose  
gift the offspring comes to be seen.” [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “is given” or “returns”; because of the following verse.]

When the seventh day had passed, the sacred retinue—camels,  
servants, and the rest—arrives.

It brings [Note: [Col. 0965] Here “carries,” ibid.] Raguel’s wealth, and the deposit entrusted to Gabael,  
to gladden the parents-in-law through the bride.

Old Anna runs about; the daughter-in-law rejoices; the household  
sweats in dutiful services for its friends.

Having met Tobias, the tribe rejoices [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: “rejoice together”]; friends  
assemble, celebrate their happiness, and exchange words.

Nabogar and Caphat [Note: [Col. 0965] Another reading: Nabaoth and Acar; Luther: Nabath and Achior.], friends of the father, arrive,  
[Col. 0966D] together with kinsmen related through the tribe.

The younger Tobias exults, tells of his successes,  
and displays both the journey’s benefits and its riches.

He magnifies Raphael’s praises: under his guidance the height  
of the Almighty enabled him to go and return in health.

After the applause of kinsmen and friends, the father  
[Col. 0967A] summons his companions; the household flourishes with a double honour. [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “the place.”]

While favour weds fortune, the fruit of honour [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “love.”]  
is fuller: favour serves here, lineage there.

Here they rejoice in the son’s return; here in the father’s restored sight [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “the sight of the father.”]—  
sight, [Note: [Col. 0967] Thus this word remains.] so the twofold cause doubles their joys.

For seven days the joyful tribe continues festive banquets,  
sweetening the feast with applause. [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “sweetening.”]

## Chapter XII

Then the father speaks to his son [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “speaks to the son.”]: “What rewards worthy  
of this man, what recompense shall we give him?

“For he proved to be your faithful companion—useful, nurturing,  
truthful, provident in counsel, powerful in skill.

“Nothing mortal flavours his conduct; the honour of his speech  
proclaims the integrity of a sacred mind.”

The son replies: “The companion is worthy of reward; rewards worthy  
[Col. 0967B] of his labour ought to correspond to his labour.

“How great his faithfulness, what honour, what gratitude are due him—  
no tongue and no effort can establish.

“The worker is worthy of his payment. Consider how great  
a benefit he has bestowed.

“He guided and directed our journey, faithfully and devoutly returned me  
safe, went before our steps, and attended us in our home.

“He rescued me from the fish’s bite, advised me to marry Sarah,  
drove the demon away [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “expelled.”], and thereby brought salvation.

“Proceeding to Rages [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “going on after Rages.”], he brought Gabael  
the talents that were sought; father, you see this through his help.

“He restored three benefits: he comforts you in sorrow,  
restores sight to you when blind, and makes you a father through offspring.

“He was gentle in service, modest in speech,  
[Col. 0967C] steadfast in purpose, sacred in religion.

“Whoever undertakes to bring forth his praises prepares  
to outshine the sun with famous [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “smoky.”] torches.

“What fitting wages shall we give the man? A dowry demands  
that dowry be repaid by dowry, favour by favour.

“Go, I pray [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “ask.”], father; may he deign to receive  
half the estate—give more generously to one who deserves it.

“Since faithfulness deserves a final harvest, let him receive it;  
when much has been sown, the harvest is small.” [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “days.”]

“What [Note: [Col. 0967] Or “what.”] he has sown, let him reap; let him enjoy the fruit  
of the vineyard he cultivated; he broke the soil with the plough, let him harvest grain.”

After these words, father and son summon Raphael;  
they come together and sit within the house.

Thus says the father: “May God grant you worthy wages  
for your merits; live in the honour of a harvest you deserve.

“What our poverty cannot do, may divine power  
[Col. 0967D] supply, lest honour suffer eclipse.

“Receive half the estate; take with cheerful countenance
