what is given. The gift bears the fragrance of the giver’s honour.”

The angelic splendour is revealed [Note: [Col. 0967] In the margin of the manuscript: “is revealed.”]; the angel makes ready; error  
[Col. 0968A] departs, truth returns, and the lamp becomes visible.

Splendour rises from darkness; grain is drawn from chaff,  
the kernel from its husk, brightness from cloud.

The seeker after truth puts off ambiguity; day emerges  
from opaque night; a flame buried in smoke gleams.

The angel says: “I do not desire a mortal price [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “I do not desire the price.”], nor do I  
need these things; I seek a spiritual gift.

“Bless the Lord who gives; let the work confess its maker,  
and the work acknowledge its author.

“A royal secret calls for the king; the mystery lay hidden for a time;  
let the work be displayed.” [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “honour.”]

For one who fasts, almsgiving, a just life  
joined together [Note: [Col. 0967] In the margin, “joined.”] can reconcile the guilty to God.

Almsgiving frees from the snares [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “punishments.”] of death, washes away filth,  
[Col. 0968B] and makes sweet plea to the Author [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “actor.”] through its work.

It bestows life everlasting to come, bodily honour,  
and spiritual glory.

Its companions are devotion, trust, the applause  
of the mind, sobriety, and unblemished faith.

Whoever commits wicked deeds enslaves the soul, pursues  
the honourable, condemns the just, and lacks honour.

Alas, alas! Death is the recompense of sin; anxiety its heir,  
grief its armour-bearer, anger its companion.

I desire to reveal what is hidden; God willed  
that I should lie concealed under a human appearance.

Whenever you used to clothe the naked, bury the dead,  
and feed beggars, I stood beside you.

Consider that I poured out prayers for you [Note: [Col. 0967D] Beware here of the papist intercession of angels for human beings, as in what is inserted here and elsewhere concerning almsgiving: [Col. 0968D]],  
[Col. 0968C] and, compassionate toward one praying, the grace of the Lord sent help.

Do not let divine scourges trouble you: the Father’s honour [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “love.”] wished  
to test [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “to be tested.”] you by a healing wound.

God sent me here so that Sarah might marry, once  
the demon had been driven away, and so that you might not lack sight as a needy man.

I am one of the seven spirits to whom it is granted  
to stand before the presence of the supreme ruler. [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “president.”]

There was a double cause [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “the cause was double,” as in the following verse.] of my coming: Sarah’s prayer  
and yours; there was one concern, a double ruin.

I am Raphael, angel of the supreme Father.” Both hear [Note: [Col. 0967] That is, father and son.]  
and marvel; terror entreats with astonished mouth.

They prostrate themselves and bow their faces; the angel comforts  
the distressed, restores the fearful, and says this:

“May peace remain with you [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “I advise”; therefore a semicolon must be placed before.]; do not fear. The will  
of the Lord sent me; I follow the Father’s [Note: [Col. 0967] Another reading: “heavenly.”] commands.

[Col. 0968D] Heavenly compassion cared for you; it is fitting that you  
continually offer thanks to God.” [Note: [Col. 0967] In the margin of another manuscript is found: “prayers.”]

“I appeared to you mortals to be a man, using  
delights, drink, clothing, sleep, and food.

[Col. 0969A] I do not taste mortal foods; worship feeds me;  
spiritual seasoning sustains me.

The Lord’s radiance shines upon me; the sight of the supreme  
ruler’s lamp cannot satisfy me.

The time asks that I return; therefore I shall return to him  
who sent me. It is fitting that we celebrate him.

This I exhort: bless the Lord, sing psalms,  
chant praises, and celebrate God’s [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “to God.”] glory.” [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “God,” in both places, with the punctuation transposed.]

Having said this, he vanishes from their sight; no use of vision  
can make known his being carried back to his homeland. [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “from his homeland.”]

For three hours they lie prostrate on the ground; ecstasy seizes both;  
they multiply vows and pour out [Note: [Col. 0969] Perhaps “flow out.”] prayers.

Each labours earnestly over the Lord’s wonders,  
and they are wet with praises [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “things to be praised”; perhaps “praising,” with *and* omitted.] and more mournful weeping.

But because Raphael has returned, whether he answered  
[Col. 0969B] truthfully, he prepares to make plain by deserved inquiry. [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “is wont.”]

A serious and fertile question arises, worthy  
of resolution, lest what should be disclosed remain hidden.

Let it be examined whether he is a true angel. Far be it—  
far be it—that deceit should sin in an angelic mouth.

The companion-messenger [Note: [Col. 0969] *Paranymphus*, “messenger,” as above.] could speak only truth, moistened by the pleasant  
fountain from which streams of truth flow.

He had said: “I am called Azariah,  
son of Ananias.” Once the bark is cut, the grains are visible.

Ash wraps a small fire, a lantern wraps a lamp,  
a voice wraps meaning, a shell the kernel, a spark its radiance.

May grain shine forth from straw, the essence of form from its covering,  
the reality from shadow, flame from ash, lamp from clay.

Consider what lies hidden; let the riddles be opened. Let what the spirit recounts  
be truth to you—kind *nois*. [Note: [Col. 0969] Greek, for “divine mind,” as above.]

[Col. 0969C] Azariah is called “helper,” Ananias  
“grace,” or “glory of God”: fix [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “join.”] your faith upon this.

For God, through angelic ministry, bestows his gifts,  
foretokens signs, and supplies [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “administers.”] assistance.

While nature serves God and fulfils heavenly  
commands, vessels assist the potter and limbs the head.

For divine power may rightly use creatures, by right of power,  
for its own rights [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “commands.”].

Those whom the adoption of the supreme Father exalts as little sons,  
the Lord’s commands ought to assist.

Consult the Scriptures; read Paul’s teachings. Paul  
asserts that we [Note: [Col. 0969] There: “these.”] are God’s fellow-workers.

Every human being [Note: [Col. 0969] That is, “man.”] is Azariah, son of Ananias,  
when, through his service, God’s grace—δόξα, “glory” [Note: [Col. 0969] Greek, for “glory.”]—is made manifest.

[Col. 0969D] Thus the sleeping doubt lies still; clouds shine,  
the reality gleams, the spirit speaks, the shadow is silent.

## Chapter XIII

The aged woman and the old man, more mature in years  
[Note: [Col. 0969] That is, Anna and Tobias, ibid.] and understanding, marvel; the old man prays and says this:

“King, eternal God, to you be praise, glory, and  
[Col. 0970A] an immortal kingdom; to you be honour without end.

You alone are powerful everywhere; you alone rule all things; you alone are  
King [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “sun.”] of justice, a sun shining without cloud.

Air, fire, water, and place contained within locality [Note: [Col. 0969] That is, what is contained; “container” for earth.]  
revere and worship you alone as the God without end.

Whatever has been, is made, or is, may confess you; and let every  
tongue desire to magnify your name.

You are king, and will be, without beginning and without end: creating all  
created things, you cannot have a predecessor.

The ruler neither had nor can have beginnings,  
from whom the beginning itself takes its origin.

God neither began nor will begin [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “will begin.”] to be: his power  
was the source and origin of beginning.

The cause of causes cannot have begun, the creator  
of the city, origin of good, and prior to beginning.

He who made all things is before all [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “all things, and.”]; offspring cannot  
be before father, nor what is sown before its sower.

You lead to hell; in pity you bring us back from bitter things;  
Father, you help us out of [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “from.”] sins by your mercy.

No one powerful can flee you; your power  
reigns everywhere: you press down the mighty and tame the fierce.

Your honour knows no eclipse, your glory [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “grace.”] no end;  
light overcomes darkness, life death, the crown the yoke.

May the nation which does not [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0969] In the manuscripts the word could not be read.]  
know with steadfast diligence that God can be, has been, and will be.

The father’s mercy chastises our sins, makes them friendly  
by punishments [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “by punishment.”], heals by wounding, and teaches by calamity.

I confess him and give him thanks: the fall  
of the sinner does not please him, but rather salvation.

Magnify the Lord, Israelite people; praise him;  
[Col. 0970C] confess him, and do not deny that you remember God.

The Lord’s indignation scattered us [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “dispensation.”], so that  
a hostile nation might worship God by our example.

You ought to recount the Lord’s mighty works; the great God  
has been able to earn magnificent praises.

Consider what good things he has bestowed upon us; exalt the king;  
let the work confess faith.

Turn from vices; strive to be just before the Father;  
let sin cease [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “be absent”]; love abounds.

You chosen of the Lord, bless the Lord; with heart,  
voice, and hand make known praises to God.

May fear of the Lord be in you; and may honour be wedded  
to chaste fear and advance into fruit. [Note: [Col. 0969] This and the preceding couplet are transposed in another manuscript.]

Jerusalem, the Lord rightly chastises you; your wicked  
[Col. 0970D] people lie scattered, grieving, exiled, destitute.

The evils you suffer were earned by your excess; a punishment  
worthy of you torments you, fitting retribution presses you down.

God afflicts the reprobate; the provident care of the Father  
is moved by mercy to chastise his own. [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “of God.”]

The Lord’s clemency does not punish with the sword [Note: [Col. 0969] Another reading: “He restrains the reprobate with the sword.”]; God inflicts  
[Col. 0971A] no material punishment upon anyone. [Note: [Col. 0971] This hemistich restored from another manuscript; otherwise corrupt.]

Thus God afflicts the reprobate: he does not incite [Note: [Col. 0971] In the margin of the manuscript: “visits.”] the enemy,  
but exposes them, withdraws gifts, and turns back aid [Note: [Col. 0971] That is, toward himself.].

For when our Father sees himself despised, he does not refuse  
to let us serve our enemy.

You are devout and patient; no disturbance of anger  
[Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “none.”] can stir wars against the author of peace.

He is said to be angry because, when the son withdraws himself from anger,  
the cruel enemy attacks, exacerbates, and harms.

Jerusalem, the Lord God gave you much [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “God the Lord gave.”]; you dared  
to reject God and despise faith.

The abundance [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “flood.”] of wealth invited contagions,  
the destruction of life, the burden of deserved perdition.

You were an enemy of faith, corrupted by luxury, dissolved  
in delights, drunk with vices, devoid of the law.

[Col. 0971B] Therefore God provided for you: you reject heavenly  
commands and repay the gift with destruction.

Alas, you endure the Gentile yoke; captive, you labour  
under a master and groan oppressed in the Lord’s prison.

There is none to console you in misery, to bring  
a ready refuge or protective aid.

Behold, Jacob is oppressed while Esau rules; Joseph is restrained  
in fetters, exposed to the Ishmaelite.

The Hebrew wails [Note: [Col. 0971] Or “is exiled.”]; Egypt rules; the accumulation of faithlessness presses on;  
ailing faith is despised.

Alas, robbed of your fruits! As protection  
for orchards ceases, with citizens slain you lie bereft. [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “lying.”]

Through calamities God invites you to pardon; he seeks  
that you enjoy true religion.

God filled you with wealth; all excess makes  
[Col. 0971C] the loss of moral character abound.

You were free and rich, flourishing in success and delights,  
happy in your ruler and powerful in your citizens.

God torments you for your own transgressions; such a plague presses upon you  
[Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “stands forth.”] as you were wont to shine forth greatly. [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “makes.”]

Dissension is innate in you, first drenched in blood  
[Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “of the fathers.”]; you sow schisms and stir up wars.

Jerusalem, your offspring compel you to misuse  
your name, while the vision of peace lacks peace. [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “you lack.”]

Your evil, worse, utterly discordant people prevent you  
from following the meanings of the peace-making word. [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “of the peace-making voice.”]

It does not know [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “you do not know.”] how to express the effect of its name; through repeated  
slaughter it may possess its name by antiphrasis.

You have become a mockery to your neighbours; the slaughtered entrails  
[Col. 0971D] of fathers are given as food to birds.

Take comfort; do not complain; rejoice. The antidote to sorrow  
is ready, as the Lord brings reconciliation. [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “prepares reconciliation.”]

Nourish hope; confess the Lord and return; multiply praises,  
and uninterrupted salvation will be given.

Protection without delay will be given you; the Lord  
will restore citizens, walls, fields, and houses.

[Col. 0972A] Your former jurisdiction will be restored [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “jurisdiction.”]; when nations are broken  
and schism expelled, there will be rejoicing.

The rage of the Gentiles, now victorious [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “nurse.”], once conquered,  
will pay tribute [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “pay”], bound and compelled to suffer punishment. [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “joined.”]

Sing psalms to God; fulfil holy vows to God. God will sustain  
you and redeem the cross with prosperity.

The remnant of our race will see you presiding;  
throughout the world, ample salvation will be granted by your salvation.

Faith formerly despised [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “plundered.”] will become the plunderer  
of its plunder, bound and destitute. [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “you will become.”]

May those who despise you [Note: [Col. 0971] Or “abandon you,” ibid.] be cursed;  
whoever blesses you shall be blessed by the Almighty’s aid.

Rejoice in your children, holy city: the Lord will bring  
them back to you by a more favourable path.

Bright emerald or sapphire shall be yours, so that from it  
[Col. 0972B] you may build many walls. [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “walls many.”]

The encircling walls shall be made in design from precious stones,  
so that the costliness of the design may adorn [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “horrify.”] the work.

By as much as injury previously surpassed, by so much  
shall you be granted a freer [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “more flourishing.”] enjoyment of success.

A nation will arise [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “which will come.”] to pour out gifts for you in vows;  
with its resources it will worship God religiously.

A diverse [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “scattered.”] people will return to you, I know not from what excess,  
sober, just, pleasing, and dutiful toward God. [Note: [Col. 0971] Or “you are given,” ibid.]

Through streets the people will sing Alleluia; the squares  
will smile with varied flower, favour, and games.

The people will compose proclamations of the Lord; the work  
of devoted minds will make known their jubilation.

Blessed be the King whose mercy regards the lament  
of oppressed Jerusalem and provides aid.

[Col. 0972C] Let every spirit love, bless, worship,  
glorify, celebrate, and reverently serve the Lord.

Both merciful and mighty, Father and Lord:  
in the Father we worship you as ruler, and in the ruler the Father.

To you be majesty, praise, renown, power, strength,  
and dominion; let every spirit resound, Amen.

## Chapter XIV

Thus speaks the father [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “the old man.”]; nor do his words lack force: in the present  
time part of their fulfilment is manifest. [Note: [Col. 0971] Or “shines,” ibid.]

The other part, which promises aid, remains under judgment  
and uncertain; let faith rejoice when the enemy is conquered.

After the restoration of sight, the old man spends the remnant  
of his life in peace and unblemished religion.

The sun distributes its rays at evening; the evening hour is wont  
[Col. 0972D] more fully to name the day. [Note: [Col. 0971] That is, “praise”; Tobias does the same in old age, ibid.]

The field of virtue labours [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “may labour.”] to multiply the heavenly talent  
and fills the Father’s granaries with harvest.

He obeys the king, chastises his children’s shameful acts [Note: [Col. 0971] Another reading: “crimes.”],  
instructs them by examples, and teaches religion.

He rebukes the proud, calms the angry,  
pities the sick, and visits the wretched in word and deed.

[Col. 0973A] Joining [Note: [Col. 0973] That is, uniting, ibid.] merit to merit, and end  
to beginning, the holy man strives to become holier.

Now the old man is heavy with age; the irrevocable harshness  
of death exacts its tribute from the flesh.

The old man’s life languishes; old age, akin to death,  
foretells its arrival with a more mournful trumpet.

Very many symptoms of death become clear; as though  
conspiring, many wearinesses press the old man.

The old man’s frame contracts [Note: [Col. 0973] Or “stature,” ibid.], his voice is hoarse, his eyes  
are smaller, his nose wet [Note: [Col. 0973] That is, moist, ibid.], his saliva frequent.

His trembling foot staggers, his hand is shaking [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “and his hand staggers”]; the stepmother  
of the chest—cough on this side, catarrh on that—harms him.

A stomach of iron, a jaw without tooth, eyes weak  
in sight, a forehead bare of hair. [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “lacks.”]

[Col. 0973B] A hump burdens his back, scabies his head [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “presses,” with the preceding punctuation transposed.], a hernia his buttocks [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “loins.”],  
a wrinkle his breast, a swelling his chest, rheumatism his steps.

Believe that these are not the troubles of Tobias’s old age [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “these troubles are not Tobias’s in old age.”];  
what I say are not the epithets—that is, the properties [Note: [Col. 0973] That is, “properties,” ibid., in the margin.]—of that man’s age.

At death’s approach the old man rejoices and longs  
for his homeland; he prays to the Father and asks aid.

With death standing open before him, he fears the Lord—not, I say,  
with servile fear, but with that reverence which love bears. [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “loves.”]

Death stands at the doors and knocks at the entrance;  
the provident care of the father [Note: [Col. 0973] Or “old man,” ibid.] summons all his offspring together. [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “assembly.”]

Therefore he prepares to set in order for his household what he considers  
dangerous to the Ninevites and to his offspring, and relates it.

At his father’s command, the son and seven grandsons  
assemble; the father admonishes them with tear-wet speech:

[Col. 0973C] “Destruction threatens Nineveh; the Ninevite people labour  
toward their fall; a near punishment is evident.

“The wonderful word of the Lord, whose word is followed by fulfilment  
of its will, has not failed.” [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “are followed.”]

“Jerusalem will renew [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “recall.”] its course; the scattered brethren  
will joyfully return, and Israel will be mighty.

“For the house of the Lord will be rebuilt in a better state;  
though it lies scattered, when built it stands.

“The provident conversion of kings to the king  
will believe, worship in voice and favour, and make gifts.

“Hear your father, whose persuasion [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “persuasion.”] loves you  
and diligently teaches you concerning your homeland.

“This I exhort: serve the Lord with fear; with trembling  
exalt [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “rejoice in.”] God and seek to please him with a devout mind.

[Col. 0973D] Let deed conform itself to words; teach our prayers  
to bear fruit for justice in practice.” [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “tribes.”]

“Son, I entreat and exhort you, in desires, words, and deed,  
give yourself—your things, your whole self—as a burnt offering to God.

“Trust counsel, I pray; do not despise your father’s footsteps  
or wish to degenerate from your father.

“Contract marriage: let prayer be the bride, and fasting  
the delightful love of the husband.

“Let almsgiving not prove barren; let kindly offspring arise;  
strive, father, to bear fruit through offspring.” [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “let them live”; another reading: “equal.”]

“This is the threefold cord which no storm  
breaks; here the enemy is present, bound in a net.” [Note: [Col. 0973] Perhaps “by this.”]

“Thus rest of life, pleasant old age, constant  
[Note: [Col. 0973] That is, unceasing, in another manuscript.] prosperity, and enduring [Note: [Col. 0973] For “eternal,” ibid.] salvation will be given.

“Bless God with mindful heart; let love, gratitude, renown,  
and honour be offered to him in praise.

“Behold, the confusion of the Ninevites is evident; the city will endure  
its fall, collapsing in deserved destruction.

“I beg you, depart hence from that place, so that after your mother is buried,  
immediate [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “continued.”] rest [Note: [Col. 0973] Or “salvation.”] may contain us.” [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “may continue us.”]

“Live happily; may the abundant blessing of the supreme  
[Col. 0974B] Father govern you in your homeland’s prosperity.” [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “us.”]

“I return, ash, into ash; I willingly pay the mortal tribute.  
Death pleases me through love for the Father.

“Live devoted to the Lord, without sin [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “bless.”], just,  
of one mind, humble [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “humble ones.”] in heart; fear God.

“May your offspring increase without measure. Farewell,  
steadfast in the Lord—in peace, health, and faith.”

Having said this, the old man sets his household in order, longs  
for his homeland, despises the prison, and desires the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “thirsts.”]

The father receives the Lord’s judgment with serene countenance,  
joyful mind, devout praise, and steadfast fear. [Note: [Col. 0973] That is, “firm,” ibid.]

His affairs arranged and his offspring blessed, he rests in peace;  
his soul enriches heaven, his body the earth. [Note: [Col. 0973] That is, “heaven,” ibid.]

Alas, what is man, whose light shadow oppresses, whose corpse is stench,  
whose delights are tombs, whose condition is ruin? [Note: [Col. 0973] Here begins a certain digression.]

[Col. 0974C] Why does nature—stepmother and mother—bear man and destroy him,  
kindly in birth, harmful in death?

What was, is, and will be he but the vilest dregs [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “dregs, worst dregs.”], although  
the flesh be dear, alas, flesh not lacking decay [Note: [Col. 0973] That is, putrefaction, ibid.]?

Not born, I cannot escape death; born,  
I cannot enjoy a condition free from misery.

The law of flesh is grievous: its life is passage; to exist  
is to be bound to fail oneself and to suffer tombs.

Alas, through how many vices, with what heavy burden of a modern  
exile, do we seek to prolong our delay! [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “delays.”]

You are born, therefore, ash; you will be ash. You begin to be; you are held.  
After non-being, life is given in order that you may grasp death.

Nature draws us toward death; compulsion delays us.  
This life is brief, slippery punishment, sorrow. [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “labour.”]

[Col. 0974D] Tobias has more consolations against death: everlasting  
light, continual life, joyful rest.

He does not die, but changeable things are changed for fixed ones:  
earth for heaven [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “lands.”], groaning for peace, labour for rest. [Note: [Col. 0973] Another reading: “sorrow for salvation.”]

The ray returns to the sun; the exiled son to the Father;  
the victor to his homeland; to the diadem.

[Col. 0975A] The righteous man dies yet does not die: he dies to the world and is reborn among the stars;  
the joyful stars possess a new star.

The righteous man dies yet does not die, but departs; leaving the flesh as a lodging,  
he seeks [Note: [Col. 0975] That is, the homeland of God the Father.] the homeland and delights of the Father. [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “he seeks.”]

He was great; now he will be greater; but greatest he seeks the world beyond the world—  
good in the world, better, best, he seeks the stars. [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “inhabits the heights,” namely Tobias.]

A Moses in teaching, another David, another Elijah:  
Jacob in the world, Israel in heaven, he dwells among the stars. [Note: [Col. 0975] Or “seeks them,” ibid.]

He was an exile; now he will be ash [Note: [Col. 0975] Perhaps *civis*, “citizen.”]; he does not die, but obeys  
the Father, while longing for the riches of homeland and Father.

For he is father of his homeland, father and patriarch, patron;  
indeed, he cannot fail in the patronage of the law.

He does not die—can one die whose fame pleads for him,  
whose praise follows [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “speaks.”], whose fruit is fragrant, whose love abounds?

[Col. 0975B] Thus man grieves where the angel sings,  
where the stars grow bright and earth grows pale.

He sleeps with the fathers [Note: [Col. 0975] Or “saints,” ibid.], sleeps in the Father’s [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “saints.”] dwelling, sleeps,  
and reaps in his homeland the heavenly gains of the journey.

Whoever strove to establish the Lord’s mighty works  
ought to be numbered among the number of saints. [Note: [Col. 0975] Or “continued,” ibid.]

Whoever honoured the Lord by example, teaching, and vows  
ought to be honoured with corresponding praise.

Tobias lies at Nineveh: his fame [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “his.”] shines upon his descendants,  
his spirit upon heaven, his bones upon earth.

The father had lived fifty-six years  
when the height of the Almighty blinded him. [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “love.”]

He recovered sight at sixty years of age;  
[Col. 0975C] afterward he lived forty, add two.

Add two years: a hundred years is the measure  
of Tobias’s days, as certain reckoning makes clear.

His sorrowing kindred pity the father, multiply lamentations,  
and their cheeks are wet [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “water.”] with more copious rain.

The tribe and relatives assemble; one death presses the homeland  
[lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0975] A word difficult to read; it appears to be *plurali*, “in the plural.”] while the father lies dead.

Tobias mourns [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “groans.”], Anna groans [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “mourns.”], Sarah weeps,  
the grandchildren lament, and the people strive to redouble their groans.

For the tenor of faith, mirror of virtue, refuge  
of justice, anchor of the law, lies submerged.

As the precepts of the law command, diligent offspring,  
endeavour to bury your father. [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “for the father.”]

After time had passed and the mother had died,  
the son strives to join the tombs of both.

After his mother’s funeral, Tobias hastens on the journey to his parents-in-law;  
[Col. 0975D] Tobias departs, and the tribe departs with him.

Sarah follows her husband; the household goods destined to make him a father,  
and the whole household [lacuna] accompany the journey.

Anna runs about; kindly old age grows young in its step;  
[Col. 0976A] you would believe the old people had not aged in service. [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “He strives through service to honour the old people,” though that verse follows below.]

Raguel runs about and meets them [Note: [Col. 0975] Another reading: “meeting them.”]; love for his arriving offspring  
redeems the torpor of old age.

The son-in-law’s mercy sympathizes with his parents-in-law and supplies—
Whatever long-standing infirmity cannot do,

she obeys, is gracious, loves, and reveres in every way;

she strives by service to celebrate the old people.

When her parents-in-law had died, as time passed,

compassionate love buries both Tobia­ses.

She distributes tears, the manifold fruit of devotion through love [variant: *honore*, “honour”; *multiplicat*, “multiplies”];

nor does honourable love feel the burden [variant: *honor*, “honour”].

With these persons already deceased [that is, the deceased], Tobias, as heir, claims

by right [or: rights, if the comma is placed thus] the property, estates, fields, and oxen [or: houses].

He claims the maidservants and servants, and distributes everything else

to the poor; in name and mind he recalls his father.

[Col. 0976B] Prudent and harmless, he dispenses teachings and instructs his offspring

with pious diligence to be like their father.

Prosperity smiles upon him, heaped up; the fifth

generation of descendants that he sees makes the father blessed.

After ten years had passed from then [or: thereafter], less one,

the irrevocable day of death arrives.

He returns to ashes; already ash, his spirit, sated, makes the stars serene;

the earth blossoms with his innocent body.

Death dares to snatch Tobias, refuge of devotion;

the earth engulfs him, and his mournful shade darkens the day.

The Law lies buried with the lawgiver—that is, the father with the son—as a fleet without its rower [or: ship],

a stream without its spring, a ray without its lamp, a day without its sun.

An eclipse takes away the ray, ashes the mirror, shadow its brightness;

destructive death carries off the father of his country.

[Col. 0976C] For him homeland is exchanged for the road, tumult for peace,

clouds for light, earth for heaven, labour for rest.

Give lamentation [*gemitus*; variant *gemitum*], Judaea; grieve, Synagogue: bereft of two

rays, you grow pale, lacking brightness.

You suffer a double eclipse [or: a double eclipse suffers you]; alas,

the twofold lamp lies submerged in the darkness of death.

Bereft of double protection, mourn with double lamentation;

when the legitimate ones are buried, grieve that the Law lacks the support of the law [or: that the Law’s support is present].

Behold, the second Tobias dies in name, imitating his father

in the lamp of character, teaching, praise, and standing.

Alas, the course [or: fear] of lawful religion expires, both Tobia­ses

being buried, bereft of religion’s robe.

O sparing Death—by antiphrasis—begin to spare; let

the antiphrasis cease and strive to bear its true name. [In the other manuscript, the following lines through the word “spare” were absent.]

Do you wish to spare the good, the just, or the holy? Spare them:

[Col. 0976D] spare them, for both were good, just, and holy.

While each lived in the other, each was one

with the other’s wishes; each was the other.

While it distinguishes them, the number two seems itself

false: though two in number, they are the same in reality. [This couplet is absent in the other manuscript.]

[Col. 0977A] The number two lies when, daring to divide them,

it joins half of one to its whole [variant: *connumerare*, “to count”].

Recall the titles of both, Nature: give to the poor [or: rewards];

take back what you have given, and you will be rich.

Both are good: this one was devout, that one devotion itself;

this one was faithful, that one faith; this one holy, that one sacredness.

Each drank from your torrent; received

in their homeland, they drink spiritual nectar.

Alike in name and reality, heavenly peace—peace in complete unity—

feeds them, and rest that will have no sunset.

Holy offspring imitate their holy father; honourable offspring, the innocent;

the sober imitate the steadfast, the just the devout.

Their worthy life and holy observance indeed follow:

the twig follows the trunk, the limbs the head.

The offspring of Tobias are pleasing to the Lord; with the savour [or: sleep]

[Col. 0977B] of the root the branches are fragrant, and scent breathes forth.

The supreme Father cherishes them, so that in the course of time

they abound in their father’s help and in the praises of men.

## AUTHOR’S EPILOGUE

I moor my vessel, because the harbour is at hand: from the blessed Jerome’s brow [*fronte*; variant *fonte*, “spring”]

this present little pitcher draws water.

Live on, O Tobiases, subjects of my work; may no envy overshadow you,

no blight, no storm oppress you.

I seek neither favour nor the trumpet of fame—that is, vain glory. I write

for all; I write by God’s gift; I write for God.

Let the hexameter of Walter of Châtillon be lacking to you,

as the poet of Vendôme delights in elegiac pentameters.

I have chosen elegiacs rather than other verse, because I judge you,

friends of the Law, to be read by the metrical law of metre.

Walter was a poet, sufficiently elegant amid the barbarism of his age; he wrote the books of the *Alexandreis*, or history of Alexander the Great, and is frequently cited by Barthius.

[Col. 0977C] Concise elegiacs are required [variant word order: *elegis opus est*]; lame elegy [variant: *elegaegia*],

claims its adornment from the completeness of its feet.

Hyperbaton does not please—and should not please—in elegiacs; *uti* is uncertain here [variant: *imo*, “rather”],

while clear-cut brevity gives succinct delight.

The pentameter, shorter than the hexameter, like an attendant,

unfolds or [variant: and] closes the course of the preceding verse.

The hexameter goes before as a lord, closing his footsteps;

the attendant turns aside [or: obeys], moving with a more languid pace.

Who would mutilate a metre, or Baucis’ kisses? Verse

made discontinuous possesses the greater integrity.

[Baucis means the old woman of that name.]

A long heap of words, the stepmother of favour,

displeases; it runs on [variant: *exquatitur*, perhaps *excutitur*, “is shaken out”], slips, and the listener’s ear is absent.

A banquet departs more quickly across a platter full of fragments;

poems in small morsels lie open [the reading *coela* is uncertain; variant: *placent*, “please”].

[Col. 0977D] Separate these elegiacs and they please [variant: *patent*, “lie open”]; let distinction cease,

and the fruit is absent, the cadence goes astray, the sense is dulled [or: the reckoning is absent].

Let no regard be paid to the author [or: actor]; let the reader test this work

by the merit of its theme.

[Col. 0978A] Its own [variant: sacred] theme makes a work festive, not its author; the worthiness

of a celebrated subject aids the material made from it.

If any spark of good appears, it drips from goodness’ face or brow [*fronte*; variant *fontes*, “springs”]:

God gives good things; every human being is His minister.

The creature supplies service; God bestows welcome increase;

the tongue supplies ministry, God the gift of grace.

God bears fruit in His servants; man is divine equipment:

man plants the seeds; God provides the grains.

The potter distributes his art through vessels; with broken ones

he works toward the work of enduring wholeness.

Thus Caiaphas has prophecy; thus Pilate, through the Father’s love,

utters words that bring good out of evil.

Read at Paris the verses which the female pupil of Vendôme gives you, Tours [*alumna* is printed for the masculine *alumnus*];

Orléans, receive them.

A little dry stream from a poor vein flows richly

[Col. 0978B] into small beds with a poorer course [or: into little channels].

The leanness of words pleased me [variant word order: *macies placuit*]—an infancy of metre,

poor in flower, lacking figure, naked of tropes.

Speaking truth [or: being bare liquid], I do not paint my metre, lest the painted furnishing

of song incur the burden of ambition.

A tale flourishing in metaphors, epithets, and trifles,

is a drunken hunter [*venator*; variant *venatur*, “hunts”] for the help of credulity.

Truth refuses to be painted, because a true arrangement of words [or: a true relation of the word]

does not know how to flatter with a more florid sound.

The letter does not deceive [variant: “will deceive”]; a perverse letter destroys its reader;

spiritual fragrance gives life.

Like a harlot, the letter bends [variant: fashions] its course toward every rival,

having put aside its spouse, meaning.

[Col. 0978C] When a word sins adulterously with a forbidden meaning,

two-headed ambiguity turns doubtful cases.

Ambiguity harms [or: shines], and equivocation harms: one sound

equivocates several meanings.

As *summus* (“supreme”; variant inflection *summis*) Aristotle, as he declares in the *elenchis* [variant: *elenchi*],

teaches that six phantasms—that is, fallacies—lie hidden in speech.

Whether it should be called so, consider why: for the mind of the worker

gives every work its title.

Let empire be yours, O King Christ—power, strength,

glory, majesty, praise, diadem, and splendour.

Existing as another, not as another thing, than the Father—indeed,

not the same as the Father in persons, yet one and the same with the Father in substance—

the Father and the Son and the Spirit are God—one

and many; three, not three things; three and the same.

There is a threefold distinction of persons, but one [*una*; variant *unum*]

[Col. 0978D] essence—Greek *ousia*—one God, one *nois*,

that is, mind or knowledge.

You were born, God, of a handmaid, so that humankind

may be reborn and renewed in the life-giving font of baptism.

You were born: root from branch, sun from star, whole from

[Col. 0979A] part, potter from vessel, farmer from field.

The summit ascends from the valley, purple from a sack,

king from a maidservant, lamp from ashes, olive from bramble.

Lest the hostile wolf scatter [variant: destroy] riches, with the hinge closed,

the shepherd enters and leaves as sheep, and the lamb as sheep.

The sower comes forth [variant: is lost] from the harvest; may the mother be the Father’s daughter,

and the Virgin daughter nurse her own begotten Father.

Blessed marriage, when sacred words wed themselves:

for Mary’s golden ear the Word—the Son of God—becomes flesh, lacking a father.

The angel is midwife, the Father an infant, speech the husband,

the ear the bride, the parent a daughter, the creator a man.

Wholly within and without, because wholly in the Virgin,

wholly with the Father, wholly everywhere, God.

Blessed birth, in which the gracious Virgin, whose womb is more capacious than the world,

bore God, accessible to the sun, accessible only to God.

[Col. 0979B] Blessed birth, in which the chamber of modesty gives birth, open

though closed, like glass when the sun shines. [In the other manuscript these couplets are transposed.]

The flesh assumed from the Virgin excludes [variant: *exclusit*, “excluded”] the sins of frail nature,

retaining punishment but not guilt.

[Col. 0980A] Why, retaining punishment, did He come to be punished—why

did He choose to suffer reproaches, spittle, scourges, and the cross?

O pious King, mighty King, best King, may all things,

bearing witness to their Creator, bless You.

Praise be Yours, because I live; I speak because I write a few

verses: I am bound to celebrate Your glory.

What I bear, I hold from You; I render You thanks, although

human praise cannot magnify God.

No praise sings You adequately, because the meaning of words

fails to signify its own maker.

The poverty of words concerning Your power compels

us to speak as though our cry were failing.

Three and One, be present to the writer; Three in One,

One in Three, be blessed. Amen.

Innocent elegiacs, sleep and rest; I sympathize with you,

[Col. 0980B] wearied by equality of feet.

Here ends [variant: “the completed”] Tobias. Whoever has read it to completion should strive

to follow Tobias with meritorious devotion.

[Col. 0979] In the year of the Lord 1315 [the word “day” is understood, or was omitted through carelessness], on the feast of Tiburtius and Valerian [a little later, on the same side of the other manuscript, was written: “Here ends the Book of Tobias of Master Conrad” (*Mri* perhaps means *Magistri*, “Master,” *Martini*, “Martin,” or *Ministri*, “Minister”). Whoever he may be—owner, copyist, or reader—the true author is Matthew of Vendôme; thus he lived and flourished before that man.].

[Col. 0979]

# MISCELLANEOUS POEMS OF MATTHEW OF VENDÔME

(Wright and Halliwell, *Reliquiae Antiquae: Scraps from Ancient Manuscripts, Illustrating Chiefly Early English Literature and the English Language*, London, 1843, octavo, vol. II, p. 257, from a fifteenth-century paper manuscript from Krems, preserved in the Imperial Library at Vienna, communicated by Dr. Endlicher of Vienna.)

## PRAISE OF THE POPE

[Col. 0979C]

The world proceeds after the Pope’s example: honour shines,

reason serves as a soldier, order flourishes.

He is holy in religion, modest in speech, a cultivator

of uprightness, prudent in counsel, summit of the world.

With him as leader reason advances; anger, cooling, settles

into peace; active devotion flourishes.

His conduct does not savour of what is merely human: he disdains

human sin and conceives God.

He grieves with the afflicted, has pity on the wretched, longs

for the laws, restrains crimes, and cherishes rights.

The Pope teaches what must be taught, forbids what must be forbidden,

punishes offences, and holds the spiritual sceptre.

He binds and looses souls; in loosing and binding,

he performs the duties of the heavenly shepherd.

[Col. 0979D] We are his children, his sheep, his limbs; he protects us:

the head its limbs, the begetter his pledges, the shepherd his sheep.

[Col. 0980C] In the Pope an assembly of virtues debates; each virtue competes

to take precedence over the others.

The conflict of virtues contends for a share, pressing

to take first place in the holy man’s heart.

Justice strives to be first; moderation competes;

gentle devotion claims the father for itself.

The fifth among the three [or: the fifth virtue, in a group of three] strives to be first: wisdom competes;

let her be a dowry for the father, sister with sister as dowry.

The laws are stern; devotion softens; moderation calms;

judgment governs each thing under its balance.

The Pope, squared by these four, consists of four virtues;

the square gives stability and perpetuates faith.

Trusting in this square, he does not trifle for the use

of sin, and, knowing God, does not know how to be ignorant of Him.

The Pope rules kings, exercises lordship over lords, and by firm right

commands stern princes to command [or: commands them to obey].

Human worth comes forth; banishing fragile

[Col. 0981A] affections, he strives to empty out the human being.

His life extends beyond human steps; from a lodging-place

he contemplates in advance the road to heaven, his homeland.

He seeks to exchange the transient for the fixed, vain things for certain ones,

earth for heaven, lodging for home.

His holy mind disdains the sick vessel; spiritual dignity complains

of being bound in the prison of flesh.

The mind thirsts for its eternal seat; the shepherd dwells often

in earth’s lodging in body, in heaven in mind.

Sacrilegious crimes do not blacken his holy heart,

nor may they debase its worth.

He is good, better, best; and, if it may be said, he seeks

to possess goodness in a fourth degree.

## PRAISE OF A KNIGHT (L. CAESAR)

[Col. 0981B] Caesar’s constancy flashes in war: it withstands opponents,

breaks the strong, and tames the fierce.

His compassion warms toward the afflicted; toward enemies he proves himself an enemy,

yet he strives to be gentle with the gentle.

He outshines commanders in virtue; he flourishes as an example

of knightly service in worth, and surpasses in honour.

He advances upon the forbidden path; he longs for a soldier’s employment,

grows sluggish at rest, and flies to arms.

He thirsts for war, has made the sword companion to his side;

his courage knows no failure, and his back no flight.

It delights him to trust in the sword; he measures law with iron as judge,

and under the sword’s presidency he cuts out a path.

At Caesar’s nod two-faced Fortune nods;

chance has, as it were, the appearance of prosperity.

Caesar rises in adversity, nor does he join honour to

[Col. 0981C] the face of angry prosperity’s winter.

He crushes the fierce, cherishes the wretched, and by the offering of justice

balances the turns of peace and wickedness.

Moderation joins law to mercy; by the gentleness

of compassion, the judicial sword grows mild.

Thus measure serves in arms, lest mercy make justice languish,

lest the life of a boy disown the work.

The weight of empire does not impoverish his mind; rather,

virtue flies, divided among its offices.

He flourishes in gifts of intellect; the arts are not exiled,

nor does imperial rule drive away study.

Ambitious thirst does not detract from faith; rather,

in the ruler faith is deliciously wise.

Caesar takes his name from achievement, yielding all things,

[Col. 0981D] his hand expounding the meanings of his name.

For him rest is to be deprived of rest; to lack labour;

for him labour is passion, to suffer nothing.

For him fear conquers while absent; fame labours;

at whose tomb battles give voice to his name.

Caesar’s arrival speaks for Caesar; the shadow

of his armed name serves in war and bears arms.

Energetic, unconquered, combative, he presses, maintains, drives on

enemies, wars, and the accused—with sword, severity, and fear.

Bold, fearless, upright, he equips, enlarges, fills

arms, honour, countenance—with blood, battle, and threats.

Vigilant, tireless, persistent, he conceives, restores, establishes

wars, certainties, and the accused—with hope, doubtful matters, and sword.

Virtue, beauty, and faith fill, assist, and instruct his actions—

virtue, mind, and strength—with power, praise, and rank.

[Col. 0982A] For this worth Rome served him under the authority of a tribune,

daring to behold in him a head greater than her own.

## PRAISE OF A KNIGHT

Speech makes Ulysses illustrious, thought makes him festive,

grace of character gives him a title, fame makes him blessed.

Keen Ulysses overflows with the delights of language,

prudent in eloquence and thought, mighty in skill.

Lest the honour of his mind grow weak, flourishing eloquence

enlarges and restores whatever may be lacking.

Lest the powerful tongue be bereft of thought, the honour

of inward understanding marries itself to the tongue.

It joins talent to study, and, as husbandman,

strives to make cultivation bear seed into harvest.

[Col. 0982B] Talent conceives as thought dictates; reason, the teacher, distinguishes;

the ministering tongue gives voice.

Talent sows, study cultivates, practice confirms;

reason polishes, and counsel cherishes.

Understanding, the forerunner, and reason, the precursor,

make the tongue heir to their doctrine.

In Ulysses the chambers of the head are not empty: they hold

their official office, first, second, and following.

The first sees, the middle distinguishes, the third preserves;

the first receives, the middle judges, the lowest binds.

The first sows, the middle recollects, the last harvests; finally,

the first begins the way, the second takes it up, the third closes it.

The first supplies work to the others: thus the first is the door,

the middle the hall of guests, and the last the house.

The first, second, and following parts enclose, judge, and repel

[Col. 0982C] things that meet them, things seen, and flight—by pestilence, taste, and a bolt.

Reason’s summit stands in the middle, and on either side [the reading *salu at* is corrupt or uncertain]

the door of the forepart and hindpart of the head has its bolt.

He surpasses nature by virtue, and the faithful master

is the inward man of the inner human being.

In character he goes beyond humanity; the honour that comes to aid

outweighs, though with difficulty, natural inclination.

Wisdom weighs doubtful cases; whether a deed is just

or wicked hangs upon the judging balance.

He undertakes action only with the counselled release of law;

the hand, friend of the mind, acts with counsel.

By contrary turns he compares contrary things, and makes

deeds answer in harmony to his words.

He binds intention to the associated deed; the hand,

matching the speech in colour, expresses the mind.

[Col. 0982D] Age does not impoverish the mind’s virtue; rather,

a mature scent breathes from tender bark.

He masters age by virtue; his grey youth

smells of an elder’s inward counsel.

He surpasses the desires of youth by the virtue of age;

by honouring his mind, he goes beyond its laws.

The grey hair of the mind chastens the reins of age,

and the mind marvels to anticipate tender days.

Pride does not strip the mind’s flower; no blight

oppresses the delights of so great an honour.

Fortune does not oppress the brave man; though moved and unstable,

two-faced Fortune finds him single-minded and firm.

Neither Antiphates nor Circe nor Charybdis

can weaken the fidelity of Ulysses’ mind.

[Col. 0983A] Strong, prudent, honourable, he conquers, sustains, and heaps up

hardships, laws, and faith—by force, reason, and position.

Prudent, eloquent, generous, he blesses, adorns, and honours

hearts, words, and hand—with mind, beauty, and gifts.

A Tully in eloquence, a Caesar in conflict, an Adrastus

in counsel, a Nestor in mind, a Cato in severity.

## CENSURE OF THE FOOL

A wandering buffoon, a greedy parasite, the dregs of the people:

he is Davus, disgrace of things, a sickly plague;

nourishment of wickedness, cesspool of the world, ruin

of justice, violation of laws, mighty in deceit;

seed of evil, starved of truth, abundant

in trifles, misshapen in body, harmful in mind;

Thersites in appearance, Argus in fraud, Tiresias in justice,

[Col. 0983B] Verres in crime, Simon in deceit.

He serves vice, ignorant of virtue, enemy

of nature; he condemns the just and crushes the honourable.

He directs his harmful talent to harmful uses;

he claims his whole self as a dwelling of wickedness.

He breathes toward what is unlawful, confusion of peace,

schism of love; among the bad he strives to be worse, the worst.

He flows here and there, full of cracks, overflowing

with trifles; he suppresses just deeds and recounts what should be silent.

A vessel of crime, a well of vices, full of vinegar,

ignorant that he is ignorant of his own wickedness.

A mind steeped in evils does not know how not to know guilt,

and a hand may be the teacher of sinning.

It is hard to unlearn familiar vices; the harmful man inclines

toward the path of customary harmfulness.

[Col. 0983C] Habit springs up into the likeness of nature, of the same colour,

and can be, as it were, nature’s son.

Davus cannot fail to be harmful; born to harm,

he thinks that he would be degenerate if he could not be harmful.

Crime is inborn in Davus; every fraud flows together into one,

and he claims every crime as his own.

He who lacks faith and law, who labours in deceit,

who flies toward what is forbidden, who lacks devotion—

whose honour is to lack honour; whose settled course is to be

without constancy; whose fidelity is not to have had fidelity;

for whom it is crime to avoid crime, wrongdoing to lack

wrongdoing, shame to be ashamed of deceit;

whom fear proves a hare, prey a lion,

[Col. 0983D] a tail a goat, thefts a fox, robbery a wolf;

under whose leadership reason begs, and under whose rule virtue

goes into exile, while sickly faith springs up.

Only the inflection of the word “called” will spare Davus;

there an articulated utterance is silent.

Davus is the sole dregs of bronze, worthy of chains,

worthy of Jupiter’s three-pronged thunderbolt, worthy to die by lightning.

He restrains caresses with threats, love with hatred,

good with plague, gifts with plunder, faith with deceit.

Behold the sum of evils: his mind is wicked, his body profane,

his tongue deceitful, his hand abominable.

He denies that he is a hypocrite; nut and shell agree; they are foul

with equal corruption, the place with like plague.

Lest the same name be applied in his place, he is foul alike within

[Col. 0984A] and without in Davus; metonymy perishes.

He grieves at seeing laughter, and laughter balances his grief;

yet he groans when events turn out more prosperously.

A mass of dregs, nature’s shame, earth’s burden,

an abyss of tables, a sickly house of dung.

His foul mind is cooked by the goads of envy; the plague

enslaves the mind’s colour and migrates into his face.

He runs about to tables; after meals he grows torpid; friend

of his belly, he consumes rich foods and despises vegetables.

He is not evil, but a grievous evil, born to consume

crops; he makes what is not numerical into a number.

At his arrival cups are drained; the table begs food from the needy,

the flask begs wine.

For him the belly is god, the kitchen temples, the cook

[Col. 0984B] priest, and smoke has the taste of Sabæan incense.

He sits upon the dish and imprisons tables and foods, whence

Venus, too friendly to the belly, springs up excessively.

He is intent upon bowls and platters; amid belching tumult

and the shrill trumpet of his belly, it thunders on both sides.

His swollen mass, distended with foods he has swallowed,

conceives winds, and Davus strives to be Aeolus.

Gaping and sick, Davus, his prison broken by the whirlwind of winds,

releases those which he cannot hold back.

He proceeds to incest; sick Venus arouses the two-pound

brothers; the other limbs are warm, the tail stiffens.

The first syllable of dactylic metre enters; short syllables

with frequent thrust shake the foul walls.

Wickedness proclaims slavish rage; in deed it fully displays

[Col. 0984C] the work of a slave’s condition.

The bland woman urges him; rebellious, he rages against free backs,

lest he pursue the straight course along the forbidden boundary.

He infects the innocent with vices; the plague of his sick heart,

divided among many, overflows.

A sack of wickedness, darkness of light, tempest

of the market, savage pestilence, gaping whirlpool:

harmful, sick, sluggish, he changes, destroys, presses upon

joys, laws, and good people—with schism, fraud, and guile.

Naked, poor, empty of price, virtue, and honour,

he rejoices in quarrel, madness, and faith; he abounds in them and lacks them.

He chooses, desires, loves, corrupts, despises, abhors

quarrels, reproaches, crime, covenants, temples, and gods.

When Virtue discovers at his birth her own enemy,

[Col. 0984D] “I see wars for myself; wars are being prepared,” she says.

## DESCRIPTION OF THE SEASONS

Rosy spring sports with tender flower; it labours

to paint Rhea with a more flowering mane.

Summer, friend of the sun, grows warm and overflowing with heat;

it strives to be the interpreter of its own name.

Autumn, the vintner and Bacchus’ cupbearer, serves up

the delights of the grape; harvest fills the granaries.

Winter bristles, clad in a threefold covering, stepmother

of flowers, sick companion of the wanton heart.

The year has twice two parts: spring is mild, summer

burns, autumn gives grapes, winter is cold.

Spring is father of flowers, summer their nurse, autumn richer

in fruit, winter lavish in clothing.

Spring disturbs the loins; in spring Diogenes rages;

[Col. 0985A] spring entangles youths and old men in Venus.

Lucifer, forerunner of the sun, drives away the stars; at dawn

the day breathes again, better now that night is exiled.

May Dawn send darkness into exile, making Titan’s bed widowed;

she dyes Jove’s face purple.

Accompanied by shaggy frost, light and sunrise creep forth;

old age strives to anticipate the seasons.

Phoebus distributes his rays more abundantly; four-footed creatures pant,

his chariot dividing the day in half.

Phoebus migrates to the Antipodes; the lower pole

slopes toward sunset on a more languid wheel.

## DESCRIPTION OF A PLACE

This place is Nature’s labour, where the delights of spring abound,

[Col. 0985B] spring’s grace and spring’s riches.

The earth luxuriates in grass with leafy tresses; the grass

blooms with flowers; the soft breeze is warm; fragrance breathes.

Nature caresses the place, lavish in granting favours;

she may lack the things she has bestowed.

Exceeding the measure of giving and reserving nothing for herself,

she purples the place with more flourishing adornment.

Zephyr makes the flowers enduring, and bristling winter

does not assail the earth with a poorer mane.

The ground sprouts into flowers; the damp clod mates

with clod; the little flower is fragrant, the herb savoury.

Neither the rage of dog nor crab changes the honour

of the flowering bloom into a poorer garment.

The sweet rose, rich in apparel, blooms upon its native mound,

a delicious companion in fragrance.

[Col. 0985C] Curled fennel grows green, rich in scent,

which is accustomed to chastise spiritual evil.

Soft bilberries darken, friends of the nostril;

lilies come forth with whiter tresses.

The blue flower turns to the sun, grievous wound of love;

the obedient herb proclaims Phoebus’ nod.

Sage appears, wedded to mild pepper,

which makes great banquets luxuriate.

Artemisia flourishes, pale-green in appearance, and is accustomed

to make the flavour of Bacchus’ delights luxuriant.

The narcissus, fragrant with chaste love, grows pale,

bearing in its paler face love’s indication.

Hyssop, powerful to entitle vessels full of God, rises,

far from Bacchus’ revelry.

The herb that sheep or deer commend to the common people by its taste

[Col. 0985D] grows at crossroads, with sparse hairs.

Parsley, contending with the bee in appearance (so the text),

denies that similar appearance entails similar flavour.

Clover, short in stature, sits as food for common folk

and a festive little supper for the fasting man.

Lettuce, the stepmother of Venus, which bids the loins cease,

rises up as a lover of religion.

Rocket (*eruca*), a mother tending toward Venus, stiffens,

so that the powerful white onion may awaken seed.

Plantain, seated close to the ground, restrains

the swelling of flesh and bids it subside.

The poppy, seeking to sleep, comes forth from the earth; dill’s

delights bloom, a fragrance beloved of the nostril.

A cleanser of the stomach and producer of rumbling, it cleanses;

[Col. 0986A] it rises, bearing a name from its function.

The lanceolate plant follows lilies in the whiteness of its garment;

bound to a wound, it lies there as a remedy.

Redness pales in violets, and some middle, I know not what,

neutral colour seems to stand between the two.

Sharp ginger, delight of the mouth, comes forth

and strives to prolong its flowering tresses.

Thymes bloom, enriching the dwellings of bees in twofold fruit—

the eyes with beauty, the throat with flavour.

A conflict of fragrances contends and breathes more sweetly;

what individual things cannot do, many accomplish.

The bee tastes the flower in plucking it, showing, with labour as teacher,

the way of human usefulness.

No tribute is paid from the flower to the plundering north wind;

the place remains inviolate in its gifts.

[Col. 0986B] Lest the flower’s infancy perish, lacking its nurse,

a life-restoring spring supplies it fostering waters.

Tree-like beauty clothes the ground, and the warm shade, bestowing coolness,

strives to banish the sun.

The oak, nourished by its own, weds heaven with its summit

and with devotional mouth looks toward its Jove.

The laurel, honour of the poet, despises winter’s anger

and rejoices in the wholeness of its foliage.

The broad elm grows green, shade at the crossroads; O Tityrus,

the beech, friendly to you, rises beneath its shade.

The palm’s foliage grows pale; its branch hears “hosanna”

when a Christ-worshipping man cries it aloud.

The holm-oak, reaching toward the stars, sprouts into spreading branches,

[Col. 0986C] accustomed to be the home of the honey-making bee.

The first seed of evil and stepmother of life,

the fig is present, harmful to the first father in the beginning.

The box-tree stands close to earth; from its spoils it provides

musical instruments and a ministerial covering for the cross.

By the craftsman’s hand it gives vessels for Lyaeus;

the maple is strengthened in its many knots.

The bent pear appears, bearing evening meals

and preventing Bacchus’ cups from resting.

The apple tree comes forth, giving nourishment to the hoarse throat;

*Hersula* is to be prepared with wine over coals.

Cherries blush full red, but delicious worth

redeems the loss caused by their short duration.

The cypress rises, queen of the tree-kind,

worthy to touch the King of kings.

[Col. 0986D] Witness of Paris’ love and of the nymph’s rejection,

the white poplar sprouts into soft foliage.

The plane-tree puts forth leaves; knotty cornel, yew—the stepmother

of bees—fragrant bean, and wet willow.

Myrrh has outstanding effect, with life-giving liquid,

able to make flesh luxuriant.

The tall pine raises its lofty head toward the clouds,

to expose ships to the judgement of waves.

The frankincense-bearing shoot rises, to offer God

the honour of a votive mind.

The almond fruit comes forth, which the hereditary fever

torments; it is a wholesome diet for the sick man.

The alder rises, excellent for drawing colour from its bark,

[Col. 0987A] providing the artisan with material for garments.

It blooms red with savoury flower; its red scent softens

the fierceness of arms and the harshness of clothing.

The tall mulberry appears; its momentary offspring, white,

blushes stained by Pyramus’ blood.

The chestnut comes forth, preserving through great age

its honeyed fruit in the hollow of its cup.

The vine is present, greater in our time than Jupiter: delight,

glory, and love of the people.

Many more trees remain, but the Muse presses her lips shut,

and brevity, friend of the ear, pleases.

The sun’s warmth does not assail the waters; rather, the rounded

row of branches sounds forth coolness.

The moisture, joining its own properties to the sun’s friendship,

sets out to make the tresses of flowers fruitful.

A further beauty remains, freely bestowed; birds excellently

add splendour with their diligent chatter.

[Col. 0987B] The nightingale, crying “Kill!”, sings its complaints,

and sings its own losses with delightful grief.

The blackbird’s voice resounds; it is made domestic,

and is accustomed to be ennobled by imitation of our speech.

The parrot cries “Farewell,” a word intended for Caesar’s triumphs,

its tongue made lowly.

The lark, striving toward crime and conflict, arms itself with wings,

and happily sings the day with prophetic voice.

The proud peacock, starred with Argus’ eyes,

shines in the honour of its painted garment.

The dove, consecrated to Venus, nests in the branches,

redeeming incest by its simpler plumage.

The friendly turtle-dove moans, pledged to its first husband,

loving the pledge of enduring affection.

[Col. 0987C] Here the spotted quail sings and dwells,

and the partridge, to be tortured on a stiff spit.

The swan, which sings its own funeral rites and, near death,

despises the critical moment, resounds from the spring.

The magpie, providing matter for logical dispute,

covers its limbs in some intermediate colour, I know not what.

The dwarf *birex* is present, which gives its short stature

distinction through the nobility of its name.

Nor is the carpenter woodpecker absent; its beak is described by the uncertain reading *ovi fabrica*,

while, a stranger, it digs sheltering roofs for itself from its companions.

[Col. 0988A] The chatterbox and greedy jackdaw grows sluggish, accustomed

to celebrate our homes in exile.

The sparrow either suffers or acts—the bird to which restless Venus,

flowing through the loins, gives its names.

No crow, raven, or owl is present to blaspheme

the sacred place by the harshness of its cry.

The eagle’s primacy is not absent, unless the royal dignity

of its condition disrupts the songs of the common flock.

Therefore, while the birds’ complaint moves their corresponding songs,

you would think an instrumental melody was present.

The flower is fragrant, the herb green, the tree bears, fruit abounds,

the bird chatters, the stream murmurs, the breeze is warm.

Birds please by voice; shade by coolness; breeze by warmth;

spring by drink, stream by murmur, ground by flower.

[Col. 0988B] Pleasant is water’s murmur, harmonious birdsong, the flowers’

sweet fragrance, the cold river, the warm wave.

The grace of the place feeds the five senses, if you consider

each of the things noted in relation to the others.

Water delights touch, flavour taste, sound the ear;

the bird gives pleasure to sight, fragrance to the nostril.

The elements are not idle, for earth conceives, air caresses,

heat brings forth, and moisture nourishes.

Ciceronian Muses, let us sing somewhat greater things;

trusting in you, we give the sea favourable sails.

Not every grove and low tamarisk pleases;

rather, it pleases to share in the laurel’s lot.

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF A PLACE

[Col. 0988C] Here the genius strives toward what is better; spring, painted with grass,

presents an outstanding garment to earth’s bosom.

Little grass sprouts; the soft breeze announces spring’s honour;

the flowerlet flashes, and the newly risen rose proclaims warmth.

The glassy surface, the nectar-like spring, gives life to, cherishes, and enlarges

the new shoots of flowers, breathing fragrance.

No hostile, cruel frost despoils or devalues

their mildness; the flower, friend of spring, retains its beauty.

## GAUFRID, SUBPRIOR OF THE REGULAR CANONS

### Letters
## LETTERS

**LETTER I.—From John, abbot of Baugezé, to Geoffrey, abbot.—**He laments the pastoral burden imposed upon him. 827

**LETTER II.—From Geoffrey to John.—**He replies to the preceding letter. 829

**LETTER III.—From Geoffrey to the monks of Baugezé.—**He congratulates them upon having at last arrived at the recently founded monastery, [Col. 1021] and praises their solitude. 831

**LETTER IV.—To John, abbot.—**He urges him courageously to rebuke vices in the monastery and punish offences. 832

**LETTER V.—To the same.—**He asks him to visit him at least by letter. 833

**LETTER VI.—From John to Geoffrey.—**He replies to the preceding letter. 835

**LETTER VII.—From Geoffrey to John, abbot.—**He complains of the letter’s brevity; states that he will amend the library at Caen if John wishes; and announces the death of his cellarer. 835

**LETTER VIII.—To Richard, priest.—**He gives him various admonitions. 836

**LETTER IX.—To G., chaplain of the bishop of Worcester.—**He exhorts him to contempt for the world. 837

**LETTER X.—To Geoffrey, his friend.—**He announces that peace has been made between the king of England and his son. 837

**LETTER XI.—To a brother weak in the knees and differing from him on certain matters.** 838

**LETTER XII.—To Bartholomew.—**He teaches how one ought to walk in the way of the Lord. 838

**LETTER XIII.—To Peter, his friend.—**He exhorts him to constant reading of Holy Scripture. 840

**LETTER XIV.—To the chaplain of the bishop of Worcester.—**On the familiar writing of letters and contempt for the world. 840

**LETTER XV.—To Peter of Buxeria.** 841

**LETTER XVI.—From John, abbot of Bugezé, to Geoffrey.—**He complains that Geoffrey has not written for a long time, and asks him for letters of exhortation. 842

**LETTER XVII.—From Geoffrey to John.—**He replies to the preceding letter. 842

**LETTER XVIII.—To Peter Mangot.—**He congratulates him on the permission granted him to build a monastery, and discusses the necessity of acquiring a library for it. 844

**LETTER XIX.—To Master R.—**He congratulates him on entering the order and teaches what sort of person he ought to be within it. 845

**LETTER XX.—To W., formerly prior of St Stephen’s at Caen.—**On contemplation. 846

**LETTER XXI.—From John, abbot of Baugezé, to Geoffrey.—**He asks Geoffrey to retain the library for him. 847

**LETTER XXII.—From Geoffrey to John.—**He asks him to obtain from God, through his prayers, a blessed death for himself. 848

**LETTER XXIII.—From John to Geoffrey.—**He replies to the preceding letter. 849

**LETTER XXIV.—From Geoffrey to John, abbot.—**He regrets that, having been summoned to the Council of Paris, he was not present when John, abbot of Baugezé, came to Sainte-Barbe in 850. 850

**LETTER XXV.—To the same.—**Apparently of the same subject. 850

**LETTER XXVI.—From Roger, formerly prior of St Abraham’s, to Geoffrey.—**He congratulates him on what he had written concerning the vision of God and exhorts him to humility. 851

**LETTER XXVII.—From Geoffrey to Roger.—**He replies to the preceding letter. 852

**LETTER XXVIII.—To the brothers of Baugezé.—**He sends them the Life of Blessed Hamo. 853

**LETTER XXIX.—To John, abbot.—**In the monastery of John, abbot of Baugezé, he finds represented to himself an image of future blessedness. 853

**LETTER XXX.—To R., precentor of the church of Troarn.—**That he may visit him at least by letter. 855

**LETTER XXXI.—From N. . . . to Geoffrey.—**It appears to be a reply to the preceding letter. 856

**LETTER XXXII.—From Geoffrey to a certain young hermit.—**He gives him salutary admonitions. 861

**LETTER XXXIII.—To Hugh, prior of St Martin’s at Sées.—**He extols the virtues of Hugh, prior of St Martin’s at Sées, and teaches how they ought to prepare themselves for the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. 863

**LETTER XXXIV.—To R., priest.—**What the priest’s station at the right in the Mass signifies, and concerning certain other rites. 864

**LETTER XXXV.—To John, abbot.—**He sympathizes with him over the misfortune that had befallen him. 867

**LETTER XXXVI.—To Simon, his friend.—**On the praise of a certain virgin. 868

**LETTER XXXVII.—To R., priest.—**He is troubled by the praises bestowed on himself. 870

**LETTER XXXVIII.—To W., abbot of St Andrew’s.—**He congratulates the abbot of St Andrew’s, of the Cistercian order, on his promotion. 870

**LETTER XXXIX.—To Peter of Buxeria.—**He says that the vow of his profession and the office of provost hinder him from remaining in solitude. [Col. 1022] 871

**LETTER XL.—To John, abbot.—**He explains the infrequency of his letters. 872

**LETTER XLI.—To Hugh, prior of St Martin’s at Sées.—**He extols his virtues and exhorts him to write the Life of Walter. 873

**LETTER XLII.—From Hugh, prior of St Martin’s at Sées, to Geoffrey.—**He replies to the preceding letter. 874

**LETTER XLIII.—From Geoffrey to Hugh, prior of St Martin’s at Sées.—**He exhorts him to write the Life of Walter and praises his abstinence from wine. 875

**LETTER XLIV.—To Augustine, his friend.—**He praises Augustine and exhorts him to pursue spiritual things. 876

**LETTER XLV.—To Geoffrey, priest.—**Small gifts ought not to be despised because they are small; rather, one should consider with how great a spirit they are given. 878

**LETTER XLVI.—To H., his friend.—**He sympathizes with his friend in his adversities. 879

**LETTER XLVII.—To Nicholas, subprior of St Victor’s.—**He gives thanks for his friendship. 880

**LETTER XLVIII.—To John, abbot.—**He praises John, abbot, for the grace of his speech. 881

**LETTER XLIX.—To Hugh, prior of St Martin’s at Sées.—**He again exhorts him to write Walter’s Life. 882

**LETTER L.—To Andrew, archdeacon of Tours.—**He gives him various admonitions. 883

**LETTER LI.—To R., his friend.—**He praises his friend R.’s zeal for contemplation. 884

**LETTER LII.—From N. to N.** 885
